# TO RODOLFO OF CARPI, OF THE 
# HOLY ROMAN CHURCH, OF THE TITLE
## OF SAINT MARY IN TRASTEVERE, <note>Rodolfo Pio da Carpi (1500–1564) was an influential Italian cardinal, humanist, and patron of the arts and learning.</note>
## Most Distinguished Cardinal, Gentian Hervet <note>Gentian Hervet (1499–1584) was a French humanist and prolific translator of Greek patristic texts into Latin.</note> 
->Sends Heartiest Greetings.<- <note>original: "S. D. P." for *Salutem Dicit Plurimam*.</note>

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'C' depicting a seated figure in robes, likely a scholar or theologian, within an ornate rectangular frame featuring classical scrollwork and motifs.</image-desc>SINCE there is nothing more beautiful, nothing more noble, nothing more illustrious for praise and glory than to so order one's life that all reason, all counsel, and finally all actions are directed toward the public benefit: certainly no one seems to me to serve the commonwealth more than those who bring forth into the clear light, rescued from the darkness, the outstanding monuments of the ancients—those who excelled others in virtue and learning. In my judgment, these people far surpass others in their beneficence; for however great the benefits of others may be, they certainly deserve well only of those who are living. But the signal merits of these men bind to themselves not only the living, but also those who have departed from life. For great gratitude is earned from the ancient writers who have left this life when the things they wrote divinely for the public benefit are shared with everyone; and those who are studious, perceiving great fruit from their labors, acknowledge that they owe a great deal both to the authors themselves and also to those by whose work the authors were brought into the light. 

But if any ancient writer, having been buried for a long time, has finally come out into the light from whom the greatest utility has flowed to the public: it must be that Clement of Alexandria—who was the disciple of Pantaenus the Martyr <note>Pantaenus (died c. 200) was the head of the Catechetical School of Alexandria and Clement's predecessor.</note> and the teacher of Origen—is by far the most useful to all because of his admirable erudition. And while I could bring forth the testimonies of Eusebius of Caesarea, Theodoret the Bishop of Cyrus, Saint Jerome of Stridon, and several other illustrious men regarding his distinguished doctrine, for the present the one Cyril, Patriarch of Alexandria, shall suffice for me. He writes about him thus against Julian: <note>Refers to Cyril of Alexandria's work *Against Julian the Apostate*.</note> *Clement also, an eloquent man, and indeed a polymath, said this about the gods and temples: For we shall not keep silence on this, but rather we shall prove that those very things which are called "temples" by a fair-sounding name were actually tombs, and these tombs were renamed as "temples."* <note>original Greek: "Εφη δὲ καὶ Κλήμης, ἀνὴρ ἐλλόγιμος, καὶ μέν τοι καὶ πολυΐστωρ, περί τε θεῶν καὶ ναῶν ὧδί. οὐ γὰρ οὐδὲ τοῦτο σιωπήσομεν, πρὸς δὲ καὶ αὐτὸ ἐλέγξομεν νέως μὲν εὐφήμως ὀνομαζομένους τάφους δὲ γενομένους τούτους καὶ τάφους νέως ἐπικεκλημένους."</note> That is: *Concerning the Gods and the temples, Clement, a man eloquent and endowed with knowledge of many things, spoke thus. For we will not hide this, and to such an extent we will prove that the temples are called by a beautiful name, yet those which are called temples were actually tombs.* And again: *Clement, an eloquent and studious man, who searched the depths of unknown Greek matters with such care and study as perhaps few of those who preceded him, makes mention of this history separately in his Miscellanies.* <note>original Greek: "ταύτης τ᾽ ἰδίᾳ μέμνηται ἱστορίας ἐν τοῖς στρωματεῦσι ὁ Κλήμης, ἀνὴρ ἐλλόγιμος καὶ φιλομαθὴς, καὶ τῶν ἀγνωσμάτων ἑλληνικῶν πολυπραγμονήσας βάθος, ὡς ὀλίγοι τάχα που τῶν πρὸ αὐτοῦ."</note> *Of this history,* he says, *Clement makes mention separately in the <term>Stromata</term> <note>From the Greek word for "patchwork" or "tapestries," used by Clement to describe the layered, diverse nature of his theological writings.</note>, a man eloquent and primarily studious, and one who investigated the depth of those things read among the Greeks with that care and study which certainly few of those who preceded him utilized.* How useful he will be in the future can be clearly seen from this. Are there any who are delighted by ancient things and those sought from the depths of history...

<meta>This page continues the dedication of a translation of Clement of Alexandria's works, specifically addressing his value to historians, theologians, and moralists of the 16th century.</meta>

histories. Let those who love history read Clement, for he held all ancient stories in such high regard and knowledge that nothing performed in the entire world seems to have escaped his notice. Are there those who venerate the songs of ancient poets as if they were divine responses from oracles? They must necessarily hold Clement in high esteem, for he cites the testimonies of many poets whose works have completely perished today. Are there those who wish to know the ancient rites and ceremonies used in sacrifices to the gods? Let them go to Clement, who reveals all the rituals—the "orgies"—and the unspeakable mysteries of the ancient gods in such a way that if there is still anyone among Christians who praises and admires the <unclear>vain</unclear> and ancient customs and institutions of the pagans—and would that there were none!—that person, upon reading Clement, must be stupider than a stone if they do not cast away every false opinion about false gods. It is inevitable that they will feel ashamed of the madness of those who once worshipped such gods. 

Are there those who wish to learn the decrees of the ancient philosophers? Let them look to Clement, who hands down and describes the origin of all philosophy, the families of all philosophers, their sects, successions, and decrees in such a way that, since a man so remarkably learned preferred <term>Christian philosophy</term> <note>In this context, "Christian philosophy" refers to the comprehensive Christian way of life and theology as the ultimate truth exceeding Greek thought.</note> above all others, even the unbelieving or the unwilling must admit that it is clearly divine, truly inspired, and promulgated by God. 

Are there those who desire to know the dogmas of the ancient heretics who disturbed the Church of God at the very beginning of its birth? They will hear them explained and refuted by Clement. Are there those who desire the authorities of the ancients against the <term>Lutherans</term> <note>A reference to the followers of Martin Luther; the author is framing the 2nd-century Clement as a weapon against the 16th-century Protestant Reformation.</note> and other heretics of our time? Clement will also dismiss them well-instructed by his own testimony on many points. Are there those who desire that wicked and corrupt morals be corrected? There is no one who pursues vice more sharply, no one who exhorts toward virtue better, and no one who better demonstrates the way to rightly establish one's life. 

Are there those who hope for fallen discipline to be restored to its integrity? They will rightly praise Clement’s teaching and the holiness of his life; for although he was only a <term>presbyter</term> <note>A priest or elder in the early church hierarchy, below the rank of bishop.</note>, he was the kind of man that, if many of the Bishops in our own times were like him, the Christian commonwealth would be in an excellent state. Such people, I say, will ask Christ to inspire a holy mind through His Holy Spirit in those who today preside over the flock committed to them. 

Since, therefore, Clement of Alexandria is going to be so useful to the Christian commonwealth, let it be acknowledged that much is owed to those, and it is right that great thanks be felt and given to those, by whose labor it was brought about that so great a man should come out into the public. Indeed, his *Stromata* <note>meaning "Miscellanies"</note> and *Paedagogus* <note>meaning "The Tutor"</note> came forth into the light from the **Medici Library**, supplied by that most illustrious Prince and greatest lover of virtue and learning, **Cosimo, Duke of Florence**. 

However, by you, most distinguished Cardinal, that book was kindly supplied which is called the *Exhortation* <note>original: "προτρεπτικός" (Protreptikos). This is one of Clement's most famous works, urging Greeks to abandon paganism for Christianity.</note>. This is an oration in which he discourages the Nations from the worship of idols and exhorts them to the true religion. Since it was recently published, and it seemed to some of my friends that I would be doing something worthwhile if I translated it into Latin, I undertook that province more confidently because I was aided by your most ancient manuscript, which was illustrated with many <term>Scholia</term> <note>Ancient marginal notes or comments made by a teacher or scribe to explain the main text.</note> added to it. For which reason, since both I and those who will receive some benefit from my labor owe you much, I decided to leave this testimony in these letters of mine to you, and to dedicate and offer to you this work of Clement’s—small in size, yet filled with various and manifold learning. I ask you again and again to receive it with a grateful heart. 

Farewell, most distinguished Cardinal. Rome, the day before the Kalends of January, 1550. <note>December 31, 1550.</note>

## EXHORTATORY ORATION
### TO THE GREEKS, OR TO THE GENTILES.

**AMPHION** of Thebes and **Arion** of Methymna were both indeed endowed with the art of singing, and in the chorus of the Greeks, both the fable and the song concerning them are still sung to this day: how one enticed a fish with his bait <note>original: "piscem inescauerit" — a reference to Arion, who was famously saved from drowning by a dolphin charmed by his music</note>, while the other built the walls of Thebes through his song <note>Amphion was said to have moved stones into place for the city's walls using the power of his lyre</note>. There was also another Thracian Master <note>original: "Sophista" — Clement refers here to Orpheus</note> (this is another Greek fable) who by his song alone made wild beasts tame, and even transplanted trees and beeches from their places by the power of his music. I can tell you yet another story, as much a brother to this one as one sibling is to another, concerning the singer **Eunomus** of Locri and the **Pythian Cicada**. A festival was being celebrated at a great gathering of Greeks 

<margin>C</margin>
at Pytho <note>The ancient name for Delphi</note> in honor of the dead Dragon <note>The Python, the great serpent slain by Apollo</note>, where Eunomus was singing a funeral song for the serpent; I know not whether his song was a hymn or a lamentation for the beast. A competition had been arranged, and Eunomus was playing his lyre in the heat of the day, at the time when the cicadas, warmed by the sun, were singing under the branches upon the mountains. They were singing not to the dead Dragon, but to the most wise God, a truly free song, superior even to the melodies of Eunomus. A string broke for the Locrian; a cicada flew onto the bridge of the lyre and chirped upon the instrument as if upon a branch. The musician, adapting his harmony to the cicada's song, supplied the missing string. Thus the cicada was led by the song of Eunomus, as the fable suggests, which has placed a bronze statue of Eunomus at Pytho with his lyre and his partner in the contest. Yet the creature flew there of its own accord and sang of its own accord. To the Greeks, however, he appeared to be an actor and an imitator of music.

<margin>D</margin>
For what reason, then, have you believed in empty fables, thinking that living creatures are soothed by music? Yet the joyful and beautiful face of truth alone, it seems, appears to you to be a pretense, and is viewed with eyes of unbelief. **Cithaeron** and **Helicon**, and the **Odrysian mountains**, and the mysteries of the Thracians which initiate men into error, have been treated with divine honors and celebrated with hymns and praises. For my part, even if it be mere fiction, I find it difficult to endure the many and great calamities recounted by the Tragedians. To you, even the descriptions of evils have become the performances of Poets. But let us leave these performances—and the Poets who celebrate the festival of the wine-press <note>original: "Lenæum" — the Lenaia, an Athenian festival in honor of Dionysus</note>, who are now utterly raving, crowned with ivy, and acting foolishly beyond measure in the Bacchic mysteries, along with the Satyrs and the insane troupe <note>original: "Thyaso"</note> and the rest of the chorus of demons who have grown old on Helicon and Cithaeron—and let us bring down from the heavens above 

<margin>E</margin>
the **Truth**, together with the brightest wisdom, to the holy mountain of God and the holy prophetic chorus. May Truth, shining with a light far more brilliant, illuminate on all sides those who wallow in darkness, and free men from error, stretching out her heavenly right hand—which is to say, intelligence—for their salvation. And they, having returned to their senses, should renounce and abandon Helicon and Cithaeron, and instead dwell in **Sion**.
<margin>Isaiah 2.</margin>
*For out of Sion shall go forth the Law, and the Word of the Lord from Jerusalem.* <note>Quoting Isaiah 2:3</note> This is the heavenly Word <note>original: "Verbum" — The Logos</note>, the true and genuine competitor, who is crowned in the theater of the whole world. My Eunomus sings not in the style of Terpander, nor the style of Capito, nor in the Phrygian, Lydian, or Dorian modes, but the eternal mode of the new harmony, which takes its 

<margin>F</margin>
name from God—the **New Song**, the **Levitical Song**. <note>A reference to the songs of the Levites in the Hebrew Temple, here linked to the "New Song" of Christ</note>

<meta>catchword: that (ille)</meta>

<margin>on the <unclear>stages</unclear></margin>
That Orpheus, and the Theban <note>Amphion</note>, and the Methymnaean <note>Arion</note>, were certain men—or rather, not men at all, but deceivers. Under the pretext of music, they brought ruin to human life. Through certain artful illusions, they demonically incited men to corruption, celebrating shameful acts in their rites <note>original: "orgiis"</note>, and turning mourning into songs for the Gods. They were the first to lead men toward idols; indeed, they used stones and wood—that is, images and sketches—to rouse the savage customs of the people. Through their chants and poems, they reduced that truly beautiful freedom of those who lived under heaven to the lowliest slavery. But my singer is not like that; he came shortly after to dissolve the bitter slavery of the demons who held tyrannical power. Leading us toward the sweet and kind yoke of religion and piety toward God, he calls back to heaven those who had been cast down to the earth. Surely he alone, out of all who have ever existed, has tamed those most difficult of wild beasts: human beings. The "birds" he tamed were the flighty among them; the "serpents" were the deceivers; the "lions" were the high-spirited and those easily moved to anger; the "swine" were those devoted to pleasure; and the "wolves" were the rapacious. As for the "stones and wood," these are the foolish. Furthermore, a person steeped in ignorance is even more senseless than a stone. Let the prophetic voice come forward as our witness, harmonizing with the truth, which takes pity on those who are worn down in ignorance and madness.

<margin>Matthew 3</margin>
For **GOD IS ABLE** from these stones to raise up children for Abraham. Pitying the great ignorance and hardness of heart of those who had become like stones against the truth, He raised up a seed of piety toward God, which perceives virtue, from among those "stones"—namely, the Gentiles who had put their faith in stones. Again, therefore, He called certain venomous impostors and hypocrites who lay in wait for justice a

<margin>Luke 3</margin>
"brood of vipers." But if any of these serpents should be led by repentance, following the Word <note>original: "Verbum" — referring to Christ as the Logos</note> willingly and of his own accord, he is made into a man of God. Others he 

<margin>Matthew 7</margin>
calls "wolves in sheep's clothing" allegorically, gesturing to those who are rapacious while in human form. All these most savage beasts, and such stones as these, the heavenly song itself has transformed into gentle men.

<margin>To Titus 3</margin>
For **WE WERE**, we too were once foolish, disobedient, led astray, slaves to various pleasures and desires, living in malice and envy, hateful, and hating one another, as the Apostolic scripture says. But when the kindness and humanity of God our Savior appeared, not by the works of righteousness 

<margin>D</margin>
which we have done, but according to His mercy, He saved us. See how much the New Song has been able to do! It made men out of stones, and men out of wild beasts. Those who were otherwise as if dead, who did not participate in that which is truly Life, revived as soon as they became mere listeners to this song. He has adorned this entire universe for you in a rhythmic and fitting way, and He reduced the discord of the elements into an orderly consonance, so that the whole world might become a harmony for Him. He let the sea flow free, yet prohibited it from invading the land; the land, which was once drifting, He made stable and solid, and He fixed the sea as its boundary. Now, He also softened the violence of fire with air—as if tempering a Dorian musical mode with a Lydian scale—and He soothed the harsh coldness of the air with the embrace of fire, harmoniously and fitly blending these extreme sounds of the universe. And this 

<margin>E</margin>
incorruptible song, the firmament of all things and the harmony of everything, extending from the center to the edges and from the extremities to the center, has harmonized this entire universe. This was done not according to Thracian music (which is like the music of Tubal), but according to the paternal will of God, 

<margin>Psalm 8</margin>
which David admired. But He who was born from the line of David, and yet existed before him—the Word of God—despising inanimate instruments like the lyre and the cithara, has harmonized this world, and even the "small world" (namely, man, both his soul and body) by the Holy Spirit. He sings to God through an instrument of many voices, and He sings to this instrument: man. For "You are my cithara, and my flute, and my temple"—a cithara because of harmony, a flute because of the spirit, and a temple because of the Word; so that the first might ring out, the second might breathe, and the temple might contain the 

<margin>F</margin>
Lord. Certainly King David, the player of the cithara whom we mentioned a moment ago, who exhorted men toward the truth and urged them away from idols, was far from praising 

<margin>1 Kings 16. <term>μελωδία</term> <note>Melody or song</note></margin>
demons. On the contrary, the demons were driven away by him with true music; for when Saul was vexed by a demon, David played...

# TO THE GREEKS

<margin>To be read cautiously. <note>original: "Cautè legenda." This is a common Renaissance-era editorial mark, often used to warn readers of potential theological errors in early Church writings.</note></margin>
▲ He alone, by singing, has cured him <note>referring to humanity</note>. As a beautiful-sounding instrument, the Lord fashioned man after his own image. Surely he himself is also the harmonious, fitting, and holy instrument of God—the otherworldly Wisdom and the heavenly Word. What then does this instrument, the Word of God, the Lord, and the New Song desire? To open the eyes of the blind, to open the ears of the deaf, and to lead those who are lame or wandering in their steps back to justice; to show God to foolish men, to restrain destruction, to conquer death, and to reconcile disobedient sons to their father. As the kind instrument of God, the Lord shows mercy, disciplines, exhorts, warns, preserves, and protects us; and from a certain overflowing abundance, he promises us the kingdom of heaven as the reward for his teaching.

<margin>
John 1.
Herodotus.
</margin>
B The only fruit he gathers from us is that we are saved. For the vice of men feeds on destruction, but truth—like a bee—brings no harm to anything that exists, but rejoices solely for the salvation of men. You have, therefore, a promise; you have kindness; become a partaker of grace. And do not think of my "saving song" as being "new" in the same way you think of a vessel or a house; for it existed "before the Morning Star," and "in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." <note>John 1:1</note> Error is old, but truth appears as a new thing. Perhaps the Phrygians are taught by their fabled goats <note>A reference to the story in Herodotus where the Phrygians were deemed the oldest race via a language experiment</note>, or the Arcadians, whom the poets describe as being "older than the moon"; or perhaps the Egyptians, who dream that this land appeared first, bringing forth both Goddesses and men. But none of them existed before this world. We, however, existed before the foundation of the world; because we were meant to exist, we were first born within God himself.

C We are the rational creations of the Word of God, through whom we are ancient, since "in the beginning was the Word." But because the Word—who was and is the divine principle of all things—derived his origin from on high, and because he has now taken a name formerly sanctified and worthy of power, "Christ," he has been called by me a "New Song." This Word, Christ, was the cause both of our existence long ago (for he was in God) and of our well-being. Now, this very Word has appeared to men—he who alone is both God and man—and he is the cause of all our good things. Having been taught by him to live rightly, we are sent onward to eternal life. For as that divine Apostle of the Lord says: "The saving grace of God has appeared to all men, teaching us that, denying impiety and worldly desires, we should live moderately, justly, and piously in this age, awaiting the blessed hope and the coming of the glory of our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ."
<margin>To Titus, chapter 2.</margin>

D This is the New Song: the manifestation, now shining among us, of the Word who was in the beginning and existed before. The Savior, who existed before, has recently appeared; he who is "the One who Is" has appeared in him who is "the One who Is," because the Word, who was with God, appeared as a Teacher, through whom all things were fashioned. The Word, who in the beginning gave life as our Creator <note>term: opifex (artificer/creator)</note> when he formed us, has now taught us to live well by appearing as our Master, so that later, as God, he might provide us with life eternal. He did not pity our error for the first time just now; rather, he has pitied us from the very beginning, and now, when we were on the verge of perishing, he has appeared and preserved us. <margin><unclear>Revelation 12.</unclear></margin> For that malignant and serpentine beast, blinding our eyes, reduces us to slavery and afflicts men even to this day—punishing us, it seems to me, in the manner of barbarians who are said to chain captives to corpses until they rot away together with them.

E Therefore, this evil tyrant and dragon, whoever he could claim for himself from their birth, binds them with the wretched chains of superstition to stones, wood, images, and various idols of that sort. He leads the living, as they say, and buries them together with these things until they perish alongside them. # EXHORTATION TO THE GREEKS
A

<margin>A</margin> Through Moses, who was perfected in every measure of wisdom, and through Isaiah, the lover of truth, and the whole choir of prophets, the Word <note>original: "Verbum" / "Logos"</note> turns those who have ears toward reason—or rather, toward Himself. Sometimes He attacks with rebukes, sometimes He even threatens, and He weeps for some men while singing to others. He acts just like a good Physician treating sick bodies: molding some parts with poultices, smoothing others, draining some, dividing others with a blade, cauterizing others, and sometimes even amputating, if there is any way a person might be healed at the cost of a part or a limb. The Savior has many voices and methods for the salvation of men: by threatening He warns, by rebuking He converts, by weeping <margin>B</margin> He shows mercy, and by singing He speaks through the bush. For those people <note>The ancient Israelites</note> required signs and wonders. He also terrifies men with fire, kindling a flame from the pillar—which is a dual sign of both grace and fear: if you obey, light; if you do not obey, fire.

However, since the flesh is more precious than both the pillar and the bush, the Prophets speak after those things. It is the Lord Himself speaking in Isaiah, Himself in Elijah, Himself in the mouths of the Prophets. But if you do not believe the Prophets, and think that these men and the fire are merely a myth, the Lord Himself will speak to you. <margin>To the Philippians 2.</margin> Who, though He was in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal with God. Instead, the merciful Lord emptied Himself, desiring to save man. And now the Word Himself speaks to you clearly, grieving at your unbelief. I certainly speak as the Word of God made man, so that you too may learn from a man in what way, finally, <margin>C</margin> a man may be made God <note>This refers to theosis or divinization, a central theme in early Eastern Christian theology: God became human so that humans might become divine.</note>.

Therefore, is it not absurd, O friends, that God is always exhorting us toward virtue, yet we refuse what is useful and postpone our salvation? Does not John also exhort us to salvation, being entirely a voice of encouragement? Let us ask him: "Who among men are you?" He will say he is not Elijah; he will deny being the Christ; but he will confess to being "a voice crying in the wilderness." Who then is John? To describe him as best I can, let it be said: he is the exhortatory voice of the Word, crying in the wilderness. <margin>Isaiah 40. John 1.</margin> "What do you cry, O voice? Tell us also." "Make straight the ways of the Lord." John is the forerunner, and the voice runs before the Word—an exhorting voice, preparing for salvation, a voice urging us toward the heavenly inheritance, through which the barren and deserted is no longer unfruitful. 

The voice of the Angel foretold this conception for me. That voice also ran before <margin>D</margin> the Lord, announcing a sterile woman <note>Elizabeth, the mother of John the Baptist</note>, just as John announced the deserted one <note>Symbolizing the Gentile world or the soul without God</note>. Through this voice of the Word, therefore, the sterile woman has many children, and the deserted one bears fruit. These two voices running before the Lord—the Angel’s and John’s—signify to me the salvation laid up for us: namely, that when this Word appeared, we would receive the fruit of a good offspring: eternal life. Scripture, gathering both these voices together, opens the whole matter. <margin>Isaiah 54.</margin> **REJOICE**, O you who do not bear; break forth into a cry, you who do not travail; for there are more children of the deserted than of her who has a husband. The Angel announced a husband to us; John exhorted us to think of the Farmer, to seek the Husband. For this is one and the same Husband of the sterile woman and the Farmer of the deserted one, who filled both the sterile <margin>E</margin> and the deserted with divine power. 

For while the noblewoman <note>Referring to the Jewish Synagogue or the Hebrew people</note> had many children, she lacked children because of unbelief—the Hebrew woman who had many children from the beginning. The sterile one among them, and the deserted, lacked a Farmer. Then, while the former produced fruits, the latter produced believers; but both are mothers through the Word. To the unbelieving, however, she remains both sterile and deserted even to this day. John, the herald of the Word, exhorted in that way so that men would be ready for the arrival of God the Christ. This was what the silence of Zacharias <margin>Luke 1.</margin> secretly signified: waiting for the fruit of Christ’s forerunner, so that the Word, the light of truth, might end the mystical silence of the prophetic riddles by becoming the Gospel. 

But if you truly desire to see God, be a partaker of the purifications <note>original: "piaculorum." In a pagan context, these were expiatory sacrifices; Clement repurposes the term for Christian holiness.</note> that are fitting to God—not of laurel branches, or wreaths made of wool and purple, but crowned with justice and clothed in the leaves of temperance, seek Christ diligently. <margin>John 11. F</margin> "**I**," He says, "am the door," which those who wish to understand God must learn, so that He may open all the gates of heaven to us at once. For the gates of Reason <note>original: "rationis" / "Logos"</note> or of the Word are rational, and they are opened by the key of faith. <margin>Matthew 11.</margin> No one knows God except the Son, and he to whom the Son has revealed Him. I know well that He who then opens the closed door, later reveals...

# EXHORTATION TO THE GREEKS

<margin>4 A</margin> things that are within, and reveals those things that could not be known before, except by those who walked through Christ, through whom alone God is perceived. Therefore, do not investigate the impious sanctuaries <note>Latin: "adyta", the innermost private shrines</note>, nor the mouths of the pits full of trickery, nor the Thesprotian cauldron, nor the Cirrhean tripod, nor the Dodonian bronze. As for the "Old Oak" <note>Latin: "Gerandryon"</note> honored in the desert sands, and the oracle there—which withered away along with the oak itself—leave these to old wives' tales. Surely the Castalian spring is now committed to silence, as is the spring of Colophon; and other divining streams have perished in a similar way. Though full of pride, they have finally been proven false—late, perhaps, but at last—as they have flowed away along with their own myths. Tell us also the oracles of other divinations—or rather, of insane vanity: the Clarian, the Py-

<margin>B</margin>thian, the Didymean, the Amphiaraus, and the Amphilochus of Apollo. If you wish, consecrate alongside them the inspectors of monsters, the augurs <note>diviners who read the flight of birds</note>, the soothsayers <note>aruspices; those who read animal entrails</note>, and the interpreters of dreams. Bring forward too the flour-diviners and barley-diviners <note>those who predicted the future by throwing grain or flour</note>, and those who are still held in honor by many: the ventriloquists <note>literally "belly-speakers," believed to be possessed by spirits</note>. Now indeed, let the inner shrines of the Egyptians and the necromancy of the Etruscans be consigned to the shadows. These are truly the insane inventions of unfaithful men. Into the business of this trickery they even bring goats, trained for divination, and crows, which are taught by men to give responses. Why should I recount the mysteries to you? I will not betray them, as they say Alcibiades once did, but through the Word of truth, I will rightly uncover the trickery hidden within them. I will bring forth and unroll those who are called your Gods, whose sacred rites are mysteries, as if on the stage of life, for those who contemplate the truth.

<margin>C</margin> They celebrate Dionysus "the Mad" <note>Latin: "Mænolen"</note> in Bacchic orgies, practicing a sacred insanity by eating raw flesh; they perform the distribution of slaughtered meats, crowned with serpents, howling "Eva, Eva"—that same Eve through whom error followed <note>Clement is making a pun between the Bacchic cry "Eua" and the biblical "Eve"</note>. The sign of the Bacchic orgies is a serpent initiated into the mysteries. Indeed, if the Hebrew language is examined accurately, the name *Hevia* <note>original: "Heuia"</note>, when aspirated, is explained as "female serpent." Furthermore, Ceres <note>Demeter</note> and her daughter Proserpina <note>Persephone</note> have now become characters on the stage; the city of Eleusis illustrates their wandering, their abduction, and their grief with torches. It seems to me necessary to give the etymology of these words, "orgies" <note>orgia</note> and "mysteries" <note>mysteria</note>. "Orgies" are named after the *anger* <note>Greek: "orgē"</note> of Ceres against Jove. "Mysteries," however, come from the *abomination* <note>Greek: "mysos"</note> and filth that occurred regarding Dionysus. Even if they are named after a certain Maon the Attic, whom Apollodorus says died in a hunt, I have no desire to begrudge your mysteries the honor of being a tomb. 

<margin>D</margin> These "mysteries" can also be understood in another way, as "little myths" <note>Greek: "mytharia"</note>, by swapping the letters; for they "hunt" <note>Greek: "thēreuousin"</note>—if any other fables do—the most barbarian among the Thracians, the most senseless among the Phrygians, and the most superstitious among the Greeks. Perish then the man who was the leader and author of this fraud for humanity, whether it was Dardanus, who displayed the mysteries of the Mother of the Gods, or Eetion, who suggested the orgies and sacred mysteries of the Samothracians, or that Phrygian Midas, who learned from the Odrysian <note>likely referring to Orpheus</note> and then passed this artful fraud to those under his rule. For the islander Cinyras of Cyprus will never persuade me that he, daring to pass the lustful 

<margin>E</margin> orgies of Venus <note>Aphrodite</note> from night into the light of day, did so for any reason other than wanting to turn a local prostitute into a goddess. Others say that Melampus, son of Amythaon, brought the festival of Ceres—the grief celebrated with praises—from Egypt into Greece. I would say these were the leaders and authors of impious myths, and the fathers of a deadly superstition, who sowed the seed of vice and corruption in life: the mysteries. Now indeed, for it is time, I will prove that these orgies of yours are full of fraud and trickery; and if you have been initiated into the mysteries, you will laugh all the more at these fables you hold in honor. I speak openly of things that are hidden, not blushing to say what you are not ashamed to worship. For she who was born from the foam and in Cyprus, the lover of Cinyras—I mean Venus—

<margin>Cinyras was King of Cyprus.</margin> is called "lover of genitals" <note>Greek: "philomēdēs"</note> because she arose from the "genitals" <note>Greek: "medea"</note>,

<margin>F</margin> from those lustful genitals, I say, which were cut off from Heaven <note>referring to the myth of Uranus being castrated by Cronus</note>, and which after the cutting did violence to the waves. As a fruit worthy of your lustful parts, Venus appears in the sacred mysteries. 

<margin>The mysteries of Venus.</margin> As a sign of the birth of this sea-born pleasure, a handful of salt and the Phallus are handed to those who are initiated into this art of adultery.

He provides controversial etymologies for religious terms to argue that pagan worship is rooted in historical crimes, filth, and human vice rather than divine truth.</summary>

# ORATION OF EXHORTATION

<margin>A</margin>
Those who are being initiated bring these things forth, like lovers to their mistresses. The mysteries of Ceres <note>The Roman name for the Greek goddess Demeter, associated with grain and the harvest</note>, moreover, consist of the lustful couplings of Jupiter <note>Zeus</note> with his mother, and the wrath of—I know not what to call her next, his mother or his wife—Ceres. For this reason she is said to have been called <gloss>g</gloss> Brimo <note>original: "Brimo," a title meaning "the terrifying" or "roaring one"</note>; there are the entreaties of Jupiter, the drink of gall, the tearing out of hearts, and operations unspeakable to tell. These mystical rites are performed by the Phrygians for Attis and <gloss>h</gloss> Cybele <note>The Great Mother goddess of Phrygia</note> and the Corybantes. They also boast that Jupiter, having torn the testicles from a ram, threw them into the lap of Ceres, paying a false penalty for his violent union, as if he had castrated himself. These symbols of this initiation, added more than enough, will, I know well, move you to laughter, even if the thought of laughing does not occur to you because you are being refuted. "I have eaten from the drum;
<margin>B</margin>
I have drunk from the cymbal; I have carried the sacred vessel <note>Latin: "temperatum," referring to the *kernos* or vessel used in the rites</note>; I have entered the bridal chamber." Are these symbols not a disgrace? Are these mysteries not ridiculous? But what if I were to add the rest? Indeed, Ceres carries a womb, and Proserpina <note>Persephone, daughter of Demeter</note> is nourished. But again, this Jupiter who fathered her, sleeps with Proserpina, his own daughter, after her mother Ceres—forgetting his prior crime. Jupiter is both the father and the corrupter of the girl, and he couples with her having become a Dragon <note>or Serpent</note>, having been caught for who he was. <gloss>i</gloss> Certainly the sign of the mysteries of Sabazius <note>A Thracian/Phrygian god often identified with Dionysus</note> for those who are being initiated is "the God who passes through the lap." This is a Dragon that is drawn through the lap of those being initiated, a clear proof of Jupiter’s lack of self-control. Moreover, Proserpina gives birth to a son in the form of a bull.
<margin>Idolatrous</margin>
Certainly, says a certain Poet devoted to the cult of idols: "The bull is the father of the Dragon, and the Dragon is the father of the bull. On the mountain, the ox-herd's hidden goad." The "ox-herd's goad," as I believe, refers to that beautiful wand <note>Latin: "ferula," the *thyrsus*</note> which they brandish. Do you also
<margin>C</margin>
want me to tell you how <gloss>k</gloss> Proserpina gathered flowers, and about her basket and her abduction by Pluto, and the gaping of the earth, and the swine of Eubuleus that were swallowed up by the Goddesses? For which reason, those sacrificing at the Thesmophoria <note>A festival held by women in honor of Demeter and Persephone</note> cast out pigs. Women celebrate the festival day of this fable in various ways—the Thesmophoria, the Scirophoria—tragically singing of the abduction of Proserpina in many modes. For the mysteries of Dionysus are plainly inhuman. While he was still a boy, with the Curetes <note>Armed youths who protected the infant god</note> leading a dance with the motion made in arms, the Titans stealthily approached with a trick. Deceived by certain childish toys, the Titans tore him apart while he was still an infant, as the poet of the mystery, Orpheus the Thracian, says:

> golden apples sent by the Hesperides.

It would not be useless to bring forward the useless symbols of this mystery to condemn them: the knuckle-bone, the ball, the pine cone, apples, the top, the mirror, and the fleece. And Minerva <note>Athena</note>, indeed, who took up the heart of Dionysus, was called Pallas from the word *pallein*, that is, from "vibrating" or "brandishing," because she made the heart vibrate and brandish. But the Titans, who had torn him apart, placed a certain cauldron upon a tripod and, throwing in the limbs of Dionysus, they first boiled them, and then, having fixed them on spits, they held them over the fires of Vulcan <note>The god of fire/the forge</note>. But Jupiter, when he later appeared—if indeed he was a God, as one who perhaps had smelled the steam of the roasted flesh, of which prize your Gods confess they are sharers—
<margin>E</margin>
punished the Titans with a thunderbolt and commanded his son Apollo to bury the limbs of Dionysus. And he, for he was not disobedient to Jupiter, carried them to Parnassus and laid the mangled corpse there. But if you also wish to consider the Orgies of the Corybantes: they, when they had killed their third brother, covered the head of the dead man with purple cloth and buried him crowned, carrying him on a bronze shield to the base of Mount Olympus. And these are, to put it briefly, the mysteries: slaughters and burials. Moreover, the priests of these things, whom those who care to name them call *Anactotelestas* <note>Initiators of the Kings/Lords</note>, bring certain portents to the calamity, forbidding people to place celery <note>or parsley</note> with its roots on the table. For they think that from the Corybantic blood which flowed out, celery has grown. Just as surely the women who <gloss>m</gloss> celebrate the Thesmophoria abstain from eating the seeds of the pomegranate, thinking that
<margin>F</margin>
pomegranates germinated from the drops of the blood of Dionysus. Calling the Corybantes "Cabeiri," they also announce the death of the Cabeiri. For these two fratricides, having taken up a chest in which the private parts of Dionysus were stored, carried it into Etruria, merchants of noble wares, and there they dwelt as exiles, [preaching] the venerable...

# TO THE GENTILES

<margin>A</margin> Commending the "venerable doctrine of piety," they offer shameful objects and a chest to be worshiped to the Etruscans <note>The people of ancient Tuscany, often associated in early Christian thought with superstitious practices</note>; for this reason, some not improbably claim that Dionysus is called Attis, as one who has been deprived of his genitals <note>original: "Atis, ut qui sit privatus pudendis," suggesting a linguistic link between the name and the Greek word for ruin or deprivation</note>. And what wonder if the barbarian Etruscans fall into such foul habits, when even for the Athenians and others of Greece—I am ashamed even to say it—the story of Ceres <note>The Roman name for the Greek goddess Demeter, the deity of grain and the harvest</note> is full of disgrace and dishonor.

For while Ceres was wandering in search of her daughter Proserpina <note>Persephone, who was abducted by Pluto</note>, she became exhausted near Eleusis (a place in Attica) and, overcome with sorrow, sat upon a well. To this very day, those being initiated are forbidden to sit there, lest they seem to imitate her in her mourning. At that time, there lived in Eleusis the "Earth-born," or sons of the earth. Their names were Baubo, Dysaules, and Triptolemus. Furthermore, there were Eumolpus and Eubuleus. Triptolemus was a cowherd, Eumolpus a shepherd, and Eubuleus a swineherd; from these families, the Eumolpidae and the race of Heralds who announce the sacred rites flourished in Athens.

Now Baubo (for I will not restrain myself from telling the story), when she had received Ceres as a guest, offered her a prepared drink. When Ceres refused to take it and would not drink because she was in mourning, Baubo took it badly, feeling she had been slighted. She exposed her private parts and showed them to the Goddess. Ceres was delighted by the sight, and at last took the drink, cheered by the spectacle. These are the secret mysteries of the Athenians. These things Orpheus <note>The mythical poet and musician to whom many "mystery" verses were attributed</note> also describes. I will bring before you the very verses of Orpheus, so that you may have that famous guide to the mysteries as a witness to this impudence:

<margin>C</margin> *Thus she spoke, lifting her robes, and showed the whole*
*Foul shape of her body; and Iacchus* <note>A minor deity associated with the procession to the Eleusinian mysteries</note> *was then*
*Of a boyish age, and Baubo’s right hand was thrust*
*Into her lap as she laughed; then the Goddess, with a cheerful mind,*
*Smiled and received the varied vessel that held the drink*
*Into the chest.*

The sign <term>Synthema</term> <note>A password or formula used by cult members to prove their initiation</note> of the Eleusinian mysteries is: "I have fasted, I have drunk the prepared potion, I have taken from the chest. After I did this, I placed it in the basket, and from the basket back into the chest." These are indeed "beautiful" spectacles, fitting for a Goddess! Mysteries truly worthy of the night and of fire, and of the great—or rather vain—spirit of the people of Erechtheus <note>A mythical king of Athens; here referring to the Athenians themselves</note>, and even other Greeks, for whom there remain after death things they do not even hope for.

To these people Heraclitus of Ephesus prophesies—to these night-wanderers, I say, these Magicians, Bacchic revelers, and Mystics—he threatens them after death, and prophesies fire for them. For they are initiated into what are considered mysteries among men in an unholy way; for they are a vain law and opinion, and they are the mysteries of the Dragon <note>likely referring to the snake-god Sabazios or the serpent associated with Dionysus</note>, a kind of fraud that worships truly profane rites and exhorts people to cursed sacraments with a corrupt religion.

What sort of things are in their mystic chests? For it is necessary to reveal their "holy" things and announce their secrets. Are they not sesame seeds and pyramids <note>cakes shaped like pyramids</note>, and well-worked wool, and cakes marked with many navels, and handfuls of salt, and the Dragon, the ritual object of Dionysus Bassareus? Are there not pomegranates, and also hearts, wands, and ivy, and furthermore cakes and poppies? These are their holy things. They even have the secret symbols of Themis: oregano, a lamp, a sword, and a woman’s comb—which is a polite and mystical way of saying the female genitals.

<margin>E</margin> O manifest impudence! In the past, silent night was a covering for the pleasures of moderate men. But now, for those being initiated, the sacred night is a speaker of incontinence, and the fire that shines in the torches exposes their vices and the disturbances of the soul. Extinguish the fire, O Priest! Show reverence for the lamps, O you who carry the torches; the light exposes your Iacchus. Turn away, hide the mysteries in the night, and let the rituals be honored by darkness. The fire does not hide; it exposes and punishes what it is commanded to. 

These are the mysteries of the impious, and of those who are plainly without God. And I rightly call them impious and without God, because they are ignorant of Him who is truly God, but impudently worship a boy who is torn apart by Titans, and a mourning woman, and parts that truly, out of shame, should not even be mentioned. They are held by a twofold impiety: the first, by which they are ignorant of the true God, not acknowledging Him who truly exists. The second, by which they think those who are not gods are gods, and call those "gods" who truly are not, rather...

<meta>catchword: rather</meta>

<summary>Clement of Alexandria ridicules the Eleusinian mysteries, specifically the myth of Baubo cheering the mourning Ceres (Demeter) through indecent exposure. He lists the mundane and "shameful" objects found in the sacred mystic chests to prove that these rites are fraudulent and godless.</summary>

# EXHORTATORY ORATION

<margin>Ephesians 2</margin>
...but those who do not even exist, but only possess a name. For this reason, the Apostle <note>Saint Paul</note> certainly reproves us also, saying: <insert>A</insert> AND *you were*, he says, *strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world.* <note>Ephesians 2:12</note> May many good things come to the King of the Scythians, whoever that Anacharsis <note>A famous 6th-century BCE Scythian philosopher who traveled to Greece</note> was. He shot with arrows his own citizen, who was imitating among the Scythians the sacred rites of the Mother of the Gods which take place at Cyzicus—beating a drum and clanging a cymbal, as <gloss>m</gloss> a priest of Cybele <note>original: "Menagyrtes," a wandering beggar-priest of the goddess Cybele</note> might, having it hung from his neck—on the grounds that he himself had become effeminate among the Greeks and was teaching the <gloss>n</gloss> "feminine disease" <note>A historical term used to describe the ecstatic, sometimes self-castrating practices associated with the cult of the Mother Goddess</note> to other Scythians. For which cause—since it must be hidden in no way—it comes to my mind to wonder how <gloss>r</gloss> Euhemerus of Agrigentum, Nicanor of Cyprus, <gloss>f</gloss> Diagoras, Hippo of Melos, and that Cyrenaic after these, whose name was Theodorus, and many others, who lived temperately and with self-control, and who perceived more sharply than other men <insert>B</insert> this error concerning these gods, were nicknamed impious and *atheists* <note>original: "ἀθέους," meaning "without God"</note>; even if they did not contemplate the truth itself, they certainly suspected the error, which is no small seed for sparking the glimmer of understanding the truth. Of these men, one <note>Euhemerus</note> instructed the Egyptians: "If you believe they are gods, do not mourn for them nor wail for them. But if you mourn them, do not think them to be gods." Another <note>Diagoras of Melos</note>, when he had taken an image of Hercules fashioned from wood, and happened to be cooking something at home (as is likely), said: "Come now, Hercules, now is the time that you, just as you did for Eurystheus, should serve us also by performing this thirteenth labor," and he prepared it for Diagoras by throwing the god, like a piece of wood, into the fire. Thus, the extremes of <insert>C</insert> <margin>Deut. 23</margin> ignorance are impiety and superstition, and one must strive to stay clear of both. Do you not see Moses, the sacred interpreter of truth, commanding that a eunuch, and one whose genitals have been cut off, shall not enter into the assembly? And furthermore, he who is born of a prostitute? <note>Referring to Deuteronomy 23:1-2</note> He signifies by the first two categories those impious characters who are deprived of divine virtue and the power to generate [truth]; and by the third, the one who, in place of the one and only God, ascribes to himself many gods with false names—just as he who is born of a prostitute ascribes to himself many fathers due to his ignorance of his true father. But there was a certain ancient kinship with heaven naturally implanted in men, obscured indeed by ignorance, but which nevertheless suddenly leaps out and shines forth from the darkness, as was said by someone:

> <insert>D</insert> -> Do you not see this one who, high above the infinite ether, <-
> -> Holds the earth in his moist arms? <-
> -> For whom the earth is a chariot, and the world a dwelling. <-
> -> Who you are is difficult to guess. <-
<note>This poem is traditionally attributed to Euripides</note>

And whatever other such things the poets sing. But perverse opinions, which have turned away from the right path, are truly ruinous; they have diverted man, who is a "heavenly plant," away from the heavenly way of seeing and have prostrated him on the ground, persuading him to attend to human fictions. For some, being immediately deceived while contemplating the sky and trusting in sight alone, watched the movements of the stars, marveled, and judged them to be gods—naming the stars "gods" [*theoi*] <note>original: "θεοὺς"</note> from the word for "running" [*thein*] <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ θεῖν"</note>, and they worshipped the Sun, like the Indians, <insert>E</insert> and the Moon, like the Phrygians. Others, gathering the mild fruits of what grows from the earth, called grain "Ceres" [Demeter], as did the Athenians; and the vine "Dionysus," as did the Thebans. Others, having considered the punishments for vice, turned these into gods, worshipping punishments and calamities. Hence the scenic poets fashioned the Furies and the Eumenides, and those they call "Avengers" [*palamnaious*] <note>original: "παλαμναίους"</note> and "Averters" [*potropaious*] <note>original: "προτροπαίους"</note> as if they were warders-off and drivers-away of evil; and furthermore "Alastors" [*alastoras*] <note>original: "ἀλάστορας"</note>, that is, evil demons or wicked spirits. Now indeed, some of the philosophers themselves, following the poets, established figures and images of the emotions that are within us: namely Fear, and Love, and Joy, and Hope—just as certainly the ancient <gloss>u</gloss> Epimenides did, who erected altars to Insult and Impudence in Athens. Others, driven by these same things, are turned from men into gods, and are <margin>Auxo from "to increase." Thallo from "to sprout."</margin> sculpted in the likeness of a body: a certain Justice, and Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos <note>The three Fates</note>, <insert>F</insert> and the goddesses of Destiny, and Auxo and Thallo of the Athenians. The sixth way of introducing and acquiring the deception of the gods is that by which they number the gods as twelve. Of these, Hesiod also sings the "Theogony," or the origin of the gods, and whatever others have discussed theologically about the gods...

He uses a mix of biblical citations and classical anecdotes to show how humanity has lost its natural connection to the true God.</summary>

# TO THE HEATHENS

<margin>A</margin> Homer says <note>The OCR reads "Arit," likely a typo for "Ait" (he says).</note>. There remains the last—for these are all seven modes <note>Clement has been categorizing the various ways humans fell into the error of worshiping false gods</note>—which proceeds from the divine benefit given to men. For since they did not understand the God who bestows benefits, they fashioned certain "Saviors"—Castor and Pollux, and Hercules the <term>Averter of Evil</term> <note>original: ἀλεξίκακον (alexikakon)</note>, that is, a helper in times of trouble, and the physician Aesculapius. These are indeed slippery and deadly digressions from the truth, which drag a man down from heaven and thrust him into the abyss. But I wish to show you to the life what sort of beings these gods were, and who they were, so that you might finally cease from your error and return again to heaven. For we too were once children of wrath, just like the rest. But God, <margin>Ephesians 2</margin> since He was rich in mercy, through His great love with which He loved us, even when we were dead in our sins, brought us to life together with Christ. For the Living Word, <margin>B</margin> buried together with Christ, is exalted together with God. But those who are still unbelieving are called children of wrath, as those who are nourished by wrath. We are no longer foster-children of wrath, we who have been torn away from error and strive toward the truth. By that reasoning, we who were once children of iniquity have now, through the mercy of the Word, become children of God. As for you, your own poet, Empedocles of Agrigento, has addressed you:

->For it is difficult; for those whom a wicked life tortures,<-
->There will be no ceasing from wretched sorrow for you.<-

Indeed, very many things have been handed down to you about the gods that are fictional and legendary. But whatever things are reputed to have actually been done, these were written about shameful men who lived <margin>C</margin> petulantly and disgracefully. You walk with a certain arrogance and madness; having left the straight path, you depart through thorns and briars.

->Why do you wander? Cease from human affairs.<-
->And casting aside the darkness of night, take hold of the light.<-

The prophetic and poetic Sibyl <note>The Sibylline Oracles were often cited by early Christians as pagan prophecies that pointed toward the one true God</note> commands these things to you; Truth also commands it, which exposes the crowd of gods from behind these terrible and awe-inspiring masks, proving that these adopted opinions are merely synonyms for error. Indeed, there are those who say there are three Jupiters: one the son of Aether in Arcadia, and the others the sons of Saturn—one of these in Crete, and the other again in Arcadia. There are those who posit five Minervas: one the daughter of Vulcan, the Athenian; <margin>D</margin> another the daughter of the Nile, the Egyptian; a third, daughter of Saturn, the inventor of war; a fourth, daughter of Jupiter, whom the Messenians named Coryphasia after her mother; and the last, the daughter of Pallas and Titanis (the daughter of Ocean), who, after her father was impiously sacrificed by her, was adorned with her father’s skin as if it were a fleece. Now indeed, Aristotle lists Apollos: the first, the son of Vulcan and Minerva (here Minerva is no longer a virgin!); the second in Crete, the son of Corybas; the third, the son of Jupiter; and a fourth, an Arcadian, the son of Silenus—he was called "The Shepherd" <note>original: Nomius</note> among the Arcadians. After these, he recounts the Libyan son of Ammon. Didymus the Grammarian adds a sixth to these, the son of Magnes. And how many innumerable Apollos are there even now—mortal men, bringing aid—who were named just like those mentioned before? What if I were to tell you of the many Aesculapiuses, or the various Mercuries <margin>E</margin> that are enumerated, or the Vulcans who are handed down in fables? Will I not seem to bring you something superfluous, overwhelming your ears with these many names? But their homelands, their crafts, their lives, and furthermore their graves, prove that they were mere men. Even Mars, certainly, who was honored by the poets as much as he could be: <margin>Iliad 5</margin>

->Mars, Mars, bane of men, who shakes the walls.<-

This turncoat, who follows now this side, now that, and rises against his enemies, as Epicharmus says, was a Spartan. Sophocles, however, knew him to be a Thracian; others an Arcadian. Homer says this one was bound for thirteen <margin>Iliad 6</margin> months.

<margin>fickle</margin>
<margin>hostile</margin>
->And Mars endured it, when Otus and strong Ephialtes,<-
->Sons of Aloeus, bound him with a heavy chain.<-
->For thirteen months he was bound in a bronze jar.<-

May the Carians be increased with many blessings, for they sacrifice dogs to him. And may the Scythians not cease—

For this reason, Megaclo, as a way of returning thanks to them on her mother's behalf, erected bronze columns and ordered them to be honored in all the sacred rites. Such is the true nature of the Muses. This history is found in Myrsilus of Lesbos.

# TO THE GENTILES
### B ii

<margin>Commonly read as Aethia.</margin>
**A** ...was an old counselor. But Sterope does not say these things, nor Arethusa, nor Arsinoë, nor Zeuxippe, nor Prothoë, nor Marpissa, nor Hypsipyle. For only Daphne escaped both the prophet and his vice. <note>Daphne fled from Apollo (the prophet) to preserve her virginity, eventually turning into a laurel tree.</note> And after all these, let Jupiter himself come forward—who, by your own estimation, is the father of men and gods—who was so abandoned to Venus <note>Lust</note> that he desired everyone and satisfied his lust upon them all. He was satisfied by women no less than the goat of the Thmuitans <note>The city of Thmuis in Egypt was known for the cult of the goat-god Mendes, associated with fertility and sexual license.</note> is by she-goats. Indeed, Homer, I admire your poems:

<margin>Iliad, book 1.</margin>
> *The son of Saturn <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note> spoke, and nodded with his dark brows,*
> *And the ambrosial locks of the King streamed down*
> *From his immortal head, and he shook great Olympus.*

**B** You fashion a grave and venerable Jupiter, O Homer, and you attribute to him a nod that must be honored. But if you were to show him only a *cestus* <note>The enchanted girdle of Venus that inspired irresistible desire.</note>, O man, Jupiter is exposed, and his hair is covered in disgrace. Into what great lust did that Jupiter fall, who spent so many nights in delight with Alcmene? For even nine nights were not long enough for his intemperance. Furthermore, his whole life was a brief span of intemperance, so that he might father for us that "Averter of Evils," Hercules, the son of Jupiter—truly the son of Jupiter!—who was born from that long night. He bravely endured twelve labors over a long time, yet in a single night he violated the fifty daughters of Thestius, acting as both the adulterer and the bridegroom of so many virgins at once. It is not without reason, then, that the poets call him wretched and <term>asyldorgon</term> <note>original: "ἀσυλόδοργον," meaning a perpetrator of wicked or lawless deeds.</note>, that is, a doer of nefarious things. It would be a long task to recount his adulteries of every kind and the outrages committed against boys. For your gods did not even abstain from boys;

**C** one loved Hylas, another Hyacinthus, another Pelops, another Chrysippus, and another Ganymede. Let your wives adore these gods! Let them pray that their own husbands be just like them—so temperate as to be similar to the gods, pursuing similar things! Let your sons grow accustomed to worshipping them, so that they too may become men, accepting the gods as the sacred image of fornication. But perhaps among the gods, only the males are driven toward Venus? No, for the female goddesses stayed at home, as Homer says, each of them blushing out of modesty to see Venus caught in adultery. <note>A reference to the Odyssey, where the gods watch Ares and Aphrodite caught in a net.</note> Yet they themselves behave impudently, being even more violently entangled in adultery: Aurora for the sake of Tithonus, the Moon for Endymion, a Nereid for Aeacus, and Thetis for Peleus; Ceres <note>Demeter</note> for the sake of

**D** Jason, and Proserpina <note>Persephone</note> for Adonis. Venus herself was covered in shame and disgrace because of Mars; she moved on to Cinyras, married Anchises, laid snares for Phaethon, and loved Adonis. She even contended with Juno, who is called <term>boopis</term> <note>original: "βοῶπις," meaning ox-eyed or cow-eyed—a standard Homeric epithet for Juno/Hera.</note>, that is, with the eyes of a cow. And when they had stripped off their divine garments for the sake of an apple, they submitted themselves to a shepherd <note>Paris</note>, who was to judge which of them was beautiful. Come now, let us also briefly survey the Games, and let us dissolve those "panegyric" gatherings at the tombs: the Isthmian, Nemean, Pythian, and the Olympic games that follow them. At Pytho, the Pythian Dragon is worshipped, and the gathering of the serpent is called the Pythia. At the Isthmus, the sea vomited up a miserable piece of refuse, and the Isthmian games mourn for Melicertes. At Nemea, funeral rites were performed for another boy, Archemorus, and the funeral oration for the boy is called the Nemea. Pisa, 

**E** O Greeks, is for you the tomb of a Phrygian charioteer, and the Olympic games are funeral offerings for Pelops. Jupiter, sculpted by Phidias, claims the Olympics for himself. It seems, therefore, that the mysteries were actually games undertaken for the sake of the dead, just like the oracular responses, and both became public affairs. But the things that are <term>Sagra mysteries</term> <note>Refers to the mysteries at the river Sagra.</note> and those in Alimus of Attica have been restricted to Athens. <margin>lamps</margin> They are a shame and disgrace to the world—both the games and the Phalli consecrated to Dionysus, which have evilly taken hold of life. For when Dionysus desired to descend to the underworld, he did not know the way. A certain man named Prosymnus promised he would tell him, but not without a price. The reward was not a beautiful one, though it seemed beautiful to Dionysus: it was a sexual favor that was demanded of him.

**F** This was demanded of a god who was willing, and he promised to give it if he returned, confirming the promise with an oath. When he had learned the way, he departed and then returned, but he did not find Prosymnus, for he was dead. To perform the "just rites" for his lover, Dionysus went to his tomb and was seized by a violent desire to endure the female role. Therefore, when he cut a branch from a fig tree that he happened upon, he shaped it into the likeness of a male member; he then sat upon the branch...

<margin>Iliad, Book 1</margin> > *The son of Saturn spoke and nodded with his dark brows,*

<margin>B</margin> You portray a venerable Jupiter, O Homer, and you grant him a nod to be honored. But if you only show the man his girdle, <note>The "cestus" or girdle of Venus, which inspired irresistible desire.</note> Jupiter is exposed, and his hair is covered in shame. To what extent did that Jupiter’s lust proceed, he who spent so many nights in delights with Alcmene? For even nine nights are not long enough for an intemperate man. Again, his whole life was but a brief span of intemperance, so that he might father for us that "Warder-off of Evils," Hercules, the son of Jupiter—truly the son of Jupiter!—who was born from that long night. He who bravely endured twelve great labors over a long time, yet defiled the fifty daughters of Thestius in a single night, acting as both the adulterer and the bridegroom of so many virgins at once. Not without reason, then, do the poets call him wretched and <term>aischrologon</term> <note>original: "ἀισχρολόγον," meaning a speaker of foul words or a perpetrator of shameful deeds.</note>—that is, a doer of abominable things. <margin>C</margin> One loved Hylas, another Hyacinthus, another Pelops, another Chrysippus, and another Ganymede. Let your wives adore these gods; let them pray that their own husbands be like them—so "temperate" that they are just like the gods, pursuing similar things! Let your sons grow accustomed to worshipping them, so that when they become men, they may accept the gods as a sacred image of fornication. But perhaps among the gods, only the males are driven by lust? No, the female goddesses remained at home, as Homer says, each of them "blushing for shame" to see Venus caught in adultery. <note>A reference to the episode in the Odyssey where Venus (Aphrodite) and Mars (Ares) are caught in a net by Vulcan.</note> Yet they themselves behave shamelessly, deeply entangled in adultery: Aurora for Tithonus, the Moon for Endymion, Nereis for Aeacus, Thetis for Peleus, Ceres for

Come now, let us also briefly survey the athletic contests and dissolve those celebratory funeral assemblies: the Isthmian, Nemean, Pythian, and the Olympic games that follow them. At Delphi <note>original: "Pythone"</note> the Pythian Dragon is worshipped, and the assembly gathered for the serpent is called the Pythian games. At the Isthmus, the sea spat out a miserable corpse, and the Isthmian games are a lament for Melicertes. At Nemea, funeral rites were performed for another boy, Archemorus, and the funeral oration for the boy is called the Nemean games.

<margin>E</margin> And for you, O Greeks, Pisa is the tomb of a Phrygian charioteer, and the Olympic games are the funeral offerings for Pelops. Phidias’s Jupiter claims Olympia for himself. These "mysteries," it seems, were actually contests undertaken for the sake of the dead, just like the responses of the oracles, and both became public spectacles. But the mysteries that are among the <margin>oracles</margin> Sagra, and those in Alimus of Attica, are confined to Athens; yet the world’s shame and disgrace are the contests and the Phalli consecrated to Dionysus, which have evilly taken over our lives. For when Dionysus desired to descend to the underworld, he did not know the way. A certain man named Prosymnus promised to tell him, but not without a reward. The reward was not a beautiful one, though it was "beautiful" to Dionysus: it was a sexual favor <note>original: "venerea gratia"</note> that was demanded of Dionysus.

<margin>F</margin> Since the god was willing, he promised to give it to him if he returned, confirming the promise with an oath. When he had learned the way, he departed; but when he returned, he did not find Prosymnus, for he was dead. To fulfill the duty to his lover, Dionysus went to the tomb and was seized by a powerful desire to perform the feminine role. When he had cut a branch from a fig tree that he happened upon, he shaped it into the likeness of a male member, and sat upon the branch...

...fulfilling a promise to a dead man. There is a mystical monument to this event: throughout the cities, <margin>A</margin> phalli are raised in honor of Dionysus. For unless they held a procession for Dionysus and sang a song to the shameful parts, Heraclitus says, <margin>Heraclitus in the Letter to Hermodorus</margin> they would be performing the most impudent of acts. This "Hades" and "Dionysus" (or Bacchus) are the ones for whom they go mad and rave—not only because of bodily drunkenness, as I believe, but because of the disgraceful and lustful interpretation of their sacred rites. Therefore, your gods are rightly such as they were, being themselves servants to vice. Furthermore, they were even servants to those the Spartans call Helots. Apollo underwent the yoke of slavery to Admetus at Pherae. Hercules served Omphale at Sardis. Neptune and Apollo were hirelings to Laomedon, just like useless slaves who could not even obtain freedom from their former master. At that time, they even built the walls of Troy for the Phrygian king. Homer is not ashamed to say that Minerva shone a light before Ulysses, <margin>B</margin> holding a golden lamp in her hands. We read that Venus, like some immodest little maidservant, placed a seat <note>original: "lecticam," a couch or litter, referring to the scene in the Iliad where Aphrodite places a seat for Helen before Paris.</note> for Helen opposite her lover to lead them into intercourse. Panyassis, moreover, records that many other gods besides these served mortal men, writing thus:

> *Ceres suffered, and the famous Mulciber suffered,*
> *Neptune suffered, and Phoebus Apollo himself*
> *Endured hiring out his labors for a mortal’s wage.*
> *Even fierce Mars suffered, forced by his angry Father.*

And so it follows from these things. It is quite logical that these gods of yours, who <margin>C</margin> languish with love and are vexed by the perturbations of the soul, are shown to be entirely subject to human emotions. For their bodies are mortal. Homer conjectures quite correctly when he introduces Venus crying out with a sharp and loud voice because of a wound, and when he narrates that the most warlike Mars was wounded in the belly by Diomedes. Polemo says Minerva was wounded by Ornytus. Furthermore, Homer says Pluto was wounded by Hercules, as was Augeas of Elis. Panyassis also reports that Juno, the goddess of marriage, was wounded by the same Hercules in sandy Pylos. Sosibius says Hercules was wounded in the hand by the sons of Hippocoon. If there are wounds, there is also blood. But the poetic discharge which they call <term>ichor</term> <note>original: "ἰχῶρα" (ichor), the fluid that flows in the veins of the gods instead of blood.</note> is even fouler than blood, for ichor is understood to be the putrefaction of blood. <margin>D</margin> Therefore, it is necessary to provide them with the cures and nourishment they require. Thus they need tables, drunkenness, laughter, and intercourse; for men would not indulge in sexual things nor labor for children, nor would they even need sleep, if they were truly immortal, lacking nothing and free from old age. Jupiter was even a participant at a human table among the Ethiopians, and at an inhuman and wicked feast: Jupiter himself was received by Lycaon, where he was surely filled with human flesh against his will. For the god did not know that Lycaon, when receiving him at a feast, had set his own slaughtered son, named Nyctimus, before him to be eaten. A remarkable Jupiter indeed! He who is the diviner, <margin>E</margin> who hears suppliants, the merciful one, the *panompheus* <note>original: "panompheus," meaning the author of all oracular voices.</note>—he who hears the voices and tongues of all, the averter and driver-off of evils. Rather, he is unjust, wicked, iniquitous, impious, inhuman, violent, a ravisher, an adulterer, and a lecher. But he was only such a thing when he was a man; now it seems to me that even your myths have grown old. Jupiter is no longer a dragon, nor a swan, nor an eagle, nor a man devoted to lust. The god does not fly, he is not possessed by the love of boys, he does not kiss, he does not commit violence—even though there are still many beautiful women more charming than Leda and fairer than Semele, and youths more handsome and refined than Ganymede, the Phrygian cowherd. Where now is that eagle? Where is the swan? Where is Jupiter himself? He has grown old along with his feathers. It is not that he repents for his loves, nor that he has been taught to be moderate and temperate. The myth is laid open for you: Leda is dead, the swan is dead, the eagle is dead. Do not search the heavens for your Jove, but the earth. The Cretan, <margin>F</margin> in whose land he is buried, will tell you. Callimachus says in his hymns: "For the Cretans, O King, built your tomb." For Jupiter is dead—do not take it badly—just like Leda, the swan, the eagle, the lecherous man, and the dragon. Now indeed, even those who are imbued with this perverse superstition seem...
