> The ancients were not born from oak or rock,
> But are from the race of men.
<note>This is a play on a line from Homer’s Odyssey, suggesting that the "gods" were actually just historical human beings.</note>

But a little later, it is found that they are even associated with oaks and rocks. Staphylus reports that a certain Agamemnon is worshipped as a version of Jupiter in Sparta. Phanocles, in his work *On Beautiful Youths*, says that Agamemnon, the King of the Greeks, was worshipped. He also mentions a temple of Venus standing at Argynnis because of her beloved Argynnus. The Arcadians worship a Diana whom they call the "Strangled One" <note>original: "ἀπάγχυμένη" (apanchymene), referring to a myth where children tied a noose around the neck of a statue of Artemis</note>, as Callimachus says in his *Causes*. Another Diana, called "Condylitis" <note>From "kondylos," meaning a knuckle or fist</note> because of a fist, was worshipped in Methymna. There is also a temple to another Diana "of the Gout" in Laconia, as Sosibius says. Polemo, meanwhile, knows of an image of the "Gaping" Apollo, and another 

<margin>B</margin> of Apollo the "Caterer" <note>original: "obsonatoris," referring to a provider of food</note> who is worshipped in Elis. Here, the people of Elis sacrifice to "Fly-Averting" Jupiter <note>original: "ἀπομύίῳ" (apomyio)</note>. The Romans also sacrifice to a "Fly-Averting" Hercules—that is, the driver-away of flies—as well as to Fever and Terror, whom they also enroll among the number of those who accompanied Hercules. I will pass over the Argives who worship Venus the "Grave-Digger" <note>original: "τυμβώρύχον" (tymborychon), she who digs up tombs</note>. The Argives, the Laconians, and even the Spartans worship Diana "Chelidytis," because the act of coughing is called "chelidotyzein" <note>original: "χελίδοῦίζειν"</note> by them. Where do you think these records come from? These things are brought forward from your own sources; do you not even recognize your own writers, whom I summon as witnesses to your unbelief? O wretched ones, who have filled your entire life—which is truly not a life at all—with such mockery. Is there not a "Bald Jupiter" honored in Argos, and another "Avenger" in Cyprus? And do not the Argives sacrifice to Venus 

<margin>C</margin> the "Promiscuous" <note>original: "πειβάσίη" (epibasia), referring to sexual accessibility</note>? Or the "Courtesan" <note>original: "ἑταίρᾳ" (hetaira)</note> among the Athenians? Or even "She of the Beautiful Buttocks" <note>original: "καλλιπύγῳ" (kallipygos)</note> among the Syracusans, whom the poet Nicander somewhere called "the one with the beautiful haunches"? I will remain silent now regarding Dionysus "the groper" <note>original: "χοιροψάλαιν" (choiropsalan), a crude term for sexual touching</note>; the Sicyonians worship him, placing Dionysus over the female parts so that he might take charge of such indecency, worshipping him who is the author and prince of shame and petulance. Such are their Gods! And such are the people themselves, playing at being gods, or rather mocking themselves and covering themselves in shame and disgrace. How much better are the Egyptians, who worshipped brute animals in their villages and towns, than the Greeks who adore such Gods! For those animals, even if they are wild, are at least not adulterers, nor are they given to debauchery and fornication. But as for these gods, what 

<margin>D</margin> need is there to say more when we have already sufficiently convicted them? Furthermore, the Egyptians I just mentioned are divided into various cults and religions. Among them, the people of Syene worship the Phagrus fish. Those who live in Elephantine worship the Maotes (which is also another fish). The inhabitants of Oxyrhynchus similarly worship a fish, from which their region is named. Moreover, the people of Heracleopolis worship the Ichneumon. The people of Sais and Thebes worship the sheep. Those of Lycopolis worship the wolf. The people of Cynopolis worship the dog. The inhabitants of Memphis worship the Apis bull, and those of Mendes worship the goat. But you, who claim to be altogether better than the Egyptians—though I fear to say you are actually worse—you do not stop laughing at the Egyptians every day, yet what are you like toward brute animals yourselves? Some among you, the Thessalians, have bestowed honor upon storks out of custom. The Thebans honor 

<margin>E</margin> weasels, because of the birth of Hercules <note>Referring to a myth where a weasel—or a woman turned into one—helped during Alcmene's labor</note>. And what of this: the Thessalians are again said to worship ants, because they learned that Jupiter, taking the form of an ant, coupled with Eurymedusa the daughter of Cletor, and fathered Myrmidon? Polemo reports that those who live around the Troad worship the mice of those regions, whom they call "Sminthian" <note>original: "σμίνθεα"</note> because they gnawed the strings of war-bows; and they named Apollo "Sminthian" after those mice. Heraclides says that during the building of temples in Acarnania, where the promontory of Actium and the temple of Actian Apollo are located, an ox is first sacrificed to the flies. Nor will I forget the Samians, who worship the sheep, as Euphorion says. Nor even those Syrians who inhabit Phoenicia, of whom some worship 

<margin>F</margin> doves, and others worship fish as intensely as the people of Elis worship Jupiter. Come now, since these things you worship are not Gods, it seems to me we must consider whether they are in truth demons, assigned to this second rank as you say. If they are indeed demons—greedy and wicked—then local demons can also be found openly in cities...

Who then are these guardians? <margin>B</margin> O man of Boeotia <note>Referring to the poet Hesiod, who was from Boeotia.</note>, do not be reluctant to say. Is it not clear who they are, and who are even more honored than these—the great demons: Apollo, Diana, Latona, Ceres, Proserpina, Pluto, Hercules, and Jupiter himself? But let us not flee; these guardians from Ascra <note>Hesiod’s birthplace; Clement is mocking the idea of the gods as moral protectors.</note> watch over us, lest perhaps we sin—those who are certainly not strangers to sin themselves. Here one might speak that which resembles a proverb: "A father who cannot correct himself, corrects his son." If these are indeed our guardians, it is not because of any goodwill they feel toward us; rather, they press for our destruction, and like flatterers, they cling to our lives, lured by the smoke of our sacrifices. The demons themselves certainly confess their gluttony for libations and the smell of burnt meat, as those who say, "we have received this smoke as our reward" <note>A reference to Homer’s *Iliad* where gods describe their share of sacrifices.</note>. What other voice would the gods of the Egyptians—namely cats and weasels—utter, if they received a voice, other than this Homeric and poetic one which delights in the smell and seasoning of meat? Such are your <margin>C</margin> demons and gods; and if any are called "demigods," they are named like "demi-asses" <note>A pun on the word for mule (mulus), suggesting demigods are hybrid absurdities.</note>. For you lack no names for the composition of your impiety. Come now, let us also add this: your gods are inhumane and man-hating demons; they not only take joy in offending human minds but also delight in human slaughter. At times they find pleasure in armed contests in the stadiums, and at other times in the countless struggles for glory in wars, so that they might be filled to the brim with human blood. Indeed, when they have invaded cities and nations like plagues, they have demanded cruel sacrifices. Aristomenes of Messene slaughtered three hundred men for Jupiter Ithometes, believing that he was rightly sacrificing so many "hecatombs" <note>A grand sacrifice, literally of a hundred oxen, but here used for human victims.</note>, among whom was King Theopompus of the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans.</note>, a most illustrious victim. The people of the <margin>D</margin> Tauric Chersonesus <note>The modern-day Crimean Peninsula.</note>, whoever they capture among those who have wandered from the sea, they immediately sacrifice to the Tauric Diana. Your Euripides <note>A famous Greek playwright.</note> sings of these sacrifices tragically upon the stage. Monimus, in his *Collection of Wonders*, reports that in Pella of Thessaly, an Achaean man is sacrificed to Peleus and Chiron. Anticlides also proclaims in his *Returns* that the Lycians (who are a Cretan race) likewise slaughter men to Jupiter. And Dosidas says the Lesbians offer a similar sacrifice <gloss>q</gloss> to Dionysus. The former sacrificed his daughter to Persephone, as Demaratus <margin>E</margin> writes in the first book of *Tragic Matters*; the latter, namely Marius, sacrificed to the "Gods who avert evil" <note>original: "Diis Aueruncanis," Roman deities invoked to ward off misfortune.</note>, as Dorotheus writes in the fourth book of *Italian Matters*. From these things, the demons are shown to wish humanity well! How then are they not holy, who are devoted to the cult and superstition of demons? Some follow demons with good words as if they were saviors, while others seek safety from those who plot against safety itself. While they think they are sacrificing to them rightly, they do not notice they are killing humans. For a slaughter does not become a holy victim just because of the location; nor if someone kills a man for Diana or Jupiter in a sacred place, rather than for anger or greed or other such demons on altars or in the streets, is it a "sacred victim." Such a sacrifice is simply slaughter and homicide. Why then, O men, wisest of other men, do we flee other wild beasts, and if we encounter a bear or a lion, do we turn away? <margin>F</margin>

-># EXHORTATION TO THE HEATHENS<-

### Page 19

<margin>A</margin> Since you have first perceived and understood that these are demons, do you not turn away? Do you not recoil from them? What truth have these wicked ones ever spoken, or what benefit have they brought? I can now show you a man who is better than these gods of yours—these demons, I mean; specifically, I show you Cyrus and Solon as better than the prophet Apollo. Your Phoebus <note>A common name for Apollo, meaning "bright" or "radiant."</note> loves gifts, not men. He betrayed <margin>r</margin> his friend Croesus, and forgetting his reward, he was so greedy for glory that he led Croesus to the funeral pyre across the Halys <note>The river Halys marked the boundary of Croesus’s kingdom; the oracle famously told him that by crossing it, he would "destroy a great empire," which proved to be his own.</note>. Thus do these "loving" demons lead men to the fire. But you, O man, who are more loving of humanity and more truthful than Apollo, have mercy on him who is bound upon the pyre! And you, Solon, prophesy the truth. And you, Cyrus, command the pyre to be extinguished. Finally, you, O Croesus, learn wisdom, now that you have learned it through your own suffering. He whom you adore is ungrateful. <margin>B</margin> He takes his payment, and having accepted your gold, he lies. O Solon, look again at the end; is it not a man, and not a demon, who speaks to you? Solon does not prophesy in riddles; you will understand him well, but you, O Barbarian <note>Clement refers to Croesus as a "Barbarian" in the Greek sense, meaning a non-Greek (Lydian).</note>, will only experience the truth of this answer while upon the pyre. 

Whence does it occur to me to wonder by what <margin>s</margin> visions men were led away—those who, being deceived, announced the superstition and worship of demons to others, commanding by law the worship of these criminal spirits? Whether it was that <margin>t</margin> Phoroneus, or Merops, or some other who established temples and altars for them, and who are also fabulously said to have been the first to offer sacrifices to them. For in later times, certainly, they fashioned the gods they would adore. Surely this Love or Cupid, who is said to be among the <margin>u</margin> oldest of the gods, <margin>C</margin> no one worshipped until a certain youth took Charmus as his lover and placed a more elegant altar in the Academy—after his lust was satisfied, they called the excess of his disease "Love," raising intemperate desire to the rank of the gods. The Athenians, moreover, did not even know who Pan was until <margin>x</margin> Philippides <note>Better known as Pheidippides, the runner who claimed to have met the god Pan on his way to Sparta.</note> told them. Rightly, therefore, since the worship of demons had its beginning somewhere, it became a fountain of foolish vice. Then, because it was not cut off but grew larger and flowed in a great channel, it established many demons, sacrificing hundreds of oxen, celebrating assemblies, erecting images, and building temples. These things I shall not pass over in silence; indeed, I will prove that while they are called "temples" by a beautiful name, they were actually tombs—that is, tombs were called temples. But you, at least even now, forget the worship and superstition <margin>D</margin> of demons, blushing to worship at graves. 

In the temple of Minerva <note>Athena</note> at Larissa, in the citadel, is the tomb of Acrisius. At Athens, in the citadel, is the tomb of Cecrops, as Antiochus says in the ninth book of his *Histories*. And what of Erichthonius? Was he not buried in the temple of Polias? And Immarus, the son of Eumolpus and Daira, was he not buried in the precinct of the Eleusinium, which is beneath the citadel? And the daughters of Celeus, are they not buried in Eleusis? Why should I list for you the wives of the Hyperboreans? Hyperoche and Laodice are buried in the Artemisium in Delos; that is, in the temple of Delian Apollo. Leandrius says that Clearchus was buried at Miletus in the <margin>y</margin> Didymaeum. Here <margin>z</margin> it is right not to overlook the monument of Leucophryne, following Zeno <margin>a</margin> of Myndus, who was buried in the temple of Diana <note>Artemis</note> at Magnesia. Nor should we forget the altar of Apollo in Telmessus, <margin>E</margin> which they write is the monument of the prophet Telmissus. Ptolemy, the son of Agesarchus, in the first book of his writings on Philopator, says that Cinyras and his descendants were buried in Paphos in the temple of Venus <note>Aphrodite</note>. Truly, if I were to pursue all the tombs that are worshipped, even all of time would not suffice. 

But you—if no shame for these things you dare to do comes over you—do you wander about as the truly dead, believing in the dead? O wretched ones, why do you tolerate this evil? In the night, your heads are shrouded. But if, beyond these things, I place the images themselves before you to consider, truly looking into them, you will find that these customs are nonsense, as you worship the senseless works of human hands. Anciently, the Scythians worshipped a <term>scimitar</term> <note>original: "acinacem," a short Persian/Scythian sword</note>. The Arabs worshipped a stone. The Persians worshipped a river. And among other men, those who were <margin>F</margin> even more ancient would set up distinguished logs and place columns of stone, which were called <term>xoana</term> <note>original: "ξόανα," primitive wooden images carved or scraped out of raw material</note> because they were scraped and polished from raw matter. In Icarus, certainly, the image of Diana was an unworked log, and <margin>Thespiae, a place in Boeotia sacred to Juno.</margin> that of Cithaeronian Juno <note>Hera</note> at Thespiae was a cut tree trunk; and that of Samian Juno, as Aethlius says, was at first merely a wooden plank.

<summary>Clement argues that pagan temples are actually tombs of dead mortals and critiques the evolution of idols from primitive objects like logs and stones (xoana) into the statues worshipped in his day.</summary>

<header>ORATION TO THE HEATHENS</header>

<margin>A</margin>
Later, however, when Procleus was Archon <note>A chief magistrate in ancient Greek city-states.</note>, the image was shaped into the form of a statue. Once statues began to be modeled after human beings, they were called *brete* <note>original: βρέτη</note>, which is the same as "statues," taking their name *ek broton* <note>original: ἐκ βροτῶν</note>, which means "from mortals." In ancient Rome, the writer Varro says the statue of Mars was originally a spear, before craftsmen had reached this beautiful but wicked level of skill. Once art flourished, error increased. It is clear then that stones and wood—and to put it simply, mere matter—were made into images resembling humans, which you present as forms of piety while slandering the truth. Since the topic requires some proof, I must not refuse it. It is well known that Phidias made the Olympian Zeus and the Athena Polias at Athens out of gold and ivory.

<margin>B</margin>
Olympicus, in his *History of Samos*, records that the statue of the Samian Juno <note>The Roman name for the Greek goddess Hera.</note> was made by the chisel of Euclides. 
<margin>This passage is corrupt.</margin>
Do not doubt then, if Scopas made two of the "Venerable Goddesses" <note>The Semnai, or Eumenides/Furies.</note> at Athens from the stone called *lychneus* <note>original: λυχνεὺς; likely Parian marble, named for being quarried by lamplight.</note>, while Polemon shows in the fourth book of his writings to Timaeus that Calos made the one they say is in the middle. Nor should you doubt the statues of Jupiter and Apollo in Patara, Lycia, which Phidias again fashioned as images, just like the lions dedicated with them. 
<margin>As if he were saying, whether it was the art of Bryaxis or Phidias.</margin>
If, as some say, it was the work of Bryaxis, I will not argue; you have him as a sculptor too. Attribute it to whichever you wish. Furthermore, as Philochorus says, the images of Neptune and Amphitrite worshipped on Tenos are the work of Telesius the Athenian. 

<margin>C</margin>
Demetrius, in the second book of his *History of Argos*, writes that the statue of the Tirynthian Juno was made of pear-wood, and the craftsman was Argus. Many will perhaps be amazed to learn that the "Palladium" <note>A wooden statue of Pallas Athena believed to protect the city that held it.</note> called *Diopetes* <note>original: Diopetes; meaning "fallen from Zeus/Heaven."</note>—which Diomedes and Ulysses are said to have stolen from Troy and deposited with Demophoon—was actually constructed from the bones of Pelops, just as the Olympian statue was made from the bones of an Indian beast <note>Likely ivory from an elephant.</note>. I bring forward Dionysius as a witness to this in the fifth part of his *Circle*. Appellas, in his *Delphic History*, says there were two Palladia, and both were manufactured by men. But so no one thinks I have skipped over anything through ignorance, I will add this as well: 
<margin>Morychus is one of the names for Bacchus.</margin>
the statue of Bacchus Morychus was made from the stone called *Phellata* <note>original: Phellata; a type of hard stone.</note>, and was the work of Sicon, also called Eupalamus, as Polemon says in a certain letter. 

<margin>D</margin>
There were also two other Cretan sculptors, I believe, named Scyles and Dipoinos. They made the images of Castor and Pollux at Argos, the effigy of Hercules at Tiryns, and the statue of Diana <note>The Roman name for Artemis.</note> Munychia in Sicyon. Why do I linger on these, when I can show you who that "great demon" really was—the one we hear is considered worthy of worship and veneration by everyone above all others? Some have dared to say that the Egyptian Sarapis <note>Also known as Serapis, a Greco-Egyptian deity who combined features of Osiris and Zeus/Pluto.</note> was not made by human hands. Others write that he was a gift sent from the people of Sinope to Ptolemy Philadelphus <note>A king of Ptolemaic Egypt (r. 283–246 BC).</note>, who had saved them from famine by sending grain from Egypt. They say this statue was an image of Pluto, which he received and placed on the promontory now called Raestis, where there is a temple of Sarapis held in high honor. 

<margin>E</margin>
There is an estate near those places. When Blistiche, a mistress, died at Canopus, Ptolemy had her moved and buried beneath the previously mentioned temple. Others say the statue of Sarapis is a Pontic image, brought honorably to Alexandria by a great gathering of people. Isidore alone records that the statue was brought from the people of Seleucia (near Antioch), who had also suffered from a lack of grain and were fed by Ptolemy. However, Athenodorus, son of Sandon, wishing to show the antiquity of Sarapis, somehow slipped up and proved the statue was manufactured. He says that the Egyptian King Sesostris, after conquering many Greek nations, returned to Egypt and brought many craftsmen with him. He ordered a magnificent and skillfully varied image of Osiris, from whom he claimed descent, to be fashioned. 

<margin>F</margin>
The craftsman Bryaxis (not the Athenian, but another of the same name) constructed it, using a mixture of various materials for the work. It contained filings of gold, silver, copper, iron, and lead; nor was any Egyptian stone missing from it, nor Sapphires and...

<header>TO THE GENTILES</header>

<margin>A</margin>...emery and hematite fragments, but no emeralds or topazes. All these materials were smoothed, ground, and mixed together, and he [the artist] coated the statue with a blue color. For this reason, the color of the image is quite dark. When he had mixed all these things with the embalming fluid <note>original: pharmaco; used here to mean the medicinal or chemical substances used in mummification.</note> left over from the burial of Osiris and Apis, he created Sarapis. His name also signifies the fellowship of the funeral and the work that resulted from the burial—so that which was composed of Osiris and Apis became "Osirapis." Furthermore, the Roman Emperor [Hadrian] introduced another new god to Egypt—one who is worshipped almost by the Greeks themselves—his favorite, Antinous, who was most beautiful. He consecrated him just as Jupiter did Ganymede. For desire that lacks fear is not easily restrained. And men now adore the "sacred nights" of Antinous, which his lover, who stayed awake with him, knew were shameful. 

<margin>B</margin>Why do you present to me as a god a man who was honored through debauchery? Why did you command that he be mourned as if he were a son? Why do you speak of his beauty? Beauty is shameful when it has withered through insult and disgrace. Do not exercise tyranny, O man, over beauty; do not bring disgrace upon a flowering youth. Keep it pure so that it may be truly beautiful. Become a king of beauty, not its tyrant; let it remain free. Only then will I recognize your beauty, because you preserved the image pure; then I will adore true beauty, which is the pattern <note>original: exemplar</note> of all beautiful things. But now, the tomb of the beloved is the temple and the city of Antinous. Just as there are temples, so too are certain tombs held in admiration: the Pyramids, the Mausoleums, and the Labyrinths—other temples of the dead, just like those tombs of the gods. But for you, I will bring forward the prophetess Sibyl as a teacher.

<margin>C</margin>> These are not the lying oracles of Phoebus <note>Apollo</note>,
> Whom foolish men called a god and falsely named
> A prophet; but this is the voice of the true God, who is unlike images
> Which the hands of men have made, lacking the power of speech.

She indeed predicts for you the ruins of temples, signifying that the Temple of Diana at Ephesus will be swallowed up by cracks and movements of the earth, in these words:

> And Ephesus, cast down and sorrowful, shall weep on the shore,
> Searching for her temple, which then no one shall inhabit.

<margin>D</margin>She also says the temple of Isis and Sarapis in Egypt is to be destroyed and burned:

> Goddess Isis, you shall remain unlucky in the waters of the Nile,
> Alone and voiceless, a Maenad <note>A frenzied female follower of Bacchus/Dionysus.</note> on the sands of Acheron.

Then she adds:

> And you, Sarapis, a huge stone mass erected high,
> A great disaster hangs over you in miserable Egypt.

But if you do not listen to the Prophetess, then listen to your own philosopher, Heraclitus of Ephesus, who reproached images for being senseless. People offer prayers to images just as if someone were speaking to houses. For are they not monstrous who adore stones? 

<margin>E</margin>Furthermore, they even set them before their doors as if they were living and effective. They adore Mercury as a god, calling him <term>aguia</term> <note>original: ἀγυιά; a term for a protector of streets or neighborhoods</note>, which is to say the overseer of the streets or the neighborhood, making him a gatekeeper. If they treat them with such insult as if they were senseless, why do they adore them as gods? If they think they possess senses, why do they make them gatekeepers? The Romans, who attribute their greatest and most noble deeds to Fortune and think she is the greatest goddess, placed her in a manure heap <note>original: sterquilinium; referring here to a latrine or refuse pile, mocking the placement of certain shrines.</note>, assigning a sewer as a worthy temple for the goddess. Truly, the senseless stone, wood, and rich gold care nothing for the smell of fat, nor blood, nor smoke, by which they are blackened while being honored and fumigated. 

<margin>F</margin>They care for neither honor nor insult. These images are viler than any animal. It makes me wonder how things that are senseless could be treated with divine honor, and I pity the madness of those who wander like wretched people. <margin>σμυρίς</margin> <note>original: smyris; emery, used for polishing.</note> For even if some animals do not have all the senses—like worms and caterpillars, and whatever appears crippled and mutilated from its very birth, such as moles and the shrew-mouse (which Nicander calls blind and deaf)—they are still better than these statues...

<summary>Clement of Alexandria critiques the deification of humans and senseless objects, specifically mocking the origins of Sarapis and the Roman deification of Antinous. He cites the Sibylline oracles and the philosopher Heraclitus to argue that idols are merely inanimate matter, inferior even to the lowest animals.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Clement of Alexandria’s polemic against the worship of physical idols. Having previously described the mundane and often "unclean" materials used to construct statues (like the mixture used for Sarapis), he now contrasts the sensory life of even the lowliest animals with the complete lifelessness of man-made images.</meta>

<header>EXHORTATION TO THE GREEKS</header>

...to images that are utterly deaf. For living creatures certainly have at least one sense— <margin>A</margin>
for instance, hearing or touch, or a sense that corresponds and agrees with
smell or taste. But idols share in no sense at all. There are, however, many 
living things that have neither sight, nor hearing, nor voice—such as the race 
of oysters—yet they live and grow, and are even affected in unison with the Moon. 
But statues are idle, ineffective, useless, and senseless; they are bound, fixed 
with nails, hammered together, cast, filed, cut, scraped, and carved. The 
sculptors vex the deaf earth and treat it insultingly, moving it away from its 
proper nature by their art and persuading people to worship it. In my opinion, 
those who make these "gods" do not actually worship gods or spirits, but rather <margin>B</margin>
the earth and their own art—which is exactly what these images are. An image 
is truly dead matter, shaped by the hand of a craftsman. To us, however, an 
image is not something perceived by the senses, nor is it the image of sensible 
matter, but rather that which is perceived by the intellect. God, who alone 
is truly God, is perceived by the mind, not the senses. And again, when 
superstitious worshippers of stones have learned through actual cases and 
misfortunes not to worship senseless matter, they are overcome by the very 
experience and perish through their superstition. And yet, while they 
secretly despise the idols but are unwilling to appear to despise them entirely, 
they are proven wrong by the very "gods" to whom these images are dedicated. 
For Dionysius the Younger, the Tyrant <note>Dionysius II of Syracuse, 4th century BCE.</note>, after he had stripped the golden 
cloak from the statue of Jupiter in Sicily, ordered him to be dressed in a woolen 
one, saying wittily that it was better than the gold: it was lighter in summer 
and warmer in winter. And Antiochus of Cyzicus <note>Antiochus IX Cyzicenus, a Seleucid king.</note>, when he was in need of money, <margin>C</margin>
ordered the golden statue of Jupiter—which was fifteen cubits high—to be 
melted down, and replaced it with a statue of cheaper material made to look 
like it, covered in gold leaf. Furthermore, swallows and many birds often fly 
in and defile these images, showing no concern for Olympian Jupiter or 
Aesculapius of Epidaurus <margin>Epidaurus is a town of the Argives, sacred to Apollo.</margin>. 
Nor do they care for Athena of the City <note>original: Poliadis; Athena Polias, the protector of the city of Athens.</note> or the Egyptian Sarapis, 
from whom even you do not learn that these images are senseless. Instead, there 
are certain wicked robbers or enemies who, breaking in for the sake of base 
profit, have plundered the sacred sites and snatched away the offerings, 
or even melted down the statues themselves. And if some Cambyses or Darius, 
or another madman, has done such things—or if someone killed the Egyptian 
Apis <note>The sacred bull of Memphis.</note>—I laugh because he killed their god, though I am indignant if he 
sinned for the sake of profit. I would gladly forget this crime, considering it <margin>D</margin>
a proof of greed rather than the weakness of the idols. But neither fire nor 
terrible earthquakes fear or respect these spirits or their images, any more 
than they do the pebbles piled up by the waves on the shore. I know that fire 
can provide proof and a cure for superstition, if you are willing to cease from 
your madness. Fire will lead you to the light. This fire burned the temple that 
was at Argos along with its priestess Chrysis; it destroyed the temple of Diana 
at Ephesus (the second one after the Amazons); and at Rome, it has often 
plundered the Capitol, nor did it abstain from the temple of Sarapis in 
Alexandria. It also demolished the temple of Dionysius the Liberal in Athens; 
and as for the temple at Delphi, first a storm snatched it away, and then a 
"wise fire" <note>original: ignis sapiens; a Stoic concept of fire as a purifying or rational force.</note> and a tempering one destroyed it. This is shown to you as a 
preface of what the fire promises. Do not those who manufacture the statues <margin>E</margin>
admonish those of you who are wise to despise the material? Phidias the 
Athenian <note>One of the most famous sculptors of classical Greece.</note> wrote on the finger of Olympian Jupiter: "Pantarkes is beautiful" 
<note>original: παντάρκης καλός; Pantarkes was a young athlete loved by Phidias.</note>. 
For to him, it was not Jupiter who was beautiful, but the one he loved. 
And Praxiteles, as Posidippus declares in his book on Cnidus, when he was 
constructing the image of Venus of Cnidus, made it in the likeness of his 
beloved Cratina, so that the wretched people might worship the girlfriend 
of Praxiteles <margin>Some say Phidias did this.</margin>. And when Phryne, the courtesan of Thespiae, 
was in her prime, all the painters modeled their images of Venus after 
Phryne’s beauty. Just as, in turn, the stonecutters also shaped the 
statues of Hermes <note>original: Mercurios; referring to the "Hermae" or bust-pillars of Athens.</note> in Athens after the likeness of Alcibiades. It remains 
now for you to apply your judgment, if you wish to worship even courtesans. 
I think it was for this reason that the kings of old, despising these fables, <margin>F</margin>
declared themselves to be gods, acting freely because they faced no danger 
from men; by this logic, they taught that they too had become immortal 
through glory. Ceyx, the son of Aeolus, was called Jupiter by his wife 
Alcyone; and Alcyone in turn was called Juno by her husband. Ptolemy IV 
was called Dionysius, and Mithridates of Pontus was also called Diony...

<meta>This page continues Clement of Alexandria’s argument that "gods" are merely divinized humans. After discussing the physical materials of idols, he now provides historical examples of rulers and private citizens who claimed divinity, as well as the mythological contradictions found in Homer.</meta>

<header>EXHORTATION TO THE GREEKS</header>
<page-num>23</page-num>

<margin>A</margin> Alexander the Great also wanted to be seen as the son of Ammon <note>Ammon was an Egyptian deity often depicted with ram horns, later identified with Zeus/Jupiter.</note>, and he insisted on being depicted by sculptors with horns, eager to disgrace the beautiful face of a man with such a shameful mark. Truly, it is not only Kings, but even private citizens who boast of divine titles—like Menecrates the Physician, who was nicknamed Jupiter. Why need I mention Alexarchus? As Aristus of Salamis writes, though he was a scholar of grammar by profession, he fashioned himself into the image of the Sun. Why need I also recall Nicagoras? He was of the Zelian race, born in the time of Alexander; he was called Mercury and wore the clothing of Mercury. Even entire nations, along with their leaders, use flattery to turn these cheap and contemptible myths about gods into reality, making themselves <margin>B</margin> equal to the gods—inflated by glory and decreeing for themselves honors that exceed all measure. Even now, they decree that the Macedonian from Pella, Philip the son of Amyntor, should be worshipped in the Cynofarges <margin>Cynosarges was an Athenian gymnasium dedicated to Heracles.</margin>, even though he had a broken collarbone, a fractured leg, and an eye that had been cut out. And again, they call Demetrius [Poliorcetes] himself a god; where he dismounted his horse to enter Athens, there stands a temple to "Demetrius the Descender" <note>original: "Demetrii καταιβάτου" (kataibatou), meaning one who descends.</note>. Everywhere, altars and "marriages" to Minerva [Athena] were prepared for him by the Athenians. He, however, despised the goddess, as he could not truly marry a statue; instead, taking the prostitute Lamia with him, he ascended to the Acropolis and wallowed in Minerva’s bedchamber, showing to the old Virgin the poses and habits of a young harlot. We should not, then, begrudge Hippo <note>Hippo of Messana, an early Greek philosopher often labeled an atheist.</note> for making his own death immortal. For Hippo ordered this elegiac verse <margin>C</margin> to be inscribed upon his monument:

> ->*This is the tomb of Hippo, whom fate made equal*<-
> ->*To the eternal gods, now that he is bereft of light.*<-

You have done rightly, O Hippo, in showing us human error! For if they did not believe you while you spoke, let them become your disciples now that you are dead. This is the "oracle" of Hippo; let us understand it ourselves. Those who are worshipped by you were once men, and eventually they died. It was time and myth that bestowed honor upon them. For somehow, things that are present tend to be despised due to familiarity; but things that are past, separated from the evidence of the present, are held in honor due to the uncertainty of time and the power of fiction. Some things are not believed, while others are even held in admiration. Now, these ancient dead, having marketed themselves through a long era of error, are considered gods by posterity. Your own mysteries, famous assemblies, stories of chains and wounds, and weeping gods, provide the proof of these things.

<margin>Iliad, Book 8</margin>
> ->*Woe is me, that Sarpedon, the one dearest to me of all men,*<-
> ->*Is fated by the gods to be subdued by Patroclus.*<-

The will of Jupiter [Zeus] was overcome! Having been defeated, your Jupiter mourns for Sarpedon. You yourselves, therefore, rightly call them idols and "daemons" <note>In this context, Clement uses "daemons" to mean lesser, often malevolent spirits, rather than the neutral Greek term for a guiding spirit.</note>, since even Homer—who honored them so improperly—called Minerva herself and the other gods "daemons."

> ->*But she ascended to Olympus,*<-
> ->*To the house of Aegis-bearing Jupiter, and to the other daemons.*<-

How then are these statues and "daemons" still gods? They are truly abominable and unclean spirits, whom everyone admits are earthbound and muddy <note>original: "lutulentos"</note>, lingering and wallowing around graves and monuments, weighed down by their own gravity. Around such places, ghostly spectra appear, thin and vanishing like shadows. These are your gods: idols and shadows. And besides these, there are those "lame, wrinkled, and squint-eyed" figures <margin>Iliad, Book 9</margin>, who are more likely the daughters of Thersites <note>Thersites was a notoriously ugly and insolent soldier in the Trojan War.</note> than the daughters of Jupiter. This is why it seems to me that Dion spoke so wittily when he asked how men could rightly seek good offspring from Jupiter, when he could not provide them for himself. O pure impiety! You bury the divine essence—which should be foreign to destruction—as much as you can, and you overwhelm that which is undefiled and holy of the true essence, robbing God. Why then have you granted gifts to those who are not gods? Why have you abandoned heaven to honor the earth? For what else is gold, or silver, or adamant, or iron, or bronze, or ivory, or precious stones? Are they not earth, and from the earth?

<summary>Clement of Alexandria argues that Greek gods were merely mortal men—such as Alexander the Great and Philip of Macedon—who were granted divinity through flattery and the passage of time. He uses Homeric poetry and historical anecdotes to mock the "unclean" and physical nature of these supposed deities.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Clement of Alexandria’s critique of idolatry. Having previously argued that "gods" were merely humans, he now turns his focus to the physical materials of statues—stone, ivory, and gold—arguing that worshipping these objects is a rejection of the rational mind in favor of artistic deception.</meta>

<header>EXHORTATION TO THE GREEKS</header>
<page-num>24</page-num>

Are not all these things you see the offspring of one mother, the earth? Why then, O **A** foolish ones devoted to empty thoughts (for I shall return to my purpose), do you assault the heavenly place with curses and drag piety and religion down to the soil? By fashioning terrestrial gods for yourselves and pursuing these created things instead of the uncreated God, 
<margin>Parian stone, which is wonderfully white.</margin> 
have you not fallen into a deeper darkness? Parian stone is beautiful, but it is not yet Neptune. Ivory is beautiful, but it is not yet the Olympian <note>A reference to the massive gold and ivory statue of Zeus/Jupiter at Olympia, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.</note>. Matter always stands in need of art. God, however, stands in need of nothing. The art came first, then the figure was added. While the richness of the material and the substance might lead to profit, they are only considered venerable because of their shape. Your statue is gold, it is wood, it is stone, it is earth; if you consider its beginning, it received its form from a craftsman. But I have learned to walk upon the earth, not to adore it. **B**

For it is not lawful for me to ever entrust the hopes of my soul to inanimate things. One must go as close as possible to the images themselves. For the error peculiar to them is proven even by their appearance. The images express the passions of demons most openly. If anyone were to go about and contemplate the paintings and images, they would immediately recognize your gods from the figures, which are full of filth, ignominy, and disgrace. Dionysus is known by his dress; Vulcan by his craft; Ceres by her calamity <note>A reference to Ceres (Demeter) mourning the abduction of her daughter Proserpina.</note>; Ino by her headband; Neptune by his trident; Jove by the swan; and the funeral pyre points to Hercules. And if anyone sees a depicted naked woman, he understands it to be the "golden" Venus. Thus did Pygmalion the Cypriot fall in love with an ivory statue; it was an image of Venus, and it was naked. The Cypriot was overcome by the shape and attempted to unite with the image. Philostephanus records this. There was **C** another Venus in Cnidus made of stone, and she was beautiful; another man fell in love with her and had relations with the stone of Venus, as Posidippus relates—the former in his work on Cyprus, the latter in his work on Cnidus. So great was the power of art to deceive, which lured men devoted to lust into the abyss. The skill of the craftsman has an effective power, but it cannot deceive one who is endowed with reason, nor those who have lived according to reason. For by means of painting, because of a sketched resemblance, pigeons have flown to painted pigeons, and horses have neighed at correctly painted mares. They say a youth fell in love with an image, and a beautiful young man with the Cnidian statue. But the sight had deceived the spectator. For no one of sound mind would have had intercourse with a goddess, nor would someone have been buried with a dead woman, nor would someone have loved a demon and a stone. **D**

But art deceives you with other tricks, even if it does not lead you to love, it leads you to cherish and adore statues and paintings. Let the painting be "like" the original, let the art be praised, but let it not deceive a man as if it were the truth. The horse stood still: the pigeon was not at all disturbed, and its wing remained idle. The cow of Daedalus, which had been fashioned from wood, caught a wild bull; art forced the beast, having deceived it, to mate with a woman who loved it <note>Referring to the myth of Pasiphaë, who used a wooden cow made by Daedalus to mate with the Cretan Bull.</note>. Such a frenzy did the arts, which use wicked artifice, bring upon the foolish. But those who nourish and train monkeys marvel that they are not fooled by likenesses of wax, or clay, or maidenly ornaments. You, however, turn out to be worse than monkeys when you devote your soul to little images and paintings of stone, wood, gold, and ivory. A great and varied crowd of such ruinous mockeries is **E** introduced by craftsmen, stone-cutters, sculptors, painters, smiths, and poets: Satyrs in the fields; Oread and Hamadryad nymphs through the forests; and indeed Naiads in the waters, rivers, and springs; and Nereids in the sea. Now the Magi boast that they have demons as ministers of their own impiety, as if they had enrolled them into the number of their own servants and made them slaves, driven by necessity through their chants. Therefore, the marriages of the gods, the procreation of children, the childbirths, and the sung adulteries, and the banquets recited by comic poets, and the laughter induced during drinking, all incite me to cry out, even if I wished to remain silent. O impiety! You have made heaven a stage, and God has become a dramatic act for you, and that which is holy you have mocked with the "masks" of demons in comedy, 
<margin>playing the satyr <note>original: "σατυρίζοντες" (satyrizontes)</note> in such a way.</margin>
lustfully and obscenely polluting the true worship of God and religion with the superstition of demons. **F**

<meta>This page continues Clement of Alexandria’s "Exhortation to the Greeks." Having previously argued that the physical material of idols is merely earth and stone, Clement now attacks the immoral myths depicted in Greek art and literature, contrasting them with the "living image" of God found in the Christian believer.</meta>

# TO THE GREEKS

<margin>A</margin>
> *The secret love of fair Venus and of Mars,*
> *How first they met within the house of Vulcan,*
> *And with many gifts defiled the marriage bed*
> *Of King Vulcan.*
<note>original: "Furtiuum pulchræ Venerisq; & Martis amorem..." These lines are a Latin translation of a famous passage from Homer's Odyssey, describing the adultery of Aphrodite (Venus) and Ares (Mars) and their subsequent entrapment by the cuckolded Hephaestus (Vulcan).</note>

<margin>B <note>References to 2 Peter 2, Exodus 19, and John 6.</note> <term>shameful passion<note>original: πασχηπασμὸς (paschepamos). A term likely referring to the performance or witnessing of lewd acts.</note></term></margin>
Stop your song, O Homer, for it is not beautiful. It teaches adultery. We, however, do not wish to stain even our ears with debaucheries and fornications. For it is we, we who carry the image of God around with us in this living and moving likeness—the human being. This image dwells within us, counseling us, speaking with us, living as our companion; it is moved by our feelings and yet is superior to all passions. We have been given and dedicated to God for the sake of Christ. We are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a peculiar people, who once were not a people, but are now the people of God. As John says, we are not from those who are below, but we have learned the whole truth from Him who comes from above. We have grasped with our minds the "economy" of God <note>The "economy" (oeconomia) refers to God's plan for salvation, specifically the incarnation of Christ.</note>, or the administration of the flesh He assumed, and we have trained ourselves to walk in newness of life. 

But the great mass of the common people do not think on these things. Instead, casting aside all shame and fear, they decorate their homes with the shameful lusts and titillations of demons in the form of Venus. By hanging up painted tablets in high places, they apply their minds to these scenes and decorate their bedchambers with unchastity. They consider intemperance to be a form of piety, and while reclining in their beds, even in the midst of their own embraces, they look upon that naked Venus who was bound in chains because of her tryst <note>A reference to the myth where Vulcan caught Venus and Mars in a bronze net.</note>. They approve of the bird flying toward Leda, welcoming it as a lover of women, and they engrave the picture into the bezel of their rings, using a seal that matches the lewdness of Jupiter. These are the models for your soft and delicate life.

<margin>C</margin>
These are the theologies full of disgrace and insolence. These are the doctrines of gods who commit fornication right alongside you. For "whatever any man wishes, that he also believes," as the Athenian orator says <note>Referring to Demosthenes.</note>. What sort of other images do you have? Certain little Pans, and naked girls, and drunken Satyrs, and phallic displays, which are laid bare in paintings and proven to originate from intemperance. Indeed, looking openly and publicly at the figures of every kind of lust and unchastity, you do not blush. Rather, you keep them placed and standing tall, as if you had consecrated the images of your gods as columns of impudence in your homes. You paint the figures and gestures of Philaenis <note>Philaenis of Samos was a Greek author traditionally blamed for writing a famous manual on sex positions.</note> just as you do the labors of Hercules. We announce to you that you must cast away the memory not only of the use of these things, but even the sight and the hearing of them. Your ears have played the harlot, your eyes have committed fornication, and what is more strange, your looks have committed adultery even before the physical embrace. 

<margin>D <note>original: "Græcè ita puto legēdum καὶ τὸ εἴθεῖον τῷ πλάσμαθός ἐλέγχῳ ἀπαρκάσαντες." The translator notes a Greek reading: "And having rejected the divine by the proof of the fiction."</note></margin>
O you who have brought violence upon humanity and have torn away divinity by the proof of your own fictions! You are entirely faithless, so that by following the disturbances of your own souls, you may have leisure for your pleasures. You believe in idols because you seek their intemperance; but you do not believe in God because you cannot bear moderation and self-control. You have hated those things which are superior and honored those which are worse, acting as observers of virtue but as champions of vice. Therefore, to speak once and for all, they alone are blessed who, according to the opinion of the Sibyl <note>The Sibylline Oracles were a collection of Greek prophecies, often used by early Christian writers to show that even "pagan" prophets predicted the downfall of idolatry.</note>:

<margin>E</margin>
> *Will altogether deny the temples they have seen,*
> *The altars, seats of the deaf and of stones,*
> *The images made by hands in the likeness of men,*
> *Stained with the living blood of heavenly things,*
> *Of four-footed beasts, birds, and the slaughter of wild animals.*

<margin>F <note>Reference to Exodus 20.</note></margin>
For we are openly forbidden to practice this deceptive art. "For you shall not make," says the Prophet, "the likeness of anything that is in heaven, or in the earth below." For in truth, Ceres, Proserpina, and the Iacchus of Praxiteles <note>Praxiteles was one of the most famous sculptors of ancient Greece, active in the 4th century BC.</note> are merely figures where the material has been subjected to the initiation of art. But while you work very hard to ensure a statue is fashioned as beautifully as possible, you do not care if, through your lack of perception, you yourselves become like those images. Most clearly and briefly does the prophetic word argue this point:

<meta>This page continues Clement of Alexandria’s critique of idolatry. Having previously contrasted the true "image of God" within humans against the lewd myths of the Greek gods, he now argues that even the "sophisticated" worship of nature and the elements by philosophers is merely a form of error that mistakes the creation for the Creator.</meta>

# EXHORTATION TO THE GREEKS

...custom, saying that all the gods of the nations are idols of demons. <margin>A</margin> God, however, made the heavens and everything that is in heaven. From this, it has come to pass that some, wandering I know not how, adore the divine workmanship indeed, but not God. They worship the Sun and the Moon and the rest of the choir of stars, irrationally considering them to be gods, when they are merely instruments of time. <margin>Psalm 33</margin> <note>original: "Pfal. 32" – In the Latin Vulgate, this is Psalm 32; in English Bibles, it is Psalm 33:6.</note> For by His word they were established, and all their power by the breath of His mouth. While human art builds houses, ships, cities, and paintings, how shall I describe what God does? Look at the entire world. It is His work; the sky, the Sun, the Angels, and men are the works of His fingers. How great is the power of God? The mere will of God is itself the creation of the world. For God alone made it, because He alone is truly God. He operates by His will alone, and the result follows immediately upon His mere desire.

Here, the choir of philosophers is overturned. <margin>B</margin> They beautifully confess that man was made to contemplate the heavens, yet they adore those things that are seen in the heavens and grasped by sight. Even if those things in the sky are not the works of human hands, they were nonetheless created for the benefit of humans. Let none of you adore the Sun, but rather long for the Sun’s Creator; nor should one judge the world to be God or worship it as such, but rather seek the world's Architect. To the one who approaches the gates of salvation, the only refuge remaining, it seems, is divine wisdom. From here, as if from a sacred sanctuary, no person can ever be led astray again, provided they strive for salvation with great zeal.

Let us pursue, if you wish, the opinions which the philosophers boast about regarding the gods. <margin>C</margin> We may find that their philosophy—building idols out of matter for the sake of empty glory, or even ascribing divine honor to certain demons—is merely dreaming of the truth. Thus, they left behind the "principles" they themselves praised: Thales of Miletus chose water; Anaximenes, also of Miletus, chose air; and Diogenes of Apollonia followed him. Parmenides of Elea introduced fire and earth as gods. Of these, Hippasus of Metapontum and Heraclitus of Ephesus considered fire alone to be God. Empedocles of Agrigentum, having encountered the multitude of things, added "Strife" and "Friendship" <note>The Greek concepts of Neikos (Strife) and Philia (Love/Friendship) were used by Empedocles to explain how elements combine and separate.</note> to the four elements.

These too are impious men, who in their foolish wisdom adored matter. <margin>D</margin> While they did not honor stones or wood, they thought the earth, their mother, should be worshiped as a goddess. They do not fashion an image of Neptune, yet they worship water itself. For what else is Neptune but a certain moist substance? <note>original: "ἀπὸ τῆς πόσεως" (apo tēs poseōs) - from drinking.</note> In Greek, he is called *Poseidon* from the word for "drinking," just as the warlike Mars is called *Ares* in Greek <note>original: "ἀπὸ τῆς ἀρσεως καὶ ἀναιρέσεως" (apo tēs arseōs kai anaireseōs).</note> from the words for "rising up" and "killing." For this reason, it seems to me that many people, by simply planting a sword in the ground, sacrifice to it as if to Mars. This is a custom of the Scythians, as Eudoxus says in his second book *On the Circuit of the Earth*. Among the Scythians, the Sarmatians adore the scimitar <note>original: "acinacem" – a short Persian/Scythian sword.</note>, as Hicesius says in his work *On the Mysteries*.

This same error befell Heraclitus and his followers, who worship fire as the principle from which all things arise. Some have named this fire <margin>E</margin> *Hephaestus* (Vulcan). The Persian Magi have also worshiped fire, as do many who inhabit Asia, and even the Macedonians, as Diogenes says in the first book of his *Persian History*. Why should I bother to list the Sarmatians, who Nymphodorus reports in his book *On Barbarian Laws* worship fire? Or the Persians, Medes, and Magi? Dinon says they sacrifice in the open air, believing fire and water to be the only images of the gods.

I will not hide their ignorance. For even if they think they are fleeing from error, they fall into another. They did not consider wood and stone to be images of the gods as the Greeks do, nor mongooses and ibises like the Egyptians, but they chose fire and water like the philosophers. <margin>Berosus was the father of the Sibyl, as Justin Martyr reports.</margin> Yet after many cycles of years had passed, <margin>F</margin> Berosus shows in his third book of *Chaldaean History* that they began to worship images in human form. This was introduced by Artaxerxes, the son of Darius and grandson of Ochus. He was the first to set up an image of Venus Tanaidis <note>A reference to the goddess Anahita, often identified with Venus/Aphrodite.</note> in Babylon, Susa, Ecbatana, Persia, Bactra, Damascus, and Sardis, and he commanded that she be worshiped. Let the philosophers therefore admit that their teachers were the Persians, the Sarmatians, or the Magi, from whom they learned their impiety...

<summary>Clement critiques the Greek and "barbarian" philosophers for worshiping the physical elements (fire, water, air) instead of the Creator. He traces the history of idolatry from the worship of nature to the introduction of human-shaped statues by the Persian king Artaxerxes.</summary>
<keywords>elements, creation, Thales, Heraclitus, Artaxerxes, Berosus, fire worship, Mars, Neptune, idolatry, philosophy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Clement of Alexandria’s refutation of Greek philosophy and pagan worship. On the previous page, he argued that while the universe is a masterpiece, philosophers mistakenly worship the creation (the Sun, Moon, and stars) rather than the Architect. He now proceeds to list specific philosophers and their errors before pivoting to Plato and the poets, who he believes came closer to the truth through a "divine influx."</meta>

# TO THE GENTILES

<margin>A</margin> ...they are ignorant of the author of those principles they hold venerable, the prince of all effects and the craftsman of the principles themselves: God, who lacks any beginning. Instead, they adore these "beggarly and weak elements," <note>original: "egena & infirma"</note> as the Apostle <margin>Galatians 4</margin> says, which were made for the use and service of mankind. Among other philosophers who looked beyond the elements to investigate what is higher and more excellent, some praised the "infinite." Among these were Anaximander of Miletus, Anaxagoras of Clazomenae, and Archelaus of Athens. These two latter thinkers placed "Mind" <note>the Greek concept of *Nous*</note> over the infinite. Leucippus of Miletus and Metrodorus of Chios also seem to have left behind two principles: the "fullness" and the "void." To these two, Democritus of Abdera added "images" or the "appearances of things." Alcmaeon of Croton, however, thought the stars were gods <margin>B</margin> because they were animate.

Nor shall I be silent about the impudence of Xenocrates (he was from Carthage), who signifies seven "Planetary Gods," and an eighth—the world itself—which consists of all these. Neither should I pass over the Stoics, who claim that God permeates all matter, even the most vile and abject; they openly bring disgrace upon their own philosophy. Nor will it be troublesome, I think, since I have reached this point, to mention the Peripatetics <note>The school of Aristotle</note>. The father of this sect <note>Aristotle</note>, because he did not understand the Father—the one called "the Supreme"—believed that God is the soul of the universe; that is, he thought the world's soul was God, and thus he is pierced by his own logic. For he who limits God’s providence only as far as the Moon, <margin>C</margin> and then considers the world to be God, is overturned, as he thinks that which is devoid of God is God himself. That man from Eresus, Theophrastus, a companion of Aristotle, thinks in some places that heaven is God, and in others that God is "spirit." As for Epicurus, I would gladly forget him alone, for he impiously claims that God has no care for human affairs. And what of Heraclides of Pontus? Is he not also pulled down toward "images"?

A great crowd of this sort flows toward me, introducing a kind of mask of demons—absurd tales of the "outsiders" <note>non-Christians</note>, shadowed by old wives' nonsense. We are far from permitting men to hear such fables; we do not even habituate our own weeping children to such stories to comfort them, for we fear that we might nourish in them the same impiety announced by those who think themselves wise—men who <margin>D</margin> know the truth no more than children.

For why, O "Truth," do you make those who believe in you subject to heavy and disordered flux and destruction? Why do you fill my life with idols, fashioning winds, air, fire, earth, stones, wood, or this world as "gods"? And why do you speak loftily and talk nonsense about the "wandering stars" as gods—to men who have truly "wandered" <note>A play on the Greek word *planetes* (wanderer)</note>—through this commonly boasted "astrology," rather than true astronomy? I desire the Lord of spirits, the Lord of fire; I seek God the Architect of the world, who provides light to the Sun, not the works of God themselves.

Whom shall I take as a helper in this inquiry? We do not entirely reject <margin>Plato in the Timaeus.</margin> Plato, if you wish. By what reasoning, then, O Plato, is God to be searched out? "For the Father and Maker of this entire universe is difficult to find, <margin>E</margin> and when you have found Him, it is impossible to declare Him." <note>A famous quote from Plato's *Timaeus* 28c.</note> But why, by Him? <margin>Speak of God by Himself, says Plato.</margin> For He is by no means to be spoken of. 

You have rightly touched upon the truth, O Plato; but do not shrink from the labor. Take up the inquiry into the Good with me. For into all men—to speak once and for all—and especially into those who occupy themselves with learning and letters, a certain "divine influx" has been instilled. For this reason, even against their will, they confess that God is one, free from destruction and unbegotten, and that He truly exists forever in the height of heaven, in His own watchtower. Tell me, what kind of God must I conceive of?

> He who sees all things, but is not seen Himself,

says Euripides. Therefore, it seems to me that Menander erred when he said:

> O Sun, for it is right to adore thee
<margin>F</margin>> As the first of the gods, through whom the others are seen.

For the Sun will never show the true God. Nor will it show the true Word <note>The *Logos* or Christ</note>, who is the "Sun of the soul." If this Sun alone rises within, in the depths of the mind, the eye of the mind itself is illuminated. Whence Democritus not improbably says that a few of the learned...

<meta>This page continues Clement of Alexandria’s argument that the best insights of Greek philosophy were actually borrowed or "stolen" from Hebrew scripture. Having previously critiqued the worship of elements and stars, he now examines specific philosophers like Plato, Xenophon, and Cleanthes, attempting to show that when they spoke truly of a single, invisible God, they were echoing the wisdom of Moses and the prophets.</meta>

# EXHORTATION TO THE GENTILES

<margin>A</margin> ...that men have raised their hands to the sky, and that this which we now call the "air" <note>original: "aërem"</note> is entirely filled with fables; for they claim it knows all things, gives and takes away, and is the King of all. For this reason, Plato also, when contemplating God, indicates He is the King of all things and is the cause of all good. Who, then, is this King, the God of the universe? He is the measure of the truth of all things that exist. For just as those things that can be measured are understood by a standard, so too, by contemplating God, truth comes into our measurement and is understood. Truly, the holy Moses says: <margin>Leviticus</margin> **"There shall NOT be," he says, "in your bag a great or small weight, but a true and just scale,"** <note>Clement is paraphrasing Deuteronomy 25:13-15 and Leviticus 19:35-36</note> considering God to be the scale and measure of all things. For unjust and unequal idols are hidden at home in the bag—and in the "filthy soul," to put it simply. But what is the only just measure? He who alone is truly God, always equal and always remaining the same, <margin>B</margin> who measures and weighs all things as if on a scale of justice, <margin>unwaveringly</margin> <note>original Greek: "ἀῤῥεπῶς" (arrhepōs), meaning without tilting or bias</note> holding and sustaining the nature of the universe in balance. Indeed, as the ancient saying goes, God holds the beginning, the end, and the middle of all things that exist, and He proceeds in a straight line according to nature as He goes about. Justice always follows Him, taking vengeance on those who fall away from the divine Law.

From where, O Plato, do you derive this truth? From where does this abundant supply of reasoning come that foretells piety and the true worship of God? "These races of barbarians," he says, "are wiser than these." <note>Plato often referred to non-Greeks, including Egyptians and potentially Hebrews, as "barbarians."</note> I know your teachers, even if you wish to hide them. You learned geometry from the Egyptians; astronomy from the Babylonians; you received the right and healthy incantations from the Thracians. <margin>C</margin> The Assyrians also taught you much. But your laws, as many as are true, and your opinion concerning God, were supplied to you by the Hebrews—who do not worship vain errors, nor do they adore the golden, bronze, silver, ivory, wooden, and stone images of dead men made by human hands, which are worshipped by men through empty counsel. Instead, they lift holy arms to heaven; in the morning, rising from their beds, they always cleanse their bodies with water and worship the immortal one who reigns forever.

And I ask you, O Philosophy, not only to bring this one man, Plato, into our midst, but many others as well, who speak of the one true God alone, whenever they have grasped the truth through His inspiration. For Antisthenes <note>A pupil of Socrates and founder of the Cynic school</note> did not think of this in a "Cynic" way, but as one who was an intimate friend of Socrates; he says that God is like no one else, and therefore no one can learn of Him from an image. <margin>D</margin> Xenophon of Athens also <margin>Xenophon, Memorabilia of Socrates</margin> writes openly about the truth, intending to bear witness just as Socrates did, had he himself not feared the poison <note>The hemlock used to execute Socrates</note>. Nevertheless, he signifies it silently. "He," he says, "who moves all things and brings them to rest, is indeed great and openly powerful; but of what form He is, does not appear." Not even the Sun, which appears bright and conspicuous from every side, allows itself to be seen; if anyone gazes at it impudently, they are deprived of their eyesight. From where, then, was the son of Gryllus <note>Xenophon</note> instructed? Was it not, perhaps, from the prophetess of the Hebrews, who prophesies in this way?

> *What flesh can look upon the true and heavenly One,*
> *The God who has no part in human fate, who dwells* <margin>E</margin>
> *Upon the peak of heaven? Mortal men cannot even*
> *Endure the opposing rays of the Sun and its flashing light.*

Cleanthes of Assos <note>Original says "Pisadeus," likely referring to his origin near the Gulf of Adramyttium</note>, the Stoic philosopher, who displayed a true Theology rather than a poetic Genealogy of the Gods, did not hide what he felt about God. If you ask me what the "Good" is like, listen: it is ordered, just, holy, pious, self-containing, beautiful, proper, severe, constant, always beneficial, free from fear, care, or pain, pleasant, safe, friendly, honored, which all confess to be glorious, far from pride, caring, moderate, vigorous, long-lasting, having no affinity for blame, and always remaining. He is filthy and illiberal who looks to public opinion as if he were to gain something good from it. Here, as I judge, he openly teaches <margin>F</margin> what God is like, and shows that common opinion and custom lead those who follow them into slavery—but not those who seek God. Nor should Pythagoras be kept silent, who says: "God is indeed one. He is not, as some suppose, outside the administration of the world; rather, He is entirely within it, the observer of all things in the whole circle."

<meta>catchword: whole (totiu.)</meta>

<summary>Clement argues that Greek philosophers like Plato, Xenophon, and Pythagoras derived their monotheistic insights from Hebrew wisdom, asserting that God is the invisible, just measure of all things who cannot be represented by idols.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Clement of Alexandria's argument that pagan authors occasionally glimpsed the truth of the one true God. Following his discussion of philosophers like Plato, he now turns to the Greek poets and dramatists to demonstrate that they, too, confessed the existence of a single Creator, often in contradiction to their own mythological traditions.</meta>

# AD GENTES
<sig>C iii</sig>
<meta>catchword: cu-</meta>

<margin>A</margin>
...of generation, the tempering of all things, he who always exists and leads his powers to their work, is illustrated in all works in heaven; he is the father of all, the mind and life-breath <note>original: "animatio"</note> of the whole circle, the motion of all things. And these things indeed suffice for the knowledge of God—things which were written by those men under God’s inspiration, and selected by us for anyone who is able to perceive even a little of the truth. But let poetry also be added—for philosophy alone is not enough—poetry, which is admittedly occupied entirely with falsehood, yet at last, after a long time, testifies to the truth, or rather confesses to God its own fabled digressions. Let whatever poet you wish come forward. And first, Aratus <note>A Greek didactic poet (c. 315–240 BC) famous for his poem on astronomy, the Phaenomena.</note> understands that the power of God pervades all things:

<margin>B</margin>
> And so that all things may remain firm,
> They offer him sacred rites and prayers, first and last.
> O wondrous father, hail, greatly useful to the world.

Hesiod of Ascra <note>An early Greek poet (c. 700 BC) often ranked alongside Homer.</note> likewise silently signifies God:

> He himself contains all within his own kingdom and power.
> Nor does any of the other immortals hold this command.

Now, indeed, they also reveal the truth on the stage. One says:

> When you have looked up into the ether and the sky,
> See him, and consider him to be God.

<margin>C</margin>
So says Euripides. And Sophocles, the son of Sophillus:

> In truth there is one, there is one God:
> Who built the framework of the sky and the earth,
> The wide waves of the sea, and the violence
> Of the winds. But we men, wandering for profit,
> Seeking comfort for the heavy accidents that befall us,
> Have set up images of bronze and wood,
> And stone and ivory.
> And by offering sacrifices to these gods, and celebrating
> Feast days for them, we believe ourselves to be pious.

<margin>D</margin>
This man [Sophocles] introduced the truth to his audience on the stage with such boldness and confidence. Furthermore, the Thracian interpreter of sacred rites and poet, Orpheus, the son of Oeagrus—after he had spoken of the sacred rites of the Orgies <note>The "Orgia" were the secret ecstatic rituals of the mystery cults, particularly those of Dionysus.</note> and set forth the "theology" of idols—sang a recantation <note>original: "recantationem," likely referring to the *Palinode* of Orpheus, a poem where he supposedly retracted his polytheism.</note> of the truth that was truly sacred, though sung late:

> I will speak to those for whom it is lawful; close the doors, profane ones,
> Whoever you are. But you, child of the bright Moon <note>A reference to Musaeus, the legendary polymath and pupil of Orpheus.</note>,
> Listen, for I shall speak true things; let not the things which once appeared
> In your breast deprive you of the light of a dear life.
> But gazing upon the divine Word <note>original: "Verbum diuinum," translating the Greek "Logos."</note>, never cease

<margin>E</margin>
> To attend to it; direct your mind and heart rightly,
> And enter upon the path; look toward the King of the world,
> Who alone is immortal.

Then, adding further below, he says clearly:

> He is one, born of himself, and all things are born from one.
> He moves within them; and no mortal
> Sees him, but he himself gazes upon all.

Thus Orpheus, though he had wandered, at last understood:

> But man, do not delay with wise counsel:
> But hasten to appease God, having yourself soon returned.

<margin>F</margin>
For if the Greeks, even at their best, received certain illuminations of the divine Word and spoke a few things of the truth, they testify to its power (which is not hidden), but they also prove their own weakness, as those who did not reach the goal. For now I consider...

# EXHORTATORY ORATION
<sig>C iii</sig>
<meta>catchword: tiu.</meta>

<margin>A</margin>
...men having raised their hands, here what we Greeks now call the "air" <note>original: "aërem"</note> is entirely filled with myths, because it knows all things and gives and takes away, and is the King of all. For this reason, Plato also, when thinking of God, signifies the King of all, and he is the cause of all good things. Who then is the King? God of the universe. He is the measure of truth for those things that exist. For just as things to which dimension applies are understood by measure, so also by our thinking of God, truth comes into dimension and is understood. Indeed, the holy Moses says: <margin>Levit.</margin> **There shall not be, he says, in your pouch a large or a small weight, but a true and equal weight,** <note>Clement is quoting Leviticus 19:35-36, interpreting the "just weight" as a metaphor for God Himself.</note> considering God to be the weight and measure of all things. For unjust and unequal idols are hidden at home in the pouch and, to put it simply, in a filthy soul. But what is the only just measure? He who alone is truly God, always equal, and always behaving in the same way, who measures and weighs all things as if on the scales of justice, containing and supporting the nature of the universe in equilibrium. Certainly God, as the ancient saying goes, containing the beginning, the end, and the middle of all things that exist, always moves straight forward according to nature. Justice always follows Him, taking vengeance on those who fall away from the divine Law. 

From where, O Plato, do you derive the truth? From where does the abundant supply of arguments predict piety and the true worship of God? These things, he says, are the wisdom of the barbarian races. <note>In the language of the time, "barbarians" referred to non-Greeks, specifically the Hebrews and Egyptians.</note> I know your teachers, even if you wish to hide them. You learned Geometry from the Egyptians; Astronomy from the Babylonians; you received right and healthy incantations from the Thracians. The Assyrians also taught you many things. But whatever laws are true, and the opinion concerning God, were supplied to you by the Hebrews—those who do not adore idols of men who have died (made by the empty plans of men from gold, bronze, silver, ivory, wood, and stone), but rather lift holy arms to heaven. They always cleanse the body with water in the morning upon leaving their beds, and they worship the immortal One who reigns forever. 

Do not bring forward only this one Plato to me, O Philosophy, but take care to bring many others into the open as well, who speak of only one true God, wherever they might have grasped the truth through His inspiration. For Antisthenes <note>A pupil of Socrates and founder of the Cynic school.</note> did not think this as a Cynic, but as a familiar friend of Socrates, saying that God is like no one else. Therefore, no one can learn of Him from an image. Xenophon of Athens also wrote openly about the truth, intending to give testimony just as Socrates did, had he not himself feared the poison. <note>A reference to the hemlock that killed Socrates.</note> But nevertheless, he signifies it silently. <margin>Xenophon, Memorabilia of Socrates</margin> HE, he says, who moves all things and makes them rest, is indeed great and openly powerful; but of what sort His form might be does not appear. Even the Sun, which appears bright and conspicuous from every side, does not permit itself to be seen. If anyone should gaze upon it impudently, he is deprived of his eyesight. From where, then, was the son of Gryllus <note>Xenophon.</note> educated? Surely from the prophetess of the Hebrews, who prophesies in this manner:

<margin>B</margin>
<margin>steadfastly <note>original Greek: ἀῤῥεπῶς</note></margin>

<margin>C</margin>

<margin>D</margin>

> *What flesh could ever behold the celestial and true One,*
> *The God who is exempt from human lot in the heights of heaven?*
> *Mortal men are not even able to look upon the opposing rays*
> *Of the Sun, and its flashing light.*

<margin>E</margin>
Furthermore, Cleanthes of Pisada, the Stoic philosopher, who displays not a poetic <term>Theogony</term> <note>A story of the birth/origin of gods.</note> but a true <term>Theology</term>, <note>The rational study of God.</note> did not hide what he felt about God. If you ask me what the "Good" is like, listen: ordered, just, holy, pious, self-contained, beautiful, decorous, serious, constant, always beneficial, free from fear, care, and grief, pleasant, safe, friendly, honored, which all confess to be glorious, free from pride, caring, moderate, vigorous, long-lasting, not at all prone to reproach, always remaining. He is filthy and illiberal who looks to public opinion as if he were to obtain something good from it. Here, as I see it, he openly teaches of what sort God is, and that common opinion and custom reduce those who follow them to slavery, but not those who seek God. Nor should Pythagoras be kept silent, who says: God is indeed one. He is not, as some think, outside the administration of the world, but is entirely within it, the observer of all things in the whole circle.

# TO THE GENTILES
