<margin>A</margin> ...of generation, the contemplation of all things, He who always exists and directs His powers to His work, is illustrated in all His works in heaven; the father of all, the mind and the life-giving spirit <note>original: "animatio"</note> of the whole circle, the motion of all things. And indeed, these things suffice for the knowledge of God—things which were written by these men through the inspiration of God, and selected by us for anyone who is able to perceive even a little of the truth. But let us also call upon poetry, for philosophy is not enough; and though poetry is almost entirely occupied with what is false, yet at last it sometimes bears witness to the truth, or rather, it confesses to God the error of its mythical digressions. Let any poet you wish come forward. And first, Aratus <note>Aratus (c. 310–240 BC) was a Greek poet famous for his astronomical poem, the 'Phaenomena'.</note> understands that the power of God pervades all things:

<margin>B</margin>
> *And so that all things may remain firm,*
> *To the first and the last they offer sacred things and prayers.*
> *Hail, O wonderful father, greatly useful to the world.*

The man from Ascra, Hesiod <note>Hesiod was one of the earliest Greek poets, often paired with Homer.</note>, likewise silently signifies God:

> *He himself contains all in his kingdom and jurisdiction.*
> *Nor does any other of the immortals hold this command.*

Now truly, they also reveal the truth upon the stage. One says:

> *When you have looked up into the ether and the heavens,*
> *Look upon Him, and judge Him to be God.*

<margin>C</margin> So says Euripides. And Sophocles, the son of Sophillus:

> *In truth there is one, there is one God:*
> *Who fashioned the machinery of heaven and the earth,*
> *The wide waves of the sea, and the violence*
> *Of the winds. But we men, wandering for gain,*
> *As a comfort for the heavy calamities that fall upon us,*
> *Have set up images of bronze and wood,*
> *And of stone and ivory.*
> *And by offering sacrifices to these, and celebrating*
> *Festive days for them, we claim to be pious.*
<note>This fragment, while attributed to Sophocles by Clement and other early Church Fathers, is considered by modern scholars to be a "pious fraud"—a Jewish or Christian composition inserted into Greek literature to support monotheism.</note>

<margin>D</margin> This poet indeed boldly and confidently introduced the truth to his audience on the stage. Now the Thracian, at once an interpreter of sacred rites and a poet, Orpheus the son of Oeagrus, after he had spoken out the sacred mysteries of the <term>Orgia</term> <note>The 'Orgia' were the secret, ecstatic religious rituals or "mysteries" associated with Orpheus and Dionysus.</note> and explained the "theology" of idols, sang a recantation of the truth—a truly sacred song, though sung late.

> *I will speak to those for whom it is lawful; close the doors, O profane,*
> *Whoever you are. But you, son of the bright Moon-Muse,*
> *Listen, for I shall speak truths; let not the things which were once*
> *Seen in your heart deprive you of the dear light of life.*
> *But looking to the divine Word, never cease*

<margin>E</margin>
> *To attend to Him; direct your mind and heart aright,*
> *And enter upon the path, and look toward the King of the world,*
> *Who alone is immortal.*

Then, adding further below, he says clearly:

> *He is one, self-begotten, and all things are born from the One.*
> *He moves among them, and no mortal*
> *Sees Him, but He Himself beholds all people.*

Thus spoke Orpheus, and though he had wandered in error, at last he understood:

> *But man, do not delay with your wise counsel:*
> *But hasten to appease God, having soon returned to Him.*

<margin>F</margin> For if the Greeks received certain flashes of the divine Word even when they were most at error, and spoke a few things of the truth, they certainly testify to its power, which is not hidden; yet they convict themselves as being weak men who did not reach the goal. For now I think...

# EXHORTATORY ORATION
30

<margin>A</margin>
...it has clearly come to pass that those who do anything or speak without the Word of truth are like those who attempt to walk without feet. Let the very reproaches of your gods—which your poets, compelled by the truth, used to attack them in comedies—shame you into seeking salvation. Menander the comic poet certainly does this in *The Charioteer*, in the act called *The Counterfeit* <note>original: "Supposititius"</note>.

> No God pleases me, he says, who walks about outside 
> With an old woman, nor one entering into houses 
> *On a painted tablet like a begging priest.* <note>The "Metragyrtes" were wandering priests of the goddess Cybele who carried tablets or images and begged for alms.</note>

<margin>B</margin>
For such were the begging priests. Wherefore, when they were begging, Antisthenes <note>A Greek philosopher and a pupil of Socrates, often considered the founder of Cynicism.</note> rightly said to them: "I do not support the mother of the gods, whom the gods themselves support." Furthermore, the same comic poet in the act called *The Priest*, resenting such customs, tries to refute the impious arrogance of error, speaking wisely:

> For if any man can draw a God 
> To where he wishes by the clanging of cymbals, 
> He who does this is surely more powerful than the God. 
> But these instruments were found to be 
> Mere inventions for the audacity of men.

<margin>C</margin>
And truly, not only Menander, but also Homer and Euripides, and many other poets, convict your gods, and do not fear to pursue them with insults in the slightest. Now they call Minerva a <term>dog-fly</term> <note>original Greek: "κυνομυιαν" (kynomyian). A term of extreme insult in the Iliad.</note>, and Vulcan <term>lame in both feet</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀμφiγυῆ" (amphigueis). Referring to his physical deformity in mythology.</note>. And Helen says to Venus:

> And may there be no return for your feet to Olympus.

<margin>11. f</margin>
Regarding Dionysus, or Bacchus, Homer says openly:

> And he who once pursued the nurses of the raving Bacchus 
> Through the holy mountain of Nysa; and they all together 
> Cast their thyrsi <note>A staff topped with a pine cone, carried by followers of Dionysus.</note> as the savage Lycurgus struck them.

<margin>D</margin>
Euripides is truly worthy of the Socratic school, looking toward the truth and despising the spectators; sometimes he openly rebukes Apollo (who dwells in the center of the world <note>Referring to the Oracle at Delphi, believed to be the navel of the earth.</note> and delivers oracles to men) by saying:

> Obeying him, he slew his own mother; 
> Consider him impious and kill him; 
> He committed the sin, not I; I was less 
> Knowing of what is honorable and of justice itself.

<margin>E</margin>
At other times he introduces Hercules as a madman, and elsewhere as a drunkard and a glutton. For how was he not such a one, who at a banquet ate green figs with meat, "barking" so foolishly that even a barbarian would notice? Now truly, in the act named *Ion*, with his head bare <note>Meaning he speaks plainly or without the mask of religious reverence.</note>, he exposes the gods to the theater:

> How can it be fair, you who gave laws 
> To men, that you yourselves are guilty of injustice? 
> For if (though it will never happen, and I speak of an impossibility) 
> You should pay the penalty for the women you have ravished, 
> You, Neptune, and Jupiter who holds the heavens, 
> In paying for your crimes, you would empty your temples.

<margin>F</margin>
It is time, therefore, having finished with these other matters in order, to come to the prophetic scriptures. For the responses of the prophets, providing us clearly with the material for the worship of God and religion, lay down the foundation for the truth. The divine scriptures and the instructions for an honorable and moderate life—which are shortcut paths, stripped of the artificial dyes <note>original: "fucis" (rouge or pretense).</note>, ornaments, flatteries, and allurements of words—raise up the man who is being suffocated by vice. Contemning the accidents of those things that pertain to daily life, they offer many remedies with one and the same voice, discouraging us from harmful deception, but leading us toward the foreseen salvation.

<margin>A</margin> ...openly exhorting us to salvation. Therefore, let the prophetess Sibyl <note>The Sibyls were legendary female figures in the ancient world believed to possess prophetic powers. Christian writers often cited the "Sibylline Oracles" as pagan witnesses to the truth of monotheism.</note> first sing for us a song of salvation.

> *He is the Prince of heaven, the Lord of the earth; He truly exists.*

---

<margin>B</margin> Divinely indeed, she likens error to darkness, but knowledge to the Sun and the light of God. By bringing both into comparison, she teaches us the necessity of choice. For falsehood is not exterminated by the mere presentation of the truth, but is put to flight when it is driven out by the force of putting truth into practice. But Jeremiah, that most wise Prophet—or rather the Holy Spirit speaking through Jeremiah—reveals God: <margin>ch. 23</margin> "I am a God at hand," he says, "and not a God afar off. If a man be in any secret place, shall I not see him? Do I not fill heaven and earth? says the Lord." And again through Isaiah: "Who has measured," he says, "the heaven with a span, and the whole earth with a fist?" <margin>ch. 40</margin> Behold the <margin>c</margin> greatness of God, and wonder. Let us worship Him of whom the Prophet says: <margin>Ibid. 64</margin> "At your presence the mountains shall melt, like wax before the face of fire." This, he says, is the God whose throne is heaven, and the earth the footstool of His feet; who, if He opens heaven, terror shall seize you. <margin>Ibid. 66</margin> Do you also wish to hear what this Prophet says about idols? "They shall be exposed," he says, "before the Sun, and their carcasses shall be food for the birds of heaven and the beasts of the earth, and they shall rot under the Sun and Moon." They loved those things which they also served, and their city shall be burned. He says that it will come to pass that even the elements and the world will perish with them: "The earth," he says, "shall grow old, and the heaven shall pass away." But the Word of the Lord remains forever. What of when God wished again to reveal Himself through Moses: "See, see that I am He, and there is no other God besides me. <margin>Deut. 32</margin> <margin>D</margin> I will kill and I will make alive; I will strike and I will heal, and there is none who can deliver out of my hands." But do you still wish to hear another giving answers? You have the whole prophetic choir, those who sing in harmony with Moses. What does the Holy Spirit say to them? I shall not fear to speak through the Prophet Hosea: "Behold, I am He who strengthens the thunder and creates the spirit, whose hands also founded the host of heaven." Furthermore, through Isaiah, I will bring this voice also to your memory: "I am," he says, "the Lord; I am He who speaks justice and announces truth. Assemble yourselves and come. Consult together, you who are saved from the Gentiles. They have no knowledge who carry the wood of their sculpture, and pray to gods who will not save them." <margin>Isa. 45</margin> Then a little further down: "I am God," he says, "and there is no just one besides me, and there is no Savior except me. <margin>E</margin> Turn to me, and be saved, you who are from the ends of the earth: I am God, and there is no other; I swear by myself." But He is indignant with idolaters, saying: <margin>Isa. 40</margin> "To whom have you likened the Lord, or to what likeness have you compared Him? Has a craftsman made an image, or has a goldsmith overlaid it with cast gold?"—and so on. No more, then, O you idolaters, but even now beware of these threats. For the carved images and the things made by hand shall wail—or rather, those who have placed their trust in them; for the matter is senseless. Furthermore, he says, "the Lord shall shake the inhabited cities, and with His hand He shall grasp the whole world like a nest." Why should I announce to you the mysteries and words of wisdom from a certain learned Hebrew <note>Clement refers here to Solomon, the traditional author of the Book of Proverbs.</note>? "The Lord created me as the beginning of His ways for His works." <margin>Prov. 8</margin> And "the Lord gives wisdom, and from His face comes knowledge and understanding." "How long do you lie there, you sluggard? When will you be roused from sleep?" <margin>F</margin> But if you are diligent, your harvest shall come like a fountain: the Father's Word, a good lamp, the Lord who brings the light of faith and salvation to all. For the Lord who made the earth by His power, as Jeremiah says, has established the world by His wisdom... <margin>ch. 27</margin>

<meta>This page continues Clement of Alexandria’s argument against the Greek gods. Having previously cited the Sibylline Oracles and Hebrew prophets to establish the one true God, he now turns back to the Greeks' own literature—specifically their comic and tragic poets—to show that even their own writers mocked the absurdity and immorality of the Olympian pantheon before he returns to the "prophetic scriptures" as the final authority.</meta>

# EXHORTATION ADDRESS
### TO THE GENTILES

<margin>A</margin> It has become clear that those who act or speak without the Word of truth are like people trying to walk without feet. Let the very criticisms of your gods also move you toward salvation out of a sense of shame—criticisms which your own poets, compelled by the truth, use to attack them in comedies. Menander the comic poet certainly writes in *The Charioteer*, in the act called *The Supposititious*:

> *No God pleases me,* he says, *who walks about outside*
> *With an old woman, nor one who enters houses*
> *As a begging priest upon a painted tablet.* <note>The "begging priests" (original: *Metragyrtes*) were wandering collectors of alms for the Great Mother goddess Cybele, often viewed with suspicion or contempt in antiquity for their perceived charlatanism.</note>

<margin>B</margin> For such were the begging priests. Hence, when they were begging, Antisthenes <note>A Greek philosopher and a pupil of Socrates, often considered the founder of Cynic philosophy.</note> rightly said to them: "I do not support the Mother of the gods, whom the gods themselves should support." But again, the same comic poet in the play called *The Priest*, being pained by the custom, attempts to refute the impious arrogance of their error, speaking wisely:

> *For if a man can drag a god*
> *To whatever he desires by clashing cymbals,*
> *Then he who does this is surely more powerful than the god.*
> *But these instruments were both invented*
> *As tools for the audacity of men.*

<margin>C</margin> And truly, not only Menander, but also Homer and Euripides, and many other poets, expose your gods and do not fear to pursue them with insults, even in the slightest degree. They call Minerva a "dog-fly" <note>original: *kynomyian* (κυνομυῖαν)</note> and Vulcan "lame in both feet" <note>original: *amphigye* (ἀμφιγυῆ)</note>. Moreover, Helen says to Venus:

> *May you never return to Olympus on your own feet.*

<margin>n. l</margin> Regarding Dionysus, or Bacchus, Homer says openly:

> *And he who once drove the nurses of the raving Bacchus*
> *Into holy Nysa; <note>A legendary mountain where Dionysus was raised.</note> all of them together*
> *Threw down their wands while the cruel Lycurgus struck them.*

<margin>D</margin> Euripides is truly worthy of the Socratic school; looking toward the truth and despising the spectators, he sometimes openly rebukes Apollo (who dwells in the center of the earth and gives oracles to men), saying:

> *Obeying him, he killed his own mother;*
> *Consider him impious and kill him:*
> *He sinned, not I; for I was less knowledgeable*
> *Than he of what is honorable and of justice itself.* <note>This refers to Orestes, who killed his mother Clytemnestra on the orders of the god Apollo.</note>

<margin>E</margin> At other times, he introduces Hercules as a madman, and elsewhere as a drunkard and a glutton. For how was he not such a man, who at a banquet ate green figs with meat, barking so clumsily that even a barbarian would notice? Furthermore, in the play named *Ion*, he exposes the gods to the theater with an uncovered head:

> *How can it be just that you, who gave laws*
> *To men, are yourselves guilty of injustice?*
> *But if (for it will never happen, and I speak of an impossibility)*
> *You were to pay the penalty for your rapes of women,*
> *Then you, Neptune, and Jupiter who holds the heavens,*
> *Would empty your temples by paying for your crimes.*

<margin>F</margin> It is time, therefore, having finished with these other matters in order, to come to the prophetic scriptures. For the responses of the prophets, providing us with clear material for the worship of God and religion, place a foundation under the truth. The Divine Scriptures and the instructions for an honorable and moderate life—which are short paths, stripped of the dyes of words, ornaments, flatteries, and allurements—raise up the man who is being suffocated by vice. Despising the accidents of those things pertaining to daily life, and bringing many remedies with one and the same voice, they discourage us from harmful deception and lead us toward the salvation previously foreseen.

# TO THE GENTILES

<margin>A</margin> ...openly exhorting them to salvation. Therefore, let the prophetess Sibyl <note>The Sibyls were legendary prophetesses in the ancient world. Early Christian writers like Clement frequently cited the "Sibylline Oracles"—a collection of Greek hexameters—believing they contained genuine divine revelations given to the pagans to lead them to monotheism.</note> be the first to sing for us a song of health:

> *Behold, He is altogether clear, and wanders in no error.*
> *Come now, having at last abandoned the mists and the darkness:*
> *The pleasing and most brilliant light of the Sun shines out.*
> *Let excellent wisdom be fixed within your souls.*
> *There is one God who sends the rains, the lightning, the quakes,*
> *The thunderbolts, plagues and famines, and all mournful things,*
> *And ice, and snows. Why must I tell you each thing one by one?*
> <margin>B</margin>*He is the Prince of heaven, the Lord of the earth; He truly exists.*

Most divinely indeed, she likens error to darkness, but knowledge to the Sun and the light of God. By bringing both into comparison, she teaches us the choice we must make. For falsehood is not banished merely by the presentation of the truth, but is put to flight when it is cast out by the force of the practical application of truth. Moreover, the most wise prophet Jeremiah—or rather the Holy Spirit in Jeremiah—reveals God: <margin>ch. 23</margin> "I am a God at hand," He says, "and not a God far off. If a man is in a secret place, shall I not see him? Do I not fill heaven and earth? says the Lord." And again through Isaiah: "Who," He says, "shall measure the heaven with a span, and all the earth with a fist?" <margin>ch. 40</margin> See the <margin>C</margin> greatness of God, and marvel. Let us adore Him of whom the prophet says: <margin>Ibid. 64</margin> "At your face the mountains shall melt, like wax before the face of fire." This is the God, he says, whose throne is heaven and the earth is His footstool; who, if He opens the heaven, terror shall seize you. <margin>Ibid. 66</margin> Do you also wish to hear what this prophet says about idols? "They are exposed," <note>original: *Traducuntur*</note> he says, "before the Sun, and their carcasses shall be food for the birds of the sky and the beasts of the earth, and they shall rot under the Sun and the Moon. They loved those things which they also served, and their city shall be burned." He says also that even the elements and the world shall perish with them: "The earth," he says, "shall grow old, and the heaven shall pass away. But the word of the Lord remains forever." And what of when God wished to show Himself again through Moses: "See, see that I am He, and there is no other God besides me. <margin>Deut. 32</margin> <margin>D</margin> I will kill and I will make alive, I will strike and I will heal, and there is no one who can snatch from my hands." But do you wish to hear yet another giving answers? You have the whole choir of prophets, those who sing in harmony with Moses. What does the Holy Spirit say to them? I shall not fear to speak through the prophet Hosea: <note>The quote "establishing the thunder and creating the spirit" is actually found in Amos 4:13; Clement, writing from memory or using a different lectionary, attributes it to Hosea.</note> "Behold, I am He who strengthens the thunder and creates the spirit, whose hands also founded the host of heaven." Furthermore, through Isaiah, I will bring this voice also to your memory: "I am," He says, "the Lord; I am He who speaks justice and announces the truth. Be gathered and come. Consult together, you who are saved from among the Gentiles. They have no knowledge who carry the wood of their carving <margin>Isa. 45</margin> and pray to gods who will not save them." Then a little further down: "I am," He says, "God, and there is no one besides me; I am a just God and a Savior, there is none except me. <margin>E</margin> Turn to me, and be saved, you who are from the ends of the earth: I am God, and there is no other; I swear by myself." But He is indignant with idolaters, saying: "To whom <margin>Isa. 40</margin> have you likened the Lord, or to what likeness have you compared Him? Has a craftsman made an image, or a goldsmith spread it over with cast gold?" and so on. Therefore, O you idolaters, do not persist, but even now beware of His threats. For the carvings and the things made by hand shall wail—or rather, those who placed their trust in them; for the material itself is without feeling. Furthermore, he says, the Lord shall shake the inhabited cities, and His hand shall grasp the whole circuit of the earth like a nest. Why should I announce to you the mysteries of wisdom and the words from a certain learned Hebrew? "The Lord created me as the beginning of His ways for His works... and the Lord gives wisdom, and from His face comes knowledge and understanding. <margin>Prov. 8</margin> How long will you lie there, you sluggard? When will you be awakened from sleep? <margin>F</margin> But if you are diligent, your harvest shall come like a fountain"—the paternal Word, the good lamp, the Lord who brings light, faith, and salvation to all. For the Lord, who made the earth by His power, as Jeremiah says, has raised up the world in His wisdom. <margin>ch. 27</margin>

<summary>Clement of Alexandria transitions from Greek literature to the higher authority of the Sibyl and the Hebrew Prophets to argue for monotheism. He uses a series of scriptural citations to contrast the living, creative power of God with the lifelessness and impending destruction of idols.</summary>

# ORATION OF EXHORTATION

<margin>Deut. 6. Matth. 4. Psal. 2.</margin>
<margin>A</margin> ...by His own [wisdom]. For we who had fallen down before idols, wisdom—which is His Word—raises us up to the truth; and this is the first resurrection from the fall. Wherefore divine Moses, exhorting against all idolatry, most beautifully cried out: <note>original: "AVDI Israël, Dominus Deus tuus, Dominus unus est..."</note> HEAR, O Israel, the Lord your God is one Lord, and you shall worship the Lord your God, and Him only shall you serve.

NOW, O men, understand, according to the opinion of that blessed Psalmist David: embrace discipline, lest the Lord be angry at some time, and you perish from the righteous way, when His fury shall be quickly kindled. Blessed are all they who trust in Him. Now indeed, the Lord, taking pity on us in a wonderful manner, delivers to us a way of salvation, like a rhythmic measure which they call <term>ἐμβατήριον</term> <note>original Greek: embatērion; an "entrance song" or "marching song" used by soldiers or during processions to encourage advancement.</note> because it exhorts us to enter in: SONS of men, how long will you be heavy-hearted? Why do you love vanity and seek after a lie? <margin>B</margin>

<margin>Ibidem. 4.</margin>
<margin>Rom. 1.</margin>
What then is this vanity, and what is the lie? The holy Apostle of the Lord, in rebuking the Greeks, shall explain it to you: that although they knew God, they did not glorify Him as God, nor did they give thanks; but they became vain in their thoughts, and they changed the glory of God into the likeness of the corruptible flesh of man, and they served the creature rather than the Creator. And yet this is the God who in the beginning made heaven and earth. But you do not understand God, and instead you worship the heaven; and how is it that you do not act impiously? Hear again the Prophet who says: The Sun indeed SHALL FAIL, and the heaven shall be darkened, but the Almighty shall shine forever; and the powers of the heavens shall be moved, and the heavens shall be rolled up like a skin <note>Clement refers here to the prophetic imagery of the sky being rolled up like a scroll or a parchment tent-cover.</note>, as those things which are stretched out and contracted (for these are the Prophetic voices), and the earth shall flee from the face of the Lord. I can <margin>C</margin> bring forward to you innumerable scriptures, of which not even one "jot or tittle" <note>original: "apex"; referring to the smallest marks in writing.</note> shall pass away without being perfectly fulfilled.

<margin>Heb. 12.</margin>
For the mouth of the Lord, the Holy Spirit, has spoken these things: Therefore, he says, my son, do not neglect the discipline of the Lord any longer, nor be weary when you are rebuked by Him. O what remarkable kindness! Not as a master to his disciples, nor as a Lord to his servants, nor as God to men: but as a father, how benignly does He admonish His sons? Then Moses indeed confesses that he fears and trembles when he hears the Word. But you, hearing the divine Word, do you not fear? Are you not anxious? Do you not at the same time both revere Him and strive to learn—that is, do you not hasten toward salvation, fearing His wrath, loving His grace, and embracing hope with wonder, so that you may decline His judgment? Come, come, O gathering of my young men! For unless you become again as children, and are born again, as the Scripture says, you shall not receive Him who is truly the Father, nor shall you ever enter into the kingdom of heaven. <margin>D</margin> For how is a stranger permitted to enter? But when, as I believe, he has been enrolled, and made a citizen, and has accepted the Father, then he shall be in the number of the Father’s sons; then he shall be held worthy to become an heir; then the Father shall impart the paternal kingdom to his legitimate and beloved son. For this is the firstborn church, which consists of many good children. These are the firstborn, who are written in the heavens, and together with so many thousands of Angels celebrate the feast day. And we are the firstborn sons, we who are the pupils of God, who are the legitimate friends of the Firstborn, we who were the first among other men to understand God, who were first torn away from sins, and who were first separated from the Devil. But now some are as much more impious as God is more benign and kind. <margin>E</margin> For God wants us to become sons instead of servants. But they have even despised becoming sons. O, what great arrogance! You put the Lord to shame. He promises liberty: but you flee away into slavery. He grants salvation for free: but you descend to man <note>Likely referring to trusting in human idols or mortal philosophies rather than divine grace.</note>. He gives eternal life: but you look for punishment, and wait for the fire which the Lord has prepared for the devil and his angels.

<margin>Ephe. 4.</margin>
Therefore the blessed Apostle says: I TESTIFY in the Lord, that you no longer walk as the Gentiles walk in the vanity of their mind, darkened in thought, and alienated from the life of God, because of the ignorance that is in them, because of the blindness of their heart: who indeed have given themselves over, being hardened in their indecency, to the working of all uncleanness and greed. With such a witness refuting the ignorance of men and calling upon God, what else remains for the unbelievers but <margin>F</margin> judgment and condemnation? But the Lord does not neglect us, persuading, terrifying, exhorting, exciting, and admonishing. He certainly rouses us from sleep, and makes those who have wandered away rise from the very darkness: <margin>Ibidem. 5.</margin> AWAKE, He says, you who sleep, and arise from the dead,

<summary>Clement of Alexandria argues that the divine Word acts as a fatherly guide, calling humanity away from the "vanity" of pagan idolatry toward a "first resurrection" as sons of God. He contrasts the voluntary slavery of the heathens with the inheritance offered to the "church of the firstborn."</summary>

<meta>This page continues Clement of Alexandria’s "Exhortation to the Heathen." Having previously discussed the Word (Logos) as the source of light, he now uses the concept of "Today" to urge immediate conversion, contrasting the wandering of the Israelites in the desert with the eternal rest offered through Christ.</meta>

# TO THE GENTILES

<margin>A</margin> ...from the dead, and Christ the Lord shall enlighten you—the Sun of the resurrection, who was begotten before the morning star <note>original: "ante Luciferum"; here referring to the dawn or the planet Venus as a symbol of the beginning of creation, rather than the fallen angel.</note>, and who has bestowed life by His own rays. Let no one, therefore, despise the Word, lest he unawares be despised himself. 

<margin>Psalm 84 <note>This citation follows the older numbering; in modern Bibles, this text is found in Psalm 95 and famously quoted in Hebrews 3.</note></margin> For Scripture says in a certain place: *Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts, as in the provocation on the day of testing in the desert, where your fathers tempted Me in their trial.* 

And what is this trial? If you wish to learn, the Holy Spirit will explain it to you: *And they saw My works,* He says, *for forty years. Therefore I was near to this generation, and I said, "They always err in their heart." But they did not know My ways, as I swore in My wrath, "They shall not enter into My rest."* 

<margin>B</margin> Behold the threats! Behold the exhortation! Behold the honor! Why, then, do we still change grace into wrath? Why do we not receive the Word with open ears and welcome God as a guest in chaste souls? For the grace of His promise is great, if today we hear His voice. 

That "Today," however, is renewed in each of its days, as long as it is called "Today." Until the final consummation, the teaching remains; and then that which is truly "Today"—the Day of God which does not fail—is extended together with the ages. Let us, therefore, always hear the voice of the divine Word. For "Today" is the image of the eternal age, and the day is a sign and symbol of light. 

And the Word is the Light for men, through which we contemplate God. Deservedly, therefore, for those who have believed and obey, grace has superabounded. But for those who have not believed and err in their hearts, and have not known the ways of the Lord—which John <note>John the Baptist</note> commanded them to make straight and prepare—

<margin>C</margin> to them the Lord was near, and He threatens. Indeed, the ancient wanderers of the Hebrews received the end of those threats in a riddle <note>original: "ænigmaticè"; meaning their physical wandering was a symbolic warning.</note>. For they are said not to have entered into rest because of their unbelief, until they followed the successor of Moses <note>Joshua, whose name in Greek is "Iesous," the same as Jesus.</note> and finally learned, though late, that they could not be saved in any other way than by believing in Jesus. 

But since the Lord is kind, He exhorts all men to the knowledge of the truth, and He sends the Comforter. What then is this knowledge? It is piety and the worship of God. 

<margin>1 Timothy 4</margin> Now, piety is profitable for all things, according to the opinion of Paul, having the promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come. At what price, O men, would you profess yourselves to be buyers, if eternal salvation were for sale? Not even if someone gave the river Pactolus <note>A river in Lydia famous in antiquity for its gold-bearing sands, associated with King Midas.</note>—which, as the fables say, flows entirely with a golden stream—would he have paid a just price for salvation. 

<margin>D</margin> Therefore, do not be loath to have labored; you may, if you wish, buy this most precious salvation with your own treasure: with love, and with the faith of life, which is indeed the just price. This is the price God willingly accepts. For we have hoped in the living God, who is the Savior of all men, especially of those who believe. 

But other men, who have clung to the world like certain little creatures called <term>φῶκαι</term> <note>original: phōkai; seals. Clement compares worldly people to seals clinging to sea-rocks.</note> cling to marine rocks, despise immortality. They are like the old man of Ithaca <note>Odysseus, who in Homer’s Odyssey famously desired to see the smoke of his home more than immortality offered by Calypso.</note>, who desired not the Truth and the heavenly fatherland, nor the light which truly is, but merely smoke. 

But piety, which makes a man like God as far as is possible, claims a teacher fitting for itself: namely God, who alone is able, according to His dignity, to make man like God. 

Since the Apostle knew this doctrine was truly divine, he said: *But you, O Timothy, from infancy have known the Sacred Letters which are able to instruct you unto salvation, through faith in Christ.* 

<margin>E, 2 Timothy 3</margin> For they are truly sacred letters which make men sacred and "deify" <note>original: "deificant"; a common patristic term (theosis) for the process of becoming more like God through grace.</note> them. From these letters and sacred syllables, the same Apostle consequently calls the composed scriptures and works "divinely inspired," being useful for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for instruction in justice, so that the man of God may be perfect, equipped for every good work. 

One will not admire the exhortations of other saints as much as the Lord Himself, who is kind and loves mankind. For He has no other work except this alone: that man may be saved. He Himself, therefore, cries out, urging us toward salvation: *The kingdom of heaven has approached.* He converts men who are approaching in fear. 

<margin>Philippians 4</margin> For that reason the Apostle of the Lord also, exhorting the Macedonians, becomes the interpreter of the divine voice, saying: *The Lord has approached; beware lest we be found empty.* 

<margin>F</margin> But you who are so needy—or rather, so unbelieving—neither believing the Lord Himself nor Paul, and especially [Paul] pleading on behalf of Christ: 

<margin>Psalm 33</margin> *Taste and see that Christ is God.* <note>Clement adjusts the Psalm text ("Taste and see that the Lord is good") to identify the Lord specifically as Christ.</note> Faith will introduce you, experience will teach you, and Scripture will instruct you. *Come,* it says, *O sons, hear me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord.*

<summary>Clement uses the scriptural concept of "Today" to urge the reader to seek salvation immediately through Christ. He contrasts the Israelites' failure to enter God's rest with the opportunity for modern believers to achieve "deification" and eternal life through faith and the "Sacred Letters" of Scripture.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Clement of Alexandria’s "Exhortation to the Heathen." Having previously discussed the Word (Logos) as the source of light and the importance of "Today," Clement now addresses the call to those who already believe and begins a sharp critique of "custom"—the pagan tradition that keeps men from the truth.</meta>

### EXHORTATION TO THE GENTILES

<margin>A</margin>
Then, as if briefly addressing those who have already believed, he adds: *Who is the man who desires life, and loves to see good days?* <note>original: "QUIS eft homo qui vult vitam..."; a quotation from Psalm 34:12.</note> It is we, we shall say—we who are the worshippers of good, the emulators and followers of good things. Listen then, you who are far off, and listen, you who are near. The Word is hidden from no one; it is a common light that shines upon all men. There is no <term>Cimmerian</term> <note>The Cimmerians were a legendary people described by Homer as living in perpetual mist and darkness; Clement uses them here as a metaphor for those in spiritual darkness.</note> in the Word. Let us hasten to salvation, to regeneration. Let us many be gathered into one love, through the union of the <term>monadic essence</term> <note>A philosophical term referring to a single, indivisible unity—here meaning the oneness of God.</note>; let us hasten. Having received this benefit, let us suitably pursue union, seeking after that good unity. And what is this union of many? When, out of a multitude of voices and dispersions, it receives a divine harmony, it becomes one assembly, following one leader of the choir and teacher: the <margin>B</margin> Word, resting in the same truth, saying "Father, Father." <note>original: "Abba pater"; "Abba" is Aramaic for Father, and "Pater" is Latin for Father.</note> God embraces this true voice, hearing it as the first thing from His children. 

<margin>to live for a long time <note>original Greek: "εἰς πολὺ ζῶμεν"</note></margin> But, you say, it is not right for us to overturn the custom handed down to us by our fathers. Why then? Do we not use milk as our first food, a thing to which nurses certainly accustomed us when we were first born? Why do we increase or diminish our father’s wealth, rather than keeping it exactly as we received it? Why do we no longer sob at our father’s breast, or do those other things we did as infants while being nourished by our mothers—things that provoked laughter? We corrected ourselves, even if we had no <term>Pedagogues</term> <note>In antiquity, a "pedagogue" was a slave who supervised a child's conduct and accompanied them to school.</note> to guide us. 

Furthermore, while excesses in our passions are sweet, they fall away even if they are harmful and dangerous. In life, shall we not turn toward the truth and seek Him who is truly our Father, even if our fathers <margin>C</margin> take it badly? Shall we not abandon a wicked, faulty, and impious custom as if it were some deadly poison? For this itself is the most beautiful argument to show you that piety and the worship of God have been hated because of insanity and this most unhappy custom. For such a great good—of which no greater has been given by God to the human race—would never have been hated or prohibited, unless you were carried away by custom and then, with ears closed (like hard-necked horses refusing the reins and biting the bit), you fled from reason. You desire to shake us off—we who are the charioteers of your life—but instead, through your ignorance, you cast yourselves headlong into destruction, considering the holy Word of God to be something to be cursed. And so, the rewards of your own choice follow you, according to the sentiment of <term>Sophocles</term>:

->Vain mind, useless ears, fruitless cares.<-

<margin>D</margin>
And you do not know this to be the truest thing of all: that the good and pious obtain a good reward, as those who have honored the Good; but those who are the opposite, <margin>Zechariah 3</margin> the wicked, receive a fitting punishment. Does punishment not even loom over the prince of vice? Certainly Zechariah threatens him with punishment: *May He who chose Jerusalem punish you! Behold, is this not a brand plucked from the fire?* <note>Quoting Zechariah 3:2.</note> Why then does this desire for a voluntary death still dwell in men? Why have they fled to this death-bearing fire-brand with which they will be burned, when it is possible to live rightly according to God, and not according to custom? For God grants life. But an evil custom, after one departs from this <margin>Hesiod</margin> life, brings a vain repentance along with punishment. "The fool learns by suffering," <note>A famous Greek proverb found in Hesiod’s *Works and Days*.</note> <margin>E</margin> that the superstition of demons destroys, but the true worship of God gives salvation. 

Let any of you look at those who worship idols: their hair is filthy, they are deformed by ragged and torn clothes, they abstain entirely from baths, they are made wild by overgrown nails, and many are even deprived of their private parts <note>A reference to the *Galli*, the self-castrated priests of the goddess Cybele.</note>—showing by their very state that the temples of idols are actually tombs or prisons. To me, they certainly seem to be in mourning rather than worshipping gods, suffering things that are more worthy of pity than of divine worship or religion. And seeing these things, are you still blind? Will you not look back toward the Lord of the universe? Will you not flee from the prisons found here and take refuge in the mercy that comes from the heavens? For God, out of great kindness and clemency, holds and embraces man, just as when a chick falls from the nest, the mother bird flies down from the nest. And if <margin>F</margin> a serpent gapes to devour the chick, the mother flies around it, mourning for her children, her most dear pledges. So too God the Father seeks His own handiwork, and heals that which has fallen, and pursues the wild beast, and receives the chick back into the nest, inciting it to fly again. 

Then even dogs that have wandered off, seeking with keen scent for their master... <margin>Isaiah 1</margin>

<summary>Clement of Alexandria argues against adhering to pagan traditions ("custom") merely for the sake of heritage, comparing spiritual growth to the way a child outgrows nursing. He paints a grim picture of the physical degradation of idol-worshippers and contrasts it with God’s fatherly desire to rescue and restore humanity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Clement of Alexandria’s "Exhortation to the Heathen" (Protrepticus). After discussing the unity of the Word (Logos), Clement shifts focus to a stinging critique of those who refuse to recognize their Creator, comparing them to animals who show more loyalty to their masters than humans show to God.</meta>

### EXHORTATION TO THE GENTILES 35

<margin>A</margin> They seek the Lord; but He says, "the ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s manger, but Israel has not known me." <note>original: "nouit... bos possessorem suum"; a quotation from Isaiah 1:3.</note> What then does the Lord do? He forgets the injuries He has received; He still shows mercy, and He still demands repentance. I wish to ask you, does it not seem absurd to you that you—who are God's own handiwork, who received your soul from Him, and belong entirely to Him—should serve another Master? And furthermore, that you should worship a tyrant instead of the King, and choose the evil one instead of the Good? For who, in truth, if they were of sound mind, would leave the Good and live with vice? Who is there that, fleeing from God, lives together with demons? Who, when he could be a son of God, delights in slavery? Or who, when he could be a citizen of heaven, pursues the underworld? Who, when it is permitted to him to cultivate 
<margin>B</margin> paradise, and to traverse the heights of heaven, and to be a partaker of the living and pure fountain—walking in the footsteps of that bright cloud through the air and contemplating, like 
<margin>3 Kings 17</margin> Elijah, the saving rain? <note>Clement references 1 Kings 17 (numbered as 3 Kings in the Vulgate), where the prophet Elijah prays for rain to end a drought, symbolizing spiritual refreshment.</note> Instead, like worms, they wallow in filth and mud—namely, in the flowing stream of pleasure—and feed on useless and foolish delights, like swinish men. For "pigs," it is said, "delight more in filth than in clean water," and to wallow in a heap of collected chaff is a certain insane delight for them, as 
<margin>They waste away on their burdens <note>original Greek: "Ἐπὶ φορτῷ μαραίνονται"</note></margin> <term>Democritus</term> <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher famous for his atomic theory; Clement uses his observations on animals to mock human behavior.</note> says. Let us not, therefore, become slaves, nor be made like pigs; but as true-born sons of light, let us look toward the light and look upward, lest the Lord should find us to be illegitimate, just as the Sun tests the eagles. <note>According to ancient lore, eagles tested the legitimacy of their young by making them look directly into the sun; those who blinked were cast out.</note> Let us therefore be led by repentance, and be brought over from ignorance to knowledge, from foolishness to wisdom, from 
<margin>C</margin> lack of self-control to temperance, from injustice to justice, and from impiety and lack of religion to God. It is a beautiful danger to flee to God. <note>original: "Pulchrum est periculum"; a reference to Plato's *Phaedo*, suggesting that the "risk" of believing in the divine and the soul's immortality is a noble and rewarding one.</note> Many other good things can we obtain, we who are lovers of justice and who pursue eternal salvation. Furthermore, there is an inheritance for those who worship the Lord, which God Himself silently signifies when speaking through Isaiah. It is indeed a beautiful and lovely inheritance—not gold, not silver, not clothing which moths eat; nor earthly things which a thief breaks in to steal while blinded by worldly riches—but that treasure of salvation, toward which those who are 
<margin>lovers of the Word <note>original Greek: "φιλόλογοι"</note></margin> ought to strive. From this place, our good works depart with us, and fly away on the wings of truth. This inheritance the eternal covenant of God hands down to us, supplying an eternal gift. Here, our Father—truly a Father, filled with love for us— 
<margin>D</margin> does not cease to exhort, to warn, to teach, and to love. For He never ceases to offer salvation. He counsels that which is best: "BE MADE righteous," says the Lord. 
<margin>Isaiah 55</margin> "You who thirst, go to the water, and whoever has no money, go, and buy, and drink without money." He exhorts us to the washing, to salvation, and to enlightenment, almost crying out and saying: "I give to you, O son, the earth and the sea and the heaven, and all the living creatures in them I bestow upon you. Only, O son, thirst for your Father; God shall be shown to you for free." Truth is not sold like merchandise. <note>original: "Non cauponatur veritas"; literally "Truth is not huckstered," contrasting the free gift of God with the paid lessons of the Sophists.</note> He gives you the creatures of the air, the water, and the earth. 
<margin>with thankful nourishment <note>original Greek: "εὐχαρίστοις τροφῆς"</note></margin> These your Father has created for your nourishment, to be taken with thanksgiving. The illegitimate child and the son of perdition—whose purpose is to serve <term>Mammon</term> <note>A biblical term for wealth or property, often personified as a false god that competes with God for human devotion.</note>—will buy these things with money. But to you, He permits what is yours. He speaks to the true son who 
<margin>E</margin> loves the Father, through whom He still works, and to whom alone He promises, saying: "And the earth shall be stretched out for a firmament." For it is not strengthened for destruction or corruption. "For the whole earth is mine," and it is yours also if you receive God. Whence the Scripture rightly announces to those who have believed: "The saints of the Lord shall be heirs 
<margin>Isaiah 64</margin> of God's glory and power." Tell me, O blessed one, what sort of glory is this? "That which eye has not 
<margin>1 Corinthians 2</margin> seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man," and they shall rejoice in the kingdom of their Lord forever, Amen. You have, O men, the divine promise of grace; you have also heard the other side, the threats of punishment, through which the Lord gives salvation, instructing man through both grace and fear. Why do we hesitate? Why do we not escape the punishment? Why do we not receive the gift? Why do we not choose those things which are better, preferring God to the evil one, and wisdom to 
<margin>F</margin> <margin>Ecclesiasticus 15</margin> idolatry, exchanging death for life? "Behold," He says, "I have set before your face death and life." The Lord tests you so that you may choose life. He counsels you as a Father: "Obey God." "For if," He says, "you hear me and are willing, you shall eat the good things of the earth." 
<margin>Isaiah 1</margin> Grace belongs to obedience. "But if you do not obey me, and are not willing..."

### EXHORTATION TO THE HEATHEN

<margin>A</margin> Then, for those who have already believed, he briefly adds: "Who is the man who desires life, and loves to see good days?" <note>original: "Quis est homo qui vult vitam...?" from Psalm 34:12.</note> It is we, we shall say, who are the good worshippers, the emulators and followers of good things. Hear, then, you who are far off, and hear, you who are near. The Word is hidden from no one; He is the common light that shines upon all men. In the Word, there is no Cimmerian <note>The Cimmerians were a mythical people said to live in perpetual mist and darkness; Clement uses this to mean there is no spiritual darkness in the Word.</note>; let us hasten toward salvation and toward rebirth. Let us many hasten to be gathered into one love, through the union of the Monadic essence <note>The "Monadic essence" refers to the absolute, indivisible unity of God.</note>. Having received this benefit, let us appropriately pursue union, seeking after a good unity. And what is this union of many? When, from a multitude of voices and dispersions, it receives a divine harmony, it becomes one assembly, following one leader of the chorus and teacher—the Word—resting in the same truth and saying, "Abba, Father." <margin>B</margin> God embraces this true voice, hearing it first from His children.

<margin>To wash away / To cleanse</margin> But, you say, "it is not right for us to overturn the custom handed down by our fathers." Why then? Do we not use milk as our first food, to which the nurses certainly accustomed us when we were brought into the light? Why do we increase or diminish our paternal estates, and not preserve them exactly equal to how we received them? Why do we no longer sob in our father's lap, or do those other things which moved people to laughter while we were infants and being fed by our mothers? Instead, we have corrected ourselves, even if we had no Pedagogues <note>A "Pedagogue" was a household slave in antiquity who supervised a child's conduct and accompanied them to school.</note> to guide us. Furthermore, while the excesses of the passions are harmful and dangerous, they are sweet and eventually pass away. But in life, shall we not turn toward the truth and seek Him who is truly our Father, even if our earthly fathers are displeased, by abandoning an wicked, corrupt, and impious custom <margin>C</margin> as if rejecting some lethal poison? For this is the most beautiful argument to show you that piety and the worship of God are hated only because of insanity and this most unhappy custom. For so great a good—greater than any other given by God to the human race—would never be hated or prohibited, unless you were carried away by custom and then, with ears closed (like hard-necked horses refusing the reins and biting the bit), you fled from reason. You desire to shake us off as the charioteers of your lives, but through your own ignorance, you cast yourselves headlong into destruction, considering the holy Word of God to be something to be cursed. Therefore, the rewards of your own choice follow you, according to the sentiment of Sophocles:

<margin>D</margin> ->Vain mind, useless ears, futile cares.<-

And you do not know that this is the truest thing of all: that the good and pious obtain a good reward, as those who have honored the Good; but those who, on the contrary, are evil, receive a fitting punishment. Does not punishment also loom over the prince of vice? <margin>Zechariah 8</margin> <note>Though the margin cites Zechariah 8, this refers to the vision in Zechariah 3:2.</note> Zechariah certainly threatens that he will be punished: "The Lord rebuke you, he who has chosen Jerusalem! Is not this a brand plucked from the fire?" What then is this lingering desire among men for a voluntary death? Why have they fled to this deadly firebrand with which they will be burned, when it is permitted to live rightly according to God, and not according to custom? For God grants life. <margin>Hesiod</margin> But a bad custom brings a vain repentance with punishment after one departs from this life. <margin>E</margin> "Even a fool knows by suffering" <note>A famous proverb from Hesiod’s *Works and Days*.</note> that the superstition of demons brings ruin, and the true worship of God gives salvation. 

Let any of you look at those who worship idols: their hair is filthy, their clothing is tattered and torn, they are deformed, and they completely abstain from washing; they are made wild by overgrown nails, and many are even deprived of their private parts <note>A reference to the Galli, the self-castrated priests of the goddess Cybele.</note>, showing by the very facts that the temples of idols are like tombs or prisons. These people certainly seem to me to be in mourning rather than worshipping gods, appearing as objects of pity rather than religious devotion. Seeing these things, do you still remain blind and refuse to look back to the Lord of the universe? Will you not flee from these earthly prisons and take refuge in the mercy that comes from the heavens? For God, out of great kindness and clemency, holds and embraces man, just as a mother bird flies to the nest when a chick falls out. If a serpent gapes to devour the chick, the mother flies around, <margin>F</margin> weeping for her dear offspring. So God the Father both seeks His own handiwork, and heals that which has fallen, and pursues the beast, and receives the chick back into the nest, encouraging it to fly again. <margin>Isaiah 1</margin> Furthermore, even dogs who have wandered off seek their master with keen scent, and the...

<summary>Clement of Alexandria argues that "ancestral custom" is a poor excuse for avoiding the truth of God. He compares God's care for humanity to a mother bird protecting her young from a serpent and contrasts this divine love with the wretched, self-mutilating practices of pagan idol worshippers.</summary>

### AD GENTES 35

<margin>A</margin> They seek the Lord, yet He says: "The ox knows its possessor, and the donkey its master's manger, but Israel has not known me." <note>original: "Isaïas 1:3"</note> What then does the Lord do? He forgets the injury He has received; He still shows mercy, and still demands repentance. I wish to ask you: does it not seem absurd to you that you—who are God's own handiwork, who received your soul from Him, and who belong entirely to Him—should serve another Master? Furthermore, why do you worship a tyrant instead of a King, and a wicked one instead of the Good? For who, in the name of truth and a sound mind, would leave the good to dwell with vice? Who is it that, fleeing from God, lives together with demons? Who, when he could be a son of God, delights in slavery? Or who, when he could be a citizen of heaven, pursues the underworld? Who would do this when he is permitted to cultivate paradise, to traverse the heavens, and to be a partaker of the living and pure fountain, walking through that bright cloud in the air in the footsteps of the Lord, beholding—just as 
<margin>B</margin> Elijah did—the rain of salvation? <margin>3 Kings 17 <note>1 Kings 17 in modern Bibles</note></margin> But these people, like worms in the mud and marshes—wallowing in the flowing gutters of pleasure—feed on useless and foolish delights; they are "swinish" men. For as Democritus says, "Swine delight more in mud than in clean water," <margin>They waste away in filth <gloss>original: Ἐπὶ φορτῷ μαραίνουσι</gloss></margin> and it is a kind of insane delight for them to roll in a heap of piled-up chaff. Let us not, therefore, become slaves, nor be made like pigs; but as true-born sons of the light, let us gaze upon the light and look upward, lest the Lord find us to be illegitimate—just as the Sun is said to test the eagles. <note>A common ancient belief held that true-born eagles could stare directly into the sun without blinking; if they failed, the parent birds rejected them as illegitimate.</note> Let us be led by repentance, and be brought from ignorance to knowledge, from foolishness to wisdom, from 
<margin>C</margin> lack of self-control to temperance, from injustice to justice, and from impiety and lack of religion to God. It is a beautiful risk to flee to God. <note>original: "Pulchrum est periculum." This is a nod to Plato's *Phaedo*, suggesting that the "risk" of believing in the soul's immortality is a noble one.</note> We who are lovers of justice and seekers of eternal salvation can obtain many other good things. Indeed, the inheritance for those who worship the Lord is among those things which God Himself silently signifies when speaking through Isaiah. It is a beautiful and lovely inheritance indeed—not gold, not silver, not clothing which moths consume; nor are they earthly things which a thief breaks into, blinding himself with terrestrial riches. Rather, it is that treasure of salvation, toward which those who are lovers of the Word <margin>Lovers of the Word <gloss>original: Φιλόλογοι</gloss></margin> must strive. From this life, our good works depart with us, flying upward on the wings of truth. The eternal testament of God hands down this inheritance to us, supplying an eternal gift. Our Father, truly a Father and filled with love for us, 
<margin>D</margin> does not cease to exhort, warn, teach, and love. For He never ceases to offer salvation. He has counseled the best things: "Become just," says the Lord. "You who thirst, go to the water; and you who have no money, go and buy, and drink without money." <margin>Isaiah 55</margin> He exhorts us to the washing, to salvation, to illumination—almost crying out and saying: "I give to you, my son, the earth, and the sea, and the sky, and I bestow upon you all the living creatures within them. Only, my son, thirst for your Father; God will be shown to you freely." Truth is not bartered. <note>original: "Non cauponatur veritas." God's truth is not sold like goods in a shop or tavern.</note> He gives you the birds of the air, the fish of the sea, and the animals of the land. The Father has fashioned these for your nourishment, to be received with thanksgiving; <margin>with thankful food <gloss>original: εὐχαρίστοις τροφαῖς</gloss></margin> though the man who is illegitimate—a son of perdition whose habit is to serve Mammon <note>A term for wealth or property, often personified as a false god or evil influence.</note>—must buy these things with money. But to you, He permits what is yours. He speaks to the true-born son 
<margin>E</margin> who loves the Father, through whom He still works, and to whom alone He promises, saying: "The earth shall be stretched out for a firmament." For it is not made firm for destruction or corruption. "The whole earth is mine," says the Lord; and it is yours as well, if you receive God. Whence the Scripture rightly announces to those who have believed: "The saints of the Lord shall be heirs of the glory and power of God." Tell me, O blessed one, what is this glory? "What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man," <margin>Isaiah 64; 1 Cor. 2</margin> and they shall rejoice in the kingdom of their Lord forever, Amen. You have, O men, the divine promise of grace; you have also heard the threats of punishment. Through both of these, the Lord grants salvation, instructing man through both grace and fear. Why do we hesitate? Why do we not escape the punishment? Why do we not receive the gift? Why do we not choose what is better, preferring God to evil, and 
<margin>F</margin> wisdom to idolatry, exchanging death for life? "Behold," He says, "I have set before your face death and life." <margin>Ecclesiasticus 15</margin> The Lord tests you so that you may choose life. He has counseled you like a Father: Obey God. "For if you hear me," He says, "and are willing, you shall eat the good things of the earth." <margin>Isaiah 1</margin> Grace belongs to obedience. "But if you will not obey me, nor be willing..."

->### ORATION OF EXHORTATION<-

<margin>A</margin> "...a sword and fire shall devour you." <note>original: "Isaïas 1:20"</note> For this is the judgment of disobedience. "For the mouth of the Lord has spoken these things." The Law of truth. The Word <term>Verbum: The Latin translation of the Greek 'Logos,' referring here to Christ as the Divine Reason and Voice of God.</term> of the Lord. Do you wish for me to be a good counselor to you? Then listen. I will show you, if it is possible. It was necessary for you, O men, when thinking about the Good itself, to bring forward a witness implanted by nature and worthy of trust—namely, that faith which openly chooses from itself and its own household that which is best and most excellent, rather than seeking or laboring over whether it ought to be pursued. For instance, should one even doubt whether a person ought to become drunk? And yet you get drunk before you even consider the matter. Nor are you very concerned about whether an injury is being committed, but you commit the injury as quickly as possible. Yet, you only question whether God is to be worshiped; and whether the Wise One—that is, God and Christ—is to be followed, you think this must be <margin>B</margin> debated and considered. Believe us, so that if drunkenness has invaded you, you may become sober and moderate. Believe, if you have been affected by injury, so that you may live. But if you wish to believe, looking up to the evident faith of the virtues: from a certain redundant abundance, I will bring to you persuasion regarding the Word.

But you—for ancestral customs still lead you away, preoccupied, from the truth—should now hear how the following matter stands. Do not let the shame of this name <note>The "name" likely refers to being called a Christian, which was often a source of social stigma.</note> seize you, which brings the greatest loss to men. <margin>This shame, specifically, is accustomed to greatly harm those who are of great and strong spirit. For he calls them such men.</margin> Therefore, stripping ourselves openly in the stadium of truth, let us compete genuinely and lawfully, with the Holy Word as the marshal <note>original: "designatore"</note>, and with the Lord of all things presiding as the judge <term>agonotheta: The official who presided over the Greek games and awarded prizes.</term> who proposes the contest and the prize. For no small prize of the contest is proposed to us: immortality.

Therefore, do not care if certain scraps of the courtroom-rabble disparage you, <margin>C</margin> leading an impious choir of demonic superstition, driven by madness and insanity into the very pit of destruction—those makers of images and worshipers of stones. For they dared to enroll men among the Gods, ascribing the thirteenth <note>Alexander was famously deified as the "thirteenth god" alongside the twelve Olympians.</note> Macedonian, Alexander, into the number of the Gods, whom Babylon proved was a dead man. Therefore, I admire that divine Sophist; his name was Theocritus. Mocking those vain opinions which men held about the Gods, this Theocritus said to the citizens: "O men, be of good heart, as long as you see the Gods dying before men."

But he who worships these Gods who fall under our sight, and who adores this promiscuous filth of those who were born, and flatters them, is far more unhappy than those very demons. For God is in no way unjust like the demons, but is as just as can be, <margin>D</margin> and nothing is more like Him than the one among us who is most just.

Go on your way, all you people who practice the illiberal art of hands, you who worship Minerva <note>Athena</note>, the daughter of Jove, as "Gorgon-faced" and "The Worker" <note>original: "Gorgopin & Ergatin"</note> with established winnowing-fans—you foolish makers of stones and worshipers of the same! Let your Phidias and Polycletus come, and again Praxiteles and Apelles, <note>Famous Greek sculptors and painters.</note> and whoever else handles illiberal and sordid arts, who are earthly workers of the earth. For then, says a certain Prophecy, things here will go unhappily, when they put their trust in statues. <margin>petty craftsmen <gloss>original: μικροτέχναι</gloss></margin> Let them come again, therefore (for I will not cease to call them), those vile and abject artisans. Not one of them ever fabricated a breathing image. Nor did they make soft flesh out of the earth. Who melted the marrow? Or who caused the bones to grow together? Who stretched the nerves? Who inflated the veins? Who poured the blood into them? Or who <margin>E</margin> stretched the skin? Where did any of them ever make eyes that see? Who breathed in the soul? Who granted justice? Who promised immortality? Only the Father, the Creator of all things, whose art is by far the best and most excellent. He made such a living image: us, namely, man.

But your Olympus—an image of an image far removed from the truth—is the deaf work of Attic hands. For the image of God is His Word and Son, that genuine divine Word of the Mind, the light of light, the exemplary and archetypal. But the image of the Word is man: the true mind which is in man, who for that reason is said to have been made in the image and likeness of God, assimilated to the divine Word by the prudence in his heart, and by that reasoning, a partaker of the Word and of reason. But of the earth-born man who is seen, the earthly image <margin>F</margin> are those effigies which bear the likeness of a man. That which is expressed and shaped for a time is seen far from the truth. Therefore, life seems to me to have been nothing else but full of madness, which occupied itself with such zeal in material things. But custom, born of vain opinion, has been permitted, which [leads us away...]

<summary>Clement critiques the Greek worship of idols and deified mortals like Alexander the Great, arguing that true divinity is found in the "Word" (Logos). He contrasts the dead statues made by famous artists like Phidias with the living "image of God"—humanity—created by the Father.</summary>

# TO THE GENTILES

<margin>A</margin>...it certainly made one taste servitude, and a care that is superfluous and alien to reason.
<margin>Let them be subject <note>original: "ὑποκείσθων"</note></margin>
The cause of unjust laws and deceptive imitations is ignorance. This ignorance, when compared to the human race, devised many forms of fatal Fates and abominable images of demons, and impressed the stain of a long death upon those who follow it. Therefore, receive the rational water, that is, the water of the Word <term>Verbi: Referring to the 'Logos' or Christ as Divine Reason.</term>. Be washed, you who are defiled. Sprinkle yourselves with true drops and cleanse yourselves from custom. Pure men must ascend to heaven. You are a man; seek that which is most common to all, Him who fabricated you. You are a son; acknowledge that which is most your own, your Father.

But you still remain in sins, wasting away and melting in pleasures. To whom shall the Lord speak? "Yours is the kingdom of heaven," if you will it—you who have directed the free will of your soul toward God. <margin>B</margin> It is yours, if only you wish to believe and follow the shortcut of the preaching. When the Ninevites <note>The people of Nineveh in the Book of Jonah, who repented at the prophet's warning.</note> heard this, though they were expecting destruction, they exchanged it for an excellent salvation through genuine and sincere repentance.

<margin>Matthew 7</margin>
"How then," one says, "shall I ascend the heavens?" The Lord is the Way: narrow indeed, but from the heavens; narrow indeed, but sending one to the heavens; narrow, as it is despised on earth; wide, as it is adored in the heavens. Next, he who has not received the Word by hearing is granted pardon due to his ignorance. But he who drinks it in with his ears, and yet of his own accord brings unbelief into his soul—the more "prudent" he seems to be, the greater evil he will be in; for he has used his prudence as an accuser, not choosing that which is best.

<margin>C</margin> For otherwise, there is something innate in man by nature, a certain connection that intervenes between him and God. Just as we do not force a horse to plow, nor a bull to hunt, but we draw each animal toward that for which it is naturally fit; so surely man, who was born for the contemplation of heaven and is truly a **heavenly plant**, we exhort to the knowledge of God. We grasp that which is his own, excellent, and peculiar to him, advising that he prepare for himself a sufficient provision for the ages: piety and the worship of God.

"Till the earth," we say, "if you are a farmer; but know God while tilling the earth." And "sail, you who are held by the love of navigation, but take on the heavenly Pilot." Knowledge finds you even while you are serving as a soldier; listen to the Commander who signals what is just to you. Therefore, as those who are heavy with the hangover and drunkenness of the past, return to sobriety. <margin>D</margin> When you have looked a little more clearly, think within your souls what those stones signify which you worship, and what you spend on material things with vain zeal. In ignorance, you consume both your faculties and wealth, as well as your very life, in death; when you find this to be the only end of your vain hope, you cannot even pity yourselves.

But you are not even fit to believe those who pity your error, enslaved as you are to evil custom; hanging from it, you go toward destruction by your own will even to your last breath. <margin>John 3</margin> "For light has come into the world, and men loved darkness more than light" <note>John 3:19</note>, even though they might remove those things which hinder salvation: pride, riches, and fear. They might utter this poetic line: *Whither shall I carry this great weight of money? And where do I myself wander?* <margin>Homer, Odyssey <gloss>uninitiated</gloss> <gloss>you were caught</gloss></margin> <note>Clement quotes Odyssey 13.203-204, where Odysseus is confused by his return to Ithaca.</note>

<margin>E</margin> If you wish, therefore, having cast aside these vain visions and fantasies, to renounce custom itself, say to vain glory: "Farewell, false dreams; you were, after all, nothing." For what, O men, do you think Typhon, and Andocides, and Mercury, and Amyetus are? <note>Clement is listing names associated with famous statues or mythological figures to show they are merely physical objects.</note> Is it not manifest to anyone that they are stones, just as Mercury <note>The "Herms" or stone pillars of the god Hermes.</note> is? Just as an altar is not God, and as a rainbow is not God, but they are certain conditions of the air and clouds; and just as a day is not God, nor a month, nor a year: so neither is the Sun, nor the Moon, by which each of the aforesaid units of time is defined.

Who then of sound mind would think that Punishment, Supplication, Justice, and Nemesis <note>The goddess of retribution.</note> are gods? For neither are the Furies, nor the Fates, nor Fate [gods], since neither is a Republic, nor Glory, nor Plutus (that is, Wealth), whom even painters depict as blind. But if you count Modesty, and Love, and Venus among the gods, let Shame, and Appetite, and Beauty, and Intercourse follow them into the pantheon. <margin>F</margin> No longer then will **Sleep** and **Death** be rightly considered by you as twin Gods, since they are merely conditions that naturally happen to living creatures. But neither will you rightly call Fate or the Fates "gods." If Strife and Battle are not gods, then neither is Mars a god, nor Enyo <note>A goddess of war.</note>. Furthermore, since lightning and thunderbolts and rains are not gods, how can fire and water be gods? How or what...

### EXHORTATORY ORATION

<margin>A</margin> Those "shooting through" <note>original: "Διαΐσσοντες" (diaissontes)</note>—that is, running through the air—are called both shooting stars and comets; do they not arise from a mere atmospheric condition? If one calls Fortune a goddess, let him also call "action" a goddess. If, therefore, none of these are reckoned to be God—nor those unfeeling, man-made figments—but rather a certain providence of divine power is seen toward us, it remains for us to confess nothing else than this: that He alone truly exists and stands firm, who is truly the only God. 

Indeed, those who have drunk mandrake <term>mandragoram: A plant used in antiquity as an anesthetic or poison, often associated with a state of stupor or spiritual "sleep."</term> or some other drug have turned out like fools. <margin>Demosthenic. <note>A reference to the powerful, persuasive style of the Greek orator Demosthenes.</note></margin> May God grant that you be awakened from this sleep at last and understand God—and that you do not fashion for yourself gold, or stone, or wood, or action, or affection, or disease, or fear, as a God. 

<margin>Ex Hesiodo. <note>Hesiod was an early Greek poet; Clement here references a famous passage from "Works and Days."</note></margin> <margin>B</margin> For truly, on the nourishing earth there are "three ten-thousands" <note>original: "myriades"</note> of demons—not immortal, yet not mortal either; for they are not even endowed with sensation so as to be sharers of death, but are stony and wooden "masters" of men, who violate and injure human life through mere custom. 

But "the earth," says the Scripture, "is the Lord’s, and the fullness thereof." Why then, while indulging in the pleasures and delights that belong to the Lord, do you dare to ignore the Master? "Leave my earth," the Lord will say to you; "do not touch the water I give you; do not share in the fruits I cultivate." O man, acknowledge that the food you receive is from God; recognize your Master; you are God's own handiwork <note>original: "figmentum," suggesting man is a vessel shaped by a potter.</note>. How can that which is His own rightfully become another's? For that which is alienated, when it is deprived of its ownership, is deprived of truth. 

Have you not, in a way, like Niobe <note>In Greek myth, Niobe was turned to stone by the gods as she wept for her children.</note>, or—to speak more mystically to you—like the wife of the Hebrew man (whom the ancients called Lot), become void of all sense? <margin>C</margin> We have learned that this woman was turned to stone because she loved Sodom. But the Sodomites were impious, and those who still dwell in impiety are hard of heart and senseless. 

Think of these voices as being spoken to you by divine inspiration. Do not think that stones and wood and birds and serpents are sacred, while men are not; on the contrary, consider men to be truly sacred, and beasts and stones to be exactly what they are. For wretched and unhappy men think God cries out through the crow and the jackdaw, but is silent through man! They have honored the crow as God’s messenger, but they persecute God’s man—who does not croak or cluck, but, alas, speaks from reason, and instructs by sounding forth with kind and humane voices. They inhumanly attempt to kill him while he calls them to justice.

<margin>They are instructed <note>original: "Κατηχοῦνται" (Katechountai)</note></margin> <margin>D</margin> They neither receive the grace that descends from above nor shun the punishment. For they do not believe God, nor do they learn His power. Just as His humanity is beyond words, so His hatred of wickedness is beyond grasping. Anger nourishes punishment because of sin, but humanity does good because of repentance. To be deprived of God’s help is by far the most miserable thing. 

The loss of eyes and the deafness of ears bring greater pain than other physical ills. <margin>By a heavenly sight, that is, the spectacle of divine beauty.</margin> For the former is deprived of the heavenly sight; the latter is robbed of heavenly doctrine. But you—who are crippled regarding the truth, blind in mind, and deaf in understanding—you do not grieve! You do not take it hard that you have failed to desire to see heaven and the Maker of heaven, nor have you sought to hear and learn of the Father and Architect of all things, joining your purpose and the free will of your soul to salvation.

<margin>E</margin> <margin>He prefers the good of teaching over any other good.</margin> No impediment stands in the way of him who strives toward the knowledge of God—not the loss of children, nor poverty, nor disgrace, nor lack of possessions. No one wishes to cut off that which is truly "True Wisdom," or to trade it for bronze or iron. For a man chooses this above anything else. Christ is a savior everywhere. For he who is an emulator of the Just One, as a lover of Him who lacks nothing, is in need of little; for he has stored his treasure of happiness in no other place than in himself and in God, where there is no moth, no thief, no pirate, but the eternal Giver of good things.

<margin>In the good itself, namely, of teaching.</margin> Rightly, therefore, you are likened to those serpents who have ears closed to the charmers. "For their WRATH," says the Scripture, "is after the likeness of a serpent, like a deaf asp that stops its ears, which will not hear the voice of the charmers." <margin>F</margin> But you, revere holiness, and receive our gentle word, and spit out the lethal venom, so that it may be granted to you also to cast off destruction, just as those serpents cast off their old age <note>A common ancient belief that serpents regained youth by shedding their skin.</note>. Listen to me, and do not block your ears, nor your hearing...
