### TO THE HEATHENS

<margin>A</margin> Stop up your ears against [wicked] hearing, but imprint what is being said upon your mind. It is a beautiful medicine of immortality; finally, stop these crawling and snake-like turnings. "For the enemies of the Lord shall lick the earth," says the Scripture <note>original: "Scriptura"; a reference to Psalm 72:9 or Micah 7:17</note>; be raised up from the earth into the air, look back toward heaven, wonder at it, and cease lying in wait for the "heel of the righteous" <note>An allusion to the curse of the serpent in Genesis 3:15</note> and hindering the way of truth. Be prudent and innocent; perhaps the Lord will indeed give you the wing of simplicity. He wishes to clothe the earth-born with wings so that, leaving behind their dens, you may dwell in the heavens. Only let us be led by repentance with our whole heart, so that we may be able to grasp the Lord with our whole heart. "Hope in Him," it says, "all the assembly of the people; pour out all your hearts before Him." He speaks to those who are fresh from wickedness; He has mercy, and He fills them with justice. Believe, O man, in man and in God. Believe, O man, in the living God who suffered and is 
<margin>B</margin> adored. Believe, O servants, in the one who died; all men, believe in Him who alone is God among all men. Believe, and receive the reward of salvation. "Seek God, and your soul shall live." He who seeks God is concerned for his own salvation. If you have found God, you have life. Let us seek, therefore, so that we may also live. The reward of finding Him is life with God. "Let all those who seek Thee exult and be glad in Thee, and let them say forever: Let God be magnified." A beautiful hymn of God is immortal man, who is built up by justice, and in whom the words of truth are inscribed. For where else is justice to be inscribed than in a temperate and moderated soul? Where is charity? Where is shame? And where is gentleness? It is necessary, as I think, that those who are sealed by these divine scriptures should consider 
<margin>C</margin> them to be the best starting gates <note>original: "carceres"; literally "prisons" or "stalls," but often used for the starting gates of a racecourse</note> from which wisdom is sent forth, to whatever part of life they may turn; and they should consider wisdom to be a harbor of salvation, tossed by no waves. Through wisdom, indeed, there are good fathers to their children, who have fled to the Father; and there are good sons to their parents, who have understood the Son; and there are good husbands to their wives, who have remembered the Bridegroom; and there are good masters to their servants, who have been liberated from the ultimate slavery. O, the error that is in men! The beasts are more blessed, for they possess ignorance just as you do, yet they never falsely imitate or feign the truth. Among them, there are no types of flatterers. Fish do not worship demons in superstition; birds do not adore idols. They only stand 
<margin>D</margin> amazed at the one heaven, since they cannot apprehend God with intelligence, as those to whom reason has not been granted. Then, are you not ashamed that you have made yourselves less rational than fish—you who have been worn down in impiety through so many ages? You were infants, then boys, then youths, then men—but never good. At least respect old age. Since you are at the sunset of life, return to your senses; become moderated and temperate, and even at the end of life acknowledge God, so that He may take up for you a beginning of salvation. You have grown old in the false religion of demons; come as youths and newcomers to the worship of God and the true religion, and God will restore you to the number of simple children. Let the Athenian follow the laws of Solon, the Argive those of Phoroneus, and the Spartan those of Lycurgus. But if you enroll yourself with God, then heaven is your fatherland, and God is your legislator. And what are the laws? "Thou shalt not kill," "thou shalt not commit adultery," 
<margin>E</margin> "thou shalt not commit lust with a boy," "thou shalt not steal," "thou shalt not bear false witness." "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God." The fulfillment of these are the rational laws and the holy words. If you are inscribed with these in your very hearts, you will "love your neighbor as yourself," and "to him who strikes you on the cheek, offer also the other." "Thou shalt not covet," for by desire alone you have committed adultery. How much better it is for men to not want to desire what they ought not from the beginning, than to obtain those things which you have desired? But you indeed cannot endure the bitterness of salvation. Just as we are delighted by sweet foods, valuing them more for the lightness of the pleasure they give, yet bitter things cure and heal us, even though they sharpen the senses. But for those who have a weak stomach, the sharpness of medicine strengthens them; so does custom <term>consuetudo: the Greek "ethos," referring to the ingrained habits of pagan culture.</term> delight and tickle with a pleasant sensation. 
<margin>F</margin> But that custom hurls one down into the abyss, whereas truth leads to heaven—truth, which is indeed harsh at first, but is a good educator of children. And indeed, the assembly of women is honorable and venerable, and the senate is prudent and moderated. Nor is truth difficult of access, nor such that it...

# EXHORTATORY ORATION

...extremely difficult, but it is right here in our homes, as Moses <margin>A</margin> suggests—being most wise—living in our three parts: our hands, our mouth, and our heart. This is indeed the true and genuine "wood of truth," which is completed in three things: in counsel, in action, and in word. Do not fear that many pleasant things, through visions and fantasies, might lead you away from wisdom; for wisdom herself will gladly leap over the trifles of custom, just as children, when they reach manhood, cast away their toys. With an unstoppable speed and a benevolence that offers easy access, the divine power that has shone upon the earth has filled the universe with the seed of salvation. For the Lord—who appeared despised in outward look but is in reality adored—did not accomplish such a great work in so short a time without divine care and providence. He is the one who purifies, the savior, the kind and merciful one <margin>B</margin>; the Divine Word <term>Logos: the creative and mediating principle of God</term> who is truly the most manifest God, who is made equal to the Lord of all, since He was His Son, and the "Word was in God." Nor was He disbelieved when He was first preached, nor was He unknown when He took on the person of a man, nor when He was formed in the flesh and performed the saving act of humanity. For He was a true and genuine champion, and the defender of His own creation. Most quickly was He delivered to all men, having risen from the Father’s will swifter than the Sun, and most easily did He cause God to shine upon us. He showed whence He came and who He was through what He taught and demonstrated—the initiator of the covenant, our reconciler and Savior, the Word who is a life-giving and peace-making fountain, poured out over the entire face of the earth, through whom, to put it simply, all things have become a sea of blessings. But if you wish, look back for a moment from on high <margin>C</margin> at this divine benefit. The first man, when he was in Paradise, played freely, for he was God’s child. But when he subjected himself to pleasure—the serpent is an allegory for pleasure <note>original: "Serpens allegoricè dicitur voluptas"</note>, crawling on its belly, nourished by earthly materials—the child was enticed by desires. He became a man through disobedience, and by not listening to the Father, he brought dishonor upon God. How much power does pleasure have? Man, who was free because of his simplicity, was found bound by sins. The Lord wished to loose him again from those chains, and so He Himself was bound in the flesh—O divine mystery!—He subdued this serpent and reduced the tyrant, namely Death, into slavery. And what is most beyond expectation, He showed that man—who had been seduced by pleasure and bound to destruction and corruption—was set free by His extended hands. O mystic miracle <margin>D</margin> <margin>With hands extended on the cross.</margin>. The Lord indeed bowed down, but man rose up; and he who fell from Paradise receives a greater reward for obedience: the heavens. Therefore, as it seems to me, since the Word Himself has come to us from heaven, we no longer need to go to human teaching—to Athens, or the rest of Greece, or even Ionia—searching inquisitively. For if we have Him as our teacher, who has filled all things with holy powers—with craftsmanship, salvation, benefit, legislation, prophecy, and doctrine—all things now echo with the Teacher, and the whole world has already become Athens and Greece through the Word. For you did not believe the poetic fables that write of Minos the Cretan enjoying the familiar company of Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note>; will you then not believe us, who have been disciples of God, and who have received that philosophy <margin>E</margin> which is truly true? What the most eminent philosophers only darkly hinted at, the disciples of Christ have understood and proclaimed. And the whole Christ, to say it once, is not divided. There is neither Barbarian, nor Jew, nor Greek, nor male, nor female; but there is the "new man" transformed by the Holy Spirit of God. Furthermore, other counsels and admonitions are both troublesome and concern specific things: whether one should marry, whether one should take part in public affairs, whether one should procreate children. But this general exhortation alone, which pertains to the whole of life at every time and in every event, directs life toward its highest point: piety and the worship of God. By this principle alone, it is necessary to live so that we may live forever. Philosophy, as the ancients say, is the long-term counsel of Wisdom <margin>F</term>, which encompasses eternal love. But the commandment of the Lord is clear, enlightening the eyes. Receive Christ, receive sight, receive light, so that you may rightly know both God and man. The sweet Word, who has enlightened us more than gold and precious stones, is more desirable than honey and the honeycomb. For how can that which gives life to the mind...

# TO THE HEATHEN
D iii

<margin>A</margin> ...truth buried in darkness, has He made it active and effective, and sharpened the light-bearing eyes of the soul? For just as if the Sun did not exist, all things would be as night as far as the other stars are concerned; so, unless we had known the Word <note>original: "Verbum", referring to the Greek "Logos", the Divine Reason or Christ</note> and been illuminated by Him, we would differ in no way from birds that are being fed, in that we would be fattened in darkness and nourished for death. Let us take hold of the light, so that we may take hold of God. Let us take hold of the light, so that we may be disciples of the Lord. This indeed He promised to the Father: **I WILL TELL** of your name to my brothers; in the midst of the church I will praise you. Praise Him, and I will tell you of your father, God. Your narrations bring salvation. Your song will teach me that until now I have wandered seeking God. But since you lead me to the light, O Lord, and I find God through you, and receive the Father from you, I become your co-heir, since you were not <margin>B</margin> ashamed of your brother. Let us therefore put away, let us put away the forgetting of the truth; let us remove ignorance and darkness, which obstruct the eyes like a mist, so that we may contemplate Him who is truly God, acclaiming Him first with this voice in a hymn: "Hail, light!" For light has dawned upon us from heaven, we who were buried in darkness and shut up in the shadow of death; a light, I say, purer than the Sun and more pleasant than this present life. That light is eternal life, and whatever participates in it lives. But night fears the light, and setting because of fear, it yields to the day of the Lord. All things have become a light that cannot be put to sleep, and the setting has given way to the rising. This is what the "new creation" <note>referring to the Christian concept of being made new in Christ</note> willed. For the Sun of Righteousness, who rides over all things, likewise oversees humanity, imitating the Father who makes His sun rise equally over all men and drops the dew of truth. He has turned the sunset into sunrise, and fixed death to the <margin>C</margin> cross; having snatched man away from destruction, He suspended him in the upper air, transplanting decay and corruption into the emptiness of incorruption. He changes earth into heaven—God’s husbandman—signifying with His right hand, rousng the people to good work, bringing the true life back to memory, and bestowing upon us an inheritance that is truly great, divine, and which cannot be taken away; making man a god <note>original: "hominem Deum faciens", a reference to "theosis," the early Christian idea that humans are transformed by grace to share in the divine nature</note> through heavenly doctrine, putting a law into their minds and writing them on the heart. What laws does He write? That all shall know God from the great even to the small. "And I will be merciful to them," says God, "and I will not remember their sins." Let us receive the laws of life; let us obey God who exhorts us. Let us learn of Him, so that He may be merciful. Let us return to Him, <margin>D</margin> though He is in need of nothing, a grateful reward: well-ordered affections. As if paying rent for a house we inhabit, let us give to God piety and His worship for our habitation here. "Bronze for gold, and the weight of nine for the weight of a hundred bulls" <note>A reference to Homer’s Iliad (6.236), suggesting God gives an infinitely better bargain than we deserve</note>. In exchange for a little faith, He gives you such a great land to cultivate: water to drink and other water to sail upon; air to breathe; fire for your work; and a world to inhabit. From here He has granted you to send a colony into the heavens. These so many and so great works and gifts He has <margin>He placed, that is, he handed over and bestowed.</margin> bestowed for a little faith. Then there are those who have believed in tricksters, receiving amulets and incantations as if they brought health. But you—will you not even bind the heavenly Word Himself, who is the Savior, to yourselves? Believing in God’s "incantation," you will be freed from vices and disturbances, which are the diseases of the soul, and be torn away from sin. <margin>E</margin> For sin is eternal death. You are plainly toothless and blind like moles; you do nothing else but eat, spending your lives in darkness, overflowing with ruin and corruption. But there is Truth which cries out: "From darkness light shall shine." Therefore, let the light shine in the hidden part of man, namely in the heart, and let the rays of knowledge arise, revealing and illuminating the man who is hidden within—the disciple of light, who is Christ’s companion and co-heir. This is especially true when the name of the good Father comes to the knowledge of a pious and good son—a name to be most honored and worshipped—of Him who commands gentle things and orders for His son those things which lead to salvation. He who obeys Him perceives great advantages in all things: he follows God, he obeys the Father, he recognizes his own error, he loves God, he loves his neighbor, he fulfills the commandment, he seeks the reward, and he demands the promise. <margin>F</margin> It has always been God's purpose to save the flock of men, and therefore the good God sent the Good Shepherd. And the Word, having explained the truth, showed men the height of salvation, so that they might either be saved by being led to repentance, or be judged if they did not obey. This is the preaching of justice: to those who obey, it is the Gospel, or good news...

->### TO THE GENTILES<-
<note>Latin: Ad Gentes. This is part of Clement of Alexandria's "Exhortation to the Heathen."</note>
->D iii<-

<margin>A</margin> ...and what was once buried in darkness, He has made active and effective, and He has sharpened the light-bearing eyes of the soul. For just as if the Sun did not exist, everything would be night as far as the other stars are concerned; so too, if we had not known the Word <note>original: "Verbum", translating the Greek "Logos", meaning Divine Reason or Christ</note> and been illuminated by Him, we would differ in no way from birds that are being fed—mere creatures fattening ourselves in the darkness and nourished by death. Let us take hold of the light, so that we may take hold of God. Let us take hold of the light, so that we may be disciples of the Lord. This is surely what He promised to the Father: **I WILL TELL** of your name to my brothers; in the midst of the church I will praise you. Praise Him, and I will tell you of your Father, who is God. Your narrations bring salvation. Your song will teach me that until now I have wandered in search of God. But since you lead me to the light, O Lord, and I find God through you, and receive the Father from you, I become your co-heir, because you were not ashamed to call me brother.

<margin>B</margin>
Let us therefore put away, let us put away the forgetfulness of truth! Once ignorance and darkness are removed—which block the eyes like a thick mist—let us contemplate Him who is truly God, first crying out this greeting to Him in a hymn: "Hail, O Light!" For light has dawned upon us from heaven, we who were buried in darkness and shut in the shadow of death; a light, I say, purer than the Sun, and more pleasant than this life here. That light is eternal life, and whatever participates in it truly lives. Night, however, fears the light, and setting because of fear, gives way to the day of the Lord. All things have become a light that cannot be put to sleep, and the setting of the sun has yielded to its rising. This is what the "new creation" desired. For the Sun of Righteousness, who rides over all things, visits humanity equally, imitating the Father <margin>C</margin> who makes His sun rise over everyone equally, and drops the dew of truth. He has turned the "sunset" of our lives into a "sunrise," and fixed death to the cross, turning it into life. Having snatched man away from destruction, He suspended him in the upper air, transplanting ruin and corruption into the emptiness where ruin and corruption cannot exist. God, like a divine farmer, changes the earth into heaven with His right hand, rousng the people to good work, bringing to memory the true life—the truly great and divine inheritance that cannot be taken away—and making man into a god through heavenly doctrine, "placing the law in their minds and writing it on their hearts." What laws does He write? That "all shall know God, from the great to the small." And God says, "I will be merciful to them, and I will not remember their sins." Let us receive the laws of life; let us obey God as He encourages us. Let us learn of Him, so that He may be merciful. Let us return to Him <margin>D</margin> a grateful reward (though He needs nothing), namely, well-ordered affections; and as a sort of rent for the house we inhabit here, let us give God our piety and worship. "Bronze for gold, and the weight of nine for the weight of a hundred bulls." <note>This is a reference to Homer's Iliad, where a character foolishly trades gold armor for bronze; Clement uses it to suggest that the "trade" we make with God—our small faith for His great gifts—is an infinitely better bargain for us.</note>

<margin>He "leased," that is, He handed over or bestowed.</margin>
For a modest faith, He gives you such a vast land to cultivate: water to drink and other water to sail upon; air to breathe; fire to work with; a world to inhabit. From here, He has permitted you to send out a colony into the heavens. These works and gifts, so many and so great, He has "leased" for a modest faith. Yet there are those who believe in sorcerers and receive amulets and incantations as if they were life-saving. But you—will you not even bind yourselves to the heavenly Word Himself, who is the Savior? Will you not, by believing in God’s "incantation," be freed from the vices and disturbances that are diseases of the mind, and be torn away from <margin>E</margin> sin? For sin is eternal death. You are plainly toothless and blind like moles; you do nothing else but eat and live in darkness, surrounded by ruin and corruption. But it is the Truth that cries out: "Out of darkness, light shall shine." Let light therefore shine in the hidden part of man, namely in the heart, and let the rays of knowledge arise, revealing and illuminating the man who is hidden within—the disciple of light, who is Christ’s familiar friend and co-heir. This happens especially when the name of the good Father—which is to be most honored and worshiped—comes to the knowledge of a pious and good son, for the Father commands gentle things and orders for His son those things which bring salvation. He who obeys Him perceives great advantages in all things: he follows God, obeys the Father, recognizes his own errors, loves God, loves his neighbor, fulfills the commandment, seeks the prize, and asks for the promise.

<margin>F</margin>
It is always God’s purpose to save the flock of men, and therefore the good God sent the Good Shepherd. And the Word, having explained the truth, showed men the height of salvation, so that they might either be saved by being led to repentance, or be judged if they did not obey. This is the preaching of justice: to those who obey, it is the Gospel, or...

<summary>Clement describes the Word (Christ) as a divine light that rescues humanity from the darkness of ignorance and the "shadow of death." He contrasts the "modest faith" required by God with the vast natural and spiritual gifts He bestows in return, urging readers to choose the Gospel over superstition.</summary>
<keywords>Clement of Alexandria, The Word, Logos, Sun of Righteousness, Light and Darkness, Salvation, New Covenant, Good Shepherd, Repentance, Gospel</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discourse on the illumination provided by the Word. The opening phrase "good news" completes the description of the Gospel as a message of salvation for the faithful and judgment for the disobedient.</meta>

->### EXHORTATORY ORATION<-

...good news, but for those who have not obeyed, it is judgment. But while the terrifying trumpet
<margin>A</margin>
sounding the call to arms <note>Latin: "classicum canens." In ancient Rome, the *classicum* was the specific trumpet signal used to assemble the army for battle.</note> has gathered soldiers and announced war, shall not Christ—who has breathed a peaceful melody to the ends of the earth—gather His own peaceful soldiers? He has indeed gathered, O man, an unbloody army through His Blood and His Word, and has handed over the kingdom of heaven to them. The trumpet of Christ is His Gospel. He has sounded the trumpet, and we have heard it. Let us arm ourselves peacefully, putting on the breastplate of righteousness, taking up the shield of faith, and placing on our heads the helmet of salvation; and let us sharpen the sword of the spirit, which is the Word of God. Thus the Apostle <note>Saint Paul, referencing the famous "Armor of God" passage in Ephesians 6:14-17.</note> arrays us in peace. These are our invulnerable weapons. Armed with these, let us join the battle in a well-ordered line against the Evil One; let us extinguish the fiery darts of the wicked one with the water-soaked points provided by the Word, returning benefits
<margin>B</margin>
for free blessings, and honoring God with the divine word.
<margin>Isaiah 58</margin>
For while you are still speaking, He will say: "Behold, I am here." O holy and blessed is this power through which God dwells together with men! It is therefore better and more excellent to become at once an imitator and a worshiper of the best and most excellent of all beings. For no one can imitate God except by worshiping Him holily, nor can one worship and venerate Him without imitating Him. For this is the celestial and truly divine love which comes to men in this way: when that which is truly honorable in the soul itself, having been awakened by the divine Word, is able to shine forth. And what is greatest of all is that salvation runs together with a genuine and sincere will, and—to put it simply—salvation is joined 
<margin>C</margin>
<margin>Joined together, that is, agreeing with one another.</margin>
together with a free choice of the mind and a way of life. Therefore, this exhortation to truth alone is like the most faithful of friends, remaining until the final breath; it is a good leader and companion for the soul with its whole and perfect spirit, for those who are reaching toward heaven. Why then do I exhort you? I urge you so that you may be saved. This is what Christ wants; in a single word, He bestows life upon you. And what is this word? Learn it in brief: the Word of truth, the Word of incorruption, who regenerates man by leading him back to the truth—the stimulus of salvation which drives away destruction, which pursues death, and which has built a temple in men so that He might place God within men. Make sure that the temple is chaste and pure; and leave pleasures and delights, like a fading and brief flower, to the wind and the fire. Wisely cultivate the fruits of temperance and moderation, and consecrate yourself to God
<margin>D</margin>
as the first-fruits, so that it may be not only your work, but also the grace of God. It is fitting for both: to appear familiar to Christ and worthy of the kingdom, and to have been deemed worthy of that kingdom. Let us therefore flee custom <note>Latin: "consuetudo." Clement uses this to mean the habitual pagan traditions and mindless rituals of the past.</note>; let us flee it as if it were a dangerous reef, or the threats of Charybdis, or the mythical Sirens. It suffocates a man, turns him away from the truth, and leads him away from life. Custom is a snare, an abyss, a harmful winnowing-fan. As that famous poet says:

<margin>Homer's Odyssey</margin>
<margin>He is referring to Circe.</margin>
> "Keep the ship away from the smoke and the savage wave." <note>A quote from Homer’s *Odyssey*, where Odysseus is warned to steer clear of the dangers of the sea.</note>

Let us flee, let us flee, O companions! This wave belches fire; it is an evil island heaped with bones and corpses. On it sings a beautiful little harlot—Pleasure—who delights in public music.
<margin>E</margin>
<margin>The Sirens say these words to Ulysses.</margin>
> "Come here, famous Odysseus, glory of the Greeks,
> Stop your ship, so that you may hear our divine songs." <note>A Latin translation of the Sirens' song from the *Odyssey*.</note>

She praises you, O sailor, and calls you famous and illustrious; the harlot claims the glory of the Greeks for herself. Let her keep the corpses; the divine Spirit brings you help. Pass by the pleasure; drive it away:

<margin>Hesiod</margin>
> "And beware that the dressed-up woman does not deceive you, 
> speaking sweetly, seeking to overturn your nest." <note>A quote from Hesiod's *Works and Days*, warning against seductive distractions.</note>
<margin>F</margin>
Sail past the song; it works death. If only you will it, you have conquered destruction; and bound to the wood <note>A dual reference: Odysseus being tied to the mast of his ship to resist the Sirens, and the Christian being "bound" to the wood of the Cross.</note>, you will be released from all ruin. The Word of God will steer you, and the Holy Spirit will lead you to the harbor of the heavens. Then you shall look upon my God and you shall be initiated into those holy mysteries, and you shall enjoy those things which are hidden in the heavens, which are reserved for me, "which no ear has heard, nor have they entered into the heart of any man." I seem to see two suns, and a double Thebes <note>A reference to the play *The Bacchae* by Euripides, where the character Pentheus, driven mad or drunk by Dionysus, sees double.</note>, said a certain man raving in the grip of idols, drunk with pure ignorance. But I would pity him in his madness, and I would exhort him who is so senseless to seek a moderate and temperate salvation, since the Lord also...

<summary>Clement uses vivid maritime and military metaphors to urge his audience to abandon pagan "customs" (the Sirens) and join the "unbloody army" of Christ. He contrasts the madness of idolatry with the temperate, light-filled salvation offered by the Word.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Clement’s exhortation to the Greeks, moving from the metaphor of spiritual armor to a direct comparison between the wild, drunken mysteries of Bacchus and the "sober" mysteries of the Divine Word (Christ). ->## TO THE GENTILES<-
<center>D iiii</center>

<margin>A</margin> He also desires the repentance of the sinner and not his death. Come, O frenzied one, leaning no longer on your thyrsus <note>The thyrsus was a staff topped with a pine cone and wrapped in ivy, carried by the followers of Bacchus.</note>, nor crowned with ivy. Cast away the headband, cast away the fawn-skin <note>The *nebris*, or fawn-skin, was the traditional garment of the Maenads (Bacchic revelers).</note>; be temperate and moderate. I will show you the Word, and I will recount the mysteries of the Word in a manner suited to your own customs. This is the mountain beloved by God, which is not the subject of tragedies like Cithaeron <note>Mount Cithaeron was the setting for many Greek tragedies involving Bacchus, including the slaughter of Pentheus.</note>; rather, it is dedicated to the acts of truth—a sober mountain, shaded by chaste woods. Upon it, those who revel are not the sisters of Semele who were struck by lightning, nor the Maenads who are initiated through the unholy devouring of raw flesh; instead, they are the daughters of God, beautiful lambs who celebrate the venerable rites of the Word, assembling a well-ordered choir. This choir is the assembly of the righteous.

<margin>B</margin> Their song is a hymn to the King of all; the maidens play the psaltery, the Angels give glory, the Prophets speak, the sound of music is sent forth, and they follow the sacred procession <note>Latin: *Thiasum*. Originally a wild procession for Bacchus, Clement reclaims the term for the Christian journey.</note> with haste. Those who are called hasten with great zeal, desiring to receive the Father. Come you also to me, O old man, leaving Athens behind, casting away your divination and your Bacchic arts, that I may lead you to the truth. See, I give you a staff to lean upon. Hasten, Tiresias <note>A famous blind seer of Thebes; Clement invites him to regain his sight through Christ.</note>, and believe! Christ will illuminate your vision more splendidly than the Sun, through whom the eyes of the blind see; night shall flee from you, the fire shall be terrified, and death shall perish. You shall see the heavens, O old man, you who cannot even look upon Thebes. O truly holy mysteries! O pure light! Torches are carried before me; when I look upon the heavens and God, I become holy through my initiation. The Lord Himself is the interpreter of these sacred rites; He seals the initiate while illuminating him, and commends the believer to the Father, to be preserved for all ages. These are the "revels" of my mysteries. If you wish, you too may be initiated, and you shall lead the dance

<margin>C</margin> with the Angels around Him who is unbegotten and free from decay, and who alone is truly God, while the Word of God sings the hymn along with us. This is the eternal Jesus, the one great High Priest of the one God, who is also the Father; He prays for men and exhorts men. Listen, you innumerable nations—or rather, whoever among men is endowed with reason, both Barbarians and Greeks! I call upon the whole race of mankind, of whom I am the creator by the will of the Father. Come to me, to be gathered under one God and one Word of God; do not merely surpass the irrational animals by your reason, but from among all mortals, I grant you the enjoyment of immortality. For I wish, I truly wish, to impart this grace to you, providing a full and complete benefit. I bestow upon you the freedom from destruction and corruption, and I grant you Reason—that is, the Word—and the knowledge of God.

<margin>D</margin> I bestow my perfect self upon you. This is what I am, this is what God wills. This is the harmony, this is the symphony and the music of the Father. This is the Son, this is Christ, this is the Word of God, the arm of the Lord, the power of the universe, the will of the Father. Of these things there were once images, but not all were like the original. I wish to restore you to the archetype, so that you may also be like me. I will anoint you with the ointment of faith, through which you strip off destruction and corruption; and I will show you the naked form of justice, through which you ascend to God.

<margin>Matthew 11</margin>
> Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.

Let us hasten, let us run, O you who are godly and like the Word of God; O men, who are His images, let us hasten, let us run,

<margin>E</margin> let us take up His yoke, let us enter into incorruption. Let us love Christ, the beautiful charioteer of men. He led the colt with the old animal under the same yoke <note>A reference to Christ's entry into Jerusalem on a donkey and a colt, often interpreted by early theologians as the joining of the Jews and the Gentiles.</note>, and having yoked the pair of men, He directs the chariot toward immortality, hastening toward God, so that He might clearly fulfill what He had silently signified: first in Jerusalem, and now by leading us into the heavens. It is a most beautiful spectacle for the Father—the eternal Son, the victor. With great zeal and effort, therefore, let us be carried toward what is honorable, and let us become godly and religious men; let us acquire God and life, which is the greatest of those things that are free from passions and disturbances. The Word is our helper; let us be of good courage and place our trust in Him. Let a desire for gold, silver, and glory never take hold of us as much as the desire for the Word of truth itself. For it is not pleasing to God if we

<margin>F</margin> treat those things which are of the greatest value as if they were of the least worth, while we value more highly follies, ignorance, laziness, pleasures, and the worship of idols—which are manifest shames, disgraces, and extreme impiety. For it is not without reason that the Philosophers consider that whatever the foolish do is done impiously, and that they themselves are impious. Furthermore, they consider...

<summary>Clement of Alexandria contrasts the chaotic, violent Bacchanalia of Greek myth with the "sober" and rational mysteries of Christ, the true Word. He invites all people, Greeks and Barbarians alike, to trade their pagan idols for the immortality offered through the yoke of Jesus.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Clement of Alexandria’s *Exhortation to the Heathen*. In the previous section, Clement contrasted the wild, destructive rituals of Bacchus with the "sober" and orderly worship of the Divine Word. He now moves into a philosophical and theological argument about the nature of true "sanity" and the relationship between God and humanity.</meta>

# ORATION OF EXHORTATION

<margin>A</margin>
...describing a kind of ignorance belonging to infancy <note>Clement uses "infancy" to denote spiritual immaturity or the state of those who have not yet been enlightened by the Word.</note>, they admit nothing other than that many are insane. It is not to be doubted, then, says the Word <note>original: *Verbum*; the Greek *Logos*, referring to Christ as the Divine Reason</note>, which of the two is better: to be wise and moderate, or to be insane. It is necessary, then, for those who adhere firmly to the Truth to follow God with all their strength, conducting themselves with moderation, and to recognize that all things belong to Him, just as they are. Furthermore, once we have learned that His possession is a thing of most beautiful excellence, we ought to entrust ourselves to God—loving the Lord God and considering this to be our duty throughout our entire lives. If, moreover, "the things of friends are common" <note>A famous Greek proverb attributed to Pythagoras and cited by Plato, which Clement here applies to the relationship between God and the believer.</note>, and the religious man is a friend of God through the mediation of the Word, then all things become the property of man because all things belong to God; for all things are common to both <margin>B</margin> friends, God and man. It remains for us now to say that he alone who is pious and religious is the true Christian, and is truly wealthy, and temperate, and noble. By this reasoning, it is just and holy to say and believe that he is the image of God with His likeness, as one who has been made by Jesus Christ with wisdom, and thus is already like unto God. And so the Prophet does not hide this grace, saying: 
<margin>Psalm 81</margin>
**I said, "You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High."** <note>original: "Ego dixi Dii estis, & filii excelsi omnes." This is Psalm 82:6 in modern Bibles.</note> For He has adopted us, and He wishes to be the Father of us alone, not of those who do not have faith. Our affairs, therefore, stand thus for us who are the ministers of God. As are the counsels, so are the words; as are the words, so are the actions; and as are the works, so is the life. The entire life of those who have known Christ is good.

<margin>C</margin>
I have spoken enough words, I think, even if I have proceeded at length because of my humanity and benevolence, pouring out what I held concerning God, seeing as I was exhorting you to the greatest of all goods, namely salvation. For concerning that life which has no end or interruption, those who announce the sacred mysteries <note>original: *sacra enuntiantes*; here referring to the proclamation of the Gospel</note> do not wish their speeches ever to be interrupted.

->There remains for you still this end: that we should choose<-
->that which is useful, whether<-
->judgment or grace.<-
<margin>D</margin>
->For I do not even think there should be any<-
->doubt as to which of them is better. Nor<-
->is it right to compare life<-
->with destruction.<-

<summary>Clement argues that the believer becomes a "friend of God," sharing in His possessions and likeness through the Word (Christ). He concludes by urging his audience to choose the path of salvation and life over the path of spiritual insanity and destruction.</summary>

<meta>This page contains scholarly commentary (scholia) on Clement of Alexandria’s *Exhortation to the Heathen*. It clarifies mythological references, provides Greek etymologies for technical terms, and identifies historical figures mentioned in the preceding text, such as the atheists Euhemerus and Diagoras. The notes are organized by "Gatherings" (Ternionis), referring to the physical sections of the printed book.</meta>

## EXPLANATORY NOTES.

->Gathering A<-

<margin>A</margin>
^a Error is an ancient thing, but the salvation offered through Christ is a new thing.
^b He is speaking of the pillar of fire that appeared to the Israelites when they were leaving Egypt under the leadership of Moses.
^c A flour-diviner <note>original: αλευρομάντις</note> practices divination with flour, while a barley-diviner <note>original: κριθομάντις</note> practices it with barley.
^d Dardanus, who was a son of Jupiter and the King of the Phrygians, is said to have been the first to initiate the mysteries of Ceres <note>The Roman name for the Greek goddess Demeter</note>.
^e Odrysus was the King of the Thracians, from whom the people derive their name.

<margin>B</margin>
^f A phallus <note>original: φαλλός</note> is a piece of wood shaped into the likeness of the male member.
^g To roar or rage <note>original: βεμβῶ</note>, which comes from the phrase "he shall roar" <note>original: αρ' τε βεμβῶ</note>.
^h Rhea is called Cybele because Cybela are the mountains of Phrygia where she is worshipped.
^i The Sabazian mysteries were performed for Dionysus, whom Proserpine <note>Persephone</note> bore to Jupiter; they also called him Sabazius and Zagreus.
^k Proserpine called the Dionysus-Zagreus by the name "The Bull" <note>original: Taurus</note> or gave him a bull-like appearance because he was extremely wild.
^l A "cone and a rhombus" <note>original: κῶνος καὶ ῥόμβος</note>, which signify both a pine nut and a spinning top <note>or bullroarer</note>; these are also names for types of dances.
^m The Thesmophoria is a festival day for Ceres, so named because laws—which are called *thesmoi* <note>original: θεσμοὶ</note>—were devised along with the discovery of the fruits of the earth, whereas previously men lived like wild beasts.

<margin>C</margin>
^n The ancients called this well "the place of the beautiful dance" <note>original: καλλίχωρον</note>. For Callimachus says: "unknown to the child, she sat down at the beautiful-dance well."
^o A *bassara* is the name for a Bacchic garment.
^p The priests of Rhea were called *Menagyrtæ* because they collected money every month <note>from the Greek *men* (month) and *ageiro* (collect)</note>, wandering through villages, cities, and houses as beggars and carrying idols on their shoulders. They are also called *metragyrtæ* because they collect money while carrying the "Mother of the Gods" on their shoulders.
^q He is speaking, I believe, of the "feminine disease," which pertains to women; or perhaps he means pleasure, which softens and makes the hearts of brave men effeminate.
^r This is Euhemerus, whom some say was from Messene; Callimachus mentions him in his Choriambics, saying, "the old braggart dries out his unjust books," as he had a bad reputation for being an atheist <note>original: ἄθεος</note>.

<margin>D</margin>
^s Diagoras was a philosopher of the Melian race; though he was pious at first, he later turned to impiety. This happened because a man who had accepted a deposit from him denied it under oath; Diagoras then claimed that the Higher Power does not watch over human affairs, for it would not have tolerated such a wicked man. Aristophanes mentions him when he calls Socrates "the Melian," meaning Diagoras. Hippon, who was also impious, is mentioned by Cratinus.
^t In Greek the word is *dysēpatos* <note>original: δυσηπατος</note>, meaning difficult to guess or comprehend. It is derived from *topos*, which means "place," but it plays upon the word "contains" which he had used previously.
^u This Epimenides purified Athens; he was a Cretan, a very wise man, mentioned by Menander in the *Kozanomenoi*.

<margin>E</margin>
->Gathering B<-

^a "To the quick," <note>original: Ad vivum</note> or "to the skin" <note>original: χρω</note>; that is, closely or truly. Thus Jeremiah says, "I am a God drawing near," meaning a true God.
^b A jar <note>original: dolium</note> in Greek is *keramos* <note>original: κέραμος</note>, but *keramos* was also a prison; for that is what it is called in the language of the Cyprians.
^c The "Cyprian poems" are what we call the Cyclic poems. They contain the abduction of Helen. The author of these Cyclic works is unknown. They are called "Cyclic" because they composed accounts of events around the *Iliad*, either before or after it, based on the Homeric works themselves.

<margin>F</margin>
^d Slender <note>original: σχλιας</note> or graceful among the Attics, as Diogenes says, or thin and subtle.
^e Homer also mentions Macaris when he says "as much as Lesbos, the seat of Macar, encompasses."
^f Sagra is a city in Italy, from which the proverb comes: "Truer than the things at Sagra."

<meta>This page continues the scholarly commentary on Clement of Alexandria's "Exhortation to the Greeks." ## ORATION TO THE GREEKS.
<note>original: ORAT. AD HORTA.</note>

<margin>A</margin>
<sup>g</sup> They are called Helots <note>original: εἵλωτες</note>, the Messenians, either from a swamp that is located near Lacedaemon <note>Sparta</note>, or from the verb "to seize" <note>original: εἵλειν</note>. For when the Lacedaemonians captured them, they condemned them to cultivate the swamp, which is a base and slavish duty. Just as the Penestae were among the Thessalians, and the Thetes (that is, the hirelings) were among the Athenians, so the Helots were among the Lacedaemonians.

<sup>h</sup> Rock <note>original: Petra</note>, as in the fables where it is said that humans were born from rocks.

<sup>i</sup> Poribasis <note>original: πόριβασις</note>; perhaps read as Epibasie <note>original: ἐπιβασίη</note>, "Venus who makes one ascend." The Scholia <note>ancient commentaries</note> interpret this as indecency <note>original: ἀσχημοσύνη</note>, that is, she who creates shameful forms.

<margin>B</margin>
<sup>k</sup> Choiropsalas <note>original: χοιροψάλας, likely a crude epithet</note>: Dionysus is worshipped in Sicyon of Boeotia, as Polemon says in his letter to Attalus. Moreover, "choiropsalon" is taken to mean "plucking." However, *choiros* <note>piglet</note> is a slang term for the female genitalia, as Aristophanes testifies in *The Acharnians*, saying: "Piggy, piggy, come now, would you eat a chickpea?"

<sup>l</sup> History records that when Alcmena was laboring in childbirth, a weasel passed by and she immediately gave birth to Hercules; for this reason, the Thebans worship the animal.

<sup>m</sup> When the Cretans went on an expedition against the Trojans and camped near the Troad, mice gnawed the leather straps of their shields during the night. Because of this, they built a temple to Apollo, and in their own Cretan tongue, they called him Smynthian <note>Smintheus</note>, for the Cretans call mice *mynthoi*.

<sup>n</sup> Phalerum was a port of Attica. The Hero who was on the prows of the ships was Androgeus, the son of Minos, so named because he was stationed at the prows. Callimachus also mentions this in the fourth book of his *Causes* <note>original: Aetia</note>.

<margin>C</margin>
<sup>o</sup> Boeotian, that is: "O Hesiod," for he was Boeotian by birth.

<sup>p</sup> Ithome is a city in Lacedaemonia, which they also say is Messene, or rather the place where the citadel of Messene is located, just as the citadel of the Argives was once called Larissa.

<sup>q</sup> This is the title of a book which contains the account of the return of those who came back from Troy <note>Referring to the lost epic poem "Nostoi" or "The Returns"</note>.

<sup>r</sup> When Croesus was upon the pyre, he spoke thus, as Herodotus says. "The things that have happened to me are indeed unpleasant, but they have taught me that what Homer says is true: 'A fool learns by suffering'" <note>original: παθὼν δέ τε νήπιος ἔγνω</note>.

<sup>s</sup> Phoroneus was Argive by birth. Merops, however, was from Cos. It is written that the oracle near Lebadia in Boeotia was first discovered by Phoroneus when he sacrificed to those who are considered Gods; a similar account is written by Merops.

<margin>D</margin>
<sup>t</sup> Hesiod says that the most ancient Love <note>Eros</note> was born along with Chaos and Earth, when he says: "First of all, Chaos came to be, but then the broad-breasted Earth, and Love" <note>original: ἢ τοι μὲν πρώτιστα χάος γένετ᾿ αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα γαῖ᾿ εὐρύστερνος, ἠδ᾿ ἔρως</note>.

<sup>u</sup> This Philippides <note>Pheidippides</note> was a day-runner <note>original: ἡμεροδρόμος</note>, that is, a courier or messenger, as Herodotus says. Later, when Xerxes led his expedition into Greece, Philippides set out to announce the arrival of Xerxes to the Spartans; on Mount Parthenius, he saw a vision of Pan in that place and heard the power of whatever spirit it was, saying that he would come to bring aid to the Greeks. From that time on, Pan was considered a God by the Athenians, and when they had built him a cave above the Areopagus, they sacrificed a gelded goat to him every year.

<sup>x</sup> For Didymean Apollo is worshipped at Miletus, either because he was born at the same time as his sister Diana <note>Artemis</note>, or because there are double sacrifices to him there.

<sup>y</sup> Diana is called Leucophryne in Magnesia.

<sup>z</sup> Myndian: Myndus is a city in Caria. Telmissus is a city in Caria which had the best seers. From there came Aristander, who accompanied Alexander the Great when he built Alexandria.

<sup>aa</sup> Some call "Phellatas" stones from Mount Phelleus—rough stones—as the comic poet Aristophanes says: "goats from Phelleus" <note>original: αἰγὰς ἐκ Φέλλεος</note>, as it is a rugged place.

<sup>bb</sup> Munichian Diana is worshipped in Piraeus <note>the port of Athens</note>. From this, a part of the harbor was called Munichium.

<margin>E</margin>
<sup>cc</sup> Dolias Minerva <note>Athena</note> is worshipped at Athens, she who is also called the "guardian of the city" <note>original: πολιῦχος</note>; she is placed upon the citadel <note>The Acropolis</note>.

It covers diverse topics from the origin of the Helots to the runner Philippides' encounter with the god Pan.</summary>

# TO THE NATIONS
<note>original: AD GENTES</note>

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>aa</margin> Liberal Dionysus <note>original: Liberalis Dionysus; a reference to the Roman god Liber, identified with Dionysus</note>, who was worshipped by the "Free-men," is associated with that place in Boeotia.

<margin>ee</margin> Others say [the name was written] on the finger of Minerva <note>Athena</note>, among whom is also Gregory the Theologian <note>Gregory of Nazianzus</note>, when he says: "And Phidias, who depicts his darling on the finger of the Maiden, [writing] 'Pantarces is beautiful.'" <note>original Greek: κἤ φειδίας τὰ παιδικὰ ἐν τῷ δακτύλῳ τῆς παρθένου γράφοντα παντάρκης καλός</note> This refers to the sculptor Phidias, who paints his youth on the finger [of a statue] with the words "Pantarces is beautiful." However, Libanius the Sophist says Phidias painted this on the finger of Venus <note>Aphrodite</note>.

<margin>ff</margin> Alcibiades was a general of the Athenian army, a man of both elegant form and youthful age, so much so that many women loved him to the point of madness.

<margin>gg</margin> Demetrius <note>Demetrius Poliorcetes</note> was King of the Macedonians and Greeks. Driven by a certain irrational madness <note>original: oestro, literally a 'gadfly's sting'</note>, he sought to take the goddess Minerva <note>Athena</note> as his wife.

<margin>B</margin>
<margin>hh</margin> This was indeed Lamia, after whom the phantoms called "lamiae" <note>monstrous female spirits or bogies</note> are named. She was terrifying to infants; for when she had lost her own children, driven as if by a sting of envy, she was carried away into the slaughter of the children of others.

<margin>ii</margin> Hippo was one of the ancient wise men; he believed that the gods do not exist, but are only thought to exist by men.

<margin>kk</margin> The Barathrum is a very deep pit in Athens into which the condemned were thrown, and their bodies were never seen again. There were also places designated for punishment elsewhere, such as the Ceatas in Lacedaemon <note>Sparta</note>, and the prison in Rome.

## Section C
<note>original: Ternionis C; 'ternio' refers to a gathering of three sheets of paper</note>

<margin>C</margin>
<margin>a</margin> Abdera is a town in Thrace, so named after Abderus, one of the companions of Hercules. He was devoured there by the horses of Diomedes; Hercules then killed those horses and named the town after Abderus, whom he loved. The same is written regarding Perithous, who was also loved by Hercules; the city of Perinthus was named after him when he died and was buried there by Hercules.

<margin>b</margin> According to the most ancient Greeks—if Herodotus of Halicarnassus is to be believed—eight gods were first brought into their religion from Egyptian myths. Later, when the Greeks were reduced to excessive superstition, they came to believe in twelve in total.

<margin>c</margin> "Fierce-eyed" <note>original Greek: γορῶπις / goropis</note> and "The Worker" <note>original Greek: ἐργάτις / ergatis</note> are epithets of Minerva; the first signifies one with a grim gaze, the second one who delights in handicrafts.

## Section D
<note>original: Ternionis D</note>

<margin>D</margin>
<margin>a</margin> He calls the other senses the "benefits of the Malignant one," because entering through the senses, he affects man with injury.

<margin>b</margin> Bloodless. For he says, "Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers of darkness, against spiritual wickedness." <note>A quotation of the New Testament, Ephesians 6:12</note>.

<margin>c</margin> By the "eating of raw flesh" <note>original: visceratione</note>. For those being initiated into the rites of Dionysus used to eat raw meat, performing this as a sign of the tearing apart of Dionysus which was done by the Maenads.

# TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS AND REVEREND
# JEAN DE HANGEST, BISHOP AND COUNT
## OF NOYON,
### PEER OF THE KINGDOM OF FRANCE,

->Gentian Hervet sends many greetings.<- <note>The Latin abbreviation "S. D. P." stands for *Salutem Dicit Plurimam*, a standard Renaissance greeting.</note>

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'C' containing a scene of a seated scholar at a lectern within an architectural setting, framed by an ornate square border.</image-desc>
**W**HEN the *Tutor* of Clement of Alexandria, recently translated into Latin by me, was about to be published, and I had long reflected on whom I might best choose from everyone, relying on whose happy auspices it might safely undergo the multifaceted and varied judgment of learned men: you first occurred to me, to whom Clement himself might deservedly desire to be sent, and by whom he would be kindly received, lovingly embraced, and strongly defended—as I have persuaded myself for just reasons, as I believe. For since a similarity of character and studies is very powerful in winning and maintaining friendship, and since Clement's learning is so great, his knowledge of various matters so remarkable and almost incredible, that the by far most learned man Theodoret <note>Theodoret of Cyrus (c. 393–458 AD) was an influential theologian and bishop of the Byzantine church.</note> did not hesitate to call him a "holy man," endowed with the greatest experience and learning, in his little book *On Divine Dogmas* <note>original: *de Diuinis dogmatibus*</note>: to whom rather should he be sent than to him who is so well-versed in every kind of literature that he excels in each? Nor indeed do I fear that I might be thought to attribute more to you than is proper, led by some desire for flattery, since I should fear more that learned men—who both formerly in France and now in Italy have known you intimately because of your great kindness, and continue to do so daily—might argue that I am too sparing and stingy in praising you, than fearing that I seem to have exceeded the limit in your praises. These praises I would indeed pursue at length and extensively at present, were it not that I must meanwhile take account of your modesty, who, although you are most worthy to be celebrated by all, yet allow yourself to be praised to your face by no one willingly. I will say only this, which is in a way necessary for me as I send Clement to you: that you are both merciful <note>original: *clementem*. Hervet is making a pun on the author's name, Clement, and the Latin adjective for 'merciful' or 'kind.'</note> and most worthy of Clement. Nor do I doubt that once some familiar acquaintance has come between you, it will happen that each—namely, you him and he you—will in turn admire the other. For since, besides his skill in Sacred Scripture, in which his principal effort was spent, he possessed knowledge of all the liberal arts and all humanities, but especially of philosophy, and foremost that of Plato, which...

<summary>This page is a formal dedication by the translator Gentian Hervet to Jean de Hangest, the Bishop of Noyon. Hervet praises the Bishop's learning and character, arguing that he is the perfect patron for this new Latin translation of Clement of Alexandria's work.</summary>
<keywords>Jean de Hangest, Gentian Hervet, Clement of Alexandria, dedication, Bishop of Noyon, Theodoret of Cyrus, Platonic philosophy, Renaissance humanism, patronage</keywords>

--- Page 66 ---
<meta>This page continues the dedicatory epistle from Gentian Hervet to Jean de Hangest, Bishop of Noyon. The previous page established Clement of Alexandria’s reputation for immense learning; here, Hervet compares the ancient author’s skills to those of his patron.</meta>

<page-num>4</page-num>
<sig>ii</sig>

...you, because his teaching seems not to differ much from the Christian faith in many respects, are greatly delighted by it, and I do not doubt that you must judge him a great man, one to be held in the highest esteem. But when he understands that all these things are held in common between you and him, and learns that you possess this additional advantage—that while he mastered only that most beautiful but singular language, namely Greek: you, on the other hand, are remarkably skilled in Greek, Latin, Hebrew, and Chaldean <note>In the Renaissance, "Chaldean" typically referred to Aramaic or Syriac.</note> (not to mention Arabic, which you have touched upon quite successfully, and French, which you have known from infancy, and Italian, which you studied as a young man), and have joined the knowledge of Civil and Canon Law <note>original: *iuris Ciuilis ac Pontificii*</note> to all the liberal disciplines and the study of philosophy and medicine; and when he realizes your mastery of administering the state and rendering judgment, gained as much through long practice and experience as through the remembrance of ancient examples and monuments—I do not doubt that he will grant you every highest honor and will be deeply grateful to have been sent to such a great man. 

But what am I doing, straying into your praises against my own resolution? For I should labor more to ensure that you receive Clement *clemently* <note>Hervet is making a pun on the name "Clement" and the Latin word *clementer*, meaning "kindly" or "mercifully."</note>, rather than risk being seen as taking too much away from one while comparing the two. However, your kindness persuades me that he will be welcome to you; since easy access is open to all learned men, I am far from thinking that a man so very learned and excellent should be excluded by you.

Since he now comes to light in both Greek and Latin, if his native language delights you more, you will be able to read him in Greek. But if you wish to hear him speaking a little more familiarly at times, you will hear him discoursing in a Latin speech—not perhaps so ornate and elegant, but one which nevertheless faithfully expresses his thoughts. For I believe that I have sufficiently maintained the translator’s fidelity, if nothing else. When you easily notice this, as I hope, it will remain for me to ask and demand that when you have received this *Tutor* <note>The title of Clement's work is the *Paedagogus*, or *The Tutor*.</note> with a grateful hand, you will defend me—or rather, our Clement—with your patronage from the slanders of malicious and wicked men. Though they themselves perform no useful work for the Christian commonwealth, they take great pleasure in themselves if they can securely disparage the labors of others. I believe I can easily repel, or rather despise, their insults if you receive this work with the benevolence I hope for and defend it with the supreme authority of your name. Farewell, and deign to enroll me in the number of your humble clients.

->Bologna, July 10, 1549.<-

<meta>This page provides scholarly commentary (scholia) on Clement of Alexandria’s "The Instructor." It follows the Table of Contents and serves to explain the philosophical and psychological framework Clement uses to describe how the Divine Word (the Logos) trains the human soul through character, action, and emotion.</meta>

<page-num>6</page-num>

### SOME SCHOLARLY NOTES ON THE INSTRUCTOR.

Those things considered in the human makeup: character comes first, as it is the material and catalyst for both good and evil movements. Since some movements are actions and others are passions <note>The author uses "passions" here to mean things we experience or suffer, rather than just strong emotions.</note>, actions are more divine because they reside in that which holds command over us [the soul or reason]. Passions, however, belong to what is weak and material. Now, character is rightly placed first, as the foundation of actions; actions and mental affections are subject to it, as they are naturally formed by reason.

"Give heed, O children." For this is said *elliptically* <note>original: *ἐλλιπῶς*; meaning with something left out or implied</note> to make young people more attentive to the gravity of what is being said. A base has been established for us—or by us—a base of truth, or a base of the great holy temple of God. And what is this base, if not the unbreakable foundation of knowledge? It is a beautiful exhortation to a life consistent with reason through obedience—an eternal longing directed toward an intellectual estate.

Since exhortatory speech—which deals with character—serves as the foundation or the keel for building up piety, it is aided by two other types of speech: prescriptive speech, which provides commands for actions; and consolatory speech, which addresses the affections or disturbances of the soul.

For since three things are considered in man—character, actions, and the soul’s disturbances—the Instructor’s word is one and the same, yet shaped to each of these. To correct and improve, it is applied appropriately to all three: to character by encouraging; to actions by providing precepts <note>Rules or instructions for conduct.</note>; and to the soul’s disturbances by consoling. 

Therefore, when it deals with character to provide salvation, it is called "exhortatory" or "persuasive" speech. When it deals with actions, it is called *preceptive* <note>original: *ὑποθετικός* (*hypothetikos*); refers to speech that lays down rules or hypotheses for living.</note>—that is, delivering rules—and *healing* <note>original: *θεραπευτικός* (*therapeutikos*); the root of our word "therapeutic."</note>—that is, curing or caring. When it transforms the soul's affections, it is "consolatory." 

And when it incites one to undertake these things, it then takes up the office of the <term>Instructor</term> <note>original: *Paedagogus*. In Greek culture, this was a trusted slave who raised a child; Clement uses it for Christ, who raises humanity.</note>, urging them to become better. Through exhortation, he encourages the shaping of character. Through the giving of precepts, he introduces symbolic themes, and through clear explanation, he beautifully suggests to posterity the errors committed by others. Hence, he is also called "the healer" or "the physician." Through consolation, he brings about a return through repentance, so that one may be restored to their original, proper state. Sometimes he also proceeds by way of doctrine, which there is no time to discuss at present, as it deals with dogmas <note>Formal theological principles.</note>.

<summary>This page explains the three methods the Divine Instructor uses to guide humanity: exhorting character, commanding actions, and healing the emotions. It defines the "Paedagogus" as a divine healer and teacher who uses different rhetorical modes to lead the soul to virtue.</summary>
<keywords>Clement of Alexandria, Scholarly notes, Ethics, Character (mores), Actions, Passions, Exhortation, Healing (Therapeutic), Precepts, Repentance, Logos</keywords>

# CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA
## THE INSTRUCTOR
### BOOK ONE.

<margin>B</margin>

->Chapter I. What the Instructor Professes.<-

<margin>C</margin>
<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'C' containing a circular portrait of a bearded man in classical robes, presumably representing Clement of Alexandria, holding a book and a staff. The circular frame is surrounded by a square border containing architectural and foliate motifs.</image-desc>A foundation of truth has been established, O children, for us ourselves—who are the holy temple of the great God—an unbreakable foundation of knowledge. This is a beautiful exhortation through obedience to a way of life that is consistent with reason <note>original: "rationi consentaneæ"; Clement is referring to the Logos, the Divine Reason or Word</note>, an eternal longing directed toward an intellectual estate. Since there are three things in man—character, actions, and the soul’s affections or disturbances—exhortatory speech <note>original: "sermo exhortatorius"; refers to the first stage of Christian guidance</note> has been assigned to character. This speech is a guide to piety and religion, which, like a keel, lies beneath the building up of faith. Greatly rejoicing in this, and renouncing our old opinions, we are made youthful and eager to lay hold of salvation, singing in harmony with the prophetic psalm: <margin>Psal. 72.</margin> **HOW GOOD IS THE GOD OF ISRAEL** to those who are upright in heart <note>The Latin cites Psalm 72, which corresponds to Psalm 73 in modern English Bibles.</note>. Moreover, the speech that is concerned with handing down precepts <margin>D</margin> presides over all actions; while the consolatory speech heals the movements and disturbances of the soul. This same word <note>original: "sermo"; here used for the Logos</note>, though it is one, snatches a person away from the worldly habits in which he was raised and nurtured, and trains him in the simple and singular salvation of faith in God. This celestial guide—the Word—when he exhorts us toward salvation, is given the name of "Exhortatory." This specific type of speech is properly called "inciting," named after the part for the whole. Indeed, all religion and the pious worship of God is exhortatory, since it produces in the kindred mind a desire both for a life lived rightly here and for the life to come. 

But now, since the Word is engaged both in healing and in handing down precepts—and since he simultaneously exhorts the one he admonishes toward both of these goals—he promises in short the healing of the diseases of the soul within us. Let him, therefore, be appropriately called by us by one name: the **Instructor** <note>original: "Paedagogus"; in the ancient world, a pedagogue was a guardian or tutor who guided a child's moral development, distinct from a teacher of academic subjects</note>. For the Instructor is concerned with action, not with the precise delivery of systematic doctrine. His purpose is to make the soul better, not merely to teach; and to guide one toward a moderate and temperate life, not a life defined solely by academic knowledge. Although this same Word <margin>E</margin> is indeed capable of teaching, he does not employ that role at this present moment. For the Word that declares and reveals matters pertaining to dogma <note>technical religious doctrines</note> is the "Teaching Word." However, because the Instructor is concerned with action, he first exhorts us to arrange our character, and then he exhorts us to the performance of what is necessary, handing down pure and sincere precepts, and holding up for future generations the images and likenesses of those errors committed in the past. Both methods are most useful. The exhortatory style leads to obedience. The use of images and likenesses is twofold: on one hand, we are to imitate the good by choosing it, and on the other, we are to turn away from the evil by rejecting it. From this follows the healing of the soul’s <margin>F</margin> diseases. The Instructor strengthens our souls with the comforts provided by these examples and precepts—like gentle medicines—leading those who suffer through human instructions toward a perfect knowledge of the truth. There is, however, a great difference between health and knowledge. For the latter is acquired through instruction, while the former is gained through healing. Therefore, one who is suffering must first be healed before he can...

<summary>Clement of Alexandria introduces the "Instructor" (the Logos/Word) as a divine guide who heals the soul and shapes human character through practical ethics and moral examples before moving on to higher theological teaching.</summary>
<keywords>Clement of Alexandria, The Instructor, Paedagogus, Logos, Divine Word, Christian Ethics, Character, Healing the Soul, Psalm 73, Pedagogy</keywords>

--- Page 70 ---
<meta>This page continues from page 7, finishing the introductory discussion on the different roles of the Word (Logos). It moves from "exhortation" to the specific role of the Instructor as a healer of the soul, then transitions into Chapter II which discusses the sinless nature of the Instructor (Christ) and the nature of human sin.</meta>

# THE INSTRUCTOR

<margin>A</margin>
...has learned what pertains <note>original: "tinent"; likely the end of "pertinent"</note> to health, and how perfectly healthy he was. For every precept is not delivered in the same way to those who are learning and to those who are struggling; rather, to the former, they are for knowledge, but to the latter, for healing. Therefore, just as those whose bodies are sick have need of a physician, so those whose souls are sick have need of an instructor <note>original: "pædagogo"; here referring to Christ as the Pedagogue or Instructor who disciplines and heals the soul</note>, so that he may heal the diseases of our souls. Afterward, indeed, they need a Teacher <note>original: "Doctore"; referring to the higher stage of spiritual education</note>, who may lead the purified soul toward an aptitude for knowledge, so that it might perceive the revelation of the Word. Furthermore, while he strives to make us perfect and complete by a healthy degree of effective discipline suited to us, he employs a beautiful economy. In every respect, the Word is kind and loves humanity; exhorting us from the heavens, then performing the office of the Instructor in all things, and teaching us.
<margin>B</margin>

### *That the Instructor guides us because of our sins. Chapter II.*

<margin>C</margin>
Our Instructor, O children, is like God His Father, whose son He is, in whom no sin at all falls, and who is related to no reproach, being impassible in his soul: God in the form of man, undefiled, serving the Father’s will, God the Word, who is in the Father, who is at the right hand of the Father, and who, along with his <gloss>a</gloss> form <note>The gloss "a" likely refers to his physical or human appearance</note> is God. He is for us an image in which there is no blemish. We must strive with all our strength to make our soul like Him. But He indeed is free from all human disturbances of the soul.
<margin>John 1.</margin>
<margin>1 Pet. 2.</margin>
For this reason, He alone is Judge, because He alone is one in whom sin does not fall. We, however, should strive, as far as is possible, to sin as little as possible. For nothing should be of greater care and study than first to be freed from the disturbances and diseases of the soul, and then to prevent ourselves from sliding easily into the habit of sinning. And indeed, the best thing is not to sin at all, which we say belongs to God. The second best is to touch none of the voluntary wrongs, which is characteristic of the wise man, and not to fall into too many involuntary ones. The third best—which is characteristic of those who have been well-brought up and rightly instituted by the Instructor—is not to remain too long in sins; let this be placed in the last position.
<margin>D</margin>
But it will also be healthy for a person if he does not resist those who call him to repentance. And to me, it seems the Instructor speaks most beautifully through Moses:
<margin>Numbers 6.</margin>
**IF ANYONE IN HIS PRESENCE** <note>original: "SI QUIS IN EO"; citing the Latin Vulgate of Numbers 6:9</note> should die suddenly, immediately his head will be polluted and it shall be shaved; here he calls involuntary sin a "sudden death." He says that this pollutes, as it sprinkles the soul with a stain. And therefore, he applies the medicine as quickly as possible, advising that his head be shaved immediately—that is, persuading him to remove and wipe away the "hairs of ignorance," which cast a shadow over reason. Therefore, the Word as Instructor has obtained moderation to prohibit irrational sin. Consider this from the Scripture: **FOR THIS REASON** the Lord says these things. That which was a sin before is shown by rebuking it through the following speech, because a just judgment follows. And this is openly shown through the Prophets when they say: **IF YOU HAD NOT SINNED**, he would not have threatened these things. And for this reason, the Lord says: "Because you have not heard these words, therefore the Lord says these things"; and, "Behold, for this reason, the Lord says."
<margin>Isaiah 66.</margin>
<margin>Jeremiah 7.</margin>
<margin>Ezekiel 33.</margin>
For prophecy exists for this reason: namely, because of obedience and disobedience.
<margin>F</margin>

For the aid given to the diseases of the body is properly called Medicine, which is taught by human wisdom. # BOOK ONE

<margin>A</margin> <margin>Psalm 86 <note>original: "Psal. 85" (Vulgate numbering). The verse is from Psalm 86:2–3.</note></margin> He is the enchanter for the sick soul. **"Save your servant," he says, "my God, who hopes in you. Have mercy on me, Lord, for I will cry out to you all day long."** For medicine, as Democritus says, heals the diseases of the body, but wisdom frees the soul from disturbances. But the good Instructor—who is Wisdom, who is the Word of the Father, who fashioned the heavens—takes care of all his creation. He heals both the body and the soul of that creature, being a physician of human nature who is sufficient in every respect: our Savior. <margin>Mark 2.</margin> **"Rise,"** he says to the Paralytic, **"and taking up the mat on which you lie, go home."** And he who was previously weak immediately became healthy and strong. And to the dead man, Lazarus, he said, <margin>John 11.</margin> "Come out." Then he who had been dead came out of the tomb just as he was before he died, having practiced <note>original: "meditatus"; suggesting the miracle was a rehearsal or foretaste of the final resurrection</note> the resurrection. 

<margin>B</margin> Furthermore, he also heals the soul itself with precepts, gifts, and graces. But he certainly differs in the way he acts through precepts and warnings: being rich in gifts and graces, he says to us sinners, "Your sins are forgiven you." But as soon as he had this thought, we were made into infants <note>The author uses "infants" or "children" to describe those new to the faith who are being shaped by the Instructor.</note>, having obtained the best and most stable place through his excellent and clearly ordered moderation. This moderation first revolves in the circuits of the world, the heavens, and the sun, and is involved in the movements of the other stars, for the sake of man. Then, it works within man himself, upon whom all his care is bestowed. Considering man to be his greatest and most beautiful work, he directed his soul with prudence, moderation, and temperance. He tempered his body with beauty and a just and well-measured proportion of members; and <margin>C</margin> in the actions of human nature, he inspired in them the beautiful order that is rightly and virtuously performed, according to his own nature.

### *That the Instructor is Kind and a Lover of Humanity. Chapter III.*

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'I' within a square frame. The background of the letter depicts a detailed landscape with a river or canal, a bridge with multiple arches, and a town with several buildings, including a prominent tower or church steeple.</image-desc>
<margin>D</margin> **In** all things the Lord is profitable, and in all things he helps, both as man and as God. As God, he forgives sins; but as man, he instructs us in the manner of an Instructor <note>term: Instructor (original: "Pædagogi ritu") - Christ is viewed as the spiritual tutor who guides the believer's character, much like a 'paedagogus' guided a child in ancient Greece or Rome.</note>, so that we might not sin. Therefore, man is rightly dear to God, since man is his own handiwork. Other things he made by a mere command, but man he fashioned by himself with his own hand, and inspired in him something of his own. Therefore, that which was made by him and in <margin>Genesis 1.</margin> his own image, was either fashioned by God because it was to be chosen for its own sake, or it was made because it was to be chosen for the sake of something else. If, then, man is a thing to be chosen for his own sake, since he is good, God loved what is good. And within man is that quality of being loved, which is called the inspiration or breathing-in of God. 

If, however, man was made to be chosen for the sake of other things, God had no other reason for making him than that without him, God could not be a good creator, nor could man arrive at the knowledge of God. For God would not have made that for the sake of which man was made, if man had not been made. And the power which God held hidden by his will, he fulfilled through the external power of creation <margin>E</margin> received from man, he who made man. And he saw what he had, and what he willed was done—for there is nothing that God cannot do. Man, therefore, whom God made, is a thing to be chosen for himself. Now, whatever is to be chosen for itself is special and familiar to the one who chooses it. That thing is to be sought after and loved. But if something is to be loved, it cannot be unloved by the one who loves. It has been shown that man is to be loved; therefore, man is loved by God. For how can he not be loved, for whose sake the Only-begotten is sent down from the bosom of the Father, the Word of faith? Faith from superabundance, the Lord himself, who openly confesses and says: **"For the Father himself loves you, because you have loved me."** <margin>John 16.</margin> And he says again: **"And you have loved** <margin>Ibid. 17.</margin> **them, just as you have loved me."** 

What the Instructor wants, what he <margin>F</margin> professes, and how he is disposed in both deeds and words—both in prescribing what ought to be done and in forbidding what is contrary—is now surely clear. It is evident, however, that there is another kind of discourse whose purpose is to teach; this is subtle and spiritual, following an accurate method of treatment, and is concerned with secrets...

THE INSTRUCTOR

<margin>A</margin>
