We should strive to reflect a likeness of the Instructor's deeds through our own actions, so that we may fulfill what was said: **"In our image and after our likeness."** <note>original: "Ad imaginem & similitudinem"; a reference to Genesis 1:26.</note> For as we wander in life as if in deep darkness, we have need of a leader who is the best, and who never wanders or stumbles.
<margin>Matthew 15.</margin>

<margin>B</margin>
Therefore, just as there is no light that does not illuminate, nor anything moving that does not
<margin>John 1.</margin>
move, so there is no one who loves who does not show love, nor anything good that does not benefit and lead toward salvation. Let us, therefore, fulfill the precepts through the works and deeds of the Lord. For the Word himself was openly made flesh, showing at once the same power for both action and contemplation. Thus, considering his speech, precepts, and warnings as law, let us learn the short and direct paths to eternity. For his precepts are full of persuasion, not fear.

### BOOK ONE

<margin>A</margin>
...He says, bringing the children for the laying on of hands and blessing. When his acquaintances and friends tried to prevent them, Jesus said: "Let the little children be, and do not forbid them to come to me. For of such is the kingdom of heaven." What he meant by this, the Lord himself declares, saying: <margin>Matthew 18.</margin> **UNLESS YOU ARE CONVERTED** and become like these little children, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven. He does not here signify the "regeneration" <note>A reference to being "born again."</note> in an allegorical sense, but rather commends the simplicity inherent in children, urging us to reflect a likeness of it. The Prophetic Spirit also chooses us as "children." **WHEN THEY HAD PLUCKED**, he says, the children took branches of olive or palm and went out to meet the Lord, crying out <margin>Matthew 21.</margin> <note>The source text erroneously cites Mat. 12.</note> and saying: **Hosanna to the son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!** Light and glory and praise with supplication to the Lord—for this is what "Hosanna" <note>original: "Osanna"</note> signifies when explained in Latin. It seems to me that the Scripture, in bringing forth this prophecy, silently reproaches those who spoke of it <margin>B</margin> as a matter of shame. <margin>Psalm 8.</margin> **HAVE YOU NEVER** read: "Out of the mouth of infants and nursing babes you have perfected praise"? In this same way, the Lord stimulates his friends, inciting them to attend to him diligently as one who was already hastening to the Father; he prepares his listeners to hear him with greater desire, foretelling that he would soon be absent. He hints that it is necessary for them to enjoy the truth more richly and profusely, since the Word would soon withdraw into heaven. Therefore, he calls them "little children" once again. For he says: <margin>John 13.</margin> **LITTLE CHILDREN**, yet a little while I am with you. And again, he compares the kingdom of heaven to children sitting in the marketplace and saying: <margin>Matthew 11.</margin> **WE PLAYED THE FLUTE** for you, and you did not dance; we lamented, <margin>C</margin> and you did not mourn—and whatever else he added in agreement with these words. Nor is this the view of the Gospel alone; prophecy is of the same opinion. Thus David says: <margin>Psalm 112.</margin> **PRAISE THE LORD, O children**, praise the name of the Lord. Furthermore, he also says through Isaiah: <margin>Isaiah 8.</margin> **BEHOLD I AND THE CHILDREN** whom God has given me. 

Are you amazed to hear that men among the Gentiles are called children by the Lord? You do not seem to hear the Attic voice <note>Referring to the refined Greek of Athens.</note>, from which one can learn that elegant and beautiful young women, who are also free-born, are called "young maidens" <note>original: "paidiskas"</note>, while servant-girls are called "little maids" <note>original: "paidiskaria"</note>; and even these young women are honored with the diminutive name of "little girls" because of the vigor of their youthful age. Now, when he says, "Let the lambs stand on the right," <margin>Matthew 25.</margin> <margin>D</margin> he signifies simple children, as if they were lambs and sheep in nature, not merely men. He judged the "lambs" worthy of privilege, preferring that gentleness, tenderness, simplicity of character, and innocence of mind found in such people. 

And again when he says: <margin>Jeremiah 46.</margin> **LIKE CALVES leaping with joy**, he signifies us again allegorically. And when he says: <margin>Deuteronomy 14.</margin> **LIKE A SIMPLE DOVE** without gall; and when he again commands us through Moses to offer two young pigeons or a pair of turtledoves for sin <margin>Numbers 6.</margin>, he is saying that the innocence of the young ones—who have no affinity with sin because of their tenderness and who hold no memory of injuries received—is acceptable to God, explaining that like is expiated by like. Furthermore, the timidity of the turtledoves signifies a caution that must be used so that one does not sin. That he calls us "chicks" <note>The Latin "pullus" can mean a chick or a young animal/foal.</note>, the Scripture is witness: <margin>Matthew 23.</margin> **JUST AS A HEN gathers her chicks under her wings.** Thus we are the Lord’s chicks, the discourse describing the simplicity of the soul through the stage of childhood in a truly wonderful <margin>E</margin> and mystical way. For in some places he calls us "sons" <note>original: "huioi"</note> as children, in other places "chicks," sometimes "infants," and elsewhere "children" <note>original: "tekna"</note> or "little sons," and often "sons," a "recent people," and a "new people." <margin>Isaiah 56 and 65.</margin> **BUT UPON MY SERVANTS**, he says, a new name shall be imposed. He calls it a "new name" because it is fresh, eternal, unpolluted, simple, childlike, and true, which shall be blessed on the earth. By allegory, he again calls us "colts" <note>original: "pōlos", a young horse or foal</note>, we who do not submit to the yoke of vice, who are not tamed by wickedness, but are simple and leap <margin>term: "pōlos" (a young foal)</margin> toward the Father alone. We are not like yoked horses who neigh after their neighbors' wives and are held by insane love for women, but we are free and recently born: who exult because of faith, who run swiftly toward the truth, who are fast toward salvation, and who tread upon and trample underfoot the things of the world. <margin>Zechariah 9.</margin> <margin>F</margin> **REJOICE GREATLY, daughter of Zion!** Proclaim it, daughter of Jerusalem! <margin>Matthew 21.</margin> Behold, your King comes to you, just, gentle, and bringing salvation; he is meek, and riding upon a beast of burden and a **new colt**. It was not enough for him to say only "colt," but he added "new" to it, to show the newness of the humanity united in Christ...

# THE INSTRUCTOR
<meta>catchword: may be called</meta>

<margin>A</margin>
...showing eternity, which is free from old age, through simplicity. Our divine trainer of colts nourishes us as such new colts, we who are infants. For even if a "new donkey" appears in Scripture, here too that donkey is a colt.
<margin>Genesis 49.</margin>
**AND THE COLT**, he says, **HE TIED TO THE VINE**. He binds this simple and infant people to the Word, whom he calls a "vine" allegorically. For the vine produces wine, just as the Word produces blood. Both are a drink for the salvation of men: wine indeed for the body, but blood for the spirit. That he also calls us lambs is shown by the faithful witness of the Spirit speaking through Isaiah:
<margin>Isaiah 40.</margin>
**AS A SHEPHERD HE WILL FEED HIS FLOCK**, and with his arm he will gather the lambs; by focusing on the most tender among the sheep, namely the lambs, he signifies simplicity allegorically. <margin>B</margin> Indeed, we certainly honor the most beautiful and perfect possessions in life with a name derived from childhood, calling discipline in Greek *paideia* <note>original: "παιδείαν"</note> and the art of guidance *paidagogia* <note>original: "παιδαγωγίαν"</note>. We acknowledge that "pedagogy" <note>The art or profession of teaching.</note> is the good training of children in virtue. Thus, the Lord revealed more clearly and evidently to us what is meant by the name of "children." When a question arose among the Apostles as to which of them was the greatest, Jesus placed a little child in the midst, saying:
<margin>Matthew 18.</margin>
**WHOEVER HUMBLES HIMSELF** like this little child, he is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven. Therefore, he did not use the term "children" as if they were reckless due to their age and unable to use reason, as some have thought; nor should it be understood as an unlearned thing <margin>C</margin> when he says, **UNLESS YOU BECOME** like these little children, you shall not enter the kingdom of God. We, therefore, who are infants, no longer roll upon the ground; nor do we crawl upon the earth in the manner of serpents as we did before, wallowing with our whole body in foolish desires. Instead, with our minds raised upward, renouncing the world and our sins, touching the earth with a light step only so far as we seem to be in the world, we pursue holy wisdom. This, however, appears to be "folly" to those who have sharpened themselves for cunning and craftiness. Rightly, then, are they called "children" who know God alone as Father—simple, infant-like, pure, and innocent—who are lovers of the "horns of unicorns" <note>A traditional metaphor for the singular, focused power of Christ or the soul's upward devotion to the One God.</note>. To those who have progressed in the Word, he announced this voice, commanding them to cast aside the care of things and business here below, and persuading them to look to the Father alone, imitating little children. And therefore he says in the following passage: <margin>Matthew 6.</margin> **DO NOT BE** anxious for tomorrow. For sufficient for the day is its own trouble. Thus he commands us to cling to the Father alone, having set aside cares for food and life. <margin>D</margin> Whoever fulfills this command is truly an infant and a child to God and to the world: to the latter, he seems as one led astray and wandering, but to the former, he is as one beloved.
<margin>Matthew 23.</margin>
Now indeed, if there is but one Master in heaven, as the Scripture says, it is confessed that all who are on earth are called disciples. For this is the truth: that which is perfect is found with the Lord, who is always teaching; while that which is childlike and infant-like is found with us, who are always learning. Furthermore, prophecy has likewise honored that which is perfect with the title of "Man." And through David, concerning the Devil, <margin>Psalm 5.</margin> **THE MAN** of blood, he says, the Lord abominates. He calls him a "Man" as one who is perfect in vice. The Lord is also called a "Man," as one who is perfect in righteousness. For now the Apostle, writing to the Corinthians, <margin>2 Corinthians 11.</margin> says: **FOR I HAVE BETROTHED** you to one man, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ <margin>E</margin>—whether as infants and holy ones, yet only to the Lord.
<margin>Ephesians 4.</margin>
Writing to the Ephesians, he revealed most clearly what is sought, saying in this manner: **UNTIL WE ALL ATTAIN** to the unity of faith and the knowledge of God, to a perfect man; to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ, so that we may no longer be infants, tossed by waves and carried about by every wind of doctrine, by the trickery of men, by craftiness in deceitful schemes; but speaking the truth in love, let us grow up into him in all things. He says these things for the building up of the body of Christ, who is the head and the man, who alone is perfect in righteousness. We, however, are infants, who avoid the blowing winds of heresies that cause inflation, and who do not give credit to those who teach us otherwise than our fathers did; then we are made perfect <margin>F</margin> when we are the Church, having received our head, which is Christ. Here, however, it is right to attend to the meaning of this word *nēpios* <note>original: "νήπιος"</note>, which signifies "infant," so that it may be understood that *nēpios* is not said of the foolish. For he who is foolish is called *nēputios* <note>original: "νηπύτιος"</note>. But a *nēpios* is one who is truly an infant, such as a *nēpios* who is gentle and soft-spirited. Thus it is that such a person is called...

<meta>This page continues the exploration of spiritual childhood. Clement of Alexandria is arguing that being an "infant" in Christ is not about being foolish or uneducated, but about possessing a "new" and "tender" spirit that is receptive to God's Word, contrasting this with the "hard-heartedness" of the old ways.</meta>

# BOOK ONE

<margin>A</margin> ...may be called an infant <note>original: "νήπιος" (nepios)</note>, one who has recently emerged as mild and gentle in character. The blessed Paul most clearly signified this, saying: **ALTHOUGH WE COULD HAVE BEEN A BURDEN** as Apostles of Christ, **WE WERE GENTLE IN YOUR MIDST, JUST AS A NURSE CHERISHES HER CHILDREN**. <margin>1 Thessalonians 2</margin> Therefore, an infant is mild and gentle, and for that reason more tender and soft. And he is tender and soft who is simple, free from deceit and fraud, far from pretense, and possessed of a right and upright soul. This is the foundation of simplicity and truth. **UPON WHOM**, he says, **SHALL I LOOK, IF NOT UPON THE GENTLE AND QUIET?** <margin>Isaiah 66</margin> Such is the virginal word, tender and soft, and not prone to fiction. Whence we are also accustomed to call a tender bride a "young wife," and a child "tender-minded" <note>original: "ἀπαλόφρονα" (aphalophrona)</note>, <margin>tender-minded</margin> that is, of a tender and soft spirit.

<margin>B</margin> We are tender and soft, we who do not resist persuasion, and are easily cultivated by goodness; we are free from bitterness, and are not at all mixed with malice and perversity. For the old generation is perverse and hard-hearted. But the chorus of infants—I mean us, who are the new people—is soft and delicate like a child. Because of the hearts of the simple and innocent, the Apostle professes to rejoice in the Epistle to the Romans, and hands down what I might call a definition of infants, saying: **I WANT YOU TO BE WISE INDEED CONCERNING GOOD, BUT SIMPLE CONCERNING EVIL**. <margin>Romans, last chapter</margin> Nor is the name of "infant" <note>original: "τοῦ νηπίου" (tou nepiou)</note> understood by us as a lack or deprivation, even though Grammarians state that *ne-* <note>original: "νη"</note> is a privative particle <note>In linguistics, a particle that expresses negation or absence.</note>. For if any mock infancy, they call us "unwise": see how they attack the Lord with blasphemies and curses, while they consider those who have fled to God to be unwise. 

<margin>C</margin> But if—which is more worthy of being heard—they themselves take "infants" to mean the "simple ones," we rejoice in the name. For infants are "new minds" in the midst of "old folly," those who have recently become prudent, having arisen in the New Testament. Surely God has recently been made known through the coming of Christ. For **NO ONE HAS KNOWN GOD EXCEPT THE SON, AND HE TO WHOM THE SON HAS REVEALED HIM**. <margin>Matthew 11; Luke 10</margin> Therefore, the "new people" are young, so they may be distinguished from the "old people." These are those who have learned new blessings; and for us, youth itself is the prime of life, free from old age, in which we always flourish in understanding and the movement of the mind—always young, always gentle, and always fresh and new. For those words must be new which have partaken of the New Word. But that which has partaken of eternity is accustomed to be likened to that which is far from destruction. 

<margin>D</margin> Thus the name of childhood is for us the "spring" of all life, because the truth that is in us is free from old age, as are our characters, which are bathed in truth. Moreover, wisdom is always budding, always remaining the same and in the same way, and never changing. **THEIR CHILDREN**, he says, **SHALL BE CARRIED UPON SHOULDERS, AND UPON KNEES THEY SHALL RECEIVE CONSOLATION. JUST AS IF A MOTHER CONSOLES SOMEONE, SO I ALSO WILL CONSOLE YOU.** <margin>Isaiah 49 & 66</margin> A mother indeed brings children to herself; and we seek our mother the Church. Therefore, whatever is weak and tender, such as that which needs help because of its weakness, is pleasing, pleasant, and delightful—the spirited part of the soul bringing help to that which is so small. 

<margin>E</margin> For just as fathers and mothers more gladly look upon the foals of horses, the small calves of oxen, the lion's cub, and the fawn of a deer, and the child of a man; so also the Father of all receives those who flee to him, and recognizes those regenerated by the Spirit into the adoption of sons as "gentle ones"; and he loves them alone, and brings them help, and fights for them and defends them: and for this reason he calls them "child." I indeed also refer Isaac to the "child." "Isaac" is interpreted as "laughter." <margin>Genesis 26</margin> A curious king saw him playing with his wife and helper, Rebecca. Now the king, whose name was Abimelech, seems to me to be a certain "super-mundane wisdom," which considers the mystery of childish play and discipline <note>original: "παιδεία" (paideia)</note>. <margin>discipline</margin> They interpret "Rebecca" as "endurance." O wise play and discipline! Laughter is aided by endurance, and the King, who watches these things, is stunned and admires the spirit of those who are children in Christ, who lead their lives in endurance. 

<margin>F</margin> And this is the divine play and discipline. Heraclitus says his Jupiter <note>referring to Zeus</note> plays such a game. For what else is more fitting for a wise and perfect man than to play and rejoice together? Through the endurance of honorable things and the administration of good things, celebrating feast days with God...

# THE INSTRUCTOR

<margin>A</margin>
Furthermore, what is signified by the prophecy can be understood in another way: namely, that we rejoice and laugh because of our salvation, just as Isaac did. <note>The name "Isaac" in Hebrew means "laughter." Clement is playing on this etymology to connect the Old Testament figure to Christian joy.</note> He also laughed after being released from death, playing and exulting with his bride, who is the Church, our helper unto salvation. To her has been given the firm and solid name of Endurance <note>original: "Tolerantia," likely translating the Greek "Hypomone," meaning patient perseverance</note>: either because she remains throughout the ages, always rejoicing; or because she is composed of the endurance of the believers, who are the members of Christ, and of those who have maintained their testimony to the end, and the thanksgiving that arises because of it. This is a mystic play and discipline, and a salvation that brings help with a grave and honorable comfort. Thus, Christ the King watches our laughter from the heavens; and when he had looked out from the window (as the Scripture says) upon the thanksgiving, <margin>B</margin> the blessing, the exultation, and the joy—and also upon the endurance working together with them and their union—he looks upon his Church alone. He reveals his own face, which the Church lacked, and she is made perfect by her royal Head. But where was the window through which the Lord was shown? It was the flesh, through which he was made manifest. He himself is Isaac (for we may take it this way) who is a type and figure of the Lord. He was a child as a son (for he was the son of Abraham, just as Christ is the Son of God) and he was a victim just as the Lord was. However, he was not sacrificed as the Lord was. Isaac only carried the wood for the sacrifice, just as the Lord carried the wood of the cross. He laughed mystically, prophesying that the Lord would fill us with laughter—we who have been redeemed from destruction and corruption by the blood of the Lord. But Isaac did not suffer, rightfully so, yielding the first part of the passion to the Word. <margin>C</margin> Moreover, his not being killed signifies the divinity of the Lord. For Jesus rose after the funeral rites were performed; he did not remain in suffering, just as Isaac was released from the sacrifice.

<margin>Isaiah 9</margin>
Furthermore, to defend what has been proposed, I will bring forward another great point. The Spirit, prophesying through Isaiah, calls the Lord himself a child: **BEHOLD, A CHILD** is born to us, and a son is given to us, whose sovereignty is upon his shoulder, and his name is called the Angel of Great Counsel. What, then, is this child? An infant, in whose image we are infants. Through the same Prophet, he narrates his greatness: **WONDERFUL** Counselor, Mighty God, Eternal Father, Prince of Peace; because he fulfills both play and discipline; and of his peace there is no end. O great God! O perfect child! The Son is in the Father, and the Father is in the Son. And <margin>D</margin> how is the childhood discipline and instruction of this child not perfect? It is this that persuades us all to be children, instructing us in the manner of an Instructor <note>original: "Paedagogus," the Greek term for a tutor or guardian who guided a child’s moral development</note>, we who are his infants. He expanded his hands toward us, which were openly and evidently believed. Concerning this child, John also bears <margin>John 1</margin> witness, he who is the greatest Prophet among those born of women: **BEHOLD THE LAMB of God**. For since Scripture calls boys and infants "lambs," he called the God who is the Word—who became man for us and who wished to be like us in all things—the Lamb of God, the Son of God, the infant of the Father.

# BOOK ONE

<margin>A</margin>
It was necessary for him to learn something; but since he was God, it was appropriate that he learned nothing. For no one could be greater than the Word. Nor is there any master or teacher for him who is the only Master. Will they not then admit, even against their will, that the perfect Word, born of the perfect Father, was perfectly reborn <note>original: "regeneratum." In this context, Clement refers to Christ’s baptism as a "rebirth" or manifestation to the world.</note> according to the divine arrangement of preordination? And if he was perfect, why was he who was perfect baptized? <note>original: "tingebatur," literally "was dipped" or "was dyed."</note> It was necessary, they say, to fulfill the human profession. Very well. I say the same. As soon as he is baptized by John, he becomes perfect. Clearly. So he learned nothing from him? Not at all. He is perfected by the washing <note>original: "lauacro"</note> alone, and sanctified by the coming of the Spirit. This is how it is. This same thing happens to us as well, for whom the Lord was the pattern. Being baptized, we are illuminated. Being illuminated, we are adopted as sons. Being adopted, we are perfected. Being perfected, we are made immortal.

<margin>Psalm 81</margin>
<margin>B</margin>
"I have said," he says, "You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High." <note>This refers to Psalm 82:6 in modern numbering; Clement uses the Septuagint numbering.</note> This work is called by many names: <gloss>a</gloss> Grace, Illumination, Perfection, and Washing. It is called "Washing" because by it we wipe away our sins; "Grace," because by it the punishments due for sins are forgiven; "Illumination," through which we behold that holy and saving light—that is, through which we clearly see what is divine. We call it "Perfection" because nothing is lacking to it. For what is lacking to one who knows God? It is indeed absurd for something to be called God’s grace if it is not perfect and complete in every way. He who is perfect will surely bestow perfect things. Just as everything happens at once when he commands it, so it follows that because he willed only to show favor, the grace was full. For what is to come

<margin>C</margin>
in time is anticipated by the will of his power. Added to this is the fact that liberation from evils is the beginning of salvation. Therefore, only we who have first reached the goals of life are already perfect. We already live, having been separated from death. To follow Christ is therefore salvation.

<margin>John 1</margin>
<margin>Ibid. 5</margin>
"For what was made in him is life." "Amen, amen, I say to you," he says, "He who hears my words and believes him who sent me has eternal life and does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life." Thus, simply to have believed and to have been reborn is perfection in life. For God is never weak.

<margin>Romans 8</margin>
<margin>2 Thess. 3</margin>
Just as his will is a work, and that work is called "the World," so also his will is the salvation of men, and that is called "the Church." He knows those whom he has called and those whom he has saved; he called and saved at the same time. <gloss>b</gloss> "For you yourselves," says the Apostle,

<margin>D</margin>
"are taught by God." It is therefore wrong to think that what is taught by him is imperfect. What is learned from him is the eternal salvation of the eternal Savior, to whom be grace for ages of ages. Amen. And he who is simply reborn, just as he is also called illuminated, is immediately freed from darkness and has received light from that time onward. Just as those who have shaken off sleep are immediately awake within; or rather, like those who try to remove cataracts from the eyes: they do not provide light from the outside which the eyes do not have, but by removing the hindrance to the eyes, they leave the pupil free. So also we who are baptized, having wiped away our sins—which were spread like a mist over the divine spirit—have a free, unhindered, and clear eye of the spirit. With this alone we behold what is divine, as the Holy Spirit flows into us from heaven.

<margin>E</margin>
This is the eternal tempering of splendor, which is able to see the eternal light, since like is a friend to like. That which is holy is a friend to him from whom holiness comes, which is properly called Light.

<margin>Ephesians 4</margin>
"For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord." From this, I think, the ancient Greeks called man *phota*, <note>original: "φῶτα" (phōta). Clement is playing on a Greek pun where "phōs" can mean both "light" and "man" depending on the accent.</note> that is, "light." "But," they say, "he has not yet received the perfect gift." I also agree. But he is in the light, and the darkness does not grasp him. Between light and darkness, there is no middle ground. The final end is reserved for the resurrection of believers. This end is not to obtain something else, but to attain the promise previously agreed upon. For we do not say that both exist at the same time:

<margin>Eternity</margin>
<margin>F</margin>
namely, the arrival at the end and the anticipation of that arrival. For eternity <note>original: "æuum" (aeon), representing timeless existence</note> and time are not the same. Nor is the desire by which we are driven toward something the same as the end toward which we strive. Both involve one thing, and one person is involved in both. Faith, which is generated in time, is, so to speak, the inciting desire.

-> THE INSTRUCTOR <-

...let us add after a short space. <margin>A</margin> **AS IF TO INFANTS.** We should understand the meaning through the phrasing of the reading: "I have catechized <note>original: "Cathechizaui," referring to basic oral instruction in the faith.</note> you," that is, I have instructed you in Christ through hearing, with a simple and naturally spiritual nourishment. For such is the nature of milk, which is the substance that nourishes living creatures, flowing from loving breasts. Thus, the whole passage is understood this way: just as nurses nourish newborn infants with milk, so I also have dripped into you the milk of Christ, which is spiritual nourishment. Therefore, milk is a perfect food and leads to the end <note>The "end" here refers to the goal or completion of the spiritual journey.</note> that will never cease. For this reason, the same milk and honey are promised in the land of rest. Rightly then, the Lord promises milk again to the righteous, so that the Word <note>original: "Verbum," referring to the Logos/Christ.</note> may be clearly shown to be both Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end—the Word, I say, which is allegorically called milk. <margin>B</margin> Even Homer, perhaps unintentionally, divined something like this when he called righteous men "milk-eaters" <note>original: "γαλακτοφάγους" (galaktophagous).</note>. <margin>1 Corinthians 3</margin> The Scripture can also be understood in this way: **AND I, brothers, could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal, as infants in Christ.** <margin>Taught by God <note>original: "θεοκατήχητοι" (theokatechetoi).</note></margin> This is so that those who were recently instructed—the catechumens <term>catechumens: those receiving basic instruction before baptism</term>—and were still infants in Christ might be understood as "carnal." For he called those who have already believed in the Holy Spirit "spiritual." But the "carnal" are those who have been recently instructed by hearing and are not yet purified; he rightly calls them carnal because, just like the Gentiles, they still thought of the things of the flesh. <margin>1 Corinthians 3</margin> **FOR WHERE there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not carnal and walking according to human ways?** Therefore he also says, **MILK I gave you to drink,** <margin>C</margin> meaning I infused you with knowledge that is given through catechesis—that is, instruction through hearing—which nourishes one for eternal life. Furthermore, the phrase "I gave you to drink" is a symbol and sign of perfect participation. For those who are perfect are said to drink, while infants suckle. **FOR MY BLOOD,** says the Lord, **is true drink.** Did he not then, when he said "I gave you milk to drink," signify the perfect joy found in the Word-as-Milk, which is the knowledge of the truth? As for what follows, **NOT SOLID FOOD, for you were not yet able,** this may signify the clear revelation that will be in the future age, like solid food, "face to face." **FOR WE SEE now as through a mirror,** says the same Apostle, **but then face to face.** Therefore he also added this: <margin>D</margin> **BUT NEITHER can you do so now.** For you are still carnal, thinking of the things of the flesh—desiring, loving, envying, being angry, and jealous. We are no longer in the flesh in that way, as some have thought. For with the flesh, having faces equal to those of the Angels, we shall see the promised vision face to face. <margin>1 Corinthians 2</margin> **HOWEVER,** if that promise is truly for after we depart from here—**what eye has not seen, nor has entered into the heart of man**—how can they say they know it, when they have not understood it by the Spirit, but received it from mere discipline? This is what "no ear has ever heard," except for that one which was caught up into the third heaven <margin>2 Corinthians 12</margin>, and even that one was commanded to cover it in secret silence. But if it can be understood as human wisdom (which is what remains), it is a boasting of knowledge. <margin>Jeremiah 9; 1 Corinthians 1</margin> Hear the law of Scripture: **LET NOT the wise man glory in his wisdom, and let not the strong man glory in his strength, but let him who glories glory in the Lord.** But we are taught by God, and we glory in the name of Christ. How then can we not think that the Apostle understands the "milk of infants" in this way, if indeed we who preside over the churches are shepherds in the image of the Good Shepherd, and you are the sheep? Does not the Lord, who also speaks of the "milk of the flock," maintain consistency by using an allegory? Now, the saying must be applied to the mind again: **MILK I gave you to drink, not solid food, for you were not yet able.** This does not mean they thought food was something other than milk, but that it is the same in substance. In the same way, the Word itself is either relaxed, gentle, and mild like milk, or it is solidified and compressed like food. Indeed, if we accept it this way, we can understand "milk" to be the preaching which is widely spread. "Food" then is the faith which, from the starting point of basic instruction, is compressed and converted into a foundation. Since it is more solid than mere hearing, it is likened to food, having become a "body" within the soul itself. Elsewhere in the Gospel according to John, the Lord explained such nourishment differently through symbols and signs <margin>John 6</margin> when he said: **EAT my flesh and drink my blood,** evidently...

He uses physiological metaphors to explain that faith is simply instruction that has become solid and foundational within the soul.</summary>

# BOOK ONE
<sig>b iiii</sig>

<margin>A</margin>
...nourished by faith and the promise, which is food and drink. He speaks allegorically, through which the church—like a human being consisting of many members—is irrigated and increased, and is forged and joined together by both: in body, by faith; in soul, by hope; just as the Lord is also composed of flesh and blood. For in truth, hope is the blood of faith, in which faith is contained, just as faith is held by the soul. When hope expires, it is just as if the blood has flowed out; the vital power of faith is dissolved.

<margin>B</margin>
If some wish to argue, saying that milk signifies the first lessons as if they were the first nutrients, while solid food signifies spiritual knowledge <note>original: "cognitiones," referring to Gnosis or higher insights.</note> to which they raise themselves because of their "science," let them know this: when they call solid food a "nourishment," they are actually leading the flesh and blood of Jesus—through their own boastful wisdom—down to a true simplicity. For blood is found to be the "first-born" substance in a human, which some have dared to call the very substance of the soul. This blood, converted by natural digestion after a mother has conceived and carries the womb, blossoms and matures—with love consenting and in a way suffering along with it—so that the infant may be without fear. That which is the more fluid part of the flesh is blood, which is like a kind of liquid flesh; and milk is that part of the blood which is more pleasant and refined. For whether it is the blood supplied to the fetus in the womb and sent through the mother’s umbilical cord, or whether the menstrual flow itself is redirected by a natural spreading—commanded by God, the nourishing author of generation—to the swelling breasts, the blood is changed for the

<margin>C</margin>
infant and becomes a pleasant and sweet nourishment. For of all the members, the breasts have the greatest sympathy with the womb. When the vessel through which blood was carried to the fetus is cut at birth, the passage is closed, but the blood is urged toward the breasts. When much has flowed there, the breasts are extended and the blood is changed into milk, not unlike how blood changes into white matter <note>original: "pus," here used as a biological comparison of transformation rather than infection.</note> in a wound. Or, perhaps the blood is transfused into the natural cavities of the breasts from open veins located there, through the infant's nursing; there it is mixed with the "spirit" <note>original: "spiritus," meaning breath or air in ancient medical theory.</note> emitted from nearby arteries. While the underlying substance of the blood remains intact, it becomes white by being agitated, similar to how the sea changes into foam—as the Poets say that the sea, stirred by the insults of the winds,

<margin>D</margin>
spits out the "refuse of the salt" <margin><gloss>salt froth</gloss></margin>. Nevertheless, it still possesses the substance of blood. In the same way, when rivers are carried with great force, they squeeze out foam with a roar because they are mangled by the interception of the surrounding air; even the moisture in our own mouths turns white from the breath. How absurd is it, then, not to admit that blood is converted by the spirit into that brightness and whiteness, receiving a change in quality but not in substance? Certainly, you will find nothing that nourishes better, nor anything sweeter or whiter than milk. Therefore, it is in every way similar to spiritual nourishment, which is sweet because of grace, nourishing like life, and white like the day of Christ; and the blood of the Word <note>original: "Verbum," the Logos.</note> has been shown to be like milk. For that reason, milk is dispensed and supplied to the infant at birth; and the breasts,

<margin>E</margin>
which previously looked straight toward the husband, now incline toward the child. Nature has perfected this nourishment so that it may be easily offered for the child to take, for an education in salvation. For the breasts are not like fountains full of ready-made milk flowing in; rather, by transforming the nourishment within themselves, they produce and exhale milk. This nourishment—which is appropriate and useful for the recently formed and born child—is crafted by God the Nourisher and Father of those who are generated and regenerated. Just as manna used to flow down from heaven for the ancient Hebrews, the celestial nourishment of Angels. <margin>Exodus 16, Deuteronomy 8</margin> Indeed, even now, nurses call the first milk that is poured out for drinking by the same name as that ancient nourishment: "manna." Furthermore, while pregnant women emit milk once they have become mothers, the Lord Christ, the fruit of the Virgin, did not consider human breasts "blessed," nor did he choose them for nourishment.

<margin>F</margin>
Instead, when the loving and kind Father rained down the Word, the Word itself became the spiritual nourishment for good and temperate men. O mystic miracle! There is indeed one Father of the universe. There is also one Word of the universe, and one Spirit...

He concludes by linking this natural process to the miracle of the Word being "rained down" by the Father as the ultimate food for humanity.</summary>

# THE TUTOR
<sig>iiii d</sig>
<meta>catchword: cretum</meta>

...is one holy spirit, and he is everywhere. But there is only one virgin mother: I <margin>A</margin>
prefer to call her the Church. This mother alone did not have [human] milk, because she alone
was not [merely] a woman. Yet she is at once a virgin and a mother—unspoiled as a
virgin, yet loving as a mother. Calling her little children to her, she nurtures them with holy milk, namely the Word
for infants <note>original: "verbo infantili," the Logos adapted for those new to the faith</note>. She did not have milk because the milk was this beautiful and 
suitable infant himself: that is, the body of Christ, who nourishes the new assembly with the Word—an assembly which 
the Lord himself brought forth through the labors of his flesh, and which the Lord himself bound in swaddling clothes with his
precious blood. O holy birth-pangs, O holy birth, O holy swaddling clothes! The Word
is everything to the infant: father, mother, tutor, and nourisher. <margin>John 6</margin> <margin>B</margin> **EAT**, he
says, *my flesh, and drink my blood.* These are the suitable and appropriate
nourishments the Lord supplies to us; he offers his flesh and pours out his blood,
and nothing is lacking for the growth of his little children. O wonderful mystery! He
commands us to cast off the old and fleshly corruption, just as we do with our old
nourishment, and to participate in the new diet of Christ. By receiving him, if it were possible, 
we lay him up within ourselves and embrace the Savior within our breast, so that
we may render the affections of our flesh pure and perfect. But perhaps you do not wish to understand it 
this way, but in a more common sense. Hear it this way as well: The Holy Spirit 
signifies "flesh" to us allegorically, for by the Spirit, flesh was fashioned. "Blood" 
designates the Word to us, for like rich blood, the Word of life has been infused. The Lord <margin>C</margin>
is the mixture of both. The nourishment of infants is the Lord, who is spirit
and word. This nourishment—that is, the Lord Jesus, the Word of God—is the 
incarnate spirit, the sanctified heavenly flesh. This nutrient is the Father's milk, by which alone
little children are fed. Thus, he who is the beloved and our nourisher, the Word, poured out
his blood for us, bringing salvation to human nature. Through him, we who have believed in
God flee to the Father’s breast—which brings forgetfulness of cares—namely, the Word.
He alone, as is fitting, supplies us infants with the milk of love. And truly blessed 
are those who suckle at this breast. And for this reason, <margin>1 Peter 2</margin> Peter also says: <margin>D</margin> **HAVING LAID ASIDE** *therefore all malice, and all guile, and hypocrisy, and envy, and slander, like newborn infants, crave the rational milk <note>original: "verbale lac," likely referring to the Greek "logikon gala," milk that is of the Word or logical</note>, so that by it you may grow into salvation, if indeed you have tasted that the Lord is Christ.* Even
if someone were to grant them that food is something other than milk, how
would they not be proven wrong by the very nature of things? For nourishment—when 
the condensing cold of winter contains it and provides no exit for the heat trapped within—is 
digested and, having turned into blood, flows into the veins. Because these veins
are not allowed to breathe out, they become filled and taut, and they throb. For this reason, 
nurses are also most full of milk at that time. We have shown a little earlier that 
blood in pregnant women is drawn off into milk; it is changed indeed, but its substance is by no <margin>E</margin>
means converted—much like how, in the elderly, blonde hair changes into gray. 
In summer, on the other hand, the body is more porous, which allows the nourishment to be more easily 
dispersed; thus, milk is less abundant because neither the blood nor the nourishment 
is entirely contained. Therefore, if the processing of food produces blood, and blood 
becomes milky, then blood is the preparation for milk, just as the blood of a human is like the juice of the vine. 
With milk, then—the Lord's own nourishment—we are fed immediately after we are born. 
As soon as we have been reborn, we are honored with the promise of rest, 
the Jerusalem above, in which it is written that honey and milk rain down, while we are 
betrothed through this holy, material nourishment. <margin>1 Cor. 6</margin> For **FOODS**, as the Apostle says, <margin>1 Cor. 3</margin> *shall be destroyed.* But the nourishment that comes through milk leads to the heavens, 
nurturing the citizens of heaven who will lead the dances with the Angels. Since the **WORD**
is the gushing fountain of life and is called a river of oil, Paul rightly speaks allegorically 
when calling him "milk," and adds: <margin>F</margin> **I GAVE** *you drink.* For the Word is drunk as the
nourishment of truth. Certainly, liquid nourishment is also called "drink." 
The same thing can be both food, if considered in one state, and drink, if considered 
in another; just as cheese is the curdling of milk, or milk congealed...

<summary>Clement explains the metaphor of Christ as milk, mother, and father, arguing that the "milk" of the Word is the same spiritual substance as the "blood" of the Eucharist, adapted for the nurturing of new believers. He uses ancient biological theories to explain how food becomes blood and blood becomes milk to support his theological claims.</summary>

<margin>A</margin> ...[dis]cerned; for I am not concerned with catching at words at this moment, except to show that one substance provides both forms of nourishment. Furthermore, for nursing infants, milk alone is enough to be both drink and food. <margin>John 4</margin> "I," says the LORD, "have food to eat that you do not know. My food is to do the will of Him who sent me." See here another kind of food, which, like milk, is described allegorically: namely, the will of God. <margin>Matt. 20 and 26</margin> Furthermore, he colloquially called the completion of his own passion a "cup," when it was necessary for him alone to drink it down, drain it, and fulfill it. Thus, for Christ, his nourishment was the fulfillment of the Father’s will; but for us infants, Christ himself is the food, as we suckle the Word of the heavens. From this, the Greek word "to seek" is said to be *masasthai* <note>original: μασᾶσθαι</note>, because the breasts of paternal kindness supply milk to infants who seek the Word. Moreover, the Word himself confesses to being the bread of the heavens. <margin>John 6</margin>

<margin>B</margin> "For it was NOT Moses," he says, "who gave you bread from heaven; but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven: for the bread of God is he who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world; and the bread that I will give is my <margin>To chew/seek (*masasthai*) from *mathos* <note>original: μασῶσθαι ἀπὸ μαθός</note>, which signifies a nipple.</margin> flesh, which I will give for the life of the world." One should note the mystery of this bread, in that he calls it "flesh," as something which rises through fire—just as wheat rises from corruption and sowing—and indeed something which consists through fire for the joy of the church, like bread that is baked. But this will be discussed by us more clearly again in our book *On the Resurrection*. Now, since he said, "AND THE BREAD which I will give,"

<margin>C</margin> "is my flesh": and flesh is irrigated by blood; and blood is allegorically called wine. It should be understood that when bread is broken into wine, it seizes the wine and leaves the watery part behind. In the same way, the flesh of the Lord—which is the bread of the heavens—drinks up the blood, nourishing those among men who are heavenly unto incorruption, while leaving those carnal desires alone to corruption. Thus the Word is described allegorically in many ways: as food, flesh, nourishment, bread, blood, and milk. The Lord is everything to us, so that we who have believed in him may enjoy him. Let no one think it strange that we call the blood of the Lord "milk" allegorically. For is wine not also described allegorically? <margin>Genesis 49</margin> "He who washes," it says, "his garment in wine, and his robe in the blood of the grape." In his

<margin>D</margin> spirit, he says he will adorn the body of the Word, just as he will nourish with his spirit those who hunger for the Word. That the blood is the Word is testified by the blood of Abel the just, <margin>Ibid. 4</margin> who calls out to God. For blood would never emit a voice unless the blood was understood to be the Word. For the ancient righteous man is a type of the new righteous man; and the ancient blood that calls out, calls out on behalf of the new blood. The blood which is the Word speaks to God, because it signified the Word who was to suffer. Furthermore, the flesh itself, and the blood within it, is irrigated and increased by milk as if by a certain reward. Moreover, the formation of that which is conceived happens when the seed is mixed and tempered with the pure remains of the menstrual purgation. For there is a power in it that collects the nature of the blood,

<margin>E</margin> just as rennet <term>original: coagulum; a substance used to curdle milk into cheese</term> makes milk curdle, and thus produces the substance of the formation. A good temperament produces growth easily, but extremes are prone to the sterility of offspring. Even in the earth itself, that which is inundated by excessive rain sees the seed washed away; yet it dries up from a lack of moisture. It is the viscous juice that contains and produces the seed. Now, some even maintain that the seed of an animal is the "foam of the blood" in substance, which, being agitated by the innate heat of the male during union, foams up through ventilation and is deposited in the seminal veins. From this, Diogenes of Apollonia <note>A Pre-Socratic philosopher known for his theories on air and biology</note> suggests that sexual matters <term>original: aphrodisia</term> are named so in Greek from "foam" <note>original: aphros</note>. From all these things it is clear that blood is the substance of the human body. Furthermore, that which <margin>Sexual matters (*aphrodisia*) or intercourse from "foam" (*aphros*).</margin>

<margin>F</margin> is in the womb is first a milky curdling of fluid. Then this curdling, having been converted into blood, becomes flesh. Having been condensed in the womb by the natural and warm spirit by which the fetus is shaped, it is brought to life. But even after it is brought forth into the light, the infant is nourished by the same blood. For the flow of milk is the nature of blood, and the source of nourishment is milk, by which a woman is shown to have truly given birth and to be a mother...

Therefore, each of us who are infants is permitted to boast in the Lord and declare: *I boast that I am from a good Father, and from equally good blood.* <note>Clement is likely adapting a classical poetic line here to a Christian context.</note> Now, that milk is made from blood through a process of change is already clear; indeed, this can be observed even in cattle and oxen. For in the springtime—when the surrounding air is more humid and the grass and pastures are more succulent and dewy—these animals are first filled with blood, as can be seen from the distension of the veins. From this blood, milk is poured out more abundantly. Conversely, in the summer, the blood—scorched and dried out by the heat—stops this transformation, and therefore they produce less milk.

<margin>C</margin>

Thus, those who swallow a little cold water in the aforementioned milk are immediately refreshed. For the fellowship that milk has with water does not allow it to turn sour; it matures not through any conflict, but through an inherent affection joined to it. The same fellowship that the Word has with baptism, milk has with water. For this alone of all liquids accepts a mixture with water, receiving a cleansing, just as baptism is for the remission of sins. It is also aptly and suitably mixed with honey, again for the sake of cleansing, along with sweet nourishment. For the Word, when mixed with kindness, simultaneously heals the affections of the soul and purges sins.

Furthermore, milk is also mixed with sweet wine, and this is a useful mixture: like a tempered affection leading toward incorruption. For the milk is separated from the whey by the wine, and whatever in it is "adulterated" <note>impure or watery</note> is drawn off as if through a water-pipe. In the same way, the fellowship of spiritual faith acts upon the vulnerable human being. By "wheying off" <note>separating out</note> carnal desires, it draws the person toward eternity, making the mortal soul immortal by divine means.

### Who is the Instructor, and concerning His Method of Instruction. Chapter VII.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'Q' depicting figures in a classical or biblical landscape.</image-desc>
**SINCE** we have shown that we are all called "children" by Scripture—and not only that, but that we who have followed Christ are called "infants" allegorically—and that the Father of all things alone is perfect (for the Son is in Him, and the Father is in the Son), it remains for us, following the proper order, to say who our Instructor is. He is called Jesus. Sometimes He calls Himself a Shepherd, saying:

<margin>B</margin> <margin>John 10</margin> **I** am the good shepherd. This is a metaphor taken from shepherds who lead sheep. An instructor <term>paedagogus: literally a "child-leader" in Greek culture, a tutor who looked after a boy's conduct</term> who leads the intellect of children is like a shepherd who cares for infants.
<margin>Ibid. 2</margin> For infants are called "sheep" allegorically because of their simplicity. AND THERE SHALL BE, He says, one flock and one Shepherd. Therefore, the Word <note>original: "Verbum", translating the Greek "Logos"</note> is rightly called the Instructor, for He leads us children toward salvation. Most clearly, the Word says of Himself through the prophet Hosea:

<margin>Instructor, in Greek παιδευτής (paideutes), which is an allusion to "children" (παῖδας) and "instructor" (παιδαγωγόν).</margin> **I AM** your instructor. Pedagogy <note>original: "Paedagogia"</note> is divine religion, which is the teaching of divine worship, the education for attaining the knowledge of truth, a right training, and a way of living that leads to heaven. Now, "pedagogy" is a term used in many ways. First, it is the pedagogy of the one who is led and learns; second, the pedagogy of the one who leads and teaches; third, pedagogy is the act of guidance and training itself; and fourth, pedagogy refers to the things that are taught, such as precepts. However, the pedagogy which comes from God is the direction of truth toward the contemplation of God, and a clear and evident description of holy actions to be maintained forever. Just as a Commander <term>Dux: a general or military leader</term> directs a phalanx, caring for the safety of his soldiers, and as a Pilot <term>gubernator: a ship's steersman</term> directs the rudder to save his passengers, so also the Instructor leads children to a saving way of life, taking care of us. In short, whatever we justly ask from God will be ours if we obey the Instructor. Just as a pilot does not always yield to the winds but turns the prow against them to resist the storms, so the Instructor never yields to the laws of this world.
<margin>D</margin> Nor does He allow the child to be driven like a small boat into a beast-like and lustful way of living. Instead, lifted high by the favorable spirit of truth alone, He holds firmly to the "rudder" of the child—by which I mean the ears—until He brings the unharmed child safely into the harbor of heaven. For the customs of our fathers, as they call them, pass away in a moment; but the divine institution of life is a possession that remains forever.

They say that the instructor of Achilles was Phoenix, and Adrastus was the instructor of Croesus' sons. For Alexander, it was Leonidas, and for Philip, it was Nausithous. But Phoenix was gripped by an insane love for women; Adrastus was an exile; Leonidas
<margin>Philip of Pella: from Pella, a city in Macedonia.</margin> did not cut back the pride of the Macedonian; and Nausithous did not cure the vice of drunkenness in the man of Pella. Nor could the Thracian Zopyrus restrain the womanizing of Alcibiades. But Zopyrus was a 
<margin>E</margin> purchased slave; and Sicinnus, the instructor of Themistocles' children, was a lazy servant. They say he used to dance, and that he invented the kind of dance called the *Sicinnis* in Greek. We are also aware of those called Royal Instructors among the Persians, four of whom the Persian Kings chose from among the most noble to put in charge of their children. But their sons learn only the art of archery; once they reach puberty, they have intercourse with their sisters, mothers, and countless women—both wives and concubines—trained like goats for sexual encounters.

Our Instructor, however, is the holy God Jesus, the Word who is the leader of all human nature; He Himself is the kind and merciful God who is our Instructor.
<margin>F</margin> <margin>Deut. 32</margin> Concerning Him, the Holy Spirit says somewhere in a song: He provided for the PEOPLE sufficiently in the desert, in the heat of thirst; He surrounded them in a waterless place, and He educated them and guarded them as the apple of His eye; as an eagle protects its nest and yearns for its young, He spread His wings and took them up, carrying them on His back. The Lord alone led them, and there was no foreign god with them. Clearly, as it seems to me,

<summary>Clement identifies Jesus as the "Instructor" (Pedagogue) of humanity, defining divine pedagogy as a spiritual training that leads to heaven, contrasting it with the failed or immoral instructors of classical history.</summary>

<margin>Ibidem</margin>
<margin>D</margin>

<margin>Ezekiel 18</margin>

<margin>E</margin>
That in their anger they killed men, and in their lust they hamstrung a bull: Their anger is to be cursed. Who, then, could have educated us more kindly and humanely than He? Therefore, previously for the ancient people there was the Old Covenant, and the Law educated the people with fear, and the Word was an Angel; but for the new and recent people, a new and recent covenant has been given, and the Word was begotten, and fear has been turned into love, and that mystical Angel, Jesus, is brought forth.
<margin>Romans 8; Deuteronomy 6; Matthew 22; Isaiah 1; Psalm 36; Ibid. 44</margin>

You have loved justice: you have hated iniquity.** This is my new covenant, impressed upon the old letter. Therefore, the novelty of the Word is not to be reproached.
<margin>Jeremiah 1</margin>
<margin>F</margin>

Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you came forth from the matrix I sanctified you.** Among us, this prophecy can signify those who were known to God for faith before the foundation of the world: but by name they are infants, having recently fulfilled the recently revealed will of God...

<margin>A</margin> ...age, insofar as we have been newly born for the sake of calling and salvation. On this account, he also 
<margin>Ibidem <note>Refers to Jeremiah 1:5 mentioned previously</note></margin> adds: I have appointed you a **prophet** to the nations, saying that it is necessary to predict that the name "recent" <note>meaning "new" or "young" in the faith</note> should not seem like a reproach to those who appear to be infants. For the Law 
<margin>John 1</margin> is the old grace given by the Word through Moses. Therefore, Scripture also says: **the law was given through Moses**. It was not *from* Moses, but *from* the Word, though *through* Moses His servant. And for that reason, it was for a time. But eternal grace and truth were realized through Jesus Christ. Look at the words of Scripture regarding the Law: it says it was "given" only. But the truth, which is the grace of the Father, is the eternal work of the Word; it is not said to be "given," but to *be realized* <note>original: "fieri", meaning to come into being or be made manifest</note> through Jesus, without whom nothing was made. Now indeed, Moses, prophetically yielding to the perfect 
<margin>B</margin> Instructor <note>original: "Pedagogo"</note>, namely the Word, predicts both His name and His method of instruction <note>original: "Pædagogiam"</note>, and commends the Instructor to the people, delivering to them precepts of obedience: God, he says, 
<margin>Deut. 18</margin> will raise up for you a **prophet** like me from among your brothers—referring to Jesus [Joshua], the son of Nave [Nun], as a sign of Jesus [the Son] of God. For the name of Jesus, which was proclaimed in the Law, was a foreshadowing of the Lord. He therefore adds, providing what would be useful for the people: you shall **hear him**, he says. And he threatens the man who will not hear this Prophet. Such is the name of the saving Instructor that he predicts for us. For this reason, Prophecy adds a "rod" to him—the Rod of discipline, of rule, and of power—so that those whom the Word does not heal through persuasion and admonition, threats may heal. Those whom threats do not heal, the Rod shall heal. 
<margin>Isa. 11</margin> And those whom the Rod does not heal, fire shall consume. A **rod**, it says, **shall go forth** 
<margin>C</margin> from the root of Jesse. See the care, wisdom, and power of the Instructor: **not according to** opinion, it says, will he judge, nor according to speech will he reprove; but he will judge the humble with judgment, and reprove the sinners of the earth. And through David: the Lord 
<margin>Psalm 117 <note>Modern Psalm 118:18</note></margin> **has chastened me severely**, but he has not given me over to death. For to be chastened by the Lord, and to be educated as if by an Instructor, is to be liberated from death. And he says through the same Prophet: you shall shepherd them 
<margin>Ibidem 2 <note>Modern Psalm 2:9</note></margin> **with a rod** of iron. The Apostle also, moved by this in the letter to the Corinthians, 
<margin>1 Cor. 4</margin> says: **what** do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love and a spirit of gentleness? 
<margin>Psalm 119 <note>Modern Psalm 110:2</note></margin> But also, the Lord will send the **rod** of power out of Zion, he says through another Prophet. 
<margin>Ibidem 22 <note>Modern Psalm 23:4</note></margin> Moreover, this instructional **your rod** and your staff have comforted me, someone else said. This is the power of the Instructor: venerable and grave, yet consoling and saving.

<margin>D</margin> ### *Against those who think that he who is just is not good. Chapter VIII.*

Here some people arise who say that the Lord is not good because of the rod, and the threats, and fear—neither listening to the Scripture 
<margin>Ecclus. 21</margin> which says: **and he who fears the Lord** will return to his heart—and forgetting that which is greatest: His kindness, in that for our sake He became human. And yet the Prophet prays to Him familiarly 
<margin>Job 10, Psalm 102 <note>Modern Ps 103:14</note></margin> through these words: **remember** us, for we are dust. That is: Have mercy on us, because You Yourself suffered and experienced the weakness of the flesh. For that reason, the Lord is the best Instructor, subject to no reproach, who out of extraordinary kindness and clemency has mercy on the 
<margin>E</margin> nature of every single human being. For there is nothing that the Lord hates; for He does not hate a thing and yet wish that which He hates to exist. Nor does He wish for something not to exist, while being the cause of that thing's existence which He wishes not to be. But neither does He *not* wish for something not to exist while it actually exists. Therefore, if the Word hates anything, He wishes it not to exist. But there is nothing for which God does not provide the cause of its existence. Therefore, God hates nothing. Neither does the 
<margin>John 1</margin> Word. For both are one, namely, God. For He said: **in the beginning** was the Word, and the Word was in God, and the Word was God. If, then, He hates nothing of those things which were made by Him, it remains that He loves them. But by right, He will love the human being far more than other things, who is the most beautiful animal of those things created by Him, and one endowed with piety and religion. 
<margin>F</margin> Therefore, God loves the human being. Therefore, the Word also loves the human being. Now, whoever loves something wishes to benefit it. But that which benefits is certainly more excellent than that which does not benefit. And nothing is more excellent than the Good. Therefore, that which is good benefits. It is, however, confessed by all that God is good.

# THE INSTRUCTOR

<margin>A</margin>
God, therefore, does good. But the good, insofar as it is good, does nothing else but benefit. God, therefore, benefits in all things. And does He not indeed benefit man in some specific way? Does He not take care of him? Or if He takes care of him, is He not also concerned for him? For that which benefits of its own accord is more excellent than that which does not do so of its own accord. Moreover, nothing is more excellent than God. And to benefit of one’s own accord is nothing else than being concerned for man. God, therefore, takes care of man and is concerned for him. Indeed, He shows this in reality when He instructs him by the Word, who is the true and genuine co-helper of God’s benevolence toward men. Now, God is said to be "good" not because He possesses virtue as a quality <note>In ancient philosophy, possessing virtue implies a potential for change; Clement argues God *is* the Good essentially</note>: for justice also is said to be a good, not because it possesses virtue, but because it is itself virtue; rather, He is good because He is good in and of Himself.

<margin>Matthew 6</margin>
<margin>B</margin>
"Good" is also defined in another way: as that which is useful, not because it delights, but because it profits. Justice possesses all these qualities: it is a virtue, it is a good to be chosen for its own sake, and it is something that does not necessarily delight. For Justice does not judge to show favor, but distributes according to the merits of each person. Furthermore, that which is useful follows from that which benefits. Therefore, in all aspects by which the "good" is judged, justice also takes on the form and character of the good; they are equal and similar to one another. Justice, therefore, is a good. "How then," they ask, "if the Lord loves humans and is good, does He become angry and punish?" It is necessary, therefore, to discuss these matters as briefly as possible. For this treatment is beneficial in some part, holding the place of a necessary aid for the right upbringing <note>original: "puerorum eductionem," referring to the training of those young in the faith</note> of children.

<margin>C</margin>
For many affections <note>passions or illnesses</note> of the soul are cured by punishment, and by the harsher command of precepts, and even through the teaching of certain contemplations. Indeed, rebuke is like a kind of surgery for the affections of the soul. 

<margin>An abscess in Greek is ἀπόστασις <note>original: "apostasis," meaning a standing away or a separation</note>, that is, an aposteme, which is a localized collection of humors.</margin>
The "abscesses" of the soul are the departures from the truth, which one must rebuke by cutting them away with a sharp incision. The casting of reproach is similar to the drinking or application of medicines; it dissolves the affections that have already become hardened, purges the filth of an immodest and lustful life, and levels out the overgrown flesh of pride and arrogance, repairing and restoring the man to a healthy and true state. Now, truly, admonition is like a certain diet for a sick soul, advising what should be taken and forbidding what should not. All these things tend toward eternal safety and health. Furthermore, just as a general of an army, when he punishes those who have committed a crime with fines, or with penalties involving chains and extreme disgrace that reach even to the body—and sometimes even punishes some with death—has as his goal that which is good, so that the leaders who obey his command may be warned. So also that great General, the Leader of the universe, the Word, warns those who are carried away by an unbridled impulse against His Law and do not obey the Charioteer. To free them from slavery, error, and the captivity of the Adversary <note>the Devil</note>, He warns them to restrain the disturbances of the soul, peacefully leading them to the sacred harmony of the commonwealth.

<margin>D</margin>
Just as the exhortatory and consolatory styles are joined to persuasive speech, so also the vituperative <note>insulting or blaming</note> and reproachful styles are joined to the laudatory <note>praising</note>. This genre is a certain cleansing art. To rebuke is a sign of benevolence, not of hatred. For both a friend and an enemy offer a reproach: but the enemy does so mocking, while the friend does so out of goodwill. It was not, therefore, out of hatred that the Lord attacked men with rebukes—men whom He Himself suffered for, though He could have destroyed us for our own crimes.

<margin>E</margin>
<margin>Hebrews 12</margin>
For the Instructor, since He is good, very skillfully uses even a curse to creep toward a rebuke; He is good, like a whip waking the sluggishness of the mind. Then again, He tries to encourage those same people in turn. For those whom praise did not move, rebuke incited; and those whom rebuke did not rouse to salvation as if they were dead, a curse awakens to the truth. For "Whips and rebukes are at all times part of Wisdom."

<margin>Ecclesiasticus 22</margin>
> HE WHO glues a potsherd together and teaches a fool, is like one who leads the earth to sensation, and sharpens one who is hopeless toward prudence. On this account he openly added: AWAKENING one sleeping from a deep sleep, 

which is more like death than anything else.

<margin>F</margin>
Furthermore, He Himself explains most openly about Himself, signifying by an allegory a diverse cultivation that is useful in many ways, when He said:

<margin>John 15</margin>
> I AM the true vine, and my Father is the Farmer.

The Word, who is a sword, prunes the lush and clinging shoots, constraining our desires so they do not seek to bear [excessive] fruit. For those who sin, rebuke has salvation as its goal, with the Word fittingly adapting itself to the specific character of each person—in some cases being vehement and intense, in others gentle and relaxed. Most clearly, then, it was said through Moses: <margin>Deuteronomy 8</margin> **BE OF GOOD** courage, for God has come to test you, so that His fear may be in you, and you may not sin. Since those who are corrected by the just one **RECEIVE BENEFIT**, even according to Plato’s opinion <note>Plato, *Gorgias* 477a</note>, it is admitted that what is just is also good. Therefore, fear itself is profitable and was devised for the good of mankind, since the spirit that fears the Lord shall live. For hope is in Him who saves them. This very one, I mean the Word, who imposes penalties, is the Judge. # THE INSTRUCTOR

<margin>to punish <note>original Greek: τιμωρῖσθαι</note></margin> for the benefit of the one who is chastised. <margin>A</margin> For correction is for the one who resists; however, He does not wish to take revenge. Vengeance is the retribution of an evil that is sent out for the benefit of the one who takes revenge. But He who taught us to pray for those who do us wrong would not desire to take revenge. And yet, all confess that God is good. Moreover, that this same God is also just, I have no need for many words if I bring forward the Lord’s own voice from the Gospel. Indeed, He says this one thing: <margin>Matthew 5</margin> <margin>John 17</margin> **THAT THEY ALL may be one, as you, Father, are in me, and I in you; that they also may be one in us: so that the world may believe that you have sent me. And the glory which you gave me I have given them, that they may be one, even as we are one; I in them, and you in me, that they may be made perfect in one.** Now, God is One, and beyond one, and above unity itself. And therefore, that small word **"YOU"**, having a demonstrative <margin>B</margin> emphasis, points out Him who truly is alone, who was, and is, and shall be—God. In these three times, one name is placed: namely, **BEING**. <note>original: ENS; Greek: ὅ ὤν. This refers to the divine name revealed to Moses, "I Am who I Am."</note> <margin>He who is</margin> But that He who is the only God is also Himself the only and truly just one, the Lord will testify in the Gospel, saying: <margin>Ibid.</margin> **FATHER, I will that they also, whom you have given me, be with me where I am; that they may behold my glory, which you have given me: for you loved me before the foundation of the world. O righteous Father, the world has not known you; but I have known you, and these have known that you have sent me. And I have declared unto them your name, and will declare it.** This is He who returns the sins of the fathers upon the children to those who hate Him, and shows mercy to those who love Him. <margin>Exodus 20</margin> For He who sets these on the right hand, and those on the left, is conceived of as the Father who is good; <margin>C</margin> insofar as He is called "good," it is for that reason alone. But insofar as the Son, His Word, is in the Father, He is called "just" based on the mutual relationship and disposition between them, so that the name of power is measured by an equality of love. **A MAN**, He says, **He shall judge according to his works, when God has made Jesus known to us by the level scales of justice,** <margin>Proverbs 31</margin> <margin>Wisdom 6</margin> through whom, as if by an equal balance, we have come to know God. Regarding this, Wisdom also speaks openly: **FOR MERCY and wrath are with Him.** <margin>Ecclesiasticus 18</margin> For the Lord alone is powerful in both these things: pouring out wrath for the sake of reconciliation out of His great mercy. So it is also with His rebuke. For the goal of mercy and rebuke is the salvation of those who are rebuked. Now, that the same God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ is good, the Word again will confess, saying that He is good to the ungrateful and to the wicked; and furthermore, while He says: <margin>D</margin> **BE merciful, as your Father is merciful:** <margin>Matthew 5</margin> <margin>Mark 10</margin> <margin>Matthew 5</margin> <margin>Ibid.</margin> and even when He says openly: **NO ONE is good except my Father who is in heaven.** Then again: **THE FATHER,** He says, **makes His sun to shine upon all.** Here it must be noted that He confesses His Father, who is good, to also be the artisan <note>original: opificem, referring to God as the "Craftsman" or "Demiurge" of the universe.</note> and creator. That the creator is just is beyond controversy. And again: **MY FATHER,** He says, **sends rain upon the just and the unjust.** <margin>Psalm 8</margin> Insofar as He sends rain, He is the artisan of the waters and clouds; but insofar as He does so upon everyone, He is just, and there is a balance joined with His power. But as a good one, He does so upon the just and unjust alike. Most clearly, then, we conclude by reasoning that God is one and the same in this way: **I WILL behold the heavens, the works of your fingers;** and, **HE WHO created the heavens, dwells in the heavens;** <margin>E</margin> **and: THE HEAVEN is your throne,** the Holy Spirit sang. Moreover, the Lord says in prayer: **OUR FATHER, who art in heaven.** <margin>Ibid. 2</margin> <margin>Ibid. 10</margin> <margin>Ibid. 102</margin> <margin>Isaiah 62</margin> <margin>Matthew 6</margin> <margin>Romans 3</margin> Now, the heavens belong to Him who created the world. Therefore, it cannot be contradicted that the Lord is the Son of the Creator. If it is confessed by all that the creator is just, and the Lord is the Son of the artisan, then the Lord is the Son of Him who is just. On which account Paul also says: **BUT NOW the righteousness of God without the Law is manifested.** And again, that you may better judge God: **THE RIGHTEOUSNESS of God through the faith of Jesus Christ unto all who believe.** For there is no distinction. And furthermore, bearing witness to the truth a little later, he adds: **IN THE FORBEARANCE of God, to show that He is at once just, and the justifier of him who is of the faith in Jesus.** That what is just is known to be good is seen by him who says: <margin>F</margin> **WHEREFORE THE LAW is indeed holy, and the commandment holy, and just, and good:** <margin>Ibid. 7</margin> placing both names under the same power. And yet, no one is good except His Father. Therefore, His Father is the same one, who though He is one, is signified by many powers. And this is what that [verse] intended: **NO ONE knows the Father, who indeed was He himself...** <margin>Matthew 11</margin>

But it is not foreign to the Word of salvation to speak harshly when He is caring for someone; for this, too, is a medicine of divine kindness, from which the blush of shame blossoms, and a sense of modesty regarding sin arises. For if it is necessary to criticize, it is also necessary to speak sternly. In such a case, it is time not to wound the soul mortally, but to heal it with a small amount of pain, gaining liberation from eternal death. In His <term>Instruction <note>original: Pædagogia; the art or method of the "Pedagogue" or household tutor.</note></term>, there is great wisdom, and the method of His administration for our salvation is varied. For the Instructor bears witness to those who are good.

<margin>B</margin>

For there is no other who is without witness than the one to whom witness is born; and the greatest grace is that which proceeds from such witness. Furthermore, even anger—if His admonition should be called anger—is an affection of kindness and benevolence toward men, since God "descends" to human emotions for the sake of man, for whose sake the Word of God became man.

### That it belongs to the same power both to do good and to punish justly: In which is also stated the method of the Word’s instruction. Chapter IX.

With all His strength, therefore, the Instructor of human nature—our Divine Word—using all the machines of wisdom, has set out to preserve His children: admonishing, blaming, rebuking, arguing, threatening, healing, promising, and bestowing favors, binding the irrational desires of human nature with many "reins," as it were. Admonition is therefore a "caring criticism" that imparts understanding. <margin>A</margin>...they sacrificed with the initiated, and the people who understood were joined with the harlot. He shows their sin more clearly by professing that they "understand," as those who sinned by their own will and deliberation. For understanding is the eye of the soul. And for this reason, **Israel** is "one who sees God": that is, one who understands God. A **complaint**, however, is a censure, as if directed toward those who are contemptuous or negligent. In this way, the use of <term>Instruction <note>original: Paedagogia; the method of the divine tutor.</note></term> is seen through Isaiah, saying: *HEAR, O HEAVENS, and give ear, O earth, for the Lord has spoken. Instead, the ox and the donkey, which are dull and foolish animals, know the one who feeds them, while Israel is found to be more estranged from reason than they are? <margin>B</margin>

rebuke, or a driving censure. The Instructor also used this medicine through Isaiah, saying: *WOE, rebellious children. These things says the Lord. You have made a plan, but not through me, and entered into covenants, but not through my spirit.* He uses a most bitter "seasoning" in each case—namely, **fear**—through which He simultaneously opens and converts the people toward salvation. It is just as wool that is to be dyed is usually constricted and compressed while being prepared, so that it may take the color better. **Reproof**, on the other hand, is the bringing forth of sin, dragging it into the light. He uses this as a most necessary mode of Instruction because the faith of so many has become weakened and loose.
