<margin>A</margin>
...He provides under a veil. This method was used through Jeremiah: <margin>Lamentations 1</margin> *HOW the city sits alone, which had been full of people! She has become like a widow, she who ruled the regions: she has been placed under tribute. Weeping, she has wept in the night.* **Detraction**, however, is a disparaging reproach. The divine **Instructor** <note>original: "Pædagogus"; the Word acting as a tutor.</note> used this help when He said through Jeremiah: <margin>Jeremiah 3</margin> *YOU HAD the look of a harlot: you were shameless toward everyone, and you did not call me into your house, nor your father, nor the prince of your virginity... a beautiful and pleasant harlot, a mistress of poisons.* Quite skillfully, after He had insulted her with the name of a harlot while she was yet a virgin, He calls her back again, exhorting her toward honor. **Indignation**, on the other hand, is a lawful rebuke, or a rebuke of "children" who have raised themselves up more than is proper. He uses this form of instruction through Moses, saying: <margin>Deuteronomy 32</margin> *Blameworthy children, a depraved and perverse generation.*

<margin>B</margin>
*Is this how you repay the Lord? Are these the foolish and unwise people? Did not this same Father possess you?* And through Isaiah He says: <margin>Isaiah 1</margin> *YOUR PRINCES do not obey; they are companions of thieves, loving gifts, pursuing rewards, and not judging for the orphans.* To speak in summary: His skill in instilling fear is a fountain of salvation. It is the nature of a good being to give salvation. The mercy of the Lord is over all flesh, while He argues, chastises, and teaches, just as a shepherd does his flock. He has mercy on those who receive discipline, and He joins to Himself those who are of an ardent zeal. By this method of leading, He kept the six hundred thousand footmen—who were driven by the hardness of heart they possessed—protecting them through mercy and discipline, by whipping, pitying, striking, and healing. For just as His mercy is great, so also is His correction. For while it is certainly a beautiful thing not to sin, it is also good that he who sins is led to repentance; just as being always healthy is the best state, but recovering from a disease is also good.

<margin>C</margin>
For this reason He also commands through Solomon: <margin>Proverbs 23</margin> *YOU INDEED strike your son with a rod, and you shall deliver his soul from death.* And again: <margin>Ibid.</margin> *DO NOT SPARE to chastise the boy: correct him with the rod, for he shall not die.* For rebuke and censure—as the Greek name itself, namely, <term>epiplexis <note>original: ἐπίπληξις; literally "striking upon."</note></term> signifies—are the very blows of the soul which chastise sins and prohibit death. They lead those who are carried toward intemperance back to moderation and self-control. <margin><term>epiplexis</term> from <term>to plesso</term> which is "I strike."</note></margin> Certainly, for this reason, Plato—knowing that rebuke possesses the greatest power for correction and is the chief form of purification—suitably said that he who is most impure had turned out uneducated and base because he could not be rebuked, <margin>D</margin> just as it was fitting for him who was to be blessed to be most pure and beautiful. For if magistrates and princes are not a terror to a good work, how shall God, who is good by nature, be a terror to him who does not sin? <margin>Romans 13</margin> *BUT IF you do evil, be afraid,* as the Apostle says. And therefore the Apostle himself, following the likeness of <margin>Ibid.</margin> the Lord, attacked the churches one by one quite sharply, being conscious of his own freedom and the weakness of those who heard him. Thus he says to the Galatians: <margin>Galatians 4</margin> *HAVE I BECOME your enemy by telling you the truth?* Just as those who are healthy have no need of a doctor insofar as they are strong, but those who are sick need the art: so we too, who labor in this life with shameful desires, blameworthy intemperance, lusts, <margin>E</margin> and the inflammations of other vices, have need of a **Savior**. He applies not only smooth and mild medicines, but also sharp ones. Indeed, the bitter roots of fear stop the creeping corrosions of sins. Therefore, fear is salutary, even if it is bitter. Rightly then do we who are sick need a Savior; and we who have wandered, one who will lead us back; and we who are blind, one who leads us to the light; and we who are thirsty, the vital fountain—those who share in it will thirst no more; and we who are dead need life; and as sheep, a shepherd; and as children, an **Instructor**; indeed, all of human nature needs Jesus: lest we who are insolent and sinners fall into the end of condemnation, but rather be separated from the chaff and stored in the Father’s storehouse. <margin>F</margin> <margin>Matthew 3</margin> For the winnowing fan is in the hand of the Lord, by which the chaff destined for the fire <margin>Luke 3</margin> is separated from the wheat. If you wish, it is permitted to learn the supreme wisdom of the most holy Shepherd and Instructor, the almighty and Paternal **Word**, where He uses allegory, calling Himself the Shepherd of the sheep. But He is also the Instructor of infants. He says—

<margin>A</margin>
...I speak through Ezekiel, directing my speech to the Elders, and setting out for them a certain healthy description of just concern: <margin>Ezekiel 34</margin> *AND THAT WHICH is lame I will bind up, and that which is sick I will heal, and that which wanders I will lead back: and I myself will feed them on my holy mountain.* These are the precepts of a good shepherd. Feed us, your infants, like sheep. Yes, Lord, fill us with your pastures of justice. Yes, Instructor <note>original: "Pædagoge"</note>, feed us toward your holy mountain, toward the church: which is on high, which surpasses the clouds, which touches the heavens. <margin>Ibid.</margin> *AND I WILL BE,* he says, *their shepherd, and I will be near them,* like a tunic near their body. He wishes to give health to my flesh, clothing me in a tunic of incorruption, and he has anointed my body. *THEY SHALL CALL ME,* he says, *and I will say, "Behold, I am here."* You have heard us more quickly <margin>Zechariah 13; Isaiah 58. B</margin> than I expected, Lord. *AND IF THEY CROSS OVER, they shall not fall,* says the Lord. For we who cross over to incorruption shall not fall into corruption, since he himself will hold us. For he himself has spoken, and he himself has willed it. Such is our Instructor, <margin>Matthew 20; John 4.</margin> who is good by the best of rights: *I HAVE NOT COME,* he says, *to be served, but that I myself might serve.* Therefore, in the Gospel, Jesus is introduced as one who is weary for our sake, promising to give his own life as a ransom for many. For he alone is confessed to be the "good shepherd." He is therefore generous and magnificent, giving that which is greatest—his own life—for us. He is exceedingly useful to men and kind toward them, because he willed to be a brother as a man, though he could have been their Lord. Indeed, he was even so good as to die for us. Furthermore, his justice cried out: <margin>Jeremiah 7, 17, 18; Malachi 2. C</margin> *IF YOU COME STRAIGHT to me, I also will come straight to you. If you walk crookedly, I too will walk crookedly, says the Lord of hosts,* signifying the rebukes of sinners through these "crooked ways." For his goodness is straight and according to nature—signified by the letter **I** in the name of **Iesu** <note>The Greek letter Iota (Ι) is a single straight vertical stroke, symbolizing the straight path of the Savior’s truth.</note>—which is firm and immovable toward those who have believed by hearing. <margin>Proverbs 1.</margin> *BECAUSE I CALLED, and you did not listen,* says the Lord, *but you made my counsels void; you did not attend to my reproofs.* In this way, the Lord's reproof is most useful. <margin>Psalm 77.</margin> Of these people David also says: *A perverse and exacerbating GENERATION, a generation that did not direct its heart; and its spirit was not faithful with God: and they did not keep the covenant of God, and they refused to walk in his Law.* These are the causes of the "exacerbation" <note>provocation or bitterness</note> because of which the Judge comes to impose penalties on those who did not wish to choose a good life. <margin>D</margin> And for this reason, he dealt with them somewhat more harshly <note>literally "more thickly" or "more roughly"</note> here, if by some means he might pull them back from that momentum by which they are carried toward death. Thus, through David, he speaks the most obvious cause of his threats: <margin>Ibid.</margin> *THEY DID NOT BELIEVE in his wonders. When he slew them, they sought him, and they turned back, and in the morning they kept watch for God, and they remembered that God is their helper, and the Most High God is their redeemer.* Thus he knew that they turned back because of fear, having despised his kindness. For the "Good" is generally despised because it is always beneficial, but that which warns through the fear of "benevolent justice" is revered. Now, there are two kinds of fear. <margin>Ecclesiasticus 30. E</margin> One kind is joined with shame <note>or respect/reverence</note>, which citizens use toward good Princes, and we toward God—just as good and moderate sons behave toward their parents. *For a horse,* it says, *left untamed becomes hard, and a son left to himself becomes headstrong.* The other kind of fear is joined with hatred, which slaves use toward difficult Masters, and which the Hebrews used, who made God a Master rather than a Father. In matters concerning religion and piety, there is a great—even total—difference between that which is spontaneous, free, and voluntary, and that which is done out of necessity. <margin>Psalm 84; Hosea 14.</margin> *FOR HE HIMSELF,* it says, *is merciful, he will heal their sins, and will not destroy, and he will abound so as to turn away his anger, and will not kindle all his indignation.* See how the "justice" of the Instructor is shown in his rebukes, and the "goodness" of God in his mercies. <margin>Psalm 88.</margin> Wherefore David—that is, the Spirit who speaks through him—embracing both, <margin>F</margin> sings of the same God: *JUSTICE and judgment are the preparation of your throne. Mercy and truth shall go before your face.* He confesses that it belongs to the same power both to judge and to do good. For the power of both exists at once: the judgment of the Just One which discerns, and the same one is both Just and Good, who is truly God; who is himself all things, and all things are him, since he is God, who is the only God. Even as a mirror...

<summary>Clement explains how Christ, as the "Good Shepherd" and "Instructor," uses both gentle care and firm justice to lead humanity. He distinguishes between the reverent fear a son has for a father and the fearful hatred a slave has for a harsh master, arguing that God's discipline is always rooted in his goodness.</summary>

# BOOK ONE
33

<margin>A</margin>...it is not an evil for a deformed person that someone shows him what he is like; just as it is not a doctor's fault for announcing a fever to a sick man. For the doctor is not the cause of the fever, but he identifies the fever. Likewise, he who reproves does not wish ill upon the person who is suffering in their soul. He does not add faults to the person, but shows the sins that are present, so that he may turn them away from such pursuits. For this reason, God is indeed good in himself. He is just for our sake, and for that reason, he is also good. What is just, however, he shows to us through his own Word <note>original: "Verbum," referring to the Logos/Christ</note>, from those heights where he was the Father. For before he was the creator, he was God, and he was good; and therefore he willed to be both the Creator and the Father, and that condition and relation of love was the beginning of justice, when he both made his Sun to shine <margin>B</margin> and sent his own Son. And he first announced from the heavens that good justice, saying: <margin>Matthew 24 <note>modern: Matthew 11:27</note></margin> NO ONE knows the Son except the Father, nor the Father except the Son. This reciprocal knowledge, which is repaid in equal measure, is a symbol of ancient justice. Then justice descended to humans, both in writing and in body, in Word <note>original: "Verbo"</note> and in Law, urging human nature toward a saving repentance. For justice was good. But do you not obey God? Ascribe the blame for that to yourself, for you draw the Judge to you.

->*Chapter 10: That the same God, through the same Word, both restrains us from sins by threats and grants salvation to human nature by exhortation.*<-

---

<margin>C</margin><image-desc>Ornate woodcut decorative initial 'S' featuring interlacing vine and knot-work patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>If, therefore, we have shown that the administration involved in guiding human nature is good and saving, and was necessarily taken up by the Word for repentance and the prohibition of sins, we must next consider the Word’s mildness and gentleness. For it has been shown that he is just; he sets forth his own teachings which exhort us to salvation, through which he wishes to signify what is good and beneficial according to the Father's will. Consider these things. The <term>Encomiastic style<gloss>a rhetorical style focused on praise and blame</gloss></term> deals with what is honorable. But the <term>Suasory style<gloss>a rhetorical style focused on persuasion or advice</gloss></term> deals with what is useful. Indeed, the nature and relationship of the Suasory style is hortatory <note>encouraging</note> and dehortatory <note>discouraging</note>. The Encomiastic style, however, is laudatory <note>praising</note> and vituperative <note>censuring</note>. In a certain way, when the Suasory <margin>D</margin> sentiment is applied, it becomes hortatory, and in another way, dehortatory. Similarly, the Encomiastic genre, when applied in one way, is vituperative, and in another, laudatory. In these styles the just Instructor <note>original: "Pædagogus"</note> is most engaged, for he has set before himself as a goal that which is useful to us. But truly, while the vituperative and dehortatory styles have been shown to us before, we must now again approach the Hortatory and Laudatory styles; let us weigh the scales of the just balance as if we were standing at the weighing-scales. <margin>Proverbs 4, 5</margin> The Instructor, therefore, uses exhortation regarding things that are useful in this manner through Solomon: I exhort you, O men, and I give my voice to the sons of men; hear me. For I will speak of excellent things, and so forth. Moreover, he gives counsel on what is salutary, since counsel is suited for choosing <margin>E</margin> and avoiding, just as he does through David, saying: <margin>Psalm 1</margin> BLESSED is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, and has not stood in the way of sinners, and has not sat in the seat of pestilence: but his will is in the Law of the Lord. Now, there are three parts of giving counsel: One, which takes examples from time past, as for example, what happened to the Hebrews who, through the crime of idolatry, <margin>Exodus 32</margin> adored the gold in the calf, and what they suffered when they committed fornication, and similar things. The second is that which is understood from the present time, which is perceived by the senses, like that which was said to those who asked the Lord: "Are you the Christ himself, or do we look for another?" GO, and tell John: the blind see, the deaf hear, the lepers are <margin>Matthew 11</margin> cleansed, the dead rise again, and blessed is he who shall not be offended in me. This <margin>F</margin> therefore was what David said in prophecy: AS we have heard, so also have we seen. <margin>Psalm 47</margin> The third part of giving counsel consists of future things, by which he commands us to beware of what is to happen, just as that which was also said: BUT THOSE WHO have fallen into sins <margin>Matthew 8, 22; Luke 13</margin> shall be cast into outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth, and what follows...

<meta>catchword: Which</meta>

...thousands, so that from all these examples it is clear that the Lord, proceeding through every method of healing, calls human nature to salvation. By consolation, he soothes our sins, indeed lessening our desires, while at the same time offering hope for salvation.

<margin>Ezekiel 18</margin>
For he says through Ezekiel: IF YOU ARE CONVERTED with all your heart and say "Father," I will hear you as a holy people. And again he says: <margin>Matthew 11</margin> COME to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you; and the things that follow, the Lord says in his own person. Most clearly, however, he calls us to goodness through Solo<margin>Proverbs 3</margin>mon, saying: BLESSED is the man who finds wisdom, and the mortal who finds prudence. For what is good is found by the one who seeks it, and is usually seen by the one who finds it. <margin>Jeremiah 31. The Word <note>original: "λόγος" (logos)</note> is reason.</margin> Now indeed, through Jeremiah he also describes prudence: BLESSED are we, O Israel, he says, because the things pleasing to God can be known by us. But they can be known through the Word <note>original: "Verbum," referring to Christ as the Logos</note>, through whom we are blessed and prudent. For prudence and know<margin>Jeremiah 11. Baruch 3. Luke 11.</margin>ledge <term>cognitio</term> are signified by the same Prophet saying: HEAR, O Israel, the mandates of life; listen so that you may know prudence. Through Moses, however, because of his benevolence toward humans, he also promises a gift to those who strive toward salvation. For he says: AND I WILL INTRODUCE you into a good land, which the Lord swore to your Fathers. And furthermore: <margin>Deuteronomy 4, 8. Isaiah 56.</margin> I WILL INTRODUCE you to my holy mountain, and I will fill you with joy, he says through Isaiah. Now indeed there is also another type of Instruction <term>Pedagogy</term>, namely beatifi<margin>Psalm 1</margin>cation: BLESSED is he, he says through David, who has not sinned: and he shall be like a tree planted by the streams of water, which will give its fruit in its season, and its leaf shall not fall away. By this he also silently signified the resurrection. AND ALL THINGS whatsoever he does shall succeed rightly. He wants us to be such, so that we may be blessed. But again, showing that which corresponds to justice on the opposite side of the scale: BUT NOT SO THE UNGODLY, he says, not so, but like the dust which the wind throws from the face of the earth. When the Instructor <note>original: "Paedagogus"</note> had shown the punishments of sins and their easy dissipation (as if blown by winds), he discouraged them from the cause of sin through punishment; and while he had threatened a penalty according to their deserts, he showed the kindness of his own beneficence, so that we might prepare good things for ourselves and enjoy them, rousing us through this with the highest skill.

<margin>Jeremiah 6</margin>
Furthermore, he exhorts us to knowledge through Jeremiah, saying: THE WAY OF GOD, if you had walked in it, you would have lived in peace forever. For by showing them the reward of knowledge, <margin>Ibid.</margin> he rouses the prudent to the love of it. And to the one who has wandered, granting pardon: TURN BACK, turn back, he says, like one who gathers grapes into his basket. You see the good of justice, which advised that one be moved by repentance. <margin>Ibid.</margin> Furthermore, through Jeremiah he illuminates those who wander from the truth: THESE THINGS says the Lord. Stand in the ways, and see, and ask for the eternal paths of the Lord, which path is the good one, and walk in it, and you will find sanctification for your souls. But he leads to repentance for the sake <margin>Jeremiah 18. Ezekiel 18, 33, 36.</margin> of our salvation. Therefore he says: IF YOU REPENT, the Lord will cleanse your heart and the heart of your seed. I could indeed bring forward the Philosophers in defense of this question, who say that only the one who is perfect is praiseworthy, while the one who is evil is blameworthy. <margin>E</margin> But since some slander that which is "blessed" <note>A reference to the Epicurean view that God is too "blessed" to care about human affairs</note>, as if it neither has any trouble itself nor causes any to others—not understanding his benevolence toward men—it is for their sake, and for the sake of those who do not attribute justice to what is good, that what we have said was added. For it would follow that we should say the rebuking and blaming kind of instruction <term>Pedagogy</term> is suitable for humans, since they say all men are fools, and only God is wise—from whom comes wisdom—and he alone is perfect, and therefore he alone is also praiseworthy. But I do not use this speech. I say, therefore, that praise and blame, or what is similar to praise and blame, are medicines most necessary for humans. Those, therefore, who are difficult to cure are driven like iron by fire, hammer, and anvil: that is, by threats, reproof, <margin>F</margin> and rebuke. But those who attend to faith itself, as if taught by themselves and driven by the free choice of the mind, are increased by praise. For virtue, once praised, grows just like a tree. Understanding this, it seems to me that the Samian Pythagoras gave this instruction.

# BOOK ONE

<margin>A</margin>
*Do not rejoice in doing things that are evil, but in doing good.*
Rebuking <note>original: "reprehendere"</note> is also called admonition, which in Greek is <term>νουθέτησις (nouthesis)</term>. The etymology of "admonition" is <term>νοῦ εἰσθετισμός (nou eisthetismos)</term>, which means "putting into the mind"; it is a type of correction intended to produce understanding in the mind. Furthermore, countless other precepts can be found concerning the pursuit of good and the avoidance of evil: <margin>Isaiah 48, Proverbs 1.</margin> "THERE is no peace for the wicked," says the Lord. Therefore, through Solomon, He instructs children: "MY SON, do not let sinners lead you into error, nor walk in the paths with them, if they urge you, saying: 'Come with us, let us share in innocent blood; let us hide the just man unjustly in the earth, let us take him from our midst like the grave takes the living.'"

<margin>B</margin>
This, therefore, is also a prophecy concerning the passion of the Lord. Furthermore, through Ezekiel, He provides us with the mandates of life. <margin>Ezekiel 18.</margin> "THE SOUL that sins shall die: but the man who is just, who does what is right, shall live. He does not eat upon the mountains, he does not cast his eyes upon the thoughts of the house of Israel, he does not defile his neighbor’s wife, he does not approach a woman in her period of impurity, he does not oppress a man with power, he returns the debtor’s pledge, he does not commit robbery, he gives his bread to the hungry, and covers the naked with a garment. He does not lend money at usury, he does not take a profit, he turns his hand away from iniquity, and executes true judgment between a man and his neighbor. He has walked in my precepts and kept my justifications to do them. This man is just; he shall surely live," says the Lord.

<margin>C</margin>
These things contain the description of the instruction of the Christian life, a fitting exhortation to the blessed life, and the reward of that life: eternal life.

## How the Word performed the office of the Instructor through the Law and the Prophets. Chapter XI.

<margin>D</margin>
<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'E' containing a scene with classical or biblical figures in a landscape with foliage and architectural elements.</image-desc>
The manner of His benevolence and instruction <note>original: "pædagogiæ"</note> toward humanity has been shown, as far as we were able to express it. Therefore, beautifully explaining Himself, He compared Himself to a grain of mustard seed, <margin>Matthew 13.</margin> signifying that in the word which is sown, there is a spiritual element, a multifaceted nature, and a magnificence and sanctity of rational power. Moreover, there is a <margin><term>δριμύτης (drimytēs)</term> <note>meaning pungency or sharpness</note></margin>—a biting quality of rebuke—and a capacity for cleansing that is useful because of its sharpness. Thus, through this tiny grain, which is used allegorically, He bestows a great deal of salvation upon the whole of human nature. For while honey is the sweetest of things, it generates bile, just as that which is "good" can lead to contempt, which is a cause of sinning. Mustard, however, diminishes bile (that is, anger) and cuts through phlegm (that is, arrogance and pride). From this Word comes true health of the soul and an eternal, good temperament. Long ago, through Moses, the Word performed the office of the Instructor <note>original: "Pædagogi"</note>. Then He did so through the Prophets. Indeed, Moses was also a Prophet. <margin>Exodus 32.</margin> For the Law is an "Instruction" for insolent boys who are not easily held back by reins.

<margin>E</margin>
"BEING SATED, therefore," he says, "they rose up to play." In Greek, the word for "sated" is <margin>1 Corinthians 10.</margin> <term>χορτασθέντες (chortasthentes)</term>, which is like saying "filled with hay." This is because he does not call the fullness of food "sustenance" for those devoid of reason, but rather <term>χόρτασμα (chortasma)</term>, meaning "fodder" or "animal feed." Because they were sated without reason and played without reason, the Law and fear followed them to cut away their sins and to urge them toward honorable things and virtuous behavior. This prepared their ears to obey the true Instructor, who is the one and the same Word <note>original: "Verbum," referring to the Logos</note> who harmonizes with the Law that urged them. For Paul says <margin>Galatians 3.</margin> the Law was given as an "Instructor" <note>often translated as "tutor" or "schoolmaster"</note> to lead us to Christ. Thus, from this it is clear that there is only one who is true, good, and just: the Son who is in the image and likeness of the Father, Jesus, the Word of God. He is our Instructor, to whom God has handed us over, just as a benevolent Father commits and commends his children to a true and natural Instructor, so that He might clearly instruct us.

<margin>F</margin>
"THIS IS my beloved Son, listen to him." The divine Instructor is worthy of our trust, being adorned with three beautiful things: knowledge, benevolence, and freedom of speech. <margin>Matthew 17.</margin> He possesses knowledge because He is the Wisdom of the Father. For all wisdom is from the Lord, and...

### That the Instructor appropriately used fatherly affection, severity, and kindness.
### Chapter XII.

<margin>B</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative historiated initial 'H' featuring a seated figure, likely a scholar or teacher, in a classical setting.</image-desc>
Having completed these matters, it follows that our Instructor, Jesus, should describe the true life for us and train the person who is in Christ. His form and character are neither excessively difficult, nor so lax as to be indulgent through kindness. At the same time, He gives commands and impresses the character of those commands so that they can be fulfilled. And indeed, He seems to me to have driven out the [old] man, but to have regenerated him by the **word** <margin>word <note>original Greek: ῥήματι (rhēmati)</note></margin>, and increased him by the spirit. Through the Word <note>original: "Verbum," referring to the Logos/Christ</note>, He has instructed us in the manner of a teacher, directing us by holy precepts toward the adoption and salvation of children. Thus, when He had transformed the one born of earth <margin>Genesis 1.</margin> into a holy and heavenly person at His coming, He would fully fulfill that divine voice: LET US MAKE man in our image and likeness. And Christ was indeed the fulfillment of what God said. But the other <margin>C</margin> man is understood only through the image. 

We, therefore, O children of the good Father, pupils of the good Instructor, let us fulfill the Father’s will. Let us listen to the Word and express the truly salvific life of our Savior, practicing here the heavenly form of living. Through this, having been made gods <note>The concept of "Theosis" or deification, where humans become like God through grace and virtue.</note>, let us be anointed with the ever-blooming joy and the incorruptible perfume of good fragrance, having the form of the Lord's life as clear evidence of incorruptibility, and following in the footsteps of God. To Him alone it belongs to consider, and He alone cares for, how and by what means the life of humanity may be made healthier. 

Furthermore, He prepares us for this so that we are easily content with food and neglect what is superfluous. Ready, unencumbered, and prepared for the eternity of a good life, He teaches each of us to be the provider of our own needs. DO NOT BE ANXIOUS, <margin>D</margin> He says, about tomorrow, <margin>Matthew 6.</margin> saying that the one enrolled in Christ's number must be content with his lot, serving himself by himself, and choosing enough food for the day. For we are trained not for war, but for peace. War indeed requires great preparation, and luxury requires great and lavish expense. But peace and love—sisters who are simple and flee from strife and business—need neither weapons nor lavish preparation. Their nourishment is the Word. 

The Word is the one to whom the leadership of demonstrating and teaching has fallen, from whom we learn frugality, simplicity, and the rejection of pride, the love of liberty, kindness, and the pursuit of honor. And if we are made like God in a single word through the union of virtue, we must not turn to sluggishness or <margin>E</margin> negligence, but work hard; do not grow weary. For you will be what you do not expect, nor could you even guess. 

Just as there is one way of life for philosophers, another for orators, and another for wrestlers, so there is a noble and liberal disposition, fitting for the free will of the soul that is studious of honor, which comes from the Instruction of Christ. Those who have been taught to act with honor and gravity—in their walking, sitting, eating, sleeping, lying down, and their whole way of life and discipline—reflect this. For this kind of upbringing by the Word is not overly intense or violent, but moderate, remaining within a just and right course. 

In this way, the Savior was called the Word, who found these verbal and rational <margin>F</margin> medicines <note>A play on the Greek "Logos," which means both "Word" and "Reason."</note> for humanity’s salvation, so that we might be endowed with good and sound sense. He observes the opportunity, rebuking harm and offense, explaining the causes of the soul’s affections, and cutting out the roots of irrational desires, commanding what we must abstain from, and offering all the antidotes of salvation to the sick. For this is the greatest and most royal work of God: to save human

# BOOK ONE
37

<margin>A</margin> ...nature. Patients are indeed angry with a physician who provides no advice for their health; how then can they not admit they owe the greatest thanks to the Divine Instructor <note>The "Divine Instructor" refers to the Logos, or Christ.</note>, who does not remain silent, nor keep within the hidden places of the soul those threats which lead away from destruction? Instead, He reproves those threats, cuts away the desires that lead toward them, and teaches what belongs to the right administration of the community. Therefore, great thanks must be given to Him. For what else do we say a "rational animal"—that is, a human being—ought to do, other than contemplate that which is divine? Furthermore, I say that he ought to consider human nature as well, and to live just as truth commands and dictates, admiring the Instructor and His precepts in a wondrous way, as they <margin>B</margin> agree and harmonize with one another. Since we must adapt ourselves to this Instructor, it is fitting that we, as His image and likeness, live in such a way that our speech truly matches our deeds.

### That just as what is done rightly and according to virtue is done through right reason, so conversely, sin is contrary to reason. Chapter XIII.

<margin>C</margin> <image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter Q featuring a landscape with architectural ruins and foliage.</image-desc>WHATEVER is contrary to right reason is sin. For the philosophers <note>Clement is referring here to the Stoics, who defined emotions as "perturbations" of reason.</note> believe that the general affections or disturbances of the soul should be defined in this way: Lust is a desire that does not obey reason; Fear is a collapse of the soul that does not obey reason; Pleasure is an elation of the soul that does not obey reason. If, therefore, disobedience toward reason generates sin, how does obedience to reason—which we call faith—not necessarily produce and <margin>"The Word" (logos/ratio) is necessarily used here to mean the Son of God.</margin> bring forth that which is called honorable and fitting? For virtue itself is a harmonious and consistent state of the soul, which is subject to reason throughout one's whole life. Furthermore, what is the highest of all, they define Philosophy itself as the "Study of Right Reason," so that whatever happens through an error of reason is necessarily a fault. It is rightly called in Greek *hamartēma* <note>original Greek: ἁμάρτημα</note>, which means an "error" or "sin." Indeed, when the first man sinned and did not obey God, man was compared to a lustful horse <note>The Latin text uses "EQUVS ad coitum" to emphasize animalistic instinct over human reason.</note>; having wandered away from reason, he was rightly considered to be without reason <margin>D</margin> and compared to the beasts. Hence Wisdom also says: <margin>Jeremiah 5:8</margin> *They were as fed horses in the morning: every one neighed after his neighbor's wife.* And therefore it adds: *He neighs after whoever sits upon him.* It no longer says "the man speaks," for he who sins against reason is no longer a partaker of reason, but is a beast without reason, given over to desires, in whom all pleasures take root. However, that which is done rightly and according to virtue out of obedience to reason, the Stoics call "the fitting" <note>original Greek: προσῆκον (prosēkon)</note> and "duty" <note>original Greek: καθῆκον (kathēkon)</note>, that is, what is consistent and appropriate. Therefore, what is becoming and consistent—namely, duty—is also appropriate. Obedience is founded upon commandments. These commandments are the same as admonitions; they propose truth as their goal and aim for the ultimate desired end. The end of <margin>E</margin> piety and religion is eternal rest in God. Moreover, the beginning of eternity is our end. Therefore, that which is an honorable deed of piety, done rightly and virtuously, is what is becoming and appropriate; it brings about "duty" through works. Thus, duties rightly consist in actions, not in mere words. Indeed, the action of a Christian is the operation of a rational soul, resulting from a sincere and prudent judgment and a desire for truth, which is carried out through the connected help of the body. What is becoming—I mean "duty"—is the single will in life that follows God and Christ, which conducts itself rightly and virtuously for the sake of eternal life. For the life of Christians, which we are now establishing, is a certain assembly and gathering of rational actions: that is, an operation taught by the Word <note>original Latin: "ratione," here meaning the Logos</note> that does not stumble, which we have called faith. This assembly and gathering are the commandments of the Lord, which, <margin>F</margin> since they are divine pronouncements and spiritual warnings, are written for us so that they may fit well for both ourselves and our neighbors. Furthermore, these things also return to us...

[the previous actions] are used, just like a ball which, because of the rebound, returns to the one who throws it. From this also arise those things which are becoming and suitable—namely, the duties <note>original: "officia," referring to the Stoic concept of "kathekon" or appropriate actions</note> necessary for the divine Instruction, as they have been commanded by God and handed down for our salvation. And since among those things which are necessary, some pertain only to leading this life here, while others truly raise and lift us up so that we may live well both here and there; consequently, some duties are ordered toward living, and others toward living rightly. Therefore, whatever things are commanded for living like the pagans <note>original: "gentiliter viuendum," referring to the lifestyle of non-Christians or "Gentiles"</note> are commonly published among the masses. But those things which are suitable for living well, from which that eternal life is acquired, may be considered here as if sketched out from the Scriptures themselves by those who collect them.

# SCHOLIA
<note>Scholia are ancient or medieval marginal notes and commentaries used to explain a primary text.</note>

->Chapter II.<-

<margin>C</margin> <margin>c</margin> **IN THE FIGURE.** *That phrase, "in the figure," is not to be understood as those who introduced "phantasm" or "vision" wanted it to be, but as Paul understood it. For Paul himself, saying: "Found in appearance as a man," <note>Philippians 2:7</note> frees us from the error of the Docetists <note>original: "Docitarum," an early Christian sect that believed Jesus's body was an illusion or "phantasm" rather than physical flesh</note> who establish a phantasmal body in Christ. Paul signifies that just as He was a true man, He also took on the true form of a man.*

<margin>b</margin> *The faculty of reasoning is located in the brain, anger in the heart, and desire in the liver.* <note>This reflects the ancient Greek "tripartite" theory of the soul, famously described by Plato and later adopted by medical writers like Galen.</note>

->Chapter III.<-

<margin>D</margin> <margin>a</margin> *IF INDEED. For since God, in His own wisdom which cannot be grasped, foresaw that this world would decline toward destruction and would necessarily have need of being corrected; lest He should have established such a great work in vain, He judged that it would not happen otherwise than through the handling of His one creation—using that creation as an instrument, as it were, to correct that which had fallen. Therefore, He first established man, a work worthy of His own reformation, through whom the will of His economy <note>original: "oeconomia," meaning God's plan or management of the world</note>—which surpasses all reason—was fulfilled.*

<margin>b</margin> **THE WORD OF FAITH.** *That is, the Lord is the confirmation of those things which are spoken.*

->Chapter V.<-

<margin>E</margin> <margin>a</margin> *The Gospel does not have it thus; for it says: "To what shall I compare this generation?" and subjoins the Parable of the children playing in the marketplace.* <note>Referencing Matthew 11:16-17.</note>

<margin>b</margin> *Nor does the Book of the Lord have it this way, for it does not say that the Lambs stood at the right hand, but the Sheep.* <note>A textual correction regarding the imagery in Matthew 25:33.</note>

->Arethas the Archbishop<-
<note>Arethas of Caesarea (c. 860–935) was a prominent Byzantine scholar and commentator.</note>

<margin>F</margin> <margin>a</margin> *Binding his foal to the vine, and his donkey's colt to the choice vine. <note>Genesis 49:11</note> He calls the "foal" the new people of the Christian commonwealth. The "Vine" refers to the People who, from the Mosaic Law and its planting, used to boast of their knowledge of God. And that this is so, Isaiah the son of Amoz and David the son of Jesse can be witnesses worthy of faith. From these, the former says: "The Vines of the Lord are the House of Israel"; and David, the son of Jesse, says: "You have transplanted a Vine out of Egypt." <note>Isaiah 5:7 and Psalm 80:8</note> To this vine, the present discourse says He binds His foal—He himself who, when those to whom the command from the tribe of Judah fell were failing, was to be the one who would preside. He was to be the "expectation of the nations" <note>Genesis 49:10</note>; yet, because He is the expectation of the nations, He does not alienate or abolish the confirmed glory of the Old Testament. Rather, because He hoped that He would suppress pagan superstition, He abolished none of the Legal rituals. Hence, the first preachers of the faith in Christ—as those who were still said to belong to the Mosaic Pedagogy <note>The "Mosaic Pedagogy" refers to the laws and customs given to Moses as a preparatory education for the Gospel.</note>—thought that nothing of the Old Testament ought to be abolished by the New: not circumcision, nor the keeping of the Sabbath, nor abstinence from certain foods.*

<margin>A</margin> ...abstinence. Specifically, they demonstrate that this is the "foal" which must be bound to the vine. <note>This refers to Genesis 49:11, a prophecy often interpreted by early Christians as Christ (the vine) and the Gentiles or the soul (the foal).</note> And these matters remained in this state until James, the brother of the Lord according to the flesh, and the divine Apostle Paul, cut away the excessive purification and the overly anxious concern regarding foods from the Law. For the Gentiles, they permitted the "ship" to be steered by only a very few rules—namely, that they should abstain from sexual immorality, things sacrificed to idols, and from what is strangled. <note>This refers to the Council of Jerusalem in Acts 15, where the Apostles decided which Jewish laws Gentile converts must follow.</note> This happened when the one who was predicted to be bound to the vine’s tendrils—the "foal"—arrived for his work. He is now freed from the yoke of the Law and brought into a free commonwealth.

### Chapter VI.

<margin>a</margin> Gregory, surnamed "the Theologian," <note>Gregory of Nazianzus (c. 329–390 AD), one of the great Cappadocian Fathers.</note> took his method of treatment from these points in his Oration titled *On the Holy Lights*. <note>original Greek: εἰς φῶτα (Eis phōta). <margin>b</margin> This also agrees with the Prophecy of Jeremiah which says: *All shall know me, from the least of them to the greatest.* <note>Jeremiah 31:34.</note>

<margin>C</margin> <margin>c</margin> **BUT THAT ALSO.** Regarding what the Apostle said about "words which it is not lawful for a man to speak," <note>2 Corinthians 12:4, where Paul describes his vision of Paradise.</note> it should not be understood as meaning that the things he said must be kept silent. For how could that be, since he himself brings forth many such things in his own Epistles? For who was not an Apostle while Christ was active in this life of ours? How can he say: *I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you?* <note>1 Corinthians 11:23.</note> And again: *concerning virgins, I have no command of the Lord?* <note>1 Corinthians 7:25.</note> Therefore, "it is not lawful" does not mean it must not be announced, but rather that those things were spoken with such authority and dignity that human nature cannot fully attain or replicate them. This is confirmed by what is said in the Gospel about the Teaching of Christ: that he taught the crowds with power, and not like the Scribes and Pharisees (who taught, it is implied, with mere flattery).

### Chapter IX.

<margin>D</margin> <margin>a</margin> **FEAR IS TWOFOLD.** There is one kind of fear that initiates, which actually converts a person; this is the fear felt by those who turn away from sins because they dread punishment. But there is another kind which "perfects" or completes us, about which David also says: *Fear the Lord, all you his saints, for nothing is lacking to those who fear him.* <note>Psalm 34:9.</note>

### Chapter X.

<margin>a</margin> **FATHER.** And how does Gregory of Nyssa, in his exposition of the Lord’s Prayer, say that those held by sins—if they say "Our Father"—call not the good God "Father," but rather an adversary? This is because they either are not truly converted so as to call Him Father, or they do not do so with their whole heart.

# THE INSTRUCTOR BY CLEMENT

## BOOK TWO.

### How one ought to conduct oneself regarding food. Chapter 1.

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>B</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut drop cap 'P' featuring floral motifs and a background landscape.</image-desc>
THEREFORE, the goal and the aim we have set for the following 
sections must be described in summary: we must present the 
scriptures to those who love the part of Instruction <note>original: "Paedagogiae" — referring to the divine guidance of the soul.</note> that will 
be useful for life, explaining what sort of person the one who is 
called a Christian ought to be throughout their entire life. We 
must, then, begin with ourselves and how we ought to compose 
and moderate ourselves. Thus, for those considering the 
balance and moderation of a composed person, we must speak 
on how each of us should behave toward our own body, or 
rather, how we should direct it. For when someone—having 
been led by reason away from external things and from the 
mere physical training of the body toward the mind—has 
learned accurately and perfectly to contemplate the things 
<margin>C</margin>
that happen in a human being according to nature, they will know that effort should not be 
bestowed on external things. Rather, it is proper to a human being to purify the eye of the 
soul and to keep their own flesh chaste and holy. For he who has been purely cleansed 
and freed from those things through which he is still dust, what else would he have within 
himself more conducive to entering the right way toward the comprehension of God? 
Indeed, other people live to eat—which certainly also happens to animals devoid of reason, 
for whom life is nothing but the belly—but the Instructor commands us to eat so that we 
may live. For pleasure is neither our task, nor our purpose, nor our goal; rather, nutrition 
is for the sake of our stay here on earth, which reason has established for the sake of 
incorruption. And for this reason, food is to be sorted and selected. It is simple, and not 
to be obtained with too much effort or too much curiosity; rather, it is the truth, fitting and 
<margin>D</margin>
applied to simple and least inquisitive "children." <note>original: "puellis" — while literally "girls," Clement often uses this term to refer to the innocent or the "children of God" regardless of gender.</note> This is because food should be 
suitable for living, not for luxury and delights. Living itself is made of two things: 
health and strength; for which the accessibility of food is most suitable, as it is useful 
for digestion and the lightness of the body. From these come growth, health, and 
<margin><term>Base eating</term> <note>original Greek: αἰσχροφαγία (aischrophagia) — referring to gluttony or shameful eating habits.</note></note>
just strength—not the unjust, slippery, and miserable kind, such as those that come

# THE INSTRUCTOR
<meta>catchword: of joy</meta>

...these insatiable, worried, and anxious seekers of food, who entangle the world in their delights and pleasures, <margin>A</margin> surrounding themselves everywhere with the sound of hissing frying pans, and spending their entire lives around the spoon and mortar—voracious and indeed all-consuming men, catching hold of food just as fire catches fuel. Moreover, they even weaken simple and easily obtained food, namely bread, by sifting out the nourishing part of the grain, so that what is a necessary nutrient becomes a shameful luxury. Among men, however, delicate gluttony has no limit. For it has progressed into pastries, cakes, and sweets, finding a multitude of additions to lunches and dinners, and hunting for every possible quality of flavor. But it seems to me that a man of this sort is nothing other than <margin>Proverbs 23</margin> <margin>B</margin> a mouth or a jaw; **DO NOT DESIRE**, however, says the Scripture, the food of the rich. For these things are joined to a life that is not true and is shameful. For they bestow their effort on side dishes which the dung receives shortly after; but for us who hunt for heavenly food, it is necessary to rule the belly <margin>1 Corinthians 6</margin> which is under heaven, and much more so to rule those things which are friendly and pleasing to it: **WHICH** God will destroy, says the Apostle, rightly cursing the greedy desires of the throat. For life depends on the belly, from which this fleshly life—the kind that brings destruction—hangs; <margin>In Clement’s time, some called lunches and banquets "agapai," that is, charities.</margin> some dare to call this "charity" <note>original: "agapas" — a Greek term for the highest form of love, also used for communal Christian meals.</note>, using an unbridled tongue, namely by calling certain little lunches that smell of steam and broth by the beautiful and salvific name of the Word's work. They do wrong to sanctified charity with little pots and flowing broth, pursuing that name with a curse through drinking, delights, and smoke. They are deceived in their estimation, as those who expected to be able to buy the promised kingdom with little lunches. For regarding those gatherings which are made for the sake of joy, <margin>C</margin> we might also rightly call this assembly "refreshments," "little suppers," "lunches," or "feasts," following reason. These feasts, however, the Lord did not call <term>agapai</term> <note>original: "αγαπας" — Clement is distinguishing between a common meal and the spiritual concept of Love.</note>, that is, charities. <margin>Luke 14</margin> Thus He says in one place: **WHEN** you are invited to a wedding, do not sit in the first place, but when you are called, sit in the last place. And in another place: **WHEN** you make a lunch or a supper. And again: **BUT WHEN** you make a feast, invite the beggars, for which reason a supper is most especially to be made. <margin>Ibid.</margin> And furthermore: **A CERTAIN MAN** made a great supper, and invited many. But I perceive from where the grand name for these suppers flowed: namely, from the throat. "The fan of the madness of lunches," says the Comic poet. For truly, for many people, many things exist for the sake of the supper. For they have not yet learned that God prepared food and drink for His own work—I mean for man—for the purpose <margin>D</margin> of preservation, but not for the purpose of being affected by pleasure. For it is not even naturally implanted in bodies that they should be helped by a manifold variety of foods. On the contrary, those who use the cheapest foods are altogether stronger, healthier, and more noble: as servants are to their masters, and farmers to their landlords; and they are not only stronger, but also wiser, as Philosophers are to the rich. For they have not overwhelmed their minds with nutrients, nor have they deceived the mind with pleasures. Charity, however, is truly heavenly nourishment, a rational feast: <margin>1 Corinthians 13</margin> **IT ENDURES ALL THINGS**, it bears all things, it hopes all things; charity never fails. Blessed is he who eats a meal in the kingdom of God. But it is the gravest fall of all if that charity which cannot fail is cast down from the heavens above into the broths of the earth. And do you think I consider that a supper which is to be destroyed? <margin>Ibid.</margin> <margin>Matthew 22</margin> <margin>E</margin> **IF I DISTRIBUTE**, he says, my possessions, but have not charity, I am nothing. On this universal charity depend the Law and the Word, if you love the Lord your God and your neighbor. In the heavens, however, is this heavenly banquet, which in Greek is called <term>agape</term> <note>original: "αγαπα"</note> from a "good sitting" <note>Clement uses a wordplay here; the Greek "agape" (love) sounds similar to "agathe sesis" (good sitting/assembly).</note>. The earthly version, however, is called a supper, as has been shown from Scripture; and a supper is indeed made for the sake of charity, but the supper is not charity itself; rather, it is a sign of social benevolence and of one who willingly imparts what is theirs. Therefore, let not that which is our good be attacked by curses: **FOR THE KINGDOM OF GOD IS NOT** food and drink, <margin>Romans 14</margin> says the Apostle (so that a fleeting and momentary lunch may be understood), **BUT JUSTICE**, and peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. He who eats of this meal will possess the best of those things which exist, namely the kingdom of God, having practiced here for the holy <margin>F</margin> assembly of charity, which is the heavenly Church. Charity, therefore, is a pure thing and worthy of God; its work, truly, is communication. Moreover, charity is the care of discipline, as Wisdom says: <margin>Wisdom 6</margin> **CHARITY** is indeed the observation of her laws. These are the things of joy...

<summary>Clement of Alexandria distinguishes between the holy concept of "Agape" (spiritual love/charity) and the physical act of banqueting, arguing that true Christian nourishment is found in the Spirit and the Word rather than in luxurious food.</summary>

# BOOK TWO 43
d iiii

<margin>A</margin> ...of joy have a certain incentive to charity from public nourishment, which accustoms us to eternal delight. Charity, therefore, is not a dinner. Rather, let the feast depend on charity. For he says, "Learn, your children whom you have loved, O Lord, that it is not the <margin>Deuteronomy 8</margin> types of fruit that nourish man, but your word preserves those who believe in you"; for the just man shall not live by bread alone. But let our supper be light and quickly prepared, suitable for keeping watch <note>Clement values "vigils" or late-night prayers, which are difficult if one has overeaten.</note>, unmixed with diverse qualities, and in no way foreign to the discipline of the Instructor. For charity is a good nurse for fellowship and communication, possessing a plentiful provision for the journey—namely, sufficiency—which, when set over nourishment in a just and measured quantity, administers the body healthily and even distributes <margin>B</margin> something from it to our neighbors.

However, a diet that overflows and overwhelms sufficiency greatly harms a man: it renders the soul sluggish and inert, while making the body sickly and prone to falling into diseases. Furthermore, those pleasures which are anxious and difficult when it comes to judging spiced and seasoned dishes brand one with disgrace and curses. These include daintiness, gluttony, greed, voracity, insatiability, and other such things. Flies also most aptly correspond to these names, as do weasels, flatterers, gladiators, and that monstrous tribe of parasites: some sell their reason for the pleasure of the belly, others their friendship, and others even their life itself—crawling upon their bellies, beasts in the likeness of men, made in the image of their father, that gluttonous and voracious beast. And those who called them prodigals—which in Greek is <term>asotous</term> <note>original: "ἀσώτους"</note>—well <margin>C</margin> seem to me to have signaled their end. For they understood them as <term>asotous</term>—that is, "alienated from salvation" <note>Clement is using a Greek pun: "asōtos" (prodigal) sounds like "a-sōtos" (unsaved or without health).</note>—through the removal of the letter 's'. 

For are they not like those who busy themselves with pots and multiple varieties of exquisite seasonings, who are of a low and abject mind, clearly children of the earth, who hunt for their daily food as if they were not going to live? The Holy Spirit pronounces them miserable through Isaiah, since the name of Charity had gradually been taken from them in some way, because the feast was not consistent with reason: <margin>Isaiah 22</margin> **BUT THEY** made joy, killing calves and sacrificing sheep, saying: "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die." And because he considers such delights a sin, he adds: **AND THIS** sin of yours shall not be forgiven until you have died. He does not mean that death is the forgiveness of sin <margin>D</margin> without feeling; rather, he is setting apart the retribution for sin—which is indeed death—from salvation. **DO NOT REJOICE**, however, in execrable delights, says Wisdom. <margin>Proverbs 4; Ecclesiasticus 2</margin> 

Here, mention must also be made of things sacrificed to idols—that is, those things offered to false gods—since he now commands us to abstain from them. Those things seem to me execrable and abominable, over whose blood they fly. Underneath is Erebus <note>A mythological place of darkness or the underworld.</note> and the souls now deprived of this light. **FOR I DO NOT** <margin>1 Corinthians 10</margin> wish you to become participants with demons, says the Apostle. For the nourishments of those who are saved and those who perish are separate. We must therefore abstain from these things, not because we are afraid—for there is no power in them—but for the sake of our conscience, which is holy, and for the sake of <margin>E</margin> those who indiscriminately judge many things and fear weakness, by which their infirm conscience is defiled. 

**FOR FOOD** <margin>1 Corinthians 8; Matthew 15; 1 Corinthians 8</margin> will not commend us to God. Nor do **THOSE THINGS** which enter defile a man, but those which come out of the mouth, he says. For the use of nourishment is indifferent: **FOR NEITHER** if we eat, he says, do we have more; nor if we do not eat, do we lack. But it is not fitting for those of us who have been deemed worthy of divine and spiritual nourishment to be participants at the table of demons. **DO WE NOT HAVE** <margin>Ibid. 9</margin> the power to eat and drink, says the Apostle, and to lead about women? <note>Referring to the Apostle Paul's mention of the right to be accompanied by a wife.</note> But, ruling over pleasures, we certainly restrain our desires. <margin>Ibid. 8</margin> See to it, then, that this power of ours does not bring an offense to the weak. We must not, therefore, like those living prodigally and profusely—as in the Gospel parable of the rich man's son—abuse the <margin>F</margin> <margin>Luke 15</margin> gifts of the Father, but use them as those who constantly rule over them. For we were ordained to hold kingship and dominion over food, not to be its servants. It is therefore a noble thing and greatly to be desired, looking up at that which is true, to pursue heavenly nourishment and to be filled with the inexhaustible sight of that which truly exists—firm, stable, and pure...

### THE INSTRUCTOR, BOOK II.

<margin>A</margin> ...enjoying pleasure. For the food of Christ shows that we ought to embrace this charity <note>The Latin *charitatem* refers to the *Agape* or "love-feast," a communal meal in the early church intended to foster fellowship rather than gluttony.</note>. It is completely contrary to reason and not human at all to be nourished for death, fattened like cattle; looking down toward the earth, always stooping from the ground over tables, pursuing a luxurious and delicate life, burying that which is good here in a life that will not last, and flattering only the devouring of food—a practice because of which cooks are held in higher value than farmers. We do not forbid the serving of various dishes, but we view the descent into such habits as a calamity. Therefore, luxury must be avoided by those who take only the few things that are necessary. And if any of the unbelievers invites us and we decide to go: <margin>1 Cor. 10</margin> <margin>B</margin>—for it is good not to associate with insolent men—the Apostle commands us to eat whatever is set before us, asking no questions for the sake of conscience. Similarly, he commanded us to buy what is in the market without any scruple or curious investigation. Therefore, we should not entirely abstain from various foods, but we should not place our focus upon them. We should take what is served, as becomes a Christian, honoring the one who invited us through a harmless and moderate participation in conversation and company. We should consider the costly dishes brought in as indifferent <term>indifferent (Greek: adiaphora)</term><note>A Stoic term for things that are neither morally good nor bad in themselves, but depend on how they are used.</note>, despising the delicacies as things that will soon cease to be. <margin>Rom. 14</margin> **HE WHO EATS**, let him not despise him who does not eat. And he who does not eat, let him not judge him who eats. As he progresses a little further, he also explains the reason for the precept. <margin>C</margin> **HE WHO EATS**, he says, eats for the Lord, and gives thanks to God. And he who does not eat, for the Lord he does not eat, and gives thanks to God. So let thanksgiving be our just nourishment. Furthermore, he who always gives thanks is not occupied with pleasures. And if we invite some guests for the sake of neighborliness, we must all the more abstain from these refined and delicate foods, showing ourselves as an example, just as we have Christ as our example. <margin>1 Cor. 8</margin> **IF ANYTHING**, for instance, of such food offends a brother, I will never eat, he says, lest I offend my brother. <margin>Ibid. 9</margin> By a small amount of restraint, I gain a man. <margin>Ibid. 8</margin> **DO WE NOT** have the power to eat and drink? **AND WE KNOW THE TRUTH**, he says, that an idol is nothing in the world, but there is in truth only one God, our Father, from whom are <margin>D</margin> all things, and one Lord Jesus. But by your knowledge, he says, the weak brother for whom Christ died has perished. But those who wound the conscience of weak brothers sin against Christ. By this reasoning, the Apostle, taking care for us, distinguishes between types of suppers: <margin>Ibid. 5</margin> commanding us **NOT TO ASSOCIATE**, if anyone who is called a brother is found to be a fornicator, or an adulterer, or an idolater; with such a person, do not even eat, suspecting the speech or the food that comes from there as having defilement, just like the "tables of demons." Both he and the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras, known for their strict dietary rules, including vegetarianism and avoiding wine, believing it kept the soul "clear."</note> admit that it is good neither to eat meat nor drink wine. For this is more the mark of a wild beast, and the steam that rises from them, being thicker and more turbulent, darkens the soul. But if someone does partake of them, he does not sin, provided he partakes moderately and temperately, not being overly devoted to them or dependent on them, <margin>Rom. 14</margin> <margin>E</margin> nor devouring and gulping down delicacies. For a voice will sound to him, saying: **DO NOT DESTROY THE WORK OF GOD FOR THE SAKE OF FOOD.** It is the mark of a fool to be greatly amazed and stunned by the things served at public feasts, especially after you have tasted the delights perceived through the Word; it is even more foolish to be seen as a slave to side-dishes, to the point that one rises—so to speak—at their smells, almost throwing one's face into the pots, peering out from one's seat as if from a nest, so that (as the common saying goes) they may catch the wandering steam through their breathing. How is it not contrary to reason to dip one's hands into seasonings, or to perpetually stretch them toward the delicacies, not in the manner of those tasting, but snatching them immoderately <margin>F</margin> and filling oneself in an unseemly way? For one may see those who are like this being compared to swine or dogs because of their voracity, rather than to men; who are in such a hurry to be satiated that both cheeks are inflated at once, the vessels on the face are raised, and moreover, sweat is poured out because they are tightly packed by their insatiability and because of...

### BOOK TWO

<margin>A</margin> On account of their intemperance, they pant with an unseemly haste that is far removed from honorable custom; they thrust nourishment into their bellies as if they were storing up provisions for a journey <note>Latin: *viaticum*, referring to the supplies or money one takes when traveling</note> rather than for digestion. And while immoderation is always an evil, it is most severely condemned in the matter of food. Therefore, voracity—which in Greek is called <term>opsophagia</term> <note>original: ὀψοφαγία; literally "relish-eating," referring to a gluttonous craving for expensive delicacies</note>—is nothing other than immoderation in the use of side-dishes. It is also called <term>laimargia</term> <note>original: λαιμαργία</note>, which is a madness concerning the throat, and <term>gastrimargia</term> <note>original: γαστριμαργία</note>, which is intemperance in nourishment and, as the name itself indicates, a madness of the belly. For in Greek, an insane person is called <term>margos</term> <note>original: μαργὸς</note>. Therefore, the Apostle, rebuking those who intended to do wrong at feasts, says:
<margin>1 Corinthians 11</margin>
> FOR EVERYONE takes his own supper first in eating, and one indeed is hungry,
<margin>B</margin> while another is drunk. Do you not have houses for eating and drinking? Or do you despise the church of God, and put to shame those who have nothing?

Among those who have much, the insatiable ones who eat without any shame bring disgrace upon themselves. Both groups do wrong: the first by burdening those who have nothing, and the second by displaying their intemperance in the presence of those who do have. Necessarily, therefore, the Apostle erupted a second time into an indignant voice against those who have cast off shame and are insatiable—those for whom nothing is enough and who use feasts shamelessly:
<margin>Ibid.</margin>
> WHEREFORE, MY BRETHREN, when you come together to eat, wait for one another. If anyone is hungry, let him eat at home, so that you do not come together for judgment.

We must, therefore, abstain from every slavish and unrefined action and from intemperance. We should handle what is served honorably,
<margin>C</margin> keeping the hand, the couch <note>In the ancient world, diners typically reclined on couches rather than sitting in chairs</note>, and the beard unpolluted. We should maintain a steady grace of the face, not turning it this way and that, nor behaving unseemly while eating; rather, we should stretch out the hand in an orderly fashion at certain intervals. One must also take care not to speak while eating. For the voice becomes ungraceful and not sufficiently clear or meaningful, as it is constricted in the narrow space of full jaws; the tongue, pressed by food and hindered from its natural operation, produces a muffled utterance. Furthermore, it is not fitting to eat and drink at the same time; for it is a sign of the greatest intemperance to confuse the times of these actions, whose uses do not belong together.
<margin>1 Corinthians 10</margin>
> AND WHETHER you eat, he says, or drink, do all for the glory of God,

proposing true frugality and simplicity as the goal. The Lord also seems to me to have
<margin>D</margin> signified this when he blessed the loaves and the cooked fishes with which he entertained his disciples, introducing a beautiful example of food that was not too exquisite. That fish, which Peter caught at the Lord’s command, also signifies a moderate and frugal nourishment, easily obtained and divinely granted. By those who "ascend from the water to the food of justice," he warns us to remove luxury and greed, just as the coin was removed from the fish <note>Refers to the miracle in Matthew 17:27, where Peter finds a four-drachma coin (a stater) in a fish's mouth to pay the temple tax</note>: so that he might set aside vain glory and, by giving the coin to the tax collectors—rendering to Caesar what is Caesar’s—he might preserve for God what belongs to God. This coin <note>Latin: *stater*</note> has other interpretations as well, which are by no means unknown. But it is not the time to treat those now; this admonition is sufficient for our present purpose, as it does not disagree with the "flowers of the Word." Indeed, we have often done this, drawing from the most useful spring of the question at hand,
<margin>E</margin> so that what is planted by the Word might be watered.
<margin>1 Corinthians 10</margin>
For although "I am permitted to partake of all things, yet not all things are expedient." For those who do everything that is permitted are quickly led to do what is not permitted. Just as justice is not reached through greed or the desire to have more, and temperance is not reached through intemperance, so too the Christian way of life is not prepared by luxury and delicacies. For the table of truth is far from foods that titillate and incite lust. For even if all things were made primarily for humans, it is not good to use all things—nor to use them always. For the time, the occasion, the manner, and the relation to something else bring no small momentum to what is useful for the person being instructed. This principle is fitting and has great power to abolish a life devoted to the belly, to which riches incite us—not the kind of riches with sharp eyes, but the excessive
<margin>F</margin> abundance that is blind toward the madness of the gullet. No one is poor regarding the things that are necessary, nor is any human ever despised [by God]. For he who nourishes the winged and swimming creatures—and, to speak simply, all irrational animals—is the one God, and they lack for nothing.
<margin>Matthew 6</margin>
<margin>Wealth: <term>ploutos</term>. Plutus, however, is imagined as blind.</margin>

This rightly brings back to our memory what was said before: that vegetables are not love itself, but meals are fruitful when they are with love, in which a middle disposition is good in all things, but especially in the preparation of a banquet. For the extremes are dangerous, but the middle ways are good; and the middle is whatever does not lack necessary things. For those appetites which are according to nature are bounded by what is sufficient. Furthermore, frugality was announced to the Jews through the Law with the highest wisdom.

<margin>Leviticus 11</margin>
As for the things he permitted them to touch, he again forbade those that had died of themselves, and those sacrificed to idols, and those that had been strangled; for not even these are permitted to be handled. Since it is impossible for one who uses pleasant things to abstain from receiving them, he set against him a contrary way of life, until the impulse that proceeds from custom toward pleasure and delight should be dissolved. For pleasure has oftentimes produced loss and

# BOOK TWO

<margin>A</margin> ...blocks the path of nourishment. For this reason, Plato—that seeker of the truth of the philosophers who Kindled a spark of Hebrew truth—spoke of the luxurious life flowing with delights: "As for me," he said, "when I had arrived, that which is called the 'blessed life' there, filled with Italian and Syracusan tables, pleased me in no way at all. To live being stuffed twice a day, and never to sleep alone at night, and whatever studies follow this way of life. For from these things, no man among those under heaven can be prudent if he practices these things from his youth, nor will his admirable nature be overcome." <note>original: "MIHI autem... nullo modo placuit." Clement suggests Plato’s wisdom in his Seventh Letter was influenced by "Hebrew truth" (the Old Testament).</note> For had Plato not heard of David? Who, when he placed the holy Ark in the middle of a tent in his city, and created joy for all who obeyed his rule, distributed to all the hosts of Israel, from man <margin>1 Chronicles 16.</margin>

<margin>B</margin> to woman, to each a loaf of bread, a cake baked in the ashes, and a pancake from the frying pan. This is sufficient and "Israelite" nourishment; that which is superfluous is "Gentile." He who uses the latter will never labor to be wise, as one who has buried his mind in his belly, much like the fish which in Greek is called <term>onos</term> <note>original: "ὄνος", meaning "donkey-fish," likely a species of hake or cod.</note>, that is, the "donkey": which Aristotle says is the only one among the animals to have its heart in its belly. The comic poet Epicharmus calls such a one <term>ektenelogastron</term> <note>original: "ἐκτενελόγαστρον", meaning "one with a stretched-out belly."</note>, that is, one who departs from the common custom of the belly. Such are those men who have put their faith in their bellies: **WHOSE God is their belly, and their glory is in their shame, who think on earthly things.** To them, the Apostle predicted no good things, saying: **WHOSE end is** <margin>Philippians 3.</margin> **destruction.**

### How one ought to conduct oneself in drinking. Chapter II.

<image-desc>Decorative initial V within a square frame decorated with scrollwork and foliage.</image-desc>

<margin>C</margin> <margin>1 Timothy 5.</margin> **USE a little wine,** the Apostle says to Timothy, who was a water-drinker, **for the sake of your stomach,** fittingly providing help for a body that was quite sick and weak, that it might be strengthened and corroborated. Yet he decreed it should be "a little," lest, while it went unnoticed, this remedy might require another cure due to its abundance. Therefore, the natural and sober drink necessary for those who are thirsty is water. The Lord supplied this to the ancient Hebrews as the unique and simple drink of temperance, flowing from the jagged rock. For it was necessary for them, as they were wanderers, to be <margin>Exodus 18.</margin> especially sober. Afterward, the holy vine sprouted the prophetic cluster of grapes. This is a sign for those who have been trained to find rest from their wandering—the great cluster, namely the Word

<margin>D</margin> <margin>Numbers 20.</margin> squeezed for us, when the "blood of the grape"—that is, the Word—willed to be mixed with water. Thus also His blood is tempered for salvation. For the blood of the Lord is twofold. One is carnal, by which we have been redeemed from destruction. The other is spiritual, with which we have been anointed. And this is to drink the blood of Jesus: to be a participant in the Lord's incorruption. Moreover, the power of the Word is the Spirit, just as blood is to the flesh. Therefore, by a moderate proportion and suitability, wine is mixed with water, but the Spirit is mixed with man. And indeed, the tempered wine receives one into a banquet for faith; but the Spirit leads one to incorruption. Moreover, the mixture of both—the

<margin>E</margin> drink and the Word—is called the **Eucharist**, which is both praised and is a "good grace" <note>A play on the Greek roots of "Eucharist" (eu-charis), meaning good grace or thanksgiving.</note>. Those who participate in it by faith are sanctified in both body and soul, since the divine will has mystically tempered the divine mixture (the Spirit and the Word) with the human being. For truly, something of the Spirit is joined to the soul that is carried by it and becomes familiar to it. The flesh, however, is joined to the Word, for the sake of which "the Word was made flesh." I therefore praise and admire those who have chosen an austere life and desire water as the medicine of a moderate life; but wine, like the threats of fire, they flee as far as possible. It is pleasing, therefore, that boys and girls should mostly abstain from this "medicine." For it is not fitting to pour wine—the hottest of all liquids—into a boiling age, as if one were pouring fire into fire, from which wild

<margin>F</margin> and monstrous appetites, burning desires, and "fiery" characters are Kindled. For adolescents, being heated from within, become prone to lusts, so that the foreseen damage to them is proven through the body, with the limbs of desire ripening faster than they ought. For when the wine effervesces, the breasts luxuriate and swell...
