# THE INSTRUCTOR

<margin>A</margin> ...and shameful things, already foreshadowing the image of fornication. It forces the body to become a wound to the soul, and impudent impulses pursue a restless and unnecessary obsession, provoking temperance and moderation toward iniquity. From this, it happens that much of our youth leaps over the boundaries of shame. It is necessary, however, as much as possible, to try to extinguish the cravings of the young, taking away the Bacchic fuel <note>original: "bacchicum fomitem"—a reference to Bacchus, the god of wine, suggesting wine fuels the fire of passion.</note> of threats, and pouring in a remedy contrary to the heat, which will restrain the burning soul, hold back the swelling limbs, and soothe the stimulus of desire that is already being stirred up. But those who are in the very flower and vigor of their age, when they have taken lunch during the day—those for whom lunch is appropriate—having tasted bread alone, should abstain entirely from drink, so that their <margin>B</margin> superfluous moisture may be swallowed up, exhausted by the eating of dry foods as if by a sponge. For constant spitting, blowing the nose, and rushing to ease oneself are signs of intemperance caused by the immoderate intake of liquids, which are poured into the body more than is proper. But if thirst should also come, this condition should be treated with a little water. For it is not fitting to be filled too profusely with water, lest the nourishment be overwhelmed. Instead, it should be broken down to facilitate digestion; while the food rises in bulk, there should be little that proceeds to excretion. In any case, it is otherwise fitting that divine thoughts not be weighed down by wine. For as the Comic poet says, "Pure wine forces the mind to grasp very few things," <note>original: "merum comprehendere." Clement likely quotes a lost fragment of Greek comedy to show that heavy drinking dulls the intellect.</note> far be it from being able to make a man temperate.

In the evening, however, at the time of dinner, wine may be used. For since we are no longer attending to somewhat more sober <margin>C</margin> and serious readings, let that which surrounds us by day be cooler then, so that the innate warmth which is failing may be cherished by introduced heat. But here, too, wine must be used sparingly; for one must not approach the "bowls of insolence." <note>Clement warns against the large mixing bowls used at parties that lead to abusive behavior.</note> However, those who are already of a more advanced age may be permitted to enjoy drink more cheerfully, reviving the chill of age—which in a way withers with time—with the medicine of the vine without harm. For the cravings of the elderly no longer fluctuate greatly around the shipwrecks of drunkenness. Being grounded in the harbor by reason and time as if by anchors, they more easily endure the storm of desires stirred up by intoxication. For these men, it is even permitted to speak somewhat politely and wittily at banquets. Yet for them too, the limit of drinking is this: that they preserve their reason <margin>D</margin> unshaken, their memory performing its duty, and the body unmoved and unconfused by wine. Those who are skilled in these matters call such a person <term>akrothōraka</term> <note>original: "ἀκροθώρακα"—literally "armed to the chest." In ancient Greek slang, it referred to being "slightly tipsy" or "chested with wine," a state where one is merry but still in control.</note>, that is, one who has notably armed his chest with wine. It is better, therefore, to stop before you slip. A certain Artorius <note>Artorius was a famous physician, possibly the doctor to Augustus Caesar.</note>, in his book *On Long Life*—for so I remember it—thinks that drink should only be provided until the food is moistened, so that we may prepare a longer life for ourselves.

It is fitting, therefore, that some should use wine as a medicine for the sake of health alone; others, however, to relax and cheer themselves. For first, wine makes him who drinks more than is usual to be fair and merciful to himself, <margin>E</margin> mild to his servants, and more pleasant to his friends; but when affected by insult, he returns like for like. Since wine is hot and has sweet juices moderately tempered, it liquefies foul wastes by its heat, and tempers sharp and bad juices with its good scent. Therefore, that saying is well put: **WINE WAS CREATED** from the beginning for the **EXULTATION** of the soul <margin>Psalm 103. Ecclesiasticus 31.</margin> and the heart, if it be drunk in sufficient quantity. <note>original: "EXVLTATIO animæ...". Clement combines the sentiment of Psalm 104:15 (Vulgate 103) with the specific wording of Ecclesiasticus (Sirach) 31:27-28.</note> It is best, however, to mix wine with a great deal of water, and not to seek it out as if it were water itself, rendering it dull and blunt toward intoxication; nor should it be poured like water for the sake of wine-bibbing. For both are the works of God, and for that reason the mixture of both—namely water and wine—conduces to health: since life consists of that which is necessary and that which is useful. Therefore, to that which is necessary—namely, mostly water—something from the useful should be mixed in. However, with immoderate wine, the tongue is indeed impeded; <margin>F</margin> the lips are loosened; the eyes are distorted and turned aside, since from the multitude of moisture the sight swims as if in a pool; and being forced to see falsely, they think that everything is being driven in a circle, and they cannot count things far off as if they were single objects. **AND YET** I seem to see two suns, said the drunkard...

<margin>A</margin> ...the Theban old man used to say. <note>original: "Thebantus senex"—likely a reference to a Cynic philosopher or a character from ancient comedy used to illustrate a moral point.</note> For the sight, moved by the heat of the wine, often perceives a single thing as having a multiple substance. It makes no difference whether the sight moves or the object being seen moves. The same thing happens to the sight from both causes: because of the fluctuation, it cannot perfectly comprehend the subject. Now indeed, his steps falter as if driven by a wave; they cannot hold their place. Belching, hiccups, vomiting, and follies follow as if for sport and delight. For whoever is intoxicated, as the tragedy says:

> *When anger conquers, wisdom is lacking.*  
> *And when the tongue has poured out many crimes,*  
> *One is forced to hear what one spoke wrongly by choice.*

<margin>B</margin><margin>Proverbs 2; Ecclesiasticus 19 & 31</margin> And indeed, Wisdom cried out even before the tragedy: "Wine that is drunk in excess fills one with irritation and every kind of fall." For this reason, many say that one ought to relax at a banquet and put off serious matters until dawn. But I, however, judge that reason should then especially be introduced into the banquet to correct drunkenness, acting like a **Tutor** <note>original: "Paedagogi"—referring to the 'Instructor' or household guide who supervised the moral conduct of children.</note>, lest the banquet slip away into intoxication while we are unaware. For just as no one who is wise would think it right to close their eyes before they go to sleep, so no one would rightly wish for reason to be absent from a banquet, nor would they rightly choose to put it to sleep before actions are performed. But reason can never cease from its duty, not even if we sleep. Indeed, it is to be invited even into sleep. For **perfect wisdom**—which is the knowledge of divine and human things, embracing and containing all things—insofar as it cares for the flock of men, becomes the art of living. By that logic, as long as we live, it is perpetually present, always performing its own duty: namely, the good life.

<margin>C</margin> Miserable are those who demand "temperance" from a banquet, yet think a life of intemperance spent in drinking bouts is a blessed one. Their life is nothing other than revelry, hangovers, baths, strong wine, the idleness of the chamber pot, and drinking. One may therefore see the hearts of the proud: they are stumbling, wearing garlands around their necks, and pouring pure wine into each other like wine jars under the name of "goodwill." Others are full of the effects of a hangover, filthy, pale and livid in the face, and pouring yet another intoxication on top of yesterday’s drunkenness.

<margin>D</margin> It is good, it is good, O friends, that when we have learned to stay as far away as possible from this image—which is both ridiculous and miserable—we may compose and fashion ourselves toward that which is better, fearing lest we too perhaps become a similar spectacle to others and turn out ridiculous. It was truly said wittily: "A furnace tests the edge of iron during tempering; but wine tests the heart of the proud." And drunkenness is indeed the more vehement use of wine. But **debauchery**—which in Greek is <term>methe (μέθη) — the state of being drunk</term>—is the disgrace incurred from its use by speaking beyond what is proper. Moreover, the **hangover**—which is the distress and nausea received because of drunkenness—is called <term>kraipale (κραιπάλη) — the "head-shaking" or nausea of a hangover</term> in Greek, because it makes the head vibrate and shake.

<margin>E</margin><margin>Proverbs 23; Ecclesiasticus 19</margin> This life—if indeed it should be called a life—which is lazy and idle, devoted to lust and pleasure, admiring and looking up to drunkenness, divine Wisdom despises it and warns her sons: "DO NOT BE a wine-bibber, nor extend your hand to the buying of meats. For every drunkard and fornicator shall be a beggar, and every sleepy person shall be clothed in rags and tatters." For everyone who does not stay awake for wisdom, but is submerged from drunkenness into sleep, is "sleepy." And the debauched man, it says, shall be clothed "in rags," and through drunkenness shall be struck with shame before those who look on. For those "holes" are the sins of the sinner, which are torn out from the *fleshly garment* <note>A common early Christian metaphor for the body or the soul's moral covering.</note>, perforated by lusts, through which the disgrace within the soul is seen—namely, sin. Because of this, the garment will not easily be preserved, being torn and mangled on every side, withering with many desires, and rent away from salvation.

<margin>F</margin><margin>Proverbs 23</margin> And for that reason, Wisdom adds most aptly as a warning: "FOR WHOM is woe, for whom is tumult, for whom are judgments, for whom are unpleasant words, for whom are unnecessary bruises?" See the wine-drinker, entirely torn apart, who despises reason itself and has surrendered himself to drunkenness—see how many and how great are the threats the Scripture has made against him. But after the threats, it adds again: "WHOSE are livid eyes? Are they not those of people who consume their time in wine? Are they not those who go...

The pilot—namely, the human mind—is tossed about by the wave of overwhelming drunkenness: and living in such a sea, he grows dim-sighted, and because of the darkness of the storm, he wanders from the harbor of truth, until rushing onto rocks hidden in the sea, he destroys himself, having been driven into pleasures. But the dry soul itself is the wisest and the best; for that reason it is also contemplative, and not being moistened by those exhalations that rise from wine, it is not forced into a bodily mass like a cloud. Therefore, Chian wine is not to be sought with great care if it is absent, nor Arethusian wine if it is not at hand. For thirst is an affection of some lack, and to satisfy it one seeks a suitable remedy, not a burning and smoky wine. ### BOOK TWO
<page-num>51</page-num>

**A** Let us drink from a stable vessel that does not tilt this way or that, not drawing the liquid in too greedily; nor, before we have finished drinking, should we force our eyes to behave unbecomingly by gulping immoderately out of lack of self-control, so that the chin is entirely soaked, washing our faces with the cups and nearly drowning ourselves. Indeed, the whispering sound made when a drink is carried with great force and drawn in with much breath—much like water poured into an earthenware jar—while the throat resounds because of rapid engorging, is a shameful and unseemly spectacle of intemperance. Added to this is the fact that such eagerness for drink is harmful to the person who practices it. Do not hasten, O friend, toward that which brings you harm. The drink is not being snatched from you; it has been given to you and awaits you. Do not hurry to burst yourself by drawing it in with a gaping mouth. Your

**B** thirst is satisfied even if you drink more slowly, behaving honestly and decorously, provided the drink is divided into portions as is proper. For that which is snatched away by intemperance is not saved by time. <margin>Ecclesiasticus 31. Isaiah 5.</margin> **IN WINE**, he says, do not show yourself to be a strong man. For wine has rendered many useless. The Scythians, Celts, Iberians, and Thracians—all of whom are warlike nations—indulge heavily in drunkenness, and they believe they are practicing a beautiful and blessed way of life. We, however, who are a peaceful race, feasting for utility and not for impudence or insult, drink sober draughts for the sake of friendship, so that our cups of friendship may truly be called by a fitting name. How do you think the Lord drank when he became a man for our sake? Was it as shamelessly as we do? Was it not honestly and temperately, was it not with consideration? For you know it well: He also used wine, for he

**C** was also a man; and he blessed the wine when he said: <margin>Matthew 26.</margin>
> **TAKE**, drink, this is my blood, the blood of the vine. The Word, which is shed for many for the remission of sins, allegorically signifies the holy flow of joy.

And he clearly showed that the one who drinks ought to be sober and moderate through the things he taught at feasts. For he did not teach while drunk. Furthermore, he showed that it was wine that was blessed by saying again to his Disciples: <margin>In the same place.</margin>
> **I WILL NOT DRINK** of this fruit of the vine until I drink it with you in the kingdom of my Father.

Moreover, that it was wine which was drunk by the Lord, he says again of himself, reproaching the hardness of the hearts of the Jews: <margin>Luke 7.</margin>
> **FOR THE SON** of man came, he says, and they say: Behold a gluttonous man and a wine-drinker, a friend of tax collectors.

Let these things be firm and fixed for us against those who are called Encratites. <note>The Encratites were an early Christian ascetic sect who practiced total abstinence from wine, meat, and marriage. Clement argues here that because Christ drank wine, it is not inherently evil if used in moderation.</note>

**D** Furthermore, let women, looking toward what is honest and decorous, avoid spreading their lips over wide cups or bursting their mouths open wide; nor should they drink unbecomingly from very narrow-necked alabaster jars <note>Alabastra were elongated vessels without handles, often used for perfumes or oils, but here used as fancy drinking vessels.</note> by tilting their heads back, for they expose their necks in a way that does not seem honest to me. By extending their throats and engorging the drink, they reveal what they can to the other guests, and by drawing in manly—or rather, slave-like—belches, they consume their time in luxury and delights. For nothing that brings disgrace or blame is fitting for a man endowed with reason, and much less for a woman, for whom the mere awareness of who she is should bring a sense of modesty. <margin>Ecclesiasticus 26.</margin> **WRATH**, he says, is great in a drunken woman; like the wrath of God is a woman who is intoxicated. Why? Because she does not hide her own shame.

**E** For a woman is easily drawn toward dishonest behavior if she permits her free choice of mind to be ruled solely by pleasures. We do not strictly forbid drinking from alabaster jars, but we forbid the *eagerness* to drink only from them, so that we may cut away pride and arrogance. We advise them to use whatever vessels are available without any emotional attachment, cutting away from afar the appetites into which they might fall. Now, the impulse of air <note>original: "aëris impulsus" — a polite reference to a belch or gas.</note> which, by a returning fluctuation, urges one to belch, should be passed through gently. In no way should women be permitted to appear to expose any part of the body, lest both fall: the men, by being incited to look, and the women, by drawing the gaze of men upon themselves. One must always live honestly, as if in the presence of the Lord;

**F** lest the Apostle say to us, as he did when angry with the Corinthians: <margin>1 Corinthians 11.</margin>
> **WHEN YOU MEET**, it is not possible to eat the Lord’s Supper.

It seems to me that the one called the "Headless One" <note>original: "Acephalus" — likely a reference to a headless constellation or an astronomical figure used as a moral metaphor for those without reason.</note> by the Mathematicians, who is counted before the wandering star with his head pressed into his chest, signifies gluttonous and pleasure-seeking men, etc.

# THE INSTRUCTOR

<margin>A</margin>
...those prone to drunkenness. For in these people, the faculty of reasoning is located not in the head, but in the intestines, serving anger and desire. For this reason, just as Elpenor <note>A companion of Odysseus in Homer’s Odyssey who, while drunk, fell from a roof and died.</note> broke his heel when he fell because of drunkenness, so too their brain, clouded with mist from intoxication, falls toward the heart and the liver—that is, toward pleasure and anger—with a greater crash than the poets say Vulcan <note>The Roman name for Hephaestus, the god of fire, who was cast down from heaven to earth by Jupiter.</note> was thrown from heaven to the earth. **LABOR**, however, and sleeplessness, as the scripture says, and bile, and torment, are with the insatiable man. <note>original: "LABOR autem, vigiliæ... et tormentum est cum homine insatiabili," from Ecclesiasticus 31:23-24.</note> On this account, the indecency of Noah <margin>Genesis 9.</margin> was recorded so that we might avoid drunkenness as much as possible, having a clear image of his lapse set down in writing; because of this, those who covered the shame of his drunkenness are blessed by the Lord. Therefore, the Scripture, summarizing most briefly, said everything in one word: *Wine is sufficient for a man of education, and he will rest in his bed.* <note>original: "Quod homini erudito satis est vinum, & in eius cubili requiescet," from Ecclesiasticus 31:22.</note> <margin>B</margin>

### That one’s zeal should not be spent on expensive household vessels. Chapter III.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring ornate foliage and scrollwork within a square border.</image-desc>
The use of silver and gold and gem-studded cups is vain and useless, being merely a deception of the sight. <margin>C</margin> For if you pour a hot mixed liquid into them, the handling of the heated vessels is troublesome; if, on the other hand, you pour in something cold, the material transfers its quality, spoiling the liquid, and the "rich drink" becomes harmful. Farewell, then, to Thericleian cups, <note>Vessels named after the famous Corinthian potter Thericles.</note> Antigonides, Labronian tankards, and *lepastae*, and the innumerable kinds of cups; and furthermore, to ladles, wine-coolers, <note>original: "psŷcteres"</note> and wine-pourers. For gold and silver, whether in private or in <margin>Concerning these, see Athenaeus, book 11.</margin> public, are—to put it simply—enviable possessions if they exceed common use; they are rare to acquire, difficult to guard, and not well-suited for use. Furthermore, the vain glory of those who turn intricate designs in glass, which is more ready to break because of its artistry and which teaches one to both fear and drink at the same time, must be banished from our good institutions and laws. Silver chairs, <margin>D</margin> basins and vinegar cruets, platters and dishes, and moreover, vessels of gold and silver—some indeed for the service of food, but others for uses I am ashamed to mention—tripods fashioned from carved cedar, frankincense wood, ebony, and ivory; beds with silver feet and those joined with ivory, bed-doors inlaid with gold and variegated with tortoiseshell, and purple rugs and other colors difficult to produce: all these are proofs of insolent luxury, the insidious comforts of envy and soft idleness. They are all to be sent away, as they possess nothing for which one should rightly put much effort into them; for **THE TIME** is short, as the Apostle says. <margin>1 Corinthians 7.</margin> It remains, therefore, that we do not bear before us some ridiculous habit or outward form, just as in processions some appear so anointed and smeared on the outside for the sake of gravity that they cause stupor and admiration, yet inside they are clearly miserable. Explaining this more accurately, he added: **IT REMAINS** that both those who have wives should be as though they had none, <margin>E</margin> <margin>Ibid.</margin> and those who buy as though they did not possess. <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 7:29-30.</note> If he said these things regarding marriage, in which <margin>Genesis 1.</margin> God said, "Increase and multiply," how do you think arrogance and pride are not to be banished by the authority of the Lord? On this account the Lord also says: <margin>Matthew 19, Mark 10.</margin> **SELL** what you have, and give to the poor; and follow me here. Follow God, naked of arrogance, naked of momentary pomp, possessing that which is yours, which is good, and which cannot be taken away: faith in God, confession of His passion, and beneficence toward men—which is indeed a most precious possession. I also accept Plato, who, having proposed a law, clearly decrees that one ought not to labor to have gold or silver riches, nor any useless vessel which is not also moderate for necessary use, so that the same thing is suited for many purposes; and let multiple and varied possessions be purged away. Thus, divine Scripture says most beautifully in a certain place, directing its words to those who are lovers of themselves and arrogant: <margin>F</margin> <margin>Baruch 3.</margin> **WHERE ARE THEY** who ruled over the nations, and who dominated the wild beasts that are upon the earth? Who made sport of the birds of the heaven, who gathered treasures of silver and gold in which men placed their trust, and of which there is no end?

# SECOND BOOK

<margin>A</margin>Is there an end to their acquisition—those who forged gold and silver and were so anxious? There is no discovery of their words: they have vanished and descended to the underworld. <note>original: "Est finis acquisitionis eorum... euanuerunt, & ad inferos descenderunt." This is a reference to Baruch 3:17-19, describing the transience of those who trust in wealth.</note> This is the reward of arrogant pride. For if we who till the field have need of the hoe and the plow, but no one has ever forged a silver hoe or a golden scythe, and we use material that is suited for doing the work rather than what is costly in agriculture: what prevents those who consider what is appropriate from feeling the same way about domestic vessels? Let their measure be use, not expense and magnificence. 

Tell me, I ask you, does the little knife placed on the table not cut if it does not have silver studs, or if the handle is not made of ivory? Or must we forge Indian iron for us to divide meat, as if calling for some special assistance? 

<margin>B</margin>What if it is a clay basin? Will it not catch the filth washed from the hands? And the clay vessel in which we wash our feet—will it not hold the dirt of the feet? Will the table, then, even if it is built with ivory feet, be indignant if it carries a loaf of bread worth only one obol? <note>An *obol* was a small coin of low value; the author is highlighting the contrast between expensive furniture and simple food.</note> Nor will the lamp provide less light because it is the work of a potter and not a goldsmith. 

I say that even a humble pallet provides no worse a sleep than an ivory bed. Since it is enough to spread out sheep or goat skins for bedding—so much so that there is no need for purple or Phoenician fabrics—what a great error and vain persuasion of what is "honorable" and "beautiful" it is to condemn frugality because of the folly of those first luxuries which brought about ruin! 

Look: Christ ate food from a cheap dish, and made His disciples recline on the grass. <margin>towel</margin> <note>original: σαβανω (*sabano*), a Greek term for a linen cloth or apron.</note> He washed their feet wrapped in a linen towel—a God far removed from pride, and the Lord of all. <margin>Matthew 14.</margin> <margin>C</margin> Did He bring down a silver washbasin from heaven? 

<margin>Mark 6.</margin> And He asked for a drink from the Samaritan woman, who was drawing water from the well with a clay vessel, <margin>John 13.</margin> not requiring royal gold, but teaching that thirst is easily quenched. <margin>Ibid. 4.</margin> For He established use as the goal, not excessive and useless magnificence. In His banquets, He ate and drank without digging up the earth's metals, nor using vessels that smelled of the rust of gold and silver. For in a way, the rust of burnt material breathes out a scent. 

In short, food, clothing, vessels, furniture, and whatever is in the home—and to say it once for all, life itself—ought to be consistent with the right upbringing of a Christian, adapted as it may be useful for the person, their age, their pursuit, and the time. Since we are ministers of the one God, it is proper that our possessions and the furniture within them show the signs of a single honorable life. <margin>D</margin> Every person, with an indistinct and non-differing faith, should be seen to act in accordance with this uniform upbringing through this single affection. 

We praise those things which we neither acquire with difficulty and which we use easily, and we guard them and share them easily; moreover, those things which are useful are better. Those things which are cheaper and more frugal are better for the rich. In summary, wealth that is not rightly administered is a "fortress of vice" and crime, in which many, being blind, will never be able to enter the kingdom of heaven, being sick indeed in worldly matters, but living proudly and arrogantly because of their luxuries. 

It is necessary for those who strive for salvation to have already anticipated with this mind: that every possession exists for the sake of use. <margin>E</margin> A possession that someone provides even from a few things will suffice for the sake of sufficiency. But those are vain who, because of their insatiability, take delight in stored-up precious things. "He who gathers wages," it says, "has gathered them into a bag with holes." <note>A reference to Haggai 1:6, suggesting that wealth gained through greed is quickly lost.</note> He is the one who gathers and excludes the seed, and is affected by loss, giving nothing to anyone. 

It is a clearly ridiculous thing, and most worthy of being mocked, for men to bring in silver urine receptacles and glass chamber pots, just as they introduce their counselors; and for these women, who are rich without reason, to make receptacles for excrement out of gold, so that it is not even permitted for them to relieve themselves without pride. I wish indeed that they would consider gold to be dung for their whole lives! Now, however, the "fortress of vice" <margin>1 Timothy 6.</margin> <margin>F</margin> has been found to be the love of money, which the Apostle says is the root of all evils. Those who long for this have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves through with many sorrows. True wealth is the poverty of desires; and true greatness of soul is not to be pleased with oneself because of riches, nor to take on great airs, but to despise them.

## How one should behave at feasts. Chapter IV.

<margin>revelry <note>original: κῶμος</note></margin>
<margin>A</margin>
From a rational feast, however, let riotous revelry <note>original: "comessatio"</note> and youthful wantonness be absent. Furthermore, avoid empty vigils <note>sleepless nights spent partying</note> that delight in insolence, shameful insults, and abusive language. For this revelry is like a drunken flute, a chain of lack of restraint caused by the sudden drinking of love-potions. Let love, drunkenness, and irrational passions be sent far away from our company. Along with insolence, song is also found in revelry. In drinking, indeed, night-watches summon drunkenness,
<margin>song <note>original: μῳδία</note></margin>
<margin>B</margin>
and excite lust, which is a boldness devoted to doing shameful things. But if people studiously occupy themselves with flutes, and psalteries <note>ancient stringed instruments similar to harps</note>, dances, leaps, the clapping of Egyptians, and similar dissolute idleness, they will become immodest, insolent, and utterly estranged from good discipline, as those whom cymbals and drums surround with noise, and the instruments of deception resound about them. For truly, as it seems to me, a feast of this kind is a theater of drunkenness. For when we have cast off the works of darkness, the Apostle <note>St. Paul</note>
<margin>Romans 13</margin>
<margin>C</margin>
wants us to put on the armor of light, so that we may walk decently as in the day: not in reveling and drunkenness, not in debauchery and impurity. Therefore, let the reed pipe be given to shepherds, and the flute <note>original: "tibia," the aulos or double-pipe</note> to superstitious men who hurry to the worship of idols. Indeed, these instruments are to be banished from a sober feast, as they are more suitable for beasts than for humans, and for those humans who are most far from reason. For we have heard that deer are charmed by reed pipes, and led into snares by hunters with song. And when horses mate, a song is played on a flute like a sort of wedding hymn. This, musicians have called the "horse-leaping" tune <note>original: ἱππόθορον</note>. Every shameful sight and every shameful sound—and to put it simply, every shameful sensation of excess, which is truly a deprivation of sense—we must especially
<margin>D</margin>
cut out, for it tickles the eyes and ears and makes us effeminate, while we guard against pleasure. The various spells of broken melodies and mournful Carian <note>original: "Caricæ Musæ," referring to Caria, a region known in antiquity for professional mourners and dirges</note> tunes corrupt morals with an unrestrained and perverse musical art, dragging us toward the emotion of this revelry. But the Spirit, setting apart the divine ministry, sings psalms
<margin>Psalm 150</margin>
saying: PRAISE Him with the sound of the trumpet. For with the sound of the trumpet He will raise the dead. PRAISE Him on the psaltery, for the tongue is the Lord’s psaltery. AND praise Him on the harp. By the harp let the mouth be understood, which is struck by the spirit as if by a plectrum <note>the small tool used to pluck a string instrument</note>. WITH THE TIMBREL and dance, praise Him. He refers to the Church, which meditated on the resurrection of the flesh in the resonating skin <note>of the drum</note>. WITH STRINGS and the organ, praise Him.
<margin>E</margin>
He calls our body the "organ" and its nerves the "strings," through which it is tuned rhythmically and harmoniously, and when struck by the spirit, it gives forth human voices. PRAISE Him on the cymbals of jubilation. He calls the tongue the "cymbal" of the mouth, which resounds when the lips are struck. And thus He called out to human nature: let EVERY spirit praise the Lord. Because He cares for every spirit He has made. Indeed, man is an instrument of peace. But if someone inquires more curiously, they will find other instruments of war that inflame desires, or kindle loves, or irritate the mind and anger. In their wars, the Etruscans use the trumpet, the Arcadians the reed pipe, the Sicilians the instruments they call *pektides* <note>original: πίκτιδας, an ancient Greek stringed instrument</note>, the Cretans the lyre, the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note> the flute, the Thracians the horn, the Egyptians the drum
<margin>F</margin>
and the Arabs the cymbal. We, therefore, use only one instrument: the peaceful Word alone, by which we honor God; no longer the old psaltery, and trumpet, and drum, and flute, which were the custom of those practiced in war. They despised the fear of God and used to gather in choruses to use such modes so that a loose and dejected mind might be excited. Let our goodwill in drinking be twofold...

### BOOK TWO
<sig>e iiii</sig>

<margin>A</margin> Therefore, the invitation comes from the Law: "If you love the Lord your God," and then, "your neighbor." <note>A reference to the Great Commandment found in Deuteronomy 6:5 and Leviticus 19:18.</note> The first invitation, which is benevolent toward God, should be expressed through thanksgiving and the singing of Psalms. The second, which concerns one's neighbor, should be expressed through an honorable way of living. <margin>Colossians 3</margin> "Let the WORD of the Lord dwell in you richly," says the Apostle. This Word adapts itself and conforms to the times, persons, and places. And so, even now, it is present at our banquet. For the Apostle adds again: <margin>Ibid.</margin> "teaching and admonishing yourselves in all wisdom, singing in your hearts to God with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs in grace." And again: "WHATEVER you do, whether in word or in deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God and His Father."

<margin>B</margin> This is our gracious and pleasant revelry. <note>original: "comessatio"</note> And if you know how to sing and play to the lyre or the cithara <note>A cithara was a professional version of the lyre, a stringed instrument often used in religious and classical music.</note>, no blame shall fall upon you. You will be imitating the righteous Hebrew King, who was pleasing and acceptable to God. <margin>Psalm 32</margin> "REJOICE, you righteous, in the Lord; praise befits the upright," says the prophecy. "GIVE THANKS to the Lord on the cithara; play to Him on the ten-stringed psaltery. Sing to Him a new song." <margin>The letter I signifies ten among the Greeks.</margin> <note>The letter Iota (Ι) is the numeral for 10 in Greek and is also the first letter of Iesus (Jesus), creating a symbolic link between the instrument and Christ.</note> Does the ten-stringed psaltery not signify the Word, Jesus, who is revealed through the symbol of the number ten? Just as it is fitting for us to praise the Maker of all things before we take our food, so too is it fitting for us to sing to Him while drinking, since we are made partakers of His creatures. For a psalm is a rhythmic and modest form of praise.

<margin>C</margin> The Apostle called the psalm a "spiritual song." <margin>To the Colossians 3</margin> Finally, before sleep comes upon us, it is a pious and holy thing to give thanks to God, so that we, having obtained His kindness and grace, may go to our sleep with a certain divine inspiration. And "to confess to Him," he says, "in the songs of the lips," because whatever He deems fit happens by His command, and nothing is lacking or diminished for His salvation. <margin>Psalms 62 & 118</margin> Furthermore, among the ancient Greeks, at banquets prepared for drinking where the cups were flowing, they used to sing a song called a *skolion* <note>original: "σκολιὸν", meaning "crooked" or "oblique," referring to the way the song was passed irregularly around the table.</note>—which means "oblique"—in imitation of the Hebrew psalms. They would all cry out a *paean* <note>A song of triumph or thanksgiving, originally dedicated to Apollo.</note> together in one voice, and sometimes even pass the toast around in turns according to the song. Those among them who were a little more skilled in music would also sing to the lyre. But let songs of love be far away. Let our songs be praises of God.

<margin>D</margin> "LET THEM PRAISE His name in dance," he says, "let them sing to Him with the drum and the psaltery." <margin>Ibid. 149</margin> And what is this "chorus" <note>The author distinguishes between a secular dance and the "chorus" or assembly of the church.</note> that sings? The Spirit himself will tell you: "His PRAISE is in the assembly of the saints. Let them exult because of their King." And again he adds: "FOR the Lord is well-pleased with His people." For modest and chaste harmonies are to be admitted, while we send as far away as possible those truly soft and effeminate harmonies from our strong and vigorous thoughts; these use a wicked artifice of vocal trills and lead to a delicate and lazy way of life. But grave melodies, and those which pertain to temperance, bid farewell to the insolence of drunkenness. Therefore, chromatic harmonies <note>In ancient music, the chromatic scale was often associated with excessive emotion or lack of discipline, unlike the more "stable" scales like the Doric.</note> should be left to the impudent insolence of wine, and to the flower-crowned music of harlots.

### On laughter. Chapter V.

<margin>E</margin> <image-desc>Large decorative initial 'R' containing foliage and floral patterns within a square border.</image-desc>Those who imitate ridiculous things—or rather, ridiculous actions—must be banished from our Commonwealth. Since all words emanate from thought and character, it is impossible for any ridiculous words to be uttered that do not proceed from a ridiculous character. For that saying: <margin>Matthew 7</margin> "A good tree DOES NOT produce bad fruit; nor does a bad tree produce good fruit," must be applied here as well. For speech is the fruit of thought. If, therefore, those who provoke laughter <margin>F</margin> are to be exterminated from our Commonwealth, it is far from being the case that it is permitted for us to provoke laughter. For it would be absurd to be found as imitators of those whom we are forbidden to hear. It would be much more absurd to study how to make yourself ridiculous, which is to be subjected to insults and mockery. For if one finds a ridiculous appearance...

<meta>This page continues the instructions of Clement of Alexandria regarding social conduct, specifically transitioning from the proper use of music and speech to the discipline of laughter and the dangers of excess in wine.</meta>

# THE INSTRUCTOR

<margin>A</margin>
If we would never dream of appearing like certain people who make a spectacle of themselves in public processions, how could we rightly allow our "inner man" to take on an even more ridiculous figure? If we would never willingly turn our own person into something laughable, why should we strive to be and appear ridiculous in our words? By doing so, we treat speech and reason—which are by far the most precious gifts within a human being—as mere objects of mockery. It is therefore absurd to practice such things, especially since the speech of such ridiculous men is not even worthy of being heard; it only serves to habituate one toward shameful deeds through these names. Therefore, one must speak with urbanity <note>original: "Vrbanè," referring to the sophisticated and polite speech of a city-dweller as opposed to a rustic.</note> and wit, rather than seeking to provoke laughter.

<margin>B</margin>
Indeed, laughter itself must be kept under control. For if laughter is expressed in the proper way, it displays a sense of grace and honor; but if it breaks out otherwise, it indicates a lack of self-control. To put it simply: whatever traits are natural to human beings should not be abolished, but rather, they must be applied with due measure and at the right time. For just because a human is an animal endowed with the power of laughter, it does not mean one must laugh perpetually, just as a horse does not neigh constantly even though neighing is its natural trait. As rational animals, we ought to compose ourselves with temperance, relaxing the sharp focus and intense strain of our studies with moderation, rather than dissolving into unseemly behavior. The graceful relaxation of the face, which like an instrument is tuned to harmony, is called in Greek *meidiama* <note>original: "μειδίαμα"</note>, that is, a smile. This is the term for the spreading of the features, the cheerfulness, and the laughter of those in whose countenance modesty resides. However, the immoderate and ungraceful dissolution of the face, if it occurs in women,

<margin>C</margin>
<margin>Ecclesiasticus 21</margin>
is called in Greek *meidiasmos* <note>original: "μειδίασμος"</note>, which is an immodest and lascivious laugh, the kind used by harlots. If it occurs in men, it is called *kagchasmos* <note>original: "καγχασμός"</note>, which is a loud cackle or mocking laughter. This is the insolent and bold laughter of suitors. For "a fool," says the Scripture, "lifts up his voice in laughter, but a clever man will hardly smile quietly." <note>Quoting Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 21:20.</note> By "clever" here, the text means a prudent man, who is affected in the opposite way of a fool. Yet, on the other hand, one should not be gloomy, but rather grave and thoughtful. I would sooner accept a person who smiles while maintaining a serious expression than one who does not. For that kind of smile is less likely to be mocked. Laughter itself must be taught and disciplined: if it arises from shameful things, one should appear to blush rather than smile, so as not to seem to be joining in the enjoyment by consent. If it concerns painful matters,

<margin>D</margin>
it is more appropriate to appear saddened than to rejoice. The former is a sign of human consideration; the latter shows a reputation for cruelty. Furthermore, one must not laugh at all times, for that is immoderate; nor should one laugh in the presence of elders or those whom it is right to revere, unless perhaps they themselves say something witty and graceful to cheer us up. One should not laugh in front of just anyone, nor in every place, nor with everyone, nor because of everything. For especially among young people and women, laughter is prone to being slandered. To present a terrifying or rigid expression from a distance may repel those standing around, but gravity of character can, by its very look, break and repress the sudden outbursts of insolence.

<margin>E</margin>
> To all fools, to say it in a single word, wine
> Bids them laugh softly, and dance willingly,
turning effeminate manners toward a state of softness. One must consider how the license of speech proceeding from this point increases and amplifies shamefulness to such an extent that it leads to foul language.
> He uttered a word that would have been better left unsaid.
Thus, the character of wicked men is most clearly seen in wine, for they are stripped of all pretense because of the undignified license of wine’s insolence in speech. Through this, reason is put to sleep, being oppressed and weighed down by drunkenness within the soul itself; meanwhile, wild passions, lacking all urbanity, are awakened and easily seize dominion over the weakness of the mind.

<margin>F</margin>

<header>BOOK TWO</header>

## On Foul Language. Chapter 6.

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>Matthew 15.</margin>
<margin>The word "defile" [coinquinant] in Greek is <term>κοινοῖ</term>, which means to make common or profane.</margin>
We must also completely abstain from **foul language** [turpiloquio]. We should shut the mouths of those who use it—using a stern look, a turning away of the face, or a "sneer" <note>original: "subsannatione," a gesture of contempt often involving wrinkling the nose.</note>, and often even with sharp words. For "the things," he says, "which come out of the mouth, defile a person." They show him to be a common, pagan, unlearned, intemperate, and insolent man; not someone who is self-possessed, modest, honorable, and temperate.

<margin>B</margin>
Since shameful things are found equally in hearing and in seeing, the divine **Instructor** [Paedagogus] provides modest and virtuous speeches to children as they struggle—like protective armor for the ears—so that their hearing is not offended. This is to prevent the "pounding of fornication" from persuading them to break the soul. He directs the eyes toward the sight of honorable things, saying it is better to slip with the feet than with the eyes. The Apostle, repelling this foul language, says:

<margin>Ephesians 4.</margin>
"Let no **evil word** proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good." And again: "As becomes saints, let not **filthiness**, and **foolish talk** [stultiloquium],

<margin>Ibid. 5.</margin>
or **crude joking** [scurrilis vrbanitas], which are not fitting, even be named among you, but rather thanksgiving." If he who called his brother a "fool" is liable to judgment, what shall we pronounce regarding him who speaks foolish things?

<margin>Matthew 5.</margin>
Is it not also written of him: "For every **idle word** a man speaks,

<margin>Ibid. 12.</margin>
he will give an account to the Lord on the day of judgment"? And again: "By your **word**

<margin>Ibid.</margin>
you will be justified, and by your word you will be condemned." What, then, are the healthy defenses for the ears, and what are the disciplines for slippery eyes? They are conversations with the righteous, which occupy the ears and block those who wish to lead them away from the truth. "Evil communications corrupt good manners," says the Poet <note>Clement is quoting the poet Menander, a line also famously quoted by St. Paul in 1 Corinthians 15:33.</note>. The Apostle says it even more excellently: "Abhor that which is evil,

<margin>C</margin>
<margin>Romans 12.</margin>
cleave to that which is good." For he who associates with the holy shall be made holy. We must completely abstain from shameful hearing, words, and sights; but much more is it necessary to be pure from shameful deeds. This includes both the exposing and stripping naked of certain parts of the body that are not fitting to see, and the gazing upon

<margin>D</margin>
<margin>Genesis 9.</margin>
private parts. For the modest son <note>Shem or Japheth, the sons of Noah.</note> did not allow his mind to look upon the shameful nakedness of the righteous man; rather, his modesty covered what drunkenness had bared, hiding the slip of ignorance from view. We must be no less pure in the sounds we produce, which should have no entry into the ears of those who have believed in Christ. For this reason, it seems to me, the **Instructor** permits us to speak nothing unseemly or dishonorable, fortifying us long in advance against **lack of self-control** [incontinentiam]. For He is accustomed to cut out the roots of **vices** [vitiorum] with wonderful art; just as "You shall not commit

<margin>Exodus 20.</margin>
adultery" is preceded by "You shall not **covet**." For adultery is the fruit of **lust** [concupiscentiae], which

<margin>Matthew 5.</margin>
is the evil root. Similarly, here too the Instructor rebukes the careless freedom of names as if it were the act itself, cutting off the careless approach to intemperance.

<margin>E</margin>
For behaving insolently in the names we use makes us practice acting dishonorably. To be modest in speech is to train oneself to firmly withstand the pressure of lust. In a deeper discourse, we have argued that the name of what is truly shameful is not found in the names of parts pertaining to intercourse or the marriage union—where names are used that are rarely spoken in common use. For the knee, the leg, and such limbs—and the names given to them—are not shameful, nor is the action performed through them. The limbs and a human's **private parts** <note>original: "verenda," literally "things to be revered" or "venerable parts," used as a modest euphemism.</note> should be considered full of modesty, not shameful. The shameful thing is their **illegal operation**, which is worthy of reproach and punishment. For the only truly shameful thing is **vice** [vitium], and the deeds done through it.

<margin>F</margin>
Consequently, the term **foul language** [turpiloquium] is rightly applied to speech about **vicious deeds**—such as discussions of adultery or the "love of boys" <note>original: "puerorum amore," a reference to pederasty, which Clement strongly condemns.</note> and similar things. Even foolish trifles should be passed over in silence. "In the **multitude of words**,"

<margin>Proverbs 10.</margin>
it says, "you shall not escape sin." Therefore, the vice of the tongue shall pay the penalty.

<summary>Clement argues that Christians must avoid foul language and shameful sights, explaining that the body itself is not shameful, but rather the "vicious" misuse of it and the speech that encourages such vice.</summary>

<margin>A</margin>
For there is a silent person who is found to be wise, and there is one who is hated for their excessive talkativeness. Furthermore, the idle talker brings upon himself both weariness and a sense of being fed up. <margin>Ibid. 10.</margin> For he who multiplies his speech hates his own soul.

### What things those who live together honorably ought to observe. Chapter VII.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' showing a seated scholar or teacher at a desk.</image-desc>
But let us also refrain from **mockery**, from which insults first begin, and from which disputes, fights, and enmities break out. We have already said that insult is the servant of drunkenness. <margin>B</margin> For a man is judged not only by his deeds, but also by his words. <margin>Ibid. 31.</margin> **In a banquet**, it says, **do not argue with your neighbor**, and do not speak a word of reproach to him. For if we are commanded above all to live among the holy, then mocking a holy person is a sin. <margin>Proverbs 20.</margin> **From the mouth of the foolish**, says the Scripture, **comes a rod of insult**. By saying "rod," it means the foundation of the insult, upon which the insult itself leans and rests. <margin>Ephesians 5.</margin> Hence I admire the **Apostle** <note>Clement refers to St. Paul as "the Apostle."</note>, who here also persuades us not to pour out scurrilous words or things that have no bearing on the matter at hand. For if people gather at banquets for the sake of **charity** [love], and the end goal of the banquet is benevolence toward those who are together, and food and drink follow that charity: how then is it not necessary to behave as <margin>C</margin> reason demands, and not to doubt because of charity? For if we meet to increase the benevolence between us, how do we provoke enmities by mocking? It is better to be silent than to contradict, bringing sin upon sin. <margin>Ecclesiasticus 14.</margin> Truly blessed is he who has not slipped with his mouth, or has not been stung by the trouble of sin, or led to repentance because of the sinful things he spoke—or because what he spoke caused no one any trouble.

In summary, therefore, young men and young women should abstain entirely from such banquets, lest they fall into things that were not fitting. For unfamiliar things heard and unseemly sights—while their faith is still wavering—fan the flames of their minds. The instability of their age helps push them headlong toward their desires. Furthermore, they should never provide others with causes for offense while they display the "flower of their age," which is especially slippery and dangerous. For Wisdom seems to command rightly: <margin>Ibid. 9.</margin> <margin>D</margin> **Do not sit at all with a woman subject to a husband** <note>original: "cum muliere quae viro subiecta est," referring to a married woman.</note>, **and do not recline on your elbow with her.** This means: Do not dine with her frequently, nor eat with her. And therefore it adds: **Nor join with her in wine**, lest your heart should ever incline toward her, and by your blood you fall into destruction. For the liberty found in wine is a slippery thing that can burst into flame. He specified a woman "subject to a husband" because the danger is greater for him who tries to dissolve the bond of life’s partnership.

But if some necessity arises that requires them to attend, let the women be beautifully covered on the outside with a garment, but on the inside with modesty. As for those who are not subject to a husband, it is an extreme disgrace for them to be present at a banquet of men, and drunken men at that. Those who fix their eyes on the "tent" <note>likely a metaphor for the body or the dining space</note>, remaining motionless and leaning on their elbows, <margin>E</margin> should be present with their ears alone. But if they are seated, they should not frequently shift their feet, nor place one thigh over the other, nor support their chin with their hand. For it is unrefined and unseemly to be unable to support oneself; such a thing is attributed to the vice of a young person. Moving often and changing one's posture and figure is a sign of levity.

Now, it is the mark of a modest and honorable person to choose the lesser portion in both food and drink, and to do so slowly rather than eagerly, both at the start and during intervals. <margin>Ecclesiasticus 31.</margin> Furthermore, one should be the first to stop, showing oneself to be free from the passion for food: **Eat like a human being**, it says, **the things set before you; but stop first for the sake of discipline.** And if you sit in the midst of many, do not stretch out your hand before them. One should never leap forward <margin>F</margin> out of greed, nor—even if desiring it—should one reach out except after some time, acknowledging their lack of self-control by the long delay. Nor, in the meantime, should they appear to cling to the food like wild animals or seize it greedily. Furthermore, one should not stuff oneself with a great deal of "relish" <note>term: "obsonium," meaning side-dishes or delicacies eaten with bread.</note>. For man was not born to devour delicacies, but to eat grain. To rise before many others and leave the banquet is the sign of a very modest person. **When it is time to rise**, it says, **do not be the last, but return...**

<margin>A</margin> ...bring into your house. Even the twelve Apostles said, when they had called together the multitude of the disciples: <margin>Acts 6</margin> "It is not good for us to leave the word of God to serve tables" <note>original: "Non est bonum nos relicto verbo Dei ministrare mensis." This refers to the appointment of the first deacons to handle food distribution so the Apostles could focus on preaching.</note>. If they carefully avoided this task, they avoided gluttony even more. These same Apostles, writing to the brothers in Antioch, Syria, and Cilicia, said: <margin>Acts 15</margin> "It has SEEMED good to the Holy Spirit and to us to impose no greater burden upon you than these necessary things: to abstain from things sacrificed to idols, from blood, from things strangled, and from fornication; by keeping yourselves from these, you will do well." 

One must flee from petulance in wine no differently than from hemlock <note>A poisonous plant famously used to execute Socrates; Clement compares the "deadliness" of social misconduct to physical poison.</note>. Both lead toward death. One must also restrain excessive laughter and immoderate tears. For often those who are drunk, 

<margin>B</margin> after letting out a massive guffaw, then descend back into tears, persuaded by I know not what insolence of the wine. For it is alien to reason to be either effeminate or petulant. 

Now, elders, looking upon the young as if they were their own sons, may very rarely—yet occasionally—joke with them, directing some playful remark at them to teach them what is decorous. With a silent and bashful youth, one may act wittily and urbanely in this way: "My son here" (speaking of the one who is silent) "never stops talking." Such playfulness increases the youth’s modesty, elegantly showing the good qualities he possesses through a false accusation of the faults he does *not* possess. This is a certain invention of a Master teacher, confirming what *is* present by mentioning what is *absent*. Certainly, he who calls a man who drinks water and is sober and temperate "drunk" and "petulant" intends to do something similar. 

<margin>C</margin> But if there are some who gladly mock others, we must remain silent, and their superfluous words should be passed over by us like overflowing cups. For that kind of play is slippery and dangerous. "The mouth of the rash man approaches destruction" <note>A paraphrase of Proverbs 10:14.</note>. You shall not accept a vain report; neither shall you sit with the unjust to be a false witness, nor join in slanders, nor in curses, nor in wickedness. 

And indeed, I believe I can set a limit for the voices of the more modest, who are permitted to speak when conversing with another. Silence is the virtue of women, and staying removed from danger is the duty of the young; but in those of proven age, speech is good. Speak, Elder, at the banquet, for it becomes you; but speak without hindrance and with perfect knowledge. 

<margin>D</margin> Young man, Wisdom also permits you: speak if <margin>Ecclesiasticus 32</margin> there is need of you, and even then, hardly when you have been asked twice. Summarize your speech into a few words. Let each person who discusses a matter measure his voice with just proportion and moderation. For a loud, shouting style of pronunciation is a most insane thing; yet to speak to those nearby so that you are not heard is the mark of one devoid of sense. For they will not hear; the latter is a sign of a small and abject spirit, while the former is a sign of arrogance. Let there also be no vehement contention for the sake of an empty victory of words. For our goal is to be strangers to tumult and perturbation, and this is what the greeting "Peace be to you" means. Before you have heard, do not answer a word. 

Now, a broken and weakened voice is characteristic of a woman; but moderation in the voice is characteristic of a modest man, keeping his speech from excessive volume, length, speed, or quantity. For one 

<margin>E</margin> must never use long-winded speech, nor talk much, nor babble. Neither should one converse in a voluble and headlong manner. For the voice itself, so to speak, must be given its due right, and the mouths of untimely noisemakers and shouters must be stopped. For that reason, the moderate Ulysses punished Thersites with blows. <note>Clement references Homer's *Iliad*, where the Greek hero Odysseus (Ulysses) strikes the vulgar and talkative soldier Thersites to restore order.</note>
*He alone was confusing everything with immoderate words.*
*In his mind he held many things confusedly and at random.*
But certainly with no order. For a talkative man is terrible in his own destruction. Therefore, just like old shoes, the other parts of babblers are worn away by vice, and only the tongue is left to do damage. For that reason, Wisdom prescribes the things most useful for life: <margin>Ibid.</margin>

<margin>F</margin> DO NOT BABBLE in the multitude of elders. Furthermore, cutting out our trifles by the roots, and beginning from God, and establishing that we should conduct ourselves moderately, it says: Do not repeat your WORDS in your prayer. <margin>Ecclesiasticus 7</margin> As for "popping" sounds <note>original: "Poppyismata." This refers to clicking or clucking sounds made with the tongue or lips.</note>, whistling, and sounds made with the fingers <note>snapping</note> to summon servants, these are devoid of reason...

# THE INSTRUCTOR

...[these] signs must be avoided by men endowed with reason. One must also frequently avoid
<margin>A</margin>
spitting, coughing up phlegm with violence, and even blowing the nose at a banquet. Indeed, 
consideration must be shown for one's fellow guests, lest they turn away in disgust from such 
indecency, which proves a lack of self-control. For many people blow their noses, spit, and dine 
all at the same time. If someone happens to sneeze, just as with a belch, they should not 
startle those nearby with a loud noise, which would bear witness to a poor upbringing. 
Instead, a belch should be let out quietly by exhaling air, with the mouth held in a 
decorous manner, not opened wide and gaping like the masks used by <term>tragic actors</term> 
<note>original: "personarum tragicarum"</note>. As for the irritation of sneezing, the 
disturbing noise should be suppressed by gently holding back and retaining the breath. 
In this way, the gathered force of the breath should be extinguished internally as 
honourably as possible, ensuring it passes so that it remains hidden from others—even 
<margin>B</margin>
if the air, forced out by necessity, brings some discharge with it. Indeed, it is a sign 
of arrogance and insolence to wish to add anything to these sounds, rather than to 
diminish them. Furthermore, those who pick their teeth or make their sores bleed are 
both a nuisance to themselves and hateful to those nearby. Moreover, the scratching of 
ears and the irritations of sneezing are like the <term>swinish itching</term> 
<note>The author uses this harsh comparison to suggest that scratching oneself or making 
loud animalistic noises is beneath human dignity.</note> and rubbing that lead toward 
unrestrained sexual immorality. One must also flee from indecencies that meet the eye, 
and the shameful talk that arises from them. Let the gaze be serious, the turning and 
movement of the neck be honorable and decorous, and the gestures of the hands in 
speaking be likewise. In short, quiet, peace, and 
<margin>C</margin>
tranquility are the proper characteristics of the Christian.

### Whether one should use perfumes and wreaths. Chapter VIII.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial "C" depicting a robed figure, possibly a scholar or saint, seated in a room with a window and a desk, gesturing as if teaching or writing.</image-desc>
<margin>Luke 7</margin>
The use of <term>wreaths</term> <note>In the ancient world, guests at parties often wore 
crowns made of flowers or ivy</note> and perfumes is not necessary for us. Indeed, they 
drive one toward lust and pleasures, especially when night is near. I know that when 
a woman brought an alabaster jar of perfume to the holy supper, she anointed the 
Lord’s feet and delighted Him. I also know 
that the ancient Kings of the Hebrews wore <term>diadems</term> adorned with gold and

<margin>D</margin>

most beautiful in her possession, namely perfume. With the ornament of her body, 
namely her own hair, she wiped away the excess perfume, offering to the Lord the 
tears of her repentance. Therefore her sins were forgiven. However, this event can 
be seen as a sign and symbol of the Lord's teaching and His passion. For the 
feet that are anointed with fragrant perfume signify the divine teaching, which 
traverses the world with remarkable glory. For "their sound has gone out into 
all the earth," and 
<margin>Psalm 18. Romans 10.</margin>
therefore—if I do not seem too bold—the feet of the Lord are the Apostles, 
anointed by prophecy, who are partakers of the sweet-smelling perfume, which 
is the Holy Spirit. Thus the Apostles, who traveled the whole world and 
preached the Gospel, 
<margin>E</margin>
are called the "feet of the Lord" through allegory. Concerning them, the Lord 
also foretold through the Psalmist: 
<margin>Ibid. 131.</margin>
"LET US WORSHIP in the place where his feet have stood." That is, where His 
feet reached: the Apostles, through whom the preaching came to the ends of the 
earth. The tears are the signs of repentance; and the loosened hair

the affliction to be endured with patience for the Lord's sake along with the 
preaching, once that old vain glory was dissolved by the new faith. 
Furthermore, it signifies the Lord's passion. To those who understand it 
mystically in this way, the oil is the Lord Himself, from whom mercy reaches 
us. But the perfume—by which I mean an "adulterated" or artificial oil—is 
Judas the Traitor, by whom the Lord's feet were anointed while He was being 
released from His 
<margin>F</margin>
life in the world. For the dead are anointed. We sinners who have believed 
in Him are the tears, and to us He has forgiven our sins. And the loosened

which there were prophetic lamentations. But 
<margin>Matthew 26</margin>
the Lord Himself will teach us that Judas is false and "adulterated" oil, 
saying: "HE WHO DIPS his hand with me in the dish, he will betray me." 
You see the deceitful guest. This very Judas...

# BOOK TWO

<margin>A</margin> Judas betrayed the Lord with a kiss. He was a hypocrite and a pretender, offering a fraudulent and deceitful kiss. In this, he imitated another ancient hypocrite <note>Likely a reference to Joab or perhaps the Serpent in Eden</note> and stood as an indictment of that people of whom it was said: <margin>Isaiah 29</margin> **THIS PEOPLE** honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me. It is therefore quite probable that the oil signifies the Disciple who obtained mercy, while the fraudulent betrayal is signified by oil that is tainted and poisonous. This was what the feet anointed with ointment foretold: namely, the betrayal of Judas, as the Lord proceeded toward His passion. Furthermore, the Savior Himself, by washing the feet of the Disciples and sending them toward honorable actions, signaled their entry into the service of the nations; He prepared their path, which was beautiful and pure, by His own power. The ointment breathed its fragrance upon them, and the work of that sweet odor reached out to all, celebrated by them. For the passion of the Lord filled us with a good odor, but the Hebrews it filled with the stench of sin. The Apostle shows this most clearly, saying: <margin>B</margin> <margin>2 Corinthians 2</margin> **THANKS BE TO GOD** who always leads us in triumph in Christ, and through us manifests the odor of His knowledge in every place; for we are the sweet odor of Christ to God, among those who are being saved and those who are perishing. To the latter, an odor from death to death; to the former, an odor from life to life. Furthermore, the Kings of the Jews—using gold, gems, and complex, varied crowns—bore a symbolic "Christ" <note>original: "Christi Christum," likely playing on 'Christ' as 'Anointed One'</note> upon their heads, though they were unwise to the Lord who adorned their heads. Certainly, a precious stone, whether a pearl or an emerald, signifies the Word itself. Gold, likewise, is the Word, which is alien to destruction and does not receive the poison of corruption. And to the newborn King, the Magi offered gold, which is the symbol of a kingdom; but <margin>Matthew 2</margin> this immortal crown remains in the image of the Lord, for it does not wither like a flower. Now, I also know of Aristippus of Cyrene <note>A philosopher who founded a school teaching that pleasure is the highest good</note>. He was devoted to a soft and luxurious life. <margin>C</margin> Aristippus used to propose a Sophistic argument of this sort: "A horse that is smeared with ointment is not hindered in its excellence as a horse, nor is a dog so smeared hindered in its excellence as a dog." He added, "Therefore, neither is a man," and thus he concluded his syllogism. Yet, a horse and a dog have no capacity of reason to judge ointment. Those whose senses are endowed with reason ought to be more severely blamed for the use of such things, as they display a childish fondness for scents.

Of these ointments, there are infinite varieties: Brenthium, Metallium, Royal ointment, Plangonian, and Egyptian *Psagda*. Even Simonides <note>A Greek lyric poet</note> does not fear to say in his Iambic verses: **I WAS ANOINTED** with ointments and incense and baccar <note>A fragrant root used in ancient perfumes</note>; for a certain merchant <margin>D</margin> was present. Furthermore, they also use ointment made from lilies, and Cyprian ointment; nard is held in the highest prize among them, as well as ointment made from roses, and other types used by women—liquid, dry, those that are sprinkled, and those used for fumigation. Every day they devise new ones to satisfy an unquenchable desire <margin>lack of taste <note>original Greek: ἀπειροκαλία, meaning a lack of aesthetic or moral judgment</note></margin> with an insatiable craving for sweet smells. Consequently, they reek of an excessive sort of beauty. They fumigate and sprinkle their clothes, their bed-coverings, and their houses; indeed, the delights of their perfumes almost compel their very chamber pots to smell sweet. Therefore, it seems to me that some were right to be annoyed that so much effort is spent on ointments that they even effeminate manliness itself; such people would expel the makers of these—the perfumers—from cities governed by good laws and <margin>E</margin> institutions, and would likewise expel the dyers of brightly colored wools. For it is a sin for "deceitful garments" and ointments to enter the City of Truth. Above all, it is necessary that the men among us do not smell of perfumes, but of the integrity of life. Let a woman breathe of Christ, the royal unction, rather than ointments and powders; let her always be anointed with the divine unction of modesty, delighting in the holy ointment, which is the Spirit. Christ compares this unction of sweet odor to His followers, composing this ointment from heavenly spices. With this ointment the Lord Himself is also anointed, as He remembers through David: <margin>F</margin> **THEREFORE** God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your fellows. Myrrh, and stacte, and cassia are upon your <margin>Psalm 44</margin> garments. However, lest we perhaps shrink from ointments like vultures or beetles—for they say these creatures die if smeared with rose ointment—a few of these ointments may be chosen by women, provided they do not make a husband listless. For excessive...

<meta>Catchword: f (for "fragrance" or a similar word starting with 'f' in the following text)</meta>

<summary>Clement of Alexandria argues that physical perfumes are often a sign of moral decay or "lack of taste," contrasting the deceptive "scent" of Judas with the spiritual "sweet odor" of Christ and a virtuous life. He calls for a rejection of luxury in favor of the "ointment" of the Holy Spirit and modesty.</summary>

### THE INSTRUCTOR
<sig>q</sig>

<margin>A</margin> The anointing of perfumes smells more like the rites performed for the dead than the familiar customs of daily life. Although oil itself is an enemy to bees and insects, it is beneficial to certain men. Indeed, it rouses some to combat; those who were previously friends are led into the stadium once they are anointed, where they fight in competition with all their might and effort. But as for ointment—which is a softened, scented oil—do you not think it can effeminate noble character? Just as we have removed luxuries from the sense of taste, we must certainly drive away the tickling pleasure of the senses from sight and smell. We must not allow the intemperance we have put to flight to find a way back into the soul through the senses, as if through gates that lack guards. 

<margin>B</margin> If people say that the High Priest—namely the Lord—offers the incense of a sweet odor to God, they should not understand this to be a literal sacrifice or a physical incense, but rather the pleasing and acceptable gift of charity <note>The Latin 'charitatem' implies the theological virtue of love/charity</note>, the spiritual sweetness of the fragrance which the Lord offers at the altar. Therefore, plain oil is sufficient for moisturizing the surface of the skin, relaxing the nerves, and suppressing the heavier odors of the body, if we even have a need for oil for such a purpose. However, the pursuit of "sweet odors" is the food of idleness and softness, which gradually draws one toward lustful and intemperate desire. For the man who lacks self-control is led and dragged about by everything: by food, by his bed, by his conversation, by his eyes, by his ears, by his jaws, and even by his nostrils. Just as oxen are led by rings and ropes, so the intemperate man is dragged by incenses, perfumes, and the sweet scents of flower-crowns. 

<margin>C</margin> Since we grant no place to pleasure that is designed for no useful purpose in life, come, let us make a distinction here as well, choosing that which is useful. For there are certain sweet scents which do not bring about a stupor, nor drive one toward amorous desires, nor smell of unchaste unions and the company of harlots, but are instead healthy when used with temperance; they nourish the brain when it is unwell and strengthen the stomach. It is far from necessary to use flowers for "cooling" when someone simply wishes to make their nerves light and agile. Their use is not to be entirely banished, but ointment should be used like a medicine or a relief—to stir up flagging strength, or to treat catarrhs <note>A buildup of mucus in the nose or throat</note>, chills, and exhaustion. 

<margin>D</margin> As the Comic poet says somewhere: "The hands are anointed with ointment, which is a great part of health, so that it may create good odors for the brain." Furthermore, the rubbing of the feet through anointing with things that warm or cool is practiced for the sake of utility: namely, so that for those who suffer from "fullness" <note>Congestion or pressure</note> in the head, there may be a certain attraction and diversion of fluids toward the less vital parts of the body. But pleasure to which no utility is added is a disgrace to the morals of a harlot and a drug used for provocation. In every way, there is a great difference between <term>μυραλοιφεῖν</term> <note>myraloiphein: to be drenched or smeared in perfume</note>—that is, being drenched in perfume—and simply being anointed with oil. The former is effeminate. To be anointed with oil, however, is sometimes useful. Thus Aristippus the Philosopher, when he had been anointed with ointment, said that those "bad men who are destined for a bad end"—the effeminate <note>original: "Cinædos" – a derogatory term for men perceived as soft or sexually passive</note>—had caused the utility of ointment to have a bad reputation. 

<margin>Eccleſi. 38.</margin> **HONOR THE** Physician because of his utility, says the Scripture. For the Most High created him. From the Lord comes medicine. 

<margin>E</margin> Then it adds: **AND THE PERFUMER** <note>original: "VNGVENTARIVS" – an ointment-maker or apothecary</note> shall make the mixture. Clearly, ointments were given for utility, not for the sweet tickling of the senses. One should by no means devote study to the incitements of perfumes; rather, one should choose what is useful in them, since God even permitted oil to be produced for men to alleviate their labors. 

But foolish women—who dye their gray hairs and anoint their locks—turn gray more quickly because of the drying properties of aromatics. For this reason, those who are anointed are drier; and dryness makes one more gray. Whether grayness is the drying out of the hair, or a lack of heat, the dryness drinks up the proper moist nourishment of the hair and produces grayness. 

<margin>F</margin> Why then should we love the perfumes that cause the very gray hair we flee? Just as dogs with keen noses track wild beasts by their scent, so those who are moderate and temperate "hunt down" the intemperate by the overly curious fragrance of their perfumes. Furthermore, such use of crowns for feasting and for insolence in wine...

He distinguishes between the "sweet odor" of spiritual charity and the physical indulgence of the senses, even noting that perfumes can physically damage the hair.</summary>
