### BOOK TWO
->f ii<-

<margin>A</margin> ...has flowed out, compared to insolence. Do not encircle my head with a crown; it is Spring. It is beautiful to dwell in dewy meadows among soft and various budding flowers, enjoying their natural and sincere sweetness of scent in the manner of bees. However, to carry around a crown woven from a pure meadow as an ornament in the home is not the behavior of temperate men. For it is not fitting to cover the hair—which is preparing itself for drunken petulance—with the berries of roses, or violets, or lilies, or any other such flowers, variegating it with herbs and blossoms. For a crown placed around the head also chills the hair, both because of its moisture and its coldness. For this reason, physicians, knowing through diligent contemplation of nature that the brain is cold, feel that the chest <margin>B</margin> and the upper parts of the nose should be anointed, so that the warm exhalation passing through may rightly cherish its coldness. It is far, then from the truth that the head should be chilled with flowers.

Added to this is the fact that those who are crowned also lose the delight of the flowers. For those who have a crown bound above their eyes do not enjoy the sight. Nor do they enjoy the sweetness of the scent, since the flowers are positioned above the respiratory organs. For since scent is naturally emitted and exhaled upwards, the breath above the head enjoys no delight, as the sweetness of the odor is carried away. Therefore, just as beauty delights while it is seen, so does the flower; and it is necessary that we, enjoying the sight of those things which are beautiful, should bestow praise and glory upon the Creator <note>original: "Opificem," literally the Craftsman or Maker, a common way early Christians referred to God as the designer of nature</note>. But the use of them as crowns is harmful and quickly passes away, afflicted by the punishment of regret. The brevity of their life is immediately proven. For both wither: both the flower and beauty. Furthermore, as for those who handle them, the flower chills them, while beauty burns and inflames them. To sum it up in a single word, <margin>C</margin> any use of them perceived through enjoyment beyond the sight is petulance and <margin>1 Cor. 11.</margin> injury, not delight.

We ought to delight ourselves honorably as if in a paradise, truly following the Scripture. A man must be considered the crown of a woman. <margin>Prov. 17. Matt. 23.</margin> But the crown of a man is marriage. The flowers of marriage are the children of both, whom the divine farmer gathers from the carnal meadows. "The crowns of old men are their children's children" <note>A reference to Proverbs 17:6</note>. But for children, he says, their glory is their fathers. For us, however, the crown of the Father of the universe and of the whole Church is Christ.

Just as roots and herbs have their own qualities, so too do flowers: some are useful, others harmful, and others dangerous. Thus, ivy is cooling. The walnut <note>original: "Nux"</note>, however, emits a spirit that <margin>D</margin> brings on numbness and lethargy, as the etymology of the name itself shows. <margin>In Greek, the walnut is called "karya," from "karos," which means torpor or heaviness of the head.</margin> The Narcissus is a flower of heavy scent: the very name implies this, as one which brings *narkē* <note>Greek: νάρκην</note>, that is, numbness, to the nerves. But the scents emitted by roses and violets, since they are moderately cool, suppress and restrain heaviness in the head. We, however, are permitted by no means to become intoxicated together, nor even to use unmixed wine <margin>to be under the influence of wine</margin>. Furthermore, the crocus and the flower of the privet lead to a sleep that is not at all troublesome. <margin>The rose, "rhodon," is named from the "rhysis" (flow) of scent.</margin> Moreover, many of these cherish the brain—which is cold by nature—with their scents, while making the secretions of the brain thin and small. Hence they also say the rose was named *rhodon* in Greek because it emits a great flow <note>original: "fluxum"</note> of scent, and therefore it quickly withers.

<margin>E</margin> Furthermore, among the ancient Greeks, there was not yet any <margin>gift, acclamation, scattering of leaves</margin> use of crowns. Neither the Suitors nor the Phaeacians, who lived a luxurious life, used them. In the games, it was first a gift for athletes; second, it was for applause and excitement; third, for the throwing of leaves. Finally, it became a crown, when a great addition was made to luxuries in Greece after the Persian Wars <note>original: "tempora Medica," referring to the wars with the Medes/Persians</note>. Therefore, those who are instructed by the Word <term>Reason/Word: the "Logos" or divine instruction of Christ</term> are kept away from crowns, nor do they think it right for their reason—which is situated in the brain—to be bound. This is not only because the crown is a symbol of convivial petulance through wine, but because it is dedicated to idols <note>original: "simulachris," meaning images or statues of pagan gods</note>. Sophocles certainly called the Narcissus the ancient crown of the Great Gods, saying this of the gods of the earth; and Sappho crowns the Muses with the rose: "You have no share in the Pierian roses." They say that Juno <margin>F</margin> delights in the lily, and Diana in the myrtle. For even if flowers were made primarily for the sake of man, when foolish people received them, they did not put them to their proper use (which they could have used with a grateful heart), but abused them in the ungrateful service of demons. Therefore, one must abstain from them for the sake of conscience.

He promotes spiritual "crowns" such as marriage, children, and Christ instead of physical luxury.</summary>

# THE INSTRUCTOR

<margin>A</margin> ...the wreath is a sign of a crown. For this reason, they also crown the dead; by which very act and testimony they assert that idols are dead. Indeed, those who engage in Dionysian revelry <note>original: "bacchantur", referring to the wild festivals of Bacchus/Dionysus</note> do not celebrate their secret rites without crowns. Furthermore, after they have surrounded themselves with flowers, they are finally inflamed in a wonderful manner. We must have no communication with demons. 

Moreover, the living image of God <note>The human being</note> is not to be crowned in the manner of dead idols. For a beautiful <margin>2 Corinthians 6. <note>The text likely intends a reference to 1 Peter 5:4</note> Unfading (Greek: *amarantos*). The "amarantum" flower signifies that which is unfading.</margin> crown of **amaranth** <note>A legendary flower that never fades; the name literally means "unfading" in Greek</note> is laid up for the one who has conducted themselves rightly. This flower the earth cannot bear; heaven alone is able to produce it. Added to these points is the fact that it is alien to reason <margin>Matthew 27</margin> for us—having heard that the Lord was crowned with thorns—to have our own heads encircled with flowers, mockingly insulting the venerable passion of the Lord through our play. For the Lord’s crown prophetically signified us, <margin>B</margin> who were once unfruitful, and who were placed around Him through the Church, of which He is the head. Furthermore, it is a type <note>A "type" is a symbolic foreshadowing</note> of faith: of life, because of the substance of the wood; of joy, because of the name "crown"; and of danger, because of the thorn, for one cannot approach the Word without blood. But the woven crown withers, and the garland twisted from wickedness is dissolved, and the flower dries up. For the glory of those who have least believed in the Lord withers away. 

In their ignorance, they crowned Jesus as He was lifted up on high. For this very reason, being hard of heart, they do not understand the wisely uttered prophecy, which they themselves call the Lord’s reproach and insult. The people who went astray did not know the Lord; they were not circumcised in reason and consideration; their darkness was not illuminated; they knew not God; they denied the Lord. <margin>C</margin> They lost the right to be called the true Israel; they persecuted God; they hoped to treat the Word with contempt; and Him whom they crucified as a criminal, they crowned as a King. 

Therefore, the Man in whom they did not believe, they shall recognize as the kind God, Lord, and Just One. Him whom they provoked so that He might show Himself as Lord, they testified to when He was lifted on high, granting a crown of righteousness to Him who is exalted above every name, through the ever-flowering thorn. This crown is an enemy to those who plot against Him, but a friend to those who dwell together in the Church; it has hedged them in and fortified them. This crown is the flower of those who have believed in Him who has been glorified, but it bleeds and punishes those who have not believed. 

Furthermore, this is also a sign of the deed successfully accomplished by the Lord, since He, in His own head and the principal part of His body, bore all our evils <margin>D</margin> by which we were pricked. For when He had freed us from offenses and sins, and thorns of that kind, through His own passion, and had weakened and abolished the Devil, He said with merit in prayer: *WHERE, O death, IS THY STING?* <margin>Hebrews 2. 1 Corinthians 15.</margin> And while we indeed gather grapes from thorns and figs from thistles, they—those to whom He extended His hands, namely the unfaithful and unfruitful people—are wounded and torn. 

I could tell you another mystical thing. For when the almighty Lord of all <margin>Exodus 3. In Greek, "light" is *phōs*, which also signifies "man".</margin> began to give the Law through the Word, and wished to manifest His power to Moses, a divine vision of formed light was shown to him in a burning bush. Now, the bush is a thorny plant. After the Word ceased to give the Law and to dwell among men, <margin>E</margin> the Lord is again mystically crowned with a crown, departing from here to where He had descended, restoring the beginning of His ancient descent, and gathering it together again as if into a sum <margin><term>Recapitulation</term> (Greek: *anakephalaiōsamenos*), a theological concept of Christ "summing up" or restoring all things.</margin>, so that what had first been seen as the Word through the bush, might be shown again through the thorn—taken up to show that all things are of one power, since He is one, and the Son of the Father who is one, the beginning and the end of the age. 

But I have digressed from the "Pedagogical" style <note>Moral instruction for daily life</note> into the kind of discourse concerned with teaching dogmas <note>Theological doctrines</note>. Let me, therefore, return to the purpose at hand. We have shown, therefore, that the delight felt from flowers—and the benefit received from ointments and incenses—should not be rejected when used in the place of medicine, for the sake of healing, and sometimes even for moderate recreation. But if some should ask: "What further grace is there in flowers for those who do not use them?" let them know that ointments are also composed from them, and these are quite useful. **Susinum** <margin>F</margin> is composed from lilies and iris. It is heating, opening, drawing, moistening, cleansing, made of subtle and thin parts, moving the bile, and softening. **Narcissinum**, which is composed from Narcissus, helps just as much as Susinum. **Myrrhinum**, truly, which is from myrtles...

# BOOK TWO

<margin>A</margin> <margin>Myrtle-oil <note>original Greek: μύρρινα</note></margin> consists of myrtles and the myrsine plant; it is astringent and restrains the odors that are emitted from the body. That which is made from roses, however, is cooling. In short, all these things were created so that we might use them for our good. <margin>Ecclesiasticus 39</margin> **Listen to me**, he says, **and bud forth like a rose planted by streams of water. Give forth a sweet smell like frankincense, and bless the Lord for His works.** <note>Clement is quoting Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 39:13–14</note> Much could be said about these things, since we maintain that flowers and aromatics were made for necessary utility, not for the insolence of luxury. Even if something must be granted to the senses, it is enough to enjoy the scent of flowers; but by no means should people be crowned with them. For the Father cares for humanity, and provides His own specific art to him alone. <margin>Ibidem <note>referring to the same passage in Sirach 39</note></margin> As the Scripture says: **Water, fire, iron, milk, the finest wheat, honey, the blood of the grape, oil, and clothing: all these things are for good to the godly.** <margin>B</margin>

## How one should behave in sleep. ### Chapter IX.

---

<margin>C</margin> <image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'Q' with floral and scrolling leaf patterns.</image-desc> HOW we should next betake ourselves to sleep, mindful of the precepts of modesty, must now be discussed. For after the banquet is finished and we have blessed and praised God—because He has supplied what was necessary for our use and granted us the passage of that day—our prayer must then be turned toward sleep. We should say farewell to the magnificence of bedding: pillows interwoven with gold, gold-variegated smooth garments, coverlets, <margin>xystides, gaunacae, rhegea <note>original Greek: ξυσίδες, γαύνακες, ῥήγεα</note></margin> purple <term>xystides <note>Fine, light robes often used by athletes or the wealthy</note></term>, the most precious <term>gaunacae <note>Thick, shaggy Babylonian cloaks or rugs</note></term>, and the poetic purple <term>rhegea <note>Fine tapestries or rugs often mentioned in Homeric poetry</note></term>, as well as garments that are soft and delicate on top, and beds softer than sleep itself. 

For besides the fact that this soft and sense-tickling pleasure is to be blamed, sleeping on downy feathers is harmful; the bodies fall as if into a vast gap because of the softness of the bedding. Such beds do not support those who roll about in their sleep, because the bedding rises up like a mound on either side of the body. Nor do they permit food to be properly digested, but rather they overheat it, which corrupts the nourishment. On the other hand, lying on flat and level beds—which are like a natural gymnasium for sleep—helps the body digest its food. Those who are able to turn themselves in such beds, having this natural gymnasium of sleep, <margin>D</margin> digest their food more easily and make themselves more fit for all circumstances. 

Furthermore, litters <note>portable couches or sedan chairs</note> that have silver feet reveal great arrogance. As for the ivory found in beds, once the elephant’s body has left its soul, it is not appropriate for holy men to use it as an idle and lazy instrument of rest. Therefore, one’s zeal should not be spent on such things. It is not the possession of these items that is prohibited, but the excessive zeal and devotion placed in them; for happiness is not located in such things. 

On the other hand, it is a mark of the vain glory of the <term>Cynics <note>A school of Greek philosophers who lived in extreme poverty to show their independence from worldly needs</note></term> to train oneself for sleep as Diomedes did, **"spreading beneath him the hides of a wild ox,"** <note>A reference to Homer's Iliad, Book 10</note> unless perhaps some necessity compels it. Even Ulysses, because the bed of his bride was uneven, corrected it by placing a stone beneath it. <note>A reference to the Odyssey; Ulysses (Odysseus) built his bed around an olive tree, demonstrating craftsmanship and stability</note> Such frugality and native simplicity—not sought from expensive outside sources—was practiced not only among private citizens but even among the leaders of the ancient Greeks. <margin>E</margin> 

<margin>Genesis 28</margin> Though why do I need to speak of these? Jacob slept on the ground, and a stone was his pillow. And yet, he was deemed worthy to see a vision that surpassed human understanding. <note>The "Ladder of Jacob," reaching to heaven</note> For us, as fits reason, a simple and frugal bed should be used, providing what is moderate and convenient to help us. If there is heat, something to protect us; if there is cold, something to warm us. Let the bed not be skillfully or curiously carved, and let it have flat and smooth feet. For too-exquisite carvings often become paths for crawling creatures, as they wind around the artistic incisions and cannot be easily swept away. 

Above all, the softness of the bed must be moderately and suitably manly. <margin>F</margin> For sleep ought not to be a total dissolution of the body, but only a relaxation. Therefore, when I say sleep is to be taken, it is not for the sake of idleness or sloth, but for rest from business and actions. Thus one must sleep so that we are easily awakened: **"Let your loins be girded,"** He says, **"and your lamps burning."** <margin>Luke 12</margin>

The crown is a sign. For this reason, they also crown the dead; by this name and practice, they testify that idols are effectively dead, just like those who join in Bacchic revelries and never celebrate their secret rites without crowns. Added to this is the fact that it is contrary to reason for us—who have heard that the Lord was crowned with thorns—to have our own heads bound with flowers, mockingly insulting the venerable passion of the Lord through our playfulness.

<margin>B</margin>
For the Lord’s crown prophetically signified us, who were once unfruitful, but who have been placed around Him through the Church, of which He is the head. For this very reason, being hard of heart, they did not understand the wisely uttered prophecy, which they themselves called the Lord's "disgrace" and "insult." The people who went astray did not know the Lord; they were not circumcised in reason or consideration; their darkness was not illuminated; they did not know God; they denied the Lord.

<margin>C</margin>
They lost the right to be called the true Israel: they persecuted God; they hoped to treat the Word with contempt. And the one they crucified as a criminal, they crowned as a King. Therefore, the one in whom they did not believe as a man, they shall recognize as the kind God and Lord, and the Just One. Him whom they provoked to offend the Lord, they testified about when He was raised on high, granting Him the <term>diadem of righteousness</term> <note>a crown symbolizing moral perfection and divine authority</note>—exalted above every name—through the ever-blooming thorn. This diadem is an enemy to those who plot against Him, but a friend to those who dwell together in the Church; it has hedged them in and protected them. This crown is the flower of those who have believed in Him who has been glorified, but it draws blood and punishes those who have not believed. Furthermore, this is also a sign of the Lord’s great achievement: that He, with His own head and the principal part of His body, bore all our evils, for which we were being pricked.

## Chapter IX.
### How one ought to conduct oneself in sleep.

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'Q' depicting a seated figure in a scholar's or classical robe within a square frame decorated with foliage.</image-desc>
We must now speak of how we should thereafter commit ourselves to sleep, mindful of the precepts of modesty. For after we have blessed and praised God at the end of the banquet—because He has supplied what was necessary for our use and permitted us to pass through that day—our prayer must be turned toward sleep. We must bid farewell to the magnificence of bedding, to pillows woven with gold, and to smooth garments variegated with gold, to coverlets and <margin>fine robes <note>original Greek: ξυστίδες (xystides)</note>. thick cloaks <note>original Greek: γαύνακες (gaunakes)</note>. rugs <note>original Greek: ῥήγεα (rhegea)</note>.</margin> purple **xystides** <term>xystides: long, flowing robes often worn by actors or the wealthy</term>, and most precious **gaunacae** <term>gaunacae: heavy, shaggy wool cloaks of Persian origin</term>, and the **purple rugs** of poetry, and garments that are soft and delicate on top, and beds softer than sleep itself. For besides the fact that this soft and sense-tickling pleasure is to be blamed, it is harmful to sleep on downy feathers; the body falls as if into a vast hollow because of the softness of the bedding. Such beds do not support those who sleep in them, because the bed rises up like a mound on both sides of the body; nor do they permit food to be digested, but rather they cause it to overheat, which corrupts the nourishment. However, lying on flat and level beds, which are like a natural gymnasium for sleep, helps in the digestion of nourishment. Those who are able to roll about in other beds, having this natural gymnasium for sleep,
<margin>D</margin>
digest their food more easily and make themselves more fit for all circumstances. Furthermore, couches that have silver feet reveal great arrogance, and the ivory found in small beds—after the elephant’s body has left its soul—is not so much permitted to holy men as it is an idle and lazy artifice of rest. Therefore, one should not devote effort to such things. For the use of these possessions is not forbidden to the owners, but the obsession placed in them is forbidden. For happiness does not reside in them. On the other hand, it is a matter of empty Cynic pride to practice sleeping as Diomedes did: *And he spread beneath him the hide of a wild ox*, unless perhaps some necessity compels it. Ulysses, because his wife’s bed was unsteady, corrected it by placing a stone beneath it. Such frugality and natural simplicity of work—not sought from the outside—was practiced not only among 
<margin>E</margin>
private citizens, but even among the leaders of the ancient Greeks. Yet why do I need to speak of them? Jacob used to sleep on the ground, and a stone was his pillow. And indeed, he was deemed worthy to see a vision that surpassed human understanding. <margin>Genesis 28.</margin> We, as is fitting for reason, should use a simple and frugal bed, which possesses that which helps us in a moderate and convenient way. If there is heat, it should protect; if there is cold, it should warm. Let the bed not be crafted with elaborate or curious skill, and let it have feet that are flat and smooth. For overly curious and exquisite carvings are often the paths for crawling creatures, as they wind through the incisions of the art and do not slip off. Above all, the softness of the bed should be moderately and appropriately manly and masculine. For sleep ought not to be a perfect dissolution of the body, but only a remission. And therefore, when I say it should be taken, I mean not for idleness and laziness, but for rest from business and actions. We must sleep in such a way that we are easily awakened: <margin>Luke 12.</margin> > "For let your loins," it says, "be girded, and your lamps burning."

<header>THE INSTRUCTOR</header>

...and you should be like people waiting for their master to return from the wedding <margin>A</margin>, so that when he comes and knocks, they may open to him immediately. Blessed are those servants whom the Master finds watching when He comes. For a sleeping person is of no use, just like a dead one. For this reason, we should even rise from bed often at night and praise God. For blessed are those who keep watch for Him, making themselves like the Angels, whom we call <term>watchers <note>original Greek: ἐγρηγόρους (egrēgorous)</note></term>, which means those who are vigilant. A sleeping person is of no value, no more than one who is not alive. But whoever has the light is awake, and the darkness does not overcome them; nor does sleep, since it is not darkness. Therefore, he who has been illuminated has kept watch for God. Whoever is such a person, lives. For **THAT** which was made <margin>John 1. Proverbs 8.</margin> in him was life. **BLESSED** is the man, says Wisdom, who hears me, and the man who <margin>B</margin> keeps my ways, watching at my gates, observing by day the post of my entrance. Therefore, let us not sleep as others do, but: **LET US WATCH**, and be sober. For <margin>1 Thessalonians 5.</margin> those who sleep, sleep at night, and those who are drunk are drunk at night: that is, in the darkness of ignorance. But let us, who are of the day, be sober. For you are all children of the light and children of the day. We do not belong to the night or the darkness; but he who takes the greatest care of us so that we may truly live, and think rightly and sincerely, has remained awake for a great deal of time, reserving for himself only what was useful for his health.

This is not so common, but the practice of discipline produces perpetual vigils through labor. Let food not weigh us down, then, but lighten us, so that as much as possible we are least harmed by sleep—just as swimmers are weighed down when burdens are hung on them. On the other hand, <margin>C</margin> like something rising from the depths below, sobriety will lift us up to the prepared station of watchfulness. For sleep, which weighs us down, is like death, leading us through ignorance into a lack of sensation: it cuts off the light by closing the eyelids. This light, then—we who are children of the true light—let us not shut it out; but turning inward toward ourselves, illuminating the sight of the <term>hidden man <note>The "hidden man" refers to the inner, spiritual self or the soul.</note></term>, and contemplating truth itself, and being made partakers of its flow, let us reveal true dreams clearly and wisely.

The belching of those weighed down by a hangover, the yawning of those burdened by too much food, the snoring muffled in blankets, and the rumblings of tightly compressed stomachs—all these bury the keen eye of the soul, filling one's thoughts with various visions. The cause is superfluous nourishment, which drags the rational faculty of the soul <margin>D</margin> down to the point where it is entirely deprived of sense. For excessive sleep brings no benefit to our bodies or souls, nor is it at all suitable for actions concerning the truth, even if it is natural. Just Lot, however (for the present, I will skip the explanation <margin>Genesis 19.</margin> of the spiritual meaning of that restoration), would not have been led into that shameful intercourse had he not been made drunk by his daughters, and overcome and weighed down by sleep. Therefore, if we cut away the causes that drive us to long and deep sleep, we shall sleep more soberly.

For it is not proper for those who have Reason inhabiting them and keeping watch within to sleep the whole night. Instead, one should wake up especially at night when the day ends; and one person should apply himself to literature, while another should begin his craft. Women should take up their wool-work. For all of us, to put it simply, <margin>E</margin> must fight against sleep, gradually accustoming ourselves by degrees so that we may participate in life through watchfulness for the greater part of the time. For sleep, no differently than a <term>tax collector <note>original Latin: publicanus. Clement compares sleep to a tax collector because it "seizes" or "divides" half of a person's life away from them.</note></term>, divides and takes half of our life. It is far from permitted for those who cut away the greatest part of the night for vigils to sleep during the day. Boredom, drowsiness, stretching, and yawning are the unstable distastes of the soul.

Finally, it must be known that it is not the soul that needs sleep: for the soul itself is always in motion. Rather, it is the body that is given over to rest and relaxed while the soul no longer operates through the body, but dwells within itself through the mind. Thus, those dreams that are true are the thoughts of a sober soul to one who considers rightly—a soul that is not dragged down by the affections of the body through its consent, but <margin>F</margin> consults for itself what is best. It is the death of the soul if it rests entirely within itself. And therefore, by always dwelling upon God in the mind, and by bringing watchfulness to the body through constant habit, one makes a human being equal to angelic grace: receiving the eternity of life through the meditation of watchfulness.

<header>BOOK TWO</header>

### *Which matters are to be treated regarding the procreation of children. Chapter X.*

<margin>A</margin>
The appropriate time for sexual union is a matter to be considered only by those who are joined in marriage. For those who are joined in marriage, the aim and purpose is the reception of children. The ultimate goal, however, is that these children be good—just as the goal of a farmer in sowing his seeds is the need for sustenance, for which he takes care to provide nourishment. The end of that agriculture is the harvesting of crops. But far better is the farmer who cultivates "living soil" <note>A common ancient metaphor for the womb or the wife.</note>. For while the former seeks food for a season, the latter acts as a farmer to ensure the permanence of the whole universe; the former plants and sows for his own sake, but the latter does so for the sake of God. For God said: <margin>Genesis 1.</margin> "INCREASE and multiply," and it is understood: by this means, man becomes the image of God, insofar as man cooperates in the generation of another human being. Not every "soil" is suitable for receiving seed. And even if it were, it is not suitable for every farmer. Indeed, one must not sow upon a rock, nor should the seed be treated with insult—for the seed is the leader and prince of generation, and is a substance that contains within it the implanted designs of nature. To treat these natural designs with dishonor and disgrace by committing them to unnatural passages <note>A reference to non-procreative sexual acts.</note>, acting without reason, is truly wicked and impious. See, therefore, how the most wise <margin>C</margin> Moses symbolically rejected unproductive sowing. <margin>Leviticus 11. Deuteronomy 14.</margin> "YOU SHALL NOT EAT," he says, "the hare, nor the hyena." He does not want men to participate in the qualities of these animals, nor to taste a lust equal to theirs. For these animals are driven to fulfill the sexual act by a kind of insane frenzy. They say the hare increases its sexual capacity every year, having as many orifices as the years it has lived; and for this reason, while he forbids the eating of the hare, he signifies a warning against the love of boys <note>The "love of boys" refers to pederasty, which Clement and other early Christian writers strongly condemned.</note>. Of the hyena, it is said that it changes its sex from male to female every single year. By abstaining from the hyena, he signifies that one must not break out into adulteries. Now, I agree that the most wise Moses, through this prohibition, undoubtedly meant that we should not be like these animals; however, I do not agree with the literal explanation of these symbolic sayings. For the force of nature can never be brought to change. What has once been formed within nature itself cannot be refashioned into its opposite by a mere condition. For a "condition" is not the same as "nature." A condition can corrupt the character of what has been formed, but it cannot transform the form itself. For even if many birds are said to change both their voice and color with the turning of the seasons—just as the blackbird <note>original Latin: merula</note> is said to turn from black to yellow, and from a sweet singer to one that makes a harsh and turbulent sound, becoming what is called a <term>kottuphos <note>original Greek: κόττυφος (kottuphos), which simply means blackbird or thrush</note></term>. Likewise, the nightingale is asserted to change both its color and its voice when the solstices occur. However, they do not change their actual nature so that a male becomes a female through a change in shape. Rather, the recent growth of feathers, like a new garment, sends out a certain tint of plumage like flowers; but shortly after, this is breathed away by the winter storms, just as a flower fades when its color withers. In the same way, the voice itself, badly afflicted by the cold, decays. For when the outer skin is thickened by the surrounding air, the arteries in the neck are compressed and clogged, which also compresses the breath. The breath, forced into a very narrow space, produces a stifled and oppressed sound. Then again, it adapts to the surrounding air, and in the spring the spirit is relaxed and freed from its straits, carried through the dilated arteries that were previously closed. Thus, it no longer produces a withered and thin song, but now sends forth a melodic one, and their voice is spread more widely; the song of the birds' voice emerges in the spring. Therefore, one should by no means believe that the hyena ever changes its nature. For the same animal does not have both male and female genitals at the same time, as <margin>F</margin> some have thought, telling monstrous tales of Hermaphrodites, and inventing a nature consisting of both man and woman between the male and female sexes. They are greatly deceived, as they have not noticed how the mother and begetter of all things, Nature, is a lover of her children. Because this animal, I mean the hyena, is extremely lustful, under...

# THE INSTRUCTOR

<margin>A</margin>
Near the tail, before the passage for waste, there is attached to the hyena a certain fleshy tubercle <note>A small, rounded swelling or prominence.</note> that is very similar in shape to the female private parts. However, this fleshy shape has no passage leading to any functional use—neither into a womb, I say, nor into the rectum. It possesses only a deep hollowness which receives empty lust when the passages occupied in conceiving offspring have been turned away. This same feature is attached to both the male and female hyena, because it is remarkably "pathic" <note>original: "pathica"; in this context, it refers to a creature that takes a passive or unnatural sexual role.</note>. For the male, in turn, both acts and is acted upon. This is why a female hyena is so very rarely found. For this animal does not conceive frequently, since an unnatural sowing of seed is commonly practiced among them.

<margin>B</margin>
For this same reason, it seems to me that Plato in the *Phaedrus*, rejecting the love of boys, calls it a "beast." He suggests that those who give themselves over to pleasures, biting at the bit of restraint, are lustful and walk in the manner of four-footed animals, attempting to sow children unnaturally.

<margin>Romans 1</margin>
God gave up the ungodly, as the Apostle says, to shameful passions. For even their women changed the natural use into that which is against nature. Likewise, their males, leaving the natural use, burned in their desire for one another: men working shame with men, and receiving in themselves the reward that was fitting for their error. And yet, nature did not grant an extra waste passage even to the most lustful of living creatures. For urine is excreted into the bladder, moist nourishment into the belly, tears into the eye, blood into the veins, wax into the ears, and mucus is carried into the nostrils. The seat of the rectum is connected,

<margin>C</margin>
through which excrement is cast out. Therefore, only the diverse nature in hyenas devised this extra part for extra-marital union; and for that reason, it is also somewhat hollow,

<margin><note>original: "ἐπιθοροῦν" (epithoroun)</note> mounting</margin>
so that it may serve the itching parts; however, from that point, the cavity is closed off, for it was not fashioned for generation. From this, it is manifest and even confessed by us that intercourse with males must be avoided, as well as unfruitful sowings, and "preposterous venus" <note>A term for unnatural or "backward" sexual acts.</note>, and those unions of Androgynes <note>literally "man-women," referring here to those who blur sexual roles or biological distinctions</note> which cannot hold together by nature. We should follow nature itself, which prohibits such things through the very constitution of our parts, having made the male not to receive seed, but to be the man who pours it forth. And when Jeremiah says—that is, the Spirit speaking through him:

<margin>chapter 12</margin>
<margin>D</margin>
> My house has become a hyena's cave,

he was expressing an abhorrence for nourishment taken from dead bodies. With a wise allegory, he rebukes the worship of idols. For truly, the house of the living God ought to be pure from idols. Again, Moses prohibits eating the hare. For the hare mates at all times, and the male leaps upon the female, approaching her from behind, for it is among those that mount from the rear. It conceives every month and "superfetates" <note>original: "superfœtat"; to conceive a second fetus while already pregnant.</note>. It both mates and gives birth. But after it has given birth, it is immediately mounted in whatever rabbit-warren it may be, for it is not content with one marriage; and it conceives again while still nursing, for it has a womb with two chambers. A single empty chamber of the womb is not a sufficient seat for it to receive intercourse. For whatever is empty is held by desire and rages with lust. On account of this, superfetations occur in them.

<margin>E</margin>
The prohibition of this riddle <note>Clement views the dietary laws of Moses as "riddles" or allegories for moral behavior.</note> exhorts us to abstain from violent appetites, mutual encounters, unions with pregnant women, alternating matings, the corruption of boys, adulteries, and lust. Therefore, Moses prohibited these things openly and not through riddles, while his head was still bare <note>Meaning he spoke clearly and without a veil of allegory.</note>:

<margin>Exodus 20</margin>
> YOU SHALL NOT FORNICATE, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not bring corruption to boys,

he says. Thus, the command of the Word is to be observed by every means: nothing should be done against the laws in any way, nor should the mandates be weakened. For the name of evil desire is "wanton injury," and Plato, having read the scriptures, called the "horse of desire" wanton and insolent,

<margin>Jeremiah 5, Ezekiel 23, Genesis 19</margin>
when he read:

> You have become to me like horses raging for females.

<margin>F</margin>
Furthermore, the Angels who came to Sodom signified the punishment for shameful and wanton injury. They burned those who wished to afflict them with shame and ignominy along with the city itself, describing with this evident sign the fire which is the fruit of lust. For the things that happened to the ancients, as we have said before, were written to warn us, so that we might not be held by the same vices and may take care lest we fall into similar punishments.

# BOOK TWO

<margin>A</margin>
...avoid. It is necessary to regard sons as children and to look upon the wives of others as if they were one's own daughters. To restrain pleasures and to exercise mastery over the stomach and the parts below the stomach is the highest form of command. For if reason does not permit the wise man to move even a finger at random—as the Stoics <note>A school of ancient Greek philosophy that taught the development of self-control and fortitude as a means of overcoming destructive emotions.</note> admit—how much more must those who pursue wisdom obtain mastery over that part of the body used for union? Indeed, for this very reason, it seems to me that the "pudendum" <note>original: "pudendum"; the Latin term for the private parts, derived from "pudor," meaning shame or modesty.</note> was so named, because that part of the body must be used with more modesty than any other. For nature has permitted us to use what is necessary and fitting, just as with food, so also with lawful marriage. Nature has permitted us to desire the procreation of children. But whoever pursues what exceeds moderation falls away from what is according to 
<margin>B</margin>
nature, harming themselves through unions that are contrary to the laws. For it is entirely right never to engage in sexual intimacy with young men as if they were women. And therefore, he who became a Philosopher through Moses <note>A reference to Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish philosopher who sought to harmonize the Torah with Greek philosophy.</note> says that one should not "sow among rocks and stones," because the seed will never take root or receive a generative nature. Therefore, the Word <note>The "Logos" or Divine Reason, often identified here with the pre-incarnate Christ speaking through the Law.</note> most clearly commanded through Moses:
<margin>Leviticus 18</margin>
> YOU SHALL NOT SLEEP WITH A MALE as with a woman, for it is an abomination.

To this is added that the noble Plato, gathering from the divine scriptures, advised against sowing in any "female field" except one's own, having accepted the law from there:
<margin>Ibid.</margin>
> AND TO THE WIFE of your neighbor you shall not give your seed for union, lest you be defiled with her.

For the seeds of concubines are fruitless and illegitimate. Do not sow where you do not wish that which is sown to be born. Nor should you touch any woman at all except your own wife, from whom alone you are permitted to receive the pleasures of the flesh for the sake of obtaining a legitimate succession. For these 
<margin>C</margin>
things alone are lawful according to reason. Certainly, for those who are sharers in the divine gift—namely, the work of creation—seed is not to be cast away, nor treated with injury, nor should it be sown as if you were committing seed to "horns." <note>A metaphor for a fruitless or hard place where nothing can grow.</note> Here Moses himself also prohibits union with <term>κερασβόλα</term> <note>original: "kerasbola"; literally "struck by horns," used here to refer to wives who are "refractory" or specifically those in their menstrual period, which was seen as a "stony" or "barren" state.</note> wives, if they happen to be detained by their menstrual cleansings.
<margin>Ibid.</margin>
For it is not fitting to pollute with a cleansing of the body that which is most generative in women, and which will soon become a human being; nor is it right to flood and overwhelm it with a foul flow of matter and the impurities that are being purged. Moreover, the seed of generation 
<margin>D</margin>
degenerates and is rendered unfit if it is deprived of the furrows of the womb. Truly, none of the ancient Hebrews ever approached his wife while she was pregnant. For pleasure alone, even if one uses it within marriage, is contrary to the laws, unjust, and alienated from reason. Again, Moses leads men away from pregnant women until they have given birth. For in reality, the womb—located below the bladder but positioned above the intestine called the Rectum—extends its neck between the shoulders into the bladder: and the mouth of the neck, into which the seed comes, is closed up when full, and is rendered empty again after the birth is cleansed: then, once the fruit has been deposited, it receives the seed. It is not shameful for us, for the benefit of the listeners, to name the parts in which the conception of the fetus occurs, which God was certainly not ashamed to fashion. And so the womb, thirsting for the procreation of children, receives the seed, but 
<margin>E</margin>
refuses shameful and blameworthy intercourse, closing its mouth entirely after conception and excluding lust. Its desires, which were previously occupied in loving embraces, turn inward and, being occupied with the procreation of offspring, work together with the Creator. It is therefore a sin to trouble nature while it is already working, by breaking in superfluously for the sake of wanton injury. This wanton injury has many names and is multifaceted. After it has turned toward this sexual immoderation, it is called in Greek <term>λαγνεία</term> <note>original: "lagneia"; meaning lust, lewdness, or lasciviousness.</note>, that is, "lasciviousness," a name signifying a lustful, common, and unchaste inclination toward intercourse. When this has increased, a great multitude of diseases follows: a craving to see, wine-drinking, a love for women, luxury, and simultaneously a zeal for all pleasures. Over all these things 
<margin>F</margin>
desire holds tyranny. Kin to these, innumerable affections increase, from which intemperate habits are carried to the extreme. As the Scripture says:
<margin>Proverbs 3</margin>
> SCOURGES ARE PREPARED for the intemperate, and punishments for the shoulders of the foolish,

calling the strength of intemperance and its constant endurance "the shoulders of the foolish." Wherefore...

# THE INSTRUCTOR BOOK II

<margin>Ecclesiasticus 23</margin>
<margin>A</margin>
"Remove from your servants vain hopes," it says, "and turn away from me unbecoming desires. Let not the appetite of the belly nor sexual intercourse <note>original: "coitus"; refers to sexual union</note> seize me." Therefore, the many wicked traps of those who lie in wait must be kept far away. For it is not only to the pouch of Crates <note>Crates of Thebes was a Cynic philosopher who famously gave up his wealth to live in poverty; his "pouch" symbolized a life free from worldly desire.</note> that the foolish parasite does not sail, but also to our city. Neither does the lustful fornicator who exults in his lewdness, nor the deceitful harlot, nor any other such beast of pleasure find a home here. Therefore, let a good and honorable occupation be sown for us throughout our entire life.

<margin>B</margin>
In short, one must either be joined in marriage or remain entirely pure and clean from marriage. This is the question at hand, and we have explained this in the book *On Continence*. But if this very question—whether one should take a wife—comes into consideration: how shall it be freely permitted to always use sexual union as a necessity, just as one uses food? 

<margin>C</margin>
<margin>Genesis 2</margin>
From this, the nerves may be seen to be spread out like threads, and in the violent tension of the encounter, they are broken apart. Indeed, it even casts a mist over the senses and interrupts one's strength. This is evident both in animals devoid of reason and in those bodies engaged in athletic exercise. Among the latter, those who abstain surpass their adversaries in contests; while the former are led away from intercourse and can scarcely be turned or pulled along, being perfectly emptied of all strength and all spirit of the soul. The Sophist of Abdera <note>Democritus, a Greek philosopher known for his atomic theory and observations on biology.</note> called sexual intercourse a "small epilepsy," regarding it as an incurable disease. For do not weaknesses follow, which are attributed to the magnitude of the emptying and that which departs? For man is born from man and is torn out from him. See the magnitude of the loss: the whole man is drawn away through the emptying of intercourse. For it says: *THIS IS NOW bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh.* <note>Genesis 2:23</note> Thus, a man is as much emptied by his seed as he appears to be in his body; for that which departs is the beginning of generation. Furthermore, the boiling of the matter disturbs and weakens and shakes the frame of the body. Therefore, that man spoke gracefully who, when asked how he still enjoyed the things of Venus <note>A common euphemism for sexual activity, named after the Roman goddess of love.</note>, replied: "Good words, I pray! Indeed, I have most gladly fled from there as if from a wild and insane Master."

<margin>D</margin>
<margin>Ezekiel 43. Hosea 2.</margin>
<margin>E</margin>
<margin>F</margin>
Otherwise, let marriage indeed be introduced and chosen. For the Lord wishes the human race to be replenished, but He does not say: "Be lustful," nor did He wish you to surrender to pleasure as if you were born only for intercourse. Let the Instructor <note>original: "Paedagogus"; the Word/Christ acting as a teacher of conduct.</note> strike us with shame, crying out through Ezekiel: "CIRCUMCISE your fornication." Even animals devoid of reason have a certain seasonable time for sowing. But not to come together for the procreation of children is to do an injury to nature. We ought to take nature as our teacher and diligently observe the considerations of time which she prudently introduces—I mean old age and childhood. For to the latter she has not yet granted it, and the former she does not wish to take wives any longer. 

But He does not want men to always devote their efforts to marriage. For marriage is the desire for the procreation of children, not a disordered and uncertain discharge of seed, which is both against the Laws and foreign to reason. Our entire life will proceed according to nature if we both restrain our desires from the beginning and do not destroy the human race, which is born from divine providence, by wicked and malicious schemes. For there are those who, under the pretext of fornication, use drugs that lead to total destruction <note>A reference to ancient contraceptives or abortifacients.</note>, consuming all humanity along with the fetus. 

Furthermore, for those to whom it is permitted to take wives, they will need the Instructor so that the mystic rites of nature <note>A metaphor for the private acts of marriage.</note> are not celebrated during the day; nor should one, returning in the morning from the church or the marketplace, for example, mate in the manner of a rooster, when it is the time for prayer, reading, and the productive works that are done during the day. In the evening, however, it is fitting to rest after the feast, and after the thanksgiving which is made to God for the good things we have received. Nature does not always grant time for the marriage encounter to be performed; for the union is more desirable the longer it is deferred. Nor should one behave immodestly and intemperately at night as if in the dark, but modesty, like the light of reason, should be shut within the soul. For we shall differ in nothing from Penelope weaving her web <note>In Homer's *Odyssey*, Penelope wove a shroud by day and unraveled it by night to delay her suitors.</note> if by day we weave the doctrines of temperance, but by night we unravel them when we come to the bed. For if it is necessary to practice honor, much more must honor be shown to your wife...

# THE INSTRUCTOR

<meta>catchword: luxuries</meta>

...it is never right to cast off. For behold, "this corruptible puts on incorruption," <margin>A</margin> when insatiable desire—which is carried toward lust by a certain flux—is chastened by self-control and, being estranged from the love of corruption, delivers the man over to eternal temperance. For in this world they marry and are given in marriage; but once the works of the flesh are abolished, and we are clothed in the pure flesh of incorruption, we pursue that which is balanced in proportion to the Angels. <margin>Matthew 22. Luke 20.</margin> For this reason Plato also, in the *Philebus*, who had been a student of "barbarous philosophy" <note>Clement frequently argues that Greek philosophers like Plato derived their best ideas from the "barbarous" (non-Greek) wisdom of the Hebrew prophets.</note>, mystically called those "impious and estranged from God" who corrupt the God dwelling within them—namely, Reason—and, as much as lies in them, pollute Him by the conjunction of their own vices. <margin>Logos: Word and Reason.</margin> Therefore, those who are sanctified to God must never live in a mortal fashion, nor, as Paul says, should the members of Christ be made the members of a harlot, nor should the temple of God be made a temple of shameful affections. <margin>B</margin> <margin>1 Corinthians 6.</margin>

Remember that twenty-four thousand were cast out on account of fornication. <margin>Numbers 25. 1 Corinthians 10.</margin> Moreover, those things which happened to those who committed fornication are, as I have already said, figures <note>original: "figurae," meaning types or symbolic warnings</note> which correct our lusts. Furthermore, the Instructor warns most openly: **FOLLOW NOT** your own desires, and be restrained from your appetites. For wine and women will make even wise men fall away, and he who clings to harlots will become more reckless. Rottenness and worms shall be his heirs, and he shall be held up as a greater mockery. <margin>Ecclesiasticus 18, 19. Luke 12.</margin> And again: <margin>Public exposure.</margin>

For He does not cease to help: "He who gazes upon pleasure with averted eyes crowns his life." <margin>Galatians 5.</margin> It is therefore not right to be conquered by sexual matters, nor to gape foolishly at lusts, nor to be moved by appetites estranged from reason, nor to desire to be polluted. But to him alone who has taken a wife, like one who is then a farmer, it is permitted to sow when the time allows for the seeding. <margin>C</margin> Against other forms of intemperance, reason is indeed the best medicine. Help is also brought by the "poverty of satiety" <note>meaning a lack of over-indulgence or fasting</note>, through which inflamed lusts leap toward pleasures. Therefore, one should not take up expensive clothing, just as one should not seek varied food. Indeed, the Lord Himself, dividing His precepts between the soul, the body, and thirdly, external things, advises that external things be acquired for the sake of the body; but He administers the body through the soul, and He instructs the soul, saying: **BE NOT ANXIOUS** for your soul, <margin>Matthew 6.</margin> what you shall eat, nor for your body, what you shall put on. For the soul is more than food, and the body more than clothing. And He adds a clear sign of His teaching: **CONSIDER THE RAVENS**, that they neither sow nor reap, they have neither storehouse nor barn, and yet God feeds them. <margin>D</margin>

Are you not of much more value than the birds? And these things He says regarding nourishment. Similarly, He also gives instructions regarding clothing, which holds the third place among external things: **CONSIDER**, He says, the lilies, how they neither spin nor weave. But I say to you, that not even Solomon was clothed like one of these. Now, King Solomon used to boast greatly about his riches. What then is more beautiful or more flourishing than flowers? What is more delightful than lilies or roses? **BUT IF GOD** so clothes the grass, which is in the field today and tomorrow is cast into the oven, how much more you, O you of little faith? **AND DO NOT** seek what you shall eat or what you shall drink. <margin>E</margin> Here, this specific word—"**WHAT**"—excludes the variety of foods. For this is what is signified by the Scripture. Do not be anxious about *what kind* of things you eat or *what kind* of things you drink. For to be anxious about these things is an excessive desire to have more, and it proves a love of luxuries. But if eating is considered only in itself, it is an argument of necessity and the fulfillment of a deficiency, as we have said. Whatever is more than this is superfluous. And the Scripture has declared that what is superfluous is from the Devil. The following saying makes the sense plain: for when He had said, "Do not seek what you shall eat and what you shall drink," He added: **AND BE NOT LIFTED UP** on high. <margin>Ibid. (Matthew 6)</margin> For arrogance and luxuries lift one up away from the truth, and the delight that is occupied with unnecessary things leads away from the truth. Wherefore He also says most beautifully: **FOR ALL THESE THINGS** the nations of the world seek. Those who are immoderate and foolish are the "nations."

But what things does He say these are? Luxuries, pleasure, delicacies, the devouring of side-dishes, and gluttony. These are that "**WHAT**." But regarding simple nourishment alone—namely, the dry and the moist, as they are necessary—He says: your Father **KNOWS** what you have need of. But if it is entirely innate in us to seek, let us not seek the faculty of seeking in luxuries... <margin>F</margin>

<summary>Clement of Alexandria argues for extreme temperance, likening the human body to a temple of God and warning that luxury in food and clothing leads away from spiritual truth. He uses the Gospel teachings on the "lilies of the field" to advocate for a life of necessity over one of superfluous desire.</summary>

# BOOK TWO

<margin>A</margin> ...let us not lose [the soul] through luxuries, but let us rouse it to the inquiry of truth. For "seek," he says, "the kingdom of God, and those things which pertain to nourishment shall be added to you." <note>A reference to Matthew 6:33.</note> If, therefore, he removes care for clothing and luxuries and superfluous things as being not at all necessary, what must we think he says about an excessive zeal for adornment: about the dyeing of wool, the variety of colors, the superfluous care for gems; the elaborate working of gold; artificial hair and twisted locks? What of the painted coloring of the eyes, what of pluckings [of hair], purple dyes and lead-white paints, and the dyed colors of the hair, and the wicked frauds of such artifices? May it not also be rightly inferred that what was said a little before concerning "grass" can best be said of these lovers of ornaments, who are <margin>B</margin> estranged from temperance and true ornament of the soul? For the world is a field, and we are the herb, who are watered by the dew of God's grace. Having been shorn, we spring up again, as will be shown more fully in the book on the resurrection. Moreover, "grass" is said allegorically of the promiscuous crowd, which applies itself to momentary joy: which flourishes for a short time, which follows superfluous ornaments, glory, and anything rather than the truth, and which is fit for nothing other than the burning of fire. <margin>Luke 16.</margin> "THERE WAS A CERTAIN MAN," says the Lord while narrating, "who was very rich, who was clothed in purple and fine linen, who feasted sumptuously every day." This man was the grass. "But a certain beggar named Lazarus was cast at the rich man's gate, full of sores, desiring to be filled with the crumbs that fell from the rich man's table." This is the herb; but that rich man was punished in the lower regions, as one who was a <margin>C</margin> partaker of fire. This one [Lazarus], however, sprouted again in the bosom of the Father. 

I praise, therefore, and admire the ancient city of the Lacedæmonians <note>The Spartans, famous for their austere and disciplined lifestyle.</note>, which permitted only prostitutes to wear floral garments and pure gold, taking away the zeal for ornament from virtuous women by conceding that only prostitutes might adorn themselves. On the contrary, however, were the Princes of the Athenians, who had expelled the civic form of life; forgetting the manly toga, they wore gold and were clothed in tunics reaching to the ankles: <gloss>*</gloss>They were clothed in the "Crobylus"—which is a type of hairstyle or bound garment—adorned with attached golden cicadas <note>The Athenians wore golden grasshoppers (cicadas) in their hair to claim they were "autochthonous," meaning they were born directly from the earth like the insects.</note>, showing their truly earthly origin with a certain effeminate <note>original: "Cynedico," referring to a "cinaedus," a term for a man perceived as lacking masculine dignity.</note> pride and arrogance. Moreover, the emulation of these Princes spread to the other Ionians, whom Homer shows to be effeminate, calling them "garment-trailers" <note>original: "ἕλκεσιπέπλους" (elkesipeplous), referring to long, dragging robes.</note>. Those, therefore, who attend to the image of the beautiful—that is, excessive zeal for ornament—but not the beautiful and honorable itself, bringing back the worship of images under a handsome name, are to be banished far from the truth; for they dream of the nature of the beautiful by opinion, not by knowledge, and the life they lead here is a deep sleep of ignorance. 

Annon ought we not to be awakened to that which is truly beautiful and strive for its adornment? And desire to attain that alone, leaving behind the things that are of this world, rejoicing in the <gloss>*</gloss>ornament <note>Clement plays on the word "mundo," which in Latin can mean both "the world" and "cleanliness/ornament."</note>—that is, in true ornament—before we fall perfectly asleep? I say, therefore, that man has need of garments for no other reason than that the body might be covered, to repel great cold and vehement heat, lest the immoderation of the surrounding air harm us. But if this is the purpose of clothing, see whether one kind of clothing should be given to men and another to women. For covering is common to both, just as drinking is. Since the use is common, we approve of a similar construction. For just as it is common to both that they need those things which cover them, so the things by which they are to be covered ought to be similar—even if it is necessary to adopt a covering of this sort by which the eyes of women are to be hidden. <margin>D</margin> For even if the woman, on account of weakness, should desire far more things, this must be attributed to the custom of a bad education, through which men, educated in evil institutes of life, have often turned out more effeminate than women. Therefore, one must not yield to them in this matter. But if it is necessary to accommodate them a little, they may be permitted to use garments a little softer, provided that works labored with the greatest folly and too much fineness <margin>E</margin>—and curious folds in the weaving—be sent far away: bidding farewell to gold threads, and Indian silks <note>original: "Seres," referring to the people of the East who provided silk.</note>, and laborious silkworms. <margin>Taken from the tragedy of Euripides' Hecuba.</margin> For the silkworm <margin>F</margin> is first a worm, then from it is born a rough caterpillar, after which in a third metamorphosis it is renewed into a butterfly, which some call in Greek "the spirit of the dead" <note>original: "νεκύδαλον" (nekydalon), referring to the pupa or silkworm.</note>. From this a long thread is born, just as a spider's web from a spider. # THE INSTRUCTOR

<margin>A</margin> By the lure of panderers, they invite the disgrace of the body. For a soft and delicate garment is no longer a covering when it cannot hide the naked form. Indeed, such a garment, falling against the body, is pressed and applied more softly to the skin itself, clinging like a mold of the flesh; it expresses the shape of a woman in such a way that the entire constitution of the body is manifest even to one who does not wish to see. The dyeing of garments must also be rejected. For these are far removed from both practical use and truth, quite apart from the fact that they give rise to a moral reproach. Nor is their use beneficial: for they are not suited for warding off the cold, nor do they provide any more covering than any other garment, except for bringing only blame. The pleasing sweetness of the color affects those who are greedy for it, driving them toward a foolish blindness of the eyes <note>original: "lippitudinem," usually meaning eye inflammation, here used metaphorically for being blinded by vanity</note>.

<margin>B</margin> And for those who are pure, and not counterfeit on the inside, it is most appropriate to use white garments that are not curious or over-wrought. Certainly, the Prophet Daniel says openly and purely: <margin>Chapter 7.</margin> **THE THRONES** were placed, he says, and he sat upon them, as the Ancient of Days, and his garment was white as snow. The Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note> says that it saw the Lord in a vision wearing such a garment: <margin>Chapter 6.</margin> **I SAW** the souls of those who had been witnesses under the altar, and a white garment was given to each one. But if it is necessary to seek some other color, the natural dye of truth itself is sufficient. Garments that are like flowers, however, are to be left to Bacchic trifles and the mysteries of the initiations. Furthermore, purple and silver vessels are, as the comic poet says, useful for tragedies and not for life.

<margin>C</margin> Our life should be considered anything but a parade. Therefore, Sardian dye <note>A deep red or brownish-red color</note>, and another called Omphacine <note>A greenish dye made from unripe olives</note>, and others of green, rose, and scarlet, and countless other dyes, have been devised by destructive pleasures. Thus it happens that the sight is now fixed on the garment rather than the person's integrity. Those things which are skillfully made of gold, and those dyed with purple, and those delights of animals <note>likely referring to silk or expensive furs</note> carried by the wind, and that saffron-colored robe <note>original: "Crocotus," a yellow robe often associated with luxury or effeminacy</note> smeared with ointments, and the enormous prices of admirable skins, and variegated clothes which have animals depicted in the purple—all these should be told to bid farewell along with the art itself. For what wise or noble thing have those women done who, as the comedy says, sit dyed with flowers, wearing saffron robes, and painted with makeup?

<margin>D</margin> Therefore, the Instructor <note>The "Paedagogus," or the Divine Word</note> openly advises: <margin>Ecclesiasticus 11.</margin> **IN THE WEARING** of a garment do not glory, nor be puffed up in any glory that is contrary to the laws. Certainly mocking those who are dressed in soft garments, he says in the Gospel: <margin>Matthew 11.</margin> **BEHOLD**, those who live in glorious clothing and delights are in the palaces of earthly kings. He calls the earthly palaces mortal and corruptible, where there is a vain opinion of honor, an ambition for empty glory, error, and flattery. But those who observe the heavenly court which surrounds the King of all, sanctify the incorruptible garment of the soul—namely, the flesh—and through it they put on incorruption. Therefore, just as a woman who does not marry devotes her work to God alone, and her care is not divided; so the modest woman who has married divides her life between God <margin>1 Corinthians 7.</margin> and her husband. But she who is carried away otherwise becomes entirely a creature of her marriage—that is, of vice.

<margin>E</margin> In the same way, a modest woman, as I indeed feel, who devotes herself to her husband, is pious and religious without any fiction. But she who is held by an immoderate zeal for adornment falls away from both God and a modest marriage, as one who would exchange her husband for an ornament. Like that Argive harlot, Eriphyle I mean: *Who took the price of gold for her dear husband.* <note>A reference to the myth where Eriphyle was bribed with a necklace to betray her husband, Amphiaraus.</note> For this reason, I rightly approve of the "Blind Sophist" <note>Probably a reference to Prodicus of Ceos, though "Blind" may be a transcription error for "Cean." He wrote the famous "Choice of Hercules."</note> who describes the fitting images of virtue and wickedness. Of these, he made one standing simply, dressed in a white garment and pure—namely, Virtue—adorned only with modesty. Such a woman should the faithful woman be: endowed with virtue along with modesty. But the other he introduces on the contrary—namely, Wickedness—clothed in a superfluous and varied garment, exulting in a borrowed color; her movement and habit are described as being prepared for pleasure, no differently than harlots. Therefore, he who follows Reason <note>original: "λόγος" (Logos), referring to both divine Reason and Christ the Word</note> will adhere to no shameful pleasure. And for that reason, what brings utility to a garment is to be preferred; and if the Word sings this, through David saying concerning the Lord:

<margin>F</margin> <margin>Psalm 44.</margin> **THE DAUGHTERS** of Kings have delighted you in honor. The queen stood at your right hand in a gilded garment and surrounded by golden fringes: he signified not luxurious and delicate clothes, but the whole and incorruptible ornament, woven from faith, of those who have obtained mercy—namely, the church. In which Jesus, far from all deceit, shines like gold, and the fringes...

Even if Miletus <note>a city famous for high-quality wool</note> boasts of itself, even if Italy is praised, even if the wool is kept under skins <note>referring to the practice of covering sheep with jackets to keep their fleece clean and fine</note>—about which some are seized with an insane passion—certainly we should devote no effort to such things. ### XI. On Footwear.

<margin>C</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'S' featuring intricate foliate and floral patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>
Similarly, in the matter of footwear, proud and arrogant women display great softness. Truly shameful are those sandals featuring golden ornaments. They even think it right to drive decorative nails into the soles. Many women even stamp "amorous greetings" onto them, so that as they walk rhythmically upon the ground, they engrave their lustful spirits into the very path they take. 

We must, therefore, bid farewell to the vain craftsmanship of golden and jeweled sandals, to Attic and Sicyonian slippers, and to Persian and Etruscan <term>cothurni</term> <note>high-laced boots traditionally worn by tragic actors</note>. With a straight goal in mind, as is the custom of our Truth, we must choose that which is according to nature. For the use of shoes is this: first, to cover the feet; and second, to ward off injury and protect the sole of the foot from the ruggedness of the mountains. 

Therefore, white shoes may be granted to women, unless they are embarking on a journey; in that case,

they should use oiled footwear. It is not becoming for a woman to show her foot; and besides, a woman’s senses are delicate and easily harmed. The best kind of exercise is to go with bare feet, both for health and for ease of movement, where necessity does not forbid it. But if we are not on a journey and cannot bear to walk with bare feet, we should use light sandals. <margin>F</margin>

# BOOK TWO

<margin>A</margin>
...enclosed in necklaces: amethysts, "thunder-stones" <note>original: "Ceraunitae," likely referring to prehistoric stone tools or specific glossy minerals believed to fall from the sky</note>, jaspers, topaz, and the emerald from Miletus—the most expensive of merchandise. But it is the pearl that has, with the height of wantonness, invaded women’s finery in a truly astonishing way. This pearl is born in a certain oyster not unlike a <term>pinna</term> <note>a type of large saltwater clam</note>. Its size is as large as a very big fish's eye. These wretched women are not ashamed to place their entire devotion in this oyster, even though they are permitted to be adorned with a holy gem—namely, the Word of God, which Scripture indeed calls the **Pearl**. This is the translucent and pure Jesus, the eye that contemplates in the flesh, who is Reason <note>original: "Ratio," translating the Greek "Logos"</note>, who is clear, and through whom the flesh is made precious, being regenerated by water. For that oyster, born in water, covers the flesh, and from it the pearl is conceived.

<margin>B</margin><margin>Revelation 21</margin>
We have also learned that the heavenly Jerusalem was constructed from holy stones; and we admit that the twelve gates of the celestial city, likened to precious stones, signify the grace of the Apostolic voice that is to be received. For colors are placed within precious stones, and these are indeed precious, while other things remain merely earthly matter. Rightly, therefore, is the city of the saints built symbolically from these. Thus, from that incomparable "flower" of stones, they understood the flower of the spirit—that is, a holy substance free from destruction.

However, those who do not understand what is symbolic in the Scriptures devote themselves entirely to physical stones, offering that marvelous defense: "Why should we not use what the Lord has shown us?" and "I have them here, why should I not delight in them?" and "For whom were they made, if not for us?" Such are the voices of those who are utterly ignorant of God's voice. 

<margin>C</margin>
For first, God openly supplies everyone with the things that are necessary, such as water and air. Whatever is not necessary, however, He has hidden in the earth and water. And for this reason, ants dig for gold, and <term>griffins</term> <note>mythical creatures often said in antiquity to guard gold mines in the East</note> guard it, and pearls are covered by the sea. But you place unnecessary care in things where it is not required. Behold, the entire heaven is open, yet you do not seek God. Instead, those among us who are condemned to death <note>likely a reference to those working in mines as a punishment</note> are the ones who search out hidden gold and these stones. Furthermore, this contradicts Scripture, which openly cries out: **SEEK** first the kingdom of heaven, and all these things shall be added to you. 

<margin>Matthew 6</margin>
Even if all things have been given to you, and even if all things are granted to you, and if "all things are lawful for you," as the Apostle says: **BUT** not all things are expedient. 

<margin>1 Corinthians 10</margin>
God Himself brought forth our race for fellowship <note>original: "communicationem," meaning sharing or communal living</note>, since He was the first to share His own son and supplied His Word as a common gift to all, and made all things for all people. 

<margin>D</margin>
Therefore, all things are common, and the rich should not claim more for themselves than others. Consequently, the saying "I have them, and I have plenty, why should I not delight in them?" is neither human nor social. Rather, this expression proves a greater love: "I have them, why should I not share them with the poor?" For he who is like this is perfect, having fulfilled the command: **YOU SHALL LOVE** your neighbor as yourself. These are the true delights; this is the precious treasure. 

<margin>Romans 13; Galatians 5</margin>
However, those things spent on desires occupy the place of destruction, not expense. For I know that God has given us the power of use, but He has established that this use should only go as far as what is necessary, and that it should be common. It is absurd and shameful for one person to live sumptuously and luxuriously while many are hungry. 

<margin>E</margin>
For how much more glorious is it to do good to many than to live magnificently? How much more prudent is it to spend on human beings than on stones and gold? How much more useful is it to have adorned friends than inanimate ornaments? To whom have lands ever profited as much as the act of being kind? It remains for us, therefore, to resolve that objection which is raised: "Who then will possess things that are costly and magnificent, if everyone chooses things that are cheap and frugal?" 

We would say: human beings—provided we use them without any violent affection or distinction. But if it is impossible for all to be frugal and temperate, yet for the sake of the necessary use of things, we must pursue those which are easily obtained, bidding these unnecessary things to have much power elsewhere. 

<margin>F</margin>
In summary, then, ornaments—as they bring a surfeit of decoration—must be entirely banished by those who reject worldliness itself. For it is necessary for women to have their ornaments within, and to show the inner woman to be beautiful. For beauty and ugliness appear in the soul alone, and therefore only the person who is endowed with virtue is truly beautiful, good, and honorable; and it is established that only what is beautiful and honorable is good.
