Yet now, even soldiers wish to be adorned with gold, as if they had never read that line of Poetry:

<margin>Homer, Iliad</margin>
> Who, carrying gold, went into war like a foolish girl. <note>original: "Quique aurum gestans, in bellum, ut stulta puella, Ibat." Referring to Nastes in Iliad 2.872</note>

Furthermore, the pursuit of ornament—which cares nothing for virtue but claims the body for itself—must be utterly expelled, for it turns the pursuit of the good and honorable toward vain glory. By adding things to the body that do not belong to it, as if they did, this habit produces a practice of lying and a deceptive custom. It does not show honor, simplicity, or freedom from pretense, but rather displays pride, arrogance, softness, and luxury. These things obscure true beauty by overshadowing it with gold. Such people do not understand how great a crime they commit against themselves, binding themselves with innumerable chains—just as they say among the barbarians, where wicked men and criminals are bound in gold.

<margin>A</margin>
Wealthy women seem to have emulated these bound captives. For is not a golden collar a shackle for the neck? <margin>B</margin> And do not the necklaces and those things called <term>katheteres</term> <note>original: "καθετῆρες" — long hanging necklaces</note> take the place of chains? In the Attic tongue, they are even called by the same name, namely <term>haluseis</term> <note>original: "ἁλύσεις"</note>, which is to say, "chains." Moreover, Philemon, in his play *The Fellow-Youths*, called the ankle-length fetters an unseemly ornament on the feet of women:

->Transparent clothes, and a certain<-
->Golden shackle.<-

Why then is this adornment so greatly desired by you, O women, unless it is because you wish to appear bound in shackles? If the material itself could wash away shame, this vice would never perish. But to me, they seem to be bound in chains by their own will, boasting of their own great calamities. And perhaps the poetic fable even says that Venus, when committing adultery, was caught in such chains <note>A reference to the story of Ares and Aphrodite trapped in Hephaestus's net</note>, signifying nothing else than that these ornaments are the signs of adultery. For Homer said those chains were also made of gold.

Even now, women are not at all ashamed to wear the most obvious signs of the Evil One. For just as the Serpent deceived Eve, so too does a "golden world" <note>The Latin "mundus" here refers to both the "world" and a woman's "toiletries/finery"</note>—using the figure of a serpent as bait—fury-drive other women into disgraceful acts, shaping golden "eels" and serpents for their decoration. Thus the comic poet Nicostratus speaks of "chains, necklaces, rings, bracelets, serpents, anklets, and hellebore." <margin>C</margin>

Listing the entire female "world" to their great ignominy, Aristophanes shows this in *Thesmophoriazusae*. I will cite the very words of the Comedian, which clearly expose the annoying pride of your insolence: <term>Miters</term> <note>headbands</note>, <term>ribbons</term>, <term>soda</term> <note>used for washing</note>, and <term>hairpins</term>. <term>Pumice stone</term>, <term>breast-bands</term>, the <term>hair-net</term> placed behind, and the <term>veil</term> <note>original: "operculum"</term>, <term>rouge</term>, <term>necklaces</term>, and instruments for painting the eyes; a fine linen robe, a <term>fillet</term>, a <term>girdle</term>, a <term>flounce</term>, a <term>bordered robe</term>, <term>thin garments</term>, a <term>tunic</term>, a <term>voluminous gown</term> <note>original: "barathrum"</note>, a <term>circular wrap</term>, and a <term>shift</term>. And I have not yet mentioned the greatest of these: <term>earrings</term>, <term>gems</term>, <term>patches</term>, <term>grape-cluster earrings</term> <note>original: "Botrylidon"</note>, <term>buckles</term>, <term>necklaces</term>, <term>anklets</term>, <term>signets</term>, <term>chains</term>, <term>rings</term>, <term>ointments</term>, <term>flasks</term>, <term>head-bands</term>, <term>charms</term> <note>original: "olisbi"</note>, <term>sard-gems</term>, <term>fans</term>, and <term>folding chairs</term> <note>original: "clincteres"</note>. 

I, for one, am exhausted and indignant just by speaking of such a multitude of ornaments. It occurs to me to wonder how they are not crushed to death while carrying such a burden. Oh, what a truly hollow concern! Oh, what a vain and insane lust for glory! In the manner of harlots, they pour out their wealth on shames and disgraces, and with their wicked and arrogant stupidity, they corrupt and adulterate the gifts of God, imitating the art of the Evil One. <margin>D</margin>

In the Gospel, the Lord clearly called that rich man a fool who stored up goods in barns and storehouses and said to himself: "You have many good things laid up for many years; eat, drink, and be merry." **FOR ON THIS NIGHT** they require your soul. Therefore, the things you have prepared—whose will they be? <margin>Luke 12</margin>

# BOOK TWO

<sig>g iiii</sig>

<margin>A</margin>
When a painter saw one of his disciples painting a portrait of Helen <note>Helen of Troy, the mythological archetype of beauty.</note> adorned with much gold, he said, "O young man, since you were unable to paint her beautiful, you made her rich." Such are the "Helens" among women today—not truly beautiful, but fashioned and decorated with many riches. <margin>Zephaniah 1</margin> The Spirit foretells to them through Zephaniah that their silver and gold will not be able to rescue them on the day of the Lord’s wrath. However, for those women who are educated by Christ the Instructor, it is fitting to be adorned not with gold, but with reason and the Word <note>original: "Verbo," referring to the Logos/Christ.</note>, through which alone "gold" truly appears. <margin>Exodus 32</margin> The ancient Hebrews would indeed have been blessed if they had taken away and cast off the finery of women, or even just melted it down; but instead, when they had fashioned a golden calf and committed the sin of idolatry by worshipping it, they gained no benefit from the craftsmanship nor from their own purpose. Yet, they taught our women by a most vivid example <note>literally "figure," an archetype or warning.</note> to abstain from such ornaments.

<margin>B</margin>
Therefore, the desire that commits "fornication" with gold is an idol to be tested by fire. For luxury is reserved for that desire alone, being a mere shadow <note>original: "simulachrum"</note> rather than the truth. <margin>Hosea 2:13</margin> Hence the Word, through the Prophet, attacks the Hebrews with reproaches: <margin>Hosea 2</margin> "They made **SILVER** and gold," he says, meaning for the ornaments of Baal. And openly threatening, he says: "**AND I WILL VISIT** upon her the days of the Baals, in which she sacrificed to them, and put on her earrings and her necklaces." And he adds the cause of this adornment, saying: "**AND SHE WENT** after her lovers, but me she forgot, says the Lord." Therefore, let us dismiss the trifles of that wicked Sophist—the Devil—so that we are not participants in this harlot-like finery, nor commit the crime of idolatry under a beautiful pretext. Thus, the blessed Paul spoke quite beautifully: <margin>1 Timothy 2</margin> <note>The margin incorrectly cites 1 Corinthians 2, but the text is 1 Timothy 2:9-10.</note> "**WOMEN**," he says, "likewise, not with braided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly attire, but as becomes women professing godliness, adorning themselves through good works."

<margin>C</margin>
For he rightly commands that their finery be absent. If they are beautiful, nature is sufficient; let art not contend against nature. That is, let fraud by no means struggle with the truth. If, however, they are naturally ugly, they prove exactly what they lack by the things they apply to themselves. It is fitting, therefore, for those who serve Christ to embrace frugality. <margin><term>litos</term> <note>original Greek: "λιτὸς"</note> frugal and thin.</margin> For frugality truly takes care of holiness, as it levels out those things which are redundant and immoderate, and perceives the use in whatever is gained from what is otherwise superfluous. For that which is frugal and "thin"—as the name itself indicates—does not stand out, nor does it rise up or swell into a mass in any way, but is entirely flat, smooth, equal, and not at all excessive, and for that reason it is "sufficient." <margin><term>hikanos</term> <note>original Greek: "ἱκανός"</note> sufficient, from <term>hikneomai</term> <note>original Greek: "ἱκνέομαι"</note> which means 'to arrive'.</margin>

<margin>D</margin>
Sufficiency is a certain state of being <note>original: "habitus"</note> that arrives at its own goal, such that nothing is lacking and nothing is redundant. The mother of these things is justice. Their nurse, however, is that virtue which in Greek is called <term>autarkeia</term> <note>original Greek: "αὐτάρκεια"</note>, which is that by which we are content. That, therefore, is a state of being content with what is necessary, and which acquires through itself those things that contribute to a blessed life. Let there be, then, a holy ornament upon the wrists of your hands: the practice of sharing <note>original: "communicatio"</note> which is easily given, and the work of managing a household. **FOR HE** who gives to the poor lends to God, and the hands of the strong are made rich. He calls "strong" those who despise money, and who are ready to share and give generously. On the feet, let there appear a restless eagerness for doing good and a path toward justice. Necklaces and chains, however, are shame and modesty: God pours out such jewels as these. <margin>Proverbs 3</margin> "**BLESSED** is the man who finds wisdom, and the mortal who sees prudence," says the Spirit through Solomon.

<margin>E</margin>
For its trade is better than treasures of gold and silver, and it is more precious than precious gems. For this is true ornament. Let the ears not be pierced contrary to nature so that golden earrings may hang from them. For it is not right to do violence to nature beyond what she intended. There could be no better ornament for the ears, descending to the natural passages, than true Catechesis—that is, the instruction received through hearing. Then the eyes, anointed by the Word, and the ears, pierced for true perception, make one a hearer of divine things and a contemplator of holy things, with the Word truly showing that true beauty which "eye has not seen, nor has ear heard" before.

<summary>Clement argues that external jewelry is a deceptive substitute for inner virtue, using the golden calf and prophetic warnings as examples. He defines true beauty through the philosophical concepts of frugality and sufficiency, urging Christians to adorn themselves with good works and divine instruction instead of gold.</summary>

# THE INSTRUCTOR
<meta>The catchword "ctor" likely refers to the beginning of the next page's first word, "pictor" (painter), continuing the anecdote about Apelles.</meta>

<margin>A</margin>
Beauty is revealed through a graceful body and flourishes in the flesh, showing a lovely appearance of moderation when one's character shines forth in their form like a certain light. For the beauty of every plant and animal is found in its specific excellence <note>original: "virtute," referring to the inherent functional perfection or "arete" of a thing.</note>. Now, the excellence of a human being is justice, temperance, greatness of soul, and piety. Therefore, the beautiful and honorable person is the one who is just and moderate—to put it simply, the one who is good, not the one who is wealthy. Yet even soldiers now wish to be adorned with gold, as if they had never read that line of Poetry:

<margin>Homer, Iliad</margin>
> ->He who went to war wearing gold, like a foolish girl.<-

<margin>B</margin>
Furthermore, this zeal for ornamentation—which cares nothing for virtue but claims the body for itself, turning the pursuit of what is good and honorable into a pursuit of vain glory—must be utterly cast out. For by attaching things to the body that do not belong to it, as if they did, one generates a practice of lying and a habit of deception. This does not show honor, simplicity, or a rejection of pretense—which is true childhood <note>Clement often uses "childhood" to mean the innocent state of a Christian under the "Instructor."</note>—but rather displays pride, arrogance, softness, and luxury. These things obscure true beauty by overshadowing it with gold. Such people do not understand how much of a crime they commit against themselves, binding themselves with countless chains, just as they say among the barbarians that wicked and criminal men are bound in gold. These wealthy women seem to have envied those captives in their chains. <margin>C</margin> For is a golden collar not a neck-shackle? Do the necklaces and what they call *pendants* <note>original Greek: "katheteis," referring to long hanging necklaces.</note> not take the place of chains? Even in the Attic language they are called by the same name: *haluseis*, which means "chains." Indeed, Philemon in his play *The Fellow-Youth* called golden anklets an unseemly ornament for a woman’s feet:

> ->Translucent robes, and a certain golden<-
> ->shackle.<-

<margin>The "lamprey" snake. Women's ornaments.</margin>
<margin>D</margin>
Why then, O women, is this ornamentation so greatly sought after by you, unless you wish to appear as if you are bound in shackles? Even if the material itself—gold—removes the social stigma, it is still a vice that never truly vanishes. Indeed, it seems to me that those who are bound in these chains by their own choice are boasting of their own great calamities. Perhaps even the poetic myth says that Venus, when committing adultery, was caught in such chains <note>A reference to the story in the Odyssey where Hephaestus traps Venus (Aphrodite) and Mars in a golden net.</note>, signifying nothing else than that these ornaments are the signs of adultery. For even Homer said those chains were made of gold.

Now, women are not at all ashamed to wear even the most obvious signs of the Evil One. For just as the Serpent deceived Eve, so too does a "golden world" <note>original: "mundus aureus," referring to both the world and a woman's "toilette" or collection of ornaments.</note>—using the serpent’s form as bait—madly drive other women into disgrace, fashioning golden "lampreys" and serpents for decoration. Thus, the comic poet Nicostratus lists: "Chains, necklaces, rings, bracelets, serpents, anklets, and hellebore." <margin>E</margin> Aristophanes, in his play *The Women at the Thesmophoria*, lists the entire world of women’s gear to their great ignominy. I will quote the very words of the comic poet, which clearly expose the tiresome pride of your insolence:

"Miters, hair-ribbons, soda-soap, and needles. Pumice stone, breast-bands, the hair-net that is placed behind, the back-veil, rouge, collars, tools for painting the eyes, fine linen robes, head-bands, girdles, gown-borders, purple-bordered robes, thin garments, tunics, the 'pit' <note>original: "barathrum," likely a deep-folded or plunging garment.</note>, circular capes, and shifts. And I have not yet mentioned the greatest of these: earrings, gemstones, patches, grape-shaped pendants, buckles, necklaces, foot-shackles, signets, chains, rings, ointments, perfume flasks, head-bindings, dildos, sardian stones, fans, and couches."

I am truly exhausted and indignant just saying the names of such a multitude of ornaments. It occurs to me to wonder how they are not crushed to death while carrying such a heavy burden. O truly empty care! O vain and insane desire for glory! # BOOK TWO

<margin>A</margin> A painter <note>original: "Actor," likely a transcription error or variant for "Pictor" (painter), referring to a famous anecdote about the artist Apelles.</note>, when he saw that one of his disciples had painted Helen of Troy adorned with much gold, said: "O young man, since you were unable to paint her beautiful, you made her rich." <meta>This page provides explanatory notes (Scholia) on Book Two of Clement of Alexandria's "The Instructor." It moves from the previous page's discussion of luxury and idolatry into technical explanations of terms used in the chapters, particularly focusing on the distinction between spiritual love and physical feasting, the shapes of ancient drinking vessels, and the cultural context of hairstyles and perfumes.</meta>

# SCHOLIA <note>These are "scholia," or marginal commentaries and explanatory notes written by later scholars to help readers understand the main text.</note>

### Chapter One

<margin>a</margin> Just as it is an unworthy thing to drag divine love down from heaven, so too is it a matter of excess to turn a lavish dinner into "charity"—namely, the *agape* <note>original: "αγαπην" (agape). This refers to the early Christian communal "love-feast," which Clement argues should not be confused with mere gluttony.</note> feast.
<margin>b</margin> ON FLOWERS. He does not mention flowers out of season, but because a little later he was going to introduce the use of plants, fountains, and irrigation, he rightly first mentions the flower which is born from those plants. <margin>A</margin>

### Chapter Three

<margin>B</margin>
THRACIAN CUPS. These are types of drinking vessels. The **Theraclean cup** <note>original: "Theracleum," named after the famous Corinthian potter Theracles.</note> is one that is placed upon a spherical base and has a shape like a funnel, from which it is easy to drink. The **Antigonium** is a cup that ends in a sharp point without a spherical base. The **Cantharus**, however, is similar to a basin but is covered on top with a lid; its opening in the middle is of a proper symmetry, and at the edge of the circumference is a small door <note>original: "ostiolum," likely a spout or hinged opening.</note> from which whoever opens it can drink. The **Labronium** is a cup made in the shape of a shield <note>original: "aspidis," referring to a round shield.</note>, from which one who drinks can swallow a full draught. The **Lepaste** is in the shape of a pot and is held by a single handle. The **Phycter** is a segment of a cylindrical figure which rests on a small cylindrical column, by which it can both stand and be gripped. The **Prochois**, which is also called an *oinochoe* <note>original: "οινoχοε" (oinochoe), a Greek wine-pitcher.</note>, is a certain spherical vessel with one handle and one spout; from these, it is gripped by the handle, and the liquid hidden inside is poured out through the spout. <margin>C</margin>

### Chapter VI

<margin>a</margin> Through these words, he seems to signify something like this: that there is no inherent filthiness in the names of body parts. For neither the shins nor the knee, for example, signify anything shameful, just as neither the mouth nor the tongue do. In the same way, the private parts are not shameful, but one must accurately weigh the purpose; a certain honor is attributed to the name, signifying that "venerable" thing <note>original: "verendum," literally "that which is to be revered," a common Latin euphemism for the private parts.</note> of which it is spoken. Thus we also call a father or any superior "venerable," just as even Helen in Homer addresses her father-in-law <note>A reference to the *Iliad*, where Helen addresses Priam with respect despite the war.</note>. <margin>D</margin>

### Chapter VII

<margin>a</margin> And how is it that Hannah, the mother of Samuel, often repeats the same things in her prayer? And how are we, when repeating "Lord have mercy" <note>original: "Kyrie eleison."</note> many times, not at all disapproved of? I believe the text does not say this to forbid repetition, but to say that those things we have vowed to God must be rendered to God immediately. We should not wait to promise the same thing again, as if we were bargaining with words for grace to be fulfilled, or as if we wished to display the arrogance of our habits by adding to an already made promise.

### Chapter VIII

<margin>E</margin>
<margin>a</margin> BRENTHIUM. So called from a certain sweet-smelling type of flower. METALLUM, named after a certain Metallus who discovered it.
<margin>b</margin> PLANGONIUM, named after its inventor, Plagon.
<margin>c</margin> BACCARI, a type of foreign <note>original: "Barbarici" (Barbaric), meaning non-Greek or non-Roman.</note> ointment.

### Chapter X

<margin>a</margin> Thucydides also mentions this **Crobylus** in the preface to the fourth book of the Peloponnesian War. The *crobylus* was a type of hair-net, extending the hair from the edges to the crown, then drawing it into a point; it was fastened with a perforated golden cicada <note>term: "cicada" (grasshopper). Ancient Athenians wore golden grasshopper pins in their hair as a symbol that they were "autochthonous," or original inhabitants of their land.</note> so that the hair would not flow downward.
*Kosmos* <note>original: "κοσμος" (kosmos).</note> signifies both the "world" and "adornment," just as in Latin the word *mundus* refers to a woman's "world" <note>A play on the Latin word "mundus," which means both "the world/universe" and "a woman's toiletries/finery."</note>.

This page moves into a detailed explanation of ancient clothing styles, the cultural differences between Spartan and Athenian women, and a natural history of gemstones used in jewelry.</meta>

<margin>A</margin>
<margin><sup>a</sup></margin> A *xystis* <note>original: "Xystis"</note> is a type of garment that is extremely delicate; for this reason, it is said to be named from "scraping" or "polishing" <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ ξέειν" (apo tou xeein)</note> because it is as if it has been shaved down due to its thinness. An *ephaptis* <note>original: "Ephaptis"</note>, however, is the same thing as a *lena* <note>a heavy woolen cloak</note>. Both are types of garments similar to a hooded cloak <note>original: "penule"</note> which is worn over other clothes. However, the *ephaptis* is more precious than the *lena*.

<margin><sup>d</sup></margin> Like the insane Nicolaitans <note>An early Christian sect mentioned in the Book of Revelation, here accused of immoral behavior</note> who imitate the evil demon itself as their leader.

<margin>B</margin>
<margin><sup>e</sup></margin> **ANKLE-LENGTH ROBE** <note>original: "TALAREM"</note>. He refers to the Priestly garment of the Law; but this was a mystical sign. It signifies, I believe, that none of the divine mysteries should be revealed to the profane. Indeed, the feet signify the movement of our actions, just as David says the heel is watched by the wicked, and elsewhere says that in the evil day he fears the iniquity of his heel.

<margin><sup>f</sup></margin> **LACEDÆMONIAN WOMEN** <note>Spartan women</note>. Because they revealed their thighs, they were called "thigh-showers" <note>original: "φαινομηρίδες" (phainomērides)</note>.

<margin><sup>g</sup></margin> **THE ELBOW** <note>original: "CVBITVS"</note>. Someone said this upon catching sight of the elbow of a Spartan woman, who replied: "But it is not public." For they also used to dance without sleeves, to such an extent that from the shoulders one could see both the arm and the wrist—this is still seen today in ancient statues. Those who did not use sleeves were said to "act like Dorians" <note>original: "δωριεῖν" (dōriein)</note>, for the Spartans were Dorians. Those who did use them were said to "act like Ionians" <note>original: "ἰανίζειν" (ianizein)</note>, like the wives of the Athenians. (The Athenians were called Ionians because of the colony they sent out). The Spartans did this to make their women more masculine, while the Athenians did it to make them more effeminate.

## Chapter XII.

<margin>C</margin>
<margin><sup>a</sup></margin> A "dark" <note>original: "fuscus"</note> color is said to be one that is not quite white; such are the stones called sardonyx. These are natural stones; they do not have a very bright white unless they are artificial. Furthermore, sapphires may be added to these, for they also lean toward a white mixed with dark. There are also many green stones: jaspers, emeralds, and many others. Those things expelled by the tide of the "Outer Sea" <note>The Indian or Atlantic Ocean</note> are what are called pearls; for they grow from the oysters of the Persian Gulf. All gems, however, are fragments of the earth. Such are the lychnites <note>a type of bright, sparkling gem</note>, carbuncles, and amethysts. Besides these are beryls, emeralds, hyacinths, and almost all gems. Topazes, however, if we are to believe Agatharchides <note>A 2nd-century BC Greek historian and geographer</note> who wrote about the Red Sea, are found on the cliffs located in the middle of it.

<margin>D</margin>
<margin><sup>b</sup></margin> This refers back to what was said above: and they do not blush, failing to understand spiritually the things said symbolically—namely, that women should provide those things which were mentioned: the creatures, the gems, and the colors of the gems.

<margin><sup>c</sup></margin> These are the names of women's ornaments found in the works of Aristophanes; what they were and of what kind they might be is unknown, and they cannot be translated into Latin.

<margin><sup>g</sup></margin> If women are beautiful, nature is sufficient; art should not strive to compete with nature. If, however, they are naturally ugly, they prove it against themselves by the very fact that they apply what they do not possess.

<meta>This page begins the third and final book of Clement of Alexandria’s *The Instructor* (Paedagogus). # CLEMENT’S THE INSTRUCTOR
## BOOK THREE.

<margin>A</margin>

->On true beauty. Chapter I.<-

---

<margin>B</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop-cap 'E' containing a woodcut illustration of two figures in a landscape with trees; one figure is seated on the ground while the other stands nearby.</image-desc>
It is then, as it seems, the most beautiful and greatest of all disciplines to know oneself. For if anyone knows himself, he knows God. And if he knows God, he will be made like Him—not by wearing gold, nor by wearing a robe that reaches his ankles, but by doing good, and by being in need of as few things as possible. For God alone needs nothing at all, and He rejoices most of all when He sees us clean in the ornament of the mind; and then also in that ornament which embraces the chaste clothing of the body, namely, moderation and temperance.

<margin>C</margin>
Since, therefore, the soul is threefold in its nature: intelligence—which is called the faculty of reasoning—is the internal man, who commands this visible man, and whom God Himself leads. Anger, however, which is wild and cruel, lives not so far from madness. The third is desire, which changes itself into various forms; more varied than Proteus, the sea-demon, it assumes now this figure, now that, and now another, and entices one toward lusts, debauchery, and adultery. <note>Proteus was a Greek sea-god known for his ability to change shape at will; Clement uses him as a metaphor for the unstable and deceptive nature of human cravings.</note>

> *And first he becomes a lion, with a handsome beard.*
> *Still bearing grooming and ornament. For the hairs of the beard show him to be a man.*
> *But after those things, a dragon, or a leopard, or a great boar.*

The excessive study of grooming has fallen away into intemperance. Thus, the man no longer displays a strong beast before him.

<margin>D</margin>
> *Flowing water, or a tree with high and lofty branches.*

Affections are poured out; pleasures are overwhelmed; beauty fades, and falls to the ground more quickly than leaves when the storms of its amorous petulance have breathed their last; and before autumn has even arrived, it withers and perishes. For desire becomes all things, and fashions all things, and wishes to apply makeup <note>original: "fucum facere." This refers to the use of dyes or cosmetics to create a false appearance.</note> so that it may hide the man. But that man, with whom Reason or the Word <note>original: "Verbum." In early Christian philosophy, the "Word" or "Logos" is the divine logic of God made manifest in Christ.</note> dwells, is not varied, is not faked; he has the form of reason. He is made like God. He is beautiful; he is not groomed so that he may merely appear beautiful. It is true beauty: for it is God. And that God becomes man, because God so wills it. Rightly, then, did Heraclitus say: *Men are Gods. Gods are men.* <note>Heraclitus was a pre-Socratic philosopher; Clement adapts his cryptic style to suggest the union of the divine and human in Christ and the Christian soul.</note> For this Reason is an evident mystery.

<margin>E</margin>
God in man, and man as God: and the Mediator fulfills the will of the Father. For the Mediator is Reason or the Word, which is common to both: indeed the Son of God, but the Savior of men; and truly His minister, but our Instructor. And since the flesh is indeed a servant, as Paul testifies: how could anyone rightly adorn a handmaid in the manner of a harlot?
<margin>To the Philippians 2.</margin>
For regarding that which is of the flesh, that it is the "form of a servant," the Apostle says of the Lord that He emptied Himself, having taken the form of a servant; calling the external man a servant before he had served, and before the Lord had taken on the flesh. But merciful God Himself made the flesh free, and when He had liberated it from destruction and bitter, lethal slavery, He joined it to incorruption, bestowing upon the flesh this holy and eternal ornament—namely, immortality.
<margin>To the Galatians 4. Hebrews 2.</margin>
There is also another beauty of men: charity. For CHARITY, as the Apostle says, is patient and kind, it does not envy, it does not act wrongly, it is not puffed up.
<margin>1. Corinthians 13.</margin>

<margin>F</margin>
For grooming is said to "act wrongly" when it clearly indicates excess and uselessness. And therefore he adds: it DOES NOT BEHAVE UNBECOMINGLY. For an alien figure, and one which is not according to nature, is unbecoming. But that which is faked is alien. This he explains clearly when he says: it DOES NOT SEEK its own things. For that which...

<summary>Clement argues that true beauty is internal and spiritual, stemming from self-knowledge and likeness to God, rather than external grooming. He contrasts the stable "form of reason" in a virtuous person with the deceptive, shape-shifting nature of worldly desire.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Book Three of Clement of Alexandria’s *The Instructor*. On the previous page, Clement argued that the highest form of beauty is knowing oneself and, by extension, knowing God. He here concludes that initial argument by citing the physical plainness of Christ as proof that external appearance is irrelevant to holiness, before launching into a critique of excessive cosmetics and jewelry.</meta>

# THE INSTRUCTOR

<margin>c. 53.</margin>
...what belongs to Him is the truth. Therefore, He calls what is His own. <margin>A</margin>
But that which is foreign seeks an excessive passion for adornment, which is far removed from God, from reason, and from love. The Spirit testifies through the mouth of Isaiah that the Lord Himself was plain in appearance: 
> AND WE SAW HIM, and He had no form nor beauty; but His form was lowly, diminished among men. <note>original Latin: "ET VIDIMVS ipsum, & non habebat speciem nec pulchritudinem, sed species eius vilis, diminuta præ hominibus." This is a reference to Isaiah 53:2-3, commonly cited by early Church Fathers to argue that Christ’s divinity was not found in physical attractiveness.</note>

Yet, who is more excellent than the Lord? He did not display the beauty of the flesh, which is perceived by sight, but rather He showed the true beauty of both soul and body: of the soul, through his benevolence; and of the body, through his immortality.

## That one should not use external adornment. <margin>Chapter II. B</margin>

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'N' containing a landscape scene with figures and architecture within a square border.</image-desc>
Therefore, it is not the outward appearance of the person that should be adorned, but the soul that must be decorated with the ornament of goodness. It could even be said that the flesh should be adorned with the ornament of self-control. However, those women who obsess over their outward appearance do not notice that the things deep within them are utterly uncultivated, wild, and barren. They are like the decorations of the Egyptians. Among them, the temples—their porticoes, entrances, and sacred groves—are magnificently constructed. Their courtyards are surrounded by many columns, and the walls shine with foreign stones and are skillfully painted so that nothing is lacking. The buildings glow with gold, silver, and electrum <note>Electrum: a naturally occurring alloy of gold and silver, highly prized in antiquity.</note>, and sparkle with various glittering gems from India and Ethiopia. The inner sanctums are shaded by veils woven with gold. <margin>C</margin>

But if you pass into the interior of the temple enclosure, hurrying toward the sight of that which is supposedly more excellent, and seek the image that inhabits the temple, a priest—one of those who sacrifices in the temple—looks at you with a grave and venerable face, singing a hymn <note>original: "Pæanem," a song of praise or triumph.</note> in the Egyptian language. But when he draws back the veil a little as if to reveal the God, he provides us with a great reason to laugh at the deity. For the God you sought, the one you were hurrying to see, is not found within; instead, there is a cat, or a crocodile, or a local serpent, or some such beast—unworthy of a temple, but better suited to a den, a cave, or a mud pit. The God of the Egyptians appears as a beast rolling around on a purple rug. 

It seems to me that women are just like this. <margin>D</margin> They wear gold, spend their time curling their hair, and are occupied with anointing their cheeks, painting their eyes, and dyeing their hair. They pursue other forms of softness through wicked arts, decorating their physical exterior and truly imitating the Egyptians to attract unfortunate lovers. But if one were to open the veil of the "temple"—I mean their life, their clothing, their gold, their makeup, their dyes, and all that is smeared and plastered on them—which is the veil woven from these things—thinking he would find true beauty within, I know well that he would find it abominable. He will not find the image of God dwelling within, as would be fitting; instead, a harlot and an adulteress has occupied the inner shrine of the soul. The true beast will be revealed: a monkey smeared with makeup and plaster, and that deceiving serpent, devouring the intelligence of the mind. Through the desire for vain glory, this dragon <margin>E</margin> holds the soul as its cave, and when it has filled everything with deadly poisons and vomited the venom of its error, it transforms women into prostitutes, acting as a pimp. For that excessive passion for adornment belongs not to a wife, but to a harlot.

Indeed, such women take very little care of the house, of serving their husbands, or of managing the family. But when the husband's purse is opened, they turn the money they are supplied with toward their own cravings, so that they might have many witnesses to their perceived beauty. They sit all day long with slaves bought with money, busy with the art of decoration. Because their natural flesh is unpleasant to look at, they try to make it soft and sweet. During the day, they stay in their chambers, fixed to the art of grooming, lest they be caught with their "painted" colors showing. But at evening, this "adulterous" beauty creeps out toward the lamp as if from a cave. <margin>F</margin> For drunkenness and the dim, flickering light provide aid to their plastered-on faces. Even Menander the Comedian drives such a woman, who was dyeing her hair, out of the house:

> *But now, get out of this house; for a modest woman*
> *should not make her hair yellow.* <note>Clement quotes from a lost play by Menander to emphasize that even secular poets recognized that altering one’s natural appearance was a sign of vanity or lack of virtue.</note>

<meta>The catchword "Sed" (But) at the bottom indicates the first word of the next page.</meta>

<summary>Clement uses a vivid analogy comparing women who wear heavy makeup and jewelry to Egyptian temples—grand on the outside but housing only a lowly beast within. He argues that true beauty is internal and that Christ himself chose a plain physical form to emphasize the priority of the soul.</summary>

# BOOK THREE

<margin>A</margin> But they should neither rouge their cheeks nor paint their eyes. These wretched women do not understand that they lose their own natural beauty when they introduce an artificial one. For in the early morning, they spend their time pulling and stretching themselves, shaping their faces with various and messy concoctions. They chill the natural color of the skin, while eroding the flesh with poisons; through obsessive and excessive scrubbing, they ruin the natural flower of their beauty and make it wither. Because of this, they appear pale when wearing these poultices, yet they are easily seized by diseases, as they possess flesh that is a mere shadow, already dissolved by toxins. They insult the Creator of humanity, as if He had not granted them beauty according to their merit. Rightly, then, in matters pertaining to the care of the home and the management of 
<margin>B</margin> the household, they are idle; they sit like painted figures for a show, not born for the protection of the home or the administration of the family. And so, in the works of the Comic poet, a sensible woman says:

> What wise thing have we women done, 
> Or what thing of splendor, we who sit scattered 
> With flowers of so many colors, utterly 
> Destroying the form and figure of free women—
> The ruin of houses, the destruction of marriages,
> And the begging disgrace of our children.

For this same reason, Antiphanes the Comic poet in *Malthaca* mocks the habit of prostitutes, saying words that apply to all regarding their 
<margin>C</margin> rubbing and smearing: “She comes, she passes by, she approaches, she does not pass, she comes, she is present, she 
" wipes herself, she approaches, she is cleaned with soap <note>original Greek: σμῆγμα (*smēgma*), used here to mean a cleansing detergent or soap</note> or lye, she is combed, she goes out, she is rubbed, she is washed, she 
" contemplates herself, she composes herself, she is drenched with ointments, she is adorned, she is anointed, and if she 
<margin>soap</margin>
" lacks anything, she is tormented to death.” For they are worthy to perish not once, but thrice, who use 
" crocodile dung, and anoint themselves with the foam of cuttlefish, and smear their eyebrows with soot, 
" and rub their cheeks with rouge. If these things were hated even by ethnic <note>i.e., Pagan</note> poets because of such customs, 
why should they not be even more rejected by the Truth? Another Comic poet, Alexis—I shall cite his words—reproves them, showing how their obsessive and superfluous explanation of things causes him shame because of their perpetual and unchangeable impudence. 
<margin>D</margin> For he was not as obsessive as he should have been, but I am ashamed that women are so 
" mocked in comedies; if only I could offer them some help. “Then indeed, she brings ruin to her husband. 
" First, in profit, and in the plundering of neighbors. All other works are done by them in passing. 
" Is one woman a little short? Cork is sewn into her shoes. Is one tall? She wears a thin sole and 
" walks with her head drooping toward her shoulder; this takes away from her height. Are another’s hips and thighs 
" too flat? Something is added to them, so that those who walk by exclaim that she has a beautiful backside. 
" Does she have a soft and protruding belly, like the nurses in comedies? She props it up by applying certain items. 
" Is the belly too flat? By using certain stays, she makes it proceed forward. 
" Does one have yellow eyebrows? They paint them with soot. Does it happen that another’s are black? 
<margin>E</margin> White lead <note>original: *cerusa*, a common but toxic lead-based cosmetic used to whiten skin</note> removes the blackness. Are they too white? She rubs away the whiteness with flour. Does she have 
" some white part of her body? She shows it bare. Does she have beautiful teeth? She must laugh 
" so that those present may see how charming her mouth is, and even if she is not happy, she laughs 
" the whole day. Having a thin sprig of myrtle in her lips, she is eventually forced to part them whether she wants to or not.” 
I have brought these things forward from worldly wisdom to discourage an excessive zeal for adornment, since the Word <note>Christ, the Logos</note> wishes to preserve us in every way. Soon I shall also fortify this with the divine 
Scriptures. For one who is not hidden usually refrains from sins due to the 
disgrace of being rebuked. Just as someone wearing a poultice, or 
one whose eyes are anointed, offers a suspicion of disease by their very appearance, so too do rouges, dyes, 
and smeared colors signify that the soul is sick within. The Instructor persuades us 
<margin>F</margin> not to approach a "foreign river." By a foreign river, he allegorically signifies a "foreign wife" 
given over to lust, who flows toward everyone and is poured out for the pleasure of all through 
prostituted intemperance. <term>FROM A FOREIGN</term>, he says, water <margin>Proverbs 9. <br/> Ecclesiasticus 25.</margin> 
abstain, and from a foreign fountain do not drink, for the stream of tickling delight...

# THE PAEDAGOGUE, BOOK II
<note>While the header indicates Book II, this text is part of Book III of Clement’s "Paedagogus," which focuses on the vanity of clothing and jewelry.</note>

<margin>A</margin>
...admonishing us to avoid [vice], so that we may live for a long time. Years of life will be added to us if we do not hunt for the pleasures of others, or if we turn away from heresies. Indeed, though being a drunkard or a wine-bibber are great vices, they are not so great as the excessive desire for self-adornment. A full table and frequent cups are enough to satisfy gluttony. But for those who are held by an excessive desire for gold, purple, and gems, neither the gold above the earth nor that which is beneath the earth will suffice; nor the Tyrian sea <note>Famous for the expensive purple dye extracted from murex snails.</note>, nor the cargoes brought from the Indians and Ethiopians; nor even the Pactolus <note>A river in Lydia famed for its golden sands.</note>,
<margin>wealth <note>original: πλοῦτος</note></margin>
whose streams are golden. Even if one of them should happen to turn out like Midas, he cannot be satisfied, but remains poor, desiring other riches; they are even prepared to die together with their gold.
<margin>B</margin>
But if riches are blind—as indeed they are—how are they not also blind who are stunned by them, and admire them, and are affected by them? Therefore, while they set no limits on their greed, they crash into impudence. For they have need of the theater, and pomp, and a multitude of spectators, and errors in sacred rites, and long delays at the crossroads, so that their [wealth] might be manifest to everyone. For they adorn themselves to please others, "boasting in appearance and not in the heart." <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 5:12.</note> For just as branded marks indicate a runaway slave, so do florid colors
<margin>Jeremiah 4</margin>
indicate an adulteress. "For even if you clothe yourself in scarlet, and deck yourself with gold ornaments, and paint your eyes with antimony <term>stibium: a dark mineral powder used as eyeliner</term>, your beauty is in vain," says the Word through Jeremiah. Is it not
<margin>C</margin>
truly absurd that horses, and birds, and other animals rise and fly out from the grass and meadows rejoicing in their own natural ornament—their manes, their natural color, and their varied feathers—while woman, as if she were inferior to the beasts, thinks herself so deformed that she needs external, bought, and shadowed beauty? Surely ribbons, and their many varieties, and the curious and unnecessary braiding of the hair, and the innumerable shapes of locks, and the costly structures of mirrors by which they arrange themselves—while they hunt for those who, like children, admire the beauty of fools—these are the marks of women who have cast off all shame. He who calls them prostitutes would not be
<margin>2 Corinthians 4
faces <note>original: προσώπων; refers here to "masks" or "outward appearances"</note></margin>
wrong, for they make masks out of their own faces. But the Word persuades us "not to consider the things that are seen, but the things that are not seen. For the things that are seen are temporary, but the things that are not seen are eternal." Nothing can be said or imagined more absurd than that mirrors should be devised for this fake beauty of theirs, as if it were a great achievement or something to be corrected,
<margin>D</margin>
when a lid should rather be placed over such a fraud.
Truly, as it is in the Greek fables, it did not turn out well for the beautiful Narcissus that he was a beholder of his own image. Since Moses commands men to make no image that represents God by art, how can these women be acting rightly, when they imitate their own images through reflections in a deceptive fiction of a mask? Furthermore, when the Prophet Samuel was sent to anoint one of the sons of Jesse as King, and he saw his eldest son, who was handsome and tall, and Samuel rejoiced and brought out the anointing oil, the Lord said to him: "DO NOT LOOK at
<margin>Exodus 20
Deuteronomy 5
god-like <note>original: θεοείκελον</note>
1 Kings 16 <note>Samuel is categorized under Kings in the Vulgate system.</note></margin>
his appearance, nor the height of his stature, because I have rejected him. For man looks at the eyes, but the Lord looks at the heart." And he did not anoint him who was beautiful in body, but him who was beautiful in soul. If, therefore, the Lord values the natural beauty of the body less than the beauty of the soul, what does He think of the counterfeit beauty, He who
<margin>2 Corinthians 5</margin>
has utterly expelled everything that is false? "FOR BY FAITH we walk, and not by sight." The Lord teaches most clearly through Abraham that he who follows God should despise his fatherland, relatives, possessions, and all riches, when He made him a stranger. And for this reason He called him "Friend," because he had held his own resources in contempt; for he was of noble birth and very rich. Thus, with three hundred and eighteen
<margin>Genesis 14
Esther 15 <note>Refers to the Greek additions to the Book of Esther.</note></margin>
of his servants, he subdued four Kings who had led Lot away captive. We find Esther alone to be justly adorned. The woman was adorned mystically for her King, but her beauty was found to be the price by which the people who were being slaughtered were liberated. That such finery makes women into prostitutes, and men into androgynes <term>androgynos: an effeminate man or "man-woman"</term> or effeminate and adulterers, the Tragic poet is our witness, speaking thus:
<margin>E</margin>
> "But there came from the Phrygians he who
> judged the Goddesses, as the stories go in Argos," <note>A reference to the Judgment of Paris, which led to the Trojan War; Paris is often depicted by Greeks as an effeminate, over-dressed easterner.</note>

# BOOK THREE

<margin>A</margin>
> To Lacedaemon <note>The ancient name for the region of Sparta.</note>, in superb attire,
> Splendid with barbaric luxury and gold:
> Loving the one who loved him, he departed by force, carrying away
> Helen to the stalls of Mount Ida, while from home was absent
> Menelaus.

O, beauty that incites one to adultery! The barbaric zeal for self-ornament and effeminate delights overturned Greece. Spartan modesty was corrupted by fine clothing, luxury, and a fair appearance; the barbaric zeal for self-adornment proved the daughter of Jove <note>Referring to Helen of Troy, daughter of Zeus/Jupiter.</note> to be an adulteress. They had no Pedagogue <note>The "Pedagogue" refers to Christ as the divine teacher.</note> to cut back their lusts, nor anyone to say: "Thou shalt
<margin>B</margin>
not commit adultery," nor anyone to say: "Thou shalt not covet," nor "Thou shalt not enter upon the path to adultery through lust," nor even "Thou shalt not inflame your desires through immoderate zeal for your own adornment." But such was the end that followed these things, and how many evils did those feel who refused to restrain their excessive self-love? Because of unbridled pleasures, Greece and Asia were thrown into turmoil. Everything was stirred up by a barbaric youth <note>Paris (also known as Alexander), the prince of Troy.</note>. All of Greece takes to the sea, the narrow strait is crowded with ships carrying armies, a long war is stirred up, and violent battles break out; the fields are filled with corpses, the Barbarian mocks the fleet, injustice gains dominion, and the eye of that fictional Jove looks toward the Thracians, while the flows of the rivers are stopped by dead bodies; breasts are beaten with wailing, and grief
<margin>C</margin>
possesses the land. All the feet and all the peaks of Ida, watered by many springs, are shaken, as are the cities of the Trojans and the ships of the Achaeans <note>The Greeks.</note>. Whither shall we flee, O Homer, and where shall we stand? Show us a land that has been least moved.
> Child, do not touch the reins, you who are ignorant,
> And unskilled in driving the chariot, do not ascend.

Heaven rejoices in two Charioteers <note>An allusion to the Platonic allegory of the soul as a chariot pulled by two horses (reason and passion).</note>, by whom alone the fire of the sun is driven. For the mind is led away from pleasure, and the integrity of reason—which does not employ the Word as its Pedagogue—slides into lust: and having fallen, it receives the reward of its fall. Of these things the Angels are a sign to you, who abandoned the beauty of God for the beauty that
<margin>Isaiah 14; Ezekiel 23</margin>
withers, and thus they fell from the heavens to the earth. Furthermore, the Shechemites <note>Refers to the biblical story in Genesis 34 where Shechem violates Dinah.</note> are punished, who fell by bringing disgrace upon a holy virgin. The grave is their
<margin>D</margin>
punishment, and the monument of their penalty leads us toward salvation.

### Against men who beautify themselves. Cap. III.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'E' featuring a pastoral landscape with a figure in the foreground and a distant town or city.</image-desc>
Luxury has proceeded so far, therefore, that not only do women labor in this vain pursuit, but even men follow this vice. For those who are not pure in the care of their bodies are by no means healthy in mind: declining toward softness, they are plainly effeminated, cutting their hair in an ungentlemanly and meretricious <note>Like a prostitute.</note> fashion, dressed in fine and transparent garments, walking about everywhere in a boastful manner, chewing mastic <note>A resin used to sweeten breath, similar to chewing gum.</note>, and smelling of perfumes. What might one say of those who, like a 
<margin>E</margin>
metoscopus <note>term: metoscopus - a "face-watcher" or physiognomist who claims to tell a person's character by their facial features.</note>, divine character from appearance, when he sees these adulterers, androgynes, and effeminates, pursuing both kinds of lust <note>A reference to both heterosexual and homosexual vice.</note>, hating hair, being smooth-skinned, loathing the flower of manhood, and adorning their hair no differently than women? Living wickedly and infamously in nefarious and audacious undertakings: *They commit FOOLISH and wicked deeds,* says the Sibyl. Because of them, the cities are full of those who "pitch" <note>note: "pitching" (pication) was the practice of applying hot pitch or resin to the skin to pull out body hair.</note>, shave, and pluck these effeminates. Workshops are built and open everywhere, and the craftsmen of this meretricious fornication earn much money from those who smear themselves with pitch and offer their hairs in any way possible to the pluckers; they feel no shame before those who watch, nor those who approach, nor themselves, though they are men. Such are those who 
<margin>F</margin>
pursue foul and ungentlemanly passions, and whose bodies are entirely hairless and smooth from violent pitch-plucking. Certainly, there is nowhere further such impudence can go. If nothing is left untainted by them, I must not pass it over in silence. One of those who are truly cowardly and degenerate was rebuked in the manner of the Pedagogue...

Here, Clement transitions to specific rules regarding masculine appearance, arguing that God designed the male body to be hairy and bearded as a sign of authority and nature’s intent.</meta>

# THE PEDAGOGUE

<margin>A</margin>
**Diogenes**, when he was being sold, spoke with a great and brave spirit: "Come, young man, buy yourself a man" <note>Diogenes the Cynic was a Greek philosopher known for his extreme honesty and rejection of social norms. Here, Clement recounts a story where Diogenes, captured by pirates, asserts his masculinity and virtue even in slavery.</note>, correcting the buyer’s lewd way of life with this double-edged speech. For those who are men, how is it not shameful and utterly unfree to be shaved and smoothed? As for dyeing one's hair, anointing gray hairs, and smearing them with colors—practices used by ruinous, effeminate, and androgynous men—these and feminine hairstyles must be entirely abandoned. For they think that, like a serpent, they can cast off the old age of their head while they transform and renew themselves by painting their skin. But even if they skillfully disguise their hair, they will not escape wrinkles, nor will they hide from death, even if they deceive time through artifice. The more a man hastens toward his end, the more truly venerable he is, as one who has only God as his senior. For He also is the eternal elder, who is more ancient than all things that exist. Prophecy called Him the **Ancient of Days**.

<margin>Daniel 7</margin>
<margin>Matthew 5</margin>
<margin>B</margin>
> **AND THE HAIR** of his head was like pure wool, says the Prophet. **BUT NO ONE ELSE**, says the Lord, can make a hair white or black.

How then do the impious manufacture a work contrary to God, or rather, violently oppose Him, by changing the hair which has been made gray by Him? 

<margin>Sirach 25</margin>
> The crown of old men, says the Scripture, is much experience, and the gray hair of his face is the flower of much experience. <note>original Latin: "Ecclesi. 25" refers to the Book of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus).</note>

But those men bring disgrace upon the dyer of gray hair, which is the chief gift of age. It is impossible—I say, it is impossible—for a man to show a true soul when he has an adulterated head.

<margin>Ephesians 4</margin>
<margin>C</margin>
> **But you have not so** learned Christ, if indeed you have heard Him and been taught in Him, as the truth is in Jesus, that you put off the old man according to your former conversation. 

He does not mean to put off gray hair, but the man who is corrupted according to the desires of deception. **Be renewed**, He says—not by dyes and ornaments, but in the spirit of your mind, and **put on the new man**, who is created according to God in justice and the holiness of truth. For a man to be combed and shorn, to arrange his hair at a mirror, to shave his cheeks, and to be plucked and smoothed—how is this not plainly feminine? Indeed, unless one saw them naked, one would think they were women. For even if they are not permitted to wear gold, yet through feminine lust, they hang certain fringes of gold and wrap threads around leaves, or make certain spherical figures of the same material, and wear them with their necks held high.

<margin>D</margin>
This is the invention of broken men who are dragged into the women's quarters <note>original: "gynæceum", the part of a Greek house reserved for women.</note>, men of a double-edged life and beasts prone to lust. This is a fornicating and impious method of treachery. For God willed that the woman should be smooth and soft, with her hair alone exulting by nature’s own accord like a horse's mane. But when He had adorned the man with a beard like a lion, He also made him masculine with a hairy chest, which is a sign of strength and command. In the same way, He adorned the roosters who fight for the hens with crests like helmets. God values these hairs so much that He commands them to be present on men alongside prudence; and being greatly delighted by honor, He has honored gravity with venerable gray hair. Wisdom and accurate, exact reasoning—the "gray" of the intellect—attain their peak vigor with time, and they strengthen and corroborate old age with the intense forces of much experience, bringing forth the lovely flower of venerable prudence to rightly produce trust: namely, gray hair.

<margin>E</margin>
This sign of a man—the beard—by which the man appears, is older than **Eve**, and is the sign of a superior nature. God deemed it right for him to be hairy, and He scattered hair over the whole body of the man; whatever was smooth and soft in him, He took from his side to manufacture the pliable woman for the reception of seed, so that she might be a helper in procreation and in the keeping of the house. But he (from whom the smooth part had been cast out) remained a man and shows himself as a man; and it is granted to him to act, just as it is granted to her to endure. For by nature, those things that are hairy are drier and warmer than those that are smooth. Therefore, the masculine are hairier and warmer than the feminine, the uncastrated than the eunuchs, and the perfect than the imperfect. To violate that which is the sign of masculine nature—namely, its hairiness—is therefore an impious act against the law.

<margin>F</margin>
The adornment of smoothness or hairlessness (for I am inflamed by the Word) in men is for a weak woman; in women, however, it is for an adulteress. Both must be banished far from our republic.

<margin>Matthew 10</margin>
> Moreover, even all the hairs of your head are numbered, says the Lord—

<summary>Clement argues that masculine features like beards and gray hair are divinely ordained signs of authority and wisdom. He condemns shaving, dyeing hair, and effeminate grooming as acts of impiety that go against the natural order established by God.</summary>

# BOOK THREE

<margin>A</margin> Indeed, even the hairs of the beard are numbered, and so too are those of the whole body. Therefore, nothing should be plucked away contrary to God's institution, which has been accounted for in His will. <margin>John 14 <note>The margin cites John 14, though the quote "Do you not recognize yourselves..." is from 2 Corinthians 13:5. Clement often synthesized various scriptures from memory.</note></margin> **Unless**, the Lord says, you do not recognize yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you. If we had known that He dwells within us, I do not know how we could have brought ourselves to treat Him with such dishonor. As for being treated with pitch <note>original: "Picari"; a method of hair removal using hot resin or pitch, similar to modern waxing but much more painful and associated with effeminacy in the ancient world.</note> and being plucked, I fear to say how unbecoming and foul a practice it is. Turning away, bending over, and openly exposing the secrets of nature, leaping about, and nearly dislocating the joints of the hips—and while their postures are shameful, they themselves do not blush. Behaving so indecorously in the very assembly of youths and in the middle of the gymnasium where the virtue of men is exercised—how is pursuing this unnatural exercise not a sign of extreme lack of self-control?

<margin>B</margin> For those who do these things in the open would hardly respect anyone at home. Furthermore, the lack of restraint shown in public testifies to that which is done in secret with total license for lust. For he who denies being a man under the rays of the Sun will clearly be proven a woman by night. <margin>Deuteronomy 23</margin> **There shall not be**, said the Word through Moses, a harlot among the daughters of Israel, nor shall there be a male prostitute among the sons of Israel. "But the pitch helps," they say; on the contrary, it makes one have a bad reputation. No one who is wise would want to appear as a male prostitute if he does not suffer from that disease, nor would he strive to have a beautiful image slandered. For God foreknew that those who are called according to His purpose would be conformed to the image of His Son, for whom, as the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul.</note> wishes, He preordained and predestined blessedness.

<margin>C</margin> So that He might be the firstborn among many <margin>Romans 8</margin> brothers. How are they not impious who treat the body, which is conformed to the Lord, with injury and dishonor? To him who wishes to be beautiful, that which is most beautiful in man must be adorned—namely, the mind, which ought to be shown more beautiful and more decorous every day. It is not hairs that should be plucked, but desires. I, for my part, feel pity even for those young boys who are sold by slave-traders. And yet, they are not treated with dishonor and injury by their own choice; but, poor wretches, they are ordered to be groomed for the sake of foul profit. But those who do these things of their own accord, willingly and gladly—things for which those who ordered them would be punished by death if they were men—how are they not to be cursed? But now life has proceeded to such a point of intemperance, with iniquity insulting and behaving wantonly, that whatever is immodest and lustful has spread through the cities and is now even held as law.

<margin>D</margin> Women stand in the brothel, selling their flesh for the dishonor of pleasure, and boys, taught to deny nature, pretend to be women. Luxury has changed all things; it has treated man with dishonor and disgrace. A soft, luxurious, and superfluous curiosity seeks all things, attacks all things, and constrains nature; men endure womanly things, and women act as men contrary to nature; and women marry and take wives. There is no passage to which the entrance of immodesty does not lie open. Now indeed, "common Venus" <note>A reference to common or profane lust/prostitution as opposed to "celestial" or virtuous love.</note> is publicized even to them, as the delight of banquets. O piteous spectacle! O unspeakable pursuit! These are the trophies shown for our city’s lack of restraint. The crimes which stand for sale in the brothels prove it. O, how great is this iniquity! But the wretches do not even understand how many tragedies uncertain sexual union often excites. Fathers often lie with their sons who are for hire, and with daughters who are prostitutes, not remembering the sons they exposed <note>The practice of "exposure" (leaving unwanted infants in the wild or public places) often led to those children being rescued and raised as slaves or prostitutes, leading to the risk of accidental incest.</note>; and the excessive license of lust causes them to forget that they are the men who fathered them.

<margin>E</margin> Wise laws permit these things; it is allowed for them to sin by law, and they call unspeakable pleasure "ease." They think themselves free from adultery, yet they are those who adulterate nature. But the avenging justice for those things which they have shamefully committed follows them, and by drawing inevitable calamity upon themselves, they buy death with a small coin. The wretched merchants of these goods sail about, importing fornication like grain or wine. Others, far more miserable, procure pleasures as if they were bread or a side dish. And not even that word of Moses comes to their mind: <margin>Leviticus 19</margin> **You shall not profane** your daughter to make her a harlot, lest the land fall into fornication and the land be filled with iniquity.

<margin>F</margin> These things were spoken prophetically long ago, but the outcome is now manifest. All the earth is now full of both fornication and iniquity. I look with suspicion and wonder upon the ancient Roman legislators. They held the womanish and effeminate pursuit of life in hatred, and the bodily custom with a woman contrary to the Law of nature...

# THE INSTRUCTOR

<margin>A</margin>
...that it should be buried in the earth <note>The hair plucked or shaved was often discarded; Clement argues even this waste should be treated according to the "Law of justice," perhaps implying it should be returned to the earth naturally.</note> they have judged to be fair. For it is a sacrilege to pluck the beard, which is a natural beauty, a noble and refined beauty.

<margin>Psalm 132 <note>Original: "Pſal. 132." This refers to the oil running down Aaron's beard.</note></margin>
<margin>Batalus was a most effeminate man <note>Batalus was a nickname given to the orator Demosthenes by his rivals to imply he was soft or unmanly.</note></margin>
<margin>Ecclesiasticus 19</margin>
<margin>Ibid. 19</margin>
*First there is the downy hair, which makes for the most pleasing youth.*
As he matures, he is then anointed with the prophetic ointment <note>A reference to Psalm 133 (132 in the Vulgate), where the sacred anointing oil flows down the beard of Aaron the High Priest.</note> while the beard is cherished, through which Aaron is honored. It is necessary for him who is rightly instructed by the Instructor—upon whom peace has dwelt—to be at peace even with his own hair. What, then, will women prone to lust not attempt when they see men daring such things? Indeed, these are not to be called men, but "Bataluses" and "man-milliners," <note>original: "fœminelli," a diminutive for "little women" or "effeminate men."</note> whose voices are squeezed and thin, and whose garments, in both touch and dye, are effeminate. These men are openly exposed by their external manners—by their dress, their shoes, their figure and posture, their haircut, and their gaze. <margin>B</margin> For, as the Scripture says, **"A man shall be known by his look, and a man shall be recognized by his meeting with another. A man's clothing, the step of his foot, and the laughter of his teeth shall tell the truth about him."** For even if these men are quite grey in other hairs, they take care only of those on the head, binding their locks with ribbons almost exactly like women. In contrast, lions boast of their shaggy manes, but they are armed by them in battle. Even goats take pride in their chin-tufts, and hunters fear them when they bristle with hair.

*The wool-bearing sheep are also weighed down by a thick fleece.*
<margin>C</margin>
And yet the kind Father has multiplied their hair also for your use, O man, by teaching you to shear the wool. Among the nations, the Gauls and the Scythians <note>Ancient nomadic peoples of Central Asia and Eastern Europe, often viewed as "noble savages" by Greek writers.</note> let their hair grow long, but they do not groom themselves excessively; indeed, the dense hair of the barbarian offers something terrifying to behold, and that reddish-yellow color threatens war, appearing as if it were kin to blood. Both these Barbarian groups hated luxury. The German provides the Rhine as an open witness to this, and the Scythian his wagon. Sometimes it happens that the Scythian even despises his wagon. To the barbarian, his wealth seems to be his greatness, and leaving behind luxuries, he leads a frugal life. Boarding his horse—which is a sufficient home and swifter than any other horse—the Scythian leads it wherever he wishes. When suffering from hunger, he seeks food from the horse. The animal offers its veins, providing its master with the only blood it possesses. Furthermore, to the Nomad, the horse is both vehicle and food. <margin>D</margin> Among the Arabs (who are other Nomads), those of an age fit for fighting mount camels; they lead out pregnant camels, which graze and run at the same time. While carrying their masters, they also carry their master's home. If drink should fail the barbarians, they milk them; and when the nourishment is exhausted, they do not even spare the blood, as is said of wolves driven by madness. Yet these animals are gentler than the Barbarians, for even when injured, they do not remember the harm received; instead, they confidently traverse the wilderness, simultaneously carrying and feeding their masters. Let those monstrous beasts perish, then, whose food is blood. For it is not lawful for men—whose body is nothing other than flesh cultivated by blood—to touch blood. Human blood has been a partaker of the Word, and has communion with grace through the Spirit. If anyone treats it with injury, he shall not remain hidden; even if he is stripped of his outward form, he may address the <margin>E</margin> Lord himself. I approve of the frugality of the Barbarians. Loving a ready way of life, the Barbarians have left behind luxuries. The Lord calls us to be such as these: naked of pride and arrogance, naked of vain glory, torn away from sins, carrying only the wood of life <note>A common patristic metaphor for the Cross of Christ.</note>, and obtaining salvation alone.

->IV. On those with whom we should associate.<-

<margin>F</margin>
<image-desc>Square ornamental woodcut initial 'E' featuring two figures in a landscape setting framed by intricate vine and leaf motifs.</image-desc>
**BUT INDEED**, I have inadvertently skipped over the logical sequence in my spirit, to which I must now return: the possession of many servants must be rebuked. For fleeing from working with their own hands and serving themselves, people take refuge in a crowd of domestics, buying a great multitude of caterers, table-setters, and those who skillfully carve meat into pieces. These hirelings are divided into many and various roles. And some of them labor in those tasks required to fulfill...

<summary>Clement argues that the beard is a natural mark of male dignity and contrasts the effeminacy of Roman grooming with the rugged, frugal lifestyle of "barbarian" tribes. He then begins a critique of the decadence of wealthy households that rely on excessive numbers of slaves rather than self-reliance.</summary>

# BOOK THREE

<sig>h iiii</sig>

<margin>A</margin> ...pertaining to the gluttony of the throat <note>original: "gulæ ingluviem." Clement uses vivid language to describe the insatiable nature of refined dining.</note>, there are organizers and seasoning-makers of foods; some are composers and architects of sweets, others of cakes and pastries, and others of pottages and broths. Others spend their labor on superfluous clothes. Others guard gold like Griffins <note>A reference to the mythical creatures said to guard gold mines in Scythia.</note>. Others keep the silver, wipe the cups, and prepare the apparatus for banquets. Others rub down the beasts of burden, and from them is trained a crowd of cup-bearers, and herds of handsome youths like cattle, from whom they "milk" beauty <note>Clement is likely alluding to the sexual exploitation of young male slaves in wealthy households.</note>. Orators and talkers serve in adorning women: some with mirrors, some with headbands, while others are in charge of combs. Many are eunuchs, and these are pimps; because it is probable that they cannot engage in lust themselves, they serve those who wish to be free for pleasure without any suspicion. <margin>B</margin> A true eunuch, however, is not one who *cannot*, but one who *will not* engage in pleasure. When the Jews overstepped through Samuel the Prophet, the Word protesting to the people asking for a king, the Lord did not promise a humane master, but threatened that He would give them a certain insolent Tyrant, devoted to lust and pleasure: <margin>1 Samuel 8 <note>Original: "1. Regum. 8." In older Latin bibles, 1 & 2 Samuel were titled 1 & 2 Kings.</note></margin> **WHO WILL TAKE YOUR daughters**, he says, **to be perfumers, cooks, and bakers**, as one who has invaded them by the laws of war, rather than following a peaceful administration of the state. And those who lift the litters of women on high and carry them swiftly are many "Gauls" <note>original: "Galli." Clement likely refers to strong Gallic slaves used as porters, but there is a pun intended on the "Galli" or emasculated priests of Cybele, continuing his theme of effeminacy.</note>; but wool-working, the art of weaving at the loom, the work of women, and the administration and guarding of the home, is nowhere to be found. Instead, there are those who tell false stories to the women and spend the whole day with them, <margin>C</margin> foolishly recounting amorous tales, killing their bodies and souls with false deeds and lying words.

<margin>Ecclesiasticus 7, Isaiah 17 <note>original: "Ecclefi. 7. Eſa. 17."</note></margin>
**YOU SHALL NOT**, he says, **be with the many on account of vice, nor shall you be added to the multitude**, because wisdom is found in the few. Confusion and lack of moderation are seen in the many. And those men who carry the litters do not do so out of a sense of honesty because they do not wish to be seen. It would be well if they offered this as a pretext for such an affection; but instead, women are carried by servants for the sake of extreme luxury, desiring to be paraded about. With the curtain open, they look out at those staring back at them, showing off their manners. Often they even peek outside, bringing shame upon their outward modesty by this excessively slippery and superfluous care. <margin>Ecclesiasticus 9</margin> **DO NOT LOOK AROUND**, he says, <margin>D</margin> **in the streets of the city, nor wander in its lonely places.** For it is truly a "lonely place" even if there is a crowd of the incontinent, provided there is no modest man there. These women are carried about through the temples, sacrificing and divining, accompanied by charlatans and peddlers, and with wicked old women <note>original: "vetulis." These were often neighborhood figures who acted as intermediaries in illicit affairs.</note> who bring ruin to houses, every day parading together and enduring old wives’ whispers over their cups, reciting certain amorous songs composed by charlatans for the destruction of marriage. They have these men as husbands, but they cling to those others; other prophets are promised to them, yet they do not know they are being deceived, surrendering themselves—as if they were vessels of pleasure—to those who wish to fulfill their lust. Exchanging their modesty for the foulest disgrace, they consider a shameful ruin to be a great gain. There are many ministers of harlot-like immodesty, <margin>E</margin> approaching from one side or another. For the intemperate are easily carried toward lust, like pigs to the part of the trough that is lowest. Whence the Scripture most firmly warns: <margin>Ibid. 11 <note>Ecclesiasticus 11:29.</note></margin> **DO NOT BRING every man into your house**, for the snares of a deceitful man are many. And elsewhere: <margin>Ibid. 9 <note>Ecclesiasticus 9:16.</note></margin> **LET JUST MEN be your guests**, and your glorying shall remain in the fear of the Lord. Let fornication go to a bad end. <margin>Ephesians 5</margin> **FOR KNOW THIS**, says the Apostle, **that every fornicator, or unclean person, or covetous man, who is an idolater, has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God.** These women delight in the company of effeminate men; within the house flow crowds of "catamites" <note>original: "cinædorum." A technical term for men who took the passive role in same-sex relations, often associated with luxury and decadence in this period.</note> with unbridled tongues, wicked in body and wicked in speech, acting as men only for immodest services, serving adultery. They laugh <margin>F</margin> shamelessly and whisper, and produce a sound of fornication and effeminacy through their noses in their wantonness; they strive to please with immodest words and gestures, provoking that laughter which is the precursor of fornication. Sometimes, whether incensed by any sort of anger, or being themselves whores, or those who even consider the crowd of effeminate men to be something happy and blessed...

### ->Chapter V. How one should behave in the baths.<-

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'V' featuring a figure in a circular medallion surrounded by scrollwork and foliage.</image-desc>
**WHAT** sort of baths do they have? Houses skillfully joined together, transparent, and portable, covered with fine linen. <margin>D</margin>

They prove that they cannot even meet or sweat without a multitude of vessels. Indeed, poor women, although they do not participate in such pomp, enjoy the baths equally. Thus, the rich have the filth of wealth and the excessive riches of those who are cursed. With this bait they ensnare the miserable, who admire the splendor of gold with mouths agape. <margin>A</margin>By wearing loincloths <note>original: "subligaculis," a type of simple undergarment or loincloth.</note> they preserved their modesty.
