->That Only the Christian is Rich. Chapter VI.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' depicting scrolling foliage and organic patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>
Wealth, therefore, is to be held as is consistent with reason, and it is to be shared generously, not in a stingy or insolent manner. Nor should the pursuit of honor be consumed in self-love, pride, and arrogance, lest someone might say to us: "His horse is worth fifteen talents <note>A "talent" was a massive unit of currency in the ancient world, representing a huge sum of gold or silver.</note>, or his estate, or his slave, or his gold; but he himself is worth less than three obols <note>An "obol" was a small coin of very low value; Clement is contrasting the value of the man's soul with his expensive property.</note>." For if you remove the finery from the women and the slaves from the masters, you will find that the masters differ in no way from the bought <margin>C</margin>slaves—not in their walk, nor their look, nor their speech; so similar are they to their chattels. Indeed, they differ only in this: that they are weaker than the slaves and have been so raised as to be more prone to illness. This, therefore, is the best of doctrines to be sung perpetually: that the good man, who is moderate and just, stores up a treasure of money in heaven. <margin>Matthew 6.</margin> <margin>Ibid. 19.</margin>He who has sold earthly things and given to the poor finds a treasure that does not perish, "where neither moth nor thief is found." He, then, is truly blessed, even if he is small, weak, and without fame; for he truly possesses great riches. But if one were <margin>D</margin>wealthier even than Midas or Cinyras <note>Midas was the mythical king whose touch turned everything to gold; Cinyras was a legendary wealthy king of Cyprus.</note>, yet were unjust and insolent—like the man who dressed luxuriously in purple and fine linen but despised Lazarus—he is both miserable, <margin>Luke 16.</margin>lives in sorrow, and shall not truly live. Wealth, then, is like a serpent: if one does not know how to pick it up harmlessly from a distance, hanging the beast safely by the end of its tail, it will wrap around the hand and bite. These creeping riches know well how to cling and bite, whether they are grasped by the skillful or the unskillful. But if someone, showing himself magnificent, uses them rightly and knowingly, he shall charm the beast away with the song of the Word and remain unharmed. However, it seems we do not notice enough who is the only rich man: he who possesses those things which are by far the most precious. For things of great value are not gems, nor silver, nor clothing, nor beauty of body, but virtue. This is the reasoning handed down by the Instructor <note>original: "Pædagogum." Clement's title for Christ as the teacher of humanity.</note> for our training. This is the reason that renounces luxuries, calls into service the labor that one performs for oneself, <margin>E</margin>and praises frugality, the daughter of temperance.

<margin>Proverbs 8.</margin>
> Receive instruction, he says, and not silver; and knowledge rather than choice gold. For wisdom is better than precious stones, and whatever is valuable is not worthy of her.

And again: <margin>Ibid.</margin>

> Gather me rather than gold, and precious stones, and silver. For my fruits are better than choice silver.

For if it is necessary to distinguish, the one who possesses many things and is burdened with gold like a filthy purse becomes "rich"; but in the just man, there is certainly that which is honorable and becoming. For "becomingness" is an order, defined by administering and giving as one ought. For there are those who sow and reap more. Of whom it is written: "He has dispersed, he has given to the poor; his justice <margin>Psalm 111.</margin>remains forever and ever." Therefore, it is not he who has and keeps, but he who imparts, who is <margin>F</margin>rich; and it is the imparting and sharing, not the possession, that makes one blessed. The fruit of the soul is sharing. Wealth, therefore, is in the soul. And yet, good things can only be possessed by the good. And Christians are the good. But the foolish or intemperate man has neither the sense nor the possession of it. Therefore, only by Christians...

### That the Christian alone is rich. Chapter VI.

<image-desc>Decorative historiated initial 'S' depicting a landscape scene within a square frame with floral ornamentation.</image-desc>
Wealth, therefore, is to be held in a way that is consistent with reason; it is to be shared generously, not in a sordid or insolent manner. Nor should the pursuit of what is honorable be consumed by self-love, pride, and arrogance, lest someone might say of us: "His horse is worth fifteen talents <note>A talent was a massive unit of currency, equivalent to about 6,000 denarii; Clement is highlighting the absurdity of valuing objects over people.</note>, or his estate, or his slave, or his gold; but he himself is cheaper than three obols <note>A small coin of very little value.</note>." For if you take away the finery from women and <margin>C</margin> the servants from the masters, you will find that the masters differ not at all from the slaves bought at auction—not in their gait, nor their look, nor their speech—so similar are they to the slaves. Indeed, they differ only in this: that they are weaker than the servants and have been raised to be more sickly. Therefore, this best of doctrines should be sung perpetually: that a good man, who is moderate and just, stores up a treasure of money in heaven. <margin>Matthew 6; Ibid. 19</margin> He who has sold earthly things and given to the poor finds a treasure that does not perish, where there is neither moth nor thief. D</margin> lives in sorrow, and indeed, he shall not live. Wealth, therefore, is like a serpent: if one does not know how to pick it up harmlessly from a distance, hanging the beast safely by the tip of its tail, it will coil around the hand and bite. Riches, creeping like serpents, are beautifully skilled at clinging and biting, whether they are grasped by the expert or the unskilled. ->That Frugality is a Beautiful Provision for the Christian. Chapter VII.<-

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'D' at the beginning of the chapter, featuring floral and vine patterns.</image-desc>
But luxuries wandering amidst pleasures are a heavy and dangerous shipwreck for men. This pleasant life, which is devoid of glory and praise, is alien to the true pursuit of honor and those things which befit a good man. For a human being is by nature a high and upright animal, held by the desire of seeking and finding the truth, as one who is the work and creation of the One <note>Referring to the Creator/God.</note>. But the pursuit of lust and pleasure is alien to the divine life, for it is much like the feeding of sparrows or the mating of goats and swine. To consider pleasure a "good" <margin>C</margin> is a sign of complete ignorance of what is honorable. Furthermore, an excessive desire for riches moves a man away from the right way of living, persuading him to cast off all shame for the sake of base things—if only he might be allowed, like a wild beast, to eat whatever he wants, drink in the same way, and satisfy his lust in sexual matters by any means possible. Therefore, such a person is very rarely an heir to the kingdom of God. To what end are so many delicacies prepared? Is it not to fill one single belly? The dunghills prove how filthy a thing gluttony is, for into them our bellies spit out the remains of the feast. Why do they gather so many cup-bearers, when they could be satisfied with one cup? Why boxes of clothes? Why gold vessels? And why ornaments? These things are prepared for thieves and wicked <margin>D</margin> men, and for eyes that cannot be satisfied. But ALMS <margin>Eccl. 7.17. and. 29. 1 Kings 19.</margin> and faith, says the Scripture, shall not desert you. Behold, therefore, we also have Elijah the Tishbite as a beautiful example of frugality: when he sat under the broom tree, and an Angel brought him nourishment. It was barley bread baked in the ashes, and a jar of water. The Lord sent such a meal to him. Therefore, as we set out toward the truth, we must be unencumbered: the Lord says, "CARRY NEITHER," <margin>Matth. 10. Luke 9.</margin> purse, nor bag, nor sandals. This means: Do not possess riches that are merely hidden away in a purse; do not fill your storehouses as if planting seeds in a bag, but share also with those who are in need. Do not be overly anxious about beasts of burden and servants, which are spoken of allegorically as the "sandals" <note>Clement interprets the 'sandals' mentioned by Jesus as the heavy material burdens of the wealthy, such as excess servants or livestock, which slow down one's spiritual journey.</note> of the wealthy when they carry burdens. <margin>E</margin> Therefore, the multitude of vessels and gold and silver cups must be cast away, along with the crowd of servants, since we have received beautiful and venerable handmaidens from the Educator: namely, industrious labor <term>operationem</term> and frugality. Now, one must walk in such a way as to enter appropriately with the Word; and if one has a wife and children, the household is by no means a burden, for it has learned to travel with a wise wayfarer. A wife who loves her husband is also to be restrained and composed, so that she may enter the journey just like her husband. Frugality, when joined with a single, moderate gravity, is a beautiful provision <term>viaticum</term> for the way that leads to heaven. Just as the foot is the measure for the shoe, so the body is the measure for each person's possession. But as for that which overflows—what they call the "ornaments" and "furniture" of the rich—these are not truly ornaments of the body. One must climb into the heavens with strength, carrying the beautiful staff of beneficence <note>Charity or doing good deeds.</note>, and perceive true rest by giving generously to those who are afflicted. <margin>F</margin> <margin>Proverbs 13.</margin> For the Scripture confesses that a man’s own riches are the ransom for his soul. <margin>A</margin> are turned. Thus also generosity, which is a good fountain of kindness, sharing drink with the thirsty, is again increased and refilled, just as milk is accustomed to flow into breasts that are sucked or even milked. For he is least in need who possesses the all-powerful Word <note>original: "Deum Verbum" - referring to the Logos/Christ</note> of God, and he never lacks any of those things which he needs. For the Word is a possession to which nothing is missing, and is the cause of all abundance. If anyone should say he has often seen a righteous man who lacked bread, this is indeed rare, and it occurs where there is no <margin>Deuteronomy 8; Matthew 4</margin> other righteous person to help; yet let him also read this: THE JUST SHALL NOT LIVE BY bread alone, but by the word of the Lord: who is the true bread, the heavenly bread. Therefore, a good man never suffers from want as long as he keeps his confession of God intact. For it is permitted for him to ask and receive those things which he lacks from the Father of all things, and to enjoy his own, if he guards the son. <margin>B</margin> This also belongs to him: to feel no lack. This Word of ours, performing the role of the Educator <note>term: "Paedagogus" — the tutor or guide who leads a child to school and supervises their moral development</note>, gives us riches, and there is no envy in becoming rich for those who possess through Him so that they lack nothing. He who has these riches shall become an heir of the kingdom of God.

## ->That parables and examples are the greatest part of right doctrine.<-
# ->VIII.<-

<margin>C</margin> <image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial S</image-desc>If any of you should perpetually flee luxuries, led by frugality, he will meditate on sustaining involuntary labors more easily, considering voluntary afflictions as perpetual exercises for persecutions: so that when he comes to necessary labors, and pains and fears, he is not untrained in enduring them. And therefore we have no homeland on earth, so that we may despise earthly possessions. Frugality is thus most rich, being equal to non-failing expenses, which it is fitting to pay for those things which are necessary and in the amount necessary. For expenses are like installments. <margin>again, a proverb</margin> And how a wife ought to live together with her husband, and concerning the administration of the home, and the use of servants, and how it is fitting for her to work by herself, and regarding the time of marriage, and those things which pertain to women, we have discussed in the book *On Marriage*. But those things which pertain to Educational instruction, those must now be added by us in the place of a description, as we depict the Christian life. And many things have indeed <margin>D</margin> already been said and reduced into the form of Educational instruction. What remains, we shall add below. For examples are of no small importance for salvation.

> See the wife of Ulysses (says the tragedy) she did not give him to death
> Nor did Telemachus join a husband to her,
> For her husband, the holy bed remains in the house.

By rebuking shameful adultery, the poet shows a beautiful image of temperance and love for one’s husband. The Spartans, however, forcing the Helots <note>original: "Ilotas" — a subjugated population in ancient Sparta, used here as a moral object lesson.</note> (the Helots are the name for slaves) to become drunk, showed to themselves while sober those things which drunkenness does, as a form of <margin>E</margin> correction and cure. Therefore, observing their foulness, they were taught not to fall into the same vice they condemned, gaining the fruit of not sinning themselves from the drunkards' disgrace. For among men, some are saved through being taught: others, however, have either embraced or sought virtue of their own accord.

<margin>Hesiod</margin>
> He is the best who perceives all things by himself.
> He is good again who obeys one who advises rightly.

<margin>Genesis 17; Luke 6</margin>
These are the Disciples, who have believed the Word. And therefore that one [Abraham] was called a friend: but these were called Apostles. Seeking the one and the same God, the former with great care and study <margin>F</margin>; the latter indeed preaching. Both, however, are peoples. Of both of these, the listeners—one attained benefit through seeking, while the other escaped safe through finding.

> But he who neither learns for himself, nor takes to heart the one who advises rightly,
> that man is, in turn, clearly useless.

The other people is the Gentile, the useless one; this is the people who does not follow Christ. Ma-

<header>BOOK III OF THE EDUCATOR</header>

<margin>A</margin>Helping in many ways, the Educator <note>term: "Paedagogus" — the divine guide, referring to the Word or Christ</note>, who is mild and kind, persuades us in some matters and reproaches us in others. Now, by showing us the foulness of others who sin and the punishment that follows it, he shows himself to be both kind and gentle by simultaneously consoling and <margin><unclear>Matthew 5</unclear></margin> admonishing us. His purpose is to turn us away from vice by showing what those others have suffered. Through these images and likenesses, he has caused those who were poorly inclined to stop; he has prohibited those who dared to do similar things; he has grounded others in endurance; he has restrained others from vice; and he has even cured others <margin><unclear>Matthew 11</unclear></margin> by leading them toward what is better through the contemplation of what is similar. For who, following someone on a path, would not be careful if the person in front fell into a ditch, so that he might avoid the <margin>B</margin> danger by fleeing the consequence of sin? What if someone, training himself, should learn the way that leads to glory, and seeing the athlete who preceded him receive the prize, does he not strive for the crown, imitating the one who went before? There are many such likenesses of divine Wisdom. I shall remember one example and set forth in a few words what <margin>Genesis 19</margin> happened to the Sodomites. For it was a judgment upon those who had committed the crime, but a pedagogical instruction to those who hear of it. When the Sodomites had stumbled into the vice of lust and intemperance because of many luxuries—committing adulteries without concern and burning with an insane love for boys—the Word <note>original: "Verbum" — the Logos</note> who sees all things looked upon them, for those who commit wicked acts cannot be hidden from Him. Nor did the vigilant guardian of human nature overlook their lust. <margin>C</margin> Instead, turning us away from imitating them and training us toward His own moderation and temperance, He fell upon certain sinners; lest, if unchastity were left unpunished, it might enjoy too much security, He ordered Sodom to be burned, pouring out some of that providential fire upon their intemperance. This was done so that if their lust were not chastised, it would not open the doors too wide for those who are carried with full force toward pleasure. Therefore, the punishment of the Sodomites was just, an image of salvation well-considered by men. For those who do not sin in the same way as those who were punished will never suffer similar penalties, as they were careful not to suffer by virtue of not sinning.

<margin>Jude v. 5</margin>> FOR I want you to know, says Jude, that God, who once saved the people out of Egypt, afterward destroyed those who did not believe, and the angels who did not keep their own domain, but left their proper dwelling, He has kept in eternal chains under darkness for the judgment of the <margin>D</margin> great day, under the gloom of wild angels.

And little by little, he explains the images of those who are judged in a manner very well-suited for teaching.

<margin>v. 11</margin>> Woe to them! For they have walked in the way of Cain, and have run greedily into the error of Balaam, and perished in the rebellion of Korah <note>original: "Core" - the leader of a rebellion against Moses</note>.

For the fear of acting insolently restrains those who cannot bear the freedom of being adopted as children of God. For this reason, there are threats and punishments, so that by fearing the penalties, we may abstain from sins. I could tell you of the punishments for an excessive desire for finery and for empty glory—not only for intemperance—and furthermore bring curses upon those who, because of riches, think and act wrongly, in which God prohibits evil deeds by terrifying them. However, sparing the length of this work, I will bring forward the Educator’s precepts which follow, so that they may avoid the threats.

### IX. For what reason a bath should be taken.

<margin>E</margin><image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'B' featuring floral and vine-like scrolls within a square frame.</image-desc>
**B**aths, therefore (for the discourse departed from this topic), are taken for four reasons. We approach them either for the sake of cleanliness, or heat, or health, or finally, for pleasure. Therefore, bathing for the sake of pleasure must be rejected. For shameful pleasure must be cut out entirely. A bath should be taken by women for the sake of cleanliness and health; but for men, for the sake of health alone. To bathe for the sake <margin>bathing.</margin> of heat is superfluous, since one who has become stiff with cold can be refreshed in other ways. Furthermore, the frequent use of baths takes away strength and relaxes the natural intensity of vigor; it often dissolves it and causes one to <margin>F</margin> faint. For in a certain way, bodies, not unlike trees, drink during bathing—not only through the mouth, but also through the passages which are in the whole body. An indication of this fact is that those who have often been thirsty and then go down into the water find a remedy for thirst...

<margin>A</margin> ...found a remedy. Therefore, unless a bath serves some useful purpose, we ought not to give ourselves over to it. The ancients called these places <term>human-fulling shops</term> <note>original Greek: ἀνθρωπογραφεῖα (anthropographeia) — shops where cloth is cleaned and thickened; here used metaphorically for baths that "wear down" the human body</note>, because they turn bodies into ragged things sooner than is natural, and force them to grow old before their time; for the heat softens the flesh, much like iron is softened by fire. For this reason, we have need of cold water, as if for a kind of tempering and strengthening. Indeed, one should not always be bathing; if you are somewhat hungry or, conversely, a bit too full, the bath should be avoided. It must certainly be used with consideration for one's age, physical condition, and the season of the year. For it does not benefit everyone at all times, as those who are experts in these matters admit. For us, however, <term>balance</term> <note>original: symmetria</note> is sufficient, which we always call upon to assist us in our lives. Nor should the bath be used so excessively that we require the helping hand of another to stand.

<margin>B</margin> Nor should one bathe constantly and many times a day, as frequently as we might go to the marketplace. Furthermore, to have many attendants to serve one in the bath is to wrong one's neighbors through luxury; it is the mark of those who do not understand that a bath should be common to all those who are washing. One ought primarily to wash the soul through the purifying Word, and only occasionally the body, on account of the dirt that clings to it. Moreover, labors must sometimes be relaxed:

<margin>Matthew 23</margin>
> "WOE to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites," says the Lord, "for you are like whitewashed tombs. The tomb appears beautiful on the outside, but inside it is full of dead men’s bones and all uncleanness."

And again he says to the same people:

<margin>Ibid.</margin>
<margin>C</margin>
> "WOE to you, for you clean the outside of the cup and the dish, but inside they are full of uncleanness. Clean first the inside of the cup, so that the outside may also be clean."

Therefore, the best washing is spiritual, for it purges the filth of the soul. Of this the Prophecy speaks openly:

<margin>Isaiah 4</margin>
> "THE LORD has washed away the filth of the sons and daughters of Israel, and shall purge the blood from their midst—the blood of iniquity and the slaughter of the Prophets."

The Lord added the method of this purging, saying:

> "BY THE SPIRIT of judgment, and by the spirit of burning."

As for the fleshy part of the body, it may be washed by water alone, as is often done in the countryside where there is no bathhouse.

### That exercises are also to be chosen by those who live a life according to reason.
#### Chapter X.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring a pastoral scene with a figure and classical architecture inside the letterframe.</image-desc>

<margin>E</margin>
FOR YOUNG MEN, the gymnasium is sufficient, even if a bath is available. Indeed, it might not be a bad thing to prefer these gymnasiums far above baths for men, as they offer something that contributes to the health of the youth, and they encourage diligence and a desire for praise, so that they might care not only for a good physical condition but also for greatness of soul. If this is done without being distracted from better things, it is skillful and not useless. Nor should women be kept away from physical labor here, though they are not to be encouraged toward wrestling or running; rather, they should be exercised in wool-working and at the loom, and should assist at the flour-mill if necessary. Furthermore, it is proper for wives to fetch from the storehouse the things we need themselves, and it is not a disgrace for them to approach the oven or the mill. Nor is it shameful to be occupied in cooking food, provided it pleases her husband; it is a disgrace for a woman to be anything but a guardian and helper of the household. Indeed, she may most honorably shake out the bedding herself, provide drink for her thirsty husband, and set out food, and in doing so she will exercise herself toward a moderate state of health. The <term>Educator</term> <note>original: Pædagogus — referring to the Word/Christ</note> approves of such a woman, who extends her arms to useful tasks and rests her hands upon the spindle; she opens her hands to the poor and reaches out her arm to the beggar. Not even in imitating Sarah does she blush to perform the duty of serving travelers. For Abraham said to her:

<margin>F</margin>
<margin>Genesis 18</margin>
> "HURRY and mix three measures of fine flour, and make cakes baked under the ashes."

And Rachel, the daughter of Laban, came, it says, with her father's sheep. Nor was that enough, for to show how far she was from all pride, the scripture added:

<margin>Ibid. 29</margin>
> "FOR SHE herself tended her father's sheep."

Scripture provides us with countless other examples of frugality, labor, and even exercise. Among men, however, some may wrestle naked, while others play with a small ball...

...let them play that game called *Phenis* <note>original: *Phenis*, likely referring to *phaininda*, a Greek ball game involving deceptive tossing and quick movement</note>, especially in the sun. For others, however, a walk is sufficient when going into the country or down into the city. But even if they should handle a hoe, this is not an illiberal or dirty task of household management, as it is an exercise pertaining to the farmer. Furthermore, I almost forgot to mention that the famous King Pittacus of Mytilene <note>One of the Seven Sages of Greece</note> used to grind at the mill, using that effective exercise. It is also a fine thing to draw water <margin>sun</margin> for oneself and to chop the wood that one will use. Jacob, moreover, tended the sheep of Laban <margin>Genesis 30</margin> that had been left to him, holding a royal sign: a rod of storax, which through the wood meditated upon changing nature for the better <note>A reference to Jacob's use of peeled branches to influence the breeding of the flocks</note>. For many, reading aloud with a high voice is also an exercise. Now, as for the wrestling which we have selected, let it not be undertaken for the sake of useless <margin>B</margin> contention and a desire for vain glory, but so that manly sweat may be excreted. Nor should one labor to show off artistic skill in that matter, but one should contend in honest wrestling, with necks, hands, and sides entwined. For such an exercise, when done in this way with decent strength, is more honorable and more manly, and is undertaken because it is useful and conducive to health. Others, who teach gymnastics, profess a study of life that is not based on liberal pursuits. However, moderation must be observed everywhere. For just as it is best for labor to precede food, so to labor beyond measure is both worst and laborious, and is a cause of disease. Therefore, one ought neither to be entirely idle nor entirely over-worked. For just as we spoke concerning nourishment, so must it be said everywhere in all things. <margin>C</margin> Life is not to be led for pleasure and a luxurious way of living, nor again for the contrary, which has no balance, but for that life which holds the middle place between these, and is temperate and moderate, and pure from both vices—namely, from delicacies and from stinginess. Now, as we also said before, that virtue of **self-sufficiency** <margin><gloss>self-sufficiency</gloss></margin> by which we are content is an exercise removed from pride; it involves putting on one's own shoes, washing one's own feet, and rubbing oneself down after being anointed with oil. Furthermore, to provide mutual help to one who has rubbed you is also an exercise in communal justice; as is sleeping near a sick friend, or one who cannot serve himself, and setting out necessary things for the needy. "And he set out a meal for them," it says, for the three <margin>Ibid. 18. John 21. Matthew 4.</margin> men, namely Abraham under the tree, and he stood by them as they ate. Fishing also, as it was for Peter, if we have leisure from our studies; but this is a better fishing, which the Lord granted to the Disciple, who taught how to fish for men through the water as if they were fish. <margin>D</margin>

### A Concise Treatment of the Best Life. Chapter XI.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter Q featuring floral patterns and vine-like scrolls within a square frame.</image-desc>
For this reason, neither the wearing of gold nor the use of softer clothing is to be entirely cut off. But the affections which are devoid of reason must be bridled, lest by too much dissolution they snatch us away and drive us toward a soft and <margin>E</margin> luxurious life. For those delicacies which have struck against satiety exult in a marvelous way and resist; they throw off the charioteer and the Pedagogue, who, holding the reins from afar, carries and drives the "human horse" toward salvation—that is, the part of the soul separate from reason, which is carried away toward pleasures, blameworthy appetites, jewels, gold, varied clothing, and other luxuries. That point, however, must be kept most firmly in memory, which was holily said: "Keep your **conduct** among the Gentiles <margin>1 Peter 2</margin> honorable, so that in the thing in which they speak ill of you as evildoers, they may, by seeing your good works, glorify God." Therefore, the Pedagogue permits us to use frugal clothing, white in color, as we have said, so that we accommodate ourselves not to a variegated art, but to the nature that generated us, rejecting whatever is deceptive and lies against the truth, so that we may embrace that <margin>F</margin> which is simple and of a single kind of truth. Rebuking one who lives too luxuriously and delicately, Sophocles says:
> "Women who are clothed in garments,"

<margin>A</margin>
...which actors represent. For just as there is a proper dress for a soldier and a sailor, so too there is a specific dress for a modest woman, which is minimally elaborate, decent, and clean. This is why the law regarding leprosy delivered by Moses <note>Referring to the detailed laws in Leviticus 13–14 regarding skin diseases and "leprosy" in fabrics</note> rejects that which is "varied" <note>original: *varium*, meaning spotted, multicolored, or variegated</note> and marked with many spots as if it were an abomination—likening it to the varied scales of a serpent. Therefore, he decreed that a person who does not bloom with a variety of colors, but is white from the crown of the head to the tips of the toes, is clean. Just as in the body, once we have abandoned the varied and shifting affections of the mind, we should love the simple color of truth, which is neither variegated nor wavering. Plato, who in this matter is a most excellent imitator of Moses, also allows for that type of weaving in which no more 
<margin>B</margin>
labor is employed than a modest woman would require. White colors are truly suited to dignity. Elsewhere he also says: "In weaving, do not employ dyes except for the ornaments of war." Therefore, white is appropriate for men of peace and for those who are "bright" <note>original: *lucidis*, implying clarity of mind and spirit</note>. Just as signs that closely precede causes indicate the effect of the thing itself, or rather point it out—just as smoke indicates fire, and a good color and pulse indicate health—so too the kind of clothing we wear indicates the constitution of our character. Pure moderation and temperance are simple, since cleanliness is a habit that prepares a pure way of life, one that is least mixed with shameful things. Simplicity is the habit that removes the superfluous. Solid clothing is quite foreign to the art of the fuller <note>A professional who cleaned and thickened cloth</note>, and it protects the heat which 
<margin>C</margin>
is in the body. It is not that the garment possesses heat in itself, but that it calls back the heat exiting the body and provides it no exit. If by chance any heat is inside it, the garment contains and encompasses it, and having been warmed by that heat, it warms the body in turn. For this reason, it is especially to be used in winter. Such clothing is easy <note>original: *facilis*, meaning manageable or simple</note>. Ease is a habit alien to things that are superfluous, which, in order that nothing be lacking, takes up those things that are sufficient for health and for a blessed life. Furthermore, let a woman also use frugal and honest clothing, perhaps softer than what is appropriate for a man, but not such that it entirely casts off shame, nor should it flow with total softness. Let garments be consistent with age, person, appearance, nature, and pursuits. For most beautifully
<margin>Romans 13</margin>
the divine Apostle commands us to "put on Jesus Christ," and not to make provision 
<margin>D</margin>
for the flesh in its desires. The Word <note>The *Logos* or Christ as the Instructor</note> also forbids us from piercing our ears, which offers violence to nature. For why not the nose as well? This would fulfill what was said: 
<margin>Proverbs 11</margin>
"Like a gold ring in a pig's snout, so is the beauty of a wicked woman." In short, if anyone thinks themselves adorned by gold, they are inferior to the gold. But whoever is inferior to gold is not its master. To admit that one is less honorable and inferior to Lydian shavings <note>original: *Lydio ramento*, referring to gold dust or scrapings from Lydia, a region famous for its wealth</note>—is that not the height of absurdity? Just as gold is polluted by the filth of a pig stirring up mud with its snout, so too women who are somewhat given to luxury, if they are incited to lust and immodesty by excessive wealth, they afflict true beauty with disgrace and dishonor, polluting it with the stains of sexual vice. He <note>The Instructor/The Husband</note> gives them a gold ring, then, not for ornament, but so that she may seal those things at home that are worthy of being guarded, because the care of keeping the house
<margin>E</margin>
belongs to her. Indeed, if nearly everyone followed the right instruction of the Instructor, there would be no need for seals, since everyone—servants and masters alike—would be equally just. But because ignorance and a poor upbringing provide the opportunity for a leaning toward wrongdoing, seals were necessary. However, sometimes there must be a relaxation of that severe and accurate way of life. For sometimes it must be conceded to those women who happen upon less self-controlled husbands that they may adorn themselves to please their husbands. But let this limit be set for them: that they strive to be praised by and to please their husbands alone. Indeed, I would not want them to practice bodily beauty, but rather to win over those to whom they are married with the modest love of their husbands—which is a powerful and just medicine. But since those men choose to have a miserable and unhappy soul, let the women be permitted, if they wish 
<margin>F</margin>
to be modest and chaste, to gradually soothe and calm the irrational desires and appetites of their husbands. The husbands themselves are to be led toward frugality by degrees, gradually becoming accustomed to that which is more moderate and temperate. For dignity is not found in...

### THE TUTOR

-> Book 3, Chapter 11 <-

<margin>A</margin>
[Grace] does not come through troublesome and immoderate additions, but by the removal of what is superfluous. Therefore, those things which women collect for the sake of luxury should be plucked away like feathers, for they breed unstable pride, softness, and empty pleasures. Once stirred up and, as it were, "winged" by these things, women often leap away from their marriages. For this reason, women must be adorned with honor and bound by modest shame, lest they drift away from the truth because of their own softness. Furthermore, it is honorable for men to have faith in their wives and permit them to keep the house, as they were given to men as helpers for that very purpose. But if we too, while managing public affairs or performing other labors in the fields, must often be away from our wives, it may be necessary to seal certain things for greater security. For this purpose, we are granted a single signet ring. All other rings are to be cast aside, for as the Scripture says: *To a wise man, disciplined instruction is a world of gold.* <note>original: "Aureus prudenti mundus est disciplina." A variation of Proverbs 17:6 in the Septuagint/Old Latin tradition.</note> <margin>B</margin> 

However, women who wear gold seem to me to fear that if someone took the gold from them, they would be mistaken for servant girls <margin>Proverbs 3</margin> because they are not "decorated." But the nobility of truth—which is judged in the soul by that which is naturally beautiful and honorable—is not determined by buying and selling, but distinguishes itself from servitude by a mind that is truly free. It is fitting for us not merely to *seem* free, but to *be* free, we who have been instructed by God as our Tutor and adopted by God as His children. And therefore, our posture, our movements, our gait, our clothing, and in a word, our entire life, must be undertaken with the greatest possible freedom. 

<margin>C</margin>
Men should not wear the ring on their finger joint, for that is a womanly habit; rather, it should be placed on the little finger, and even then, pushed down to its base. In this way, the hand will be most ready for work in those matters where we need it, and the seal will not easily fall off, being protected by the larger part of the finger. 

Let our seal-emblems be a dove, or a fish, or a ship running swiftly before the wind, or a musical lyre (which Polycrates <note>The tyrant of Samos, famous in legends for his ring</note> used), or a ship's anchor (which Seleucus <note>Founder of the Seleucid Empire</note> had engraved). And if someone is a fisherman, let him remember the Apostle <note>Referring to Peter, the "fisher of men"</note> and the children who are drawn up out of the water <note>A reference to those newly baptized, often called "fish" in early Christian symbolism</note>. We must not engrave the faces of idols, for it is forbidden even to look upon them. Nor should we use a sword or a bow, as we follow peace; nor drinking cups, for we are moderate and temperate. Many lustful people have engravings of their lovers or mistresses naked, so that they cannot forget their passions even if they wanted to, as their lust and intemperance are perpetually recalled to their minds.

<margin>D</margin>
Regarding hair, this is the view. The hair on a man’s head should be thin, unless perhaps he has curly hair, but the beard should be shaggy. Twisted hair should not be allowed to hang down too far from the head, as it slides into a womanly hairstyle. For men, the beard is enough. Even if someone trims a bit of the beard, it must not be completely stripped away; for it is a shameful sight, and a beard shaved right down to the skin seems little different from plucking or smoothing the skin. Indeed, the Psalmist was delighted by the hair of the beard: <margin>Psalm 132</margin> **AS** the ointment, he says, which descends upon the beard, the beard of Aaron. Since he praised beauty by mentioning the growth of the beard, he cheered his face with the ointment of the Lord. 

<margin>E</margin>
Now, since hair is not cut for the sake of beauty, but for practical reasons, the hair of the head should be trimmed so that it does not grow down and block the sight. Perhaps the hair on the upper lip, which becomes soiled while eating, should also be trimmed—not with a razor, for that is ungentlemanly <note>original: *illiberabile*, meaning unbecoming of a free man</note>, but with barber’s scissors. However, the hair of the beard, which causes no trouble, should not be disturbed, as it brings gravity to the face and inspires a certain "paternal terror" <note>Meaning a look of authority and fatherly respect</note>. 

Furthermore, a man’s appearance and habit often teach many not to sin, as they cannot easily go unrecognized. For those who wish to sin, it is most pleasing to hide their appearance and remain unremarkable. Fearing this, those who are allowed to sin because they are not recognized have successfully imitated many disguises so they might sin securely. Therefore, thin hair not only shows a serious man, but also ensures that the skull is less easily harmed, as it accustoms it to both cold and heat, and repels the discomforts arising from them; long hair, like a sponge, absorbs moisture into itself and inflicts constant harm upon the brain. <margin>F</margin> For women, it is enough to soften the hair and frugally bind the locks with a small pin, nurturing modest hair into true and genuine beauty through simple grooming.

### BOOK THREE

->The Tutor<-

<margin>A</margin> For the intricate braiding of hair and the joining of chains <note>referring to elaborate hairpins or woven jewelry</note> not only makes them unsightly but also tears the hair, plucking it out with artificial bindings. This results in women not even touching their own heads, fearing they might mess up their hair. Indeed, they even go to sleep in fear, lest they accidentally spoil the shape of the woven design. But the addition of hair from others <note>wigs or hairpieces</note> is entirely to be rejected; it is highly impious to apply foreign locks to the head, covering the skull with dead hair. For upon whom does the Priest lay his hand? Whom will he bless? Not the woman who is adorned, but the foreign hair, and through it, another's head. If the head of the woman is the man, and the head of the man is Christ, how is it not impious for them to fall into a double sin?

<margin>B</margin> <margin>1 Corinthians 11</margin> For by excessive hair they deceive men, and as much as lies within them, they bring dishonor upon the Lord while they are adorned like harlots to the betrayal of the truth, and they insult the head which is truly beautiful with curses. Therefore, hair should not be dyed, nor gray hair colored. For just as varying the color of clothing is not permitted, so especially the old age of one's years—to which great trust is given—must not be hidden. Rather, God's beauty must be brought into the light so that the youth may honor it. For when gray hair appears like a Tutor <note>original: "Pædagogi," referring to the ancient guide who led children to school and supervised their behavior</note> to those behaving shamelessly, it leads them to modesty, and the brightness of its appearance terrifies and restrains youthful desire. Neither should the allurements of wisdom be craftily smeared upon their faces. We will show them a modest ornament.

<margin>C</margin> For the best beauty is first the beauty of the soul, as we have often indicated, when the soul has been adorned by the Holy Spirit and with those things that spring from Him: joy, justice, prudence, fortitude, temperance, the love of good things, and modesty—than which no brighter color was ever seen. Afterward, let the beauty of the body also be cultivated, through the moderation of the limbs and parts with a healthy color. This is the appropriate and composed adornment of health, through which one moves from an artificial image toward the truth, in accordance with the form given by God. For adorning according to nature, the tempering of drink and the moderation of food are endowed with great skill. For not only does the body obtain health from these, but it also causes beauty to appear from them. For from that which is fiery comes glow and splendor; from that which is moist, shine and grace; from that which is dry, strength and stability; from the air, the ability to breathe and a balanced equilibrium.

<margin>D</margin> From these, this statue of the Word or of reason <note>original: "verbi seu rationis," likely referring to the Logos forming the human person</note> is handsomely adorned. Beauty is the noble flower of health. For health works within, but beauty, blooming outward, shows a good color clearly. Therefore, the ways of living a most beautiful and healthy life, by exercising the body, produce a genuine and firm beauty, as the spirit draws all moisture and cold breath into itself. Heat, fanned by movement, draws this to itself; after it has drawn it, it gradually exhales the excess of nourishment through the flesh, with some moisture but significant heat. Thus, the nourishment is also used up sooner. Food hardly sticks to an immobile body, but falls away, just as bread falls from a cold oven,

<margin>E</margin> either entirely or leaving only the bottom. Justly, therefore, for those who do not expel waste through the cleansing of exercise, both urine and feces abound. Other excrements also abound for them, and furthermore, sweat, since the nourishment is not distributed to the body at all, but is poured out into what is superfluous. From this, lusts are also stirred up in the genital parts, when the overflow flows in without moderate movement. Therefore, it is necessary to melt away this superfluity and pour it out through digestion <note>original: "concoctione," an ancient medical term for the "cooking" of food in the stomach through heat</note>, through which the appearance becomes ruddy. It is absurd for those who were made in the image and likeness of God to bring in external adornment as if despising the original model, preferring wicked human craftsmanship to God's handiwork. The Tutor

<margin>F</margin> <margin>1 Timothy 2</margin> commands them to adorn themselves in decent clothing with shame and modesty, subject to their own husbands, so that if any do not obey the word, they may be won over without a word through the conduct of their wives. <margin>1 Peter 3</margin> When they see, he says, your chaste conduct which is in the Word. Their ornament should not be the outward braiding or the wearing of gold, or the putting on of robes, but the hidden person of the heart in the incorruptibility of a gentle and quiet spirit...

He emphasizes that exercise and moderation in diet prevent the buildup of bodily waste and lust, maintaining the body as a true reflection of God's image.</summary>

# THE TUTOR: BOOK 1
## On Adornment and Grooming

[This beauty] is not something troublesome or excessive by addition, but rather comes about through the removal of what is <margin>A</margin> superfluous. Therefore, those things which women acquire for luxury should be plucked away from them like feathers, for they give rise to an unstable pride, soft temperament, and empty pleasures. Once excited and, in a sense, "winged" by these things, women often leap away from their marriages. For this reason, women should be adorned honorably and bound by a modest sense of shame, lest they drift away from the truth because of their softness. It is indeed honorable that men, having faith in their wives, should entrust them with the guardianship of the home, as they were given to men as helpers for that very purpose. But if it is necessary for us—while we are managing public affairs, working in the fields, or frequently away from our wives—to seal certain things to keep them safer, he <note>God or the Law</note> gives us a single signet ring for this purpose. Other <margin>B</margin> rings, however, are to be cast aside, for as the Scripture says in <margin>Proverbs 3</margin>:

> To the prudent, a world of gold is instruction. <note>original: "Aureus prudenti mundus est disciplina." This reflects the Septuagint version of Proverbs 3:22 or 17:6, suggesting that for the wise, discipline is more valuable than any ornament.</note>

Those women who wear gold seem to me to fear that if someone took the gold away, they would be mistaken for servant-girls because they are not "decorated." But the nobility of truth, which is judged in the soul by what is naturally beautiful and honorable, does not distinguish servitude by buying and selling, but by an unfree mind. It is fitting for us not merely to *seem* free, but to *be* free, we who have been instructed by God as our Tutor <note>term: Pædagogo; the ancient guardian who led a child to school and taught them morals</note> and adopted by God. Therefore, our posture, movements, gait, clothing, and—to put it simply—our entire life must be undertaken with the greatest possible freedom. Furthermore, a ring is not to be worn by men on the joint of the finger—for that is the manner of women—but on the little finger, and even then, it should be placed at the <margin>C</margin> very base. In this way, the hand will be most ready for work when we need it, and the seal will not easily fall off, being protected by the larger joint of the finger.

Let our seals be a dove, or a fish, or a ship running before the wind, or a musical lyre—which Polycrates used—or a ship's anchor, which Seleucus had engraved. And if someone is a fisherman, let him remember the Apostle <note>referring to Peter and the "fishers of men"</note> and the children who are drawn up out of the water <note>a reference to baptism</note>. We must not engrave the faces of idols, for even looking at them is forbidden to us. Nor should we engrave a sword or a bow, as we follow peace; nor drinking cups, as we are moderate and temperate. Many lustful people have images of their naked lovers or mistresses engraved, so that they cannot forget their passions even if they wanted to, as their lust and intemperance are perpetually recalled to their minds.

Regarding hair, this is the rule: The heads of men should be thin [on top], unless <margin>D</margin> perhaps one has curly hair, but the beard should be shaggy. Twisted locks of hair should not hang too low from the head, sliding down into a womanly mane. For men, a beard is sufficient. If someone trims a bit of his beard, it must not be stripped entirely bare, for that is a shameful sight; a beard shaved right down to the skin seems not far removed from plucking and smoothing the skin [to look like a woman]. For the Psalmist, delighting in the hair of the beard, says in <margin>Psalm 132</margin>:

> **...like** the ointment, he says, which descends upon the beard, the beard of Aaron. <note>original: "sicut vnguentum, inquit, quod descendit in barbam, barbam Aaron." From Psalm 133:2 (132 in the Vulgate).</note>

By praising the beauty of the flowing beard, he gladdened the countenance with the Lord's ointment. Since, however, hair is trimmed not for the sake of beauty but due to circumstance, the hair of the head should be cut so that it does not grow long enough to block the sight, and perhaps the hair on the upper lip, which gets soiled while eating, should be <margin>E</margin> trimmed—not with a razor (for that is ungentlemanly), but with barber's scissors. However, the hairs of the beard, which cause no trouble, should not be disturbed, as they bring a gravity to the face and inspire a certain paternal awe. Furthermore, a man’s appearance and dress teach many not to sin, as they will be easily recognized. To those who wish to sin, it is most pleasing to hide their appearance and not be noticed. Those who fear being caught sinning because they might be recognized have often disguised themselves to resemble many others so they could sin securely.

Therefore, thinning hair not only shows a serious man, but it also makes the skull less easily injured, as it accustoms it to both cold and heat, and repels the discomforts that come from them; for a long mane, like a <margin>F</margin> sponge, soaks up moisture and inflicts perpetual harm upon the brain. For women, it is enough to soften their hair and frugally bind the mane with a simple pin, nourishing their modest locks into a true and natural beauty with simple care.

Meretricious <note>The text ends mid-sentence with the catchword "Meretricii," indicating the next page will discuss the hairstyles or habits "of harlots."</note>

# BOOK THREE

<margin>A</margin> For the harlot-like braiding of hair and the linking of chains not only make them look deformed but also tear the hair, pulling it out with skillfully inserted bindings. It happens that they do not even touch their own heads, fearing they might disrupt the hair’s arrangement. Furthermore, they do not even sleep without fear, lest they accidentally ruin the shape of the texture while slumbering. The addition of someone else’s hair <note>Referring to wigs or hairpieces.</note> is to be entirely rejected; it is most impious to apply external locks to the head, covering the skull with dead hair. For upon whom does the Priest <term>Presbyter</term> <note>original: "Presbyter". Literally an "elder," here referring to the clergy member performing a ritual blessing.</note> lay his hand? Whom will he bless? Not the woman who is thus adorned, but someone else’s hair, and through that, another person's head. If the head of the woman is the man, and the head of the man is Christ, how is it not impious for them to fall into a double sin?

<margin>B</margin> <margin>1 Corinthians 11</margin> For by excessive hair they deceive men; and as far as it lies within them, they bring dishonor upon the Lord, for they adorn themselves like harlots to defraud the truth, and they insult the head which is truly beautiful with curses. Therefore, hair is not to be dyed, nor is gray hair to be colored. For it is not permitted to vary one's clothing <note>i.e., to change its natural appearance to deceive others</note>; and especially the old age of one's life—which is held in great trust—must not be hidden. Rather, the honor given by God should be brought into the light so that the youth may honor it. For when gray hair appears, like a Tutor <term>Paedagogus</term> <note>The title of this work, referring to the one who guides children or the soul in proper conduct.</note> to those who behave shamelessly, it leads them back to modesty; its bright appearance terrifies and restrains youthful desire. Nor should the allurements of clever wisdom be smeared upon their faces. We shall show them a modest adornment. For the best beauty is first the beauty of the soul, as we have

<margin>C</margin> often indicated; when the soul is adorned by the Holy Spirit and by those things which arise from Him—joy, justice, prudence, fortitude, temperance, the love of good things, and a sense of shame—than which no color was ever seen more radiant. After this, however, let the beauty of the body also be cultivated through the moderation of the limbs and parts, combined with a healthy color. This is the fit and composed adornment of health, through which a transition is made from a manufactured image toward the truth, according to the form given by God. For adorning according to nature, there is great skill in the proper temperature of drink and the moderation of food. For the body obtains health from these things, and it also makes beauty appear through them. For from the fiery element comes brightness and splendor; from the moist, shine and grace; from the dry, strength and stability; from the air,

<margin>D</margin> the faculty of breathing and a steady equilibrium. From these things, this graceful and beautiful statue of the Word <note>original: "verbi seu rationis". Refers to the human person as a rational creation of the Logos.</note> is adorned. Beauty is the flower of noble health. For health works within, and beauty, blossoming outwardly, shows a manifest good color. Therefore, the most beautiful and healthy ways of leading one's life, by exercising the body, produce a genuine and firm beauty, as the spirit draws all juice and cold vapor into itself. Heat, fanned by movement, draws things to itself; and after it has drawn them, it gradually exhales the excess of nourishment through the flesh, warmed by a certain moisture but significant heat. Thus, the nourishment is emptied out sooner. But food hardly clings to an immobile body, but falls away; just as bread from a cold oven either falls out entirely or leaves only its bottom stuck behind. Rightly, therefore, for those who do not clear away waste through

<margin>E</margin> the cleansing of exercise, both urine and feces abound. Other excrements also abound in them, and furthermore sweats, since the nourishment is not distributed to the body but flows into that which is superfluous. From this, lusts are also stirred up in the genital parts when the surplus flows there due to a lack of moderated movements. Therefore, it is necessary to melt away this surplus and pour it out through digestion <note>original: "concoctione". In ancient medicine, digestion was viewed as a "cooking" or "concoction" of food.</note>, through which the appearance becomes ruddy. It is absurd that those who were made in the image and likeness of God, as if despining the original model, should bring in external adornment, preferring the wicked human artifice to the craftsmanship of God. But the Tutor

<margin>F</margin> <margin>1 Timothy 2</margin> commands them to adorn themselves in respectable clothing with shame and modesty, being subject to their own husbands, so that if any do not obey the word, they may be won over without a <margin>1 Peter 3</margin> word through the behavior of their wives. **WHEN** they see, he says, your chaste conduct in the Word. Their adornment should not be the external braiding of hair or the putting on of gold or the wearing of clothes, but the hidden man of the heart in the incorruptibility of a gentle and quiet spirit.

# THE TUTOR

...spirit, <note>Continuing from the previous page: "a quiet spirit."</note> which is precious in the sight of God. The work which women perform by their own hands brings them a true and most genuine beauty, as it exercises their bodies and adorns them through their own efforts. It does not offer a "world" of ornaments <note>original: "mundum." In Latin, *mundus* refers both to the world and to a woman's collection of jewelry and toiletries.</note> produced by the labor of others—which is often unclean, shameful, illiberal, and fit for harlots—but rather the clean adornment of every chaste woman, which is supplied and woven by her own hands when it is most needed. For it is never fitting for those who arrange their lives according to God’s laws to appear adorned in things bought from the marketplace, but rather in their own domestic works. For it is a most beautiful thing for a woman to be the guardian of the home, clothing both herself and her husband in their own finery, through which all may rejoice: the children because of their mother, the husband because of his wife, the wife because of them, and all of them because of God. To put it briefly: <sig>B</sig>

<margin>Proverbs 31</margin> It is the storehouse of virtue: a brave woman who does not eat her food in idleness; the laws of mercy are in her mouth; she who opens her mouth wisely and lawfully. Her children rose up and called her blessed, and her husband praised her, as the holy Word says through Solomon. For a pious woman is blessed; let her praise the fear of the Lord. And <sig>C</sig>

<margin>Ibid. 12</margin> again: **A VIRTUOUS WOMAN** is a crown to her husband. Furthermore, one’s posture, gaze, gait, and voice must be corrected as much as possible. For women ought not to behave like some who, imitating the gestures of a comedy and maintaining the broken movements of dancers, come forward as if onto a stage with effeminate motions, soft steps, and feigned voices—looking about with sparkling eyes, prepared to bait someone’s pleasure. <sig>D</sig>

</margin> For honey drips from the lips of a harlot, who, speaking with grace, makes her throat smooth; but in the end, you will certainly find it more bitter than gall and sharper than a two-edged sword. For the feet of folly lead those who follow her down to the underworld after death. Certainly, a harlot conquered the noble Samson, and another woman shaved her husband. But another woman did not thus trample Joseph; instead, <sig>E</sig>

<margin>Genesis 39</margin> the Egyptian harlot was defeated, and he, though taking up the chains of self-control, appeared more powerful than her loose authority. That which has been said seems to be in the best state: "In short, I do not know how to whisper, nor how to walk with a broken gait and a neck bent sideways, as I see many other effeminate men <term>cinaedos</term> <note>original: "cinaedos." A derogatory term for men perceived as effeminate or passive, often used in social critiques of the era.</note> here in the city, plucked of hair and treated with pitch." <note>Pitch was used as a form of painful hair removal in antiquity.</note> Womanish movements, luxury, and delicacies are to be entirely avoided. For a soft movement in walking, and a gait that is effeminate and enervated—as Anacreon <note>A Greek lyric poet known for themes of wine and love.</note> says—are very much the marks of a harlot. It is said, <sig>F</sig> as it seems to me in a comedy, that a harlot's footsteps leave behind a shape of luxury. But the footsteps of fornication are by no means fixed in truth, for they do not walk the paths of life. Her tracks are slippery and dangerous, and they are not easy to recognize. Furthermore, the eyes must be especially guarded, since it is better to slip with the feet than with the eyes. Therefore, the Lord heals this vice as concisely as possible:

<margin>Matthew 5</margin> **IF YOUR EYE**, He says, offends you, pluck it out, pulling out the desire from the very bottom. For a lascivious gaze, and looking with rolling or blinking eyes, is nothing other than committing adultery with the eyes, since through them desire enters as the first skirmish of the battle. For before the whole body, the eyes are corrupted. But an eye that gazes upon things beautiful and good fills the heart with joy. That is, he who has learned to gaze rightly fills it with joy. But he who winks the eye deceitfully gathers sorrows for men. They introduce such an effeminate man as Sardanapalus, <note>The legendary last king of Assyria, often cited in antiquity as the ultimate example of decadence and effeminacy.</note> King of the Assyrians, sitting on a bed with his feet turned up, plucking purple wool and rolling the whites of his eyes.

<margin>Matthew 6</margin> Women who practice these things are the seducers of their own gaze. For the **LAMP** of the body is the eye, says the Scripture, through which internal things appear, illuminated by the light that is perceived. **FORNICATION** in a woman is found in the lifting of the eyes.

<margin>Colossians 3</margin> **MORTIFY** therefore your members which are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, passion, evil desire, and covetousness, which is the service of idols. For because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the children of disobedience, cries the Apostle. But we stir up the passions of the soul and do not blush. Some women among them, devouring mastic gum <note>original: "mastichem." A resin used as chewing gum in antiquity to sweeten breath or clean teeth, here associated with vanity.</note> as they go about, smile with parted lips at those who approach them. Others, as if they had no fingers, delight in scratching their heads with the hairpins <term>fibulis</term> they wear, choosing those made from tortoise shell, ivory, or some other dead animal...

<header>BOOK THREE</header>

<margin>A</margin> they take great care with intense study. Others, however, as if they possessed certain budding flowers so that they might appear beautiful to onlookers, defile their faces by smearing them with colors. Through Solomon, he calls a woman of this sort foolish and bold, one who <margin>Proverbs 9</margin> knows no shame:

> SHE SAT at the doors of her house openly upon a seat, calling to those who pass by on the road, namely those who direct their ways. She calls, moreover, through her appearance and her entire way of life, saying: “Who among you is the most foolish? Let him turn aside to me.” To those who lack wisdom, she commands, saying: “Touch the hidden breads with joy, and the sweet water of theft.”

He calls this "stolen love." <note>original: "venerem." Referring to Venus, the goddess of love, used here as a metonym for sexual desire or acts.</note> Guided by this, the Boeotian <margin>,, B</margin> Pindar says:
> Sweet, he says, is the stolen care of Venus. <note>original: "furtiua cura Veneris"</note>
But the wretched man does not know that serpents dwell with her, and that she goes toward the snare of hell. But "leap back," says the Tutor, "do not stay in that place any longer, nor fix your eyes upon her." For in this way, you shall cross foreign water and pass over Acheron. <note>Acheron: One of the rivers of the Greek underworld; Clement uses it here to signify death or spiritual ruin.</note> Wherefore the Lord says this through Isaiah: <margin>Isaiah 3</margin>

> BECAUSE the daughters of Zion walked with outstretched necks, and with winking eyes, and trailing their robes as they walk, and tripping with their feet; God will humble the daughters of Zion, and will reveal their form—an unseemly form.

I certainly believe that not even the maidservants who follow virtuous women should speak or do shameful things; rather, they themselves ought to be corrected by their masters. Thus, the comic poet <margin>,, </margin> Philemon says quite sharply:
> When it is permitted, after a free woman, to follow a beautiful maidservant looking back, and for someone following from the Plateans <note>original: "Platæico." Likely referring to a resident of the Plataea district or a stock character type.</note> to look at her askance.
<margin>C</margin> For the lack of restraint of the maidservant is reflected back upon the mistress, who allows those who attempt lesser things not to fear climbing to greater ones; by ignoring shameful acts, the mistress shows she does not condemn them. To not be angry with those who surrender themselves to lust is a sign of a mind inclined toward similar things. For as the mistress is, so—as it is said in the proverb—is the little dog.

As for our walking, a frantic gait must be banished far from us; instead, a dignified and slow pace is to be chosen, though not excessively slow. One should not sway in the street, nor look back with a tilted neck to see if those they meet are looking at them—as if leading a pageant parade on a stage and showing off rings. Nor, if pushed into a lower spot, should they need to be led back to their former place by servants, as we see some more delicate men do; they seem robust, but are <margin>D</margin> effeminated by the softness of their souls. In the face of a strong man, there should be no sign of softness, nor indeed in any part of his body. Therefore, let the disgrace of a great and lofty soul never be found in movement or in dress. 

Truly, one who is of sound mind should not use servants like pack animals. For just as they are commanded to be subject to their masters with all fear—not only to the good and gentle, but also to the moody and wicked, as <margin>1 Peter 2</margin> Peter says—so equity, patience, and kindness are beautifully fitting for masters. In short, he says:
> BE ALL of one mind, merciful, loving the brethren, endowed with good hearts, humble, and so forth: SO THAT you may be heirs of a certain good and lovely blessing.

Wishing to describe the image of a young girl, Zeno <margin>,, E</margin> of Citium <note>Zeno of Citium: The founder of Stoicism. Clement often integrates Stoic ethics into Christian teaching.</note> depicts her thus:
> Let there be, he says, a pure face, the eyebrow not lowered, nor the <margin>,, </margin> eye haughty or broken; the neck not tilted back, nor the limbs of the body <margin>,, </margin> relaxed, but upright, like one in a high tension—a right tone. Let there <margin>,, </margin> be sharpness in speech, and a good memory of those things which were <margin>,, </margin> said; and a carriage and motion that gives no hope to the unchaste.

Let modesty reside in the face, and let her display a womanly strength in her look. Let the gloom of the perfume-sellers, goldsmiths, wool-workers, and other workshops be far away, in which women, adorned in harlot's finery, spend the whole day as if sitting in a brothel. Neither should men, spending time in barbershops and taverns, chatter with sweet and flattering words, nor should they ever cease hunting for women who sit there—men who do not stop speaking evil even to provoke a laugh. 

By now, the game of dice must also be forbidden, and furthermore, the pursuit of profit from the game of knucklebones, <note>knucklebones: An ancient form of dice made from the tarsal bones of sheep or goats.</note> which some pursue sharply. <margin>F</margin> Such delights, by no means hidden, are found by those vexed by bile. The cause is idleness. For one loves empty things that are separated from the truth. For they cannot otherwise refresh the mind without damage. Of the mind of every man...

<header>THE TUTOR</header>

<margin>A</margin> ...the fellowship that exists with good men. On the other hand, the most wise Moses, our Tutor, recognizing that a life lived among wicked men is plainly like that of swine, <margin>Leviticus 11. Deuteronomy 14.</margin> forbade the ancient people from eating pigs. By this, he signified that those who call upon God ought not to associate with impure men who, like pigs, itch for bodily pleasures, obscene foods, and shameful stimulations, and are drenched in the harmful pleasure of lust. <note>original: "veneris voluptate." Venus, the goddess of love, is used here as a metaphor for sexual desire.</note> Furthermore, he says that one must not eat the kite, nor any bird that lives on prey, nor the eagle; "YOU SHALL NOT DRAW NEAR," he says, to those who acquire their livelihood through plunder. Moreover, other laws also contain a similar allegory. But as to those with whom we should share our lives—namely, the just—he speaks again through allegory: <margin>In the same place.</margin> <margin>B</margin> "Whatever has a split hoof and chews the cud is clean." The fact that it has a split hoof represents the balance of justice. <note>The "split hoof" is interpreted here as the ability to distinguish between good and evil, or the balance required in a just life.</note> "Chewing the cud," however, refers to the proper nourishment of justice: namely, the Word. <note>original: "Verbum." This refers to the Logos, or Christ, as the Divine Reason.</note> This Word enters from the outside through instruction <term>catechesis: formal religious instruction given to converts</term> just like food, but through meditation, it is recalled from within—as if from the belly—to a rational remembrance. The just man "chews" this spiritual nourishment when he has the Word in his mouth. Justice is rightly "split" because it both sanctifies us here in this life and sends us forward into the age to come.

Therefore, the Tutor will not lead us to public spectacles; nor would one be out of place to call the stadiums and theaters a "seat of pestilence." <note>This is a reference to Psalm 1:1, "nor sits in the seat of the scornful," which Clement links to the Roman theater.</note> For here, too, there is a wicked counsel, just as there was against the Just One, and therefore the assembly gathered against him is devoted to curses. These gatherings are full of great <margin>C</margin> confusion and injustice, and the very reason for the assembly is a cause of disgrace, as men and women gather together indiscriminately to look at one another. In such a place, the assembly acts wrongly. For while the eyes wander lewdly, desires grow hot; the eyes, having become accustomed to looking at one's neighbors more shamelessly because they have been granted this idle leisure, intensify their lusts. Therefore, let public spectacles and performances <note>original: "acromata." These were musical or theatrical performances, often of a worldly or decadent nature.</note> be forbidden, for they are full of wickedness and of obscene and vain words recklessly poured out. For what shameful act is not shown in the theaters? What shameless word do the jesters and actors not bring forth to stir up laughter? Those who have perceived some delight from the vice within themselves carry home clear images of it impressed upon their minds. Conversely, those who cannot be soothed or affected by these things will be the least likely to fall into lazy pleasures.

If people say that these spectacles are taken up as a game to refresh the mind, we shall say that those <margin>D</margin> cities are not wise which treat a game as a serious matter. For the cravings of vainglory are not games; they are so merciless that they lead to death. Nor are they games when they involve vain pursuits, reckless ambitions, and the wasting of one's resources. Furthermore, the riots stirred up for these reasons are games no longer. Leisure must never be bought with a vain pursuit. For a wise man will never prefer that which is merely pleasant over that which is better.

"But," someone says, "not all of us are philosophers." Do we not then all pursue life? What are you saying? How then did you believe? Moreover, how do you love God and your neighbor if you do not "philosophize"? <note>Clement argues that "philosophy" is not just for scholars, but is the lived practice of Christian wisdom.</note> How do you love yourself if you do not desire life? "I have not learned letters," he says. But even if you have not learned to read, you cannot excuse yourself from hearing, since hearing does not need to be taught. Faith is the <margin>E</margin> possession not of those who are wise according to the world, but of those who are wise according to God. That wisdom is learned even without letters. Its scripture—which applies even to the unrefined and ignorant, and is divine—is called "charity" (love), which is a spiritual decree.

It is permitted to hear divine wisdom; it is permitted to be involved in the administration of the state; it is even permitted to take up the things of the world honorably according to God’s will—this is by no means forbidden. Let whoever sells or buys something never state "two prices" for what they are selling or buying. <note>This refers to the practice of haggling or having one price for the rich and another for the poor; Clement demands a single, honest price.</note> By stating one simple price and striving to speak the truth, even if he does not get his price, he is nonetheless rich in the right disposition of the soul because he has attained the truth. Let the oath—the author of all that is sold—be absent. Let the oath be absent in other matters too, and let the marketplace traders and tavern-keepers "philosophize" in this way: <margin>Exodus 20.</margin> <margin>F</margin> YOU SHALL NOT TAKE the name of the Lord in vain. For when the greedy, the liars, and the hypocrites who trade in the truth do this, they do not act out of their Father's...

<summary>Clement provides an allegorical reading of Mosaic dietary laws to guide Christian social associations and delivers a sharp critique of theaters and stadiums as sources of lust and civil disorder. He argues that even the uneducated can live "philosophically" through faith and love, and he mandates strict honesty and the avoidance of oaths in business transactions.</summary>

She herself will never stumble if she places both modesty and her veil before her eyes; nor will she provoke another to the slip of sin by exposing her face. Those who are initiated into Christ <note>A term used for baptized Christians.</note> ought to appear and be shaped throughout their entire lives in the same way they compose themselves in church for the sake of gravity and decency. The Apostle called it "holy." <note>The "Holy Kiss" or "Kiss of Peace" was a liturgical greeting in the early church.</note> Having tasted the Kingdom worthily, let us show the goodwill of the soul with a modest and closed mouth, through which the gentleness of our character most exerts itself. <margin>Chapter 4.</margin>

# THE TUTOR

<margin>Ecclesiasticus 35.</margin>

<margin>A</margin>
shall I crown Him, or anoint Him with ointment, or what kind of incense shall I offer to the Lord? "An odor of sweetness to God," He says, "is a heart that glorifies Him who made it." And concerning the administration of the state: "Render the things that are Caesar's to Caesar; and the things that are God's to God." Regarding the swearing of oaths and the memory of an injury received: <margin>Leviticus 19.</margin> <margin>Ecclesiasticus 10.</margin> <margin>Isaiah 3.</margin> <margin>Luke 14.</margin> "Did I ever command your fathers when they went out from the land of Egypt to offer me burnt offerings and sacrifices?
