To the former, in this way: "Woe to those who call sweet bitter, and bitter sweet." To the latter, thus: "Woe to those who are prudent in themselves, and knowing in their own sight." "For he who humbles himself shall be exalted, and he who exalts himself shall be humbled." And He pronounces the merciful <margin>C</margin> blessed, because they shall obtain mercy. But Wisdom pronounces anger to be wretched: <margin>Matthew 5.</margin> <margin>Ecclesiasticus 30.</margin> "Because it will destroy even the prudent themselves." Now, He also commands us to love our enemies, and to bless those who curse us, and to pray <margin>Matthew 5.</margin> for those who insult us and treat us injuriously: "To him who strikes you," <margin>Ibid. 21.</margin> He says, "on the cheek, offer him the other also. And if anyone takes away your tunic, do not forbid him from taking your cloak as well." Concerning faith: "Whatever you ask in prayer believing, you shall receive," He says. But to the unfaithful, nothing is trustworthy, as Pindarus says <note>original: "Pindarus." Clement often blends classical Greek poetry, like that of Pindar, with Christian doctrine to appeal to educated readers.</note>. And indeed, we must treat our servants as we treat ourselves. For they are human beings, just as we are. For God is equal to all, both free and slave, if you consider it. Moreover, it is necessary not to punish brothers who sin, but to rebuke them: <margin>D</margin> <margin>Proverbs 13.</margin> "For he who spares his rod," He says, "hates his son." Furthermore, He drives out the desire for glory, <margin>Matthew 23.</margin> <margin>Ibid. 11.</margin> <margin>Luke 7.</margin> <margin>1 Peter 2.</margin> saying: "Woe to you Pharisees, because you love the first seats in the synagogues, and greetings in the marketplace." But He embraces the repentance of the sinner, loving the repentance that follows sins. For only the Word <note>original: "Verbum" (the Logos/Christ).</note> is He upon whom sin does not fall. For to sin is innate and common to all by nature. But to recover one's senses after a sin is not the mark of just any man, but of one who is rightly to be considered magnificent. Concerning fellowship: <margin>Matthew 25.</margin> "Come," He says, "to me, all you blessed, be heirs of the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry, and you gave me to eat; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink. I was a stranger, and you gathered me in; naked, and you covered me; sick, and you visited me; I was in prison, and you came to me." And when did we do <margin>E</margin> any of these things for the Lord? The Lord himself will say in return, kindly turning the benevolence shown to the brothers toward himself, and saying: "Whatever you did for these little ones, you did for me." And those who are such shall go into eternal life. Such are the laws of the Word, consoling words, not written on stone tablets by the fingers of the Lord, but written in the hearts of men, upon which alone destruction does not fall. Therefore, the tablets of those who were hard of heart were broken, so that the faith of children might be imprinted on tender minds. Both Laws, however, served the Word for the instruction of human nature: the former through Moses, the latter through the Apostles. Now, what kind of "childish instruction" was handed down through the Apostles, it seems to me necessary to discuss that kind also. Rather, the Tutor says, remembering his own. And I will set out his precepts again, <margin>F</margin> <margin>Zechariah 8.</margin> <margin>Ephesians 4.</margin> as if in a seed: "Putting away lying, speak the truth, each one with his neighbor, because we are members of one another. Let not the sun go down upon your anger, nor give place to the Devil. He who stole, let him steal no longer,"

<summary>Clement compiles a series of ethical precepts from the Old and New Testaments, framing them as the "Tutor’s" instructions for daily life. He emphasizes that the New Law is written on the heart rather than on stone, demanding mercy, humility, and the fair treatment of servants.</summary>

# THE TUTOR

<margin>A</margin>
...that we are in him. He who says he remains in him ought himself also to walk just as he walked. <note>original: "Qui dicit in ipso manere..."; a reference to 1 John 2:6.</note> O pupils of this blessed Tutelage, let us fulfill the beautiful character of the church and run like infants to our good mother. If we are hearers of the Word, let us glorify the blessed economy—that is, the divine plan of the assumed human flesh—through which man is instructed by the Tutor, yet sanctified as God's own child. <term>Economy</term><note>original: "œconomiam"; in early Christian theology, this refers to God's strategic plan for the salvation of humanity, specifically through the Incarnation of Christ.</note> Though he is formed from the earth, he lives in the heavens, finding there the Father whom he learns of while on earth. The Word does everything: he acts, he teaches, and he instructs. A horse is led by a bridle, a bull by a yoke, and a wild beast is caught in a snare; but man is transformed by the Word, by which wild beasts are tamed, swimming creatures are baited, and birds are drawn down. 

<margin>B</margin>
This Word, or Reason, truly constructs the bridle for the horse, the yoke for the bull, the snare for the wild beast, the rod for the fish, and the trap for the bird. This Word governs the republic, tills the fields, commands and serves, and fashions all things.

->He created the earth, and the heaven, and the high reaches of the sea,<-
->And all the beautiful stars which crown the heaven on every side.<-

O divine works! O divine precepts! Let this water ripple within itself; let this fire restrain its anger; let this air wander through the ether; and let the earth both grow firm and bear fruit. When I wish to form a man, the elements are my material; I dwell together with my own handiwork. If you know me, the fire will serve you. Such and so great is the Word.

<margin>C</margin>
This is the Tutor, the creator of the world and of man; and for his sake, he is now also the Tutor of the world. By his command we both exist, awaiting judgment. For he does not bring a deceptive spoken word to men. As Bacchylides says: "The word shall be wisdom." <note>Bacchylides was a Greek lyric poet from the 5th century BCE.</note>

<margin>To the Philippians 2.</margin>
"Be blameless and sincere, and beyond reproach before God," as Paul says, "children in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation; appear as lights in the world." <note>A translation of Philippians 2:15.</note> What remains, then, after such a celebration of the Word, is that we shall pray to the Word. Be gracious to your children, O Tutor, Father, Charioteer, Son of Israel, and Father—both are one, O Lord. Grant to us who follow your precepts that we may fulfill the likeness of your image, and that we may perceive, as much as we are able, the good God and a Judge who is not harsh. Grant that all of us who live in your peace may be transferred into your city, having sailed through the waves of sin without being tossed. May we come together in tranquility with the Holy Spirit and ineffable wisdom,

<margin>D</margin>
praising by night and by day until the perfect day. Let us give thanks and praise the one Father and the Son—the Son, I say, the Tutor and Teacher, together with the Holy Spirit, who is one in all things, in whom are all things, through whom all things are one, through whom is that which always exists, of whom we are all members, and to whom belong glory and the ages. He is entirely good, entirely beautiful, entirely wise, and entirely just. To him be glory now and forever. Amen. Since the Tutor has led us into

<margin>A</margin>
### Chapter Two.

ᵃ This passage is indeed corrupted in the Greek, but I believe this to be the intended meaning.

<margin>B</margin>
### Chapter III.

ᵃ **Chewing mastic**, <note>original: "Mastichen rodentes"</note> specifically so that they may clean the filth from their teeth.
ᵇ **A physiognomist**, <note>original: "Metoposcopus"</note> one who judges a person's nature by inspecting their forehead.
ᶜ **Of the hips**, in Greek *lordoumenous* <note>original: "λορδουμένους"</note>, which means to thrust the chest forward by pulling in the back parts of the loins. For *lordos* <note>original: "λορδὸς"</note> signifies the opposite of the word *kyrtos* <note>original: "κυρτόσ"</note>, which means convex or hunched.
ᵈ He understands **wicked women** <note>original: "Sceleratas"</note> to be the *Tribades* <note>A term used in antiquity for women who engaged in same-sex intimacy.</note>, whom they also call Lesbians and *Heteristrias*.

<margin>C</margin>
### Chapter IIII.

ᵃ To the **mountebanks**, in Greek it is *metagyrtai* <note>original: "μητραγύρταις"</note>. These are the beggar-priests dedicated to Rhea, the mother of the Gods; they perform deceptions and compose love potions. They are also called *Galli*, men who have castrated themselves and are prepared to endure the most shameful acts.
ᵇ A **Maltese dog**, <note>original: "Melitæus catellus"</note> a small and low-to-the-ground puppy which they call a *navidion* <note>original: "ναυίδιον"</note>, because it does not grow tall. For *navidion* is the diminutive of *nanos* <note>original: "νανος"</note>, which signifies a small man or dwarf. It is called "Maltese" after the island of Melite in the Tyrrhenian Sea.

### Chapter VI.

ᵃ **Cinyras** was by far the wealthiest King of the Cyprians. It is said that, driven by an angry Venus, he committed incest with his daughter Myrrha, from whom Adonis was born.

<margin>D</margin>
### Chapter VII.

ᵃ Scripture speaks of being "under the juniper" and of **spelt bread** <note>original: "panem ὀλυρίτην"</note>. The word is *olyra* <note>original: "ὄλυρα"</note>, which many call *bromos* <note>A type of grain, often identified as oats or wild rice.</note>.

<margin>E</margin>
### Chapter X.

ᵃ The **game of Phenis** <note>original: "Phenis ludus"</note> is of this sort: Among boys playing, one holding a ball would show it to one person first and then throw it to another. It was so named either after Phenicida, who first invented it, or from the verb *phenakizein* <note>original: "φενακίζειν"</note>, which means to deceive. For he would deceive his playmates by showing the ball to one but handing it to another.

<image-desc>A large historiated woodcut initial 'C' containing a scene within an oval border. The scene depicts two figures in a landscape; one appears to be reclining on the ground while another stands or bends over them. The initial is surrounded by dense ornamental foliage and scrollwork.</image-desc>Since the eight books of the *Stromata* <note>meaning "Miscellanies" or "Tapestries," Clement’s most famous work</note> by Clement of Alexandria <note>a Christian theologian and philosopher of the 2nd century</note>, which are filled with diverse and manifold learning, were brought forth from your library and published in Greek by your printer, and have now been translated into Latin by me, Most Illustrious Prince, I thought it wrong that when they soon come into the hands of scholars, they should not know to whom they ought to be grateful for this treasure. For while those who delight in the study of literature owe you much for many reasons, they must certainly confess themselves so obligated to you for the edition of this truly admirable author that no forgetfulness will ever erase the memory of this divine favor. 

Certainly, this work of his is of such a kind that it contains such great and countless riches of every branch of learning, that there is no one gifted in any arts or disciplines who will not receive the greatest benefit from it. If it had perished, and had not been—I might almost say—called back to life by your help, the Christian Commonwealth <note>original: "Christiana respublica," referring to the collective community of the Christian world</note> would have suffered an incredible loss. For this reason, it is fitting to believe that Clement himself—who naturally rejoices that his work, written for the public good, has been rescued from destruction—will both be deeply grateful to you and will return that thanks through his prayers to God. 

It is indeed a great honor, best of Princes, to bind to yourself with your immortal favor not only the living, but also those who have departed from life. There are surely many things, the greatest and most distinguished, which many people rightly look up to, praise, and admire in you; yet there is nothing that everyone proclaims more with one voice—and even praises to the skies—than both your remarkable love of learning and your exceptional kindness toward scholars. 

And deservedly so. For since you have set this goal for yourself in the administration of this most beautiful state, granted to you by divine providence, and have directed all your actions toward this end—as is the duty of the best and truly Christian prince—that your citizens might live well and happily (which only happens when, after vices have been expelled, there is a place for virtue and dignity): what could be more honorable and useful than to seek from the monuments of the ancients noble principles and...

Since the eight books of the *Stromata* <note>original: "Stromatum"; literally "Miscellanies" or "Patchwork," referring to the varied subject matter of the work</note> by Clement of Alexandria, filled with varied and manifold learning, were brought forth from your library and published in Greek by your printer, and have now been translated into Latin by me, Most Illustrious Prince, I thought it should not be allowed that when these books come into the hands of scholars shortly, they should be ignorant of to whom they ought to be grateful for this treasure. For while those who delight in the study of letters owe you much on many accounts, they must certainly confess themselves so obligated to you for the edition of this truly admirable author, that no forgetfulness shall ever erase the memory of this divine benefit. 

Certainly, this Commentary of his is of such a kind, containing such great and innumerable riches of every branch of learning, that there is no one endowed with any arts or disciplines who will not receive the greatest utility from it. If it had perished, and had not been—I might almost say—restored to life by your help, the Christian commonwealth <term>respublica: the community of Christian nations and scholars</term> would have suffered an incredible loss. On which account it is pious to believe that Clement himself—whom it is reasonable to think rejoices that his work, written for the public good, has been rescued from destruction—will both feel great gratitude toward you and return it through his prayers to God. 

This is indeed a great glory, best of princes: to bind to yourself by your immortal benefit not only the living, but also those who have departed from the living. There are indeed many things, and those the greatest and most distinguished, which many people rightly look up to, praise, and admire in you; yet there is nothing that everyone proclaims with one voice and even extols to the heavens more than your remarkable love of learning and your exceptional benevolence toward the learned. And rightly so. For since, in this administration of a most beautiful state <note>Florence</note> bestowed upon you by divine providence, you have set this before yourself and directed all your actions toward it—namely, that which is the goal of a best and truly Christian prince: that your citizens may live well and happily—which happens only when, with vices expelled, there is a place for virtue and dignity; what is more honorable and useful than [to seek] from the monuments of the ancients both excellent institutions and fa- <meta>catchword: fa- (likely leading to 'fata' or 'facere' on the following page)</meta>

<meta>This page continues Gentian Hervet’s dedication to Cosimo I de' Medici. Hervet moves from praising the Duke's library to a metaphor of the Duke as a physician of the state, before discussing his own labor in translating Clement of Alexandria from Greek into Latin.</meta>

...to have been taught to learn, and by your example, zeal, and assistance, to incite your citizens toward honorable pursuits? By this means, it has certainly come to pass that, like a most skilled physician, you have taught those in good health the things that pertain to maintaining their well-being, and you have cured the sick—partly with gentle and partly with sharp medicines, as the illness required—so that the long-desired health has been restored to your republic <term>respublica: the state or political community of Florence</term>. 

But where am I being carried away? Contrary to what I had intended, I run off into your praises, which are neither suited to a talent so small as mine, nor to such a meager faculty of speaking; they certainly cannot be celebrated within the brevity of this letter. Should I not rather return to our Clement? For why should I not call him "ours," since each of us has contributed what we could to him? You received him liberally, nourished him, restored him, and ordered him to go out into the public eye polished and well-tended <note>Hervet refers to the Duke's patronage of the first Greek edition of Clement’s works</note>. I, however, having immediately entered into no common friendship with him, was not satisfied to hear him speaking Greek, unless I also taught him to speak "Roman" <note>original: "Romanè"; meaning Latin</note> so that he might become familiar to all Latin speakers. 

How well I have succeeded, let others judge. For I am not so unaware as to not know how difficult it is for an old Greek to learn a foreign tongue, especially if the teacher himself is a stranger to the language he teaches. However the matter may stand, I have tried diligently, and I believe I have performed the task so that—if nothing else—he certainly expresses his thoughts faithfully and familiarly in Latin. 

And so, since the extant works of this Clement were recently brought to light by your great benefit, and since I had translated them into Latin and sent them to Florence to be published in the most beautiful types <note>original: "typis"; referring to the printed typeface of the printing press</note>, I decided that this divine work of the *Stromata* <note>original: "Stromatum"; Clement’s "Miscellanies"</note> should be sent forth under your most fortunate auspices. I was moved to do this all the more gladly because Petrus Victorius <note>Piero Vettori (1499–1585), a famous Italian philologist and editor of classical texts</note>, a man of extraordinary learning, had dedicated all of Clement's works to Marcello Cervini <note>1501–1555; then Cardinal of Santa Croce and later Pope Marcellus II</note>, a man of primary piety and learning, in whose distinguished circle of clients he had kindly supplied Clement's *Protrepticus* <note>Clement's "Exhortation to the Greeks"</note>. Therefore, I thought it would not be foreign to my duty if, by consecrating these *Stromata* to your fortunate name, I left a testimony of how pleasing it is to all good men, and how celebrated with immortal praise is this your zeal for learning and your inexhaustible liberality in promoting the noble arts and disciplines.

->ears for a little while to Clement speaking Latin. At Gubbio,<-
->July 6, 1551.<-

<margin>A</margin>...so that you may read them at hand, and be able to preserve them. But is it the case that writing should not be permitted at all, or should it be allowed for some? And if the former: what is the use of letters? But if the latter: should it be for good men, or those who are not of that sort? It would certainly be ridiculous if, while the writings of those who are good and studious are rejected, the compositions of those who are not such men were admitted. But if Theopompus and Timaeus <note>Theopompus of Chios and Timaeus of Tauromenium were Greek historians often criticized for their biting or gossipy styles.</note>, who compose fables and slanders—and even Epicurus <note>The philosopher Epicurus was frequently targeted by early Christian writers as the "author of impiety" because of his materialist views and denial of divine providence.</note>, the leader and author of impiety—and furthermore Hipponax and Archilochus <note>Ancient Greek poets famous for their aggressive, often insulting iambic verse.</note>, are permitted to write so shamefully, then must he who preaches the truth be forbidden from leaving behind something useful for those who come after? I consider it beautiful and honorable to leave behind good sons for those who are to come. And while sons are the offspring of bodies, discourses are the offspring of the soul. Indeed, we call those "Fathers" who have instructed us in the <term>catechesi: the basic oral instruction of the Christian faith</term>. Philosophy, however, is human and shares itself willingly. ...that faith may work through love? <margin>A</margin> God is entirely free from blame for the fault of one who does not choose what is best, and He is in no way the cause of it. Now, it is indeed the duty of some to "lend out" the word <note>The Latin *fœnerari* suggests lending at interest; here, it refers to the spiritual investment of teaching.</note>; of others, however, it is to test it, and either receive it or not. The judgment, moreover, is judged within themselves. But the knowledge of preaching is in some sense Angelic, helping in whichever way it might work, whether by hand or by tongue. For "he who sows in the spirit, from the spirit shall reap eternal life." As we are doing what is good, let us not be of a small and dejected spirit. Upon the person who, by divine providence, has come upon these things, God confers the greatest gifts: the beginning of faith, a prompt and eager desire for a rightly ordered life, a longing for truth and an impulse toward it, the movement of inquiry, the footprint of knowledge, and—to put the matter briefly—He gives the material and the opportunity for salvation. <margin>B</margin> Furthermore, those who are genuinely and sincerely educated in the words of truth, having received the <term>viaticum<note>Originally a Roman term for provisions or money for a journey; in a Christian context, it refers to spiritual nourishment for the journey to the afterlife.</note></term> of eternal life, are carried up to the heavens. <margin>To exhort. <note>original: προτρέψαι</note></margin> Therefore, the Apostle speaks quite wonderfully: <margin>2 Corinthians 6</margin> **Always showing yourselves as ministers of God... as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing all things. It is necessary, therefore, for both parties to test themselves: the teacher, to see if he is worthy to speak and leave behind these monuments; and the student, to see if he may rightfully hear and read. Even when some have divided the **Eucharist** <note>The central Christian rite of the Lord's Supper.</note> according to custom, they permit each of the people <margin>C</margin> to take a portion of it. For the conscience is the best guide for accurately and perfectly choosing or avoiding things. Its firm foundation is a righteous life combined with the appropriate doctrine; and to follow others who have already been tested and who have conducted themselves rightly is the best path, both for understanding the truth and for following the commandments. Therefore, whoever eats <margin>1 Corinthians 11</margin> the bread and drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of the bread and drink of the cup. Consequently, the person who takes up the care of benefiting his neighbors must consider whether he has rushed into teaching boldly and recklessly, or driven by some rivalry toward others; whether he seeks glory from the communication of the word; or whether he accepts this reward alone: the salvation of those who hear him. He must consider whether he has escaped the charge of speaking only to please, and the foul <margin>D</margin> accusation of receiving gifts, if he is one who speaks through written monuments. **For we were never found in the speech of flattery, as you know,** says the <margin>1 Timothy 2 <note>This is likely a citation error in the original text; the quote is actually from 1 Thessalonians 2:5.</note></margin> Apostle, **nor in the pretext of greed. God is witness; neither seeking glory from men, nor from you, nor from others, when we might have been a burden as Apostles of Christ; but we were gentle in your midst, just as a nurse cherishes her children.** By the same reasoning, those who are partakers of the divine words must observe whether they approach them led by the vice of an overly curious mind—as if they were merely looking at the buildings of cities—or whether they come to be partakers of secular benefits, having heard that those who are consecrated to Christ willingly share the necessities of life. Such people are hypocrites, and should therefore be sent away. But if anyone wishes not just to *seem* <margin>E</margin> righteous but to *be* so, it is necessary that he possess the best conscience. If, therefore, the harvest is indeed great, but the laborers are few, one must truly pray that there be a very great abundance of laborers. However, there is a twofold agriculture: one which is not contained in writings, and another which is. In whichever way the laborer of the Lord sows the noble grain, increases the ears of corn, and reaps them, he will appear a truly divine husbandman. **Work,** says the Lord, **not for the food that perishes, but for that which remains <margin>John 6</margin> unto eternal life.** Nourishment is taken both through food and through words; and <margin>Matthew 5</margin> indeed, "blessed are the peacemakers," who, by teaching the opposite, transform those who are attacked by ignorance in this life and error, and lead them to the peace which is in the Word and the life which is from God; and who nourish those who hunger for righteousness by the distribution of bread. For even souls have their own proper nourishments: some are <margin>F</margin> increased through recognition and knowledge, while others are fed by **Greek Philosophy**, of which—as with nuts—not everything is edible. It will bring forward the decrees established by notable heresies and speak against them, whatever must be dispensed before 

<margin>B</margin> <margin><gloss>outlined</gloss></margin> prophetic contemplation. This contemplation will proceed for us from the glorious and venerable rule of tradition <note>original: "traditionis regula." This refers to the "Rule of Faith," the shared core of Christian belief used to measure truth.</note>, starting from the beginning of the world, bringing forward first those things which must necessarily be treated through natural contemplation—just as a farmer first prepares the ground by clearing away thorns and weeds before planting a vineyard. For the contest has its prelude, and there are mysteries that precede the mysteries. Our commentaries will not be afraid to use the most beautiful elements of philosophy and the preparatory disciplines. For it is right to become a Jew to the Hebrews and those under the law, but also a Greek to the 

<margin>C</margin> <margin>1 Corinthians 9</margin> <margin>Colossians 1</margin> Greeks, so that we may win them all. And in the Epistle to the Colossians, he says: **"ADMONISHING every man and teaching in all wisdom, that we may present every man perfect in Christ."** Although the splendor of contemplation is appropriate for a certain description of commentaries, the very abundance of good disciplines is like a kind of seasoning mixed with an athlete’s food—not for one seeking delicacies, but for one acquiring a healthy appetite and a love of praise. <margin><gloss>useful learning</gloss></margin> <margin><gloss>exercises</gloss></margin> Just as when we sing, we temper a too-intense sound of gravity into a melodic tone.

<margin>D</margin> Just as those who wish to address a crowd often do so through a herald so that the words spoken may be better heard, so too here: since our discourse which precedes the tradition must be held for many, we must bring forward the opinions and voices that resonate among various people, through which those who listen will be more readily converted. To put it briefly: among many pearls, there is one; in a great catch of fish, there is one "beautiful-fish" <margin><gloss>beautiful-fish</gloss></margin> <note>original: "callionymus" or "καλλιχθύς." Ancient naturalists believed this fish was especially sacred or medicinal.</note>. In time and with labor, the truth will shine out, if a good helper is found. For many benefits are supplied by God through men. All of us who use our sight contemplate the things that fall before us, but some for one reason and others for another. A cook and a shepherd do not contemplate a sheep in the same way. The cook examines closely whether it is fat, but the shepherd observes whether the sheep’s milk is of good quality. One may milk it if he needs food; another may shear the fleece if he needs a covering. In this same way, let the fruit of the good learning of the Greeks proceed for me. 

<margin>E</margin> For I consider no writing so fortunate as to have no one contradict it at all; rather, that writing should be considered reasonable which no one contradicts with justice. Both the action and the design together must be accepted, not because they are free from criticism, but because no one criticizes them justly. If someone does not act directly, it does not immediately mean they are avoiding the task; rather, they act by wisely applying a certain divine "dispensation" <note>An "economy" or strategic adaptation of truth to suit the audience's capacity.</note>, <margin><gloss>according to the circumstance</gloss></margin> accommodating themselves to circumstances and turning in every direction. <margin><gloss>accommodating oneself</gloss></margin> For one who possesses virtue no longer needs the path to virtue, nor does one who is strong in strength need restoration. For just as farmers first water the earth, so we too—with that which can be drunk from the discourses of the Greeks—

<margin>F</margin> first water that in them which is "earthly," so that it may receive the spiritual seed that is cast down and be able to nourish it easily. These discourses shall be called <term>Stromateis</term> <note>original: "στρωματεῖς." Literally "patchwork quilts" or "miscellanies." It implies a varied, unsystematic collection of deep thoughts.</note>, that is, "patchwork-coverlets" woven with variety, containing truth mixed with the decrees of philosophy—or rather, covered and hidden, just as the edible part of a nut is covered by a shell. For it is fitting, I believe, that the seeds of faith be preserved only for the "farmers of the faith." I am not unaware of the things tossed about by certain ignorant and noisy people, who say that one should only deal with the most necessary things and those which...

<margin>A</margin> ...indeed contain; but to leap over those external and superfluous things which wear us out in vain and hold us back in things that contribute nothing to the final goal. Other people, even some philosophers, think that Philosophy entered into life from an evil source for the destruction of men, as if it were the product of some malignant inventor. I, however, will show throughout these entire discourses which are called *Stromatēis* <note>original: "stromatēis," meaning "Miscellanies" or "Patchwork Tapestries." Regarding those commentaries which, in necessary times, have embraced the opinions of the Greeks, I say only this to those who take pleasure in the zeal of rebuking: First, even if Philosophy were useless, if confirming that it is useless is useful, then it is a useful pursuit. <note>Clement uses a classic logical paradox here: to prove philosophy is useless, one must use philosophy, thereby proving its utility.</note>

<margin>B</margin>
Next, it is impossible for those who use only bare words regarding their decrees to condemn the Greeks, unless they descend to opening them up one by one until they reach full understanding. For the most trustworthy proof is that which comes through experience, since the knowledge of things that are condemned is found to be the most perfect demonstration of them. Thus, many things may not contribute directly to the end goal, but they bring ornament to the craftsman. Furthermore, the very conflict between different doctrines, when they are compared with each other, reconciles the truth, from which knowledge follows. This is not because Philosophy entered through the primary reason, but because through the fruit gathered from knowledge, we receive a firm and stable persuasion of true understanding, owing to the science of those things which are understood beneath the surface. ->**THE STROMATA, BOOK I.**<-

<margin>A</margin>...leads to the preparation of wisdom. For **Philosophy** is indeed an exercise. <margin>The Greek text says "of philosophy" <note>original: "φιλοσοφίας"</note> but I think it should read "of wisdom" <note>original: "σοφίας"</note>.</margin> **Wisdom**, however, is the knowledge of things divine and human, and of their causes. Therefore, Wisdom is the mistress of Philosophy, just as Philosophy is the mistress of those preparatory disciplines <note>likely referring to the "liberal arts" like grammar or geometry</note> that are heard first. For if Philosophy professes to master the tongue, the belly, and the passions below the belly, and is to be chosen for its own sake, it will appear much more venerable and excellent if it is practiced for the honor and knowledge of God. <margin>Genesis 11 and 17.</margin> The Scripture will provide testimony for these things through what follows. 

<margin>B</margin> Sarah was once sterile. As the wife of Abraham, when she did not bear children, Sarah allowed her Egyptian handmaid, named Hagar, to go to Abraham for the sake of conceiving children. Thus **Wisdom**, who dwells with the believer (and Abraham was accounted faithful and just), was still sterile and without offspring in that generation. This is because she had not yet brought forth for Abraham any fruit of virtue. Rightly, however, she wished that he—who still had time to make progress—should first engage with the discipline of the world. (By "Egypt," the world is signified allegorically). Afterward, when he finally approached Wisdom herself through divine providence, she gave birth to Isaac. 

Now, Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish philosopher who heavily influenced Clement</note> interprets **Hagar** as "sojourning" <note>staying as a guest in a foreign land</note>, for it is said: "Do not stay too long with a stranger." **Sarah**, however, he interprets as "my princedom" <note>or "authority"</note>. It is permissible, therefore, for one who has first been instructed in the secular disciplines to come to Wisdom, who holds the highest sovereign power, and through whom the race of Israel is increased. From this, it is shown that Wisdom is endowed with the power of teaching; Abraham reached her by passing from the contemplation of the heavens to the faith and justice that comes from God. 

<margin>C</margin><margin>Genesis 32.</margin> Through **Isaac**, that which is learned by itself <note>or "self-taught" knowledge given by God</note> is indicated. For this reason, he is even found to be a "type" or symbol of Christ. He was a man of only one wife, namely Rebecca, whose name they translate as "Patience" or "Endurance." <margin>Ibid. 32.</margin> **Jacob**, on the other hand, is said to have consorted with many, as he is portrayed as the "practitioner" or "athlete"; for exercises are carried out through many different doctrines. This is why he is also named **Israel**, which truly means "the power of seeing," as one who is experienced in many things and fit for spiritual exercise. There may also be something else signified by those first three fathers <note>Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob</note>: that they represent the firm and valid seal of knowledge, which consists of Nature, Teaching, and Exercise. 

<margin>Genesis 38.</margin> You may also find another likeness of these things in **Tamar**, who sat at the crossroads and appeared to be a prostitute. The studious **Judah**—whose name is interpreted as "Powerful," one who leaves nothing unconsidered or unsearched—considered her and turned aside to her, yet he preserved the <margin>D</margin> confession he held toward God. 

<margin>Genesis 16 and 21.</margin> Hence even Abraham, when Sarah was jealous of Hagar (who was held in higher esteem than herself), chose from secular Philosophy only that which was useful. **"BEHOLD,"** he said, **"your handmaid is in your hands; use her as you please."** It was as if he were saying: "I embrace secular teaching as a younger woman and a fellow-servant, but your knowledge I honor and cherish as my perfect Mistress." And Sarah **AFFLICTED** her, which is to say she corrected and admonished her. <margin>Proverbs 3; Hebrews 12.</margin> Thus it is rightly said: "Do not neglect the discipline of the Lord, nor grow weary when you are rebuked by Him. For whom the Lord loves He corrects, and He scourges every son whom He receives." These aforementioned scriptures, when examined in other places, signify that other mysteries are present.

<margin>E</margin> From this, we say that Philosophy uses bare reason to investigate the truth and the nature of things. This is the truth of which the Lord Himself said: <margin>John 14.</margin> **"I am the truth."** Again, the discipline which precedes the rest found in Christ exercises the mind and awakens the intelligence, producing a sharpness of intellect fit for inquiring through true Philosophy. Once this is found—or rather, received—the **Mystae** <note>Initiates into the divine mysteries/believers</note> hold it from Truth itself. A readiness to see what is necessary through exercise contributes much. The exercises of the mind are those things which can be perceived by the intellect. Their nature is threefold, considered in continuous quantities, discrete quantities, and in the art of discourse <note>referring to Geometry, Arithmetic, and Dialectic/Logic</note>. 

<margin>F</margin> For the speech which is constructed from demonstrations <note>logical proofs</note> creates a perfect faith in the soul regarding the conclusion; it prevents one from thinking that what has been demonstrated could be otherwise, and it does not allow the soul to succumb to those errors that attack us through fraud. In these disciplines, therefore, the soul is purged of sensory things and awakened so that it may perceive the truth. For education, and the good erudition that is preserved,

He argues that mental exercise in the arts and sciences sharpens the soul to eventually recognize and hold fast to the ultimate Truth found in Christ.</summary>

<margin>A</margin> ...produces good natures; and good natures, by receiving such instruction, become even better than before—both in other respects and in reproduction, just as is seen in other animals. Whence it also says in <margin>Proverbs 6</margin>: "Go to the ant, O sluggard, and become wiser than she," who stores up much food of every kind during the time of harvest against the threats of winter; or <margin>Ecclesiasticus 11 <gloss>treasury</gloss></margin>: "Go to the bee, and learn how she is a worker." For she, feeding upon every meadow, produces a single honeycomb. If, however, you pray in your inner room—just as the <margin>John 4</margin> Lord taught us to worship in spirit—then this "economy" <note>This refers to *oikonomia*, the careful management and stewardship of a household or, in this case, the inner life of the soul.</note> will not only be practiced in the house, but also in the soul: what things should be given to it, and how, and how much; and what things should be stored up and hidden within it, and when they should be brought forth, and before whom. For men do not become good and honorable by nature, but by discipline, just as <margin>B</margin> physicians and pilots do. We all see a vine or a horse in common; but the farmer knows whether a vine is good or bad for bearing fruit, and he who has knowledge of horses easily discerns the lazy from the swift. While some are more naturally suited to virtue than others, as shown by the pursuits of those with better natural dispositions, this does not mean those with better natures possess perfection from the start. Even those least suited to virtue by nature, once they have attained the proper discipline, may reach every kind of integrity and honor; conversely, those naturally suited to virtue may turn out poorly through negligence and carelessness. We, in turn, were fashioned by God to be naturally suited for society, communication, <margin>C</margin> and justice. Hence, we should not say that justice arises solely from external imposition; rather, we should understand that the goodness of the "workmanship" <note>Clement views the human soul as God's masterwork, containing innate potential that must be "awakened" by divine commands.</note> is stirred up by a command when the soul has learned through discipline to choose the good. 

But just as we say a person can be faithful even without literacy, so we admit that one who has not studied can still understand the things of faith. For it is not faith alone, but faith engaged with discipline, that allows one to accept what is said well and reject what is foreign <margin><gloss>simply</gloss></margin>. If ignorance, lack of skill, and lack of knowledge regarding divine and human things were to bring about science just as much as learning does, then there would be no difference; but just as one may live rightly in poverty, so too may one live rightly in abundance. We confess that one can hunt for virtue more easily and quickly with <margin><gloss>divine education</gloss></margin> preceding liberal studies—though virtue is not of such a kind that it cannot be grasped without them, but even then, it is grasped by those who have <margin>D</margin> <margin>Proverbs 11</margin> learned and have their senses exercised. For "Hatred," says Solomon, "stirs up strife." But discipline guards the paths of life, so that we are not deceived nor circumvented by those who practice a wicked art for the ruin of their listeners. Discipline, he says, wanders "unrefuted." One must pursue a method of arguing and refuting so that the deceptive opinions of the Sophists <note>Sophists were professional teachers in ancient Greece often criticized by philosophers for using clever but fallacious arguments to win debates rather than seeking truth.</note> may be repelled. Anaxarchus writes rightly and divinely in his book *On Kingship*: "Much and varied learning <margin><gloss>erudition</gloss></margin> helps much, but also harms much the one who possesses it. It helps the one who is worthy, but harms the one who says whatever he pleases, even before the whole people. One must know the measure of time. This is the end of wisdom." Those who sing before the gates, even if they sing something learned, are not considered wise but fall into the reputation <margin>E</margin> of folly. And Hesiod says:

> [The gifts] of the Muses, which make a man speak much,

<margin><gloss>speaking much, vocal, divine</gloss></margin> "divine, vocal." For by "copious in words" he means one who speaks much, and by "sharp and vehement" he means "vocal," and "divine" refers to the one who is skilled, a philosopher, and a knower of truth. It appears, therefore, that those earlier liberal disciplines of the Greeks, together with Philosophy itself, come from God to men—not as the primary source, but just as rains break upon good land, and upon manure, and upon houses. Similarly, both grass and grain sprout, and even a fig tree grows among monuments, or any tree that is more "impudent." These things that grow emerge in the likeness of those that are true, since they have obtained the same power of the rain; yet those that grow in rich soil do not have the same favor <margin>F</margin> as those that are either dried up or uprooted. Furthermore, the parable of the seed, which the Lord <margin>Matthew 13, Mark 4</margin> interpreted, is useful here. For there is one farmer of the soil that is within men, who sows from on high...

<meta>catchword: sows from</meta>

<summary>Clement argues that while humans have a natural capacity for virtue, discipline and "divine education" (theopaideia) are necessary to perfect the soul. He compares Greek philosophy to rain that falls on all soils, providing a useful but secondary preparation for the true seed of divine word.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Clement’s argument from the previous section, where he compared the cultivation of the soul to the cultivation of the land. He transitions from discussing the diversity of "seeds" (the Word) to defining true philosophy and critiquing the empty rhetoric of the Sophists.</meta>

<header>STROMATA, BOOK I.</header>

<margin>A</margin> ...born from the constitution of the world are nourishing seeds; He who at every time rains down the primary Word. But the times and places that received it produced differences. Moreover, the farmer does not only sow wheat—though of that there are many different types—but also other seeds: barley, beans, peas, chickpeas, and seeds that produce garden plants <margin>vetch, garden plants, and Ethiopian legumes</margin> and flowers. It belongs to the same science of agriculture to plant, to perform the duties of the nursery, and to work whatever pertains to the seedlings themselves, the gardens, and orchards, and in sum, to the producing and nourishing of every kind of tree. Similarly, it is not only the art of feeding sheep, but also of cattle, horses, and dogs, and the arts of tending bees—in a word, all those engaged in caring for flocks and nourishing animals—differ from each other in degree. But they are all useful for life. Now, by "Philosophy" I do not mean the Stoic, nor the Platonic, nor the Epicurean and Aristotelian; but whatever has been said rightly by these sects, which teach justice along with a pious science—this whole selection I call Philosophy. But whatever things they have butchered from human thoughts and corrupted, these I would never call divine.

<margin>B</margin> Now let us also consider this: if those who do not know how to do good occasionally live rightly (for it happens that they do good), while others are carried toward the word of truth through intelligence as toward a target; and if Abraham was justified not by works but by faith; then nothing will profit them after the end of life, even if they now work rightly, unless they have faith. For this reason, the Scriptures were set forth in the Greek tongue <note>original: "Gręca voce," referring to the Septuagint translation of the Hebrew Bible</note>, so that they could never bring forward any pretext of ignorance, since they are able to hear our teachings if only they wish to.

<margin>C</margin> One person speaks about the truth in one way, while the truth interprets itself in another. A conjecture about truth is one thing; truth itself is another. A likeness is one thing; the thing itself is another. One is attained through discipline and exercise; the other through power and faith. For the gift of teaching comes from piety, but faith is a grace. For by doing the will of God, we know His will. "Open then," says the Scripture <margin>Psalm 117</margin>, "the gates of justice, so that entering into them I may confess to the Lord." But since God saves in many ways—for He is good—there are many and various paths to justice that lead to the Lord's way and gate. If you seek the royal road and the entrance fortified with strong authority, you will hear: "THIS is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it." Therefore, while many gates of justice are open, this one was in Christ; all the blessed who have entered through it have directed their path in the holiness <margin>D with the power of knowing <gloss>gnostically</gloss></margin> endowed with the power of knowledge. Now Clement <note>Clement of Rome, writing to the church in Corinth</note>, in his letter to the Corinthians, explains the difference between those who are approved in the church in these words <margin>vigorous. they were zealous.</margin>: "LET a man be faithful, let him be powerful in explaining knowledge, let him be wise in the discernment of words, let him be wonderful in his works."

But the Sophistic art, which the Greeks pursued as <margin>as a defining art.</margin> something noble and to be magnified, is a deceptive power—or one perceived through appearances—implanting false opinions through words as if they were true. For it provides the art of speaking for the sake of persuasion, but for the sake of strife, it provides the art of litigation and combat.

<margin>E</margin> Therefore, if the arts are not joined with Philosophy, they will be destructive to anyone. Thus Plato openly called sophistry an "evil art," and following him, Aristotle pronounces it a kind of contentious art <note>original: "iurandi artem," likely a reference to eristic or litigious reasoning</note>, as one that plausibly strips away the whole duty of wisdom and professes a wisdom in which it is not practiced, nor has it placed any study. To speak briefly: just as the beginning of the art of speaking is that which is probable, its duty is the argument, and its end is persuasion; so the beginning of the art of litigation and strife is that which is seen, its duty is contention, and its end is victory. In the same way, the beginning of the Sophistic art is that which appears to be true; its duty is twofold: one part from the art of speaking, which <margin>detailed. extensive.</margin> is seen pursuing a matter with a continuous speech; the other part from Dialectics, which proceeds by questioning. Its end is to strike one dumb and to lead them to wonder.

<margin>F</margin> And Dialectics, which is commonly bandied about in the schools, is shown to be an exercise for the philosopher in what is "probable," for the sake of the faculty of contradiction. Rightly, therefore, did the noble Apostle disparage these superfluous arts of words: "IF ANYONE," he says, <margin>1 Timothy 6</margin> "does not approach sound words, but is puffed up with some doctrine, knowing nothing, but laboring..."

<summary>Clement defines true philosophy as the collection of universal truths found across different sects and contrasts this with the deceptive "Sophistic art." He emphasizes that while varied arts and schools of thought exist, faith and the "gate of Christ" are the essential requirements for true righteousness and knowledge.</summary>
<keywords>Philosophy, Sophistry, Dialectics, Faith vs Works, Abraham, Clement of Rome, Plato, Aristotle, Gospel as Gate, Greek Scriptures</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Clement’s critique of empty rhetoric, following the previous page's discussion on the "seeds" of truth. Here, he contrasts the "disease" of Sophistry—mere verbal sparring—with the "saving speech" of true philosophy and Scripture, using his recurring metaphor of agricultural cultivation to describe the labor required to reach spiritual maturity.</meta>

# CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

<header>STROMATA, BOOK I</header>

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>discussions</margin> <note>original: διατριβαί - philosophical pastimes or lectures</note>
...wandering around questions and strifes of words, from which come envy, strife, blasphemy, evil suspicions, and the wranglings of men who are corrupt in mind and deprived of the truth. <note>Clement is quoting 1 Timothy 6:4-5 here.</note> You see how he attacked them, calling their Logic—that is, the art which is concerned with speech—a "disease." Because of this art, those who take to heart this talkative and wicked skill puff themselves up and look around grandly, whether they be Greeks or even barbarian <term>Sophists</term> <note>professional teachers of rhetoric who were often accused of prioritizing style and persuasion over truth.</note>. Therefore, the tragic poet Euripides says most beautifully in the *Phoenissae*:

> "A word that is sick in itself needs wise medicines;
> But an unjust speech..."

<margin>B</margin>
For speech is called "healthy" when it is "salutary" or saving, since truth itself is that which is always healthy and remains immortal. However, any separation from that which is healthy and divine is impiety and a lethal condition. These are ravenous wolves covered in sheep’s clothing, kidnappers and <margin>soul-guides</margin> <note>original: ψυχαγωγοί - literally "leaders of souls," here meaning those who lead souls astray through deception.</note> who drive away the deserted souls; they steal in secret, but are proven to be thieves. They try to overcome us by both craft and force—we who do not delight in superficial things, since we are perhaps less powerful than they are in speaking, as the tragedy says:

> "A man often hindered by a child-like tongue,
> Though he speaks what is just, possesses less eloquence.
> But from a mouth that flows beautifully, they steal
> The very truths, so that things seem as they should not."

<margin>C</margin>
<margin>cursed words
unfruitfulness
sleight of hand
To Titus 1.
mind-deceivers
Matthew 6.</margin>
Such are these litigious men, whether they follow certain sects or practice I know not what dialectical arts. These are the ones who "pull the ropes," as the <term>Scripture</term> <note>likely referring to Isaiah 5:18</note> says, and weave nothing, making much of vain labor. The Apostle himself called this "imposture" and "cunning," fit for the snares of error. "For there are," he says, "many disobedient, vain-talkers, and <margin>deceivers of the mind</margin>." Not to everyone, therefore, was it said: "YOU ARE the salt of the earth." For there are some even among those who hear the word who are like sea fish; although they are nourished in the salt water from their very birth, they still need salt to be seasoned for eating. I therefore most gladly admit the tragedy which says: "O son, false speeches can also be spoken well, and by the appearance of words they may conquer the truth. But this is not the most perfect truth by nature or fact." Whoever is wise in tongue, I always consider that the actual reality is superior to the words.

<margin>D</margin>
Therefore, to please the many is not at all to be sought after. For the things that are pleasing to them, we do not practice; and the things we know are far from their affections. "Let us not be," says the <margin>Galatians</margin> Apostle, "desirous of empty glory, provoking one another, envying one another." Thus, that lover of truth, Plato, as if inspired by God, says: "I am the kind of man who obeys nothing else of mine but the reason which, upon consideration, seems best to me." He therefore rebukes those who believe in opinions without mind and knowledge, since one ought not to abandon right and sound reason to believe in that which partakes of falsehood. For to have wandered from the truth is an evil. But to speak true things, and to hold opinions on things as they really are, is good. Men are deprived of good things against their will—either circumvented, or deceived by illusions, or coerced, even when they did not believe.

<margin>E</margin>
And while he who believes is caught by his own will, he is circumvented who is led into a contrary persuasion, forgetting that time takes some things away and reason takes others from the unwary. Often pain, anguish, and again contention or anger force a man after an opinion has been adopted. Finally, they are deceived by illusions who are either led by pleasure or terrified by fear. All such changes are voluntary. Yet knowledge would never have accepted any of those things. Some, however, who think themselves ingenious, wish neither to touch Philosophy nor Logic, nor even to discern natural contemplation, but they demand "naked faith" alone—just as if they wanted to harvest clusters of grapes immediately from the start without having exercised any care for the vine.

<margin>F</margin>
The Lord is called the "Vine" <margin>John 15.</margin> allegorically; from Him the fruit must be gathered with diligence and the art of cultivation, which is done through reason and speech. One must prune, dig, tie, and do the rest. As I see it, the pruning hook, the hoe, and other rustic tools are needed for the care of the vine so that it may produce edible fruit for us. Just as in agriculture, [the work is varied...]

<summary>Clement critiques Sophists and "mind-deceivers" who prioritize eloquent but empty speech over truth, arguing that faith must be cultivated through reason and study rather than remaining "naked" and unexamined. He uses the metaphor of a vine to explain that spiritual fruit requires the "tools" of philosophy and diligent labor to grow.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Clement’s argument for the necessity of a broad education. Having previously warned against the "disease" of sophistry, he now balances that by explaining how diverse fields of study—when properly directed toward the truth—actually strengthen a Christian's faith and ability to interpret Scripture.</meta>

# CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

## STROMATA, BOOK I

<margin>A</margin>
...just as in the cultivation of the earth, or indeed in medicine, the person who has studied various disciplines learns usefully, so that they might better cultivate or cure. In the same way, I consider a person to be well and usefully educated <margin>desirous of useful learning <note>original: χρησομαθής</note></margin> who refers all things to the truth. By gathering what is useful from Geometry, Music, Grammar, and even Philosophy itself, they safeguard their faith so that it is not intercepted by any traps. Furthermore, as was said before, an athlete is looked down upon if they have not first trained themselves for the contest. Now, we also praise a pilot who has experience in many things and knows the ways of many men, and a physician who has experienced many cases—which is how they even form the category of the "empirical" doctor. So, the one who refers every detail to a right life, bringing examples from both the Greeks and the barbarians, is a highly skilled investigator of the truth and a person of truly great counsel.

<margin>B</margin>
Like the "touchstone"—which is the <term>Lydian stone</term> <note>a dark stone used since antiquity to test the purity of gold by the color of the streak it leaves</note> believed to be able to distinguish counterfeit gold from the genuine—so the one among us who has great experience and knowledge of things is fit to separate and discern. They can distinguish <term>Sophistry</term> <note>deceptive, clever sounding arguments</note> from true Philosophy, the art of cosmetics from gymnastics, <margin>cosmetics <note>original: κομμωτικώ</note></margin> and cookery from medicine, and the art of rhetoric from <term>Dialectic</term> <note>the art of logical discussion and investigation of truth</note>. Indeed, such a person can even distinguish the various heresies found in "barbarian" <note>Clement often uses "barbarian philosophy" to refer to Hebrew or non-Greek wisdom, including Christianity</note> philosophy from the truth itself.

How can it not be necessary for someone who wishes to reach the power of God to philosophize about things perceived by the intellect? And how is it not also useful to distinguish words that are ambiguous, or those used equivocally in the Testaments? For it was through <term>amphiboly</term> <note>a grammatical ambiguity where a sentence can be interpreted in two ways</note> that the Lord wisely eluded the devil during the time of His temptation. <margin>to be successful <note>original: ἐπίβολον γένεσθαι</note>; to outwit <note>original: σοφίζεται</note>; Matthew 4</margin> I certainly do not see here how the "inventor of Philosophy and Dialectic," as some believe him to be, is shown to be deceived by a turn of ambiguity.

<margin>C</margin>
Now, if the Prophets and Apostles did not know the technical arts through which the exercises of Philosophy are demonstrated, yet the mind of the Prophetic and teaching Spirit—speaking secretly because not everyone has ears that understand—requires "artful doctrines" for its explanation. The Prophets and the disciples of the Spirit knew the meaning of those words securely. For the Spirit spoke from faith and with an ease that cannot be described, yet those who have not learned cannot perceive it so easily. "Write the precepts," it says, "in a twofold way," namely, for the will and for the knowledge of how to respond with words of truth to those who propose them to you. What, then, is the science of responding, or even of questioning? This would be Dialectic.

<margin>D</margin>
<margin>by the Word/Reason <note>original: λόγω</note>; John 1</margin>
What then? Is not every action also a matter of <term>Logos</term> <note>a Greek term meaning both "word" and "reason/rationality"</note>? Are not actions done according to the Word or Reason? If we do not act according to Reason, we act without reason. A rational work is produced by God. "And nothing was made without Him," it says—meaning the Word/Reason of God. Did not the Lord also make all things by the Word? Even beasts of burden work, but they are driven by the compulsion of fear. Do those who are called "Orthodoxists" <margin>those with "right opinion" <note>original: ὀρθοδοξασταί</note>; Matthew 26; 1 Corinthians 11</margin> also perform good works without knowing what they are doing?

For this reason, when the Savior took the bread, He first spoke and gave thanks; then, having broken the bread, He set it out so that we might eat <margin>rationally <note>original: λογικῶς</note></margin> according to Reason, and so that once we have recognized the Scriptures, we might establish our lives through obedience.

<margin>E</margin>
Just as those who use speech badly are no different from those who act badly—for calumny is the servant of the sword and brings the pain of a curse, which leads to the destruction of life—these are the works of wicked speech. In the same way, those who use speech well come close to those who perform good deeds. Therefore, speech recreates the soul and exhorts it toward honesty. "Blessed is the one who uses both hands as if they were the right hand." Therefore, the one who can act well should not be attacked with curses by the one who can speak well; nor should the one who can speak well be blamed by the one who can act well. Let each do that which is implanted in them by nature. What one person shows through action, the other speaks, preparing the way for beneficence and leading listeners to work well. For there is such a thing as "saving speech," just as there is a "saving work."

<margin>F</margin>
And certainly, justice does not exist without speech. Just as the benefit of an act is lost if we take away the "doing well," so also obedience and faith are lost if neither the precept nor the person who is to explain it are present together. Now, for the sake of one another, we abound in both words and deeds. But the contentious and <term>Sophistical</term> art is to be utterly rejected, since the very style of the Sophists not only blinds the eyes of many and leads them astray, but...

<sig>bb</sig>

<summary>Clement argues that secular studies like philosophy and dialectic are essential tools for Christians to interpret Scripture accurately and distinguish truth from clever deception. He highlights the "Logos" as both Word and Reason, suggesting that true faith requires both right action and a rational understanding of God's commands.</summary>

<margin>Psalm 48 <note>Modern Psalm 49</note></margin>

...sometimes even using force, they bring back a <term>Cadmean victory</term> <note>A "Cadmean victory" is a Greek idiom for a victory that is as costly as a defeat, referencing the tragic fate of the house of Cadmus.</note>. <margin>Proverbs 10</margin>
**YOU WILL SEEK** wisdom among the wicked and you will not find it. And if you ask again what that wisdom is, he says: "The mouth of the righteous will drop wisdom for you." Now, the art of <term>Sophistry</term> <note>The use of clever but false arguments, especially for persuasion rather than truth.</note> is called "wisdom" only in an ambiguous sense compared to the truth. My own aim, as I see it, is a worthy one: to live in a way that is consistent with the Word <note>original: λόγῳ (Logos)</note> and with Reason, and to understand the meaning of things. I do not value eloquence highly; I am content if the meaning of what is understood is simply conveyed.

<margin>B</margin>
<margin>by the Word <note>original: λόγῳ</note></margin>
I do not care what name is used for what I want to explain. For I believe it is best to provide help so that those who wish to be saved may be saved, rather than to compose little phrases as if they were mere ornaments.

<margin>Ornaments <note>original: Τὰ κόσμια</note></margin>
*And if you were careful,* says Pythagoras in Plato’s *Statesman*, *not to be too anxious about names, you will appear richer in wisdom in your old age.* And again, you will find in the *Theaetetus*: "A certain ease with names and words, and not examining them with too much precision, is for the most part not vulgar or ill-bred, but rather the opposite; and sometimes it is even necessary." This is what the Scripture expressed as briefly as possible, saying:

<margin>be not wordy <note>original: μὴ πολὺς γίνου</note></margin>
**DO NOT BE** much occupied in words. For speech is like the clothing on a body.

<margin>C</margin>
The "flesh" and "nerves" are the actual things themselves. One should not, therefore, take more care for the clothing than for the health of the body. Not only should a frugal way of life be practiced, but also a style of speech that is free from unnecessary decoration and finery, especially for the person who has chosen the true life. Indeed, we reject luxuries as deceptive and indulgent, just as the ancient <term>Lacedaemonians</term> <note>The Spartans, famous for their austerity and simple speech.</note> rejected perfumes and purple cloth. They rightly considered and named these "deceptive clothes" and "deceptive ointments." Just as a meal is not honest if it has more seasonings than nutrients, so the use of speech is neither beautiful nor refined if it delights the listeners more than it helps them. Pythagoras warns that the Muses are more pleasant than the Sirens, teaching us not to pursue wisdom for mere pleasure,

<margin>D</margin>

One should never "enlarge their phylacteries" <note>A reference to Matthew 23:5, criticizing those who display religious symbols merely to be seen by others.</note> by seeking after and magnifying vain glory. It is enough for the person gifted with the power of knowing if even a single listener is found for them. In this, the Boeotian writer Pindarus may be heard:

**IT IS NOT** permitted to open the ancient word to everyone, except by the most faithful paths of silence. For a dominant speech is the sting of a fight. Therefore, the blessed Apostle very rightly warns us not to contend with words for no useful purpose, which only leads to the ruin of the listeners, and to avoid profane novelties of speech,

<margin>E</margin>
<margin>2 Timothy 2</margin>
<margin>1 Corinthians 3</margin>
for these lead mostly to ungodliness, and their talk spreads like gangrene. Thus, this wisdom of the world is foolishness before God. And God knows the thoughts of these "wise" men, that they are vain. Let no one, therefore, boast in superior human thought. For it is rightly written in Jeremiah:

<margin>Jeremiah 9</margin>
**LET NOT** the wise man glory in his wisdom, and let not the strong man glory in his strength, and let not the rich man glory in his riches. But let him who glories glory in this: that he understands and knows that I am God, who works mercy, judgment, and justice upon the earth.

<margin>1 Corinthians 2</margin>
**FOR** in these things is my will, says the Lord. I also hear these words of his:

<margin>F</margin>

# THE MISCELLANIES, BOOK I.

He <note>Likely referring to Epicurus, who Clement often critiques for prioritizing pleasure.</note> relates the number of the Gods to pleasure, and if he has honored any other elements, he does not establish them as an efficient cause, nor does he even perceive the Craftsman <note>original: opificem; referring to God as the creator or Demiurge</note> through vision. Furthermore, the Stoics <note>A school of philosophy that held that God was a physical "spirit" or breath (pneuma) pervading the universe.</note>, whom he also mentions, are not correct when they say that God, being a body, has permeated the lowliest matter. Moreover, he calls "human tradition" those musical trifles which are concerned with mere speech. For this reason, he also writes: **FLEE** from youthful questions. For disputes of this kind are childish. But virtue, says the philosopher Plato, is not held by the "love of the young," and our contest—as Gorgias of Leontini <note>A famous Greek Sophist and rhetorician.</note> would have it—requires two virtues: boldness and wisdom. Boldness to face the danger, and wisdom to discern the riddle.

<margin>B</margin>
<margin>Matthew 7.</margin>
<margin>Colossians 2.</margin>
For the Word <note>original: Verbum; translating the Greek "Logos," which means both "Reason" and "Word."</note>, like a herald at the Olympic games, calls whoever is willing, but crowns the one who is able to remain undefeated; for in truth, the Word does not want the one who has believed to be idle. **SEEK**, He says, **AND YOU SHALL FIND**, but He ends the search with finding, having driven out recent trifles and inserted the contemplation that confirms our faith. **NOW I SAY THIS** so that no one might deceive you with persuasive speech, says the Apostle <note>Paul</note>, so that you may learn to discern what they say and be taught to meet the objections they raise. **AS YOU HAVE THEREFORE RECEIVED** Jesus Christ the Lord, walk in Him, rooted and built up in Him, and confirmed in the faith. Now, the confirmation of faith is persuasion. **SEE** that no one leads you away from faith in Christ through philosophy and empty deceit, which removes providence <note>original: providentia; the belief that God actively guides the world.</note>, according to human tradition. For the philosophy that is according to divine tradition establishes and confirms providence.

<margin>C</margin>
<margin>the ruling principle <note>original: ἡγεμονικὸν; the Stoic term for the commanding part of the soul.</note></margin>
If providence is removed, the Economy <note>original: Oeconomia; the "divine plan" or "dispensation" of salvation through Christ.</note> of the Savior appears to be a mere fable, since we would be carried along according to the elements of this world and not according to Christ. For the doctrine which is in agreement with Christ both asserts that God is the Craftsman and extends His providence even to particular things. It knows the nature of the elements to be such that they are subject to birth and change, and it teaches that they are ruled by God so that they may have a power that assimilates and distributes, so that the primary Mind precedes all teaching. However, some worship the elements: Diogenes <note>Diogenes of Apollonia, who taught that air was the primary substance.</note> worshipped Air; Thales worshipped Water; Hippasus worshipped Fire. And those who propose "indivisible principles" <note>The Atomists, such as Democritus or Epicurus.</note>, though they take up the name of philosophy, are but impious little men devoted to pleasure.

For when we were children, says the Apostle, we were serving under the elements of this world. But a child, even if he is an heir, differs in nothing from a slave until the time appointed by the father. Therefore, even the Philosophers are children unless they become men through Christ. For if they are not to be heirs with the son of the free woman, they are certainly at least the seed of Abraham, which received its own gift, though not according to the promise. But solid food is for the perfect, who because of habit have their senses trained to discern good and evil. For whoever partakes of milk is unskilled in the word of righteousness, since he is a child and does not yet know the Word through which he believed and works, nor can he give an account of it.

He says this to the spiritual ones, who judge all that is said by the truth to see if it only seems so, or if it truly coheres with the truth. An unrefuted discipline wanders, but blows and rebukes provide the discipline of wisdom—that is, rebukes which are given with love. For a righteous heart seeks knowledge, because he who seeks God finds knowledge with justice. He writes this attacking those who are wise in their own opinion and think they are someone, but are not actually wise. For the kingdom of God is **NOT IN SPEECH**. Not, I say, in that which is not true, but only plausible in opinion. But He said it is "in power" or "in strength." For truth alone...

He uses Pauline metaphors of "milk" and "solid food" to describe the transition from basic human learning to mature Christian wisdom.</summary>
