<header>14 CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA</header>

<margin>A</margin>
Sometimes even using force, they bring back a **Cadmean victory**. <note>A "Cadmean victory" is a Greek idiom for a pyrrhic victory where the winner is as damaged as the loser.</note> For that Psalm is by far the most true: <margin>Psalm 48.</margin> **THE JUST** shall live to the end, for he shall not see destruction when he sees the wise dying. <note>Clement refers to Psalm 49:10 in modern numbering.</note> But who he calls "the wise," hear from the **Wisdom of Jesus**: <note>Referring to the Book of Sirach or Ecclesiasticus.</note> **WISDOM IS NOT** the knowledge of wickedness. But he speaks of that wisdom which the arts have devised, those which are occupied with speaking and debating. <margin>Proverbs 10.</margin> **YOU SHALL SEEK** therefore wisdom among the wicked, and you shall not find it. And if you ask again what kind it is, he says, "the mouth of the just shall distill wisdom for you." However, the art of **Sophistry** <note>The practice of using clever but fallacious arguments.</note> is called "wisdom" only equivocally when compared to the truth. 

But my own purpose—which is reasonable, as I believe—is to live in a way consistent with the **Word** <margin>by the Word <note>original: λόγῳ (logō)</note></margin> and with reason, and to understand those things which are signified; for while I never make much of eloquence, I am content if that which is understood is clearly expressed. For what name is used to explain what I wish to set forth is of no concern to me. <margin>B</margin> For I think it is best to bring help so that those who desire to be saved may be preserved, rather than to compose little phrases like mere ornaments. And "if you are careful," says **Pythagoras** in Plato’s *Statesman*, "not to be too troubled about names, you will appear more wealthy in prudence in your old age." And again, you will find in the *Theaetetus*: "The easy use of names and words, and a not too accurate examination of them, is for the most part not sordid or illiberal, but rather its opposite; and it is sometimes even necessary." <margin>the worldly things <note>original: τά κόσμια (ta kosmia)</note></margin>

<margin>C</margin>
The Scripture has declared this as briefly as possible, saying: <margin>not many words <note>original: μή πολύς ῥίνος (mē polys rhinos)</note></margin> **DO NOT** be much occupied with words. For diction is like a garment on the body, but the facts themselves are the flesh and the nerves. One ought not, therefore, to take more care for the clothing than for the health of the body. For not only a frugal way of life must be practiced by one who has chosen the true life, but also a style of speech that is a stranger to unnecessary refinement and decoration. Indeed, we repudiate luxuries as deceitful and extravagant, just as the ancient **Lacedaemonians** <note>The Spartans, famous for their austere and simple lifestyle.</note> rejected perfume and purple cloth. They rightly considered and named them "deceitful garments" and "deceitful ointments," because a preparation of food is not honorable if it has more condiments than nutrients, nor is a use of speech beautiful or refined if it can delight the listeners more than it can help them. 

<margin>D</margin>
**Pythagoras** warns us to consider the **Muses** more pleasant than the **Sirens**, <note>The Muses represented divine inspiration and arts, while the Sirens represented deadly, seductive temptation.</note> teaching us to practice wisdom without mere pleasure, and rebuking the deceptive delight of the soul. <margin>soul-leading <note>original: Ψυχαγωγίαν (Psychagogian)</note></margin> One person is enough who has sailed past the Sirens, and another who answered the **Sphinx**—or even, if you wish, no one at all. One must never, therefore, "widen their phylacteries" <note>A biblical metaphor for performing religious acts for public show (Matthew 23:5).</note> by seeking and magnifying vain glory. It is enough for one who is endowed with the power of knowing if even one listener is found for him. Thus, **Pindar** the Boeotian writer may be heard: **IT IS NOT** permitted to open the ancient word before everyone, except by the most faithful paths of silence. For a dominant speech is a stimulus for battle. 

<margin>2 Timothy 2.</margin>
<margin>E</margin>
Therefore, the blessed Apostle very rightly warns us vehemently not to contend with words for nothing useful, to the subversion of the listeners, and to avoid profane novelties of words; <margin>1 Corinthians 3.</margin> for they lead to much impiety, and their speech spreads like a cancer. This "wisdom of the world" is therefore foolishness with God. And God knows the thoughts of these "wise men," that they are vain. Let no one, therefore, glory in surpassing human thought. For it is rightly written in **Jeremiah**: <margin>Jeremiah 9.</margin> **LET NOT** the wise man glory in his wisdom, and let not the strong man glory in his strength, and let not the rich man glory in his riches. But let him who glories, glory in this: that he understands and knows that I am God who performs mercy, judgment, and justice upon the earth. **FOR IN THESE** is my will, says the Lord. 

<margin>1 Corinthians 2.</margin>
Let us not trust in ourselves, but in God who raises the dead, says the Apostle. He who has snatched us from such great death, so that our faith might not be in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God. For the spiritual man judges all things, but he himself is judged by no one. I also hear these words of his: "I say this so that no one may deceive you with persuasive speech, nor let anyone enter who would plunder you." <margin>Colossians 2.</margin> <margin>F</margin> And again: "See that there be no one who seduces you through **Philosophy** and empty deceit, according to the tradition of men, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ." He is rebuking not all philosophy, but the **Epicurean** <note>Followers of Epicurus who believed the world was made of atoms and that gods did not intervene in human affairs.</note> kind (which Paul also mentions in the Acts of the Apostles), which removes providence and places pleasure in the position of the Gods...

<summary>Clement argues that true wisdom consists of living by the divine Word (Logos) rather than practicing Sophistry or ornate speech. He uses a mix of Pythagorean philosophy and Pauline scripture to warn that secular "wisdom of the world" is often a deceptive "Cadmean victory" that lacks spiritual substance.</summary>

<margin>A</margin> He accounts pleasure among the number of the gods, and treats other elements with honor as if they were divine; yet because he does not establish an efficient cause for them, he does not even perceive the Creator through vision. For even if one is not to be an heir with the son of the free woman <note>A reference to Sarah and the promise to Abraham</note>, he is certainly of the seed of Abraham, though he did not receive his own gift from the promise. But solid food is for the perfect, who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern good and evil. For whoever partakes of milk is unskilled in the word of righteousness, being a child who does not yet know the word through which he believed and works, nor can he 
<margin>E</margin> give an account of it. But PROVE ALL THINGS, says the Apostle, and hold fast to what is good. <margin>1 Thessalonians 2 <note>Correctly 1 Thess. 5:21</note></margin> He speaks to the spiritual ones, who judge all that is said by the truth to see whether they only seem so, or whether they truly adhere to the truth. For discipline wanders about irrefutably, and stripes and rebukes provide the discipline of wisdom—that is, the rebukes which are given with love. For a righteous HEART seeks knowledge, since he who seeks God finds knowledge with justice. And those who have sought it rightly have found peace. AND I will know not the speech of those who are puffed up, but the power: those <margin>1 Corinthians 4</margin> who are wise in their own opinion, and think they are something when they are not, he writes this rebuking them. <margin>rebuking <note>original Greek: ἐπιῤῥαπίζων (epirrhapizōn), literally "slapping" or "striking back" at their pride</note></margin> For the kingdom of God is NOT in speech. Not, I say, in that which is not true, but in that which is plausible in opinion. But he said it is in "virtue," or power. For truth alone 
<margin>F</margin> is powerful. And again: IF ANYONE thinks he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know. For opinion is never the truth. But the opinion of knowledge puffs up and fills one with pride, whereas charity builds up; for charity is not concerned with opinion but with truth. Hence, if anyone loves, he is known [by Him], he says. Since, however, it is not only tradition... <margin>1 Corinthians 8</margin>

# CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

<margin>A</margin> Eloquence is a public matter for those who have a sense for the grandeur of speech. However, the wisdom that is spoken in mystery, which the Son of God taught, must be kept hidden. For already Isaiah the Prophet had his tongue purified with fire <note>Referencing Isaiah 6:6-7</note> so that he might be able to declare the vision; and it is fitting for us to have not only a pure tongue but also chaste ears if we attempt to become partakers of the truth. These things were an obstacle to my writing, and even now I still fear, as the saying goes, to "throw pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet and, turning, tear us to pieces." <margin>Matthew 7</margin> For it is difficult to show that the words concerning the true light were truly pure and clear to unlearned listeners. Indeed, to the common crowd, almost nothing sounds more ridiculous than these things; <margin>more divinely inspired <note>original Greek: ἐνθουσιαστικώτερα</note></margin> yet to the ingenious, they are more admirable and more full of God's inspiration. But the unspiritual man <note>original: "animalis homo," often translated as the "natural man" who lacks the Spirit</note> does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him. However, the wise do not carry in their mouths what they ponder in assembly. But what you hear, says the Lord, in the ear, preach upon the rooftops; <margin>Matthew 10</margin> <margin>B</margin> bidding us to receive the secret traditions of true knowledge <note>original: "cognitionis," here implying "Gnosis"</note>—which are explained excellently and for excellent men—and just as we have heard them in the ear, so also to hand them down to those to whom it is proper, rather than passing them on to everyone indiscriminately, as he commanded that they were spoken to those people in parables. <margin>sketch or outline <note>original Greek: ὑποτύπωσις</note></margin> <margin>I have agreed <note>original Greek: συνημολόγησα</note></margin>

But in truth, the description of these commentaries or memoirs is like seeds of truth scattered here and there, so that they might remain hidden from those who, in the manner of "Greeklings" <note>original: "graecurulũ," a diminutive often used dismissively of shallow Greek scholars</note>, carry words about everywhere and at random. But once they have found a good farmer, each of these seeds will sprout and produce grain. Since truth is one—for falsehood has innumerable side-paths—just as the Bacchantes <note>Followers of Bacchus/Dionysus in Greek myth</note> tore apart the limbs of Pentheus and scattered them, so the sects of philosophy, both Barbarian <note>Non-Greek, often referring to Hebrew or Egyptian wisdom</note> and <margin>C</margin> Greek, each boast that the portion they have obtained is the whole truth. But by the rising of the light, I believe, all things are illuminated. Therefore, all Greeks and Barbarians who have desired the truth can be shown to possess a certain part of the Word of Truth—some many parts, others only a small portion, if any at all. And indeed, they treat the age—the future, the present, and even the past—as if it were a single moment. But the truth of the age is much more powerful <margin>unseemly <note>original Greek: ἀικελίως</note></margin> at gathering its own seeds, even if they have fallen into foreign soil. For through many examples we find that among the heresies there are opinions received that are not entirely absurd, nor do they lack a natural logical sequence; even though they have cut themselves off from Christ like a woman from a man, <margin>just as the women from the hemp-plant sect have cut themselves off from Christ <note>original Greek: καθάπερ ἐν αὑτῷ αἱ γυναῖκες αἱ ἀπὸ κωνίτιδος ἀποκεκομμέναι τὸν χριστόν. This obscure reference likely concerns a specific heretical group or ritual practice.</note></margin> it is certain and beyond controversy that they are different in kind and in the whole of truth. <margin>D</margin> For truth is gathered into one either as a limb, or as a species, or as a genus. For instance, even the *Hypate* <note>The lowest note in the Greek musical scale</note>, though it is the opposite of the *Nete* <note>The highest note</note>, is still part of one harmony; and in Arithmetic, an even number differs from an odd one, yet both agree in the science of numbers, just as the circle, the triangle, the square, and other figures differ from one another. Furthermore, in the whole world, all the parts, even if they differ from each other, preserve their connection and agreement with the whole. In this way, then, both Barbarian and Greek philosophy have plucked a certain torn-off fragment of eternal truth, not from the mythology of Bacchus, but from the Theology of the Word <note>The Logos/Christ</note> which exists forever. He who can put the divided parts back together again and make the Word one and perfect, you may be sure, will contemplate the truth without danger. Thus it is written in Ecclesiastes: AND I ADDED wisdom <margin>E</margin> <margin>Ecclesiastes 1</margin> <margin>choice or purpose <note>original Greek: προαίρεσις</note></margin> <margin>a Gnostic or Knower <note>original Greek: γνωστικός</note></margin> above all who were before me in Jerusalem, and my heart saw much wisdom and knowledge; I knew parables and science besides. And this indeed is the choice of the spirit, because in the multitude of wisdom is the multitude of knowledge. He who is endowed with every kind of wisdom would be the one who has properly attained the virtue of knowing. And it is also written: The abundance of the knowledge of wisdom will give life to him who is of it. And again, this saying confirms more clearly what has been said: ALL things are in the sight of those who understand. <margin>before the face <note>original Greek: ἐνώπια</note></margin> <margin>Proverbs 7</margin> <margin>The Greek text has "right," but I think it should read "before the face." <note>original: ὀρθὰ habet exẽplar Græcũ, sed puto legendum ἐνώπια.</note></margin> Now, "all things" means both Greek and Barbarian wisdom. Neither one alone constitutes "all." They are "in the sight" of those who wish to receive understanding. CHOOSE discipline and not silver, and knowledge above tested gold. Choose also understanding more than pure gold. For wisdom is better than precious stones. Whatever is precious is not to be compared with her in value. <margin>F</margin> <margin>nothing is worthy of her <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἔστιν ἄξιον αὐτῆς</note></margin> The Greeks say that after Orpheus and Linus, and the poets who were the most ancient among them, the "Seven Sages" were held in admiration for their wisdom; four of whom were from Asia: Thales of Miletus and Bias of Priene...

He justifies the study of various philosophies by citing biblical praise for universal wisdom and begins a history of the Seven Sages of Greece.</summary>

### MISCELLANIES, BOOK I.

<margin>A</margin> ...Bias of Priene, Pittacus of Mitylene, and Cleobulus of Lindos. Two others were from Europe: Solon the Athenian and Chilo the Lacedæmonian <note>Lacedæmonian is another name for Spartan</note>. For the seventh member, some name Periander of Corinth; others, Anacharsis the Scythian; and still others, Epimenides the Cretan.
<margin>Titus 1 / epistle <note>original Greek: ἐπιστολῇ</note></margin>
This is the same Greek prophet whom Paul recognized and mentioned in his epistle to Titus, saying: **A CERTAIN ONE** of them, their own prophet, said: "Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons." And this testimony is true. You see how he grants a certain amount of truth even to the prophets of the Greeks? He is not ashamed to use Greek poems for the sake of edification and to reach those he cares for.
<margin>1 Corinthians 15 / bad company ruins good morals <note>original Greek: φθείρουσιν ἤθη χρηστά ὁμιλίαι κακαί</note></margin>
Thus, when speaking to the Corinthians (for this is not the only instance) regarding the resurrection of the dead, he used a tragic iambic verse, saying: **WHAT** does it profit me if the dead do not rise? "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die. Do not be deceived: bad company ruins good morals." 

<margin>B</margin> Others, however, have included Acusilaus of Argos in the number of the Seven Sages; others, Pherecydes of Syria. But Plato, considering Periander unworthy of wisdom because he was a tyrant, substituted Myson of Chenae. That the Greek sages lived long after the time of Moses will be shown a little later. We must now consider that the style of philosophy used among them was Hebrew-like and enigmatic. For they embraced a brevity that was both advisory and highly useful. Plato says this style was zealously and diligently followed by all Greeks in common, but especially by the Lacedæmonians and Cretans, who lived under the best laws. 

<margin>C</margin> Regarding that famous saying, *Know thyself*, some think it belongs to Chilo. Chamæleo, in his book *On the Gods*, attributes it to Thales; Aristotle attributes it to the Pythia <note>The priestess of the Oracle at Delphi</note>. This command may urge one to pursue true knowledge, for the individual parts cannot be known without understanding the substance of the whole universe. It is necessary to diligently investigate the origin of the world, through which the nature of man can also be learned. 

Again, they attribute *Nothing in excess* to Chilo the Lacedæmonian. However, Strato, in his work *On Inventions*, ascribes this saying to Stratodemus of Tegea. Didymus believes it belongs to Solon, just as he also attributes *Moderation is best* to Cleobulus. Regarding the saying *A pledge, and ruin is near*, Cleomenes says in his book *On Hesiod* that it was first said by Homer in these words: 
*Worthless are the pledges of worthless men.* <note>original Greek: δειλαί τοι δειλῶν γε καὶ ἐγγυάασθαι</note>
Some think this was a saying of Chilo, while 
<margin>D</margin> Didymus says it was an admonition from Thales. Furthermore, the saying *All men are evil*, or *Most men are evil* (for this is stated in two ways), Sotades of Byzantium attributes to Bias; and *Diligence overcomes all*, they claim is from Periander. Similarly, they say the advice *Know the opportunity* belongs to Pittacus. 

Solon gave laws to the Athenians, and Pittacus to the Mitylenæans. Eventually, Pythagoras, a close associate of Pherecydes, was the first to call himself a "Philosopher" <note>Literally "a lover of wisdom," rather than claiming to be "wise" (Sophos) himself</note>. Thus, after the men mentioned before, there were three successions of philosophy, taking their names from the places where they practiced. First, the **Italic** school, derived from Pythagoras; second, the **Ionic**, from Thales; and third, the **Eleatic**, from Xenophanes. 

<margin>E</margin> Furthermore, Pythagoras, the son of Mnesarchus, was a Samian according to Hippobotus; but Aristoxenus in his *Life of Pythagoras*, along with Aristarchus and Theopompus, says he was a Tuscan. Neanthes says he was Syrian or Tyrian; so that, in the opinion of many, Pythagoras was a "barbarian" by race. Moreover, Thales, as Leander and Herodotus report, was a Phoenician, though some consider him a Milesian. He alone seems to have associated with the prophets of the Egyptians. No teacher is recorded for him, just as none is recorded for Pherecydes the Syrian, who was the teacher of Pythagoras. The Italic philosophy of Pythagoras flourished in the town of Metapontum in Italy. 

Anaximander, son of Praxidamus, a Milesian, succeeded Thales. He was followed by
<margin>discourse <note>original Greek: διατριβή</note></margin>
Anaximenes, son of Eurystratus, also a Milesian. After him came Anaxagoras of Clazomenae, son of Hegesibulus. He transferred the school from Ionia to Athens. He was succeeded by Archelaus, who was the teacher of Socrates. 

<margin>F</margin> <margin>stone-cutter <note>original Greek: λιθοξόος</note></margin>
**From** these, the smooth-talking stone-cutter turned away—the charmer of the Greeks—as Timon says in his *Silli* <note>A work of satirical poems</note>. This was because Socrates turned away from natural philosophy <note>Physics and the study of the external world</note> 
<margin>gave birth <note>original Greek: ἐκύησεν</note></margin>
to those matters which pertain to ethics. When they had heard Socrates, Antisthenes founded the Cynic sect, while Plato withdrew to the Academy. Following Plato...

# CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

<margin>discordant <note>original Greek: ἀπωιδὸς</note></margin>

<margin>A</margin>
After Aristotle finished his studies and moved to the Lyceum, he founded the Peripatetic school <note>The "walking" school, named after the covered walkways of the Lyceum</note>. He was succeeded by Theophrastus, then Straton, then Lycon. After them came Critolaus, and then Diodorus. To Plato, Speusippus succeeded. Then came Xenocrates, then Polemon. The students of Polemon were Crates and Crantor, with whom the "Old Academy" came to an end. Arcesilaus was a companion of Crantor, and from him until the time of Hegesilaus, the "Middle Academy" flourished. Then Carneades succeeded Hegesilaus, followed by those who came after. Of the Eleatic discipline, the leader was Xenophanes of Colophon; Timaeus says he lived during the time of Hiero, who held power in Sicily, and the poet Epicharmus. Apollodorus, however, says he was born in the fortieth Olympiad <note>A four-year period used for dating; the 40th Olympiad was roughly 620–617 BCE</note> and lived until the times of Darius and Cyrus. Parmenides was a student of this Xenophanes.

<margin>B</margin>
Parmenides’ student was Zeno, then Leucippus, then Democritus. The students of Democritus were Protagoras of Abdera and Metrodorus of Chios, who taught Diogenes of Smyrna, who taught Anaxarchus. His student was Pyrrhon, followed by Nausiphanes. Some say Epicurus was a disciple of the latter. This is the succession of those who were philosophers among the Greeks, presented as a summary. The dates of those who were the founders and authors of their philosophies must be told next, so that by comparison we may show that the philosophy of the Hebrews was older by many generations. We have already spoken of Xenophanes, who was the leader of the Eleatic philosophy. Regarding Thales, Eudemus says in his *Astrological Histories* that he predicted the eclipse of the sun that occurred at the time the Medes and Lydians engaged in battle—specifically when Cyaxares, father of Astyages, ruled in Media, and Alyattes, father of Croesus, ruled in Lydia.

<margin>C</margin>
Herodotus also agrees with this in his first book. Those times are around the fiftieth Olympiad. Pythagoras is found to be in the time of the tyrant Polycrates, around the sixtieth Olympiad. It is written that Mnesiphilus was a rival of Solon, and Themistocles associated with him. Solon flourished in the forty-sixth Olympiad. Heraclitus, son of Bauson, persuaded the tyrant Melancomas to give up his tyranny. He even looked down upon King Darius when the king urged him to come to the Persians. These are the dates of those who were the most ancient of the wise men and philosophers among the Greeks. But what need is there to say that most of them were both foreign by birth and educated by foreigners? Since

<margin>D</margin>
it has been shown that Pythagoras was a Tuscan <note>an Etruscan from Italy</note>. Antisthenes was a Phrygian, and Orpheus was an Odrysian or a Thracian. Many show that Homer was an Egyptian. Thales, though he was a Phoenician by race, is also said to have met with the prophets of the Egyptians, just as Pythagoras did with those same people. It was because of them that Pythagoras was even circumcised, so that he might enter the inner shrines <note>original Latin: adyta</note> and learn the mystic philosophy of the Egyptians. He also associated with the most excellent of the Chaldeans and the Magi. The word <term>homakoeion</term> <margin>homakoeion: an auditorium, from the phrase "to hear together" <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τοῦ ὁμοῦ ἀκούειν</note></margin> used by him signifies what is now called a church. Furthermore, Plato does not deny that he "purchased" the most excellent parts of his philosophy from foreigners <note>The Greeks used the word "Barbarian" for anyone not Greek</note>, and he admits that he went to Egypt. In the *Phaedo*, he writes that a philosopher can find help from any quarter: "Greece is a large place, O Cebes," he says, "in which there are men

<margin>E</margin>
who are good in every respect, but there are also many races of foreigners." Thus Plato believes there are some philosophers even among the foreigners. Epicurus, however, thinks the opposite—that only Greeks are capable of philosophizing. But in the *Symposium*, Plato truly speaks when he praises the foreigners for having practiced philosophy with distinction. In many other places, both among the Greeks and the foreigners, many sacred rites have already been established because of such "sons" <note>i.e., great thinkers</note>. It is clear that foreigners have always honored their lawgivers and teachers exceptionally, calling them gods.

<margin>Plato in the Phaedo.</margin>
For they believe that noble souls, as Plato says, leaving their super-celestial place, endured coming into this Tartarus <note>the underworld or the physical world of suffering</note>; and having taken on a body, they shared in all the evils found in the physical realm out of a concern for the human race. These souls brought forth laws and preached philosophy, than

<margin>F</margin>
which no greater good has ever come, nor will ever come, to the human race. And it seems to me that when the foreigners felt the great benefits brought by these wise men, they both honored them and practiced philosophy publicly—including all the Brahmins <note>original Latin: Brachmanes</note>, the Odrysians, and the Getae.

# STROMATA, BOOK I

<margin>A</margin>
The Getae <note>A Thracian tribe residing near the lower Danube.</note>. Furthermore, the Egyptian people most diligently counted those men among the Gods; so too did the Chaldeans and the Arabs of what is called *Arabia Felix* <note>Latin: "Happy Arabia," referring to the fertile southern part of the Arabian Peninsula.</note>, and all those who inhabit Palestine, along with a significant portion of the Persian race, and countless other nations besides these. It is clear that Plato is always found to hold the barbarians <note>In this context, "barbarian" is the standard Greek term for any non-Greek person or culture, often used here with respect for their ancient wisdom.</note> in high regard, as he remembered that both he and Pythagoras had learned many of their most excellent and noble doctrines among the Barbarians. Therefore, he even spoke of "races of barbarians," recognizing these groups as "races of barbarian philosophers." In the *Phaedrus*, he shows us that the Egyptian King and Thoth <note>original: "Thoyth"</note>—whom he knew to be Mercury <note>The Greek god Hermes, associated with the Egyptian Thoth as the bringer of writing and wisdom.</note>—were wiser than us. Furthermore, in the *Charmides*, he appears to know certain Thracians who are said to make the soul immortal.

<margin>Pythagoras.</margin>
It is told that Pythagoras was a disciple of Sonchis, the Egyptian High Prophet, while Plato studied under Sechnuphis of Heliopolis. Eudoxus of Cnidus was a student of Conuphis, who was also an Egyptian.

<margin>B</margin>
In the dialogue *On the Soul* <note>Referring to the "Myth of Er" in Plato's *Republic*.</note>, Plato again seems to acknowledge prophecy when he introduces a Prophet delivering the speech of Lachesis <note>One of the three Fates in Greek mythology.</note>, who foretells the destinies to the souls who are being allotted their lives.

<margin>Plato.</margin>
And in the *Timaeus*, he introduces the most wise Plato learning from a Barbarian. The passage goes like this: "O Solon, Solon, you Greeks are always children; there is no such thing as an old Greek. For you possess no ancient discipline." <note>This famous quote emphasizes the Egyptian priest's view that Greek culture was young compared to the ancient civilizations of the East.</note> Democritus also wrote Babylonian books on ethics. These influences can be observed in his work.

<margin>C</margin> <margin>Democritus.</margin>
Democritus says these things when writing about himself and boasting of his great learning: "Of those who lived in my time, I have wandered through more lands, inquiring into things far remote; I have seen the most regions of air and earth, and heard the most learned men. In composing lines with demonstration <note>Referring to geometry.</note>, no one has yet surpassed me, not even those among the Egyptians called the <term>Arpedonaptae</term> <note>Literally "rope-stretchers," these were Egyptian surveyors who used knotted ropes to perform complex geometric calculations for land measurement.</note>." He was in foreign lands for eighty years in total. Indeed, he visited Babylon, Persia, and Egypt, presenting himself as a disciple of the Magi and the Priests.

<margin>Zoroaster.</margin>

<margin>Pythagoras.</margin>

<margin>D</margin>

<margin>Sibyl.</margin>
Thus, they say that at Delphi, in the assembly hall, a certain rock is shown upon which the first Sibyl <note>An ancient prophetess.</note> is said to have sat; she had come from Mount Helicon, raised by the Muses, being the daughter of Lamia. Serapion says in his verses that even after death, the Sibyl did not cease from the art of divination. He writes that the part of her that vanished into the air after her death is what divines through lots and omens. From that part of her body which turned into the earth, grass grew; whatever beasts ate of it while in that place would reveal a perfect knowledge of the future to men through their entrails. He believes her soul is that face which appears in the Moon. So much for the Sibyl.

<margin>E</margin> <margin>Numa.</margin>
Numa, the King of the Romans, was a Pythagorean. Aided by the things handed down by Moses, he forbade the Romans from making any image of God resembling a human or an animal. Therefore, when they built temples during the first one hundred and seventy years, they made no image, neither sculpted nor painted. For Numa had secretly indicated to them that the "Best Being" <note>God</note> cannot be reached by any other means than through the mind alone.

Philosophy, therefore, a very useful thing, flourished long ago among the Barbarians, shining through the nations, and only afterwards did it come to the Greeks. Its leaders were the Prophets of the Egyptians, the Chaldeans of the Assyrians, the Druids of the Gauls,

<margin>F</margin> <margin>The Magi.</margin>
the Samanaeans <note>likely "Sramanas," Indian forest ascetics</note> of the Bactrians, the philosophers of the Celts, and the Magi of the Persians—who indeed even signaled the birth of our Savior, coming to Judea with a star leading them—along with the <term>Gymnosophists</term> <note>Literally "naked philosophers," a group of Indian ascetics admired by the Greeks for their endurance and wisdom.</note> of the Indians, and other Barbarian philosophers. There are two kinds of these: some are called Sarmanae...

others, indeed, are the Brahmins <note>original: "Brachmanes"</note>. And among the Sarmanae <note>referring to the Sramanas, a class of Indian wandering ascetics</note>, those who are called the Forest-Dwellers <note>original: "Allobii," likely a corruption of the Greek "Hylobioi"</note> do not inhabit cities, nor do they have houses or roofs; they clothe themselves in the bark of trees, eat acorns and berries from the trees, and drink water from their hands. They know nothing of marriage or the procreation of children, just like those who are now called the Encratites <note>A group of early Christians who practiced strict "self-control" or "continence," abstaining from marriage and wine</note>. There are also some among the Indians who obey the precepts of Buddha <note>original: "Buttę"</note>, whom they have honored as a God because of his extraordinary virtue. Among the Scythians there was also Anacharsis, who is recorded to have excelled many of the Greek philosophers. Hellanicus writes that the Hyperboreans lived beyond the Rhipaean mountains and were taught justice, eating no meat but only the fruits of trees. They lead those who have reached sixty years of age outside the gates and remove them from their midst. 

<margin>Dignity <note>original: "σεμνότης"</note></margin>
There are also among the Germans certain sacred women who, by gazing into the whirlpools of rivers and the sounds and eddies of the currents, divine and predict the future. These women did not permit the Germans to fight with Caesar before the new moon had shone. Far more ancient than all of these is the Jewish race, and Philo the Pythagorean <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish philosopher whom Clement views as part of the Pythagorean tradition due to his focus on numbers and ethics</note> shows with many words that the philosophy recorded in writing among them began before that of the Greeks. Furthermore, Aristobulus the Peripatetic and many others say the same, lest I linger too long in listing them by name. Most clearly, however, the writer Megasthenes, who lived with Seleucus Nicator, writes in the third book of his *Indian History*: "All things that were said about nature by the ancients are also said by those who philosophize outside of Greece—partly among the Indians by the Brahmins, and partly in Syria by those called Jews."

Some, speaking more fabulously, say that among those called the Idaean Dactyli <note>Mythical "finger-men" associated with Mount Ida, often credited with inventing metallurgy and musical rhythm</note>, the first wise men arose, to whom is attributed the invention of the "Ephesian letters" <note>Magical formulas or spoken charms</note> and the discovery of musical rhythms. For this reason, those in music are called "Dactyls." The Idaean Dactyli were both Phrygians and barbarians. Herodotus records that Hercules, being a prophet and a student of nature, received the "pillars of the world" from Atlas, the barbarian Phrygian. Hermippus of Beirut calls Chiron the Centaur wise, of whom the author of the *War of the Titans* also says:

> *He led the mortal ages to justice, showing*
> *The oath, and the sacred rites of the Gods, and the patterns of heaven.*

Under him, Achilles was trained before being led to Troy. Hippo, the daughter of the Centaur, living with Aeolus, taught him the contemplation of nature—her father's science. Euripides also testifies to Hippo in this way:

> *She who first prophesied divine things*
> *Through oracles, and by the rising of the stars.*

By this Aeolus, Ulysses was received in hospitality after the capture of Troy. Observe the dates for a comparison with the age of Moses, and the most ancient philosophy which existed in his time. Not only philosophy, but almost all arts had Barbarians as their inventors. Thus, the Egyptians first brought Astrology down to men, as did the Chaldeans. The Egyptians again were the first to teach the lighting of lamps, divided the year into twelve months, forbade sexual intercourse with women in temples, and established by law that one must not approach sacred things after being with a wife without washing. Again, they were the inventors of Geometry. There are some who say the Carians discovered the foreknowledge gathered from the stars. The Phrygians were the first to observe the flights of birds. Those who were neighbors to Italy <note>referring to the Etruscans</note> perfectly mastered the art of inspecting entrails for divination. The Isaurians and Arabs studied augury, just as the Telmessians studied the divination that comes through dreams. The Etruscans invented the trumpet, and the Phrygians the flute (for Olympus and Marsyas were Phrygians). Cadmus was a Phoenician, and he was the inventor of letters for the Greeks, as Ephorus says; hence Herodotus writes that the letters were called "Phoenician." Others say the Phoenicians and Syrians were the first to devise letters. As for medicine, they say Apis the native Egyptian discovered it before Io came to Egypt, and later Aesculapius expanded the art.

<summary>Clement argues that the roots of philosophy, science, and the arts are found in "barbarian" (non-Greek) cultures, citing early references to Buddha, Indian ascetics, and the antiquity of Jewish law as being superior and prior to Greek thought.</summary>

For at that time, the theft had some utility which returned to humanity, not because the one who stole it intended to be useful, but because Providence directed the outcome of that bold attempt toward something beneficial. I know many people constantly rise up against us, claiming that he who does not prohibit an act is the cause of it. They say the cause of a theft is the one who did not keep watch, or the one who did not prohibit it; just as the cause of a fire is the one who did not extinguish it when it started, or the cause of a shipwreck is the pilot who did not pull in the rope. Now, those who are the causes of these things are punished by law.

<margin>E</margin>
For the fault of what happens is attributed to the one in whose power it was to prohibit it. To them we say: "Cause" is understood in the context of doing, working, and acting.

<margin>To act on oneself. <note>original: "αὐτὸν ἐνεργεῖν"</note></margin>
But that which does not prohibit is, by that very fact, removed from the operation. Furthermore, a cause is involved in the operation, just as a shipbuilder is involved in the making of a boat, or a housebuilder in the construction of a house. But that which does not prohibit is separate from the thing being made. Therefore, the act is completed because the one who *could* prohibit it does not act nor prohibit.

Nor would they blame the thief, but the one who did not prohibit the theft. Therefore, let them say it was not Hector who burned the Greek ships, but Achilles, because although he could have stopped Hector, he did not. **E** which arose from voluntary defection to remain useless or unprofitable, nor does it let it become entirely harmful. <margin>A</margin> Diodorus relates that Antiphon, of the Rhamnusian tribe, was the first to invent judicial orations and to write them for a fee to be delivered by others. <note>Antiphon (c. 480–411 BC) was the first of the "Ten Attic Orators" to take up speechwriting as a profession.</note> Apollodorus of Cuma was the first to take the title of "Critic," and was called a Grammarian. <margin>B</margin> We have already mentioned the time of Solon. Draco, who was also a legislator, is found to have lived around the thirty-ninth Olympiad. Thus, Greek philosophy attains the truth only in a partial and weak way—as some say, by chance—but it does not reach the whole truth. Others, however, claim it was set in motion by the Devil. <margin>C</margin> Some even believe that certain inferior powers inspired the whole of philosophy. But even if Greek philosophy does not comprehend the full magnitude of truth, and remains weak in fulfilling the commands of the Lord, it certainly prepares the way for the "Royal Doctrine" <note>The "Royal Doctrine" refers to the Gospel or Christian revelation.</note> by disciplining the mind, forming character, and confirming those who believe in providence to be ready to receive the truth.

<margin>John 10</margin> But, they say, it is written: "All who came before the Lord’s coming are thieves and robbers." <note>A reference to John 10:8. Early critics used this to dismiss all pre-Christian philosophy as demonic or fraudulent.</note> Therefore, all those who are contained in speech—who lived before the Word <note>original: "verbo" (Logos). Clement refers to the Incarnation of Christ.</note> took on flesh—are included in this general statement. Yet the Prophets, being sent and inspired by the Lord, were not thieves, but ministers. <margin>Proverbs 9</margin> Therefore, the Scripture says: <margin>D</margin> "Wisdom has sent her servants, calling with a high proclamation to the bowl of wine." <note>A paraphrased reference to Proverbs 9:1-3, where Wisdom invites people to a banquet.</note>

Philosophy, however, was not sent by the Lord, but "came," it is said, having been "stolen" or "given by a thief." Whether it was a power or an Angel who learned something of the truth but did not remain in it, and thus inspired these things and taught what was stolen: this happened not because the Lord was ignorant—for He knows the ends of all future things before the constitution of every essence—but because He did not forbid it. For at that time, this theft brought some utility to humanity, not because the one who stole intended it to be useful, but because Providence directed the outcome of that bold attempt toward something beneficial.

I know that many constantly rise up against us, saying that he who does not forbid an act is the cause of it. They claim the cause of a theft is the one who did not guard the item or did not forbid the thief; just as the cause of a fire is the one who did not extinguish it when it started, or the cause of a shipwreck is the pilot who did not pull in the rope. <margin>E</margin> Indeed, those who are the causes of such things are punished by law. For the blame for what happens is placed on the one who had it in his power to forbid it.

To these people we say: a "cause" is understood in the context of doing, working, and acting. <margin>Ineffectual. <note>original: "ἀνενέργητον." A Greek philosophical term for that which lacks the power to act or produce an effect.</note></margin> But that which does not forbid is, by that very fact, removed from the operation. Furthermore, a cause is involved in the action, just as a shipbuilder is involved in the making of a boat, or a housebuilder in the construction of a house. But that which does not forbid is separate from what is being done. Therefore, the act is completed because the one who *could* forbid it does not act nor forbid. <margin>The Greek says "it was in his power," but I think it should read "it was NOT in his power," to contrast with what follows about the devil, etc. <note>A translator's note on a suspected error in the Greek manuscript source.</note></margin> For what does he perform, who does not forbid?

<margin>F</margin> Indeed, their argument leads to an absurdity; for they would say that the cause of a wound is not the weapon, but the shield that did not forbid the weapon from passing through. They would not blame the thief, but the one who did not forbid the theft. Therefore, they might say that Achilles, not Hector, burned the Greek ships, because although he could have forbidden Hector, he did not. He uses logical analogies to prove that God's non-interference does not make Him the cause of human error or sin.</summary>

...He did not forbid the fire, and perhaps it was a contributing cause. However, since the Devil possessed free will and could have been led by repentance—or choose to steal—he himself is the cause of the theft, not the Lord who did not forbid it. Nor was the gift itself harmful such that a prohibition was necessary. If we must argue accurately and subtly against those who disagree, let them know that the one who does not forbid an act (as we say in the case of the theft) is in no way the cause of it. Rather, the cause and the blame are assigned to the one who does the thing that is forbidden. For he who protects with a shield is the cause of the one being protected not being wounded, for he prevents him from being struck. And for Socrates, his *daemon* was a cause, not by prohibiting, but by exhorting him—even if it did not always exhort. <note>Socrates famously claimed to have a "daimonion" or "divine sign," an inner voice that warned him against certain actions.</note> Neither praises, nor censures, nor honors, nor punishments are just if the soul does not have the free power <margin>of impulse and aversion. <note>original: ὁρμῆς καὶ ἀφορμῆς</note></margin> to both desire and act, but instead possesses vice involuntarily. Therefore, he who forbids is indeed a cause. But He who did not forbid the free choice of the soul judges justly, so that God is most certainly not the <margin>B</margin> cause of our vice. Since, then, free choice and desire are what first begin sins, <margin>Who is the source of sins? <note>original: τίς κατάρχει τῶν ἁμαρτημάτων</note></margin> and since a false opinion sometimes dominates us—from which we neglect to withdraw because of injustice and ignorance—punishments are rightly inflicted. For to have a fever is involuntary; but when someone suffers a fever through their own fault and lack of self-control, we blame them, even though the sickness itself is involuntary. For no one chooses evil insofar as it is evil, but is led astray by the pleasure inherent in it, thinking it a good thing and judging it worthy to be pursued. Since this is the case, it is within our power to be liberated from ignorance and from evil or "pleasant" choices, and above all, not to give our assent to those deceptive mental images and visions.

<margin>C</margin>
The Devil is called a robber and a thief; he mixed false prophets among the true Prophets, just as tares are mixed with wheat. Therefore, "all who came before the Lord" were thieves and robbers—not absolutely all people, but all the false prophets, and all those who were not properly sent by Him. <note>Clement is interpreting John 10:8, explaining that "all" does not include the holy Hebrew prophets, but rather those who claimed their title falsely.</note> These false prophets also possessed a stolen thing: the name of "Prophet," for they were indeed prophets, but of the one who is a liar. For the Lord says: *You are of your father the devil, and* <margin>John 8</margin> *you wish to do the desires of your father. The Angel of Repentance, known as the "Shepherd," <margin>D</margin> says to Hermas regarding the false prophet: "For he says some true things. For the Devil fills him with his own spirit, to see if he can break any of the righteous." <note>Clement cites *The Shepherd of Hermas*, a popular 2nd-century Christian text that was sometimes treated as Scripture in the early Church.</note> Therefore, all things are dispensed by the powers above for good, so that through the Church the "manifold and varied wisdom of God" may be known from the foreknowledge of the ages, which He accomplished in Christ. Nothing opposes God, nor is anything contrary to Him, for He is the Lord and the Almighty. Furthermore, the counsels and operations of those who have fallen away—though they are individual acts—arise from a bad disposition, like diseases of the body. Yet they are administered by a universal and general providence toward a healthy end, even if the immediate cause of the disease is active.

<margin>E</margin>
It is, therefore, the greatest argument for Divine Providence that it does not allow the vice which has arisen from a voluntary falling-away to remain useless or unprofitable, nor to be entirely harmful. For it is the duty of Divine wisdom, virtue, and power not only to do good (for this is, so to speak, the very nature of God, just as it is the nature of fire to warm and light to illuminate), but especially this: to lead that which was devised by the wicked to a good and useful end, and to use those things which seem evil in a beneficial way—just as he used the testimony that proceeded from temptation. There is, therefore, even in philosophy—which was stolen like the "little bit of fire" by Prometheus—something suitable for light that can be usefully kindled; it is a certain trace of wisdom and an impulse from God.

<margin>F</margin>

They took parts of the truth from the Hebrew prophets without acknowledging it, attributing these ideas to themselves as if they were their own doctrines. Some things they corrupted; others, through a kind of superfluous diligence, they pronounced unlearnedly while <margin>acting like sophists. <note>original: σοφιζόμενοι—meaning to use clever but fallacious arguments.</note></margin> Still other things they actually discovered themselves. <margin>Impulse and aversion. <note>original: ὁρμῆς καὶ ἀφορμῆς. These are technical Stoic terms for the basic movements of the soul toward or away from an object.</note></margin>
<margin>The originator of sins. <note>original: προκατάρχει τῶν ἄμαρτημάτων.</note></margin>
Neither praise, nor blame, nor honors, nor punishments are just, if the soul does not have the free power of both desire and action, but instead vice were involuntary. Thus, he who forbids is indeed a cause. But He who did not forbid the free choice of the soul judges justly, so that God is most certainly not the cause of our vice. However, since free choice and desire first begin the process of sinning, and since a false opinion sometimes dominates—from which we neglect to withdraw due to a lack of justice and ignorance—punishments are rightly inflicted. For to have a fever is involuntary, but when people have a fever through their own fault and through their own lack of self-control, we blame them, even though the state of being ill is involuntary. For no one chooses evil insofar as it is evil, but being led away by the pleasure inherent in it, and thinking it to be good, he deems it something to be pursued. Since things are so, it lies within our power to be liberated from ignorance and from a bad and "pleasant" choice, and above all, not to give our assent to those deceptive mental images and visions.

The Devil is called a robber and a thief, for he mixed false prophets among the true Prophets, like weeds among the wheat. <margin>E</margin>
It is, therefore, the greatest proof of Divine Providence that He does not allow the vice which arose from a voluntary defection to remain unhelpful or useless, nor to be entirely harmful. For it is the duty of Divine wisdom, virtue, and power not only to do good (for this is, so to speak, God’s nature, just as it is the nature of fire to warm and light to illuminate), but especially to lead that which was devised by certain evil-doers toward a good and useful end, and to use those things which seem evil for a beneficial purpose—just as He used the testimony that proceeded from temptation. Therefore, there is even in philosophy—which was snatched away by theft as if by Prometheus—a small spark of fire fit for light, which is usefully stirred up: both a trace of wisdom and a movement from God.

<margin>B</margin> 
From these things it is clear that even by using poetic examples, such as from the *Phenomena* of Aratus, Paul approves what was rightly said among the Greeks. Through the "unknown God," he signified by way of a circumlocution <note>A roundabout way of speaking.</note> that the Creator God was indeed honored by the Greeks, but that it was necessary to receive and learn of Him through the Son by means of recognition. 

"I have SENT you therefore to the nations," he says, "to open their eyes, that they may turn from darkness, and from the power of Satan to God, so that they may receive forgiveness of sins and an inheritance among those who are sanctified by faith in me." 
<margin>Acts 26</margin>

<margin>C</margin> 
Therefore, those eyes of the blind that are opened represent the recognition of the Father through the Son, which is the comprehension of the Greek circumlocution; and to be "turned from the power of Satan" is to be changed from sin, through which slavery had been introduced. Yet we do not accept all philosophy absolutely, but only that of which Socrates also speaks in Plato: "For there are, as they say in the mysteries, many who carry the wand <term>thyrsus|the staff topped with a pine cone carried by devotees of Dionysus</term>, but few are Bacchanals <term>Bacchi|true initiates who have the spirit of the god, not just the outward dress</term>." By this, he silently signifies that "many are called, but few are chosen." 
<margin>Matthew 22</margin>

Thus he openly adds: "But these, in my opinion, are none other than those who have philosophized rightly. From their company I have never, as far as I was able in life, been absent, but have applied all diligence in every way to be among them. But whether I have applied it rightly, and what we have accomplished, we shall know clearly when we arrive there <note>i.e., in the afterlife.</note>, if God wills, a little later." 

<margin>D</margin> 
Does it not seem to you that he declares from the Hebrew scriptures that hope which exists after the death of the righteous? And in the *Demodocus*, if it is indeed a work of Plato: "Do not think that I say to philosophize is to live focused on the arts, nor to desire to learn many things <gloss>unfolding/examining <note>original: "ἐκπτυκτίζοντες"</note></gloss>; for I indeed considered this a disgrace." For he knew, as I think, that he who teaches already possesses a mind knowing many things, as is the opinion of Heraclitus. 

And in the fifth book of the *Republic*: "Shall we then place all these, and others of certain such things, and the mathematicians of I know not what arts, as Philosophers?" "By no means," he says, "but they are similar to Philosophers." "But the true ones," he says, "whom do you mean?" "Those," I say, "who delight in the contemplation of truth." 

<margin>E</margin> 
For philosophy is not found in Geometry, which relies on postulates and positions. Nor is it in Music, which is indeed conjectural; nor in Astronomy, which is filled with natural, fleeting, and merely probable reasons. Rather, philosophy belongs to the Good itself through knowledge and truth. While other paths may be "of the good," they are only "toward the good." Wherefore he himself does not grant that the "circle of learning" <margin>circular <note>original: "ἐγκύκλιον"</note></margin>—which they call the "encyclopedia"—actually confers the Good, but that it brings help to excite and exercise the soul toward those things perceived by the intelligence. 

Therefore, whether people say the Greeks spoke something of divine philosophy by chance <margin>by coincidence <note>original: "κατὰ σύμπτωσιν"</note></margin>, that "chance" is actually part of the divine economy <note>The "economy" (oikonomia) refers to God's providential plan and management of human history.</note>. One should not attribute chance to the gods simply because of the disputes between us. Or if they achieved a pre-set goal <margin>necessity <note>original: "ἐνδείαν σει," likely a corruption for 'necessity' or 'destiny'</note></margin>, that achievement is not devoid of providence. Or again, if one says the Greeks had a "natural notion" <margin>by chance encounter <note>original: "κατὰ συντυχίαν"</note></margin>, 

<margin>F</margin> 
we recognize one Creator of nature, by which reason we have also said that justice is natural. Or if they had a "common mind": let us consider who its father is, and what justice is in the distribution of the mind. For whether someone has called it a "fore-announcement" <margin>fore-announcement <note>original: "προαναφώνησις"</note></margin>—that is, a pre-speaking or a prediction—it still points to the same source.

cc <meta>catchword: sis.</meta>

# CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

...and let him allege <term>appropriation <note>original: συνοικείωσιν (synoikeiosis); a term often used in Stoic philosophy to describe the natural affinity or "belonging" one feels toward something, here used to describe the connection between partial truths and the Whole Truth.</note></term>, that is, a conjoined explanation; he is speaking of the types of prophecy. <margin>
Appropriation.
Reflection.
1 Corinthians 13.
</margin>

<margin>A</margin> **FOR we see now as if through a mirror**, recognizing ourselves through that reflection which is in the mirror itself, and contemplating together, as far as is possible, the efficient cause by means of the divinity that is within us. For "you have seen," he says, "your brother, you have seen your God." I think "God" is seen definitely and comprehensively when the heart has been made pure. And by "face to face," it means then at last [one sees] definitely and comprehensively when the heart has been made pure. And indeed, those who have practiced philosophy with exactness among the Greeks see God through an **apparent and transparent form**. Reflection and transparency.

Proverbs 27.

<margin>Romans 1.</margin> 

**KNOWINGLY recognize the souls of your flock.** For when the Gentiles, who do not have the Law, do by nature the things of the Law, these, not having the Law, are a law unto themselves—with their "uncircumcision" keeping the justifications of the Law according to the opinion of the Apostle, both before the Law and before the Coming [of Christ]. He then makes a comparison of the Philosophers with those who are called Heretics, quite clearly:

<margin>C</margin>
<margin>
Proverbs 27.
Proverbs 10.

**BETTER is**, says the Word, **a friend near at hand than a brother dwelling far away.** But "he who relies on falsehoods, he feeds the winds, and pursues winged birds." I do not think the Word is now speaking of philosophy—since philosophy argues with probability and speaks with probability in many matters—but rather it pursues heresies. Thus he adds: **FOR he has left the ways of his own vineyard, and has wandered in the paths of his own husbandry.** These are the ones who leave the Church from the beginning. Now, he who has fallen into heresy passes through a desert without water, having abandoned the one who is truly God; deserted by God, seeking water where there is no water, traversing an uninhabitable and thirsty land, gathering with his hands the barrenness of fruits. And to those who lack prudence:

<margin>D</margin>
<margin>Proverbs 9.</margin>

**I COMMAND**, says Wisdom, speaking to those who are involved in heresies: **Touch hidden breads with pleasure, and stolen water is sweet.** By "bread and wine," it is not speaking of any others than those heresies which use bread and water in the offering <note>The Eucharist</note> not according to the rule of the Church; for the Scripture states openly: There are those who use only water in the Eucharist.

<margin>
These heretics are called
"Water-Offerers"

</margin>

**BUT recoil, do not linger in his place.** By "place," he called the synagogue equivocally, but not the Church. Then he exclaims: **For in this way you shall cross an alien water,** regarding heretical baptism as not being the proper and genuine water. **And you shall pass through an alien river,** which carries one down and drags one into the sea, into which is cast the one who turns away from that stability which is in the truth, flowing back again to the gentiles and the disordered waves of life. 

<margin>E</margin>

Now, just as many men who pull a ship cannot be called "many causes," but rather one cause made of many—for each individual is not the cause of the ship being pulled, but only a cause along with the others—so also Philosophy contributes to the comprehension of truth, since it is an inquiry into truth. It is not that it is *the* cause of comprehension, but a cause *along with others*, a helper, and perhaps even a "contributory cause." Just as "being happy" is one thing, but its causes are the virtues, which are many; and just as the causes of "being warmed" are the Sun, and fire, and a bath, and clothing; so also, though the Truth is one, there are many things which contribute to its inquiry, but the discovery is through the Son. 

<margin>F</margin>
<margin>Unassailable <note>original Greek: ἀνεπιχείρητος (anepicheiretos); something that cannot be attacked or refuted.</note></margin>

And if we consider it rightly, virtue is one in its power, but it happens that when it is in certain things, it is called "prudence," in others "temperance," and in others "fortitude" or "justice." By the same reasoning, although Truth is also one, in Geometry there is the "truth of Geometry," in Music the "truth of Music," and in right philosophy there would be "Greek truth." But this alone is the supreme truth, which cannot be handed over by human hands, and which we are taught by the Son of God. In this way we speak of one and the same drachma: if it is given to a sailor, it is "passage money"; if to a tax-gatherer, a "tax"; and to one who leases a house, [it is "rent"]...

# THE MISCELLANIES, BOOK I.
->CC ii<-

### A

Each thing, whether it be virtue or even truth, when called by a single name, is the cause only of that which is its own effect. <margin>conjoined use <note>original: σύγχρησιν (synchresin)</note></margin> However, through their conjoined use, one achieves a blessed life. For we shall not be blessed because of mere names, since we call the "right path" blessedness, and the "blessed man" is he whose soul is adorned with virtue. 

But if philosophy also brings aid from a distance toward the discovery of truth, <margin>incursions <note>original: ἐμβολάς</note>; logically <note>original: λογικῶς</note></margin> reaching toward our knowledge through various notions—a knowledge which closely touches the truth—it assists the one who has studied to grasp knowledge through the Word, or Reason. And yet, Greek truth is separate from our own, even if it happens to share the same name; this is because of the greatness of our knowledge, its more fundamental demonstration, its divine power, and other similar factors. 

### B
For we have been taught by God, being instructed in truly sacred letters by the Son of God. From this, they do not move souls in the same way, but through a different doctrine. But if, for the sake of those who are prone to find fault, we must make a distinction, we shall call philosophy a "contributing cause" and a "cooperator" in the true comprehension of truth, insofar as it is an inquiry into truth. We will admit it to be a discipline that precedes the power <margin>of knowing <note>original: γνωστικόν (gnostikon)</note></margin>, yet we do not designate it as the primary cause, nor the containing cause, but rather an assistant and cooperator; it is not as if truth could not exist without philosophy. 

For nearly all of us, without the "circle of disciplines" <term>Liberal Arts <note>original: disciplinarum orbe (encyclical education)</note></term> and Greek philosophy—and some even without letters—have been moved by a divine and <term>barbarian philosophy <note>The Greeks called all non-Greeks "barbarians." Clement uses this term proudly to refer to the Hebrew/Christian tradition.</note></term>. By power, we have received the word concerning God through faith, having been educated by a wisdom that works by itself. But that which works with another, since it is too imperfect to work by itself, we call a cooperating and assisting cause; it is named 

### C
a "cause" because it comes together with something else, though by itself it cannot produce the true effect. 

Although at one time philosophy by itself justified the Greeks—though not unto that universal and general righteousness—it is now found to be a cooperator and an assistant toward that righteousness, just as the first and second steps are for one ascending to an upper room, or as a <margin>grammarian <note>original: γραμματικῶς</note></margin> is to one who is about to study philosophy. It is not that if philosophy were taken away, the universal and general Word would lack anything, or that the truth would be destroyed. <margin>voiced <note>original: πεφωνώς</note></margin> For sight, hearing, and the voice all contribute to truth; but it is the Mind which perceives it appropriately and naturally. The doctrine of the Savior is perfect in itself and stands in need of nothing, since it is the "power of God and the wisdom of God." When Greek philosophy is added, it does not make the truth more powerful, but it renders the "sophistic" <note>Sophistry refers to clever but false arguments.</note> reasoning against the truth weak. Because it repels the deceitful traps set against the truth, philosophy is called the "appropriate fence and wall for the vineyard." <margin>fence-top; bit/bridle; innocent <note>originals: θριγκός (thrigkos); ψωάλιον (psualion); ἄκακος (akakos)</note></margin>

"At the end of dinner, the little cake is sweet," as Pindar the Theban says. Moreover, the Scripture says openly: "The simple man who understands shall be more CUNNING. But the wise man shall receive knowledge." And: "HE who has received from himself seeks

It says: <margin>Ecclesiasticus 17</margin> "SON, be not a liar, for a lie leads to theft." Now, a thief truly possesses what he has stolen, whether it be gold, silver, a speech, or a decree. <margin>thievish; swept along <note>originals: κεκλεπτικός; σεσυρᾶσθαι</note></margin> Consequently, those things which they have stolen are true, but they know them only by conjecture and by being moved by the necessities of logic. If they were to learn, they would recognize them through true comprehension.

# CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

<margin>
"Forty" <note>original: τεσσαράκοντα (tessarakonta)</note> is in the Greek, but it should be read as "four" <note>original: τέσσαρσι (tessarsi)</note>, as gathered from the calculation.

"Double-natured" <note>original: διφυᾶς (diphyas)</note>. 

The Greek has "fifty-two" <note>original: πεντήκοντα δυοῖν (pentēkonta duoin)</note>, but I think it should read "fifteen" <note>original: πεντεκαίδεκα (pentekaideka)</note>.
</margin>

Let us run through what has been said on this topic. So, Apion the Grammarian, who was nicknamed *the frequent victor* <margin>A</margin> <note>Apion was a famous 1st-century scholar known for his rivalry with Josephus and his victories in intellectual competitions.</note>, in the fourth book of his *Egyptian Histories*, makes mention of Amosis, King of Egypt. Even though Apion was hostile to the Hebrews—being Egyptian by birth and having even written a book against the Jews—he brings forward Ptolemy of Mendes as a witness to Amosis's deeds. His words are as follows: "Amosis excavated Avaris <note>The capital of the Hyksos in Egypt.</note>, who lived in the time of Inachus of Argos, as Ptolemy of Mendes wrote in his *Chronologies*." This Ptolemy was indeed a priest. While explaining the deeds of the Egyptian Kings in three books, he says that in the time of Amosis, King of Egypt, the Jews went out from Egypt under the leadership of Moses. From this, it is seen that Moses flourished in the time of Inachus. <margin>B</margin>

Among Greek history, the Argive records are the oldest—those, I mean, that trace their origin from Inachus, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus teaches in his *Chronologies*. Compared to these, the Athenian records are more recent by four generations, tracing their origin from Cecrops. Cecrops was said to be of a "double nature" and "indigenous" <note>Greek myths often described the first kings as "born of the soil" (indigena) or having hybrid bodies, such as Cecrops being half-man, half-serpent.</note>, as Tatian says in those same words. Nine generations later are the Arcadian affairs starting from Pelasgus, who is also called "indigenous." There are others fifteen generations more recent than these, namely the Phthiotic records which start from Deucalion. By the time of the Trojan War, twenty or more generations are counted starting from Inachus. In total, there are—to speak generally—four hundred years and more. Furthermore, the history of the Assyrians will be seen to be many years older than Greek history, based on the records of Ctesias. Moses moved out of Egypt in the thirty-second year of the reign of Amosis of Egypt and Inachus of Argos.

There occurred in Greece, <margin>C</margin> in the time of Phoroneus (who lived after Inachus), the flood that happened in the time of Ogyges, and the establishment of the kingdom at Sicyon—first under Aegialeus, then Europus, then Telchis—and the kingdom of Cres in Crete. For Acusilaus says that Phoroneus was the first of men. Hence, the poet of the *Phoronis* called him "the father of mortal men." Following Acusilaus, Plato writes in the *Timaeus*: "And when he wished to lead them to speak of the ancient things of this city, he set out to speak of the oldest things: of Phoroneus, who was called the first, and of Niobe, and of those things which happened after the deluge." In the time of Phorbas lived Actaeeus, from whom the land was called Actaea Attica. In the time of Triopas lived Prometheus, Atlas, and Epimetheus, as well as Cecrops (who had the double nature) and Ino.

In the time <margin>D</margin> of Crotopus occurred the Great Fire of Phaëthon <note>A myth describing a solar disaster caused by the son of Helios losing control of the sun-chariot.</note> and the flood of Deucalion's time. In the time of Sthenelus occurred the reign of Amphictyon, the arrival of Danaus in the Peloponnese, and the building of Dardania by Dardanus. "From Zeus who was born," says Homer, "he who knows how to gather the clouds," and the lead of Europa from Phoenicia into Crete. In the time of Lynceus occurred the abduction of Proserpina <note>Persephone</note>, the construction of the temple in Eleusis, the agriculture of Triptolemus, the arrival of Cadmus in Thebes, and the reign of Minos. In the time of Proetus occurred the war of Eumolpus against the Athenians. In the time of Acrisius occurred the crossing of Pelops from Phrygia, the arrival of Dionysus in Athens, the second Cecrops, the deeds of Perseus and Bacchus, and the time of Orpheus and Musaeus.

<margin>
"Thargelion" <note>original: Θαργηλιών (Thargēliōn)</note>. 
"Waning" <note>original: λήγοντος (lēgontos)</note>. 
This comparison is according to the Athenian custom, where after the twentieth day of the lunar month they would count down: "the eighth of the waning moon," "the seventh of the waning moon."

The number is corrupted; perhaps "three hundred" should be read instead of "six hundred."
</margin>

In the eighteenth year of the reign of Agamemnon, Troy <note>original: Ilium</note> was captured, during the first year of the reign of Demophon (son of Theseus), on the twelfth day of the month of Thargelion <margin>E</margin> <note>Roughly May/June.</note>, as Dionysius of Argos says. However, Aegias and Dercylus say in their third book it was the eighth day of the waning month of Panemus. Hellanicus says it was the twelfth of the month of Thargelion, while some Athenian historians say the eighth day of the waning moon, in the last year of the reign of Menestheus, during the full moon. "It was the middle of the night," says the author of the *Little Iliad*, "and the bright moon was shining." Others say it was on the same day of the month of Scirrophorion. As for Theseus, who was a rival of Hercules, Homer mentions that he fought at Troy.

It is shown, therefore, that Moses lived six hundred and four years before Bacchus was counted among the gods, <margin>F</margin> since Bacchus was deified in the thirty-second year of the reign of Perseus, as Apollodorus says in his *Chronicles*. From Bacchus to Hercules and those brave men who sailed in the *Argo* with Jason, sixty-three years are counted; and Aesculapius and the Dioscuri...

# THE STROMATA, BOOK I
cc iii

<margin>A</margin> The Dioscuri <note>Castor and Pollux, the twin sons of Zeus/Jupiter</note>, that is Castor and Pollux, sailed with them <note>the Argonauts</note>, as Apollonius of Rhodes testifies in the *Argonautica*. From the reign of Hercules at Argos until the deification <note>original: "relationem in Deos," literally "the reporting into the gods"</note> of Hercules himself and Aesculapius, thirty years are counted, according to the chronographer Apollodorus. From that point until the deification of Castor and Pollux, there are fifty-three years. It was during this time that Troy was also captured. If we must also trust the poet Hesiod, let us listen to him:

<margin>Mercury</margin>
> And the messenger of the Gods was born to Zeus by the beautiful Maia, daughter of Atlas,
> After she had entered the sacred marriage bed.
> But the daughter of Cadmus <note>Semele</note> bore a magnificent son,
> When she had secretly lain with him: Bacchus, who brings great cheer.

<margin>B</margin> Cadmus, the father of Semele, came to Thebes in the time of Lynceus and was the inventor of the Greek alphabet. Triopas lived at the same time as Isis, in the seventh generation from Inachus. They say Isis was the same as Io, because she wandered over the whole earth. Ister, in his book *On the Colony of the Egyptians*, says she was the daughter of Prometheus. Prometheus lived in the time of Triopas, seven generations after Moses. Therefore, Moses seems to have flourished even before what the Greeks consider the "generation of man" <note>Referring to the myth of Prometheus creating or providing for humanity</note>. Leo, who wrote about the Egyptian gods, says that Isis is called Ceres <note>the goddess of agriculture, Demeter</note> by the Greeks; she lived in the time of Lynceus, eleven generations after Moses. Apis, the King of the Argives, built Memphis, as <margin>C</margin> Aristippus says in the first book of his *History of Arcadia*. Aristeas of Argos says he was named Sarapis, and that he is the one the Egyptians worship. Nymphodorus of Amphipolis, in the third book of his *Laws of Asia*, says the bull Apis died and was embalmed, placed in a coffin—which is called a <term>soros <note>original: σορός (soros)</note></term> in Greek—in the temple of the deity being worshipped. From this, he was called "Soroapis," and later, by the local custom of those who lived there, "Sarapis." Apis is the third in line from Inachus. Now, Latona <note>Leto</note> lived in the time of Tityus. For the famous wife of Zeus <note>Hera</note> was incited against Latona. Tityus lived at the same time as Tantalus. Rightly, then, does Pindar the Boeotian also write of it. <margin>D</margin> In that time, Apollo was born. It is no wonder, since he is even found to have served Admetus for wages, alongside Hercules, during a "Great Year" <note>A mythological cycle of time</note>. Zethus and Amphion, the inventors of music, lived around the time of Cadmus. If anyone should say that Phemonoë was the first to sing oracles to Acrisius, let him know that Orpheus, Musaeus, and Linus (the teacher of Hercules) lived twenty-seven years <margin>oracle-teachers <note>original: χρησμοδίδασκαι (chrēsmididaskai)</note></margin> after Phemonoë. Homer and Hesiod lived much later than the Trojan War; long after them were the Greek lawgivers—Lycurgus, Solon, the Seven Sages, Pherecydes of Syros, and the great Pythagoras—who lived much later around the time of the Olympiads, as we have shown before. Thus, we have shown that Moses is more ancient than most of the gods worshipped by the Greeks, as well as those called Sages and Poets. <margin>E</margin> Nor is he the only one; even the Sibyl is said to be older than Orpheus. Regarding the prophecies she uttered, she is said to have been called "Diana" <note>Artemis</note> as a surname while in Phrygia, and when she came to Delphi, she sang:

> O Delphians, you who are the servants of the far-striking Phoebus,
> I have come to you to set forth the mind of mighty Zeus,
> Since I am provoked to anger against my brother Phoebus.

There is also another called the Erythraean Herophile. These are mentioned by Heraclides of Pontus in his book *On Oracles*. ### THE STROMATA, BOOK I.

<margin>A</margin> ...Indeed, all the years from that time until the death of Solomon total six hundred and eighty-three years and seven months. Hiram gave his daughter to Solomon; at that time, after the fall of Troy, Menelaus came to Phoenicia, as Menander of Pergamum and Laetus say in their *History of Phoenicia*. After Solomon, his son Rehoboam <note>original: "Roboam"</note> reigned for seventeen years. At that time, the High Priest <term>Pontifex</term> was Abimelech, son of Zadok. In his time, the kingdom was divided in Samaria, and Jeroboam <note>original: "Hieroboam"</note>, a servant of Solomon from the tribe of Ephraim, reigned there. During this period, Ahijah <note>original: "Achias"</note> the Shilonite and Shemaiah <note>original: "Sameas"</note> son of Amame <note>Likely Shemaiah the prophet (1 Kings 12:22)</note> also prophesied; the latter went from Judah to Rehoboam and prophesied over the altar. After him, his son Jehoshaphat <note>original: "Iosaphat"</note> reigned <margin>B</margin> for five years <note>The biblical record says 25, though Clement's source may differ or refer to a co-regency</note>.
