In the time of Micaiah, there was also the false prophet Zedekiah <note>original: "Sedecias"</note> son of Chenaanah. Following them was the reign of Jehoram <note>original: "Ioran"</note>, son of Jehoshaphat, for eight years; in his time Elijah prophesied, and after Elijah, Elisha <note>original: "Heliseus"</note> son of Shaphat. In his time, those who were in Samaria ate dove’s dung and their own children <note>A reference to the famine during the siege of Samaria in 2 Kings 6</note>. The time of Jehoshaphat extends from the latter part of the third book of Kings <note>1 Kings</note> through the fourth <note>2 Kings</note>. During the time of Jehoram, Elijah was taken up. Elisha, son of Shaphat, began to prophesy for six years starting when he was forty years old. Then Ahaziah <note>original: "Ochozias"</note> reigned for one year. In his time, Elisha was still prophesying, and with him Abdadonaeus <note>Likely another variation of Obadiah</note>. After him, Athaliah <note>original: "Gotholia"</note>, the mother of Ahaziah, reigned for eight years after killing her brother’s sons; for she was of the lineage of Ahab. But Jehosheba <note>original: "Iesabea"</note>, the sister of Ahaziah, stole away Joash <note>original: "Ioas"</note>, the son of <margin>C</margin> Ahaziah, and later restored the kingdom to him. In the time of this Athaliah, Elisha was still prophesying, and after her Joash reigned—as I said before—who had been saved by Jehosheba, the wife of Jehoiada <note>original: "Iodaeae"</note> the High Priest. The total years for this period come to forty. Therefore, from Solomon until the death of the prophet Elisha, some say there are one hundred and five years; others say one hundred and two. However, the chronology proposed here shows one hundred and eighty-one years from the start of Solomon's reign.

From the time of the Trojan War until the birth of Homer, according to the opinion of Philochorus, there were one hundred and eighty years after the Ionian colony was established. Aristarchus, however, in his *Commentaries on Archilochus*, says he lived at the time of the Ionian migration <margin>so as to encounter him <note>original: "ὥστ’ ἐπιβαλεῖν αὐτῷ"</note></margin> <margin>D</margin> which took place one hundred and forty years after the Trojan times. Apollodorus says it was one hundred years after the Ionian colony was established, when Agesilaus son of Doryssus was King of the Lacedaemonians; so that Lycurgus the lawgiver would have reached him while he was still a young man. Euthymenes, in his *Chronicles*, says he flourished with Hesiod during the time of Acastus, and was born in Chios around the two-hundredth year after the capture of Troy. Archemachus also holds this opinion in the third book of his *History of Euboea*. From this it follows that both he and Hesiod were more recent than the prophet Elisha. 

But if one wishes to follow the grammarian Crates and says that Homer lived around the time of the return of the Heraclidae—eighty years after the fall of Troy—he is still found to be <margin>E</margin> later than Solomon, during whose time Menelaus arrived in Phoenicia, as was said before. Eratosthenes, moreover, places the age of Homer in the one-hundredth year after the fall of Troy. <margin>The Greek text has "in forty-three Philippics," but I think it should read "in the forty-third book of the Philippics," or perhaps "in forty-three by force," that is, in the forty-three as one who does not care to express in which book.</margin> Furthermore, Theopompus, in the forty-third book of his *Philippic History*, reports that Homer lived five hundred years after those who fought at Troy. Euphorion, in his work *On the Aleuadae*, says he lived in the time of Gyges, who began to reign in the eighteenth Olympiad, and whom he also says was the first to be called a tyrant. Sosibius the Laconian, in his description of dates, places Homer in the eighth year of the reign of Charillus, son of Polydectes. Charillus reigned for sixty-four years, followed by his son Nicander for thirty-nine years. They say the first Olympiad was established in his thirty-fourth year, so that Homer would have lived ninety <margin>F</margin> years before the Olympics were established.

After Joash, the kingdom was taken up by his son Amaziah <note>original: "Amasias"</note> for thirty-nine years. He was likewise succeeded by his son Uzziah <note>original: "Ozias"</note> for fifty-two years. He died a leper. In his time, Amos and Isaiah (his son), Hosea <note>original: "Osee"</note> son of Beeri, and Jonah son of Amittai <note>original: "Amathi"</note>—who was from Gath-Hepher—prophesied.

<margin>A</margin> There was also the sign of Jonah <note>The "Sign of Jonah" usually refers to the three days in the whale, symbolizing the resurrection</note>, and Tobias, guided by the Angel Raphael, takes Sarah as his wife after a demon had killed her first seven suitors. # CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

...Arses, three years. The total years of the Persian Kings are collected together as two hundred and thirty-five years. <margin>A</margin> Therefore, when Alexander the Macedonian had removed this Darius <note>Darius III, the last king of the Persian Empire, defeated by Alexander the Great.</note>, he began to reign in the years that were added. In a similar way, the times of the Macedonian Kings are collected as follows:

Alexander, eighteen years. Ptolemy, the son of Lagus, forty years. Ptolemy Philadelphus, twenty-seven years. Then Euergetes, twenty-five years. Then Philopator, seventeen years. After him, Epiphanes, twenty-four years. He was succeeded by Philometor, who reigned thirty-five years. After him, Physcon <note>original: "Fuscon," a nickname meaning "Pot-belly"</note>, twenty-nine years. Then Lathyrus, thirty-six years. Then he who was surnamed Dionysus <note>Ptolemy XII Auletes</note>, twenty-nine years. Last of all, Cleopatra reigned for twenty-two years. After this, there was a reign of the Cappadocians for eighteen days.

The combined times of the Macedonians therefore become three hundred and twelve years and <margin>B</margin> eighteen days. It is shown, then, that those who prophesied in the time of Darius, son of Hystaspes, in the second year of his reign—namely Haggai <note>original: "Aggæum"</note>, Zechariah, and the Angel among the <margin><unclear>e.bi...</unclear></margin> twelve <note>Referring to the "Angel of the Lord" mentioned in the Twelve Minor Prophets</note>—since they prophesied in the first year of the forty-eighth Olympiad <note>A four-year period used by Greeks to reckon time; the 48th Olympiad began in 588 BCE</note>, are more ancient than Pythagoras. Pythagoras is said to have lived in the sixty-second Olympiad, and Thales, who was the most ancient of the Greek Sages, lived around the fiftieth Olympiad. The other Sages who are numbered with Thales lived at the same time, as Andron says in *The Tripod*. Indeed, Heraclitus, being later than Pythagoras, mentions him in his writings.

Thus, beyond controversy, the first Olympiad was more ancient than the age of those Prophets mentioned before, as well as those who are called the "Seven Sages." <margin>C</margin> This first Olympiad is also shown to have occurred four hundred and seven years after the Trojan War <note>original: "Iliacis"</note>. Therefore, it can easily be seen that Solomon, <margin><unclear>...</unclear></margin> who lived in the time of Menelaus (and Menelaus was at Troy), was many years more ancient than the Greek Sages. <margin><unclear>...</unclear></margin> Furthermore, how many years Moses was prior to Solomon has been declared by us in what was said previously.

Alexander, who was surnamed Polyhistor <note>meaning "Very Learned" or "Many-Sided"</note>, wrote some letters in his work *On the Jews*: those of Solomon to Vafres <note>The Pharaoh Apries, known as Hophra in the Bible</note>, King of Egypt, and to the King of the Phoenicians at Tyre, as well as their letters to Solomon. In these, it is shown that Vafres sent him eighty thousand Egyptian men for the building of the temple; the other king sent just as many along with a Tyrian architect <margin>D</margin> named Hyperon <note>Traditionally known as Hiram Abiff</note>, born of a Jewish mother from the tribe of David, as is written there.

Furthermore, Onomacritus the Athenian—to whom are attributed the poems said to be by Orpheus—is found to have lived at the time of the rule of the Peisistratids, around the fiftieth Olympiad. Orpheus was a disciple of Musaeus and sailed with Hercules. Amphion, however, preceded the Trojan War by two generations. Demodocus and Phemius were held in great esteem for their art of playing the lyre after the capture of Troy—the former among the Phaeacians, and the latter among the Suitors.

Indeed, they say that the oracles attributed to Musaeus are actually by Onomacritus. The *Crater* of Orpheus is said to be by Zopyrus of Heraclea, and the *Descent to the Underworld* by Prodicus of Chios. <margin>E</margin> Ion of Chios, in his *Trigramms*, reports that Pythagoras also attributed these works to Orpheus. Epigenes, in his writings on the poetry attributed to Orpheus, says that the *Descent to the Underworld* and the *Sacred Discourse* are by Cercops the Pythagorean, while the *Robe* and the *Physics* are by Brontinus.

Furthermore, some also place Terpander among the ancients. Hellanicus certainly reports him as living in the time of Midas. However, Phanias, placing Lesches of Lesbos before Terpander, reports that Terpander was more recent than Archilochus. <margin><unclear>...</unclear></margin> He says Lesches competed with Arctinus and won. Xanthus the Lydian lived around the eighteenth Olympiad. But as Dionysius says, Thasos was founded around the fifteenth Olympiad, so it is consistent that Archilochus was known after the twentieth Olympiad. He certainly mentions the destruction of the Magnesians which happened shortly before. It is said that Simonides lived in the time of <margin>F</margin> Archilochus, while Callinus was not much older. Archilochus mentions the Magnesians who had perished, but Callinus mentions them as still being in prosperity. Eumelus of Corinth, being older, is said to have lived until the time of Archias, who founded Syracuse. I have been led to say these things because...

# THE STROMATA, BOOK I.

<margin>A</margin> ...four years. From Shem to Abraham, one thousand two hundred and fifty years. From Isaac until the division of the land, six hundred and eleven years. Then, from the Judges until <margin>the allotment of land <note>original: "κληροδοσίαν" (klērodosian)</note></margin> Samuel, four hundred sixty-three years and seven months. After the Judges, the years of the kingdoms totaled five hundred seventy-two years, six months, and ten days. After those times, the years of the Persian kingdom were two hundred thirty-five. Then the Macedonian kingdom, until the death of Antony <note>Mark Antony, whose death marked the end of the Ptolemaic/Macedonian period in Egypt</note>, lasted three hundred twelve years and eighteen days. After that time, the Roman reign until the death of Commodus <note>The Roman Emperor who died in 192 AD, providing a contemporary anchor for Clement’s writing</note> was two hundred twenty-two years. Again, from the seventy-year captivity and the restoration of the people to their fatherland, until the captivity that occurred in the time of Vespasian <note>The destruction of the Temple in 70 AD</note>, four hundred ten years are collected. Finally, from Vespasian until the death of Commodus, there are found one hundred <margin>B</margin> twenty-one years, six months, and twenty-four days. Demetrius <note>Demetrius the Chronographer, a Jewish historian of the 3rd century BC</note> says in his book *On the Kings of Judea* that the tribes of Judah, Benjamin, and Levi were not led away in the captivity by Sennacherib, but that from this captivity until the final one, which Nebuchadnezzar conducted from Jerusalem, there were 138 years and six months. From the time the ten tribes were led away captive from Samaria until Ptolemy IV, there were five hundred seventy-three years and nine months. Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria, the famous Jewish philosopher</note> also wrote of the Kings of the Jews, but differently than Demetrius. Furthermore, Eupolemus <note>A Jewish historian of the 2nd century BC</note> says in a similar work that all the years from Adam until the fifth year of Demetrius (the 12th year of Ptolemy reigning in Egypt) total five thousand one hundred forty-nine years. From the time <margin>C</margin> Moses led the Jews out of Egypt until the aforementioned time, there are two thousand five hundred eighty years. From that time until the Roman Consuls Gaius Domitian and Casianus, one hundred twenty years are collected. Euporus <note>Likely referring to the historian Ephorus</note> and many other historians say there are seventy-five nations and languages, having heard the voice of Moses saying: "All the souls from Jacob who went down into Egypt were seventy-five." However, it appears by true reasoning that the languages or dialects, as they are called, and general modes of speech are seventy-two, as our scriptures hand down. Others are formed through the mixing of two, three, or even more dialects. A <term>dialect</term> is a way of speaking that shows the specific character of a place, or a way of speaking <margin>dialects <note>original: "διάλεκτοι" (dialektoi)</note></margin> that shows the specific or common character of a nation. The Greeks say there are <margin>D</margin> five dialects among them: Attic, Ionic, Doric, Aeolic, and a fifth, "Common"; however, the voices of the Barbarians <note>In the ancient sense, "Barbarian" simply meant any non-Greek speaker</note>, which cannot be easily categorized, are not called dialects but "languages." Plato attributes a certain dialect even to the Gods, mainly conjecturing this from dreams and oracles, and also from those possessed by daemons, who speak neither with their own voice nor dialect, but with that of the daemons who enter them. He also believes that even irrational animals have dialects which those of the same species understand. Thus, when an elephant falls into the mud and cries out, another one present, seeing this, returns a little later leading a herd of elephants and saves the one who fell. They say also that in Libya, if a scorpion <margin>E</margin> does not succeed in stinging a man, it goes away and returns with many others, hanging one from another like a chain <margin>indication <note>original: "μνύιος" (mnuios), likely a corruption of a Greek term for signaling</note></margin>, and so they manage their ambush—these beasts using no obscure nod, nor signaling to one another by shape, but, as I think, by their own dialect. Some others also say that if any fish that is being pulled up escapes by breaking the line, no more fish of that kind will be found that day. The primary and general dialects are indeed "barbaric," and their names are given by nature. For men confess that those prayers are more powerful which are uttered in a barbaric tongue. Furthermore, Plato in the *Cratylus*, wishing to interpret *pyr* <note>original: "πῦρ" (pȳr)</note>, which signifies "fire," says it is a barbaric name. He testifies that the Phrygians call it thus, declining it only slightly. It will not hurt, I think, to also list the times of the Roman <margin>F</margin> Emperors to show the birth of the Savior. Augustus, forty-three years. Tiberius, 22 years. Gaius <note>Caligula</note>, 4 years. Claudius, 14 years. Nero, 14 years. Galba, one year. Vespasian, 10 years. Titus, 3 years. Domitian, 15 years. Nerva, one year. Trajan, 19 years. Hadrian, 21 years. Antoninus <note>Antoninus Pius</note>, 21 years. Similarly, again, Antoninus and Commodus <note>Marcus Aurelius and his son Commodus</note>, 32 years. Totaling...

### CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

...from Augustus until Commodus <note>The Roman Emperor who reigned 180–192 AD</note>, all the years total 222. And the years from Adam until <margin>A</margin> the death of Commodus are 5,783 <note>Clement follows the Septuagint's longer chronology for the early biblical period</note> years, two months, and twelve days.

Some describe the times of the Roman Emperors as follows: Gaius Julius Caesar, three years, four months, and five days. After him, Augustus reigned for 46 years, four months, and one day. Then Tiberius, 26 years, six months, and 19 days. He was succeeded by Gaius Caesar <note>Caligula</note> for three years, ten months, and eight days. Then Claudius, for 14 years, eight months, and 28 days. Nero, 14 years, eight months, and 28 days. Galba, seven months and seven days. Otho, five months and one day. Vitellius, seven months and one day. Vespasian, 11 years, 11 months, and 22 days. Titus, two years and two months. Domitian, 15 years, eight months, and five days. Nerva, one year, four months, and ten days. Trajan, 19 <margin>B</margin> years, seven months, and 15 days. Hadrian, 20 years, ten months, and 28 days. Antoninus <note>Antoninus Pius</note>, 22 years, three months, and seven days. Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, 19 years and 11 days. Commodus, 12 years, nine months, and 14 days. Therefore, from Julius Caesar until the death of Commodus, there are 236 years and six months. 

All the years collected from Romulus, who founded the city <note>Rome</note>, until the death of Commodus, total 753 years and six months. Furthermore, our Lord was born in the 28th year, when they first ordered a census and tax-description to be made in the time of Augustus.

<margin>
Luke 3.
<br/>
Isaiah 71 <note>Likely a reference to Isaiah 61:2; early manuscripts often had different chapter divisions</note>.
</margin>
That this is true is written in the Gospel according to Luke: <margin>C</margin> *In the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, the word of the Lord came upon John, the son of Zechariah.* And again in the same book: *Jesus was about thirty years old when he came to his baptism.* And that he was to preach for only a single year, this also is written: *He has sent me to preach the acceptable year of the Lord.* This was said both by the Prophet and the Gospel. Therefore, the 15th year of Tiberius and the 15th year of Augustus <note>Clement appears to be harmonizing the start of the ministry with the reign of Augustus, or perhaps referring to the 15th year after Augustus's death</note> complete the 30 years until the time he suffered. From the time he suffered until the destruction of Jerusalem, there are 42 years and three months. And from the destruction of Jerusalem until the death of Commodus, there are 128 years, ten months, and three days. Thus, from the birth of the Lord until the death of Commodus, the total years are 189 and one month.

However, there are those who, with even greater curiosity, add not <margin>
Pachon <note>original: "πάχων" (Pachon) — an Egyptian month</note>.
<br/>
Perhaps the name of a month.
<br/>
<br/>
The all-night readers <note>original: "παννυϰτερεύοντες ἀναγνῶται" (pannyctereuontes anagnōstai)</note>.

only the year but also the day of the Lord’s birth, which they say was the 25th of Pachon in the 28th year of Augustus. They say it was the 15th year of Tiberius Caesar, on the 15th day of the month of Tubi <note>Roughly January</note>. Some, however, say it was the 11th of the same month. Regarding his Passion, there are different opinions; some say he suffered in the 16th year of Tiberius Caesar, on the 25th of Phamenoth <note>Roughly March</note>, while others say the 25th of Pharmuthi <note>Roughly April</note>, and others say the 19th of Pharmuthi. Some of them even say he was born on the 24th or 25th of Pharmuthi.

Furthermore, we must also relate to this chronology the days indicated by Daniel from the desolation of Jerusalem. There were seven years and seven months of Vespasian. To these are joined the two years of Otho, Galba, and Vitellius, totaling 17 months and eight days; thus it becomes three years and six months, which is the half of a "Week," just as <margin>E</margin> the Prophet Daniel said. For he said there would be two thousand three hundred days from the time the "abomination" <note>The "abomination of desolation," a prophetic term for the desecration of the Temple</note> stood under Nero against the holy city until its destruction. For thus he showed the statement which follows: *How long shall the vision stand, the sacrifice be taken away, the sin of desolation be given, and the power and the sanctuary be trodden under foot?* And he said to him: *Until the evening, two thousand three hundred days, and the sanctuary shall be cleansed.* These 2,300 days, therefore, make six years and four months, half of which was held by Nero while he possessed the Empire, and it was half of the week; the other half was <margin>F</margin> Vespasian with Otho, Galba, and Vitellius. And therefore Daniel says, *BLESSED is he who shall come to the one thousand three hundred and thirty-five days.* For the war lasted until those days, and after this, it ceased. This number is also shown from the following chapter, which reads: *And from the time of the change of the daily sacrifice, and when the abomination of desolation shall be given, one thousand two hundred and ninety days.*

Let these various accounts of the times, written by many and set forth by us, stand as they are.

They say that the scriptures of both the Law and the Prophets were translated from the Hebrew tongue into the Greek language in the time of Ptolemy, son of Lagos <note>Ptolemy I Soter</note>, or as some say, in the time of the one surnamed Philadelphus <note>Ptolemy II</note>. This occurred after Demetrius Phalereus <note>An Athenian statesman and scholar</note> had applied the greatest care to the matter and took pains to ensure they were translated. For while the Macedonians still held Asia, the King—striving with great zeal to adorn the library at Alexandria, which was under his power, with all possible writings—wished for the prophecies held by the people of Jerusalem to be translated into the Greek tongue. For even during the captivity under King Nebuchadnezzar, when the <margin>D</margin> scriptures had perished, in the time of Artaxerxes, King of the Persians, Ezra the Levite (who had become a priest) was inspired to prophesy, renewing all the ancient scriptures.

Aristobulus <note>A Jewish philosopher of the 2nd century BC who argued that Greek philosophy was derived from the Bible</note>, in his first book to Philometor, writes in these words: "Plato also followed our laws, and he shows clearly enough that he was a diligent student of the things said in them. His lineage, deeds, and life are proclaimed by the scriptures, which are worthy of trust; yet we must also say that Moses, being a Chaldean by remote ancestry, was born in Egypt, as his ancestors had migrated from Babylon to Egypt because of a long-lasting famine. Born in the seventh generation, and educated in a royal manner, he experienced a specific turn of fortune. When the Hebrews in Egypt had grown into a great multitude, the King [Pharaoh] prepared a plot against them; he ordered them to raise the females (for a woman is a weak thing in <margin>F</margin> <margin>to play</margin> war) but to kill the males, as he was suspicious of the strength of the youth. Since the boy [Moses] was born of noble rank, his parents hid and nourished him for three successive months, as natural love overcame the tyrant's cruelty. But later, fearing they might perish along with the child, they took a basket made of the papyrus that grows in those places...

For the science of tending sheep is a preliminary exercise for one who is to lead that most gentle "flock" of men, just as hunting is for those who are naturally warlike. From this occupation, God led him to be the leader of the Hebrew army. Then, the Egyptians were frequently warned, though they often remained foolish. The Hebrews, however, were spectators of the evils others suffered, learning of God’s power without any personal danger. But since the Egyptians did not accept the reports of these powerful effects—being dull-witted and unbelieving due to their folly—then, as the Proverb says, they learned only after the event <note>The sense is "learning the hard way."</note>, and later the Hebrews departed, carrying out a great deal of plunder from the Egyptians. This was not due to greed, as their accusers claim.

Moreover, the cause of the war was just. The Hebrews came to the Egyptians as suppliants due to famine; yet the Egyptians reduced their guests to slavery, forcing them to serve like bondservants without even paying them a wage. <meta>This page continues Clement’s argument that Moses was the first and greatest of all lawgivers and leaders. Having previously discussed his upbringing, Clement now shifts into a philosophical and political analysis of Moses's "royal science," comparing his leadership and military strategy to that of famous Greek and Persian figures.</meta>

->CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA<-

<margin>A</margin> Skill in battle would be a part of the military art, or the science of leading an army. The art of leading an army, in turn, is a branch of the science of ruling. Furthermore, skill in making laws is a part of the science of ruling, as is the faculty of passing judgment. Now, one part of the science of ruling is divine, such as that which comes from God and His holy Son, from whom all good things on earth and all external blessings are supplied, as well as perfect happiness. For he says, **ASK**, and great things will be added to you, and small things too. <note>This "Ask" (Petite) quote is a famous "unwritten saying" of Jesus frequently cited by Clement; it mirrors Matthew 6:33.</note> The second species of kingship, following that administration which is purely rational and <margin>the spirited part of the soul <note>original Greek: "τῷ θυμοειδεῖ τῆς ψυχῆς"</note></margin> divine, is that which uses only the spirited or "irascible" part of the soul in its ruling. By this species, Hercules was king of the Argives, and Alexander was king <margin>B</margin> of the Macedonians. The third species is that which desires only one thing: to win and to overthrow. This type cares very little whether the victory is for good or for evil; this was the style used by the Persians when they made war against Greece. For of anger, one part is merely contentious—which seeks power only to obtain dominance—while the <margin>fond of strife; fond of the noble <note>original Greek: "φιλόνεικον; φιλόκαλον"</note></margin> other is devoted to what is good and honest, where the soul uses its anger toward that which is honorable. The fourth species of kingship is the worst of all, which is established by desires, like the reign of Sardanapalus <note>A legendary Assyrian king often cited in antiquity as the ultimate example of luxury and self-indulgence.</note> and those who set this goal for themselves: to indulge their own lusts to the greatest extent.

Now, for the science of ruling—both that which conquers by virtue and that which conquers by force—the instrument is the science of military formation. This science manifests differently depending on the nature and the material. In the case of weapons and predatory animals, using animate <margin>C</margin> and inanimate things, it is the soul and the mind that do the organizing. But in the case of the soul's disturbances, over which we obtain dominance through virtue, it is <term>reasoning</term> <note>original: "ratiocinatio"</note> that is endowed with the power of organizing. It seals self-control, temperance, holiness, and good knowledge with truth, directing the end toward piety and the worship of God. For to those who use virtue in this way, it is <term>prudence</term> <note>original: "prudentia"</note> that organizes; if it is divine, it is wisdom; if human, it is politics, or the science of governing cities. But the science of ruling encompasses all of these. Therefore, a King is one who rules according to the laws, who is endowed with the science of ruling those who are willing—just as the Lord is, who accepts those who believe in Him and through Him. <margin>Phil. 2.</margin> For God handed over **EVERYTHING**, and subjected all things to Christ, our King, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven, on earth, and under the <margin>D</margin> earth, and every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.

Now, a <term>stratagem</term> <note>original: "Strategema," meaning a military maneuver or trick of leadership.</note>, or the method of leading an army, is contained in three species: caution, boldness, and that which is mixed from both. Each of these <margin>cautious and encircling <note>original Greek: "ἀσφαλεῖ καὶ τῷ περιβόλῳ"</note></margin> is composed of three things: by speech, by deeds, or by both together. All of these may be achieved either by persuading, or by compelling, or by doing injury in taking vengeance on those whom it is expedient to punish, or by doing what is just, or by <margin>interweaving <note>original Greek: "ἐμπλέξας"</note></margin> lying, or by speaking the truth—or even by using some of these at the same time. When the Greeks received all these methods and the knowledge of how to use each from Moses, they received no small benefit.

For the sake of an example, I will mention one or two instances of his generalship. When Moses led the people out, suspecting that the Egyptians would pursue them, he abandoned the short and direct route and <margin>E</margin> turned into the desert, making the journey mostly at night. For there was another <term>Economy</term> <note>original: "Oeconomia," here referring to God's pedagogical plan or management of history.</note> at work, by which the Hebrews were taught through the vast wilderness and a long period of time to believe that there is only one God, having been accustomed to it through moderate endurance. Therefore, Moses's stratagem teaches that one must foresee what is useful before dangers arise, and only then proceed. And indeed, what he suspected came to pass. For the Egyptians pursued them with horses and chariots. But they quickly perished when the sea was divided and overwhelmed them with their horses and chariots, so that no remnants of them remained. After this, a following column of fire (for it went before them) led the Hebrews through an inaccessible region, exercising and leading <margin>F</margin> them by labors and marches toward strength and fortitude. Thus, after they had experienced things that seemed difficult, the goodness of the region toward which he was leading them from the pathless way became apparent. Furthermore, he killed the enemies who had previously occupied the region, putting them to flight after he had invaded them from the wilderness and the rough road (for such is the virtue of a General). For this...

<meta>This page continues Clement’s argument that Moses was the first and greatest of all lawgivers and leaders. # STROMATA, BOOK I.
d iiii

->CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA<-

<margin>A</margin> It was a matter of skill and the science of leading an army to have occupied the enemy's territory. When Miltiades <note>The famous Athenian general who led the Greeks at the Battle of Marathon in 490 BCE.</note>, the commander of the Athenian army who defeated the Persians in the battle at Marathon, observed this, he imitated it in the following way. He led the Athenians by night, making his way through trackless places and deceiving the Barbarians <note>In this context, "Barbarians" refers specifically to the Persians.</note> who were watching him. For Hippias, who had defected from the Athenians, had led the barbarians into Attica and was guarding the advantageous positions he had seized beforehand, because he was familiar with the region. Indeed, it was difficult to escape the notice of Hippias. Therefore, Miltiades rightly made use of both trackless places and the night; having attacked the Persians under the command of Datis, he emerged superior in the contest with those whom he himself led, and managed the affair well and successfully. Furthermore, for Thrasybulus <note>The Athenian leader who overthrew the Thirty Tyrants in 404 BCE.</note>, who was bringing the exiles back from Phyla and wished to remain hidden, a column became his guide. <margin>B</margin> As Thrasybulus was entering through untrodden places at night, when the moon did not shine and the winter sky was dark and appeared gloomy, a fire went before them. After it had led them without any mishap, it vanished where the altar of the *Phosphoros* <note>original: "τῆς φωσφόρου"; translating to "The Light-bringer," a title often associated with the goddess Artemis or Diana.</note> now stands. From this, let our accounts become credible to the Greeks: namely, that the Almighty God is able to make a pillar of fire precede the Hebrews by night, to be the guide of their journey. Furthermore, it is even said in a certain oracle:

->Bacchus is a source of joy to the Thebans, and he is a column.<-

This is from the history found among the Hebrews. Moreover, Euripides says in the *Antiope*:

->Inside the Cowherd, but in the chambers,<-

->The ivy-crowned column of the God Euius,<- <note>"Euius" is an epithet of the god Dionysus or Bacchus.</note>

<margin>C</margin> The column signifies that no image of God can be fashioned. But the illuminated column, besides signifying that an image cannot be fashioned, also signifies the stability and firmness of God, and His immutable light which cannot be represented by a figure. Therefore, before the appearance of images was accurately and perfectly grasped, <margin>installations <note>original: "ἀφιδρύματα" - refers to primitive cult images or sacred objects.</note></margin> the ancients would set up columns and worship them as if they were statues. And for that reason, the author of the *Phoronis* writes thus:

->Callithoe holds the key of the Queen of Olympus,<-

->Of Argive Juno; with fillets and garlands,<-

->She was the first to adorn the Queen's column.<-

Furthermore, the author of the *Europia* signifies that the image of Apollo in Delphi <margin>D</margin> is a column, through these words:

->That we may dedicate the tenth and the first fruits to the God,<-

->From the hallowed seats and the lofty column.<-

<margin>Apollo, as if "without many" [One]. <note>original: "ἀπόλλων quasi ἄνευ πολλῶν. absque multis." Clement uses a common Greek etymology: *A-* (not) + *polloi* (many) = The One God.</note></margin>
Apollo certainly, who is understood mystically through the privation of the many, is the one God. Furthermore, that fire which was like a column, and the fire which entered through trackless places and where no path lay open, is a symbol and sign of the holy Light; this Light passes through the earth and returns again to heaven by the wood <note>In early Christian thought, the "wood" (lignum) frequently refers to the Cross of Christ, which connects earth to heaven.</note>, through which it is also granted to us to see by means of the intellect. Now the philosopher Plato, aided by Moses in the making of laws, criticized the system of administering the Republic of Minos and Lycurgus <margin>E</margin> as those which looked only toward greatness of soul and fortitude. However, he praised as more honorable and more venerable that system which speaks of a "One," and is always directed toward a single decree. For he says it is more fitting for us to philosophize with both strength, honor, and prudence, if, looking toward the dignity of heaven, we use the same judgment concerning the same things, immutably and <margin>without changing one's mind <note>original: "ἀμετανόητος" - unrepentant or steadfast.</note></margin> without any change of mind. Does he not interpret those things said in the law—that we should look toward the one God and do those things which are just—by so commanding? Moreover, he says there are two species of the "Statesman": one, indeed, is the law-giver; the other, however, is the "Statesman" properly so called. <margin>F</margin> And "Statesman" specifically signifies a "craftsman" in the book of the same name <note>Referring to Plato's dialogue, the *Politicus* or *Statesman*.</note>; and those who look toward him, and act rightly, and live justly with contemplation, he also names as "statesmen." That which is called the "political" art, just like the "legislative" art, he divides into the greatness of the mundane mind and into the private order, which he called moderation, harmony, and temperance.

<summary>Clement argues that Greek military tactics and religious symbols (like pillars) were borrowed from or prefigured by the Hebrew Exodus. He then links Moses's divine lawgiving to Plato's political philosophy, suggesting Plato's "Statesman" is modeled on Mosaic principles.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Clement’s argument that Moses was the first and greatest of all lawgivers and leaders. On the previous page, Clement illustrated Moses’s strategic brilliance by comparing him to Greek generals like Miltiades and Thrasybulus. Now, he shifts into a philosophical and theological justification of Moses’s laws, harmonizing them with the ideals of Plato and the teachings of the Apostle Paul.</meta>

### CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

<margin>A</margin> Indeed, rulers must be suited to those they govern, and those who are governed must obey their rulers. Moses strove with great zeal to ensure this occurred. Furthermore, Plato—aided by these ideas—says that "lawful" pertains to generation, while "political" pertains to friendship and harmony. In the *Epinomis* <note>A dialogue traditionally attributed to Plato or one of his students, dealing with the nature of wisdom.</note>, he joined the laws to the philosopher who understands the transitions of all generation occurring through the wandering stars. In the *Republic*, he connects another philosopher, Timaeus—who is skilled in astronomy and the movements of those stars—to the study of their mutual agreement and fellowship. Therefore, I believe the goal of both the politician and the one living according to the law is contemplation. It is necessary, then, to administer the city correctly. However, the best path is to practice philosophy. For the one who is wise lives by <margin>B</margin> referring all things to knowledge, directing his life through good deeds, despising those things which are contrary, and pursuing the disciplines that lead to truth.

Law is not simply whatever is decreed by a legal body—for just as sight is not everything that is seen, law is not just any opinion. It is certainly not a bad opinion; rather, law is a *good* opinion, and a good opinion is one that is true. A good opinion is that which finds what truly exists and attains it. <margin>Exodus 3</margin> Moses says, "**I AM** <note>original: "QUI EST"; referring to the divine name revealed at the burning bush.</note> has sent me." Consequently, regarding this "good opinion," some have said that the law is "right reason" <note>term: *recta ratio* — the Stoic and Platonic idea that true law is derived from universal, divine logic.</note>, which commands what must be done and forbids what must not be done. Hence, it is rightly said that the Law was given through Moses as a rule for the just and the unjust. We might properly call it a <margin>C</margin> <margin>Etymology of *thesmos* <note>original: θεσμοῦ</note></margin> **divine rite** <note>original: "θεσμόν" (*thesmos*); a term for law established by divine decree rather than human agreement.</note>, which was handed down from God through Moses.

It therefore possesses the power to lead one back to God. As Paul also says: <margin>Galatians 3</margin> "**THE LAW WAS ADDED** because of transgressions, until the seed should come to whom the promise was made." Then, as if explaining and following the meaning, he adds: "But before faith came, we were kept under the guard of the law, confined by fear—on account of sins—for the faith that was to be revealed. Therefore, the Law was our **tutor** <note>original: "Pædagogus"; in the ancient world, a trusted slave who supervised a child's conduct and led them to school.</note> to lead us to Christ, so that we might be justified by faith." A skilled lawgiver is one who assigns what is appropriate to each part of the soul and its actions. Moses, to put it simply, was the **living law** <note>original: "lex animata"; the idea that a perfect ruler is the embodiment of divine law.</note>, governed by the good Word <note>original: "verbo" (Logos).</note>.

<margin>D</margin> Thus, he provided a good method for administering the Commonwealth. This method is the good education of humans within society. Furthermore, he handled the judicial faculty, which is the science of correcting sins for the sake of justice. Belonging to the same order is the punitive faculty, which holds the science of moderating punishments. Since there is punishment, there is the correction of the soul. In short, the entire training of Moses consists of teaching those who can be good and honorable, and in "hunting" those who are similar to them—this being the art of ruling. The wisdom of lawgiving consists of the proper use of those things captured by reason and the Word. For it is the specific duty of the "royal science" both to acquire and to use. Therefore, the philosophers proclaim that only the wise man is King, Lawgiver, General, Just, Holy, and a Friend of God. If we find these qualities in Moses, as is shown from the Scriptures themselves, we shall rightly and persuasively say that <margin>E</margin> Moses was truly wise.

Just as we say the "pastoral art" is the care of sheep—for <margin>John 1</margin> "the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep"—so we shall say the art of lawmaking prepares the virtue of men, stirring up human goodness with all its might, as it manages the care and providence of the human flock. If the "flock" mentioned allegorically by the Lord is nothing other than a flock of humans, then the Good Shepherd and the Lawgiver are the same. There is one caretaker for the one flock—namely, for the sheep who hear him— <margin>Luke 15</margin> and he is the one who seeks and finds the lost sheep through law and reason; for the law is spiritual and leads to blessedness itself. That which is made by the Holy Spirit is spiritual. He is the true Lawgiver, who not only professes what is good and honorable but knows it. His law also belongs to the one who has the knowledge <margin>F</margin> of a saving justice—or rather, the Law is the "Just One" of knowledge. For the Reason or **Word of God** <note>original: "Verbum Dei" (Logos).</note> is both power and wisdom. And he himself is again the interpreter of the laws, through whom the law was given; he is the first interpreter of divine precepts, who explains and reveals the bosom of the Father: the Only Begotten Son. Furthermore, those who obey the law because they possess some...

<meta>This page continues Clement’s argument from Page 44, where he established that Moses was the first and greatest lawgiver. He now moves into a polemic against the Greeks who doubt the divine origin of the Mosaic Law, while simultaneously defending the "harshness" of the law as a form of divine medicine.</meta>

## STROMATA BOOK II. 3

<margin>A</margin> ...the knowledge of Him, and they cannot help but believe, nor can they be ignorant of the truth. But as for those who do not believe and have no desire to be found in good deeds and works, they—if anyone—confess that they are ignorant of the truth. What, then, is this unbelief of the Greeks? Why do they refuse to believe the truth which says that the Law was given by God through Moses? This is especially strange since they themselves honor Moses in their own writings. They report that Minos <note>The mythical King of Crete, famous for his wisdom and justice.</note> went to the cave of Jupiter <note>Original: Iouis (Zeus). Clement is comparing Moses's time on Sinai to Greek myths.</note> and received laws from him after a period of nine years. They also write that Lycurgus <note>The legendary lawgiver of Sparta.</note> frequently went to Delphi to learn laws from Apollo. Furthermore, Plato, Ephorus, and Chamaeleon of Heraclea in his work *On Drunkenness*, as well as Aristotle in his *Republic of the Locrians*, have recorded in their literary monuments that Zaleucus of Locri received his laws from Minerva <note>Original: Minerua (Athena).</note>. 

<margin>B</margin> Those Greeks who extol their own laws to make them appear most worthy of trust, attributing them to the gods in imitation of Mosaic prophecy, are ungrateful; they refuse to acknowledge the truth and the archetype <note>Clement argues that Greek culture "plagiarized" its best ideas from the Hebrew scriptures.</note> of the stories they tell. Therefore, let no one attack the law as if it were not good and honorable simply because it carries punishments. For just as someone who removes a disease from the body is seen to perform a kindness, so too the one who tries to free the soul from injustice should be seen as taking even greater care, insofar as the soul is more excellent than the body. For the sake of bodily health, we endure being cut, burned, and drinking bitter medicines; the one who applies these is called both a "savior" and a "physician." The patient does not envy him or wish him ill, even when the logic of the craft dictates that he must cut away certain parts so that the healthy parts do not perish along with them; no one <margin>C</margin> would accuse the physician’s art of being a crime. 

For the sake of the soul, then, shall we not similarly endure exile, or fines, or chains, if only one might be restored from injustice? For the Law, taking care of those who obey it, instructs them in piety toward God, dictates what must be done, and pushes back against every sin, imposing penalties for moderate offenses. However, when the Law sees someone who appears incurable—one who has been carried away into the furthest reaches of injustice—it then takes care of the others, lest they be corrupted by him. Like cutting a limb away from the whole body, the Law puts such a person to death for the ultimate health of all. 

<margin>1 Cor. 11</margin> "But when we are judged by the Lord," says the Apostle, "we are disciplined so that we may not be condemned with the world." <margin>Psalm 117</margin> For the Prophet foretold: "The Lord has surely disciplined me, but He has not given me over to death." <note>Clement is quoting Psalm 118:18 (117 in the Vulgate numbering).</note> To teach you His justice, He "disciplined you," it says, "and tested you, and afflicted you with hunger and thirst in the desert." This was so that all might know His justifications <margin>D</margin> and His judgments in your heart—whatever I command you today—and that you may know in your heart that as a man disciplines his son, so the Lord our God will discipline you. 

Because example corrects us: "The wicked man," it says, "seeing the evil man punished, is himself powerfully disciplined." For the "fear of the Lord is the generation of wisdom." <margin><gloss>to cease from doing ill</gloss> <note>original: "κακῶς πράττειν ἀποπαῦσαι"</note></margin> It is the greatest and most perfect good when someone can lead another away from doing evil and behaving badly toward virtue and good action, which is exactly what the law does. Therefore, even when someone has fallen into an incurable evil, obsessed by injustice and greed, he is actually receiving a benefit if he is put to death. For the Law is beneficent; it can make just men out of the unjust (if only they will listen), and it frees others from present evils. Indeed, it <margin>E</margin> strives to render immortal those who have chosen to live temperately and justly. 

To "know the law" belongs to a good mind. And again: "Evil men do not understand the law, but those who seek the Lord will understand every good thing." It is necessary for the power that administers providence to be both Sovereign <note>Original: Domina, emphasizing authority.</note> and Good. The power of each procures salvation: the former disciplines through punishment as Sovereign, while the latter provides through beneficence as the Good. One is permitted not to be a "son of unbelief," but to pass from darkness to life, and, having adapted oneself to the breath of wisdom, to become a legitimate servant of God—first a servant, then a <margin>F</margin> faithful attendant who fears the Lord God. If anyone ascends further, he is counted among the number of the sons. After charity (love) has covered a multitude of sins through the perfection of blessed hope, he is then permitted—having increased in charity—to be received into the chosen adoption of sons, which is called the "friend of God," already singing his vow and saying: "Let it be..."

<summary>Clement argues that the Mosaic Law is the divine archetype for all Greek lawgiving and defends its use of punishment as a medicinal "benefit" for the soul, comparing the Law to a physician who cuts away a diseased limb to save the body.</summary>

### MISCELLANIES, BOOK I.

...of the knowledge of it, and they are unable to disbelieve or remain ignorant of the truth.

<margin>A</margin> But those who do not believe, and have no desire to be involved in [good] deeds and works, these people—if anyone—confess that they are ignorant of the truth. What, then, is this "Greek incredulity"? Is it a refusal to believe the truth which declares that the Law was given by God through Moses? This is strange, since they themselves honor Moses in their own writings. They report that Minos <note>The mythical King of Crete.</note> went to the cave of Jupiter <note>Original: Iouis (Zeus). Greeks believed Minos received laws from Zeus every nine years.</note> and received laws from him over a nine-year period. They write that Lycurgus <note>The legendary lawgiver of Sparta.</note> frequently went to Delphi to learn laws from Apollo. Furthermore, Plato, Ephorus, and Chamaeleon of Heraclea in his work *On Drunkenness*, as well as Aristotle in his *Republic of the Locrians*, have all recorded in their memoirs that Zaleucus the Locrian received his laws from Minerva <note>Original: Minerua (Athena).</note>.

<margin>B</margin> Those Greeks who extol their own laws to make them seem as credible as possible by tracing them back to the gods—in imitation of the Mosaic prophecy—are ungrateful, for they do not acknowledge the truth and the original model <note>Original: archetypum (archetype). Clement argues that Greek culture is a "plagiarism" of older Hebrew wisdom.</note> of the stories they tell. Therefore, let no one attack the Law as if it were not good or honorable simply because of the punishments it prescribes. For a doctor who removes a disease of the body is seen as a benefactor; in the same way, one who attempts to free the soul from injustice should be seen as providing even greater care, insofar as the soul is more excellent than the body. To restore the health of the body, we endure being cut and cauterized <note>A common ancient medical practice of "firing" a wound to stop infection or bleeding.</note> and drinking bitter medicines; the one who administers these is called both "savior" and "physician." The patient feels no envy or ill-will toward him, even when the doctor, following the rules of his craft, cuts away certain parts so that the healthy parts do not perish with them. No one would accuse the physician's art of being a crime. If this is true for the body, should we not similarly endure exile, or fines, or chains for the sake of the soul, if indeed a person is to be restored from injustice?

<margin>C</margin> [Is it not a benefit to remove] injustice? For the Law, in caring for those who obey it, trains them in piety toward God and dictates what must be done, pushing back against every sin by imposing penalties on those of a moderate nature. However, when the Law sees someone in such a state that they appear "incurable" <note>Original: immedicabilis. A person so committed to evil that they cannot be reformed.</note>—as one who has been driven to the extreme of injustice—then, out of care for the others so they are not corrupted by him, the Law cuts him off like a diseased limb from the whole body and puts him to death in a most "salutary" <note>Clement uses "saluberrime" (most healthfully) to suggest that execution is a "healing" act for society at large.</note> manner.

<margin>A</margin> The Proverbs say: "In all your ways acknowledge her, so that she may direct your ways in a straight path, and your foot may not stumble." <note>Proverbs 3:6. The "her" refers to Wisdom.</note> Through these words, he wishes to show that our deeds must be consistent with our words. Furthermore, he shows that we ought to choose what is useful from every type of instruction. The ways of Wisdom are various, leading us by a straight path toward the way of truth. This way is faith. "Your foot shall not stumble," he says regarding those who seemed to oppose the one and only divine <term>providential administration</term> <note>original: "providentia administrationi"</note>. Whence he adds: "Do not be wise in your own eyes" through impious reasonings that stir up sedition against God's <term>Economy</term> <note>original: "Oeconomiam"; the divine plan or management of the universe</note> and dispensation. Rather, "Fear God, who alone is powerful." It follows that nothing can oppose God. In another sense, logical induction clearly teaches that the fear of God is the turning away from evil. For it says: "And turn away from <margin>B</margin> all evil." This is the discipline of the Lord. "For whom the Lord loves, he chastens," <note>Proverbs 3:11-12; Hebrews 12:6</note> making him suffer so that he might understand, yet restoring him to peace and incorruption. 

<margin>Hebrews 11</margin> Therefore, the <term>Barbarian philosophy</term> <note>Clement's term for the ancient Hebrew and Christian wisdom</note> which we follow is truly perfect and true. Thus it says in the book of Wisdom: "He himself gave me a true <margin>Wisdom 7:17-20 (Margin: Sirach 15)</margin> knowledge of the things that are, that I might know the constitution of the world and the things that follow," up to the point of "the powers of roots." In all these things, he includes the contemplation of nature, which concerns all things made in the sensory world. Next, he also silently signifies those things which are grasped by the intellect through what he adds: "And whatever things are hidden and open, I have known. For Wisdom, the worker of all things, taught me." Here, in a few words, you have what our Wisdom professes. 

<margin>C</margin> The discipline of these things, when practiced alongside a right way of life through the wisdom of the Artificer of all, raises a person toward Him who is the leader and prince of the universe. He is someone difficult to grasp or "hunt down," for He always recedes and stays far from the one who pursues Him. Yet, though He is far off, He moves very close—a truly ineffable thing. <margin>Jeremiah 23</margin> "I am a God who is near," says the Lord. He is far off in His essence <note>original: "essentia"</note>—for how can that which is created approach the Unbegotten?—but He is very near in His power, by which He embraces all things in His bosom. "If anyone does a thing in secret," He says, "shall I not see him?" Indeed, the power of God is always present, seeing us, doing us good, and teaching us by the power that touches us. 

Whence Moses, being persuaded that God could never be known by human <margin>D</margin> <margin>Exodus 33</margin> wisdom, said: "Show yourself to me." He was compelled to enter into the <term>darkness</term> <note>original: "caliginem"; the thick cloud on Mount Sinai</note> where the voice of God was—that is, into the secret and formless notions concerning that which exists. For God is not in the darkness, nor in a place, but above place, and time, and the properties of created things. Therefore, He is never in a part, neither as a container nor as one contained, whether by boundary or by division. <margin>Isaiah 66</margin> "For what house will you build for me?" says the Lord. But He did not even build a house for Himself, since He cannot be contained. And although heaven is called His throne, He is not even contained there, but rests there, delighted by His handiwork. 

It is clear, therefore, that the truth is hidden from us; and if this has been shown by one example, it will be demonstrated by many more shortly. Why should those not be rightfully welcomed who wish to learn, and who, <margin>E</margin> according to the opinion of Solomon, are able to know wisdom and discipline, to understand the reasons of prudence, to receive the <term>subtleties</term> <note>original: "strophas"; can mean turns of phrase or complex arguments</note> of speeches, and to understand true justice? For there is another kind of justice which is not taught from the truth by Greek laws and other <margin>Proverbs 1</margin> philosophers. "And to direct judgments," it says—not judicial ones, but it signifies that we ought to possess a judgment within ourselves that is <margin>law</margin> healthy and free from error. "To give shrewdness to the simple, and to the newborn child, sense and goodwill." For when the wise man hears these things, being persuaded to obey the precepts, he will become wiser through knowledge. He who is intelligent will acquire guidance, and will understand the parable and the obscure word, and the sayings and riddles of the wise. 

<margin>F</margin> For those who are inspired by God do not offer "adulterated" reasons, nor do those who learn from them. Nor do they search the "depths of God" as traps, like the ones many Sophists use to entangle young men. Rather, they are those who attain the things hidden in the prophecies. But it is forbidden to give "holy things to dogs" until the beasts have been tamed. For it is not right to offer [the truth] to the envious and the disturbed...

For this reason, he adds: "Be not wise in your own eyes" through impious reasonings that stir up rebellion against the <term>Economy</term> <note>From the Greek 'oikonomia,' referring to God's plan or management of the universe and salvation history.</note> and dispensation of God. "But fear God, who alone is powerful." It follows from this that nothing can oppose God. Moreover, induction also clearly teaches that the fear of God is the turning away from evil. For he says: "And turn away from 

<margin>B</margin> every evil." This is the discipline of the Lord. "For whom the Lord loves, He corrects," making him feel pain so that he may yet understand, and restoring him to peace and incorruption. Therefore, the <term>Barbarian philosophy</term> <note>Clement's term for the Judeo-Christian tradition, which he defends as older and truer than Greek philosophy.</note> which we follow is in truth perfect <margin>Hebrews 11</margin> and true. Thus, it says in Wisdom <note>Referring to the Book of Wisdom or Ecclesiasticus.</note>: <margin>Ecclesiasticus 15:1-2</margin> "HE HIMSELF gave me a true knowledge of the things that are, that I might know the constitution of the world, and the things that follow thereafter," up to the point: "and the powers of roots." In all these things, he includes <term>natural contemplation</term> <note>The study of the physical world or "physics" as a path to understanding the Creator.</note>, which concerns everything made in the sensory world. Next, he also silently signifies those things which are grasped by the intellect through what he adds: "I have known both what is hidden and what is open. For Wisdom, the artisan of all things, taught me." In these few words, you have what our Wisdom professes.

<margin>C</margin> The discipline of these things, when practiced alongside a right way of life through wisdom—the artisan of all—raises a person toward Him who is the leader and prince of the universe. He is a subject difficult to grasp or "hunt down," for He always withdraws and stays far from the one who pursues Him. Yet, though He is far off, He walks very near—a truly ineffable thing. <margin>Jeremiah 23</margin> "I am a God at hand," says the Lord; He is far off in essence—for how could that which is created approach the Uncreated?—but He is very near in power, by which He embraces all things in His bosom. "If anyone does a thing in secret," He says, "shall I not see him?" Even as He sees, does good, and teaches by the power that touches us, the power of God is always present. Hence Moses, being persuaded that God could never 

<margin>D</margin> be known by human wisdom, says: <margin>Exodus 33</margin> "SHOW yourself to me." And he is compelled to enter into the "thick darkness" where the voice of God was—that is, into the arcane and formless notions concerning that which exists. For God is not in the darkness, nor in a place, but above place and time, and the properties of created things. Therefore, He is never in a part, neither as a container nor as one contained, whether by boundary or by division. <margin>Isaiah 66</margin> "For what house will you build for me?" says the Lord. But He did not even build one for Himself, since He cannot be contained. And although heaven is called His throne, He is not even contained by that; rather, He rests there, delighted by His handiwork. It is clear, then, that the truth is hidden from us; and if this has already been shown by one example, it will be demonstrated by many more shortly. Why then should those not be welcomed who wish to learn, and 

<margin>E</margin> according to the sentiment of Solomon, are able to know wisdom and discipline, to understand the reasons of prudence, to receive the subtleties of speech, and to understand true justice? For there is another kind of justice which is not taught from the truth by Greek laws and other philosophers. <margin>Proverbs 1</margin> "And to direct judgments," he says—not judicial ones, but he signifies that we ought to have a judgment within us that is sound and free from error. "To give shrewdness to the simple, and to the <margin>young</margin> <note>original: νέῳ (neo)</note> child recently born, sense and goodwill." For when the wise man hears these things, being persuaded to obey the precepts, he will become wiser through knowledge. He who is intelligent will acquire guidance, and will understand a parable and a dark saying, and the words and riddles of the wise. For those who are inspired by God do not produce "adulterated" reasonings, nor do those who learn from them. Nor do they 

<margin>F</margin> set traps, with which many Sophists <note>Professional teachers in Greece often criticized for using clever but fallacious arguments.</note> entangle young men, having no time for anything that is true. But those who possess the Holy Spirit search the "deep things of God"—that is, those who attain to the things hidden in the prophecies. However, one is forbidden to give what is holy to "dogs" <note>A reference to Matthew 7:6, warning against sharing sacred mysteries with those who would despise them.</note> as long as they remain beasts. For one should not offer to the envious, the disturbed, and the...

Clement is quoting Proverbs 5:16, warning against sharing sacred mysteries with those who will misuse them.</note> For many who encounter these things do not perceive them. But even when they have learned, they do not truly know, as the eminent Heraclitus says. <note>Heraclitus was a pre-Socratic Greek philosopher known for his paradoxical views on the difficulty of human understanding.</note> Does he not also seem to you to be rebuking those who do not believe? "But my **JUST** man shall live by faith," said the Prophet. <note>Habakkuk 2:4.</note> And another Prophet also says: "**UNLESS** you believe, you shall not understand." <note>Isaiah 7:9. In the Greek version of the Old Testament used by Clement, this verse emphasizes that faith is the foundation of intellectual understanding.</note> For how could the soul grasp the wonderful and supernatural contemplation of these things if an inner unbelief fights against learning them?

<margin>Hebrews 11.</margin>
Now faith, which the Greeks slander—deeming it empty and "barbarian"—is a voluntary anticipation, an assent of piety, "the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen," as the divine Apostle <note>Saint Paul, specifically referring to the definition of faith in Hebrews 11:1.</note> has declared. For by it, especially, the elders received their testimony. "But **WITHOUT** faith it is impossible to please God." Others, however, have defined faith as the coming assent to a thing that is not apparent—just as, certainly, demonstration is the manifest assent to a thing that was previously unknown. **B**

<margin>Faith is the principle of action, the foundation of choice.</margin>
If, therefore, a voluntary choice is the longing for something, then this desire is currently engaged in the mind. Since the principle of action is voluntary choice, faith is found to be the principle of action and the foundation of prudent choice; for someone first demonstrates something to the mind through faith. To be willing to follow that which is useful is the beginning of wisdom. Therefore, voluntary choice, which cannot be torn away, brings a great momentum toward knowledge.

Indeed, the meditation on faith becomes science <note>In this context, 'science' or 'scientia' refers to certain, systematized knowledge rather than modern laboratory science.</note> when it rests upon a stable and firm foundation. **C** Philosophers therefore define science as a "habit" <note>An internal disposition or state of being.</note> which cannot be shifted by reason. There is, then, another such true state of piety and the worship of God, for which reason is the only teacher.

<margin>Theophrastus.</margin>
It is not I, but—as I believe—Theophrastus <note>The successor to Aristotle in the Peripatetic school.</note> who says that sensation is the principle of faith. For from sensation, the principles are extended to that reason and thought which reside within us.

<margin>John 20.</margin>
Therefore, he who has believed the divine scriptures, possessing a firm judgment that cannot be contradicted, receives the voice of Him who gave the scriptures as a demonstration. Faith is not, then, fortified by demonstration. "Blessed, therefore, are those who have not seen and yet have believed." <note>John 20:29.</note> Even the songs of the Sirens <note>Mythical creatures whose songs were irresistible to sailors.</note> were effective, showing a power more than human, and they amazed those who encountered them, leading them to receive what was being said almost against their will.

Here, the followers of Basilides **D** consider faith to be "natural," insofar as they place it even within [the soul's] choice, so that it might discover teachings through intelligent comprehension without the need for demonstration. The Valentinians, <note>Basilidians and Valentinians were Gnostic groups who believed that salvation was determined by one's inherent "nature" rather than by free choice.</note> however, while they attribute "faith" to us "simple" people, wish "knowledge" to belong to themselves—those who are saved by nature—claiming it arises from the abundance of an "excellent seed," and saying that this knowledge is as far separated from faith as the spiritual is from the animal. Furthermore, the Basilideans say that faith and choice are specific to each "spatial realm," and that a worldly faith for all nature follows as a consequence of a super-mundane choice, and that the gift of faith is appropriate to the measure of each person's hope.

If faith is merely a natural advantage, then it is not a duty of voluntary and free **E** choice; nor would it follow that there is a just reward, nor a fault for the one who did not believe (since he was not the cause), nor for the one who did believe (who was also not the cause). Every characteristic and difference of faith and unbelief would be subject to neither praise nor blame for those who consider it rightly, since it would possess a preceding natural necessity originating from Him who is all-powerful.

But if we are pulled by natural operations like ropes, as if we were inanimate objects, then that which is involuntary is superfluous, as is the desire that precedes it. Nor do I understand how that could be a "living being" whose power of desiring (which is moved by an external cause) has been dictated by necessity.

<margin>Repentance. Baptism. The Blessed Seal.</margin>
Where then is the repentance of him who was once an unbeliever, through which comes the remission of sins? For this reason, neither is baptism consistent with reason, nor the "blessed seal," <note>A common early Christian term for the sacrament of Baptism or Confirmation.</note> nor the Son, nor the **F** Father; instead, they hold what is, in my opinion, an impious distribution of "natures" which does not have voluntary faith as the foundation of salvation.

But we—who have received from the scriptures that the power to choose and to avoid has been given to men by the Lord with free and absolute authority—[act] by a judgment which...

<summary>Clement defines faith as a voluntary act of the will and the necessary foundation for all knowledge, refuting Gnostic thinkers who argued that faith and salvation are biologically or "naturally" predetermined.</summary>

<meta>Clement continues his bridge-building between Greek philosophy and Christian faith. # CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA
<header>CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA</header>

<margin>
Epicurus
Anticipation <note>original: πρόληψις</note>
To think <note>original: νοεῖν</note>
To grasp <note>original: καταλαβειν</note>
</margin>
...let us know; it is therefore a faithful knowledge. Moreover, divine faith can be known through a certain sequence <sig>A</sig> and mutual consequence. Indeed, even Epicurus—who prioritized pleasure above the truth—considers faith to be an **anticipation** of thought. He defines **anticipation** as an application toward something evident, leading to an evident understanding of a thing. He argues that no one can seek, doubt, or even hold an opinion, much less prove or argue anything, without this "anticipation." For how could anyone learn about the thing they seek if they do not already have an anticipation of what they desire? He who has learned has already turned his anticipation into a comprehension. If, therefore, the learner does not learn without an anticipation that allows him to receive what is being said, then he must possess ears gifted with the faculty of hearing the truth. "Blessed is he who speaks into the ears of those who hear," just as surely as he who practices obedience is blessed. To "hear," however, <sig>B</sig> is to understand. If, then, faith is nothing other than an anticipation of the mind regarding the things being said—and if this "saying" results in obedience, and this "understanding" in persuasion—then no one can learn without faith, because no one can learn without anticipation. Therefore, what was spoken by the Prophet is shown to be entirely true: <margin>Isa. 6.</margin> **UNLESS** you believe, you shall not understand. <note>original: "NISI credideritis, non intelligetis." This is a famous Latin rendering of Isaiah 7:9 from the Septuagint, which Clement frequently uses to show that faith must precede intellectual grasp.</note>

<margin>Heraclitus.</margin>
Heraclitus of Ephesus also alluded to this when he said: **UNLESS** one hopes, one will not find that which is unhoped-for, since it is both inscrutable and has no path leading to it.

<margin>Plato.</margin>
Furthermore, Plato the Philosopher says in *The Laws* that he who is to be blessed and happy must be a partaker of the truth from the beginning, so that, being true, he may live for the longest time. For such a man is faithful. But the unfaithful man is he who delights in voluntary falsehood; whereas he who is involuntarily false is mindless—and a mindless man is not truly a human being. <note>Plato suggests that the "unwillingly" ignorant are like animals rather than men.</note> Neither state is to be desired. <sig>C</sig> For whoever is unfaithful and ignorant is ungrateful. <margin>friendless <note>original: ἀφίλος</note></margin> Perhaps in the *Euthydemus* you might say he secretly identifies this as "royal wisdom"? Certainly in the *Statesman* <note>original: Politico</note> he uses these words: "Therefore, the royal wisdom belongs to the true King; and he who possesses it, whether he be a ruler or a private citizen, shall be rightly called **royal** <note>original: βασιλικὸς</note>—that is, Kingly, or skilled in the art of reigning—entirely because of this art."

Now, those who have believed in Christ are—and are called—"of Christ," which is to say "of the Anointed One," just as those who are truly Royal are the concern of the King. For just as the wise are wise by wisdom, and those who are just are just by right, <margin>lawful by law <note>original: νόμῳ νόμιμοι</note></margin> so also are kings made by Christ the King; and those who belong to Christ are Christians. Then, a little further down, he clearly adds: "That which is right shall be legitimate; and the law, since it is nature, is right reason, and exists neither in writings nor in anything else." And the Eleatic Stranger <note>A character in Plato's dialogues.</note> pronounces the Royal and political man to be a **living law**. <sig>D</sig> Such a person is one who fulfills the law and does the will of the Father, clearly inscribed upon a high wooden tablet <note>original: ligno. Clement likely alludes to the Cross here.</note>, displayed as an exemplar of divine power to those who are able to see clearly. 

The Greeks know that the *scytalae* <note>Cylindrical batons used by Spartan officials (Ephors) to communicate or record laws.</note> of the Spartan Ephors were laws inscribed on wood. But my Law, as was said before, is both royal and living, and is right reason itself. "Law is the King of all mortals and immortals," as Pindar of Boeotia sings. 

<margin>Speusippus.</margin>
Speusippus, in his first book *Against Cleophon*, seems to say things similar to Plato, writing thus: "For if kingship is a good thing, and only the wise man is a King and ruler, then the Law, being right reason, must also be good." Such is the state of these matters. Following this, the Stoic philosophers <sig>E</sig> establish that kingship, priesthood, prophecy, the science of legislation, wealth, true beauty, nobility, and freedom belong to the wise man alone. Yet they themselves admit that such a man is difficult to find. 

It appears, therefore, that all the dogmas mentioned above were handed down to the Greeks by the great Moses. Moses teaches through these things that "all things belong to the wise man," and because "God has had mercy on me, I have all things." He signifies that such a man is a friend to God, saying: "The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob." Indeed, Abraham is found clearly called a "friend." <margin>Exo. 33.</margin> He who sees God is shown to have had his name changed; and Isaac, like a consecrated victim, was allegorically chosen for himself as a type of the future economy of salvation. Even the Greeks celebrate King Minos, <sig>F</sig> who for nine years lived in familiarity with Jove <note>The Roman name for Zeus.</note>, having heard how God spoke with Moses "as a man speaks with his friend." 

Moses, then, was a wise man, a king, and a legislator. But our Savior surpasses all human nature. He is beautiful indeed, so that He alone may be loved by us who desire true beauty; for He was...
