<meta>Clement continues his argument from the previous page, where he established that faith is a form of "anticipation" or "prior knowledge" necessary for any learning. He now moves to identify Christ as the ultimate source of this truth—the King, Priest, and Lawgiver—while demonstrating how Greek philosophers like Plato and Xenocrates inadvertently supported these Christian doctrines regarding wealth, virtue, and the primacy of faith.</meta>

# STROMATA, BOOK II.

<margin>A</margin> ...the true light. But he is revealed as King, called so by unlearned children, by the unbelieving and ignorant Jews, and proclaimed by the Prophets themselves. He is so truly wealthy that he despised all the gold—and everything upon and under the earth—that was offered to him with all glory by the adversary <note>The "adversary" refers to the Devil, specifically the temptation of Christ in the wilderness.</note>. What does it profit to say that he is the only High Priest <note>original: "Pontifex"</note>, who alone holds the worship of God through true knowledge? He is Melchizedek, the King of Peace, who alone is the most fit of all to rule over the human race. He is also the Lawgiver, as the one who gives the law through the mouths of the Prophets, most clearly commanding and teaching what must be done and what must be avoided. Who could be more noble than him, whose only father is God?

Now, come, let us show that Plato also supports these same dogmas. In the *Phaedrus*, he said that the wise man is truly wealthy, saying: "O beloved Pan, and whatever other gods are present here, <margin>B</margin> grant that I may be beautiful in my inner self, and that whatever I have outwardly may be friendly to my inner qualities; may I consider the wise man to be the truly wealthy one." Furthermore, the Athenian Guest <note>Clement refers to the main speaker in Plato’s "Laws".</note>, rebuking those who thought that people possessing much money were the wealthy ones, says: "But for people to be both extremely wealthy and extremely good is impossible—at least for those whom the common crowd counts as rich." He speaks of those who possess the highest value in a few things, while even a wicked man may possess common riches. **A FAITHFUL MAN** possesses a whole world of wealth, says Solomon, but for the unfaithful, there is not even a penny. Therefore, the Scripture is much more to be believed when it says that it would be <margin>easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle, etc. Matthew 19. Mark 10.</margin> easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to "philosophize" <note>Clement adapts the Gospel verse "enter the kingdom of God" to "philosophize," suggesting that true wisdom is inaccessible to those obsessed with wealth.</note>. 

On the other hand, Plato considers the poor to be blessed, as he understood it, saying: "Poverty <margin>C</margin> should be measured not by the diminishing of one's resources, but by the increase of one's greed." For poverty is not a lack of money, but an insatiable desire. If that greed recedes, the one who is good will also be wealthy. And in the *Alcibiades*, he calls vice a slavish thing, but virtue a liberal or "free" thing. **TAKE AWAY**, says the Scripture, the heavy yoke from yourselves, and take up the light one—just as the poets also speak of a "servile yoke." And that phrase, "you were sold to your sins," agrees with what was said before. Therefore, everyone who commits sin is a slave. But he who is a slave does not remain in the house forever. <margin>John 8.</margin> But if the Son sets you free, you shall be free indeed, and the truth shall set you free.

The Athenian Guest also says that the wise man is beautiful in this way: "If anyone affirms that the just, even if they are deformed <margin>D</margin> in body, are beautiful insofar as their character is most just, such a statement would almost certainly not be seen as an error." And the prophecy foretold of Christ: <margin>Isaiah 53.</margin> "His appearance was diminished beyond all the sons of men." 

Furthermore, Plato called the wise man a King in the *Statesman* <note>original: "Politicus"</note>, as has already been mentioned. Having demonstrated these points, let us return to our undertaken discourse on faith. Indeed, Plato also shows through every demonstration that faith is necessary everywhere. "From you comes peace together." For a faithful and sincere man in times of unrest would never exist without all virtue. Many mercenaries are willing to die in war, yet most of them are bold, unjust, insolent, and lacking in prudence, with very few exceptions. If these things are said correctly, any legislator of any importance, looking <margin>E</margin> primarily toward the greatest virtue, will enact laws. That virtue is **faithfulness** <note>original: "fidelitas"</note>, which we need at all times: in peace, in war, and throughout the rest of our entire lives. For it seems to contain the other virtues within it. What is best, however, is not war or civil strife; we should pray not to have need of those. Peace with one another and goodwill is by far the best thing. 

From these points, it is clear that having peace is most desirable according to Plato's opinion, but the greatest mother of the virtues is faith. It was rightly said, therefore, by Solomon: "Wisdom is in the mouth of the faithful." For Xenocrates also, in his book *On Prudence*, says that wisdom is the science of first causes and of the essence which is perceived by the intellect. He considers there to be two types of prudence: one concerned with action, and the other with contemplation, <margin>F</margin> which he says is human wisdom. Wherefore, while wisdom is indeed a form of prudence, not every prudence is wisdom. 

It has been shown, however, that the knowledge of the principle of all things is held by faith, and not by demonstration. For it would be absurd if the followers of Pythagoras the Samian, having refused to ask for the reasons of the things they sought...

Just as playing with a ball depends not only on the person who throws the ball, but also requires someone to catch it with rhythm so that the exercise of the game is carried out according to the rules of the ball; so too, for teaching to be trustworthy, it happens when the faith of those who hear—which is, to put it simply, a natural art—contributes to the instruction. Thus, fertile earth also assists in the dropping of seeds. Therefore, since there are two kinds of vice—one which acts with fraud and secrecy, and the other which brings and draws with force—the divine Word cried out, calling everyone at once. It is necessary that this expectation be "faithful." A faithful person is one who keeps those things handed down to him without transgression. To us, the things said about God and the divine words—namely the commandments—are handed down along with the execution of the precepts. This is the "faithful servant" praised by the Lord. When God is called "faithful," it signifies that He is worthy of being believed by anyone making a declaration.

How then can faith be a mere opinion or estimation? For the Philosophers consider the things they say to be firm. Faith is not an opinion or estimation, which is a voluntary assent to a preceding demonstration, but an assent to something valid and powerful. And who could be more powerful than God? Unbelief, however, is a weak [assent] to that which is opposite...

### THE MISCELLANIES, BOOK II.

<margin>Expectation. Confidence.</margin>
**A** ...a weak, declarative opinion or estimation, just as the difficulty in believing which is called **unbelief** <note>original: "ἀπιστία" (*apistia*)</note> is a habit that accepts faith only with difficulty. Indeed, faith is a voluntary estimation and an anticipation of a prudent preconception. **Expectation**, however, is an opinion of the future. The expectation held by others is an opinion of what is uncertain. **Confidence** <note>or "trust," from the Latin *fiducia*</note> is a firm apprehension of something. Therefore, we believe in Him in whom we have placed our confidence for divine glory and salvation. We have placed our confidence in God alone, whom we know will not transgress those things which were beautifully promised to us, and thus created and kindly given to us by Him. Now, **benevolence** is the wishing of good things to another for that person’s own sake. For He lacks nothing. But toward us, benevolence is defined as

<margin>Benevolence.</margin>
**B** beneficence; it is the kindness from the Lord, since it is divine benevolence, and a benevolence directed toward doing good. For we are Israelites, who believe not through signs, but through hearing. Therefore, "rejoice, O barren one who does not bear; break forth and shout," He says, "you who are not in labor, for many more are the children of the desolate than of her who has a husband" <note>Quoting Isaiah 54:1 and Galatians 4:27 to show the growth of the Gentile church</note>. <margin>Isaiah 54. Galatians 4. Into the fullness <note>original: "εἰς τὸ πλήρωμα"</note>.</margin>

For this reason, the Apostle also says in the Epistle to the Romans: "For the **righteousness** of God is revealed in it from faith to one faith," which is perfected from Prophecy into the Gospel by one and the same Lord, teaching salvation. "This command," he says, "I entrust to you, son Timothy, according to the prophecies previously made concerning you, that by them you may wage the good warfare, having faith and a good conscience, which some, having rejected, have suffered shipwreck concerning the faith," because they polluted the conscience that comes from God with unbelief. <margin>Vision <note>original: "ὅραμα"</note>.</margin>
**D** criticized as something easy, common, or belonging to just anyone. For if it were a human pursuit, as the Greeks thought, it would have been extinguished. He does not create faith himself; rather, he who is worthy of faith is proven by faith itself. Such a change is therefore divine, so that he who was made faithful from unbelief might also believe in hope and fear.

Therefore, the helpers of our faith are fear and endurance, while those who bring us aid are long-suffering and self-control. As long as these remain chaste in things pertaining to the Lord, he says, wisdom, understanding, science, and knowledge rejoice together with them. Since, therefore, the previously mentioned virtues

# CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

<margin>An assertion of fear against those who speak ill of the law.</margin>
...but they accuse the matter itself; they attack the law. Yet if they attack the law, it is clear that they also attack the one who gave the law. <margin>A</margin> For these three things must necessarily exist in a relationship: the one who administers, the administration, and the thing that is administered. If, therefore, they remove the law through their positioning, it follows necessarily that every person led by desire, yielding to pleasure, will neglect that which is right and honorable. Such a person would despise God and, being without fear, would be simultaneously impious and unjust, having leaped away from the truth. 

But surely, they say, fear is a "deviation from reason" and a "perturbation of the mind." <note>This was a common Stoic definition of passion/emotion as something to be avoided.</note> What are you saying? How can this definition be maintained further when a precept has been given to me through reason or the Word? <margin>The precept pronounces fear.</margin> The precept pronounces fear through discipline, preparing the one who receives it to be corrected. Therefore, fear is not alien to reason; rather, it is in accordance with reason. For why should it not be, when it exhorts: "You shall not kill, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal, you shall not bear false witness"? <margin>B</margin> <margin>Critolaus of Phaselis.</margin> But if they cleverly devise names, let the philosophers call the fear of the law <term>εὐλάβειαν</term> <note>original: *eulabeia*; meaning "caution," "reverence," or "discretion."</note>, which is a deviation from harm in accordance with reason. Critolaus of Phaselis <note>A 2nd-century BCE Peripatetic philosopher.</note> not ineptly called such people <term>ὀνοματομάχους</term> <note>original: *onomatomachous*; meaning "those who fight over names."</note>. Thus, the precept appeared beautiful—and indeed most beautiful—to those who accuse us, once they devised a change of name. Caution, then, is shown to be in accordance with reason, since it is a turning away from that which harms, from which arises repentance for the sins that preceded it. <margin>Psalm 110. "They do."</margin> For "the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom. A good understanding have all those who practice it." <note>Clement is quoting Psalm 111:10 (110 in the Vulgate). The Greek margin note *poiousin* refers to "doing" or "practicing" the law.</note> He calls "wisdom" the realization which is the fear of the Lord, leading <margin>C</margin> toward wisdom. 

If, however, the law brings fear, then the beginning of wisdom is the knowledge of the law, and no one is wise without the law. Therefore, those who reject the law are fools, and it follows that they themselves are considered <term>ἄθεοι</term> <note>original: *atheoi*; meaning "godless" or "impious."</note>. Discipline, moreover, is the beginning of wisdom. But "fools despise wisdom and discipline," says the Scripture. 

Let us see, however, what things the law announces are to be feared. <margin>What things are to be feared.</margin> If it were those things that are "indifferent" <note>A Stoic term for things that are neither virtuous nor vicious in themselves.</note> between virtue and vice—such as poverty, disease, disgrace, or low birth—these are the sorts of things praised by those proposing the laws of a city, and by the Peripatetics, who introduce three types of goods and consider their opposites to be evils. <margin>To the winged ones.</margin> But the law given to us commands us to flee those things that are truly evil: adultery, petulance, the pursuit of boys, <margin>D</margin> ignorance, injustice, and the sickness of the soul, which is death—not the death that separates the soul from the body, but that which dissolves the soul from the truth. <margin>Storing up material things. Certain heresies say the law is evil.</margin> For these are the grave and truly fearful vices, along with the actions that proceed from them. Truly, however, the divine responses say that "the nets are spread in vain for the winged ones." <note>A reference to Proverbs 1:17.</note> For they themselves, while they are partakers of blood, hide away evils for themselves like a treasure. 

How then is the law still called "evil" by some heresies, who cry out that the Apostle says: "For through the law comes the knowledge of sin"? <note>Quoting Paul in Romans 3:20.</note> To them we say: the law did not *create* sin, but *revealed* it. For since it commanded the things that are to be done, it rebuked those things that are not to be done. It is the mark of a good person to teach what is healthy and show what is destructive, advising the use of the former and commanding the flight from the latter. <margin>A passage of the Apostle in the Epistle to the Romans.</margin> <margin>E</margin> Now the Apostle, whom they do not understand, said that the knowledge of sin was made manifest through the law, but not that it received its substance from it. How is the law not good, which educates and chastises, and which was given as a <margin>Pedagogically.</margin> Pedagogue <note>original: *Pædagogus*; a tutor or guardian who led a child to school.</note> to Christ? Thus, while we are directed by the reason of chastisement through fear, we may be converted to that perfection which is through Christ. 

"I do not wish," He says, "for the death <margin>Ezekiel 18. Repentance is effected by the precept.</margin> of the sinner, but for his repentance." <note>Ezekiel 18:23.</note> Now the precept effects repentance, for it prohibits those things that are not to be done, while it holds out good deeds. But by "death," I believe, He means ignorance. And "he who is near the Lord is full of lashes." <margin>Instructed.</margin> That is, he who draws near to knowledge makes use of dangers, fears, troubles, and afflictions for the sake of the desire for truth. <margin>Writings of Barnabas the Apostle.</margin> "For a chastised son turned out wise, and an intelligent son was saved from the heat." <note>A paraphrase of Proverbs 13.</note> An intelligent son will respect the precepts. <margin>F</margin> And the Apostle Barnabas says: "Woe to those who are intelligent in their own eyes, and knowing in their own presence." And a little later he added: "Let us be made spiritual, a perfect temple for God; as much as it is in us, let us meditate on the fear of God, and let us strive to keep His precepts..."

# STROMATA, BOOK II.

<margin>A</margin> ...let us give thanks, that we may rejoice in his justifications. Hence it was divinely said that the "fear of God is the beginning of wisdom." <margin>of Phasis</margin> <note>Likely referring to the philosopher Critolaus of Phaselis mentioned previously.</note> Here the followers of Basilides <note>Basilides was a 2nd-century Gnostic teacher in Alexandria who taught a complex cosmology involving various levels of existence.</note>, explaining this saying, claim that the Prince <note>The "Prince" or Archon refers to the Demiurge, the lesser deity who created the physical world in Gnostic systems.</note> himself, when he heard the voice of the ministering spirit, was struck with amazement by what he heard and saw, since the Gospel was announced to him beyond his expectation. They claim his amazement was called "fear," which became the "beginning of wisdom," a wisdom that distinguishes between kinds, discerns, perfects, and restores. <margin>distinguishing kinds. over all.</margin> For once he had distinguished not only the world but also the "election" <note>The "election" refers to the spiritual elite or "pneumatics" who are destined for salvation in Gnostic thought.</note>, he finally sends it away. Valentinus also seems to have grasped something similar in a certain letter. For he writes in these words: "And so, through that creation, he was struck with terror," <margin>B</margin> "and became the author of the angels, when he spoke greater things than were suited to the creation, <margin>he was for the angels.</margin> because of the one who had invisibly placed in him the seed of the higher essence, and spoke freely." So also in the generations of worldly men, the works of men became objects of fear to those who made them: just as statues and images, and all things the hands produce in the name of God. For Adam, formed in the name of "Man," provided fear of the "Pre-existent Man," <note>Referring to the "Anthropos," a divine archetype in Gnostic myth.</note> as if he himself were established within him; and they were struck with amazement, and quickly destroyed the work. But since there is only one Principle, as will be shown shortly, these men seem to be fashioning musical nonsense and fables. However, because it seemed useful to God that men should first be instructed and corrected by the Law and the Prophets: the fear of the Lord was called the beginning of wisdom—that fear which was given by the <margin>C</margin> Lord through Moses to those who are disobedient and hard of heart. <margin>Fear tames those whom reason does not conquer.</margin> For those whom reason does not conquer, fear tames. When the Word, who instructs and corrects, foresaw this from on high, He fashioned this instrument, purging them for piety in both ways, aptly and conveniently. Therefore, "amazement" is fear arising from an unusual vision or appearance, or because of an unexpected sight, like a message. <margin>What is amazement? *ekplēxis*</margin> But "fear" is a profound admiration, as if for something that has been done or exists. They do not notice, therefore, that they have made the greatest God (whom they celebrate) subject to affections and disturbances through this "amazement." Furthermore, they imply He was in ignorance before the amazement, since ignorance must exist before amazement. If "amazement" and "fear" were the beginning of God's wisdom, <margin>D</margin> there is a great danger that ignorance was the cause even before God's wisdom and the creation of the whole world—and even before the restoration and the "election" itself. Is this ignorance, then, of good things or of bad things? If it is of good things, then by that amazement, the ministry, the preaching, and baptism all cease. But if it is of bad things: how can evil be the cause of the best things? <margin>scrutiny.</margin> For if ignorance had not come first, the minister would not have descended. Nor would amazement have seized the Prince, as they say; nor would the beginning of wisdom have started from fear for the "election" and the judgment of worldly things. If the fear of the "Pre-existent Man" made the Angels who fashioned him into plotters against their own creation—because a seed of the invisible higher substance was placed within the work—then they were either moved by a hollow opinion (which is incredible) or driven by envy <margin>E</margin> against the Angels, on account of the workmanship of which they were believed to be the authors (as if of a son), so that no ignorance fails to fall upon them; or they were moved while held by foreknowledge. But they would not have plotted, through what they attempted, against that which they foreknew; nor would they have been struck with amazement by their own work, if they had understood the "seed" from foreknowledge; nor finally, relying on knowledge, would they have dared to do what cannot be done, since they had learned that the one in the Pleroma <note>The *Pleroma* is the "fullness" or totality of the divine powers in Gnostic theology.</note> was plotting against man. Moreover, they assumed that which is "according to the image" (in which the archetype also exists) and that which, along with the rest of knowledge, is alien to destruction. <margin>the Pleroma.</margin> To these very people, and to some others—especially the Marcionists <note>Followers of Marcion, who rejected the Old Testament God as a lesser, vengeful deity distinct from the Father of Jesus.</note>—the Scripture cries out to those who will not hear:

> "BUT he who hears me shall rest confident in peace, and shall cease from all evil without fear."

<margin>F</margin> What, then, do these people want the Law to be? They will not say it is evil, but rather "just," distinguishing the "good" from the "just." But the Lord, commanding us to fear evil, does not liberate us from evil by evil, but dissolves the contrary by its contrary. Now, evil is the contrary to good, just as the unjust is contrary to the just. If, therefore, he said the beginning of the removal of evils is the "absence of fear" which the fear of the Lord produces: then fear is a good thing, and the fear that comes from the Law is good; for...

# CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

# CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

<margin side="left">A</margin>
...a just operation. But for those who consider themselves wise—whether they be of the barbarian <note>In this context, Clement refers to non-Greek groups, including Christians and Jews, though he is here likely critiquing heretical groups.</note> heresies or the Greek philosophers—"knowledge puffs up," according to the words of the Apostle.
<margin side="left">1 Cor. 8.</margin>
True knowledge, however, is that which consists of the science of demonstrating those things which are handed down in the true philosophy. We might say that such a demonstration is a discourse which produces faith concerning doubtful matters from those things which are certain and beyond controversy. Since faith is twofold—one kind arising from science and the other from opinion—nothing prevents there being a twofold demonstration as well: one from science, and the other from opinion. For knowledge <note>original: *cognitio*</note> and foreknowledge are also called twofold: one which is accurate and exact in its nature, and the other which is defective. But is not that demonstration alone true which is found among us, supplied as it is from the divine scriptures, the sacred letters, and from that wisdom which is taught by God,

<margin side="left">B</margin>
<margin side="left">Mark 4. Luke 17. Matt 9.</margin>
as the Apostle says? Therefore, discipline and obeying the precepts—which is to believe in God—and faith, which is the power of God and the strength of truth, immediately says: *if you have faith as a grain of mustard seed, you shall move a mountain.* And again: *according to your faith let it be done unto you.* Thus, one is cured by receiving healing through faith, while the dead man rises again through the power of the one who had believed that he would rise.

But the demonstration which is from opinion is human, consisting of rhetorical arguments or even dialectical syllogisms. For the supreme demonstration, which we have shown to be from science, produces faith through the citation and opening of the scriptures to the minds of those who desire to learn, which constitutes true knowledge. <margin side="left">C</margin> For if the premises assumed for the matter under inquiry are taken as true, being divine and prophetic, it is certainly clear that the conclusion drawn from them will also be true, and thus demonstration will rightly be knowledge for us.

<margin side="left">Exod. 17.</margin>

This is, I believe, the true and just measure from God, which measures those things that come into dimension: the "Decad" <note>The number ten, signifying completion.</note> which contains the man, which the three previously mentioned measures signified in summary. This would include the body, the soul, the five senses, the power of speech, the procreative power, and the intellectual or spiritual faculty—or whatever other name you wish to call it. It is necessary, to put it in a single word, that we transcend all other things and stand firm in the mind; just as in the universe, when we have leaped beyond the nine parts—first the one consisting of the four elements (placed in one category due to their changeability), then the seven wandering stars <margin side="left">E</margin> [planets], and the ninth, the non-wandering sphere—we come to the perfect number which is above the gods <note>Likely referring to celestial powers or planetary spirits.</note>, namely the tenth part; and, to say it once, to the knowledge of God, desiring the Creator after the creature.

For this reason, tenths <note>Tithes</note> of the ephah and of the sacrifices were offered to God, and the feast of the Passover began from the tenth day, which represents the transition from every disturbance and every sensible thing. Therefore, he who is endowed with the power of knowing stands firm by faith. But he who considers himself wise does not reach the things of truth, using weak and unstable impulses. <margin side="left">F</margin>

Rightly, therefore, it is written: *And Cain went out from the face of God, and dwelt in the land of Naid, opposite Eden.* The interpretation of "Naid" is "fluctuation" <note>Nod, often interpreted as wandering or tossing.</note>. "Eden," however, means "delights." Faith, knowledge, and peace are delights, and he who does not listen to them is cast out. He who considers himself wise does not even wish to hear the divine precepts, but as one who has learned for himself, he is carried away unbridled into the tossing <margin side="left">G</margin> billows, descending toward mortal things and those subject to birth, away from the knowledge of the Unbegotten, holding now one opinion, now another. <margin>A</margin> The principal part of the soul, and that which leads and rules it, is called its governor <note>original: *gubernator*, a translation of the Greek term *hegemonikon*, referring to the ruling part of the mind</note>. <margin>Genesis 18. Exo. 34.</margin> For in truth, it is an unchangeable leading toward that which is unchangeable. Thus Abraham stood upright before the Lord, and approaching, he spoke. And it is said to Moses: "But you, stand here with me." The followers of Simon <note>Simon Magus, a sorcerer mentioned in the Book of Acts, whom later writers identified as a father of heresies</note>, however, wish to become like the "Standing One" <note>The "Standing One" was a title Simon Magus used for himself to suggest his own divinity and permanence</note> whom they worship in their conduct. Therefore, faith and the knowledge of truth bring it about that the soul which has received them remains in the same state and is always similarly disposed. But transition, turning away, and failure are joined by kinship to falsehood, just as tranquility, rest, and peace are joined to the power of knowing. Therefore, just as arrogance and a boastful self-persuasion pursue philosophy, so also false knowledge—which is called so by a misleading name—pursues true knowledge.

<margin>B</margin> <margin>2. Tim. 1.</margin> Concerning this, the Apostle writes: "O Timothy, guard the deposit, avoiding the profane novelties of words and the oppositions of knowledge falsely so called, which some, promising, have fallen away concerning the faith." <margin>The Epistles of Paul to Timothy were not approved by the Heretics because they were convicted by them.</margin> Since Heretics are convicted by this statement, they reject the epistles to Timothy. Come then, if the Lord is truth, and wisdom, and the power of God, as indeed he is: let it be shown that he who has known him, and through him his father, is truly endowed with the power of knowing. <margin>Prov. 10.</margin> For he perceives together with the one who speaks. **THE LIPS** of the righteous know high things. <margin>Faith is twofold: of things past and things future.</margin> Since faith, just like time, is twofold, we find two virtues that live together. For memory belongs to the time which is past, while hope belongs to that which is future. For we believe that past things occurred, and that those things which are future will be. And again, we love, being persuaded by faith that past things are so, and expecting future things through hope. For love has persuaded the one endowed with the power of knowing of all things, as one who knows the one God.

<margin>C</margin> **AND** behold, all things whatsoever he had built were very good; and he knows and admires them. <margin>godly-piety <note>original: *theosebeia*</note></margin> Piety adds length to life, and the fear of the Lord adds days. Therefore, just as days are part of a life that continues to ascend, so also fear is the beginning of love, which comes through the increase of faith, and then love. But I do not fear a father whom I fear and love in the same way I fear and hate a wild beast. Again, fearing lest I be punished, I love myself, choosing fear. He who fears to offend a father loves himself. Blessed therefore is he who is found faithful, tempered by love and fear. Faith is a virtue leading to salvation, and a power leading to eternal life.

<margin>D</margin> Again, Prophecy is foreknowledge, but knowledge is the understanding of prophecy. It is like the knowledge of those things which were previously known to them from the Lord, who manifests all things beforehand. Therefore, the knowledge of those things which were predicted shows a threefold outcome: either that which was once, or that which is now present, or that which is to come. Then the extremes fall under faith, either of those things which are completed or those which are hoped for. However, to confirm both extremes, present operation brings persuasion. For if, since prophecy is one, one part of it is being perfected while another part has been fulfilled, from this both that which is hoped for and the truth of what has passed become credible. For it was previously present, then it passed for us, so that there is even a faith of past things—the comprehension of the past—and a future hope, the comprehension of a future thing.

<margin>E</margin> Not only the Platonists, but also the Stoics say that assents <note>original: *assensiones*, referring to the mental act of accepting something as true</note> are in our own power. Therefore, every opinion, and judgment, and estimation, and discipline by which we live, and are always with the human race, is an assent. And this would be nothing other than faith. <margin>loss of understanding, non-existence, but I read it as "of non-existence" <note>This marginal note seems to be a philological correction of a Greek term in the source text</note></margin> And incredulity or infidelity, which is the undoing or destruction of faith, shows that assent or faith can exist. For there would be no deprivation of that which could not exist. And if one considers the truth, he will find that a man is indeed spoken ill of because he assents to what is false; yet he has many things which move and incite him to true faith. Therefore, that which contains the Church, as "The Pastor" <note>A reference to *The Shepherd of Hermas*, an early Christian work popular in Clement's time</note> says, is the virtue of self-control. ### CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

<margin>examining/torturing <note>original: βασανίσων (basanisōn). This refers to the soul’s painful self-examination during penance.</note> Forgiveness of sins differs from repentance.</margin>
<margin>The first repentance is before baptism.</margin>
<margin>A</margin> ...restored the reading. Moreover, the fear of the devil's works also possesses a cohabiting hatred <note>Meaning that true fear of evil results in a natural hatred for it.</note>. He likewise says that repentance is a "great understanding." For he who is moved by repentance for what he has done, no longer does or says such things. Instead, by examining <note>original: *torquens*, literally "twisting" or "torturing"</note> his soul for the sins he committed, he performs good deeds. Therefore, the forgiveness of sins differs from repentance. Yet he shows that both are within our power. It is necessary, then, for him who has received the forgiveness of sins to sin no more; specifically, in that first and only repentance for sins, which was for those committed in the former life as a Gentile. That repentance purges the place of the soul from sins so that faith may be established as a foundation. Since the Lord is the knower of hearts and foreknows the future, he saw from the beginning the human tendency toward easy change and the inclination to return [to sin], as well as the cunning of the devil from on high. The devil, <margin>B</margin> envying man because of the forgiveness of sins, suggests certain causes of sin to the servants of God, craftily striving so that they might also fall along with him. Therefore, since He is of great mercy, He has granted a second repentance even to those who, being in the faith, fall into some sin. <margin>Second repentance after baptism.</margin> If anyone is tempted after their calling, being forced or cleverly circumvented, they have received one "un-repented-of" repentance <note>A technical term from the *Shepherd of Hermas* meaning a single, final opportunity for penance after the washing of baptism.</note>. For if we sin willfully after we have received the knowledge of the truth, there <margin>Hebrews 10.</margin> no longer remains a sacrifice for sins, but a certain fearful expectation of judgment and a zeal of fire which is to devour the adversaries. Continuous repentances that follow one after another <margin>Successive <note>original: ἐπάλληλοι (epallēloi)</note>. The difference between those who have not believed and those who stumble in the faith.</margin> because of sins differ in no way from those who have not believed at all, except only in the fact that they realized they were sinning. I do not know which is <margin>C</margin> worse: to sin knowingly and with foresight, or, having been moved by repentance for past sins, to sin once again. For sin is made manifest because it is rebuked on both sides: the former is condemned because it was done by a worker of iniquity; the latter because he who foreknows what is to be done approaches it as an evil. The former perhaps obeys anger or pleasure, not being ignorant of what he is indulging; but the latter, who returned to pleasure after being moved by repentance for having indulged in it, is joined to him who sins willfully from the beginning. For he who performs again the very thing he previously condemned—having been moved by repentance—does so by his own choice. Thus, the man from the Gentiles who was stirred to faith from his former life obtained forgiveness of sins once. But he who <margin>D</margin> sins even afterward, and then is moved by repentance—even if he obtains pardon—ought to feel shame, <margin>One who sins after baptism and repents, even if he obtains pardon, is no longer washed for the forgiveness of sins. It is not true repentance to seek pardon often for sins we often commit.</margin> as one who is no longer washed for the forgiveness of sins <note>Referring to the belief that the "washing" of Baptism is a unique, unrepeatable event.</note>. For it is necessary not only to abandon the idols he formerly held as gods, but also the deeds of his former life; he who is not born of blood, nor of the pleasure of the flesh, but is regenerated in the spirit, should be led by repentance in such a way that he does not roll back into the same sin. For to repent often, and to have a readiness for easy change due to a lack of discipline, is merely a rehearsal of sins. Therefore, to frequently seek pardon for things we frequently commit appears to be repentance, but is not.

JUSTICE, moreover, protects the ways that are free from reproach. <margin>Proverbs 13. Psalm 103. Psalm 126. Psalm 112. Psalm 49.</margin> And again: "The justice of the innocent man shall direct his way." Furthermore, as a father <margin>E</margin> has mercy on his children, the Lord has had mercy on those who fear him, as David writes. Therefore, those who sow in tears shall reap in joy—speaking of those who make confession in repentance. "For blessed are all who fear the Lord." You see a similar beatitude in the Gospel. "Fear not," it says, "when a man becomes rich, and when the glory of his house is multiplied. For when he dies, he shall take nothing with him; nor shall his glory descend with him." "But I, in your mercy, will enter into your house; I will worship at your holy temple in your fear. O Lord, lead me in your justice." Indeed, fear is an impulse of the mind toward something or away from something. But an "affection" or "passion" <note>original: *perturbatio*, used here to translate the Greek *pathos*</note> is an excessive impulse, either one that extends beyond the measures of reason, or an impulse that is carried away and does not obey <margin>On free will.</margin> reason. Therefore, movements of the soul that are contrary to nature, arising from that disobedience to reason, are passions. <margin>F</margin> Furthermore, defection, withdrawal, and disobedience are in our power, just as obedience is also in our power. Wherefore...

<summary>Clement discusses the doctrine of "second repentance," explaining that while baptism offers a total washing of past sins, those who stumble afterward have only one additional opportunity for formal penance. He also defines the passions as impulses that disobey reason and asserts the reality of human free will.</summary>

### MISCELLANIES, BOOK II.
ff ii

<margin>A</margin> ...voluntary acts are also judged. Indeed, if one were to examine every disturbance of the soul, they would find them to be alien to reason. Therefore, that which is <margin>The involuntary is twofold.</margin> involuntary is not judged. This is of two kinds: one which happens through ignorance, and the other through necessity. For how can you judge those who are said to sin in involuntary ways? Either a person was ignorant of themselves, like Cleomenes and Athemas who were seized by madness; or they were ignorant of the thing they were doing, like Aeschylus, who spoke of the mysteries <note>The Eleusinian Mysteries, which were sacred secrets.</note> on stage and was acquitted in the court of the Areopagus <note>The high court of Athens.</note> when he proved he had never been initiated into the mysteries. Or perhaps a person is ignorant of the actual deed, such as one who threw a projectile at an opponent but killed a family member instead, mistaking him for an enemy. Or they are ignorant of the instrument, such as one who practices with blunt-tipped <margin>B</margin> spears but kills someone because the spear-head flew off. Or they might be ignorant of the manner of doing it, such as one who kills an opponent in the stadium; for he did not fight to kill, but to win. Or they might be ignorant of the purpose for which the act is done, such as a doctor who gives a healthy antidote and yet kills the patient; he did not give it for that reason, but to save him. Indeed, the law used to punish even those who killed unintentionally, just as it did those who suffered from involuntary bodily discharges, but not in the same way as those who did so by choice. However, even such a person will be punished as if for a voluntary act if they allow their soul’s disturbance to overcome the truth. For in reality, he who is "incontinent of the procreative word" <note>original: *verbi genitalis*. This likely refers to a lack of spiritual discipline or loose speech.</note> deserves punishment, as this is an affection of the soul alien to reason, which comes close to useless chatter. But the faithful man chooses to "conceal matters in the spirit." Therefore, those things undertaken by choice and election are punished. For the Lord <margin>C</margin> searches the hearts and kidneys, and he who looks with lust is judged. For this reason He also says, "Do not covet." And "This people," He says, "honors me with their lips, but their heart <margin>Exodus 20.</margin> is far from me." For God looks upon the intention. For even Lot’s wife, who <margin>Mark 10; Genesis 19; <note>original Greek: λίθον ἁλάτινον (pillar of salt)</note></margin> turned back toward worldly vice of her own will, He left as a senseless thing, making her a pillar of salt. He set her there to go no further, not as a foolish or useless statue, but as one who could "season" and "confirm" those who are able to see spiritually. Now, a voluntary act is either that which comes from desire, or from purpose and choice, or from deliberate thought. These three things are situated close to one another in a certain way: sin, misfortune, and crime (or an unjust deed). <margin><note>original Greek: ἁμάρτημα (sin/error). ἀτύχημα (misfortune). ἀδίκημα (crime/unjust deed).</note></margin> <margin>D</margin> Sin is, for example, to live luxuriously and intemperately. Misfortune is to kill a friend unknowingly, as if he were an enemy. Crime is the digging up of graves or sacrilege. It is established that "to sin" comes from not knowing how to judge what one ought to do—just as someone might fall into a ditch either because they did not know it was there, or because they were unable to jump over it due to physical weakness. But it is certainly within our power to be led to our own discipline and to obey the commandments; for unless we wish to be participants, giving ourselves over to anger and pleasure, we will sin—or rather, we will inflict injury upon our own souls. For the character Laius says in the tragedy:

> None of these warnings were hidden from me at all.
> Yet nature brings force upon me, though I know better.

<margin>E</margin> That is, he gives himself over to the disturbance of his soul. Medea herself cries out similarly on the stage:

> I know well what evils I am about to do.
> But my anger is more powerful than my plan.

Nor is Ajax silent, but as he is about to lay hands on himself, he cries out:

> There is no matter that so bites the mind 
> Of a free man as unfair and unjust infamy.
> I myself have been so affected; a thick stain,
> Stirred from the depths, involves me
<margin>F</margin> > Driven by the sharpest stings of madness.

And while anger drives these men, desire drives countless others into tragedy, such as Phaedra, Anthia, and Eriphyle:

> Who had accepted the precious gold for her beloved. <note>Refers to Eriphyle, who betrayed her husband for a golden necklace.</note>

Quæ

<summary>Clement distinguishes between voluntary and involuntary actions, arguing that while accidents and ignorance may lessen guilt, the soul is ultimately judged by its internal intentions and its ability to govern its passions.</summary>

### THE MISCELLANIES, BOOK II

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>The ancient saying "Follow God," and where it was taken from.</margin>
...until that point, and "there was no one who sought, or turned away." <note>original: "et non erat qui requireret, nec auerteret"</note> For there is great joy with the Father when one sinner is saved, says the Lord. For that reason, Abraham is even more to be praised, because he walked just as the Lord had spoken to him. Since one of the wise men of the Greeks had drawn from this source, he brought forth that famous saying, "Follow God." <note>original: "Deum sequere"; a maxim often attributed to the Seven Sages or Pythagoras</note> "But the pious," says Isaiah, "have consulted wisdom regarding the things that are." <note>Isaiah 32:8</note> Now, "counsel" is an inquiry into how we might rightly conduct ourselves in present circumstances. <term>εὐβουλία</term> <note>original: "euboulia"; good counsel or sound deliberation</note> however, is prudence in deliberation. Furthermore, did not God also, after granting pardon to Cain, shortly thereafter introduce Enoch, who had been led by repentance? This signifies that repentance is accustomed to generate pardon.

<margin>B</margin>

<margin>
The ancient saying: "Pardon is better than punishment," and where it was taken from.
"Give a pledge, and ruin is at hand," and where it was taken from.
Proverbs 6.
"Know thyself," and where it was taken from.

Pardon <note>original: "venia"</note> does not consist of mere remission, but of a healing remedy. This very thing occurred with Aaron during the fashioning of the [golden] calf. From this, one of the Greek sages said, "Pardon is better than punishment," <note>attributed to Pittacus of Mytilene</note> just as surely as that other saying: "Give a pledge, and ruin is at hand," <note>original: "Sponde, noxa præsto est"</note> which comes from the voice of Solomon saying: "My son, if you become surety for your friend, you will hand over your hand to an enemy." <note>Proverbs 6:1</note> For a strong snare to a fault is one's own lips, and one is caught by the words of one's own mouth. And what was taken from there is now more mystically expressed by Paul as: "Know thyself." If you have seen your brother, you have seen your God. For by this logic, you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and your neighbor as yourself. He says that on these commandments depend the whole law and the prophets. These also harmonize with the words: "These things I have spoken to you that my joy might be fulfilled." <note>John 15:11</note> "And this is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you," for the Lord Christ is merciful and compassionate to all.

<margin>
Sins are purged by almsgiving and faith.

Joys.
<unclear>ἀχάμιοι</unclear> <note>The Greek term in the margin is unclear; likely referring to a specific group or a corruption of "those without joy."</note>
</margin>
Moses, commanding that "Know thyself" more openly, often says: "Take heed to yourself." Therefore, by almsgiving and faith, sins are purged. But by the fear of the Lord, everyone turns away from evil. "The fear of the Lord is discipline and wisdom." <note>Proverbs 1:7</note> Here again, accusers arise, saying that joy and sadness are perturbations of the soul. For they define "joy" as an elevation [of the soul] consistent with reason, and "to exult" as to rejoice because of things that are good; but "mercy" they define as sadness on account of one who suffers evils unworthily. They claim that such things are changes and movements of the soul. <note>Clement is referencing Stoic definitions of emotions/passions.</note>

<margin>D</margin>
<margin>Matthew 12.</margin>
But we, it seems, do not cease to understand these things carnally, deducing the Scriptures from our own mental affections, and assuming the will of the impassible God <note>original: "Dei impatibilis"; the theological concept that God does not suffer or feel human passions</note> is similar to our own movements. If we think that the Almighty possesses feelings in the same way we hear them described, we fall into impious error. Rather, the Prophets spoke to us in the way we—who are bound in the flesh—were able to hear, the Lord healthfully accommodating and lowering Himself to the weakness of men. Therefore, since it is God's will that he who obeys the commandments and is led by repentance for his sins should be saved, and since we rejoice because of our own salvation, the Lord (who spoke through the Prophets) attributed to Himself that which brings us joy, just as He speaks in human terms in the Gospel: "I was hungry, and you gave me to eat; I was thirsty, and you gave me to drink. For what you did for one of these least, you did for me." <note>Matthew 25:35-40</note> Just as, therefore, He is nourished who is not [literally] nourished, because the one whom He wills is nourished; so too He, without being changed, rejoiced because the one who was led by repentance rejoiced, as He willed.

<margin>E</margin>
<margin>Abundantly.</margin>
Because God is abundantly merciful since He is good, giving commandments through the law and the Prophets, and now more closely through the coming of the Son, He saves and pities those whom He has pitied. Properly speaking, a greater person pities a lesser one. And while no man is "greater" than another man insofar as he is born human, God is greater than man in all things. If, therefore, the one who is greater pities the lesser, only God will have mercy on us. For a man becomes [merciful] through justice, freely sharing and imparting those things which he received from God, both because of natural benevolence and disposition, and because of the commandments he obeys. But God has no "natural" disposition or relation <note>original: "habitudinem seu relationem"</note> toward us, as the founders of heresies <note>Likely referring to Gnostics who claimed humans are consubstantial with God.</note> would have it—not even if He makes us from nothing, or fashions us from matter.

<margin>F</margin>
Indeed, since that [nothingness] does not exist at all, and this [matter] is different from God in every way—unless one dares to say that matter is a part of Him, and that we are of the same essence <note>original: "essentię"; Greek: ousis</note> as God. I do not know how anyone who accepts this could endure to say they "know God," seeing that our lives are turned toward such evils. For if that were the case, it would mean—which is a wicked thing to say—[that God sins].

He also refutes the Gnostic idea that humans share the same essence as God, maintaining the distinction between the Creator and the created.</summary>

# CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

<margin>A</margin>
...to say, God sinning in individual parts: since parts are parts of a whole, and they complete the whole. But if they do not complete it, they would not even be parts. But in truth, since God is by nature rich in mercy, He takes care of us because of His goodness—we who are neither parts of Him nor His children by nature. And this is certainly the greatest proof of God's goodness toward us: that even though we behave this way toward Him, and are by nature completely alien to Him, He nevertheless takes care of us. A natural affection exists in living creatures toward their own offspring, and a friendship arises from habit among those who share the same mind. But God's mercy toward us is abundant, we who have nothing to do with Him, neither in our essence, I say, nor in our nature, nor in the specific power of our essence, but only in the fact that we are the work of His will.

<margin>B</margin>
And so, for the one who has voluntarily received the knowledge of the *truth* through practice and teaching, He calls this *adoption*, which is the greatest progress of all; but "iniquities seize the wicked," <margin>Proverbs 5</margin> and each person is bound by the chains of their own sins, and the cause for these is not to be attributed to God. And truly "blessed is the man who fears all things" for the sake of piety. <margin><term>scientific habit</term> <note>original: "ἐπιστητικὴ ἕξις" (epistētikē hexis); a stable philosophical disposition for knowledge</note></margin> Therefore, just as knowledge is a habit that creates stability, from which "to know" happens (and for which there is a comprehension that cannot be moved by reason), so also ignorance is a fading imagination <margin><term>dwelling within</term> <note>original: "συνοικημένον" (synoikēmenon); something that has taken up residence in the mind</note></margin> or vision, which can be moved by reason. But what is moved, like that which is established and confirmed by reason, is in our own power. Associated with knowledge are experience, and what is called in Greek *eidesis* <note>original: "εἴδησις"; a seeing or perceiving of forms</note> and *epinoia* <note>original: "ἐπίνοια"; reflection or conception</note> and intelligence, and recognition. And *eidesis* would be the knowledge of all things through their specific form.

<margin>C</margin>
Experience, however, is a comprehensive knowledge, so that it even diligently investigates the quality of each thing. Intelligence is the knowledge of that which is understood by the mind. And *synesis* <note>original: "σύνεσις"; understanding or sagacity</note> is the knowledge of that which is comparable, or a comparison that cannot be moved, or the comparative faculty of those things which belong to prudence and knowledge—both of each individual thing and of all things which are brought into a single reason. Recognition is the knowledge of that which is knowledge itself, or the knowledge that corresponds to existing things. Truth, however, is the knowledge of what is true. The habit of truth is the knowledge of true things. Knowledge consists through reason, and cannot be moved by another reason, <margin><term>investigates</term> <note>original: "πολυπραγμονεῖ" (polypragmonei); to be a busybody or to inquire deeply</note></margin> and here he diligently inquires about recognition. Now, those things which we do not do, we either do not do because we cannot, or because we do not want to, or because of both.

<margin>D</margin>
We do not want to, therefore, because we neither can nor want to. For example, we do not swim right now because we *can*, but we do not *want* to. We are not, however, like the Lord, because we *want* to be, but we *cannot*. For "no disciple is above his master." It is enough, however, if we have been made like the Lord—not in essence. For it is impossible for that which exists by adoption to be equal in essence to that which exists by nature; but rather, it is because we have been made eternal, and have known the contemplation of the things that exist, and have been called children, and see the Father only from those things which are <margin><term>from His own</term> <note>original: "ἀπὸ τῶν οἰκείων" (apo tōn oikeiōn); from His related attributes or household</note></margin> joined to Him. Therefore, the "will" precedes everything. For the rational faculties are the ministers of that "will." "Will it," he says, "and you shall be able." For the one who is endowed with the power of knowing, the will, the judgment, and the practice are all one and the same.

<margin>E</margin>
For if the propositions are the same, the dogmas and judgments are also the same, so that the words, life, and character are consistent with the established argument <margin><term>He introduces</term> <note>original: "τῆς εἰσάγει" (tēs eisagei)</note></margin>. "The upright heart seeks out knowledge," and hears them. "God taught me wisdom, and I have known the knowledge of the saints." It is clear, therefore, that all the other virtues written in the books of Moses provided the Greeks with the starting point for the entire field of ethics: I mean the virtue of greatness of soul, temperance, prudence, justice, courage, endurance, honesty, self-control, and that which surpasses religion.

<margin>F</margin>
But religion <margin><term>of those things upon these</term> <note>original: "τῶν ἐπὶ τούτοις" (tōn epi toutois)</note></margin> is manifest to anyone; it teaches us to worship and honor the supreme and most ancient Cause. The same Law also displays justice, teaching even prudence through abstinence from sensible idols, and a calling toward the Maker and Source of the universe; from this source, like a fountain, every insight of judgment is increased. "For the sacrifices of the wicked are an abomination to the Lord. But the vows of those who walk in the right way are accepted by Him." For justice is more acceptable to God than sacrifice.

<summary>Clement argues that humans are God's children through adoption and His will rather than being "parts" of His essence. He defines various levels of philosophical knowledge and asserts that the Greek ethical virtues were originally derived from the laws of Moses.</summary>

# THE MISCELLANIES, BOOK II

<margin>Isaiah 1</margin>
**A** Similar points are also found in the writings of Isaiah: 
> "What to me is the multitude of your sacrifices, and the whole burnt offerings of rams?" and the rest that follows. "Loose every bond of wickedness." 

For this is the sacrifice acceptable to God: a heart that is contrite and seeks the One who formed it. 
<margin>Pythagoras's saying: "Do not step over the balance." Proverbs 11. Proverbs 10. *Phaulos* <note>original Greek: "φαῦλος" meaning base, cheap, or easy-to-do evil.</note></margin>
> "A deceitful balance is an abomination before the Lord, but a just weight is acceptable to the Lord." 

From this, Pythagoras advises "not to step over the balance." <note>This Pythagorean maxim was a common ancient metaphor for not overstepping the bounds of justice.</note> Furthermore, the "deceitful justice" mentioned refers to the public profession of heresies. 
> "And the tongue of the unrighteous shall perish, but the mouth of the righteous distills wisdom." 

Yet, for their part, the "wise" and "prudent" of the world call such people fools. It would be a long task to bring forward all the testimonies concerning these virtues, since the entirety of Scripture celebrates them. Since the great-souled define the virtue of **magnanimity** <note>original: "magni animi virtutem," translating the Greek *megalopsychia*</note> as the knowledge of things that are serious, things that are not serious, and things that are intermediate; and **temperance** <note>original: "temperantiam"</note> as a stable habit which, by choosing and avoiding, preserves the judgments of prudence; there is added to this virtue of a great and lofty soul also 
<margin>*Hypexairesis* <note>original: "ὑπεξαίρεσις," a Stoic term for "acting with a reservation" or exception.</note> *Megalopsychia* <note>original: "μεγαλοψυχία," greatness of soul.</note></margin>
**B** **tolerance**—which they call **fortitude**, the knowledge of what is to be endured and what is not—and a loftiness of mind, which is the knowledge of the things that happen, rising above them. Furthermore, to temperance is added **caution**, which is a rational turning away from evil. The **guarding of the commandments**, being a harmless observation of them, is the acquisition of a secure life. Nor can anyone be "tolerant" without the virtue of a great soul, nor "continent" <note>self-controlled</note> without temperance. These virtues follow one another in turn, and in whomever these consequences of the virtues are found, in him also is **salvation**, which is the preservation of that which is in a right state.

<margin>Gnostically <note>original: "γνωτικῶς," meaning with the insight of a true knower or Gnostic.</note></margin>
**C** Therefore, it is right that if we have treated these virtues so far, we have considered them all, because he who possesses one virtue through knowledge possesses them all through their mutual connection. Now, **continence** is an internal state that does not overstep what has been judged by right reason. The "continent" person is he who restrains those desires that are contrary to right reason, or who restrains himself so that he is not carried away by desire beyond right reason. But temperance itself does not exist without the virtue of a great soul, since it arises from the commandments, following the God who ordained them, and from **prudence**, and from that **justice** which imitates the divine state. Through this justice, we are made continent and cleansed for piety and religion; following God, we aim toward action, becoming assimilated to the Lord as far as is possible for us who are fleeting and subject to death. 

<margin>*Epikourois* <note>original: "ἐπικούροις," referring to the Epicureans.</note></margin>
**D** This goal is to become just and holy with prudence. For God is in need of nothing and is "impassible" <note>incapable of suffering or being moved by passion</note>. Hence, He is not "continent" in the strict sense, for no passion or disturbance ever falls upon Him such that He would need to overcome it. But our nature, which is subject to passions and disturbances of the soul, has need of continence. Through this exercise, as we learn to need few things, our habit of life attempts to approach the divine nature. For a good man needs few things, as one who stands on the border between a mortal and immortal nature; he is needy because of the body and the process of birth, but he is taught to need little because of the continence he has adopted through reason. 

<margin>Deuteronomy 22</margin>
For what reason does the Law forbid a man to wear a woman's garment? Does it not want us to be "men," and to be effeminated neither in body, nor in deeds, nor in mind, nor in words? It wants him to be masculine who devotes himself to the truth, in enduring labors and sufferings, in life and character, and in speech and training, by night and by day—and even if there should be a need for testimony or **martyrdom**, which proceeds through blood. Again, if someone, 
<margin>Deuteronomy 24. Exempt from military service.</margin>
**E** says the Law, has recently built a house and not yet lived in it; or has planted a new vineyard and not yet shared in the fruit; or has betrothed a virgin and not yet married her: the human law wants these men to be exempt from military service. It does this prudently, as befits a Commander, so that we do not engage in the work of warfare with a cowardly or dejected soul while we are being pulled away by our desires. For those who go into any grave danger without excuse are free from such cravings. But speaking in human terms, since you consider the uncertain outcomes of war, the Law deemed it unjust that while one man did not enjoy his own labors, another should receive the fruits of those who labored 
**F** without any labor of his own. The Law also seems to indicate **greatness of soul**, establishing that it is proper for the one who planted to receive the fruit, the one who built to live there, and the one who courted the girl to take her as his wife. For to those who have trained themselves, hope does not render their efforts vain, based on the reason of their knowledge.

He argues that the Mosaic Law’s prohibitions—such as cross-dressing and military exemptions—are actually spiritual lessons designed to foster a "masculine" soul focused on God and martyrdom.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: On the previous page, Clement began a systematic defense of Christian ethics, defining virtues like magnanimity and temperance. This page continues that argument by showing how the Mosaic Law (the Old Testament law) actually trains the soul in these virtues, using both historical examples and specific legal statutes regarding social welfare.</meta>

<header>CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA</header>

<margin>A</margin>
For the hope of a good man, whether dead or living, does not perish. **I** love those who love me, says Wisdom. But those who seek me shall find peace, and so forth. Indeed, did not the women of the Midianites <note>The Midianites were a neighboring people of the Israelites; this refers to the events in Numbers 25 where Midianite women seduced Hebrew men into idolatry.</note> use their beauty to wage war on the Hebrews? 
<margin>Num. 25.</margin>
By means of incontinence, they led them away from temperance and into impiety. For by using the allurements of harlots to bait them away from grave and honest exercise toward the pleasures of prostitution, they led them—as if driven by a kind of madness—to the sacrifices of idols and to foreign women. Being conquered at once by women and by pleasure, they fell away from God and from the law, and almost the entire people fell into the hands of their enemies through a "womanly stratagem," <note>original: "muliebri strategemate"</note> until a warning fear rescued them from the danger into which they had been brought. But then, those who remained took up the struggle for piety and religion with great and willing courage in the face of danger, and they emerged superior to their enemies.

<margin>B</margin>
Therefore, the "beginning of wisdom" is religion <note>original: "religio," often translated as the "fear of the Lord" in this scriptural context.</note>. Moreover, "understanding" is the providential care for holy things. To know the law is the mark of a good mind. Therefore, those who have thought that the law produces only a fear characterized by "perturbation" <note>Clement is likely arguing against the Stoic view that fear is a negative "perturbation" of the soul, or against Gnostic critics who claimed the Old Testament Law was based only on cruel fear.</note> are neither intelligent, nor have they truly perceived the law. For the fear of the Lord gives life. But he who errs shall be afflicted by labors which knowledge <note>original: "cognitio," often referring to "Gnosis" or spiritual insight.</note> neither considers nor accounts for. Truly, Barnabas <note>Referring to the *Epistle of Barnabas*, an early Christian text Clement highly valued.</note> says mystically: "May God, who is the Lord of the whole world, give us also wisdom, intelligence, science, the knowledge of His justifications, and endurance." Become, therefore, God-taught, seeking out what the Lord requires of you, so that in the day of judgment you may find those who lie in wait for these things. He called them "sons of love and peace" because of their knowledge.

<margin>C</margin>
Regarding the granting of gifts and sharing, although much could be said, it will suffice to say this: 
<margin>Deut. 23. Who is a brother.</margin>
that the law forbids charging interest <note>original: "fœnerari," referring to usury or lending money at interest to those in need.</note> to a brother. He names as "brother" not only someone born of the same parents, but also anyone of the same tribe, the same mindset, and anyone who shares in the same Word. The law does not think it right to take interest from money, but rather to favor the needy with open hands and minds. For God is the founder of such a gift. Now, he who gives willingly receives interest great enough—the things most precious among men—namely, gentleness, kindness, magnificence, a good reputation, praise, and glory. Does this not seem to you to be a precept of humanity, just like that other command: to return the wages of a poor man on the very same day? It teaches that it is necessary to pay the wages to servants without delay.

<margin>D</margin>
For, as I see it, the eagerness of the poor man to do the work that follows is diminished if his nourishment is missing. Furthermore, the law says that the lender should not enter the house of the debtor to take a pledge by force; rather, he should wait for the debtor to bring it out, and the one who has it should not refuse. 
<margin>Lev. 19.</margin>
And during the harvest, the law forbids owners to pick up the stalks that fall from the bundles, just as it commands them to leave some parts unharvested. Through this, the law trains owners to practice sharing and magnificence <note>original: "magnificentiam," meaning noble generosity.</note> by letting go of some of their own property for the needy, while providing the poor with a way to seek their own sustenance. You see how the law of God simultaneously announces justice and goodness, for He supplies nourishment abundantly to everyone. Even in the grape-harvest, the law forbids going back to pluck what was left or gathering the grapes that fell.

<margin>E</margin>
It also prescribes the same for those gathering olives. Moreover, the tithes of fruits and cattle taught them both to be pious toward God and not to be entirely devoted to profit, but to make their neighbors participants in their humanity. For from these things, as I believe, the Priests were also fed, along with the firstfruits. Thus, we now understand that we are being educated through the law toward piety, sharing, justice, and humanity. For does it not also command that every seventh year the field be left idle? It commanded that the poor should safely enjoy the fruits that were produced by divine power, with nature cultivating the field for those who wished. How then is the law not good and a teacher of justice? And again, in the fiftieth year <note>This refers to the Jubilee Year described in Leviticus 25.</note>, it commands the same things to be done as in the seventh, while also returning to each man his own property if his field had been taken by some accident. It limits the greed of those who desire to possess everything by measuring the time of their enjoyment, and it refuses to let those who have paid the penalty of long poverty be punished perpetually.

<margin>Levit. 25. F</margin>
Moreover, alms and faith are the guards of the kingdom. A blessing is upon the head of him who gives, and he who has mercy on beggars shall be blessed, because he shows charity toward one who is like 
<meta>catchword: himself</meta>

### STROMATA, BOOK II.

<margin>A</margin> ...likeness to Him, because of the love he has for the Creator <note>original: "opificem," literally the "craftsman" or "maker"</note> of the human race. Those things which were said previously also have other, more natural explanations regarding rest and the receiving of the inheritance, but they have not been spoken of at this time. Now, love <note>original: "charitas"</note> is understood in many ways: through gentleness, through kindness, through patience, through the absence of envy and jealousy, through the removal of hatred, and through the forgetting of injuries. This love is of such a kind in all things that it cannot be divided or distinguished, gladly sharing what it possesses. Again, he says: "If you see the beast of burden belonging to your relatives, or friends, or those people whom you know, wandering in the wilderness, lead it back and return it." And if the owner is far away, after you have kept it with your own animals until he returns home, return it. This teaches a natural social responsibility <note>original: "naturalem societatem"</note>; namely, that we should consider a found object to be a trust <note>original: "depositum," a legal term for property held in trust</note>, and that we should not be mindful of an injury received from an enemy.

<margin>B</margin> <margin>Deut. 24. 28.</margin> <margin>Levit. 19.</margin> This commandment of the Lord, which is truly a "source of life," causes one to turn away from the snare of death. Indeed, does He not command us to love strangers, not only as friends and relatives, but even as ourselves, in both soul and body? Furthermore, He has even honored the foreign nations, and is not hostile even toward those who have done wrong. Thus He says clearly: "You shall not abhor an Egyptian, because you were a stranger in the land of Egypt." Whether He calls a pagan or any worldly person an "Egyptian," He even desires that we do not consider enemies to be enemies—even if they are threatening the walls and attempting to capture the city—until we have first invited them to peace by sending ambassadors to them. <margin>Deut. 21.</margin> Furthermore, He does not want one's conduct toward a captive woman to be insolent or 

<margin>C</margin> insulting. But He says: "When you have permitted her to mourn for thirty days as she wishes, and when she has afterwards changed her clothes, then approach her according to the law as a wife." For then it will no longer be an insulting relationship. He does not want the relationship to be for hire, like that of a prostitute, but solely for the sake of the procreation of children. You see here humanity combined with self-control. He does not permit the master who loves a captive woman to fulfill his pleasure immediately. Instead, He cuts back <note>original: "resecat"</note> desire by a pre-set span of time; moreover, He even has the captive's hair shaved so that the master might turn away from a love based on shameful appearance. For if his reason persuades him to take her as a wife, he will keep her even if she becomes unattractive. Then, if someone, having satisfied his desire, no longer wishes to have a relationship with the captive: He established that it is not permitted to sell her, nor to keep her any longer as a slave, but He wants her to be free and released from servitude, lest if another woman enters the house, something heavy and intolerable should happen to her out of jealousy.

<margin>D</margin> He also commands us to lighten the load and lift up the fallen beasts of our enemies, teaching us from afar that the Lord does not embrace gloating over evils, nor should we insult the miseries of enemies and rejoice in them; thus, being practiced in these things, we may be taught to pray even for our enemies. For it is not fitting to be envious or to be pained by a neighbor's good fortune, nor to derive joy from a neighbor's misfortunes. "If," He says, <margin>Exo. 23.</margin> "you find the wandering beast of any enemy: having left behind the internal fire of contention, lead it back and return it." For the true integrity of life follows the forgetting of injury, and the dissolution of enmities follows that integrity. From here, we are led perfectly and wholly toward concord, and she, as if by the hand, leads us to blessedness. And if you judge someone 

<margin>E</margin> an enemy because of his character, yet you catch him being deceived either by desire or by irrational anger, turn him back toward the integrity of life. Does not the law now seem humane and kind—a Pedagogue <note>original: "Paedagogus," a tutor or guardian who leads a child to school; a reference to Galatians 3:24</note> to Christ? And is not God the same, being both good and just, who from the beginning until the end has used every kind of thing fittingly for our salvation? "SHOW MERCY," says the Lord, "so that you may obtain mercy." Forgive so that it may be forgiven you; as you do, so it shall be done to you. As you give, so it shall be given to you. As you judge, so you shall be judged; as you are kind, so kindness shall be shown to you. By the measure you use to measure, it shall be measured back to you. <margin>Mar. 4.</margin> Furthermore, He altogether forbids bringing infamy upon those who serve for their livelihood, and for those who are in servitude because of debts, He gives a total release <note>original: "inducias," a truce or stay of execution</note> in the seventh year. Moreover, He forbids that suppliants be handed over to punishment. 

<margin>F</margin> Therefore, that saying is most true: "Just as gold and silver are tested in the furnace, so the Lord chooses the hearts of men." And a merciful man is indeed long-suffering, and in anyone who is diligent, there is wisdom. For into a man of understanding...

<summary>Clement demonstrates that the Mosaic Law is not merely a set of rigid rules but a humane "pedagogue" designed to train the soul in charity, mercy, and self-control. He highlights laws regarding the treatment of enemies, animals, and captive women to show that the Law shares the same benevolent spirit as the Gospel.</summary>
