He now transitions into how this same Law demands mercy toward animals as a training ground for human compassion.</meta>

# CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

...likewise anxiety will fall away, and he who is anxious and takes care will seek life; and he who seeks God will find knowledge with justice. Those who have sought Him rightly have found peace. It seems to me that even Pythagoras <note>Pythagoras (c. 570–495 BC) was a Greek philosopher known for his belief in the transmigration of souls and his vegetarianism; Clement argues here that Pythagoras' famous kindness toward animals was actually borrowed from the Jewish Law.</note> adopted his own gentleness toward irrational animals from the Law. For the Law immediately forbade using the young born from flocks of sheep, goats, or herds of oxen—not even under the pretext of sacrifice—for the sake of the fathers and mothers. In this way, the Law leads man toward gentleness, starting with even the lowest of brute animals.

> GRANT, he says, the offspring to the mother for at least the first seven days.

If nothing happens without a cause, and milk flows in those animals that have given birth to nourish their offspring, then whoever tears the offspring away from that supply of milk treats nature with contempt. Therefore, let the Greeks (and anyone else who attacks the Law) feel shame: for if the Law is kind even to beasts, yet they themselves "expose" <note>Infant exposure was the ancient practice of leaving unwanted newborns in the wild to die, a practice Clement contrasts with the Law’s mercy.</note> human infants. Long ago and prophetically, the Law intended to cut away their ferocity through this very precept.

<margin>Deuteronomy 14</margin>
For if it prohibits the offspring of beasts from being separated from the mother before the flow of milk, much more does it provide a remedy for the cruel and monstrous human mind—ensuring that even if people neglect nature, they certainly do not neglect discipline. For kids and lambs are permitted to be filled by these mothers. And perhaps there might be some excuse for one who separates an offspring from its mother; but what cause could there be for the exposure of an infant? From the beginning, it was better for a man not to take a wife if he did not desire to procreate children, rather than becoming the murderer of his child through the intemperance of pleasure. Again, the kind Law prohibits sacrificing the offspring and the mother on the same day.

<margin>Law regarding pregnant women, in the Digest on punishments <note>original: "l. pregnātis. ff. de pœnis." This refers to the Roman Digest (Pandects), a compendium of legal writings. Clement is noting a parallel between Mosaic Law and Roman Law.</note></margin>
From this, even the Romans, if any pregnant woman has been condemned to death, do not allow her to undergo punishment until she has given birth. Thus, the Law clearly does not permit any animals carrying a womb to be slaughtered until they have given birth, checking from a distance the human inclination toward doing harm. It extends kindness even to brute animals so that, when we have practiced it among those of a different species, we might exercise a far greater humanity toward those of our own kind. However, those who strike the bellies of animals before birth so that they might eat meat seasoned with milk <note>A reference to a culinary practice where an unborn animal was essentially cooked in its mother's milk or fluids before birth; Clement finds this practice particularly gruesome.</note> turn the womb, which was created for generation, into a tomb for the offspring carried within—even though the Law clearly commands:

> BUT you shall not cook a lamb in its mother’s milk.

For it says that the very thing which is the nourishment of the living should not become the seasoning for the slaughtered animal; nor should that which is the cause of life assist in the consumption of the body.

<margin>Deuteronomy 23</margin>
The same Law also proclaims that the mouth of an ox treading the grain should not be bound. For it is right to judge the worker worthy of his nourishment. It also prohibits yoking an ox and a donkey together at the plow, perhaps guessing at the lack of compatibility between these animals, but simultaneously signifying that no one should be treated with injustice from among different peoples, nor be subjected to a yoke, if we can accuse them of nothing else than being of a different race. This is a matter which lacks fault, is not caused by vice, and does not proceed from vice. To me, this word also seems to signify by allegory <note>Clement often uses "allegory" to find hidden Christian meanings in Old Testament laws. Here, the ox and donkey represent the believer and the unbeliever.</note> that the cultivation of the word should not be shared equally between the clean and the unclean, the faithful and the unfaithful; for the ox is clean, while the donkey is counted among the unclean. Using a certain overflowing humanity, the good Law teaches that trees which are domestic and of a mild nature should not be cut down, nor should the crop be harvested before the season to its own destruction; nor should mild fruit be destroyed entirely, whether of the earth or of the soul. For it does not even permit the cutting down of the fields of enemies.

<margin>Leviticus 19</margin>
Truly, those who are students of agriculture can also receive benefit from the Law. For it commands that trees recently planted be cherished and nourished for three successive years, by cutting away the superfluous shoots that grow, lest being too heavily weighed down they be overwhelmed, or become weak through lack of food if the nourishment is divided into tiny parts. It commands one to plow and dig around them, so that nothing budding or sprouting nearby prevents their growth. It does not allow the fruit to be gathered in an imperfect state from imperfect trees, but only after three years, when in the fourth year the firstfruits are consecrated to God, after the tree has reached perfection. This figure of agriculture might be a method of teaching, showing...

<meta>catchword: showing (docens)</meta>

<summary>Clement argues that the Mosaic Law’s commands regarding the humane treatment of animals and plants are actually pedagogical tools designed to instill "humanity" and "gentleness" in people. He contrasts these merciful laws with the "ferocity" of those who practice infant exposure or animal cruelty.</summary>

# THE MISCELLANIES, BOOK II.

<margin>A</margin> <margin>Hence the error of Nestorius. <note>original: "Hinc error Nestorii." <margin>B</margin> and to make those who approach us good and honorable: just as the one who is most temperate makes others self-controlled; he who is of a great and lofty mind makes others brave; the wise man makes others intelligent; and the just man makes others just. This is the person who, according to the "image and likeness," is endowed with the power of knowing; who imitates God as far as is possible, omitting nothing that contributes to that attainable likeness—being self-controlled, enduring, living justly, ruling over the perturbations of the soul, sharing what he has, and doing good according to his power in both word and deed. <margin>Matthew 5.</margin> "This man," he says, "is greatest in the kingdom, who has done and taught," imitating God in that he bestows favor in a similar manner. <margin>C</margin> disorder and poor harmony toward a better transformation, through these three: the mouth, the heart, and the hands. These shall be the symbol and the sign: the hands of action; the heart of counsel; and the mouth of speech. For since he is a part of the people, he completes it, being restored into that whole from which he came. Moreover, the part is also called the "whole." Furthermore, nobility itself is shown in the fact that he chooses and practices those things which are most beautiful and honorable. What

<margin>D</margin> indeed did such nobility profit Adam, or the fact that he had no mortal father? For the very father of men who are in the cycle of generation chose shameful things with a prompt and eager mind, following his wife, and neglected what was true and honorable. By this, it happened that he exchanged an immortal life for a mortal one, though not forever. But Noah, who was not made like Adam, is preserved by divine care and providence. For he offered and dedicated himself to God. And to Abraham, who had fathered children by three wives—not for the sake of enjoying pleasure, but because he hoped, as I think, to multiply the race in the beginning—only one heir succeeds to the paternal goods, while the others were separated from the kinship. And when twins were born from him, the younger heir is the one who pleased the father and received the vows, while the one who was older in age serves him. For to the bad man, the greatest good is that which is not in his own power. This "Economy" <note>The 'Economy' (Oeconomia) refers to God's plan for the salvation of humanity throughout history.</note> is both prophetic and typical. Moreover, he clearly indicates that "all things belong to the wise man" by saying:

<margin>E</margin> "BECAUSE God has had mercy on me, I have all things." For he teaches that one must seek the One through whom all things were made; from those who are worthy, He grants the promised things. He describes the man who is good as the heir and citizen of the kingdom through divine Wisdom, along with those who were formerly just—who lived justly both under the Law and before the Law—whose actions serve as laws for us. And teaching again that the wise man is a King, he makes those of a different race say to him: "A King from God you are among us," <margin>Genesis 23.</margin> those who are ruled by him obeying the good man of their own accord because of his zeal for virtue. Moreover, the philosopher Plato, in defining the end of happiness <note>original: "beatitudinis."</note>, says it is "assimilation to God" as far as possible, thus concurring in a way with the decree of the Law. For great natures, free from the perturbations of the soul, are somehow carried toward the target of truth—as Philo the Pythagorean says when describing the deeds of Moses—or perhaps even having been taught by some of the divine oracles that existed then.

### CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

**A** **B** **C** **D** **E** **F**

We should be content with those things that are according to nature and do not exceed its limits, by avoiding that which is excessive or contrary to nature, wherein the power to sin is born. <margin>Ephesians 6</margin> Therefore, it is necessary for us to put on the armor of God so that we may be able to resist the snares of the Devil. For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but powerful through God for the destruction of strongholds, destroying arguments and every high thing that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of faith, as the divine Apostle says. Truly, a man is needed who can use these things—from which the disturbances of the mind arise—in an admirable and steady way; things such as wealth and poverty, glory and ignominy, health and disease, life and death, labor and pleasure. For to use "indifferent" things <note>A Stoic term for things that are neither morally good nor bad in themselves, but depend on how they are used.</note> indifferently, we need great discernment, since we were previously poorly affected by much weakness and were formerly occupied with bad education and instruction in ignorance. It is therefore a lawful consequence that some are indeed thrown down in the struggle. However, those who approach the contest more like athletes, fighting with all their might, reach even to the crown. Those aforementioned powers <margin>In much filth. <note>original Greek: ἐν πολλῷ τῷ λύθρῳ</note></margin> then fail amidst much sweat and blood, admiring the victors. For of those things that move, some move out of appetite and vision, like animals; others move by being moved by something else, like inanimate objects. Among the inanimate, they say that plants also move by passing into growth, if anyone grants them that plants are indeed inanimate. Stones have "habit" <note>the basic physical state of existence</note>, while plants have "nature." Animals share in appetite and vision, as well as the things mentioned before. But the power of reasoning, which is proper to the human soul, ought not to be driven in the same way as animals lacking reason; rather, it should discern the visions that urge it on and not be led away by them. These powers of which we spoke hold out beauties and glories, and adulteries and pleasures, and such bait-like visions to those souls that can be easily seduced, <margin>A green branch. <note>original Greek: θαλλός</note></margin> just as those who drive cattle hold out green branches to them. Then, when they have circumvented by trickery those who cannot discern true pleasure from false, and the fleeting, falling, and injurious from holy beauty, they lead them away into slavery. Every deception that constantly presses upon the soul imprints a vision upon it; and the imprudent and ignorant soul carries around the image of disturbance and vice, since the cause arises from the baiting and our own assent. However, the followers of Basilides <note>A prominent Gnostic teacher in Alexandria in the 2nd century.</note> are accustomed to calling vices and disturbances of the mind <term>appendages</term> <note>original Greek: προσαρτήματα</note>. They claim these are certain spirits attached to the rational soul in its essence through a primal disturbance and confusion. They say other adulterated and diverse natures of spirits grow onto these—such as those of a wolf, a monkey, a lion, or a bear. The properties of these animals, which are grasped by the soul through vision, are said to make the soul's desires similar to those of the animals. For they imitate the works and deeds of those animals whose properties they carry. And they not only enter into union and familiarity with the appetites and visions of unreasoning animals, but they even emulate the movements and beauties of plants, because they carry the attached properties of plants as well. They claim one may even have the properties of "habits," such as the hardness of a diamond. But we will discuss this dogma later when we treat the soul. For now, it must only be noted that according to the opinion of Basilides, man preserves the image of the Trojan Horse <note>original Latin: Durii equi. Literally "Doric horse," referring to the wooden horse used by the Greeks to infiltrate Troy.</note>, as it is in the poetic fables, so that...

### MISCELLANIES BOOK II

<margin>Isidorus, son of Basilides.</margin>
...as one who has an army of so many different spirits insinuated into a single body. Thus Isidorus himself, the son of Basilides <note>Basilides was a prominent Gnostic teacher in Alexandria; his son Isidorus followed his teachings but wrote his own treatises.</note>, in his book *On the Attached Soul*, having observed this dogma, writes in these very words, as if accusing himself: "For if you persuade anyone that the soul is not a single entity, but that the vices and disturbances of the worse parts are 'attachments,' <note>The Gnostic concept of *prosartēmata*, or external spirits/passions that "clump" onto the rational soul.</note> then wicked men will have no small pretext for saying: 'I was forced, I was led away, I acted under compulsion, I worked against my will,' even though he himself led the way in his evil desires and did not fight against the violence of these attachments. We must, however, having become superior through our rational part, show ourselves to overcome the lesser creature within us." For he, too, posits two souls within us, just like the Pythagoreans, whom we shall consider later.

<margin>B</margin>
<margin>Valentinus.</margin>
Furthermore, Valentinus <note>A famous Gnostic philosopher who founded the Valentinian school.</note>, writing to certain people, speaks of these attachments in these words: "There is one who is good, whose confidence is the manifestation made through the Son; and through him alone can the heart be made pure, once every evil spirit has been driven out of the heart. For many spirits dwelling in it do not allow it to be pure. Each of them performs its own works, often insulting it with unseemly desires. To me, the heart seems not unlike an inn. For an inn is pierced and dug out, and often filled with dung, since men behave wantonly there and take no care for the place at all, as it belongs to someone else. In the same way, the heart also, as long as no care is taken for it, remains unclean and a habitation for many demons. But when the Father, who

<margin>C</margin>
alone is good, visits it, it is sanctified and shines with light. And thus, he who possesses such a heart is blessed, for he shall see God." What then is the reason, let them tell us, that care and providence are not exercised over such a soul from the beginning? For either it is not worthy—and how then does providence come to it as if by repentance—or is it saved by nature, as he himself wishes? If so, it would be necessary that care be taken for it from the beginning because of its kinship to God, and it should give no entry to unclean spirits unless it were forced and proved weak. For if it were to give entry, though led by repentance, to choose the better things, then he would be saying—unwillingly—exactly what our own Truth decrees: that salvation comes from a change through obedience, and not from nature.

<margin>D</margin>
<margin>Muddy impressions <note>original Greek: πηλμάτων</note></margin>
<margin>Images <note>original Greek: εἰκώσεις</note></margin>
For just as exhalations that arise from the earth and from marshes and pits condense into a mist and a cloudy gloom, so also the vapors of carnal desires brand a bad habit onto the soul, representing and pouring out before it the phantoms of pleasure. Thus they pour darkness over the light of the intellect, as the soul draws in the vapors arising from desire, and the persistence of pleasures thickens the mists of vice. Gold is not taken from the earth as a pure nugget; rather, it is smelted and filtered. Then, when it is pure, it is called gold, as it is earth that has been cleansed. "Ask, and it shall be given to you" is said to those who are able to choose for themselves those things which are best. How we might say that the operations of the Devil and unclean spirits sow

<margin>E</margin>
<margin>Barnabas.</margin>
seeds into the soul of a sinner, I do not need many words to explain, if I bring forward as a witness the Apostolic Barnabas <note>Referring to the author of the *Epistle of Barnabas*, traditionally identified as the companion of St. Paul.</note> (who was one of the seventy and a helper of Paul), speaking in these words: "Before we believed in God, the habitation of our heart was subject to destruction and weakness, truly a temple built by hands. For it was full of the worship of idols and was a house of demons, because it did whatever was contrary to God." He says, therefore, that sinners perform operations suitable to demons, but he does not say that the spirits themselves dwell in the soul of the unbeliever. And therefore he adds: "Take heed that the temple of the Lord be gloriously built. Learn that you have received the remission of sins, and have 

<margin>Remission of sins.</margin>
hoped in the name. Let us be made new again, created from the beginning." For it is not that demons are expelled from us, but he says that sins are remitted, which we used to commit just as they do before we believed. Rightly, therefore, he opposed those things which

<margin>F</margin>
follow. "Wherefore, in our habitation, God truly dwells." In us there is...

<meta>This page continues Clement’s critique of Gnostic and philosophical views on the soul and morality. ### CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

<margin>A</margin>
...provided that it is the Word of his faith, the calling of his promise, the Wisdom of his justifications, and the mandates of his teaching. I know that I have encountered a certain heresy whose leader claimed to fight against pleasure through the use of pleasure. This "distinguished Gnostic" <note>Clement uses "Gnostic" here sarcastically or to refer to a specific group, likely the followers of Carpocrates, who claimed that true knowledge allowed them to indulge in worldly things without sin.</note> fled toward pleasure through a simulated battle. For he called himself a "Gnostic," that is, one endowed with the power of knowing. He claimed it was no great feat to abstain from pleasure if one had not experienced it, but rather that the truly great man is he who engages in it and yet is not conquered by it. For this reason, he claimed he "exercised" himself in pleasure for its own sake.

<margin>To the lover of pleasure <note>original: "φιληδόνῳ"</note></margin>
<margin>B</margin>
But the wretched man, in his foolishness, deceived himself with the art of pleasure. In this way, as is evident, Aristippus of Cyrene <note>A Greek philosopher who founded the Cyrenaic school, which taught that pleasure is the highest good.</note> arrived at the same opinion as this sophist who boasts of holding the truth. Thus, when it was held against him as a disgrace that he was constantly in the company of the Corinthian prostitute, <margin>I possess Lais; I am not possessed by Lais. The response of Aristippus.</margin> he said, "I possess Lais, but I am not possessed by her." Such also are those who say they follow Nicolaus <note>Nicolaus was one of the seven deacons mentioned in Acts 6:5; later traditions linked him to a "heresy" of the Nicolaitans mentioned in Revelation, though Clement often defends Nicolaus himself while blaming his followers for twisting his words.</note>, <margin>From a memoir <note>original: "ἀπομνημονεύματι"</note></margin> citing a certain monument of his writings that has been distorted by them— <margin>From a perversion <note>original: "ἐκ παρατροπῆς"</note></margin> namely, that "One must abuse the flesh." <margin>To abuse/use up <note>original: "παραχρᾶσθαι"</note></margin> But that distinguished man meant that it was necessary to ward off pleasures and desires, and by this exercise to make the appetites and assaults of the flesh weak and withered. <margin>They live in luxury <note>original: "καθηδυπαθῶσιν"</note></margin> But those who are as profuse in pleasure as goats, as if showing contempt for the body, enjoy sweet delight, not knowing that while pleasure is by nature fleeting, it renders its offspring squalid and tattered: <margin>Rags <note>original: "ῥάκεται"</note></margin> for their own soul is buried in the mire of vice, as those who follow the decree of pleasure itself rather than that of the Apostolic man. For how do these people differ from Sardanapalus <note>A legendary Assyrian king, often cited by ancient authors as the ultimate example of decadence and effeminacy.</note>, <margin>The Epitaph of Sardanapalus.</margin> whose life is described by this epigram?

<margin>C</margin>
> ->What I ate, I have; and what saturated lust<-
> ->Drained; but those many and noble things lie abandoned.<-

The affection for pleasure is not at all necessary, but is a certain addition and attraction to certain natural uses, such as hunger, thirst, cold, and marriage. <margin>Following <note>original: "ἑπομένης"</note></margin> Therefore, if it were possible to drink, to take nourishment, or to procreate children without it, no other use for it could be shown. For pleasure is neither an operation, nor an affection, nor even a part of us. Rather, it entered life for the sake of an auxiliary service, just as they say salt was added for the sake of digesting food. But when pleasure is unbridled and usurps the management of the household by force, it generates the primary craving, which is desire—an appetite alien to reason <margin>D</margin> on the part of the one who gratifies it. This is what persuaded Epicurus <note>A philosopher who taught that the absence of pain (ataraxia) was the goal of life, often misinterpreted as a promotion of simple physical pleasure.</note> to place pleasure as the goal of the philosopher. <margin>He treats as divine <note>original: "θειάζει"</note></margin> Thus he established that a firm and stable good constitution of the flesh, and a trustworthy hope that it will remain so, is a divine thing. <margin>Greed/Gluttony <note>original: "λιχνεία"</note></margin> For what is luxury other than a lustful licking, and the superfluous redundancy <margin>Lecardia <note>Likely a reference to 'leicardian' or heart-licking, signifying excessive indulgence.</note></margin> of those who are dissolved into the sweet sensation of delight? Diogenes <note>Diogenes the Cynic, known for his extreme asceticism and biting social critiques.</note> writes significantly in a certain tragedy,

<margin>Diogenes. The laughter of the smoky-faced ones <note>original: "φλισοκαπνο- γελώνης"</note></margin>
> ->To the effeminate and the lewd ones,<-
> ->My heart is bound with sweet delights,<-
> ->Who do not wish to labor in the slightest,<-

<margin>E</margin>
And those things which follow, which are indeed spoken shamefully, but according to the merits of those who are devoted to pleasure. It seems to me, therefore, that the Law divinely willed that fear should hang over us of necessity, so that through caution and attention, the philosopher might prepare and preserve for himself <margin>Freedom from care <note>original: "ἀμεριμνίαν"</note></margin> a state of being least solicitous, far from a fall, and not akin to sin, remaining so in all things. For peace and liberty do not arrive in any other way than through a perpetual and indefatigable resistance against the movements of our soul. For these adversaries are thick and "Olympic" <note>Meaning they are formidable opponents, like athletes in the Great Games.</note>, and to put it in a word, sharper than wasps. This is especially true of pleasure, which lies in wait and bites <margin>F</margin> not only by day, but even by night in dreams, baiting us with illusions. How, then, can the Greeks still rightly attack the Law, when they themselves also teach that pleasure must serve fear? Socrates therefore...

### MISCELLANIES, BOOK II.

<margin>Xenophon, in the *Sayings of Socrates*.</margin>
**A** [Socrates] commands us to beware of those things which persuade us to eat when we are not hungry and to drink when we are not thirsty. He also warns against beautiful sights and kisses, as these naturally emit a poison more dangerous than that of scorpions and spiders. Antisthenes <note>A pupil of Socrates and a founder of the Cynic school, known for his extreme asceticism.</note> goes even further, stating that he would "rather go mad than feel pleasure." And Crates of Thebes <note>A famous Cynic philosopher who gave away his wealth to live in poverty.</note> says:

> May you conquer these things, exulting in upright character,
> Never selling yourself to gold nor becoming a slave
> To greedy loves; for there are no longer any such merchants.

And he gathers the whole matter as if into a concluding summary:

> He whom shameful pleasure does not touch or enslave
> Loves an immortal kingdom and freedom as well.

**B** This same man [Antisthenes] writes very correctly elsewhere that the "poultice" <note>original: "cataplasma," a medical dressing or remedy.</note> for the unbridled desire of sexual things is hunger; but if that does not work, then a noose <note>Suggesting suicide as a final resort to avoid moral corruption.</note>. As for the doctrine of Zeno the Stoic <note>The founder of Stoicism, known for teaching that virtue is the only good.</note>, the comic poets testify to it—even while mocking him—in this manner:

> This man Zeno practices a philosophy
> That is empty; for he teaches the hunger of Aegis-bearing Jupiter. <note>original: "Iouis egiferentis." A mocking reference to Zeno's extreme fasting, comparing his meager diet to the divine but intangible nature of the gods.</note>
> Let there be but one loaf of bread, a dried fig, and a drink of water.

Indeed, all these men are not ashamed to openly confess the utility that comes from caution. However, true and rational wisdom does not rely on words and decrees alone, but on invulnerable coverings and effective mysteries; meditating and exercising itself in divine precepts, it receives divine power from the Word <note>original: "verbo seu ratione," referring to the *Logos*.</note> through that part of the soul which is inspired by Him. Even the poets describe the "Aegis" <note>The shield or breastplate of Zeus/Jupiter, often associated with protection and terror.</note> of Jupiter:

> Terrible it is, draped all around with white fear.
> Strife is within it, and pressing Force, and chilling Horror.
> And the Gorgon’s head <note>A mythical monster whose gaze turned men to stone; here used as a symbol of the law's power to terrify the wicked.</note> is there, that once-mighty monster,
> Terrible and horrendous, a portent of Aegis-bearing Jupiter.

To those who are able to rightly perceive what is healthy for the soul, I do not know if anything will seem more lovable than the honor and gravity of the Law, and its daughters: Caution and Reverence.
<margin>Caution or Reverence. <note>original: "εὐλάβεια"</note></margin>
Nevertheless, when something is said to be "too intense," exceeding the proper pitch, it is like when the Lord speaks against certain people. He does this so that those who
<margin>Over-pitched or too intense. <note>original: "ὑπέρτονον"</note></margin>
strive to follow Him do not "sing" anything that is out of tune or discordant with the harmony of the strings. I hear this not as something that is inherently too intense or exceeding a just tone,
<margin>Out of tune and unstrung. <note>original: "ἔκτονον καὶ ἄχορδον"</note></margin>
but as something that seems so to those who refuse to take up the divine yoke. For to those who are lax and weak, that which is moderate seems too intense and over-pitched; they see the highest justice as "harsh." For because they are held by a love for sin, they seek indulgence; they think the truth is a nuisance, severity is cruelty, and the man who does not sin alongside them
**E** and is not dragged down with them, they call "unmerciful." Therefore, a tragedy correctly writes this concerning Pluto <note>The god of the Underworld, often associated here with unyielding justice.</note>:

> You ask what sort of Spirit <note>original: "Daemonem"</note> is coming toward you?
> One who knows neither fairness nor any grace.
> For justice alone is what pleases him.

Even if you are not yet able to do what the Law commands, nevertheless, by considering that these most beautiful examples are set before us, we can nourish and increase the love of freedom within ourselves. In this way, we will be helped by a more ready and eager spirit—challenging ourselves with some examples, imitating others, and revering others. For those ancient ones who lived according to the Law were not, as the saying goes,

**F** Born from an aged oak or a jagged rock. <note>A reference to Homer’s *Odyssey*; Clement means the ancient heroes were human beings like us, not mythical or inanimate objects, and thus we can imitate their virtue.</note>

<margin>A</margin>
But because they wished to practice philosophy sincerely and genuinely, they offered and dedicated their whole selves to God and were brought into the account of faith. Zeno <note>The founder of Stoicism.</note> used to say beautifully regarding the Indians that he would rather see one Indian being roasted <note>A reference to Indian gymnosophists (naked philosophers) who practiced extreme asceticism, including self-immolation.</note> than learn all the proofs concerning the perfection of labor. For us, however, there are daily overflowing fountains of Martyrs (or witnesses) seen by our own eyes, who are roasted, tortured, and beheaded. The fear of the law, acting as a **pedagogue** <note>original: "pædagogus," a slave who escorted children to school and supervised their conduct; here, the Jewish Law leading people to Christ.</note>, led and trained all of them so that they might show their piety even through their blood. "God stood in the assembly of the Gods; <margin>Psalm 81 <note>Psalm 82 in modern Bibles.</note></margin> in the midst, however, He judges the Gods." Which ones? Those who are superior to pleasure, who conquer the movements and disturbances of the soul, and who know each of the things they do—those who are **Gnostics** <note>Clement uses "Gnostic" to mean the "true seeker of knowledge" or the perfect Christian, rather than the heretical groups often associated with the name.</note>, that is, those endowed with the power of knowing, who are greater than the world. <margin>B</margin> <margin>Ibidem <note>In the same place (the Psalm).</note></margin> And again, "I said: You are Gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High." To whom does the Lord say this? To those who, as much as is possible, repudiate all mortal things. And the Apostle says: <margin>1 Corinthians 15 <note>The OCR says 11, but the context of corruption refers to chapter 15.</note></margin> <margin>Romans 8</margin> "But YOU are no longer in the flesh, but in the spirit." And again he says, "Though we are in the flesh, we do not war according to the flesh." For flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God, nor does corruption possess incorruption. "Behold, you shall die like men," the Spirit said, rebuking us. Therefore, it is necessary for us to train ourselves to avoid those things that are prone to vices, fleeing—like those who are truly Philosophers—those foods which incite lust and that dissolute relaxation and delight found in the bedchamber. We must act so that those things which happen in the fulfillment of pleasure and the enjoyment of delights might be a great reward to others, but not the same for us. <margin>C</margin> For **temperance** is the greatest gift of God. For He Himself said, "I will NOT leave thee, nor forsake thee," as one who has judged you worthy because of your true and genuine election. Thus, as we strive to approach piously and cautiously, the kind and sweet yoke of the Lord will receive us, leading each of us from faith to faith, with one Charioteer driving us toward salvation through progress, so that he who is fit may approach. This is the fruit of blessedness. Let there be, <margin>Hippocrates of Cos: <gloss>Unwearied labor. Not being over-sated with food.</gloss></margin> according to the opinion of Hippocrates of Cos <note>The famous Greek physician.</note>, an exercise not only for the health of the body, but also of the soul: an unwearied undertaking of labors and not a too-great saturation of nourishment. Epicurus <margin>The impious saying of Epicurus.</margin> however, placing happiness in not being hungry, nor thirsty, nor cold, shouted that voice equal to a God, saying impiously that he would fight for these things even against Father Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus.</note>, as if he were speaking of pigs feeding on dung and not of those endowed with reason <margin>D</margin> and philosophers, decreeing it a "blessed victory." For among those who obey pleasure, it is established that there are the Cyrenaics <note>A school of philosophy that taught pleasure is the supreme good.</note> and Epicurus. For they openly say that the end of life is to live pleasantly, and that pleasure is the only perfect good. Epicurus also says that the removal of pain is pleasure; he says that which is to be chosen and sought after is that which first draws one from oneself to oneself, which is obviously entirely in motion. Dinomachus and Callipho said that the end was to do whatever is in one's power for the sake of attaining and enjoying pleasure. And Hieronymus the Peripatetic said the end was indeed to live without annoyance or disturbance; but the ultimate good, or that looking toward the end, was happiness. And Diodorus, who was likewise from the same sect, declares the end to be living honorably and without any annoyance. And indeed Epicurus <margin>E</margin> and the Cyrenaics say that pleasure is the first thing that is proper and suitable to nature. For they say that **virtue**, approaching for the sake of pleasure, produced pleasure. According to the opinion of Callipho, virtue approached for the sake of pleasure, but in the course of time, when she had seen her own beauty, she made herself equal in honor to the principle—that is, to pleasure. But they hand down that for Aristotle, the end is to live according to virtue. Yet they say that neither happiness nor the end is present to just anyone who possesses virtue. For the wise man who is tortured, and falls into various misfortunes against his will, and therefore wishes to escape from life, is neither blessed nor happy. For virtue also has need of a certain amount of time. For it does not arrive in one day, as it consists in perfection; for as they say, a child is never "happy." <margin>F</margin> Perfect time, then, would be the life of a man; and so happiness is completed from a triple kind of goods. Therefore, he is not poor, nor inglorious, nor sickly; nor if anyone were

a slave, <note>This "catchword" at the bottom indicates the first word of the next page.</note>

<meta>This page continues Clement’s survey of philosophical opinions regarding the "ultimate goal" or "end" of human life. Having previously discussed the Christian view of suffering and faith, he now provides a catalog of pagan definitions of happiness and the purpose of existence to show the diversity—and potential insufficiency—of human wisdom compared to divine truth.</meta>

### MISCELLANIES, BOOK II. ###

<margin>A</margin> even a slave is happy according to their opinion. On the other hand, Zeno the Stoic <note>The founder of the Stoic school.</note> thinks the end is to live according to virtue. But Cleanthes says the end is to live in conformity with nature <margin>*in reasoning well.* <note>original: "ἐν τῷ εὐλογισθεῖν"</note></margin>—which he established as consisting of choosing those things that are in accordance with nature. And his associate, Antipater, thinks the goal lies in the constant and unwavering selection of things according to nature, and the rejection of things contrary to nature. Furthermore, Archedemus explained the end thus: that in choosing the greatest and most important things according to nature, one must not be able to overstep them. In addition to these, Panaetius defined it as living in accordance with the impulses given to us by nature. Finally, Posidonius said the end is to live contemplating the truth and order of the universe, and to fashion oneself as much as possible so that in no
<margin>B</margin> respect is one led by that part of the soul which lacks reason. Some of the more recent Stoics have taught that the end is to live consistently with the constitution of man. Why should I list Aristo for you? He said the end was **indifference** <note>original: "ἀδιαφορίαν" (adiaphoria). The state of being indifferent to external circumstances like wealth or health.</note>. Yet that which is truly indifferent leaves the end itself indifferent. Or shall I bring forward the words of Herillus? He places the end in living according to knowledge. Indeed, some of the more recent members of the Academy <note>Plato’s school, which in its later years turned toward skepticism.</note> wish to define the end as a firm and stable withholding of assent from appearances. Furthermore, Lyco the Peripatetic <note>A follower of Aristotle.</note> used to say that the true joy of the soul is the end, just as Leucimus said it is the joy which proceeds from honorable things. Critolaus, who was also a Peripatetic, said the end was the perfection of a life flowing according to nature, which is completed by three kinds of goods, signifying the perfection handed down from the ancestors. But we must not rest satisfied with these; rather, we must
<margin>C</margin> strive as much as possible to bring forward what the natural philosophers <note>The "Physici," early Greek philosophers focused on the nature of the physical world.</note> have decreed on this subject. For they say that Anaxagoras of Clazomenae said that contemplation is the end of life, and the freedom that proceeds from it. Heraclitus of Ephesus said it was **contentment** <margin>*contentment.* <note>original: "εὐαρέστησις" (euarestesis)</note></margin>. Heraclides Ponticus reports that Pythagoras taught that the knowledge of the perfection of the virtues of the soul is happiness. Moreover, the followers of Democritus teach that the end is tranquility of mind, which Democritus called **well-being** <note>original: "εὐεστώ" (euesto)</note> in his book *On the End*; he often exclaims: "Delight and its absence are the boundaries <margin>*what "well-being" is for those in their prime.* <note>original: "εὐεστώ quid περιμανότων"</note></margin> for those who have reached the very flower of life." Hecataeus, however, says the end is self-sufficiency. Furthermore, Apollodotus of Cyzicus says it is the delight of the mind, just as Nausiphanes says it is "unshakeability" or "freedom from wonder." For he says that what Democritus called <margin>*unshakeability.* <note>original: "κατάπληξιν" (kataplexin)</note></margin>
<margin>D</margin> "fearlessness" <note>original: "ἀθαμβίην" (athambien)</note> is the same thing. Besides these, Diotimus pronounced the end to be the absolute perfection of all goods, which he says is called **well-being**. Again, Antisthenes said it was the absence of pride <margin>*absence of pride.* <note>original: "ἀτυφίαν" (atuphian)</note></margin>. Those called the Annicereans, from the Cyrenaic succession, established no single fixed end for the whole of life; rather, they said each individual action has its own proper end—namely, the pleasure resulting from the action. These Cyrenaics invalidate and abolish Epicurus’s definition of pleasure (which is the removal of pain), calling that the "condition of a corpse." They claim we are affected with joy not only because of physical pleasures, but also because of social habits and honors. Epicurus, however, thinks that all joy is produced primarily from the flesh. But Metrodorus, in the work
<margin>E</margin> entitled *That the Cause of Happiness Which Comes from Ourselves is Greater than That Which Arises from Things*, says: "What else is the good of the soul than the firm and stable constitution of the flesh, and the faithful hope that it will remain so?" But truly, Plato the philosopher says the end is twofold. One is the "Participable" and the primary Good among the **Forms** <note>Plato’s "Forms" are the eternal, perfect archetypes of all things.</note>, which he calls the Good itself. The other is that which participates in it and receives a likeness proceeding from it, which is found in men who claim virtue and true philosophy for themselves. Therefore Cleanthes also, in his second book *On Pleasure*, says that Socrates teaches everywhere that the just man and the happy man are the same. He says Socrates cursed the man who first divided the just from the useful, as one who had committed an impious act. For they are indeed impious who separate the "useful" from the "just" which comes from the law. Plato himself says that happiness, which is **Eudaimonia**, consists in "having a good Spirit" <note>A play on the Greek word "eudaimonia": *eu* (good) and *daimon* (spirit/divinity).</note>.
<margin>F</margin> He says that the "Spirit" (*Daimon*) is the principal part of our soul. And happiness is...

<margin>How it should be understood that man was created according to the image and likeness of God. Luke 14 & 18.</margin>
<margin>A</margin>
the most perfect and fullest good. At other times, however, he calls it a life that is consistent and in harmony with oneself; and sometimes that which is most perfect by virtue. This he places in the knowledge of the good, and in that likeness to God which consists in being just and holy with wisdom. Do not some of our own people likewise understand that man received "the image" immediately at his birth, but that he is to receive "the likeness" later through achieving perfection? Now indeed, Plato, teaching that this likeness will belong to the good man through humility, interprets it thus: *Everyone who humbles himself shall be exalted.* <note>original: "Omnis qui seipsum humiliat, exaltabitur." This is a reference to Luke 14:11 and 18:14, showing Clement's habit of finding Christian truths in Platonic philosophy.</note> Therefore, he says in *The Laws*: "God indeed, as the ancient saying goes, holding the beginning, the middle, and the end of all things, proceeds straight ahead, circling according to nature. Justice always follows Him, as the avenger of those who fall away from the divine law." You see how he himself also <margin>B</margin> introduces reverence for the divine law. He adds, therefore: "He who is to be happy, adhering to this law, follows it humbly and moderately." Then, having joined to these things their consequences, and having given a warning with fear, he adds: "What action, then, is dear to God and in harmony with Him? One, which follows one ancient word: namely, that the similar is a friend to the similar which is moderate; but those things which are immoderate are friends neither to each other nor to those that are moderate. By this reasoning, our temperate man is a friend of God, for he is like Him. But he who is not temperate is unlike Him and different." In saying that this is an "ancient decree," he quietly signaled the doctrine that reached him from the Law. And in the *Theaetetus*, having granted that evils must necessarily haunt mortal nature and this region, he adds: <margin>C</margin> "Therefore, one must try to flee from here to there as quickly as possible. Now, flight is assimilation to God as far as is possible. And assimilation is to become just and holy with wisdom." And **Speusippus**, the son of Plato’s sister, says that happiness <term>beatitudo: "blessedness" or "happiness," the ultimate fulfillment of human life</term> is a perfect habit in those things which are according to nature, or a habit of good things; a state which all men indeed desire, but which the good aim for as a freedom from trouble and disturbance; and he held that the virtues were the causes of this happiness. **Xenocrates** of Chalcedon defines happiness as the possession of one's own virtue and the faculty that serves it. Then, as to where it resides, he seems to say the soul; as to what causes it, the virtues; and as to the parts it is made of, good actions, honorable habits, affections, movements, and dispositions—since without these <margin>D</margin> the things of the body and external things cannot exist. For **Polemo**, a companion of Xenocrates, seems to want happiness to be the sufficiency of all goods, or of the most and greatest of them. He decrees, therefore, that happiness can never exist without virtue, but that virtue is sufficient for happiness even without the goods of the body and external things. And let these things be as they are. What might be said against these opinions shall be said at the proper time. For us, however, the proposal is to reach the "end that has no end," following the commandments—that is, following God—and living by them, without reproach and with knowledge, through the understanding of the divine will. Now, assimilation to the Right Reason (or the Word) <note>original: "Recte autem rationi seu verbo." Clement uses "Verbum" to refer to the Logos, or Christ.</note>, as far as is possible, is the end, and the restoration into perfect adoption through the Son, always glorifying the Father through the Great <margin>E</margin> High Priest who deigned to call us brothers and co-heirs. And the Apostle indeed, briefly describing the end in the Epistle to the Romans, says: <margin>Rom. 6</margin> **BUT NOW** being made free from sin, and become servants to God, you have your fruit unto holiness, and the end, everlasting life. And since he knew a twofold hope—one which is expected, and the other which is intended for threats—he now teaches that the end of faith is restoration. <margin>Rom. 5</margin> For **PATIENCE**, he says, brings proof; and proof, hope. And hope does not confound us, because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Spirit, which is given to us. On account of this love, there is also a restoration into hope, which he says elsewhere is the "rest" laid up for us. You will find similar things <margin>Ezek. 18</margin> in Ezekiel, which go like this: *The soul that sins, it shall die. But the man who <margin>F</margin> is just, and does judgment and justice, and has not eaten upon the mountains, and has not [lifted up] his eyes*

# THE STROMATA, BOOK II.

**A** But truth comes with good consent and harmony. For while the marriage of others focuses on the agreement of pleasure and delight, the marriage of those who practice philosophy <note>In Clement's writing, "philosophy" often refers to the lived Christian faith or the pursuit of divine wisdom.</note> leads to that harmony which is in the **Word** <note>original: "Verbo," referring to the *Logos* or Christ</note>. This allows women to adorn their character rather than their outward form, and it commands husbands not to treat their wives merely as objects of passion—as if their only goal were to bring shame upon the body—but to use marriage as a help for the whole of life and for the highest form of self-control. For I believe that a human being, who is "sown" and for whom all things are produced by nature, is far more excellent and precious than the seeds of wheat and barley which are cast down at the appropriate seasons. And just as sober farmers cast those seeds, **B** so too must every foul and filthy passion be purged from marriage. This ensures that we cannot be put to shame by the fact that the mating of brute animals is more in accord with nature than the human union in the very heat of desire. Indeed, many animals immediately withdraw once they have fulfilled their duty, leaving the work of procreation to the governance of nature.

The tragic poets have written that **Polyxena** <note>Polyxena was the daughter of King Priam of Troy; according to legend, she was sacrificed at the tomb of Achilles but insisted on dying with dignity.</note>, even as she was being killed, took great care in her dying moments to fall decently, covering those parts of a woman that should not be seen. For her, even calamity was a kind of marriage <note>Clement suggests her death was a "wedding to death," a common tragic trope, yet she maintained her modesty.</note>. To succumb and yield to vices and the disturbances of the mind is the extreme of slavery, just as to conquer them is the only true freedom. Therefore, the Divine Scripture says that those who have leaped over the commandments have been "sold to foreigners"—that is, to sins which are not according to nature—**C** until they turn back and perform penance. Marriage must therefore be preserved like a **sacred statue** <note>original: "sacra statua." Clement uses this image to describe marriage as something holy that represents a higher reality.</note>, kept clean from things that pollute it; for we should wake from sleep with the Lord, go to sleep with thanksgiving and prayer.

Moreover, where the Scripture counsels one to take a wife, and never permits one to depart from the union, it openly establishes a law: *You shall not divorce your wife, except for the sake of fornication.* Furthermore, it considers it adultery to be joined in marriage while another of the separated parties is still living. The Scripture shows that a wife is free from suspicion and accusation when she does not adorn or deck herself out more than is becoming, attending diligently to prayers and petitions; she should guard the many exits of the house, excluding from her sight, as much as possible, those who do not belong there, considering the guarding of the home more profitable than untimely trifles.

But what does the Law say? To restrain the inclination toward vice, it commands that a woman who is an adulteress and has been convicted of adultery be removed from the midst. If she is the wife of a **Priest**, it commands her to be handed over to the fire. The adulterer is also crushed with stones, but not in the same place, so that even death is not shared between them. Truly, the Law does not fight against the Gospel, but agrees with it. And why not, since the Lord is the one provider of both? For she who has committed fornication lives indeed in sin, but is dead to the commandments. But she who has been led by penance, as one who is regenerated through a conversion of life, has a regeneration of life. ### MISCELLANIES. <note>original: "STROMATEON." The title means "patchwork" or "tapestries," referring to the varied and woven nature of the topics discussed.</note>

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial 'A' featuring a bird perched on a branch within a landscape scene, framed by a decorative border.</image-desc>

<margin>B</margin>
And the Valentinians <note>Followers of Valentinus, a 2nd-century Gnostic teacher who believed in "aeons" or divine pairings.</note> indeed, who derive their divine pairings from above from the celestial emanations, accept marriage. But the followers of Basilides <note>A Gnostic teacher in Alexandria; his followers often took a more ascetic or complex view of morality.</note> say that when the Apostles asked whether it were better not to marry, they claim the Lord replied: <margin>Matthew 19.</margin> **NOT ALL** can accept this word. For some are eunuchs from birth, others by necessity. They interpret this saying as follows: Some from birth have a natural aversion to women; those who use this natural temperament act rightly if they do not marry. These, they say, are the eunuchs from birth. But those who are so by necessity are the theatrical performers who, in order to gain a good reputation and glory, practice self-restraint. <margin>C</margin> And those who have been castrated because of some compelling necessity are eunuchs by necessity. Therefore, those who become eunuchs by necessity do not do so by the "word" or by reason. But those who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven do so, they say, because of the consequences of marriage, taking up this thought because they fear the business of providing for the necessities of life. <margin>1 Corinthians 7.</margin> And concerning that phrase, "It is better to marry than to burn," they say the Apostle means: "Do not cast your soul into the fire by resisting day and night, fearing lest you fall away from continence." For when the soul is occupied with resisting, it is divided from hope. <margin>Having shaken off the fire <note>original: "πῦρ ἀποκομματίσας" (pyr apokommatisas).</note></margin> Therefore, Isidorus <note>The son of Basilides.</note> says in his *Ethics*: <margin>D</margin> "Take a strong wife, so that you are not torn away from the grace of God; and when you have expelled the fire from the seed, pray with a good conscience." But he says, "When your thanksgiving turns into a petition, and you subsequently cease <margin>Unreasonably prone to lust <note>original: "κατωφερὴς παρὰ λόγον" (katōpherēs para logon).</note></margin> to act rightly, but not as if you are wandering into error, then take a wife." But if there is some young man, either poor or prone to sexual desire, and he does not wish to marry in accordance with the "word" or reason, let him not be separated from his brother. Let him say: "Having entered into the holy places, I can suffer nothing." But if he has a suspicion, let him say: "Brother, lay your hand upon me, so that I may not sin," and he will receive help that is both intellectual and sensible. Let him only wish to seek what is good, and he will attain it. But sometimes we say with our mouths: "We do not wish to sin," while our thoughts are fixed on the sin. <margin>E</margin> One who is like this does not do what he wants because of fear, lest a punishment be imposed upon him. Human nature, however, has certain necessary and purely natural needs. That it needs clothing is both necessary and natural; <margin>Sexual matters are natural, but not necessary.</margin> but the sexual act is natural, yet not necessary. I have cited these words to rebuke those Basilidians who do not live rightly—either as those who believe they have the power to sin because of their "perfection," or that they will be saved by nature even if they sin because of their innate "election"—since the very founders of their dogmas do not allow them to do these things. Let them not, therefore, while taking up the name of Christ and living more intemperately than the pagans, bring a curse upon that name. <margin>2 Corinthians 11.</margin> For such men are false apostles, deceitful workers, and so on, until the phrase: "Whose end will be according to their works." <margin>The vow of chastity.</margin> Continence <note>original: "continentia." In this context, it refers to self-control or sexual restraint.</note> is therefore <margin>F</margin> a disregard for the body in accordance with the agreements made with God. For continence is concerned not only with sexual matters, but also with other things which the soul wrongly desires when it is not content with necessities. There is also continence of the tongue, in acquiring wealth, in its use, and in desire. But it does not only teach us to be temperate, for it offers us temperance as a divine power and grace. We must therefore say what our people think regarding the subject at hand. We indeed regard chastity <note>original: "castitas."</note>...

Clement argues against using spiritual perfection as an excuse for immoral behavior and begins to define true Christian continence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Clement’s examination of different sectarian views on marriage. Having discussed the Valentinians and Basilidians on the previous page, he now turns to the more radical group known as the Carpocratians, who argued for the "community of wives."</meta>

# CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

<margin>Chastity. Monogamy.</margin>
And those to whom this has been given by God, we call blessed. However, we admire **monogamy**, <margin>A</margin> which consists in only one marriage, as a thing of honor. Nevertheless, we say that one must have mercy on others and "bear one another’s burdens" <note>Galatians 6:2</note>, lest someone who seems to stand upright should himself also fall. <margin>Polygamy.</margin> Regarding second marriages: "If you are burning," says the Apostle, "join in marriage." <note>1 Corinthians 7:9. In this context, "burning" refers to being consumed by sexual desire.</note> But those who descend from **Carpocrates** <note>A 2nd-century Gnostic teacher in Alexandria who taught that all things should be shared in common.</note> and **Epiphanes** think that wives should be common property; from these men, the greatest disgrace has spread to the name <note>The name of Christian.</note>. This Epiphanes, whose writings are still circulated, was the son of Carpocrates and a mother named Alexandria. On his father's side he was Alexandrian, but on his mother's side, a Cephalenian. He lived only seventeen years and was honored as a god in Sama, a city of Cephalenia. In that place, a temple of huge stones, altars, shrines, and a museum were built and consecrated to him. When it is the new moon, the Cephalenians gather <margin>B</margin> to sacrifice to Epiphanes in honor of his "apotheosis" <note>His transformation into a god.</note>; they offer libations, feast together, and sing hymns. He was taught by his father both the standard curriculum of education and the philosophy of Plato. He was the author and leader of "monadic" knowledge <note>The belief that all reality is a single, unified substance, used here to justify total communal sharing.</note>. From him also <margin>Carpocrates</margin> flowed the heresy of those now known as Carpocratians. In his book *On Justice*, he says that the "justice of God" is a certain communion based on equality. Certainly, the sky is extended equally in every direction and contains the whole earth in its circle; and the night displays all the stars equally. The Creator poured out the Sun—the author of day and the father of light—from on high as an equal gift to all who can see. All people look upon it together, for it does not distinguish between rich or poor, or the ruler of the people, the foolish and the wise, females and males, free men and slaves. <margin>C</margin> Nor does it act differently toward the unreasoning animals. Since God poured out the sun equally for all living creatures, for both the good and the bad, He made justice firm and solid, as no one can have more than another, nor take it away from a neighbor so that he might have double the light for himself. The Sun makes common nourishment rise for all living beings, with common justice given equally to all. This is similarly true for the herds of cattle, such as oxen, and for swine, and for sheep, and all the rest. For justice appears in them as "community." Then, through this community, all things are sown similarly in their kind, and common nourishment is open on the ground for all beasts that graze, and for all equally; because it is held by no law, but by the supply of the One who commands the gift, it is present for all appropriately and justly. <margin>D</margin> Nor do they have a written law regarding procreation, for it would be abolished <note>original: "μετεγράφη γὰρ ἂν" (metegraphē gar an). This suggests that a written law would interfere with the natural, unwritten law of communal sharing.</note>. They sow and procreate equally, having an innate communion from justice. The creator and father of all provided the eye for seeing equally to all in common, by His own justice making a law; He did not distinguish female from male, nor that which is rational from that which lacks reason, and—to say it once—nothing from anything else. Rather, by dividing vision similarly with equality and community, He bestowed it upon all with a single command. But the laws of men, he says, because they could not punish ignorance, taught people to act against the laws. For the "propriety" of laws <note>The concept of private property or individual rights.</note> cut apart the community of the divine law and gnaws at it, not understanding the saying of the Apostle: "Through the law I knew sin." <margin>Rom. 3.</margin> And he says that "mine" and "thine" entered through the laws, so that people no longer <margin>E</margin> enjoy things in common (though they are common)—not the land, nor possessions, nor even marriage. For He made vines for all in common, which do not refuse the sparrow or the thief; and wheat similarly, and other fruits. But the violation of community and equality generated the thief of livestock and fruits. Therefore, since God made all things in common for man, and joined the female with the male in common, and joined all living beings together similarly, He proclaimed justice as community with equality. But those who were born this way have denied the community which brings about their procreation. And he says, "if a man takes one woman and keeps her, let him do so, though they could be shared by all," just as He made the other animals. Having said these things in these words, <margin>F</margin> he again adds the following: "For He implanted in males a deep and violent desire for the continuation of the race, which neither law, nor custom, nor anything else can abolish. For it is the decree of God." And how much further this [is to be] examined...

<meta>catchword: examinetur (to be examined)</meta>

<meta>This page continues Clement’s examination of sectarian views on marriage. Having previously introduced the Carpocratians and their leader Epiphanes, Clement now critiques their theological justifications for the "community of wives" and contrasts their libertinism with the asceticism of the Marcionites.</meta>

# MISCELLANIES, BOOK III

<margin>A</margin> ...be examined in this discourse, since through these arguments he openly destroys both the Law and the Gospel. For the Law says, <margin>Exodus 20</margin> "You shall not commit adultery," but the Gospel says, <margin>Matthew 5</margin> "Whoever looks with lust has already committed adultery." The command "You shall not covet," <note>original: "Non concupisces"</note> which is spoken by the Law, shows that there is one God who is preached through the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospel. For the Law says, <margin>Deuteronomy 5</margin> "You shall not covet your neighbor's wife." Now, a "neighbor" is not just a Jew to a Jew, for that person is a brother and shares the same spirit. It remains, therefore, that "neighbor" <note>original: "propinquum," meaning one who is near or related</note> refers to one of another nation. For how is one not a neighbor who is able to partake of the Spirit? For Abraham is the father not only of the Hebrews, but also of the Gentiles. If, then, the woman who commits adultery and the man who fornicates with her are punished by death, it is clear that the precept which says, "You shall not covet your neighbor's wife," speaks of the <margin>B</margin> Gentiles; so that when someone has abstained, according to the Law, from both his neighbor's wife and his own sister, he may clearly hear from the Lord:

> But I say to you, do not covet.

The addition of this little word, "I," shows that the application of the precept is even more intense. Furthermore, that Carpocrates and Epiphanes wage war against God is evident from that book commonly circulated, titled *On Justice*, where Epiphanes adds these words: "Hence, as one who has said something ridiculous, this word of the Lawgiver is to be heard: 'You shall not covet'—and to say it even more ridiculously—'your neighbor’s property.'" For Epiphanes argues that the very One who gave the desire to sustain <term>procreation</term> <note>original: "generationem," the act of begetting children</note> now orders that desire to be taken away, though He takes it away from no other animal. And that phrase, "Your neighbor's wife," he says is even more ridiculous, as it forces what should be common into private ownership. These are the dogmas that the "excellent" Carpocratians establish. They say that these men and some other followers of similar evils, when they meet for dinner (for I would not call their gathering an <term>Agape</term> <note>A "love feast" or communal meal practiced by early Christians to express fellowship.</note>), both men and women together, after they have sated themselves <margin>C</margin> and their lust is excited by fullness, they overturn the lamp—which would have put their fornicating "justice" to shame—and in the darkness they couple however they want and with whomever they want. Having practiced "community" in this kind of Agape, they then demand by day from whichever women they please a shameful obedience to the "Carpocratian Law" (for it is a sin to call it a "divine" law). Such laws, I feel, Carpocrates ought to have proposed for the lusts of dogs, pigs, and goats. It seems to me that Plato has also been misunderstood in his *Republic* when he says that the wives of all should be common. He meant that women who were not yet married should be common to those who were going to seek them—just as a theater <margin>D</margin> is common to the spectators—but that once a woman has married, she belongs to the one who took her first and is no longer common. Xanthus, <margin>Xanthus</margin> in his writings titled *Magica*, says that the Magi <note>Ancient Persian priests or wise men.</note> have intercourse with mothers and daughters, and that it is lawful to have intercourse with sisters; he also claims wives are common, not by force or in secret, but by mutual consent when one wishes to marry the wife of another. Regarding these and similar heresies, I believe Jude spoke prophetically in his epistle: <margin>Epistle of the Apostle Jude</margin>

> Likewise indeed these dreamers also (for they do not apply themselves to the truth in reality)... [and so on] until the part: And their mouth speaks proud things. <note>Jude 1:8-16</note>

Now, if Plato himself and the Pythagoreans—and later the Marcionites—regarded <term>procreation</term> as evil, they were far from suggesting that wives should be common. But the Marcionites say that nature itself is evil, <margin>E</margin> created from bad matter by a "Just Creator" <note>The Marcionites distinguished between a "Just" but harsh God of the Old Testament and a "Good" God of the Gospel.</note> or Craftsman. For this reason, because they do not wish to fill the world made by this Creator, they choose to abstain from marriage, resisting their Creator and striving toward the "Good One" who called them—who is not, as they say, God in the same way. Thus, since they wish to leave nothing of their own here, they are not continent by choice or by moral training, but because of a hatred conceived against the One who created them, being unwilling to use the things He created. But these people—who, because of the impious war they wage against God, have wandered from thoughts that are according to nature—scorn the long-suffering and kindness of God. Even if they do not wish to marry, they still eat created food and breathe the Creator's air; they are His works and they remain in His domain, yet they <margin>F</margin> announce a "new and alien knowledge," as they call it. For this reason, they ought to give thanks to the Lord of the world that they received the Gospel here. But we shall argue more accurately against them when we treat the subject of "First Principles." Philoso—

<meta>This page continues Clement’s argument against the Marcionites, an early Christian sect that viewed the physical world and procreation as inherently evil. Here, Clement demonstrates that the Marcionites did not invent this pessimistic view but borrowed it from ancient Greek philosophers and poets who viewed the soul as a divine prisoner within the "tomb" of the physical body.</meta>

# CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

...philosophers <note>The text continues a list of Greek thinkers whose ideas were adopted by later sects.</note> whom we have mentioned. The Marcionites, having impiously learned from them that birth is evil, boast of this as their own doctrine. However, those philosophers do not claim that birth is evil by its very nature, but only for the soul which has passed on that which is true. For they lead the soul, which is divine, down into this world as if into a place of punishment. According to their opinion, it is necessary for souls sent into bodies to be purified. But this doctrine no longer fits the Marcionites; rather, it belongs to those who believe that souls are thrust into bodies, <margin>to be embodied<br/>to enter into<br/>to be transferred</margin> and are bound to them, and draw near to them. There will be another time to speak against these people when we treat the subject of the soul. It appears, then, that Heraclitus pursues birth with curses. He says, "Since those who are born wish to live and to have their fates <note>original: "mortes" (deaths/fates); Greek: "moroi"</note>, or rather to rest, <margin>fates</margin> they also leave behind children so that more deaths may come to be." It is clear that Empedocles also agrees with him when he says: <margin>B</margin>

> *I wept and wailed when I saw the unfamiliar region.* -> And further: <-
> *For he made dead things from living, and changing them in turn.* -> And again: <-
> *Woe to me! How unhappy and wretched is the race of men,*
> *From what great strifes and lamentations were you born!*

And the Sibyl <note>The Sibylline Oracles were a collection of Greek oracular utterances often cited by early Christians.</note> also says:
> *Mortal humans, who are only flesh and nothing.*

Similarly, the Poet <note>Homer.</note> writes:
> *The life-giving earth nourishes nothing more miserable than man.*

Furthermore, Theognis shows that birth is evil, speaking in this way: <margin>C</margin>
> *The best thing for those on earth would be not to be born,*
> *Nor to enjoy the glittering light of the bright Sun.*
> *But once born, to pass as quickly as possible through the gates of Hades.* <note>Hades refers to the underworld or the state of the dead.</note>

Following these, the tragic poet Euripides also writes:
> *For we ought to gather in a great assembly*
> *To weep for the newborn, who comes into so many evils.*
> *But for the dead, to whom rest from evils has been given,*
> *We should carry him from the house with joy and happy songs.* -> And again: <-
> *Who knows if living is actually dying,*
> *And dying is living?* <margin>D</margin>

Herodotus also seems to introduce Solon saying the same thing as these men: "O Croesus, every human being is nothing but calamity." Indeed, the story of Cleobis and Biton <note>A famous Greek legend where two brothers die in their sleep after performing a virtuous act, which was considered the greatest gift from the gods.</note> clearly intends nothing else than to disparage birth and praise death.

<margin>*As is the generation of leaves, so is that of men*</margin>
So says Homer. Plato, in the *Cratylus*, attributes to Orpheus the saying that the soul is punished in the body. In fact, some say the body itself is the monument <note>original: "monimentum"</note> of the soul, as if it were buried in the present; and because the soul signifies what it signifies, <margin>The word *sema* (tomb) comes from *semainein* (to signify).</margin> it is therefore rightly called a *sema* <note>Clement is noting a Greek pun: "sema" can mean both "tomb" and "sign/signal."</note>. It certainly seems that Orpheus gave it this name especially so that the soul might pay the penalty for those things for which it is being punished. It is also worthwhile to remember the words of Philolaus. For this Pythagorean says: "The <margin>E</margin> ancient theologians and prophets also testify that the soul is joined to the body for the sake of certain punishments to be paid, and is buried in it as if in a monument." Furthermore, Pindarus, speaking of the things in the Eleusinian mysteries, adds: "Blessed is he who, having seen those things common under the earth, knows indeed the end of life, and knows the divine empire given by Jupiter." And Plato, following this in the *Phaedo*, does not hesitate to write in this way: "Furthermore, those who established these mysteries for us meant something else," and so on, until: "And he dwells with the Gods." But what about when he says: "As long as we have a body, and our soul is confused with such an evil, we shall never sufficiently possess that which we desire"? Does he not mean that birth is the cause of the greatest evils? Indeed, in the *Phaedo* he also testifies: "For it happens that <margin>F</margin> those who practice philosophy rightly are not noticed by others; they pursue nothing else than to die and to be dead." And again...

<summary>Clement argues that the Marcionite rejection of physical birth is a derivative of ancient Greek philosophy and poetry, citing thinkers like Plato, Heraclitus, and Empedocles who viewed the body as a tomb (sema) for the divine soul.</summary>
