<meta>This page continues Clement’s argument that the Marcionites (a sect that rejected the material world) misinterpreted Greek philosophy. Clement argues that while philosophers like Plato spoke of the soul's struggle with the body, they did not consider the physical world "evil" in the way Marcion did.</meta>

### STROMATA BOOK III
<sig>hh iii</sig>

<margin>A</margin> The philosopher <note>referring to the Platonic ideal</note> holds the body in the greatest contempt and flees from it, seeking instead to exist by the soul alone. Does he not, then, agree with the divine Apostle, who says: <margin>Romans 7</margin> "Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death?" <note>original: "INFELIX ego homo quis me liberabit de corpore mortis huius"</note> Unless, perhaps, he uses the phrase "body of death" figuratively <note>original: "tropicè"</note> to refer to the consensus of those who are dragged down into vice. Even sexual union, which is the beginning of procreation, seems to have been shunned by Plato in the first book of the *Republic* even before Marcion existed. For in praising old age, he remarks: "I would have you know that the more the other pleasures wither away, the more the desires and pleasures of study and learning grow." And when the subject of sexual matters <note>original: "rei venereæ," literally "the things of Venus"</note> was brought up, he said, "Hush! I have gladly escaped from that, as if from some mad and savage master." Again, in the *Phaedo*, he pursues the idea of birth with curses.

<margin>B</margin> Therefore, what is said about these things in the secret teachings <note>original: "arcanis"</note> is this: that we humans are in a kind of custody. Those who are seen to have excelled in living a holy life are the ones who are freed and released from these places on earth as if from prisons, and they arrive above at a pure habitation. But nevertheless, although this is how things stand, he perceives a well-conducted administration and providence, and says: "One must not release oneself or flee." And to say it briefly, he did not give Marcion any occasion to think that matter is evil, since he himself spoke piously about the world. For from the one who constructed it, the world has all its good things; but from its prior state, whatever heavy and unjust things happen in heaven, it has from that [former state] and produces them in living beings. Furthermore, he adds more clearly: "The cause of these things for it is the corporeal temperament <note>The physical makeup or "mixture" of matter</note>, which was joined with

<margin>C</margin> that nature which was of old, because it shared in great confusion and disorder before it came into the world that now exists." Nevertheless, in the *Laws* as well, he laments the human race, saying: "The gods, pitying the human race which was born for labor, established for them the alternations of feast days so that they might rest from their labors." And in the *Epinomis*, he likewise pursues the reasons why they are pitied, saying: "From the beginning, to be born itself is a heavy thing for any living being. First, to share in the things carried in the womb; then to be born; and further to be nourished and educated—all these things happen through innumerable labors, as we all say." What then? Does not Heraclitus also say that birth is death?

<margin>D</margin> Pythagoras says the same, as does Socrates in the *Gorgias* when he says: "Death is whatever we see when awake; whatever we see when sleeping is sleep." But enough of these things. When we treat the subject of first principles, then we shall consider these contradictions which the philosophers signify silently and which the Marcionites decree in their dogmas. For the rest, I think it has been shown clearly enough that Marcion ungratefully and unlearnedly took the occasions for his external and foreign dogmas from Plato. But let our discourse proceed to the topic of continence <note>original: "continentia," meaning self-control or chastity</note>. We were saying that the Greeks, having a suspicion of the difficulty in the use [of the body], said many things regarding the procreation of children; <margin>Aeschylus</margin> and when the Marcionites received these things impiously, they were ungrateful to the Creator. For the tragedy says:

<margin>E</margin>
> It is better for men not to be born than to be born.
> Then I labor to bring forth children with bitter pains;
> And having labored, if I should give birth to fools,
> I am afflicted seeing them become wicked, when nothing helps.
> And again, if I lose the good ones, so that they may be safe,
> My poor heart melts with fear.
> What good is this, truly? Is it not enough to lose
> One soul, unless you afflict yourself further?

And still similarly:

<margin>F</margin>
> This shall become my old conviction:
> A man ought never to plant <note>i.e., beget</note> children,
> Seeing as he perceives to how many evils we beget them.

<summary>Clement argues that Marcion's rejection of the physical world is a crude misunderstanding of Plato and other Greek thinkers, who viewed the body as a challenge but still recognized the world's providential order. He cites various philosophers and tragic poets to show that the "misery of birth" was a common theme they used to encourage virtue, not to spite the Creator.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Clement’s argument from the previous page, where he discussed how Greek philosophers like Plato viewed the body. He now transitions into how poets and other philosophical schools, such as the Pythagoreans, viewed the hardships of life and the physical world, contrasting these views with the heretical stance of Marcion.</meta>

# CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

In the passages that follow, he also clearly traces the cause of evils <margin>A</margin> back to first principles, saying:

> *O man, born wretched and subject to misfortunes,*
> *You were brought forth; from that beginning you held the misery of your life,*
> *From the moment the ether began to provide*
> *The breath that nourishes all mortals.*
> *Since you are mortal, do not be unmindful of this.*

And again, he passes down similar sentiments in this way:

> *No one of all mortals has ever been blessed,*
> *And no one has ever been free from trouble.* <margin>B</margin>

And then again:

> *Alas, how many and how great things happen to the human race,*
> *How many types of evils, and no end is given.*

And still in a similar vein:

> *Among men, no one is perpetually blessed.*

For this reason, they say that even the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras, who combined mathematics with mystical philosophy</note> abstain from sexual matters <note>original: "rebus venereis," literally "the things of Venus," the goddess of love</note>. However, it seems to me, on the contrary, that they take wives in order to raise children, but they wish to restrain themselves from sexual pleasure after children have been born. For this reason, they forbid the use of beans in a mystical sense, not because it is a legume that causes flatulence and is difficult to digest and causes turbulent dreams, nor because it is shaped like a human head, as that well-known verse claims: <margin>C</margin>

-> *Eating a bean is the same as gnawing your father’s head.* <-

<margin>Beans make women sterile.</margin>
But rather because beans, if eaten, make women sterile. Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle, known as the father of botany</note> certainly reports in his book *On Natural Causes* that the pods of beans, if placed at the roots of trees that have recently been planted, dry out the plants. Moreover, domestic hens that eat them constantly are made sterile. Among those who are led by heresy, we have already mentioned Marcion of Pontus <note>A 2nd-century Christian leader who taught that the God of the Old Testament was a lesser, evil creator</note>, because of the struggle he took up against the Creator, as one who rejects the use of worldly things. But for him, the cause of "continence"—if indeed it should be called continence—is the Creator himself, whom he thinks he is opposing. This "Giant" fighting against God is continent against his will, railing against creation and the work of God. 

If they use the voice of the Lord who says to Philip: <margin>D</margin>
<margin>Matthew 8</margin>
"LET the dead bury their own dead, but you, follow me," <note>original: "SINE mortuos sepelire mortuos suos"</note> let them consider this: that Philip also carries a similar physical form <note>original: "carnis figmentum," suggesting the physical body</note>, yet he does not have a "corrupt corpse." How then, while he had flesh, did he not have a "dead body"? Because he rose from the tomb of the Lord, which put his vices to death, and he spoke to Christ.

We also remember the wicked community of women <note>Clement refers to the practice of "wife-sharing" or free love attributed to certain radical sects</note> according to the opinion of Carpocrates. But when we were speaking of the saying of Nicolaus, we passed over this: They say that since he had a beautiful wife, and after the ascension of the Savior he had been reproached by the Apostles for his jealousy, he brought the woman into their midst and permitted anyone who wished to marry her. For they say this action was consistent with that saying which states that "one must abuse the flesh." <note>This was a controversial slogan among early Gnostic groups; Clement argues it meant "disciplining" the flesh, while others took it to mean "indulging" it.</note> Those who follow his heresy follow his deed and saying absolutely and without consideration, and they fornicate shamelessly and excessively. <margin>E</margin> 

However, I hear that Nicolaus indeed used no other wife than the one who had married him, and of his children, his daughters grew old as virgins, and his son remained incorrupt. Since things are so, the bringing of his wife into the midst of the Apostles was a rejection and purging of his vice—the jealousy he was said to suffer from—and his "continence" from those pleasures that are sought with great zeal taught this lesson: To "use the flesh" is to "train the flesh." For they did not wish, as I believe, to serve two masters—pleasure and God—in accordance with the Lord's precept. 

They say that Matthias <note>The apostle chosen to replace Judas Iscariot</note> also taught in this way: <margin>Matthew 6</margin> to fight against the flesh and use it, <margin>F</margin> <margin>The teaching of Matthias.</margin> granting it nothing immodest for the sake of pleasure, but to increase the soul through faith and knowledge. There are those, however, who even proclaim public sexual union <note>original: "publicam venerem"</note> to be a "mystical communion." For just as doing something good is called "working," so also doing something evil is called—

<sig>iii dd</sig>
<meta>Catchword: militer (the first part of "similiter," meaning "similarly")</meta>

He argues that true "continence" involves disciplining the body to serve God, rather than rejecting creation as evil or indulging in licentiousness.</summary>

# STROMATA, BOOK III.

<margin>A</margin> ...to act equivocally in a similar way. In the same manner, "communion" <note>original: "communio," meaning sharing or fellowship</note> is a good thing when it refers to the sharing of money, food, and clothing. However, those people have impiously called any kind of sexual union "communion." Thus, they say that one of them, having approached a certain virgin of ours who was beautiful in appearance, said: "It is written, *Give to everyone who asks of you*." She, however, responded quite honorably, as one who did not understand the man’s lewdness: "But you should go and meet my mother concerning marriage." O the impiety! Even the words of the Lord are forged by these "communicators of intemperance" and "brothers of lust." They are a disgrace not only to philosophy but to the whole of life; they adulterate and corrupt the truth as much as lies within them—or rather, they bury it. These most unhappy of all men proclaim that the union of the flesh and intercourse is <margin>B</margin> a "sacred communion," <margin>High priests of communion</margin> and they believe it leads to the kingdom of God.

Indeed, this "communion" leads to brothels and dens of prostitution, and pigs and goats would be participants in it alongside them. Prostitutes who preside over brothels would have greater hope than they do, for they shamelessly admit anyone who wishes. But you have not learned Christ in this way, if indeed you have heard him and been taught in him, just as <margin>Eph. 4</margin> the truth is in Christ Jesus: that you put off the old self <note>original: "veterem hominem," literally "the old man"</note> which belongs to your former way of life and is corrupted according to deceitful desires. Be renewed in the spirit of your mind and put on the new self created <margin>Eph. 5</margin> according to God in righteousness and the holiness of truth, in the likeness of God. Therefore, become <margin>C</margin> imitators of God, as beloved children, and walk in love, just as Christ also loved us and gave himself up for us as an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweet-smelling aroma. But fornication, and all impurity or greed, let it not even be named among you, as is proper for saints, nor filthiness nor foolish talk. For the Apostle, teaching us to be chaste even in our speech, writes: *For know this, that every fornicator...* and so on, up to the point: *But rather expose them.*

Moreover, their dogma flowed out of a certain secret text, and I will even quote the phrasing, which is the "mother of their lack of self-control." Whether they themselves were the authors of this book’s writing—notice the arrogance, if indeed they lie about God for the sake of their own lack of restraint—or whether they happened upon it through others and suffered perversely from the disease of this famous dogma, this is how the passage goes: "All things were one. But after it seemed good to its Unity not to be alone, inspiration went out from it, and entered into a union and <margin>D</margin> communion with it, and created the 'Beloved.' From this point, inspiration went out from itself, and when it had shared intimacy and union with it, it created the Powers, which can neither be seen nor heard, until each was given its own name."

If these people, like the Valentinians <note>A prominent Gnostic sect following Valentinus</note>, had posited spiritual communions, perhaps someone might have accepted their opinion. But to raise a communion of carnal disgrace to the level of sacred prophecy is the mark of one who despairs of salvation. Such are the things they establish.

The followers of Prodicus <margin>E</margin> also behave this way; they falsely call themselves "Gnostics," claiming they are by nature the children of the first God. Abusing their nobility and freedom, they live as they wish. And they wish to live lustfully, considering themselves to be held by nothing, as "Lords of the Sabbath" and "royal sons" who are superior to every class of people. "For a king," they say, "there is no written law."

<margin>Something seems to be missing here. How false their claims are is clear from these points: first, etc. Or perhaps he deliberately omitted it using a brevity similar to Thucydides. 2 Peter 2.</margin>

First, however, they do not do everything they wish. For many things will prohibit them even if they desire and attempt them. Furthermore, what they do, they do not as kings, but as slaves who deserve the whip <note>original: "mastigiae," a term for a slave who is frequently beaten</note>. For they commit adulteries in secret, fearing lest they be caught, avoiding condemnation, and fearing lest they be punished. How can a lack of self-control and filthy speech be a "free" thing? "For everyone who sins is a slave," says the Apostle. But how can someone establish a life from God who has surrendered himself as a captive to every lust, when the Lord said: "But I say, do not lust"? <margin>F</margin> Does a man wish to sin of his own accord, and pass a decree that he may commit adulteries, and fill himself with pleasures and delights, and violate the marriages of others? While we should pity others who sin unwillingly, if those who have come into the external world are not faithful in what belongs to another, faith will not be kept with them. A guest treats the citizens with insolence and does them injury, not using what is necessary as a traveler... <margin>Exo. 20</margin>

...in various ways, lives without offending fellow citizens? How is it that they—while doing the same things as those who are <margin>A</margin> hated by the nations because they do not follow the commands of the laws (namely, being unjust, lacking self-control, being greedy, and committing adultery)—claim that they alone know God? For it would be necessary for them to live rightly even when among strangers, so that they might truly demonstrate a "royal virtue." <note>Clement refers to "royal virtue" as the supreme, self-governing character of a true philosopher-Christian.</note> But as it is, they are hated by both human legislators and the divine law, since they have chosen to live unjustly and contrary to the laws. <margin>Num. 25</margin> Certainly, the one who stabbed the fornicator <note>Phinehas, who killed an Israelite man and a Midianite woman to stop a plague, as recorded in Numbers 25.</note> is shown by God to be pious in the book of Numbers. <margin>1 John 1</margin> But "if we walk in the light, as he himself is in the light, we have fellowship with him, and the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from sin." <margin>B</margin> How then are these people better than the men of this world or age, when they are similar even to the worst of this world? For I believe that those who are made to be alike are alike by nature. Those whom they judge themselves to be superior to in nobility, they ought also to surpass in character, so that they may avoid being shut up in prison. For truly, as the Lord said: <margin>Matt. 5</margin> "UNLESS your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of God." Regarding abstinence from certain foods, this is demonstrated by Daniel. But to speak plainly: regarding obedience, the psalmist David says: <margin>Psalm 118</margin> <note>Psalm 119 in modern Bibles.</note> "How shall a young man direct his way?" And immediately he hears: "By keeping your words with his whole heart." And Jeremiah says: "Thus says the Lord: Do not walk according to the ways of the nations." <margin>C</margin> Driven by this, certain others, small and of no value, say that man was formed by different powers; they claim that the parts down to the navel are of a more divine craftsmanship, but the parts below are of a lesser one, for which reason those parts crave sexual intercourse. They do not notice, however, that the upper parts also crave nourishment and, in some cases, are prone to lust. They also oppose Christ, who told the Pharisees that the same God made both our internal and external man. Furthermore, desire does not belong to the body, even if it is enacted through the body. Certain others, whom we also call <term>Antitactae</term> <note>original: "Antitactas," meaning "The Opponents" or "The Rebels." These were a Gnostic sect that believed they should break the Old Testament laws to spite the creator-god.</note> (that is, "adversaries" or "those who stand in opposition"), say that God indeed, the Father of all, is ours by nature and all things whatever that are good are his. However, one of those who was made by him sowed weeds, generating a nature of evils, in which he has entangled us all, making us adversaries to the Father. <margin>D</margin> Therefore, they say, we ourselves oppose this creator to avenge the Father, by acting against the will of the second [the creator]. Since he [the creator] said: "You shall not commit adultery," they say: "We commit adultery to dissolve his commandment." We would say to them as well: if we have learned that false prophets and those who fake the truth are known by their works, and your works are ill-reputed and blamed, how can you still say that you possess the truth? For either there is no evil, and thus the one you accuse of being opposed to God is not worthy of blame, nor was he the maker of any evil; for a tree is destroyed along with its bad fruit. Or, if evil exists and persists, let them tell us what they say about those precepts that were given concerning justice, self-<margin>E</margin>control, endurance, patience, and things of this sort—are they good or evil? If the commandment is evil, which forbids the doing of many shameful things, then vice would be passing a law against itself to dissolve itself—which is impossible. But if the commandment is good, then since they oppose good commandments, they confess that they are opposing what is good and doing what is evil. Furthermore, even the Savior himself—whom alone they think should be obeyed—forbade us to hate or to pursue others with curses. And he said: "While going with your adversary, <margin>Matt. 5, Luke 12</margin> try to depart as his friend." Either, therefore, they will also deny the persuasion of Christ by opposing the adversary, or if they are friends, they will not treat him with injury in return. What of this? Do you not know, you "distinguished" men (for I shall speak as if you were present), that by fighting against precepts that are rightly established, you resist your own salvation? For you <margin>Matt. 5</margin> do not overturn those things which were usefully decreed, but rather yourselves. And the Lord says: "Let <margin>F</margin> your good works shine," but you make your lusts and lack of self-control manifest. And besides, if you wish to dissolve the legislator's precepts, for what reason do you follow the one that says "You shall not commit adultery" and "You shall not bring defilement upon a boy,"

### THE MISCELLANIES, BOOK III. ###

<margin>A</margin> You attempt to dissolve the very things and practices that contribute to self-control <note>Original: *continentiam*. Clement refers to the discipline of the body</note> because of your own lack of restraint. Yet you do not dissolve the winter that comes from Him so that you might make it summer in the middle of winter; nor do you make the land navigable or the sea passable on foot, as historians say the barbarian Xerxes wished to do. Why then do you not resist every commandment? For since He says:
> Increase and multiply,
it would be necessary for you, who set yourselves in opposition, to abstain from sexual intercourse entirely. And when He said:
> I have given you all things for food and enjoyment,
you ought to have enjoyed nothing. Furthermore, when He says "an eye for an eye," you should not have repaid a contest with a contrary contest. And when He ordered a thief to pay back fourfold, you should have added even more to what was given to the thief. Again, in the same way, regarding the commandment:
> You shall love your God with all your heart,
if you were to resist this, you ought not even <margin>B</margin> to love the God of the universe. And again, when He said:
> You shall not make a graven or molten image,
it would follow that you ought to worship graven images. How then are you not acting impiously—you who resist the Creator (as you say), but follow after things that are characteristic of harlots and adulterers? How do you not realize that you make Him greater whom you regard as weak? For if what He wills happens, and not what the "Good One" willed, then it is shown by your own actions that your "father" is weak. They also recount certain phrases plucked from Prophetic passages and poorly stitched together—things that were spoken allegorically—taking them as if they were spoken directly and without figure.

<margin>Malachi 3</margin>
<margin>C</margin> For they say it is written:
> They resisted God and were saved.
They attribute this "impudence" even to God <note>Clement is refuting a Gnostic reading of Malachi 3:15 where they interpreted "resisting God" as a heroic act of salvation against a "lesser" Creator-God</note>, and they take this speech as if it were a command of advice, attributing it to their own salvation that they resist the Creator. But it is not written that God is impudent. If it is understood this way, however, you must understand "the impudent one" to be the one called the devil—either as one who accuses sinners, or as one who fell and is an apostate. Therefore, the people of whom this was said—when they were punished for their sins, being distressed and groaning—were murmuring with these words, complaining that other nations were not punished while behaving wickedly, while they themselves were harassed in every matter, just as Jeremiah also said:

<margin>Jeremiah 12</margin>
<margin>Anthypophora</margin>
<margin>Romans 3</margin>
<margin>D</margin>
> Why does the way of the impious prosper?
This is similar to what was said in Malachi: "They resisted God and were saved." For those called Prophets do not only say that they hear certain things from God, but they are also shown to announce through <term>anthypophora</term> <note>A rhetorical device where the speaker voices a common objection or question from the public in order to answer it</note> those things commonly tossed about by the people, bringing forward questions posed by men, among which is the saying proposed here. Was it not regarding these people that the Apostle, directing his words, wrote in the Epistle to the Romans:
> And not as we are slandered, and as some say that we say: "Let us do evil that good may come," whose damnation is just.
These are the people who, in reading, pervert the scriptures with their tone of voice to suit their own pleasures; and by the transposition of certain accents and punctuation marks, they twist what was commanded moderately and usefully to serve their own luxuries.

<margin>Malachi 2</margin>
<margin>Onychizontes</margin>
<margin>E</margin> "You who weary God with your words," says Malachi. And you say, "In what way have we wearied Him?" While you say:
> Everyone who does evil is good in the sight of the Lord, and He is pleased with them; and where is the God of justice?
Therefore, let us not <term>dig further into this spot with a nail</term> <note>Original: *vngue amplius fodicantes* (literally "scratching/digging with a nail"). It refers to over-scrutinizing or obsessively probing a point</note> by remembering more absurd heresies. Nor, on the other hand, should we feel ashamed or make these Commentaries too long by being forced to speak against each one in detail. Come, let us divide all heresies into two types and answer them. For they either teach people to live indifferently <note>i.e., that moral choices don't matter</note>, or, exceeding all measure and tone, they profess a "continence" out of impiety and hatred. First, however, we must treat the first group.

<margin>Accountable</margin>
<margin>1 Corinthians 6</margin>
<margin>F</margin> If any life is permitted to be chosen, then certainly that life which is lived with self-control <note>Original: *continentia*</note> is also permitted. And if any life is free from danger, then a life chosen with virtue and temperance is much more so. For if no account is to be rendered for a life lived without restraint—granted the power given to the "Lord of the Sabbath"—then much more will he who conducts his life moderately and temperately be <term>accountable</term> <note>Original: *ὑπεύθυνον* (hypeuthynon). Clement argues that if the libertines think they are safe from judgment, the virtuous are even safer</note> to no one.

<meta>This page continues Clement’s argument from the previous page, specifically addressing the Gnostic misuse of the concept of "indifference" (*adiaphora*) to justify sexual immorality. Clement transitions from philosophical logic to direct scriptural refutation using the Epistles of Paul and John.</meta>

# CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA #

<margin>1 Cor. 6</margin> ...he is liable to give an account to reason. **All things** are lawful, but not all things are expedient, says the Apostle. But if all things are lawful, then clearly it is also lawful to be moderate and temperate. Just as he is to be praised who used his liberty to live according to virtue, so much more is He to be venerated and adored who gave us free power over ourselves and our own law <note>The Latin *nostri iuris potestatem* refers to "free will" or "autonomy."</note>, and allowed us to live as we wished, for He did not permit our choosing or avoiding to be a matter of necessity. However, even if both paths were equally safe—both for the one who chose lack of restraint and the one who chose self-control—they are still not equal in honor and dignity. For he who crashes into pleasures merely gratifies the body. But the temperate man frees the soul—the mistress of the body—from vices. And if they say we were "called to liberty," let us only take care not to provide liberty as an "opportunity for the flesh," according to the opinion of the Apostle.

But if desire must be obeyed, and if a life that is shameful and foul must be chosen as "indifferent" <term>indifferent: *indifferens* (Greek *adiaphoron*), a Stoic term for things that are neither morally good nor bad</term>, as they themselves claim, then either every desire must be obeyed—and if this were so, one must perform even the most shameless and nefarious acts by following those who persuade us—or there are some desires that must be declined, and we can no longer live "indifferently." We should not shamelessly serve the most vile and abject parts of ourselves—the belly and the genitals—by flattering our own corpse <note>Original: *nostro blandiendo cadaueri*. A common philosophical trope viewing the physical body as a "corpse" that the soul must carry.</note> because of desire. For desire is nourished and kept alive while it is served so that it may enjoy what it wishes; conversely, if it is restrained and disrupted, it withers. How can it be possible for one who is conquered by pleasures to be likened to the Lord, or to have the knowledge of God? For the beginning of every pleasure is desire. And desire is trouble and anxiety, which craves something because of a state of lack. Therefore, those who undertake this way of life seem to me to be nothing other than what is said in the proverb:

<margin>Gal. 5</margin>

---

->*To feel cruel pains beyond ignominy.*<-

---

As those who choose to draw evil upon themselves both now and in the future. If, then, all things were lawful and there was no fear of falling away from our hope because of evil actions, they might perhaps have some pretext for living wickedly and miserably. But since a certain blessed life has been shown to us through the commandments, all who follow them must not listen wrongly to anything that has been said, nor must they despise any of the things that are fitting, even the smallest, but must follow where the Word leads. For if we fall away from it, we must necessarily fall into immortal evil. If, however, we follow the Divine Scripture, through which those who have believed enter in so that they may be likened to the Lord as far as possible, we must not live "indifferently." Instead, we must be clean from pleasures and desires according to our strength, and care must be taken for the soul.

For a mind that is clean and free from every vice is, in a way, fit to receive the power of God, since the divine image arises in it; and "whoever has hope in the Lord," he says, "makes himself clean and chaste, even as He is chaste." <margin>1 John 3. Clement reads *hagnizei* (purifies); our translator reads *hagiazei*, for he translates it as "sanctifies."</margin> That those who are still led by vices should receive the knowledge of God is quite impossible. Therefore, it is also impossible for those who have no knowledge of God to attain the Goal <note>The "Goal" or *finis* refers to the ultimate purpose of human life, usually defined as union with God.</note>. The ignorance of God seems to accuse the one who does not attain this end. Furthermore, a man's way of life is what causes God to be ignored. For it is completely impossible for someone to be endowed with knowledge and yet not blush at flattering the body. Nor can it ever be agreed that pleasure is "the good" when only the beautiful and honorable is good—or even when the Lord alone is beautiful, and God alone is good and alone lovable.

**In** Christ you were circumcised with a circumcision not made by hands, in the stripping off of the body of the flesh, in the circumcision of Christ. <margin>Col. 2</margin> If then you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, savor the things that are above, not the things that are on the earth. For you are dead, and your life is hidden with Christ in God—but not that life which is practiced by fornication. Put to death, therefore, your members which are on the earth: fornication, uncleanness...

<meta>This page continues Clement of Alexandria’s defense of marriage and the physical world against Gnostic extremists. On the previous page, he argued against those who used "liberty" as an excuse for immoral behavior. Here, he shifts to refuting those who claim that marriage and procreation are inherently evil or "worldly," using the teachings of the Apostles and the sayings of Jesus to prove that the body and its functions can be sanctified.</meta>

# THE MISCELLANIES, BOOK III #

<margin>A</margin> ...added passion and desire, because of which wrath comes. Let them also, therefore, put away anger, indignation, vice, slander, and foul talk from their mouths, stripping off the **old man** with its lusts, and putting on the **new man** who is renewed in knowledge according to the image of Him who created him. For a person’s way of life clearly proves whether they truly know the commandments. Indeed, as the speech is, so is the life. **A tree is known by its fruits**, not by its flowers, leaves, and branches. Knowledge <note>original: "cognitio," likely referring to "Gnosis"</note>, therefore, comes from the fruit and the way one lives, not from mere words and outward show. For we do not say that knowledge is merely words, but a certain divine science, and that light which is born in the soul from obedience to the commandments, which makes manifest all things that exist in the realm of generation <note>The physical world of birth and change</note>, and instructs a man so that he may **know himself**, and teaches him to direct his thoughts toward God.

<margin>B</margin> For what the eye is to the body, knowledge is to the mind. Nor should they call that "liberty" which is actually a slavery to pleasure, like those who claim that bitter bile is sweet. We have learned of the liberty with which our Lord sets us free, releasing us from pleasures, desires, and other vices and disturbances of the soul. <margin>1 John 2</margin> **He who says, "I know the Lord," and does not keep His commandments, is a liar, and the truth is not in him**, as John says.

Moreover, there are those who, using certain beautiful-sounding words to promote "continence," are actually impious toward both the creation and the holy Creator—the only Almighty God. They say that one should not accept marriage or the procreation of children; they argue that we should not bring other miserable souls into the world, nor provide "food for death." To these people, we must say the following. First, that word <margin>C</margin> <margin>1 John 2</margin> of John’s: **And now many Antichrists have arisen, by which we know that it is the last hour. They went out from us, but they were not of us. For if they had been of us, they would surely have remained with us.**

Next, the arguments they bring forward must be overturned and dissolved in this way: When Salome asked how long death would hold power <note>This refers to an apocryphal dialogue often attributed to the lost *Gospel according to the Egyptians*</note>, the Lord—not as if life were evil, or the creation were bad—replied: **"As long as you women give birth."** He said this as one teaching a natural consequence: for destruction always follows birth. 

Indeed, the Law intends to lead you away from luxuries and every shame and disgrace. This is its goal: to lead from injustice to justice, by choosing honorable and moderate marriages, the procreation of children, and a good way of life. <margin>D</margin> The Lord, however, did not come to abolish the Law, but to fulfill it; and to fulfill it not as if it were lacking anything, but because the prophecies of the Law were completed at His arrival. For a right way of life was preached through the Word even to those who lived justly before the Law.

The common crowd of men, therefore, who do not know continence, live by the body, but not by the spirit. Without the spirit, however, the body is merely earth and ash. Now, the Lord judges even adultery from the thought. For why? Is it not also permitted to use marriage with self-control, and not try to dissolve what the Lord has joined? For such are the teachings of those who divide marriages, which is why the name [of Christ] is attacked with insults and slander among the Gentiles. These men say that sexual intercourse is a crime; yet since they themselves exist because of intercourse, how can they not be <margin>E</margin> criminals in their own eyes? But for those who are sanctified, I believe the "seed" is also holy. 

For us, it is not only the spirit that must be sanctified, but also our character, our life, and our body. For by what reasoning does the Apostle Paul say that a woman is sanctified by her husband, or a husband by his wife? <margin>1 Cor. 7</margin> And what of the fact that the Lord also spoke to those who asked about divorce—whether it was lawful to put away a wife, since Moses permitted it? He said: **"Moses wrote this because of the hardness of your hearts."** <margin>Matt. 19; Mark 10</margin> Have you not read that God said to the first-formed man: **"You two shall be in one flesh"**? Therefore, he who divorces his wife, except for the cause of fornication, makes her commit adultery.

<margin>F</margin> But they argue that after the resurrection, <margin>Luke 20</margin> **they neither marry nor are given in marriage.** Indeed, it was also said concerning the belly and food: <margin>1 Cor. 6</margin> **Food is for the belly, and the belly for food; but God will destroy both it and them.** He was attacking those who, like goats and rams— 

<summary>Clement refutes ascetic Gnostics who reject marriage, arguing that "true knowledge" (Gnosis) leads to a sanctified life within creation rather than a rejection of it. He explains that while birth naturally leads to death, marriage and procreation are part of God's law and can be practiced with Christian self-control.</summary>

<margin>
He will abolish; <note>original Greek: "katargēsei"</note> he will render idle and cause to cease.
</margin>
<margin>A</margin>
...they think they must live for themselves, so that they might not eat and mate securely and without fear. If they have therefore received the resurrection, as they themselves say, and for this reason they weaken and abolish marriage, then let them also neither eat nor drink. For the Apostle <note>Saint Paul</note> says that in the resurrection the belly and foods will be made idle and cease to be. Why then do they hunger and thirst, and suffer the affections of the flesh, and other things which will not be suffered by the one who, through Christ, has received the perfect resurrection for which we hope? Furthermore, even those who worship idols abstain from certain foods and from sexual intercourse. <margin>Romans 14</margin> "But the kingdom of God," he says, "is not food and drink." Certainly, it is also a concern for the Magi <note>Persian priests/astrologers</note>, who worship angels and demons, to abstain simultaneously from wine, from the flesh of living creatures, and from sexual matters. But just as humility is gentleness, and not the mere affliction of the body, so also continence is a virtue of the soul, which is not found in what is manifest outwardly, but in what is hidden within.

<margin>B</margin>
There are also those who openly call marriage "fornication," and decree that it was handed down by the devil. These boastful pretenders say they are imitating the Lord, who neither took a wife nor possessed anything in the world, glorying that they have understood the Gospel better than others. But the Scripture says to them: "God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble." Furthermore, they do not know the reason why the Lord did not take a wife. First, He had His own bride, the Church. Second, He was not a common man, such that He had need of a helper according to the flesh. Nor was it necessary for Him to procreate children, He who remains for eternity and was born as the only Son of God.

<margin>C</margin>
The Lord Himself says: <margin>Matthew 19, Mark 10</margin> "What God has joined together, let no man separate." And again: <margin>Matthew 24</margin> "As it was in the days of Noah, they were marrying and giving in marriage, building and planting; and as it was in the days of Lot, so shall be the coming of the Son of Man." And that He might show He is not speaking only to the Gentiles <note>non-Jews</note>, He adds: <margin>Luke 18</margin> "When the Son of Man comes, will He find faith on the earth?" <margin>Luke 21</margin> And again: "Woe to those who are pregnant and nursing in those days." Although these things are also spoken allegorically. For this reason He did not predefine the times which the Father has placed in His own power, so that the world might continue through generations. As for that saying: <margin>Matthew 19</margin> "Not all can accept this word. For there are eunuchs who were born so, and there are eunuchs who were castrated by men, and there are eunuchs who castrated themselves for the sake of the kingdom of heaven.

<margin>D</margin>
He who can accept it, let him accept it." They do not know that after He had spoken about divorce, when some had asked: "If such is the case of a man with his wife, it is not expedient to marry," then the Lord said: "Not all can accept this word, but those to whom it is given." Now, those who were asking this wanted to know from Him whether, if a wife were condemned and cast out because of fornication, He would grant permission to marry another. They say that not a few athletes also abstain from sexual pleasure for the sake of physical training, practicing continence, such as Ascylus of Croton and Crison of Himera. Furthermore, Amoebeus the lyre-player, though he had recently married, abstained from his bride; and Aristotle of Cyrene <note>Likely referring to the philosopher Aristippus of Cyrene, who was famous for his relationship with the courtesan Lais</note> was the only one to despise Lais when she loved him.

<margin>E</margin>
Therefore, when he had sworn to the harlot that he would take her away to his fatherland if she gave him some help against his opponents in certain contests, after he had accomplished this, he wittily fulfilled the oath he had written by setting up an image of her as like her as possible in Cyrene, <margin>Ister</margin> as Ister writes in the book *On the Peculiarity of Contests*. <margin>eunuch-hood <note>original Greek: "eunouchian"</note></margin> Wherefore, even chastity is not a "good" or a "virtue" unless it is done for the sake of the love of God. <margin>1 Timothy 4</margin> Now, concerning those who abhor marriage, the blessed Paul says: "In the last days some will depart from the faith, giving heed to spirits of error and doctrines of demons, forbidding to marry and to abstain from foods." <margin>Colossians 2</margin> And again he says: "Let no one seduce you by insisting on humility and religion and the harsh treatment of the body."

<margin>F</margin>
He also writes those same things elsewhere: <margin>1 Corinthians 7</margin> "Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek a release. Are you free from a wife? Do not seek a wife." And again: "Let each man have his own wife, lest Satan tempt you." What then, did not even the righteous men of old participate in the created world with thanksgiving? <meta>This page continues Clement’s discussion of "continence" (self-control), moving from the examples of the Apostles to a philosophical and comparative religious analysis. He distinguishes Christian self-control from both Greek philosophy and the extreme asceticism or moral laxity of various sects.</meta>

### CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

I say, the view which comes from the opinion of the Greek Philosophers, professes to fight against <margin>A</margin>
desire and not to serve it in one's deeds. However, the continence according to our own view is not to feel desire at all; it is not that a man should act bravely while feeling desire, but that he should restrain himself even from the act of desiring. This continence, however, cannot be attained in any other way except <margin>Matthew 7; Luke 11</margin> by the grace of God. And for this reason He said: "Ask, and it shall be given to you." Moses also received this grace, he who was clothed in a needy body, so that for forty days he neither hungered nor thirsted. Just as it is better to be healthy than for a sick man to discourse about health, so too it is better to be the light than to speak about the light. And the continence which comes from the truth is better than that which is taught by the Philosophers. For where there is light, there is no darkness. But where desire alone sits within, even if it rests from the operation that occurs through the body, the memory certainly still clashes with that which is not present. In short, and let our <margin>B</margin> discourse proceed generally for us regarding marriage, food, and other things: let us do nothing out of desire, but let us will only those things which are necessary. For we are not children of desire, but of the will; and he who has taken a wife for the procreation of children ought to exercise continence, so that he does not even lust after his own wife, whom he ought to love, giving his effort to children with an honorable and moderate will. For we have not learned to "make provision for the flesh for its lusts," but walking honorably as in the day of Christ, and in the bright, Lordly instruction and conversation of life; "not in carousing and drunkenness, not in sexual promiscuity and indecency, not in strife and jealousy." <note>Clement is quoting Romans 13:13-14 here.</note> Truly, indeed, one ought not to consider continence in one <margin>C</margin> kind alone, namely in sexual matters, but also in whatever other things the soul lustfully desires, not content with necessities but anxious for luxuries. Continence is to despise money, pleasure, and possessions; to look down upon the public spectacles with a great and lofty soul; to restrain the mouth; and to conquer by reason those things which are evil. Now, indeed, even certain angels, when they had been incontinent, overcome by desire, descended here from heaven. <note>A reference to the "Watchers" or fallen angels from the Book of Enoch who desired human women.</note> Valentinus, however, in his letter to Agathopus, says: "Jesus, having sustained all things, was continent. He worked by his divinity. He ate and drank in a particular way, not returning the food." <note>original: "non reddens cibos." This refers to the Docetic belief that Jesus did not excrete waste because his body was not fully human/corruptible.</note> So great was the power of continence in him that the nourishment in him did not perish, because he himself had no perishing. We, therefore, because of love for the Lord and for the sake of what is honorable itself, embrace continence, sanctifying the temple of the spirit. For it is honorable, for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, to castrate oneself <margin>D</margin> from all desire, and to cleanse the conscience from dead works to serve the living God. But those who, because of a hatred taken up against the flesh, desire to be freed from the conjugal union and from the participation in common foods, are unlearned and impious, and are continent without reason, like many other nations. The Brahmins <note>original: "Brachmanes"</note> certainly eat no living thing and drink no wine. But some of them take food daily as we do; others, however, every third day, as Alexander Polyhistor says in his book *On Indian Affairs*. They despise death and make nothing of living, for they believe there is a regeneration <note>Clement refers here to the concept of reincarnation or Saṃsāra.</note>. Some worship Hercules and Pan. Those among the Indians who are called <term>semnoi</term> <note>original: σεμνοὶ, meaning "venerable" or "holy ones." These are likely Buddhist monks or Shramanas.</note>, which means "honorable and venerable," spend their whole lives naked. These men practice the truth, predict the future, and worship a certain pyramid <margin>E</margin> under which they think the bones of some God are laid. <note>This is one of the earliest Western descriptions of a Buddhist Stupa.</note> Neither the Gymnosophists <note>literally "naked philosophers"</note> nor those called <term>semnoi</term>, that is, "venerable," use women. For they think this is against nature and unjust. For this reason, they keep themselves chaste. There are also women who are called <term>semnai</term> <note>original: σεμναὶ, the feminine form of the previous term</note>, that is, "venerable," who are virgins. They seem to observe the heavens and, through their signs, predict certain future things. Since, however, those who introduce "indifference" <note>A term for the heretical belief that physical actions do not affect the soul's salvation.</note>, twisting a few scriptures, think they support their own itching pleasure—specifically that one: "For sin <margin>Rom. 6.</margin> shall not have dominion over you; for you are not under the law, but under grace," and some others of this kind, of which it is not consistent with reason for me to make mention here. For I do not equip a ship for the purpose of piracy; so let us break the argument of those few men. For the excellent Apostle himself, subjoining to the aforementioned saying, will bring the solution to the intended crime. <margin>F</margin> "WHAT then? Shall we sin because we are not under the law, but under grace? God forbid!" Thus, in the same footsteps, he dissolves the art of divine and prophetic pleasure...

### STROMATA, BOOK III.

<margin>A</margin>...adapted sophistry. They do not understand, therefore, as it seems, that "we must all be made manifest before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive the things done through the body, according to what he has done, whether <margin>2 Corinthians 5</margin> good or evil," <note>original: "bonum, siue malum"</note> so that someone may receive what he has done through the body. Therefore, if there is any "new creature" in Christ, that person is no longer devoted to sins. "Old things have passed away." <margin>sinful <note>original: "ἁμαρτητικὴ"</note></margin> We have stripped off the old life: for behold, "new things have been made," chastity out of fornication, and self-control out of lack of control; justice out of injustice. For "what participation is there between justice and injustice, or what fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement is there between Christ <margin>2 Corinthians 6</margin> and Belial? What part has a believer with an unbeliever? What agreement has the temple of God with idols?" Having these promises, therefore, "let us cleanse ourselves from all <margin>1 Corinthians 7</margin> defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God." <margin>B</margin> But those who resist God’s creation through that "fair-sounding" self-control <note>Clement is being sarcastic about their extreme asceticism.</note> also say those things which were spoken to Salome, <note>Salome appears in apocryphal texts as a disciple who asks Jesus deep philosophical questions.</note> which we mentioned earlier. They are found, I believe, in the *Gospel according to the Egyptians*. <note>A lost "apocryphal" gospel used by early Egyptian Christians but not included in the New Testament.</note> For they say that the Savior himself said: <margin>Gospel according to the Egyptians.</margin> "I CAME to dissolve the works of the woman." By "the woman," he meant desire; and by "works," he meant generation and decay. What then? Would they say this arrangement of the world has been dissolved? They would not say so. For the world remains in the same administration. But the Lord did not speak a falsehood. For in truth, he dissolved the works of desire: greed, strife, the lust for glory, the insane love for women, pederasty, gluttony, luxury and wastefulness, and things similar to these. The birth of these things is the destruction of the soul, since we are made dead by our transgressions. Indeed, that "woman" is intemperance. <margin>C</margin> But it is fundamentally necessary for birth and decay <note>Generation and death.</note> to occur in creation, until the perfect and completely absolute distinction and restoration of the "election" <note>The "elect" or the community of believers.</note> is achieved, through which even those substances which are mixed and confused in the world are restored to their own proper nature. Whence, rightfully, when the Word had signified something regarding the end of the world, Salome said, "How long shall men die?" The scripture calls "man" in two ways: both the one who is seen (the body) and the soul; and again, the one who is saved and the one who is not. Sin is called the death of the soul. Therefore, the Lord responds carefully and considerately: "As long as women bear children," that is, as long as desires are at work. And therefore, "just as through one man sin entered <margin>D</margin> into the world, so through sin death spread to all men, <margin>Romans 5: in whom <note>original: "ἐφ' ᾧ"</note></margin> inasmuch as all have sinned." "And death reigned from Adam until Moses," says the Apostle; but by the natural necessity of the divine Economy, death follows generation, and the dissolution of the body and soul follows their joining together. If, however, birth exists for the sake of learning and knowledge, and dissolution is for the sake of restoration: then, just as a woman is thought to be the cause of death because she gives birth, so too she shall be called the leader of life for the same reason. Now, she who first began the transgression was called "Life" <note>A reference to Eve (Zoe), whose name means "Life."</note> because of the cause of succession; and she is the mother of those being born, both the just and the unjust, with each of us either justifying himself or, on the contrary, making himself disobedient. Hence, I certainly do not think the Apostle abhorred the life which is in the flesh, when he says: "BUT in all confidence, as always, <margin>E</margin> so now also, Christ shall be magnified in my body, whether by life <margin>Philippians 1</margin> or by death. For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain. But if to live in the flesh is also the fruit of work for me, what I shall choose I know not; and I am hard pressed between the two, desiring to be dissolved and to be with Christ: for that is much better; but to remain in the flesh is more necessary for your sake." For through these words, as I think, he clearly shows that the departure of the body is a perfection of love toward God; but his presence in the flesh is an endurance proceeding from a grateful heart, for the sake of those who have need to be saved. But what of this? Do they not also add the things that follow after what was said to Salome—those people who follow anything rather than the Gospel rule which is from the truth? <margin>F</margin> For when she had said, "I did well then, that I did not bear children" (on the assumption that birth was not to be taken up as it should), the Lord replied, saying: "Eat of every herb, but that which has bitterness, do not eat." For by these words he signifies that it is in our power, and is not a necessity—

<meta>This page continues Clement’s argument that marriage is part of God's providential design. He is specifically refuting the Gnostic groups who viewed the physical world and procreation as evil. The catchword "as if" connects to the previous discussion of how these groups misinterpret the purpose of the body.</meta>

# CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

...as if <margin>A</margin> <margin>it is joined with the acquisition [of a wife] according to reason, for the sake of the pleasing tasks of necessity <note>original Greek: "συμφράζεται τῆ κτήσει κατά λόγον διά τάς χρείας ἀσχολίας εὐάρεστον"</note></margin> marriage brings some help to the work of creation, as he further explains. Therefore, let no one consider marriage a sin when it is conducted according to reason—which is the Word <term>Logos; Clement often uses "reason" and "the Word of God" interchangeably</term>—unless one considers the upbringing of children to be a bitter thing. On the contrary, for many, to be without children seems the most difficult burden. Nor should the procreation of children seem bitter to anyone because it draws one away from divine things through the business of managing necessary affairs. For the man who does not easily bear a solitary life desires marriage, since that which is close to the heart is harmless when joined with temperance. Each of us has the power to choose whether we wish to father children.

I observe, however, how some who have abstained from marriage under the pretext of its difficulties have not acted in accordance with <margin>hatred of mankind <note>original Greek: "μισανθρωπίαν"</note></margin> holy knowledge, but have instead fallen away into inhumanity and a hatred of men; <margin>B</margin> and among them, charity has perished. Others, however, who have embraced the concessions of the law, have become bound and steeped in the tingling pleasures of the senses; they have become, as the Prophet says, "like onto the beasts."

<margin>Matthew 18</margin> Now, who are those "two or three" who are gathered in the name of the Lord, in whose midst the Lord is? Does he not mean by the three a man, a woman, and a child, since a woman is joined to a man through God? But if a man wishes to be unencumbered and <margin>unmarried <note>original Greek: "ἄγαμος"; referencing 1 Corinthians 7</note></margin> unhindered, not wishing to procreate children because of the trouble and occupation involved in raising them, let him remain, says the Apostle, "celibate as I am."

Some explain the Lord’s meaning by saying that He is the Creator and God of generation when with the many, but with the "one"—namely the elect—He is the Savior, who is the Son of a different God, a "Good God." <note>Clement is refuting the Marcionite heresy, which claimed there were two different gods: a harsh Creator God of the Old Testament and a Good Savior God of the New.</note> But this is not the case. <margin>C</margin> Rather, God is present through His Son with those who have lived honestly and moderately in marriage and have raised children. And the same God is likewise present with the one who has remained continent <margin>otherwise <note>original Greek: "λοιπῶς"</note></margin> in a manner consistent with reason and the Word. 

Furthermore, these "three" might be understood in another way: as anger, desire, and reason; or in another sense as flesh, soul, and spirit. Perhaps the "triad" mentioned earlier also quietly signifies the calling, the election, and the third class which is placed in the first honor. <margin>without division <note>original Greek: "ἀμερίστως"</note></margin> With these is the power of God, which watches over all things, descending without being divided into that which is divided.

He who uses the operations of the soul according to nature as he ought, desires those things that are appropriate and hates those things that are harmful, just as the commandments order: "You shall bless him who blesses," it says, "and curse him who curses." <margin>D</margin> When, however, he moves beyond these things—namely anger and desire—and truly loves the creation for the sake of Him who is God and the Maker of all, he shall live by right knowledge. He does not gain a habit of self-control through labor, but through an assimilation to the Savior, a union of knowledge, faith, and love. As one who is "one" in his final judgment, and truly spiritual, he does not admit thoughts arising from anger or desire. This "perfect man," fashioned by the Master Architect Himself in the image of the Lord, is worthy to be called a brother by the Lord; he is both friend and son.

Thus, "two and three" are gathered in the same place: namely, in the man endowed with knowledge. Furthermore, the harmony of many might also be counted as "three," with whom the Lord is: the one Church, the one man, the one race. Was the Lord not with the one Jewish people when He gave the Law? <margin>E</margin> And now, by prophesying and sending Jeremiah to Babylon, and even calling those from the Gentiles through prophecy, He has gathered two peoples. The third is the "one" who is created out of the two into a "new man," in whom He walks and dwells within the Church itself. The Law and the Prophets, together with the Gospel, are gathered into one knowledge in the name of Christ.

Therefore, those who do not marry because of hatred, or who use the flesh indifferently because of lust, are not among those who are saved and with whom the Lord is. Having shown these things, come now, let us bring forward whatever Scriptures oppose those Sophists who arise from heresies, <margin>F</margin> declaring the rule of self-control that is observed in accordance with reason and the Word. Each heresy brings forward the Scripture that seems to favor it. But he who understands will use it at the right time to refute those who establish decrees contrary to the commandments. And so, to repeat the matter from the beginning: the Law indeed...

<summary>Clement of Alexandria interprets the "two or three gathered" (Matthew 18:20) as the Christian family or the internal harmony of the soul, refuting Gnostic claims that marriage is unholy. He argues that true spiritual perfection comes through loving God's creation with reason, rather than through extreme asceticism or total license.</summary>

### STROMATA, BOOK III.

<margin>A</margin> ...as we said before, that commandment, *You shall not covet your neighbor's wife*, was proclaimed long before the similar and connected voice of the Lord, who says in his own person: <margin>Matthew 5</margin> *YOU HAVE HEARD the law commanding, "You shall not commit adultery." But I say, "You shall not even lust."* <note>Clement is arguing that Jesus did not abolish the Old Testament law but intensified it by focusing on the internal desire (lust) rather than just the outward act.</note> For it is clear that the law intended for men to use their wives with moderation, and solely for the purpose of conceiving children, from the fact that it forbids a man who does not have a wife from immediately having relations with a female captive. If he should desire her, he must allow her to shave her hair and mourn for thirty days. If, after this, his passion has not faded, only then may he devote himself to producing children; for the impulse that dominates him will have been tested over a set time, making his desire consistent with reason. From this, <margin>It cannot be shown from Scripture that the ancients were accustomed to have relations with pregnant women. <note>original Greek: γαλακτοχίαν - referring to the period of nursing/lactation</note></margin>

<margin>B</margin> you will not find anyone among the ancients in Scripture who had relations with a pregnant wife. Only after she had carried the womb to term, and after the child was born and weaned from milk, were the wives again known by their husbands. You will find that the father of Moses maintained this aim and practice; for he waited three years after the birth of Aaron before fathering Moses. Again, the tribe of Levi, by observing this law of nature delivered by God, entered the promised land smaller in number than the others. For a race does not multiply easily when men who enter into legitimate marriage sow their seed and then wait not only for the duration of the pregnancy, but also for the weaning from milk. Thus, Moses also rightly led the Jews toward self-control by degrees, for he commanded them to hear the words of God only after they had abstained from sexual pleasure for three consecutive days.

We, therefore, are the temples of God, as the Prophet says: *I will dwell in them, and walk* <margin>Leviticus 26. 2 Corinthians 6.</margin>
<margin>C</margin> *among them; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people*, if we arrange our lives according to the commandments, whether individually or as the whole church together. *WHEREFORE come out from among them, and be separate, says the Lord. And touch no unclean thing. and I will receive you, and I will be a Father to you. And you shall be my sons and daughters*, says <margin>Isaiah 51. 2 Corinthians 6.</margin> the Lord Almighty. He commands us prophetically to separate ourselves—not from those who have married, as some claim, but from the heathens who were still living in fornication, and moreover from the previously mentioned heresies, as being impure and impious. For this reason, Paul also addressed those who were like the people mentioned: *Since we HAVE* <margin>2 Corinthians 7.</margin> *these promises, beloved, let us cleanse our hearts from every defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God.* For I am jealous for you with the jealousy <margin>2 Corinthians 11.</margin>
<margin>D</margin> *of God, for I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.* The Church, possessing a bridegroom, is not joined in marriage to another. But each of us has the power, if we wish, to marry a legitimate wife—in a first marriage, I mean. *But I fear lest, as the serpent deceived Eve by his craftiness, your senses should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ.* The Apostle spoke this very piously and in the manner of a teacher.

Wherefore the admirable Peter also says: *DEAREST ONES, I beseech you as* <margin>1 Peter 2.</margin> *strangers and pilgrims, to abstain from carnal desires, which war against the soul, keeping your conduct good among the Gentiles: for such is the will of God, that by doing good you may silence the ignorance of foolish men, as free people, and not using your liberty as a cloak for malice,* <margin>The Greek text of Clement has "practice" <note>original Greek: ἐργασίαν</note></margin>
<margin>E</margin> *but as servants of God.* Similarly, Paul also writes in the epistle to the Romans: *WE WHO* <margin>Romans 6.</margin> *died to sin, how shall we still live in it? Since our old man was crucified with him, that the body of sin might be destroyed...* and so on, until the point: *Neither yield your members as instruments of unrighteousness to sin.* And so, having come to this place, I do not think I should leave it unnoted that the Apostle preaches the same God through the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospel. For that phrase, *You shall not covet*, which <margin>The Law also forbade covetousness.</margin> is written in the Gospel, he attributes to the Law in the epistle to the Romans, knowing that He who preached through the Law and the Prophets is the same as the Father who is announced through Himself. <margin>Romans 7.</margin> For he says: *WHAT shall we say? Is the law sin? God forbid. But I did not know sin except through the law. For I would not have known lust if the law had not said, "You shall not*
<margin>F</margin> *covet."* Even if those who hold a different opinion, being contentious, think that Paul said the words that follow as an attack against the Creator: *For I KNOW that no good thing dwells in me, that is, in my flesh.* But let them read what follows...

### CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

...what was said before and those things that follow. For he first said, <margin>A</margin> **BUT it is sin dwelling in me.** For which reason it was consistent to say, **good does NOT dwell in my flesh.** Consequently, he added: "But if I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but the sin that dwells in me." This sin, he says, "fighting against the law of God and the law of my mind, takes me captive to the law of sin which is in my members. **Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death?**" <margin>to say in addition <note>original Greek: ἐπιλέγειν</note></margin> And again (for he never grows weary of helping in any way possible), he does not hesitate to conclude, as it were: **For the LAW of the spirit has set me free from the law of sin and death.** For through his Son, God condemned sin in the flesh, so that the justification of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the spirit. Beyond these things, still explaining what was said before, he cries out, <margin>B</margin> **The body indeed is dead because of sin**, signifying that the body is not a temple, but a "sepulcher" <note>or "tomb"</note> for the soul. For when it has been sanctified to God, the spirit of Him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in us. <margin>Romans 8</margin> **He will also give life to your mortal bodies through His spirit dwelling in you.** Therefore, rebuking those devoted to pleasure once again, he adds those words: **For the wisdom of the flesh is death.** For those who live according to the flesh think on the things of the flesh, and the wisdom of the flesh is to be at enmity with God; for it is not subject to the law of God. "Those who are in the flesh," however—not as some decree <note>referring to heretical groups who taught the physical body was inherently evil</note>—"cannot please God," but rather as we said before. Then, to distinguish them, he says to the church: **But you are not in the flesh but in the spirit, since the spirit of God dwells in you. But if anyone does not have the spirit of Christ, he is none of His.** <margin>C</margin> **But if Christ is in you, the body indeed is dead through sin, but the Spirit is alive through righteousness. Therefore, brothers, we are debtors, not to the flesh to live according to the flesh. For if you live according to the flesh, you are going to die. But if by the spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live. For as many as are led by the spirit of God, these are the sons of God.** And against that "nobility" and "freedom" which is execrably introduced by those of a different opinion <note>Clement refers to Gnostic sects who claimed spiritual "freedom" as an excuse for licentiousness</note>, who boast on account of their lust and intemperance, he adds, saying: **For you did not receive the spirit of slavery again unto fear, but you received the spirit of adoption as sons, in which we cry, "Abba, Father."** <margin>1 Corinthians 7 / Something is missing.</margin> That is, we received it for this purpose: that we might know Him whom we pray to, who is truly the Father—who is the sole Father of all things that exist, who instructs and corrects for our salvation like a father, and threatens with fear. <margin>D</margin> As for the fact that marriage "by mutual consent" is vacant from sexual relations "for a time" for the sake of prayer, this is a teaching of self-control. For he added that phrase **by mutual consent** so that no one should dissolve a marriage; and **for a time**, lest the one who has taken a wife, practicing continence out of necessity, should eventually fall into sin—that is, falling into a state where he spares his own marriage but lusts after another's. For this reason, even concerning the man who thinks he is behaving improperly or unseemly because he supports a virgin, the Apostle rightly says he should give her in marriage. But the purpose of each person—both of the one who has "castrated himself" (that is, who has chosen chastity) and of the one who, on the other hand, has joined himself in marriage for the sake of procreating children—ought to remain firm, not yielding or giving in to that which is lesser and inferior. <margin>E</margin> For if a man is able to add some growth to his life, he will acquire for himself a greater dignity in God, as one who has been self-controlled both purely and confidently. But if he goes beyond the rule he has chosen, he will later fall back from that hope into a greater glory <note>Clement likely means the person will lose the special reward of celibacy if they cannot maintain the standard they set for themselves</note>. For marriage, just like chastity, has its own proper gifts and ministries which pertain to the Lord—namely, taking care of children and a wife. For what is honorably pleaded by the man who is "perfect" in marriage <margin>1 Timothy 3</margin> is the necessity of the union, as one who has shown care and foresight for everyone in a shared home. **Bishops**, he says, **ought to be appointed who, having practiced in their own home, are prepared to preside over the whole church.** Let each person, therefore, perform the ministry in the work in which he was called, so that he may become free in Christ. <margin>Romans 7</margin> And again, discussing the law and using an allegory: **For the woman who is under a husband is bound to the law while the husband lives**, and so forth. <margin>F</margin> And again: **A woman is bound as long as her husband lives. But if he dies, she is free to marry, only in the Lord. But she is more blessed if she remains as she is, in my opinion.** But in the earlier section he says, **You are put to death to the law...**
