### STROMATA BOOK III

<margin>A</margin> ...not from marriage, so that you may belong to another—to Him who was raised from the dead—as the bride and the **Church**. This Church must be chaste, both from the internal thoughts that are contrary to the truth and from those who attempt to influence it from the outside. That is to say, from those who follow heresies and try to persuade you to commit "fornication" away from your one husband, namely, the Almighty God. We must take care that, just as the serpent deceived Eve (who is called "Life"), we too are not led astray by the clever allurements of heresies to transgress the commandments. 

Furthermore, the second part of the passage establishes **monogamy** <note>the practice of being married to only one person</note>. For we should not think, as some have supposed, that the "binding" of a woman to a man signifies the connection of the soul to the destruction of the flesh. Such people openly attribute the invention of marriage to the Devil, and their views represent a direct attack on the Creator. In doing so, the Lawgiver <note>God</note> is in danger of being pursued with insults. I believe it is Tatian the Syrian <margin>Tatian</margin> who dares to decree such dogmas. 

<margin>B</margin> He certainly writes these things in his book *On Perfection According to the Savior*. He claims that "agreement" <note>concord</note> joins one to prayer, but that "communion" or sexual union is "destruction" and dissolves the act of petitioning. He very cautiously tries to forbid marriage while appearing to grant it. For when he mentions that the Apostle permitted a couple to "come together again" because of Satan and a lack of self-restraint, he declares that whoever obeys this is "serving two masters": through agreement, they serve God, but through disagreement <margin>Greek: *asymphōnias* (discord)</margin> they serve lack of restraint, fornication, and the Devil. 

He says these things while interpreting the Apostle Paul. However, he sophistically evades the truth, using a truth to confirm a falsehood. For we also confess that lack of restraint and fornication are Diabolical vices and passions. Yet, in a **moderate marriage**, there is an agreement of the will that leads temperately toward prayer and joins the couple together for the procreation of children with honor. 

<margin>C</margin> Indeed, the Scripture uses the word **"knowledge"** to describe the time of procreating children, when it says: **"ADAM KNEW Eve his wife, and she conceived, and bore a son, and named him Seth. For God has raised up for me another seed in place of Abel."** Do you see whom they are attacking with their insults? They insult honorable and moderate procreation and attribute generation <note>the act of bringing life into being</note> to the Devil. The text does not simply say "god," but uses the definite article—**the God** <note>original: *ho Theos*</note>—signifying the Almighty. 

As for what the Apostle adds—**"And again, come together"**—because of Satan, he adds this so that they may never fall away into other desires. He does not completely reject the natural appetites of someone who has been moved by modesty to a temporary agreement of abstinence. Rather, he re-introduces <margin>D</margin> the union of marriage, not for the sake of lack of restraint or fornication or the work of the Devil, but so that the person is **not** subjected to such things. 

Tatian also separates the "Old Man" from the "New Man," but not as we do. He claims the "Old Man" is the Law and the "New Man" is the Gospel. We agree with him in saying this, but not in the way he intends it—namely, by dissolving the Law as if it came from a "different God." In truth, the same Man and Lord makes the old things new; He no longer permits **polygamy** <note>having multiple spouses</note>. At one time, God required that, when it was necessary for humanity to "increase and multiply." But now He introduces monogamy for the sake of procreating children and for the care of the household, for which the woman was given as a helper. 

And if the Apostle, because of a lack of restraint, allows a second marriage as a concession, <margin>E</margin> such a person does not sin against the Covenant (for it is not prohibited by the Law), but he does not fulfill that highest perfection of life which is driven by the Gospel. However, he who remains as he is—keeping that union which was dissolved by death unpolluted—acquires for himself celestial glory. Such a person obeys the **Economy** <note>God's management or plan</note> with a grateful and willing spirit, which ensures he cannot be pulled away from the service of the Lord. 

Furthermore, the divine providence of the Lord does not now command that someone who rises from the marriage bed must wash themselves <note>ritual bathing</note> as they did in the past. The Lord does not necessarily lead people away from procreation; rather, He washes those who believe through **one baptism** toward a habit of life that is perfect in every way. He has encompassed the many washings of Moses into this single baptism. 

<margin>F</margin> In the past, the Law used those washings to predict our spiritual rebirth through physical generation, specifically because of the procreative power of women. The Law did not abhor the generation of a human being. For the fact that a human appears through generation is what the shedding of seed achieves. Therefore, there are not "many" genital intercourses, but rather the reception by the womb professes... <margin>Greek: *dysōpei* (shames or constrains)</margin>

<margin>A</margin> ...not through marriage, so that you may become the bride and the church to Another, even to Him who was raised from the dead. This church must be kept chaste, protected both from internal thoughts that are contrary to the truth, and from those who tempt from the outside—that is, the followers of heresies. These people try to persuade you to commit "fornication" from your one husband, namely Almighty God. We must not be led astray by the clever allurements of heresies, as the serpent deceived Eve (whose name signifies "Life" <note>The Hebrew name *Hawwah* is related to the word for "living."</note>), and thereby transgress the commandments. 

This second part of the passage establishes monogamy <note>The practice of being married to only one person at a time.</note>. For one should not think, as some have, that the "binding" of the woman to the man refers to a connection of the flesh with destruction. This idea belongs to impious men who openly attribute the invention of marriage to the Devil; by saying this, they risk attacking the Lawgiver <note>Moses, viewed as the author of the Old Testament Law.</note> with curses. I believe it is Tatian the Syrian who dares to decree such 

<margin>Tatian.</margin>
<margin>B</margin> dogmas. Indeed, he writes these very words in his book *On Perfection According to the Savior*: "Agreement indeed joins one to prayer, but the communion of sexual union—being destruction—dissolves that petition." He restricts marriage very cautiously by framing it as a "concession." For when Paul permitted a couple to "come together again because of Satan and a lack of self-control" <note>1 Corinthians 7:5</note>, Tatian pronounced that the one who obeys this will serve two masters: through agreement, he serves God; but through "disagreement" <margin>disagreement <gloss>original: ἀσυμφωνίας</gloss></margin>, he serves lack of self-control, fornication, and the Devil.

<margin>C</margin> honorable procreation of children. Scripture certainly uses the word "knowledge" to describe the time of procreating children, when it says: *Adam KNEW Eve his wife, and she conceived, and bore a son, and called his name Seth.* For God said, "He has raised up for me another seed in place of Abel." 

See whom they attack with curses when they attack honorable and moderate sowing [of seed] and attribute generation to the Devil? For God did not speak in a general sense; by adding the article—namely saying <term>the God <note>original: ὁ θεός</note></term>—he signified the One who is Almighty. As for what the Apostle adds, *And again, come together, because of Satan*, that was said to prevent them from ever declining into other desires. He does not perfectly reject the natural appetites of one who is moved by modesty to a temporary agreement [to abstain]; through this, he reintroduces 

<margin>D</margin> the marriage bond, not for the purpose of lack of self-control, fornication, or the work of the Devil, but so that the couple is not subjected to those things. 

Tatian also separates the "old man" and the "new man" <note>A common Pauline theme referring to the self before and after conversion.</note>, but not as we do. We agree that the "old man" is the Law and the "new man" is the Gospel, but not in the way he wants, which is to dissolve the Law as if it belonged to another God. Rather, the same Man and Lord makes the old things new. He no longer permits polygamy <note>Having multiple spouses.</note>. Back then, God required it when it was necessary for people to "increase and multiply." But now He introduces monogamy for the procreation of children and the care of the household, for which the woman was given as a helper. And if the Apostle, because of a lack of self-control and its consequences, grants a second marriage by way of pardon, 

<margin>E</margin> such a person does not sin against the Covenant (for it is not prohibited by Law). However, he does not fulfill that highest perfection of life which is lived according to the Gospel. But he who remains single, keeping that union which was dissolved by death unpolluted, acquires heavenly glory for himself. He obeys the Divine Economy <note>The unfolding plan of God's administration of the world.</note> with a grateful and willing heart, which ensures he cannot be pulled away from the service of the Lord. 

Furthermore, the divine providence of the Lord does not now command that someone rising from the marriage bed must be washed <margin>Shameful <gloss>original: Δυσώπεϛ</gloss></note> as in the old days. For the Lord, who cleanses believers through one baptism into a way of life that is perfect in every part, does not necessarily lead them away from procreation. He encompassed the many ritual washings of Moses into a single baptism. Formerly, therefore, the Law—predicting our spiritual rebirth through physical generation—

<margin>F</margin> prescribed washings for women because of their reproductive capacity. This was not because the Law abhorred the generation of a human being. For the discharge of women is simply the material of a human being to be generated. With spiritual insight <note>original: γνωσικῶς (*gnōstikōs*)</note>.

If the Lawgiver and the Evangelist are one and the same, He is never at war with Himself. For the Law lives, since it is spiritual and is understood with true spiritual insight. But we have "died to the Law through the body of Christ," so that we might be born to another—to Him who rose from the dead—who was foretold by the Law, so that we might bear fruit for God. Therefore, the Law is indeed holy, and the commandment is holy, just, and good. We have died to the Law in this sense: we have died to the sin that is identified by the Law. The Law reveals sin but does not create it; by commanding what must be done and forbidding what must not be done, it exposes the underlying sin so that sin might be made manifest. Now, if the marriage sanctioned by the Law were a sin, I do not know how anyone could claim to know God while saying that God’s own command is a sin. If the Law is holy, then marriage is holy. The Apostle <note>Saint Paul</note> relates this sacred mystery to Christ and the Church. Just as that which is born of the flesh is flesh, so that which is born of the spirit is spirit—not only in the act of giving birth, but also in the act of learning.

"And you therefore have died to the Law through the body of Christ, that you might be born to another, who rose from the dead." At the same time, it is understood that we shall bear fruit by being obedient, since we obey the same Lord who commanded from afar through the truth of the Law.

To sum up, all the Apostle’s epistles teach moderation and self-control; they contain countless precepts about marriage, the procreation of children, and the management of a household, yet they never forbade or abolished honest and moderate marriage. Instead, preserving the harmony of the Law with the Gospel, they admit both: the man who uses marriage moderately while giving thanks to God, and the man who, as the Lord wills, lives in chastity, just as each was called, choosing his path without offense and with perfection. -># MISCELLANIES, BOOK III<-

<margin>A</margin> And to those who ask, if anyone considers the matter carefully <note>original: *ruminauerit*, literally "ruminates" or "chews the cud," a metaphor for meditatively Digesting scripture</note>, he will find that the Lord does not reject marriage, but provides a remedy for the expectation of carnal desire in the resurrection. When He spoke of the "Sons of this age," He did not say this to distinguish it from some other age <note>Clement is arguing against Gnostics who claimed there was a "bad" creator god of this age and a "good" god of another</note>, but as if to say: "Those born in this age, being sons by virtue of generation, both beget and are begotten." For no one passes through this life without the process of generation. But this generation, which undergoes a similar death, no longer awaits the one who has been separated from this life. There is, therefore, only one Father of ours, who is in heaven. But He Himself is also the Father of all through creation. <margin>Matthew 23</margin> "Do not call anyone on earth your father," <margin>B</margin> He says. This is as if to say: Do not think of the one who sowed you with carnal seed as the author and primary cause of your essence, but rather as a helping cause of your birth—or better yet, a minister. Thus, He wants us to be turned back again and become like children, recognizing Him who is truly the Father, as those who have been reborn through water <note>A reference to Christian baptism as a "second sowing" or spiritual birth</note>, since this is a different kind of sowing within creation.

But, someone says, "The man who is unmarried cares for the things of the Lord, while he who has taken a wife considers how he may please his wife." <margin>1 Corinthians 7</margin> But what of this? Is it not permitted even for those who please their wives in a godly way to give thanks to God? Is it not allowed for the man who has taken a wife to be concerned with the things of the Lord alongside his marriage? Just as the woman who has not married is concerned with the things of the Lord—to be holy in body and spirit—so too the married woman is concerned in the Lord with the things of her husband and the things of the Lord, that she may be holy in both body and spirit. For both are holy in the Lord: one as a wife, the other as a virgin. 

<margin>C</margin> Now, to shame and restrain those who are prone to second marriages <note>Clement generally approved of first marriages but, like many early Church Fathers, viewed second marriages after widowhood with some skepticism</note>, the Apostle speaks aptly in a loftier tone. "Already," he says, <margin>1 Corinthians 6</margin> "every sin is outside the body, but he who commits fornication sins against his own body." If anyone dares to call marriage "fornication," they are again attacking the Law and the Lord with insults. For just as greed and the desire to have more is called "fornication" because it opposes self-sufficiency—and just as idolatry is the distribution of the one God among many idols—so too is fornication a lapse from one marriage into many. For "fornication" and "adultery" are used in three ways by the Apostle, as we have said. Of these, the Prophet says: "You were sold for your sins." And again: "You are defiled in a foreign land," <note>original: *POLLVTVS es in terra aliena*</note> regarding a wicked union as one made with a foreign body, and not with <margin>D</margin> that which is given in marriage for the procreation of children. 

Hence the Apostle also says: <margin>1 Timothy 5</margin> "I desire that the younger women marry, bear children, and manage their households, giving the adversary no occasion for slander." For already some have turned away after Satan. Indeed, he also admits a man of only one wife <note>The "husband of one wife" rule for clergy</note>, whether he be a Presbyter, a Deacon, or a <margin>1 Timothy 3</margin> Layman, using marriage without blame. <margin>1 Timothy 2</margin> "But she will be saved through the procreation of children." And again, <margin>Matthew 12</margin> when the Savior calls the Jews an "evil and adulterous generation," He teaches that they did not know the Law as the Law intended. Instead, by following the traditions of the elders and the commandments of men, they "adulterated" the Law, failing to treat it as a husband and master of their virginity. Perhaps He also knew they were enslaved to foreign desires, because of which they were constantly serving sins and being "sold" to foreigners. <margin>E</margin> For among the Jews, common women <note>meaning prostitutes or public women</note> were not permitted; indeed, adultery was forbidden.

As for the man who says, <margin>Luke 14</margin> "I have married a wife, I cannot come" to the divine supper, this is an example used to rebuke those who abstain from the divine command for the sake of pleasures. For by that logic, neither the righteous who lived before the Advent, nor those who married after the Advent, would be saved—even if they were Apostles. And if they bring up what the Prophet says: "I have grown old among all my enemies," <note>Psalm 6:7</note> let them understand "enemies" to mean sins. Sin is one thing; marriage is another. Marriage is not a sin; fornication is. They should not speak of generation (birth) and the Creator of that generation as a sin. 

Such arguments are also used by Julius Cassianus, who was the leader of the school of "Appearance" or Phantasia <margin>of the *dokesis* <note>original: τῆς δοκήσεως</note>, that is, the sect of the Docetists, who said the Lord took on a phantasmagorical body.</margin>. In his work *On Continence* or *On Chastity*, <margin>F</margin> he says these words: "Let no one say that because we have such parts—the female shaped one way and the male another, the one to receive and the other to sow—that this practice is granted by God. For if this were from the God toward whom we strive..."

# CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

<margin>The Legislator and the author of the Gospel are the same. Romans 7, interpreted with spiritual knowledge <note>original: *gnostikōs*, referring to the deeper insight of a true Christian scholar</note>.</margin>
<margin>A</margin> ...generation, formed in the workshop of nature in a feminine way into a fetus. How can it be that marriage is merely an ancient invention of the Law, while the marriage according to the Lord is something alien, since we serve the very same God? For what God has joined, let no man rightfully put asunder. Moreover, the Son will also observe those things which the Father commanded. If, then, the Legislator and the Evangelist <note>The author of the Gospel</note> are one and the same, He is never at war with Himself. For the Law lives, since it is spiritual and is understood through spiritual knowledge. But we are "dead to the law through the body of Christ," so that we might be born to another who rose from the dead—who was foretold by the law—so that we might bear fruit for God. Therefore, the law is indeed holy, and the commandment is holy, and just, and good. We have died to the law, then— <margin>B</margin> that is, to the sin which is made known by the law. The law reveals sin, but does not create it; by commanding what must be done and prohibiting what must not be done, it rebukes the underlying sin so that sin might be made apparent. If marriage, which is according to the law, were a sin, I do not know how anyone could say they know God while claiming that God’s own command is a sin. But if the law is holy, then marriage is holy. The Apostle <note>Paul</note> thus leads this mystery <note>original: *sacramenta*</note> toward Christ and the church. Just as that which is born of the flesh is flesh, so that which is born of the spirit is spirit—not only in giving birth, but also in learning.

<margin>You will be well-pleasing to God.</margin>
Now the children are holy, being the "well-pleasing delights of the Lord's words" which have betrothed the soul. Therefore, fornication and marriage are separate things, just as the devil is far removed from God. "And you, therefore, have died to the law through the body of Christ, so that you might be born to another, who rose from the dead." At the same time, it is understood that <margin>C</margin> we are heard most closely if we are obedient, since even by the truth of the law, we obey the same Lord who commands from afar.

<margin>1 Timothy 4. Deceivers <note>original: *planis*, from the Greek *planoi*, meaning wandering impostors</note>.</margin>
Does not the Spirit rightly and openly say of such men: "In the later times some will fall away from the faith, giving heed to spirits of error and doctrines of demons, through the hypocrisy of speakers of lies, having their consciences seared, and forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from foods which God created for participation with thanksgiving by the faithful and those who have known the truth; for every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected that is taken with thanksgiving. For it is sanctified through the word of God and prayer"?

<margin>Romans 14. 1 Corinthians 7.</margin>
<margin>D</margin>
Necessarily, then, one must not forbid joining in marriage, nor eating meat, nor drinking wine. For it is written: "It is good not to eat meat, nor to drink wine, if one eats it as a cause of offense." And: "It is good to remain as I am." But also, he who uses these things does so with thanksgiving, and he who does not use them likewise does so with thanksgiving, and let him live with a moderate and temperate perception, in accordance with reason. To speak summarily, all the epistles of the Apostle which teach moderation and self-control—while containing innumerable precepts about marriage, the procreation of children, and the management of a household—never prohibited or abolished honorable and moderate marriage. Instead, preserving the harmony of the Law with the Gospel, they admit both: the man who, giving thanks to God, uses marriage with moderation, and the man who, as the Lord wills, lives in chastity <margin>E</margin> according to how each was called, choosing blamelessly and perfectly. "And the land of Jacob was praised above every land," says the Prophet, himself a vessel of the Spirit bringing glory.

<margin>Mark 6. Luke 12.</margin>
But someone might attack procreation, saying that "corruption" falls upon it and that it perishes. Someone might even use force and twist the words, saying that the Savior spoke of the procreation of children when He said: "One ought not to lay up treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy." Nor do they blush to add to these the words of the Prophet: "All of you shall grow old like a garment, and the moth shall eat you up." But we do not contradict the scripture; corruption does indeed fall upon our bodies, and they are fleeting. But perhaps the Prophet predicts destruction for those with whom he argued, seeing as they were sinners. The Savior, however, was not speaking of the procreation of children, but was exhorting people to share and communicate their wealth, addressing those who wish only to abound in riches but refuse to bring help to the needy.

<margin>John 6. Matthew 22. Luke 20.</margin>
For this reason He says: "Work not for the food which perishes, but for that which remains unto eternal life." Similarly, they bring forward that saying about the resurrection of the dead: "The sons of that age neither marry nor are given in marriage." But concerning this question...

### STROMATA, BOOK III

<margin>A</margin> And to those who ask, if one considers it carefully, he will find that the Lord does not reject marriage, but brings a remedy to the expectation of carnal desire in the resurrection. When he spoke of the **"sons of this age,"** <note>original: *Filii huius seculi*; referring to Luke 20:34</note> he did not say this to distinguish it from some other age <note>Clement is refuting the Gnostic idea that there is a "bad" creator-god of this world and a "good" god of another</note>, but as if he were saying: "Those born in this age, being sons by virtue of procreation, both beget and are begotten." For no one passes through this life without procreation. But this generation, which undergoes a similar death, no longer waits for the one who has been separated from this life. There is, therefore, only one Father of ours who is in heaven. But He is also the Father of all through creation. <margin>Matthew 23:</margin> **"Call no man father on earth,"** he says. It is as if he said: "Do not consider him who sowed you with carnal seed to be the author and cause of your essence, but rather a helping cause of ge-
<margin>B</margin> neration, or rather a minister." Thus, he wants us to be turned back again as children, acknowledging Him who is truly Father, as those who have been reborn through water, since this is a different kind of sowing in the act of creation. But, it is said, "the unmarried man cares for the things of the Lord." "But he who has taken a wife, how shall he please his wife?" What then? <margin>1 Corinthians 7:</margin> Is it not also permitted for those who please their wife according to God's will to give thanks to God? Is it not also permitted for the man who has taken a wife to be concerned, even within marriage, for the things of the Lord? But just as the woman who is not married is concerned with the things of the Lord—that she may be holy in body and spirit—so also the married woman is concerned in the Lord for the things of her husband and the things of the Lord, so that she may be holy both in body and spirit. For both are holy in the Lord: the one as a wife, the other as a virgin. But to put to 
<margin>C</margin> shame and restrain those who are prone to second marriages <note>Clement, like many early Church Fathers, looked upon second marriages—even after widowhood—with some disapproval, though he defended the first marriage</note>, the Apostle speaks aptly with a certain high tone. **"Every sin,"** he says, **"is outside the body."** <margin>1 Corinthians 6</margin> But he who commits fornication sins against his own body. If anyone dares to call marriage "fornication," he attacks the Law and the Lord with curses. For just as avarice and the desire to have more is called "fornication" <note>original: *fornicatio*; here used metaphorically for greed</note>, as it is contrary to being content, and just as idolatry is the attribution of the one God to many, so also is fornication a falling away from one marriage into many. For in three ways, as we have said, "fornication" and "adultery" are understood by the Apostle. Of these the Prophet says: "You were sold for your sins." **"You are polluted in a foreign land,"** <note>referring to Baruch 3:10-11</note> regarding a wicked union as that which is made with a foreign body, and not with
<margin>D</margin> that which is given in marriage for the procreation of children. Whence also the Apostle says: <margin>1 Timothy 5:</margin> **"I wish for the younger women to marry, to procreate children, to rule the household, and to give no occasion to the adversary for the sake of reproach."** For already some have turned aside after Satan. Indeed, he certainly admits a man of only one wife, whether he be a Presbyter, or a deacon, or a <margin>1 Timothy 3</margin> Layman, using marriage without blame. He shall be saved through the <margin>1 Timothy 2</margin> procreation of children. And again, when the Savior calls the Jews a "wicked and adulterous generation," <margin>Matthew 12</margin> he teaches that they did not know the Law as the Law intended. Instead, following the tradition of the elders and the commandments of men, they "adulterated" the Law, not treating it as that which was given as their husband and master of their virginity. Perhaps he also knew that they were enslaved to foreign desires, on account of which, being constantly enslaved to sins, they were sold to
<margin>E</margin> foreigners. For among the Jews, "common women" <note>prostitutes</note> were not permitted; moreover, adultery was forbidden. But he who says, "I have taken a wife, I cannot come" to the <margin>Luke 14</margin> divine supper, is indeed an example to rebuke those who, for the sake of pleasures, abstain from the divine command. For by this reasoning, neither those who were righteous before the Coming [of Christ], nor those who married wives after the Coming, would be saved, even if they were Apostles. And if they should bring up what the Prophet also says, **"I have grown old among all my enemies,"** let them hear "enemies" as sins. For there is one specific sin—not marriage, but fornication. Let them not likewise call procreation a sin, nor the creator of procreation. Such arguments are also used by Julius Cassianus, who was the leader of the "Apparition" or "Illusion" <gloss>the sect of the Docetae, that is, the sect of the Docetists who said the Lord assumed a phantom body</gloss> <note>Docetism taught that Christ did not have a real physical body, but only "seemed" to have one. Because they hated matter, they often hated marriage too.</note>.

<meta>This page continues Clement of Alexandria’s refutation of the Encratites—extreme ascetics who viewed marriage and procreation as inherently sinful. Clement is specifically engaging with Julius Cassianus, a Gnostic teacher who argued that the division of humanity into male and female was a result of a "fall" from a divine state.</meta>

->CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA<-

<margin>A</margin>
...if this constitution were evil, he would not have called the Eunuchs blessed, nor would the Prophet have said they are not an unfruitful tree <note>referring to Isaiah 56:3-5</note>: transferring the metaphor from the tree to the man who, by his own choice and by a settled purpose, castrates himself from such carnal thoughts. Yet, still fighting for his impious opinion, he [Cassianus] adds: "How could anyone not rightly find fault with the Savior, if he transformed us and freed us from error, and from the joining of parts and appendages and genitals?"—decreeing in this the same things as Tatian <note>Tatian was a 2nd-century Christian writer who became the leader of the Encratites, a sect that rejected marriage</note>. This man [Cassianus] came out of the school of Valentinus <note>Valentinus was a famous Gnostic teacher in Rome; his followers believed in a complex hierarchy of divine beings</note>. Therefore, Cassianus says: When Salome asked when the things she was inquiring about would be known, the Lord said, "**When you have trodden underfoot the garment of shame, and when the two have become one, and the male with the female is neither male nor female.**" <note>original: *Quando pudoris indumentum conculcaueritis...* This famous quote comes from the lost "Gospel according to the Egyptians," an apocryphal text used by Gnostic groups</note> In the first place, we do not have this saying in the four 
<margin>B</margin>
Gospels handed down to us, but rather in the one called "according to the Egyptians." Secondly, it seems to me that he [Cassianus] is unaware that "male" signifies anger, while "female" signifies desire. When these are active, repentance and shame follow. When a person, therefore, obeys neither anger nor desire—which, increased by habit and bad education, overshadow and cover the reason—but strips away the darkness arising from them and, feeling shame through repentance, unites the spirit and the soul in obedience to reason: then, as Paul says, there is **neither male nor female** in us. For the soul, departing from that form by which male and female are distinguished, is translated into union, being neither. However, this "illustrious" man [Cassianus] thinks more Platonically than is fitting, imagining that the soul, which is divine from the beginning, 
<margin>C</margin>
is made effeminate by desire and comes down here to generation and destruction. Indeed, he almost forces Paul to say that procreation consists of error, when he says: **I FEAR** 
<margin>2 Cor. 11</margin>
**lest as the serpent deceived Eve, your senses may be corrupted from the simplicity which is in Christ.** But it is certain that the Lord also came to those things which had gone astray. They had gone astray, however, not by a repetitive origin from on high into this earthly generation. For generation is a creation of the Almighty, who would never lead the soul from better things to worse. But to those who had gone astray in their senses or thoughts, the Savior came to us, I say: whose faculties were corrupted by our disobedience to the commandments while we greedily pursued pleasure; since our first-formed father <term>protoplastus<gloss>The Greek word for the first-created human, Adam</gloss></term> anticipated the proper time, and sought the grace of marriage before the right time, and thus went astray: for whoever looks at a woman to 
<margin>D</margin>
lust after her has already committed adultery in his heart, as one who did not wait for the time of the [divine] will. It was the Lord himself, therefore, who even then condemned the desire that 
<margin>Eph. 4</margin>
precedes marriage. Therefore, when the Apostle said, "**Put on the new man who is created according to God,**" he speaks to us who were fashioned by the will of the Almighty. He spoke of the "old man," not looking at generation and regeneration, but at the life spent in disobedience and obedience. Cassianus thinks that the "tunics of skins" <note>referring to Genesis 3:21</note> are physical bodies: regarding which we shall later show that both he and those who think like him have gone astray, when we undertake an exposition on the origin of man, following those things which must be said first. "For," he says, "those who are ruled by earthly things both beget and are begotten: but our citizenship is in heaven, from which also 
<margin>E</margin>
we expect the Savior." Rightly, then, we know these things were said, since we must order our lives as strangers and pilgrims: "**Those who have a wife, as though they had none; those who possess, as though they did not possess.**" Those who procreate children, doing so as begetters of mortals, as those who will leave behind possessions, as those who will live even without a wife if necessary; not using their possessions with emotional attachment, but with thanksgiving, and 
<margin>1 Cor. 7</margin>
contemplating great and noble things in their minds. ### THE STROMATA, BOOK III. ###

<margin>A</margin>
...he [the Apostle Paul] contends against them, wishing to lead them back to their own ranks: through laborious self-restraint, he wishes to offer them an opportunity. Rightly, therefore, he says, "It is better to marry than to burn" <note>1 Corinthians 7:9</note>, so that the husband may render what is due to the wife, and the wife to the husband, and that they do not deprive one another of this divine help given for procreation. <margin>Luke 14</margin> **"WHOSOEVER,"** they say, "does not hate his father, or mother, or wife, or children, cannot be my disciple." He does not command us to hate our kin. <margin>Exodus 20</margin> For he says, "Honor your father and mother, that it may be well with you." But he means: do not be led away by desires that are alien to reason; do not be joined to the customs of the world. For a house is made of kin, and cities are made of houses, just as Paul said that those who are occupied in marriage "please the world." <margin>1 Corinthians 7</margin> Again, the Lord says: he who has taken a wife should not cast her out, and he who has not taken one should not 
<margin>B</margin> <margin>The vow of chastity.</margin> take one. Let him who, by a purpose of chastity, has professed not to take a wife, remain celibate. To both, therefore, the same Lord gives fitting promises through the Prophet Isaiah, saying: "Let the eunuch not say, 'I am a dry tree.'" <margin>Isaiah 56</margin> For the Lord says this to the eunuchs: "If you keep my Sabbaths and do whatever I command, I will give you a place better than sons and daughters." For chastity alone does not justify, nor does the "Sabbath" of the eunuch, unless he performs the commandments. He also brings in those who have taken a wife, and says: "My chosen ones shall not labor in vain, nor shall they procreate children for a curse, because their seed is blessed by the Lord." For him who has procreated and raised children according to reason, and has educated them in the Lord—just as for him who has "begotten" someone through true catechesis <term>catechesis: the oral instruction of new converts to the faith</term> and training—a certain reward is set forth, as it is for the "chosen seed." 
<margin>C</margin>
But others interpret the procreation of children as a "curse," and they do not understand that the Scripture is speaking against those very people. For those who are truly the chosen of the Lord do not decree false dogmas, nor do they produce "children who are for a curse," such as heresies. Therefore, a "eunuch" is not one who has had his parts cut off by force, nor is it simply one who is celibate, but one who does not "beget" falsehood. The tree of truth was formerly dry here; but if it obeys the Word and keeps the Sabbaths by abstaining from sins and performs the commandments, it will be more honorable than those who are educated only by the Word without a right way of life. <margin>John 13</margin> **"LITTLE CHILDREN,"** says the Teacher, "I am with you only a little longer." Wherefore Paul also, writing to the Galatians, says, <margin>Galatians 4</margin> **"MY LITTLE CHILDREN,"** for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you. "For if you have ten thousand tutors in Christ," he says, 
<margin>D</margin>
"you do not have many fathers. For in Christ, through the Gospel, I have begotten you." <note>1 Corinthians 4:15</note> Therefore, the "eunuch" who shall not enter the church of God is he who is sterile and bears no fruit, neither in his way of life nor in his speech. But those who have "made themselves eunuchs" from all sin for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, these are the blessed ones who "fast from the world." <margin>Jeremiah 20</margin> **"CURSED"** be the day on which I was born, and let it not be desired, says Jeremiah. He is not saying that procreation is absolutely cursed, but he is grieving over the sins and disobedience of the people. Therefore he adds: "For why was I born to see labors and sorrows, and my days have been in perpetual reproach?" For all who preached the truth were sought out for punishment and came into danger because of the disobedience of those who heard them. **"WHY"** was my mother’s womb not my grave, so that I might not see the 
<margin>E</margin>
affliction of Jacob and the labor of the race of Israel? says the Prophet Esdras. <margin>Job 25</margin> **"NO ONE"** is clean from filth, says Job, not even if his life were but one day. Let them tell us, then, where a newborn infant has committed fornication? Or how has he fallen under the curse of Adam, he who has done nothing? It remains for them [the heretics], it seems, to say consequently that procreation is evil—not only that of the body, but also that of the soul, for the sake of which the body exists. This is why David said, "In sins was I conceived, and in iniquities did my mother conceive me." <margin>Psalm 50</margin> <note>Psalm 51 in modern Bibles</note> 
<margin>Original sin was not sufficiently known by Clement.</margin> 
He speaks prophetically of his "mother" Eve, for Eve was the "mother of the living"; and if he was conceived in sins, yet he himself was not in sin, nor was he himself sin. But if anyone turns from sin to faith, he turns from a custom of sinning—as if from a mother—to life. One of the twelve Prophets shall bear witness to me, who said: 
<margin>F</margin>

<summary>Clement argues that procreation is not inherently sinful, interpreting difficult passages from Jeremiah, Job, and David to show that biblical "curses" refer to human disobedience and spiritual fruitlessness rather than the act of birth itself. ...through whom we do not know God, he utters impieties. If anyone says that procreation is evil for that reason, let him also say it is good for the same reason—insofar as we come to know the truth in it. "Be sobered justly, and do not sin; for some have an ignorance of God" <note>1 Corinthians 15:34</note>, specifically those who sin. For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against spiritual powers. The princes of the darkness of this world are able to tempt us, and for this reason, mercy is given. And thus Paul also says, 
<margin>1 Corinthians 9</margin>
"I buffet my body, and lead it into servitude." For he who competes abstains from all things—that is, he is self-controlled <term>continent; from the Latin *continens*, meaning holding oneself in</term> in all things, not by avoiding all things, but by using those things he has judged proper to use in a self-controlled manner. Those people do so to receive a corruptible crown, but we to receive an incorruptible one, conquering in the struggle, but not receiving a crown without the dust of the arena. Now, some even prefer a widow over an incontinent virgin, as the widow has despised the pleasure she has experienced with a great and lofty mind. But if procreation is evil, let them say that the Lord was in evil, for he was a partaker in procreation; and let them say the Virgin who gave him birth was in evil. 
<margin>
"Alas for the evils!" <note>original Greek: οἴμοὶ ἳ κακῶν</note>

The "Docetists" <note>original Latin: *Dokeisis*</note> are the name given to those Heretics who claimed that Christ had a phantasmal body <note>From the Greek *dokein*, "to seem"; they believed Jesus only seemed to have a physical body.</note>.
</margin>
Alas, how many and how great are the evils! They attack the will of God and the mystery of creation with curses while they rail against procreation. And for this reason, [the body] is a vision or a phantom to Cassianus. For this reason also, to Marcion and to Valentinus as well, it is an "animal body" <note>In the sense of being purely biological/brutish rather than spiritual.</note>; for they say that man became like the cattle when he came to sexual intercourse. But when a man, driven by true madness, wishes to enter "alien beds" <note>A reference to adultery or illicit lust.</note>, then truly such a man is turned into a beast. 
<margin>Jeremiah 5</margin>
"They became as horses raging after females; each one neighed after his neighbor's wife." And if the serpent took the logic of his treacherous counsel from the brute animals and persuaded Adam to consent to a union with Eve—on the grounds that the First-Formed <term>Protoplasts; the first humans created by God</term> would not have otherwise used this natural function, as some think—then creation is again attacked with curses, as if it had made humans weaker than the nature of the unreasoning animals, a nature which those first formed by God followed. But if nature led them to the procreation of children as it does the brutes, yet they were moved to it sooner than they should have been—having been led astray by fraud while they were still young—the judgment of God is indeed just upon those who did not wait for His will. Yet procreation itself is holy, through which the world consists, through which the essences, through which the natures, through which the Angels, through which the powers, through which souls, through which the commandments, through which the Law, through which the Gospel, through which the knowledge of God exists. 
<margin>Isaiah 40</margin>
"And all flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of the grass; and the grass indeed withers, and the flower falls. But the word of the Lord remains," which has anointed the soul and united it to the spirit. For how could the Economy <term>The divine plan or administration of salvation</term> which is among us in the church have reached its end without the body, since he himself who is the head of the church passed through life in the flesh, though without outward form or beauty <note>A reference to the "Suffering Servant" in Isaiah 53:2.</note>, teaching us to look toward that which is formless and incorporeal in the divine cause? For "the tree of life," says the Prophet, "is in good desire" <note>Proverbs 13:12</note>, teaching that good and pure desires are in the living Lord. Now indeed, these men wish for the intimacy of a man with his wife in marriage, which is called "knowledge," to be a sin; for they claim this is signified by the eating from the tree of good and evil, using the significance of this word "He knew" <note>Genesis 4:1</note> to signify a transgression of the commandment. But if this is so, then the knowledge of truth is also a partaker of that tree of life. Therefore, an honorable and moderate marriage can also be a partaker of that tree. But it has been said by us before that one may use marriage well or ill. and this is the "tree of knowledge," if we do not transgress the laws of marriage. Did not our Savior, just as he healed the soul, also heal the body from its afflictions? 
<margin>
1 Corinthians 15.
The Greek has "overshadowing" <note>original: ἐπισκιάζων</note> but I think it should read "equipping" <note>original: ἐπισκευάζων</note>.
</margin>
Truly, if the flesh were an enemy to the soul, he would not have fortified an enemy against it by equipping it with health. 
<margin>Galatians 3</margin>
"But this I say, brethren, that flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God, nor does corruption possess incorruption." For since sin is corruption, it cannot have fellowship with incorruption, which is righteousness. "Are you so foolish," he says, "that having begun with the spirit, you are now perfected by the flesh?" Therefore, as we have shown, some have stretched the harmony of justice and salvation—which is venerable, firm, and stable—too far, taking up a form of self-restraint <term>continence</term> with every kind of impiety, blasphemy, and cursing, when it was permitted to choose chastity according to a healthy rule and with piety. # OF CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA,

## THE MISCELLANIES, BOOK

### FOUR.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'C' depicting a landscape with a fortified town or buildings, trees, and distant hills.</image-desc>

I believe it is now the proper sequence for us to treat of martyrdom, and who the "perfect" person is. This will include the necessary discussions that follow from those topics: that philosophy is equally for the slave and the free, for the male and the female; and after we have completed the subsequent sections on faith and inquiry, we shall introduce the symbolic style. Once we have concluded the discourse on ethics, we will show in summary the utility that was brought to the Greeks by "barbarian philosophy" <note>original: *barbara philosophia*. Clement uses this term to refer to Jewish and Christian wisdom, which the Greeks considered "barbaric" or foreign.</note>. After I have placed this before your eyes, a concise exposition of the Scriptures will be delivered against both Greeks and Jews. This will include whatever we had originally intended to complete in a single commentary at the start of the preface, but which we were unable to contain there because we were necessarily bound to the great multitude of subjects. After this, as far as we are able to fulfill the declaration of the proposed matters, we must review what has been handed down regarding natural principles—both by the Greeks and by other "barbarians"—as these opinions have reached us, and argue against the chief points of what the philosophers have devised. Following this, after we have briefly run through Theology, we shall treat what has been handed down in the prophecies, so that when we have shown the Scriptures in which we believe to be valid and ratified by almighty authority, we may proceed through them in an orderly way. From there, we can demonstrate to all heresies that there is one God and almighty Lord, who was sincerely and genuinely preached through the Law, the Prophets, and the blessed Gospel. Much remains to be said against those who hold different opinions, as we attempt to dismantle the arguments asserted in their writings and persuade them—even against their will—by convicting them through the Scriptures themselves. Therefore, once our entire purpose has been completed in these commentaries as the Spirit wills, and having been aided by them for our immediate use (for certain things must absolutely be prefaced before the Truth), then we shall truly approach the "Gnostic" nature—that is, the contemplation suitable for a person endowed with the power of knowing.

<margin>Hierophancy. <note>original: *ἱεροφαντεία*. The act of revealing or interpreting sacred mysteries.</note></margin>
We have been initiated into the minor mysteries before the great ones, so that nothing may stand in the way of the truly divine interpretation of sacred things, once those matters which must be known and handed down beforehand have been purged and formed. This contemplation of the nature of Gnostic tradition, according to the rule of truth—or rather, a certain celestial speculation—depends on that discourse which is handed down

<margin>The study of nature, or rather, a God-enlightened contemplation. <note>original: *φυσιολογία μᾶλλον δὲ ἐποπτεία θεοφωτισμένη*. The term *epopteia* refers to the highest stage of initiation in the Greek mysteries, here applied to Christian spiritual vision.</note></margin>
concerning the origin of the world. From here, it ascends to the theological form, or that which consists in the contemplation of divinity. Thus, from that origin which was committed to writing prophetically—namely, from Genesis—we shall take the beginning of the tradition in part, bringing forward and, as far as we are able, dissolving the claims made by those who think differently. But this indeed shall be written soon, if God wills and inspires us. Now, however, we must approach what has been proposed, and the discourse pertaining to ethics must be finished. As we have often said, let our *Commentaries* <note>These are the *Stromata* or "Miscellanies."</note> be varied—for the sake of those who might approach them impudently or unskillfully—and, as the name itself indicates, "woven together," passing continually from one thing to another, and through the sequence and context of the words, signifying one thing but indicating another. For "those who seek gold," says Heraclitus, "dig up much earth and find little." But those who examine that which is truly akin to the golden race will find much in little. For the Scripture will find one who is meant to understand it. They are helpful, therefore, both for calling back—

# CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

...for a memorial, and to openly declare the truth to those capable of seeking with <margin>A</margin> reason, these *Miscellanies of Commentaries*. It is also necessary for us to labor and to discover other things added to these; for to those who travel a path they do not know, it is enough merely to point out the way that leads there, but afterwards they must enter upon it and find the remainder of the way for themselves. As they say, when a servant once asked what he should do to please his master, the Pythian <note>The Pythian refers to the Oracle of Delphi, the priestess of Apollo.</note> replied: "You will find it if you seek." And indeed, as it seems, it is truly difficult to find the beautiful and honorable thing that lies hidden, since "sweat is placed before virtue."

->The way is long and steep towards it.<-

<margin>Hesiod.</margin>
<margin>B</margin>
> For it is arduous at first, but when the summit is reached,
> it becomes easy, though it was exceedingly difficult before.

For the way of the Lord is indeed "strait and narrow," and the "kingdom of God belongs to the violent." <margin>Matthew 7.</margin> Therefore "seek," He says, "and you will find," keeping to the truly royal road and not running past it. <margin>Matthew 11.</margin> There is, then, in a small space a great and fertile abundance of the seeds of doctrines contained in this work—just like "a field full of all herbs," as the Scripture says. # MISCELLANIES, BOOK IV

<margin>A</margin> Solomon. <note>original: "Solomon." This likely references the Wisdom literature's focus on the "proper work" of humanity.</note> For if every nature has its own particular function—just as there is a specific task for the ox, and likewise for the horse and the dog—what shall we say is the specific function of a human being? It seems to me that man is like a centaur <note>original: "centauro." In Greek mythology, the centaur was a hybrid of man and horse, representing the dual nature of the human condition.</note>, that Thessalian fiction, composed of a part that shares in reason and a part that lacks reason—the soul and the body. While the body works the earth and is drawn toward the earth, the soul is raised up to God. Having been educated through true philosophy, the soul strives toward its kin in the heavens above, turning away from the desires of the body and, furthermore, from toil and fear. Nevertheless, we have shown that both endurance and fear can be good. <margin>Rom. 3. Rom. 5.</margin> For "if through the law comes the knowledge of sin," as those who attack the Law say, and "until the law, sin was in the world," yet "apart from the law sin is dead," let us answer them in return. Much more so do you remove punishment when that which is innate—the tendency to lust—is absent. <margin>B</margin> <margin>1. Tim. 1.</margin> For as the Scripture says, "The law is not laid down for the righteous." Heraclitus spoke beautifully on this: "They would not have known the name of Justice if these [injustices] did not exist." And Socrates says that the Law was not made for the sake of good men. But those who accuse the Law have not understood how the Apostle says that "he who loves his neighbor does no evil." <margin>Rom. 13.</margin> For those commands—"You shall not kill," "You shall not commit adultery," "You shall not steal," and any other precept—are reduced to this single statement as a summary: "You shall love your neighbor as yourself." By this same reasoning, he says: "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and you shall love your neighbor <margin>Matth. 22.</margin> <margin>C</margin> as yourself." Indeed, if he who loves his neighbor does no evil, and every commandment is summed up in this—in loving one’s neighbor—then those precepts which result in a looming fear actually give birth to love, not hatred. Therefore, the law which produces fear is not a vice. <margin>Rom. 7.</margin> Wherefore "the law is holy," and truly "spiritual," according to the opinion of the Apostle. It is necessary, therefore, as is consistent, that when we have diligently investigated both the nature of the body and the essence of the soul, we understand the purpose of each, and not consider death to be an evil. <margin>Rom. 6.</margin> "For when you were slaves of sin," says the Apostle, "you were free in regard to righteousness. What fruit did you have then from those things of which you are now ashamed? For the end of those things is death. But now, having been set free from sin and having become slaves to God, you have your fruit leading to holiness, and the end is eternal life. For the wages of sin is death, but the grace of God <margin>D</margin> is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord." The matter, therefore, seems to be brought to this point: it has been shown that "death" is that union of the soul with the body when it is devoted to sin, while "life" is the separation from sin. Many ramparts and ditches of desire hinder us, as do the whirlpools of anger and hot-temperedness, which must be leaped over; one must escape every engine of ambush if they are to see the knowledge of God no longer "through a glass darkly."

# CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

...it happens in vain when someone is stirred by rivalry against one who is faithful through love. <margin>A</margin> But to the Lord, the persuasion of doctrine is inspired by God, and from this, the faithful will not falter even through the fear of death. Furthermore, such a person confirms the truth of their preaching by their actions, showing that the One toward whom they strive is truly powerful. You might marvel at the love he teaches so clearly: he is united with a grateful spirit to that which is kindred and of the same nature, and he even puts unbelievers to shame by the sacrifice of his precious blood. Therefore, out of fear regarding the commandment, he refuses to deny Christ, so that through this "fear" he might become a witness. Yet, he does not sell his faith for the hope of prepared gifts; rather, because of his love for the Lord, he will most gladly be liberated from this life. He feels gratitude perhaps both to the one who provided the cause for his departure from here, and to the one who laid the traps; for they provided an honorable opportunity—which he did not create himself—to show who he truly is: to the persecutor through his endurance, and to the Lord <margin>B</margin> through his charity. Through this love, he was known to the Lord, who even before a person is born knows their purpose and the free will of the soul that bears witness. And so, with a good heart, he comes to his friend, the Lord, for whom he gave up both body and soul, as the judges expected; he is addressed by our Savior—O beloved brother, to speak poetically. 

We now call martyrdom a "consummation," <margin><gloss>perfection</gloss></note> <note>original: "τελείωσιν" (teleiōsin). In early Christian thought, this term referred to both the completion of a spiritual journey and the finality of death through martyrdom.</note> not because a person has received the end of life like others, but because they have shown the **perfect work of love**. Furthermore, even the ancient Greeks praise the end of those who died in war, not because they favor a violent death, but because such a person ends their life in battle, departing without fearing death. They are severed from the body without their mind having previously suffered or been softened, as usually happens to people in sickness. <margin>C</margin> For those who die of illness often depart in a weakened state, desiring to live, and therefore do not release a pure soul; instead, the soul carries away its desires like "leaden marks" unless they were trained and thoughtful in virtue. There are also those who die in war still filled with desires, which is the same as if they had wasted away from disease. 

If, then, the confession made before God is a "testimony," then every soul that has conducted itself purely and sincerely with the knowledge of God, and which has obeyed the commandments, is a witness both in life and in speech—regardless of how it is released from the body. Such a soul pours out faith like blood throughout its entire life and even at its departure. Now the Lord says in the Gospel: "Whoever has left father or mother or brothers," and what follows, "for the sake of the gospel and my name," <margin>Matth. 10.</margin> <margin>D</margin> is blessed. He does not mean just any testimony, but that which comes from **knowledge**, as one who has lived life according to the rule of the Gospel out of love for the Lord. For the "perception of the name" and the "understanding of the Gospel" signify knowledge, not a bare and simple title. To "leave" one's worldly kin means to leave behind the habits of the world; to "leave" means to give up resources and all possessions, because one lives without any attachment to them. 

Indeed, one's native land is figuratively called "mother and nurse," <margin><gloss>In Greek, the word for "Law" is of the masculine gender.</gloss></note> <note>original: "νόμος lex græcè est masculini generis." The author is explaining an allegorical point: if "mother" represents the land, "father" represents the "laws."</note> while "fathers" represent the civil laws. These things must be disregarded with a grateful spirit by a just man who is of a great and lofty soul, so that he may become a friend of God and obtain the "right-hand portion" of sanctification, just as the Apostles did. <margin><gloss>slain in war</gloss></note> <note>original: "ἀρηϊφάτους" (arēiphatous), literally "slain by Ares," the god of war.</note> Next, Heraclitus says: "Gods and men honor those slain in war." And Plato writes in the fifth book of *The Republic*: <margin>E</margin> "Of those who die in war, shall we not say that he who dies after behaving nobly belongs first of all to the **golden race**?" Most certainly. The "golden race," by the judgment of the gods, consists of those who are in heaven and in the "unwandering sphere," <note>The "unwandering sphere" refers to the outermost celestial sphere of fixed stars in ancient cosmology.</note> who hold the greatest leadership over the providence of humanity. 

However, some of the heretics, having misunderstood the Lord, are held by a desire for life that is both impious and cowardly. They say that "true testimony" is simply the knowledge of the true God (which we also admit), but they claim that anyone who confesses through death is a "self-murderer" and brings death upon themselves. They bring forward other such sophistries and clever excuses for cowardice. We shall speak against them when the time requires, for they differ from us in their basic principles. Yet we also say that those who deliberately seek death—for there are some who are not ours but only share the name, who strive with great zeal to hand themselves over because they desire death out of a wretched hatred for the Creator—<margin>F</margin> we say that these people bring themselves forward without any true martyrdom or testimony,

<summary>Clement defines true martyrdom as the "perfect work of love" and a lifelong "confession" of faith, contrasting it with the Greek glorification of falling in battle and refuting heretics who either fear death or seek it out of hatred for the physical world.</summary>

### STROMATA, BOOK IV.
<sig>kk iiii</sig>

<margin>A</margin> ...sanctification, even if they are punished publicly. For they do not preserve the character of a faithful witness, those who have not known Him who is truly God. They hand themselves over to a vain death, just as the **Gymnosophists** <note>literally "naked philosophers," a group of ancient Indian ascetics known for their endurance and practice of self-immolation</note> of the Indians rashly cast themselves into the fire. But since those who have taken a false name for themselves <note>likely referring to heretics who courted death to "escape" the material world</note> attack the body, let them learn that a good physical structure and proper composition contribute to the soul's sharpness of wit. Therefore, in the third book of the *Republic*, **Plato**—whom they cite most as a witness to disparage procreation—said that one must take care of the body for the sake of the soul's harmony, through which one who announces the preaching of truth is permitted both to live and to live rightly. For by entering through life and health, we learn knowledge. 

<margin>B</margin> For how is "living rightly" not to be chosen by one who is not permitted to advance toward the heights at all without those things which are necessary, and who through them does all things that tend toward knowledge? In living, therefore, "living well" behaves correctly; and he who has exercised himself through the body toward living well is transmitted to the state of eternity. It is also right to admire the **Stoics** <note>a school of philosophy that taught virtue is the only good and external things are indifferent</note>, who say the soul is affected by nothing from the body—neither toward vice by disease, nor toward virtue by health—but they say both of these are **indifferent** <note>original: *indifferentia* (Greek: *adiaphora*); things that are neither morally good nor bad in themselves</note>. Although **Job** also is proposed to us as a most noble example because of his remarkable self-restraint and extraordinary faith; he who became poor from being rich, abject from being illustrious, deformed from being beautiful, and <margin>Job. 1.</margin> sickly from being healthy, put to shame the one who had tempted him, while blessing the one who had formed him. He bore his second circumstances just as his first, rightly teaching the **Peripatetics** <note>followers of Aristotle, who believed external goods and health were necessary for a happy life</note> that he who is endowed with knowledge can use all things rightly. 

<margin>C</margin> And the Apostle shows that those things which were done rightly and virtuously by the ancients are set forth as images for our own good actions. <margin>Phil. 1.</margin> "So that my bonds," he says, "were made manifest in Christ in all the **praetorium** <note>the Roman imperial guard or the governor's palace</note> and elsewhere; and many of the brothers in the Lord, gaining confidence from my bonds, dared to speak the word of God more abundantly without fear." Since martyrdoms are also gloriously sanctified examples of conversion. "For WHATEVER," he says, "was written, was written for our <margin>Rom. 15.</margin> instruction, so that through patience and the consolation of the scriptures we might have hope of consolation." Moreover, if pain is present, the soul seems in some way to turn away from it and makes much of being freed from present trouble. At that time, it certainly rests even from disciplines, when other virtues are also disregarded. However, we do not say that virtue itself suffers; for virtue does not fall ill. 

<margin>D</margin> But he who partakes in both—virtue and disease—is pressed by that which urges him; and if he who has not yet acquired the habit of self-restraint is not of a great and lofty mind, he is displaced from his position and is found like a fugitive, unable to endure. The same reasoning applies to poverty. For poverty itself forces the soul to cease from necessary things—I mean contemplation and the pure removal of sin—inasmuch as it brings the necessity of being occupied in acquisition to one who has not dedicated himself entirely to God. Just as, on the other hand, health and an abundance of necessary things keep the soul free, having no impediment, and knowing how to use present things rightly. "For such as these," says the <margin>1. Cor. 7.</margin> Apostle, "shall have TRIBULATION in the flesh. But I spare you. For I want you to be without concern, so that you may sit by the Lord decently and honestly without distraction." 

<margin>E</margin> These things, therefore, are to be held not for their own sake, but for the sake of the body. Moreover, care for the body exists for the sake of the soul, to which it is related. For it is necessary for him who has established a life based on knowledge to learn in it those things which are appropriate. For it is clear that pleasure is not "the good" from the fact that certain pleasures are evil. By this reasoning, it would appear that good is evil and evil is good. Furthermore, if we seek certain pleasures but flee others, not every pleasure is an evil. Similarly, the same reasoning applies to pains, some of which we endure and others of which we flee. Choice and avoidance come from knowledge, so much so that **knowledge** is the good, not **pleasure**, for the sake of which we also sometimes choose a certain pleasure. 

<margin>F</margin> Now the **Martyr**—that is, the witness—chooses and seeks that pleasure which is grasped through hope, by means of present pain. But if pain is understood in thirst, and pleasure in drinking, then the pain that preceded would be the producer of the pleasure. But the evil of a good thing would not be its producer. Therefore, neither is evil. And **Simonides** <note>a Greek lyric poet</note>, just as also **Aristotle**...

# CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

<margin>A</margin> **Aristotle** <note>a Greek philosopher and student of Plato who founded the Lyceum</note> writes that the best thing for a human being is to be healthy. Second is to be naturally and intellectually inclined toward what is good and honorable. Third is to be wealthy without using deceit or fraud. **Theognis of Megara** <note>a 6th-century BC Greek poet known for his elegiac verses on morality and social class</note> also speaks on this:

<margin>Electra</margin>
> To flee poverty, cast yourself into the depths of the fish-filled sea,
> Or, O Cyrnus, down from the steep and jagged cliffs.

On the other hand, the comic poet **Antiphanes** says: "Plutus—that is, Wealth—when he takes on people who can see better than others, makes them blind." For it has been proclaimed by the poets that Wealth is blind from birth. And **Euphorion of Chalcis** <note>a Hellenistic poet known for his complex and dark style</note> says that Wealth "begot a son who never saw the Sun":

> Virtue is very poorly taught by riches,
> And by those luxuries that exceed the proper measure for men.

<margin>B</margin> **Euripides** said this regarding Alexander. It has certainly been said that "Wisdom fell to the lot of Poverty because of their kinship," but the "love of money has captured not only Sparta, but every city." Therefore, as **Sophocles** says, it is not only coins, white silver, or gold that serve as currency for mortals, but also virtue.

Our holy Savior, however, placed both poverty and wealth—and things similar to them—within both the spiritual and the sensory realms. For when He said, "Blessed are those who suffer persecution for the sake of righteousness," He openly teaches us to seek the martyr <note>original: "martyrem," meaning a witness who testifies through suffering</note> in every situation. If one is poor for the sake of righteousness, they testify that the justice they love is a good thing. And if one hungers and thirsts for the sake of righteousness, they testify that attaining righteousness is the highest goal.

<margin>C</margin> Similarly, the one who weeps and mourns for the sake of righteousness testifies that the highest law is beautiful and honorable. Therefore, just as He calls those who suffer persecution "blessed," so too does He bless those who hunger and thirst for righteousness—those who take up a sincere and genuine desire that not even hunger can break; if they thirst for justice itself, they are blessed.

Furthermore, the poor are blessed, whether in spirit or in possessions, provided it is for the sake of righteousness. Does He not then mean those who are not merely poor in an absolute sense, but those who *willed* to become poor for the sake of righteousness? He calls those blessed who have despised the honors found here in this world so that they might acquire the Good.

Similarly, He blesses those who, having had beautiful characters and bodies, have become distinguished and illustrious through their chastity—those who have been advanced to the status of adopted children <margin>John 1.</margin> for the sake of righteousness. Therefore, they have received the power to become children of God, to walk upon serpents and scorpions, and to obtain dominion over demons and the forces of the adversary.

<margin>D</margin> To speak summarily, the Lord’s discipline <note>original: "Dominica exercitatio," referring to the spiritual training of a Christian</note> gracefully and willingly leads the soul away from the body, provided the soul itself pulls away by transferring its focus. For "whoever loves his soul <note>original: "animam," meaning life or soul</note> will lose it, and whoever has lost it will find it," <margin>Matthew 10, Mark 8, Luke 9, John 12.</margin> if only we apply our fragility to the incorruptibility of God. Now, the will of God is the knowledge of God, which is the communication of incorruptibility. Therefore, the one who recognizes their sinful soul through the process of repentance "loses" that soul by separating it from the sin from which it was torn; but having "lost" it, they find it through obedience, so that it may live for faith but be dead to sin.

<margin>E</margin> This, then, is what it means to "find the soul": to know oneself. Regarding the soul's conversion toward divine things, the **Stoics** <note>philosophers who emphasized self-control and detachment from emotions</note> say this happens through "change," the soul being changed into Wisdom. **Plato**, however, calls it the "turning around" <note>referring to the *periagoge* in the Allegory of the Cave</note> of the soul toward better things, which receives its "turning" away from a kind of "nocturnal day."

Even the philosophers allow a good man to "lead the soul out" <note>a euphemism for suicide or death</note> for a just cause, if someone has been so removed from the ability to act that no hope of action remains for him. But the judge who applies force to make one deny their Beloved <note>referring to Christ</note> actually proves who is a friend of God and who is not. In this case, no comparison is even left to be made: which should one choose more—the threats of men or the love of God?

Abstaining from evil actions is found to be, in a way, the diminishing and extinction of evils, while their operation is removed by ceasing from the act. <margin>Matthew 19, Mark 10.</margin> And this is the meaning of "Sell all that you have, and give to the poor, and come, follow me"—that is, follow the things spoken by the Lord.

<margin>F</margin> Since the Greek word used is <term>ὑπάρχοντα</term> <note>original: "hyparchonta," meaning both one's "possessions" and "the things that exist/belong to one's nature"</note>, which signifies both the things that *are* and the resources we possess, some say He meant the "alien things" within the soul—though they can hardly explain how one "distributes" such things to the poor. But indeed, God distributes all things to everyone according to their merits, since His dispensation is just...

<summary>Clement interprets the Beatitudes and Christ’s commands on wealth, arguing that true "poverty" and "losing the soul" involve a spiritual detachment from sin and worldly honors to achieve self-knowledge and divine kinship.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Clement’s exploration of Christian ethics and the proper use of wealth.
