### STROMATA, BOOK IV

<margin>Action and stewardship.</margin> "Therefore," He says, "having looked down upon the resources which God distributed for your magnificence, follow the things spoken by me; strive toward the ascent of the spirit, not only justified through abstinence from evils, but also perfected by the Lord’s benevolence." Now, He refutes the man who boasted that he had perfectly fulfilled the precepts of the law, as one who had not truly loved his neighbor. For love, which rules over the Sabbath through the ascent of knowledge, professes benevolence. I believe, moreover, that it is necessary to approach the saving Word neither out of fear of punishment, nor because of some promise of a gift, but for the sake of the good itself. Those who are such stand at the right hand of the sanctuary. But those who, in exchange for the giving of things subject to corruption and death, think they will receive incorruption in return, are called "mercenaries" in the <margin>image</margin> <margin>Luke 15</margin> parable of the two brothers. And might not the concept of "likeness and image" be reduced to this? So that those who dwell with the Savior are there because of their *likeness* to Him. But those who stand on the left are according to the *image*. There are, then, three states, although for both groups there is one underlying root in the truth; yet the choice is not equal, or rather, the difference resulting from the choice is not equal. For there is a difference, I believe, between choosing out of imitation and choosing out of knowledge—just as there is a difference between something that is ignited and something that is illuminated. Therefore, the light of that *likeness* found in the scriptures is Israel; but the other is the *image*. 

What does the parable of <margin>Luke 19</margin> Lazarus <note>originally: "Lazari parabola"; likely referring to the rich man and Lazarus in Luke 16, though Clement or the scribe notes Luke 19</note> intend, showing through the Lord the likeness of the rich man and the poor man? And what of: "No one can <margin>Matthew 6</margin> <margin>C</margin> <margin>Luke 4</margin> serve two masters, God and Mammon" <note>a Syriac word for "wealth" or "property"</note>—since the Lord called the love of money by this name. Now, those who were held by the love of their own possessions do not come when called to the supper; not because they possessed things, but because they possessed them with an emotional attachment. 

Thus, <margin>Matthew 8</margin> <margin>Luke 9</margin> "FOXES have holes"—He called those evil men who are clearly "sons of the earth," occupied in digging out and burying riches, "foxes." Similarly, He said regarding Herod: "Go, tell that fox: Behold, I cast out demons and perform cures today and tomorrow, and on the third day I am perfected." For <margin>Matthew 13</margin> "BIRDS of the air"—He called those who are distinguished from other birds by the "heavenly air," who are truly pure and able to fly toward the knowledge of the heavenly Word. For there are innumerable anxieties not only for wealth, glory, and marriage, but also for poverty, for the one who cannot endure it. And He signified these very cares in the parable of the fourfold seed, saying that the seed which fell <margin>D</margin> <margin>Matthew 13</margin> <margin>Luke 8</margin> among thorns and hedges was choked by them and was unable to produce fruit. 

Therefore, it is necessary to learn how to use each of the things that happen to us, so that through a good life lived out of knowledge, we may be trained for the habit of eternal life. <margin>Psalm 36</margin> "For I have seen," it says, "the wicked man highly exalted and lifted up above the cedars of Lebanon; and I passed by," says the scripture, "and behold, he was not; and I sought him, and his place was not found. Keep innocence, and behold righteousness, for there are remnants for the man of peace." But such a man would be one who believes without hypocrisy, with his whole heart, and is tranquil in his whole soul. For "another <margin>Isaiah 29</margin> <margin>Mark 7</margin> <margin>Psalm 77</margin> <margin>Psalm 30</margin> people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from the Lord; they bless with their mouth, but in their heart they curse. They loved Him with their mouth, and they lied to Him with their tongue. But their heart was not right with Him, nor were they faithful in His covenant." 

<margin>E</margin> And therefore, "let deceitful lips become mute," and the "boastful tongue," those who have said, "we will magnify our tongue, our lips are our own; who is our Lord?" <margin>Psalm 11</margin> "Because of the affliction of the needy and the groaning of the poor, I will now arise," says the Lord; "I will place them in safety, I will act freely with them." For Christ belongs to those who carry themselves <margin>Mark 6</margin> humbly, not to those who lift themselves up over His flock. "Therefore, do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy, and where thieves dig through and steal." Perhaps the Lord says this to rebuke those held by the love of possessions; perhaps also even those who are absolutely anxious and affected by cares. Now, it also applies to those held by the love of the body. For <margin>F</margin> loves, diseases, and evil thoughts "dig through" the reason and the whole man. But in truth, our treasure is where there is a kinship of the mind, since it hands over a sharing and distributing power to justice—indicating that it is necessary to return to the custom of the old way of life those things acquired by it, and to run back to God, seeking mercy. <header>CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA</header>

<margin>Exodus 33. Romans 9. Matthew 7. Luke 12.</margin>
<margin>A</margin>
... truly a purse <note>original: "crumena"</note> that does not grow old, provisions for eternal life, and a treasure in heaven that never fails. For the Lord says: "I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy." <note>Exodus 33:19; Romans 9:15</note> Moreover, they say these things even to those who wish to be poor for the sake of justice. For they have heard through the commandment that the way is wide and spacious which leads to destruction, and many are those who pass through it, speaking of nothing else but luxury, the love of women, the desire for glory and ambition, and similar vices and disturbances of the soul. For "Fool," He says, "this night they require your soul. But the things you have prepared, whose will they be?" <note>Luke 12:20</note> And the commandment indeed presents itself in these words and in this manner.

<margin>B</margin>
<margin>Matthew 6.</margin>
BEWARE, therefore, of all avarice and the desire to have more, since a man’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions. For what does it profit a person if they gain the whole world, but suffer the loss of their own soul? Or what price will a person give in exchange for their soul? And therefore He says: "Do not be anxious for your soul, what you shall eat, nor for your body, what you shall wear. For the soul is more than food, and the body more than clothing." And again: "For your Father knows that you have need of all these things. But seek first the kingdom of heaven and its justice, for these are the great things; but the small things, which pertain to food and life, these shall be added to you." <note>Matthew 6:25–33</note> Does He not clearly command us to pursue the life which is established through knowledge, and by word and deed exhort us to seek the truth? Christ, therefore, in training the soul, teaches that a person is rich not because of a gift, but from their purpose and will.

<margin>C</margin>
<margin>Luke 19. Luke 21.</margin>
Thus, regarding Zacchaeus—though others say it was Matthias, the chief of the tax collectors—when he had heard the Lord, who had deigned to be at his house, he said: "Lord, half of my goods I give as alms, and if I have defrauded anyone of anything through false accusation, I restore it fourfold." Of him the Savior also said: "Today, the Son of Man, having come, has found that which was lost." <note>Luke 19:8–10</note> And again, when He saw a rich man cast something into the treasury in accordance with his means, but a widow cast in two small coins, He said the widow had cast in more than them all. For the former contributed out of abundance, but she out of her poverty. This is because He reduced all things to the training of the soul.

<margin>D</margin>
<margin>Matthew 5. Matthew 10. Matthew 20.</margin>
BLESSED, He says, are the meek, for they shall possess the earth. <note>Matthew 5:5</note> The "meek" are those who have quelled the untrustworthy war within the soul—the war of anger, desire, and the things that fall under them. He praises the meek: those who are such by choice and by the soul’s purpose, rather than those who are so out of necessity. For with the Lord there are many rewards and mansions, according to the proportion of their lives. For He says: "He who receives a Prophet in the name of a Prophet shall receive a Prophet’s reward; and he who receives a righteous man in the name of a righteous man shall receive a righteous man’s reward; and whoever receives one of these little ones as a disciple does not lose his reward." <note>Matthew 10:41–42</note> And again, He shows the differences in rewards for virtue, and the noble remunerations, through the hours that were not equal in number. <note>Referring to the Parable of the Workers in the Vineyard, Matthew 20:1–16</note> Furthermore, to each of the workers He gives an equal reward, which is salvation—signified by the "denarius"—indicating equal right even through those who worked at hours that did not agree with each other. They shall work, therefore, in accordance with the mansions that correspond in proportion to the prizes of which they have been deemed worthy, acting as helpers of an ineffable stewardship and gift.

<margin>E</margin>
Plato says: "Those who appear to have been signally called forth to live holily, these are they who are liberated and released from those things which are on the earth, as if from prisons, and come upward to the heavenly dwelling." <note>Plato, Phaedo 114b–c</note> And again, he says the same thing more clearly: "But from among these very ones, those who have been sufficiently purified in Philosophy live entirely without bodies for all time." Although he adds certain forms to them, to some of them "airy" forms, and to others "fiery" forms. He adds further: "And they come into dwellings even more beautiful than these, which are neither easy to explain, nor is the present time sufficient for it."

There are two modes of one who is led by repentance: one is the more common fear because of things done; the other, more proper to the soul, is a modesty or shame before itself arising from conscience. Whether here or elsewhere, for no place is void of God’s mercy. <meta>This page continues Clement’s exposition of the Beatitudes from Matthew 5, moving from the concept of poverty and desire to the virtues of mercy, purity of heart, and peacemaking. He frames these Christian virtues using the language of Greek philosophy, particularly contrasting the Stoic view of emotion with the Christian view of divine character.</meta>

<header>STROMATA, BOOK IV</header>

<margin>To show mercy <note>Greek: ἐλεεῖν (eleein)</note> in Greek implies being polite or civil, but read it here as "divine" <note>Greek: θεῖον (theion)</note>. Hosea 6. Matthew 9.</margin>

**A** According to the wise <note>referring to Stoic philosophers who viewed pity as a rational weakness</note>, mercy is a distress caused by the misfortunes of others; but it is instead something divine, as the prophets say: "I desire mercy," He says, "and not sacrifice." <note>Hosea 6:6; Matthew 9:13</note> Moreover, He wishes those to be merciful who not only perform acts of mercy, but also those who *wish* to show mercy, even if they are unable to do so. These are the people who act with a spontaneous and free will. For sometimes we wish to show mercy—either by giving money or by physical effort, such as bringing aid to the needy, serving the sick, or being present for someone in calamity—yet we cannot fulfill our purpose due to poverty, illness, or old age (for old age is also a natural illness). Even if we are unable to carry out the actions we desire and toward which we are moved by an internal impulse of the soul, we are still judged by that intent.

**B** Therefore, those who have the *will* shall receive the same honor as those who had the *ability*. Their will is equal, even if the others surpass them in resources. Since there are two paths found that lead to the perfection of salvation—action and knowledge—He called those "blessed" who are pure in heart, for they shall see God. And if we truly consider the matter, knowledge <note>original: "cognitio," likely referring to "Gnosis" or spiritual insight</note> is the purification of the ruling part of the soul, and it is a good action in itself. Some things are good in their own right; others are good because they participate in what is good, such as the actions we call "good." Without the presence of intermediary things, which occupy the place of "matter," actions are neither good nor bad—take, for example, life, health, and other things that are either necessary or circumstantial. 

<margin>circumstances <note>Greek: περιστατικῶν (peristatikōn)</note>.</margin>

Therefore, He wants those who come to the recognition of God to be pure from bodily desires and from unholy thoughts. This happens when the ruling faculty of the soul has nothing adulterated to block its view or hinder it. 

**C** When, therefore, a person has dwelt and lingered in contemplation, maintaining a pure relationship with God—sharing in a holy quality through knowledge—he approaches closer to a state of impassible identity <note>a state where the soul is no longer tossed by passions</note>. At this point, he no longer merely "has" science or "possesses" knowledge, but he *is* science and knowledge.

<margin>identity <note>Greek: ταυτότης (tautotēs)</note>.</margin>

Blessed, therefore, are the peacemakers, who have tamed and quieted the law of the mind that rebels against our judgment—the threats of anger, the baits of desire, and other passions that war against reason. Having lived with the knowledge of good works and true reason, they are restored to the more beloved and gracious status of adoption as sons. Perfect peacemaking is that which keeps a person tranquil in every situation, calling the administration of divine and human affairs holy and honorable. Through this knowledge, one comes to see the conflicts within the world as the most beautiful harmony and concord of creation. 

**D** They also bring peace to those who are attacked here by the leader of the war—sin—teaching them to cross over to faith and peace. The sum of all virtue, I believe, is the Lord teaching that we ought to despise death through knowledge, because of our love for God. "Blessed," He says, "are those who suffer persecution for the sake of justice, for they shall be called the sons of God." Or, as some of those who rearrange the Gospels <note>likely referring to non-canonical versions or specific scholarly arrangements of the text</note> put it: "Blessed are those whom justice pursues, for they shall be perfect," and "Blessed are those who suffer persecution for my sake, for they shall have a place where persecution shall not reach," and "Blessed shall you be when men hate you, when they shut you out, and when they strike out your name as evil, on account of the Son of Man." 

**E** This applies if we do not detest those who persecute us, but endure the punishments they inflict without hating them, reflecting that we have been tested later than we expected. But we should also know that every trial is an opportunity for martyrdom. Furthermore, if a person has lied and shown himself to be unfaithful, fleeing to the army of the devil, consider what a great evil he dwells in. He lies to the Lord—or rather, he lies to his own hope and frustrates it—by not believing in God. And he does not believe who does not do what He commanded. Indeed, does a person not deny himself when he denies the Lord? For he does not take away the Lord's mastery, but he deprives himself of the relationship that exists with Him. 

**F** Therefore, he who denies the Savior denies life; for light was life. He does not say such people have "little faith," but that they are unfaithful and hypocrites—those who take the inscription of the Name upon themselves but deny that they are faithful. Yet, the "faithful" one is called both a servant and a friend. Therefore, if anyone loves himself...

<summary>Clement interprets the Beatitudes, defining mercy as a divine state of will and "purity of heart" as the soul's transition into becoming "knowledge" itself. He characterizes peacemaking as the internal mastery of passions and views persecution as an opportunity for martyrdom and a test of true faith.</summary>

# CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

<header>STROMATA, BOOK IV</header>

<margin>A</margin> ...loves the Lord and confesses salvation so that he may save his own soul. Yet if you should die for your neighbor out of love, consider that our Savior is near. For God is called "the one who approaches," He who saves and is saved, choosing death for the sake of life, and suffering for your sake rather than for His own. And has He not been called a "brother" for this reason—He who suffered for His own love for God, who suffered for His own salvation, and who dies again for His own salvation, enduring it for the love of the Lord? For even though He was Life itself, He willed to suffer for us, so that by His suffering we might live. <margin>Matthew 7</margin>
> "Why do you call me 'Lord, Lord,'" He says, "and not do what I say?"

For the people who love with their lips but keep their hearts far from the Lord are persuaded by one another and have willingly sold themselves. <margin>Matthew 15</margin> However, those who carry out the Savior's commands are martyrs—that is, <term>witnesses</term> <note>original: "martyres, id est testes." Clement is emphasizing the Greek root *martus*, which means a witness in a legal or factual sense, not just someone who dies for a cause.</note>—in every action. They do what He wills, following the Lord's name, and testifying in reality to Him in whom they believe. They have "crucified the flesh with its vices and desires." If we live by the Spirit, he says, let us walk by the Spirit. <margin>Galatians 6</margin>
> "He who sows in his flesh will reap corruption from the flesh. But he who sows in the spirit will reap eternal life from the spirit."

To wretched men, the testimony of the Lord offered through blood appears to be a most violent death, for they do not know that this door of death is the beginning of true life. They do not wish to understand the honors that follow the deaths of those who lived holily, nor the punishments of those who lived unjustly and lustfully. I say this not only from our own scriptures—for almost all our <margin>C</margin> commandments signify this—but they will not even lend an ear to the writings of their own people. For Theano the Pythagorean <note>Theano was a female philosopher of the 6th century BCE, often identified as the wife or student of Pythagoras.</note> writes: "Life would truly be a banquet for those who lived wickedly and then died, if the soul were not immortal; then death would be a gain." And Plato says in the *Phaedo*: "If death were a release from everything," and so forth.

Therefore, one should not think—according to the opinion of Telephus in the works of Aeschylus—that "a simple and single path leads to the underworld." For there are many paths, and many sins that lead away. Aristophanes, mockingly playing with these wandering infidels in a comic style, says:
> "Come now, you men of obscure life, like the generation of leaves, weak, figures of wax, leaves resembling shadows, fleeting, wingless, possessing life for only a single day."

And Epicharmus <note>A Greek dramatist and philosopher</note> says: "The lives of men are themselves like inflated wineskins." <margin>D</margin> But to us, the Savior said:
> "The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak,"

since the "wisdom of the flesh" is an enemy to God, as the Apostle explains: <margin>Matthew 26; Romans 8</margin>
> "For it is not subject to the law of God, nor indeed can it be. Those who are in the flesh cannot please God."

And explaining this further, he adds—lest anyone with an ungrateful mind, like <term>Marcion</term> <note>Marcion of Sinope was a 2nd-century heretic who taught that the physical world and the human body were inherently evil creations of a lesser god. Clement is careful here to distinguish between "sinful flesh" and the "creation" itself.</note>, should take it that the created world is evil: "But if Christ is in us, the body is indeed dead because of sin, but the spirit lives because of righteousness." And again:
> "For if you live according to the flesh, you will die. For I consider that the sufferings of this world are not worthy of the glory that is to be revealed in us, if indeed we suffer with Him, so that we may also be glorified with Him as co-heirs with Christ."

And we know that for those who love God, all things work together for good, for those who are called according to His purpose. <margin>E</margin> For those whom He foreknew, He also predestined to be conformed to the image of the Son of God, so that He might be the firstborn among many brothers. Those whom He predestined, He also called; those whom He called, He also justified; and those whom He justified, He also glorified.

You see that martyrdom is taught through love. But if you wish to be a martyr and bear witness only for the sake of the reward of good things, you will hear again: "For in **HOPE** we are saved. But hope that is seen is not hope. For what a man sees, why does he hope for it? But if we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it with patience." But even if we suffer for the sake of righteousness, Peter says, "you are blessed. Do not fear their terror, nor be troubled. But sanctify the Lord Christ in your hearts." <margin>1 Peter 3</margin> Always be ready to give a defense to everyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you, but <margin>F</margin> do so with modesty and fear, keeping a good conscience, so that in the things they disparage you, those who slander your good conduct in Christ may be put to shame.

For it is better, if the will of God wills it, to suffer for doing good than for doing evil. And if anyone...

<summary>Clement defines martyrdom as a lifestyle of "witnessing" through action and love rather than just a violent death. He integrates Platonic and Pythagorean philosophy with Pauline theology to argue that the soul's immortality makes earthly suffering and "crucifying the flesh" meaningful.</summary>

<margin>A</margin>
We labor, working with our own hands; we are cursed, and we bless; we suffer persecution, and we endure it. We have become like the refuse of this world. <note>Clement is quoting the Apostle Paul in 1 Corinthians 4:12–13.</note> Such also are the things which Plato says in the *Republic*: even if the just man is tortured, even if his eyes are gouged out, he will still be happy. <note>Plato, Republic II, 361e. Charity sustains all things and bears all things, because he is persuaded that divine providence administers everything rightly. "I beg you,"

<margin>1. Cor. 4</margin>
he says, "be imitators of me." Thus, the first step of the body is instruction joined with fear, through which we abstain from doing wrong. The second is hope, through which we desire

<margin>B</margin>
what is best; but charity brings perfection, as is fitting, for it now teaches through the way of knowledge. For the Gentiles—I know not how—when they attribute what happens to a necessity that lacks reason, they confess that they obey against their will. Certainly, Euripides says:

> *Accept the advice I give you, woman,*
> *No mortal exists who does not labor.*
> *One buries children, and then bears new ones,*
> *And then meets death. Men bear these things with grief.*

->Then he adds:<-

> *It is necessary to suffer what Nature requires. But it is fitting*
> *To migrate there, where no necessity is heavy.*

<margin>C</margin>
But for those who strive toward perfection, rational knowledge is set before them, the foundation of which is the Holy Trinity: faith, hope, and charity, but the greatest of these is charity.

<margin>1. Cor. 10</margin>
"All things are indeed lawful, but not all things are beneficial. All things are lawful, but not all things build up," says the Apostle. And: "Let no one seek what is his own only, but also what belongs to another," so that he may be able both to act and to teach at the same time, building and building upon. For it is certain and beyond controversy that the earth is the Lord's and its fullness. But the conscience of the weak is sustained. I say conscience, however, not his own, but that of the other. For why is my liberty judged by another's conscience? If I participate by grace,

<margin>D</margin>
why am I reviled for that for which I give thanks? Therefore, whether you eat, or drink, or do anything, do all for the glory of God. For though we walk in the flesh, we do

<margin>1. Cor. 10</margin>
not wage war according to the flesh. <note>The marginal note lists 1 Corinthians 10, but this is a quotation from 2 Corinthians 10:3–5.</note> For the weapons of our warfare are not fleshly, but powerful in God for the destruction of fortresses, destroying arguments and every high thing that exalts itself against the knowledge of the Lord. Armed with these weapons, he who is gifted with knowledge says: "O Lord, give me misfortune and affliction, and receive the demonstration; let this heavy and formidable thing come. I despise dangers because of my love for you."

> *For virtue alone, in the affairs of mortals,*
> *Does not take its rewards from the shields of war,*
> *But has itself as the reward for its labors.*

<margin>E</margin>

<margin>F</margin>

Theodotus the Pythagorean did something similar, as did Paulus, the associate of Lacydes, as Timotheus of Pergamum says in his book *On the Greatness of Mind of Philosophers*, and as Achaicus says in his *Ethics*.

### STROMATA, BOOK IV.

<margin>A</margin> Furthermore, the Roman Posthumus <note>Clement likely refers to a legendary Roman figure such as Mucius Scaevola, known for his endurance, though he names him Posthumus here.</note>, after being captured by Peucetion, not only revealed nothing of what was hidden, but even when he had placed his hand into the fire as if it were bronze, he stood with a firm and completely unchangeable expression. I will not dwell on Anaxarchus <note>Anaxarchus (c. 340 BC) was a Greek philosopher who, when being tortured by the tyrant Nicocreon, famously shouted that his body was merely a shell.</note> exclaiming: "Pound the pouch of Anaxarchus; for you do not pound Anaxarchus," <note>original: "tunde Anaxarchi capsam; Anaxarchum enim non tundis"</note> while he was being crushed with iron pestles by the tyrant. Therefore, neither the hope of happiness nor love toward God feels bitterness at those things which happen. The soul remains free, even if it falls among the most savage beasts or into the most devouring fire; and even if it is worn down by the torments of a tyrant, it hangs upon divine friendships, not at all reduced to slavery, and it moves through the heavenly regions, leaving the body to those who are only able to hold it.

<margin>B</margin> It is said that a certain barbarian tribe, not a stranger to the taste of philosophy, chooses a legate every year for the hero Zalmoxis <note>Zalmoxis was a legendary social and religious reformer among the Getae (Thracians); Clement notes the tradition that he was a student or slave of Pythagoras.</note>. This Zalmoxis was one of the associates of Pythagoras. Therefore, the one who is judged most worthy is sacrificed, while those who have also practiced philosophy but were not chosen grieve as those who have been rejected from a blessed ministry. Thus, the whole Church is full of those who throughout their entire life have meditated on death, which rouses us to Christ—both temperate men and women alike. For it is possible for someone who has ordered their life according to our custom to practice philosophy even without being learned, whether they be a barbarian, a Greek, a slave, an old man, a boy, or a woman. For temperance is common to all people who have chosen it by their own will. Among us, it is beyond controversy that the same nature in every species also possesses the same virtue. Therefore, a woman does not have one nature regarding her humanity and a man another, but rather the same.

<margin>C</margin> For which reason they also share virtue. If, indeed, the virtue of a man is temperance and justice, and whatever qualities are thought to follow them, then it would follow that only a man should be endowed with virtue, while a woman should be intemperate and unjust—but it is shameful even to say this. Therefore, both man and woman, free and slave, must similarly take care for temperance and justice and every other virtue, since it happens that there is one and the same virtue for the same nature. And yet, we do not say that the nature of a woman is the same as that of a man insofar as she is a woman. For it is entirely necessary that there be some difference in each of them, through which one of them is made female and the other masculine.

<margin>D</margin> We say, therefore, that carrying a womb and giving birth belongs to the woman insofar as she is a female, not insofar as she is a human. If there were no difference between a man and a woman, both would do and experience the same things. Insofar, then, as they are the same—because there is the same soul—they will arrive at the same virtue. But insofar as they are different by the property of the body, they are destined for the carrying of offspring in the womb and for the keeping of the house.

<margin>1 Cor. 11</margin>
> "For I want you to know," says the Apostle, "that Christ is the head of every man, and the man is the head of the woman. For the man is not from the woman, but the woman from the man. But neither is the woman separate from the man, nor the man separate from the woman in the Lord." <note>1 Corinthians 11:3, 8, 11.</note>

For just as we say that a man ought to be temperate and overcome pleasures, so we should also judge that a woman ought to be temperate and practiced in the struggle against pleasures.

<margin>E</margin> I say then, "Walk in the spirit, and you shall not fulfill the desire of the flesh," as the Apostolic precept advises.

<margin>Gal. 5</margin>
> "For the flesh lusts against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh. These, therefore, are opposed, not as evil to good, but as those which fight usefully. Therefore he adds: "So that you do not do what you want. Now the works of the flesh are manifest, which are: fornication, uncleanness, indecency, idolatry, witchcraft, enmities, contentions, rivalries, anger, brawls, dissensions, sects, envies, drunkenness, revelries, and things similar to these; of which I tell you beforehand, that those who do such things shall not possess the kingdom of God. But the fruit of the spirit is charity, joy, peace, patience, kindness, self-control, goodness, faith, gentleness." <note>Galatians 5:16–23.</note>

By "flesh," I believe, he meant the sinners, just as by "spirit" he meant the righteous.

<margin>F</margin> Now, indeed, we must take up fortitude and the virtue of a great soul, for the sake of the soul’s confidence and endurance, so that to the one who strikes the cheek, the other may be offered; and to the one who takes away the cloak, even the tunic may be yielded, by bravely restraining anger. For we do not train women to be like Amazons <note>Legendary female warriors of Greek mythology.</note> in warlike virtue, since we even wish men to be peaceful. But I hear that the Sauromatian <note>A nomadic tribe related to the Scythians, where women famously participated in warfare.</note> women also go to war no less than the men, and other Sacian women who

# STROMATA, BOOK IV.
### A, B, C, D, E, F

<margin>A</margin>...or an wicked Master, the slave pursuing virtue with a brave and noble spirit. For just as it is a beautiful and honorable thing for a man to die for virtue, for liberty, and for his own sake, so it is also for a woman. For this is not a property of the male nature, but of the nature of good people. Therefore, both the old and the young, the woman and the slave who is obedient to the commands, will live faithfully, and if necessary, will die—which is indeed to be made alive through death. We certainly know for a certainty that children, women, and slaves have often turned out to be the best of people, even against the will of their parents, husbands, and Masters. Therefore, those who are to lead a pious life ought to be no less ready and eager in spirit when some appear to hinder them; indeed, it is much more fitting to strive and to contend exceptionally, lest, being defeated, they fall away from the best 

<margin>B</margin>and most necessary counsels. For I do not think any comparison can be admitted as to whether it is better to be enrolled in the fellowship of the Almighty or to choose the darkness of demons. For those things which we do for the sake of others, we should always do by looking toward those for whose sake they seem to be done, taking as our measure that which is pleasing to them. But those things which are done for our own sake rather than for others should be performed by us with equal zeal, whether they seem to please some people or not. But if some of those things which are "indifferent" <note>In Stoic and early Christian ethics, "indifferent" things (Greek: *adiaphora*) are those that are neither inherently good nor evil, such as wealth or health.</note> have attained such honor that they seem worth seeking and choosing even against the will of some, how much more must we think that we must contend for virtue, looking to nothing else but that which can be done rightly and honorably, whether it seems so to others or not. 

<margin>C</margin>Beautifully, therefore, Epicurus also says, writing to Menoeceus: "Neither if one is young, let him delay practicing philosophy; nor if he is old, let him grow weary of philosophizing. For no one is immature, nor of too advanced and exhausted an age, for attaining the health of the soul. He who says that the time for philosophizing has not yet come or has passed is like one who says that the time for happiness is either not yet present or has passed. Therefore, both the young man and the old man must practice philosophy." <note>original: "Nec si sit aliquis iuuenis, differat philosophari..." A famous passage from Epicurus's Letter to Menoeceus regarding the universal need for wisdom.</note> To the latter, so that as he ages he may grow young in good things through the grace of what has been done; to the former, so that he may be at once young and old through the absence of fear regarding the future. But concerning martyrdom—or "testimony"—the Lord spoke openly; we shall join together those things which were written in different places.

<margin>Matthew 10</margin>
<margin>D</margin>I SAY to you, whoever confesses in me before men, the Son of Man will also confess in him before the Angels of God. 
<margin>Mark 8</margin>
But whoever denies me before men, I will deny him before the Angels. 
<margin>Matthew 10</margin>
For whoever is ashamed of me or of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation, of him also the Son of Man will be ashamed when he comes in the glory of his Father with his angels. 
<margin>Luke 12</margin>
Therefore, whoever confesses in me before men, I also will confess in him before my Father who is in heaven. When they bring you into synagogues, and to magistrates and powers, do not be anxious beforehand how you shall answer or what you shall say. For the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you should say. Explaining this passage, Heracleon <note>A prominent Gnostic teacher and commentator on the New Testament, belonging to the school of Valentinus.</note>, who was held in the highest esteem in the school of Valentinus, says in these words: "One confession is in faith and conduct of life, but the other is by the voice."

<margin>E</margin>And that confession which is made by the voice also takes place before the authorities, which alone, he says, many people incorrectly think is the only confession. But even hypocrites can use this confession. Nor will this saying be found to have been spoken universally and generally. For not all who are saved have used that confession which is made by the voice and then departed [this life], among whom are Matthew, Philip, Thomas, Levi, and many others; and the confession made by the voice is not universal and general, but particular. But He calls "universal and general" that which is made by deeds and works, corresponding to the faith in Him. Moreover, the particular confession made before authorities follows this [general] confession, if the need arises and reason compels it. For he will also confess rightly with his voice who has first rightly confessed with his inner disposition. Beautifully, moreover, regarding those who confess:

<margin>F</margin>in those who confess, He said "In me." <note>Clement (and Heracleon) notes the specific phrasing in the Greek/Latin text: "confess *in* me" rather than just "confess me."</note> But in those who deny, He added that word "me." For even if they have confessed Him with their voice, they deny Him by not confessing through action. Only those confess "in Him" who live in that confession and action which is directed toward Him; since he is entwined in the things he confesses and is held by them. Wherefore, never...

<meta>This page continues Clement’s exploration of Christian ethics, specifically transitioning from the universal capacity for virtue to a detailed theological debate on the nature of "confessing" one's faith. # CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA
### Page 126

...He cannot deny Himself. But those who are not in Him deny Him. For He did not say, "Whoever shall deny *in* me," but "me." <note>Clement is analyzing the specific phrasing of Matthew 10:32-33. The Greek text uses a construction that can be literally translated as "confess *in* me," which the Gnostic Heracleon interpreted as an internal, spiritual union rather than just a vocal statement.</note> For no one who is in Him ever denies Him. 

<margin>A</margin> Regarding the phrase "before men," this applies to those who are being saved, and similarly even to the Gentiles: among some, confession is made by their way of life, and among others, it is also made by their voice. Therefore, those in Him can never deny Him; however, those who are not in Him are the ones who deny Him. 

These are the views of Heracleon, and in other matters he seems to agree with us in this part. However, he does not notice that even if some have not confessed Christ before men through a specific action or way of life, the very fact that they confess with their voice in the law courts, and do not deny Him even when tortured unto death, shows they have believed from the heart. 

A confessing heart—and <margin>B</margin> especially one that is not changed even by death—entirely cuts away all the vices that were produced through the desires of the body. It is, to put it simply, a suddenly accumulated repentance through action, and a true confession in Christ, with the voice serving as the witness. 

But if the Spirit of the Father testifies within us, how can we still be the hypocrites whom He said testify with the voice alone? Moreover, it will be granted to some, if it is beneficial, to answer and defend themselves, so that through both their testimony and their confession everyone may be helped—while those in the Church are strengthened, those from the Gentiles who have curiously sought salvation are marveled and led to the faith, and the rest are struck with awe. 

Therefore, it is absolutely necessary to confess. For that is placed within our power. To answer and defend oneself, however, is not entirely so, for that is not placed within our power. "But he who endures to the end will be saved." <margin>Matth. 24.</margin> For who among those who are wise would not rather choose to reign in God than to serve? 

<margin>C</margin> <margin>Tit. 1.</margin> Certain people "claim to know God," as the Apostle says, "but by their deeds they deny Him, being abominable, disobedient, and unfit for any good work." Yet even if those people have only confessed this one thing, they have performed at least one good deed at the end. Therefore, it appears that Martyrdom is a purification of sins accompanied by glory. 

Now, indeed, the Shepherd says: "You will escape the working of the wild beast if your heart is pure and free from all blame." <note>Clement is quoting the *Shepherd of Hermas*, a popular early Christian text (Vision 4.2.4) that used the "wild beast" as a symbol for coming persecution.</note> Furthermore, the Lord Himself says: "Satan has desired you, that he might sift you, but I have prayed." <margin>Luc. 22.</margin> 

Therefore, the Lord alone drank the cup for the purification of those men who plotted against Him and for the unbelievers. The Apostles, imitating Him—as those who were truly gifted with <term>gnosis</term><note>The Greek term for "knowledge." Clement uses this to describe the "perfect" Christian who understands the deeper truths of faith, reclaiming the word from the Gnostics.</note> and were perfect—suffered for the churches they founded. Thus, those who are gifted with this knowledge, following in the Apostolic footsteps, ought to conduct themselves <margin>D</margin> so that sin does not fall upon them, and because of their love for the Lord, they should also love their neighbor; so that if some circumstance calls them to act for the Church, they may drink the cup, suffering afflictions without offense. 

However, those who bear witness by their deeds in life and by their words in court, both waiting in hope and shrinking in fear, are better than those who confess salvation with their mouth alone. But if someone has also passed over into love, he is a truly blessed and genuine witness <note>The word "martyr" in Greek literally means "witness."</note>, as one who has perfectly confessed both to the commandments and to God, through the Lord. Loving Him, he has shown Him to be his brother, and has handed over his whole self for the sake of God—like a deposit—returning the man who is required of him with gratitude and affection. 

When, on the other hand, He said, "When they persecute you in this city, <margin>Matth. 10.</margin> flee to another," He does not advise fleeing as if suffering persecution were an evil thing; nor does He command us to avoid death by flight because we are terrified of it. <margin>E</margin> Rather, He wants us to be the authors of no evil, nor helpers in the cause of any evil—neither to ourselves, nor to the one who persecutes, nor to the one who kills. For He is, in a way, warning us to be careful. 

He who does not obey is bold and reckless, and thoughtlessly casts himself into manifest dangers. If he who kills a man of God sins against God, then he who offers himself to the judgment is also held guilty of his own murder. Such would be the person who does not avoid persecution, but through boldness offers himself to be captured. He is one who, as much as it is in his power, assists the wickedness of the persecutor. 

Furthermore, if he himself provides the cause—plainly provoking the "wild beast"—or if he provides any cause for a fight, or for loss, or for a trial, or for enmities, then he has given birth to the occasion of the persecution. And for this reason, we are commanded <margin>F</margin> to retain nothing of those things which belong to this life; but to him who takes the cloak, to give the tunic besides. This is not only so that we may remain subject to no disturbances of the soul, but also so that by not claiming these things, we do not turn those who are contending in court into enemies against us.

<summary>Clement debates the nature of confession and martyrdom, arguing that while vocal testimony in court is vital, true "martyrdom" is a life of love and purification. He warns against reckless self-sacrifice, noting that provoking one's own death makes a person complicit in the persecutor's sin.</summary>

# STROMATA BOOK IV
### Page 127

<margin>A</margin> ...wild men, and through our own actions we provoke them to attack the Name <note>The "Name" refers to the name of Christ, the profession of being a Christian.</note> with curses. But they say: "If God cares for you, why do you suffer persecution and are put to death? Does He Himself hand you over to them?" However, we do not think that the Lord wills for us to fall into these disasters, but rather that He prophetically foretold the things that would happen—namely, that we would suffer persecution, be killed, and be hanged for the sake of His name. Therefore, He did not desire for us to suffer persecution, but He signaled beforehand what we were going to suffer through that prediction of what would happen, training us for endurance, to which He promised the inheritance. Nevertheless, we are not the only ones punished, but we suffer along with many others.

<margin>B</margin> But they say: "Since they are evildoers, they rightly pay the penalty." Therefore, even against their will, they grant us justice by their own testimony—we who are punished unjustly for the sake of justice. But neither does the injustice of a judge affect the providence of God. For a judge must have the decision of his own mind in his own power; he is not like a puppet pulled by strings, as if he took his opportunities only from some external cause. Therefore, he himself is examined and tested just as we are, in the way he judges, through his choice of what is to be preferred and through his patience. Although we do no wrong, the judge looks upon us as if we were evildoers. For he does not know our affairs, nor does he wish to know them, but is carried away by a certain empty, preconceived prejudice. For this reason, he is also judged. They persecute us, then, not because they have found us to be unjust, but because they think we do an injustice to human life by being Christians—both ourselves who live such a life, and others whom we exhort to live a similar life.

<margin>C</margin> But why, they ask, is no help brought to you when you are persecuted? For what injury is done to us, as far as we are concerned, when we are dissolved by death to go to the Lord, undergoing a change of life, as if it were a change of age? If we are wise, we will be grateful to those who have provided us the opportunity for a swift migration, if we bear witness <term>witness: "martyrium" or martyrdom</term> because of love. If we have seemed to many to be evil men, yet if they themselves had known the truth, all would have leaped onto the path, and there would have been no "choice" <note>Clement suggests that if the truth were obvious to all, faith would not be a virtuous choice but an inevitability.</note>. But indeed our faith, being the light of the world, convicts their unbelief. For "Anytus and Meletus may kill me, but they cannot harm me in any way." <note>A famous quote attributed to Socrates during his trial, recorded in Plato's *Apology* (30c). Clement uses the pagan philosopher's defiance of his accusers as a model for Christian courage.</note> For I do not think it is right that what is better should be harmed by what is worse; so much so that each of us may say securely and confidently:

<margin>Psalm 118, Wisdom 3</margin>
<margin>D</margin> "The Lord is my helper, I will not fear what man shall do to me." <note>original: "Dominus mihi adiutor, non timebo quid faciat mihi homo." (Psalm 118:6)</note> For "the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, and no torment shall touch them." <note>original: "Iustorum enim animæ in manu Dei sunt, & non tanget eas tormentum." (Wisdom of Solomon 3:1)</note> 

However, Basilides <note>An early 2nd-century Gnostic teacher in Alexandria who proposed a complex system of cosmology and ethics.</note>, in the twenty-third book of his *Expositions* <note>original: "Exegeticōn"</note>, says the following about those who are punished in martyrdom: "I say that whoever falls into these so-called afflictions—if they have sinned unknowingly in other lapses—are led to this good end by the kindness of Him who leads them, even if other specific charges are brought against them, so that they may not suffer for things that are certainly evil and beyond all controversy. They are not attacked with curses as an adulterer or a murderer, but are accused for being Christians; this will comfort them so that they do not even seem to suffer. And if someone who has not sinned at all should come to suffering—which is rare—not even he will suffer anything from the snares prepared by the power, but will suffer as an infant suffers who seemed to have committed no sin." Then a little further down he adds:

<margin>E</margin> "Therefore, just as the infant who has not previously sinned, or has not actually sinned in himself, but has within him the capacity to sin, is treated with a benefit when he is cast into suffering—as one who gains many things that are difficult—so also if even a 'perfect' man, who has not sinned in action, should suffer, he has suffered similarly to the infant. For he has within himself the power of sinning, but because he did not receive an opportunity to sin, he did not sin. Therefore, it is not to be credited to him that he did not sin. For just as he who wants to commit adultery is an adulterer even if he does not achieve the effect, and he who wants to commit a murder is a murderer even if he cannot kill; so also I call that man a 'sinner' if I see him suffering, even if he has done nothing evil; I will call him evil because of his *desire* to sin. For I will say anything rather than call Providence evil." Then below, he speaks openly about the Lord as if about a man.

<margin>F</margin> "But if, setting aside all these discourses, you should come to the point of saying to me..."

<meta>This page continues Clement’s critique of the Gnostic teacher Basilides. On the previous page, Clement argued that God does not desire the suffering of Christians but foresees it and uses it to train them in endurance. Here, he specifically addresses Basilides' controversial theory that martyrdom is a punishment for sins committed either in this life or a previous one.</meta>

# CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA
### Page 128

<margin>A</margin> If, out of reverence for certain persons, you should say, for example: "This man sinned, and for this reason he suffered"; or "This man sinned, for he endured this." If you allow it, I will say: "He did not sin, but he was like an infant who suffered." But if you press the point more vehemently, I will say that whomever you might name, he is a man; but God is just. "For no one is clean from filth," <note>original: "Nullus enim est mundus à sorde" — a reference to Job 14:4, suggesting that all humans possess some degree of imperfection or sin.</note> as someone once said. But the fundamental argument of Basilides <note>Basilides was a prominent Gnostic teacher in Alexandria (2nd century AD) who taught that souls undergo transmigrations.</note> is that the soul which previously sinned in another life suffers its punishment here; the "elect" soul is punished through martyrdom, while others are purified by their own specific punishments. How can this be true, however, when it remains within our own power either to confess or not, and thus to be punished or not? For in the case of one who is going to deny his faith, the very providence <note>Divine care or guidance.</note> that Basilides describes is rendered void. I will ask him then, regarding the man who is <margin>B</margin> held as a "confessor" <note>A "confessor" is a Christian who publicly acknowledges their faith in the face of persecution, often leading to martyrdom.</note>: will he bear testimony and be punished by providence, or not? 

For if he denies his faith, he will not be punished. But if the outcome—and the fact that he should not be punished—means the destruction of those who deny the faith, then by his logic, this happens through providence; thus, he would bear testimony against his will. Furthermore, how could a most glorious reward be stored in heaven for the one who bore witness, simply because he was a witness? If providence does not allow the one who had the power to sin to actually reach the point of sinning, then providence is unjust in both respects: both because it does not liberate the one who is dragged to punishment for the sake of justice, and because it would have liberated the one who wanted to do wrong. The latter would have done wrong because he willed it, while providence would have prohibited the deed, thereby unfairly favoring one who still possessed the power to sin. <margin>C</margin> How is he not truly impious and a stranger to God who would rank the devil among the gods, yet dares to call a man possessed of the power to sin "Lord"? 

For the devil is a tempter; he knows what we are, but he does not know if we will endure. Wanting to shake us from the faith, he tries to draw us to himself. This is the only thing permitted to him—and this is so that we might receive the opportunity for salvation through the commandments by our own efforts, and for the shame and ignominy of the one who tempted us but did not succeed. It also serves for the strengthening of those in the church and for the conscience of those who have admired such endurance. If martyrdom is merely a retribution through punishment, then so too are the faith and the teaching through which martyrdom comes. Therefore, these would also be <margin>D</margin> assistants to punishment—and what could be more absurd than that? 

But regarding those doctrines—whether the soul migrates from body to body <note>Referring to "metempsychosis" or reincarnation, a key part of Basilides' system.</note> and concerning the devil—we shall speak at the proper time. For now, let us add this to what has been said: where is faith anymore, if martyrdom is undergone to pay the penalties of prior sins? Where is the love for God, which suffers and sustains persecution for the sake of the truth? Where is the praise for the one who confessed, and the blame for the one who denied? To what end is a virtuous life still useful, or the putting to death of desires, or the refusal to hate any creature? 

If, as Basilides himself says, we think that one part of what is called "God's will" is to love all things because all things contribute a logic and proportion to the universe, and another part is to desire nothing, and a third is to hate nothing—then punishments would also exist by the will of God, which is an impious thought. For the Lord did not suffer by the [active] will of the Father, nor do those who suffer <margin>E</margin> persecution suffer it by the will of God. For one of two things must be true: either persecution is something good and honorable because of God's will, or those who afflict and torment the martyrs are innocent. 

But nothing happens without the will of the Lord of the universe. It remains, therefore, to say briefly that things of this sort happen without God prohibiting them. This alone preserves both providence and the goodness of God. We must not think, then, that He brings about afflictions by His own working (for it is not permitted to think this), but we should be convinced that He does not prohibit those who carry them out, and that He uses the audacious attempts of adversaries for good. "I will destroy the wall," He says, "and it shall be trodden down," <note>Isaiah 5:5.</note> since providence itself is a kind of <term>ars erudiens</term> <note>A "teaching art" or "educational method."</note>; in some cases for the sake of each person's own sins, but in the case of the Lord and the Apostles, for the sake of ours. <margin>F</margin> <margin>Ephesians 4, 1 Thessalonians 4</margin> Indeed, the divine Apostle says: "For THIS is the will of God, your sanctification, that you should abstain from fornication, and that each of you should know how to possess his own vessel in sanctification and honor, not in the passion of lust like the Gentiles who do not know God."

<summary>Clement refutes the Gnostic Basilides' view that martyrdom is a punishment for past sins, arguing instead that suffering is permitted by God (though not willed by Him) as a means of moral training and demonstrating faith.</summary>

# THE MISCELLANIES, BOOK IV
### Page 129

<margin>A</margin> ...know the Lord, and let no one overstep or through greed defraud his brother in business, because the Lord is an avenger of all these things, just as we have also told you before and testified. For God has not called us for impurity but in sanctification. Therefore, whoever rejects this does not reject man, but God, who has given us His Holy Spirit. <note>Clement is quoting 1 Thessalonians 4:6–8 to emphasize that moral conduct is tied to God's direct call to holiness.</note> It was for the sake of this sanctification of ours that the Lord was not prohibited from suffering. But if someone from among them, in response, should say that a **Martyr** is indeed punished for sins that were committed before this migration into the body, but that he will again receive the fruit of the life led here—for such is the established administration—we will ask him whether this reward happens through providence. <margin>B</margin> For if it is not a matter of divine administration, the plan and arrangement of expiation perishes, and the very argument and foundation of their opinion falls away. But if these expiations are from providence, then punishments are also from providence. Now providence, even if it begins to move from the "First Principle," <note>original: "a Principe" — meaning the highest God or the beginning of all things.</note> as it were, is nevertheless mixed into and inherent in substances, since even the substances themselves were made by the God of all. Since things are so, they must necessarily admit either that the punishment is not unjust—meaning those who condemn and persecute the Martyrs act rightly and justly—or that persecutions are carried out by the will of God. It is certainly not the case, then, that labor and fear happen to things as they say, like **rust on iron**, <note>A Gnostic metaphor suggesting that suffering is a natural, mechanical byproduct of material existence rather than a moral trial.</note> but rather they come to the soul by its own will. But concerning these matters, many things are reserved to be said later when we treat these considerations in their proper time.

<margin>C</margin> Now **Valentinus**, <note>Valentinus was a 2nd-century Gnostic teacher who taught that only certain people possess a "divine spark" and are naturally saved.</note> in a certain Homily, writes in these words: "From the beginning you are immortal, and you are children of eternal life, and you wished to distribute death among yourselves so that you might consume it, and that death might die in you and through you. For when you dissolve the world, but you yourselves are not dissolved, you are lords of the creation and of all destruction." For he too, similar to **Basilides**, posits a race that is saved by its very nature, <note>The Gnostic idea that certain people are "spiritual" by nature and cannot lose their salvation, while others are purely "material."</note> and says that this "different race" came down here from above to abolish death, and that the origin of death was the work of him who created the world. For this reason, he interprets that scripture in this way: <margin>Exodus 33</margin> *No one shall see the face of God and live*, <note>original: "Nemo videbit faciem Dei, & viuet"</note> as if the Creator were the author and cause of death. <margin>αἰών</margin> <note>original Greek: "aiōn" — referring to an eternal being or age in Gnostic cosmology.</note> Concerning this God, he hints secretly, writing in these words: <margin>eternal age</margin> "By as much as the image is inferior to the living face, by so much is the world inferior to the living **Aeon**." <note>An "Aeon" is a divine emanation in Gnostic thought; Valentinus is arguing that our physical world is a poor, dead copy of the true divine realm.</note> What then is the cause of the image? The majesty of the face, which provided the pattern to the painter so that it might be honored through his name. <margin>D</margin> For the form was not found from itself or its own authority, but it filled the name which was lacking in breadth. Moreover, the fact that God is invisible aids in the faith of that which has been fashioned. For he [Valentinus] called the **Creator**, insofar as he is called God and Father, the "image" and "prophet" of the true God. And he called the "painter" **Wisdom** <note>original: "sapientiam" (Sophia) — in Gnostic myth, Sophia is the emanation whose error led to the creation of the material world.</note>, whose handiwork is the image, to the glory of him who is invisible. For whatever things proceed from a "pairing" <note>original: "coniugatione" — referring to the Gnostic concept of *syzygies*, or divine male-female pairs.</note> are **pleromata** (that is, "fullnesses"), but whatever comes from one alone are "images." Because, therefore, that which appears is not the whole, the soul that comes from the "half" <margin>E</margin> came into being—namely, that which is "different"—and this is the breathing-in of the different spirit; and in short, that which is inspired into the soul is the image of the spirit. And to speak briefly: what is said about the Creator, who was made according to the image, they say was predicted about the generation of man in the sensible image. Furthermore, they transfer this likeness to themselves, handing down the idea that the "interjection of the different spirit" was unknown to the **Creator**.

Now, when we treat the fact that there is indeed **one God**, who is preached through the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospel, we shall also argue against this; for that is the principal discourse. But we must meet the point that is pressing. If the "different race" came to dissolve death, then **Christ** did not abolish death unless He Himself is said to be of the same essence as them. But if one person abolished it so that the "different race" was not affected, then those who are rivals of the Creator do not abolish death—those who breathe a supernal life into the image of their "half-soul," <margin>F</margin> according to the dogma they have adopted, even if they say this happens through the "Mother" [Sophia]. But even if they say they are warring against death together with Christ, let them confess their secret decree: that they dare to attack the divine power of the Creator, attempting to correct His creation.

But a son would never contend with his father, especially among Gods. However, as to the fact that this Creator of the universe, the Almighty Lord, is the Father of the Son, let us defer that to the discussion in which we promised to speak against heresies, showing that He is the only one who has been <margin>Philippians 1</margin> proclaimed by Him. But if he is sacrificed upon the sacrifice and service of faith, rejoicing and congratulating those to whom the Apostle speaks—the Philippians—calling them partners and sharers in grace, how can he call them "unanimous" <note>original: *vnanimes*</note> and "soulish"? <note>original: *animales* (Latin) / *psychikoi* (Greek). In Gnostic thought, "soulish" or "psychic" people were a middle class of Christians who lacked the higher "spiritual" spark.</note> Similarly, he writes regarding Timothy and himself: "For I have no one," he says, "so like-minded <note>original: *vnanimem*</note> who will sincerely be anxious for you. Indeed, even the Phrygians <note>The Phrygians refers to the Montanists, a prophetic movement that called mainstream Christians "psychic" for rejecting their new revelations.</note> now call those who do not attend to the "New Prophecy" <margin>C</margin> "soulish"; we shall argue against them when we treat the subject of Prophecy. Therefore, he who is perfect must practice love, and from there strive toward divine friendship, carrying out the commandments through love. Now, "to love enemies" does not mean to love evil, nor impiety, nor adultery, nor theft; rather, it means to love the thief, the impious, and the adulterer—not insofar as he sins and defiles the name of "man" by some action, but insofar as he is a human being and the work of God. Certainly, "to sin" is placed among actions, not among substances. <note>Clement argues that evil is a choice/act, not a physical "thing" created by God.</note> For this reason, sin is not a work of God. Sinners are called "enemies of God," being enemies of the commandments which they do not obey, just as those who listen are "friends." The latter are called so because of their union, the former because of an alienation proceeding from the free will of the <margin>D</margin> mind. For enmity and sin are nothing without an enemy and a sinner. And when he teaches "to covet nothing," it is not as if the things desired were alien <note>i.e., belonging to a different, "evil" God.</note>—as those who decree that the Creator is different from the First God have thought—nor as if generation were execrable and evil. For those are impious opinions. We call the things of the world "alien" not because they are absurd, nor because they do not belong to the God who is Lord of all, but because we do not remain in them throughout eternity; they are "alien" in terms of possession (belonging to successors), though in use they are the property of each of us, for whose sake they were made—but only insofar as it is necessary for us to be among them. Therefore, in accordance with natural appetite, one must rightly use those things which are [otherwise] forbidden, taking care not to slip into excess in any way <margin>Luke 6</margin> <margin>Matthew 5</margin> or be affected by them beyond measure. Furthermore, how great is His kindness? "Love your enemies," He says. "Bless those who curse you, and pray for those who treat you with contempt," and similar things. To which He adds: <margin>E</margin> "That you may be like your Father who is in heaven," signifying that assimilation which happens to God. Again, He says: "Be quickly well-disposed toward your adversary, while you are on the way with him." The "adversary," however, is not the body, as some would have it, <note>Some Gnostics taught the body was an enemy to be hated.</note> but the Devil and those who are like him, who walk with us on the way through the men who imitate his deeds in this earthly life. It is impossible, therefore, for those who confess themselves to be of Christ, yet dwell in the works of the Devil, not to suffer the most hostile things. <margin>Matthew 5</margin> <margin>Romans 8</margin> For it is written: "Lest perhaps he deliver you to the Judge." Now, the "Judge" refers to the minister of the Devil’s empire. For I am persuaded that neither death, which those who persecute us bring, nor the life lived here, nor the angels who fell, nor <margin>F</margin> principalities—and the "principality" of Satan is the life he chooses; for such are the principalities and powers of darkness—nor things present, in which we are during the time of this life (like the hope of a soldier or the profit of a merchant), nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, which through man's own...

...to taste knowledge. Wherefore, showing even more clearly the nature of <margin>A</margin> knowledge <note>original: "cognitionis" — refers here to *gnosis*, or deep spiritual insight.</note>, he added:
> Since these things are manifest to us, and we have looked into the depths of divine knowledge, we ought to do all things in order, whatever the Lord has commanded us to perform at their appointed times. Let the wise man, therefore, show his wisdom not in words alone, but in good works. Let the humble man not bear witness to himself, but let him allow testimony to be borne to him by another. He who is pure in the flesh, let him not be boastful, knowing that it is another who grants him his continence. See, brothers: the greater the knowledge we have been deemed worthy of, the greater the danger we undergo.

Therefore, the venerable and pure instruction of our kindness, according to the opinion of Clement <note>Clement of Alexandria is here quoting the Epistle of Clement of Rome to the Corinthians.</note>, seeks that which is commonly useful, whether one bears testimony or teaches by deed and word—and that in a twofold way, both <margin>B</margin> unwritten and written. This is charity <note>original: "charitas" — the Greek *agape*, meaning selfless, divine love.</note>: to love God and one's neighbor. It exalts to a height that cannot be described. Charity covers a multitude of sins. Charity sustains all things; it is patient in all things. Charity glues us to God. It performs all things in concord. In charity all the elect of God are made perfect. Without charity, nothing is pleasing to God. Of its perfection, he says, there is no explanation. Who is fit to be found in it, except those whom God Himself has deemed worthy? Now indeed, the Apostle <margin>1 Cor. 13</margin> Paul says:
> If I deliver my body to be burned, but have not love, I am a resounding brass and a tinkling cymbal.

If I bear witness, he says, not out of a chosen affection through love <margin>C</margin> endowed with knowledge, but perhaps because of fear or the reward that is expected—moving my lips to testimony and confessing the Lord—I am a common man, sounding the Lord's name but not knowing Him. For there is also a people who loves with their lips. There is also another who delivers his body to be burned. "And if I distribute all my goods to feed the poor," he says, not out of the principle of fellowship which proceeds from love, but for the sake of a reward expected either from the recipient of the benefit or from the Lord who promised it; "and if I have all faith, so as to move mountains," and cast away the vices which pour forth darkness, but am not faithful to the Lord because of love; I am nothing—as one who, if compared with him who bears witness to the world out of true knowledge, would be considered of no account. Moreover, all generations from Adam even unto this day have passed away. But those who by God's grace have been perfected in love have a place among the godly, who will be made manifest <margin>D</margin> in the visitation of Christ's kingdom. Love does not allow one to sin. But if, even against his will, one falls into such a case through the suggestion of the adversary, he shall sing, imitating David: <margin>Psalm 68</margin>
> I will confess to the Lord, and it shall please Him more than a young calf that produces horns and hoofs.

<margin>Psalm 116</margin> "Let the poor see and be glad." For He says: <margin>Psalm 80</margin>

<margin>Psalm 50, John 4</margin> For a sacrifice to God is a contrite spirit. Therefore, God is also called Love, since He is good; His love works no evil toward a neighbor, neither doing injury nor returning it, but—to put it simply—doing good to all, after the image of God. <margin>Rom. 13</margin> Therefore, the fullness of the law is love, just as Christ is; that is, the presence of the Lord who loves us, and the doctrine of love and the way of life which is ours from Christ. <margin>E</margin> Love, therefore, perfects the commandment against committing adultery and the commandment against coveting a neighbor's wife, which had previously been prohibited by fear. Therefore, it refers to the same act, whether it is done through fear, or perfected through love, or whether it is practiced through faith or even out of knowledge. Justly, therefore, and accordingly, different things are prepared for their differences: for him who is endowed with knowledge, things are prepared "which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have they entered into the heart of man." <margin>A</margin> ...indeed, those who have written histories record such a judgment of the just Bocchoris <note>original: "Bonchoridis" — referring to Bocchoris, a legendary king and judge of Egypt known for his wisdom.</note>. A young man, seized with love for a harlot, persuaded her for a certain agreed-upon price to come to him the following day. However, when his desire overtook him in his sleep, and his lust was satisfied beyond hope, he barred the entrance to the girl he loved when she came to him as had been arranged. But when she learned what had happened, she demanded the payment, saying that by that means she had satisfied the lover's desire. They went, therefore, to the Judge. He, having ordered the young man to hold out the purse in which the payment was kept in the sun, commanded the harlot to grasp the shadow, cleverly decreeing that he should return a phantom of payment for a phantom of an embrace. And indeed, one dreams with the soul assenting to a vision.

<margin>B</margin> But he truly "dreams" who looks with lust—and not only, as that Gnostic <note>The "Gnostic" in Clement's writing refers to the "true" or "perfected" Christian who possesses deep spiritual knowledge (*gnosis*), rather than the heretical sects usually associated with the name.</note> used to say, if as soon as he sees her, he conceives a relationship with the woman in his mind, for this is already the work of desire, as desire. But if he has looked upon the beauty of the body, the Word says, and the flesh appears beautiful to him out of libido and desire—seeing with a carnal and inclined mind toward sinning—he is condemned because he admired her. On the contrary, he who looks through chaste affection does not judge the flesh, but the soul to be beautiful; he admires the body, in my opinion, as if it were a statue through which he transmits himself to the Craftsman <note>A common Platonic and Christian metaphor: admiring the beauty of a created thing (the "statue") as a way to praise the Creator (the "Artificer" or God).</note>. He shows that which is truly beautiful—a holy sign, a bright character of justice—to the Angels who preside over the ascent. I speak of the "anointing" of a well-composed

<margin>C</margin> and God-pleasing mind: the quality of affection implanted in the soul which exults and triumphs because of the indwelling of the Holy Spirit. This glory, which had shone in the face of Moses, the people were not able to gaze upon; and therefore he took up a veil of glory for those who looked carnally. For those who introduce anything from worldly things are detained by those who exact a tax from those burdened by their own vices and perturbations of the soul. But he who is naked of those things upon which a tax falls, and is full of knowledge and that which comes from the works of justice, they transmit the man with a prayer, pronouncing him blessed along with his work. And "his leaf shall not fall away"—of the tree of life, I say—which is nourished "beside the runnels of waters" <margin>Psalm 1.</margin>. The just man is compared to fruitful trees, not only to those which are carried on high for sacrifices. There were also, in the

<margin>D</margin> offerings of sacrifices under the law, those who considered the defects of the victims. Therefore, those who are beautifully practiced in knowing these matters distinguish "appetite" from "lust." They attribute lust to pleasure and intemperance, but they establish that "appetite" exists in those things which are according to nature, as a movement that arises from reason. Of this perfection, both man and woman can equally be a participant. Now indeed, it was not only Moses who heard from God, "I have spoken to you once and twice," saying:
> I have seen this people, and behold, it is a stiff-necked people. Let me destroy them, and I will blot out their name from under heaven, and I will make you into a great and admirable nation, far greater than this one. <margin>Exodus 32.</margin>
He responds by pleading, not looking to his own benefit, but to the common salvation:
> By no means, Lord; forgive the sin of this people, or else blot me out 

<margin>E</margin> also from the Book of the Living. Such was his perfection that he preferred to die together with his people rather than be saved alone. But there is also Judith, who was perfected among women: when the city was besieged, having prayed with the elders, she entered into the camp of the foreigners, despising every danger for her fatherland and handing herself over to the enemies in faith in God. She soon received the rewards of faith when, as a woman, she bore herself excellently against the enemy of the faith and gained the head of Holophernes. And again, that woman perfected in faith, Esther, liberating Israel from tyrannical power and from the cruelty of the Satrap <note>A regional governor or official in the Persian Empire.</note>; a lone woman, afflicted by fasts, she resisted innumerable armed forces, dissolving the tyrannical decree through faith. She mitigated the tyrant, repressed Haman, and preserved Israel unharmed through perfect prayer to God. I pass over Susanna and the sister of Moses;

<margin>F</margin> for the latter indeed led the army together with the Prophet, the leader of all the women who were distinguished for wisdom among the Hebrews. The former, proceeding even unto death through the highest honor when she was condemned by intemperate lovers, remained a firm and constant witness of modesty. Dion the philosopher certainly records...
