### CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

<margin>A</margin>...a certain woman named Lysidisa, out of her remarkable modesty, was said to have washed herself while still wearing her tunic. Philotera, too, when she was about to enter the bath, would draw her tunic down little by little so that as much of her as was naked was covered by the water, and then again, as she stepped out, she would put it on gradually. Did not the Athenian "Lioness" <note>original: "Leæna Attica"—Leæna was a famous heroine who, according to legend, bit off her tongue so she could not reveal the secrets of the plot against the tyrant Hipparchus under torture.</note> also endure tortures bravely? Although she was aware of the plot being prepared by Harmodius and Aristogiton against Hipparchus, she spoke nothing at all, even though she was cruelly tormented. They say also that the women of Argos, led by the poetess Telesilla, put to flight the Spartans—who were known for great military courage—as soon as they showed themselves, and they made it so that those women feared death not at all. He who wrote the *Danaid* says similar things about the daughters of Danaus.

<margin>B</margin>> And then quickly the daughters of Danaus took up arms,
> On the banks of the beautifully flowing River Nile. ->And what follows.<-

<margin>C</margin>The other poets sing of the speed of Atalanta in the hunt, the extraordinary friendship of Anticlea, the love of Alcestis for her husband, and the great and lofty spirit of Macaria and the daughters of Hyacinthus. Why, did not even Theano the Pythagorean advance so far in philosophy that when someone looked at her inquisitively and remarked, "What a beautiful elbow," she replied, "But not a public one"? Another saying of the same gravity is recorded: for when a woman was later asked how long it took after being with a man to be pure enough to enter the Temple of Demeter <note>original: "Thesmophorium"—a temple or site for the Thesmophoria, a festival honoring Demeter and Persephone restricted to women.</note>, she replied, "From one's own husband, immediately; from a stranger, never." Furthermore, Themisto, the daughter of Zoilus of Lampsacus and wife of Leontieus, devoted herself to Epicurean philosophy, just as Myia, daughter of Theano, followed the Pythagorean way, along with Arignete, who wrote a history of Dionysius. The daughters of Diodorus (who was nicknamed "Saturn" <note>referring to Diodorus Cronus, a famous dialectician of the Megarian school</note>) were all expert in logic, as Philo the Dialectician says in his work *Menexenus*; their names are said to be Menexene, Argia, Theognis, Artemesia, and Pantaclea. I also remember a certain woman of the Cynic school: her name was Hipparchia of Maroneia, the wife of Crates, because of whom the "Cynic Wedding" <note>original: "Cynogamia"—referring to the public, unconventional marriage practices of the Cynic philosophers.</note> was celebrated even in the Painted Stoa. Arete of Cyrene, the daughter of Aristippus, educated her son Aristippus, who was nicknamed <term>taught by his mother</term> <note>original: "μητροδίδακτος" (metro-didaktos).</note>. In Plato's circle, Lasthenia of Arcadia and Axiothea of Phlius also studied philosophy. Even Aspasia of Miletus—about whom the comic poets wrote much—was consulted by Socrates for philosophy and by Pericles for rhetoric.

<margin>D</margin>I pass over others, lest the discourse be too long, and I shall not list the poetesses like Corinna, Telesilla, Myia, and Sappho, nor the painters like Irene daughter of Cratinus and Anaxandra daughter of Nealces (as Didymus says in his *Symposiacs*). Even the daughter of Cleobulus the Wise (the ruler of Lindos) was not ashamed to wash the feet of her father's guests. Indeed, the blessed Sarah, wife of Abraham, herself prepared hearth-baked bread for the Angels, and the young girls among the Hebrews used to tend the sheep. This is why Nausicaa in Homer's poems had gone out to wash the laundry. Therefore, let a modest woman first, if possible, persuade her husband to be her companion in those things which lead to true happiness.

<margin>E</margin>If she cannot achieve this, let her strive for virtue alone, obeying her husband in all things, so that she does nothing against his will—except for those things which are judged to belong to virtue and salvation. But if anyone, without any pretense, should keep a wife or even a maidservant from such a pursuit of virtue, he seems at that moment to be doing nothing else but deciding to lead his household away from justice and self-control, and wishing to make his home both unjust and unrestrained. It is impossible, therefore, for either a man or a woman to be learned in life if they have not used discipline, meditation, and practice. We say that virtue is situated not in some external things, but most especially within ourselves. Thus, a person can prevent other things by waging war; but that which is placed within our own power can by no means be stopped, not even if one insists most strongly. For it is a gift given by God and is not subject to anyone else. Hence, lack of self-control cannot be seen as anyone's evil except the one who behaves unrestrainedly. Conversely, self-control is the good of the one who can restrain themselves.

<margin>F</margin>Euripides describes the woman who loves her husband with honor, advising her thus:

->To follow him with good words.<-

He concludes with advice for wives on pursuing virtue even if their husbands do not share their spiritual goals.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Clement’s discourse on the nature of Christian virtue. Having previously discussed the role of women and the sanctity of marriage, he now transitions into a deep exploration of spiritual perfection, the relationship between the Mosaic Law and the Gospel, and the ultimate witness of martyrdom as a culmination of "Gnosis" or spiritual knowledge.</meta>

# CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

### THE MISCELLANIES, BOOK IV.

<margin>A</margin> In the same way, one is made complete and perfected: as one who is pious and religious, as one who is patient and self-controlled, as a worker, as a martyr, and as one endowed with <term>knowledge <note>original: "cognitione"—Clement uses this term to refer to Gnosis, the deep, experiential understanding of divine truths that goes beyond mere faith.</note></term>. Yet, I am not sure if any person, while still being human, can be perfect in all these things at once, except for the One who, for our sake, put on humanity. Although a person might be considered perfect according to the "naked" Law—meaning one who simply professes to abstain from evil—that is merely the path leading toward the Gospel and toward the doing of good.

Indeed, the perfection of the Law, achieved through knowledge, is the acceptance of the Gospel, so that the one who was perfect under the Law might become even more. For Moses, who represents the Law, predicted that He should be listened to, so that we might receive—according to the Apostle’s mind—Christ as the "fullness of the Law." In the Gospel, the one endowed with knowledge now makes progress, not only using the Law as a stepping stone, but perceiving it and understanding it with the mind, just as the <margin>B</margin> Lord, who gave the testaments, delivered it to the Apostles.

But if he also orders his life rightly (since it is certainly impossible for knowledge to encounter difficulty in doing good) and, moreover, makes a most righteous confession, he may become a martyr—meaning a <term>witness <note>original: "testis"—the Greek word "martys" literally means witness; Clement here connects the act of dying for the faith with the act of testifying to the truth of one's spiritual knowledge.</note></term>. Receiving the greatest dignity and merit possible among men, he still does not arrive at the point of being called "perfect" while in the flesh, because the end of life claims this title. This is because the witness who acts from knowledge has finally reached the point of showing a perfect work; by kindly giving his blood through the love that comes from knowledge, he yields up his spirit. He shall then be blessed from that moment and rightly called perfect, so that the "excellence of the power may be of God, and not from us," as the <margin>2 Cor 4</margin> Apostle says.

Let us only preserve our free choice and love for anyone who is afflicted; we are "troubled on every side, yet not distressed; in need, but not crushed by poverty; <margin>C</margin> persecuted, but not forsaken; cast down, but not destroyed." For it is necessary for those <margin>2 Cor 10</margin> who, according to the Apostle's intent, strive for completion to "give no offense in anything," but in everything to commend themselves not to men, but to God.

Let it also be an added benefit to obey men; for it is consistent to obey them to avoid the insults they might throw. Commendation, however, is found in <margin>1 Cor 6</margin> great endurance: in afflictions, in necessities, in distresses, in beatings, in imprisonments, in riots, in labors, in sleepless nights, in fastings, in chastity, in knowledge, in patience, in kindness, in the Holy Spirit, in unfeigned love, in the word of truth, in the power of God—so that we might be "temples of God cleansed from every defilement of <margin>2 Cor 7</margin> flesh and spirit." "And I," He says, "will receive you: and I will be a Father to you: and you shall be <margin>D</margin> my sons and daughters," says the Lord Almighty. "Let us therefore," he says, "perfect holiness in the fear of God."

For even if fear generates sorrow, "I rejoice," I say, "not that you were made sorrowful, but that you were made sorrowful unto <term>repentance <note>original: "pœnitentiam"—more than just feeling sorry, this implies a total change of mind and direction.</note></term>." For you were made sorrowful according to God’s will, so that you might suffer loss from us in nothing. For the sorrow that is according to God works repentance unto salvation that is not to be regretted. But the sorrow of the world works death. For behold this very thing—that you were made sorrowful according to God—what great diligence it worked in you: what a defense, what indignation, what fear, what longing, what zeal, what vengeance! In every matter, you have shown yourselves to be pure. These are the preliminary exercises for the training that proceeds from knowledge.

Since God Almighty Himself <margin>Ephe 4</margin> <margin>E</margin> gave "some as Apostles, some as Prophets, some as Evangelists, others as pastors and teachers, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ: until we all meet in the unity of the faith and of the recognition of the Son of God, into a perfect man, into the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ."

We must strive to emerge as men of knowledge and to be perfected as much as possible while still remaining in the flesh, through a perfect harmony and agreement here. We should meditate on aligning ourselves with the will of God toward the restoration of that which is truly perfect nobility and kinship, into the fullness of Christ, which is absolutely perfected out of perfection. Now we see by what reasoning and how and when the divine Apostle speaks of the "perfect," and how he shows the differences between those who are perfect. And again, "To each one is given the manifestation <margin>1 Cor 12</margin> <margin>F</margin> of the Spirit for the common good." To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom; to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another faith in the same Spirit; to another the gifts of healing in the same Spirit; to another the working of miracles; to another prophecy.

<summary>Clement explains that spiritual perfection is a journey from the Law to the Gospel, culminating in the "witness" of martyrdom and the attainment of divine Gnosis. He emphasizes that while the gifts of the Spirit vary, the goal is the unity and "fullness of Christ" in the body of the Church.</summary>

# THE MISCELLANIES, BOOK IV

### CHAPTER 16

<margin>A</margin> ...prophecy. To another, the discernment of spirits. To another, various kinds of tongues. To another, the interpretation of tongues. But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each one individually as He wills <note>original: "Omnia autem hæc operatur unus & idem spiritus..."—A direct quotation of 1 Corinthians 12:10-11.</note>. Since things are this way, the Prophets are indeed perfect in prophecy, the just in their justice, and the Martyrs in their confession. Others are perfected in preaching—not being void of common virtues, but conducting themselves rightly in those roles to which they were appointed. For who in their right mind would say a Prophet is not just? Or were not the just, like Abraham, also prophets?

<margin>Homer</margin>
->*For to one man God gave the duties of war as his gift,*<-
->*To another to dance, or to sound with the lyre and song.*<-

<margin>B</margin> So says Homer <note>original: "Ait Homerus"—Clement frequently quotes the Greek poet Homer to show that even the ancients caught glimpses of divine truth.</note>. But each person has his own gift from God: one in this way, another in that. The Apostles, however, were filled in all things. You will find, if you wish, in their deeds and writings, their knowledge, life, preaching, justice, chastity, and prophecy. It must be known that although Paul is more recent in time—as he flourished immediately after the Lord's ascension—his writing nevertheless depends upon the Old Testament, breathing and speaking from that source. For faith in Christ and the knowledge of the Gospel is the explanation and the fulfillment of the Law. Therefore, it was said to the Hebrews:

<margin>Isaiah 7</margin>
*Unless you believe, you will not understand.* <note>original: "Nisi credideritis, non intelligetis"—A common patristic reading of Isaiah 7:9, emphasizing that faith is the prerequisite for spiritual insight.</note> This means: unless you believe in Him who was predicted through the Law and signified by the oracles of the Law, you will not understand the Old Testament, which He himself explained by His own presence. Therefore, the person who is truly understanding and perceptive 

<margin>C</margin> is the one endowed with <term>knowledge <note>original: "cognitione"—Referring to Gnosis, the deep spiritual understanding Clement prizes.</note></term>. His work is not merely abstaining from evil—for that is only the foundation for the greatest progress—nor does he do anything good because of fear. For it is written:

<margin>Psalm 138</margin>
> *Where shall I flee, and where shall I hide from your face? If I ascend to heaven, you are there. If I go to the furthest reaches of the sea, there is your right hand. If I descend into the depths, there is your spirit.*

But neither does he act for the sake of the hope of a promised honor.
<margin>Revelation 22</margin>
For it is said: *Behold the Lord, and His reward is before His face, to render to each according to his works.*
<margin>1 Corinthians 2</margin>
*Things which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have they entered into the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love him.* But the only beneficence that is done for the sake of love, and for the sake of what is honorable itself, is to be sought by the one endowed with knowledge. Now, it was said to the Lord in the person of God: <margin>Psalm 2</margin> ASK of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance.

<margin>D</margin> This is a truly royal petition, which teaches that the salvation of men is to be sought without a price. We are to be the heirs and possess the Lord. On the contrary, to desire the science of God for the sake of some utility—namely, so that this might happen or that might not happen—is not the mark of one endowed with knowledge. For the person in contemplation, knowledge itself is a sufficient cause. Indeed, I would dare to say: it is not because he wishes to be saved that the one who pursues knowledge for the sake of holy divine science chooses it. For understanding is always in motion, and it extends toward that which is eternally active in the intellect. When that eternal intellectual activity becomes the very essence of the one who knows—joined without any intervals of time—that perpetual contemplation remains as a living substance. Therefore, if someone were to propose a choice to the one endowed with knowledge:

<margin>E</margin> whether he would prefer the knowledge of God or eternal salvation (supposing these things could be separated, though they are entirely the same), without any hesitation he would choose the knowledge of God, judging that state—which transcends faith through love into the character of knowledge—to be desirable for its own sake. This, then, is the primary beneficence of the one who is perfect: when it is not done for some use of things pertaining to himself. When he has judged it beautiful and honorable to do what is good, this vehemently stirred impulse conducts itself well in every action—not acting rightly in one thing but not in another, but being established in a habit of doing good. He does not act for the sake of glory, or as the philosophers say, <term>fame <note>original: "εὔκλειαν" (eukleian)—A Greek term for good reputation or illustrious glory.</note></term>, nor for a reward from men or from God; rather, he lives his life in the image and likeness of the Lord. And if by some reason

<margin>F</margin> some contrary thing should occur while he is doing good, he will cast aside any thought of "an eye for an eye" or repaying like for like, without any memory of the injury received; he stands as one who is just and good toward both the just and the unjust. To those who are of this sort, the Lord says: <margin>Matthew 5</margin> *Be like your Father who is perfect.* To such a man the flesh is dead, but he himself alone lives, as...

<summary>Clement describes the "Gnostic" or perfect Christian as one who seeks the knowledge of God for its own sake, rather than for the hope of heaven or fear of punishment. He argues that true spiritual perfection involves a constant state of contemplation and doing good without any selfish motive, mimicking the nature of God.</summary>

<margin>A</margin>
...who has consecrated the tomb <note>The "tomb" refers to the physical body, which the soul inhabits.</note> into a holy temple for the Lord, converting the old soul, which was liable to sins, toward God. Such a man is no longer merely self-controlled, but has reached a state of impassibility <term>impassibility: a state of being "beyond passion" (apatheia), where the soul is no longer disturbed by worldly desires or emotions</term>, so that he may put on the divine image while waiting. If you perform alms, <margin>Matthew 6</margin> He says, let no one know; and if you fast, anoint yourself, so that God alone may know, and no other man. But not even the one who shows mercy should know that he is showing mercy. For in that way, he would be merciful at one time, and not at another. But when he performs a beneficial act out of a settled habit, he will be imitating the nature of the Good. This disposition will be both his nature and his practice. Those who are elevated should not be moved away, but those entering in should reach where they ought. For this is what it means to be "drawn by the Father": to be made worthy to receive the graces of virtue from God, and to run without impediment. And even if some hate the "chosen one," he knows their ignorance, pitying the lack of understanding in their souls. Rightly, then, knowledge itself loves, <margin>B</margin> and it teaches and instructs those who are ignorant to honor every creature of the Almighty God, since it has learned to love God. Such a man will not hold virtue in such a way that it can be lost while awake or in dreams, or by any vision, because the habit never departs from himself, exceeding even the state of being a habit <note>original: "habitū... habitum excedens"—Clement suggests the Gnostic's virtue is so deeply ingrained it becomes his very nature, rather than just a practiced behavior.</note>. Whether this knowledge is called a "habit" or a "disposition," because diverse notions never enter it, the principal part of the soul remains unchangeable; it does not take on any diversity of sights which are the dream-images arising from the day’s movements. For this reason, the Lord also commands us to watch, so that our soul may never be moved by disturbances of the mind even in dreams, but He commands us to keep even the night-time conduct of life pure and immaculate, <margin>C</margin> as if one were working during the day. For this is the "likeness to God," as far as it is possible: to preserve the mind in that state and relation <margin>"Euphrone" (night) is named from "thinking well"</margin> which exists in things that are unchanging; this is the disposition of the mind, as a mind. But a varied disposition arises through an affection toward material things. For this reason, it seems to me they called the night *euphrone* <note>original: "εὐφρόνην"—a Greek word for night, which Clement derives from "eu" (well) and "phronein" (to think).</note>, because the soul, then ceasing from the senses, turns toward itself and is more a participant in prudence. Therefore, the sacred mysteries are also mostly performed at night, signifying the contraction of the soul away from the body that happens at night. Let us not sleep, then, as the others do, but let us watch and be sober. For those who sleep, sleep at night, and those who get drunk, get drunk at night. But since we belong to the day, let us be sober, putting on the breastplate of faith and love, <margin>1 Thessalonians 5</margin> <margin>D</margin> and the helmet of the hope of salvation. Whatever they say about sleep, the same must also be understood concerning death. For both signify a departure of the soul—death more so, and sleep less so—which can also be understood from Heraclitus <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher known for his paradoxical sayings about change and the soul.</note>. "A man in joy touches the light, though dead to himself and extinguished; but while alive he touches the dead when sleeping, his eyes extinguished. While awake he touches the sleeper." For "Blessed are those who have seen the Lord," according to the Apostle's sentiment. "Because it is now time for us to rise from sleep, for now our salvation is nearer than when we believed. The night is far spent, the day is at hand. Let us therefore cast off the works of darkness, and let us put on the armor of light." By "day," he allegorically means the Son and the light; and again, he calls the "commandments" the "armor of light" metaphorically. For this reason they say we must go to sacrifices and prayers cleansed, pure, and <margin>E</margin> bright; and this is done for the sake of a symbol and a sign, namely, to be outwardly adorned and purified. But true purification is to contemplate and feel holy things in the soul. Indeed, there was even an image of baptism which was passed down from Moses to the poets in this way:

> *When she had drawn water, wearing clean garments on her body,*
> *Penelope came to the prayers; but Telemachus,*
> *Having washed his hands in the sea, offered his vows to Minerva.* <note>Clement is quoting the Latin translation of Homer's "Odyssey." He suggests that the Greek rituals of washing before prayer were actually derived from the laws of Moses.</note>

This was the custom of the Jews, so that they were often even dipped while in bed. Well, then, was that other saying also spoken: "Be clean not by a bath, but in your soul." For there is a perfect cleanliness, as I see it, which is of the mind, works, and thoughts; and besides, <margin>F</margin> a sincerity of speech, and finally, a freedom from sin in one's dreams. But a sufficient purgation for a man, in my opinion, is a perfect, firm, and stable repentance—if, when we have condemned ourselves for our preceding actions, we move forward, thereafter understanding...

# THE STROMATA, BOOK IV

<margin>A</margin> ...understanding, and lifting the mind from its immersion, both from those things which delight through the senses and from prior sins. If, therefore, an etymology is to be given for "knowledge," which is called *stasis* <note>original: στάσιν; Clement is connecting the Greek word for knowledge (*episteme*) with the word for standing or stability (*stasis*).</note>, its explanation must be taken from the "standing" and "rest" that it implies, since it settles our mind—which was previously carried about in various directions—firmly upon things. Similarly, an etymology must also be given for "faith"—I mean *pistin* <note>original: πίστιν</note>—as being about the "standing" of our soul, that is, concerning that which is "stability and rest." Furthermore, we desire to know the man who is just always and in all things; one who remains just not because he fears the punishments established by law, nor to avoid the hatred of those with whom he lives or those who prosecute sins, nor because he dreads the danger hanging over him from the crimes and outrages themselves. For he <margin>B</margin> who abstains from doing something unjust because of these things is good not by his own will, but by fear. 

And indeed, Epicurus <note>Epicurus (341–270 BC) was a Greek philosopher who taught that the highest good was pleasure, often defined as the absence of pain or fear.</note> says that the man who is wise according to his opinion might wish to do an injury for the sake of some gain, but he cannot persuade himself that it will remain hidden. Therefore, if he knew it would remain hidden, he would do the injury, according to his opinion. And these are indeed dark dogmas. 

If, however, a man abstains from doing injury because of the hope of receiving a reward from God for his just deeds, even then he is not good by his own will. For just as fear makes the former man just, so a reward makes this one just—or rather, makes him *appear* just. Now, not only do those who follow the "barbaric philosophy" <note>A common term among early Church Fathers to refer to the Judeo-Christian tradition as opposed to the Greek "Hellenic" tradition.</note> know that there is a hope after death—good for the good, but the opposite for the wicked—but so do the Pythagoreans. For they also proclaimed a hope at the <margin>C</margin> end for those who lived as philosophers. Even Socrates says in the *Phaedo* <note>A dialogue by Plato depicting the death of Socrates and his arguments for the immortality of the soul.</note> that good souls depart from here with "good hope," and conversely, when rebuking the wicked, he contrasts them with this, saying they live with "bad hope." Heraclitus also seems to agree with this in what he says regarding men: "There await men when they die things they do not hope for nor expect." 

Divinely, therefore, Paul clearly writes to the Romans: *Affliction produces patience. Patience produces character. Character produces hope. And hope does not put us to shame.* <margin>Rom. 5</margin> Patience exists because of a future hope. But "hope" is also, in a manner of speaking, the return and restoration of hope, which does not put us to shame because it is no longer affected by reproaches and insults. 

The man who obeys the "naked calling" <note>The simple, direct call of God without ulterior motives.</note> insofar as he has been called, tends toward knowledge neither because of fear nor because of pleasures. <margin>D</margin> He does not consider whether any useful gain or external delight follows, but, drawn by the love of Him who is truly the "Lover," and led toward that which ought to be done, he is a pious worshipper of God. Thus, even if he were to receive from God the power to do forbidden things without any punishment, or if it were promised to him that he would receive the blessings of the blessed for doing so—even if he were persuaded that his actions would be hidden from God (which is impossible)—he would never allow his mind to do anything contrary to right reason. This is because he has once and for all chosen that which is truly honorable, which is to be chosen for its own sake, and for that reason is to be sought and loved. 

For we have not been taught that what is good lies in the "feeding of the belly." <margin>1 Cor. 8</margin> That man heard that *food will not commend us*, nor will marriage, nor indeed will abstinence from marriage in ignorance; rather, it is the work born of virtue <margin>E</margin> that is accomplished through knowledge. For even a dog, which is an animal devoid of reason, might be said to be "continent" while it fears the one who holds the stick, and therefore abstains from food. Know then, that when the promise is taken away, and the fear of the one whose threats were intended is removed, and the impending danger is separated, the true purpose is revealed. 

For such people do not properly join or adapt themselves to the nature of the thing itself so as to truly grasp through knowledge that all things created for our use are good—such as marriage, for example, and the procreation of children, if they are undertaken with temperance. They do not realize that it is better to be in the "Good" through that assimilation to God, becoming impassible <note>The state of *apatheia*, or being unswayed by passions.</note> and endowed with virtue. Instead, they abstain from some things and not from others only because of external <margin>F</margin> goods or evils. Furthermore, in their loathing of the things they abstain from, they are seen to accuse both the creature and the Creator; and though they may appear faithful in outward form, they possess a godless judgment. That commandment, *Thou shalt not covet*, does not require the necessity born of fear, which forces one to abstain from what is pleasant...

<summary>Clement discusses the internal motivations for virtue, arguing that the true "Gnostic" acts out of love for God rather than fear of punishment or hope for reward, while using etymology to link faith and knowledge to spiritual stability.</summary>

# CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

<margin>A</margin> ...nor to repress their appetites by the reward which persuades through a promise. Those who obey God for the sake of promises do not choose obedience for the sake of the commandment itself, but for the sake of the promise, being enticed by pleasure. But neither will a simple turning away from sensible things <note>rebus sensilibus: things perceived by the physical senses.</note> necessarily result in a union with those things perceived by the intellect. On the contrary, a union with the things of the intellect is brought about for the one endowed with knowledge <note>original: "cognitione præditus"; Clement is referring to the "Gnostic," his ideal of the perfected Christian scholar.</note> by a natural withdrawal from sensible things. This is the path of one who, through the selection of things that are beautiful, chooses the Good with full understanding; such a person admires the process of creation and sanctifies the Creator, while also sanctifying that state which is an assimilation to God. "But I will free myself," he might say, "from desire. O Lord, let there be a union between me and You." For the dispensation of creation is indeed beautiful, and all things are managed rightly, and nothing happens without a cause. I must be among Your things. O Almighty <margin>B</margin> One, even if I am here on earth, I am with You. I wish to be free from fear so that I may approach You, reflecting on how Your chosen path—which is just—is content with few things, selected from among good things of a similar nature.

The Apostle, teaching us in a most mystical and holy way about that choice which is truly pleasing—not that he rejects other things as if they were evil, but because he judges some things to be better than good ones—signified this by saying: <margin>1 Cor. 7</margin> **WHEREFORE both he who gives his virgin in marriage does well, and he who does not give her in marriage does better,** toward that which is honorable, providing the ability to attend to the Lord without distraction. We know, however, that those things which are prepared with difficulty are not necessary, while those things which are necessary have been made easy to obtain by the kindness of God. For this reason, Democritus <note>Democritus (c. 460–370 BC) was a Greek philosopher known for the atomic theory of the universe.</note> says well that <margin>C</margin> nature and teaching are very similar things. We can provide the reason briefly: nature arranges and composes a human being, and in doing so, it grants him his character. It makes no difference whether this character was an effect of nature or transformed by time and discipline. The Lord provided both: the former through creation, and the latter through the re-creation and renewal that comes from the Covenant. That which leads to what is most essential—that is, the most worthy of choice—is the mind <note>original: "mens"; in Greek context, "nous".</note>, which is the most essential part of all. Thus, truly honorable things seem to be the most pleasant, and they provide of themselves the fruit that men desire, namely, the tranquility of the soul. <margin>Proverbs 1</margin> **But he who listens to me,** He says, **shall rest, trusting in peace, and shall rest without fear of any evil.** Trust in God with all your heart and all your mind. In this way it is possible <margin>D</margin> for the one endowed with knowledge to have already become a "god." <margin>Psalms 82; John 10</margin> **I said, You are gods, and sons of the Most High.** Empedocles <note>Empedocles (c. 494–434 BC) was a Greek philosopher who taught that the soul could achieve divinity.</note> also says that the souls of the wise become gods, writing in this manner:

> Finally, they are prophets, and those who sing hymns in song,
> and physicians among the earthly generations of men.
> From here gods arise, whose honors are the greatest.

And indeed, the human being as a species is formed from the "idea" of the spirit which is innate. For he is not created without form or lacking a figure in the workshop of nature, where the generation of man is mystically perfected, since both the art and the essence are shared. But this particular man, or the individual human, receives his character from the form of the soul implanted by the things he has chosen. By this reasoning, we say that Adam was also <margin>E</margin> perfect, as far as his formation is concerned. For nothing was lacking to him of those things that grant the character of human form and species. But while he was being made, he received perfection and was justified through obedience. This was what "grew into a man"—namely, that which was placed in his own power, or <term>free will</term> <note>original: "liberum arbitrium".</note>. The fact that he chose, and even chose that which was forbidden, is a fault not to be attributed to God. 

For generation is twofold: one of things that are begotten, and the other of things that are made. The virtue of a man of great and brave spirit—since he is, as they say, subject by his essence to the disturbances and movements of the soul—renders him who partakes in it free from fear and invincible. Anger acts as the attendant of the mind in patience, endurance, and similar virtues. Under the category of desire, <margin>F</margin> temperance and salvific prudence are also placed. God, however, is impassible <note>impatibilis: incapable of suffering or being affected by external passion.</note>, free from anger and desire; He is not "fearless" because He overcomes fear, nor does He simply turn away from things that are painful or heavy. Neither is He "temperate" in the sense of ruling over desires, for He is not subject to any heavy...

### MISCELLANIES, BOOK IV.

<margin>A</margin> ...nor can any trouble fall upon the nature of God. For God does not flee from fear, nor does He experience desire, such that He would need to master His cravings. Therefore, that Pythagorean saying—that a man must become "one"—has also been spoken among us in a mystical sense. For the High Priest himself is "one," since God is one through an unchangeable state of being, because He always "runs" toward what is good. <margin><term>God</term><note>original: "Deus," from the Greek θέειν (theein) meaning "to run."</note> Deus, from "to run."</margin> Indeed, the Savior, by removing desire, also removed anger, which is the desire for vengeance. For in short, <term>passibility</term><note>The capacity to suffer or be affected by external emotions and desires.</note> exists through every kind of desire. But the man who is led to a state of <term>impassibility</term><note>original: "impatibilitatem"; a state of being free from passion or suffering, modeled after the divine nature.</note> becomes "God-like" without any stain; he becomes "one." Just as those who are moored in the sea by an anchor pull on the anchor—yet they do not drag the anchor toward themselves, but rather pull themselves toward the anchor—so too those <margin>B</margin> who, through a life proceeding from knowledge, "draw" God to themselves, are unknowingly and without noticing it bringing themselves closer to God. For he who worships God, worships himself <note>In the sense that he cares for the divine spark within his own soul.</note>. Therefore, in a life devoted to contemplation, one takes care of oneself while venerating God, and through sincere purification, contemplates the Holy God in a holy manner. For the virtue of temperance, which stands by, continually considering and contemplating itself, is assimilated to God as much as is possible. Now truly, this is within our power, for we are equally masters of our own choice and its opposite: such as whether to practice philosophy or not, and whether to believe or not to believe. Therefore, because we are equal participants in both of these opposing choices, it is found that what is in our power is indeed possible. Furthermore, the commandments are such that they can be performed or not performed by us, which is why it is only fair that 

<margin>C</margin> praise or blame should follow. And those who are punished for the sins they have committed are punished for those sins alone. For the things that have been done have passed away, nor can what has been done ever be "undone." Therefore, the things done before one comes to faith are dismissed—not as if they never happened, but *as if* they had not happened. However, the teacher Basilides <note>A famous 2nd-century Gnostic teacher in Alexandria whom Clement often debates.</note> does not say all sins are forgiven, but only that involuntary sins and those done through ignorance are dismissed—as if a mere man, and not God, were providing so great a gift! To such a person the Scripture says: <margin>Psalm 49</margin> "O wicked man, did you think that I would be like you?" But even if we are punished for voluntary sins, we are not punished so that they might not have happened, but because they *did* happen. Punishment does not help the one who sinned to make the act "undone," but it serves so that he may not sin any further, and so that no one else falls into similar errors. Thus, the good God chastises for 

<margin>D</margin> these three reasons: first, so that the one being chastised might become better than himself; second, so that those who can be saved might be prepared by being warned through examples; and third, so that the victim of the injustice is not held in contempt or made an easy target for further injury. There are also two methods of correction: one through teaching, and the other through discipline, which we have called "chastising." It should be known, however, that those who fall into sin after the "washing" <note>Referring to Baptism.</note> are the ones who are chastised. For the things done previously were dismissed, but the things done afterward are purged. Of the unbelievers it is said that they are considered "as dust which the wind drives from the face of the earth," and as "a drop that falls from a bucket." <margin>Psalm 1. Isaiah 40.</margin> Blessed is he who possesses the discipline of knowledge, and is driven neither to the harm of fellow citizens nor to unjust actions, but gazes upon the "unaging" <note>original: "senii expertem"; without old age/immortal.</note> order of immortal nature—by what reason, in what way, and in what manner it consists. In those who are 

<margin>E</margin> of this sort, the meditation on shameful deeds never takes root. Rightly then, Plato also says that the one who contemplates the "Ideas" <note>The eternal, perfect forms of things in Platonic philosophy.</note> will live as a "God among men." The Mind is the place of the Ideas, and the Mind is God. He said that the one who contemplates the God who cannot be seen is a "God living among men." Furthermore, in the *Sophist*, Socrates named the guest from Elea (who was a practitioner of dialectic) a "God," <margin>Hesiod.</margin> like those "who are similar to foreign guest-Gods who frequent the cities." For when the soul transcends the realm of "becoming" <note>original: "generationem"; the physical world of change and birth.</note> and exists by itself, dwelling with the "Forms" or "Ideas"—like the "leader of the chorus" in the *Theaetetus*—that person, having become like an Angel, will be with Christ, as one who dwells in contemplation, always considering the will of God. 

<margin>F</margin> In truth, "this man alone is wise; the rest flit about like shadows." For "the dead bury their dead." <margin>Matthew 8.</margin> Wherefore Jeremiah says: "I will fill it with the dead born of the earth, whom my anger has struck." And while God cannot be demonstrated <note>Proven through human logic or scientific observation.</note>, He does not produce "science" <note>original: "scientiam"; here meaning humanly acquired knowledge.</note>; however, the Son is Wisdom, and Knowledge, and Truth, and whatever else is [associated] with these...

He defends the existence of free will and explains that divine punishment is a medicinal tool for correction and the prevention of future sin.</summary>

### CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

...possess a kinship. Furthermore, it possesses demonstration and the power of reasoning. <margin>A</margin> All the powers of the spirit, when they are made into one single thing, contribute to the same end, namely to the Son. However, He is undefined in the conception of each of His powers. Although the Son is not truly "one" as a single unit, nor "many" as if made of parts, He is "one" as all things, from which all things come. For He is the same circle of all powers, which are revolved into one and united. And for this reason, the Word is called the **Alpha and Omega** <note>original: "Alpha & ω." These are the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, symbolizing that Christ is the beginning and the end of all things.</note>, whose end alone is the beginning, and again He ends in that which is the beginning from above, never receiving distance or dimension. For this reason, to believe in Him and through Him is to become unique—that is, to become indivisibly united in Him. Not to believe, however, is to doubt, to be stationary, and to be separated and divided by an interval. Therefore, the Lord says these things: 
<margin>Ezekiel 44</margin>
> every son of a stranger, uncircumcised in heart and uncircumcised in flesh—that is, unclean <margin>B</margin> in both body and spirit—shall not enter into the holy places from among the strangers in the midst of the house of Israel, except for the Levites.

By "strangers," He meant those who refused to believe but chose to remain in unbelief. Therefore, only those who lead a pure life are truly the priests of God. For that reason, when all the tribes were circumcised, those who were anointed as High Priests, Kings, and Prophets were considered more holy. Whence He commands them not even to touch the dead, nor to enter among those who are dying—not because the body is a wicked thing, but because sin and disobedience are carnal and dwell in the body, and are therefore "dead" and to be detested. Thus, the priest is permitted to enter only for a father and mother, a son and a daughter who has died, since these alone are the kin of his flesh and seed, <margin>C</margin> from whom the priest received the immediate and continuous cause of his entry into life. Moreover, these people are purified for seven days, the number of days in which a generation is completed. For on the seventh day, rest is celebrated. On the eighth day, however, he offers an atonement, as it is written in Ezekiel, through which atonement the promise can be received. Now, the perfect purging and cleansing, as I believe, is the propitiatory faith in the Gospel which comes through the Law and the Prophets, and the purity which comes through all obedience, along with the laying aside of worldly things, even to the grateful restoration of the "tabernacle" <note>The human body or soul's earthly dwelling.</note> from the soul's pleasant use. Whether it be the time which, through the seven periods that are numbered, returns to the total rest; or the seven heavens which some number by ascent; or even the "unwandering region" <note>The sphere of the fixed stars in ancient cosmology.</note> which approaches the world perceived by the intellect, called the **Eighth** <margin>D</margin> <note>The "Octave" or "Ogdoad," a term used in early Christian and Gnostic thought to describe the spiritual realm beyond the seven planetary spheres.</note>, he nevertheless says it is necessary for the man endowed with **knowledge** <term>Gnosis</term> to emerge from generation and from sin. Thus, for seven days they sacrifice victims for sins. For the caution of change still touches the seventh circuit.

<margin>Job 1</margin>
But the righteous Job says: 
> Naked I came out of my mother’s womb, and naked I shall return there. 

He does not mean naked of possessions—for that is a small and common thing—but as a righteous man he departs naked of vice and sin, and of the formless image that follows those who have lived unjustly. For this was what was said:
<margin>Matthew 18</margin>
> Unless you are converted and become like little children...

...pure in the flesh and holy in the soul through abstinence from evil works, showing that He wants us to be such as He <margin>E</margin> brought forth from the womb of water. For generation, following upon generation, wants to render us immortal through progress. But "the lamp of the wicked shall be extinguished." Furthermore, the most wise Moses, using a beautiful **epanalepsis** <note>A rhetorical device involving the repetition of a word or phrase.</note> or repetition, signified the chastity in body and soul which is pursued by the man endowed with knowledge, describing the incorruption of body and soul in **Rebecca** in this way: 
<margin>Genesis 24</margin>
> Now the virgin was beautiful, and no man had known her. 

Now, "Rebecca" is interpreted as the **Glory of God**. And the glory of God is incorruption. This is what truly constitutes justice: to refuse to have more of another's thing than is right, but to be entirely a sanctified temple of the Lord. Therefore, justice is the peace of life, stability, and tranquility, to which the Lord sent us, saying: "Go in peace." For "Salem" is interpreted as **Peace**, of which our Savior is described as King; whom Moses calls <margin>F</margin> **Melchizedek** <note>A mysterious priest-king from the Book of Genesis, regarded by early Christians as a prefiguration of Christ.</note>, King of Salem, Priest of the Most High God, who gave sanctified wine and bread as nourishment, as a type of the **Eucharist**. Furthermore, "Melchizedek" is interpreted as "Righteous King." Now, justice and peace are synonymous. However, **Basilides** <note>A famous Gnostic teacher in Alexandria (2nd century AD) whose views Clement often contrasts with his own "true" Christian Gnosticism.</note>, who fell away, believes that Justice and her daughter Peace remain stationed in the **Eighth** sphere. # STROMATA BOOK IV.

<margin>A</margin>
The second step, however, is from the more natural things to moral things, which are clearer. For the discussion regarding those [natural] matters will follow after the current treatment at hand. Truly, therefore, our Savior initiates us into mysteries, in a manner consistent with what tragedy says:
> Seeing those who see, he himself grants the Mysteries. <note>original: "Orgia" - Clement is quoting Euripides' *Bacchae*. In this context, "Orgia" refers to secret religious rites or sacred mysteries, which Clement applies to Christian teaching.</note>

But if you should ask what kind of form these mysteries have for you, you will hear in return:
> It is not permitted for those not celebrating the rites to know the secrets.

But if someone should again curiously inquire what sort of things they are, let him hear once more:
> It is forbidden for you to know, but it is worth knowing.
> To the impious, the mysteries of God are hostile.

<margin>B</margin>
God is without beginning, the perfect and completely absolute principle of the universe, the efficient cause of the principle. Insofar as He is essence, He is the principle of the efficient place; insofar as He is good, the moral principle; and insofar as He is mind, the principle of the reasoning and judging place. Hence, He alone is the teacher, who is the only [Son] of the highest pure Father, who instructs man. Therefore, they do not act rightly who hunt after a fiction and revile the body, not considering that the upright constitution of the body was made for the purpose of contemplating heaven. They fail to see that the function of the sensory organs tends toward knowledge, and the limbs and parts are aptly composed for honor, not for pleasure. Hence, this dwelling place receives the soul, which is most precious to God; and the body is deemed worthy of the Holy Spirit through the sanctification of soul and body, so that it might be perfected by the perfection of the Savior. Furthermore, a mutual consequence of the three virtues is found in the man endowed with knowledge <note>The "Gnostic" or Christian intellectual</note>, who concerns himself with God morally, naturally, and logically. For Wisdom is the science of divine and human things. Justice is the harmony of the parts of the soul. Holiness is the worship of God.

<margin>C</margin>
If anyone should say they accuse the flesh and procreation itself, citing Isaiah who says: <margin>Isaiah 40</margin> *All flesh is grass, and all the glory of man is like the flower of the grass. The grass is withered, and the flower has fallen. But the word of the Lord remains forever*: let him hear the Spirit interpreting through Jeremiah what is sought: *And I scattered them like straw which, driven by the wind, flies in the wilderness. This is the lot and portion of your unbelief, says the Lord.*

<margin>D</margin>
*Just as you have forgotten me, and hoped in false things, I too will reveal your back parts over your face, and your shame will be seen, and your adultery, and your neighing,* and what follows. For this is "the flower of the grass," and "to walk according to the flesh," and to be "fleshy" according to the Apostle’s <note>Referring to St. Paul</note> opinion—namely, those who are in sins. That the soul is the more excellent part of man is beyond controversy, while the body is the inferior part. But neither is the soul good by nature, nor again is the body evil by nature. Nor indeed is that which is not good immediately evil. For there are certain things that occupy a middle place, and among these middle things, some are preferred and some are rejected. It was necessary, therefore, for the composition of man, which exists among sensible things, to consist of diverse but not contrary elements: body and soul.

<margin>E</margin>
<margin>Preferred and not preferred are Stoic terms. Concerning which Cicero writes in the third book of *On Ends*.</margin>
Therefore, good actions, as the better ones, are always attributed to that which is more excellent, namely the governing spirit; but pleasurable and sinful actions are attributed to that which is inferior—yet not to a sinning spirit. Now indeed, the soul of the wise man, and of him who is endowed with knowledge, as one traveling in the body, uses it severely and austerely. He shows no excessive affection or indulgence toward it, as one who is about to leave the tent immediately if the time for departing and migrating calls. *I am a stranger,* he says, *on the earth, and I am a pilgrim with you.* From this, Basilides <note>A famous early Christian teacher in Alexandria who was later considered a heretic for his dualist views.</note> says the "external choice of the world" received the soul, as being supramundane by nature. But this is not so. For all things belong to the one God, and no one would be by nature a stranger to the world, since there is one essence and one God. But the chosen one lives his life as a guest, knowing all things which are to be acquired and which are to be rejected:

<margin>F</margin>
and whatever "triple goods" <note>An Aristotelian/Peripatetic concept referring to goods of the soul, goods of the body, and external goods.</note> the Peripatetics advocate, he uses them. He even uses the body, just like someone traveling far abroad uses the inns and lodgings that occur to him on the way; he takes care indeed of the worldly things of the place in which he stays, but leaves the habitation and possession, as well as the use, moved by no affection: ready and

### CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

...following Him with an eager spirit, who leads one away from this life: never turning back on any occasion, giving thanks for his temporary stay, but blessing God for his departure, and embracing the heavenly dwelling. <margin>A</margin> <margin>2 Cor. 5</margin> FOR WE KNOW that if our earthly house of this tent is dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. For in this we groan, desiring to be clothed over with our habitation which is from heaven, if indeed, being clothed, we shall not be found naked. For we walk by faith, not by sight, as the Apostle says. We prefer, rather, to be pilgrims away from the body and to be at home with God. This "preferring" <note>original: "Magis autem est in comparatione" — Clement is performing a grammatical analysis on the Latin/Greek comparative "rather/more," arguing that it implies a choice between two similar states of being.</note> is a matter of comparison. Now, comparison exists between things that fall into a similar category, as the "stronger" is stronger than the strong, and the "strongest" is the most so among the strong. Whence he added: "Wherefore we strive, whether as pilgrims or at home with Him, to be pleasing to Him"—namely, to the one God, whose work and creation are all things: the world, and the things above the world. <margin>B</margin> I admire Epicharmus <note>A Greek comic playwright and Pythagorean philosopher known for his philosophical maxims.</note> who says clearly: "If you have been pious in mind, you shall suffer no evil in death. The spirit remains above in heaven." I also admire the lyric poet who sings: "But the souls of the impious fly beneath the heaven in bloody pains, under the inevitable yokes of evils; but the souls of the pious dwell in the heavens, singing of the Great One in blessed hymns." Therefore, the soul is not sent down from the heavens to these inferior things. For God makes all things toward that which is better; rather, the soul which chooses the best life from God and justice, exchanges the earth for heaven. Justly, therefore, <margin>Job 42</margin> Job, who arrived at knowledge, says: <margin>C</margin> "I know that You can do all things, and there is nothing that You cannot do. For who announces to me things I did not know, great and wonderful things I did not understand? I have held myself in low esteem, considering myself to be earth and ashes." For he who is in ignorance is subject to sin, and is "earth and ashes." But he who stands in knowledge, having been assimilated to God as much as possible, is already spiritual and therefore chosen. That the Scripture calls the foolish and disobedient "earth" will be made plain by the Prophet Jeremiah regarding Jehoiakim and his brothers, saying: <margin>Jer. 22</margin> "Earth, earth, hear the word of the Lord, write this man down as a rejected man." And again, another Prophet says: <margin>Isa. 1</margin> "Hear, O heaven, and listen, O earth," calling "hearing" the intelligence, and the "heaven" the soul of the one endowed with knowledge <note>The "Gnostic" or spiritual seeker who possesses true understanding of God.</note> who has undertaken the contemplation of heaven and divine things, and by that reason has become an "Israelite." Conversely, he called the one who had chosen ignorance and hardness of heart "earth." And that phrase "Listen" he invoked from the ears, which are the instruments of hearing, attributing carnal things to those who attend to sensible things. <margin>D</margin> These are those of whom the Prophet Micah says: <margin>Micah 3</margin> "Hear, O people, the word of the Lord, you who dwell together with sorrows." And Abraham says: <margin>Gen. 18</margin> "By no means," said the Lord who judges the earth. <margin>John 3</margin> For he who has not believed in the saving voice has already been judged. Moreover, it is written in the books of Kings also regarding the judgment and sentence of the Lord, which holds thus: God hears the righteous, but he does not save the impious, because they do not wish to know God. For the Almighty will not do absurd things. What do the heresies <note>Clement is likely refuting Gnostic sects like the Marcionites or Valentinians who claimed the Creator God of the Old Testament was cruel or different from the Father of Christ.</note> still say to this voice, when Scripture proclaims the Almighty God to be good, and in no way the author of vice and injustice? Indeed, ignorance arises because one does not know; but God does nothing absurd. <margin>E</margin> "For this," he says, "is our God, and there is none besides Him who saves." <margin>Isa. 45</margin> For there is no injustice with God, according to the opinion of the Apostle. <margin>Rom. 9</margin> Furthermore, the Prophet clearly teaches God's counsel and the progress of knowledge through these words: <margin>Deut. 10</margin> "And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you, except that you fear the Lord your God, and walk in all His ways?" That you should both love Him and serve Him alone is asked of you who have the power of choosing salvation. What, then, do the Pythagoreans mean when they command one to pray aloud? It was not, as it seems to me, because they thought God could not hear those who speak silently, but because they wished prayers to be just, such as one would not be afraid to pour out with many people knowing them. We, however, shall treat the matter of petition in its proper time as the discourse proceeds. <margin>F</margin> But we ought to have works that cry out, as if walking in the day. <margin>Rom. 13</margin> "For let your works shine." <margin>Matt. 5</margin> And "behold the man and his works before his face." For "behold God and His works." It is necessary to imitate God,

<margin>B</margin>
For the Stoics <note>A school of Hellenistic philosophy that taught virtue as the highest good and the universe as a rational, governed city.</note> also say that heaven is truly the city, while the things here on earth are not actually cities; for they are called such, but are not. For a city is a good thing, and a "people" is an honorable assembly—a multitude of men governed by law, just as the Church is governed by the Word. This is a city that cannot be besieged or oppressed by tyranny. On earth as it is in heaven, the divine will is done. The Poets also establish images of this city in their writings. For the Hyperborean and Arimaspian cities, and the Elysian Fields <note>Mythological locations in Greek literature representing utopias or the afterlife of the blessed.</note>, are the established states and "cities of the righteous." Moreover, we know that Plato’s *Republic* is also set in heaven as a model.

# CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA,

## THE MISCELLANIES, BOOK

### THE FIFTH.

<margin>E</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'D' depicting a figure in a landscape with buildings in the background, set within a classical architectural frame.</image-desc>
Regarding the one who is endowed with spiritual knowledge, we have pursued these matters in a somewhat hurried fashion; now let us proceed to the things that follow. Indeed, the nature of faith must be considered once again. For there are those who distinguish between the two, saying that our faith concerns the Son, but spiritual knowledge concerns the Spirit. However, they have not noticed that one must truly believe in the Son—that He is the Son, that He came, and how, and for what reason, and concerning His passion—but it is also necessary to know who the Son of God is. For truly, there is neither knowledge without faith, nor faith without knowledge. Nor is the Father without the Son; for at the same time as He is "Father," He is the Father of the Son. Furthermore, the true Son is the teacher sent from the Father. And that one may believe in the Son, it is necessary to know the Father, to whom the Son is also referred. And again, that we may first know the Father, it is necessary to believe in the Son, since it is the Son of God who teaches. For from faith we come to knowledge of the Father through the Son. But the knowledge of the Son and the Father, which is

<margin>F</margin>
according to the <term>rule of knowing</term><note>Latin: "cognoscendi regula." Clement refers to the "Rule of Faith" or "Canon of Truth," a standard of orthodox Christian teaching.</note>—which is truly the rule of knowledge—is the pursuit and treatment of truth through the truth itself. We, therefore, are those who are faithful in that which is not believed [by others], and who are endowed with knowledge in that which is not known—that is, in that which is ignored and not believed by everyone else; yet we are endowed with knowledge in that...

<meta>This page marks the beginning of Book V of the Stromata (Miscellanies). Clement transitions from the moral qualities of the "Christian Gnostic" discussed in Book IV to a deeper exploration of the nature of faith, specifically distinguishing between the basic faith of all Christians and the advanced, intellectual faith of the spiritually mature.</meta>

# CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

<margin>A</margin>
...it is believed and known by few. But those <term>endowed with knowledge</term><note>Latin: "cognitione præditi." Clement uses this to describe the "Christian Gnostic," one who has moved beyond simple belief to a deep, contemplative understanding of divine truth.</note> do not describe their works through speech, but through contemplation itself. "Blessed is he who speaks into the ears of those who hear." Now, faith is the "ears" of the soul. The Lord silently hinted at this faith when He said:

<margin>Luke 8</margin>
->HE who has ears to hear, let him hear<-

so that when one has believed, he may understand what is said, in the way it is said. Furthermore, even **Homer**, the most ancient of poets, uses the specific word "hear" to mean the general concept of "perceive" when he writes: <note>original: "Cum audibant maximè & ipsi"</note> "When they themselves also heard most clearly." For in short, the harmony and agreement of the faith of both [the speaker and the listener] revolves around a single end: namely, salvation.

<margin>Rom. 1</margin>
The Apostle [Paul] is a true witness for us, saying:
> FOR I long to see you, that I may impart to you some spiritual gift, so that you may be established; that is, that I may be comforted together with you by the mutual faith both of you and me.

And again, a little further down, he adds:
<margin>B</margin>
> FOR the righteousness of God is revealed in it from faith to faith.

It seems, then, that the Apostle announces a double faith—or rather, one faith that undergoes growth and perfection. For "common faith" is laid down as a foundation. To those who certainly desired to be healed, as those who were faithfully moved, He said: "Your faith has saved you." But the faith which is built up exceptionally is completed in the believer, and is further perfected through that which comes from <term>doctrine</term><note>Latin: "doctrina." Here, Clement means systematic instruction or the deep study of scripture.</note> and the practice of performing the commandments. Such were the **Apostles**, of whom it is said that faith could move mountains and transplant trees. Thus, when they felt the greatness of this power, they asked that faith be added to them—a faith which, like a **mustard seed**, would "bite" the soul usefully and grow in it so much that the rational explanations of sublime things might find rest within it.

<margin>C</margin>
For if, as **Basilides** <note>A teacher in Alexandria (2nd century AD) who taught a form of Gnosticism that Clement argues against. Basilides believed salvation was determined by one's inherent "nature" rather than choice.</note> thinks, God made "intelligence" as a natural trait, calling it both exceptional faith and a "kingdom," and interpreting this essence as being close to the Creator (though not by power, but by essence and nature)... and if he says that faith is not the rational assent of a soul using **free will**, then the commandments in both the Old and New Testaments are superfluous. If one is saved by nature, as **Valentinus** <note>Another influential Gnostic teacher who held that humans were divided into different "natures" (spiritual, soulish, or material) at birth.</note> wants, or is "faithful and chosen by nature" as **Basilides** thinks, then it would follow that nature could eventually shine forth even without the coming of a Savior. But if they say the coming of the Lord was necessary, then their theories of "natural properties" vanish, since the "chosen" are saved by teaching, purification, and the performance of good works—not by their inherent nature.

<margin>Gen. 13</margin>
<margin>D</margin>
Take **Abraham**, for instance, who believed the voice he heard under the oak tree at Mamre, which promised: "I give this land to you and your offspring." Was he "chosen" [by nature] or not? If he was not, how did he believe immediately as if it were natural to him? But if he *was* chosen, then the heretics' foundation is destroyed, since we find a "chosen one" being saved before the coming of the Lord.

<margin>Gen. 15</margin>
For "it was credited to him as righteousness." If anyone dares to say, following **Marcion** <note>A controversial leader who taught that the God of the Old Testament was a different, lesser deity than the God revealed by Jesus.</note>, that the Creator saves those who believed in Him even before the Lord’s coming, then the power of the "Good God" [of the Marcionites] is praised more than is fitting. This would imply that the "Good God" only later attempts to give salvation through teaching or imitation, following the Creator's lead. But even if this "Good God" gives salvation in such a way, according to their opinion, he is giving salvation to those who are not his own, against the will of the one who created them—doing so by force or by fraud.

<margin>E</margin>
And how can one be "good" who acts in this way and comes after [the Creator]? Furthermore, even if the dwelling place of the Almighty is remote from the dwelling of this "Good God," the will of the one who gives salvation is not remote from the good, since he began the work first. From these points, it is shown that those who are "strangers" to the faithful are foolish:
> FOR their paths are perverse, and they do not know peace,

says the Prophet.

<margin>2 Tim. 2</margin>
The divine Paul advised us to avoid foolish and unlearned questions, because they generate strife; and **Aeschylus** <note>A famous Greek tragic playwright.</note> cries out:
> Do not labor in vain over things that do no good.

<margin>F</margin>
For we know that the best kind of inquiry is that which agrees with faith—that which builds upon the foundation of faith to reach the splendid and magnificent <term>knowledge of truth</term><note>Latin: "veritatis cognitionem," referring to the Greek "gnosis."</note>. However, we also know that we do not seek things that are already obvious (for example, "Is it daytime?" when it is clearly day). Nor do we seek things that are uncertain and will never be made clear (such as whether the number of stars is even or odd). Nor indeed those things which are...

<summary>Clement argues that faith is not a fixed natural trait as the Gnostics (Basilides and Valentinus) claim, but a growing capacity that begins as a foundation and is perfected through teaching and free will. He uses the examples of Abraham and the Apostle Paul to prove that salvation is based on belief and action rather than inherent essence.</summary>

### THE MISCELLANIES, BOOK V

<margin>A</margin>
Furthermore, arguments are refuted even by those who oppose them in discussion, depending on how they are stated—for instance, the question: **"Is the fetus in the womb a living creature, or is it not?"** The fourth method of inquiry arises when an argument is produced from one side or the other against which nothing can be said, and which cannot be untied. If, therefore, the reason for questioning is removed by every means, faith is strengthened and established. Thus, we bring forward that against which nothing can be said: that it is **God** who speaks, and He brings forth in the Scriptures a tradition concerning each of the things I seek to know. Who, then, is so impious and alienated from God as to not believe God, and to demand proofs from God as if He were a man? Again, regarding questions, some require the senses—such as if one were to ask whether fire is hot or snow is white.

<margin>B</margin>
Others, however, require a reminder or a rebuke, as **Aristotle** says, such as the question: **"Ought one to honor their parents?"** There are even some questions worthy of punishment, such as seeking proofs for whether there is a **Providence** <note>Divine Providence refers to God's intervention and guidance in the universe.</note>. Since Providence exists, it is wicked to think that prophecy, and the <term>Economy</term><note>Latin: "oeconomiam." Here referring to the "Divine Economy," the plan of God for the salvation of humanity through Christ.</note> and divine dispensation regarding the Savior, were not also produced by Providence. And perhaps one ought not even try to prove these things, since divine Providence is manifest from the sight of all the visible effects which are established by art and wisdom—some of which occur in order, while others are manifested in order. He who imparted to us being and life also gave us <term>Word</term><note>Latin: "verbum" or "rationem," translating the Greek "Logos." It refers to both speech and the underlying rational principle of the universe.</note>, desiring that we live well and in accordance with reason. For the Word of the Father of all things is not this spoken word, but

<margin>C</margin>
Wisdom and the most manifest goodness of God, and again, an almighty and truly divine power, which is not such that it cannot be understood even by those who do not confess it—a will which contains all things by its omnipotence. However, because some are unfaithful and others are contentious, not all achieve the perfection of the good. For it is not possible for us to attain it without the free choice and purpose of our own soul; nor is the whole of what is to happen placed solely in our will. **For we are saved by grace, but not without good works**; but it is necessary that one who is naturally fit for the good should apply some zeal toward it. It is also necessary to have a healthy mind, one that is not slowed down by any regret in the "hunting" of the good; for this we have the greatest need of divine grace, right doctrine, a chaste and pure disposition of the soul, and the attraction of the Father toward Himself.

<margin>D</margin>
For being bound to an earthly body, we apprehend sensible things through the body, but those things perceived by intelligence are grasped through the power of reason itself. If anyone expects to comprehend all things through the senses, he has fallen far from the truth. The Apostle [Paul] certainly writes spiritually concerning the knowledge of God:

<margin>1 Cor. 13</margin>
> <term>WE SEE</term> <note>Latin: "VIDEMVS."</note> now as if through a mirror, but then face to face.

For the spectacle of truth is given to few. Thus **Plato** also says in the *Epinomis*: "I do not say it is possible for all men to be blessed and happy, except for a few. As long as I live, I define it thus. But there is a good hope that after I have departed, I shall attain all things." The words spoken by **Moses** mean the same thing: **"No one shall see my face and live."** For it is clear that no one

<margin>E</margin>
can ever clearly comprehend God during the time of this life. But those who are pure in heart will see God after they have arrived at the final perfection. For since the soul was too weak to comprehend those things that are, and we stood in need of a divine Teacher, the Savior is sent down—the teacher and supplier of the possession of the good, the secret of great Providence, and a holy sign and indicator. **Where, then, is the scribe? Where is the inquirer of this age?** Has not God made foolish the wisdom of this world? And again: **I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the understanding of the intelligent I will reject**—namely, of those who seem to themselves to be wise and are contentious.

<margin>Jeremiah 6</margin>
Thus **Jeremiah** says most beautifully:
> <term>THUS says the Lord</term><note>Latin: "HAEC dicit Dominus."</note>: Stand in the ways, and ask for the eternal paths, which way is the good way, and walk in it, and you shall find atonement for your souls.

<margin>F</margin>
Ask, he says, and hear from those who know, without contention and strife. When we have learned the way of truth, let us enter it directly, by no means turning ourselves back, until we have attained that which is desired. Rightly, therefore, a certain King of the Romans, **Numa** was his name, since he was a Py... <note>The text cuts off, likely referring to Numa Pompilius being a follower of Pythagoras.</note>
