[Numa the Py]thagorean <note>original: "thagoreus." This refers to Numa Pompilius, the second king of Rome, whom ancient authors often mistakenly called a student of Pythagoras.</note>, first of all men, established a temple to Faith and Peace. <margin>A</margin> Regarding **Abraham**, it was written that he believed, and it was credited to him as righteousness. When he pursued the "High Philosophy" <note>Clement uses this term to describe the study of the heavens and atmospheric phenomena.</note> concerning things happening in the air and moving in the heavens, he was called **Abram**, which is interpreted as "High Father." Later, however, when he looked up into heaven—whether seeing the Son in spirit, as some explain, or a glorious Angel, or perhaps knowing God through a being superior to the rest of creation—he assumed the letter *alpha* <note>The letter 'A' added to his name.</note>, signifying the knowledge of the one and only God. He was then called **Abraham**, becoming a wise and pious friend of God instead of a mere investigator of nature. For this name is interpreted as the "father of a chosen sound." The Word <note>The Logos.</note>, after all, is what produces the sound. The "father" of this sound is the mind, and the mind of one endowed with virtue is a "chosen mind." It also occurs to me to praise the Agrigentine Poet <note>Empedocles of Agrigentum (c. 494–434 BC).</note>, who celebrates faith with these praises: <margin>B</margin>

> O friends, I know that truth resides within the words
> Which I speak; but the task is hard and very difficult,
> For the impulse of faith enters the minds of men with great toil.

<margin>1 Corinthians 2</margin>
For this reason, the Apostle also exhorts us that our faith should not rest in the wisdom of men who claim to be persuasive, but in the power of God, which alone—and without the need for formal proofs—can grant salvation through faith alone. For He knows how to save those who are most proven. Furthermore, "Justice will overtake the architects and witnesses of lies," says the Ephesian <note>Heraclitus of Ephesus (c. 535–475 BC).</note>. For he too knew, having learned from "barbarian" <note>A common term used by Greeks for non-Greeks, here referring to Hebrew or Oriental philosophy.</note> philosophy, of the purification by fire of those who have lived wickedly. This is what the Stoics later called <term>ekpyrōsin</term> <note>original: ἐκπύρωσιν. A Greek term meaning "conflagration" or "universal burning." The Stoics believed the universe was periodically consumed by fire and reborn.</note>, which is a burning-out or inflammation. <margin>C</margin> By this reasoning, they even maintain that a person possessing a specific quality will rise again, thus defending the doctrine of the **Resurrection**. **Plato** also says that at certain times the earth is purified by fire and water, speaking in this way: "There have been many destructions of men, and there will be more; the greatest by fire and water, and others lesser by countless other causes." And shortly after he adds: "In truth, there is a shifting of the things that travel through the heavens and around the earth, and at long intervals of time, a destruction of things on earth occurs by much fire." Then he adds concerning the flood: "But when the gods, purifying the earth with water, inundate it, the ox-herds and shepherds in the mountains are preserved, while those in the cities among us are carried into the sea by the rivers." We showed in the first book of the *Stromata* <margin>D</margin> that the Greek philosophers are called "thieves" because they ungratefully took their primary doctrines from **Moses** and the **Prophets**. To this we will add that those Angels who were allotted the upper realms, having fallen into pleasures, revealed secrets to women. Whatever knowledge they possessed was disclosed, while other Angels concealed these things, or rather, reserved them until the coming of the Lord. From that source flowed the doctrine of providence and the revelation of sublime things. Since prophecy had already been handed down to the Greeks, the treatment of these doctrines was taken up by the Philosophers; in some places they guessed the truth correctly, but in others they were false and went astray because they did not understand the hidden nature of prophetic allegory. Only a few people are moved to notice these urgent matters as they pursue them. Therefore, we say that faith must be shown not as something idle or solitary, but as something coupled with inquiry. <margin>E</margin> I do not say that one should not seek at all. <margin>Luke 11</margin> For He said: "Seek, and you shall find."

->*Regarding that which is sought:*<-

> What is sought can be caught, but what is neglected escapes. <note>As Sophocles says.</note>

**Menander** the comic poet says similar things. The wisest men say that whatever is sought requires zeal and care; one must direct the perceptive faculty of the soul toward discovery, clearing away everything that causes an impediment—casting out contention, envy, and that most destructive strife itself. For **Timon of Phlius** writes most beautifully: <margin>F</margin>

> Strife, the ruin of men, comes sounding a hollow note,
> Whose sister and companion is Contention, the maker of slaughter.

Concerning false and negative speech—the "horned" argument, the "hidden" one, the "crocodile," the "sorites" <note>term: Sorites (The Heap). A paradox regarding how many grains of sand make a "heap."</note> as well, and the "unveiled" argument—and concerning ambiguities and sophisms <note>term: Sophism. A clever but false argument used to deceive.</note>: to seek after God is healthy, provided it leads not to strife, but to discovery. For it is written in David: *The poor shall eat and be satisfied, and they who seek the Lord shall praise Him; their hearts shall live forever and ever.* For those who seek with a true inquiry, praising the Lord, shall be filled with the gift that comes from God—that is, with knowledge—and their soul shall live. For by allegory, the soul is called the "heart," which provides life, since the Father is known through the Son.

But we must not give our ears to everyone who speaks or writes shamelessly and rashly. For cups that are handled by many people are picked up by the "ears" <note>original: "ansas aures." In the same way, those who defile the pure hearing of faith with much nonsense eventually become deaf to the truth, become useless, and fall to the ground.

<margin>C</margin>
Therefore, it is not without reason that we instruct children, taking them by the ears, to kiss those who belong to them; this silently signifies that the sense of love is generated through hearing. For "God is love," and He can be known by those who love, just as God is "faithful" and is handed over to the faithful through instruction. It is necessary for us to become joined and familiar with Him through divine love, so that "like may contemplate like," hearing the word of truth purely and without deceit, like children who obey us. This was what was silently signified by whoever it was that inscribed this at the entrance of the temple in Epidaurus:

<margin>Entering.</margin>
> He who enters the threshold of the holy temple must be pure.

<margin>D</margin>
<margin>Matthew 18.</margin>
Purity, moreover, consists in thinking holy thoughts. "For unless," He says, "you become as these little children, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven." For here, the temple of God is seen to be founded on three foundations: faith, hope, and charity <note>or "love."</note>. Regarding faith, we have provided sufficient testimony from the Greek writings. Lest our progress be too long-winded by trying to collect everything about hope and love, it will suffice to say only this: that Socrates in the *Crito*, preferring to live and die well over mere life, believed he possessed some hope of another life after death.

Indeed, in the *Phaedrus*, he says that the soul itself, when it is by itself, is alone able to participate in true wisdom—the kind that surpasses human strength. And when the love gathered from here carries it up to heaven, reaching the goal of hope through philosophical love, he says it receives the prize of another eternal life. In the *Symposium*, he says that a natural love of generating its like is implanted in all: in ordinary men, only other humans; but in a good man, something like himself. This a good man cannot achieve unless he possesses perfect virtues, through which he is to educate the youths who frequent him, and, as he says in the *Theaetetus*, he will "generate" and make them men. For some procreate with the body, but others with the soul. For among the barbarian <note>original: "barbaros." Clement uses this term for non-Greeks, including Hebrews and Egyptians.</note> philosophers as well, to instruct and enlighten through hearing is called "to regenerate." *And I have begotten you in Christ Jesus,* says the noble

> Look upon it with the mind, nor care to discern it with the eyes.

> Yet behold things absent as present to the mind,

CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

<sig>A</sig>
<margin>archetypal <note>original: αρχετυπική (archetypikē)</note></margin>
For he who hopes, just like he who believes, sees with his mind those things that are perceived by the intelligence, and those things which are to come. If, therefore, we say that something is "just," we also say it is "beautiful" and "honorable." Furthermore, we say that "Truth" is something real. Yet, we have never seen any of these with our eyes, but only with the mind. Now, the Word of God says: "I am the truth." Therefore, the Word must be considered with the mind. "And who," he asks, "do you say are the true philosophers?" "Those," I replied, "who are devoted to the contemplation of truth." In the *Phaedrus*, Plato declared that Truth is the "Idea." The "Idea" is the intelligence of God, or that which is understood by the divine mind, which the Barbarians <note>Clement often uses the term "Barbarian" to refer to the Hebrews or Christians, acknowledging they were non-Greeks who possessed the original truth.</note> called the <term>Logos of God</term> <note>original: λόγον θεοῦ (logon theou) — the Word, Reason, or Wisdom of God.</note>, that is, the Word or Reason of God. His phrasing on the matter is as follows: *For one must dare to speak the truth, especially when one is speaking about Truth.* <sig>B</sig> For that which is without color or shape, and cannot be touched, and which is truly the essence of the soul, can be seen only by God, the pilot. Now, the "Word" brought forth is the cause of craftsmanship and creation. Then, he also generates himself when the "Word was made flesh" so that he might also come within our sight. The just man, therefore, seeks the discovery that arises from love, and by striving toward it, he becomes truly fortunate. <margin>John 1.</margin> <margin>archetypal.</margin> <margin>Luke 11.</margin> <margin>Matthew 11.</margin> For he says, "To him who knocks, it shall be opened. Ask, and it shall be given to you." For those who "take the kingdom by force" are the violent—not those who use contentious speeches, but those who, through the persistence of a right life and prayers made without ceasing, are said to apply "force," as they are the ones who wash away the stains contracted from their previous sins.

<sig>C</sig>
> *You might certainly weigh out vice in troops.*
> *For God brings aid to the one who labors.*

For the gifts of the Muses <note>A poetic way of referring to knowledge or divine inspiration.</note> are not easily captured things lying in the open, to be taken by just anyone. Therefore, the recognition of one's own ignorance is the first lesson for him who walks according to the Word or Reason. When someone realizes they are ignorant, they seek; and when they have sought, they find a teacher; and when they have found one, they believe; and when they have believed, they hope; and having loved from that point on, they are made like the one they love, striving to be that which they first loved. Socrates points out this path and method to Alcibiades when he asks: "Do you not think I can know about the things that are just in any other way?" "Certainly," Socrates says, "if indeed you find them." "But do you not think I can find them?" "Most certainly, if you seek them." "Then do you think I cannot seek?" <sig>D</sig> "I think you can," Socrates replies, "if you believe that you do not know." By this same logic, there are the lamps of the wise virgins, which are lit at night in the thick darkness of chastity—for the Scripture secretly signifies that this world is "night." Wise souls, pure as virgins, realizing they are placed in worldly ignorance, light the lamp, rouse the mind, illuminate the darkness, expel ignorance, seek the truth, and await the arrival of the Teacher. "It is impossible, then," I say, "for the common crowd to be a philosopher."

> *Many carry the wand, but few are truly Bacchic.*
> <note>A Greek proverb meaning many participate in the outward rituals, but few are truly inspired or enlightened by the god.</note>

<margin>Matthew 20.</margin>
<margin>2 Thessalonians 3.</margin>
<sig>E</sig> This is according to the opinion of Plato. For "Many are called, but few are chosen." And "Knowledge is not in everyone," says the Apostle. "Pray that we may be delivered from wicked and perverse men. For faith is not the possession of all." Furthermore, the poetic works of Cleanthes, the Stoic philosopher, record similar things in this manner:

> *Look not for fame, while you wish to be suddenly wise.*
> *Let not the opinion of the senseless crowd terrify you.*
> *The crowd possesses no wise or just judgment,*
> *And among the few, this will scarcely be found.*

And even more pithily and briefly, the Comic poet says:

> *It is not fitting to judge beautiful things in a tumult.*

For they heard, as I believe, that beautiful Wisdom which says to us: "In the midst of the foolish, watch for the right moment. But in the midst of the thoughtful, dwell continually." And again: "The wise shall hide wisdom." <sig>F</sig> For the common crowd demands a "pledge" or proof of truth; they are not satisfied with the naked salvation that comes from faith.

> *But among the wicked, those who prevail do not believe strongly,*
> *Yet the persuasion of our Muse commands you thus.*

### MISCELLANIES, BOOK V.

<margin>A</margin> *“The word, once dissected, remains within your very core.”* <note>original: “Dissecto nostras intra tua viscera verbo.” This is a poetic fragment, likely from a lost tragedy, suggesting that once the truth is internalized, it stays with a person.</note>
For according to Empedocles <note>A Greek Pre-Socratic philosopher (c. 490–430 BC) who taught that the universe was composed of four elements and governed by Love and Strife.</note>, it is characteristic of the wicked to want to overcome the truth simply because they do not believe. However, the Greeks will recognize that our teachings are probable and worthy of belief if the Word is examined more closely through its consequences. For we are taught that "like is known by like." Indeed, Solomon says: *Answer a fool according to his folly.* <margin>Proverbs 26.</margin> Therefore, to those who seek the wisdom found among themselves, we must present those things that are suitable and familiar to them, so that they may most easily come to the faith of truth through their own familiar paths, as is fitting. For the Apostle says, *I have become all things to all men, that I might win all.* <margin>1 Corinthians 9. Matthew 5.</margin> For the rain of divine grace is also sent down upon the just and the unjust. Is He the God of the Jews only, and not also of the Gentiles? <margin>B</margin> Certainly He is the God of the Gentiles too, since there is only one God, as the noble Apostle cried out. <margin>Romans 3.</margin> But because they are unwilling to believe either in the Good through justice or in the knowledge that leads to salvation, we ourselves—regarding their own traditions as belonging to God, since all beautiful and honorable things have come from us to the Greeks—shall approach them in a way that they are fit to hear. For the greater part of the common people measures wisdom or justice not by the truth, but by the things that delight them. Furthermore, they are delighted by nothing more than by things that are similar to themselves. For whatever is still deaf and blind, lacking understanding and the keen, contemplative vision of the soul—which only the Savior provides—must stand outside the divine chorus. <margin>C</margin> Just as the profane are excluded from the mysteries, or those unskilled in music from the dances, those who are not yet pure, not yet worthy of the chaste truth, and who are discordant, disordered, and still focused on material things, must remain outside. For we compare spiritual things with spiritual. <margin>1 Corinthians 2.</margin> Truly, it was for this reason—through a method of concealment that is truly divine and most necessary for us—that the truly sacred Word was laid up in the sanctuary of truth. The Egyptians signified this through what they call "shrines" (*adyta*), and the Hebrews through the "veil." This was to show that only those who were consecrated—that is, dedicated to God—were permitted to enter, those whose desires for vice had been "circumcised" through their love for the only God. Indeed, it even seemed a sacrilege to Plato for the impure to touch the pure. Hence, prophecies and divine responses are given through riddles. Nor are the mysteries shown to those who approach rashly and shamelessly, but only after certain purifications and instructions. <margin>D</margin> For the Muse was not then "greedy for gain" <note>Clement is quoting Pindar here, contrasting the ancient, pure inspiration of the Muses with the commercialized art of his own day.</note> nor a "hired worker," nor were sweet, honey-toned, soft songs sold by Terpsichore with a silvered face.

Now, those who are taught by the Egyptians learn first the style of Egyptian letters called the **epistolographic** <note>original: ἐπιστολογραφικήν (epistolographikēn) — the "letter-writing" or demotic script used for everyday business.</note>, which is suitable for writing letters. Second is the **hieratic** or "priestly" script, used by the <term>sacred scribes</term> <note>original: ἱερογραμματεῖς (hierogrammateis).</note>. Finally, they learn the **hieroglyphic** <note>original: ἱερογλυφικήν (hieroglyphikēn) — "sacred carved writing."</note>, the sacred carved script. One aspect of this script is "cyriologic," <note>original: κυριολογικήν (kyriologikēn) — "properly speaking," using letters like an alphabet.</note> which uses the primary elements or letters; the other aspect is "symbolic," which signifies through signs. Of the symbolic type, one part speaks properly through imitation, another is written "tropically" (metaphorically), and another is taken openly as allegory through certain riddles. For instance, when they wish to write the word "sun," they draw a circle; for the "moon," they draw a crescent shape <margin>E</margin> that properly resembles the form. In the "tropical" style, they record things by transferring and shifting meanings according to suitability—changing some things and transfiguring others in many ways. Thus, when they record the praises of kings in myths, as if they were gods, they engrave them in these characters. Of the third kind, which is done through riddles, take this as an example: they likened the other stars to the bodies of serpents because of their wandering, oblique paths. But the Sun they represented as a **Scarab beetle** <note>The scarab (dung beetle) was a primary symbol for the sun god Khepri in Egypt.</note>, because it shapes a round ball out of ox dung and rolls it with its face turned away. They say this animal lives six months under the earth <margin>F</margin> and spends the other part of the year above ground, emitting its seed into the globe to give birth, and that there is no female scarab. To put it briefly, all those who have treated divine matters—both Barbarians <note>Refers to the Hebrews and early Christians.</note> and Greeks—shrouded the principles of things and handed down the truth through riddles, signs, symbols, allegories, metaphors, and similar figures and modes, such as these.

<summary>Clement explains that divine truth is intentionally veiled in symbols, riddles, and hieroglyphics to ensure it is only accessible to the purified and dedicated, drawing parallels between Egyptian, Hebrew, and Greek traditions.</summary>

### MISCELLANIES, BOOK V.

<margin>A</margin>
*“...the word has been dissected within your very vitals.”* <note>original: "Dissecto nostras intra tua viscera uerbo." This likely refers to a fragment of the philosopher Empedocles regarding how truth is internalized.</note>
For according to Empedocles, it is characteristic of the wicked to wish to overcome the truth by refusing to believe it. However, the Greeks will recognize that our teachings are probable and worthy of belief if the Word is examined more closely through its consequences. For we are taught "like by like." <note>A common ancient philosophical principle that the mind can only understand things that share its nature.</note> Solomon also says: <margin>Proverbs 26</margin> *Answer a fool according to his folly.* Therefore, to those who seek the wisdom found among themselves, we must present those things which are familiar and suitable to them, so that they may come most easily through their own concepts—as is fitting—to the faith of the truth. *I have become all things to all men,* he says, <margin>1 Corinthians 9; Matthew 5</margin> *that I might gain all.* For the rain of divine grace is sent down upon both the just and the unjust. *Is God the God of the Jews only, and not also of the Gentiles? Certainly of the Gentiles also, since God is one,* cried the noble Apostle. <margin>B</margin> <margin>Romans 3</margin>

But since they do not wish to believe through goodness or through the knowledge leading to salvation, let us ourselves take up those things which are their own—considering that all things belong to God, and that whatever is beautiful and honorable has come from us to the Greeks—and let us approach them according to their readiness to hear. For the majority of the common people measure wisdom or justice not by truth, but by the things that please them. They are delighted by nothing more than what is similar to themselves. For whatever is still deaf and blind, lacking understanding and the clear, piercing vision of a soul eager for contemplation—which only the Savior provides—must stand outside the divine chorus. Like the uninitiated at the mysteries or the unmusical at a dance, such a person is not yet pure, nor worthy of the chaste truth; being unharmonious, disordered, and still material, they must remain outside. <margin>C</margin> For we *compare spiritual things with spiritual.* <margin>1 Corinthians 2</margin>

For this reason, certainly, through a truly divine method of concealment that is most necessary for us, the truly sacred Word is stored in the inner sanctuary of truth. The Egyptians indicated this through what they call "adyta" <note>Inner shrines or restricted areas of a temple.</note>, and the Hebrews through the "veil" <note>The curtain in the Temple of Jerusalem separating the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place.</note>. These signified that only those who were consecrated—that is, dedicated to God—were permitted to enter; those whose desires for vice were "circumcised" through their love for the only God. For Plato also thought it was a divine law that the "impure should not touch the pure." Hence, prophecies and divine responses are given through enigmas. The mysteries are not shown to those who approach rashly or impudently, but only with certain purifications and instructions. For the Muse was not then a mercenary or a common worker, <margin>D</margin> nor were "honey-toned, sweet songs" sold by a "silver-faced Terpsichore" <note>Clement quotes the poet Pindar here, lamenting the commercialization of art and wisdom.</note> with her soft poems.

Now, those who are educated by the Egyptians first learn the style of Egyptian letters called <term>epistolographic</term> <note>original: ἐπιστολογραφικήν; the "letter-writing" or demotic script used for everyday business.</note>. Second is the <term>hieratic</term> <note>original: ἱερογραμματεῖς; the "priestly" script used by sacred scribes.</note>, which is used by the sacred scribes. The last is <term>hieroglyphic</term> <note>original: ἱερογλυφικήν; "sacred carved writing."</note>. One type of this is <term>kyriological</term> <note>original: κυριολογικήν; "speaking literally" or using the primary elements of the alphabet.</note>, while the other is symbolic. Of the symbolic type, one part speaks literally through imitation; another is written figuratively; and another is taken openly as an allegory through certain enigmas. For example, when they wish <margin>E</margin> to write "Sun," they make a circle; for "Moon," they make a crescent shape, consistent with its primary form. In the figurative style, they transfer and shift meanings according to similarities, changing some things and transforming others in many ways. Thus, they record the praises of kings in myths, attributing them to the gods through these carved signs.

Of the third kind, which consists of enigmas, this is an example: they compared other stars to the bodies of serpents because of their oblique paths. But the Sun they compared to a <term>scarab beetle</term>, because it fashions a round ball out of ox dung and rolls it with its face turned toward it. They say this animal lives six months under the earth and the other part of the year above ground; it emits its seed into the globe and gives birth, and they say no female scarab is ever born. <margin>F</margin> To speak plainly, all who have treated divine matters, whether non-Greeks or Greeks, have hidden the principles of things. They have handed down the truth through enigmas, signs, symbols, allegories, metaphors, and other such figures and modes, such as:

<meta>This page continues Clement of Alexandria's argument from Book V of the *Miscellanies*. He is explaining how divine truth is often veiled in both Greek philosophy and Christian scripture to encourage deeper seeking. This follows his discussion on how even the Greeks recognized the need for "likeness" to perceive truth.</meta>

# CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

Even among the Greeks there were oracles, and the Pythian Apollo is indeed called <gloss>Loxias</gloss> <note>original: *λοξίας*; a title of Apollo meaning "the Ambiguous" or "the Oblique"</note>, that is, **oblique** or indirect. <margin>A</margin> Furthermore, the sayings of those who are called "sages" among the Greeks signify a greater reality with only a few words. An example is the phrase: *Be thrifty with time*. This implies either that life is short and time must not be consumed recklessly, or conversely, that one should be sparing with private expenses so that, even if you live many years, you will not lack necessities. Similarly, the famous phrase *know thyself* indicates many things: that you are mortal, that you were born a human being, and that if you compare yourself to the most excellent and outstanding things in life, you should realize you are of no account if you only claim to be famous or wealthy. Conversely, it suggests that when you are wealthy and famous, you should not boast only of the advantages by which you surpass others. Rather, he says, "know" for what purpose you were born, <margin>B</margin> whose image you are, what your true essence is, what your "workmanship" consists of, and what your connection and affinity with God might be, along with similar reflections.

The Spirit also speaks through the prophet Isaiah: <margin>Isa. 45</margin> **I will give you the treasures of darkness, the hidden ones.** For the treasures of God, the riches that never fail, are that very wisdom which is so difficult to "hunt" or track down. Even the Poets, who learned their theology from the Prophets, philosophize through secret meanings. I speak of Orpheus, Linus, Musaeus, Homer, and Hesiod, and those who are wise in that same way. For them, the "veil" used before the common people is the delight of poetry, dreams, and symbols—all of which are obscure to most men, not out of envy (for it is wrong to think of God as subject to such human passions), but so that the inquiry required to grasp the meaning of these riddles might lead one back to finding the truth. In this way, Sophocles <margin>C</margin> the tragic poet says:

> ->And such a one have I known God to be.<-
> ->He always displays divine things to the wise.<-
> ->But to the wicked He is a harsh and brief master.<-

Here, he uses "harsh" <note>original: *Malum*, "bad" or "evil," used here in the sense of a stern disciplinarian.</note> to mean "straightforward." 

Quite clearly, concerning our entire Scripture, it is written in the Psalms <margin>Ps. 77</margin> that it was spoken in a parable: **Hear, my people, my law; incline your ear to the words of my mouth. I will open my mouth in parables; I will speak propositions from the beginning.** The noble Apostle also says something similar: <margin>1 Cor. 2</margin> "We speak wisdom among those who are perfect; yet a wisdom not of this world, nor of the princes of this world who are coming to nothing. But <margin>D</margin> we speak the wisdom of God hidden in a mystery, which God ordained before the worlds for our glory, which none of the princes of this world knew. For if they had known, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory." 

Now, the philosophers did not labor to bring shame upon the coming of the Lord; therefore, it remains that the Apostle is attacking and criticizing the vain self-assurance of those who were considered wise among the Jews. And for this reason, he adds: "But we preach, as it is written, things which the eye has not seen, nor the ear heard, nor have they entered into the heart of man—the things which God has prepared for those who love Him. For God has revealed them to us through the Spirit. For the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God." 

The Holy Spirit knows the disciple who is spiritual and endowed with knowledge <term>gnosis; the deeper, experiential knowledge of divine truth</term>, who is supplied by God and possesses the mind of Christ. However, the "natural man" <note>original: *animalis homo*, referring to one guided only by the soul/intellect without the Spirit.</note> does not accept the things <margin>E</margin> that belong to the Spirit, for they are foolishness to him. 

Indeed, the Apostle, in order to distinguish the perfection that comes from "knowledge," sometimes calls the common faith a "foundation," and at other times "milk." He writes in this manner: <margin>1 Cor. 3</margin> **Brothers, I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal, as infants in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not solid food, for you were not yet able; nor indeed are you able even now. For you are still carnal.** For where there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not carnal, walking according to the ways of men? These are things chosen and taken up by sinful men. But those who have abstained from such things think on divine matters and share in the food of "knowledge." 

**According to the grace given to me,** he says, **as a wise architect, I have laid the foundation. But another builds upon it gold, silver, and precious stones.** <margin>F</margin> **These are the structures of knowledge, which are placed upon the foundation of faith which is in Christ Jesus. But the stubble, wood, and hay are those things offered and dedicated by heresies.** **BUT what each person...**

<summary>Clement explains that divine truth is intentionally hidden in riddles and symbols—found in Greek oracles, poetry, and Christian Scripture—to ensure that only the spiritually prepared can find it. He distinguishes between basic faith ("milk") and deeper spiritual knowledge ("solid food") using the metaphors of the Apostle Paul.</summary>

# MISCELLANIES, BOOK V.

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>Rom. 1.</margin>
**The fire shall test the work.** <note>original: *opus ignis probabit*; a reference to 1 Cor 3:13, though Clement links the theme to Romans</note> In his Epistle to the Romans, the Apostle also quietly hints at the "building up of knowledge" when he says: *For I long to see you, that I may impart to you some spiritual gift, so that you may be established.* Such gifts could not be openly committed to writing. Now, the Pythagorean symbols also depend, in a very hidden way, upon "barbarian" <note>Clement uses "barbarian" to refer to non-Greek cultures, specifically the Hebrews</note> philosophy. For instance, the Samian <note>Pythagoras of Samos</note> advises one "not to keep a swallow in the house." This means one should not welcome a talkative person, a whisperer, or a man with an unbridled tongue who cannot contain or grasp the things communicated to him. For "the swallow and the turtle-dove, the birds of the field, know the times of their coming," <margin>Jer. 8.</margin> as the Scripture says, and one ought never to live alongside trifles. Indeed, the turtle-dove is a grumbler, representing the ungrateful malice of complaining, and is rightly expelled from the home.

<margin>B</margin>
> *Produce not for me various whispers from here and there.*

The swallow, which silently hints at the fable of Pandion, represents things that must be prayed against and expiated—the sorts of things that common rumor says happened because of her. We have heard that Tereus suffered some of these things and committed others. <note>In myth, Tereus was transformed into a hoopoe, and his sisters-in-law into a swallow and a nightingale after a cycle of violence</note> Furthermore, the swallow hunts the musical cicadas. Therefore, anyone who persecutes the **Word** <note>the Logos</note> is rightly expelled, as is anyone who looks down upon the scepter-bearing Juno of Olympus. "I have a faithful storehouse on my tongue," say the poets and Aeschylus:

> *I too have a guarding key on my tongue.*

<margin>C</margin>
Again, Pythagoras commanded that when a pot is lifted from the fire, one should not leave its mark in the ashes, but should stir them; and that those who rise from bed should ruffle the bedclothes. By this he quietly signified not only that pride and arrogance must be erased, but that not even a trace of anger should be left behind. When the "boiling" has ceased, it should be smoothed over, and every memory of injury should be wiped away. <margin>Eph. 5.</margin> **Let not the sun go down on your wrath,** says the Scripture. And He who said, *You shall not covet,* has removed all memory of an injury received. For anger is found to be an impulse of a gentle soul’s desire, seeking vengeance without reason and beyond measure. Similarly, he advises that the bed be disturbed so that we might not remember any dream or vision of the day, nor any pleasure that occurred in the night. Perhaps he also meant that the dark fantasies of the mind should be dispelled by the light of truth.

<margin>D</margin>
<margin>Ps. 4.</margin>
**Be angry, and do not sin,** says David; teaching that we should not give in to appearances nor carry out the deed, thereby confirming the anger. Again, "one must not sail upon the land" is a Pythagorean symbol. This signifies that taxes and similar contracts, which are turbulent and unstable, should be refused. For this reason, the Word says that Tax-collectors <note>Publicans</note> achieve salvation with difficulty. Furthermore, Pythagoras commands that rings should not be worn, nor should the images of the Gods be engraved upon them. Just as <margin>Exo. 20.</margin> Moses, many centuries before, openly established the law that no graven, molten, fashioned, or painted image or likeness should be made, so that we might not attend to sensible things <note>things perceived by the physical senses</note>, but pass over to those things perceived by the intelligence. For the habit of seeing God easily makes His majesty seem cheap and contemptible; to worship the essence perceived by the intelligence through physical matter is to despise it through the senses. 

<margin>E</margin>
<margin>The Greek copy has <term>ouranos</term> <note>meaning "heaven"</note>, but I believe it should read <term>anthropo</term> <note>meaning "man"</note>; otherwise the sense is either non-existent or weak.</margin>
Therefore, the wisest of the Egyptian Priests established the temple of Minerva under the open sky, just as the Hebrews built their temple without an image. There are some who, while worshipping God, make an image of a man which contains the stars and adore it, even though our Scripture certainly says: **Let us make man in our image and likeness.** I think it is worthwhile also to bring forward the voice of Eurytus the Pythagorean, which goes like this: When he had spoken in his work *On Fortune* about the Craftsman using himself as a model to make man, he added: "The Tabernacle <note>the human body</note> is similar to the rest, as it is made from the same matter; but it was produced by the most excellent Architect, who fabricated it using himself as the archetype." And in

<margin>F</margin>
short, Pythagoras and those named after him, along with Plato most of all other philosophers, made use of the Lawgiver <note>Moses</note>, as can be conjectured from their very dogmas. And since they had encountered certain prophetic voices through a correctly-guessing reputation for divination—not without divine instinct—they reached the truth in parts and

# CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

<margin>A</margin> Those who have treated [truth] with sharp vision <note>original: *acies tractatam*</note> have honored it not with obscure names, nor with terms that stray from the declaration of things, since they received the manifestation of the union that exists with the truth. Hence, Greek philosophy is like the light from a rush-wick <note>a simple lamp made from a reed</note> which men light, artfully stealing light from the sun. But when the Word was preached, that entire holy light shone out. Thus, a theft is useful in a house at night, but during the day the fire is made clear, and the whole night is illuminated by the great sun of the light perceived by the intellect. Now, Pythagoras made a summary of what was said by Moses concerning justice when he said "the balance must not be stepped over"—that is, one must not overstep the equality used in distributions, thereby honoring justice.

<margin>B</margin>
->Equality always binds friends together,<-
->And likewise joins friends to friends, and cities to cities,<-
->And allies to allies; for the law is equality.<-
->But to men, the just is always the opposite: the greater<-
->Is the enemy of the less, and begins the day of hostile hatred.<-
->As the poetic beauty has it.<- <note>These verses are from Euripides' play, *The Phoenician Women*</note>

<margin>Matth. 11.</margin> Therefore the Lord says, "TAKE my yoke, for it is kind and light"; and to his companions who contend for the first place, he commands equality with simplicity, 
<margin>Math. 19. Gal. 6.</margin><margin>C</margin> saying that they ought to become like little children. Similarly, the Apostle writes that in Christ there is neither slave nor free, neither Greek nor Jew. For the new creation in Christ is free from contention and greed, and is a just equality. Indeed, envy stands outside the divine choir, as do rivalry and sorrow. For this reason, the initiates <note>original: *Mystæ*; referring here to the Orphic or Pythagorean traditions</note> also forbid "eating the heart," teaching that one ought not to bite and consume the soul with sloth and grief because of things that happen contrary to counsel and expectation. Miserable, therefore, is he whom Homer also says wanders alone, "consuming his own soul." Again, since the Gospel and the Apostles—like all the Prophets—set out two ways: and they call one "narrow and cramped," as it is restricted by commandments and prohibitions; but the other is the opposite, "broad
<margin>Matth. 7. Psal. 1.</margin> and spacious" and has nothing to obstruct it. And they say, "Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners." From this also comes <margin>D</margin> the fable of Prodicus the Chian <note>historically Prodicus of Ceos</note> concerning Virtue and Vice; and Pythagoras, by commanding one to enter the "royal road," is not afraid to forbid following the opinion of the common crowd, which lacks judgment and is not without controversy. Furthermore, Aristocritus, in the first book of his positions against Heracleodorus, mentions a certain letter which reads as follows: *King Ateas of the Scythians to the people of Byzantium: Do not bring harm to my revenues, lest my horses drink your water.* For the barbarian symbolically signified the war he was about to bring upon them. Similarly, the poet Euphorion introduces Nestor saying:

->We have not yet moved our horses from the river Simois.<-

And for this reason, the Egyptians also place Sphinxes in their temples, seeing as the discourse 
<margin>E</margin> concerning God is enigmatic and obscure. Perhaps it is because one ought both to love and fear God: to love Him as being kind and propitious to the holy, but to fear Him as being inexorably just to the ungodly. For the Sphinx signifies an image of a wild beast and a human at the same time. It would be a long task to pursue all the Prophetic and legal writings by bringing forward those things said through riddles. For almost the entire divine Scripture speaks in this manner. But to a person of sound mind, a few examples set forth are sufficient, I believe, to show the point proposed. Indeed, the narrative of the seven enclosures in the ancient temple already confesses this concealment, which among the Hebrews had a reference to something specific, as did the composition of the priest's robe through various symbols. These refer to visible things, signifying the composition that reaches from 
<margin>Exo. 25. and 26.</margin><margin>F</margin> heaven down to the earth. And the covering and the veil were varied with blue <note>original: *hyacintho*; likely referring to a deep sky-blue or violet</note>, purple, scarlet, and fine linen. This signified that the nature of the elements holds the revelation of God. For the purple comes from the water, and the fine linen from the earth; and the blue is likened to the air, since it is dark and obscure, just as the scarlet is likened to fire. In the middle of the covering and the veil, where it was permitted...

<meta>Continuing from the previous page, Clement is interpreting the symbolic architecture of the Hebrew Tabernacle as a precursor to both Christian truth and Greek philosophical concepts, specifically focusing on how physical structures represent spiritual realities.</meta>

### STROMATA, BOOK V

<margin>A</margin> ...where the Priests were accustomed to enter, there was situated the altar of incense <note>original: *thuribulum*</note>, a symbol of the earth which is situated in the middle of this world, from which exhalations arise. That middle place also which is within the veil, where the High Priest alone was permitted to enter on appointed days, and the outer courtyard which was open to all Hebrews, they say represent the space between heaven and earth. Others, however, say they are symbols of the world which is perceived by the intellect <note>the "intelligible world" of Platonic thought</note> and the world perceived by the senses. Therefore, the covering by which the unfaithfulness of the people was kept back was spread before five columns, keeping away those who were in the surrounding area. For that reason, in a very mystical way, five loaves are broken by the Savior and multiplied for the multitude of those who hear <margin>John 6.</margin> For many attend only to the five senses, as if they were the only things that exist. But see, looking around,

<margin>B</margin> says Plato, that no one from among those who are not initiated into the mysteries should overhear. These are the people who think nothing else exists except that which they can grasp tenaciously with their hands; they do not admit into the order of substance any actions, or generations, or anything that is not visible. Such are those who attend only to the five-fold set of senses <note>the five senses: sight, hearing, smell, taste, touch</note>. Hearing, and things of that kind, cannot approach the understanding of God. For this reason, the Son is called the "Face of the Father" <note>the visible manifestation of the invisible God</note>, the Word carrying flesh, having become effective through the five-fold senses, and who is the indicator of the Father’s unique nature. "If we live by the spirit, let us also walk by the spirit" <margin>Gal. 5.</margin> "We walk by faith, not by sight," the excellent Apostle says <margin>2 Cor. 5.</margin> Therefore, the priestly ministry was hidden within the covering, and it keeps those who labor within it far away from those who are on the outside. Again, the veil of the entrance to the Holy of Holies is held by four columns there, which declare the holy "quaternion" <note>the number four</note> of the ancient covenants. <margin>C</margin> Furthermore, there is that mystical "four-letter name" <term>Tetragrammaton: the four Hebrew letters YHWH representing the name of God</term>, which was applied only to those who could enter the inner sanctuary; it is called Jehovah <note>original: *Iehoua*</note>, which is interpreted as "He who is and who is to be." Furthermore, among the Greeks, the name *Theos* <note>original: *θεὸς*, meaning God</note> also contains a four-letter sequence. Since the Lord alone existed in the world perceived by the intellect, he entered into sufferings, undergoing the knowledge of that which is ineffable, surpassing every name known by the voice. Now truly, the lampstand <margin>Exo. 25 & 26.</margin> was also situated in the southern parts of the altar of incense, through which the movements of the seven luminaries <note>the seven classical planets</note> are declared, which perform their southern revolutions. For from each side of the lampstand three branches were inserted, and lamps were in them; because the Sun also, <margin>D</margin> placed like a lampstand in the middle of the other wandering stars <note>planets</note>, imparts light by a certain divine music to those who are above it and those who are below it. The golden lampstand has another riddle as well: it is a sign of Christ, not only in its shape, but also because he emits light in many ways and many modes into those who believe in him, hope in him, and look to him, through the ministry of those things which were first created. They say also that there are seven eyes of the Lord—seven spirits resting on the rod which blossoms from the root of Jesse <margin>Isaiah 11.</margin> On the northern parts of the altar of incense was situated the table upon which was the presentation of the loaves <note>the Showbread</note>, because the northern winds provide the most nourishment. There were also certain dwellings of the churches which breathe together into one body and one assembly. Now, those things which are told concerning the holy Ark signify the world perceived by the intellect, <margin>E</margin> which is hidden and closed off from the common people. Furthermore, those golden images <note>the Cherubim</note>, each having six wings—or "two bears" as some would have it—signify, or what fits better, the two hemispheres. The name "Cherubim" is intended to mean "much knowledge." But both have twelve wings, and through the Zodiac circle and the time that is carried within it, they signify the world of the senses. Concerning these, I believe, the tragedy speaks when discussing nature: "And tireless time, full of a perennial flow, circles around, giving birth to itself. And the twin bears <note>Ursa Major and Minor</note> keep the Atlantic pole with the swift motions of their wings." Atlas, who does not suffer, could indeed be the pole, or the sphere that does not wander. Perhaps, however, it is better understood as immobile eternity. <margin>F</margin> But I think it better that the Ark, which is called *Thebotha* from its Hebrew name <note>Tevah</note>, signifies something else. It is interpreted as "one for one" from all places. Might it therefore signify the "Octad" <note>the number eight, often symbolizing the new creation or heaven</note> and the world perceived by the intellect? Or does it signify God, who comprehends all things, is without shape, and does not fall under the sight?

### STROMATA, BOOK V

<margin>A</margin>
...they honored the subject they treated, not with obscure names nor by straying outside the explanation of things, once they had received the manifestation of the union that exists with the truth. Hence, Greek philosophy is like the illumination that comes from a wick <note>original: *scirpo*, referring to a rush-light or simple torch</note> which men light, artfully stealing light from the sun. Now, Pythagoras made a summary of what Moses said regarding justice when he said "one must not step over the balance" <note>This is a famous Pythagorean *symbolon* or maxim</note>, which means one must not overstep the equality that is practiced in distributions, thereby honoring justice.

->Join friends together, and even cities to cities.<-

As poetic beauty holds. For this reason, the Lord said: "TAKE UP <note>original: *TOLLITE*</note> my yoke, for it is kind and light," and to his followers who were contending for the first rank, he commanded equality with simplicity <unclear>ti</unclear>, saying:
<margin>Math. 19. Gal. 6.</margin>
That they must become like little children. Similarly, the Apostle also writes that in Christ there is neither slave nor free, neither Greek nor Jew. For the "new creature" <term>new creature (kainē ktisis): a theological term for the transformed life of a believer</term> which is in Christ is free from contention and greed; it is a just equality. For envy stands outside the divine choir, as do rivalry and sorrow. For this rea-

<margin>C</margin>
-son, the Initiates <note>original: *Mystæ*, referring to those initiated into the Mystery religions</note> also forbid eating the heart, teaching that one should not bite or consume the soul with sloth and grief because of things that happen contrary to one's plan or opinion. Therefore, that man is miserable, whom Homer also describes as wandering alone, "consuming his own soul" <note>Referring to the character Bellerophon in the *Iliad*</note>. Again, since the Gospel and the Apostles, as well as all the Prophets, set out two ways: and they call one "narrow and cramped" <margin>Matt. 7. Psal. 1.</margin> as it is constrained by commands and prohibitions; but the other is the opposite, "broad and spacious" and with nothing to block it; and they say, "Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners." From this also comes the fable of Prodicus of Chios <note>A famous sophist</note> concerning Virtue and Vice, and Pythagoras's command to enter by the "royal road," for he is not afraid to forbid following the opinion of the common crowd, which lacks judgment and is never without controversy. Aristocritus, in the first book of his opinions against Heracleodorus, mentions a certain letter which reads as follows: "Atas, King of the Scythians, to the people of Byzantium: Do not

<margin>D</margin>
bring harm to my tributes, lest my horses drink your water." For the barbarian signified in a symbolic way the war he was about to bring upon them. Similarly, the poet Euphorion also introduces Nestor saying:

->We have moved our horses from the river, but not yet from the Simois.<-

<margin>E</margin>
And for this reason, the Egyptians also place Sphinxes in their sacred places, because the discourse concerning God is enigmatic and obscure. Perhaps it is also because it is necessary to both love and fear God: to love Him as one who is kind and propitious to the holy, but to fear Him as one who is inexorably just toward the impious. For the Sphinx represents nearly at once the image of a man and a beast. It would be a long task to follow all the Prophetic and legal writings, bringing forward those things which were spoken through enigmas. For almost the entirety of the Divine Scripture speaks in this manner. But to one of sound mind, a few examples set forth are sufficient, I believe, to demonstrate the point proposed. Indeed, the concealment mentioned in the ancient temple—the account of the seven circuits among the Hebrews—already confesses this, as does the composition of the High Priest's robe <note>original: *talari*, the robe reaching to the ankles</note> with its various symbols, which refer to visible things, signifying the composition that reaches from heaven to the earth.

<margin>Exo. 25. and 26. F</margin>
And the covering and the veil were varied with hyacinth, purple, scarlet, and fine linen. This signified that the nature of the elements contains the revelation of God. For purple comes from the water <note>from the murex sea-snail</note>, and fine linen from the earth; and hyacinth <note>a blue or dark color</note> is likened to the air since it is dark and obscure, just as scarlet is likened to fire. ### STROMATA, BOOK V

<margin>A</margin>
...it was permitted for the priests to enter, there was placed the censer <note>original: *thuribulum*</note>, a symbol of the earth which is situated in the middle of this world, from which vapors arise. That middle place also, which is within the veil—where only the High Priest was permitted to enter on fixed days—and the outer court which was open to all Hebrews, they say is the middle between heaven and earth. Others, however, say it is a symbol of the world which is perceived by the intellect, and the world of the senses. Therefore, the cover <note>original: *operculum*</note> by which the people's lack of faith was kept back was stretched out before five columns, keeping away those who were in the surrounding area. For that reason, in a very mystical way, five loaves are broken <margin>John 6</margin> by the Savior and multiplied for the multitude of those who hear Him. For many attend only to the things of the senses, as if they were the only things that exist. "But look around you," <margin>B</margin> says Plato, "lest anyone from among those who are not initiated into the mysteries should overhear." These are the people who think nothing else exists except what they can grasp firmly with their hands, not admitting into the order of substance any actions, or generations, or anything that is not visible. For such are those who attend only to the fivefold nature of the senses <note>The five senses: sight, hearing, smell, taste, touch</note>. Hearing, and things of that kind, cannot approach the intelligence of God. Hence the Son is called the "Face of the Father"; the Word <note>The *Logos*</note> took on flesh through the five senses and became the indicator of the Father's unique nature. "If we live by the spirit, let us also walk by the <margin>Gal. 5</margin> spirit." "We walk by faith, not by sight," as the excellent Apostle says. Therefore, <margin>2 Cor. 5</margin> the priestly ministry was hidden away within the covering, and it keeps those who labor within it far away from those who are outside. Again, the veil of the entrance to the Holy of Holies—<margin>C</margin> the four columns there declare the holy "quaternion" <note>A group of four</note> of the ancient covenants. Furthermore, that mystical "tetragrammaton" <note>The four-letter name of God</note> name, which was bestowed only upon those who could enter the inner sanctuary, is called Jehovah <note>original: *Iehoua*</note>, which is interpreted as "He who is and who is to be." Furthermore, among the Greeks, the name *Theos* <note>original Greek: θεὸς</note>, that is, "God," contains four letters. Since the Lord alone existed in the world perceived by the intellect, He enters into sufferings, undergoing the knowledge of that which is ineffable, surpassing every name known by the voice. Now, the lampstand <margin>Exo. 25 & 26</margin> was also placed in the southern parts of the censer, by which the movements of the seven luminaries <note>The seven "planets" of the ancient world: Sun, Moon, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note> are shown, which make their turnings in the south. For from each side of the lampstand three branches were inserted, and lamps in them, since the Sun also, like a <margin>D</margin> lampstand placed in the middle of the other wandering stars, provides light through a kind of divine music both to those above it and those below it. The golden lampstand also holds a certain enigma: it is a sign of Christ, not in its shape alone, but also because He sends light in many parts and many ways into those who believe in Him, hope in Him, and look to Him, through the ministry of those things which were first created. For they say there are seven eyes of the Lord, seven spirits resting on the rod which blossoms from the root of <margin>a</margin> Jesse. To the northern parts of the censer was placed the table upon which was the <margin>Isa. 11</margin> "proposition of loaves" <note>The Bread of the Presence or Showbread</note>, since the northern winds especially nourish the spirits. There were also certain dwellings of the churches which breathe together into one body and one assembly. Now, the things told concerning the holy Ark signify the world perceived by the intellect, <margin>B</margin> which is hidden and closed off from the common people. Furthermore, those golden images <note>The Cherubim</note>, each having six wings—or "two bears" as some would have it—signify either, or what fits better, the two hemispheres. The name "Cherubim" is intended to mean "much knowledge." But both have twelve wings, and through the Zodiac circle and the time that is carried within it, they signify the world of the senses. Of these things, I believe, the tragedy speaks when discussing nature: "And untiring time, full of a perennial flow, circles around, giving birth to itself. And the twin bears, with the swift motion of their wings, guard the Atlantic pole." Atlas, who does not suffer, can indeed be the pole, the sphere that does not err. But perhaps it is better to understand it as the "immobile age" <note>The *Aeon* or eternity</note>. I think it better, however, that the Ark—which is called *Thebotha* <note>A transliteration of the Hebrew *tebah*</note> from the Hebrew name—signifies something else. It is explained as "one for one from all places." Is it then the "ogdoad" <note>The number eight</note>, that is, the world perceived by the intellect? Or is it He who encompasses all things, who is without form and cannot be seen, a sign of God...

CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

<margin>A</margin>
...[be sancti]fied, let its discussion be deferred for the present. Furthermore, it signifies the rest that is found among the glorifying spirits, whom the Cherubim represent. For He who advised that not even a carved image should be manufactured would never Himself have fashioned an image of the saints. Nor is there any composite or sensible <note>meaning: perceptible by the physical senses</note> animal in heaven that possesses such a form. Rather, the "face" is a symbol of the soul endowed with reason. The "wings" represent the ministries and sublime operations of the powers on the right and the left.

<margin>John</margin>
The "voice," moreover, is the glory of a grateful mind, engaged in a contemplation that cannot cease. It is enough for the mystical interpretation to proceed this far. Now, the High Priest’s long robe <note>original: *vestis talaris*, a robe reaching the ankles</note> is a sign of the world of the senses. The seven gems represent the seven wandering stars <note>the five known planets plus the Sun and Moon</note>: five specific gems, and two carbuncles for Saturn and the Moon. For the former is southern, moist, earthy, and heavy, while the latter is airy. For this reason, the Moon is called by some <term>aerotomos</term> <note>original: *ἀεροτόμος*</note>,

<margin>B</margin>
which is to say, "air-cutting," because the air is dark. Divine providence rightly describes those who contribute to the generation of things here—that is, those who preside over the wandering stars—as being placed upon both the chest and the shoulders; through them, the first grouping of seven acts as the power that effects generation. The chest is the dwelling place

<margin>Psalms, Luke</margin>
of the heart and the soul. There were also gems of various kinds representing the modes of salvation, some in the higher parts and others in the lower parts of every body that attains salvation. Furthermore, the three hundred and sixty-six bells <note>likely representing the days of the year</note> hanging from the long robe represent the span of a year. I mean "the acceptable year of the Lord," proclaiming and echoing the great advent of the Savior. Moreover, the golden miter <note>original: *pileus*</note> that is stretched out signifies the royal power of the Lord, since the Savior is the head of the church.

<margin>C</margin>
<margin>1 Cor. 11</margin>
Certainly, the miter placed upon the head is a sign of sovereign command; and elsewhere we have heard: "And the head of Christ is God," the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Now, the Breastplate <note>original: *Pectorale*</note> consists of both the "shoulder-piece" <note>original: *superhumerali*, referring to the Ephod</note>, which is a symbol of work, and the "Rational" <note>original: *rationali*, the Breastplate of Judgment</note>; this latter signifies reason <note>Clement puns on the Latin *rationalis* and the Greek *logion*, connecting the ornament to the *Logos* or Word</note>, and it is an image of heaven, which was made by the Word, and is subject to Christ, the head of all things, as it moves in a similar and consistent manner. The bright emerald gems on the shoulder-piece signify the Sun and the Moon, which are the helpers of nature. The shoulder, I believe, is the origin of the arm. Those twelve gems located in four rows

<margin>Exodus</margin>
upon the chest describe for us the circle of the zodiac, corresponding to the four turnings of the year <note>the four seasons</note>. And furthermore, it was fitting that the Law and the Prophets be placed beneath the Lord's head,

<margin>D</margin>
because the righteous are signified in both testaments. For we would speak correctly in saying that the Apostles are both prophets and righteous men, since one and the same Holy Spirit works through them all. Just as the Lord is above the whole world, and even beyond the world perceived by the intellect, so also the Name <note>The Tetragrammaton, the holy name of God</note> inscribed upon the gold plate was deemed worthy to be above every principality and power. It was inscribed both because of the precepts committed to writing and because of His sensible presence. Moreover, it is called the "Name of God," since just as the Son looks upon the goodness of the Father, He works as God the Savior—He who is the beginning of all things, who was made the first Image from the God who cannot be seen, and was before the ages.

<margin>E</margin>
He prefigured all things that were made after Him. Now, the "Rational" <note>the Breastplate</note> signifies Prophecy, which cries out and proclaims through the Word, and signifies the future judgment. For the Word is the same which simultaneously foretells, judges, and discerns individual things. They say that the garment—that is, the long robe—foretells the dispensation of the flesh He took upon Himself, through which He was seen more closely in the world. For that reason, the High Priest, laying aside the sanctified tunic—whereas the world and the creatures in the world are sanctified by Him who composed all good things that were made—is washed and puts on another "holy of holies" tunic, so to speak. This tunic enters into the sanctuary with him, showing, as it seems to me, a lightness and a nature endowed with knowledge. As he

<margin>F</margin>
becomes the leader of the other priests—while they are washed with water and clothed only in faith, and await their own dwelling place—he himself, having distinguished the things of the intellect from the things of the senses, and having surpassed the other priests, hastens to penetrate...

### STROMATA, BOOK V.

<margin>A</margin> Long ago, that which is perceived by the intellect was washed away from the things of this world; it is no longer cleansed by water, as it was before when it was assigned to the three ranks of the Levitical order. But since he is now pure in his whole heart through the word of knowledge <note>original: *verbo cognitionis*</note>, and has conducted himself with great righteousness, increasing the rule of life given by the Priest at the very end, he is truly sanctified in both word and life. Clothed in the exultation of glory, he receives the secret inheritance of that spiritual and perfect man, "which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man" <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 2:9</note>. Having become a son and a friend, he is now filled "face to face" with a contemplation that can never be satisfied. But nothing is better than to hear the Word itself, which, through the scriptures, brings a greater understanding. For it says: 

<margin>B</margin> "And he shall strip off the linen garment which he had put on when he entered into the holy place, and he shall leave it there; and he shall wash his body with water in a holy place and put on his own garment." <note>A translation of the Latin version of Leviticus 16:23-24</note> In one way, I believe, the Lord strips off and puts on as He descends to the world of the senses. In another way, the one who believes through Him strips off and puts on the sanctified garment, as the Apostle also indicated. For this reason, High Priests were chosen for the image of the Lord, being those most approved from the sanctified tribe; and those who were chosen for kingship or for prophecy were anointed. 

Similarly, the Egyptians did not entrust their mysteries to just anyone; nor did they offer the knowledge of divine things to the uninitiated. They gave it only to those who were to succeed to the throne, and to those of the priests who were judged most distinguished by their upbringing, learning, and lineage. Therefore, regarding the practice of concealment, the enigmas of the Egyptians are similar to those of the Hebrews. 

<margin>C</margin> Among the Egyptians, some represent the Sun in a ship, while others show it on a crocodile. They signify that the Sun, passing through the sweet and moist air, gives birth to time—which the crocodile enigmatically signifies through a certain other priestly story. Furthermore, in Diospolis <note>The "City of Zeus," the Greek name for the Egyptian city of Thebes</note>, a city in Egypt, on the sacred temple gate called a Pylon, there is a figure of a young boy as a sign of birth, and an old man for destruction. Again, a hawk is a symbol for God, while a fish is a symbol of hatred. In another sense, the crocodile is a sign of impudence. It seems, therefore, that this entire symbol placed together signifies this: "O you who are born and die, God hates impudence." 

They also manufacture ears and eyes out of precious materials and consecrate them, dedicating them to the gods, signifying silently by this that <margin>D</margin> God sees and hears all things. Additionally, the lion is a sign of power and strength for them, just as the ox represents the earth, agriculture, and nourishment. The horse represents a spirit of greatness, virtue, and freedom; while the sphinx represents strength combined with cleverness of mind, as it has the body of a lion but the face of a human. Similarly, a man is carved by them in sacred places to represent cleverness of mind, the intellect, strength, power, and art. 

Now, in what they call the <margin>processions of the gods <note>original: *κωμάσιαι* (komasiai)</note></margin> processions of the gods, they carry golden images: two dogs, one hawk, and one ibis. They call these four images "four letters." The two dogs are symbols of the two hemispheres <note>The northern and southern halves of the celestial sphere</note>, as those which travel around and keep watch. The hawk represents the Sun, for it is fiery and has the power to destroy; thus they attribute pestilential diseases to the Sun. <margin>E</margin> The ibis represents the Moon: the dark feathers represent the shadowed part, and the white feathers represent the bright part. There are some, however, who believe the dogs signify the tropics, which guard and observe, like gatekeepers, the Sun’s approach to the South and the North. The hawk signifies the equinoctial line, which is high and scorched, just as the ibis signifies the ecliptic or zodiac <note>original: *signiferum*</note>. For the ibis seems to have provided the Egyptians with the beginning of the discovery of numbers and measures, just as it did from the oblique circles. 

But it was not only the Egyptians who were most capable in the power of reasoning; among other barbarians <note>In the Greek sense: non-Greeks</note> as well, those devoted to the study of philosophy followed this symbolic style. They certainly say that Idanthuras, King of the Scythians, as Pherecydes of Syros relates, sent a symbol instead of a letter to Darius, who had crossed the Ister <note>The river Danube</note> and was threatening war. <margin>F</margin> He sent a mouse, a frog, a bird, a javelin, and a plow. When doubt naturally arose concerning these items, Orontopagas the Tribune said they were handing over the empire, guessing that the mouse meant houses, the frog meant the waters, and the bird meant the air...

# CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

<margin>A</margin> ...from the javelin, weapons; but from the plow, the region. <note>original: "ex iaculo autem, arma: ex aratro verò regionem"</note> However, Xiphodrus <note>A philosopher known for interpreting symbols</note> interpreted this in the opposite way. For he said: "Unless we fly away like birds, or go beneath the earth like mice, or under the water like frogs, we shall not escape their weapons. For we are not masters of the land." It is also said of Anacharsis the Scythian <note>A famous 6th-century BCE Scythian philosopher who traveled to Athens</note> that while sleeping, he held his private parts with his left hand and his mouth with his right, signifying that it is necessary to restrain both, but that it is a greater thing to restrain the tongue than to restrain pleasure. And why should I linger on recounting the customs of the barbarians <note>In this context, "barbarians" refers to non-Greeks</note>, when I can show that the Greeks themselves made extensive use of hidden meanings? Certainly, Androcides the Pythagorean <note>A follower of Pythagoras who wrote on symbols</note> says that the letters called "Ephesian," <note>Ephesian Letters were ancient magical formulas or "power words" used in amulets</note> which are widely celebrated among the common people, occupy the place of symbols. He says that *Askion* <note>original: "ἄσϰιον"</note> signifies darkness, for darkness has no shadows. *Kataskion* <note>original: "ϰατάσϰιον"</note> signifies light, since it illuminates shadows. *Lix* <note>original: "λὶξ"</note> is an ancient name for the earth, and *Tetraa* <margin>B</margin> <note>original: "τετράα"</note>—that is, the number four—signifies the year, because of the four seasons. *Damnameneus* <note>original: "Δαμναμενεὺς"</note> is the Sun, who "subdues," and *Aisia* <note>original: "αἴσια"</note> means the "true voice." The symbol signifies that the divine order of things is like an adornment: darkness when compared with light, the Sun compared with the year, and the earth compared with the generation of all kinds of nature. Furthermore, Dionysius Thrax <note>Dionysius the Thracian, a famous Greek grammarian of the 2nd century BCE</note>, in his book *On the Explanation of the Symbol of the Wheels*, says in these words: "Some signified actions not only through words, but also through symbols. Through words, as in the case of the Delphic precepts: 'Nothing in excess,' and 'Know thyself,' and others similar to these. But through symbols, such as the wheel that is turned in the temples of the gods—which was derived from the Egyptians—and the branches given to those who worship." For Orpheus the Thracian <note>The legendary poet and prophet</note> says:
<margin>C</margin>
> *Of branches, for those mortals whose cares are earthly,*
> *The fates do not stand in one place in the mind, but all things*
> *Revolve around, nor is it permitted to remain in one part,*
> *Once the course has begun, truly a part is equal to each.*

<margin>D</margin> The branches, moreover, are either a symbol of the first nourishment, or they are meant to teach the common people that while fruits altogether sprout and increase, lasting for a very long time, they themselves have received only a brief span of life; for that reason, they wish branches to be given. Perhaps it is also so they may know that just as these branches are burned again, so they too will quickly leave this life and become the work of fire. Therefore, this type of symbolic interpretation is most useful for many things: contributing to correct theology and piety, judging the cleverness of the mind, practicing brevity, and demonstrating wisdom. For as the grammarian Didymus <note>Didymus Chalcenterus, a prolific Alexandrian scholar</note> aptly says, it belongs to the wise man to use symbolic language and to explain what is signified by it. Indeed, even the education of children, which focuses on the basic elements <note>term: elements (Greek: "stoicheia"), referring both to the alphabet and the physical building blocks of the world</note>, includes an interpretation of the four elements. For he says the Phrygians call water *Bedy*, as Orpheus also does:

> *And the clear water of the Nymphs, the Bedy, flows forth.*

<margin>E</margin> Furthermore, Dion Thytes, a sacrificer, seems to write in a similar way: "And taking the *Bedy*, pour it upon the hands, and turn to divination." On the other hand, the comic poet Philydeus understands *Bedy* to mean the air, which provides life, through these lines:

> *I pray that I may draw in the healthful Bedy,*
> *Which is the most vital part of health.*

"That I may draw in," he says, "pure air, not disturbed." Neanthes of Cyzicus <note>A 3rd-century BCE Greek historian</note> also agrees with this opinion, writing that the priests of the Macedonians invoke *Bedy* in their prayers to be favorable to them and their children—which they interpret as the air. Some unlearned people have taken *Zaps* to mean fire, from the word for "boiling." <note>original: "ζέσιν"</note> But the sea is called thus, as Euphorion says in his writings against Theoridas:

<margin>Zaps.</margin>
> *It had been the destruction of ships, which he urges with songs,*
> *And now the false Zaps laments in the insane sea.*

<margin>F</margin> Similarly, Cratinus the younger, a comic poet:
> *The Zaps produces both prawns and little fish.*
->And Simmias of Rhodes:<-
> *Born from the unsown fields and the Cabiri, the bitter one*
->*Is Zaps.*<-

He specifically analyzes the symbolic meanings of the elements, such as the mysterious terms "Bedy" and "Zaps," through the lens of ancient poetry and grammar.</summary>
