### THE STROMATA, BOOK V.

<sig>oo iii</sig>

<margin>A</margin> **Earth** <note>original: "χθών"</note> is the land that is spread out in great magnitude. And the **plectrum** <note>original: "πλῆϰτρον"; a tool used to pluck or strike a stringed instrument</note> is interpreted by some as the celestial pole, but by others as the air, which strikes and moves all things according to their nature and growth, or perhaps that which fills all things. However, these people have not read the philosopher Cleanthes, who explicitly calls the Sun a **plectrum**. For by supporting the radiance in the east, the Sun—as if striking the world—brings forth light into its harmonious and proper course. Through the Sun, he signifies the rest of the stars as well. Furthermore, the Sphinx is not merely the intelligence of the universe or the rotation of the world, as the poet Aratus suggests; rather, it might be the spiritual tension that pervades and contains the world. It would be better, however, to understand it as the ether, <margin>Sphinx comes from the word 'to bind' or 'to constrict.'</margin> which contains and constricts all things, just as Empedocles also says:

<margin>B</margin>
> *Come now, I shall tell you in song the beginning of the Sun,*
> *And the source from which all things we see have arisen:*
> *The earth, and the surging sea, and the moist air,*
> *Titan, and the ether that binds all things in a circle.*

But Apollodorus of Corcyra says these verses were uttered by the prophet Branchus when he was purifying the Milesians from a famine. For while sprinkling the crowd with laurel branches, he led the hymn in this manner: <margin>“Far-worker” and “Far-shooting” are titles for Apollo and Diana, so named because they act from a distance.</margin>

> *Sing, O youths, to the Far-worker and the Far-shooter.*

Then the people shouted out these words: *Bedy, Zaphs, Chthon, Plectrum, Sphinx, Knachzbi, Chtyptes, Phlegmo, Drops.* Callimachus also mentions this history <margin>C</margin> in his *Iambics*. Now, **Knachzbi** is derived from a word meaning disease, from the terms meaning to vex or cause pain, to tear apart or scatter, and to destroy or consume by lightning. Thespis the tragedian, however, says something else is signified by these terms, writing in this way: "Behold, I pour for you a libation of white *knachzbi*, which I have pressed from the milky thistles. Behold, I place before you *chtyptes* cheese, mixed with red honey, upon <margin>Thistles.</margin> <margin>During the Pandia festival.</margin> your holy altars. Behold, I pour for you the glowing lightning of Bromius <note>A title for Dionysus, the god of wine</note>." In my opinion, this signifies first the milky nourishment of the twenty-four elements of the soul, after which the food is solid milk <note>i.e., cheese</note>. Finally, he teaches of the glowing wine, the "blood of the vine" of the Word, which represents the perfecting joy of education. **Drops**, moreover, is the effective word which, from the first catechesis <note>Instruction given to new converts or students</note>—that is, the training that comes through hearing—kindles and illuminates a person toward the growth of manhood and the full measure of age. <margin>D</margin> There is also a third description for children recorded in this way: "I seize the Sphinx, the thief, the vulture of beasts." <note>original: "μάρπτω σφίγξ, ϰλὼψ, ζὺψ, θηρῶν"</note> This signifies, I believe, that through the administration of the elements and the world, we must progress toward the knowledge of more perfect things, having overcome eternal salvation through effort and labor. For "I seize" <note>original: "μάρπτω"</note> means to comprehend. The **Sphinx** represents the structure of the world. The **vulture** <note>original: "ζὺψ"</note> signifies difficulty, and the **thief** <note>original: "ϰλὼψ"</note> represents both the hidden knowledge of the Lord and the light of day. Furthermore, does not Epigenes also, in his book on the poetry of Orpheus, explain those things peculiar to Orpheus by saying that "plows with curved bodies" <note>original: "ϰερχίσι ϰαμπύλοις φῶσι"</note> signifies the rays of the sun, and "threads" <note>original: "σημῶσιν"</note> signify the furrows? He says that "thread" <note>original: "μίτον"</note> is an allegory for seed, and that the "tears of Jupiter" signify rain. <margin>E</margin> The **Fates** <note>original: "μοίρας"</note> are the phases of the Moon—the thirtieth, the fifteenth, and the new moon. Therefore, he says Orpheus calls them "white-robed" because they are parts of the light. Again, the "flowery one" <note>original: "ἄνθιον"</note> signifies spring because of its nature. Night is called "idle" <note>original: "ἀργίδα"</note> because of rest, and the Moon is called the "Gorgon" <margin>‘Argos’ means idle. ‘Aphrodite’ from ‘aphros,’ meaning foam.</margin> because of the face seen within it. And **Aphrodite** <note>The goddess of love</note> is said by the Theologian to be the time in which one ought to procreate. The Pythagoreans also used riddles of this kind, calling the wandering stars "the dogs of Proserpina" and the sea "the tear of Saturn" in an allegorical sense. We find innumerable things said enigmatically among both philosophers and poets, just as entire books indicate the hidden intent of the writer—such as the book of Heraclitus *On Nature*, who for this very reason was called "The Obscure." The theology of Pherecydes <margin>F</margin> of Syros is similar to this book. For the poet Euphorion, the *Causes* of Callimachus, the *Alexandra* of Lycophron, and other similar works are set forth like a gymnasium for all scholars to unravel. Such things Moses also commanded, so that these...

He interprets various cryptic terms as references to the sun, the elements, and the stages of spiritual education.</summary>

### CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

...duties. Not to eat pork, nor eagle, nor hawk, nor crow. For the **pork** <margin>A</margin> indeed signifies an animal dedicated to pleasure and impurity, representing a craving for food, a lustful desire in sexual matters, and a stained lack of self-control—materialistic and lying in the mud, fattening itself for its own destruction. Again, however, he permits eating those things which have a **cloven hoof** and which **ruminate** <note>original: "ruminant"; to "chew the cud," interpreted here as meditating on divine words</note>. Barnabas says <margin>In the Epistle of Barnabas <note>original: ἐν τῇ βαρνάβα ἐπιστολῇ</note></margin> this signifies that we ought to cling to those who fear the Lord and meditate in their hearts on the distinction of the word they have received: those who speak and keep the Lord’s justifications; those who know that meditation is a work of joy, and who "ruminate" on the word of the Lord. But what is it that has cloven and double hooves? It signifies that the righteous man both walks in this world and yet looks forward to the holy age to come. Then he adds: See how beautifully Moses gave the law. But from where could they have the mental capacity to think these things, unless we, rightly understanding the precepts, speak as God willed? Therefore, He circumcised our ears and hearts so that we might understand these things.

When he certainly said: "You shall not eat the eagle, the hawk, the kite, and the crow," he meant: You shall not cling to, <margin>B</margin> nor be made like, those men who do not know how to provide a living for themselves through labor and sweat, but live by robbery and iniquity. For the **eagle** signifies robbery; the **hawk** signifies injustice; and the **crow** signifies greed and the desire to possess more. Moreover, it is written: *With the innocent man you will be innocent, and with the chosen you will be chosen, and with the perverse you will be perverted.* <margin>Psalm 17 [18:26-27] <note>original: ψ. 17. 26. 27.</note></margin> It is fitting, therefore, to cling to the holy; for those who cling to them shall be sanctified. Hence Theognis writes: <margin>C</margin>

> For from the good you will learn good things, if you stay with them,
> But the wicked will destroy the character that you once had.

And again, when he says in the song: *For he is gloriously magnified; the horse and its rider he has thrown into the sea:* <margin>Exodus 15:1 <note>original: Εξοδ. 15. 1.</note></margin> he signifies that the vice of manifold and impulsive desire, along with the **Charioteer** <note>A reference to the human intellect or "reason" attempting to guide the soul</note> who had mounted it and loosened the reins on pleasures, was cast into the sea, thrown down into the tumults and disturbances of the world. So also Plato, in his book on the Soul <margin>From Plato’s Phaedrus <note>original: ἐκ τοῦ Πλάτωνος Φαίδρου</note></margin>, says that both the Charioteer and the horse that failed—the part devoid of reason, which is divided in two, namely into anger and desire—fall down. For this reason, the myth signifies that **Phaethon** <note>The son of the Sun-god who lost control of his father's chariot</note> fell from the chariot because of his lack of restraint. <margin>D</margin>

The same applies to Joseph. When his brothers envied him as a youth, as one who foresaw something greater in knowledge, they stripped him of his **varied coat** <note>the "coat of many colors," interpreted here as various types of knowledge</note> and threw him into a pit (but the pit was empty and had no water) <margin>Genesis 37:3, 23, 24 <note>original: Γεν. 37. 3. 23. 24.</note></margin>—as if they had sent away and bid farewell to the varied knowledge of a good man acquired through diligent study; or, using only the bare faith that comes from the law, they threw him into a pit empty of water, as those who had sold the one lacking the divine word into Egypt. But the pit empty of science <note>original: "scientia"; here meaning deep spiritual knowledge</note> into which he was thrown, having been stripped of his knowledge, and appearing similar to his brothers, is the wise man who had been hidden and stripped of his recognition. In another sense, the "varied garment" might be desire, which is thrown into a vast abyss.

But if anyone, he says, opens a pit or digs one and does not cover it, and a calf or an ass falls into it, the owner of the pit shall pay the price <margin>Exodus 21:33, 34 <note>original: Εξοδ. 21. 33. 34.</note></margin> and give money to the neighbor, but the dead animal shall be his. <margin>E</margin> Connect this to that prophecy for me: *The ox knows its owner, and the ass its master’s manger; but Israel has not understood me.* <margin>Isaiah 1:3 <note>original: Ησαι. 1. 3.</note></margin> Therefore, lest anyone among them, when they fall into the knowledge taught by you, is unable to contain the truth, does not obey, and falls away, be cautious in the use of the word. Close up the spring that lives in the deep for those who approach without reason, but provide a drink for those who thirst for the truth. In the case of such people, the pit—that is, the one endowed with knowledge—will be fined, as if the fault is placed on him because the other was offended and "devoured" by the magnitude of the word, being unable to contain such riches of the word; or because he led one who was a simple worker over to contemplation, <margin>F</margin> and led him away from a simple and unlabored faith. He shall give "money" to the Almighty will, rendering an account of his deed. This, then, is the type and figure of the Law and the Prophets, which existed until John. But he, even if he spoke more openly, as one who no longer...

### STROMATA BOOK V.

<margin>A</margin> ...the prophet [John the Baptist] would foretell, but he showed as already present the one who was symbolically announced from the beginning. "I am not," he said, "worthy to untie the strap of his sandal." <margin>John 1</margin> For he confesses that he is not worthy to baptize such a great power. For it is necessary for those who make themselves clean to release the soul from the body and its sins, just as a foot is released from a shackle. But perhaps it was also the final operation of the Savior toward us—the one which I say is immediate and containing—which was hidden by the enigma of prophecy. Through his presence, he who showed the very sight of Him, by signifying that He who was foretold had come openly from afar, truly untied the end of the oracles of the flesh's dispensation <note>The "flesh's dispensation" refers to the period of Christ's physical life on earth</note> by revealing the meaning of the symbols.

And those things which are done by the Romans in the making of wills have taken their place: namely, those scales and copper coins <note>original: "librae illae, & asses"; referring to the Roman legal ritual of *mancipatio* used in wills</note> for the sake of justice; the taking of fruits <margin>καρπισμοί <note>original: "karpismoi," meaning harvest or fruit-taking</note></margin>; and the touching of ears <note>original: "aurium contrectationem"; the legal act of *antestatio*, calling a witness by touching their ear</note>. The former are done so that things are done justly; <margin>B</margin> the latter for the division of honor. The third, however, is so that he who had happened to be there when the burden was imposed might stand and hear, and hold the place of an intercessor.

But, as it seems, in my excessive zeal for demonstrating this, I have progressed further than is fitting. For life would fail me if I were to lead forth the multitude of those who philosophize symbolically. Therefore, for the sake of memory and brevity, and because they reach toward the truth, such are the writings of the "barbaric" philosophy <note>Clement uses "barbaric philosophy" to refer to the Jewish and Christian scriptures, which Greeks considered non-Greek or "barbarian"</note>. For those who often approach them and have given proof of themselves in faith and in their whole life, they wish that there be only that which is truly Philosophy and true Theology. Indeed, they even wish for us to have <margin>C</margin> some interpreter and guide. For in this way, they thought that greater study would be devoted to it, and that men would be least deceived when they receive it from those who know, and that it would benefit those who are worthy of it.

Moreover, all things that are shown through a veil show the truth to be greater and more distinguished, just as things which shine through clear water, and <margin>beautiful things <note>original: "ὡραῖα" (*horaia*)</note></margin> forms which allow some evidence of themselves through coverings. For splendors, besides being manifest, suggest that they should be understood in one way. Since, therefore, it is permitted to receive things in many ways—as we certainly do in those things said with concealment—the unlearned and unskilled man is deceived; however, he who is endowed with knowledge understands. Therefore, they do not wish all things to be exposed rashly to just anyone, nor the good things of wisdom to be communicated to those whose <margin>D</margin> souls have not even been purged in their dreams. For it is not right for any passerby to seek those things which were prepared with so many struggles, nor to tell the mysteries of the Word to the profane.

They certainly say that Hipparchus the Pythagorean was accused because he had openly written the decrees of Pythagoras; he was expelled from the school, and because of this, a pillar was erected for him as if he were dead. Wherefore, even in "barbaric" philosophy, they call those "dead" who have fallen away from the doctrines and subjected the mind to the disturbances of the soul. For "what is the participation of justice and injustice," as the divine Apostle says, "or what society has light with darkness? And what is the agreement of Christ <margin>2 Corinthians 6</margin> with Belial, or what part has the faithful with the unfaithful?" For the honors of the Olympians and the dead are separate. "Wherefore, depart from the midst of them, and be separate," says the Lord, "and <margin>E</margin> touch not the unclean thing, and I will receive you, and I will be a Father to you, and you shall be sons and daughters to me."

Not only the Pythagoreans and Plato hid many things; even the Epicureans say that there are certain secrets among them, and they do not permit everyone to read those writings. Furthermore, the Stoics say that certain things were written by Zeno first which they do not easily permit their disciples to read, unless they have first made a trial of them to see if they philosophize genuinely and sincerely. The followers of Aristotle also say that of their writings, some are <term>esoteric <note>original: "ἐσωτερικὰ"; internal or secret teachings</note></term>, that is, internal; others are common and <term>exoteric <note>original: "ἐξωτερικὰ"; external or public teachings</note></term>. Moreover, those who created the mysteries, being philosophers, obscured their doctrines with myths so that they would not be manifest to all. Then, while those men were hiding human opinions and <margin>B</margin> keeping the unlearned from approaching them, was it not much more beneficial for the holy and blessed contemplation of the things that truly exist to be hidden? But neither those things which belong to the "barbaric" philosophy, nor the Pythagorean myths, nor those things in Plato’s *Republic* by Armenius, and in the *Gorgias* by Aeacus and Rhadamanthus, and in the *Phaedo* confess...

<margin>A</margin> ...the story of Tartarus <note>Referring to the myth of the afterlife in Plato’s *Phaedo*</note>, and in the *Protagoras* the story of Prometheus and Epimetheus, and furthermore the story of the war waged between the Atlanteans and the Athenians in the Atlantic—these are not to be explained allegorically in every single name, but rather in those parts which signify a universal and general meaning. Furthermore, the custom of Pythagoras and the dual relationship he had with his associates—calling some "Listeners" <note>original: "akoumatikous"</note> and others "Mathematicians" <note>original: "mathematicos"</note>, who sincerely and genuinely touched upon philosophy—signified that one thing was spoken openly, while another was hidden from the many. <margin>Opinion and True Glory <note>original Greek: "Δόξα εὔκλεια"</note></margin>
> *To pluck the mortal flowers of honors from the age,*

The Ionian Muses <note>Refers to the philosophical poets like Heraclitus</note> say clearly that the common crowd of men, and those among the peoples who seem wise to themselves, follow the poets and use laws as those who know that many are evil; but those who are the best pursue glory. But many fill and sate themselves like cattle, with the belly and the shameful parts, and with those things among us which are most foul, measuring happiness by these. And again: "According to the stewardship <note>original: "dispensationem"</note> of God which was given to me for you, that I may fulfill the word of God, the mystery which has been hidden from ages and generations, which has now been manifested to his saints, to whom God willed to make known what are the riches of the glory of this mystery among the Gentiles." Wherefore, some mysteries were hidden until the Apostles and were handed down by them as they received them from the Lord—hidden, that is, in the Old Testament, but now manifested to the saints. But another thing is the "riches of the glory of the mystery" which is among the Gentiles, which is faith and hope in Christ, whom he called elsewhere the "foundation." # CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

<margin>1 Corinthians 3</margin> <margin>A</margin> ...[the] rulers of this age who are being brought to nothing; but he speaks the wisdom of God hidden in a mystery. Then, a little further down, he teaches a warning lest his words go out to the common people, in this way: "And I, brothers, could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as fleshly people. As infants in Christ, I gave you milk to drink, not solid food, for you were not yet able, nor are you able even now, for you are still fleshly." If, therefore, milk is for infants, while solid food—the nourishment of the perfect—is spoken of by the Apostles, milk will be understood as catechesis <note>original: "catechesis," the basic oral instruction given to new converts</note>, as it were the first nourishment of the soul. But solid food is the looking upward of contemplation, which is the very flesh and blood of the Word: that is, the comprehension of divine power and essence. "Taste and see," he says, "that Christ is the Lord." <note>original: "Christus est Dominus," a variation of Psalm 34:8 often used by Clement to refer to the experience of Christ.</note> For in this way he imparts himself to those who are partakers of such spiritual food, <margin>B</margin> when the soul nourishes itself according to the opinion of Plato. For the food and drink of the divine Word is the knowledge <term>cognitio <note>The Latin translation of the Greek "Gnosis," referring here to deep, experiential spiritual knowledge</note></term> of the divine essence. For this reason, Plato also says in the second book of the *Republic*, that when we have sacrificed—not a pig, but some great and difficult <note>original: "dubium," translating the Greek "aporon," meaning a rare or hard-to-provide sacrifice</note> sacrifice—only then is it necessary to seek after God. But the Apostle says, "And Christ our Passover has been sacrificed," truly a difficult and inexplicable sacrifice, the Son of God who is sanctified for us. Now, the sacrifice acceptable to God is the separation from the body and its passions and vices. This is, in truth, the real worship of God.

<margin>1 Corinthians 5</margin> <margin>C</margin> Is it not, therefore, for this reason that philosophy was rightly called by Socrates a "meditation on death"? <note>A famous definition from Plato's *Phaedo*.</note> For he who brings neither sight into his thinking, nor draws upon any of the other senses, but applies himself to things with the pure mind itself, he pursues true philosophy. This is also the meaning of Pythagoras’s five-year silence, which he commanded of his disciples, so that, having turned away from sensible things, they might contemplate God with a naked mind. These things, therefore, were received from Moses by the most excellent of the Greek philosophers. <note>Clement frequently argues that Greek wisdom was originally "borrowed" or "stolen" from the Hebrew prophets.</note> For he [Moses] commands that when they have skinned the burnt offerings, they should divide them limb by limb; because it is necessary that the knowing soul, when it has been stripped of its material skin, without the trifles of the body and all the vices which empty and false opinions claim for themselves, having put off fleshly desires, be consecrated to the light.

But many men, putting on that which is mortal like snails, and rolled up like a ball around their own lusts and excesses, no differently than porcupines, form such opinions about the blessed and imperishable God as they hold about themselves. <margin>D</margin> They do not notice, however, that even if he is near to us, God has given us innumerable things in which he himself does not participate: such as birth, while he himself is unbegotten; nourishment, while he himself has no need of it; and growth, while he exists in equality; and the power of old age and death, while he himself is free from age and death. Therefore, let no one suppose in any way that hands, and feet, and mouth, and eyes, and comings-in, and goings-out, and angers and threats, are called "affections" <note>original: "affectiones," referring to human-like passions or physical traits attributed to God in the Bible</note> of God among the Hebrews. It is holier and more pious to say that some of these names are used allegorically, which indeed we shall explain in their own place as we proceed.

<margin>E</margin> Of all medicines, wisdom is the most health-giving. Callimachus writes in his *Epigrams*: "One is wise from another." And "both long ago and now," says Bacchylides in his *Paeans*, "for it is not easy to find the gates of obscure verses." Thus Isocrates speaks beautifully in the *Panathenaicus*, when he had first asked: "Whom, then, do I call wise?" he adds: "First, indeed, those who rightly use the things that happen every day, and whose judgment is such that it easily keeps pace with the opportunities of the times, and for the most part conjectures what is useful. Then, those who always behave honorably and justly with those they associate with, and who bear the annoyances and indignities brought by others patiently and easily, showing themselves as little burdensome as possible and most moderate to those they deal with. <margin>F</margin> Furthermore, those who rule over pleasures and are superior to them, and are not conquered by misfortunes but bear themselves vigorously in them, and in accordance with the dignity of the nature in which they share. Fourth—which indeed is the greatest—those whom prosperity does not corrupt, nor leads away to immoderation and insolence, but who remain in the ranks of those who are modest and think rightly." Then he adds the finishing touch <note>original: "colophonem," meaning the crowning stroke or completion</note> to his speech: "But those who [attain] not only to one of these, but to all these..."

<meta>catchword: all</meta>

<summary>Clement argues that deeper spiritual truths (solid food) require the soul's separation from bodily passions, a concept he finds in both the Apostle Paul and Greek philosophers like Socrates and Pythagoras. He also warns against interpreting biblical descriptions of God literally, advocating for an allegorical understanding of God's nature.</summary>

### STROMATA, BOOK V.
### Page 167

<margin>A</margin>...all have a well-composed habit of soul; I say that these are both wise and perfect men, and that they possess all the virtues. You see how even the Greeks—although they do not know how one ought to know—celebrate with divine praises the life that is led by means of knowledge <term>cognitio <note>The Latin translation of the Greek "Gnosis," referring to a deep, experiential spiritual insight rather than just factual information.</note></term>. However, they do not even in their dreams understand what true knowledge is. If, therefore, we agree that knowledge is the rational food of the soul, then those are truly blessed who, according to the Divine Scripture, hunger and thirst for the truth, for they shall be filled with eternal nourishment. Moreover, the philosopher of the stage, Euripides, is found to agree with what has been said in a most admirable way, signifying in some silent manner both the Father and the Son through these words: "To Thee, the King of all, I offer a libation and a meal-offering, O Jupiter, <margin>B</margin> or if you prefer to be called Hades. Receive for me a sacrifice, difficult and full of every offering of fruits, poured out in abundance." For the perfect and in every way absolute offering—the "difficult" sacrifice that cannot find a way out <note>original: "sacrificium dubium," likely a reference to the complexity or the profound nature of Christ's sacrifice which surpasses human understanding</note>—is Christ, sacrificed for us. And to make it plain that he [Euripides] does not know the Savior himself, he adds: "For You, wielding the scepter of Jove among the heavenly beings, also share in the rule of earthly things from the gods." Then he says openly: "Send forth light, that the souls of men who wish to know may learn from where their struggles sprouted, what is the root of evils, and which of the blessed ones, when revealed, might provide a rest from labors." It is not without reason, then, that in the mysteries performed among the Greeks, the first place is held by expiations and purifications, just as among the Barbarians <note>Clement uses "Barbarians" here to refer to non-Greeks, specifically the Hebrews and Christians</note> there is the washing [baptism]. After these are the "minor mysteries," which possess <margin>C</margin> some foundation of teaching and preparation for things to come. In the "great mysteries," however, there is nothing left to learn about the universe, but rather to contemplate and comprehend with the mind both nature and the things themselves. We may receive the method of expiation and purification through confession, and the method of contemplation through "analysis" <note>original: "resolutione," referring to the logical process of stripping away layers to reach a first principle</note>. We proceed to the first intelligence through this analysis, beginning from those things that are subject to it: first, we strip away the natural qualities from a body; then we cut away the dimension of depth, then width, and after these, length. For what remains is a "point" <note>original: "signum," here used in the geometric sense of a point having position but no magnitude</note>, which is a unity having, so to speak, a position. If, therefore, having removed all that belongs to bodies and those things called incorporeal, we cast ourselves into the magnitude of Christ, and then proceed into His vastness and immensity through holiness, we may reach in some way the understanding of the Almighty, <margin>D</margin> knowing not what He *is*, but what He *is not*. As for figure, motion, standing, a seat, a place, or the right or left hand—these are not even to be thought of concerning the Father of the universe. And yet these things are written [in Scripture]. But what each of these signifies will be shown in its proper place. The First Cause, therefore, is not in a place, but is above place, and time, and name, and understanding. For this reason, Moses also says: "Show me Thyself most clearly," <margin>Exodus 33</margin> silently indicating that God cannot be taught, nor expressed in words by men, but can only be known by that power which proceeds from Him. For the inquiry is formless and does not fall under the sight, but the grace of knowledge comes from Him through the Son. Solomon will also most clearly <margin>E</margin> bear witness to us, saying in this manner: "The prudence of man is not in me, but God gives me wisdom, and I know holy things." <margin>Proverbs 30</margin> Furthermore, Moses allegorically named the divine providence the "Tree of Life" which was planted in Paradise. This Paradise can also be understood as the world, in which all things that proceeded from creation have arisen. In it, the Word also flourished and bore fruit by becoming flesh, and He gave life to those who tasted His kindness, since it was not without the "wood" [the Cross] that He came into our knowledge. For our life is suspended upon our faith. Furthermore, Solomon <margin>Proverbs 3</margin> also says again: "It is a tree of immortality to those who take hold of it." And for this reason, <margin>Wisdom 15, Ecclesiasticus 15, Deuteronomy 30</margin> he says: "Behold, I set before your face life and death: to love the Lord your God, and to walk in His ways, and to hear His voice, and to believe in life. But if you transgress <margin>F</margin> the justifications and judgments which I have given you, you shall perish by destruction. For this is your life and the length of your days: to love the Lord your God." Again, <margin>Genesis 22</margin> when Abraham had come to the place which God told him on the third day, looking up, he saw the place from afar. For the first day is that which is made by the sight of beautiful things...

...and of honorable things. The second is the desire of the most excellent soul. In the third stage, however, the mind <margin>A</margin> clearly perceives spiritual things, with its eyes opened by the Teacher who rose on the third day. These three days may also represent the mystery of the seal <note>likely referring to the "signaculum" or seal of baptism, or the three stages of Christian initiation</note>, through which the one who is truly God is believed in. Therefore, he [Abraham] sees the place from a distance, for the region of God is difficult to grasp—that which Plato called the "region of ideas" <note>original Greek: χώραν ἰδεῶν (chōran ideōn)</note>, meaning the field and receptacle of ideas. Plato adopted this from Moses, recognizing it as the "place" which contains all things and the universe itself. Rightly, then, is it seen from a distance by Abraham, because he exists within the realm of generation <note>the physical world of birth and change</note>, and he is continually initiated into the mysteries through an Angel nearby. Hence the Apostle says <margin>1 Corinthians 13</margin>: "We see now," he says, "as if through a mirror; but then face to face," through those pure and incorporeal applications of the mind alone. It is possible for someone, in discussing <margin>B</margin> God, to divine the truth if they attempt, setting aside all senses, to strive toward that which each thing truly is, and not depart from the things that exist until—transcending those things that stand above—they have grasped that which is "The Good" by intelligence itself. Thus, they dwell at the very end of what can be apprehended by intelligence, according to the opinion of Plato. Again, Moses, by not permitting altars and shrines to be constructed in many places, but building only one temple to God, announced that the world is "only-begotten" <note>the unique, single creation</note> (as Basilides says) and that God is one (though Basilides no longer seems to see this). Because Moses, who was endowed with knowledge, did not enclose Him who cannot be contained by any place, no image was placed in the temple to be worshipped. This signified that God does not fall under human sight and cannot be circumscribed, yet he led the Hebrews toward the knowledge of God <margin>C</margin> through the honor of the Name which dwelt in the temple. Furthermore, the Word, by forbidding both the construction of shrines and all sacrifices, silently signifies that the Almighty is not contained in any particular thing, through the words he speaks in <margin>Isaiah 66</margin>: "What house will you build for me, says the Lord? Heaven is my throne," and so on. And concerning sacrifices similarly <margin>Psalm 49</margin>: "I do not want the blood of bulls, or the fat of lambs," and other things which the Spirit of the Lord forbids through the Prophet. Most beautifully, therefore, Euripides also agrees with these points, writing:

<margin>And concerning sacrifices similarly.</margin>
->What house built by craftsmen could<-
->Contain the divine body within its walls?<-
->For God lacks nothing, if he be truly God.<-

   These are the "unhappy" words of the poets <note>Clement often calls poets "unhappy" or "unfortunate" because they stumble upon truths without having the full faith</note>. For God did not make the world because he had any need, <margin>D</margin> nor does he receive honors from men, or from other "gods" and "demons" (as Plato says), as if receiving a tax from the created world—smoke from us, and from the gods and demons their own specific gifts and ministries. Most appropriately and effectively for teaching, Paul says in the Acts of the Apostles <margin>Acts 17</margin>: "God," he says, "who made the world and everything in it, being Lord of heaven and earth, does not live in temples made with hands, nor is he served by human hands as if he needed anything, since he himself gives to all life and breath and everything." Zeno, the founder of the Stoic sect, also says in his book *On the Republic* that one ought not to build temples or images. For nothing composed by human hands is worthy of the gods. He did not fear to write these words: "There will be no need to build shrines. For a shrine <margin>E</margin> that is not of great value and holy is to be considered nothing. But no work of builders and common laborers is of great value and holy." Rightly then, Plato also, knowing that the world is the temple of God, showed the citizens a single place in the city where images should be kept. Privately, however, he forbade anyone from having images of the gods. "Let no one else," he says, "consecrate sacred things to the gods." For gold and silver, both in other cities privately and in sacred things, are matters of envy. Ivory, being from a body that has lost its soul, is a profane gift. Iron and brass are instruments of war. But from wood, let a man offer whatever he wishes, provided it is joined from a single piece. Similarly with stone for common sacred use. Rightly, then, in his *Great Epistle*, he says: "For these things cannot be explained in words like other disciplines. But when there has been long use and the long custom of life in the matter itself, suddenly, like a light kindled from a leaping fire in the soul, it thereafter nourishes itself." Are these things not similar to what was said by the Prophet Zephaniah? <margin>F</margin>

<margin>A</margin>AND THE spirit TOOK me, and lifted me to the fifth heaven; and I beheld the Angels who were called Lords, and their diadem placed in the holy spirit, and the throne of each of them was seven times brighter than the light of the rising Sun, they who dwell in the temples of salvation, and praise God the ineffable, the most high. For it is difficult to find the Father and maker of this universe, and once you have found him, it is impossible to declare him to all <note>Clement is quoting Plato’s *Timaeus* 28c, a passage frequently used by early Christian writers to describe God's transcendence</note>. For he can by no means be explained in words, like other branches of study, as Plato, the friend of truth, says. For Plato had beautifully heard that the most wise Moses, ascending the mountain for holy contemplation, reached the summit of those things perceived by the intellect; necessarily discerning this, Moses forbids the whole people from ascending with him. And <margin>B</margin> when the scripture says, "Moses ENTERED into the darkness where God was," <note>original: *INGRESSVS est autem Moses in caliginem ubi erat Deus* (Exodus 20:21)</note> this signifies to those who are able to understand that God is neither visible to the eye nor can He be expressed in words. This darkness is, in reality, the unbelief and ignorance of the many, which stands in the way of the splendor of truth. <margin>C</margin><margin>2 Corinthians 12</margin> To these things spoken, the Apostle will bear witness, saying: "I knew a man in Christ caught up to the third heaven," and from there into paradise, who "heard secret words which it is not lawful for a man to speak." Thus he silently signifies that God cannot be explained in words—not by the law or fear of some precept, for he adds "it is not lawful," but signifying that by holy power God cannot be uttered. Indeed, he begins to speak above the third heaven, as it is right to initiate chosen souls into the sacred mysteries of those who are there. Now I know that in Plato (for scripture now suggests many examples to me from "barbarian philosophy" <note>Clement uses "barbarian philosophy" to refer to the Hebrew and Christian scriptures, which the Greeks considered foreign or non-Greek</note>, in accordance with my first promises, while awaiting the time) many heavens are understood. Since he certainly hesitated in the *Timaeus* whether it is necessary to think of many worlds or just <margin>D</margin> this one, he uses the names indifferently, without any distinction of term, calling it both "world" and "heaven." The phrasing goes like this: "Have we then rightly said there is one heaven, or many and infinite? It would be more correct to say one, if indeed it was made according to the model." Furthermore, in the letter of the Romans to the Corinthians <note>A reference to the letter known as 1 Clement (20:8), written from the church at Rome to the church at Corinth</note>, it is written: "The ocean is infinite, and the worlds that are after it." Following these things, the divine Apostle exclaims: "O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!" <margin>Romans 11</margin> Was this not, then, what the Prophet silently signified, commanding them to make "ash-baked breads," which are called <term>ἐγκρυφίας</term> <note>original Greek: *egkryphias*, meaning breads baked in ashes or "hidden" things</note>, that is, "hidden," signifying that the truly sacred word concerning the Unbegotten One and His powers ought to be concealed? Confirming these things in the letter <margin>E</margin><margin>1 Corinthians 2</margin> to the Corinthians, the Apostle said openly: "But we speak WISDOM among the perfect. But not the wisdom of this age, nor of the rulers of this world who are being destroyed, but we speak the wisdom of God hidden in a mystery." And again elsewhere he says: "To the knowledge of the mystery of God in Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom <margin>Colossians 2</margin> and knowledge." Our Savior Himself seals these things, saying: "To you it is given to know the mystery of the kingdom of heaven." <margin>Matthew 13</margin> And again, the Gospel says our Savior spoke the word to the Apostles in a mystery. For the prophecy says of Him: "He shall open His mouth in parables, and utter things hidden from the foundation of the <margin>Psalms 77</margin> world." Now indeed, through the parable of the leaven, the Lord also signifies this concealment. For He says: "The kingdom of heaven is like leaven, which a woman took and <margin>F</margin><margin>Matthew 13</margin> hid in three measures of meal, until the whole was leavened." For either the soul is made safe in its three parts through obedience by the spiritual power hidden in it through faith, or it means that the power of the word given to us—being both powerful and concise—secretly and latently draws to itself everyone who has received it and possessed it within themselves, and...

...gathers His whole assembled multitude into unity. <margin>A</margin> **These things, then, were most wisely written by Solon concerning God.**

> *It is not easy to see with the mind the obscure measure,*
> *Which alone holds the limits of all things.*

For the Poet of Agrigentum <note>Empedocles (c. 490–430 BCE), a philosopher who wrote in verse and claimed that God is a "sacred and unutterable mind."</note> says concerning God:

> *It is not permitted to reach Him with our eyes,*
> *Or with our hands—the way that is truly the greatest*

<margin>John 1</margin>
<margin>B</margin> And John the Apostle says: *No one has ever seen God; the only-begotten God who is in the bosom of the Father, He has made Him known.* <note>John 1:18. Clement emphasizes that the "bosom" of the Father signifies God's invisibility and inexpressibility.</note> Now, when he named the "invisible and ineffable bosom of God," some from this point have called Him the **Abyss** <note>original: *profundum*. In early Christian and Gnostic thought, the "Abyss" or *Bythos* represented the unfathomable depth of the Divine essence before creation.</note>, as one who has comprehended all things and embraced them as if in a bosom, yet whom no one can attain, and who is infinite. This discourse concerning God is indeed the most difficult to treat. For since the "first principle" of any thing is by far the most difficult to find, surely the first and most ancient principle of all is difficult to demonstrate—He who is the cause for all other things to exist and to have been made. 

For how can He be described? He is neither a genus, nor a difference, nor a species, nor an individual, nor a number; nor is He an "accident" <note>In Aristotelian logic, an "accident" is a quality that can change without changing the essence of a thing (like being tall or tan). God has no such external qualities.</note>, nor that to which something happens. Nor would anyone rightly call Him a "whole." For "whole" is a term applied to magnitude, and He is the Father of the universe. <margin>C</margin> Neither should it be said that He has parts. For the One is indivisible, and therefore it is also infinite—not intended in the sense of being impossible to pass through, but insofar as He admits no distance or dimension, and has no limit. Therefore, He is without form and cannot be named. 

And if we ever name Him—calling Him either the "One," or the "Good," or "Mind," or "Being itself," or "Father," or "God," or "Creator," or "Lord"—we do not speak as if we are producing His actual name. Rather, because of our powerlessness, we use these beautiful names so that the mind may have something to lean upon without wandering aimlessly. For none of these names by themselves signify God, but all of them together indicate the power of the Almighty. For names are derived from things present in a subject, or from the relationship things have to one another; but none of these can be applied to God. <margin>D</margin> Neither is He grasped by demonstrative science, for such science consists of things prior and better known; but nothing exists prior to the Unbegotten. 

It remains, therefore, that by divine grace and by the Word alone which proceeds from Him, we may understand that which is unknown. <margin>Acts 17</margin> Just as Paul also in the Acts of the Apostles is recorded as saying: *Men of Athens, I see that you are in every way more superstitious. For as I passed by and beheld the objects of your worship, I found also an altar on which was inscribed: To the Unknown God. Whom therefore you worship in ignorance, Him I announce to you.* Therefore, whatever falls under a name is created, whether they wish it or not. 

<margin>E</margin> Thus, whether the Father Himself draws to Himself everyone who has lived purely and progressed to the knowledge of the blessed and imperishable nature, or whether our own free will, coming to the knowledge of the good, "leaps over the barriers" (as is said in the gymnasiums)—nevertheless, the soul is not raised and does not arise without exceptional grace. It is lifted above the heights, laying aside every weight and returning to that which is its own kind. 

Plato also says in the *Meno* that virtue is given by a divine gift, as his words show: *From this consideration, O Meno, it seems to us that virtue comes by a divine lot to those to whom it comes.* Does it not seem to you that he has quietly signaled that "divine lot" as the habit of knowing that comes to everyone? <margin>F</margin> He adds more clearly: *But if we have now sought correctly in this whole discourse, virtue would neither be by nature, nor of such a kind as can be taught; but it comes by a divine lot, not without the mind, to those to whom it comes.* Therefore, wisdom given by God, which is the "virtue of the Father," encourages our free will, welcomes our faith, and rewards our care and attention with the supreme communication of the choice. Furthermore, I will bring forward Plato himself to you, who clearly wishes it to be believed...

**A** ...to be called the sons of God. For when he <note>Plato</note> spoke in the *Timaeus* concerning the gods who do not fall under our sight and are generated, he says that to speak of other spirits <note>original: *daemones*; here referring to the lesser deities or guardian spirits of Greek thought</note> and to know their origin exceeds our human powers. Instead, he says we must believe those who spoke before us, who—as they themselves claimed—were descended from the gods and clearly knew their own parents. It is therefore impossible, he argues, to lack faith in the sons of the gods, even if they speak without probable or necessary demonstrations. I do not think a more manifest testimony could be brought forward by the Greeks that our Savior, and those who were anointed for Prophecy, were indeed called the "sons of God," and that the Lord, being the true and legitimate Son, is the true witness of divine things. And for this reason, he added that it is necessary to believe them, since they are divinely inspired, even if someone—speaking in a somewhat more tragic tone—should say they do not believe.

**B** *For it was not Jupiter who had proclaimed these things.* <note>A quote from Sophocles' *Antigone*, line 450, where Antigone argues that human laws do not override the unwritten laws of the gods.</note>
But let him know that God Himself has proclaimed the Scriptures through His Son. Moreover, he is worthy of belief <margin>Matthew 11</margin> who announces his own things, because "No one," says the Lord, "knows the Father, except the Son, and him to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him." Therefore, this must be believed even according to Plato’s opinion, even if it is proclaimed and spoken through the Old and New Testaments without "probable and necessary demonstrations." "For if you do not believe," says the Lord <margin>John 8</margin>, "you will die in your sins." <margin>John 3</margin> Conversely: "He who believes has eternal life." <margin>Psalm 2</margin> "Blessed, therefore, are all who trust in Him." Now, to have "trust" <note>original: *fiduciam*; a deeper, more personal confidence than simple intellectual assent</note> is something greater than faith alone.

**C** For when anyone has known that our Teacher is the Son of God, he conceives a trust that his doctrine is true. And just as doctrine—according to the opinion <margin><term>phrenes</term></margin> <note>original Greek: *φρένες*; the mind or the "seats of the soul," often translated as the heart or diaphragm in early physiology</note> of Empedocles—increases the "inner heart," so trust in the Lord increases faith. And we say it is the way of those people <note>referring to Epicureans or certain Sophists</note> to disparage philosophy, to attack faith, to praise injustice, and to consider the "blessed life" to be one led by desire and lust. But truly, faith—even if it is a voluntary assent of the soul—is nevertheless a worker of good things and the foundation of just action. But if Aristotle should dispute this with his technicalities, <margin><term>poiein / prattein</term></margin> <note>Clement distinguishes between *poiein* (to make/produce) and *prattein* (to act/do). Aristotle argued that "making" is found in animals and inanimate things, but "acting" involves moral choice and belongs only to humans.</note> teaching that "making" is found even in beasts and inanimate objects, but that "acting" belongs to humans alone, let him correct those who say that God is the "maker" of the universe. For that which is "acted," he says, is either good or necessary. To do an injury, therefore, is not "good."

**D** For no one does an injury except for the sake of something else. Moreover, among those things which are "necessary," nothing is voluntary. To do an injury is voluntary; therefore, it is not "necessary." The good differ from the wicked most especially in their habits, their choices, and their good desires. For every wickedness of the soul occurs with a lack of self-control, and he who acts through passion acts through lack of control and wickedness. It occurs to me, therefore, to admire that divine voice in every detail: <margin>John 10</margin> "AMEN, amen, I say to you, he who does not enter the sheepfold through the door, but climbs up another way, he is a thief and a robber. But he who enters through the door is the shepherd of the sheep; to him the gatekeeper opens." Then, pursuing the matter, the Lord says: "I am the door of the sheep." It is necessary, therefore, for those who have learned the truth through Christ to be saved, even if they have practiced the philosophy of the Greeks. For now it is openly shown: "What had not been made known to other generations has now been revealed to the sons of men."

**E** For the manifestation of God as the one Almighty was entirely natural among all who are truly wise; and many who did not completely cast off all shame toward the truth have grasped this eternal benefit from divine providence. And to speak briefly, Xenocrates of Carthage does not abandon all hope that even in animals devoid of reason there is some knowledge of God. Democritus, moreover, even if he were unwilling, will confess it by the logical consequence of his own doctrines. For he made those same "images" <note>original: *imagines*; Democritus's *eidola*, or atomic films that convey information to the senses</note> which strike humans and animals devoid of reason to be derived from the divine essence. Certainly, man is far from being devoid of a divine notion, for it is written that he was a participant in "inspiration" at his creation, as one who participated in a purer essence than other living creatures. Hence Pythagoras says that the mind

**F** comes to men by "divine lot," as Plato and Aristotle also confess. But we say that the Holy Spirit is "breathed into" the one who has believed. The Platonists, however, say that the "Mind"—which is an outflowing from a divine lot—dwells in the soul, and they place the soul in the body. For it was openly said by Joel, who was one of the twelve Prophets...

<margin>A</margin>
"To find the Father and Maker of this universe is difficult," <note>original: "Patrem huius vniuerfi inuenire est difficile"; a famous quote from Plato's *Timaeus* 28c.</note> not only because he shows the world to have been created, but also because he signifies it was brought forth from Him, as a son. He calls Him the Father because He is the one by whom it was solely begotten, and who established it out of that which did not exist. The Stoics also maintain that the world was created. Furthermore, that which is frequent in the barbarian philosophy—I mean the devil, the prince of demons—Plato calls a "maleficent soul" in the tenth book of the *Laws*, using these words: "Is it not necessary that the Soul which manages all things that are moved everywhere, should also manage the heavens?" He said: "What then? One or more? More; I will answer for you. We must posit no fewer than two: namely, the one that is beneficent, and the one that is capable of effecting the opposite." Similarly, he also writes these things in the *Phaedrus*: "And there are indeed other evils as well. But <margin>B</margin> some demon has mixed pleasure into most of them for the present moment." Furthermore, <margin>Ephesians 6</margin> in the tenth book of the *Laws*, he openly demonstrates that Apostolic saying: *Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the spiritual forces of those things which are in the heavens.* <note>Clement is correlating Plato's "cosmic battle" between good and evil souls with the spiritual warfare described by St. Paul.</note> Writing in this manner: "Since we have granted among ourselves that the heaven is full of many good things, but also of their opposites—and more of those that are not of that [good] kind—we say there is a kind of immortal fight, one which requires great caution." And again, the barbarian philosophy knows one world which is perceived by the intellect <term>intelligible world; the realm of ideas</term>, and another which is sensible <term>sensible world; the physical world perceived by the senses</term>. The former is the archetype, while the latter is the image of that which is called the exemplar. He <margin>C</margin> attributes the former to the Monad <note>original: "vnitati"; the number one, signifying unity and the divine</note>, as it is perceived by the intellect; but this sensible one he attributes to the number six. For among the Pythagoreans, the number six is called "marriage," as it is the generative number. <note>In Pythagorean numerology, 6 is the first "perfect number" and associated with the creation of the physical world.</note> In Unity, God established the invisible heaven and the holy earth, and the light perceived by the intellect. *For in the beginning,* it says, *God made the heaven and the earth. But the earth was invisible.* <note>Genesis 1:1–2. Clement uses the Septuagint's Greek phrasing where the earth is "invisible and unformed" to support his theory of an "intelligible" first creation.</note> Then he adds: *And God said, "Let there be light," and there was light.* In the birth of the sensible world, however, a "solid" heaven is fabricated. That which is solid is sensible; as are the visible earth and the light that is seen. Does it not seem to you that from this source, Plato leaves the "ideas" of living creatures in the world perceived by the intellect, and generates the sensible forms and those things perceived by the intellect to be fabricated? Therefore, Moses rightly says that the body was formed from the earth—which <margin>D</margin> Plato calls an "earthly tabernacle"—but the soul endowed with reason was breathed into the face from above. For here they say the "ruling faculty" <term>hegemonikon; the principal part of the soul</term> is located. They interpret this as the entrance of the soul into the First-Formed man through the addition of the senses; and therefore, man was made in the "image and likeness." For the image of God is the Divine and Royal Word <note>The Logos</note>, the impassible man; but the "image of the image" is the human mind. If you wish to take this "assimilation" <note>likeness to God</note> by another name, you will find in Moses what is called "divine consequence." For he says: *Walk after the Lord your God, and keep His commandments.* I believe that all who are endowed with virtue are seekers and worshippers of God. From this, the Stoics said that the end of Philosophy is "to live according to nature"; but Plato called it "assimilation to God," as we showed in the second book of the *Miscellanies*, and Zeno the Stoic took that from Plato. But Plato, <margin>E</margin> taking it from the barbarian philosophy, says that all good men are friends to one another. For Socrates says in the *Phaedrus*: "It is not destined or fated that the evil man should be a friend to the evil, nor that the good man should not be a friend to the good." Indeed, he sufficiently proved in the *Lysis* that friendship could never be preserved in injustice and wickedness. And the Athenian Guest <note>The main speaker in Plato's *Laws*.</note> similarly says that an action is dear and consequent to God, and follows one ancient reason: when it is moderate, for immoderate things are not friends to the moderate. "But God shall be for us the measure of all things." Then again, he adds further below: <margin>F</margin> "For every good man is like the good man. And by that reasoning, he who is like God is also a friend to that which is good, and to God." While I am on this topic, I am also reminded of that other saying. For he says at the end of the *Timaeus* that it is necessary "to assimilate the one who understands to that which is understood, according to his ancient nature." And when he has achieved this assimilation, he possesses "the goal of the best life, which has been proposed by the Gods to man, both for the present time and for the future."

Now, to speak once and for all, Democritus writes that there are few men under the light who stretch out their hands here—to what we Greeks now call the "Air." But more mystically, Pindar the Boeotian—as one who was a Pythagorean—says: "There is one race of men [and of gods] inspired by divinity; from one mother we both draw our breath." <note>Pindar, *Nemean Odes* 6.1.</note> He means that matter is delivered over, and there is one worker of it, whom he calls <term>ἀρισοτέχνην</term> <note>original Greek: <term>aristotechnēn</term></note>

<margin>E</margin> that is, the "most excellent and best craftsman," who also provided progress toward divinity according to merits. <margin>F</margin> I say nothing of Plato. He clearly, in his letter to Erastus and Coriscus, seems somehow to show the Father and the Son from the Hebrew Scriptures, when he exhorts them to take an oath, applying themselves with a zeal not foreign to the Muses...

# CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

<margin>A</margin> ...and by the sisterly pursuit of discipline, you should swear by God himself, the cause of all things, and the Lord, the Father of both the leader and the cause, whom you will understand if you have philosophized correctly. <note>Clement is likely referencing Plato’s *Sixth Epistle*, where he speaks of swearing by the "God who is the leader of all things."</note> And in that assembly which occurs in the *Timaeus*, he calls the Father the "Artisan," saying: *Gods of gods, of whom I am the father and the maker of works.* <note>original Latin: "Dei Deorum quorum ego sum pater & opifex operum." This is Plato’s *Timaeus* 41a.</note> Therefore, when he also says, "All things are around the King of all, and all things are for His sake," calling Him the cause of all things—and "the second around the second things, and the third around the third"—I do not understand this in any other way than that the Holy Trinity is being signified. For the "third" is the Holy Spirit, while the "second" is the Son, through whom all things were made according to the will of the Father. Furthermore, the same author mentions this in the tenth book of the *Republic*. He speaks of Er, the son of Armenius, a Pamphylian by birth, who is <margin>B</margin> Zoroaster. <note>Plato’s "Myth of Er" is found at the end of the *Republic*. Clement here identifies Er with the Persian prophet Zoroaster, a common syncretic belief in late antiquity.</note> Indeed, Zoroaster himself certainly writes these things: *Zoroaster, son of Armenius, a Pamphylian by birth, wrote this. Having died in war, while I was among those below, I learned from the Gods.* Plato says that this Zoroaster came back to life after he had been placed on the funeral pyre for twelve days. And perhaps this silently signifies a resurrection, or perhaps it signifies that souls take their path toward assumption through the twelve signs of the zodiac. He also says that the same path is the descent into generation. For that reason, one must consider that the twelve labors of Hercules were of a similar nature, after which the soul obtains liberation from the entire world. I also acknowledge Empedocles, who mentions the restoration <term>instauratio; Greek: apokatastasis; the return of all things to their original state</term> of the universe in a very naturalistic way, specifically that there will one day be a change into the essence of fire. Heraclitus of Ephesus is most clearly of this <margin>C</margin> opinion, since he judged that while one world is eternal, he knew the other would perish—namely, the one that consists of various and manifold ornamentation, as it is not different from the one that exists in a certain state. Moreover, he made it plain that he knew the world to be eternal, which is like the seed of the world's arrangement, saying: *No god or man made this same world of all things. But it always was, and is, and shall be an ever-living fire, kindling in measures and extinguishing in measures.* <note>A famous fragment of Heraclitus (DK B30).</note> That he thought it both had an origin and would fall into destruction is signified by what follows: *The transformations of fire: first, the sea. Of the sea, half is earth, and half is lightning.* <note>Heraclitus DK B31.</note> For by "virtue and power," he means that from the administering Word and God, the fire—namely all things—are <margin>D</margin> converted through the air into the liquid state, which is like the seed of the world's arrangement, and which he calls the "sea." From that, in turn, the earth and heaven and those things contained in them are born. How it returns again to its former state and turns to fire, he clearly shows through these words: *The sea is poured out, and it receives its measurement in the same proportion as existed before it became sea.* Similarly, he says the same regarding the other elements. The most learned of the Stoics also bring forth similar decrees when treating the "conflagration" <term>conflagratio; Greek: ekpyrosis; the Stoic belief that the universe is periodically destroyed by fire</term> and the administration of the world, and concerning the world which is eternally of such a quality, and concerning man, and the persistence of our souls. Furthermore, Plato, in the seventh book of the *Republic*, called the day we have here "nightly," on account of the "rulers of this darkness," as I perceive it. <note>A reference to the Allegory of the Cave, combined with the biblical "rulers of darkness" from Ephesians 6:12.</note> He interprets sleep and death as the descent of the soul into the body, in the same manner as Hera- <margin>Psalm 3.</margin> <margin>E</margin> clitus. Did the Spirit not predict this regarding the Savior, speaking through David? *I slept and was in a deep slumber; I was awakened, for the Lord will uphold me.* <note>Psalm 3:5. Clement interprets the "sleep" of the Psalmist as the Incarnation of Christ.</note> For he calls allegorically not only the resurrection of Christ an "awakening from sleep," but also the descent of the Lord into the flesh a "sleep." Now truly the same Savior commands, "Watch," <note>Matthew 25:13.</note> as if he were saying: "Practice how to live, and try to separate the soul from the body." Plato also divines the "Lord's Day" in the tenth book of the *Republic* through these words: *After seven days have passed for those who were in the meadow, it is necessary for them to depart on the eighth day and to arrive on the fourth day.* <note>Plato, *Republic* 614b-616b. Clement links the "eighth day" to Sunday, the day of Resurrection.</note> And by "meadow," one must understand the fixed sphere as a mild, calm, and kind place, the place of the pious and holy. The "seven days" refer to each movement of the seven wandering stars <note>The seven planets of antiquity.</note> <margin>F</margin> and every art of operation which tends toward the goal of rest. But the journey which happens after the wandering stars leads to heaven—that is, the eighth movement and the eighth day. He says that the souls depart on the "fourth day," signifying the journey made through the four elements. <meta>This page continues Clement’s argument that Greek philosophers and poets—including Hesiod, Homer, and Plato—possessed a "stolen" or divinely inspired glimpse of the truth found in the Hebrew Scriptures, specifically regarding the sacredness of the seventh day (the Sabbath) and the nature of the one true God.</meta>

# THE MISCELLANIES, BOOK V

<margin>A</margin> The cycle of the world turns back upon itself for all living things that are born and for all that are produced by nature. Hesiod indeed speaks of it in this way:
> *The first day is sacred, then the fourth and the seventh are sacred.* <note>Original: "Prima dies sacra est, tum quarta & septima sacra." This refers to Hesiod’s *Works and Days*, 770.</note> And again:
> *On the seventh day, there was again the brightest light of the Sun.* And Homer says:
> *But then the sacred day arrived, the seventh,*
> *And the seventh was sacred.* And again:
> *It was the seventh day, in which all things were completed.* And again:
> *On the seventh light, we depart from the banks of the Acheron.* <note>Clement is quoting lines attributed to Homer and Hesiod that were commonly cited by early Christian writers to prove the Greeks recognized the Sabbath, though some of these verses do not appear in modern editions of the *Iliad* or *Odyssey*.</note>

Furthermore, the poet Callimachus also writes:
<margin>B</margin>> *On the seventh day, all things were made perfect.* And again:
> *The seventh is among the good; the seventh is his birthday.* And:
> *The seventh is among the first; the seventh is perfect.* And:
> *In the starry heavens, seven things were made perfect*
> *By the spheres, which revolve through all the appearing years.*

Moreover, the elegies of Solon <note>Solon (c. 630 – c. 560 BCE) was an Athenian statesman and poet, one of the Seven Sages of Greece.</note> greatly celebrate the number seven. But what of this? Does not Plato—in a manner almost prophetic of the salvation-giving plan of God—speak similarly to the Scripture that says, *Let us take away the just man from us, for he is useless to us*? <note>Clement is referencing Isaiah 3:10 or Wisdom of Solomon 2:12.</note> In the second book of the *Republic*, Plato says: *The just man who is thus disposed will be scourged, tortured, bound, have his eyes dug out, and finally, having suffered every evil, he will be impaled.* <note>original Latin: "suspēdetur," literally "hung" or "crucified." Clement views this description of the "perfectly just man" in Plato's *Republic* (361e) as a pagan prophecy of the crucifixion of Christ.</note> And Antisthenes the Socratic, expressing that prophetic voice <margin>Isaiah 40.</margin> which says, *To whom have you likened me? says the Lord,* states that God is like no one else, because no one can learn of Him from a likeness or an image. Xenophon of Athens also says similar things in these words: "He who shakes all things and brings them to rest is clearly manifest as one who is great and powerful; yet what form He possesses is not apparent. Neither indeed does the Sun, which seems to illuminate all things with its light, permit itself to be seen. But if anyone tries to gaze upon it impudently, he is deprived of his eyes."
> *For what flesh could see with its eyes the heavenly,*
> *True, and immortal God, whose seat is in the height of heaven?*
<margin>D</margin>> *No mortal will be able to look upon the rays of the Sun*
> *With fixed eyes from its rising.* As the Sibyl <note>The Sibyls were ancient prophetesses; Clement frequently quotes the "Sibylline Oracles," which were often Jewish or Christian compositions using a pagan Greek prophetic persona.</note> foretold.

Rightly, then, Xenophanes of Colophon <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher (c. 570 – c. 478 BCE) famous for his critique of human-like gods.</note> also teaches that God is one and incorporeal, adding:
> *One God is greatest among the race of gods and men,*
> *Who is like mortals neither in body nor in mind.* And again:
> *But mortals believe that they have given birth to gods,*
> *And that they use their own clothing, voice, and body.* And again:
> *If oxen and lions had hands for tools,*
> *And were able to paint and perform the arts of men,*
<margin>E</margin>> *If the form of the gods were to be depicted by them,*
> *They would make such forms and bodies for them*
> *As nature had given to their own bodies.*

Therefore, let us again hear the lyric poet Bacchylides speaking of the divine nature: "They are indeed far removed from diseases and are untamable, sharing in no crime, and in no way like men." And Cleanthes the Stoic, who writes these things about God in a certain poem:
> *You ask what the nature of the Good is? Hear it from me:*
> *It is that which is ordered, religious, and pious,*
> *Just, self-controlled, decorous, and useful,*
<margin>F</margin>> *That which is severe, grave, always beneficial,*
> *Free from fear, grief, and trouble,*
> *Helping, pleasing, and beautifully consistent with itself.*

### STROMATA, BOOK V.

<margin>A</margin> ...the meeting of light and darkness. Both Euphorion and Aeschylus <note>Euphorion of Chalcis (3rd century BCE) and Aeschylus (c. 525–456 BCE) were Greek poets; the latter is the famous tragedian.</note> speak most gravity concerning God:
> Jupiter is the ether, Jupiter is the earth,
> Jupiter is the sky and all things, and whatever is above them.

I know that Plato also agrees with Heraclitus, who writes: "The One, which alone is wise, does not want and yet does want to be called by the name of Jupiter <note>Original: *nomen Iovis*. Clement refers to the Greek *Zeus*, noting that for Heraclitus, the supreme principle both fits and transcends traditional religious names.</note>." And again: "It is law and counsel to obey the One." If you wish to draw that saying toward a deeper spiritual meaning <note>original: *sensum anagogicum*</note>—"He who has ears to hear, let him hear"—you will find it declared thus by the Ephesian <note>Heraclitus of Ephesus.</note>: "Those who heard without understanding are like the deaf. The common saying testifies that they are absent even when present." But do you wish to hear of a single Principle from the Greeks as well? Timaeus of Locri <note>A Pythagorean philosopher featured in Plato’s dialogues.</note>, in his work *On
<margin>B</margin> Nature*, provides testimony to me in these words: "The one Principle of all things is unbegotten. For if it were begotten, it would no longer be the principle, but rather those things from which it was begotten would be the principle." From that source, indeed, the true opinion flowed forth: "Hear, O Israel, the Lord your God is one, and Him alone shall you serve."
> Behold, He is clear to all, bright and open, unerring.

### MISCELLANIES, BOOK V.

<margin>A</margin>
> *The earth shall remain, yet be deserted, for it*
> *Shall not produce feathered leaves, being scorched by fire.*
> *But thereafter, it shall preserve all things which it had lost.*

We find things similar to these written in the Orphic works in this manner:

> *For those whom he had hidden, he sent back again*
> *From his sacred heart into the joyful light, all full of care.*

If we live in a holy and just manner, we are indeed blessed here, but after our departure from this life, we are more blessed; not that we are happy only for a time, but that we are able to rest for eternity.

> *Dwelling together with the gods above: at the same table*
<margin>B</margin>
> *Where the brave Danaans <note>original: "Danai"—a common Homeric term for the Greeks.</note> are, enjoying a common lot.*

So says the philosophical poetry of Empedocles. There will be no one so great, even according to the opinion of the Greeks, that he may surpass justice, nor anyone so small that he may remain hidden. Moreover, the same Orpheus says these things as well:

> *But looking toward the divine Word, persist*
> *Entirely in it, and correct the cravings of your mind.*
> *Walking the straight path, look only upon the immortal*
> *King of Heaven.*

And again, speaking of God and saying that He does not fall under the gaze of the eye, he says that He was known to only one of the Chaldean race—either meaning Abraham by this, or his son—in these words:

<margin>C</margin>
> *Save for one, to whom a lineage is derived*
> *From the Chaldean race, he knew the stars of heaven*
> *And their paths, and how the sphere is moved*
> *In a circle, and revolves around the earth upon its axis.*
> *And how a Spirit rules this, both in the air and in the pouring sea.*

Then, he joins to this that verse: "Heaven is my seat, and the earth the footstool of my feet." <note>A reference to Isaiah 66:1.</note>

<margin>I think while on high.</margin>
> *But he himself is constant and firm in great Olympus.*
> *To him belongs a golden throne, and the earth is beneath his feet.*

> *Of the Ocean, and within him, his anger shakes*
<margin>D</margin>

> *He himself is in the heavens, and embraces the entire earth.*

> *It is not permitted for you to speak otherwise, for the limbs tremble.*

And those things which follow in order. For through these verses, he signified all those Prophetic sayings. "If you should open the heavens, trembling shall seize the mountains because of you; and they shall melt, just as wax melts from the face of fire" <note>Referencing Isaiah 64:1.</note>; and through Isaiah: "Who has measured the heaven with a span, and the earth with his fist?" <note>Referencing Isaiah 40:12.</note> Again, when he says: <margin>Isaiah 40.</margin>

> *Whom the Fates obey, even though he softens them not.*

> *Your order is perpetual, following your commands.*

> *Arriving with icy clouds, which your power divides.*

Then he adds, openly calling God the Almighty:

> *To speak of him alone as free from destruction and immortal*
> *Is possible only for those to whom it is innate to lack death.*
