<meta>This page continues Clement of Alexandria’s argument that Greek philosophers and poets derived their best insights from "barbaric" (specifically Hebrew) sources. On the previous page, Clement cited Aeschylus and the Psalms to show a shared recognition of God’s power; here, he expands this to include the concepts of providence, divine naming, and free will across different cultures.</meta>

<page-num>184</page-num>
<header>CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA</header>

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>Consider that those qualities which are most beautiful and exist in themselves must necessarily be present to Him.</margin>
<margin>A preconceived expression <note>original Greek: κατά πρόληψιν φράσιν</note>, which signifies a concept of the mind voiced according to the movement of the soul.</margin>
His most general operations have reached everyone equally. However, those among the Greeks who were the most inquisitive philosophers—moved by "barbaric" philosophy <note>Clement uses "barbaric philosophy" to refer to the ancient Hebrew scriptures and wisdom, which he argues predates Greek thought.</note>—ascribed providence to Him who cannot be seen, who is the only one, the most powerful, the greatest artisan, and the primary author of all that is beautiful. Yet, they remained ignorant of the consequences of these truths unless they were instructed by us. Nor did they understand how it is in our nature to perceive God through the mind, except, as we have often said, through His own clear and true revelation. Therefore, the Apostle <note>Saint Paul</note> rightly says: "Is He the God of the Jews only, and not also of the Greeks?" He says this not only to prophesy that those Greeks who believe will come to know God, but also to signify that while He was indeed the Lord and God of all by His power—truly the Almighty—He was not the Lord of all in terms of their *knowledge* of Him.

<margin>B</margin>
For they did not know what He is, nor how He is Lord, Father, and Creator, nor did they know any other part of the "economy" <note>original Latin: œconomiam; here referring to the divine plan or arrangement of truth</note> and dispensation of truth, unless they learned it from the truth itself. Similarly, the words of the Prophets carry the same weight as the words of the Apostle. For Isaiah says: *But if he says: "We trust in the Lord our God," now join yourselves with my Lord the King of the Assyrians.* And he adds: *And now we have not ascended into this region to war against it without the Lord.*

<margin>Jonah 1</margin>
Even the prophet Jonah himself silently signifies the same when he says: *And the one who governed the prow <note>the ship’s captain</note> approached him and said: "Why do you snore? Arise, call upon your Lord God, that he may save us, and we may not perish."* By saying "your God," he spoke to one who knew God through recognition; but by saying "that God may save us," he signified the consensus of the nations who

<margin>C</margin>
had turned their minds toward the Almighty, even though they had not yet believed. And again the same prophet says: *And he said to them: "I am a servant of the Lord, and I fear the Lord God of heaven."* And again: *And they said: "By no means, Lord, let us not perish for the sake of this man’s life."*

<margin>Malachi 1</margin>
The prophet Malachi openly shows God saying: *I will not accept a SACRIFICE from your hands, for from the rising of the sun to its setting, my name is glorified among the nations; and in every place, a sacrifice is offered to me.* And again: *For I am a great King, says the Lord Almighty, and my name is celebrated among the nations.* What kind of name? Among those who have believed, it is the Son signifying the Father. But among the Greeks, it is the Creator God.

<margin>D</margin>
Plato demonstrates free will through these words: *Virtue is subject to no master; as each person honors or despises it, so shall they participate in it. The fault lies with the one who chooses; God cannot be blamed.* <note>Quoting Plato’s "Republic," Book X.</note> *O warlike Trojans,* says the lyric poet, *Jupiter, the ruler of the gods who sees all, is not the cause of evils for mortals. Instead, a choice is set before all men to seize justice—chaste, holy, and the companion of Good Order <note>term: Eunomia; the personification of good law</note> and wise Justice <note>term: Themis; the personification of divine right or law</note>. O children, blessed are those who have now found her living as a companion.* Pindar openly introduces the Savior <note>God</note> living together with Themis, interpreting the "Just Savior King" in this way: *First, the heavenly Themis, endowed with good counsel, was led by the Fates in golden horses from the cliffs of Ocean to the venerable stairs of Olympus, along a rich path, to be the ancient consort of the Savior.*

<margin>E</margin>
*She, with golden reins, bearing splendid fruit, gave birth to the good Saviors.* Therefore, he who does not believe the truth, but is inflated by human doctrine, is wretched and unhappy. As Euripides says, *He who sees these things and does not perceive God in his mind, but casts far away the twisted deceits of high-flown disputation, which an untamed tongue hurls recklessly—participating in no certain opinion regarding things unseen—let him,* I say, *approach the true discipline and hear Parmenides of Elea promising:*

<margin>F</margin>
> *You shall know the ethereal nature, and all the signs*
> *In the ether, and the most bright lights of the sacred sun,*
> *Which is a truly obscure matter, and from where they were born.*
> *And you shall know the great deeds of the Moon in its orbits,*
> *And its nature; and the sky which encircles the world.*

> *For from here, that harsh Necessity has escaped.*

And consider Metrodorus, who, although he was an Epicurean, spoke these things divinely: "Remember, O Menestratus, that since you are mortal and have received a limited life, your soul may ascend until you behold eternity and the infinity of things—both those that shall be and those that have been. This is when, with the blessed choir (following Plato’s thought), we shall contemplate the happy vision and spectacle; we following with Jupiter <note>original: "Ioue," referring here to the Greek Zeus</note>, and others with other gods. We shall perform and celebrate the most blessed mysteries <note>Clement uses the language of Greek mystery cults to describe Christian spiritual heights</note>, being ourselves whole and free from the sufferings of evils which awaited us in later times. We shall gaze upon and contemplate whole and quiet visions in pure light, being ourselves pure, and by no means sealed in this which we now carry about and call a 'body,' bound to it like an oyster to its shell."

<margin>B</margin>
The Pythagoreans, moreover, call the heaven the <term>ἀντίχθονα</term> <note>original: "antichthona," meaning the "Counter-Earth," a hypothetical body in Pythagorean cosmology</note>, which is to say, the earth situated opposite. Concerning this earth, the Lord says through Jeremiah: "I will place you among the children, and give you a chosen land, the inheritance of God the Almighty"; those who have been heirs of this shall be the kings of the earth. Countless other examples flow to my mind that could be added, but so that there may be a limit to my speaking, I will bring an end to this discourse, lest that happens to us which the tragic poet Agatho says:

> *That which is said in passing, as if it were the main point,*
> *They value and pursue with great diligence.*

Since, therefore, it has been clearly shown, as I believe, how the Greeks are to be understood as "thieves" <note>Clement refers to the idea that Greek philosophers "stole" their best ideas from the Hebrew prophets</note> as spoken by the Lord, I shall gladly move past the dogmas of the philosophers. For if we were to pursue

We will, nonetheless, necessarily touch upon this contemplation when we collect the opinions of the Greeks concerning first principles. But from what has been said, we may also silently consider how the books of the Greeks are to be read, and who knows how to swim through their waves.

> Happy is he who possesses the riches of a divine mind,

CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA
A
<meta>catchword: tia,</meta>

# THE SIXTH BOOK OF THE MISCELLANIES.

<image-desc>A decorative historiated drop cap 'H' containing a woodcut illustration of a man, possibly a scholar or saint, seated in a lush landscape with trees and foliage, appearing to be in contemplation or reading.</image-desc>

Now, these sixth and seventh books of the Commentaries—which belong to the true philosophy—provide an informative shaping of knowledge <note>original: "cognitionem informatium," referring to the structured pursuit of spiritual insight</note>, called the *Stromateus* <note>The title *Stromata* means "Patchwork" or "Miscellanies," reflecting the intentionally varied and unorganized nature of the text</note>. Having described the moral reasoning handed down in these books as much as possible, and having shown the way of life of the person who is endowed with knowledge <term>Gnostic</term> <note>original: "cognitione præditus." Clement uses this term for the advanced Christian who possesses deep spiritual understanding, distinct from the later "Gnostic" heretical movements</note>, it proceeds to show philosophers that such a man is by no means impious or a stranger to the religion of God, as some have supposed. Rather, he alone is truly pious and rightly engaged in the worship of God. This work summarizes the religious mode of the one endowed with knowledge, which serves to warn and call to mind truths that ought to be printed <note>original: "imprimendam," here meaning "imprinted" on the soul or committed to writing</note> without danger. <margin>John 5. Isaiah 32. C</margin> For the Lord commanded us to "work for the food that remains for eternity." And elsewhere the Prophet says: "Blessed is he who sows upon every water, which the calf and the donkey tread upon," referring to the people gathered into one faith from both the Law and the Gentiles. <margin>Rom. 14.</margin> "But he who is weak eats vegetables," as the famous Apostle says. Previously, *The Tutor* <note>original: "Pædagogus," referring to Clement’s earlier work, *The Instructor*</note>, which we divided into three books, showed the education and training given from childhood; that is, the doctrine handed down from basic instruction <term>catechesis</term> or from hearing, which increases alongside faith. It provides a shaping of life and prepares the soul, endowed with virtue, for those who are counted among the ranks of men, so that they may receive the science that provides true knowledge. Since the Greeks will evidently learn from what we say here that they behave impiously when they wickedly persecute the man who is pious and a true worshiper of God, <margin>D</margin> then—proceeding in accordance with the style and form of the *Miscellanies*—we must resolve the doubts raised against us by both Greeks and barbarians regarding the coming of the Lord. Indeed, in a meadow, flowers of various kinds bloom, and in an orchard, the planting of trees is not separated by species from those of a different kind—even if some, having gathered various scholarly collections, have written works titled *Meadows*, *Helicons*, *Honeycombs*, or *Robes*. Instead, my description in the *Miscellanies* is varied like a meadow, as ideas have come to my mind, neither purged by strict order nor refined in diction, but intentionally scattered. Since things are so, these Commentaries will serve to stir my own memory; and for the person who is fit for knowledge, if he should happen upon them, the search for what is useful and profitable will be achieved through sweat. <margin>E</margin> For it is right that labor should precede not only food, but much more so knowledge, for those who pass through the truly narrow and cramped Way of the Lord toward eternal and blessed salvation. Our knowledge and spiritual birth is our Savior himself, into whom we are grafted, being transplanted and transformed into good soil from our old life. This change of planting contributes to the fertility and goodness of the fruits. The Lord is the Light and the true knowledge into whom we have been transplanted. Moreover, knowledge is also said to be twofold: one is common to all men, being a similar intelligence and apprehension, which appears everywhere in public because it knows each of the subjects placed before it. <margin>F</margin> Not only do rational powers possess this, but even those lacking reason; I would never call this "knowledge," as it is an innate natural ability to know through the senses. But that which is excellently and specifically named "knowledge" <term>Gnosis</term> takes its form and character from the mind and reason, through which only the powers that participate in reason can share in knowledge, as they understand those things that are apprehended.

<summary>Clement introduces Book VI of the Miscellanies, defining the "Gnostic" as the truly pious Christian and explaining his "meadow-like" writing style intended to provoke intellectual labor. He distinguishes between common sensory perception and the higher spiritual knowledge (Gnosis) found in Christ.</summary>

# THE MISCELLANIES, BOOK VI.

<margin>A</margin> ...knowledge <note>original: "scientia," completing the word from the previous page</note>, are applied purely and sincerely through the bare operation of the soul. <margin>Psalm 111</margin> *A good man is he,* says David, *who shows mercy to those who perish in error, and lends by imparting the word of truth,* not haphazardly or by chance, but *if he weighs his words in judgment,* with deep calculation and reasoning. *He has dispersed, he has given to the poor.* But before we approach that which was proposed for the end of the fifth book of the *Miscellanies*, we must provide what is missing as a sort of preface. For since we have shown that the symbolic style of writing is ancient—and that it was used not only by the Prophets among us, but also by very many of the ancient Greeks, and not a few of the other foreigners among the nations—it was also necessary to follow the mysteries of those who are being initiated. <margin>B</margin> However, I delayed declaring these things until that place where, following those things said by the Greeks about first principles, we shall refute them; for we shall show that there will be mysteries in that contemplation as well. And when we have shown that the apparent meaning of Greek thoughts was illuminated by the truth handed down to us through the scriptures—in which it signifies that the fruit of truth reached them afterward—we have shown, if it is not a burden to say so: come, let us bring forward the Greeks themselves as witnesses to the theft committed against each other. For those who so evidently steal what is their own from one another confirm that they are indeed thieves; and even against their will, they are shown by us to have used the truth they received and to have secretly handed it down to those of their own kind. For those who do not abstain even from their own people will hardly abstain from ours. And I will remain silent indeed regarding their doctrines in philosophy, since <margin>C</margin> those who are divided into sects confess in their writings—lest they be convicted of the crime of an ungrateful mind—that they received their principal decrees from Socrates. But when I have used a few testimonies from those who are celebrated in speech and held in great estimation among the Greeks, and have convicted their kind of stealing in different times, I shall turn to those things which follow next. For when Orpheus had written:

> There is nothing worse or more troublesome than a woman. ->Homer openly says:<-
> There is nothing worse or more grievous than a woman.

<margin>D</margin> And again, when Musaeus had written:
> As you see the nourishing earth bring forth leaves into the light,
> And some perish on the branches, and others arise again,
> So the generation of the age of men rolls on. ->Homer transcribes:<-
> The wind pours some leaves on the ground, and the forest again
> Produces others, turning green in the springtime.
> So the human race is born, and so it passes away.

And again, when Homer had said:
> It is by no means right to boast over those who have finished their fate <note>meaning the dead</note>.

Archilochus and Cratinus write: the former indeed says, "It is not beautiful to pursue the dead with <margin>E</margin> curses." And Cratinus in *The Laconians* says, "It is a terrible thing for men to boast greatly over young men who are dead." And again, Archilochus, transferring that Homeric line:
> I am hurt, nor do I refuse to bear it for many.

Writes in this way: "I have erred, and truly calamity has caught someone else." Just as certainly as that other verse:

He himself, transforming it, brought it forth thus: "I will do it, for in truth Mars is common to men." Furthermore, transferring this also:
> All victory is placed in the judgment of the Gods.

Through this iambic verse, he openly adds spirit even to the youth:
<margin>F</margin>
> But victory is situated in the judgment of the God.

> Sleeping on the ground with unwashed feet.

### MISCELLANIES, BOOK VI.

<margin>A</margin> I could not easily judge what I should say about shame.
> It is certainly a necessity, and not a heavy evil.
You may take instances of theft from mutual comparison, both from those who flourished at the same time and those who competed against one another in the same fields. For instance, from Euripides in *Orestes*:
> The allure of sleep, and a remedy for evil.

And Sophocles in *Minos*:

Sophocles in *Hipponous*:

<margin>D</margin> He uses these Iambic verses in *Aegeus*:

<margin>Panyassis writes:</margin> A noble gift is held from the gods for man:

Euripides writes:

<margin>F</margin> Sometimes things must just happen. And when Antimachus of Teos had said:
> From gifts, many evils arise for the race of men,
Augias wrote:
> For gifts deceive the minds of men along with their deeds.

# MISCELLANIES, BOOK VI.

<margin>A</margin> I would not easily judge what to say about shame.
> *Surely it is necessary, and it is not a heavy evil.*
<note>original: "pudore." Clement is likely quoting a poet discussing the dual nature of shame—as both a virtue and a paralyzing social anxiety.</note>

You may take instances of theft from a mutual comparison of their works, both from those who flourished at the same time and those who competed with one another in the same fields. For instance, from Euripides in *Orestes*:
> *The lure of sleep, and a remedy for evil.*

And from Sophocles in *Eriphyle*:
> *Go to sleep, the doctor of this ill.*

> *Nature gave an shameful name to the illegitimate.*
<note>original: "Nothum dedit probrosum natura nomine." The line discusses the stigma of birth versus natural character.</note>

> *Whatever is good has a similar nature.*

<meta>This page continues Clement’s detailed argument that the great Greek poets, historians, and philosophers were not original, but frequently "stole" their best ideas and phrases from earlier sources—or even from the "barbarian" (Hebrew and Egyptian) wisdom that predated them. # THE MISCELLANIES, BOOK VI.

<margin>A</margin>> *The nourishing earth is grazed upon by all.* <note>A poetic sentiment suggesting that literary material is common ground for everyone to pick from.</note>

Furthermore, you will find that when Plato had said, "For the first shoot of every plant that has grown correctly is paramount for the virtue of its nature," the Historian <note>Likely referring to a specific historical commentator or Thucydides</note> added a similar conclusion, writing: "Moreover, it is not naturally implanted in any wild plant to become tame once it has passed its tender age." And that famous line of Empedocles:

> *For I was once a boy, then a girl,*
> *A bush, and a bird, and a silent fish in the sea,*

<margin>B</margin>Euripides transcribes this in his play *Chrysippus*: "Of the things that are brought forth, nothing dies; but while one is distinguished from another, it reveals a different form." And when Plato had stated in his books on the *Republic* that women should be held in common, Euripides writes in *Protesilaus*:

> *Therefore, let the marriage bed be common.*

Furthermore, when Euripides wrote:

> *For what is enough is sufficient for the wise.*

Epicurus says openly: "Sufficiency is the wealthiest of all things." And again, when Aristophanes writes:

> *If you are just, you will have a stable life.*
> *You will live well, free from both tumult and fear.*

<margin>C</margin>Epicurus says: "The greatest fruit of justice is freedom from disturbance." Now, since these types of Greek "thefts" <note>original: *furti*</note> regarding their sentiments are of this nature, they should suffice as a clear example for one who is able to see. Indeed, they have been caught not only stealing sentiments and expressions and stating them through paraphrase, as will be shown, but they will also be clearly proven to have committed wholesale thefts. For having completely snatched up what belonged to others, they published it as their own. For example, Eugamon of Cyrene stole an entire book about the Thesprotians from Musaeus; Pisander of Camirus stole the *Heracleia* from Pisinus of Lydia; and Panyasis of Halicarnassus took the *Capture of Oechalia* from Cleophylus of Samos. You will also find that even Homer, that great poet, translated those verses:

<margin>D</margin>> *And as a man rears a branch of a flourishing olive,*

and the lines that follow, word for word from Orpheus's poem about the *Death of Dionysus*. Also, the lines written by Orpheus in his *Theogony* about Saturn:

> *And he lay with his thick neck turned aside,*
> *And sleep, which conquers all, had seized him,*

Homer transferred those lines to describe the Cyclops. Moreover, Hesiod writes regarding Melampus:

> *It is a pleasant thing to obey the deeds done by the gods*
> *For men; these are the clearest signs of the wicked and the evil.*

And the lines following those, he took word for word from the poet Musaeus. Furthermore, Aristophanes, in his first *Women at the Thesmophoria*, transferred verses from the comedy of <margin>E</margin> Cratinus titled *The Burned Men* <note>original: *Empiprameni*</note>. Plato the Comic poet and Aristophanes in his *Daedalus* steal from one another. Regarding the play *Cocalus*, which had been skillfully written by the poet Aristophanes, the comic writer Philemon acted it out after changing it only slightly in the comedy titled *The Supposititious Son* <note>original: *Hypobolimaios*</note>. Also, Eumelus and Acusilaus the historians published the poems of Hesiod as their own after they had turned them into prose. Gorgias of Leontini and Eudemus of Naxos, both historians, stole from Meleagora; and besides them, Bion of Proconnesus, who transcribed the deeds of the ancient Cadmus by reducing them to a summary; and also Amphilochus, Aristocles, Leandrius, Anaximenes, Hellanicus, Hecataeus, Androtion, and Philochorus. Dieuchidas of Megara translated the beginning of his speech from Hellanicus’s *Deucalonia*. I say nothing of Heraclitus of Ephesus, who took many things from Orpheus. From Pythagoras, Plato tore away the idea that the soul is immortal; but Pythagoras himself took that from the Egyptians.

<margin>*</margin>Many Platonists have also committed to writing works in which they show, as we said at the beginning, that both the Stoics and Aristotle took their most numerous and important dogmas from Plato.

# THE MISCELLANIES, BOOK VI.

<margin>A</margin>...from Plato. Furthermore, Epicurus stole his principal decrees from Democritus. And let these matters stand as they are. For my life would fail me if I wished to pursue in detail the thefts of the Greeks, which proceeded from an excessive love of themselves, and how they claim for themselves the invention of the most beautiful decrees among them, which they actually received from us <note>Clement uses "us" to refer to the Judeo-Christian tradition.</note>. Now, they are not only convicted of stealing dogmas from the barbarians <note>In this context, "barbarians" refers to non-Greeks, specifically the Hebrews and Egyptians.</note>, but also of imitating those things which, through divine power, were done wonderfully and beyond expectation by those among us who lived holily while caring for our people—recounting them as if they were Greek fables of the miraculous. And we shall ask them whether they say the things they write are true or false. They certainly will not say they are false, for they would not willingly condemn themselves of the greatest folly for writing falsehoods. Instead, they will confess them to be true. 

<margin>B</margin>And if so, how do the miracles performed through Moses and the other prophets still seem incredible to them? For God Almighty, caring for all men, turns some toward salvation by precepts, others by threats, some by miraculous signs, and others by kind promises. Indeed, when a long-lasting drought once afflicted Greece and there was a great sterility of crops, those who remained, they say, came as suppliants to Delphi because of the famine and asked the Pythia <note>The priestess of the Oracle at Delphi.</note> how they might be delivered from such a heavy calamity. She replied that there was one remedy for the disaster: if they would employ the prayers of Aeacus. Obeying her, Aeacus ascended the "Greek Mountain" <note>Mount Panhellenion on the island of Aegina.</note> and, stretching out his clean hands toward heaven, invoked the common God and prayed that He would have mercy on afflicted Greece. As soon as <margin>C</margin>he began to pray, a lucky thunderclap immediately sounded, and the whole air all around was covered with clouds. Violent and continuous rains broke out and filled the entire region. From this followed an abundant and copious fertility of crops, obtained through the prayers of Aeacus, which acted like a form of divine agriculture. 

<margin>1 Kings 12</margin> <note>original: 1. Reg. 12. In the Latin Vulgate, 1 & 2 Samuel are titled 1 & 2 Kings.</note> *And Samuel invoked the Lord,* it says, *and the Lord gave voices and rain in the day of harvest.* You see that there is one God who, through the powers subject to Him, rains upon the just and the unjust. Our scripture is full of God hearing and fulfilling every petition through the prayers of the righteous. Again, the Greeks relate that when the Etesian winds <note>Seasonal Mediterranean winds that provide cooling in summer.</note> once failed, Aristaeus sacrificed to Zeus Isthmius in Ceos, for the calamity was very great. When everything was burning with heat and the winds that usually cooled the crops did not blow, he easily recalled them. And the Delphians, <margin>D</margin> when Xerxes invaded Greece with war, were told by the Pythia:

->*O Delphians, appease the winds with prayer, and it will be better.*<-

Having placed an altar and made a sacrifice to the winds, they had them as helpers. For when they blew violently around the promontory of Sepias, they shattered the entire equipment of the Persian fleet. Empedocles of Agrigentum was also surnamed <term>κωλυσανέμας</term> <note>original: *kōlysanemas*, meaning "the restrainer of winds."</note>, that is, the "prohibitor of winds." It is certainly said that when a certain heavy wind once blew from the mountain of Agrigentum, which not only brought diseases to the inhabitants but was also a cause of sterility for their wives, he made it cease. Therefore, he himself also writes in his verses: <margin>E</margin>

> You shall take away the blasts of the tireless winds,
> Which, by their blowing, weary the fields, destroying the crops of men.
> And again,
> Whenever you wish, you shall set these same blasts still again.

And he used to say that some followed him who had need of divinations, and others who had long been tormented by heavy diseases. The Greeks believed that the righteous could perform healings, signs, and miracles because they had learned it from our scriptures. For if any virtues or powers move the winds and distribute the rains, let them hear the Psalmist <note>original: *Psalmographum*, the "Psalm-writer," referring to David.</note>: 
<margin>Ps. 84, Deut. 10</margin>
*How lovely are your tabernacles, O Lord of powers.* He is the Lord of powers, principalities, and authorities. Of whom Moses says: <margin>F</margin> *That we should be with Him; and circumcise your hard heart, and you shall no longer harden your neck. For the Lord is the Lord of Lords, and the God of Gods: the great and strong God,* and what follows thereafter. And Isaiah says: *Lift up your eyes on high, and see who has made all these things.*

# THE MISCELLANIES, BOOK VI.

**A** furthermore, some say that plagues, hailstorms, and tempests, and things similar to these, do not occur solely due to a material lack of order in nature, but are also often brought about by the anger of <term>demons</term><note>In the ancient world, "demons" (daimones) were often seen as intermediary spirits, not necessarily evil, though Clement views them through a Christian lens as "non-good" spirits.</note> or ill-willed angels. Indeed, they say that the Magi of Cleonae <note>A city in Greece; its inhabitants were famous for their "hail-wardens" who claimed to predict or divert storms.</note> observed the heights of the clouds that were about to hurl down hail, and attempted to drive away the wrath with chants and sacrifices. If it ever happened that they lacked an animal for sacrifice, they would even sacrifice by wounding their own finger and offering their blood. Similarly, Diotima of Mantinea <note>The priestess and philosopher who appears in Plato’s "Symposium" as Socrates' teacher on love.</note> performed sacrifices for the Athenians before a plague, which caused the disease to be delayed for ten years. Likewise, the sacrifices of Epimenides of Crete <note>A semi-mythical Greek seer and philosopher.</note> delayed the Persian War for the Athenians for a significant amount of time. These people believe it makes no difference whether we call these souls "Gods" or **B** "Angels." Furthermore, those skilled in their doctrines have placed the burial vaults of the dead in many temples as if they were statues of the Gods, calling their souls "demons." They teach that these should be worshipped by men, as if they had received power from divine providence due to the purity of their lives to serve human needs in the regions around the earth. For they knew that some souls are held to the body by nature. But concerning these matters, we shall speak more at the proper time in the following writing when we deal with the subject of Angels.

As for Democritus, by predicting many things from his observation of the heavens and celestial matters, he was nicknamed "Wisdom." Once, when his brother Damasus had kindly received him, Democritus conjectured from certain stars and predicted that there would be a great rain. Those who believed him gathered their harvests in time, for even though it was summer, the crops were still out in the **C** threshing floors. Others, however, lost everything when a massive and unexpected rainstorm rushed upon them.

<margin>Exodus 3</margin>
How, then, can the Greeks still refuse to believe that God appeared on Mount Sinai, at which time a fire burned that consumed nothing of the plants growing on the mountain? And the sound of trumpets was carried, which was breathed forth without any instruments? For that descent of God onto the mountain was the arrival of divine power, which pervades the whole world and proclaims the light that cannot be approached. Such is the <term>allegory</term> <note>Clement often uses "allegory" to mean the deeper, spiritual meaning of a physical event described in Scripture.</note> that is appropriate to the Scripture. Furthermore, fire was seen, as Aristobulus says <note>Aristobulus of Paneas, a Jewish philosopher who tried to harmonize Greek philosophy with the Torah.</note>, when the entire people (who were no fewer than one million, excluding children and those younger) were gathered around the mountain. The circumference of the mountain was no less than a five-day journey. Therefore, through the whole place of the vision, for all of them encamped in a circle, **D** a burning fire was seen all around. Thus, the descent was not limited to one specific spot, for God is everywhere. 

The historians who have written accounts also say that on the island of Britain there is a certain cave beneath a mountain, with a hole at the summit. When the wind falls into the cave and is buffeted within the hollows of the pit, the sound of cymbals being struck in rhythm can be heard. Often, too, when leaves are moved in the woods by a sudden and thick blast of wind, a sound like the singing of birds is produced. Furthermore, those who composed Persian histories report that in the higher places of the region of the Magi, there are three mountains placed one after another in a long plain. Those who pass through the place, when they reach the first mountain, hear a confused voice as if from many thousands of **E** men shouting, just as if they were in a battle line. When they come to the middle mountain, they hear a louder and clearer noise at the same time. Finally, at the end, they hear people singing a <term>paean</term> <note>original: "pæana"; a Greek song of triumph or thanksgiving.</note>, as if they were victors. 

I believe the cause of any such sound is both the smoothness and the concavity of the locations. The wind that has entered is thrown back and, proceeding into the same place, sounds more vehemently. These things are as they are. But Almighty God, even though nothing is subject to Him by necessity, can generate a voice and a vision in the hearing, demonstrating His majesty beyond those things that usually have a natural sequence, in order to convert the soul that does not yet believe and to receive the command that is given. Since there was a cloud and a high mountain, why could a diverse sound not be heard when the wind was moved by the Working Cause?

<margin>A</margin> There is also testimony to confirm that even the most excellent philosophers claimed the most beautiful of our <note>Clement refers here to Judeo-Christian or "barbarian" truths.</note> dogmas for themselves, boasting and glorying in them. First, the **Cantor** <note>original: "Cantor" (Singer)</note> comes forward, carrying one of the symbols of music. They say he must learn two of the books of Mercury <note>The Roman name for the Egyptian god Thoth, often called Hermes Trismegistus by the Greeks.</note>, one of which contains hymns to the Gods, and the other the rules for a king's life. After the cantor comes the **Horoscopus** <note>original: "horoscopus" (Time-watcher)</note>, who holds in his hand a timepiece and a palm branch, the symbols and signs of astrology. He <margin>15. B.</margin> <margin>B</margin> must always have the four books of Mercury that deal with astrology on the tip of his tongue. After all these comes the **Prophet**, who openly carries a water jar in his robe, followed by those who carry the offered loaves of bread. As the overseer of sacred matters, he learns the ten books called "Hieratic" <note>Priestly books.</note>. These contain laws, descriptions of the Gods, and the entire discipline of the Priests. For among the Egyptians, the Prophet also presides over the distribution of taxes. There are, therefore, forty-two books of Mercury which are truly necessary; thirty-six of these, containing the entire philosophy of the Egyptians, are learned by those mentioned above. The remaining six are learned by <margin>D</margin> the *Shrine-bearers* <note>original: "παστοφόροι" (Pastophoroi)</note>, as they pertain to medicine: namely, the construction of the body, diseases, instruments, medicines, the eyes, and finally, women's ailments. Such, to speak briefly, are the affairs of the Egyptians.

The philosophy of the Indians was also very celebrated. Alexander <margin>Plutarch's Life of Alexander</margin> the Macedonian, having captured ten of the Indian **Gymnosophists** <note>Literally "naked philosophers," a group of ancient Indian ascetics.</note> who seemed to be the best and most excellent, and who surpassed the others in the brevity of their speech, proposed questions to them. When he ordered the eldest among them to answer first, the one being examined was asked which he thought were more numerous, the living or the dead. He said, "The living, for the <margin>E</margin> dead no longer exist." The second was asked whether the earth or the sea bred larger beasts. "The earth," he said, "for the sea is also a part of it." The third was asked what is the most cunning of living creatures, which until now has not been known. "Man," he replied. The fourth, when asked for what reason they had moved Sabba, their prince, to revolt, answered: "Because they wanted him either to live honorably or to die miserably." The fifth <margin>Same source</margin> was asked whether he thought day or night came first. "By one day," he replied. For to difficult questions, there must also be difficult answers. The sixth was asked how a man might be most loved. "If," he said, "being most powerful, he is not terrifying." The seventh was asked how a man could <margin>F</margin> become a God. "If," he said, "he does those things which it is impossible for a man to do." The eighth was asked what is stronger, life or death. "Life," he said, "which bears so many evils." What he means by "Do not worship as the Greeks do," Peter himself will explain, adding: <margin>C</margin> "Because they are carried away by ignorance and do not know God with perfect knowledge as we do; even with the power He gave them for use, they formed wood and stones, brass and iron, gold and silver from their own materials and usage. And that we and the Greeks know the same God, though not in the same way, he further introduces in this manner: "Neither worship Him as the Jews do. For the Lord exhorts some, while to others who have already set out, He both extends a hand and <margin>A</margin> draws them to Himself. <margin>Wisdom 6</margin> For He who is the Lord of all does not respect or revere any person’s status, nor will He care for worldly greatness, since He Himself made both the great and the small, and He provides for and cares for all alike. <margin>Psalm 9</margin> David also says: "But if the nations are also sunk in the destruction they made; in this snare which they hid, their foot is caught." But the Lord was a refuge for the poor, a helper in opportunity and in affliction. Therefore, the Gospel was opportunely proclaimed to those who are in affliction. And for this reason, he says: "Proclaim His works among the nations," so they may not be judged unjustly. If, therefore, He proclaimed the Gospel to those who were in the flesh for this very reason—that they might not be unjustly condemned—how could He not also have proclaimed it for the same reason to those who departed this life before His coming? <margin>Psalm 10</margin> For the Lord is just, and He loved justice; His face beheld <margin>B</margin> righteousness. But he who loves injustice hates his own soul. If, then, all sinful flesh perished in the flood, while they were being returned to discipline through chastisement, one must believe that first, the will of God—which has the power to educate and to act—gives salvation to those who turn to Him. Furthermore, the soul, which is a far more subtle thing, could by no means be affected by water, which is coarser; because of its subtlety and simplicity, the soul cannot be overcome, and is even called incorporeal. But that which is coarse and has been thickened by sin is cast away along with the "carnal spirit" <note>original: *spiritu carnali*. In Clement's thought, this refers to a lower, irrational part of the soul associated with worldly desires.</note> which lusts against the soul.

Now even Valentinus <note>A famous 2nd-century Gnostic teacher who attempted to bridge Greek philosophy and Christian mystery.</note>, the leader of those who introduce and recommend "communion," writes word for word in his *Homily on Friends*: <margin>C</margin> "Many of the things written in public books are found written in the Church of God. For these are the common words that proceed from the heart. The law written in the heart is the people of the beloved, who is loved and who loves Him." By "common books," he means either the Jewish scriptures or the writings of the philosophers. Thus, he makes truth a shared thing. Isidorus also, who was both the son and disciple of Basilides <note>Another major Gnostic thinker from Alexandria; Isidorus followed his father's esoteric teachings.</note>, writes these words in the first book of his *Expositions of the Prophet Parchor*: "The Athenians say that certain things were signified to Socrates by a *Daemon* <note>original: *Daemone*. In Greek philosophy, a *daimon* was a guiding spirit or divine voice, not necessarily an evil demon.</note> following him. Aristotle also says that all men are attended by *daemons* who follow them at the time they migrate into a body." Isidorus claims Aristotle took this prophetic teaching and placed it in his own books, without confessing where he had taken the discourse from. And again, in the second <margin>D</margin> book of the same work, he writes: "Let no one think that what we say is the unique property of the 'elect' <note>The Gnostics often referred to themselves as the 'elect' or 'spiritually elite' who possessed special knowledge.</note>, or that it was previously spoken of by some philosophers. For this was not their own invention, but having taken it from the Prophets, they attributed it to one who is 'wise' according to their own opinion." And again in the same book: "For it seems to me that those who claim philosophy for themselves do so to learn what the 'winged oak' is, and the 'variegated cloak' upon it—all of which Pherecydes <note>An early Greek thinker (c. 6th century BC) often considered a teacher of Pythagoras; his works were highly allegorical.</note> spoke of allegorically in his *Theology*, taking them from the prophecy of Ham."

The foundation, as we have previously noted, is not what we call the way of life adopted in every heresy, but that which is truly philosophy: rightly crafted wisdom, which provides experience of the things in life. And Wisdom we define as the solid knowledge of things divine and human—a <margin>E</margin> firm, stable, and unfailing comprehension that encompasses things as they are, both past and future. The Lord taught us this through His presence and through the Prophets; it is of such a nature that it cannot fail, as it was handed down by the Word <note>original: *Verbo* (Logos).</note>. This wisdom is also entirely true in its will, as it is known through the Son; part of it is eternal, while part is useful for a time; part is one and the same, while part is manifold and diverse; part is without any passive movement, while part involves a feeling of longing; and part is perfect, while part is in need. This is the wisdom that Philosophy desires: the rectitude of the soul and the word, and the purity of life. Philosophy is well-disposed toward this wisdom and does all things to attain it. Among us, those are called "Philosophers" <margin>F</margin> who love the wisdom that is the craftswoman and teacher of all—that is, the knowledge of the Son of God. Among the Greeks, however, they are called "Philosophers" who engage in disputes about virtue. Philosophy would then be that which exists in every school of thought—I speak of those things in philosophy...

He concludes by defining true Christian philosophy as the knowledge of the Son of God.</summary>

# MISCELLANIES, BOOK VI
### 201

<margin>A</margin>
**Wisdom** <note>original: "sophia"</note> consists of those decrees which cannot be criticized, joined with a life that is consistent and focused on a single choice; these very truths, though they were stolen from the grace divinely given to the barbarians <note>Clement often uses "barbarian" to refer to the Hebrew/Jewish tradition, which he believes predates and informs Greek philosophy.</note>, were then adorned with **Greek eloquence**. For they stole some things, while they misunderstood others. In some cases, they spoke certain truths by imitation, but they did not deliver them perfectly; in other cases, they relied on human conjecture and reasoning, in which they inevitably fall into error. These men think they have attained the truth perfectly, just as we understand ourselves, but they have only caught a part of it. Certainly, they know nothing more than this world. Although **Geometry** deals with measurements, magnitudes, and figures through descriptions on flat surfaces, and **painting** seems to take over the entire field of optics—which they call **perspective**—in the things that are sketched. However, this art describes the vision falsely, using technical skill to manipulate the signs created by the intersection of visual lines.

<margin>B</margin>
From this are maintained *hypostáseis* <note>original: "ὑποστάσεις"; here meaning prominent or standing-out visions</note>, and *hypothéseis* <note>original: "hypotheses"; here meaning lower or underlying visions</note>, and *pháseis* <note>original: "φάσεις"; meaning appearances or things seen</note>. And indeed, some things seem to stand out, while others seem to recede; others are apprehended by the vision in some other way upon a smooth and level surface. In this same way, philosophers also imitate the truth in the manner of a painting. But *philautía* <note>original: "φιλαυτία"; excessive self-love or conceit</note> is always the cause of all sins for anyone. Therefore, one ought not to be too much a lover of oneself by choosing and seeking glory from men, but rather to be holy with prudence by loving God. If anyone, therefore, uses specific things as if they were universal and general, and treats that which serves as if it were the master, he falls away from the truth, not understanding what was said by **David** in his confession: <margin>Psalm 101</margin> <note>Modern Psalm 102:9. Clement uses the Septuagint/Vulgate numbering.</note> "I ate earth (or ashes) like bread." Excessive self-love, vain opinion, and mere persuasion are "earth" and "error" to such a person.

<margin>C</margin>
If this is so, then cognition and science come from instruction. If there is instruction, it is necessary to seek a **teacher**. For **Cleanthes** names **Zeno** as his teacher, and **Theophrastus** names **Aristotle**; **Metrodorus** names **Epicurus**, and **Plato** names **Socrates**. But even if I go back to **Pythagoras**, and **Pherecydes**, and **Thales**, and the very first "wise men," I stop to ask who was *their* teacher. And whether you mention the **Egyptians**, or the **Indians**, or the **Babylonians**, or the **Magi** themselves, I will not stop demanding to know who taught them. Furthermore, I lead you back to the very first origin of humanity, and from there I begin to ask who the teacher was. Certainly, it was no man, for they had not yet learned anything. But neither was it any of the **Angels**.

<margin>D</margin>
For men do not hear in the same way that Angels signal to one another as Angels. For they do not have ears as we do, nor has anyone given Angels a tongue, or lips—I mean the instruments of the voice—or the throat, the windpipe, the internal organs, the breath, and the air which is struck to create sound. Indeed, God is far removed from sounding out in that holiness which cannot be approached, He who is even separated from the **Archangels**. Now, we have indeed received that the Angels also learned the truth, as did the principalities that are subject to them, for they had a beginning to their existence. It remains, therefore, that as we ascend, we must seek their teacher. Since, however, there is only one who is **unbegotten**, namely God the Almighty, there is also only one who is **pre-begotten**, through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made. <margin>John 1</margin>

<margin>E</margin>
For there is truly one God, who created the "beginning" of all things, signifying the **first-born Son**, as **Peter** writes, clearly understanding that passage: <margin>Genesis 1; Hebrews 1</margin> "In the beginning God made heaven and earth." Moreover, He is called **Wisdom** by all the Prophets. He is the teacher of all things that have been created, the Counselor of God who foreknew all things. From on high, from the first constitution of the world, He has both taught and perfected in many portions and in many ways. Hence it was rightly said: <margin>Matthew 23</margin> "Call no man your teacher on earth." You see from where true philosophy has taken its starting points, even if the Law is but an image and a shadow of the truth. But the excessive self-love of the Greeks proclaims certain men as "teachers." Just as all fatherhood traces back to God the Creator, so also does the teaching of things that are good and honorable, which justifies and leads to this end and brings help, trace back to the Lord.

<margin>F</margin>
If, however, some people—having received the seeds of truth in whatever way from some effect—did not nourish them but committed them to sterile and dry earth, they choked them with wild weeds, just as the **Pharisees** turned away from the Law by introducing human doctrines. The teacher is not the cause of their failure, but rather those who chose to hear incorrectly. Those, however, who...

<margin>Psalm 11</margin>
**A** they believed in them <note>The "them" refers to the prophets and scriptures mentioned on the previous page.</note> and in the Lord’s coming and the explanation of the scriptures. These people are occupied in the **knowledge of the law**, just as philosophers, through the teaching of the Lord, are led to the recognition of true philosophy. For the "words of the Lord are pure words, silver tried by fire, proved by the earth, purified seven times" <note>Psalm 12:6 in modern Bibles; Psalm 11 in the Vulgate. Clement interprets "purified seven times" as the process of refining the soul.</note>; or because the just man is tested like silver that is frequently purified, having become the Lord's coin and having received the royal seal. Or perhaps it is because Solomon also says the tongue of the righteous is like refined silver, signifying that wise and proven doctrine is praiseworthy and acceptable. This occurs when the "earth" has been frequently purged—that is, when the soul endowed with knowledge <note>original: "cognitione"; referring to Gnosis.</note> has been sanctified in many ways through abstinence from earthly passions. The body in which it dwells is also sanctified when it is dedicated as its own in the purity and sincerity of a holy temple.

**B** Now, the first purification of the soul while in the body is abstinence from evils, which some consider to be the height of perfection. This is, to put it simply, the common perfection of the faithful Jew and the Greek. But for the one who is endowed with knowledge, after that perfection which is decreed for others by the Law, justice proceeds toward the practice of doing good. For the one whose growth in justice has increased toward benevolence, perfection remains in an unchangeable habit of doing good in the **likeness of God**. For those who are the "seed of Abraham" and "servants of God" are the "called." But the "sons of Jacob" are his "chosen," those who have "supplanted" <note>A wordplay on the name Jacob, which was traditionally interpreted to mean "supplanter" or "he who trips up."</note> the workings of vice.

**C** Therefore, if we call Christ himself "Wisdom," and his work that which was done through the Prophets (by which the tradition of knowledge <note>original: "traditio quae est ex cognitione"</note> can be built up), then he himself taught the holy Apostles by his presence. Wisdom would then be "knowledge," insofar as it is the science and comprehension of things that are, will be, and have been—stable and firm, as it was handed down and revealed by the Son of God. And if the goal of the wise man is contemplation, that contemplation which still belongs to the philosophers seeks divine science, but does not yet achieve it—unless it receives the prophetic voice declared to it through discipline. Through this, it understands the nature of things that are, will be, and previously were. **Knowledge** <note>original: "Cognitio" / Gnosis</note> itself is that which has come down by succession to a few of the Apostles, handed down without writing. Hence, knowledge or wisdom must be practiced until it becomes an eternal habit of contemplation, one that is not subject to change.

**D** For Paul also, in his Epistles, does not seem to condemn philosophy; rather, he does not want the person who shares in the heights of knowledge to return any longer to Greek philosophy. He allegorically calls these the "elements of the world," because they teach elementary things in a way and serve as a discipline preceding the truth. For this reason, writing to the Hebrews who were turning back from faith to the Law, he says: "Do you have need again for me to teach you what are the primary elements of the words of God? And you have become those in need of milk and not solid food." <margin>Hebrews 5</margin> Similarly, he writes to the <margin>Colossians 2</margin> Colossians who were converts from the Greeks: "See that no one plunders you <margin>Signifying: the Greek has *sylagogon* [συλαγωγῶν], meaning "invading" or "carrying off as spoil," but I read it as "signifying."</margin> through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elements of this world, and not according to Christ," signifying that a return to philosophy is a return to an elementary doctrine.

**E** But if someone should say that philosophy was discovered by the Greeks through human intelligence, I find the scriptures saying that intelligence is sent from God. The Psalmist certainly considers intelligence to be the greatest gift and asks for it, saying: "I am your **SERVANT**, give me understanding." <margin>Psalm 118</margin> Does not David write, seeking knowledge in many forms, "Teach me goodness and discipline and knowledge, for I have believed in your commandments"? That the Covenants are primary and of the greatest authority is beyond controversy, and they are given to those who are more excellent. 

**F** Certainly, the Psalm says of God: "He has not done so for any other nation, and he has not manifested his judgments to them." <margin>Psalm 147</margin> <margin>Acts 10</margin> That phrase, "He has not done so," signifies that he *did* do something, but "not in this way." Therefore, that "so" or "in this way" is placed there to create a comparison with our own excellence. The Prophet could have simply said "He did not do it" without adding "so." Furthermore, Peter says in the Acts: "In truth I perceive that the Lord is no respecter of persons; but in every nation, he who fears him and works justice is accepted by him." Therefore, it was not only in time that God...

### MISCELLANIES, BOOK VI

<margin>A</margin> ...[God] did not look back <note>The text suggests that God's goodness does not have a starting point in time where He suddenly decided to be kind.</note>, but it was from eternity. Indeed, His beneficence never had a beginning. Nor is it circumscribed by places or by any specific people. For His beneficence is not partial. "Open to me," it says, "the gates of righteousness; entering into them, I will confess to the Lord." <margin>Psalm 117</margin> <note>Psalm 118:19 in modern Bibles.</note> Explaining the prophet's saying, Barnabas <note>Referring to the author of the *Epistle of Barnabas*, an early Christian text Clement highly valued.</note> adds: "Since many gates are open, that which is in righteousness is the one in Christ, into which all who enter are blessed." To this same sentiment belongs that prophetic word: "The Lord is over many waters" <margin>Psalm 28</margin> <note>Psalm 29:3.</note>, signifying that there are not only diverse covenants, but also diverse modes of doctrine—those among the Greeks and those among the barbarians <note>In the early church, "barbarian" often referred to non-Greeks, including Jews and Christians.</note>—which lead toward righteousness. Now David also sings openly, bearing witness to the truth: "Let sinners be turned into hell, and all the nations that forget God." <margin>Psalm 9</margin> <note>Psalm 9:17.</note> They "forget," clearly,

<margin>B</margin> Him whom they once remembered; and Him whom they knew before they forgot, they now bid farewell and send away. Therefore, there was a certain obscure knowledge of God even among the nations. And let these things be so. However, it is necessary for one who is endowed with knowledge <term>Gnostic<note>original: "cognitione præditus"; referring to the "Gnostic" or the advanced Christian seeker who possesses spiritual insight.</note></term> to have learned many things. And since the Greeks say—Protagoras having been the first to start this—that a prepared speech exists to oppose any other speech, it is fitting to speak even against such speeches. For the Scripture says: "He who speaks much shall hear in turn." <note>Job 11:2.</note> But who will understand the parable of the Lord, except the wise and the knowing, and he who loves his Lord? Let such a person, therefore, be faithful. Let him be of such a kind that he can explain knowledge. Let him be wise in discerning words. Let him be admirable in his deeds. Let him be chaste and pure; for he ought to be all the more humble the greater he appears to be. Clement says in

<margin>C</margin> his letter to the Corinthians: <note>Referring to the letter known as 1 Clement, written by Clement of Rome.</note> "Let him be such as can obey the precept, and 'snatch some from the fire; and have mercy on those who differ.'" <note>A paraphrase of Jude 1:22-23.</note> Certainly, the sickle was made so that branches might be pruned, but we also use it to distinguish the tangled shoots of the vine, and we cut away the thorns which cling to the vines and make them difficult to approach. All these things refer to the pruning of vines. Furthermore, man was made primarily for the knowledge of God, but he is also a geometer, and a farmer, and he philosophizes—one of which is for the purpose of living, the second for living well, and the third for meditating on those things which can be demonstrated. Moreover, let those who say that philosophy originated from the Devil also know what the Scripture says: that the Devil transforms himself <margin>2 Corinthians 11</margin>

<margin>D</margin> into an angel of light. Doing what? Prophesying, clearly. If he prophesies as an angel of light, then he must speak the truth. If he prophesies angelic and luminous things, then he even prophesies useful things when he is transformed into the likeness of [divine] operation, even if he himself is something else—insofar as he is a subject of apostasy. For how could he deceive anyone, unless he leads the studious man through truths toward a connection and familiarity, and only then attracts him away from the truth? Otherwise, he will be found to know the truth, even if not so as to fully comprehend it, yet in such a way that he is not ignorant of it. Therefore, philosophy is not false, even if one who is a thief and a liar <note>A reference to the Devil.</note> speaks truths through a transformation of his operation. Nor, indeed, because of the one who speaks, should the things spoken be ignorantly condemned beforehand. This must also be observed in those who are now said to prophesy: we must consider whether the things they say

<margin>E</margin> adhere to the truth. Now, if we say in a universal and general discourse that whatever things are necessary and useful for life come to us from God, we shall not err. Rather, we might say that philosophy was given to the Greeks as their own proper covenant <note>original: "proprium datum esse testamentum"</note>, as it is the foundation of Christian philosophy—even if some of the Greeks who philosophize turn a deaf ear to the truth of their own accord, despising the voice of the barbarians, or even fearing the danger of death that hangs over the faithful from civil laws. Just as in the barbarian philosophy <note>meaning the Judeo-Christian tradition</note>, so also in the Greek, tares have been sown by the "farmer of tares" <note>The Devil.</note> himself. From this source, even among us, heresies have sprung up in the midst of the good and life-giving wheat. Both the impiety and pleasure-seeking of Epicurus, and whatever other things were sown contrary to right reason,

<margin>F</margin> are the adulterated fruits of the agriculture given to the Greeks by God. The Apostle calls this the "wisdom of this world" <margin>1 Corinthians 2</margin>, which is clearly focused on pleasure and held by an excessive self-love, teaching only the things of this world and what pertains to it alone. Consequently, as far as its governance is concerned, it is subject to the princes who are here [on earth]. Wherefore...

# CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

<margin>1 Cor. 2</margin>
<margin>A</margin>
This unique philosophy <note>original: "singularis hæc philosophia"; Clement refers to the Christian life as the "true philosophy."</note> provides, in a way, the basic elements of that science which is truly perfect. This science is concerned with things perceived by the intellect, and with even more spiritual things which "eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have they entered into the heart of man," <margin>1 Corinthians 2:9</margin> until our Teacher—the Word concerning these things—opens to us the holy of holies. Beyond these, He reveals even holier things through an ascent to those who are the legitimate, sincere, and non-adulterated heirs of the Lord’s adoption. For now we dare to say (for this is the "faith of knowledge") that the one who is truly endowed with knowledge knows all things and understands them with a firm grasp—even those things which seem doubtful and inexplicable to us. Such were James, Peter, John, Paul, and the rest of the Apostles. For is not prophecy full of knowledge, given that it was granted by the Lord and then declared by the Lord to the Apostles? Is not knowledge, then, the unique property of the rational soul, which is exercised for this purpose: that through knowledge it might be inscribed for immortality?

<margin>B</margin>
There are, indeed, two powers of the soul: knowledge and <term>appetition</term> <note>original: "appetitio"; also referred to as impulse or drive.</note> or impulse. This impulse is found to be a certain movement that follows a kind of mental ascent. For whoever is driven <margin><term>ὁρμὴ</term> <note>original Greek term for an impulse toward action.</note> impulse toward doing something.</margin> toward an action first acquires knowledge before the action, and secondly, the appetition or impulse. Let us also consider this: learning is more ancient than acting. For naturally, one who acts first learns what he wishes to do. Knowledge arises from having learned; acting arises from having been moved by an impulse. Knowledge is the source of learning, but appetition follows science, and action follows that. Thus, knowledge would be the principle and the craftsman of every action undertaken by reason.

<margin>C</margin>
Therefore, the property of the rational soul rightly receives its character from that form alone. In truth, impulse—just like knowledge—is moved toward things that exist. But knowledge itself is a certain perfected contemplation by the soul of things that are: either of one thing, or many, or all things together. Nevertheless, some say that a wise man is convinced there are certain things that cannot be comprehended, so that he "comprehends" a comprehension regarding them—namely, that those things which are incomprehensible cannot be comprehended. This, however, is a common trait even of those who can see very little. For such a person merely confirms that there are some things which cannot be understood. But the person endowed with knowledge <note>The "Gnostic" in Clement's terminology.</note> of whom I speak,

<margin>D</margin>
himself comprehends those things that seem to others impossible to understand. He believes that to the Son of God, nothing is incomprehensible; hence, nothing is of such a nature that it cannot be taught. For He who suffered because of His love for us would omit nothing that contributes to the doctrine of knowledge. Thus, faith itself becomes a firm, stable, and constant demonstration of the things handed down by God, and truth follows it. And if anyone desires the experience of many things, he "knows the things of old, and conjectures what is to come; he understands the subtleties of words and the solutions of riddles. He foresees signs and wonders, and the outcomes of seasons." <margin>Wisdom of Solomon 8:8</margin> Such is the man endowed with knowledge. Only those affections <note>original: "affectiones"; these are physical needs or passions.</note> which arise to maintain the body fall upon him—namely hunger, thirst, and the like. But in the case of the Savior, it would be ridiculous to think His body required such necessary services to remain in existence.

<margin>E</margin>
For He ate, not for the sake of the body (which was sustained by a holy power), but so that those who lived with Him might not think of Him in another way—as indeed some later thought He had appeared only as a vision or a phantom. <note>Clement is refuting "Docetism," an early belief that Christ only seemed to have a physical body.</note> But He was, to put it simply, <term>impassible</term> <note>original: "impatibilis"; literally "unable to suffer" or "beyond emotion." It refers to a state where one is not moved by passions like pain or pleasure.</note>; no movement of affection reached Him, neither pleasure nor pain. As for the Apostles, through the Lord's teaching, they overcame anger, fear, and desire through an abundance of knowledge. They did not even admit those things that seem to be "good" emotions—such as confidence, emulation, joy, or desire—because they were entirely unchanged due to a firm and stable state of mind. Remaining always in a state of spiritual exercise, they were foreign to all alteration, certainly after the Lord's resurrection.

<margin>F</margin>
For even if someone accepts the things mentioned previously as "good" when they are done with reason, they are certainly not to be admitted in a "perfected" person. Such a person does not possess "confidence," for he does not deal with things he considers grave or troublesome; among the things of this life, he considers nothing to be grave or troublesome...

<summary>Clement defines the "Gnostic" as a perfected Christian who possesses true knowledge of God, transcending physical passions and even the human emotions of the Apostles. He argues that Christ and the perfected soul exist in a state of impassibility, viewing the world with a stable, divine perspective.</summary>

### STROMATA BOOK VII.

<margin>A</margin> ...should think, nor can anything lead him away from the love of God. Nor does he have need of mere "tranquility" of soul, for he never falls into sorrow or mental anguish, since he is fully persuaded that all things are done rightly. Nor does he become angry, for there is nothing that could move him to anger, since he always loves God and is entirely turned toward Him alone; for this reason, he hates none of God's creatures. Furthermore, he feels no envy, for he lacks nothing necessary to become as good and honorable as possible. Neither does he love anyone with this common, worldly friendship, but rather he loves the Creator through His creatures. Thus, he falls into no worldly <term>desire</term> <note>original: "cupiditatem"; refers to misplaced or excessive craving.</note> or appetite, nor does his soul lack anything from others, since through love he already dwells with the Beloved, to whom he is now intimately joined by choice.

<margin>B</margin> Through the habit which proceeds from spiritual exercise, he approaches Him with greater self-control and is blessed because of his abundance of good things. For these reasons, he strives with the greatest effort to be made like the Lord in <term>impassibility</term> <note>original: "impatibilitate"; the state of being undisturbed by passions or suffering, often called "apatheia" in Greek philosophy.</note>. For He is the Word, or the Reason of God, which possesses understanding, through which the image and likeness of the Mind is seen in man alone. Indeed, the good man becomes God-like and similar to God through his soul; and in turn, God is similar to the form of man, for the "form" of each individual is the Mind, from which we receive our character. Consequently, those who sin against a human being are impious and accursed. It is foolish to say that one who is endowed with knowledge and is perfect should not set aside anger and bold confidence, as if without these he could neither be stirred up against incoming threats nor endure heavy burdens. But if we were to take away even desire from him, some argue he would be disturbed and overwhelmed by all painful and harsh things, and thus

<margin>C</margin> he would depart from life in the most wretched way if he did not participate in it—or, as it seems to some, if he did not feel the same longing for things that other good and honorable men feel. If, therefore, every union and reconciliation initiated with what is good and honorable is done through "appetite," then how, they ask, can he remain "impassible" while still seeking what is honorable? But these people, it seems, do not know the divinity of Love. For Love is not the appetite of the one who loves, but rather a benevolent and firm union, restoring the one endowed with knowledge to the unity of faith, having no need of specific place or time. He who, through love, already exists in those things where he is destined to be—having already grasped hope through knowledge—seeks nothing, for he possesses, as far as is possible, that which

<margin>D</margin> is to be sought. Rightly, therefore, he remains in one immutable state, loving out of knowledge. He will not burn with a vehement zeal to be made like the good, since through love he already possesses that which is good and honorable. What need has he further of confidence or desire, when he has received union and familiarity with the impassible God through love, and through that love has enrolled himself in the number of His friends? Therefore, he who is endowed with knowledge and is perfect must be removed from every passion and disturbance of the soul. For knowledge produces exercise, and exercise produces a habit or a settled state. Such a constitution produces impassibility, not merely a moderation of the soul’s feelings. He enjoys perfect impassibility through the absolute amputation of desire. Moreover, he who possesses knowledge does not participate in those things commonly boasted of as "goods"—that is, "passible goods" which are

<margin>E</margin> joined to the disturbances of the soul. For example, he does not partake in the "joy" that is joined to worldly pleasure, nor the "sadness" joined to pain, nor the "caution" that is subject to fear. Neither does he partake in "outbursts of temper," for that is rooted in anger—even if some say these things are no longer bad, but good. For it is impossible that he who has once been perfected through love, and eternally perceives the unquenchable delight of contemplation, should find pleasure in small, humble, or abject things. What just cause remains for him to return to worldly goods, when he has received that "light to which there is no access," <note>original: "lucem ad quam non patet aditus"; a reference to 1 Timothy 6:16.</note> even if not yet in time and place, then certainly in that love which is endowed with knowledge? It is because of this love that the inheritance follows—a perfect and absolute restoration—confirmed through works by Him who pays the

<margin>F</margin> reward. Because he chose this through knowledge, he who possesses knowledge anticipates the reward through love. For is he not a pilgrim journeying toward the Lord because of his love for Him? Even if his "tabernacle" <note>A biblical metaphor for the physical body.</note> is seen on earth, he does not indeed lead himself out of life (for that is not permitted), but he leads his soul away from worldly movements and passions.

### CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

<margin>A</margin> ...to him, for it has been granted to him; and again, he lives with his desires put to death, and no longer makes use of the body, except to allow it what is necessary, so that he does not give it a reason for its own dissolution. Therefore, how much more does he need the virtue of a <term>great soul</term> <note>original: "magni animi virtute"; often associated with the philosophical concept of "magnanimity" or greatness of spirit.</note>, he who does not dwell in evils, being one who is not even present there, but is entirely with the one he loves. Truly, what is the use of <term>temperance</term> <note>original: "temperantiæ"; the virtue of moderation and self-control.</note> when he no longer feels the need for it? For to have such desires that one needs temperance to restrain and curb them belongs not yet to the world of the pure, but to one who is still moved by the disturbances of the soul. But the virtue of a great and exalted soul is taken up because of fear and cowardice. For it is certainly not fitting that the friend of God, whom God predestined before the foundation of the world to be enrolled in the highest adoption of sons, should be subject to pleasures or fears, and be occupied in suppressing the disturbances of the soul.

<margin>B</margin> For I would say boldly, just as he is predestined by what he will do and what will follow: so he himself also, since he has predestined his own path because of the One he has known, holds the One he has loved. Nor does he find the future difficult to guess, as many live by guessing; but through faith endowed with <term>knowledge</term> <note>original: "cognitione"; here referring to Gnosis.</note>, he has received that which is uncertain and obscure to others, and through love, what is future is already present to him. For he has believed—both because of prophecy and because of the divine presence—in God who does not lie; and he holds what he believed, and obtains the promise. Moreover, the Truth is the one who promised, and is the end of the promise; because he who promised is worthy of faith, the believer has received it firmly and stably through knowledge.

<margin>C</margin> But he who, through the state in which he exists, knows the firm and stable comprehension of future things, meets the future through love. Now indeed, he will not even desire to obtain those things which are here, for he is persuaded that he will obtain those things which are truly good; instead, he will always desire to hold a right and rightly-conducted faith, and moreover that as many as possible might become like himself for the glory of God, which is perfected and completed through knowledge. For he is a bringer of salvation who is made like the Savior, as far as it is lawful for human nature to reach His image, by carrying out the commandments, by never transgressing them, and by conducting himself rightly. This is what it means to worship God: through that which is truly the justice of deeds and of knowledge. The Lord does not wait for his voice in prayer, saying, "Ask, and I will do it; think in your soul, and I will give." 

<margin>D</margin> In short, it is impossible for that which is immutable to grow together and be reconciled with that which turns and changes. But when the <term>ruling faculty</term> <note>original: "facultas animæ principalis"; the 'hegemonikon' or the directing part of the soul in Stoic and Christian thought.</note> of the soul is engaged in continuous change, and therefore in instability, it is not preserved as a stable "habit." For how could one who is always changed by those things that enter and strike from without hold a habit and a disposition, and—to put it simply—possess knowledge? Although philosophers also consider virtues to be habits, dispositions, and knowledges. But how is knowledge not born simultaneously with men, but is rather something mixed? Just as in the beginning there is need of attention, education, and growth so that it may be learned; so then, from diligent and uninterrupted meditation, it arrives at a stable habit.

<margin>E</margin> So also, being perfected and completed in the <term>mystic habit</term> <note>original: "habitu mystico"; a deep, settled spiritual state of union with God.</note>, because of love it remains such that it cannot fall away. For he understands not only the first cause, and the cause generated from it, and in these he is firm and stable, possessing reasons that are "stably stable," and which cannot fall away or be moved. Moreover, concerning good and evil things, and concerning the origin and generation of the universe, and—to say it once—concerning those things which the Lord has spoken, he has learned from the Truth itself the most accurate and exact truth from the foundation of the world to the end, not preferring anything to the Truth itself, even if it seemed probable or necessary from Greek rhetoric.

<margin>F</margin> But those things which were said by the Lord you will take as open and manifest, even if they were obscure to others; he has now received knowledge about all things. But among us are the divine words, and they answer concerning those things that are, as they are; and concerning future things, as they will be; and concerning those things that have been done, as they were. In those things alone which constitute knowledge, since he is endowed with knowledge, he will conduct himself excellently, and will undertake to discourse on the good, always adhering to those things perceived by the intellect. From those heavenly archetype patterns of human things, he describes the administration of life, just as those who sail direct the ship toward a star; toward every good action he always...
