<header>### STROMATA BOOK VI</header>

<margin>A</margin> **Always** ready and prepared, he is accustomed to look down upon all heavy and troublesome things whenever it is necessary to endure something. He never performs anything rashly, nor anything that does not befit himself or the <term>Commonwealth</term> <note>original: "Reipublicæ"; referring here to the community of believers or the cosmic order.</note>. He is provident and far-sighted, and is not swayed by pleasures—neither those that are real, nor those that occur in dreams at night. Being accustomed to a thin diet, which ensures he is content with little, he is <term>temperate</term> <note>original: "temperans"; showing self-control and moderation.</note> and moderate, maintaining gravity and honesty. He lacks very few of the things necessary for life; he seeks nothing superfluous. Even these necessities he does not treat as primary goals, but accepts them as part of the custom of life and as necessary for the <term>pilgrimage of the flesh</term> <note>A common early Christian metaphor for earthly life as a temporary journey.</note>, admitting only as much as is required. For his primary focus is <term>knowledge</term> <note>original: "cognitio"; often synonymous with Gnosis in Clement’s writing.</note>. Consequently, he also attends to those studies which train the mind for knowledge, taking from <margin>B</margin> each discipline that which contributes to the truth. From **Music**, he pursues the proportion found in things that are joined and composed. In **Arithmetic**, he notes the increases and decreases of numbers and their mutual relationships, observing how most things fall into numerical proportion. He contemplates **Geometry** as an essence in itself, identifying a continuous space through the intellect and perceiving an immutable essence distinct from physical bodies. And again, lifted from the earth by **Astronomy**, he is raised high in mind along with the heavens and revolves together with their motion, always considering divine things and their mutual harmony and agreement. It was by these very means that **Abraham** was led to ascend to the knowledge of the One who had created him. Furthermore, the one endowed with knowledge will use **Dialectics**, choosing the division of genera into species, and applying the distinction of existing things until he reaches the first and simplest principles.

<margin>C</margin> Many, however, fear Greek Philosophy just as children fear **scary masks** <note>original: "laruas"; masks used in theater or to frighten, implying that the fear of philosophy is irrational and childish.</note>, worrying that it might lead them astray. But if their faith is such—I will not call it knowledge—that it can be dissolved by the mere probability of an argument, then let them admit they do not possess the truth. For Truth, as they say, is invincible; it is only false opinion that is dissolved. After all, we choose purple cloth by comparing it with another purple. Therefore, if someone admits he does not have a heart rightly informed and unfolded, he lacks the "money-changer’s table" and the reason that possesses the power of judgment. How can he be a <term>banker</term> <note>original: "trapezita"; a money-changer or banker who must distinguish authentic currency from counterfeit. Clement uses this as a metaphor for the Christian discerning true and false doctrines.</note> if he cannot test and distinguish a good coin from one that is false or <margin>D</margin> <margin>Psalm 114</margin> adulterated? **David** cried out: *The righteous shall never be moved* <note>original: "In æternum non commouebitur iustus"; referencing Psalm 112:6 (numbered 111 or 114 in various traditions).</note>. He shall not be moved by deceptive speech, nor by false pleasure. Thus, he shall not be moved from his inheritance. He shall not fear a bad report, nor vain slander, nor the false opinion that surrounds him. Nor will he dread crafty and cunning speeches, for he is able to discern them through questioning and responding correctly. For **Dialectics** is like a fence, preventing the truth from being trampled underfoot by the <term>Sophists</term> <note>Professional rhetoricians often criticized by philosophers for using clever but fallacious arguments.</note>. Indeed, it is necessary for those who are praised in the holy name of the Lord, as the Prophet wills, to rejoice in their hearts while seeking the Lord. *Seek Him, therefore, and be strengthened; seek His face continually in every way* <note>original: "Quærite faciem eius perpetuo modis omnibus"; referencing Psalm 105:4.</note>. <margin>Psalm 68</margin> For since He has spoken in many fashions and in many ways, He is not known absolutely. The one endowed with <margin>E</margin> knowledge does not use these disciplines as virtues themselves, but as helpers to distinguish common and proper traits, admitting them for the sake of the truth. For the cause of all error and false opinion is the inability to distinguish how things agree with one another and how they differ. If one does not pursue a discourse according to these divisions, he will not notice that he is confusing common and specific attributes. If this happens, he must necessarily lose the way and fall into error.

The distinction of names and things in the Scriptures also brings great light to the soul. For it is necessary to understand both words that signify many things, and many words when they signify a single thing. This is how one learns to respond correctly. However, one must avoid the excessive and plainly useless abuse of time spent on things where it is not required. The one endowed with knowledge uses disciplines as <margin>F</margin> **preparatory exercises** <note>original: "præexercitationibus"; studies that prepare the mind for higher theology.</note> which serve as "assisting causes" for the accurate tradition of truth—at least as far as it can be attained—so that he cannot be pulled away from it, and to repel the artificial arguments that wickedly strive to cut down the truth. Do not leave...

# CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

<margin>A</margin>
...under those categories which lead toward the disciplines of the world and Greek philosophy. However, this is not for the primary reason, but for that which is necessary, secondary, and derived from specific circumstances. For those tools which are used wickedly and maliciously by those who devote their efforts to <term>heresies</term> <note>The word here refers to competing schools of thought or factions that Clement views as deviant from true Christian knowledge.</note> shall be used rightly by one who is endowed with true knowledge. Since there is a unique truth appearing in Greek philosophy—which is truly truth in the same way that the Sun, by illuminating colors both white and black, shows the nature of each—so too does this truth refute all mere probability of speech. Rightly, therefore, it has been proclaimed by the Greeks: "The Queen Truth is the principle of great virtue." Just as we have the example of Abraham in **Astronomy**, so too we have him in **Arithmetic**. For when he heard that Lot had been led away captive, he numbered three hundred of his household servants, attacked the enemy, and overcame a vast <margin>B</margin> number of them. They say, therefore, that the type of the <term>Sign of the Lord</term> <note>A reference to the Cross.</note>, as far as the shape is concerned, is the letter which signifies three hundred <margin>The letter T is the type of the cross, which also signifies three hundred. I. H. signifies both Jesus and eighteen.</margin>. Further, the <term>iota</term> <note>original: "ιῶτα"</note> and <term>eta</term> <note>original: "ῆτα"</note> signify the Name of Salvation. Therefore, it is shown that those who belong to Abraham's household and are joined to him—those who flee to the sign and the name of the Lord—attain salvation and overcome those who would lead them into captivity, as well as the many unfaithful nations following them. Now, the number three hundred is three times one hundred. The tenth number, without any controversy, is perfect in every respect. But eight <margin>Genesis 6.</margin>, which is the first cube, represents equality in all dimensions of length, breadth, and height. "The days of men," He says, "shall be one hundred and twenty years." This is <margin>Post. 64. These words seem to be missing. Namely eight, by odd numbers from unity. Where it says "it produces squares," it seems it should read "it produces triangles."</margin> the fifteenth number produced by the composition of units. Moreover, the Moon on the fifteenth <margin>C</margin> day is full. In another sense, the number one hundred and twenty is a <term>triangular number</term> <note>A number that can be arranged in an equilateral triangle; the sum of consecutive integers.</note>, and it consists of the evenness of the number 64. The composition of these by parts produces squares: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15. From the oddness of the number 56—namely, seven pairs starting from two, which generate those numbers which are "longer in one part"—we get 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14. In another meaning, the number 120 consists of four parts: one is a triangle, namely 15; the second is a square, namely 25; the third is a pentagon, namely 35; and the fourth is a hexagon, namely 45. For the same proportion of 5 is taken in each species. For of the triangles from unity, the fifth is 15. Of the squares, the fifth is 25, and those that follow in order according to the same proportion. Now, the number 25, which is the fifth from unity, is said to be the symbol of the <term>Levitical tribe</term>. The number 35 <margin>D</margin> is also derived from the description of doubles: Arithmetic, Geometric, and Harmonic—namely 6, 8, 9, and 12. The sum of these produces the number 35. Within these days, the Jews say the seven-month fetus is formed. The number 45 consists of the description of triples—namely 6, 9, 12, and 18—the sum of which produces 45. Similarly, within these days they say the nine-month fetus is formed. This is the form of the **Arithmetical** example. The testimony for **Geometry** is found in the Tabernacle that was constructed and the Ark that was built; these were constructed through divine discoveries and proportions that proceed with the highest reason, through the gift of understanding. This leads us from sensible things to those perceived by the intellect, or rather from those to the holy place and the Holy of Holies. For the squared timbers signify a squared <margin>E</margin> figure on every side, effecting security and stability with right angles. The length of the building was three hundred cubits. The width was fifty, and the height thirty. At the top, the Ark ends in a single cubit, sharpening from a wide base like a pyramid—a symbol of those who are purified and tested by fire. This **Geometric** proportion is provided for the purpose of passing into those holy dwellings, the differences of which are shown by the differences in the underlying numbers. The numbers introduced are "six-fold" (as 300 to 50) and <margin>The word "Or" or "twelve," as it appears in some versions, seems to be entirely superfluous and should be removed.</margin> "ten-fold" (as 300 is ten times 30) and <term>superbipartient</term> <note>original: "ἐπιδιμερῶν"; a ratio where one number contains another plus two-thirds of it (e.g., 50 to 30).</note>. For <margin>F</margin> fifty to thirty is a superbipartient ratio. There are those who say the three hundred cubits are a symbol of the Sign of the Lord. The fifty represents the hope and remission given at **Pentecost**. And the thirty—or as it is in some versions, twelve—they say signifies the preaching, since the Lord preached in His thirtieth year, and the twelve...

# STROMATA, BOOK VI. 209

<margin>A</margin> ...indeed, [ten] <note>The Latin "cim" is a fragment of "decem" (ten). Clement is likely connecting the number of Apostles to the Decalogue (Ten Commandments).</note> were the Apostles. And the building was completed at one cubit, with the progress of the righteous ending in the <term>monad</term> <note>From the Greek 'monas,' referring to the number one or a state of indivisible unity.</note> and in the unity of faith. Now, the table in the temple was six cubits long, and its four feet were each approximately one and a half cubits. Therefore, when all these cubits are added together, they total twelve, which corresponds to the twelve-month cycle that occurs through the circle of the year—during which the earth produces and perfects all things, following the established custom of the four seasons. I believe the table signifies an image of the earth, supported by four feet: summer, autumn, spring, and winter, through which the year proceeds. For this reason, it is also said that the table has "winding and twisted waves" <note>A reference to the decorative rim or "crown" of the Table of Showbread described in Exodus 25:24-25.</note>, either because all things are moved in the cycles of the seasons, or perhaps it signified the earth which the Ocean flows around.

<margin>B</margin> Furthermore, let David be presented as an example of music, simultaneously playing the harp and prophesying, praising God in a harmonious and rhythmic way. Among the musical modes, the <term>Dorian</term> <note>A Greek musical scale associated by the ancients with dignity and solemnity.</note> is the most "well-harmonized" <note>original: "εὐάρμονον"</note> (that is, concordant), while the <term>Phrygian</term> <note>A musical mode often associated with excitement or religious fervor.</note> is "diatonic" <note>original: "διάτονον"</note> (which is intense or sharp), as Aristoxenus <note>A Greek philosopher and pupil of Aristotle who wrote extensively on music theory.</note> says. Thus, the harmony of the "Barbarian" <note>In this context, "Barbarian" refers to the non-Greek, specifically Hebrew, origins of the biblical Psalms.</note> Psaltery, demonstrating the dignity and gravity of its modes, being the most ancient, served as the primary model for Terpander <note>A 7th-century BCE Greek poet and musician credited with inventing the seven-stringed lyre.</note> in developing the Dorian harmony to praise Jove in this manner: "Jupiter, the beginning of all; Leader of all; to you, Jupiter, I send this beginning of hymns."

The lyre might also be understood allegorically by the Psalmist. In its primary meaning, it represents the Lord. In its second meaning, it represents those who strike the souls [of listeners] in a disciplined way, with the Lord leading the song. The people who are saved might also be called a lyre through the inspiration of God. And whoever glorifies God through musical knowledge is heard, striking the chord of faith through the Word.

<margin>C</margin> You might also interpret "musical consonance" in another way: namely, the harmony of the Church, consisting of the Law, the Prophets, the Apostles, and the Gospel together, as well as the harmony found within each individual prophet when the spirit leaps from one person to another. 

But many, it seems, among those who bear the name [of Christian], approach doctrine in a rustic or unrefined way—not unlike the companions of Ulysses. They pass by the Sirens <note>In Greek mythology, the Sirens lured sailors with beautiful songs; here, Clement uses them as a metaphor for the "seductive" but useful beauty of Greek learning.</note>, but they also pass by the rhythms and modes, plugging their ears because of ignorance. They know that if they once lend an ear to Greek disciplines, they will never be able to return afterward. 

<margin>D</margin> However, for the person who harvests what is useful for the instruction of <term>Catechumens</term> <note>Students undergoing basic instruction in the Christian faith before baptism.</note>—and especially those who are Greek—it is not necessary to abstain from the study of doctrine like irrational animals, for "the earth is the Lord’s and the fullness thereof." We must provide as many aids as possible to those who listen. But we must by no means linger in these studies, except for the benefit that can be gained from them. Once we have secured that benefit, we should be able to "return home" to the true philosophy, which is the firm refuge of the soul and provides security from all things. 

Therefore, music should be touched upon for the sake of adorning and composing one's character. Certainly, at a banquet, we pledge one another by singing psalms, charming away our desires and glorifying God for the abundant gift of those things which humans use and enjoy, and because nourishment has been perpetually supplied for the growth of both body and soul.

<margin>E</margin> However, we must reject superfluous music that breaks the spirit and affects it in erratic ways—music that is sometimes mournful, sometimes indecent and inciting to lust, and sometimes frantic and insane. 

The same reasoning applies to **Astronomy**. For through the knowledge of sublime things—the shape of the universe, the revolution of the heavens, and the motion of the stars—it leads the soul closer to the creative power of God. It teaches us to easily perceive the yearly seasons, the changes in the air, and the rising and setting of the stars. For the art of navigation and agriculture is full of the utility that flows from it, just as it is for **Geometry**, **Architecture**, and the art of building. 

Furthermore, this discipline [Geometry] makes the soul capable of attaining the highest things: it enables it to perceive the truth, refute the false, and find certain points of agreement and proportions. It allows us to hunt for the similar in the dissimilar. It leads us to find <margin>F</margin> length without width, surfaces that lack depth, and a "point" which has no parts—thus translating us from sensible things (perceived by the senses) to those perceived by the intelligence. 

Therefore, the liberal disciplines assist philosophy, and philosophy itself assists in handling the truth. For behold, a cloak was first wool, then it was carded...

...existed, and the <term>weft and warp</term> <note>original: "subtegmen stamenque." Clement uses the metaphor of weaving cloth to describe how a soul is constructed and prepared.</note> were made. Then, it was woven together. <margin>A</margin> Therefore, the soul must first be prepared and intricately worked upon if it is to be established as something optimal and most excellent. For one part of the truth is concerned with knowledge, while the other is concerned with action. Moreover, action flows forth from contemplation. However, great exercise and experience are necessary. Furthermore, one part of contemplation is directed toward one's neighbors, while the other is directed toward oneself. For this reason, education must be so arranged that it suits both purposes. Therefore, for the person who has sufficiently learned those things that lead toward knowledge, it is permitted to remain quiet thereafter, directing all actions toward contemplation. 

But since some devote themselves to writing for the benefit of their neighbors, while others prepare themselves to hand down the Word, various teachings are useful. In particular, the reading of the <margin>B</margin> Lord’s scriptures is necessary for the demonstration of the things being said—especially if the listeners come from the background of Greek learning. David describes just such a Church: 
<margin>Psalm 44</margin> *The Queen stood at your right hand in clothing of gold, surrounded by variety.* <note>Psalm 45:9 in modern numbering. Clement interprets the "variety" or "embroidery" of the Queen's dress as the diverse branches of human knowledge that serve the Church.</note> She is surrounded and varied, I say, with Greek learning and superfluous "golden fringes." Yet the Truth is through the Lord. For, as it says, 
<margin>Wisdom 9</margin> *Who has known your counsel, unless you gave wisdom and sent your holy spirit from the highest heavens? And so the ways of those on earth were corrected, and men learned the things that please you, and were saved by wisdom.* 
For the person endowed with knowledge knows the things of old through scripture and 
<margin>Wisdom 8</margin> conjectures about things to come. He knows the <term>turns of phrases</term> <note>original: "strophas orationum." This refers to understanding complex rhetoric and figures of speech.</note> and the solutions to riddles; he foresees signs and wonders, and the outcomes of times, as we said before. You see that the fountain of all disciplines <margin>C</margin> flows from wisdom. 

Now, to those who object, asking: "What does it help us to know the causes of things—for example, how the Sun moves and the rest of the stars—or to have studied the theorems of Geometry, or Dialectics, and each of the other disciplines? For these contribute nothing to the teachings we must hand down, and Greek philosophy is merely human intelligence; for it is not taught by the truth." To them, these things must be said: first, that they are mistaken about the most important matters—namely, the voluntary choice of the mind and intelligence. For it says, *Those who keep holy things holily shall be sanctified, and those who have learned them shall find an answer.* <note>Wisdom 6:10.</note> For the person endowed with knowledge will rightly do all things holily that must be done, as he learned through the Lord’s teaching, even if he received it through men. 

And again, one may hear: *For in His hand*—that is, in His power <margin>D</margin> 
<margin>Wisdom 7</margin> and wisdom—*are both we and our words, and all prudence and knowledge of crafts.* 
<margin>Ibid. 7</margin> For God loves nothing except the one who dwells with wisdom. Furthermore, they have not read what was said by Solomon. For when he had treated the construction of the temple, he says clearly: *The craftsman built it by wisdom, but your providence, O Father, governs it.* <note>Wisdom 14:2–3.</note> And how is it not contrary to reason to value the craft of the carpenter or the shipbuilder, yet think poorly of philosophy? 

Perhaps the Lord also fed that multitude who reclined on the grass across from Tiberias with two fishes and five barley loaves, secretly signifying the earlier education of the Jews and Greeks which precedes the "divine wheat" of the nourishment cultivated through the Law. For barley ripens earlier than wheat in the harvest <margin>E</margin> time. These "fishes," which are born and carried through the waves of the Gentiles, signified Greek philosophy; they were given for the abundant conduct of life to those who lay on the ground. These fishes did not provide growth in the same way as the fragments of the loaves did; but once they had become participants in the Lord’s blessing, they possessed an inspired resurrection of divinity through the power of the Word.

# THE MISCELLANIES, BOOK VI.

<margin>A</margin> ...joined together, it grows into a holy temple of God, as the divine Apostle says. <margin>Eph. 2:</margin> <note>Ephesians 2:21: "In whom the whole building, being fitted together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord."</note> I will remain silent for the present regarding the parable in the Gospel which says: *The kingdom of heaven is like <margin>Matth. 13.</margin> a man who cast a net into the sea, and from the multitude of caught fish, chose the better ones.* <note>Matthew 13:47-48.</note> Now, indeed, the wisdom that exists among us clearly proclaims the four virtues, so that even their sources were given to the Greeks by the Hebrews. <margin>Wis. 8.</margin> <note>Clement refers to the "four cardinal virtues" (Temperance, Prudence, Justice, and Fortitude) mentioned in Wisdom of Solomon 8:7, a book he attributes to the Hebrew tradition.</note> From these, however, it can be known: if anyone loves justice, her labors are virtues. For she teaches temperance and prudence, justice and the virtue of a great and lofty soul <note>original: "magni excelsique animi virtutem," referring to Fortitude or Courage.</note>, than which nothing in life is more useful to men. 

Finally, they also needed to know this: that we are born naturally suited for virtue, but we do not possess it from birth; rather, we are suited <margin>B</margin> to acquire it. By this reasoning, that doubt raised by the heretics <note>Likely referring to Gnostic groups like the Valentinians, who believed humans were born with fixed natures (either "spiritual" or "material").</note> against us is resolved: "Was Adam formed perfect or imperfect?" But if he was imperfect, how is the work of a perfect God imperfect, and especially man? But if he was perfect, how did he transgress the commandments? They shall hear from us that he was not made perfect in his initial constitution, but suited to receive virtue. For it matters a great deal to be made capable of acquiring it. 

God wants us to be saved by our own efforts. This, then, is the nature of the soul: to be impelled and incited by itself. Furthermore, since we are endowed with reason, and <term>Philosophy</term> <note>For Clement, "philosophy" means the pursuit of wisdom through reason, which he sees as a gift from God.</note> consists of reason, we have a certain kinship with it. Now, aptitude is indeed a movement toward virtue, but it is not virtue itself. And everyone, as I said, is suited by nature for <margin>C</margin> acquiring virtue, but one person approaches training and exercise more, another less. Therefore, some have reached perfect virtue, while others have only reached a portion. On the other hand, some who were neglected, even if they otherwise had a good natural disposition, turned toward the opposite. 

Much more so is <term>knowledge</term> <note>original: "cognitio," Clement's Latin translation for the Greek "gnosis," meaning deep, spiritual insight into divine truth.</note>, which excels all disciplines in greatness and truth; it is both the hardest to acquire and is overcome with much labor. But, it seems, they did not know the mysteries of God: <margin>Wis. 2.</margin> namely, that God created man for immortality, and made him an image of His own nature; through this nature, the person who is endowed with knowledge, and is just and holy, strives with prudence to reach the measure of full maturity. 

That not only actions and thoughts, but also words, must be pure for the person who possesses knowledge, is shown here: <margin>D</margin> *You have tested my heart, you visited me by night,* he says; *you have set me on fire, and no iniquity was found in me. Let my mouth not speak the works of men.* <note>Psalm 17:3-4 (Psalm 16 in the Vulgate). Clement uses this to show that the "Gnostic" or advanced Christian is pure in every faculty.</note> And why do I say "the works of men"? He recognizes sin itself—not just that which has been brought to repentance (for this is common to other believers as well), but what sin is. For he does not condemn just this or that specific act, but to speak once and for all, he brings forward every sin; not just what someone has done wrong, but what ought not to be done. 

From this, there is also a double repentance. One is common, because one has sinned. The other, however, when one has learned the nature of sin, persuades one to desist from sin itself through foundational reason. The consequence of this is that one does not sin. Therefore, let them not say that he who does wrong and sins, does so through the <margin>E</margin> operation of demons. For in that case, he would be free of any fault. But when a man, in sinning, chooses the same things as the demons—being unstable, light-minded, and changeable in his desires like a demon—he becomes "demoniac." 

Now, he who is naturally evil, having become a sinner through vice, is rendered wicked, possessing what he chose. Conversely, the good man conducts himself rightly. Therefore, we call not only the virtues but also honest actions "good." Among good things, we know that some are to be chosen and sought for their own sake, such as <term>knowledge</term>. For we hunt for nothing else from it when it is present, except only that it be present, and that we may be in perpetual contemplation; we decide for it and because of it. 

Other things, however, are sought for the sake of something else, such as faith—both for the avoidance of punishment which follows from it, and for the utility gained from the reward. For fear is the cause for many to not sin. <margin>F</margin> The promise, however, is the occasion for pursuing obedience, through which comes salvation. Therefore, the most perfect good is knowledge, which is sought for its own sake. By consequence, those goods which follow through it are also good. And punishment, for the one who is punished, is a cause of correction; for those who can look on from a distance, it becomes an example.

<summary>Clement argues that humans are not born virtuous but with a natural "aptitude" to become so through effort and reason. He defines the highest good as "knowledge" (Gnosis), which is sought for its own sake, and distinguishes between common repentance and a deeper understanding of the nature of sin.</summary>

# CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

<margin>testing</margin> <note>original: "ἐτάσεως," referring to the scrutiny or examination of one's life.</note> ...through which they take care that they do not fall further into similar things. Let us, therefore, take up knowledge, not <margin>A</margin> desiring those things which happen, but embracing it for this very reason alone: namely, that we may know. For the first utility is the habit of knowledge, which provides innocent pleasures through exultation, both now and in the future. Now, they say that exultation is a joy which is the reputation of virtue arising from truth, through a certain cheering and expansion of the soul. Moreover, the deeds that participate in knowledge are good and honorable actions. For true riches are an abundance in those actions which come from virtue. Poverty, however, is a lack of moderate actions. For the possession and use of necessary things do not have a harmful quality, but rather that quantity which is beyond measure. Therefore, the one who is endowed with knowledge circumscribes his desires, both in possession and in use, not leaping over the limit of those things which are <margin>B</margin> necessary. This man, therefore, considering living to be necessary for the increase of science and the preparation of knowledge, will value living well most highly, rather than merely living. Preferring neither children, nor again marriage, nor parents, to the love of God and that justice which is in life. Moreover, his wife is judged as a sister to him after the conceiving of children, as if she were born of the same father; remembering her as a wife only then, when he looks upon his children, so that she may be in truth a future sister after the laying aside of the flesh—which [flesh] divides and distinguishes spiritual knowledge by the property of the sexes. For souls are by themselves equal; souls are neither, being neither male nor female, since they neither marry <margin>appearance</margin> <note>original: "σχήματος," referring to the outward form or fashion of the world.</note> nor are given in marriage. Is it not the case that a woman who is not effeminate is thus transformed into a man, being equally manly and perfect? This, therefore, was the laughter of Sarah, to whom the birth of a child was announced; not that she, as I think, would not have had faith in the Angel, but because she was ashamed again of the physical union through which she was to become the mother of a son. And is it not from that time, when <margin>Gen. 18.</margin> because of Sarah's beauty he was called into danger before the King of Egypt, that <margin>Gen. 20</margin> Abraham properly called her sister, though not yet born of the same mother and the same father? And indeed, to those who are led by repentance for sins, and have not firmly believed, God grants their petitions through prayers. But to those who live without sin and out of knowledge, He grants them even if they have only thought of it. For behold, to Hannah, who had only thought of a child, the conception of Samuel was given. "ASK," says the Scrip- <margin>D</margin> ture, "and I will do; think in your mind, and I will give." <note>A paraphrased reference to God’s responsiveness to the righteous, often linked to Isaiah 58:9 or 65:24.</note> For we have received God as the Knower of hearts, not one who guesses from the movement of the soul, as we men do. But neither [does He know] from the outcome, for it would be ridiculous to think so. Nor as the Architect praised the work once it was done, so also did God, when He had made the light and then saw it, say it was good. Rather, even before He had made it, knowing what it was going to be, He praised that which was made, as one who could make good from on high through a purpose that lacks a beginning; that which was to be good in actuality, and that which was to be, He already predicted to be good, with the word "hyperbaton" <note>A rhetorical term for a transposition of words; Clement suggests the biblical phrasing hides a deeper truth about God's timelessness.</note> concealing the truth. Therefore, the one who is endowed with knowledge prays, even in thought, joined to God at every hour through love, and made an intimate. And first, indeed, he will ask for the remission of sins. Afterward, that he may sin no more. Then, to be <margin>E</margin> able to do good, and to understand all the creation and dispensation which was made through the Lord; so that, having been made pure in heart through the recognition which is through the Son of God, he may be initiated face to face into the mystery of the blessed spectacle, hearing the Scripture which <margin>Tobit 12.</margin> says: *Fasting is good with prayer.* Now, fasts signify generally all abstinence from all evils, as much those done in deed as those in words, and in thought itself. There is, therefore, as it seems, a "square justice," equal and similar on every side, in word, in deed, in abstinence from evils, in doing good, in the perfection of knowledge, nowhere limping in any way, lest he seem unjust and unequal. Therefore, insofar as someone is just, he is also entirely faithful. But insofar as he is faithful, he is not <margin>Gen. 15.</margin> yet also just. I speak of the justice which comes through progress and consummation, through which the one who is endowed with knowledge is called just. For now indeed to Abraham, who had been made faithful, it was accounted as justice, as one who had proceeded to that which is the greatest and most perfect of faith. For not he who only abstains from an evil action is just, unless he has furthermore perfected himself so that he also does good, and knows for what cause <meta>catchword: he must abstain</meta>

<summary>Clement defines the "Gnostic" life, emphasizing that true spiritual knowledge leads to a "square justice" where deeds, thoughts, and words are perfectly aligned. He explores the transition from physical marriage to spiritual siblinghood and explains how God answers the mere thoughts of the perfected soul.</summary>

### MISCELLANIES, BOOK VI.

<margin>2 Corinthians 6</margin>
**A** One must indeed abstain from certain things, while other things must be done. Through the "weapons of righteousness on the right hand and on the left," the Apostle says the righteous person is sent forward to the highest inheritance; protected by the former <note>The "left-hand" weapons usually represent endurance in adversity or protection from sin.</note> and active in the latter <note>The "right-hand" weapons represent active works of virtue.</note>. For the mere shield of armor and the abstinence from sins are not enough for perfection, unless one also takes up the work of righteousness, which is the active practice of doing good. Then, using both hands, the one who is endowed with knowledge is revealed in righteousness. From this point onward, such a person is no different than Moses; the "face" of their soul is glorified <note>original: "facie animæ glorificatus," an allusion to Moses' face shining after speaking with God.</note>, just as we said before that the body provides the form and character to a righteous soul. For just as a dye that has been set in wool transmits its quality and change to the rest of the wool, so also in the soul: the labor passes away, but that which is good and honorable remains;

**B** and while that which is merely pleasant is left behind, that which is shameful is wiped away. These are the qualities that provide form and character to every soul, by which one is recognized as glorified, and the other as condemned. Certainly, just as a certain glorified appearance of color rested upon the face of Moses because of his righteous actions and the constant habit of conversation he had with God as He spoke, so too a certain divine power of goodness inheres in the righteous soul through contemplation, prophecy, and the service of active work. This is like an intellectual illumination—much like the heat of the sun—imprinting an open seal of righteousness, a light united to the soul through a love <note>original: "charitatem," often translated as "charity" or "divine love."</note> that is never separated by any distance, which breathes toward God and is breathed upon by God. From this

<margin>Matthew 5; John 13</margin>
**C** arises an assimilation to God the Savior for the one endowed with knowledge, who has indeed emerged as perfect, as far as is permitted to human nature. "Be like the Father," He says, "who is in heaven." It is He who said, "Little children, I am with you yet a little while." For God does not remain blessed and alien to destruction merely because He is good by nature, nor because He lacks any business or gives none to others. Rather, because He is God and the good Father, and is engaged in continual beneficence, He remains in that same goodness so that He never departs from it. For what is the use of a "good" that neither works nor affects anything good? Therefore, the one who first moderated the movements of his own soul, and meditated on becoming impassible <note>original: "impatibilis," meaning one who is not swayed by suffering or disordered passions.</note>, and grew toward the beneficence of a perfection endowed with knowledge, is indeed equal to the angels. Already luminous and shining like the sun through beneficence, such a person hastens through righteous knowledge and the love of God toward the holy dwelling,

**D** just like the Apostles. They were not chosen as Apostles because of some extraordinary natural property—for Judas was also chosen with them—but they were capable of becoming Apostles because they were chosen by Him who foresees even the ends of things. Therefore, Matthias, who was not chosen along with them initially, was substituted into the place of Judas when he proved himself worthy to become an Apostle. It is permitted even now, therefore, for those who have exercised themselves in the Lord's commandments and have lived perfectly according to the Gospel, to be enrolled in the number of the Apostles through their knowledge. Such a person is truly a Presbyter <note>A term for a church elder or priest.</note> of the Church and a true Deacon <note>A term for a servant or minister.</note> of the will of God, if he does and teaches the things of the Lord. He is not a "Presbyter" simply because he is ordained by men, nor because he is merely thought to be righteous, but because he is righteous, he is recorded in the presbyterate. And even if he is not honored with the first seat here on earth,

<margin>Revelation 4</margin>
**E** he will sit upon the twenty-four thrones judging the people, as John says in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note>. For there is in truth one saving testament which has reached us from the foundation of the world through different generations and times, even if it was thought to be different in the way it was given. For it follows that there is one immutable gift of salvation from one God through one Lord, which profits in many ways. For this reason, the "dividing wall" <note>original: "materia," here referring to the barrier of the old law or worldly distinctions.</note> is taken away which divided the Greek from the Jew, so that there might be a peculiar people. And thus both come to one unity of faith, and from both there is one election. And among the elect, he says, there are those "more elect," who are gathered from the perfect knowledge and from the Church itself, and are honored with the most magnificent glory,

**F** as judges and administrators, drawn equally from both Jews and Greeks: twenty-four in number, with a doubled grace. For here in the Church, the advancements of Bishops, Presbyters, and Deacons are, I believe, imitations of the angelic glory and of that economy and dispensation which the Scriptures say those await who, following in the footsteps of the Apostles, have lived in the perfection of righteousness according to the Gospel.

He argues that the true hierarchy of the Church is based on character and righteousness rather than human ordination, mirroring the celestial ranks of angels.</summary>

### CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

<margin>A</margin> ...following the footsteps of the Apostles, they lived in the perfection of righteousness in accordance with the Gospel. The Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul in 1 Thessalonians 4:17.</note> writes that those who are caught up in the clouds will first serve as **Deacons**, and then be co-opted into the **presbyterate** <note>The rank of elder or priest.</note> through a progression of glory. For "glory differs from glory" until they grow into a perfect man. Such people, as the blessed David says,
<margin>Psalm 15 <br/> John 1</margin>
will rest on the holy mountain of God, the supreme church, in which are gathered **God’s Philosophers** <note>Clement uses "philosophers" to describe true Christians who seek divine wisdom.</note>, who are truly Israelites, pure in heart, in whom there is no deceit. These did not remain in the "seven" of rest <note>The "septenary" represents the Sabbath or a state of peaceful cessation from sin.</note>, but by the performance of good works and divine imitation, they were raised up to the inheritance of the "eight" of beneficence <note>The "octonary" refers to the eighth day, symbolizing the resurrection and the highest heaven.</note>, attending to the pure and sincere contemplation of insatiable vision.

<margin>John 10</margin>
<margin>B</margin> The Lord says, "I also have other sheep, which are not of this fold," which are granted another fold and mansion in proportion to their faith. "But my sheep hear my voice," understanding the commandments through my **knowledge** <note>original Latin: "cognitione," translating the Greek "gnosis."</note>. This may be understood magnificently and according to the worthiness of their merits, with the reward of their works following as a consequence. Therefore, when we hear the phrase, <note>original: "Fides tua te saluam fecit"</note> *“Your faith has saved you,”* we do not take him to mean that they will be saved absolutely just because they believed in any way whatsoever, unless works followed. Indeed, he spoke these words only to the Jews who held the Law and had lived blamelessly, for whom only faith in the Lord was still lacking. Therefore, one cannot be a "believer" while remaining intemperate; even if one departs from the flesh, it is necessary to set aside vices to reach one's own mansion. To **know** is more than to **believe**, just as
<margin>C</margin> it is a greater thing to be considered worthy of the highest honor after you have been saved than it is merely to be saved. Therefore, when the believer has cast off vices through much discipline, he passes to the "greatest punishment" <note>This refers to a purifying discipline or the pain of regret after death.</note>, which is better than his previous state, bringing with it the specific repentance for those sins committed after baptism. He is tortured even more because he does not yet—or perhaps never will—attain those things which he sees others participating in. Furthermore, he is filled with shame for his failings, which are the greatest punishments for a believer. For the justice of God is good, and His goodness is just. Even if the tortures cease once the penalties are paid and the sins committed by each are expiated, they still have the greatest permanent grief: that though they were found worthy of another fold, they are not with those who were glorified for their righteousness.

Now, Solomon, calling the one endowed with knowledge "wise," says this about those who wonder at the dignity of that mansion:
<margin>D</margin> <margin>Wisdom 5</margin>
"For they shall see the death of the wise, and shall not understand what God has decreed for him, and for what purpose the Lord has established him; and they shall say of his glory: 'This is he whom we once held in derision and as a proverb of reproach, we fools. We esteemed his life madness and his end dishonorable. How is he numbered among the children of God, and his lot is among the saints?'" <note>Quoting from the Wisdom of Solomon 5:4-5.</note> Therefore, not only the believer, but even the **Gentile**, is judged most justly. Since God, possessing foreknowledge, knew that the Gentile would not believe, He nevertheless gave him **philosophy** before faith, so that he might receive his own perfection.

<margin>E</margin> <margin>Deuteronomy 4</margin>
The Law says that God gave the Sun, the Moon, and the stars for worship <note>Clement argues that God permitted celestial worship as a "stepping stone" to prevent total atheism.</note> to the nations, lest they should be entirely godless and alienated from God, and so utterly perish. But those people, though born under this mandate, were ungrateful and turned instead to carved images. If they are not led by repentance, they are judged: some because they were able to believe in God but chose not to, and others because, even when they wished to, they did not labor to become believers. Even those who did not return from the worship of the stars to their Creator are judged. For this path was given to the Gentiles: that through the worship of the stars, they might look up toward God. But those who did not even wish to remain with the stars given to them, but fell away from them to wood and stones, are counted—the scripture says—as the "dust of the earth" and a "drop from a bucket," useless for salvation and cast out from the body.

Just as "to save" in an absolute sense is among the "middle" things, but to do so rightly and as is fitting is a "perfect" duty; so also
<margin>F</margin> every action of the person endowed with **knowledge** <term>Gnostic: one who possesses spiritual insight</term> is a "right and perfect duty," whereas the action of the simple believer might be called a "middle action," as it is not yet performed according to the Word or reason, nor rightly conducted out of science <note>In the sense of certain spiritual knowledge.</note>. On the other hand...

<summary>Clement explains that the afterlife consists of different levels of glory (mansions) based on whether one possessed simple faith or advanced "knowledge" (Gnosis). He argues that God gave philosophy and the stars to the Gentiles as a preliminary form of worship to lead them toward the Creator, making their eventual judgment just.</summary>

Having previously discussed the ranks of the church reflecting celestial orders, he now addresses the nature of virtuous action, the different rewards in the afterlife, and the concept of becoming like God through the Word.</meta>

### MISCELLANIES, BOOK VI.

<margin>A</margin> On the other hand, the action of any pagan is a sin. The Scriptures show that it is not enough simply to act well, but one must perform actions looking toward a specific goal and acting according to the Word <note>original: "verbo," referring to the Logos or Divine Reason</note> or right reason. Just as those who are unskilled in playing the lyre should not touch the instrument, so also business should not be attempted by those who have not received **knowledge** <note>original: "cognitionem," translating the Greek "gnosis"</note> and do not know how to conduct them according to the Word of life. For the struggle for liberty is undertaken by warriors not only in wars, but also at banquets, in the bedchamber, and in the courts—those who have been "anointed by the Word" <note>A metaphor for being consecrated or prepared by Christian teaching</note> are ashamed to become slaves to pleasure. I would never trade virtue for unjust gain. For pleasure and pain, labor and fear, and—to put it simply—vices and the agitations of the soul are clearly unjust gains; that which is pleasant in the present moment brings distress afterward.

<margin>B</margin> <margin>Matthew 16:</margin> For "what does it profit," He says, "if you gain the whole world, but lose your soul?" It is clear, therefore, that those who do not perform good actions do not even know what is useful for themselves. If this is so, they cannot even pray to God to receive good things from Him, since they are ignorant of what is truly good. Nor, if they did receive them, would they perceive the gift, nor would they use what they know in a way worthy of its dignity; both because of their lack of skill in rightly using what has been given, and because of their excessive ignorance, not knowing how even divine gifts ought to be used. For "unskillfulness" is the cause of ignorance. Furthermore, it is the "boasting" of a soul that is perhaps boastful in speech but possesses a good conscience, to speak out against the accidents that occur. Against these things, one must conduct oneself cautiously and prudently. For that which is done well and is just will bring me aid, and I shall never be found doing evil.

<margin>C</margin> This good conscience preserves both holiness toward God and justice toward men; it keeps the soul pure with honorable thoughts, chaste words, and just deeds. Thus, when the soul has received the power of the Lord, it **meditates on being God** <note>This refers to "theosis" or deification, the process of becoming like God through grace, a central theme in early Greek patristic theology</note>, thinking nothing else to be evil except ignorance and action that does not proceed from right reason. Always giving thanks to God for all things—through righteous hearing, divine reading, true inquiry, holy offering, and blessed prayer—it is ever praising, singing, blessing, and playing the psaltery. Such a soul is never at any time divided from God. Rightly, therefore, it was said: <margin>Wisdom 3.</margin> "And those who trust in Him shall understand the truth, and the faithful in love shall abide in Him." You see how the wisdom of those endowed with knowledge differs.

<margin>D</margin> According to a system of proportion and harmony, there are various **mansions** <note>original: "mansiones," referring to John 14:2</note> based on the dignity and merits of those who have believed. For behold Solomon says: "For to him shall be given the chosen grace of faith, and a more pleasant lot in the temple of the Lord." For the comparative degree shows those things which are lower in the temple of God (which is the universal church); but it leaves us to imagine the superlative also, in which the Lord is. These three "chosen mansions" are signified by the numbers in the Gospel: **thirty, sixty, and a hundred.** <note>Referring to the Parable of the Sower in Matthew 13</note> And the perfect inheritance belongs to those who attain to the "perfect man" according to the image of the Lord. But this "likeness" is not, as some suppose, in a human physical form. For such a thought is impious. Nor is it the assimilation that is passed down regarding the power of the First Cause. For this also is an impious tradition of those who expect the power of man and God Almighty to be the same.

<margin>E</margin> <margin>Psalm 49. John 13.</margin> "You thought, wickedly," He says, "that I would be like you." For "it is enough for the disciple if he becomes like his master," says the Master. He therefore becomes like God who is adopted as a son and chosen for the number of friends, because he is a co-heir with Lords and Gods <note>original: "Dominorum & Deorum," likely referring to the angelic orders or the perfected saints</note>, provided that he has been brought to perfection through the Gospel, just as the Lord Himself taught. He who is endowed with knowledge, therefore, expresses a closer and more coherent likeness—namely, the mind of the teacher. When the teacher possessed this mind, he commanded and counseled the wise and the temperate. He expresses this likeness, I say, by understanding as the teacher intended, and having received the magnificent meaning, teaching "upon the housetops" <note>referring to Matthew 10:27</note> according to the dignity of those who wish to be built up high—but first beginning to carry out in deed the things that are spoken, in accordance with the example of his life’s discipline; for he commanded things that were possible to be done.

<margin>F</margin> And truly, it is necessary for him who is "royal" and a Christian to be able to obtain the principal power and to lead. For it was established not only that we should rule over those external wild beasts, but also over the wild agitations of the soul within ourselves. Through...

<summary>Clement discusses how true Christian knowledge (gnosis) leads to virtuous action and theosis (becoming like God). He explains that heavenly rewards are proportional to merit, using the Gospel's "thirty, sixty, and a hundredfold" to represent different levels of spiritual achievement.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Clement’s argument that "gnosis" (spiritual knowledge) is necessary to truly understand the scriptures. He moves from discussing the virtuous life of the Christian sage to the specific ways that divine truth is hidden from the unworthy but revealed to the seeker, using the metaphor of grafting trees to explain how different people—philosophers, Jews, and pagans—are brought into the faith of Christ.</meta>

# CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

<margin>A</margin> Therefore, regarding the knowledge <note>original: "scientiam," here referring to the Greek "gnosis" or spiritual insight</note> of a good and bad life, let the one who is gifted with knowledge be saved, understanding and performing more than the scribes and Pharisees. "Aim, prosper, and reign," David writes, <margin>Psalm 44</margin> <note>original: "Intende, bene prosperare, & regna." This refers to Psalm 45:4 in modern Bibles.</note> "because of truth, mildness, and justice; and your right hand," which is the Lord, "will lead you wonderfully." Who then is wise, and will understand these things? Who is discerning, and will know them? <margin>Psalm 106</margin> <note>Modern Psalm 107:43</note> For the Prophet says, "The ways of the Lord are right," signifying that only the one gifted with knowledge can understand those things which are spoken secretly by the Spirit. And "he who understands will be silent in that time," says the Scripture, <note>Amos 5:13</note> namely, in speaking to the unworthy. For the Lord says, "He who has ears to hear, let him hear," saying that it is not for everyone to hear and understand. Indeed, David says: <margin>Psalm 18</margin> <note>Modern Psalm 18:11-12</note> "Dark water in the clouds of the air. At the brightness before Him, the clouds passed, <margin>B</margin> hail and coals of fire," teaching that the holy words are hidden. To those who are gifted with knowledge, he signifies that the words are sent down from the divine like harmless hail, clear and transparent; but to the common people they are obscure, like coals extinguished from a fire, which will not burn or give light unless someone ignites and stirs them.

The Lord, therefore, says: "He gives me the tongue of discipline, that I may know the time when it is necessary to speak a word," <margin>Isaiah 50</margin> <note>Isaiah 50:4</note> not only in offering testimony, but also in questioning and answering. And "the discipline of the Lord opens my mouth." It belongs, therefore, to the one gifted with knowledge to know how to use speech: when, how, and before whom it is necessary. Indeed, the Apostle also says: "According to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ," <margin>Colossians 2</margin> <note>Colossians 2:8</note> <margin>C</margin> handing down that Greek doctrine is like the basic "elements," but the doctrine of Christ is perfect, as we have already indicated before.

Now, the wild olive is grafted into the richness of the cultivated olive. <margin>Romans 11</margin> <note>Romans 11:17-24</note> Moreover, it grows into the same species as the cultivated olive. For that which is grafted uses the tree into which it is inserted as its ground. All plants together germinated by divine command. Therefore, even if it is a rustic wild olive, it nevertheless crowns those who are victors in the Olympic games; <note>Clement refers to the "kotinos" or wild olive wreath given to Olympic winners</note> and the elm, lifting the vine on high, teaches it to be fertile. We see, however, that wild trees draw in more nourishment because they cannot "concoct" <note>original: "concoquere," a classical biological term for digesting or ripening nutrients</note> it. Therefore, those things that are wild concoct less than those that are cultivated, and the reason they are wild is the lack of this "concocting" power. Thus, the grafted olive receives more nourishment because it is planted in a wild stock. <margin>D</margin> It becomes accustomed to concocting the nourishment as it is assimilated into the richness of the cultivated tree. 

In the same way, the Philosopher—who is likened to the wild olive—possesses much that is "unconcocted," because he inquires gladly and attains things easily, yet hungers for the richness of truth. If through faith he receives divine power, being grafted into the good and mild knowledge <note>The "good olive" of the Gospel</note> like a wild olive grafted into the truly beautiful and merciful Word, he concocts the nourishment that is handed down and becomes a good, cultivated olive. For grafting makes those that were useless into noble ones, and forces those that were sterile to be fertile through the art of agriculture and the science that comes from knowledge. 

They say that grafting is done in four ways. First, where the one grafting must fit the shoot between the wood and the bark; <margin>E</margin> in this way they receive the **Catechumen** <note>A convert receiving basic instruction before baptism</note>—those simple folk from the nations who receive the Word on the surface. In the second way, when the wood is split and they insert a noble plant into it; this happens to those who have practiced philosophy. For when their dogmas are cut open, the recognition of truth is generated within them. In this way, too, when the ancient Scripture is opened to the Jews, the new and noble plant of the olive is grafted in. 

The third type of grafting concerns the wild ones and the heretics, who are drawn by force to the truth. For when they have scraped both shoots with a sharp hook until they have bared the marrow—though without wounding them—they bind them together. The fourth <margin>ἀγριέλαιον <note>original Greek: "agrielaion," meaning wild olive tree</note> ἐπίσημον <note>original Greek: "episemon," meaning a sign or a mark, here likely referring to the "eye" or bud used in grafting</margin> mode of grafting is that which is called "inoculation" <note>The process of budding, or inserting an "eye" (bud) from one tree into another</note>. For an "eye" is cut from a noble trunk, with the bark also circumscribed in a circle the size of a palm's breadth. Then the trunk is scraped away to match the eye’s circumference, and so it is inserted, bound around, and smeared with mud, with the eye kept whole, unhurt, and unpolluted. <margin>F</margin> This genus is certainly the most useful among cultivated trees. This same grafting mentioned by the Apostle can be done into the "good olive"—that is, into Christ himself—by the wild and un-

<meta>Catchword: -faithful (delis)</meta>

<meta>This page continues Clement’s discussion on how divine knowledge is imparted to the believer. He moves from the metaphor of grafting "wild" souls into the "cultivated" tree of Christ to a scriptural and philosophical exploration of how Wisdom is found and the logical steps that lead a seeker toward God.</meta>

### MISCELLANIES, BOOK VI

<margin>A</margin> ...faithful nature <note>The text continues from the previous page, likely completing the word "fidelis" (faithful).</note> which is implanted into Christ—that is, the nature of those who believe in Christ. It is better, however, for each person’s faith to be placed within the soul itself. For the Holy Spirit, being distributed through the soul in a certain way, is "transplanted" without being limited, according to the specific capacity <note>original: "circumscriptio," referring to the individual boundaries or limits of a person's nature</note> of each individual. Regarding this spiritual knowledge <note>original: "cognitione," referring to Gnosis</note>, Solomon says the following: <margin>Wisdom 6</margin> "Wisdom is radiant and does not fade; she is easily seen by those who love her, and she anticipates those who desire her so that she may be known beforehand. He who rises early to seek her will not labor. For to think upon her is the perfection of prudence. And he who keeps watch for her sake will quickly be free from care, because she goes about seeking those who are worthy of her." For this knowledge is not for everyone. "And in the paths," it says, "she is kindly perceived by them in a vision." <margin>B</margin> These "paths" refer to the way one leads their life, and the multifaceted variety found in the Covenant <note>original: "testamento," the divine agreement or Scripture</note>. Soon after, he adds: "And she meets them in every thought," suggesting she is considered in various ways—namely, through every kind of teaching. Then he introduces the idea of Love as the perfecting element, using a logical chain of reasoning <term>syllogism: a form of reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two given premises</term> and true propositions, leading to a true and demonstrative conclusion in this way: "For her truest beginning is the desire for discipline <note>original: "disciplinæ," meaning instruction or learning</note>, which is to say, the desire for knowledge. The care for discipline is love. Love is the keeping of her laws. Attention to the laws is the confirmation of those laws. The confirmation of the laws is the absence of corruption <note>original: "vacuitas interitus," literally the emptiness of destruction/perishing</note>. And the absence of corruption makes one come close to God. Therefore, the desire for Wisdom leads upward to the Kingdom." He teaches, as I see it, that true discipline is a certain desire for knowledge. <margin>C</margin> And love is indeed the keeping of the commandments which lead to that knowledge. The keeping of them is the firming up of the precepts, which results in the absence of corruption. And being free from corruption makes us near to God. If, therefore, the love of knowledge makes one a stranger to destruction and lifts the one who is of "royal" character near to God: then it is necessary to seek knowledge until it is found. "Inquiry" is the excitement and impulse toward grasping something, which finds the subject through certain signs. "Finding" <note>original: "Inuentio," or discovery</note>, however, is the end and the rest of the inquiry which has reached comprehension; this is indeed knowledge. Finding itself is properly knowledge, being the achievement of the inquiry. They say a "sign" is that which precedes, accompanies, or follows a thing—which is the grasping of it. <margin>D</margin> Therefore, in the inquiry concerning God, the "finding" is the teaching that comes through the Son. The "signs" that he is our Savior, the very Son of God, are the prophecies that preceded his coming and proclaimed him; the sensory testimonies concerning him at his birth; and furthermore, the "powers" <note>original: "virtutes," often meaning miracles or divine strengths</note> that were preached and openly shown after his ascension. That the truth is with us is indicated by the fact that the Son of God himself has taught us. If, in every question, these general factors are found—the matter and the person—it is shown that the truth is truly among us. For the *person* of the truth that is shown is the Son of God; the *matter* is the power of faith, which overcomes everything that opposes it, even the whole world itself in its resistance. But since this is already certain and confirmed beyond controversy by eternal deeds and <margin>E</margin> words—and any man who thinks there is no Providence is worthy of punishment, not of an argument, being truly impious—our purpose is to show what we must do and how we must live to reach the knowledge of Almighty God. And how, by honoring God, we become the cause of our own salvation. Since we have recognized and learned what is pleasing, just, and holy to Him, not from Sophists <note>professional teachers of rhetoric in ancient Greece often accused of valuing style over truth</note> but from God himself, we set about to do it. Our being saved—which is pleasing to Him—comes through good works and knowledge, of both of which the Lord is the Master. Therefore, if (even according to Plato’s opinion) the truth can only be learned either from God or from those descended from the Gods, we rightly boast that we learn the truth through the Son of God, selecting testimonies from the divine oracles <note>the Scriptures</note> which <margin>F</margin> were first foretold and then declared. Those things which help in finding the truth are not themselves to be rejected. Indeed, philosophy itself—which announces Providence and treats the reward of a blessed life and the punishment of a miserable one—deals with these matters in a theological way. But as for that which treats them accurately and precisely...

<meta>This page continues Clement’s argument from the previous section where he differentiates between true Christian Gnosis (knowledge) and the partial or distorted views of "barbarian" (non-Christian) philosophies and heresies. He is establishing the "Ecclesiastical Rule" as the standard for interpreting the hidden meanings of the Bible.</meta>

# CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

...[con]cluded, and those things which are held individually, it certainly does not preserve. For [heresy] does not treat the Son of God, <margin>A</margin> nor the divine arrangement <term>economy: from the Greek 'oikonomia,' referring to God's strategic plan for human salvation</term> through providence, as we do. For it did not know divine religion. Wherefore the heresies which exist in barbarian philosophy—even if they speak of one God, and even if they celebrate Christ—they do so from a [partial] comprehension, not from the truth. For they invent another God and do not receive Christ as the Prophecies handed down. Truly, the false dogmas among them, as long as they oppose the life lived in truth, are against us.

For already <margin>Acts 16</margin> Paul circumcised Timothy on account of those who believed from among the Jews, lest those who were novices <term>Catechumeni: students undergoing initial instruction in the Christian faith</term> from the Law might fall away from the faith if he dissolved those things which had previously been taken more carnally from the Law—even though he knew rightly that circumcision does not justify. For he professed to become "all things to all people," <margin>by way of accommodation <note>original: "κατὰ συμπεριφοράν" (kata symperiphoran) — a technical term for 'condescension' or adapting one's behavior to the needs of others for their benefit</note></margin> while he lowered himself and variously accommodated himself to them, preserving <margin>B</margin> those things which were the principal dogmas, in order to gain everyone. And Daniel <margin>Daniel 5</margin> wore a necklace <note>original: "torquem," a chain of office or honor</note> even though he did not neglect the fact that the people were afflicted by the King of the Persians. 

Therefore, those who are truly liars are not those who lower themselves and accommodate themselves for the sake of the divine plan of salvation; nor those who slip in some specific details; but those who fail in the most principal matters, and weaken and abolish the Lord as far as they are able. They take away the true teaching of the Lord, failing to distribute and hand down the scriptures in a manner worthy of God and the Lord. For the deposit <note>The "depositum" refers to the sacred trust of faith handed down from the Apostles</note> which is returned to God consists of the understanding and practice [of the faith], in accordance with the Lord’s teaching through the pious tradition of his Apostles. <margin>greediness / trifles <note>original: "λιχνότητας" (lichnotas)</note></margin> 

"But what you hear in the ear," <margin>Matthew 10</margin>—that is, secretly and in mystery (for things of this kind are said to be "in the ear" <margin>C</margin> allegorically)—"preach," he says, "upon the rooftops." This means they should hand it down in a sublime and exalted style of speaking, after having received it clearly and magnificently, explaining the scriptures according to the rule of truth. For neither was prophecy, nor the Savior himself, so coarse or general in speaking of divine mysteries that they could be easily grasped by anyone; instead, he spoke in parables. Certainly, the Apostles say of the Lord that "he spoke all things in parables, and spoke nothing to them without a parable." <margin>Mark 4</margin> 

But if all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made, then prophecy also and the law were made through him, and were spoken through him in parables. "Otherwise, all things are right," says the scripture, "before those who understand"—that is, those who preserve the exposition of the scriptures declared by him, receiving it from the ecclesiastical rule. <margin>D</margin> The **ecclesiastical rule** <term>regula ecclesiastica</term> is the harmony and consensus of the Law and the Prophets, in accord with the testament handed down through the Lord’s coming.

And indeed, prudence follows knowledge <note>original: "cognitionem," referring here to spiritual Gnosis</note>, and temperance follows prudence. For let it be said that prudence is divine knowledge, even in those who "become gods" <note>Clement refers to "theosis," the process of being made like God through grace and knowledge</note>. But they philosophize that temperance is mortal, belonging to men who are not yet wise. Now, if virtue is divine, or even the knowledge of it, then temperance is like an imperfect prudence—desiring prudence, working laboriously, but not yet contemplating. This is just as human justice is subjected to holiness as something common, since holiness is divine justice. For to the person who is perfect, justice comes not through civil contracts or the prohibition <margin>E</margin> of the law, but from their own action and love toward God. 

For many reasons, therefore, the scriptures hide their meaning. First, so that we might seek diligently and always remain watchful in finding the words of salvation. Furthermore, it was not appropriate for all men to understand, lest they be harmed by receiving in the wrong way what was spoken healthfully by the Holy Spirit. Therefore, for those who are chosen from among men, and for those who are adopted from faith into knowledge, the holy mysteries of the Prophecies are preserved, veiled in parables. For the style of the scriptures is parabolic. Therefore, the Lord also, though he was not of this world, came to men as if he were of the world. He bore every virtue; and the person who was nurtured in the world, he was going to raise from the world into the [spiritual] world <margin>F</margin> toward those things which are perceived by the intellect and are primary. For this reason, scripture also uses metaphor. For a parable is such a thing: a discourse leading the one who understands from something not strictly proper, but similar to the proper, to that which is true and proper. Or as some say...

<meta>This page continues Clement’s argument from the previous section where he critiques the "partial" knowledge of Greek philosophers and heretics. He now moves into a specific defense of why the Holy Scriptures use parables, enigmas, and figurative language, citing the "Preaching of Peter" to show that Christ was hidden in the Old Testament prophets to be revealed to those with faith.</meta>

### STROMATA, BOOK VI.

<margin>A</margin> [A parable is] a way of speaking which, through other things, demonstrates with great power those things that are properly meant. Indeed, the entire <term>economy: the divine plan or "household management" of God for human salvation</term> which was predicted by the Prophets regarding the Lord, truly appears as a parable to those who do not know the truth. For instance, when one person says—and others hear—that the Son of God, who created all things, took on flesh and was conceived in the womb of a virgin (at least in terms of how His perceptible physical body was born), and consequently suffered and rose again, it is "a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Greeks," <note>Clement is quoting 1 Corinthians 1:23</note> as the Apostle says. However, the Scriptures openly show the truth to those who "have ears," announcing that the very suffering of the flesh which the Lord assumed is the power and wisdom of God. Finally, since the parabolic style of Scripture is <margin>B</margin> extremely ancient (as we have shown), it rightly abounded among the Prophets. This was so the Holy Spirit might show that the [Greek] philosophers and the wise men among other non-Greeks <note>original: "barbaros" — Clement uses this term for any non-Greek culture, including the Hebrews</note> were ignorant of the Lord’s future coming and the mystical doctrine that was to be handed down by Him.

Rightly, then, did the Prophecy that proclaims the Lord use figurative language. Lest it seem to be blaspheming to some by speaking contrary to common opinions, it shaped its meanings into words that could also lead the mind toward other interpretations. Furthermore, all the Prophets who predicted the Lord's coming and the holy mysteries accompanying Him suffered persecution and were killed, just as the Lord Himself was, who explained the Scriptures to them. His companions, too, who preached the Word after He departed this life, made use of parables. Hence <margin>C</margin> Peter, speaking in his *Preaching* <note>original: "Prædicatione" — referring to the *Kerygma Petrou*, an early Christian text Clement regarded highly</note> concerning the Apostles, says:

> "But when we had unrolled the books of the Prophets which we possessed—which name Jesus Christ sometimes through parables, sometimes through enigmas, and sometimes plainly with their own authority and specific words—we found His coming, His death, the cross, and all the other punishments which the Jews inflicted on Him, as well as His resurrection and His assumption into the heavens, all written before Jerusalem was even founded. Just as it is written: 'All these things which He had to suffer, and those things which shall be after Him.' Therefore, when we recognized these things, we believed in God through what had been written concerning Him."

And a little later, he adds that the Scriptures were made by divine providence, reporting it thus: "For we knew that God had truly commanded these things, and we say nothing without the Scripture."

The Hebrew language also has certain other <margin>D</margin> <margin>dialect <note>original: "διάλεκτος" (dialektos)</note></margin> properties, just as every other language does, containing a way of speaking that reflects the style and character of the nation. They define a "dialect" as a form of speech composed according to the style and character of a specific people. But Prophecy is not characterized by those specific terms. To the Greeks, what are called "metaphorical changes" <note>original: "troporum mutationes" — referring to rhetorical figures of speech</note> are used intentionally to conceal, having been derived in imitation of our prophecies. Indeed, a "trope" is shown to be a voluntary turning away from the literal meaning, occurring either in verse or prose. Certainly, a trope is a word transferred from its proper meaning to an improper one for the sake of composition and the correct use of diction in a speech. However, Prophecy does not use figures of speech for the sake of mere ornament. Rather, because the truth is not for everyone, it hides the truth in many ways, making light to rise only for those <margin>E</margin> who are initiated into knowledge <term>gnosis: the deep, spiritual understanding of divine truths</term>, and who seek the truth through love.

A species of prophecy is called a "proverb" by the non-Greek philosophy <note>meaning the Hebrew tradition</note>. It is also called a "parable," and then an "enigma." Furthermore, it is called "wisdom," and—as something distinct from it—"discipline," and again "words of prudence," "subtleties of words," "true justice," "the doctrine of directing judgment," "shrewdness" which comes to the simple through discipline, and "perception and intelligence" which is given to the one who has been recently imbued <margin>Proverbs 1</margin> with instruction <term>catechesis: the basic teaching given to new converts</term>.

> He who hears these Prophets, it says, "will be wise and even wiser, the man of understanding will possess guidance, and he will understand a parable and a dark saying, and the words of the wise and their enigmas." <note>A paraphrase of Proverbs 1:5–6</note>

If, therefore, the "Hellenic" (that is, Greek) languages happen to be named after the Greek son of Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note> named Deucalion, it can easily be seen from the <margin>F</margin> timelines we previously mentioned how many generations the Greek languages are younger than the Hebrew tongue. As our writing proceeds, we will note the tropes used by the Prophet in each section, and we will derive a way of living from knowledge according to the "rule of truth," pursuing it diligently and skillfully...
