<meta>This page continues Clement’s argument from the previous section where he explains how spiritual truths are hidden within the literal "body" of the Scriptures. He uses the examples of Hermas, the prophets, and the transformation of Moses to illustrate that only those with spiritual insight can move beyond the "letter" of the text to the deeper "syllable" or spiritual meaning.</meta>

# CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

...demonstrating these things. For did not the Power who appeared to Hermas in a vision—acting as a <term>type: a symbolic person or thing representing a later reality</term> of the Church—give him a book to read which she wanted to be announced to the chosen? <margin>A</margin> But he says he transcribed it letter by letter, since he could not yet find out how to complete the syllables. This signified that the "letter" of the text is clear to everyone if taken as a bare reading, and that this represents the faith which holds the place of basic elements. Consequently, the literal reading also admits an <term>allegory: a story or image with a hidden spiritual meaning</term>. However, we understand that the explanation of the Scriptures arising from deeper knowledge—as faith now progresses—is likened to reading by syllables. Furthermore, the prophet Isaiah is commanded to take a new book and write in it a certain holy knowledge that would come later through the exposition of the Scriptures. By a prophetic spirit, he was foretelling that which at the time was still unwritten because it was not yet known. For it had been said from the beginning only to those who understand. But now, <margin>B</margin> since the Savior has taught the Apostles, the unwritten tradition is also handed down to us. For that reason, the most learned among the Greeks consecrate the pomegranate to Mercury (whom they say represents speech/reason), because of its interpretation. For speech, like a pomegranate, has many hidden chambers. 

Rightly, then, when Moses was being taken up, Joshua <note>original: "Iesus filius Naue" — Joshua son of Nun. In Latin, the names Joshua and Jesus are identical.</note> saw him as double: one Moses with the Angels, and another on the mountains, who was worthy of being given a proper burial in the ravines. Joshua saw this spectacle from below, having been lifted up by the spirit, along with Caleb. But they did not both see in the same way. The latter [Caleb] descended more quickly, as one who carried much weight that slowed him down. But the former [Joshua], when he had descended, later recounted the glory which he had contemplated, being one who could perceive more than the other because he was purer. This history signifies, I believe, <margin>C</margin> that knowledge does not belong to everyone. For some receive only the "body" of the scriptures—that is, the words and names—just as they might perceive the physical body of Moses. But others look through to the inner meanings and what is signified by the names, inquiring curiously after that "Moses" who is with the Angels.

<margin>Matth. 15.</margin> Certainly, even among those who called upon the Lord Himself, many said, "Son of David, have mercy on me." But few recognized the Son of God, as Peter did. <margin>Ibidem. 16</margin> The Lord even pronounced Peter blessed because flesh and blood had not revealed the truth to him, but his Father who is in heaven. This signifies that the person endowed with spiritual knowledge knows the Son of the Almighty not through His flesh, which was carried in the womb, but through the Father’s own power. <margin>D</margin> 

Acquiring the truth is not only difficult for those who merely happen upon it; history teaches that even for those to whom knowledge properly belongs, the full contemplation is not given all at once in a heap. Instead, it is given gradually, until—just as the Hebrews used to look upon the glory of Moses with veiled eyes and the holy ones of Israel saw visions of Angels—we too are able to look directly upon the splendor of the truth. 

Let us briefly set forth the evidence for declaring this knowledge: the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments</note>. It is unnecessary to say now that the number ten is sacred. But if the written tablets are found to be the work of God, they will show a natural craftsmanship. The "finger of God" is understood as the power of God, through which the creation of heaven and earth was effected. The tablets are understood to be signs of both of these. For God’s writing and formation on the underlying tablet is the creation of the world. The Decalogue, in its heavenly image, <margin>E</margin> contains the Sun, Moon, stars, clouds, light, spirit, water, air, darkness, and fire. This is the natural "Ten" of heaven. The image of the earth contains men, cattle, creeping things, wild beasts, and from the waters: fish and whales; and again, similarly from the birds: those that eat flesh and those that eat mild and tame food; and from the plants similarly: those that are fertile and those that are sterile. This is the natural "Ten" of the earth. Furthermore, the Ark which contained these things would be the knowledge and wisdom of things divine and human. 

Perhaps these two tablets were the Prophecy of the two Testaments. Mystically, they were renewed when ignorance and sin abounded. It seems the precepts are written in a twofold way for twofold spirits: namely, the "ruling" spirit and the "subject" spirit, since "the flesh lusts <margin>Gal. 5. F</margin> against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh." There is also a certain "ten" within man himself: the five senses, the faculty of speech, the power of reproduction, and then the eighth which was in the formation of the spirit, the ninth which is the faculty of the soul, and the tenth which holds the leadership...

# MISCELLANIES, BOOK VI.

<margin>A</margin> ...the ruling power, which is also called the primary part; and the tenth is the Holy Spirit, which is added through faith, a unique property that grants form and character. Added to these is the fact that the law seems to command ten specific human parts: sight, hearing, smell, touch, taste, and the organs that serve them, which are double—namely the hands and the feet. For this is the formation of a human being. However, the soul enters, and even before it, the <term>principal faculty: the 'hegemonikon' or ruling part of the mind</term> by which we reason enters; this is not generated through the discharge of seed, so that even without it, the number ten is gathered, through which the entire action of a human is completed in order. For as soon as a human is first born, he receives the beginning of life from the <term>passible parts: those parts of the soul or body capable of feeling or suffering</term>. Therefore, we say that the faculty of reasoning, and that which is the principal part, is the cause of the constitution of the living being.

<margin>B</margin> Furthermore, this part, though devoid of reason itself, becomes animated and is a part of the soul. Now the vital faculty—which contains the power of nourishing and growing, and to speak briefly, of moving—is the lot of the carnal spirit. This spirit is most easily moved, proceeding through the senses and the rest of the body, and it is through the body that it first experiences sensations. The principal faculty of the soul, however, possesses the free power of choosing, in which exist inquiry, learning, and knowledge. Indeed, the relationship of all parts is ordered toward one principal faculty; it is because of that faculty that a human both lives and lives in a certain way. Thus, through the bodily spirit, a human feels, desires, rejoices, grows angry, is nourished, and grows; furthermore, through it, he proceeds to actions in accordance with what the mind has thought and conceived.

<margin>C</margin> But after he has conquered his desires, the principal faculty reigns. Therefore, that commandment found in
<margin>Exodus 20; Galatians 5.</margin>
**"Thou shalt not covet,"**
means, he says, that you shall not be a slave to the carnal spirit, but you shall command it; because the flesh lusts against the spirit and rises up to behave basely and unbecomingly against nature. The spirit, however, obtains command over the flesh so that a human may lead a life according to nature. Is it not, then, with good reason said that man was made in the image of God? This is not regarding the shape of his physical construction, but because God architects all things by reason; and the human who has escaped into being endowed with knowledge performs good and honorable actions through the faculty of reasoning.

<margin>This passage is corrupt.</margin>
Rightly, then, the two tablets of the commandments were given to the two spirits—both to the one who is formed and to the one who is principal. These, which were handed down before the Law, are said to signify and express the movements of the senses through

<margin>D</margin> thought, and they manifest them through that operation which comes from the body. For comprehension arises from both. Again, just as the sense is to the sensible object, so is the intelligence to that which is comprehended by it. Furthermore, actions are also twofold: some through the agitation and conception of the mind, others through outward operation. And the first commandment of the Decalogue shows that there is only one God Almighty, who brought the people out of Egypt through the wilderness into their fatherland, so that through divine operations they might comprehend His power as best they could, and abstain from the idolatry of created things, having all their hope in the God who is of the truth. The second "word" <note>original: "oratio," referring to the 'Words' or Commandments</note> signified that it is not right to take up or bring down His great and all-venerable power—which is His Name—

<margin>E</margin> (for many are still capable only of learning this name) nor to transfer His naming to created and vain things which craftsmen have made; for He who *Is* cannot be placed in these. For in unbegotten identity, He who *Is* is Himself alone. The third saying is that which signifies that the world was made by God, and that He gave us the seventh day for resting because of the affliction and the suffering of evils in this life. For God is <term>untiring: indefessus</term> and <term>impassible: incapable of suffering or being affected by external forces</term>, and He stands in need of nothing. But we who carry flesh have need of rest. Therefore, the seventh day is proclaimed as rest—an abstinence from evils—preparing for that primary day, the day from which all things have sprung, which is truly our rest. This is also truly the first generation of light, in which all things are simultaneously seen and possessed. From this day, primary wisdom and

<margin>F</margin> knowledge illuminate us. For the light of truth—the true light, devoid of shadow—is the Spirit of the Lord, which is divided without being severed among those who are sanctified through faith, acting like a lamp for the recognition of things that exist. Following Him, then, we are rendered impassible through our whole life. And that is what it means to rest. Wherefore Solomon also...

<meta>This page continues Clement’s discourse on the mystical significance of numbers, transitioning from the structure of the human soul and the Decalogue to the cosmic and theological roles of the numbers six, seven, and eight in creation and the person of Christ.</meta>

### CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

<margin>A</margin> Before heaven and earth and all things that exist, the Lord says that **Wisdom** was begotten. Participation in this Wisdom—which occurs through virtue rather than by essence—teaches those who have been here to possess the knowledge of things divine and human through the path of comprehension. These matters must also be briefly recalled to memory, since the reasoning has entered upon the <term>Septenary: the number seven</term> and the <term>Octonary: the number eight</term>. For that which is the Octonary appears to be, in its own proper sense, the Septenary; and the Septenary is clearly the <term>Senary: the number six</term>, and this is indeed properly the **Sabbath**. The Septenary, however, is the "worker." For the origin of the world is completed in six days, and the movement of the Sun, which occurs from solstice to solstice—or from one tropic to the other—is perfected in six months, through which partly the leaves fall, and partly the plants sprout and the perfections of seeds are achieved. <margin>B</margin> Moreover, they say that the fetus is also perfectly completed in the sixth month—that is, in one hundred and eighty-two and a half days—as Polybus the physician writes in his book *On Eight-Month Births*. Aristotle the philosopher, in his book *On Nature*, and the Pythagoreans, believe the number six to be perfect based on the birth of the world according to the opinion of the Prophet <note>Clement refers to Moses and the account in Genesis</note>; they call it *mesythēn* and *gamon* <note>original: "μεσύθιν & γάμον"</note>. They call it *mesythēn*—that is, "the middle position"—because it is the middle of the "right" number, which is twelve. For it appears to be equally distant from both ends. They call it *gamon*—that is, "marriage." For just as marriage generates from the male and the female, so the number six is generated from the odd number three (which is called male) and the even number two (which is considered female). For twice three becomes six. Again, there are three most general movements through which all generation is carried: upward, downward, to the right, to the left, forward, and backward. <margin>C</margin> Therefore, they rightly consider the Septenary to be without mother and without offspring, interpreting it as the Sabbath and calling it, allegorically, a form of rest, in which they neither take wives nor are given in marriage anymore. For the Septenary is not produced from any number multiplied by another, nor does it produce any other number when multiplied, among those numbers within the <term>Duodenary: the number twelve</term>. They call the Octonary the "cube," numbering the fixed sphere along with the seven wandering planets, through which the "Great Year" is produced, like a certain period of reward for those things which were promised. By that same reasoning, when the Lord ascended the mountain as the fourth, He became the sixth <note>This refers to the Transfiguration, where Jesus (the 4th figure, or perhaps the 4th day) is revealed in glory, often associated with the 'six' of the world</note>, and was illuminated by spiritual light, stripped of the power that proceeded from Him—as much as could be seen by those who had been chosen to see—and was proclaimed the Son of God through the seventh voice, so that those who were persuaded concerning Him might rest. But He Himself, through the generation signified by the Senary—though He was the <margin>D</margin> distinguished Octonary—appeared as God in the flesh, showing His power, who was numbered as a man, yet who He truly was remained hidden. For the Senary is also referred to in the order of numbers. However, the sequence of the <term>Elements: the letters of the Greek alphabet</term> makes that "distinguished mark" <note>The 'episēmon' or 'stigma', a symbol used for the number 6 that was not part of the standard classical alphabet</note> something which is not written. Here, among the numbers themselves, each unit is preserved in order up to the Septenary and the Octonary. But in the order of the letters, the sixth is *hekta* <note>original: "ἕκτα"</note> and the seventh is *hepta* <note>original: "ἑπτὰ"</note>. Since the "distinguished mark" for writing was somehow stolen away, if we follow it this way, the Septenary becomes the sixth, and the Octonary becomes the seventh. On this account, man is also said to have been made on the sixth day, he who was faithful to Him who is "distinguished," so that he might immediately receive the rest of the Lord’s inheritance. Something similar is shown by the sixth hour of the salvific <term>Economy: the divine plan for salvation</term>, in which man was <margin>E</margin> perfected. Now, the middle of the eight themselves becomes seven. And seven appears to have six intervals. For that reasoning is different when the Septenary shall have glorified the Octonary, and the heavens of heavens declare the glory of God. Their sensible figures are the elements which are the vowels among us. Thus also the Lord Himself is called **A and Ω** <note>Alpha and Omega</note>, the beginning and the end, through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made. Therefore, God did not cease to act as some believe "God’s rest" to mean. For since He is good, if He should ever cease to do good, He would also cease to be God—which is a wicked thing to say. Therefore, to have "rested" is to have ordained that the order of things which were made should be preserved without any transgression for all time: and to have caused <margin>F</margin> every creature to cease from the old confusion. For the creations which occurred on different days are most accepted in their sequence, inasmuch as all things that were made—which were created simultaneously with the thought—shall hold honor from that which is more ancient, nor...

### STROMATA, BOOK VI.

<margin>A</margin> ...there would be an equal estimation of them in the future, nor would the birth of each have been declared by voice, if creation were said to have made all things simultaneously and in a heap. For it was necessary to have named something as first. Therefore, the first things were spoken prophetically, even though all things were made simultaneously in power from one essence. For there is, I believe, one will of God in one identity. But how could creation have been made in time, since time itself was made along with those things that exist? Indeed, the whole world revolves in cycles of seven—all things that are brought forth alive and all things that grow. There are seven whose power is greatest: the first-born <term>Angel princes: the seven archangels who stand before God</term>. Furthermore, the mathematicians also say there are seven wandering stars <note>the seven "planets" of the ancient world: Sun, Moon, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note> that govern the earth, by which the <margin>B</margin> Chaldeans believe all things pertaining to mortal life are brought about through harmony. This leads them to promise that they can speak even of future events. Among the fixed stars, there are the seven stars of the Pleiades. The Great Bear also consists of seven stars, by which both agriculture is practiced and ships are navigated. The Moon, truly, changes its shape every seventh day. In the first <term>hebdomad: a period of seven days</term>, it is "cut in half" <note>the first quarter moon</note>. In the second, it is full. In the third, as it wanes, it is again cut in half, and in the fourth, it does not appear. Indeed, as Seleucus the Mathematician <note>a Greek astronomer who supported the heliocentric theory</note> records, the moon changes its appearance seven times. For from being obscure and not appearing, it becomes a horned crescent. Then it is cut in half. Then it is <gloss>bulging on both sides <note>original: "ἀμφίκυρτος", meaning gibbous</note></gloss>, and then full. And again, as it wanes, it becomes bulging on both sides, and similarly cut in half, and then a horned crescent.

<margin>C</margin> > Let our seven-toned lyre sound beautiful hymns

A certain poet of no small renown writes this, teaching that the ancient lyre had seven strings. There are also seven instruments of the senses in our face: two for the eyes, two for the passages of hearing, two for the nostrils, and the seventh is the mouth. The stages of life also change through the <term>Septenary: the number seven</term>, as the elegies of <term>Solon: an ancient Athenian lawmaker and poet</term> signify in this manner:

> *Once an infant has completed seven years,*
> *The teeth, the fence of the mouth, are brought forth.*
> *After God has granted him another seven years,*
> *He becomes a youth, and the seed of generation is given to him.*
> *But after his age has grown by another seven years,*
<margin>D</margin> > *A thick harvest of beard covers his rising cheeks.*
> *When a further seven is added to him,*
> *The man will then give strong signs of his virtue.*
> *But the fifth seven-year period warns him to take a wife,*
> *And then to be mindful of his own posterity.*
> *Skillful genius and firm prudence belong to the sixth period,*
> *And after this, it is no pleasure to see foolish deeds.*
> *When the seventh seven-year period has arrived, and also*
<margin>E</margin> > *The eighth, he flourishes in tongue and genius.*
> *In the ninth, they still have some power, but already*
> *The strengths by which a man performs brave deeds are diminished.*
> *But when the tenth period has completed its seven years,*
> *The sad fates will grant a mature death.*

Again, in illnesses, the "critical day"—that is, the day that brings judgment—is the seventh and the fourteenth, on which nature struggles against the causes producing the disease. <term>Hermippus of Berytus: a 2nd-century grammarian</term> brings forward countless other such examples in his book *On the Septenary*. Clearly, the blessed <margin>F</margin> <margin>Psalm 89</margin> David hands down the mystical reasoning concerning the <term>Septenary</term> and the <term>Octonary</term> to those who understand, singing thus: *Our years shall be meditated upon like a spider. The days of our years in themselves are seventy years. But if they be in strengths, eighty years.* <note>Psalm 90:9–10 in modern numbering; Clement interprets 70 and 80 as symbols of the two spiritual numbers</note>. This, then, would be our reign. Therefore, so that we might learn that the world was created, but that we should not think God acts within time, the Prophecy added: <margin>Gen. 2:</margin> *This is the book of the generation of the heaven and the earth, and of the things in them, when they were made, in the day that God made heaven and earth.* <note>Genesis 2:4</note>

<meta>This page continues Clement’s allegorical interpretation of the Bible, specifically moving from the mystical significance of numbers into a spiritualized reading of the Decalogue (the Ten Commandments). # CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

For the phrase "when they were made" <note>original: "quando facta sunt"</note> signifies a declaration that is indefinite and exists outside of time. However, the phrase "In the day that God made" <note>referring to Genesis 2:4</note>—that is, in which and through which He made all things, and without whom nothing was made—signifies the operation that occurs through the Son. David speaks of this: <margin>Psalm 117</margin> <margin>A</margin> "This is the day the Lord has made; let us exult and rejoice in it." <note>In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 118:24. Clement interprets the "Day" not as a period of 24 hours, but as the Word (Logos) of God.</note> This means that through the knowledge handed down by Him, we may enjoy divine banquets. For "Day" is the name given to the Word who illuminates hidden things, and through whom every created thing came into the light, into birth, and into existence. <margin>Ten is written with the letter iota, which is the first letter of the name of Jesus.</margin> And in short, the Decalogue <term>Decalogue: The Ten Commandments</term>, through the letter *iota* <note>The Greek letter 'I' (iota) represents the number ten and is the first letter of 'Iesous' (Jesus)</note>, signifies the blessed name, pointing to Jesus who is the Word. The fifth discourse follows next, concerning the honor due to one's father and mother. Now, the scripture clearly calls God the Father and Lord. Therefore, it also calls those who have recognized Him "sons" and "gods."

<margin>B</margin> The Lord and Father, then, is the Creator of all things. But the "Mother" is not, as some imagine, the physical substance from which we were born; nor is it the Church, as others have explained. Rather, it is divine knowledge and wisdom, just as Solomon says, calling wisdom the "mother of the righteous," and she is to be chosen for her own sake. Furthermore, whatever is good and honorable is recognized as coming from God through the Son. Following this is the discourse on adultery. Adultery occurs if someone, having abandoned the true ecclesiastical knowledge and persuasion regarding God, approaches a false opinion that is not fitting. This happens either by attributing something to gods from among created things, or by setting up some image of something that does not exist, thereby overstepping knowledge—or rather, leaping away from it. <margin>C</margin> False opinion is alien to the person endowed with knowledge, just as truth is joined and familiar to them. Wherefore the noble Apostle <note>St. Paul</note> followed the Prophet in calling one species of idolatry "fornication," as the Prophet says: <margin>Jeremiah</margin> "He committed adultery with wood and stone." <note>Jeremiah 3:9</note> Of the wood he said, "You are my father," and to the stone, "You gave me birth." Next follows the discourse on murder. Murder is a firm and persistent taking away. Therefore, whoever wishes to take away the true discourse concerning God and His eternity in order to introduce falsehood—saying either that the universe is governed by no providence, or that the world was uncreated, or denying any of the firm and stable truths of true doctrine—is the most destructive of murderers. After this is the discourse on theft. <margin>D</margin> Just as one who steals another's property falls into the evils he deserves for such a great injustice, so too does he who claims divine works as his own through the art of sculpting or painting, saying that he himself is the maker of living creatures and plants. Similarly, those who imitate true philosophy are "thieves." Whether a man be a farmer or the father of a son, he is merely a minister in the sowing of seeds. It is God who provides the growth and perfection of all things, bringing those things that are born to their natural state. Many people, however, along with the Philosophers, attribute growth and change primarily to the stars; in doing so, they deprive the Father of the universe of His untiring and inexhaustible power. The elements and the stars—that is, the powers that administer them—were commanded to carry out the things pertaining to the divine economy <term>Economy: The "plan" or "management" of the universe by God</term>. They obey and are moved by what is commanded of them, wherever the Word of the Lord leads them, since it is within divine power to operate all things secretly. <margin>E</margin> Therefore, whoever claims to have invented or made something from among the things belonging to creation will pay the penalty for an impious and wicked undertaking. The teaching then discourses on all forms of covetousness. Just as he who lusts after improper things is forced to give an account, in the same way, one is not permitted to "covet" false things, nor to think that among created things, the animate can give salvation or harm by themselves, or that the inanimate can do so at all. If someone says that an antidote cannot heal or that hemlock cannot kill, he is secretly deceiving with a clever sophistry. For none of these things operates without the one who uses the herb or medicine, just as an axe does not work without the one who chops, nor a saw without the one who cuts. While they do not operate by themselves, they possess certain natural qualities which, through the operation of an artisan, achieve their proper work. <margin>F</margin> In the same way, by the general and universal providence of God, effective operation is transmitted to individual things through the submission of those things moved most closely by Him. But as it seems, the Greek philosophers, though they name God, do not know Him, since they by no means worship God as God. For the things they philosophize, as Empedocles <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher</note> says, such as the things through...

<meta>This page continues Clement’s argument from Book VI of the Stromata. Having discussed the symbolic meaning of the Commandments, he now moves to the relationship between worldly philosophy and divine truth, arguing that while philosophy contains sparks of truth, the full reality (the "Gnosis") is found in Christ.</meta>

### MISCELLANIES, BOOK VI.

<margin>A</margin> ...have passed haphazardly into the common tongue of the masses, they are poured out even though the multitude hardly understands their meaning. For just as art devises a way whereby the light proceeding from the Sun may catch fire through a glass vessel full of water, so too Philosophy, when it has received a certain spark of fire from the divine Scripture, perceives a vision in a few. Certainly, just as all living beings breathe the same air, but each in its own way and for a different purpose, so too many approach the truth—or rather, approach what is said *about* the truth. For they do not speak of God Himself, but they explain Him by attributing their own feelings to God. Indeed, they lead a life seeking what is probable, but not what is true. Truth is not taught by mere imitation, but by disciplined instruction. For we do not believe in order to *appear* to be like Christ, just as we do not approach the Sun merely to *appear* to be in the Sun. But

<margin>B</margin> in the former case, we approach so that we may grow warm; in the latter, however, we strive to become good and honorable men, so that we may truly be Christians. <margin>Matthew 11</margin> <note>Clement refers to Matthew 11:12: "The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent take it by force."</note> For the Kingdom belongs to those who are most "violent"—those who, through the inquiry of discipline and perfect exercise, reap the fruit of becoming Kings. He who merely imitates an opinion shows only a preconceived notion. However, when someone has received a spark of the matter and has kindled it within his soul through desire and doctrine, he thereafter moves everything in order to know it. For what a person does not grasp, he neither desires nor accepts the benefit that comes from it. Therefore, he who is endowed with knowledge <term>Gnosis: A higher, spiritual knowledge or insight into divine truths</term> later imitates the Lord for the sake of the goal of those things done rightly and virtuously, as far as is possible for humans, having

<margin>C</margin> accepted a certain quality of the Lord, looking toward assimilation to God <note>The Platonic concept of 'Homoiosis Theoi', or becoming like God, which Clement adapts for Christian theology.</note>. But those who do not know this knowledge cannot seek the truth by any certain rule. Therefore, it is impossible for us to be participants in the contemplations that are led by knowledge unless we empty ourselves of our prior thoughts. For in this way, truth is commonly spoken of in an absolute sense regarding everything perceived by the intellect and the senses. Indeed, one can see the truth of a painting as distinct from the common view, or the nobility of music as separate from the impure. Therefore, in philosophy too, there is some truth separate from other philosophers, and a true beauty beyond the adulterated kind. It is not, then, those partial truths about which "truth" is merely predicated that must be sought, but the Truth itself must be investigated with great care and zeal, not

<margin>D</margin> by seeking to know names. For what is said of God is not one single thing, but innumerable things. It matters whether you speak of God Himself or of the things that pertain to God. In short, when speaking of any matter, the accidents must be distinguished from the substance. And it is enough for me to say that God is He who is the Lord of the universe. When I say "Lord of the universe," I mean it perfectly and absolutely in itself, with nothing remaining to be excluded. Since there are two species of the "idea" of truth—namely, names and things—some people speak only of names; these are the ones concerned with the ornament and elegance of speech, such as the Greek Philosophers. The actual things <note>original: "Res"</note>, however, are found among us "barbarians" <note>Clement uses "barbarians" to refer to Christians and Hebrews, reclaiming a term Greeks used for non-Greeks to suggest they possess the ancient, raw truth.</note>. Now, the Lord did not wish to use a lowly and humble form of body for His own sake, but rather lest anyone, by praising His appearance and admiring His beauty, should turn away from what was being said, and by attending to what is left behind, be led away from the things perceived by the intellect. Therefore, we should not dwell on the diction, but

<margin>E</margin> on the things signified. The word is not believed at all by those who are capable of grasping things but have not been moved toward knowledge. For even ravens imitate human voices, though they have no notice of the thing they are saying. But an intelligent grasp follows closely upon faith. Thus even Homer said: "The Father of men and of Gods," <note>A common line in the Iliad and Odyssey.</note> without knowing who the Father is or in what way He is a Father. Just as it is natural for someone with hands to take up an object, and for someone with healthy eyes to see the light, so it is proper for him who has received faith to be a participant in knowledge—if, once the foundation is laid, he wishes to work with gold, silver, and precious stones <note>Alluding to 1 Corinthians 3:12 regarding the building of a spiritual foundation.</note> and build upon it. He does not merely promise that he wants to be a participant, but to command; not that he *will* be, but that he *is* royal, enlightened, and endowed with knowledge. It is not by name,

<margin>F</margin> but by the reality itself that it is fitting to reach for things. For since God is good, for the sake of the principal part of the whole creation, and because He wished it to be saved, He turned also to the making of all other things, offering them this first benefit from the beginning: that they should exist. For anyone will confess that it is better to be than not to be. Then, according to its capacity...

He explains that faith is the necessary foundation for this higher understanding, which transforms the believer into the likeness of the Divine.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Clement’s argument from Book VI of the *Stromata* (Miscellanies). He is discussing how Divine Providence works through all levels of human existence, specifically defending the role of philosophy as a preparatory tool for the ultimate truth found in Christ (the "Gnosis").</meta>

# CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

<margin>A</margin>...the nature of each individual, everything was made and continues to be made as it progresses toward that which is better. For this reason, it is not absurd to say that philosophy was also given by divine providence, educating us beforehand for that perfection which comes through Christ—provided that philosophy is not ashamed to learn from "barbarian" knowledge <note>original: "barbara cognitione". Clement uses "barbarian" to refer to non-Greek sources, specifically the Hebrew Scriptures.</note> the way to advance toward the truth. But even the hairs of the head are numbered, and there are even lowlier movements than these. How then can philosophy not be within the Word <note>original: "Verbo," referring to the *Logos* or Christ.</note>? Indeed, Sampson was given strength in his hair, so that even the discarded arts of those things which exist in life—those which lie low and remain on the ground after the departure of the soul—cannot be conceived of without divine power. Now truly, divine providence, from above among those things which are primary, as if from the head, permeates down to all things. <margin>Psalm 132</margin> <note>This is Psalm 133 in modern English Bibles. "Like the precious ointment upon the head, that ran down upon the beard, even Aaron's beard."</note> As the ointment, he says, which descends onto the beard of Aaron, and onto the edge of his garment—that is, the Great High Priest <note>Clement interprets the High Priest Aaron as a "type" or symbol of Christ.</note>, through whom all things were made, and without whom <margin>B</margin> nothing was made <margin>Something is missing here, as if to say: "not into the world of the body, but of the soul," or something similar.</margin> into the world of the body. From the outside, however, the philosophy of the people is like a garment. Therefore, those philosophers who have exercised their spiritual senses toward their own perception, after they have diligently searched out not just a part of philosophy, but that which is perfectly and absolutely philosophy in itself, and who bear witness to the truth with a certain love for it and without any arrogance—these have advanced toward understanding from those things rightly said by those of differing opinions. They do so through divine administration and ineffable goodness, which always leads the things of nature toward what is better, as much as possible. Then, having had dealings not only with the Greeks but also with the "barbarians," they are led <margin>C</margin> toward faith through the common exercise of their own understanding. Once the power of truth is accepted as a foundation, they also take on a further progression into inquiry; and from that point, it is pleasing for them to learn. Desiring knowledge, they strive with great zeal toward salvation. For that reason, the Scripture says that the "spirit of sense" was given by God to craftsmen. This is nothing other than <term>prudence</term> <note>Latin: "prudentia," a translation of the Greek "phronesis," meaning practical wisdom or discernment.</note>, a power of the soul which contemplates things as they are, discerns and compares what follows, identifying the similar and the dissimilar, and which commands, forbids, and even conjectures the future. This pertains not only to the arts, but even to philosophy itself. Why then was the serpent also called "prudent"? Because even in evil deeds, a certain logic, discernment, composition, and conjecture of the future can be found; and for this reason, many crimes remain hidden, because the wicked provide for themselves in every way so that <margin>D</margin> they can avoid punishment. Since this prudence is multifaceted and extended through the whole world and all human affairs, it changes its name in each of them. When it applies itself to first causes, it is called <term>intelligence</term>. When it has confirmed these things by demonstrative reasoning, it is named <term>cognition</term>, <term>wisdom</term>, and <term>science</term>. When it is occupied with things tending toward piety and has accepted a reason derived from the beginning without contemplation—through the observation of the activity within itself—it is called <term>faith</term>. And if it establishes what is seen in sensible things as if it were the truest reality among them, it is called <term>right opinion</term>. In those actions performed with the hands, it is called <term>art</term>. When it begins an impulse toward doing something without the contemplation of first causes, but through the observation of similar things and their translation into action, and establishes something thereby, it is called <margin>E</margin> <term>experience</term>. To this belongs that truly principal Holy Spirit, which the believer assumes after a firm and stable faith, finally reaching it through inspection and care. Since philosophy has shared in this more excellent sense—as has been shown from what was said before—that which is the treatment of things perceived by intelligence through reason, with choice and assent, is called <term>dialectics</term>. This confirms what is said about the truth through demonstration and dissolves the doubts that are brought forward. Therefore, those who say that philosophy does not come here from God seem to say that it is entirely impossible for God to see all individual things, or that He is not the cause of all good things, since each of these things is made of individuals. Nothing among the things that are would <margin>F</margin> consist at all if God did not will it. But if philosophy exists by His will, then it is from God, since He willed it to be exactly as it is, for the sake of those who would not otherwise abstain from evil. For God knows all things, not only those that are, but even those that are to be, and how...

He defines various levels of human knowledge—such as intelligence, science, faith, and art—as different expressions of a single, divinely-granted prudence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Clement’s argument from Book VI of the *Stromata* (Miscellanies). Having previously discussed how divine providence permeates even the smallest details of life, he now explains how God’s oversight encompasses both human agency in the arts and the specific gift of philosophy to the Greek world.</meta>

### STROMATA, BOOK VI

<margin>A</margin> ...each thing will be; and foreseeing those movements which are individual, He gazes upon all things and hears all things. Looking into the naked soul within, He possesses an eternal understanding of each particular thing. Whether it be what happens in theaters or in the various parts of every individual, He sees it by looking upon it, looking around it, and looking through it. In God, this happens simultaneously and all at once <note>original: "simul & aceruatim"</note>. For He perceives all things and individual things with a single application of His mind, though not all things occur through His primary intention. For already many things in this life take their origin through human reason as well, once they have received divine illumination. Behold, for example: health comes through medicine; a good physical condition through <term>aliptics</term> <note>the ancient art of anointing and training athletes in the gymnasium</note>; and wealth arises and is present through trade and the art of moneymaking—all through divine providence, certainly, but also through human <margin>B</margin> help and labor.

Intelligence also comes from God. And the free will of good men most especially obeys the divine will. Although many advantages are common to both good and bad men, they nonetheless become useful only to the good and honest, for whose sake God created these things. For the power of those things given by God was born for the use of good men. Furthermore, the thoughts of those endowed with virtue come about through divine inspiration, when the soul is moved in a certain way and the divine will is transmitted into human souls, while those who are the particular divine ministers <note>referring to angels</note> lend their help to such services. For the prefectures of the <term>Angels</term> <note>referring to the traditional Jewish and early Christian belief that specific angels are assigned to govern nations</note> are distributed through nations and cities; and perhaps some are even assigned to individuals. Thus, the Shepherd <margin>C</margin> takes care of individual sheep; he is held by a zeal for foreseeing and visiting especially those who are of excellent character and are able to benefit the people greatly. These are the ones who are fit for both ruling and teaching, through whom the evidence of providence is clearly shown, whenever God wishes to do good to men either through teaching or through some magistracy and administration. And He always wishes it. Therefore, He moves those who are fit to effectively bring about those things which pertain to peace, virtue, and benevolence.

Whatever comes from virtue, arises from virtue, and is referred back to virtue, is given either so that men may be good, or so that those who are good may use those advantages which are according to nature. For He helps both in universal and in particular matters. Therefore, just as it is not absurd to attribute insolence and injustice to the devil, how can they <margin>D</margin> designate him as the giver of a good thing that comes from virtue—namely, philosophy? On the contrary, I think it is the property of Law and right reason to return what is suitable to each, what is his own, and what belongs to him. For just as the lyre belongs only to the lyre-player, and the flute to the flute-player, so the advantages of good men are their possessions. Just as it is the nature of a benefactor to do good, as it is the nature of fire to warm and light to illuminate, a good man will not do evil. Light does not create darkness, nor does fire make things cold. So, conversely, vice could not produce anything that comes from virtue, for its operation is to do evil, just as the operation of darkness is to confuse the eyes. Therefore, philosophy—which makes men endowed with virtue—is not the work of vice. It remains, then, that it is the work of God, whose only work is to do good; and whatever things are given by God are both rightly given and rightly received.

<margin>E</margin> Furthermore, if the use of philosophy does not belong to the wicked, but was given to the best and most excellent of the Greeks, it is clear from this source by whom it was given: namely, by providence, which distributes to each according to their merits those things which are fitting. Deservedly, then, the Law was given to the Jews, and philosophy to the Greeks, until the Advent <note>the coming of Christ</note>. From that point on, there is a universal and general calling to a special people of justice, through the teaching that comes from faith, brought together by the one Lord, who is the one and only God of both—the Greeks and the barbarians <note>non-Greeks</note>—or rather, of the entire human race. Moreover, we have often called "philosophy" that which attains truth through philosophy, even if it is a specific instance.

Now, truly, even those things which are good <margin>F</margin> in the arts, insofar as they are arts, have their beginning from God. Just as doing something skillfully is contained within the contemplations of an art, so acting prudently is placed under <term>Prudence</term>. Prudence is a virtue; and its property is to know both other things and especially those which pertain to itself. And <term>Wisdom</term>, which is a faculty, is nothing else...

<summary>Clement argues that philosophy was a divine gift to the Greeks, acting as a "covenant" similar to the Law given to the Jews, both of which prepared humanity for Christ. He also asserts that God's providence governs both universal laws and individual human efforts in the arts and sciences.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Clement of Alexandria’s *Stromata* (Book VI). On the preceding page, Clement was discussing how divine providence operates through human intellect and labor. This page concludes that thought by comparing divine knowledge to human training and then explores the secondary role of Greek philosophy as a "dessert" to the "main meal" of Christian truth.</meta>

CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

<margin>A</margin> ...than the knowledge of divine and human goods. Since "the earth is the Lord’s and its fullness," the Scripture, in teaching that good things come to humans from God, declares that it is through divine virtue and power that this distribution reaches us for human aid. Now, there are three ways in which one person shares a benefit with another. The first is through **shaping**, just as a <term>gymnastic trainer</term> <note>original: "Pædotriba", a specialist in the ancient Greek gymnasium who molded the physical form and technique of youth</note> molds a boy. The second is through **encouragement**, as when one person urges another to grow because they themselves have already grown. In the first case, the trainer helps the learner; in the second, the teacher benefits right along with the one who receives the lesson. The third way is by **command**, occurring when the trainer no longer shapes the student nor demonstrates the wrestling moves for imitation, but instead—seeing the boy is now sufficiently practiced—commands him by name to go and wrestle. Therefore, the person who is <term>endowed with spiritual knowledge</term> <note>Clement refers here to the "True Gnostic," his ideal of the mature Christian who has reached deep intellectual and spiritual insight</note>, having received the power to help from God, assists some by **shaping** them through influence, others by **encouragement** through example, and others by **instruction** through teaching and education. 

<margin>B</margin> Certainly, he himself has been helped by the Lord in the same way. Thus we recognize the benefit that comes from God to humanity, with the <term>Angels</term> <note>Clement often highlights the role of angels as "ministers" or intermediaries of God’s providence in human affairs</note> assisting at the same time. For divine power provides good things through the Angels, whether they are seen or unseen. Such was also the manner of the Lord’s coming: when divine power inspires something through human thoughts and reasoning, it sends strength and a more perfect sense into our minds, providing a surge of readiness and mental alacrity for both asking questions and completing works. Furthermore, truly admirable and holy examples of virtue are set before us for imitation and likeness through the great deeds <margin>C</margin> written in the scriptures. Moreover, this type of divine action is most evident through the Lord’s covenants, through the laws found among the Greeks, and even through the precepts found in philosophy. To put it simply, every benefit pertaining to life is perfected by God the Almighty—the Father who presides over all—through the Son. For this reason, the Apostle says that the Son is the "Savior of all people, <margin>1 Tim. 4</margin> especially of those who believe." [1 Timothy 4:10] This aid is brought near to individuals by the command and instruction of Him who is closest to the Primary Cause—namely, the Lord. 

Now, the person among us who is endowed with spiritual knowledge is always occupied with the most important matters. But if he ever has leisure, or a time for relaxing the mind from these primary concerns, he might—as a substitute for other recreation—touch upon Greek philosophy. He does this like someone <margin>D</margin> bringing a **dessert** <note>original: "bellarium", refers to the sweetmeats or delicacies served at the end of a Roman or Greek banquet</note> to a dinner; he does not do it as one who has neglected the more excellent things, but as one who takes what is appropriate, for the reasons I have mentioned. However, those in philosophy who crave things that are unnecessary and superfluous, and who devote themselves only to the clever tricks of debate, depart from what is necessary and primary, truly chasing after the shadows of arguments. While it is good to know all things, if a person’s mind is too weak to take on the mastery of many disciplines, they should choose only those things which are primary and better. For what is truly **science**—which we say belongs only to the person endowed with spiritual knowledge—is a firm and stable comprehension, leading to the knowledge of the Cause through constant and stable reasoning. Whoever possesses knowledge of what is true in any one thing, <margin>E</margin> possesses in that same thing the knowledge of Truth itself. 

Therefore, that famous argument seems correct to me: *Should one philosophize?* For the very act of asking follows from the practice. But even if one argues that we should *not* philosophize, one cannot condemn something without first knowing it. Therefore, one must philosophize. Since this is the case, the Greeks ought to learn through the Law and the Prophets to worship the one God who is truly almighty, and then be taught by the Apostle. To us, there is **no idol** <margin>1 Cor. 8</margin> in the world, since among created things nothing can represent the image of God. [1 Corinthians 8:4] Furthermore, they should be taught that the statues they worship are not even images of the gods themselves. For the nature of souls is not of such a shape as the statues the Greeks mold. For souls do not fall under the sense of sight—not only rational souls, but even <margin>F</margin> the souls of other living creatures. Their bodies are never parts of the souls themselves, but are instruments—in some cases things in which the soul dwells, in others vehicles, and in others possessions in some other way. But it is impossible for the nature of instruments...

<summary>Clement explains how God provides for humanity through shaping, encouragement, and command, often using angels and the Son as intermediaries. He argues that while Christian scripture is the "main meal," Greek philosophy serves as a useful "dessert" or recreation for the advanced believer, provided it leads back to the primary knowledge of God.</summary>

<margin>Matthew 5</margin>

<margin>Acts 17</margin>

Wherefore, a little further down, he adds: **"Even if I am unskilled in speech, yet I am not so in knowledge."**

<margin>C</margin> Furthermore, let those among the Greeks who boast that the truth has been grasped by them tell us from whom they boast to have learned it. They certainly will not say they learned it from God. They confess they learned it from men. And if this is so, they either learned it lately from themselves—as some of them certainly boast with great insolence—or from others like them. But men, insofar as they are men, are not as worthy of belief as God. For a person, being weak and subject to death, cannot speak of God with true dignity, nor can a created work speak truly of the **Unbegotten** <note>original: "ingenito"; a technical term for God as the uncaused cause who was never born or created</note> and the one over whom destruction has no power. Furthermore, if a man cannot speak the truth about himself, is he not much more unworthy of belief concerning God? For as far as a man is removed from the power of God, so much is his speech weak, even if he speaks not of God Himself, but about God and the Divine Word. For human nature's speech is weak and unable to "speak" God—I do not mean His name, for naming Him is common not only to philosophers but also to poets; nor do I mean His essence, for that is impossible; but rather His power and His works.

<margin>D</margin> Although those who claim God as their teacher scarcely arrive at the notion of God—with grace bringing them aid toward whatever small amount of knowledge they reach—they accustom themselves to contemplate will by will, and the Holy Spirit by the Holy Spirit; for **"the Spirit searches the deep things of God."** 
<margin>1 Corinthians 2</margin>
**"But the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit."** Therefore, the only doctrine delivered by God is that which is among us, upon which all the fountains of wisdom depend, as many as are carried toward the truth as their goal. Certainly, for the Lord who was to come to men to teach us, there were innumerable signifiers, announcers, preparers, and forerunners from on high from the very foundation of the world, signifying through works and words, and foretelling that He would come, and how, and when, and by what signs.

<margin>E</margin> From a distance, certainly, the Law and prophecy meditate upon Him. Then the Forerunner <note>John the Baptist</note> showed Him as present, after whom the preachers, teaching the power of His coming, make Him known. 
<margin><insert>I have added two words that seemed to be missing in the Greek, namely "philosophers to the Greeks."</insert></margin>
**Philosophers** pleased the Greeks alone, and not even all of them. Socrates pleased Plato, Plato pleased Xenocrates, Aristotle pleased Theophrastus, and Zeno pleased Cleanthes—they persuaded only their own followers. But our Master’s Word did not remain in Judea alone, as philosophy remained in Greece, but was diffused through the whole world, persuading nations and villages and entire cities of both Greeks and Barbarians, converting whole houses and each individual listener, and even drawing not a few of the philosophers themselves to the truth.

<margin>F</margin> Indeed, if any magistrate prohibits Greek philosophy, it immediately vanishes. But our doctrine, from its very first preaching, has been prohibited by Kings and Tyrants alike, and by individual leaders and magistrates with all their bodyguards and countless men, warring against us and...

...trying to cut us down with all their strength. Yet she <note>Clement refers to the Church or Divine Truth as a feminine entity</note> flourishes all the more. <margin>A</margin> For she does not die away like human teaching, nor does she wither like a weak gift. Furthermore, concerning the Art of Poetry, Plato says that "a poet is a light and sacred thing," and cannot create verses until he has been inspired by God and has moved beyond his own mind <note>original: "mente excesserit"; referring to Plato's concept of 'divine madness' or inspiration in the dialogue *Ion*</note>. <margin>C</margin>
# THE MISCELLANIES OF CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA
## BOOK
### SEVEN.

<image-desc>A large historiated woodcut initial 'I' (beginning the word NOW) depicting a group of figures in classical robes engaged in discussion or instruction within an architectural setting with a landscape background visible through an arch.</image-desc>
NOW indeed it is time for us to show the Greeks that only the <term>one endowed with spiritual knowledge</term> is truly pious and religious. Thus, when the philosophers learn what a true Christian is really like, <margin>D</margin> they may condemn their own ignorance for having blindly and recklessly persecuted the "name" <note>The name of "Christian," which was often persecuted in the Roman Empire based on reputation rather than evidence of crimes</note>. Without any judgment, they call those "impious" and "estranged from God" who actually know the one who is truly God. We must use clearer arguments with the philosophers, so that, being trained by their own doctrines, they may be able to hear us, even if they have not yet shown themselves worthy to share in the power of faith. We shall not mention prophetic sayings for the time being, as we will use the Scriptures at a more opportune time later. <margin>E</margin> We will, however, point out what they signify, describing Christianity in summary, so as not to interrupt the flow of the discourse by including the Scriptures all at once—especially for those who do not yet understand their language. Once we have shown the underlying meanings, then, when they have come to believe, the Scriptures will be opened to them from an overflowing abundance. But if the things we say seem to some common people to be different from the Lord's Scriptures, they should know that our words breathe and live from that source; since they take their argument from the Scriptures, they profess to bring the meaning alone, and not the literal wording. For an excessive treatment that is not done at the proper time might deservedly seem unnecessary; to ignore entirely what is urgent and pressing would show great laziness and poverty of thought. <margin>Psalm 118</margin> <note>In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 119:2</note> "Truly blessed are those who search the testimonies of the Lord. They will seek Him with their whole heart." Both the Law <margin>F</margin> and the Prophets bear witness concerning the Lord. It is therefore our purpose to show that only the one endowed with spiritual knowledge is holy, and that he worships the one who is truly God in a proper way, as befits His majesty. Clement is defining the character of the "Christian Gnostic"—the person of deep spiritual knowledge—by describing their hierarchy of values and their relationship to God and the Church. He moves from the general concept of piety to the specific roles of church officers and finally to the nature of the Son of God.</meta>

<header>MISCELLANIES BOOK VII.</header>

<margin>A</margin> **Love of God and piety toward God.** Whatever is excellent and superior, the man of knowledge should deem honorable according to its dignity. Among sensible things <note>Things perceived by the physical senses</note>, he honors magistrates, parents, and every **elder** <note>original: "presbyterum"; here referring generally to seniors or specifically to church elders</note>. Among those things which are taught, he honors the most ancient philosophy and the most venerable prophecy. Among things perceived by the intellect, he honors that which is most ancient. In the order of existence, he honors the **Beginning** that lacks both time and beginning, and the first-fruits of all existing things: the **Son**. From the Son, he learns about the **Father** of the universe, the Cause which surpasses all things—the most ancient and most beneficent of all. This Father is not truly conveyed by the human voice, but is to be worshipped and venerated with holy admiration through silent devotion. This is expressed most appropriately by the **Lord**, <margin>B</margin> as far as those who are learning are able to hear; however, He is understood by those who have been chosen by the Lord for **spiritual knowledge** <note>original: "cognitionem"; referring to Gnosis</note>, who are (as the Apostle says) "exercised in their senses" <note>A reference to Hebrews 5:14 regarding spiritual maturity</note>. Therefore, the worship of God is the continual care of the soul by the one endowed with knowledge, and his perpetual occupation with God through a love that never ceases.

For of the service which concerns human affairs, one kind makes people better, while the other is subservient. Medicine makes the body better, while philosophy makes the soul better. From children to parents, and from subjects to magistrates and princes, a subservient usefulness arises. Similarly in the church: the **Presbyters** <note>Elders/Priests</note> maintain that service which makes people better, while the **Deacons** perform the service that is subservient. In both these ministries, **Angels** serve God in the management and <margin>C</margin> administration of earthly things. 

The man endowed with spiritual knowledge himself serves God, but to men he shows that service which makes them better through contemplation; in whatever way he is appointed to teach, he works for the correction of humanity. For he alone is truly pious and religious who serves God beautifully and without reproach in human affairs. Just as the cultivation of plants is best when it produces and brings in fruit—where the science and experience of agriculture brings utility to men—so the pious and religious worship of God by the man of knowledge brings in an excellent harvest through his experience. He receives the fruit of those men who have believed through him, so that many may come to the knowledge of God and be saved through it. **Godliness** <note>original: "θεοσέβεια" (theosebeia); literally "reverence toward God"</note>—for so we call the worship fitting for God's majesty—<margin>D</margin> is a habit which preserves that which is appropriate for God. 

The person of **godliness**, who worships God in a way consistent with His majesty, is the only one who is truly a "friend of God." Such a person knows what is fitting in both knowledge and life, living as one who is to be, and already is, made like unto God. By this reasoning, he is first of all a lover of God. For just as he who honors a father loves a father, so he who honors God loves God. For this reason, it seems to me there are three effects of the power of knowing: First, to know things. Second, to carry out what the **Word** <note>original: "Verbum" / "ratio"; referring to the Logos or Divine Reason</note> dictates. And third, to be able to hand down those truths which were hidden, as fits the majesty of God. 

Therefore, if a man is persuaded that God is omnipotent and has learned the divine mysteries from His only-begotten Son, how could he be an **atheist** <note>original: "ἄθεος"; literally "without God" or impious</note>? For an atheist is one who does not think God exists. However, a **superstitious** person <note>original: "δεισιδαίμων" (deisidaimon); literally "one who fears spirits/demons"</note> <margin>E</margin> is one who fears demons—one who refers everything to "gods," whether wood, stone, spirit, or a human being living a life reduced to slavery by a lack of reason. 

Faith, then, is to know God; it is the first teaching of the Savior after one has placed trust in Him. It involves doing nothing unjust and considering this conduct worthy of the knowledge of God. On earth, the most excellent thing is a human being who lives with the greatest piety toward God. In heaven, the most excellent thing is an **Angel**, who is locally closer to God and already a purer sharer in the eternal and blessed life. But the most perfect, most holy, most sovereign, most authoritative, most royal, and by far the most beneficent nature is that of the **Son**, who is closest to the only Almighty One. He is the greatest excellence, who orders all things according to the Father's will and governs the universe in the best way, performing all things with unwearied and inexhaustible power, because He acts with his gaze fixed upon secret and hidden thoughts. For the Son of God never leaves His watch-tower; He is not divided, not dissected, and does not move from place to place, but is always everywhere and contained by nothing. He is all mind, all the Father’s light...

<summary>Clement defines true piety as a combination of right knowledge and service, distinguishing between the roles of Presbyters and Deacons in the Church. He concludes by exalting the Son of God as the supreme, omnipresent governor of the universe who acts in perfect accord with the Father's will.</summary>

Having established that the "man of knowledge" honors the Son as the "Beginning" and the first-fruits of creation, Clement now describes the Son’s universal role as the Divine Word (Logos). He explains how the Word acts as the Savior for all humanity—both Greeks and non-Greeks—and manages the world through Divine Providence.</meta>

<margin>A</margin> ...all eye, seeing all things, hearing all things, knowing all things, and by his power he searches out all powers. To him is subject the entire host of Angels and Gods—subject, that is, to the paternal **Word** <note>original: "Verbo"</note> who undertook the holy **economy** <term>economy: From the Greek 'oikonomia,' referring to God’s plan for the management and salvation of the world.</term> and dispensation for the sake of the One who subjected them. Through him also all men belong to him. But some do so through knowledge, others not yet; some as friends, others as faithful servants, and still others as mere servants. 

This is the Teacher who instructs the one endowed with **spiritual knowledge** <note>original: "cognitione"; referring to Gnosis, the deep experiential knowledge of divine things</note> in the mysteries; he encourages the faithful one with good hope; and he corrects the hard-hearted with disciplined training through the judgment of their actions. From this source comes Providence—individually, publicly, and everywhere. That he is the Son of God, and that he is the Savior and Lord of whom we speak, the divine Prophecies openly demonstrate. By this reasoning, he who is the Lord of all Greeks and barbarians <margin>B</margin> persuades those who are willing. For he compels no one to receive salvation from him, because each person is able to choose, and to fulfill everything from their own side toward receiving hope.

He it is who gives wisdom to the Greeks through the lower Angels. For by divine and ancient decree, the Angels are distributed among the nations. But "the Lord's portion" is the conviction of the believers. For either the Lord does not care for all men—which would happen either because he lacks the power (which is an impious thought, for it is a sign of weakness) or because he lacks the will despite having the power (which is not the character of a good being). Therefore, he who took on suffering flesh for our sake is not idle due to a love of luxury. Either he cares for all, which is certainly fitting for the Lord of all—for he is the Savior, and not a Savior of some <margin>C</margin> while not of others.

According to the aptitude that each person possesses, he has distributed his benefit to both Greeks and barbarians, and to those among them who were predestined and called in their own time—the faithful and the chosen. Therefore, he who called everyone equally never envied anyone; rather, to those who believed in an exceptional way, he granted exceptional honors. Nor could he, who is Lord of all and who serves the will of the good and almighty Father, ever be prevented by another. Neither does envy ever touch the Lord, who is **impassible** <term>impassible: Incapable of suffering or being affected by external passions and changing emotions.</term> and was begotten without a beginning. Nor are human affairs of such a nature that the Lord could envy them. It is another who envies, one who is himself touched by passion.

Nor can it be said that the Lord is unwilling to grant salvation to the human race due to ignorance, as if he did not know how each person's care should be managed. For ignorance does not touch God, who before <margin>D</margin> the constitution of the world was the Father’s counselor. For this was the **Wisdom** in which the Almighty God delighted. The Son is the power and virtue of God, as the most primordial Word of the Father before all things were created, and his Wisdom; he might also be properly called the Teacher of those who were formed through him.

Nor does he ever abandon the care of men because of being distracted by some pleasure—he who, having taken on flesh that was by nature subject to suffering, trained it toward a state of impassibility. How is he Savior and Lord if he is not the Savior and Lord of all? But he is indeed the Savior of those who have believed, because they wished to know. Of those who have not believed, he is the Lord, so that when they are finally able to confess, they may receive the specific and appropriate benefit. Every operation of the Lord has a relation to the Almighty, and the Son is a certain paternal <margin>E</margin> operation, so to speak.

Therefore, the Savior never hates men; indeed, because of his excellent kindness and love for humanity, he did not despise the weakness of human flesh, but put it on and came for the common salvation of men. For the faith of those who have chosen is common. Nor would he ever neglect his own work, since the capacity for knowledge and mental perception was implanted in man alone among the other animals from creation; nor could there be any other better or more suitable administration of men for God than that which has been ordained. It is always fitting for that which is by nature better and more excellent to preside over that which is inferior, and for the administration of that which cannot govern anything rightly to be given to another. That which truly rules and commands <margin>F</margin> is the divine Word and his Providence, which looks upon all things and despises the care of no one among those who belong to it. Those who have chosen to belong to him and be joined to him are those who are initiated through faith. He [is the giver] of all good things...

<margin>A</margin> ...of ages, by the will of the Almighty Father, the Son is the author and cause, the primary worker of motion, a power that cannot be grasped by the senses. For he was not seen as that which he truly was by those who were unable to perceive him because of the **weakness of the flesh** <note>original: "imbecillitatem carnis"</note>. When, therefore, he had taken on sensible flesh, he came to show men that their strengths were sufficient to obey the commandments. Since he is the **paternal power** <note>original: "virtus paterna"</note>, he easily overcomes what he wills, leaving not even the smallest thing without the care of his administration. For otherwise, the whole would not have been perfectly fashioned by him. But I believe it is a mark of the greatest power to have an accurate examination of all parts, even down to the smallest, reaching up to the first administrator of the universe, who, by the Father's will, governs <margin>B</margin> the salvation of all. Others are ordained to look after others, until one arrives at the Great High Priest. For from one principle above, which works according to the divine will, depend the first, second, and third things. Then, at the highest edge of the visible world, the blessed **Angels** <note>original: "Angeli"</note> are placed; and so on down to our very selves, others are arranged under others, who are both saved and save through the One and by the One.

Just as the smallest piece of iron is moved by the spirit of the **lodestone** <term>lodestone: a naturally magnetized mineral (magnetite), used here as a metaphor for divine attraction</term>, extending through many iron rings; so too those who are endowed with virtue, being drawn by the divine Spirit, are joined to the first mansion. Then others follow in order down to the last. But those who are wicked through weakness, having fallen into an evil condition because of their unjust frailty—like those who neither hold nor are held—are tossed about, driven by the **disturbances of the soul** <margin>C</margin> and fall to the ground. 

For this Law was given from on high: that whoever wishes may choose virtue. Wherefore the precepts, which were both in the Law and before the Law, were established—not as laws for the righteous (for the law is not made for a righteous man)—so that whoever chose virtue might receive eternal life and a blessed reward. But for the one who, conversely, delighted in vice, it was granted that he should dwell with those he had chosen. Furthermore, it was granted that the soul, which continually becomes better in acquiring virtue and preparing for justice, should receive a better place in the universe, being extended through every stage of progress toward the state of **impassibility** <term>impassibility: From the Greek 'apatheia,' meaning freedom from irrational passions and disturbances, a goal of the Christian sage</term>, until it reaches the **perfect man** <note>original: "virum perfectum"; an allusion to Ephesians 4:13</note>, namely the excellence of both knowledge and inheritance.

These saving conversions are divided, according to the order of change, by times, places, honors, forms of knowledge, inheritances, and <margin>D</margin> ministries, until one reaches that which transcends even contemplation, and is closest to the Lord in eternity. That which is lovable draws to the contemplation of itself everyone who has entirely devoted themselves to knowledge through the love of knowledge. 

Therefore, the Lord gave both the earlier and the later commandments, drawing from a single fountain. He did not disregard those who lived before the Law as if they were without law, nor did he allow those who did not hear the **barbarian philosophy** <note>original: "barbaram philosophiam"; Clement's term for the Hebrew Scriptures and Christian teachings, which Greeks considered "barbarian"</note> to be carried away without restraint. For while he provided the former with commandments and the latter with **philosophy** <note>Greek philosophy</note>, he shut up unbelief until his advent, at which time anyone who does not believe is without excuse. For by a different progress, both Greek and barbarian, he leads them toward the perfection that comes through faith. 

If, however, anyone from among the Greeks, having bypassed the preliminary training of Greek philosophy, has rushed straight to the <margin>E</margin> true doctrine, even if he be entirely unlearned, he has surpassed others by a long distance, since he has chosen the shortcut of salvation through faith toward perfection. 

Therefore, whatever things did not hinder man’s free will, God brought about so that they might assist in virtue. Thus, in some way, even to those who can only see obscurely and dimly, the one who truly is the only Almighty, Good God appears, granting salvation from age to age through the Son. He, in turn, was in no way the author or cause of evil. For the salvation of the universe, all things have been ordained by the Lord of all, both generally and individually. It is, therefore, the duty of **saving justice** <note>original: "iustitiae salutaris"</note> to lead each thing toward that which is better, as far as the circumstances allow and permit. For the salvation and permanence of that which is more excellent, the lesser things are also administered in proportion to their own <margin>F</margin> character. Behold, for whatever is endowed with virtue is changed for the better, having the cause of its change within itself: the choice of **knowledge** <note>original: "cognitionis"; referring to Gnosis</note>, which the soul had in its own power. But the **chastisements** <note>original: "Castigationes"</note> which are necessary for the goodness of the great Judge who watches over us, are carried out through the nearby Angels...
