...and through various prejudices, and through a perfect and in every part complete judgment, they compel those who have slightly cast off the sense of pain to be led by **repentance** <note>original: "pœnitentia"</note>. I pass over other matters, glorifying the Lord. <margin>A</margin> But I say that those souls endowed with **knowledge** <term>knowledge: Clement uses the Greek-derived concept of "gnosis," referring here not to a heresy, but to the deep, spiritual understanding of a perfected Christian</term>, which surpass the way of life of every holy order in the magnificence of their contemplation, are counted as holy among the holy, once they have been distributed among the blessed habitations defined for the "gods" <note>Clement often uses "gods" to refer to deified saints or high-ranking angels in the presence of God</note>. Being translated entirely from one place to another, they arrive in better places than the best, no longer embracing divine contemplation in mirrors or through mirrors, but rather being received into the most evident and truly pure, sincere, and everlasting banquet of divine contemplation. There, the souls who love beyond measure can never be sated; enjoying inexhaustible joy for ages that never end, they remain honored, so to speak, by the identity of universal excellence.

<margin>B</margin> This is the contemplation that can be grasped by those who are pure in heart. This, then, is the work of him who is perfected in knowledge: to have companionship with God through the **Great High Priest** <note>Referring to Christ</note>, being assimilated to the Lord according to his strength through all piety and religion toward God. This path tends toward the salvation of men through the care of exercising beneficence toward us, and again through sacred ministries, through teaching, and through the performance of good works. Now, indeed, he also creates and fashions himself. Furthermore, he who is endowed with knowledge adorns those who hear him, making that which possesses **impassibility** <term>impassibility: a state of being unmoved by suffering or worldly passions; a core virtue in ancient philosophy and early Christian asceticism</term> by nature as similar as possible to that which possesses it by exercise—and this occurs when he cannot be torn away from the companionship and conversation of the Lord.

I believe that gentleness, kindness, <margin>C</margin> and the magnificent, majestic worship of God are the rules of this **assimilation** <note>The process of becoming "like God"</note> which arises from knowledge. I say these virtues are a sacrifice pleasing and acceptable to God: a heart free from pride and arrogance joined with right knowledge. The Scripture says this is God's **whole burnt offering** <note>original: "holocaustum"</note> when any man is taken up into holiness and illuminated toward that union which cannot be divided. For the Gospel and the Apostle both command us to take ourselves captive and to slay ourselves—killing the "old man" who is corrupted by desires and raising the "new man" from the old state of death—by putting away the disturbances of the soul and becoming entirely estranged from sin. This was what the Law also silently signified by commanding that the sinner <margin>D</margin> be removed from the midst, and that the state of impassibility which comes from faith be translated from death to life.

Because those who taught the Law did not understand this, but instead received the Law as something that delighted in strife and contention, they gave an opportunity to those who wish to rashly slander it. For this reason, we rightly do not offer sacrifice to God, who is in need of nothing and who provided all things to men; rather, we glorify Him who was sacrificed for us, sacrificing ourselves to Him who needs nothing, out of that which needs nothing, and from the impassible to that which is impassible. For God is delighted only by our salvation. Rightly, therefore, we do not offer sacrifice to Him who is not conquered by pleasures, since the exhalation of smoke from a sacrifice—if it reaches anywhere at all—remains far below the thickest clouds.

God, therefore, needs nothing, nor <margin>E</margin> is He captured by pleasure, nor is He greedy for gain or money, since He is full and provides all things to every created thing that has need. God is not invoked by sacrifices, nor by gifts, nor again by glory and honor, nor is He enticed by any such thing. But He appears only to good and honest men, who would never betray justice either because of a threatened fear or because of magnificent promises.

Those who have not perceived the freedom of the human soul—which, as far as the choice of life is concerned, cannot be reduced to slavery—become distressed by the injustices of the unlearned and think that God does not exist. Similarly, those <margin>F</margin> who fall into the intemperance of pleasures, or into vehement pains and unexpected misfortunes, lament their circumstances and say there is no God; or if there is, that He does not see all things. There are others who are persuaded that those who are thought to be "gods" can be appeased by sacrifices and gifts, thereby favoring their own lusts; they are unwilling to believe that He alone is truly God, who exists in the identity of true justice. He, therefore, is pious and religious who is...

<margin>A</margin> The one **endowed with knowledge** <term>knowledge: Clement uses "cognitio" here to translate the Greek "gnosis," referring to a deep, experiential understanding of divine truth</term> is he who, first of all, takes care of himself. Next, he cares for those closest to him, that they may become as good as possible. For just as a son gratifies a good father by showing himself to be good and like his father, so too does a subject who submits to the command of a prince or magistrate. For to believe and to obey is within our own power. 

If anyone should think that the cause of evils is the frailty of matter, or the impulses of ignorance that are not led by will, or the necessities of those lacking reason because of their lack of skill, then the one endowed with knowledge—who has surpassed these states as one might surpass the nature of wild beasts through long discipline—does good to those who are willing, to the best of his ability, thus imitating the divine plan. And if he should ever be appointed to a position of leadership, he will preside over the salvation of those <margin>B</margin> over whom he holds command, just as **Moses** <note>Clement frequently cites Moses as the archetype of the perfect leader and "Gnostic" of the Old Testament</note> did. He will tame that which is wild and unfaithful by honoring those who are best and most excellent, and by punishing the wicked—a punishment which is assigned according to reason for the sake of discipline. 

For the soul of a just man is a truly divine image, made in the likeness of God. In this soul, through obedience to the commandments, there is built up and established the Leader of all things mortal and immortal, the King and Parent of all, the truly good law and ordinance, and the **eternal Word** <note>original: "Verbum æternum," referring to the Logos/Christ</note>, who is the one **Savior** <note>original: "Seruator"</note> both for individuals privately and for all in common. 

This is truly the **Only-Begotten** <note>original: "vnigenitus"</note>, the impression of the glory of the King of all and the Almighty Father, who imprints upon the one endowed with knowledge a perfect contemplation according to His own image. Thus, there exists now a third divine image, which is assimilated as far as possible to the "Second Cause" <note>By "Second Cause," Clement refers to the Son/Logos, who proceeds from the Father, the "First Cause"</note>, who is truly life itself. <margin>C</margin> Through this life, we live the true life, as if we were sketching the likeness of the man of knowledge, who dwells among things that are firm, stable, and subject to neither change nor alteration. 

Therefore, ruling over himself and his own, and possessing a firm and stable comprehension of divine science, he approaches the truth with sincerity and purity. For the knowledge and comprehension of those things perceived by the intelligence may rightly be called a firm and stable science. That part of it which deals with divine matters has this duty: to consider what the First Cause is, and what that is through which all things were made, and without which nothing was made; what things are pervasive, and what are containing; which are joined together and which are truly disjoined; and what order each of them holds, and what power and <margin>D</margin> service each one brings. 

And again, regarding human affairs: what man himself is, and what is according to his nature or contrary to it; and how, in turn, he ought to act or to suffer; and what his virtues and vices are, concerning good, evil, <margin><unclear>Pain is also found to be useful</unclear></margin> and indifferent things. He treats also the virtue of a great and lofty soul, prudence, temperance, and that virtue which is perfect and absolute in every part following all the others: **justice**. 

He uses prudence and justice to acquire wisdom. He uses the virtue of a great soul not only in enduring accidents, but also in resisting pleasure, desire, pain, and anger—and in short, anything that entices us by force or some fraud. For one ought not to endure vices and shameful things, but rather be persuaded to endure those things that are terrible. Indeed, **pain is also found to be useful** <margin>E</margin> both in medicine and for the sake of education and chastisement; through it, character is corrected for the benefit of men. 

The forms of this greatness and loftiness of soul are endurance, high-spiritedness, magnanimity, liberality, and magnificence. Because of these, the man endowed with knowledge takes no heed of the world’s reproach or bad reputation. He is subject neither to glories nor to flatteries; and in sustaining labors while simultaneously doing what is necessary, and overcoming all accidents with a great and brave soul, he appears as a true man among other men. Again, preserving prudence, and being moderate and temperate in the stillness of his soul, he receives the commandments as things that befit him. Rejecting shameful things as foreign to him, he behaves in an orderly and decorous manner, both as a citizen of this world and of the world beyond, and in no way falling into sin. <margin>F</margin> He is exceedingly rich, because he desires nothing, as one who needs little and abounds in great stores of every good because of his knowledge of the Good. For the first duty of his justice is to embrace with love those of his own kind, and to act and dwell with them, both on earth and in heaven. In this way, he also gladly shares and communicates...

<margin>A</margin> ...shares what he possesses, and while he is kind and benign, he holds the wicked in the greatest hatred, perfectly abhorring and turning away from all wrongdoing. Therefore, one must learn to be faithful both to oneself and to one's neighbor, and to obey the commandments. For he is a servant of God who, of his own will, subjects himself to the commandments. But he who is pure in heart—not merely because of the commandments, but because of **knowledge** <term>knowledge: Latin "cognitio," translating the Greek "gnosis," referring to the highest stage of Christian insight</term> itself—he is a friend of God. For we are not born endowed with virtue by nature, nor does it come to those who are born as some other parts of the body might later grow naturally. If it were so, it would not be voluntary or praiseworthy. Nor is virtue perfected through the mere practice and habit of those who associate together, in the way that speech is learned; indeed, vice is almost generated in that very way. Nor does this knowledge come from some craft, whether from those which propose profit for themselves, or those pertaining to the care of the body. Nor does it come from those <margin>B</margin> disciplines that are of the world; for it would be well for them if they were merely able to prepare the soul and serve it. For civil laws can perhaps restrain evil actions. But speeches prepared for persuasion, since they dwell on the surface, cannot provide the permanence of truth which constitutes science. 

However, **Greek philosophy** <note>Clement viewed Greek philosophy as a "handmaid" to theology, preparing the mind for Christian revelation</note> as it were, pre-cleanses and prepares the soul for the reception of faith, upon which truth builds knowledge. This man, then, is the true **Athlete**, who in the great stadium—namely, this beautiful world—is crowned with the true victory of the soul over all the disturbances of the mind. For the Superintendent of the Games <term>Superintendent: original "Agonotheta," the official who presided over the Greek games</term> is Almighty God, and he who distributes the prizes is the only-begotten Son of God. The spectators are <margin>C</margin> Angels and gods <note>original: "Dii"; likely referring to the "deified" saints or celestial beings</note>; and the contest, diverse and consisting of every kind of combat, is not against flesh and blood, but against spiritual powers who work through the flesh to produce violent movements of vice and passion. Having overcome these great contests, and having as it were laid prostrate the threatening tempter, he has attained immortality. For the judgment of God in his most just tribunal cannot be deceived. Indeed, the theater has been called to the contest. In the stadium, the athletes fight it out. And from these, he certainly overcomes who has obeyed the trainer <term>trainer: original "alipta," one who anointed and prepared athletes</term>. For all things are proposed by God as equal to all: and He Himself is beyond reproach; but he who is able obtains mercy, and he who wills it is able. 

By this reasoning, we have also received a mind, that we might know what we do; and that saying, **"Know thyself,"** here means to know for what purpose we were born. For we were <margin>D</margin> born so that we might choose to obey the commandments in order to be saved. This is <margin>Adrasteia/Nemesis: named because she cannot be escaped. Contentment.</margin> **Nemesis**, through whom it is not permitted to escape God. It is, therefore, the duty of man to obey God, who has announced a diverse salvation through the commandments. Furthermore, the expression of a grateful heart is confession. For the Benefactor is the first to begin doing good. He who receives with a prompt and eager mind, and keeps the commands with appropriate consideration, is faithful. But he who returns thanks for a benefit received, to the best of his strength through charity, is now a friend. 

There is one primary return of gratitude from men: to do those things that are best to God. For like his own offspring, and in some way related through their effects, the Master and Savior accepts the improvements and corrections of men <margin>E</margin> as His own grace and honor; just as He considers the losses and offenses suffered by those who have believed in Him as crimes admitted against Himself, and as His own reproaches and disgraces. For what other reproach or disgrace could touch God? Therefore, thanks cannot be fully returned according to the dignity of salvation, if compared with the benefit that proceeds from the Lord. For just as those who harass possessions do an injury to the owners, and those who harass soldiers do so to their General, so too is the harassment of those dedicated to Him a contempt for the Lord. For just as the Sun not only illuminates the heaven and the whole world, shining over the land and sea, but also sends its light through a window or a small hole into the innermost chambers of houses, so the Word, poured out everywhere, looks upon even the smallest things of those done in life. 

<margin>F</margin> The Greeks, however, just as they make their gods similar to men in form, so also they make them subject to the same passions of the soul as themselves. And as each group describes their forms as similar to their own—as **Xenophanes** <note>Clement quotes the pre-Socratic philosopher Xenophanes to critique anthropomorphism in religion</note> says: "The Ethiopians make them black and flat-nosed; the Thracians make them ruddy and blue-eyed"—so they also assimilate the souls of the gods to those who fashion them. <margin>A</margin> ...though they are superior, they are still subject to movements and disturbances. Therefore, it is necessary that the wicked should hold evil thoughts about God, while the good hold the very best. For this reason, the one who possesses a truly royal mind and is endowed with **knowledge** <term>knowledge: Latin "cognitio," representing the Greek "gnosis," the deep spiritual insight Clement believes is the goal of the Christian life</term>, because he worships God piously and is far removed from superstition, is convinced that only He who is the only God is to be honored and venerated. He believes God is magnificent, embracing all with His benevolence, the prince and author of all good things, and not the cause of any evil. Regarding the false religion of the Greeks, I believe I have shown enough in the book titled *Exhortation to the Greeks* <note>original: "Protreptikos," Clement’s famous work written to convert pagans by exposing the absurdities of their mythology</note>, making abundant use of the histories that served that purpose.

<margin>B</margin> There is no need, then, to repeat what has already been clearly stated. However, as far as noting the point we have reached, it is enough to bring forward a few examples out of many to show that those who liken God to the worst of men are impious. For either their gods are harmed by men—and those who are harmed by men are shown to be inferior to them—or, if they are not harmed, they nevertheless become indignant just as a non-injured but irritable old woman is provoked to anger. This is what they say of Diana, who was supposedly enraged at the Aetolians because of Oeneus <note>In myth, King Oeneus forgot to include Diana in his harvest sacrifices, leading her to send a monstrous boar to ravage his land</note>. For how is it that she, being a goddess, did not consider that Oeneus had not acted out of contempt, but had simply forgotten or neglected the sacrifice? She is also depicted as defending her own case to Minerva, being angry because Minerva had given birth in a temple, saying:

<margin>C</margin> > You rejoice in bloody spoils
> Seeing them stripped from the dead.
> These things are not cursed by you.
> But if I have given birth, you consider it a grave offense.

And yet, other animals that give birth in temples do them no harm. Rightly, then, the superstitious, fearing gods who are so prone to anger, imagine that everything that happens is a sign or a cause of evil. If a mouse nibbles through an altar made of clay; if, having nothing else, it gnaws a leather oil-flask; if a cock that is fed in the evening should crow—they declare these to be omens. Menander mocks such a person in the comedy titled **The Superstitious Man** <term>The Superstitious Man: Greek "Deisidaimon," a stock character in Greek comedy who lived in constant fear of trivial omens</term>:

> "What good could happen to me, O good gods?
<margin>D</margin> > For as I was tying my right shoe, I snapped the lace!"

Rightly so, you trifler! It broke because it was rotten. You are simply a cheap miser who refuses to buy new ones. There is also that witty remark of Antiphon’s: when a certain man saw an omen in the fact that a sow had devoured her own piglets, and Antiphon saw that the sow was skeletal with hunger because of the owner's stinginess, he said, "Be happy for the sign—that being so hungry, she didn't eat your children!" Bion said, "What is so strange about a mouse gnawing a basket when it found nothing to eat? It would have been a wonder if—as Arcesilaus used to joke—the basket had eaten the mouse!" Diogenes also spoke rightly to the man who was amazed to find a snake coiled around a pestle: "Do not wonder," he said, "for it would be much more wonderful if you had seen the pestle coiled around the snake!" For it is natural for irrational animals to run, fight, give birth, and die; since these things are according to their nature, they can never be "against nature" for us.

<margin>E</margin> > And many birds fly beneath the rays of the Sun.

Philemon the comic poet also laughs at such things in a play. "When I see someone," he says, "watching to see who sneezes, or who has spoken, or looking back to see who is passing with a bird, immediately everyone in the market sneezes; each man walks and talks to himself, saying that things for the citizens do not turn out as their nature warrants." Furthermore, while sober people seek health, those who stuff themselves and wallow in drunkenness on feast days bring diseases upon themselves. Many also fear "suspended writings" <note>charms or amulets worn around the neck</note>. Diogenes acted very wittily when he found written over the house of a certain wicked man: *The glorious victor Hercules dwells here; let no evil enter.* "And how," Diogenes asked, "shall the master of the house enter?" These same people worship every greasy stone and every piece of wood, as the saying goes, tying up yellow wool and scraps of—

<margin>A</margin> ...and they fear torches, squills <note>A type of sea onion used in ancient Greek purification rituals to ward off evil spirits</note>, and sulfur, being enchanted by charlatans through certain impure purifications. But God, who is truly God, knows only the holy. He knows righteous characters, just as He knows the unrighteous, the impure, and the criminal. Indeed, one may certainly see that eggs, among those things used for purification, if they are kept warm, are brought to life; yet this would never happen if they shared in the evils of the person being purified. The comic poet Diphilus certainly mocks these charlatans elegantly when he writes: "Purifying the daughters of Proetus <note>In mythology, the Proetides were daughters of King Proetus driven mad for insulting Hera or Dionysus</note>, and their father Proetus, son of Abas, and a fifth one among them. With a single torch and a single squill for so many human bodies, and with sulfur and bitumen from the deep-sounding sea, flowing from the quiet but deep Ocean. But, blessed Air, send Anticyra <note>A Greek city famous for hellebore, a plant used to treat madness; the poet is calling for a cure for the 'madness' of superstition</note> through the clouds, so that I may turn a parasite into a drone." Certainly Menander also says rightly: "If you actually had some real evil, 

<margin>B</margin> you would need to apply a real medicine. But now you have none. I have found an empty remedy for an empty problem. Just imagine that it helps you. Let the women wipe you all around, and let them bring water from three springs to sprinkle you, and throw in salt and lentils. Anyone who is not conscious of any evil within themselves is pure." Now the Tragedy <note>A reference to Euripides' play *Orestes*</note> says: "Orestes, what disease is destroying you? My conscience, because I am conscious of having committed grave crimes." For in truth there is no other purity than to abstain from sins. Therefore, Epicharmus also says beautifully: "If you have a pure mind, you are pure in your whole body." Furthermore, we say that souls must first be purged of evil and wicked dogmas through right reason, and only then turn toward the commemoration of the chief points of faith. For even before the tradition of the mysteries 

<margin>C</margin> or sacraments <note>original: "sacramenta," referring here to the sacred rites and teachings of the early Church</note>, certain purifications must be offered to those who are to be initiated into the mysteries, since it is necessary to turn toward the true tradition by setting aside impious opinions. For do we not rightly and truly refuse to circumscribe in any place Him who cannot be circumscribed, nor do we shut up in temples made by hands Him who contains all things? What kind of "holy work" could come from builders, stonecutters, and a sordid or unrefined <term>unrefined: Latin "illiberalis," literally "not befitting a free person," used here to describe manual labor as opposed to spiritual contemplation</term> art? Are those people not better who thought the air and that which it contains—or rather the whole world and the universe—was alone worthy of God’s excellence? For it would be ridiculous, as the Philosophers themselves say, that man, who is the plaything of the Gods, should "make" a God, or that a God should come to be from a playful art; since that which is made becomes the same as and similar to that from which it is made—just as that which is made from ivory is ivory, and that which is made from gold 

<margin>D</margin> is golden. But the images and temples fashioned by base and sordid men are made from vain and useless matter. Therefore, they too must be vain, useless, material, and profane; and even if you perfect the art, they always participate in filth and unrefined nature. Thus, these are not sacred or divine works of art. Indeed, what could possibly be "placed" or "situated," since there is nothing that is not already placed and situated, given that all things are in a location? Now, whatever is placed or situated is so because it was not previously placed or situated. If, therefore, God is "placed" or "situated" by men, there was a time when He was not placed or situated, and thus He did not exist at all. For that which did not exist was neither situated nor placed, since whatever does not exist is then placed or situated. But that which *is* cannot be placed or situated by that which 

<margin>E</margin> is not, nor by any other thing. For He Himself truly *is*. It remains, then, that He exists through Himself. And how can something beget itself? Or how could He, who already exists, place and situate Himself? But not even in this way could it be, since that which does not exist cannot be placed or situated. And as for what is thought to have been placed and situated—how could that which already exists do to itself later what it already had before? Since all things that exist belong to Him, how could He still have need of anything? Furthermore, if God had a form similar to a human, would He not, like a man, have need of food, clothing, a house, and other things that follow as a consequence? For those who share the same form and the same affections will also need the same way of life. But if "sacred" is understood in two ways: 

<margin>F</margin> namely, God Himself, and that which is built in His honor, how could we not properly call the Church <note>original: "ecclesia"</note>—which was made for the honor of God through holy knowledge <term>knowledge: "agnitio," referring again to Gnosis or spiritual insight</term>—the "sacred place" of God? It is of great price and was not built by a sordid or unrefined art, but rather by the will of God it was made into a temple.

### STROMATA, BOOK VII.

<margin>A</margin> ...performed: but it is not a temple decorated by the hand of a charlatan <note>Latin: *praestigiatoris*; referring to those who use trickery or "magic" to impress the masses</note>, but a temple made by the will of God. For I do not now call the *place* the Church, but the congregation of the elect. This temple is better suited for receiving the greatness of God’s dignity. For a living being that is of great value—dedicated to Him who is worthy of all honor, or rather, to Him whose value nothing can match—is consecrated because of its extraordinary holiness. Now, he who is endowed with <term>knowledge</term> <note>Original: *cognitione*; Clement uses this to refer to the "Gnostic" or the advanced Christian who has deep spiritual understanding</note> is of great value; he is held in honor and esteem by God, and in him God is settled—that is, the knowledge concerning God is consecrated within him. Here we find the divine likeness and the holy image in a righteous soul, provided that the soul is blessed because it has been purified beforehand, and provided it performs blessed works. 

<margin>B</margin> Here is both that which *can* be a dwelling and that which *is* a dwelling: the latter in those who have already attained knowledge, and the former in those who are capable of attaining it, even if they are not yet worthy to receive the science of God. For whatever is destined to believe is already faithful to God; a statue is set up in honor, endowed with virtue, and dedicated to God. Therefore, just as God is not confined by space, nor is He ever likened to the form of a living creature, so too He is not subject to similar passions. He does not lack anything, as created beings do, such that He would crave a sacrifice like a hungry man craves food. Anything that is touched by passion is subject to decay; and to offer food to one who does not require nourishment is pure folly. 

Furthermore, the comic poet Pherecrates <note>A poet of Old Attic Comedy from the 5th century BCE</note> elegantly depicted the gods in his comedy titled *The Deserters*, where they complain to humans about sacrifices. He says that when men sacrifice to the gods, they first set aside the parts that are most shameful, saying: 

<margin>C</margin> "Have you not smeared the thighs with fat all the way to the groin, and made the loin very thin, and then distributed the spine itself to us as if it were filed down, like you do for dogs? Then, because you are ashamed of yourselves, you cover it with many layers of meal." 

Eubulus, who is also a comic poet, writes <margin>explains</margin> <note>Original: *ἐκλύει* (eklyei); a Greek term meaning to set free, explain, or interpret</note> about sacrifices in this way: "You sacrifice only the tail and the thigh, as if to <term>paedicones</term> <note>Likely a reference to those who practice pederasty; a biting social commentary on the 'cheapness' of the offering</note>." And in the comedy *Semele*, he introduces Dionysus as an arbiter, saying: "First of all, they sacrifice blood and the bladder to me, but not even the surface of the heart. For I do not eat sweet victims, nor do I eat thighs." Menander also wrote: "When they have placed the tips of the loins, the bile, and the bones that cannot be eaten upon the gods’ altar, they consume the rest themselves." 

<margin>D</margin> For must even wild beasts not be kept away from the smell <note>Original: *nidor*; the steam or "savor" of roasting meat</note> of the sacrifices? But if the smell is truly a gift for the gods of the Greeks, why have they not previously ranked cooks among the gods, since they are worthy of equal happiness? And why do they not worship the dog, which is much closer to this venerable smell? Even Hesiod says that Zeus, being deceived by Prometheus in the division of the meats, received:

<margin>Hesiod, in Theogony</margin>
> *With evil art, the bones of the ox covered in shining fat.*
> *From this it comes that the sons of men burn white bones for the gods upon the sacred altars, imitating the custom of ancient times.*

But they would never say that God is nourished because He is tormented by a desire arising from a lack. If they did, they would make Him like a plant, which is nourished without appetite, or <margin>E</margin> like the beasts that hide in caves. Certainly, they say those creatures are nourished either by the thickness of the air or even by the exhalation of their own bodies, and they grow without harm. But if God is nourished without any need, what is the use of nourishment for one who does not lack it? 

However, if He rejoices in being honored—even though His nature lacks nothing—then it is not without reason that we honor God with prayers. This is the best and holiest sacrifice we offer with righteousness, honoring Him through the most righteous Word <note>The *Logos* or Christ</note>, through whom we receive knowledge, and glorifying the things we have learned through Him. Therefore, our altar here on earth is the congregation of those who are dedicated to prayer, who possess, as it were, one common voice and one mind. 

Now, the nutrients received through the sense of smell, although they are more divine than those taken through the body, nevertheless imply <margin>F</margin> respiration. What then do they say of God? Does He breathe through His skin like the race of demons? Or does He only breathe in, like aquatic creatures through the dilation of their gills? Or does He breathe all over, like insects through the compression of their wing-slits? No one of sound mind would liken God to any of these. Those things that breathe through the lungs against the chest...

### CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

<margin>A</margin> ...expansion, they draw in air. Furthermore, if they assign to God internal organs, arteries, veins, nerves, and limbs, they render Him no different from a mortal. Now, "conspiration" <note>Latin: *conspiratio*; literally "breathing together." Clement is using the physical act of breathing as a metaphor for the spiritual harmony of the believers.</note> is a term properly used in the Church. For the sacrifice of the Church is the Word exhaled from holy souls, while the sacrifice and the entire mind are simultaneously opened up to God. Men have commonly boasted of the most ancient and holy altar at Delos. They say that Pythagoras approached this altar alone because it was not defiled by slaughter and death. But will they not believe us when we say that the truly holy altar is the righteous soul, and that the incense stripped from it is holy prayer? 

As I see it, the eating of meat was the pretext upon which human sacrifices were devised. Otherwise, anyone who wished to eat meat could have done so without such a cult of idols. For the sacrifices established by the Law <note>The Mosaic Law of the Old Testament.</note> signify our religion through allegory; for instance, the turtledoves and pigeons offered for sins signify that the <margin>B</margin> cleansing of the irrational part of the soul is acceptable to God. If any of the righteous do not burden their souls by eating meat, they use a logic that is quite consistent—though not for the same reasons as Pythagoras and his followers, who dream of the transmigration of the soul <note>The belief that souls are reborn into different bodies, including animals.</note>. 

Indeed, Xenocrates, in his specific treatise on animal nourishment, and Polemon, in his work *On Life According to Nature*, appear to say clearly that a diet of meat is useless, as it has already been processed and assimilated into the "souls" of beasts. For that reason, the Jews also strictly abstain from pork, considering this animal to be most wicked and accursed, since more than any other it digs up and destroys the fruits of the earth. But if they say that living creatures were given to humans, we also confess this, though <margin>C</margin> not entirely for the purpose of eating them. Nor were all given, but only those that do not work. On this point, the comic poet Plato says not badly in his comedy titled *The Feasts*: "Of the quadrupeds, we ought to kill none hereafter except for swine. For they have the sweetest meat, and nothing comes back to us from a pig except bristles, mud, and squealing." 

Hence Aesop used to say that pigs do not cry out without reason when they are being dragged away, because they understand perfectly that they are useful for nothing other than sacrifice. For this reason, Cleanthes also used to say that they possess a soul in place of salt, so that their meat does not rot <note>A famous Stoic pun; the "soul" of the pig is just a preservative to keep the meat fresh for human consumption.</note>. Some, therefore, do not eat it because it is useless; others because it destroys crops; and others do not eat it because the animal is prone to sexual excess. For that same reason, the Law does not sacrifice a goat, except for the purpose of sending away evils <note>A reference to the "Scapegoat" ritual in Leviticus.</note>, since <margin>D</margin> pleasure is the "metropolis" of vice. 

Furthermore, they say that eating goat meat contributes to the "falling sickness" <note>Epilepsy.</note>. They also say that the greatest physical growth comes from pork. Therefore, while it is useful to those who exercise the body, it is certainly not so for those who strive to grow the soul itself, because of the dullness of mind generated by eating meat. Perhaps some of those endowed with <term>knowledge</term> <note>Original: *cognitione*; here referring to the advanced spiritual practitioner.</note> might also abstain from meat for the sake of discipline, so that the flesh does not become too luxurious or be carried away with excessive impulse toward sexual matters. For as Androcydes says, "Wine and the gorging of meat make the body robust, but the soul weaker." Therefore, this kind of nourishment is impious and foreign to religion for those seeking perfect understanding. 

Consequently, the Egyptians also, in those sanctifications performed according to their rites, <margin>E</margin> do not permit the Priests to eat meat; they use only the lightest of birds, and they do not touch fish—partly because of certain myths, but mostly because that kind of food makes the flesh "moist" <note>In ancient medicine, "moist" humors were often associated with sluggishness or lack of spiritual clarity.</note>. Now, land animals and birds are nourished by breathing the same air as our souls, since they have a soul derived from the same kind of air. But they say fish do not even breathe this air, but rather the air that was mixed with water at the very first origin of the world, just as with the other elements; this is taken as a sign of their material persistence. 

We must therefore offer sacrifices to God, not expensive and splendid ones, but those that are pious and acceptable to Him—that "incense" composed in the Law, which consists of many tongues and voices in prayer, or rather, which is constructed into a unity of faith from diverse nations and sexes through the gift of the <margin>F</margin> testaments. It is gathered together in praises with a pure mind, through a just and right way of life, from holy works and righteous prayer. For who is so foolish, as the poetic wit says, and of such a cowardly spirit...

### STROMATA, BOOK VII.

<margin>A</margin> Is any man so gullible as to hope the Gods—who have no flesh on their bones, and only parched <gloss>consumed</gloss> bile—rejoice in, and demand for themselves, gifts that even hungry dogs would not eat? And that they return favor to those who do these things, whether they be pirates, robbers, or tyrants?

We, however, say that fire sanctifies not the flesh, but sinful souls. We do not speak of that gluttonous and all-consuming fire which is entirely filthy and undignified, but of the **wise fire** <note>original: *ignem prudentem*; Clement adapts this term from Stoic philosophy to describe a spiritual fire that refines the soul rather than burning physical matter.</note>, which persuades the soul as it passes through it. We are commanded to worship and honor the same one whom we are persuaded is the **Word**, the **Savior**, and the **Leader**.

<margin>B</margin> Through him, we honor the Father—not on selected days, as some others do, but continuously throughout our entire life, and in every way. Truly, we are a "chosen race, justified by the commandment." It says, "Seven times I have spoken your praise." <note>A reference to Psalm 119:164.</note> Therefore, the person endowed with **knowledge** <term>Gnosis: for Clement, this is the deep, spiritual insight into divine truths that leads to a perfected Christian life</term> does not honor God in a defined place, nor in a chosen temple, nor on certain feast days or appointed times, but throughout his whole life, in every place—even if he is by himself, or if he has others with him who believe the same. This is to give thanks through the knowledge of a righteous life. 

If the presence of a good man, because of the respect and reverence for his excellence, always shapes and molds the person who interacts with him, how much more shall he who is always in the presence of God—through knowledge, lifestyle, and thanksgiving—rightly become better in all his 

<margin>C</margin> deeds, words, and affections? Such is the man who is persuaded that God is present everywhere, and does not believe Him to be confined to certain fixed locations by human will. For if he thought he was sometimes without God, he might give himself over to excess and lust by night or day. 

Therefore, celebrating a festival throughout our whole life, and persuaded that God is present everywhere and in every part of us, we praise Him while we tend our fields, we praise Him while we sail, and we conduct ourselves in every other walk of life according to his divine art. He who is endowed with knowledge is joined more closely to God and becomes more familiar with Him, showing both gravity <note>Dignity or seriousness.</note> and joy in all things. Gravity, because he is turned toward God; joy, because he considers the human goods that God has given us. It seems the Prophet shows the excellence of knowledge this way: 

<margin>D</margin> "Teach me kindness, discipline, and knowledge," <note>Psalm 119:66.</note> increasing by degrees that which is the foundation of perfection. 

This man, therefore, is truly royal, a Priest, a holy servant of God. This status is even now preserved among the most learned of the barbarians <note>Clement often uses "barbarian" to refer to non-Greeks, including Egyptians and Hebrews, whom he respected for their ancient wisdom.</note>, who elevate the priestly class to the rank of kings. Such a man never hands himself over to the confused crowd that rules the theaters. He does not even admit in his dreams those things said, done, or seen for the sake of enticing pleasure. He does not seek those pleasures perceived by sight, nor the varieties found in other enjoyments—such as expensive and magnificent incense that charms the smell, or seasonings for food, or the delights of various wines that bait the sense of taste. Nor does he seek fragrant wreaths woven from various flowers, which soften the soul through the senses. 

<margin>E</margin> Instead, always referring the honorable use of all things back to God—food, drink, and oil—he offers the firstfruits to the Giver of all, giving thanks through the gift, the oil, and the **Word** given to him. He rarely attends banquets unless the gathering is for the sake of professing friendship, harmony, and confession, and this has persuaded him to come. 

For he is persuaded that his God knows and hears everything—not only the voice, but even the thought. For even the hearing we possess through bodily channels does not perceive by physical force alone, but through a certain vital sense and an intelligence that discerns voices signifying something. God is not, therefore, endowed with a human form so that He might hear, nor does He need senses (as the Stoics <note>A school of philosophy that believed God was a physical "breath" or fire pervading the universe.</note> pleased to think, especially regarding hearing and sight, claiming He could not otherwise perceive anything). 

<margin>F</margin> Instead, by the ease with which air is affected, the most keen **harmony of the Angels**, and the power that touches the conscience of the soul, He knows all things simultaneously with the thought, through an inexplicable power and without need for sensory hearing. If someone says that a voice rolling through the lower air does not reach God, let them know that the thoughts of the holy ones cut through not only the air, but the entire world. 

<summary>Clement describes the "True Gnostic" as one who worships God through a life of constant prayer and ethical conduct rather than physical sacrifices or specific holy days. He argues that God, being incorporeal, perceives even the unspoken thoughts of the righteous through a spiritual power that transcends physical senses.</summary>

<header>CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA</header>

<margin>A</margin>
Divine power, just like light, perceives the whole soul. What of it? Do not even our vows and inner purposes reach God, sending forth a voice of their own? Or are they not also transmitted by the conscience? What voice would He wait for, He who knew the chosen purpose even before our birth, and who knows that which is to come as if it already were? Does not the light of power make the depths of any soul shine, since—as the scripture says—the light of power searches the innermost rooms? <note>Clement alludes to Proverbs 20:27, "The spirit of man is the lamp of the Lord, searching all the innermost parts of the being."</note> God is all hearing and all seeing, if I may use these names. Therefore, the ignorant man preserves no true religion nor any worthy worship of God, neither in hymns, nor in speeches, nor in writings or doctrines; for his opinion of God is unfitting, turning toward low and unseemly notions and thoughts. Thus it happens that the praise offered by many differs not at all from a curse, because of their ignorance of the truth. And just as there are cravings, desires, and—to put it simply—impulses of the mind, so there are also prayers.

<margin>B</margin>
Wherefore no one desires a drink, but rather *to drink* the drink; nor does one desire an inheritance, but rather *to be* an heir. In the same way, one does not merely desire knowledge, but *to know*; nor a just republic, but *to govern* the republic. Therefore, prayers belong to those who have petitions, and petitions belong to those who have desires. Praying and desiring act upon one another to obtain good things and the conveniences attached to them. Thus, he who is endowed with **knowledge** <term>Gnosis: Clement’s term for the highest form of Christian insight and spiritual maturity</term> asks and prays for things that are truly good for the soul. He himself also assists in reaching a state of goodness, so that he no longer possesses "goods" as if they were external lessons to be learned, but rather he becomes good himself. Therefore, it is most fitting for those to pray who know God as they ought, and who possess the virtue that is appropriate and

<margin>C</margin>
consistent with that knowledge—those who know what things are truly good, what should be asked for, and when and how to ask for each thing. It is the height of ignorance to ask from those who are not gods as if they were gods, or to ask for things that are not beneficial, essentially asking for evils for oneself because they appear to be good in one's vision. Since there is only one good God, we and the Angels pray to Him that some good things be given, and that others remain with us. But we do not pray in the same way. For it is not the same thing to ask that a gift remain as it is to strive to receive it from the very beginning. Furthermore, the turning away and driving off of evils is a type of prayer. But that kind of prayer must never be used to the harm of other men—unless the person of knowledge, caring for justice, manages this petition for the sake of those who have lost their sense of what is evil. Therefore, to speak more boldly, prayer is a conversation

<margin>D</margin>
and a dialogue with God. Even if we speak silently, whispering and not even opening our lips, we have cried out within. For God perpetually hears every dialogue prepared within the heart. In this prayer, we stretch our head and hands toward heaven and raise our feet at the final exclamation of the prayer, following the essence of God—which is apprehended by the intellect—with the readiness and eagerness of the spirit. While trying to lead the body away from the earth along with the word, we have an upright and elevated soul through the desire for better things; we compel the soul to go forward into holy things, despising the bond of the flesh with a great mind. For we know very well that he who is endowed with knowledge gladly leaves the whole world behind, just as surely as the Jews left Egypt, showing clearly that he will be as close as possible to God.

<margin>E</margin>
Even if some people establish certain and defined hours for prayer—such as the third, sixth, and ninth <note>The traditional "canonical hours" of prayer in the early Church (roughly 9 AM, Noon, and 3 PM).</note>—the person of knowledge prays throughout his whole life, striving to live in conversation with God through his prayers. He has left behind, to put it simply, everything that is not useful, since he has already arrived at the point where he receives the perfection of one who acts out of love. Now, those who know the blessed trinity of the holy mansions <note>A reference to the varying degrees of glory or "dwelling places" in heaven.</note> understand the triple division of hours, which are honored by just as many prayers. At this point, I am reminded of certain people who think differently: specifically, the followers of the heresy of Prodicus <note>Prodicus was a 2nd-century Gnostic teacher who reportedly taught that prayer was unnecessary for the "spiritual" person.</note>, whose doctrines suggest that one should not pray at all. Lest they pride themselves on this impious wisdom of theirs as if it were some new or foreign discovery, let them know that it was previously held by the philosophers called the Cyrenaics. In due time,

<margin>F</margin>
we shall speak against the impious "knowledge" of those cursed men. We do not insert a dispute against them in this Commentary now, for such a treatment would be lengthy and would interrupt the discourse we have begun; for now, we wish only to show the truly pious and reli- <note>The word is completed on the next page as "religious man."</note>

<summary>Clement defines prayer as an internal, perpetual dialogue with God that transcends physical rituals or set times. He argues that the person of true spiritual knowledge (the Gnostic) lives in a constant state of prayer and moral ascent, contrasting this with the ignorance of pagans and certain heretical groups like the followers of Prodicus.</summary>

<page-num>243</page-num>
<header>MISCELLANIES, BOOK VII</header>

<margin>A</margin>
The holy worshiper of God is he who, according to the ecclesiastical rule, is truly endowed with <term>spiritual knowledge</term><note>Latin: *cognitio*; referring here to the Greek *gnosis*, the deep spiritual insight Clement attributes to the mature Christian.</note>. To him alone—since God distributes and shares according to His own will—is petition granted, both when he asks and even when he merely thinks of it. For just as God can do whatever He wills, so whatever is asked by the person endowed with knowledge, he receives. For God knows entirely those who are worthy of good things and those who are not; hence He gives what is fitting to each. Therefore, He will not give to the unworthy, even if they ask often. But He will surely give to those who are worthy. Yet petition is not superfluous, even if good things are given without prayer. Furthermore, both thanksgiving and petition for those things which pertain to the conversion of one's neighbors are the work of the person endowed with knowledge. Indeed, it was in this way that the Lord also prayed: giving thanks for His ministry, but asking that as many as possible might attain <margin>B</margin> <term>knowledge</term>, so that in those who are saved, God might be glorified through salvation arising from recognition; and that He who is alone good and the only Savior might be recognized through the Son from age to age. Nevertheless, the faith that one will receive is itself a species of prayer, laid up in a manner consistent with spiritual knowledge. Moreover, if prayer is an occasion for conversation with God, no opportunity for access to God should be overlooked. Certainly, for the one endowed with knowledge, holiness is connected to blessed providence; through a spontaneous confession, he reveals the perfect benefit of God. For his holiness is like a kind of care that responds to providence, which is turned back toward the benevolence of the Friend of God. For the Good is not good by necessity or against His will, in the way that fire <margin>C</margin> possesses the power of heating. Rather, the imparting of good things is voluntary, even if it anticipates a request. Nor, indeed, will anyone be saved against his will. For the soul is not inanimate, but will strive toward salvation entirely by its own will and free choice of mind. Therefore, man also received commandments, so that he might be one who can be moved and incited by himself toward whichever he wishes of those things to be chosen or avoided. God, then, does not do good out of necessity, but does good by free will to those who turn to Him by their own effort. For the providence that comes to us from the divine is not a form of servitude, as if proceeding from the inferior to the superior. Rather, out of mercy for our weakness, the nearby and continuous dispensations of providence are exercised. Just as shepherds care for their sheep, and a King for those who obey his authority, and as we obey our superiors <margin>D</margin> who rule those committed to them in the order handed down to them. Therefore, they are the servants and worshipers of God who offer the most liberal and truly royal worship, which is performed through a pious and religious mind and knowledge. Consequently, every place is truly sacred in which we receive the notion and thought of God, and every time is sacred likewise. When, however, he who possesses a good mind and a good disposition of soul and is grateful asks through prayer, he brings some help in a certain part, gladly receiving what he desires through those things he asks for in his prayers. For when He who is the giver of good things perceives our good inclination of soul, all good things follow simultaneously upon his conception of it. Certainly, through prayer, the manner in which one conducts oneself toward what is necessary is examined. If, however, voice and speech were given to us for the sake of understanding, why <margin>E</margin> would God not hear the soul and the mind itself, since surely soul already hears soul, and mind hears mind? Hence, God does not wait for tongues that produce many voices, like human interpreters, but He knows the minds of all—to put it simply—and what a voice signifies to us, our thought speaks this to God; He knew this would come into the mind even before creation. It is permitted, therefore, not to emit prayer even with the voice, but only to direct whatever is spiritual within us toward the voice perceived by the mind, through an undivided turning toward God. Since, moreover, the East is the image of the day of birth, and from there the light increases which first shone out of the darkness, the day of the knowledge of truth has also dawned for those who were wallowing in ignorance, in the same way that the Sun rises in the morning East—namely, through prayers. For this reason, even the most ancient of <margin>F</margin> temples looked toward the West, so that those who stand with their faces turned toward the images might be taught to turn toward the East.

> Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight. The lifting up of my hands as an evening sacrifice,

<margin>Psalm 140</margin> <note>Psalm 141:2 in modern numbering.</note> say the Psalms. Therefore, prayer for wicked men is not only against others, but even against themselves...

<margin>A</margin>It is most destructive, for even if they receive the favorable and prosperous things they ask for, these things harm those who receive them, as they are ignorant of how to use them. For those who pray to possess those goods which they do not have, seek things that *seem* to be good, not those that truly *are* good. However, the one who is <term>endowed with knowledge</term><note>Latin: *cognitione præditus*; Clement’s term for the "Gnostic" or mature Christian who has attained deep spiritual insight.</note> will ask for the permanence of what he possesses, for an aptitude for those things he is about to attain, and for the eternity of those things he is yet to receive. As for those things which are truly good and reside in the soul, he prays both that they be his and that they remain with him; he desires nothing of the things that are absent, being content with what is present. For he is not lacking in his own proper goods, since he already has enough for himself from divine grace and knowledge. But while he is content with his own, and does not need the things of others, he recognizes the omnipotent will, and simultaneously possesses and prays for it; above all, he clings most closely <margin>B</margin> to the Power [of God], striving to be spiritual, and is united to the Spirit through infinite <term>charity</term><note>Latin: *charitatem*; meaning divine, self-giving love (agape).</note>. Thus, he is of a great and exalted mind, possessing through knowledge that which is most excellent and best of all. He is easily moved toward and applied to contemplation, and regarding those things which fall under contemplation, he possesses a permanent force in his soul—that is, the piercing sharpness of knowledge. He contends with the greatest possible strength to possess this power, abstaining from those things which are contrary to the mind, and residing perpetually in contemplation. He exercises himself in that discipline which abstains from pleasant things and correctly performs those things that ought to be done. Furthermore, using great experience both in doctrine and in the matters pertaining to life, he possesses <term>freedom of speech</term><note>Latin: *dicendi libertatem*; translating the Greek *parrhesia*, the bold and frank speech of a free person before God and men.</note>—not the force of an unbridled tongue, but a power and faculty using simple speech. This speech hides nothing of those things which can be said at the <margin>C</margin> appropriate time, and about which it is most necessary to speak with dignity, neither for the sake of favor nor because of fear. Therefore, he who has received the things of God from the <term>mystic choir</term><note>A metaphorical reference to the community of those initiated into the deeper truths of the faith.</note> of truth itself, uses an encouraging speech that indicates the magnitude of virtue—both virtue itself and what arises from it—with dignity. Through a divine elevation of speech, he makes himself as familiar as possible with those things perceived by the intelligence and those which are spiritual, based on his knowledge. Thus, he is always kind, gentle, easy to approach, affable, patient, grateful, and endowed with a good conscience. He is not only rigid and austere so as not to be corrupted, but also so as not to be tempted. For he offers a mind that yields neither to pleasure nor to pain, nor is it <margin>D</margin> conquered by them. He is a judge, if reason calls, immovable, granting nothing at all to the movements of the soul, proceeding unchangeably where justice commands. Entering in, he is persuaded that all things are administered most beautifully, and that souls always progress toward the better until they come to the Good itself, as those who have reached the vestibules of the Father—to speak plainly—near to the great High Priest. This man, endowed with knowledge, who is faithful and persuaded that the things in the world are administered in the best way, certainly meets all that happens with an equal mind. Rightly, therefore, he requires nothing from the things pertaining to life for necessary use, as one who is plainly persuaded that God, who knows all things, supplies what is useful to the good even if they do not ask. For just as to the craftsman He provides craft-wise, and to the gentile in a manner suited to a gentile, so also to <margin>E</margin> the one endowed with knowledge, He provides each thing out of knowledge. And he who is converted from the gentiles will ask for faith; but he who ascends to knowledge will ask for the perfection of charity. But he who has already reached the summit, being endowed with knowledge, prays that contemplation may increase and remain, just as the common man prays to be perpetually healthy. Indeed, he will also pray that he may never fall away from virtue, helping and taking care to remain perpetually in such a state that he *cannot* fall away. For he knows that even some of the Angels, who fell to the ground because of <term>sloth</term><note>Latin: *socordiam*; negligence or spiritual apathy.</note>, had not yet perfectly expressed themselves in that one habit, moving away from an aptitude for duplicity. He who has exercised himself here to the summit of knowledge and the excellent height of the perfect man, has chosen to live so as to slip in no place or time. He exercises himself in this through a stability of mind that is everywhere equalized and of <margin>F</margin> <margin><gloss>monotonon</gloss><note>Greek: *monotonon*; meaning "of a single tone" or "steadfast."</note></margin> plainly one tenor. But for those in whom some heavy corner still remains turning downward, that which is lifted up by faith is also pulled down. Therefore, for him who has prepared a virtue that cannot be lost through exercise proceeding from knowledge, it becomes a natural habit.

# STROMATA, BOOK VII

<margin>A</margin> And just as weight is natural to a stone, so the <term>knowledge</term><note>Latin: *scientia*; Clement uses this to describe the deep, transformative spiritual insight of the "Gnostic."</note> of this man becomes such that it cannot be lost—not against his will, but through his own will, by the power of reason, understanding, and foresight. However, because things can be lost through a lack of care, he will maintain a sense of caution so that he does not sin, and careful reflection so that his virtue is not lost. Knowledge appears to provide this careful reflection, teaching him to perceive those things which can help ensure that virtue remains permanent. Therefore, the greatest thing is the <term>knowledge of God</term><note>Latin: *Dei cognitio*.</note>. For this reason, virtue is also preserved in such a way that it cannot be lost.

He who knows God is holy and pious. It has been shown, therefore, that only the one endowed with knowledge is truly pious and religious. He rejoices in present blessings. He is glad because of those things which have been promised, as if they were already <margin>B</margin> present. Nor are they hidden from him as if they were still absent, because he has already known beforehand what kind of things they are. Being persuaded by knowledge of how each of these future things shall be, he possesses them. For that which is lacking and defective must be measured by that which belongs to it. Therefore, if he possesses wisdom—and wisdom is a divine thing—he who participates in that which lacks nothing will not be in want. For the communication of wisdom does not happen by a mutual moving and holding between the action and the participant, nor by something being taken away or becoming needy. It is shown, therefore, that the action cannot be diminished through the act of communication itself.

Thus, all good things belong to the one endowed with knowledge in potential—though not yet in full number—for otherwise he could not be moved forward regarding the divine progress and <margin>C</margin> administrations that are his due. God also assists this man, honoring him with a closer care. For were not all things made for the sake of good men, so that they might possess them and find them useful—or rather, find salvation in them? Therefore, God will not take away from them those things created for the sake of virtue, since they are the very ones for whom these things were made. For it is clear that God, honoring their good nature and holy purpose, inspires strength for the rest of their salvation in those who have resolved to live well—exhorting some, while bringing help to others who have proven themselves worthy. For every good thing is of such a kind that it attaches itself to the one endowed with knowledge, since his goal is to know and to act knowingly in everything. <margin>D</margin> Just as a physician provides health to those who cooperate with him toward health, so also God provides eternal salvation to those who cooperate with Him and work with Him toward knowledge and good actions. And since, along with what we do, those things commanded by the precepts are within our power, the promise is also fulfilled.

And it seems to me that this was also rightly said among the Greeks. A certain athlete among the ancients, who was neither ignoble nor small-minded, after he had exercised his body for a long time for the sake of strength, went up to <term>Olympia</term><note>The site of the ancient Olympic Games.</note>. When he looked upon the statue of <term>Jupiter of Pisa</term><note>Jupiter (Zeus) of Pisa, referring to the famous statue at Olympia in the region of Elis/Pisa.</note>, he said: "O Jupiter, if I have prepared everything rightly for the contest, grant me victory as is just." So it is with the one endowed with knowledge; when he has fulfilled everything without reproach and with a good conscience—concerning teaching, exercise, the performance of good works, and being pleasing and acceptable to God—that whole effort leads his salvation to perfection.

These things are required of us because they are <margin>E</margin> within our power: the choice, desire, possession, use, and persistence in those things that pertain to us, whether present or absent. Therefore, he who converses with God must truly have a pure and immaculate soul, making himself perfectly good. If not yet perfect, he should at least be progressing toward knowledge and desiring it, and he must be entirely torn away from the works of vice. Furthermore, it is fitting for him to perform all his prayers well, and in the company of good people. For it is a slippery and dangerous thing to be counted among the sins of others. Therefore, the one endowed with knowledge will pray together with those who have more recently believed concerning the things they ought to act upon together.

His entire life is a kind of celebrated and holy festival. To him, sacrifices are prayers and praises, and the readings of the <term>Scriptures</term><note>Latin: *scripturarum*; the Bible.</note> performed before meals. There are psalms and hymns while the meal is taken. Before going to bed, and again during the night, there are prayers. Through these, he unites himself to the divine choir, out of a continuous memory, dwelling in a contemplation that must always be committed to memory. Truly, is it not...

He describes the "Gnostic" as a spiritual athlete who cooperates with God to achieve salvation, turning every aspect of daily life—meals, study, and sleep—into a continuous religious festival.</summary>

->### CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA<-

<margin>A</margin> Does he also recognize another sacrifice, namely the distribution of <term>doctrines</term><note>Latin: *dogmatum*; here referring to the sharing of spiritual truths and teachings.</note> and money to those in need? Most certainly. But he does not use wordy prayer with his mouth, like one who has learned exactly what it is necessary to ask from the Lord. Therefore, he will pray in every place, but not so as to appear openly to the people. Indeed, while he is walking, speaking, resting, reading, and performing those actions dictated by reason, he prays in every way. Even if he only thinks within the inner chambers of his soul and invokes the Father with unutterable groans, He [God] is near while he is still speaking. 

Since there are three ends to any action, he does everything for the sake of what is good and useful; <margin>B</margin> however, acting for the sake of pleasure he leaves to those who follow a common [worldly] life. He who is tested and judged in such piety is far from being prone to lying or to swearing oaths. For an oath is a definitive confession made by appealing to the divine. But how could he who is once and for all faithful show himself to be unfaithful, such that he even has need of an oath? And has he not lived his life in such a way that it is a firm and definite oath, showing the faithfulness of his confession through a constant and stable life and speech? 

If doing an injury lies in the judgment of the one who acts and speaks, and not in the suffering of the one who undergoes persecution, then he will neither lie nor commit <margin>C</margin> perjury, for he would be wronging God—knowing as he does that God is by nature such that He cannot be harmed. Nor will he lie or transgress in any way for the sake of his neighbor, whom he has learned to love, even if that person is not a close acquaintance. Much more for his own sake will he neither lie nor commit perjury, since he will never willingly be found unjust toward himself. Indeed, he does not even swear, for he has determined to use "Yes" or "Is" for affirmation, and "No" for negation. For to swear is to utter an oath, or something conceived in the mind as an oath, in an affirmative way. It is enough for him, therefore, to add "I speak truly" to his affirmation or negation, <margin>D</margin> to prove his word to those who do not perceive the stability of his response. 

For he ought to have, as I think, a life worthy of trust among outsiders, so that an oath is not even demanded of him. Among himself and those with whom he lives, he should possess fairness of mind, which is <margin>goodwill</margin><note>Greek: *eugnomosyne*; a term implying fair-mindedness, noble disposition, or voluntary justice.</note>, or voluntary justice. Now, the person endowed with <term>knowledge</term><note>Latin: *cognitio*; Clement's term for the deep, experiential spiritual insight of the mature Christian.</note> is one who swears rightly and truly, but is not prone to swearing; he rarely approaches an oath, and only in the manner we have described. Although being truthful in an oath consists of agreement with what is true, this only occurs insofar as one conducts oneself correctly in one's duties. <margin>E</margin> Where, then, is there further need of an oath for one who lives as though he has reached the height of truth? He who does not even swear is far from being about to commit perjury. 

He who transgresses nothing of what has been agreed and settled would never swear, since the observation of transgression or perfect adherence lies in deeds—just as lying and perjury consist in speaking and swearing contrary to one's duty. He who lives justly, skipping nothing of what ought to be done, swears truly and holily by his deeds whenever the judgment of truth is examined. Therefore, for him, the testimony of the tongue is superfluous. Since he is always persuaded that God is everywhere, and he would blush not to speak the truth, <margin>F</margin> and since he knows it is unworthy of him to speak falsely, he is content with the divine conscience and his own, and therefore he does not lie. Nor does he do anything contrary to what was agreed. For that reason, he neither swears if asked, nor does he ever deny the truth lest he speak falsely, even if he were to die in tortures.

The dignity of the one endowed with knowledge is greatly increased and amplified by the one who has undertaken the leadership of teaching others. Such a person has received the stewardship of the greatest good on earth in both word and deed, through which he intercedes so that union and fellowship with God may occur. Just as those who worship and venerate earthly things pray to images as if they could hear, regarding the agreements made with them as firm and stable: so, through living images—namely, human beings—the true magnificence of the Word is received from a trustworthy teacher. The benefit bestowed upon these students is referred back to the Lord himself; in whose image the teacher (who is truly a man) shapes and composes, renewing for salvation the <term>Catechumen</term><note>Latin: *Catechumenum*; a person receiving basic instruction in the Christian faith before baptism.</note>. For just as the Greeks call iron "Mars" and wine "Bacchus" for a certain reason, so the person endowed with knowledge [seeks] the neighbor's benefit...

<summary>Clement argues that the "Gnostic" Christian's life is a continuous act of prayer and integrity, making formal oaths unnecessary because their deeds and character already testify to the truth. He also describes the role of the Christian teacher as one who shapes the souls of students into the divine image.</summary>

### MISCELLANIES, BOOK VII.

<margin>A</margin>
...considering the salvation [of others] as his own benefit, he may rightly be called a living image of the Lord, not in terms of the specific shape of his body, but in terms of the symbol or sign of his power, and the likeness of his preaching. Whatever he holds in his mind, he also carries on his tongue among those who are worthy to hear, speaking and living simultaneously with assent and certain conviction. For he thinks and speaks the truth at the same time, unless perhaps he must use a lie as a form of medicine—as a doctor does for the sick—for the sake of the salvation of those who are suffering, as the <term>Sophists</term><note>The "Sophists" were ancient Greek teachers of rhetoric; Clement here refers to a common philosophical debate about the "noble lie" or "medicinal lie" used for a greater good.</note> say. For behold, the noble Apostle <margin>Acts 16; Galatians 5, 6</margin> circumcised Timothy, even though he cried out and wrote that circumcision made by hand was of no use. But he did this so that he might not suddenly and violently tear away those Hebrews who were listening from the Law to the circumcision of the heart which comes from faith, or force them to break away from the synagogue while they were still struggling. By accommodating himself to the Jews, <margin>B</margin> he became a Jew so that he might win everyone. 

Therefore, he who lowers himself to such <term>accommodation</term><note>Latin: *accommodationem*; the practice of "divine economy" or "stewardship," where a teacher adapts the truth to the level of the listener's understanding.</note> for the sake of the salvation of his neighbors is by no means forced to be a participant in any pretense, because of the danger that hangs over the righteous from those who envy them. Rather, solely for the benefit of those near to him, he will do certain things that would not primarily be done by him if he were not doing them for their sake. He gives himself up for the Church, for the friends whom he himself fathered in the faith, as an example to those who are capable of receiving the highest <term>economy</term><note>Latin: *oeconomiam*; in this context, the strategic management or "arrangement" of spiritual truths for the benefit of the community.</note> of a kind and pious teacher, to demonstrate the truth of words and the work of charity toward the Lord. He is of such a character that he is not reduced to slavery by fear; he is true in speech, patient in labor, <margin>C</margin> and never willing to lie in the discourse he delivers. In that discourse, he always conducts himself so that he does not sin, since a lie itself—being something spoken with some deceit—is not "idle talk" but is put into practice as a vice. Therefore, the one who is endowed with <term>knowledge</term><note>Latin: *cognitio*; translating the Greek *gnosis*, referring to deep, experiential spiritual insight rather than mere intellectual facts.</note> alone bears witness to the truth everywhere, both in deed and in speech. For he always conducts himself rightly in all things: in speech, in action, and in thought itself. 

This, then, to speak briefly, is the piety and religion of the Christian. If he does these things as he says, he acts piously and justly in accordance with right reason. If these things are so, then the one who is endowed with knowledge would be the only truly pious, just, religious man and a true worshiper of God. Therefore, the [mature] Christian is not impious. This was the point I intended to show <margin>D</margin> to the philosophers. Wherefore, he will never in any way perform any evil or shameful act, which is unjust. Consequently, he does not behave impiously, but he alone worships God piously and holily—Him, I say, who is truly God, the Prince and King of all, and the Almighty—worshiping purely and chastely out of true religion. 

For knowledge is, to put it simply, a kind of perfection of man as man, which is completed through the science of divine things, and is congruent and harmonious with itself and the divine Word in its manner, life, and speech. For through this, faith is perfected, inasmuch as it is only through knowledge that the believer is made perfect. Faith, therefore, is an internal good; even without seeking God, it confesses that God exists and glorifies Him as He is. From this faith, one must be led forth and grown in it by the grace of God, so that—as far as is possible—one may receive His <margin>E</margin> knowledge. 

However, we say that <term>knowledge</term> differs from the wisdom that comes through instruction. For insofar as something is knowledge, it is also entirely wisdom. But insofar as something is wisdom, it is not entirely knowledge. For the name of "wisdom" is perceived by vision only in the knowledge of the spoken word. But truly, not to doubt God but to believe is the foundation of knowledge. Christ is both: the foundation, I say, and the building, through whom is both the beginning and the end. Indeed, the extremes—namely the beginning and the end, faith and love—are not taught. But the knowledge which is given from tradition by the grace of God is committed as a kind of deposit to those who have shown themselves worthy of the doctrine; from this knowledge, the dignity of love shines forth, from light to light. For it is said, <margin>F</margin> <margin>Matthew 25; Luke 14</margin> "To him who has, it shall be given." To faith, knowledge shall be given; to knowledge, love; and to love, the inheritance. This happens when one has hung upon the Lord through faith, knowledge, and love, and has ascended together with Him to where the God and guardian of our faith and love resides. Therefore, in the end, knowledge is delivered to those who are fit and selected for this, because there is need of greater preparation and preliminary exercise...
