### CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

<margin>A</margin>The things being said must be heard, both for the ordering of life and for advancing considerately toward that justice which lies beyond the Law. This leads us to an infinite and perfect end, first teaching us the way of life suitable for God—living with the gods—once we have been freed from all punishment and penalty, which we endure from our sins as a form of saving discipline. After this redemption, rewards and honors are given to those who are perfected; they have ceased their purification and have ceased from every other ministry, even if it be a holy one among the holy. 

<margin>B</margin>Then, for those who are pure of heart, through close adherence to the Lord, there remains a restoration to perpetual <term>contemplation</term><note>Latin: *contemplationi*; the highest stage of spiritual life where the soul gazes directly upon divine truth.</note>. They are called "gods" by name <note>Clement refers to the doctrine of *theosis* or deification, where the soul becomes like God through grace and knowledge.</note>, being placed in the same seats as the other gods who were first established by the Savior. Knowledge, therefore, is swift for purification and fit for easily undergoing a change for the better. From this, it easily leads the soul to that which is its own kin—the divine and the holy—and through the mystical progress of its own light, it transmits the human being until it restores the one who is pure in heart to the supreme place of rest, teaching them to contemplate God knowingly and through comprehension "face to face." For this is the perfection of the knowing soul: that when it has overcome all purification and ministry, it may be with the Lord, where it is most near and joined to Him in subjection. 

<margin>C</margin>Faith, therefore, to put it briefly, is a short and concise <term>knowledge</term><note>Latin: *cognitio*, translating the Greek *Gnosis*. Clement famously defines faith as a summary of knowledge, and knowledge as the firm demonstration of what was first accepted by faith.</note> of urgent matters. Knowledge, however, is the firm and stable demonstration of those things which were accepted through faith, built upon faith through the teaching of the Lord; it transmits one to that which cannot fall away or change, and which can be grasped by science. Indeed, it seems to me that there is a first saving change from the nations to faith, as I said before. The second change is from faith to knowledge. This knowledge, passing into <term>love</term><note>Latin: *charitatem*, the highest virtue that unites the believer to God.</note>, then makes friend of friend—the one who knows becomes a friend to the one who is known. And perhaps such a person has already anticipated from this moment what it is to be like the Angels. Therefore, after that final excellence in the flesh, being always changed for the better as is fitting, he hastens toward the paternal court, toward the truly Lordly mansion through the holy <margin>D</margin> <term>sevenfold realm</term><note>Latin: *hebdomadem*; referring to the seven planetary spheres or heavens through which the soul was thought to ascend to reach the presence of God.</note>. He is to become, so to speak, a light that stands and remains properly, which is in every part and entirely immutable—which is the first mode of the Lord's operation, the reward we spoke of, in accordance with piety and true religion. 

From the many testimonies that exist, I will bring forward one example in summary, as spoken by the prophet David: <margin>Psalm 23</margin> **WHO** shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, or who shall stand in His holy place? The one innocent in hands and pure of heart, who has not received his soul in vain, nor sworn deceitfully to his neighbor. This one shall receive a blessing from the Lord, and mercy from God his Savior. This is the generation of those seeking the Lord, seeking the face of the God of Jacob. 

Briefly, I believe, the Prophet has signified to us the one who is endowed with knowledge; and cursorily, as it seems, David has demonstrated to us that the Savior is God, calling Him the "face of the God of Jacob," who announced and taught concerning the spirit. 

<margin>E</margin>Wherefore the Apostle also called the Son the <term>character</term><note>Latin: *characterem*; here meaning the "exact imprint" or "express image," referencing Hebrews 1:3.</note> or type of the Father's glory, who taught the truth about God and expressed that God the Father is one and the only almighty, whom no one knows except the Son, and he to whom the Son has revealed Him. Moreover, he mentions that God is one through those who "seek the face of the God of Jacob," whom our Savior and God expresses as the only good God and Father. The "generation of those seeking Him" is the chosen race, which is endowed with the power of inquiring toward knowledge. 

<margin>1 Corinthians 14</margin>And therefore the Apostle also says: "I will profit you nothing unless I speak to you either in revelation, or in knowledge, or in prophecy, or in doctrine." 

<margin>F</margin>Nevertheless, some things are also done correctly by those who are not endowed with knowledge, but not by reason; as is the case with the virtue of a "great spirit." For some, being naturally prone to anger, and then having nourished this without reason, are carried by a certain impulse to many things without reason, and they do things similar to those who are of a great and lofty spirit. Thus, even base and unrefined craftsmen sometimes conduct themselves correctly in matters of endurance. But they do so neither for the same cause as the one who is endowed with knowledge, nor with the same goal in mind...

<summary>Clement describes the soul's ascent from faith to spiritual knowledge (gnosis) and finally to love, which results in the "deification" of the believer and direct contemplation of God. He uses Psalm 23 and the writings of St. Paul to illustrate the transition from a life of discipline to a state of enlightened rest and divine friendship.</summary>

### THE STROMATA, BOOK VII

<margin>A</margin> ...not even if they give up their whole body. For they do not have charity <note>Latin: *charitatem*; referring to *agape*, or Christian love.</note>, as the Apostle says, which is generated through knowledge <note>original: *cognitionem*; Clement argues that true spiritual love is a product of deep religious understanding (*gnosis*).</note>. Therefore, whatever action is performed by one who knows is a right action. But whatever is done by one who is ignorant is evil, even if it is pursued with great intensity, because such a person is not acting from reasoned consideration, nor does he direct his action toward anything useful among those things that lead to virtue and proceed from virtue. The same reasoning holds true for the other virtues. For this reason, those who possess knowledge also behave consistently in the worship and religion of God. It is not only in holiness, therefore, that the one endowed with knowledge is such a person. Furthermore, regarding religion and the worship of God which arises from knowledge, there are consequent precepts concerning the other conduct of his life. For it is our purpose now to describe <margin>B</margin> the life of the one endowed with knowledge, rather than to bring forward a contemplation of dogmas, which we shall explain later at a fitting time, while also maintaining the proper sequence.

He has, therefore, discussed all things truly and magnificently, as one who has conceived divine doctrine. When he has taken his beginning from an admiration of creation—for knowledge can be received by taking an argument from the home <note>Likely referring to the physical world or the "household" of the cosmos as a starting point for learning about the Creator.</note>—he becomes an eager and prompt disciple of the Lord. As soon as he heard of God and providence, he believed because of the things he admired. Driven by this, he gives himself to discipline in every way, doing all those things through which he might receive the knowledge of what he desires. Now, desire—through the progress of faith—stands tempered alongside inquiry. This process makes one worthy of such great contemplation. In this way, the one endowed with knowledge will "taste" the will of God. <margin>C</margin> For he does not merely offer his ears, but his soul, to the things signified by what is spoken.

When, therefore, he has received the essences and the things themselves through the Words, he rightly leads his soul to what is required. He will accept the commands, "You shall not commit adultery" and "You shall not kill," in their proper sense, as they were spoken to the one endowed with knowledge, not as they are understood by others. He approaches, exercising himself in the contemplation that produces science <note>Latin: *scientiam*; here meaning certain or systematic knowledge of divine things.</note>, so that he may enter the contest with those things which are spoken more universally and magnificently. He rightly knows that the one who "teaches man knowledge," as the Prophet says, is the Lord, for the Lord works through the mouth of man. For that reason, He also took on flesh.

Rightly, then, he never prefers the pleasant to the useful; not even if, by some chance, a beautiful woman should provoke him by using the force of a harlot to anticipate him, since not even the wife of his master could lead Joseph away from his purpose. <margin>D</margin> He stripped himself for her as she held his tunic by force, like one who had been stripped of sin but had put on the ornament of honesty and temperance. For even if the eyes of the Egyptians—I mean the masters—did not see Joseph, the eyes of the Almighty certainly did. For we hear the voice and look upon bodies, but God examines the reality from which the voice and the gaze are produced.

Consequently, if either disease or some accident should invade the one endowed with knowledge, or even death—which is the most terrifying of all things—he remains unte rrif ied in his soul, knowing that all such things are a necessity of nature. He knows that even so, by the power of God, these things are made into a medicine of salvation; they benefit those who are less disciplined through training, and are truly distributed by a holy providence according to merit. 

Using created things, when and as much as the Word says, and giving thanks to the one who created them by his actions, he <margin>E</margin> becomes the master of their use. He never remembers an injury received; he is indignant at no one, nor does he lash out bitterly against anyone, even if they deserve hatred for what they do. For he worships the Creator and loves his companion in life, pitying him and praying for him because of his ignorance. 

He is also affected in his own body by common feeling, to which he is bound by a suffering nature, but he does not allow his primary affection to be focused upon it. In cases of involuntary accidents, leading himself away from pains toward those things which are his own <note>i.e., spiritual matters</note>, he is not led away by those things which are foreign to him <note>i.e., physical sensations</note>; rather, he yields and accommodates himself only to those things which are necessary, so long as the soul is preserved unharmed. For he does not wish to be seen as faithful merely by opinion or reputation, but by knowledge and truth, making this <margin>F</margin> both firm and stable in action and effective in speech. He does not only praise what is good and honest, but he himself is compelled to be good and honest, passing from being a "good and faithful servant" to being a "friend" through charity, because of the perfection of the habit he has acquired from true discipline and much exercise. As one who strives with great force to arrive at the peak...

<meta>This page continues the description of the "Gnostic"—Clement’s term for the spiritually mature Christian—focusing on their resilience in the face of suffering and their unique perspective on earthly life and marriage.</meta>

### CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

<margin>A</margin> ...the summit of knowledge, adorned in character and composed in bearing, possessing all those advantages belonging to one who is truly endowed with knowledge. He gazes upon beautiful images: many who conducted themselves rightly and with virtue in ages past—the Patriarchs, the many Prophets, and the innumerable Angels—and lastly, the Lord Himself, who taught us and showed us that it is possible to attain that highest life. For this reason, he does not love all the goods of the world that are ready at hand, lest he remain pinned to the ground; rather, he loves those things which are hoped for, or rather, those which are already known to him, for they are hoped for in the sense that they are still to be fully grasped. By this reasoning, he sustains labors, torments, and afflictions—not like the "strong men" among the Philosophers <note>Likely referring to the Stoics, who valued endurance but for different reasons.</note>, who endure in the hope that present pains will cease and they will again participate in pleasures. Instead, his knowledge has produced in him a most firm persuasion regarding the reception of the hope of things to come.

<margin>B</margin> Therefore, he looks down not only upon the punishments of this life, but even upon all its pleasures. Indeed, they say that the blessed Peter, when he saw his own wife being led to her death, rejoiced because of her calling and her return home. Calling out to her by name to exhort and console her, he said: "Listen, you, remember the Lord." <note>original Latin: *heus tu memento Domini*. This is a famous early Christian tradition recording the martyrdom of St. Peter’s wife.</note> Such was the marriage of the blessed, and a perfect affection even unto those most dear. For this reason, the Apostle also says that he who marries should be as though he did not marry <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 7:29.</note>, wishing for marriage to be moved as little as possible by worldly passion, and never to be torn away from love for the Lord—a love which that true man urged his wife to hold fast as she journeyed to the Lord. Is not their faith in the hope after death manifest, then, when they give thanks to God even in the very hour of their torments?

<margin>C</margin> For they possessed, I believe, a firm and constant faith, which was followed by faithful actions. Therefore, in every circumstance, the soul of the one endowed with knowledge is brave and strong; like the body of an Athlete, it is in peak condition and possesses the greatest strength. For he is of the best counsel in matters pertaining to men, setting forth his judgment on what a just man must do—namely, those principles which proceed from above from God. Toward the goal of becoming like God, he acquires a moderation of the body’s pleasures and pains. He rises boldly against fears, having his confidence in God. In truth, then, the soul endowed with knowledge is a terrestrial image of divine virtue, adorned with perfect virtue arising from all these things at once: nature, practice, and the reason that grows along with them. This beauty of the soul becomes a temple of the Holy Spirit

<margin>D</margin> when it maintains a disposition throughout life that is in harmony with the Gospel. Such a person rises above every fear, every danger, and everything formidable—not only death, but also poverty, disease, disgrace, and all things of this sort—as one who cannot be conquered by pleasure and who dominates desires that lack reason. For he knows well what must be done and what must not, as one who knows with vigor which things are truly heavy and to be feared, and which are not. Thus, he knowingly sustains what is necessary and what reason dictates is fitting, knowingly distinguishing between those things in which confidence should be placed (that is, the true goods) and those which only seem to be so; and distinguishing between things that are truly terrifying and those that only appear to be—such as death, disease, and poverty, which are matters of opinion rather than truth.

<margin>E</margin> This is the one who is truly a good man: who, through his habit or the disposition of a virtuous soul, is removed from the disturbances of the mind <note>original: *perturbationibus*; a translation of the Greek *pathe*, or "passions," which the Stoics and Clement believed should be mastered.</note> and has overcome the whole of a life subject to passions. For such a man, everything depends on himself for the attainment of his end. For those things called "misfortunes" of fate are not formidable to a good man, because they are not truly evil. But those things which are truly heavy are foreign to the Christian who is endowed with knowledge, for they are diametrically opposed to the good—namely, they are vices—and it is impossible for contraries to exist in the same person at the same time. He who leads his life without reproach, performing the role God has given him to play, knows what must be done and what must be endured.

<margin>F</margin> Since the vice of a small and abject mind consists of ignorance regarding what is or is not truly heavy, it follows that only the one endowed with knowledge has a daring and confident mind, as he knows the goods that are and will be. Along with these things, as I have said, he also knows those things which are not truly heavy, recognizing that vice alone is the enemy and the bringer of destruction to those who are progressing toward knowledge, protected by the armor of the Lord...

He highlights the martyrdom of St. Peter's wife as an example of a marriage centered on Christ rather than worldly passion.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Clement’s exploration of the "Gnostic"—the spiritually mature Christian—specifically contrasting their internal motivations for virtue and martyrdom with those who act out of fear, habit, or a desire for reward. ### MISCELLANIES BOOK VII

<margin>A</margin>...of the Lord, and thus fortified, he wages war against it <note>Referring to the "war" against worldly temptations or the devil mentioned in the previous context.</note>. For if something exists because of imprudence and the operation—or rather the cooperation—of the devil, this does not immediately make that thing "imprudence" or "the devil" itself, since no specific action is a habit. Prudence <term>Prudentia: translated from the Greek "phronesis," meaning practical wisdom or a stable disposition of the soul.</term> is indeed a habit (a stable disposition). No single action, however, is a habit. Therefore, an action that arises from ignorance is not itself "ignorance." Rather, it is a vice caused by ignorance, yet not ignorance itself. For neither the movements of the soul nor sins are themselves vices, even if they proceed from a vice. Therefore, no one who is brave without reason is truly endowed with knowledge; for one might likewise call children "brave" when they endure terrifying things because they are ignorant of the danger. Certainly, they touch fire in this way, and wild beasts run onto spears; though they are brave without reason, they would not be called <margin>B</margin> endowed with reason. Perhaps some might also call those performers brave who rotate themselves among swords, practicing a dangerous art for a meager wage out of mere experience.

But he who is truly brave, when he sees a clear danger approaching—often due to the envy and rivalry of the many—accepts it with confidence. By this reasoning, he is distinguished from others who are called Martyrs, because some provide their own occasion for death and cast themselves into dangers (to put it politely). But the ones endowed with knowledge <note>Clement refers here to the "Gnostic" Christian.</note> compose themselves according to right reason; then, when God calls them, they surrender themselves with a prompt and eager spirit. They confirm their calling by the fact that they have decided nothing regarding themselves rashly or headlong, and they present a man to be examined in that bravery which arises from rational truth. Therefore, they do not endure smaller evils out of fear of greater ones <margin>C</margin> like the rest, nor do they persist in the confession of their calling because they fear the reproach of those in the same position or opinion. Instead, because of their love for God, they willingly obey the calling, proposing no other goal for themselves except to please God—not even for the sake of the rewards of their labors.

For others suffer for the desire for glory; some to avoid another more grievous punishment; and others for certain joys and pleasures expected after death. These are "children in faith," blessed indeed, but not yet "men" in that love toward God which characterizes the one endowed with knowledge. For there are—just as in gymnastic contests—crowns for both men and boys within the Church. Love <note>original: "Charitas," translating the Greek "Agape."</note> itself is to be chosen and <margin>D</margin> sought for its own sake, not for the sake of anything else. Therefore, in the one endowed with knowledge, the perfection of bravery grows alongside knowledge through the exercise of life, which is always practiced in order to conquer the movements of the soul. Love, then, renders its "athlete" free from fear and dread, confident in the Lord, by anointing and exercising him; just as justice grants him the habit of speaking the truth throughout his whole life. For the shortcut to justice is to say: *Let your "Yes" be "Yes," and your "No" be "No."* <note>A reference to Matthew 5:37.</note>

The same reasoning applies to temperance. For the one endowed with knowledge does not present himself as temperate and moderate out of a desire for honor (as athletes do for crowns and glory), nor again out of a desire for money (as some do), while still pursuing "the good" while troubled by heavy movements and disturbances of the soul. Nor is anyone truly <margin>E</margin> temperate who is continent only because of a rustic life or because they have never tasted pleasures. Certainly, when those who spend their lives in hard labor taste pleasures, they break their rigid streak of continence for the sake of those pleasures. Such are those who are restrained only by law and fear. For if they find an opportunity, they stealthily transgress the law, fleeing from what is honorable.

But temperance that is sought for its own sake, which is perfected through knowledge and remains forever, makes a man a Master—one who rules by his own authority. Thus, the one endowed with knowledge is temperate, being neither moved by pleasures nor melted by pains; just as they say a diamond <note>original: "adamantem."</note> is not melted by fire. The cause of these things is Love, the most holy and principal part of all science. For through the worship of Him who is best and most excellent—which receives its character from the "One"—Love makes the <margin>F</margin> one endowed with knowledge both a friend and a son at the same time: a truly perfect man, as one who has grown to the measure of full age. Furthermore, the harmony and agreement concerning the same thing is "assent." That which is the same is "one." Friendship is perfected through the likeness of a community which is situated in the "One." Therefore, the one endowed with knowledge, since he loves Him...

<summary>Clement distinguishes the "true knower" (Gnostic) from "children in faith" by their motivations, arguing that true bravery, temperance, and martyrdom must be rooted in rational love for God rather than fear of punishment or desire for reward.</summary>

### MISCELLANIES BOOK VII

<header>CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA</header>

<margin>A</margin>...who truly knows the one God, and is a truly perfect man and a friend of God, adopted into the rank of a son. These are the names of nobility, of knowledge, and of perfection, achieved through the contemplation of God, which the soul receives as it recognizes its highest progress. Having been made completely pure, the soul is deemed worthy to see God Almighty "face to face" <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 13:12</note> eternally. For having become entirely spiritual, and having advanced into that which is kindred to it within the spiritual church, it remains at rest in God. (Let these things be as they are.) Since this man who is endowed with knowledge <term>Cognitio: the Latin translation of "gnosis," referring to deep, experiential spiritual understanding.</term> behaves in this way regarding both his body and his soul, he is found to be equal and consistent toward his neighbors, whether they be servants, or enemies by law, or whoever they may be. For he does not, in a manner contrary to divine law, despise a brother born of the same Father and the same Mother <note>Meaning God as Father and the Truth or the Church as Mother.</note>. He certainly lightens the burden of those who are afflicted, helping with <margin>B</margin> consolations, encouragements, and those things necessary for life. He gives to all who are in want, but not in the same way; he gives justly and according to merit. Moreover, he gives even to the one who persecutes and hates him, if that person is in need, caring little for those who say he gave out of fear—provided he did not do it for fear, but to bring him aid. For if those who do not spare their money to help their enemies also hate the wicked, how could their love not be even greater toward their own? From such a disposition he proceeds to perfect knowing: determining to whom specifically, how much, when, and in what manner he should give.

Now, who could rightfully be the enemy of a man who provides <margin>C</margin> no cause for enmity at all? Do we not say of God that He opposes no one and is the enemy of no one? For He is the creator of all, and there is nothing among the things that exist that He does not will. We say, however, that those who are disobedient and do not walk according to His precepts are His "enemies," as they harbor enmity against His covenant. In the same way, we shall find it to be with the man endowed with knowledge. He himself will never be an enemy to anyone in any way; however, those who turn to a path contrary to his might be understood as his "enemies." Furthermore, that habit of distribution within us is called justice; and indeed, the habit of discerning according to merit, whether more or less—wherein this must be done from knowledge—is a form of the highest justice. There are, to be sure, certain things rightly done by some after the fashion of the common people, such as the restraint <margin>D</margin> of pleasures. For just as among the Gentiles, restraint may arise from the inability to obtain what one sees, or from the fear of men; and as there are even those who abstain from present joys for the sake of greater pleasures later; so also in the faith, some restrain themselves either because of a promise or because of the fear of God. But such restraint is only the foundation of knowledge, a kind of leading toward that which is better, and an incentive toward that which is perfect. For it is said, "The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom" <note>Psalm 111:10; Proverbs 1:7</note>. But he who is perfect suffers all things and endures all things because of love, not to please men, but to please God. Although praise follows him as a consequence, it is not for his own benefit, but for the imitation and use of those who offer the praise. In another sense, a man is called "continent" <term>Continens: meaning self-controlled or possessing restraint.</term> not only if he suppresses the disturbances of the <margin>E</margin> soul, but also if he has "contained" (held fast) good things and has firmly and stably acquired the magnitude of knowledge, from which he produces those actions that arise from virtue.

This knowledge ensures that if any accident should happen, the man endowed with knowledge never departs from his own character. For the possession of the good which constitutes knowledge is solid and unchangeable, being the knowledge of things divine and human. Therefore, knowledge never becomes ignorance, nor does good change into evil. On this account, he eats, and drinks, and marries—not as his primary purpose, but out of necessity. I say he marries if the Word <note>The Logos, or Christ's command.</note> dictates it, and as is fitting. For he who would be perfect has the Apostles as his examples; a man is truly shown to be a man not in the fact that he has chosen a monastic life <note>original: "vitam monasticam". Clement argues that the domestic life is actually a harder and higher test of virtue than the solitary life.</note>, but he surpasses other men who, in marriage, in the procreation of children, and in the care and providence of a household, exercises himself without seeking pleasure. Amidst the care of a household, <margin>F</margin> he remains inseparable from the love of God, and he rises above every temptation brought about through children, wife, servants, and possessions. For the man who does not have a household largely avoids being tempted. Therefore, he who cares only for himself is surpassed by the man who, although he might be inferior in matters regarding his own personal safety, yet is su-

<summary>Clement argues that the "Gnostic" (the spiritually mature Christian) demonstrates true virtue not through isolation, but by maintaining a focus on God while managing the complex responsibilities and temptations of family life and social charity.</summary>

### MISCELLANIES BOOK VII

<header>STROMATA BOOK VII</header>

<margin>A</margin>Moreover, in those things which concern the management of life, a small image of the truth is preserved by providence. But for us, the soul must first be exercised in many different ways as much as possible, so that it may be easily worked upon to receive knowledge <term>Cognitio: The Latin equivalent of the Greek "gnosis," referring to deep, experiential spiritual insight.</term>. Do you not see how wax is softened and brass is purified, so that it may receive the mark that is applied to it? Now, just as death is the separation of the soul from the body, so knowledge is like a rational death, leading away and separating the soul from its impulses and disturbances, and leading it to a life of doing good and performing virtuous works, so that it may then say freely to God: "I live as you wish." For he whose purpose is to please men cannot please God, because many choose not what is beneficial, but what is delightful. <margin>B</margin> However, the one who pleases God becomes, as a consequence, pleasing and acceptable to good men. How, then, could food, drink, and sexual pleasure be any longer delightful to him, when he holds even speech that brings some pleasure, or a movement of thought, or a pleasant operation, as suspect? <margin>Matthew 6</margin> For "no one can serve two masters, God and Mammon." <note>original: "Nemo enim potest duobus Dominis servire, Deo & Mammonæ."</note> By saying this, He does not speak of money in a bare sense, but of the provision of various pleasures that comes from money. In truth, it cannot be that he who has known God magnificently and truly should serve those pleasures that oppose Him. Therefore, there is only one who is entirely free from all desire from the beginning: the kind and merciful Lord, who for our sake also became man. But those who study to be likened to the character given by Him—so that they may become free from desire—strive with great force through spiritual exercise. <margin>C</margin> For he who has felt desire and yet restrained himself—like a widow who becomes a virgin again through temperance <note>Clement often uses the metaphor of "regained virginity" to describe a soul that has returned to purity through self-discipline.</note>—has returned that knowledge to the Savior and Teacher as a reward, which he himself sought: namely, abstinence from evils and the performance of good actions, through which salvation comes. Just as those who have learned the arts acquire their nourishment through the things they were taught, so the one endowed with knowledge, acquiring life through the things he knows, is saved. For he who refuses to shut out the disturbances of the soul kills himself. But, as it seems, the lack of nourishment for the soul is ignorance, while its true food is knowledge. <margin>Matthew 25</margin> These are the "knowing souls," whom the Gospel likened to the sanctified virgins who wait for the Lord. For they are virgins in that they have abstained from evils, and they wait for the Lord because of love; and they light their own lamps for the contemplation of things, being wise virgins, saying: "O Lord, <margin>D</margin> at last we desire to receive you. We have lived according to the things you commanded, omitting nothing of what you prescribed. Therefore, we also ask for the things promised. We pray for what is useful, since it is not fitting to ask you for what is merely beautiful; and we will receive all things for our benefit, even if the exercises that come upon us seem to be evils—which your divine economy <term>Oecononmia: The "divine management" or plan by which God governs the world and trains humanity.</term> provides to us for the purpose of exercising our stability and constancy." And the one who is endowed with knowledge, because of his remarkable holiness, is more prepared not to obtain what he asks for than to obtain what he does not ask for. His prayer is his entire life and his conversation with God. If he is clean from sins, he will certainly obtain whatever he wants. For God says to the righteous: "Ask and I will give to you; <margin>E</margin> think and I will act." <note>This is a common apocryphal or paraphrased saying attributed to Jesus in early Christian writings.</note> If they are useful things, he will receive them immediately; but he will never ask for useless things, and therefore he will not receive them. Thus, what he wants will be. But if someone should say to us that even certain sinners obtain their requests: this happens rarely because of the just goodness of God. It is also given to those who are able to do good to others. Hence the gift is not made because of the one who asked, but as a presiding economy for the sake of the one who will be saved through him, making the gift just once again. But to those who are worthy, even those things which are truly good are given even without their asking. Therefore, when someone is righteous not by necessity or fear or hope, but by a free purpose of the mind, this is called the "Royal Road," which the royal race enters upon. Other turnings away from it are slippery and steep. If someone were to take away fear and honor, I do not know if those noble philosophers who speak freely would still endure their afflictions. <margin>F</margin> Desires and other sins are said to be "thistles and stakes." Therefore, he who is endowed with knowledge works in the vineyard of the Lord, planting, pruning, and watering—a truly divine farmer of those who are planted in the faith. And those who have done no evil think it fair that they receive a reward for their leisure.

<summary>Clement describes the soul's preparation for divine knowledge through self-discipline, comparing it to purifying metal. He defines true prayer not as asking for wants, but as a continuous life of conversation with God and the pursuit of spiritual maturity along the "Royal Road."</summary>

He who has done good deeds from a bare and pure intent of the soul demands a reward like a good workman. He would certainly have received a double reward, both for the evils he did not commit and for the good things he did well. This person, who is endowed with the power of <term>knowledge (gnosis): The Greek term for a higher, experiential understanding of divine truth, which Clement uses to describe the mature believer.</term>, is tempted by no one unless God permits it, and even then, it is for the benefit of those who live alongside him. It certainly confirms others in the faith by encouraging a manly endurance. And truly, for this reason, the blessed Apostles were led into experience and the testimony of perfection in order to confirm and establish the churches. Since, therefore, the one endowed with knowledge has a voice resonating in his ears saying, "Whom I have struck, do you show him mercy," <note>original: "Quem ego percussero, tu eius miserere." This appears to be an unwritten saying attributed to God or a paraphrase of the spirit of divine discipline.</note> he prays that even those who hate him may be led to repentance. For the punishment that is taken upon evildoers in the stadiums is a thing that children should not even contemplate. It is impossible for
<sig>B</sig>
the person endowed with knowledge—who has exercised himself to be good and honest from a free intent of the soul—to ever be taught or delighted by such things. Therefore, he who is not at all melted by pleasures, nor ever falls into sins, is not chastened by the examples of others' punishments. He is far from being delighted by earthly pleasures and spectacles, for he has despised worldly things even if they were presented as divine promises. Therefore, <margin>Matthew 7</margin> "not everyone who says 'Lord, Lord' shall enter into the kingdom of God, but he who does the will of God." This person shall be the workman endowed with knowledge, who conquers worldly desires even while he is still in the flesh. Concerning the future things he has known, and those which do not yet fall under his sight, he has such a certain persuasion that he considers them more present than the things that are actually before him. This is the fit and timely workman, who
<sig>C</sig>
rejoices in what he knows; yet, because he still moves about within the necessities of this life, he is constricted in spirit, not yet having been deemed worthy of the full and effective participation in those things he knows. For this reason, he uses this life as if it were a foreign land, only as much as necessity requires. He himself knows the enigmas of the fasts of these days—I mean the fourth and the sixth <note>Wednesday and Friday were traditional days of fasting in the early Church.</note>. One is called the day of Mercury, and the other the day of Venus. <note>In the Roman calendar, Wednesday was *Dies Mercurii* and Friday was *Dies Veneris*.</note> Behold, he fasts throughout his life from both greed and lust, from which all vices arise. For we have already established three supreme types of "fornication" according to the Apostle's view: lust, greed, and idolatry. Therefore, he fasts from evil actions according to the Law, and from evil thoughts according to the perfection of the Gospel. Temptations are also presented to him, not for his own purification, but, as we said, for the benefit of those near him, so that if he despises and drives away those labors and pains through the trial, he might serve as an example. The same reasoning applies to pleasure; for it is a very great thing when
<sig>D</sig>
someone has experienced it and then abstains. For what great thing is it if someone restrains himself from things he does not know? When he has carried out the commandment of the Gospel, he makes that day the "Lord's Day" whenever he casts away an evil thought and receives the thought that comes from knowledge, glorifying the resurrection of the Lord within himself. Furthermore, when he has grasped the understanding of the theorems of science, he thinks he sees the Lord, directing his sight toward those things that fall under his spiritual gaze—even if he seems to see things he does not wish to see, he chastens his faculty of sight whenever he feels himself affected by pleasure from looking. For he wishes to see and hear only that which pertains to him. Now, truly considering the souls of his brothers, the soul itself 
<sig>E</sig>
beholds the beauty of the flesh, having become accustomed to gazing only at what is honest without carnal pleasure. Those are truly brothers who, through a chosen creation, a harmony of manners, and the substance of their works, do and think and speak the same holy and honest deeds which the Lord willed them to feel as the elect. For faith consists in choosing the same things; knowledge consists in learning and feeling the same things; and hope consists in doing the same things. But if, because of the necessity of life, he consumes some time in nourishing himself, he considers himself to be defrauding a debt, like someone torn away from his proper business. From this it truly happens that he does not even see a dream that would be unbecoming of an elect person. For in truth, he is entirely a guest and a stranger 
<sig>F</sig>
throughout his whole life; though dwelling in a city, he despises the things in the city that are held in admiration by others. He lives in the city as if in a solitude, so that the place does not compel him, but his free choice of will shows him to be just. <margin>A</margin> ...accurately knowing, helping his associates, moving the "mountains" <note>likely referring to obstacles of pride or sin</note> of those close to him, and casting away the inequalities of their souls. For each of us is the worker of our own life. However, he who wishes to remain hidden from men even while doing the best things, persuades both the Lord and himself that he lives according to the commandments, preferring them because he believes them to be truly good. For where a man’s mind is, there also, it is said, is his treasure. <margin>Matthew 6</margin> He humbles himself, so that he never despises a brother who is in affliction; because of that perfection which is found in <term>charity (charitas): the Greek 'agape,' or selfless, divine love</term>, if he knows he can bear poverty more easily than his brother, he considers his brother’s pain to be his own. And if, by giving from his own scarcity, he suffers some hardship for the sake of doing good, 
<margin>B</margin> he does not take it badly, but rather increases the benefit. For he possesses a pure and sincere faith, praising the Gospel through both his works and his contemplation of reality. Yet he does not receive praise from men, but from God, by carrying out what the Lord taught. Because he is drawn by his own hope, he does not taste the "beautiful" things of the world, despising everything here with a great soul. He pities those who are disciplined after death, who are forced to confess through punishment. Having a good conscience always, he is always ready for his departure <note>meaning death or the transition to the next life</note>, living as a pilgrim and a guest among the inheritances of this world. He remembers only his own true home, considering everything here to be foreign. He does not merely admire the Lord’s commands, but, to put it simply, through <term>knowledge (gnosis): experiential, spiritual understanding</term> itself, he becomes a partaker of the divine will. He is truly an intimate of the Lord, chosen for the commandments because he is just,
<margin>C</margin> and endowed with the power of ruling and reigning because he is endowed with knowledge. He despises all the gold that is above and below the earth, and the kingdom that stretches from the ends of the earth to the boundaries of the Ocean, so that he may hold fast to the worship of the Lord alone. Therefore, whether he is eating, drinking, or marrying—if the Word <note>original: "Verbum," referring to Christ the Logos</note> so dictates—and even in his dreams, he acts and thinks holily, so that he is always pure for prayer. Indeed, he even prays with the Angels, as one who is already equal to the Angels, and he is never outside that holy watch; even if he prays alone, he has a choir of Angels standing with him. He understands a twofold operation: that of the one who believes, and that of the thing believed, according to its worthy excellence. For justice too is twofold: one kind is motivated by charity, the other by fear. It is certainly said, "the fear of the Lord is clean, enduring forever." <margin>Psalm 18</margin> For those who are converted from fear to faith and justice, 
<margin>D</margin> remain forever. Now, the person who fears works at abstaining from evils. But charity, which builds upon what is voluntary, encourages one to do good, so that he may hear from the Lord: "I no longer call you servants, but friends." <margin>John 15</margin> And now, with confidence, he approaches his prayers. This very kind of prayer is an act of thanksgiving for things past, present, and future, as if they were already present through faith. This is preceded by having received knowledge. Furthermore, he prays to live his defined life in the flesh in such a way that, as one endowed with the power of knowing and as one free from the flesh, he may attain the best things and flee the worse. He also asks for relief from the things we have sinned in, and for conversion to recognition, following the one who calls him with such intensity in his "departure" <note>his spiritual ecstasy or death</note> as the caller himself calls. To put it another way, he hastens to give thanks because of his good conscience, 
<margin>E</margin> and so that when he is there with Christ, having proven himself worthy through purity, he may possess the power of God through a blending <note>original: "contemperaturam," suggesting a mystical union or attunement</note> provided through Christ. For he is not "warm" by merely participating in heat, nor "bright" because of a fire; rather, he wishes to be entirely light. He knows accurately what was said: "Unless you hate father and mother, and moreover your own soul, and unless you carry the sign." <margin>Luke 14</margin> For he not only despises with a great soul those carnal affections which have the greatest allurements of pleasure, and everything suited to the creation and nutrition of the flesh, but he even rises up against the "corporeal soul," <note>the lower, animal soul or instincts</note> placing a bridle of reason upon the spirit that refuses to be ruled, since the flesh lusts 
<margin>F</margin> against the spirit. To "carry the sign" is to carry death around, renouncing all things while still alive; for the love of the one who sowed the flesh is not equal to the love of the one who created the soul for knowledge. When this man has reached the habit of doing good, he performs a benefit faster than it can be spoken, praying that he may even share in the sins of his brothers...

<margin>A</margin> But he who has done good things from a bare and pure intention of the mind, demands a reward like a good worker. He would certainly have received a double portion, both for those things he did not do <note>meaning sins he avoided</note> and for those things he did well. This person, who is endowed with the power of **knowledge** <note>original: "cognoscendi" — refers to Gnosis, the deep spiritual insight Clement values</note>, is tempted by no one unless God permits it, and this is for the benefit of those who live alongside him. It certainly confirms them in the faith by encouraging a manly endurance. And indeed, for this reason the blessed Apostles, to confirm and establish the churches, were led to the experience and testimony of perfection. Therefore, since the one endowed with knowledge has a voice resonating in his ears saying, *Whom I have struck, you must pity* <note>A phrase often attributed to divine instruction on showing mercy to the disciplined</note>, he prays that even those who hate him may be led to repentance. For the punishment of evildoers in the stadiums <margin>B</margin> is something that even children should not watch. For it is impossible that he who is endowed with knowledge—who has exercised himself from a free intention of the mind to be good and honest—could ever be taught or delighted by such things. And therefore, he who is not at all weakened by pleasures, nor ever falls into sins, is not corrected by the examples of others' misfortunes. He is far from being delighted by earthly pleasures and spectacles, for he has despised worldly things, even if they were divine promises. Therefore, **not everyone** <margin>Matthew 7</margin> **who says, "Lord, Lord," shall enter into the kingdom of God, but he who does the will of God.** Such a person would be a worker endowed with knowledge, who conquers worldly desires even while he is still in the flesh. Concerning the future things he has come to know, and which do not yet fall under his sight, he has such a certain persuasion that he considers them more present than the things which are actually before him. This is a fit and well-timed worker, who rejoices in the things he knows; but because he still moves within the necessities of this life, <margin>C</margin> he is narrowed in spirit, not yet having been deemed worthy of the full and effective participation in what he knows. For this reason, he uses this life as if it were someone else's, only as much as necessity requires. He himself knows the hidden meanings of the **fasts** of these days, I mean, the fourth and the sixth days <note>Wednesday and Friday, traditional Christian fast days</note>. One is said to be the day of Mercury, and the other the day of Venus <note>original: "Mercurii... Veneris" — Wednesday and Friday in the Roman calendar. Clement links the gods of these days to specific vices</note>. For behold, they fast in their life both from greed and from lust, from which all vices arise. For we have already placed the three highest forms of "fornication" according to the Apostle's opinion: lust, greed, and idolatry. He therefore fasts, according to the law, from evil actions, and according to the perfection of the Gospel, from evil thoughts. Temptations are also presented to him, not for his own purification, but for the benefit of his neighbors, as we have said—so that if a trial of labors and pains occurs, he might despise and reject them. The same logic applies to pleasure; for it is a great thing <margin>D</margin> when someone has experienced it and then abstains. For what great thing is it if one restrains himself from things he does not know? When he has carried out the commandment which is from the Gospel, he makes that day the **Lord’s Day** <note>Sunday</note>, whenever he casts away an evil thought and receives that thought which is from knowledge—that which is within himself—glorifying the Lord’s resurrection. Furthermore, when he has received the comprehension of the contemplation that comes from science, he considers himself to see the Lord, directing his sight toward those things which fall under his spiritual gaze; even if he seems to see things he does not wish to see, he punishes his faculty of sight if he feels himself affected by pleasure from the application of his vision. For he wishes to see and hear only what pertains to him. Now, considering the souls of the brothers, the soul itself looks upon the beauty of the flesh, having become accustomed to gazing only upon what is honest <margin>E</margin> without fleshly pleasure. The "brothers" are those who truly, through an elect creation, a consensus of character, and the substance of their works, do and think and speak the same holy and honest works which the Lord willed them to feel, since they are the chosen. For **faith** consists in choosing the same things. **Knowledge** <note>original: "Cognitio"</note> consists in having learned and perceiving the same things. And **hope** consists in doing the same things. But if, because of the necessity of life, he consumes some time in nourishing himself, he considers himself to be defrauding a debt, as one who is torn away from his proper business. Hence it happens that he truly does not even see a dream that would be unbecoming to one of the elect. For in truth, he is a total guest and a pilgrim throughout his whole life; though inhabiting a city, he despises those things in the city <margin>F</margin> which are held in admiration by others, and he lives in the city as if in a solitude, so that the place does not compel him, but his free choice of will shows him to be just. This man who is endowed with knowledge, to put it briefly, fulfills the **Apostolic absence** <note>Living as the Apostles did even when they are no longer present</note>, living rightly, accurately...

Because he is drawn by his own hope, he does not taste the "beautiful" things of this world, despising everything here with a great soul. He pities those who are punished after death, those who confess unwillingly through torment. He always maintains a good conscience and is always ready for his departure, living as a pilgrim and a guest among these earthly inheritances. He remembers only what truly belongs to him, considering everything here to be foreign. He does not merely admire the Lord's commandments, but—to put it simply—through <term>knowledge</term> <note>original: "cognitionem" — referring to Gnosis, the deep spiritual insight Clement emphasizes</note> itself, he becomes a participant in the divine will. He is a true friend of the Lord, chosen for the commandments as a righteous man.

<margin>C</margin>
<margin>Psalm 18</margin>
He is endowed with the power of ruling and reigning because he is endowed with knowledge. He despises all the gold that is above and below the earth, and every kingdom from one end of the Ocean to the other, so that he may hold fast only to the worship of the Lord. Therefore, whether he is eating, drinking, or marrying—if the <term>Word</term> <note>original: "Verbum" / Logos</note> dictates it—and even when looking at his dreams, he acts and thinks holily, always remaining pure for prayer. Indeed, he prays with the Angels, as one who is already equal to the Angels, and he is never outside that holy guardianship; even if he prays alone, he has a choir of Angels standing with him. He knows a twofold operation: that of the one who believes, and that of the thing believed, which possesses a worthy excellence. For justice is also twofold: one kind is motivated by love, the other by fear. For it has certainly been said: *The fear of the Lord is pure, enduring forever and ever.* <note>Psalm 19:9 in modern bibles; Clement cites the Septuagint/Vulgate numbering as Psalm 18</note> For those who are converted from fear to faith and justice remain forever.

<margin>D</margin>
<margin>John 15</margin>
Now, the one who fears works at abstaining from evil. But charity, which builds upon what is voluntary, encourages one to do good, so that he may hear from the Lord: *I no longer call you servants, but friends.* <note>John 15:15</note> And so he approaches his prayers with confidence. The very nature of his prayer is an act of thanksgiving for the past, present, and future, as these things are already present to him through faith. This is preceded by the receiving of knowledge. Furthermore, he prays to live his allotted life in the flesh as one endowed with the power of knowing—as if he were free from the flesh—so that he may attain what is best and flee what is worse. He also asks for the easing of our sins and for conversion to recognition, following the Caller into the heights as eagerly as He calls; hurrying, so to speak, to give thanks because of a good conscience. He strives to be with Christ there, having proven himself worthy through purity, so that through a "tempering" <note>original: "temperaturam" — a technical term for the soul's harmonious blending with divine virtue</note> he may possess the power of God supplied through Christ.

<margin>E</margin>
<margin>Luke 14</margin>
For he is not "hot" simply by participating in heat, nor "bright" like fire; rather, he wishes to be light itself. He accurately knows that saying: *Unless you hate father and mother, and even your own soul, and unless you carry the sign.* <note>Luke 14:26-27</note> For he despises carnal affections—which hold the greatest allurements of pleasure—and everything suited to the creation and nourishment of the flesh. But he also rises up against the "corporeal soul," placing a bridle on the spirit that refuses to be ruled, *because the flesh lusts against the spirit.*

<margin>F</margin>
To "carry the sign" is to carry death about, renouncing all things while still alive; for the love of the one who sowed the flesh is not equal to the love of Him who created the soul for knowledge. When this man has reached the habit of doing good, he bestows benefits faster than it can be spoken, praying that he might even share in the burden of his brothers' sins...

This person lives as a "pilgrim" on earth, viewing themselves as an equal to the angels and a participant in the divine will.</summary>

<margin>A</margin>...to confession and the conversion of his kin; he is most ready to share his own goods with those most dear to him. Such are his friends. By increasing the seeds deposited within him through that spiritual "farming" <note>original: "agricultura" — a metaphor for spiritual discipline and the cultivation of the soul</note> which the Lord commanded, he remains untainted by any sin, becomes self-controlled, and dwells with those of a similar spirit in the choirs of the saints, even if he is still held for a time on earth. This man, speaking and performing the Lord's commands day and night, rejoices beyond measure—not only when he rises in the morning and at noon, but also while walking, sleeping, dressing, and undressing; he even does so while teaching his son, if he has a son by birth. He is inseparable from the commandment and from hope, always giving thanks to God, like those "glorifying animals" <note>A reference to the four living creatures in the visions of Isaiah and Revelation</note> spoken of allegorically by Isaiah. He is enduring in every 
<margin>Job 1</margin>temptation. *The Lord gave,* he says, *and the Lord has taken away.* Such was Job, who, 
<margin>B</margin>because of his love for the Lord, set aside all external things that were taken from him, along with his health. For he was, it says, *just, holy, and abstaining from every wickedness.* Now, "holy" signifies those rights that pertain to God and the entire divine plan; and because he knew these things, he was endowed with <term>gnosis</term> <note>original: "cognitione" — spiritual knowledge or insight</note>. For one must neither be too devoted to good things if they are present, nor, on the other hand, be too distressed if they are bad; but one should be superior to both, trampling the latter underfoot and sharing the former with the needy. In managing his affairs, in humbling himself, and in adapting to others, the man gifted with such caution is very careful, lest he be misunderstood, or lest his temporary adaptation be mistaken for his permanent character. He never remembers the sins committed against him, but forgives them. Therefore, he also prays justly, saying: *Forgive us, for we also forgive.* For 
<margin>C</margin>this too is one of the things God wills: to covet nothing and to hate no one. For all men are the work of a single Will. Does our Savior not wish for the one gifted with knowledge to be perfect, just as the heavenly Father is? Referring to himself, he says: 
<margin>Psalm 33</margin>*Come, children, listen to me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord.* <note>Psalm 34:11 in modern numbering</note> He does not wish us to have further need of the help given through Angels, but to receive it from Him directly when one has become worthy, and to have protection from Him through obedience. Such a man asks of the Lord, rather than merely begging; and the man of knowledge will not beg for an abundance of money to share with needy brothers, but will pray that they be supplied with what they lack. For in this way, the man of knowledge gives even his prayers to those in need, and does not simply offer them ignorantly or without focus. Often, therefore, poverty and disease, 
<margin>D</margin>and such temptations, are provided for the warning and correction of past deeds, and for the care of the future. He who is of this sort, while asking for relief from these things, does so as one who possesses the excellence of knowledge—not for the sake of empty glory, but because he is a man of knowledge, he practices beneficence as one who has become an instrument of God’s goodness. They say that Matthias the Apostle said among other things: *If the neighbor of an elect man sins, the elect man has sinned.* For if he had conducted himself as the Word <note>original: "Verbum seu ratio" — the Logos or divine reason</note> commands, his neighbor would have so revered his life that he would not have sinned. 
<margin>1 Cor. 3</margin>What then shall we say of the man of knowledge? *Do you not know,* says the Apostle, *that you are the temple of God?* Therefore, the man of knowledge is divine and 
<margin>E</margin>already holy, who breathes God and is breathed upon by God. Now, the Scripture, showing that he is a stranger to sin, says that he who has offended is "sold to foreigners." <note>A reference to the Israelites being sold into captivity in the Book of Judges</note> And when it says a man should not look upon another's wife with lust, it says clearly that sin is something "foreign" and contrary to the nature of the temple of God. Now, the temple is one great thing, like the Church, and another small thing, like the man who preserves the "seed of Abraham." Therefore, he who has God resting within him will not desire anything else. Having left behind everything that acts as an impediment, and having despised all the matter that distracts him, he "cuts through the heavens" by means of his knowledge. Passing through spiritual essences and every principality and power, he touches the supreme thrones, striving for that one thing alone, for the sake of which alone he sought 
<margin>F</margin>knowledge. Having the serpent mixed with the dove <note>A reference to Matthew 10:16, "wise as serpents and innocent as doves"</note>, he lives perfectly and with a good conscience, mixing hope with faith in expectation of the future. For he feels the gift he has received, as one who has been judged worthy to obtain it, and has been translated from servitude into the adoption of sons, as a consequence of his knowledge. He has not failed to know God—or rather, he has been known by Him—and for the sake of that end, he demonstrates his works according to the merits of grace.

He emphasizes that the spiritually mature person is so influential that they bear a level of responsibility for the conduct of their neighbors.</summary>

<margin>A</margin>...actions. For works follow spiritual knowledge, just as a shadow follows the body. Rightly, therefore, nothing that happens disturbs him, nor does he fear anything that occurs by divine providence for our benefit. He does not blush at the prospect of death, for he possesses a good conscience and is ready to be shown to the heavenly powers—having been cleansed, to put it simply, of all the stains of the soul—knowing that after his departure from this life, things will be better for him. Hence, he never prefers what is merely pleasant or useful over the divine plan <note>original: "œconomiæ" — the "economy" or management of the universe by God</note> and counsel. Through the commandments, he exercises himself so that he may become pleasing and acceptable to the Lord in all things, and praiseworthy in the eyes of the world, since all things depend upon the one Almighty God. <margin>John 1</margin> *He came unto his own,* it says, *and his own received him not.* <note>original: "In propria venit filius Dei, & sui eum non receperunt"</note> Where-
<margin>B</margin>fore, even in the use of worldly things, he does not merely give thanks and admire the creation, but is also praised as is fitting, because his purpose ends in contemplation through action proceeding from knowledge, which is performed in accordance with the commandments. From this point, gathering through his science the provisions for his journey of contemplation, and having magnificently received the greatness of that contemplation, he proceeds to the holy reward of his transition <note>original: "translationis" — the passage from earthly life to the divine presence</note>. For he has heard the Psalm saying: *Walk about Zion, and go round about her; tell the towers thereof.* <margin>Psalm 47</margin> <note>Psalm 48 in modern numbering</note> This signifies, I believe, that those who have received the Word deeply will be high like towers, and will stand firmly and steadily in faith and knowledge. And these things, let it be said as briefly as possible, are like seeds sown for the Greeks concerning the man who is endowed with spiritual knowledge. It must be understood, however, that if a
<margin>C</margin>simple believer performs one or two of these things correctly, he does not perform them all, nor does he do so with that supreme science possessed by the man of spiritual knowledge. Furthermore, many other testimonies could be brought from the Scriptures to support that "impassibility" <note>original: "impatibilitatis" — a state of being unmoved by irrational passions or suffering</note> which we find in the man of knowledge, through which the perfection of the believer—advancing through love into the "perfect man"—reaches the measure of full maturity, having been made like God and truly equal to the angels. But I think it better, for the sake of the length of this discourse, to leave this praise to those who wish to labor, allowing them to work out the doctrines themselves through the citation of the Scriptures. I will mention one point very briefly, lest I leave the place unnoted. For the divine Apostle says in the first epistle to the Corinthians: *Dare any of you, having a matter* <margin>1 Cor. 6</margin>
<margin>D</margin>*against another, go to law before the unjust, and not before the saints? Do ye not know that the saints shall judge the world?* and so forth. Since this is a very great matter, we shall use the appropriate words of the Apostle's sayings, pursuing them in very few words and setting forth the speech as if by paraphrase; we shall show the meaning of the Apostolic word, through which he describes the perfection of the man of spiritual knowledge. For he does not define the man of knowledge simply by the fact that he suffers injury rather than inflicting it; but he teaches him even to forget the injury received, not permitting him even to pray for evil upon the one who did the wrong. For he knows that the Lord also openly commanded us to pray for our enemies. To say that even the one who has been wronged should go to law before the unjust is nothing other than wishing to appear to take revenge, and wishing to return the injury, which is itself a way of doing wrong. To
<margin>E</margin>say, however, that some wish to go to law before the "saints" <note>Clement interprets "saints" here as those who pray for justice to be done on their behalf</note> shows those who ask in their prayers that a "like for like" <note>An eye for an eye</note> be returned to those who did the injury. While these are better than the former group, they are not yet fully obedient unless they perfectly forget the injury according to the Lord’s doctrine and pray even for their enemies. It is beautiful, therefore, that they have received a good mind through that repentance which leads to faith. For even if Truth seems to have enemies who are envious and jealous, Truth itself is an enemy to no one. For God also *makes his sun to rise upon the just and the unjust.* Indeed, he sent the Lord himself to the just and the unjust; and he who strives to be made like God, through the greatest forgetfulness of injuries received, forgiving *seventy times seven* <note>original: "septuagesies septies"</note>—that is, through the whole of life
<margin>F</margin>and the entire conversion of the world which is signified by the weeks that are numbered—is kind and merciful toward everyone, even if someone should wrong the man of knowledge throughout this entire span of time spent in this life. For the good man does not only wish to leave his possessions to others who have wronged him; but

<margin>A</margin> He even wishes the just man to seek forgiveness from those judges for those who have sinned against him. And rightly so, since those who attempt to do him injury only cause harm in that which is external—that which pertains to the body—even if they proceed as far as death itself. None of these things are truly the "property" of the person who is endowed with <term>knowledge</term> <note>original: "cognitione" — Clement's term for "gnosis," the deep spiritual understanding of the mature Christian</note>. How, then, shall someone judge the fallen Angels if he himself has fallen away from that gentleness and that forgetting of received injury which the <term>Gospel</term> <note>original: "Euangelium"</note> prescribes? "Why do you not rather," he asks, "suffer injury? Why are you not rather defrauded? But you do injury and defraud," specifically by praying for evil to come upon those who sin through ignorance. Thus, you defraud them of God’s mercy and goodness as far as it lies within you, even though you call them brothers—meaning not only those who are in the faith, but also <margin>B</margin> <term>proselytes</term> <note>original: "proselytos" — converts or newcomers to the faith</note>. For we do not yet know whether he who is now an enemy will later become a believer. From this, it is clearly gathered that even if all are not yet brothers, they should at least appear so to us. Indeed, only He who knows the work of creation through its operations—and through whom you in turn adore the will of God—knows all men, who are the work of one God and a single image, surrounded by one substance, even if some are more obscured than others. "Do you not know that the unjust will not possess the kingdom of God?" Therefore, he who returns an injury does an injury himself, whether in deed, word, or even in the thought of the will—a thought which the Gospel circumscribes after the initial training of the Law. "And such were some of you." That is, you were like those whom you yourselves do not now forgive. "BUT you were washed." Not in an absolute sense like the <margin>C</margin> others, but when through knowledge you cast away the passions of the soul, so that, according to your strength, you might be assimilated to the goodness of God’s <term>providence</term> <note>original: "prouidentiæ"</note>, both through endurance and through the forgetting of received injury. Like the Sun, you send out the light of your words and deeds of kindness upon both the just and the unjust. The person endowed with knowledge will claim this for himself, whether through greatness of soul or through the <term>imitation</term> <note>original: "imitatio"</note> of that which is better. There is also a third cause: "Forgive, and it shall be forgiven you," as if the commandment were compelling one toward salvation because of God's remarkable goodness. "BUT you were sanctified." For it is fitting for one who has reached this state to be holy, falling in no way into any disturbance of the soul, but living as if he lacked flesh and had escaped this earth as a holy man. "Therefore you were justified," he says, "in the name of the Lord." You were made, so to speak, by Him, so that you might be just as He is, and you were <margin>D</margin> mixed and tempered with the Holy Spirit as far as it was possible. "For are all things lawful for me? But I will not be brought under the power," he says, to do or think or speak anything contrary to the Gospel. "Food for the belly, and the belly for food. Which things God will destroy." That is, He will destroy those who think and live as if they were born only to eat; they do not eat merely to live as a consequence, but they attend principally to knowledge. And does he not say that they are like the flesh of a holy body? For the <term>Church</term> <note>original: "ecclesia"</note> of the Lord is allegorically called the "Body," a spiritual and holy choir; those who are called by name alone, but live without reason, are merely "flesh." But this spiritual body—that is, the holy Church—is not for <term>fornication</term> <note>Clement interprets "fornication" here as a spiritual betrayal or a turning back to pagan habits</note>, nor for falling away from the Gospel. One must in no way enter into the customs and familiarity of the life of the pagans. <margin>E</margin> For he who lives like a pagan within the Church commits "fornication" against the Church and its body, whether in deed, word, or even in thought itself. He who clings to this harlot—that is, to an operation outside the Covenant—becomes another body, not holy, but "one flesh," sharing a pagan life and a different hope. But he who clings to the Lord in spirit is a spiritual body, a different kind of union. This man is a total Son, a holy man, <term>incapable of passion</term> <note>original: "impatibilis" — the state of *apatheia*, or being unmoved by worldly desires and emotions</note>, endowed with knowledge, perfect, formed by the doctrine of the Lord, so that when he has clung to the Lord in deed, word, and the very spirit, he may receive that dwelling place which is owed to a man who has become such as this. This specimen is sufficient for those who have ears. For the mystery is not to be fully unrolled, but only shown enough to call it to <margin>F</margin> remembrance for those who are sharers in knowledge, who will also understand how it was said by the Lord: "Be perfect as your Father is perfect," perfectly forgiving sins, forgetting received injuries, and living in a state of passionlessness. For just as we call a doctor "perfect," or a philosopher "perfect," so, in my opinion, [a person of knowledge is perfect...]
