### MISCELLANIES, BOOK VII

<sig>yy iiii</sig>

<margin>☞</margin> ...perfectly endowed with <term>knowledge</term> <note>original: "cognitione" — Clement's term for "gnosis," the deep spiritual insight of the mature believer</note>. However, none of these attributes, even the greatest of them, are assumed to be the exact likeness of God. For we do not say, as the <term>Stoics</term> <note>A school of Greek philosophy that taught virtue is sufficient for happiness and that the wise man could reach a state of divine-like perfection</note> most impiously claim, that the virtue of man and the virtue of God are the same. Must we then be "perfect," as the Father wishes? It is by no means possible for anyone to be perfect in the same way that God is. Rather, the Father wishes us to become perfect and blameless by living in obedience to the Gospel. If, therefore, a statement is uttered in such a way that it seems to lack something, and we "fill in" what is missing to complete the sense—at least for those who are capable of understanding—we will both recognize the will of God and live a life that is simultaneously pious and magnificent, worthy of His command. But since it follows that we must respond to the objections raised against us by the Greeks and the Jews—and since we are similarly criticized by certain <term>heresies</term> <note>original: "hæreses" — from the Greek word for "choices" or "sects"; here referring to groups that have broken away from the main Church</note> which follow other doctrines—it would be well to first clear away these obstacles. Once we are ready to resolve these doubts, we may proceed to the next *Stroma* (Miscellany).

<margin>☞</margin> First, then, they bring this against us: they say we ought not to believe because of the dissension among the sects. They argue that truth is delayed and hindered while different groups establish different dogmas. To these people we say: even among you Jews, and among those who were held in the highest esteem among the Greeks—the philosophers—there were very many sects. Yet you do not say that one should hesitate to philosophize or to follow Jewish discipline simply because of the dissension between your own schools. Furthermore, it was predicted by the Lord through prophecy that <term>heresies</term> would be sown into the truth just as <term>weeds</term> <note>original: "zizania" — likely darnel or tares, a weed that looks like wheat until it is grown</note> are sown among the wheat; it is impossible for that which was predicted not to happen.

<margin>☞</margin> The reason for this is that <term>Momus</term> <note>The Greek god of mockery and unfair criticism</note> follows whatever is beautiful. Now, if someone fails to observe a formal agreement and transgresses the confession we hold, shall we also abstain from the truth because of a person who did not stand by his own profession? Just as an honorable man must never be a liar, nor weaken anything he has promised even if others leap over their agreements, so too it is in no way fitting for us to leap over the <term>ecclesiastical rule</term> <note>original: "regulam ecclesiasticam" — the traditional standard of faith and practice in the early Church</note>. We observe that profession, especially regarding the most important matters, while they leap over it. Therefore, we must believe those who adhere firmly to the truth. Indeed, we may use this defense even more broadly with them: even among physicians, whose opinions differ according to their various schools, they still effectively heal people. Would any sick person in need of a cure refuse a doctor simply because of the different "sects" within medicine?

<margin>☞</margin> Therefore, let no one whose soul is sick and filled with idols ever use "heresies" as a pretext for avoiding health and conversion to God. "Certainly," he says, "there are heresies for the sake of the <term>approved</term>." <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 11:19: "For there must be also heresies among you, that they which are approved may be made manifest among you."</note> By "the approved," he means either those who, in coming to the faith, approach the Lord’s teaching with a more careful choice—like <term>skilled money-changers</term> <note>original: "probi argentarii" — a common early Christian metaphor for discernment, comparing the Christian to a banker who can spot counterfeit coins</note> who distinguish the Lord’s coin from a false impression—or those who have already become approved within the faith itself, both in their life and in their knowledge. For this reason, there is a need for greater care and foresight to examine how one must live exactly and perfectly, and what constitutes true piety and the right worship of God.

<margin>☞</margin> It is clear that since the truth is arduous and difficult, questions have certainly arisen; from these, heresies have grown among those who are afflicted with excessive self-love, ambition, and a lust for glory—people who did not truly learn or receive the truth, but merely took up a "persuasion" of knowledge for themselves. We must, therefore, search out the actual truth with greater zeal and care, for it alone is concerned with Him who is truly God. This labor is followed by a "sweet discovery" and memory. The labor of discovery must be undertaken because of the heresies, but one must not give up entirely. If fruit were set before you—some real and ripe, and others made of wax to look exactly like it—you should not abstain from both just because of the resemblance.

<margin>☞</margin> At the same time, one must distinguish the true from the apparent through comprehensive contemplation and essential consideration. It is as if there were one "King’s Highway," but also many other paths, some of which lead to a precipice, others to a rushing river or a deep sea; a person would not hesitate to start the journey because of the different paths, but would use the King’s Highway—the one that is well-trodden and free from danger. So, even though different people say different things about the truth, one must not depart, but rather exa—

# 260 CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

<margin>A</margin>
...more actively and diligently must we seek its most exact and accurate knowledge. For along with garden herbs, weeds also grow. Do farmers then refrain from cultivating their gardens? Since we have many things from nature that incite us and give us the occasion to examine the things being said, we ought also to find the logical consequence of the truth. Therefore, we are justly condemned if we do not assent to those whom we ought to obey, and if we do not discern that which is repugnant, unseemly, contrary to nature, and false from that which is true, consistent, decorous, and according to nature. Indeed, we must use these things as incentives and occasions for recognizing that which is truly the truth. For the Greeks, therefore, this pretext is empty. For to those who are willing, it will be possible to find the truth. But for those who offer reasons that lack logic, there is a judgment 
<margin>B</margin>
that has no excuse. For do they destroy the idea of demonstration, or do they agree that demonstration exists? I think everyone would confess it exists, except for those who destroy the senses. Since there is such a thing as demonstration, it is necessary to go down into the questions and learn demonstratively through the scriptures themselves how the <term>heresies</term> <note>original: "hæreses" — from the Greek word for "choices" or "sects." In this context, Clement refers to groups that have broken away from the orthodox Church.</note> have fallen away. We must learn how the most perfect knowledge is found in the truth alone and in the ancient church, and that this is truly the best "heresy"—that is, the best "choice." Among those who turn away from the truth, some try to deceive only themselves, while others try to deceive their neighbors as well. And those who are called <gloss>wise in their own opinion</gloss> <note>original: "δοξόσοφοι" (doxosophoi) — those who possess "doxa" (opinion) rather than "episteme" (true knowledge)</note>, who think they have found the truth when they have no true demonstration, they deceive themselves, 
<margin>C</margin>
thinking they have acquired it. Their number is not small. They are people who avoid questions because they fear being proven wrong, and they shun doctrine because they fear condemnation. But those who deceive the people who come to them are very clever and crafty; even if they claim to know nothing, they nevertheless obscure the truth with "probable" arguments. But the nature of "probable" arguments is one thing, and the nature of "true" arguments is another. And we recognize that the name "heresy" must be used in such a way that it is opposed to and distinguished from the truth. Since certain <term>Sophists</term> <note>Professional teachers in ancient Greece often criticized for using clever but fallacious reasoning to win arguments rather than find truth.</note> have torn away parts of the truth to the destruction of men, burying them under human inventions, they boast that they preside over a <term>school</term> <note>original: "diatribæ" — a place for philosophical debate or a specific sect's meeting place.</note> rather than the Church. But those who are prepared to expend labor on the most beautiful things will not stop seeking the truth until they have received a 
<margin>D</margin>
demonstration from the scriptures themselves. And there are indeed certain common judges of men, namely the senses. But there are others, those who have consulted and practiced the things that are true—namely, the arts of true and false speech through the mind and reasoning. The greatest thing, however, is to set aside opinion by standing in the middle between accurate and perfect knowledge on one side, and rash, opinionated wisdom on the other. We must know that he who hopes for eternal rest also knows that its entrance is laborious and narrow. And he who has once accepted the Gospel and the "saving word," he says, once he has known it, let him not turn back to the things behind him like Lot's wife, nor to his former life which gives its attention to sensible things. Neither should he run back to heresies. For they somehow accustom a person not to know God. For "he who loves father or mother more than 
<margin>E</margin>
me"—I who am truly the father and teacher of truth, who regenerates and recreates, and who cherishes and nourishes the chosen soul—"is not worthy of me," says the Son of God, who is God's disciple, and 
<margin>Luke 9</margin>
at the same time His friend and kinsman. "For no one looking back and putting his hand to the plow is fit for the kingdom of God." But, as it seems, to many even to this day Mary appears to be a woman who has given birth because of the birth of her son, though she is not such a woman. For some say that after she had given birth, she was examined by a midwife and found to be a virgin. Such are the Lord’s Scriptures to us: they bring forth the truth, yet remain "virgins" with the concealment of mysteries. "She brought forth, and did not bring forth," says the scripture, as one who conceived from herself and not from union. Therefore, for those who are endowed with knowledge, the scriptures have "conceived." But the heresies, since they have not 
<margin>F</margin>
understood, send them away as if they had not conceived. While all men have the same faculty of judgment, some follow the Word <note>original: "Verbum" / "Logos"</note> which dictates to them and they make their arguments; others, however, since they have given themselves over to pleasures, twist the scripture to their own desires. But I believe the lover of truth needs strength of soul. It is necessary...

He uses the metaphor of Mary's perpetual virginity to explain how the Bible reveals truth to the faithful while remaining "sealed" or mysterious to those who lack spiritual insight.</summary>

# 261 MISCELLANIES, BOOK VII

<margin>A</margin> For it is necessary that those who attempt the greatest tasks will slip in the most important matters, unless they hold the <term>rule of truth</term> <note>original: "regulam veritatis" — a common phrase in the early Church referring to the core set of apostolic teachings used to measure the validity of any doctrine.</note> received from the Truth itself. Those who are of this sort, having fallen away from the right path, are deservedly deceived in many specific details, because they do not have a fully trained judgment for distinguishing true things from false things in the matters they must choose. For if they had such judgment, they would obey the divine scriptures. Therefore, just as if someone were to become a beast instead of a human, much like those who were infected by <note>In Greek mythology, the sorceress Circe turned Odysseus's crew into swine with a potion.</note> Circe’s poisons; so too has a man ceased to be a "man of God" and faithful to the Lord who has kicked against the ecclesiastical tradition and leaped into the opinions of human <term>heresies</term> <note>original: "hæresum" — here meaning man-made sects as opposed to divine revelation.</note>. But he who returns from error, obeys the scriptures, and permits his life to be guided by the truth, is in a certain sense turned from a man into a God.

<margin>B</margin> For we have the Lord as the starting point of our teaching, who, through the Prophets, the Gospel, and the blessed Apostles, leads us from the beginning to the end of knowledge in many ways and in various forms. But if anyone thought they needed another starting point, that original principle could not truly be preserved. He, then, who is faithful in himself, is worthy of belief because of the Lord's scripture and voice, which is used through the Lord for the benefit of humanity. We use this very scripture as our judge for discovering the reality of things. For whatever is judged is not believed until it has been judged. Therefore, that which requires judgment is not the ultimate starting point. Rightly, then, we embrace the indemonstrable starting point by faith, and having taken demonstrations about the principle from the principle itself through a certain redundant abundance, we are educated by the voice of the Lord toward the knowledge of the truth.

<margin>C</margin> For we should not give credit to men who simply make absolute pronouncements, for it is permitted for them to pronounce the opposite as well. If it is not enough simply to state what seems right, but one must also prove what is said, then we do not wait for testimony given by men, but we prove what is sought by the voice of the Lord, which is more worthy of faith than any demonstrations—or rather, is the only demonstration. Through this science, those who have merely tasted the scriptures are made faithful. But those who have proceeded even further are the <term>perfect pointers of truth</term> <note>original: "perfecti gnomones veritatis" — a "gnomon" is the part of a sundial that casts a shadow to indicate time; here, it refers to a person who serves as an accurate indicator of the truth.</note>; these are the ones endowed with knowledge, since even in the affairs of life, skilled craftsmen surpass the unskilled, and express what is better through common notions. Thus, we also, demonstrating perfectly from the scriptures themselves about the scriptures themselves, persuade demonstratively from faith.

<margin>D</margin> But if those who follow heresies dare to use the Prophetic scriptures, they do so, first of all, by not using all of them. Secondly, they do not use them in their entirety, nor as the body and context of the prophecy dictates. Instead, selecting things that were spoken with ambiguity, they twist them toward their own opinions, plucking a few phrases scattered here and there, not considering what is signified by the verses themselves, but using the bare words. For in almost all the sayings they bring forward, you will find them attending only to the names, as those who would change the meanings; they neither recognize how things are said, nor do they use the allegations they assert in the way their nature requires. Truth, however, is not found in the changing of meanings—for in that way, they would overturn all true truth—but in considering what is perfectly fitting and appropriate for the Lord and Almighty God, and in confirming each of the things demonstrated through the scriptures from the scriptures themselves which are similar.

<margin>E</margin> Therefore, they do not wish to be converted to the truth, as those who are ashamed to set aside the advantage of their own self-love; nor do they know by what reasoning they might establish their own opinions, while doing violence to the scriptures. But when they have proceeded to bring false dogmas before the public, evidently fighting against almost all the scriptures and always being refuted by us who speak against them, what remains is this: even now they persist. Part of this involves not admitting certain things from the Prophetic writings; another part involves slandering us, claiming that we are of a "different nature" and cannot understand the things that are specifically theirs.

<margin>F</margin> Sometimes, even when they are convicted, they deny their own dogmas, being ashamed to openly confess what they boast of teaching in private. This can be seen in all heresies by following the wickedness of their own dogmas. For after they have been overturned by us, when we show they are openly opposed to the scriptures, one of two things can be seen to happen among those who lead the sect: either the logical consequence of their dogmas...

<summary>Clement argues that the "rule of truth" found in the complete context of the Holy Scriptures is the only valid starting point for knowledge, accusing heretics of cherry-picking and twisting biblical texts to suit their own self-interest.</summary>

# 262 CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

<margin>A</margin> ...opinion, or they despise Prophecy itself, or rather their own hope. For they always take for themselves whatever seems more obvious to them than what was spoken by the Lord through the Prophets, and what has been proven and confirmed by the Gospel and the testimony of the Apostles. Therefore, when they saw danger looming—not over a single doctrine, but over the preservation of their <term>heresy</term> <note>original: "hæresi" — a Greek word meaning "choice" or "sect," here used for those who choose their own path over the common faith.</note>—they did not seek to find the truth (for if they had read what is set in our midst and available to us, they would have despised those things as cheap). Instead, striving to overcome the common faith, they departed from the truth. For since they had not learned the mysteries of ecclesiastical <term>knowledge</term> <note>original: "cognitionis" — likely translating the Greek 'gnosis,' which Clement uses for the deep, spiritual understanding of the faith.</note>, nor perceived the greatness of the truth, they were lazy in searching the depths of things. Reading only on the surface, they bid farewell to the authority of the scriptures. Elated by a vain opinion of wisdom, they argue perpetually, openly showing that they care more about appearing wise than actually practicing <term>philosophy</term> <note>original: "philosofentur" — to Clement, true philosophy is the pursuit of divine truth.</note>.

<margin>B</margin> Now indeed, since they rely on principles that are not necessary, and are moved by human opinions, they arrange things so that their desired conclusion necessarily follows. They are wounded by the arguments of those who practice true philosophy, and they would endure anything and, as the saying goes, "move every rope" <note>An ancient idiom meaning to leave no stone unturned or to try every possible means.</note>, even if they are to become impious because they do not believe the scriptures, rather than be led away from the pleasant honor of their sect and the "first seat" <note>referring to positions of social or ecclesiastical status</note> tossed about by the crowd in their churches. For the sake of this status, they even embrace the "first place at the table" during the communal meal through that which is falsely called <term>charity</term> <note>original: "charitatem" — referring to the 'Agape' or love-feast, which Clement suggests heretics use for social climbing.</note>. But among us, the recognition of truth is what causes faith to be held in things not yet seen, based on things that are already credible; this is the very essence, so to speak, of <term>demonstration</term> <note>original: "demonstrationis" — logical proof used to explain the faith.</note>.

<margin>C</margin> But every heresy, it seems, has from the beginning ears that do not hear what is useful, but are open only to those things said for pleasure. For any one of them would surely have been cured if they had only wished to obey the truth. Now, there is a three-fold method for curing an opinion, just as there is for any ailment: knowledge of the cause, the method by which it can be removed, and thirdly, the exercise and habituation of the soul so that it can follow what has been rightly judged. For just as a clouded eye cannot see the light of truth perfectly, so also a soul disturbed by doctrines that are contrary to nature cannot see clearly, and even struggles to look at what is right before its feet. Thus, they say that even blinded eels are caught in muddy water. And just as naughty children shut out the <term>Pedagogue</term> <note>original: "Pædagogus" — The "Instructor." In Clement’s theology, this is Christ himself who educates the soul.</note>, so also these people keep the Prophecies away from their church, holding them in suspicion because of their rebukes and warnings.

<margin>D</margin> They certainly stuff together many lies and fictions, so that they may seem justified in not admitting the scriptures. By this reasoning they are not pious, since they do not acquiesce to divine precepts—that is, to the Holy Spirit. Just as almonds are called "empty," not because there is nothing in them, but because what is inside is useless; so also we call those <term>heretics</term> empty who are void of God’s counsel and the traditions of Christ. They become bitter like a wild almond, and are the leaders and authors of doctrines, except for those things which, because of the evidence of truth, they were unable to set aside or hide. Therefore, just as in war a soldier must not abandon the rank assigned by the General, so we must not abandon the order given to us by the <term>Word</term> <note>original: "Verbum" — translating the Greek 'Logos,' Christ as the Reason and Speech of God.</note>, whom we have received as the Prince and Leader of knowledge and life.

<margin>E</margin> The common crowd has not even examined this: whether someone should be followed, who this person is, and in what manner. For as the Word is, so should the life of the faithful person be, so that he may follow God, who from the beginning directs all things in a straight path. But if someone should transgress the Word, and through that, God—if they were weak because some sudden vision presented itself—it must be brought about that visions based on reason are ready at hand. But if someone from the common crowd has been overcome by a previously prevailing habit, as the scripture says, care must be taken that the habit comes to rest in that which is perfect and absolute in every part, and the soul must be exercised to speak against that habit.

<margin>F</margin> If, however, someone seems to be drawn to conflicting doctrines, these must be removed, and one must go to those who produce peaceful doctrines and "enchant" <note>Using the beauty of the Word to soothe and teach.</note> with the divine scriptures those who are unrefined and unskilled, and who are terrified by the noise—explaining the truth to them through the continuity of the <term>Testaments</term> <note>original: "testamentorum" — the harmony between the Old and New Testaments.</note>. But as it seems, we decline more toward things that are mere opinions, even if they are contradictory, than toward the truth; for the truth is austere, grave, and severe. And while there are indeed three...

He compares their rejection of divine instruction to children avoiding a teacher and emphasizes that true faith requires logical demonstration and the harmony of the Old and New Testaments.</summary>

<meta>This page continues from page 262, where Clement described how those who follow private sects (heresies) prioritize their own surface-level opinions over the deep, proven truths of the Gospel and the testimony of the Apostles. He now moves into a philosophical classification of these different states of mind.</meta>

### STROMATA BOOK VII. 263

<margin>a</margin> There are three states of the soul: ignorance, opinion, and knowledge. Those who live in ignorance are the pagans. Those who live in knowledge are the true church. Those who live in opinion are those who follow <term>heresies</term> <note>original: "hæreses" — from a Greek word meaning "choice," referring here to groups that choose a private path over the common tradition.</note>. Therefore, it is easy to see that those who truly know are no more emphatic about what they know than the others are about what they merely opine, at least when it comes to making assertions without proof. Thus, they despise and mock one another; it happens that the very same idea is held in the highest honor by some, while by others it is condemned as madness.

<margin>b</margin> Yet we have learned that "pleasure" is something to be attributed to the pagans; "strife and contention" are what characterize the heresies; "joy" is to be assigned as the unique property of the church; and "gladness" is to be given to the one who is endowed with true knowledge. <margin><gloss>Gladness [euphrosyne]: Joy joined with prudence.</gloss></margin> Just as someone who studies under Ischomachus will become a farmer; or under Lampis, a sailor; or under Charidemus, a general; or under Simon, a horseman; or under Perdix, an innkeeper; or under Crobylus, a chef; or under Archelaus, a dancer; or under Homer, a poet; or under Pyrrho, a debater; or under Demosthenes, an orator; or under Chrysippus, a logician; or under Aristotle, a scientist; or under Plato, a philosopher—so too, the one who obeys the Lord and follows the Prophecy given through him is transformed into the very image of the Teacher: a **God walking in the flesh.** <note>Clement refers to the concept of "theosis" or deification, where the believer becomes god-like through spiritual maturity.</note> Those who do not follow God as their guide never reach this height. And he guides us through the divinely inspired scriptures.

<margin>c</margin> Although the things done by humans are countless, there are essentially two origins for every sin: ignorance and weakness. Both of these are within our power, as we often choose neither to learn nor to restrain our desires. Of these two, one leads to poor judgment, and the other prevents us from carrying out what has been rightly judged. For if someone is deceived in their thinking, they cannot act rightly, even if they have the strength to do what they think is correct. Conversely, even someone who judges correctly what ought to be done cannot be considered blameless if they are too weak to actually do it. Consequently, two types of <term>discipline</term> <note>original: "disciplinę" — here meaning a course of education or training.</note> are provided to help with each sin. For ignorance, there is knowledge and clear proof from the testimony of the scriptures; for weakness, there is training through the Word, which is taught by "Faith" and "Fear" acting as our tutors. Both of these grow until they reach perfect love.

<margin>d</margin> For the person who possesses true knowledge, there is, I believe, a double goal. In some matters, it is contemplation based on science; in others, it is action. It might even happen that these heretics, by listening to these Commentaries, may be corrected and converted to God Almighty. But if, like "deaf serpents" (as the saying goes—an old expression for something newly heard), they refuse to hear the song, let them certainly be corrected by God. Let them patiently endure the fatherly warnings that come before the final judgment, until, moved by shame, they are led to <term>repentance</term> <note>original: "pœnitentia" — a change of mind and heart.</note>, rather than casting themselves into the final judgment through sheer disobedience. For there are also specific disciplines called "chastisements," into which many of our own people who have fallen into sin slip away from the Lord’s people; but just as a teacher or father corrects a child, so we are corrected by <term>Providence</term> <note>original: "prouidentia" — God's caring oversight of the world.</note>.

<margin>e</margin> God does not "punish," for punishment is the returning of evil for evil. Instead, he chastises, both publicly and privately, for the benefit of those being corrected. I have brought these things up because I wish to encourage the studious not to fall easily into heresies. I want to lead others away from what is merely surface-level—whether you call it ignorance, stupidity, or a bad habit. I am using these words to try to lead those who are not entirely incurable back to the truth. For there are some who will not even allow themselves to hear those who encourage them toward the truth. Instead, they resort to trifles, pouring out abusive words against the truth, arrogantly claiming to know the greatest matters when they have neither learned, nor sought, nor labored, nor discovered the logical connection of things.

<margin>f</margin> One should pity such people rather than hate them for their way of life. But if there is anyone who can be healed—someone who can endure the "fire and iron" of the freedom of truth, which cuts and burns away their false opinions—let them offer the "ears of the soul." This will happen if they do not embrace idleness and sluggishness...

<summary>Clement distinguishes between the ignorance of pagans, the unfounded opinions of heretics, and the true knowledge found in the Church, arguing that God uses corrective discipline rather than vengeful punishment to lead souls toward truth.</summary>
<keywords>ignoracy, opinion, knowledge, heresy, theosis, discipline, repentance, providence, correction vs punishment, Clement of Alexandria</keywords>

# CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

...they push out the truth, or out of a desire for glory, they pursue innovations with great intensity. <margin>A</margin> For there are those who are indolent, who, although it is possible to gather proofs consistent with the divine scriptures from the scriptures themselves, do not do so at all; instead, they choose only what supports their own pleasures. Those held by the desire for glory are those who, by their own choice and with a deceptive imitation of Wisdom, corrupt the teachings that naturally harmonize with the divinely inspired words—teachings handed down by the blessed Apostles and teachers. They do this through other interpretations, resisting divine tradition with human doctrines in order to establish a <term>heresy</term> <note>original: "hæresim" — from the Greek word for "choice," used here to describe a sect that chooses its own path over the common tradition.</note>. For among those men who were so great in ecclesiastical knowledge, what was left to be said by Marcion, for example, or Prodicus, and similar men who did not enter by the right path? For they were not able to surpass those who preceded them in wisdom, so as to invent anything beyond what was truly said by them. It would have been well enough for them if they could have simply known the things that were previously handed down.

<margin>B</margin> Therefore, for us, the only one who is truly endowed with knowledge <note>Clement uses the term "Gnostic" to describe a person with deep, spiritual understanding of the faith.</note> is he who has grown old in the scriptures themselves, preserving the Apostolic and ecclesiastical rectitude of dogmas. He lives most rightly according to the Gospel, and he finds the proofs he seeks, as one sent by the Lord, from the Law and the Prophets. For the life of the one endowed with knowledge is, I believe, nothing other than deeds and words that follow the tradition of the Lord.

<margin>1 Corinthians 10</margin>
> "But knowledge is not in everyone. For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers," says the Apostle, "that all were under the cloud, and all shared in the spiritual food and drink,"

clearly confirming that not everyone who hears the Word has grasped the magnitude of knowledge in deed and word. For this reason, he also added: <margin>C</margin>

<margin>Luke 6</margin>
> "But not in all of them was He well pleased."

By whom? By the one who said:

> "Why do you call me, 'Lord,' and do not do the will of my Father?"

This "will" is the doctrine of the Savior, which is our spiritual food and the drink that knows no thirst—the water of life for the one endowed with knowledge. But, they say, it is written: <margin>1 Corinthians 4</margin> "Knowledge puffs up." To them we say: perhaps that which *seems* to be knowledge is said to "puff up," if one thinks the word means to make one swollen and insolent. But if—as should rather be said—the voice of the Apostle means to think magnificently and truly, then the doubt is resolved. Following the <margin>Ecclesiasticus 4</margin> scriptures, let us confirm what has been said.

> "Wisdom," says Solomon, "puffed up <note>original: "inflauit" — Clement is playing on the dual meaning of the Latin and Greek terms for "puffed up" or "inflated." While it usually means prideful, he argues here it can mean "magnified" or "inspired."</note> her sons."

<margin>D</margin> For the Lord did not produce pride and arrogance in those who are unique in his doctrine; rather, he causes one to have confidence in the truth and to be magnificent in the knowledge that is handed down through the scriptures. This makes one a contemner of those things that lead to sin. This is what the expression "puffed up" signifies: it teaches the magnificence of wisdom, which is implanted in those who are sons through his doctrine. Indeed, the Apostle says:

> "And I will know not the speech of those who are puffed up, but the power,"

to see if you understand the scriptures magnificently—which is to say, truly—for nothing is greater than the truth. For in this is the power of the "puffed up" sons of Wisdom. It is as if he were to say: "Let me see if you are rightly and magnificently proud of your knowledge." <margin>Psalm 75</margin> For, as David says:

> "God is known in Judea,"

that is, to the Israelites who exist through knowledge. For "Judea" is interpreted as "confession." Appropriately, therefore, this was said by the Apostle:

<margin>Romans 13</margin>
> "You shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal, you shall not covet, and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this word: You shall love your neighbor as yourself." <margin>E</margin>

For it is never necessary—as those who follow heresies do—to adulterate the truth, nor to steal the rule of the church by serving one's own desires and glory to the deception of neighbors. Those who truly love their neighbors should instead teach them to embrace the truth. Therefore, it was clearly said: <margin>Psalm 9</margin>

> "Announce his deeds among the nations,"

so that those who have heard may not be judged, but converted. However, whoever acts deceitfully with their tongues are punished with written penalties. Those who touch upon impious discourses and use divine words not rightly but perversely, neither enter the kingdom of heaven themselves, nor do they allow those they have deceived to attain the truth. They do not possess the key to the entrance, but rather a false one, or as the custom says, an <term>antikleida</term> <note>original: "ἀντικλεῖδα" — a Greek term for a "counter-key" or "skeleton key" used for breaking in.</note>, that is, an opposing key. <margin>F</margin> Through this, they do not enter by drawing back the veil, as we do through the tradition of the Lord; instead, they cut through the door and secretly dig through the wall of the church. Transgressing the truth, they become the masters and leaders of the mysteries of the souls of the impious. For the fact that the Catholic church held its assemblies before their groups...

<meta>This page continues from page 264, where Clement argued that true knowledge belongs to those who preserve the Apostolic tradition. Here, he provides a historical timeline to prove that the "true Church" preceded all heretical sects and uses an allegory from the Old Testament to distinguish between them.</meta>

### MISCELLANIES, BOOK VII.

<margin><unclear>.c. 21. 1.</unclear></margin>
<margin>A</margin>
There is no need for many words. For the teaching of our Lord, during His advent, began under Augustus and was completed in the middle of the reign of Tiberius. The teaching of His Apostles, including the ministry of Paul, was completed by the time of Nero. However, later, around the times of the Emperor Hadrian, there were those who devised <term>heresies</term> <note>original: "hæreses" — meaning "choices" or "sects" that deviate from the established path.</note>, and they continued until the age of Antoninus the Elder; such as Basilides, even though he claims Glaucias as his teacher (as they boast), who was the interpreter of Peter. Similarly, they say that Valentinus also heard Theodas, who was a close associate of Paul. Marcion, though born in the same era as these men, lived as an old man among those who were younger. After him, Simon heard Peter preaching for a little while.

<margin>B</margin>
Since these things are so, it is clear that from the most ancient and true Church, these more recent heresies—and those even lower than them—were innovations of a corrupted nature. From what has been said, I think it is manifest that there is only one Church, that which is truly ancient, into whose catalog are enrolled those who are righteous according to God’s purpose. For as there is one God and one Lord, so also that which is most highly venerable is praised because of its unity and because it stands alone, as it is an imitation of the first principle which is One. Therefore, the Church, which is one, is assigned to the nature of the One, though heresies attempt to tear it into many parts. Thus, in substance, in thought, in origin, and in excellence, we say that the ancient and <term>catholic</term> <note>original: "catholicam" — meaning universal or encompassing the whole.</note> Church is unique. It exists in the unity of one faith, which is based on its own testaments—or rather, on the one testament given at different times—by which, by the will of God through one

<margin>C</margin>
Lord, He gathers those who have already been ordained, whom God predestined, having known them to be righteous before the foundation of the world. Furthermore, the preeminence of the Church, like the principle of its construction, is based on unity, surpassing all other things and having nothing similar or equal to itself. But these things will be discussed later. Among the heresies, some are named after a person, such as those called after Valentinus, Marcion, and Basilides, even if they boast that they follow the opinion of Matthias. For as there was one teaching of all the Apostles, so also was there one tradition. Others are named from a place, like the Peratics. Others from a nation, like the heresy of the Phrygians. Others from an activity, like the <term>Encratites</term> <note>original: "Encratitarum" — meaning 'the self-controlled,' a group that practiced extreme asceticism.</note>. Others from their own specific dogmas, like the <term>Docetists</term> <note>original: "Docitarum" — from the Greek word for 'to seem,' they believed Christ only appeared to have a physical body.</note> and the Haematites. Others from the positions and things they themselves honored, such as

<margin>D</margin>
those called Cainites and <term>Ophites</term> <note>original: "Ophiani" — from the Greek word for serpent, a group that gave special status to the serpent in Genesis.</note>. Still others are named from the wicked things they dared to do, such as those from the Simonians called Entychites. Now, for those who belong to the Church and are held by a desire for contemplation, we shall show a small opening, drawing from the Law regarding sacrifices—both concerning common Jews and the heresies that are set apart as "unclean"—based on the divine distinction between clean and unclean animals, and then we shall end this discourse. For the Scripture teaches that those animals which have cloven hooves and chew the cud are clean and acceptable sacrifices to God. This signifies that the righteous enter the path to the Father and the Son through faith. For this is the stability of those whose hooves are cloven: they meditate on the words of God day and night and "chew the cud" in the

<margin>E</margin>
receptacle of the soul’s training. This knowledge, which is provided with practice, the Law calls the "rumination" of a clean animal in an allegorical sense. But those animals that have neither characteristic, or only one of them, it rejects as unclean. And those that chew the cud but do not have a cloven hoof, silently signify the mass of the Jews, who indeed have the words of God in their mouths, but do not have the faith or the "base" which transmits them to the Father through the Son and leans upon the truth. Thus, this kind of creature falls quite easily, as its feet are not cloven, nor does it lean upon the duality of faith.

> "For no one," He says, "knows the Father except the Son, and him to whom the

<margin>Luke 10</margin>

<margin>F</margin>

They perform the works of justice in a somewhat crude manner rather than with accuracy and refinement, if indeed they perform them at all. To those who are such, the Lord says:

# CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA
## THE MISCELLANIES: BOOK
### EIGHT.

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>B</margin> <image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial 'S' depicting a man sitting by a riverbank with a city and mountains in the far background.</image-desc>BUT neither were the most ancient philosophers driven toward contention and doubting, let alone us who embrace that which is truly philosophy—whom the Scripture explicitly commands to search and investigate for the sake of discovery. However, the more recent of the Greek philosophers, moved by an empty desire for praise, are led down into useless trifles by simultaneously refuting others and engaging in conflict. In contrast, the barbarian philosophy <note>original: "barbara philosophia" — Clement uses this term to refer to the Judeo-Christian tradition, which the Greeks considered "barbarian" or foreign, but which Clement asserts is the source of all true wisdom.</note>, expelling all contention, <margin>Luke 11</margin> says: "Seek, and you shall find; knock, and it will be opened to you. Ask, and it will be given to you." And indeed, he who knocks at the doors of truth through inquiry—that is, through the kind of discourse consisting of question and answer—does so by means of what is evident. Clearly, <margin>C</margin> once the obstacle is removed by thorough investigation, a form of contemplation born of <term>knowledge</term> <note>original: "scientia" (Greek: "episteme") — in this context, it refers to systematic, certain knowledge rather than mere opinion.</note> is generated. To those who knock in this way, that which is sought is opened, as I believe. And for those who thus seek questions through the Scriptures, aiming toward that which comes from God, there is a granting of divinely given <term>cognition</term> <note>original: "cognitionis" (Greek: "gnosis") — spiritual insight or higher knowledge.</note> by comprehending through the rational inquiry that truly shines forth. For it is not possible for someone to find who does not seek, nor for someone to seek who does not investigate, explain, and open the way through questioning, leading what is sought toward clarity; nor, again, can one proceed through every examination without subsequently receiving the prize, namely the knowledge of what was sought. But he who has sought can indeed find, provided he first realizes that he does not know. Guided from this point by a desire to find that which is good and <margin>D</margin> honorable, he seeks kindly, without contention and without a desire for glory, by asking and answering, and by considering the things that are said. For it is necessary not only for those who apply themselves to the divine Scriptures, but also for those who follow common notions, to propose questions in such a way that the discovery ends in some useful goal. For a different place and a different crowd awaits turbulent men and their legalistic inventions. But it is fitting for him who is both a lover of and a familiar with the truth to be peaceful; in his inquiries, through the <term>demonstration</term> <note>original: "demonstrationem" — a formal logical proof.</note> that comes from knowledge, he should not labor from excessive self-love, but as a lover of truth, he should approach the cognition that encompasses it. What other method, then, could be better or more evident for the beginning of such teaching than to follow the proposed name so <margin>E</margin> clearly in discourse that everyone who uses the same word may understand it? Is the name for the sake of demonstration like "Blityri" <note>original: "Blityri" — a nonsense word used by ancient Greek logicians, similar to "gibberish" or "abracadabra," to illustrate a sound that has no meaning.</note>, a mere sound signifying nothing? Surely neither the philosopher, nor the orator, nor even the judge utters "demonstration" as if it were a name signifying nothing, nor is any of those who contend in a trial ignorant of what is signified. Now, philosophers devise demonstrations differently, according to how each one establishes them. Therefore, regarding any subject of inquiry, if one treats it correctly, one will not lead the discourse to any other principle that is more certain and beyond controversy than to that which everyone of the same nation and language admits is signified by the name. Then, proceeding from that point, it is necessary to ask whether that which is signified by the discourse actually exists or not. Next, if its existence has been shown, <margin>F</margin> one must accurately inquire into its nature, and whether it exceeds the given order. But if that which has been seen is not sufficient to speak absolutely about the subject of inquiry—for an opponent is equally permitted to pronounce the opposite of what he wishes—then it is necessary to confirm what has been said. And if his judgment refers to that which is similarly...

<meta>Continuing from page 267, Clement is discussing the methodology of inquiry. He has just argued that the "barbarian philosophy" (Christianity) encourages searching for truth through dialogue and evidence. He now moves into the technical requirements for a logical starting point to avoid the philosophical trap of infinite regress.</meta>

# CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

<margin>A</margin> If one doubtful thing is used to prove another, and that in turn relies on something else equally doubtful, the process will proceed to infinity, and nothing will ever be able to be demonstrated. However, if the conviction <note>original: "fides" (Greek: "pistis") — in this context, Clement uses the term to mean an intellectual starting point or a "primary conviction" that is accepted as true without further proof.</note> regarding a certain and uncontroversial matter is referred back to what all people acknowledge, that must be established as the principle of doctrine. Therefore, every term proposed must be understood in relation to an expression that is certain, uncontroversial, and manifest to those participating in the consideration; this will serve as the principle of doctrine, which will then explain the discovery of the things being sought. 

Come then, let the proposed term be "Sun." The Stoics <note>A school of Hellenistic philosophy that taught that virtue is the only good and that the universe is governed by divine reason.</note> say that it is an "intelligent bond from sea waters." Is this statement or definition not more obscure than the word itself? It requires another demonstration to prove it is true. It is better, therefore, to say in common and plain speech that the "Sun" is the name for "that which is the most brilliant of all the things that travel the heavens." For, in my opinion, this description is more worthy of conviction, clearer, and one which all men similarly acknowledge.

<margin>Demonstration</margin> In the same way, all men would acknowledge that a demonstration is consistent with reason if it creates conviction regarding doubtful matters by starting from things that are certain and uncontroversial. Not only are "demonstration," "conviction," and "knowledge" used in two ways, but even "pre-knowledge" or "foreknowledge" is spoken of in two modes: one which arises from knowledge <note>original: "scientia" (Greek: "episteme") — systematic, certain knowledge.</note> and is firm and stable, and another which arises only from hope. Strictly speaking, a demonstration is that which imparts conviction from knowledge into the souls of those who are learning. The other type is based merely on opinion. 

Just as with "man," one is truly a man who possesses common prudence, while another is wild and beastly. Thus, the Comic poet <note>Likely referring to a fragment of Greek New Comedy.</note> also said:
<margin>Chares</margin><margin>C</margin> "Chares is a man, so long as he acts like a man." The same logic applies to an ox, a horse, or a dog, according to the virtue or vice of the animal. For we look to the perfection of the species; we come to those qualities which are the primary characteristics of the thing signified. For behold, we understand a "physician" <margin>Physician</margin> as one who lacks nothing of the medical faculty. We understand one "endowed with knowledge" as one who lacks nothing of the knowledge that comes from science. 

A "syllogism" <margin>Syllogism</margin> <note>A form of reasoning in which a conclusion is drawn from two given or assumed premises.</note> differs from an "indication" insofar as that which indicates signifies one thing, being itself one thing; for example, we say that "carrying a womb" <note>i.e., being pregnant.</note> is an indication that a woman is no longer a virgin. But what is taken up in a syllogism, though it is one conclusion, follows from several things; for example, that Pytho was betraying the Byzantines <note>A reference to Pytho of Byzantium, an orator and diplomat for Philip II of Macedon; his activities were used as a standard example in logic and rhetoric textbooks.</note> is signified not by one fact, but by many things taken together. 

<margin>D</margin> To conclude from things that a person acknowledges is to reason, or to construct a syllogism. But to conclude something from *true* things is to "demonstrate." Thus, there is a certain composite utility in demonstration: it is useful because the premises it takes up are true for the sake of the things sought, and because it draws a consequent conclusion. If the first part is not true, or if the second part does not follow from it, it does not demonstrate; rather, one has merely reasoned or effected a syllogism. For to infer a fitting conclusion from assumed premises is merely to reason. But for each of the assumed premises to also be true is not only to reason, but also to demonstrate. 

<margin>To conclude</margin> To "conclude," which is <term>περαίνειν</term> <note>original: "perainein" — a Greek verb meaning to bring to an end, to limit, or to finish.</note>, as is evident from the name itself, is to lead to an end. In every discourse, the "end" is the thing being sought, which is also called the conclusion. No simple and primary statement is called a "syllogism," <margin>❦</margin> even if it is true; rather, a syllogism is composed of at least three such parts: two serving as the premises taken up, and one as the conclusion. 

<margin>B</margin> Now, either all things need demonstration, or some things are believable in themselves. If the former were true, we would proceed to infinity by seeking a demonstration for every demonstration, and thus the very possibility of demonstration would be overturned. But if the latter is true, those very things which are believable of themselves will be the "principles of demonstration." <margin>Principles</margin> Indeed, philosophers admit that the principles of the universe are indemonstrable. Therefore, if demonstration exists, it is absolutely necessary that there be something previously believable of itself, which is called "primary" and "indemonstrable." Every demonstration is thus reduced to an indemonstrable conviction. <margin>❦</margin> 

However, there may be other principles of demonstrations following that "fountain" which arises from conviction—namely, those things which are clearly apparent through the senses and the intellect. For those things which occur through the senses are simple and of such a kind that they cannot be undone. But those which come from the intellect...

<meta>catchword: ...intellect [tia]</meta>

<summary>Clement explains that all logical proof must start from self-evident principles or "primary convictions" to avoid an infinite loop of definitions. He distinguishes between simple syllogistic reasoning (logic based on premises) and true demonstration (logic based on truth).</summary>
<keywords>logic, demonstration, syllogism, primary principles, epistemology, Stoics, Byzantium, Chares, sense perception, intellect</keywords>

# STROMATA, BOOK VIII
zz iii

<margin>A</margin> ...evident, simple, rational, and primary. Those things which are produced from these are indeed composite, but no less evident and credible, and even more rational than the first principles. Therefore, that specific faculty of speech which we all possess by an innate nature is derived from what follows <note>consequence</note> and what is contradictory <note>repugnance</note>. If, then, a discourse is found of such a kind that it can produce conviction regarding things not yet probable by using things that are already credible, we shall call that very thing the essence of demonstration. It has been said that the nature of conviction <note>original: "fidei" (Greek: *pistis*) — in this logical context, it refers to intellectual certainty or the "faith" one has in a proven premise.</note> and of demonstration is twofold. One type brings only persuasion to the minds of the listeners. The other, however, effects scientific knowledge. If, therefore, someone begins from things that are evident to the senses and the intellect, and then brings in a fitting <margin>B</margin> conclusion, he demonstrates truly. But if he begins only from opinions, and not from primary principles—that is, from things neither evident to the senses nor to the intellect—even if he brings in a fitting conclusion, he will be reasoning, but he will not produce a demonstration that constitutes scientific knowledge. If, however, the conclusion is not fitting, he will not even be reasoning at all.

Now, demonstration differs from resolution. Each thing that is demonstrated is shown through certain other things which are themselves demonstrated, and those too were previously demonstrated by others, until we return to those things which are credible in themselves, or to those things which are evident to the senses and the intellect; this process is called resolution. Demonstration, however, occurs when the thing being sought follows from the first principles through all the intermediate steps. Therefore, the man who is <margin>C</margin> gifted with the faculty of demonstrating must take great care regarding the truth of his propositions, but he should not worry about the names—whether one prefers to call them "pronouncements," or "propositions," or "assumptions." Similarly, great care must be taken regarding which subjects lead to what conclusion, but whether one wishes to call the speech "concluding" or "syllogistic" <note>A form of reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two given or assumed premises.</note> is not a concern. 

For I say that he who demonstrates must observe these two things in all cases: namely, that he assumes true propositions, and from them brings in a following conclusion—which some even call <term>inference</term> <note>original: "ἐπιφορὰν" (epiphoran) — a technical term in Greek logic for the "bringing in" of a conclusion.</note>, that is, the result which is brought in for each question from the propositions regarding the matter being sought. And indeed, diverse propositions are required. For the matter proposed, it is <margin>D</margin> necessary to assume what is appropriate to the argument, and this argument must be certain and beyond all controversy for everyone. If propositions are taken that do not fit the proposed question, it is impossible for the person to find anything correctly, since the whole proposed question remains unknown—this is also called the "natural question." 

In every inquiry, there is something that is sought first, which, being entirely credible in itself, is believed without demonstration; from this, one must proceed to the investigation of other things, and this must be established as the judge of the things that appear to have been found. For every inquiry is discovered from a prior knowledge. There is knowledge that exists before any matter is sought, sometimes only regarding the essence, when its duties and functions are unknown—as, for example, with <margin>E</margin> stones and all living creatures whose operations, or passions, or powers, or in a word, the things that are within them, we do not know. At other times, however, something is known from these powers or passions, or some of them—such as the desires and passions of the soul—while the essence remains unknown and is being sought. In many cases, since our own intelligence is subject to itself, all these things are involved in the question of which substances they belong to. For when we have conceived in our thoughts the notions of both—namely, of the essence and the operation—then we approach the inquiry. 

There are also some things of which we know the operations together with the essences, but we are ignorant of the passions <note>Here referring to "affections" or the ways a thing can be acted upon.</note>. <margin>F</margin> Such then is the reason and method of discovery. For one must begin from the knowledge of the proposed questions. Often the figure of speech deceives and confuses and disturbs the thought, so that it does not easily find where the difference lies. For example: Is a fetus carried in the womb an animal? For since [definitions] of both "animal" and "fetus"...

<summary>Clement explains the technical requirements for a valid demonstration, distinguishing between mere persuasion and scientific proof while defining the process of "resolution" back to self-evident principles. He emphasizes that inquiry must begin with a clear understanding of what is already known about a subject's essence or function.</summary>

<meta>Continuing from page 269, Clement is illustrating how to conduct a logical investigation into definitions. He uses the status of a fetus as a case study to show how different philosophical schools (Platonists, Aristotelians, and Stoics) define "life" and "soul" differently, and how a dialectician must force a questioner to define their terms before proceeding.</meta>

-># CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA<-

<margin>A</margin> ...in order that we might have some notion of what is being carried [in the womb], we ask whether the fetus carried in the uterus is an **animal** <note>original: "animal" — in this philosophical context, it means a "living being" or "sentient creature" possessing an "anima" or soul.</note>. This is to ask whether there exists within the substance carried in the womb the capacity to move and, furthermore, to perceive. Therefore, the inquiry into its operations and affections concerns an essence that must first be understood. Immediately, then, the person who proposes the question must first be asked what exactly they mean by "animal." This is especially necessary when we see a name being applied to diverse uses. We must investigate whether the meaning is doubted because of the name used, or if it is beyond controversy among everyone. For if he says that he calls an "animal" anything that grows and is nourished, we will ask him in turn whether he also considers plants to be animals. Then, if he says they are, we must show what it is that is carried and nourished in the womb. For **Plato** also calls plants animals, as they participate in only the third species of the soul—namely, that which desires.

<margin>B</margin> **Aristotle**, however, believes that plants participate in both the "natural" and "nutritive" soul, but he does not think they should be called "animals." For he wishes only that which participates in the other soul—namely, the "sentient" <note>the soul capable of feeling/perception</note> soul—to be called an animal. The **Stoics**, on the other hand, do not even call the natural or vegetative faculty a "soul." But if the one who proposed the question denies that plants are animals, we shall show that he is speaking contradictions. For when he has defined an animal as that which is nourished and grows, and then pronounces that a plant is not an animal, he seems to be saying nothing else than that "that which is nourished and grows is both an animal and not an animal." Let him say, therefore, what he wishes to learn: whether the fetus in the womb grows and is nourished, or whether it participates in any sensation, or even in movement that arises from desire.

<margin>C</margin> For according to the opinion of **Plato**, a plant is both animate <note>possessing a soul</note> and an animal. According to the opinion of **Aristotle**, it is not yet an animal (for it lacks the power of sensation) but it is already animate. Therefore, as he himself holds, an animal is an "animate essence endowed with the power of sensation." According to the opinion of the **Stoics**, however, a plant is neither animate nor an animal. For an animal is an "animate essence." If, therefore, an animal is animate, and the soul is a "nature endowed with the power of sensation," it is clear that what is animate is already endowed with the power of sensation. If, then, the one who asked the question is interrogated in turn as to whether he calls the fetus in the womb an "animal" because it is nourished and grows, he has his answer.

<margin>D</margin> But if he says that what he is asking is whether the fetus carried in the womb is already endowed with the power of sensation, or if it is endowed with the power of moving itself through some desire, then the investigation of the matter is open, and the deception of the name no longer remains. If, however, he does not respond to what he was asked in turn, and does not wish to say what he understands or to what thing he is attributing the name "animal" when he made his proposition, but instead orders us to divide the definitions, he can be recognized as being **contentious** <note>original: "contentiosum" — referring to "eristic" or "sophistic" argument, where one seeks to win a debate rather than find the truth.</note>. If, when there are two modes—one which proceeds by interrogation and response, and the other by pursuing and explaining at length—he refuses the one, let him listen to us pursuing all things pertaining to the proposed question. Then, after we have finished, it will be permitted for him to treat each point in turn. But if he tries to interrupt the examination by questioning, it is plain he wishes to hear nothing. But if he prefers to respond, he must first of all be asked to what thing he attributes the name "animal."

<margin>E</margin> And when he has answered this, he must again be asked what he means by "the fetus carried in the womb"—whether he means things already in the uterus, or those things which are already formed and expressed in limbs, which are called **embryos** <note>original: "ἔμβρυα" (embrya)</note>. When he has answered this as well, it is necessary to conclude and teach what was proposed. But if he wants us to speak without him responding, let him listen: "Since you do not wish to say in what sense you mean what you proposed (for in that way I would not be speaking about words but considering the things themselves), know that you have acted just as if you had proposed the question of whether a 'dog' is an animal; for I would have rightly asked:

<margin>F</margin> 'Which dog?' For I speak of the terrestrial dog, and the marine dog, and the celestial star, and even of **Diogenes** <note>Diogenes of Sinope, the "Cynic" philosopher—"Cynic" literally means "dog-like."</note>, and other dogs in succession. For I cannot divine whether you are asking about all of them, or about one in particular." Therefore, what you will eventually have to do, do it now that you have learned: say clearly about which...

<summary>Clement uses the definition of a "fetus" and an "animal" to demonstrate the necessity of clear definitions in logic. He contrasts the views of Plato, Aristotle, and the Stoics on whether plants and fetuses possess souls and sensation.</summary>

<meta>Continuing from page 270, Clement is further refining the dialectical method of inquiry. He has been using the status of the fetus—whether it is an "animal" (a living, sentient being) or merely a "plant" (living but not sentient)—to demonstrate how to define terms and establish the starting points of a logical proof.</meta>

->### MISCELLANIES, BOOK VIII<-

<margin>A</margin> ...For you might ask: if you enjoy examining names, it is clear that the very name "fetus" is neither an animal nor a plant, but a name, a voice, a physical entity, a "something," and indeed anything rather than an animal. If this was your proposition, you have your answer. However, the thing signified by the name "fetus" is also not the animal itself. Rather, that concept is incorporeal, and should be called both a "thing" and a "thought," and anything rather than an animal. There must be some other nature of an animal. For it has been clearly shown by the very thing under inquiry—namely, the nature of the fetus in the womb—that the question of what this nature is differs from the question regarding the <margin>B</margin> meanings of the name **animal** <note>original: "animal" — in this philosophical context, it refers to any "animated" being possessing a soul/anima, not just non-human creatures.</note>. 

I say, therefore, if you define an "animal" as that which can perceive and move by **appetite** <note>original: "appetitio" — a technical term for the internal impulse or desire that leads to voluntary movement</note>, then an animal is not simply that which *is* moving and perceiving by appetite at this moment. For it can also be asleep, or it might not perceive if there are no sensible objects present. Rather, that which has the *capacity* to be impelled by appetite or to perceive is the sign given by nature by which an animal is recognized. Something of this sort is signified by these terms. 

First, we must consider whether the fetus carried in the womb can perceive or move by appetite. This is the matter proposed for consideration. Second, we ask whether the fetus carried in the womb *ever* perceives or moves by appetite. In this latter sense, no one asks the question, as it is evident. <margin>C</margin> But the original inquiry was whether the fetus is already an animal, or still a plant. 

Next, the name "animal" was brought into the definition so that it would be manifest that once we found sensation and movement proceeding from appetite, we had distinguished the animal from the non-animal. We then distinguished this again from related things, saying that one thing is such by **potential** <note>original: "potestate" — the capacity to become something or act in the future</note> (which does not yet perceive or move, but will eventually do so), while another is such in **actuality** <note>original: "actu" — the state of currently exercising a faculty</note>. Of the latter, one type is already acting, while the other is able to act but is currently resting or asleep. This is the heart of the inquiry. 

<margin>D</margin> We must not say a fetus is an animal simply because it is nourished; that is the error of those who depart from the **essence** <note>original: "essentia" — the fundamental nature of a thing</note> and fix their minds on things that are merely accidental. In everything that is said, a **demonstration** <note>original: "demonstration" — a formal logical proof</note> must be found; this is a discourse that proves one thing from other things. Those things from which the matter of inquiry is proved must be acknowledged and known by the student. The principle of all these things is that which is evident to the senses and the intellect. 

Indeed, a primary demonstration consists of all these elements. However, a proof that concludes something else based on things already demonstrated is no less credible than the first, yet it cannot be called "primary" because it is not concluded from the very first propositions. 

Thus, the first species of the difference between things under inquiry has been shown (there being three species in total). I mean the case where the essence is known, but <margin>E</margin> some action or affection of it is unknown. 

The second species of the proposed questions was that in which we know all the actions and affections, but are ignorant of the essence—for example, in which part of the body the principal part of the soul is located. The same method of demonstration is employed in this question as well. Some say it is impossible for there to be multiple principles for a single animal. While it is impossible for there to be multiple principles of the same *kind* for one animal, it is not absurd for there to be principles that are different in *kind*. 

Among the **Pyrrhonists** <note>Followers of Pyrrho, a school of Skeptical philosophy</note>, they say, there is **epoche** <note>original: "ἐποχὴ" — the suspension of judgment or "holding back" of assent</note>, which is the withholding of assent. This view maintains that nothing is firm or stable. But if this principle begins with itself, it is clear that it will first weaken itself. For either it grants that something is true (and thus assent is not to be withheld from everything), or it persists in saying nothing is true (and it is clear that it cannot claim its own statement is true). <margin>F</margin> For either it speaks the truth, or it does not. If it speaks the truth, it concedes, even if unwillingly, that something is true. But if it does not speak the truth, it leaves as true those very things it wished to remove. For insofar as the suspension of judgment is shown to be false, the things it tried to destroy are shown to be true—much like a dream that says all dreams are false. For when it destroys itself, it confirms the others. In short, if it is true, it must take its principle from itself, since it is not the suspension of assent for something else, but first of all for itself. Then, if it comprehends that it is a human being...

<meta>This page continues Clement’s discussion on dialectic and the importance of clear definitions. He uses the biological status of the fetus—a common topic in ancient philosophy—to illustrate how to resolve ambiguities in language before proceeding with a logical argument. He specifically contrasts the views of the Platonists, Peripatetics (Aristotle), and Stoics on what constitutes a "living being" (animal).</meta>

->### CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA: MISCELLANIES, BOOK VIII<-

...carried in the womb, so that we might have some notion of it, we ask whether the fetus carried in the womb is an **animal** <note>original: "animal" — here meaning a living, sentient being with a soul.</note>. This inquiry asks whether the substance carried in the womb exists in such a way that it can then move and, furthermore, perceive. Therefore, the investigation into its operations and affections concerns an essence that is already recognized. Immediately, then, the person who proposes the question must first be asked what exactly they call an "animal." This is especially necessary when we see a name being applied to diverse uses. We must investigate whether the meaning is doubtful because of the name itself, or whether it is beyond controversy for everyone. For if he says that he calls anything an "animal" that grows and is nourished, we will ask him in turn whether he considers plants to be animals as well. Then, since he has spoken in this way, it is necessary to show what it is that is carried and nourished in the womb. For Plato also calls plants "animals," insofar as they participate in only the third species of the soul—namely, that which **desires** <note>original: "concupiscit" — referring to the appetitive or vegetative part of the soul in Platonic tripartition.</note>.

<margin>B</margin> Aristotle, however, judges that plants participate in both the natural and the nourishing soul, but he does not believe they should be called "animals." For he wants only that which participates in the other soul—namely, the sentient soul—to be called an "animal." The Stoics, on the other hand, do not even call the natural or vegetative faculty a "soul" at all. But if the person who proposed the question denies that plants are animals, we will show that he is saying things that contradict himself. For since he defined an "animal" as that which is nourished and grows, and then pronounced that a plant is not an animal, he appears to be saying nothing other than that "that which is nourished and grows" is both an animal and not an animal. Therefore, let him say what he wishes to learn: whether the fetus in the womb grows and is nourished, or whether it participates in some sensation, or even in movement that arises from **appetite** <note>original: "appetitione" — the internal impulse toward an object.</note>. 

<margin>C</margin> According to the opinion of Plato, a plant is both animate and an animal. In the opinion of Aristotle, it is not yet an animal (for it lacks the power of sensation) but it is already animate. Therefore, as he himself holds, an "animal" is an animate essence endowed with the power of sensation. According to the Stoic view, however, a plant is neither animate nor an animal. For an animal is an animate essence; and if an animal is animate, and the "soul" is a nature endowed with the power of sensation, it is clear that what is "animate" is already endowed with the power of sensation. If, therefore, the one who asked the question is interrogated in turn as to whether he still calls the being in the womb an "animal" because it is nourished and grows, he has his answer. But if he says that what he is asking is whether the fetus carried in the womb is already endowed with the power of sensation, or even with the power of moving itself through some appetite, then the investigation of the matter becomes clear, and the deception of the name no longer remains.

<margin>D</margin> However, if he does not answer the question asked in turn, and does not wish to say what he understands or to what thing he attributes the name "animal" when he made his proposition, but instead orders us to divide the definitions, he can be recognized as being **contentious** <note>original: "contentiosum" — someone arguing for the sake of winning rather than finding truth.</note>. Now, since there are two methods—one which proceeds through interrogation and response, and the other by pursuing and explaining at greater length—and if he rejects the former, let him hear us pursuing all the things that pertain to the proposed question. Then, after we have finished, it will be permitted for him in turn to treat each point. But if he tries to interrupt the examination by questioning, it is plain that he wishes to hear nothing. But if he prefers to answer, first of all he must be asked what the "fetus carried in the womb" signifies to him: does he mean those which are already formed and are animals, or does he want the term to signify the **cast seed** <note>original: "semen deiectum"</note> in the womb, 

<margin>E</margin> or those which are already formed and expressed in their limbs, which are called <term>ἔμβρυα</term> <note>original Greek: "embrya" — embryos, specifically those showing physical development.</note>? When he has answered this as well, it is necessary to conclude and teach the matter that was proposed. But if he wants us to speak without him responding, let him listen: "Since you do not wish to say in what sense you speak of what you proposed (for in that way I would not be talking about meanings, but would be considering the things themselves), know that you have acted just as if you had proposed whether a 'dog' is an animal; for I would have rightly asked, 'Which dog?' For I might speak of the terrestrial dog, or the marine dog [the shark], or the celestial star [Sirius], or even of **Diogenes** <note>Diogenes of Sinope, the famous philosopher known as 'the Dog' (Cynic).</note>, and other dogs in succession. 

<margin>F</margin> For I could not divine whether you are asking about all of them, or about one in particular. Therefore, what you would have done later, do now that you have learned: speak openly about which..."
