<meta>This page continues Clement’s exploration of logic and definitions within his "Miscellanies." He is currently using the status of a fetus—whether it is a "living being" (animal) or a "plant"—as a case study for how to define terms before engaging in a formal proof. He then transitions into a critique of the Pyrrhonian Skeptics.</meta>

### MISCELLANIES, BOOK VIII.

<margin>A</margin> ...as you might ask. But if you prefer to delight in examining the names of things: it is clear that the name "fetus" itself is neither a living being nor a plant, but is a name, and a voice, and a physical thing, and "that which is," and "something"—indeed, anything rather than a living being. If this was your proposal, you have your answer. However, even that which is signified by the name "fetus" is not a living being. Instead, that signified thing is incorporeal; it should be called a "matter" or a "concept," or anything else rather than a living being. Yet, there might be some other nature belonging to a living being. For it has been clearly shown, starting from the very thing under investigation—that is, the nature of the fetus in the womb—what its quality is. This is a different question from the one proposed concerning the various meanings of the word **living being** <note>original: "animal" — in ancient philosophy, this refers to any "animated" entity possessing a soul, distinct from plants.</note>. I say, then, if you define a "living being" as that which can perceive <margin>B</margin> and move by **impulse** <note>original: "appetitione" — the internal drive or desire that leads to action.</note>, then a thing is not a "living being" in an absolute sense just because it moves and perceives by impulse. For it is also possible for it to sleep, or, if there are no objects to perceive, not to perceive at all. Rather, the *capacity* to be driven by impulse or to perceive is the sign given by nature by which a living being is recognized. This is what is signified by these terms. 

First, we must consider whether the fetus carried in the womb can perceive or move by impulse. Secondly, we must ask if the fetus in the womb can *eventually* perceive or move by impulse. In this second meaning, no one asks the question, for it is obvious. But the original inquiry was whether the fetus is *already* a living being, or is still a plant. Then, the name "living being" was brought into the definition so that it would be clear that—through sensation and the motion that proceeds from impulse—<margin>C</margin> we had found how it differs from a non-living thing. We then distinguished this again from related concepts, saying that one thing is "potentially" such—meaning it does not yet perceive or move, but will eventually do so—while another thing is "actually" such. Among those that are "actually" such, one is currently acting, while another is capable of acting but is at rest or asleep. This is the heart of the inquiry. We should not say a fetus is a living being simply because it is nourished; that is a mistake made by those who wander away from the **essence** <note>original: "essentia" — the fundamental nature of what a thing is.</note> of a thing and pay attention only to its accidental properties. 

In every statement made, a **demonstration** <note>original: "demonstratio" — a formal logical proof.</note> must be found; this is a discourse that proves one thing from other things. However, the person speaking must admit to and recognize those things used to prove the point of inquiry. The starting point for all of these <margin>D</margin> is that which is evident to the senses and the intellect. A primary demonstration consists of all these elements. However, a demonstration that concludes something else based on things already proven by a previous demonstration—though no less credible than the first—cannot be called "primary," since it is not concluded from the very first propositions. 

Thus, the first type of difference among the things being investigated has been shown (there being three types in total). I mean the case where the essence is known, but some of its actions or **affections** <note>original: "affectionem" — how a thing is acted upon or its internal states.</note> are unknown. The second type of difference in the questions proposed is that in which we know all the actions and affections, but we are ignorant of the essence; for example, in which part of the body the "ruling part" of the soul is located. The same method of demonstration <margin>E</margin> applies to this question as well. 

Some say it is impossible for there to be multiple principles for a single living being. While it is impossible for there to be multiple principles of the same *kind* for one living being, it is not absurd for there to be principles that are different in *kind*. 

Among the Pyrrhonians, they say, there is **epoche** <gloss>suspension of judgment</gloss> <note>original: "ἐποχὴ" (epoche) — the core Skeptic practice of withholding assent to any claim to achieve tranquility.</note>, which is the suspension of assent; this view holds that nothing is firm or stable. If this principle begins with itself, it is clear that it will first undermine itself. For it either grants that something is true (in which case assent should not be suspended for everything), or it persists in saying nothing is true (in which case it is clear that this statement itself is not true). Either it speaks the truth, or it does not. But if it speaks the truth, it concedes—even against its will—that there is something true. If it does not speak the truth, it leaves as "true" those very things it wanted to remove <margin>F</margin> from consideration. For to the extent that the things being destroyed (or the suspension of assent itself) are shown to be false, those things being destroyed are shown to be true—much like a dream that claims all dreams are false. For by destroying itself, it confirms the others. In short, if this view is true, it takes its starting point from itself; it is not the suspension of assent regarding something else, but first regarding itself. Then, if it comprehends that it is a human being...

Here, he moves into the logical paradoxes of radical doubt and the formal process of definition.</meta>

# CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

<page-num>272</page-num>

<meta>catchword: solum</meta>

<margin>A</margin>...or because he suspends judgment: it is clear that he does not suspend judgment on that very point. How, then, does he even answer when he is asked a question? For it is clear that regarding this, he does not suspend his judgment. But if a man declares that he suspends judgment—if it follows that we ought to suspend judgment about all things—we must first of all suspend judgment about the *suspension of judgment itself*, to determine whether it should be believed or not. Furthermore, if it is true that he knows nothing of the truth, then nothing of the truth can be granted by him at all. If, however, he says that he is ignorant of the truth because it is "doubtful," he thereby grants that the truth *can* be known, because he seems not to confirm his own suspension of judgment regarding it. 

Now, if a **heresy** <note>original: "hæresis" — from the Greek *hairesis*, meaning "choice" or "school of thought." In this period, it refers to any philosophical or theological sect, not necessarily a "heretical" one in the modern sense.</note> is an inclination toward certain **doctrines** <note>original: "dogmatum" — fundamental principles or tenets.</note>, or as some say, an inclination that provides a logical sequence between many doctrines <margin>B</margin> and appearances, aiming toward living rightly—and if a doctrine is a reasoned grasp of the mind, and grasping is a habit and an **assent** <note>original: "assensio" — the mental act of accepting something as true.</note> of the soul—then not only the **Skeptics** <note>original: "Ephectici" — literally "those who hold back," referring to the Pyrrhonian Skeptics who practiced the suspension of judgment (epoché).</note>, but any **Dogmatist** <note>original: "dogmaticus" — a philosopher who asserts specific truths.</note> (that is, one who hands down doctrines) is accustomed to suspend judgment in some matters, either because of the weakness of the mind, the obscurity of the things themselves, or because the arguments on both sides are of equal strength. 

But before we reach definitions, demonstrations, and divisions, we must first establish how many ways the subject of inquiry can be spoken of; **homonyms** <note>words that sound the same but have different meanings</note> must be handled, and **synonyms** <note>different words with the same meaning</note> must be placed appropriately and distinctly in their own significance. Next, we must ask whether the proposed subject is categorized by its relation to other things, or whether it is taken by itself. After this: *Whether it is*. *What it is*. *What its properties are*. Or even in this way: *Whether it is*. *What it is*. *Why it is*. <margin>C</margin>To contemplate these things, it helps to have a knowledge of individual things and of the whole, as well as things that come prior, the differences, and the divisions of those differences. 

Indeed, **induction** <note>original: "inductio" — the logical process of moving from specific instances to a universal rule.</note> brings forth the universal and the definition. **Divisions** <note>original: "divisiones" — the process of breaking a broad category (genus) down into sub-types (species).</note> bring forth the species, the "what it is," and the individual. Contemplation, by which we consider in how many ways a thing may be spoken of, brings about the identification of what is unique to it. Doubts, however, bring forth the differences within the things themselves and the demonstrations. In other ways, too, the consequences of the contemplation increase the study itself. From all these things, knowledge and truth are revealed. 

Again, that which is reduced to a summary through division is called a **definition**. For we take the prior distinction of the division and the posterior. The prior is taken when a point is granted or proposed; the posterior, when it has been demonstrated. Furthermore, <margin>D</margin>through the senses, the universal and general is gathered into a summary from that which is singular. For the beginning of induction is sense-perception, but the end is the universal and general. And induction does not show *what* a thing is, but *that* it is or is not. Division shows *that* it is; and distinction, similar to division, teaches the essence and *what* it is, but not *whether* it is. **Demonstration** <note>original: "demonstratio" — a formal logical proof.</note>, however, opens up three things: *whether* it is, *what* it is, and *why* it is. 

There are also some definitions that contain the **cause**. Since "to know" is to have seen the cause—and there are four causes: **matter**, the **mover** <note>the efficient cause</note>, **form**, and the **end** <note>the final cause or purpose</note>—there will be a distinction in four ways. First, one must take the **genus** <note>the broad category</note> in which those things closest to the highest things reside. Afterward, the nearby and containing **difference**. <margin>E</margin>The continuation of these differences, which are split and divided, fulfills the "what it is to be," or the essence and definition of the thing. It is not necessary, however, to state all the differences of each thing, but only those that grant it its specific form. 

Geometric resolution and composition are similar to **dialectical** <note>logical</note> division and definition. From division, we return to those things that are simpler and more fundamental. We divide the genus of the thing being sought into the species that exist within it. For example, in "man," we divide **living being** <note>original: "animal" — in ancient logic, this refers to any "animated" creature with a soul.</note>, which is the genus, into the species that appear within it, namely **mortal** and **immortal**. And כך, always cutting the genera that seem to be composite into simpler species, we approach the thing being sought until it no longer admits of division. For when we have divided "living being" into mortal and immortal; then <margin>F</margin>mortal into **terrestrial** and **aquatic**; and again terrestrial into **winged** and **pedestrian**; and thus we have divided the species nearest to the thing being sought, which also encompasses the thing itself: by cutting, we shall arrive at the simplest species, which is nothing else, but that alone...

<summary>Clement outlines the logical contradictions of radical Skepticism, arguing that the act of suspending judgment on all things is itself an assertion. He then details the systematic methods of Induction, Division, and Demonstration used to define the essence and causes of any subject.</summary>

# THE MISCELLANIES, BOOK VIII

<page-num>273</page-num>

<margin>A</margin> ...it only comprehends that which is sought. For again, we divide **walking** into that which partakes of reason and that which is void of reason. Then, from those species that are selected through division, choosing those which are more closely related to man, and once we have composed them into a single statement, we produce the definition of man, which is: "a mortal animal, terrestrial, walking, and a partaker of reason." <note>This is the classic Aristotelian method of definition by genus and specific difference.</note> Thus, the division occupies the place of the raw material, seeking the simplicity of the name for the definition. But the definition, which composes and constructs, acts as the craftsman and builder, and demonstrates the knowledge of that which exists. Definitions are not of these specific divisions, nor of the **Ideas** <note>original: "idearum" — referring to Platonic Forms</note>, but of the things for which we hold universal and general notions in the mind. We say that definitions are the statements that interpret these notions; for divisions are also made of these mental concepts.

<margin>B</margin> From these divisions, one type divides that which is being divided into its species, such as a genus. Another divides into parts, as one divides a whole. Yet another divides into **accidents** <note>original: "accidents" — non-essential qualities, like being "tall" or "musical," which can change without the thing ceasing to be what it is.</note>. Now, the division of a whole into parts is mostly considered in terms of magnitude. However, the division into accidents can never be fully grasped, since the **essence** <note>original: "essentiam"</note> of the things that exist must also be present in every single thing. For this reason, both of these types of division are rejected; only the division of a genus into species is approved. From this, the identity existing in the genus receives its form and character, as does the diversity found in the specific differences.

A species is always considered as a certain part. However, it does not work in reverse: if something is a part of another, it is not necessarily a species. For a hand is a part of a man, but it is not a species of man. <margin>C</margin> And while the genus is present in the species—for "animal" is present in both "man" and "ox"—the whole is not present in its parts. For "man" as a whole is not present in the feet. Therefore, the species is more primary than the part. Whatever is predicated of the genus is also predicated of the species. It is best to contemplate the genus in two species; if not, then in three. Therefore, species that are divided more generally receive their character from the "same" and the "other." Then, once they are divided, they receive their character through those things which are signified generally.

For every species is either an **essence** <term>Substance or being; what a thing is in its fundamental nature.</term>—as when we say that among existing things, some are bodies and others are incorporeal—or it is a quantity, or a relation, or a place, or a time, or an action, or a **passion** <note>original: "pati" — the state of being acted upon by an external force.</note>. Whoever, then, has knowledge of a thing <margin>D</margin> will also be able to give a definition of it; just as he who cannot grasp and define something in words has never truly had knowledge of that thing. 

From the ignorance of definition, many doubts and deceptions arise. For if he who knows a thing holds the knowledge of it in his mind, and can also explain in words what he holds in his mind—and the explanation of what is thought in the mind is a definition—it is necessary that he who knows a thing can also give its definition. A **difference** <note>original: "differentia"</note> is also assumed in definitions, which serves as a sign within the definition. Thus, adding "endowed with the power of laughter" to the definition of man completes the whole: "an animal partaking in reason, mortal, terrestrial, walking, and endowed with the power of laughter." For those things added to a definition through difference are signs of specific properties; they do not indicate the nature of the things themselves. 

<margin>E</margin> Now, they say that a difference is the rendering of a property, and to the extent that it differs from others, that which has the difference—which belongs to it alone and is predicated interchangeably with the thing—it is necessary in definitions to first assume the genus as the primary principle and that which can stand firm. In longer definitions, there is a multitude of species found through the **ten predicaments** <term>Aristotle's ten categories: substance, quantity, quality, relation, place, time, position, state, action, and passion.</term>; in the shortest, those which are taken from proximate and containing species signify the essence and nature of the thing. The smallest definition consists of three parts: the genus and two most necessary species. This is done for the sake of brevity. We say, then: "Man is an animal endowed with the power of laughter." 

<margin>F</margin> Then one must assume that which chiefly belongs to the thing being defined, either its own particular virtue, or its own function and office, or something else of that kind. Therefore, a definition that sets forth the essence of a thing cannot indeed accurately grasp the nature of the thing in its entirety, but it declares the essence through its primary species. Moreover, a definition almost holds the essence within its **quality**. 

There are two supreme causes which bring about the maintenance of **assent** <note>The mental act of accepting a proposition as true.</note>. One...

<meta>This page continues Clement’s discussion on the foundations of knowledge and logic. Following the explanation of how definitions are constructed from species and genus, he now addresses why humans struggle to agree on the truth and introduces the linguistic and categorical tools used to organize reality, heavily drawing on Aristotelian logic.</meta>

<page-num>274</page-num>
<header>CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA</header>
<meta>catchword: therefore</meta>

<margin>A</margin>
Furthermore, the human mind is complex and unstable; it is inherent in its nature to generate dissension, either among people or within a person’s own self. Secondly, there is the discrepancy found in things themselves, which is the primary cause for the **suspension of assent** <note>original: "sustentatio assensionis" — a technical term for the Skeptical practice of withholding judgment (epoché) when faced with equal arguments for and against a point.</note>. For since we cannot believe all appearances because they conflict, nor can we disbelieve all appearances (for the claim that "all things are untrustworthy" would itself be untrustworthy as part of "all things"), nor can we believe some and not others due to their equal weight, we are led to suspend our judgment. Among these principal causes for the suspension of assent, the instability of thought produces dissension. Dissension, in turn, is the 
<margin>B</margin>
immediate cause for the suspension of assent. Thus, life is full of trials and cares; in short, the choice between what are called "good" and "evil" provides evidence of a doubting mind that limps along due to the weakness of opposing facts. Consequently, libraries are full of books, treatises, and commentaries by those who disagree with one another regarding doctrines, each having persuaded themselves that they alone possess the truth. In speech, there are three factors involved: first, **names**, which are primarily signs of what is conceived in the mind and, by extension, signs of the subject matters; second, **thoughts**, which reflect and express the subject matters. Therefore, thoughts are the same for everyone, because the same form and impression are generated in all people by the underlying objects; however, names are not the same, owing to different languages. Third, there are 
<margin>C</margin>
the **subject matters** themselves, from which our thoughts are imprinted. **Grammar** reduces names into twenty-four universal and general elements <note>Clement refers to the 24 letters of the Greek alphabet.</note>. For it is necessary for elements to be defined; there is no scientific knowledge of individual things, as they are infinite. It is characteristic of science to rely on universal and general theorems that are defined. Thus, individuals are reduced to universals and generals. The investigation of philosophers is concerned with both what is conceived in the mind and the subject matters. Since the individual instances of these are infinite, certain elements have been discovered to which everything being sought can be reduced. If a thing appears to fall under one or more of these elements, we declare that it exists; if it escapes them all, we say it does not exist. Of the things spoken, some are said without connection, such as "man" or "runs," and whatever does not complete a sentence 
<margin>D</margin>
that holds truth or falsehood. Others are said with connection. Of those words spoken without connection: some signify **substance**; others **quality**; others **quantity**; others **relation**; others **place**; others **time**; others **position**; others **state** <note>original: "habere"</note>; others **action**; and others **passion** <note>These are the ten Categories of Aristotle, the basic building blocks of logical thought.</note>. We say these are the elements of things that exist, which exist in matter and after the first principles. They can be considered in this way. Those things that lack matter can be apprehended by the mind alone through the first application of thought. Of those things placed under the ten categories: some are said "in themselves," like nine of the categories; others are "relative to something." And again, of those things under these ten 
<margin>E</margin>
categories, some are **synonymous** <note>In ancient logic, synonyms are things that share both a name and a definition, like a "man" and an "ox" both being called "animal."</note>, where the name is common to both and the definition is the same—for example, "living being" <note>original: "animal"</note> and its definition, "animated substance." **Heteronyms** are those things which have different names for the same subject, such as "ascent" and "descent"; for it is the same path, whether going up or down. There is another species of heteronyms, such as "horse" and "black," which have different names and definitions and do not share the same subject; these should be called "other" rather than heteronyms. **Polyonyms** are those which have the same definition but different names, such as "blade," "brand," and "sword" <note>These are what we call synonyms in modern English.</note>. **Denominatives** are those named from something else, such as "brave" from "bravery." **Homonyms** are those that use the same name but do not have the same definition, such as "man" 
<margin>F</margin>
referring to a living person and "man" referring to a painted figure. Of homonyms, some share a name by chance, like "Ajax the Locrian" and "Ajax the Salaminian" <note>Two different heroes from the Trojan War with the same name.</note>. Others share a name by design. Of these, some are by resemblance, like a living man and a painted man. Others are by proportion and analogy, such as the "feet" of Mount Ida and our own "feet."

<summary>Clement explains that human disagreement arises from the mind's instability and the complexity of the world, leading to a suspension of judgment. He then outlines the logical framework of the ten Categories and the classification of names (synonyms, homonyms, etc.) as tools for scientific inquiry.</summary>
<keywords>logic, epistemology, suspension of assent, Aristotelian categories, grammar, synonyms, homonyms, Ajax, linguistics</keywords>

# STROMATA BOOK VIII.

<margin>A</margin> ...because they are lower down. Others are named from their operation, such as the "foot" of a ship <note>original: "pes navis" — in Latin, this refers to the sheet or rope used to trim a sail, but the word "pes" also means a human foot.</note> by which a ship sails, and our own foot, by which we move. There are also things called "homonyms" <note>Words that sound the same but have different meanings.</note> which originate from the same source or tend toward the same end; for example, a "medical" book and a "medical" scalpel are both named from the doctor who uses them and in accordance with medical theory. Among causes, some are called **preliminary** <margin><term>prokatarktika</term> <note>original: "$\pi \rho \omicron \kappa \alpha \tau \alpha \rho \kappa \tau \iota \kappa \alpha \acute{\iota}$"</note> and primordial, <term>synektika</term> <note>original: "$\sigma \upsilon \nu \epsilon \kappa \tau \iota \kappa \alpha \acute{\iota}$"</note> or containing.</margin>, while others are **containing**, some are **assisting**, and others are **necessary conditions** <note>original: "sine quibus non" — literally "without which [it could] not [happen]."</note>. Preliminary causes are those that first provide the occasion for something to happen, just as beauty provides the occasion for love in those who lack self-control. For the mere sight of it generates the affection of love in them, though not by necessity. Containing causes (which are also called "perfect in themselves" by synonymy) are those where the cause itself is sufficient to produce the effect. Next, all causes should be demonstrated in the one who speaks. A father is the preliminary, or primordial, cause of education. But the teacher is the containing cause—that is, the one who holds it together.

<margin>B</margin> The natural talent of the student is the assisting cause. Time, however, holds the role of the necessary condition. A "cause" is properly defined as that which, by acting, provides something or is endowed with the power of providing. Just as we say iron is <term>cutting</term> <note>original: "$\tau \mu \eta \tau \iota \kappa \omicron \acute{\nu}$"</note>, meaning it is endowed with the power of cutting, not only while it is actually cutting, but even when it is not. In the same way, the <term>passive</term> <note>original: "$\pi \alpha \theta \eta \tau \iota \kappa \omicron \acute{\nu}$"</note>—that is, being endowed with the power of being provided for—signifies both that which is already being operated upon and that which is not yet being operated upon but has the capacity to be. Furthermore, some say that causes consist of bodies; others say they are incorporeal. Some say that a body is properly a cause, while an incorporeal thing is a cause only by a misuse of terms or in a causal sense. Others, however, turn this around:

<margin>C</margin> they say that incorporeal things are properly the causes, while bodies are called causes only by a misuse of terms. For example, they argue that the "cutting," which is an action, is incorporeal; and that this action is the cause of being cut, while the sword and the person cutting are merely the bodies involved. For some things, the cause is described in three ways: one is the cause *as* the sculptor; another is the cause *for the sake of which* the statue is made; and another is the cause *from which* it is made, such as the material. For bronze is the cause for the statue to be made. Therefore, "to be made" and "to be cut," which are the causes of what they are, are incorporeal since they are actions. For this reason, **predicates** <note>original: "categoremata" — a logical term for what is said about a subject.</note>, or as some call them, **sayables** <note>original: "lekta" <term>$\lambda \epsilon \kappa \tau \alpha \acute{}}$</term> — a technical Stoic term for the meaning or "sense" of a statement.</note> (as Cleanthes and Archedemus call them), are causes. Or rather, some are called causes of predicates—such as "it is being cut," the case of which is "to be cut." Others,

<margin>D</margin> however, are causes of **pronouncements**, such as "a ship is being built," the case of which is "for a ship to be built." Aristotle, however, uses these names for the things themselves: House, ship, burning, cutting. It is beyond controversy that a "case" <note>The state of affairs or the event itself.</note> is incorporeal. Therefore, that famous Sophism is solved in this way: "What you say passes through your mouth," which is true. "But you say 'house'." "Therefore, a house passes through your mouth," which is false. For we do not say the "house" which is a physical body, but the "case" which is incorporeal, which the house possesses. Likewise, we say a builder builds because of the relationship he has to what is to come. In this way, we say "a cloak is being woven." For the act of doing signifies the operation. Now, it is not the case that the act belongs to one thing

<margin>E</margin> while the cause belongs to another; rather, the cause belongs to the same thing, both the cloak and the house. For insofar as it is the cause of being made, it is also the producer of its being made. The cause is the same as the producer and the "for the sake of which." And if something is a cause and a producer, it is also entirely the "for the sake of which." However, if something is a "for the sake of which," it is not necessarily the cause. Many things certainly contribute toward a single effect, for the sake of which the end is achieved, but not all of them are causes. Medea would not have killed her children if she had not been angry; nor would she have been angry if she had not suffered from jealousy; nor would she have been jealous if she had not loved. Nor would she have loved if Jason had not sailed to Colchis. Nor would he have sailed to Colchis if the *Argo* had not been built; nor would the *Argo* have been built if the timbers had not been cut from Mount Pelion. In all these instances, although they are things "for the sake of which," they are not all causes of the slaughter of the children; only Medea is the cause. Therefore, that which does not prevent an action does not perform it. Consequently,

<margin>F</margin> that which does not prevent is not the cause, but rather that which *does* prevent. For a cause is understood to be something that acts and operates. Furthermore, that which does not prevent is separate from what happens. But a cause is directly related to what happens. Therefore, that which does not prevent cannot be the cause...

<meta>catchword: pro-</meta>

<summary>Clement distinguishes between different types of causes (preliminary, containing, assisting) and necessary conditions. He argues that only active agents are true causes, illustrating this with the legal and logical chain of events leading to Medea's crimes.</summary>
<keywords>causality, Stoicism, logic, Medea, Jason, Aristotle, predicates, sayables, incorporeals, preliminary cause, containing cause</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Clement’s exploration of the nature of causality, building on the definitions of "preliminary" and "containing" causes. He is transitioning from a discussion of things that prevent an action to a systematic classification of the four types of causes, heavily influenced by Aristotelian and Stoic logic.</meta>

# CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA

...prevents it. Therefore, it is certainly perfected because that which could prevent it is not present.

<margin>A</margin>
Now, a cause is spoken of in four ways: the **efficient** cause, such as the sculptor; the **material** cause, such as the bronze; the **formal** cause, such as the shape; and the **final** cause, such as the honor of the gymnasist <note>The "gymnasiarch" was the official in charge of the gymnasium, often sponsoring games or statues.</note>. Therefore, the bronze holds the status of "that without which it cannot be" <note>original: "sine quibus non"</note> in order for the statue to exist. In this sense, it is also a cause. For whatever is necessary for an effect to happen is necessarily a cause. However, it is not a cause in an absolute sense. It is not the **sustaining** <note>original: "synectica"</note> or containing cause, but rather an **assisting** cause. Whatever acts, produces an effect in conjunction with the suitability of that which is acted upon. For the cause indeed produces an effect, but each thing is acted upon according to its own natural disposition, provided that this disposition exists and meets the requirements of a "necessary condition." Thus, a cause is ineffective without this suitability. It is not the primary cause, but rather an assisting cause.

<margin>B</margin>
Every cause is considered in the act of doing. But the earth did not create itself; therefore, it could not be its own cause. It is ridiculous to say that the wood, rather than the fire, is the cause of burning; or the flesh, rather than the sword, is the cause of a cut; or that the athlete's own weakness, rather than the opponent's strength, is the reason he was defeated. A **containing cause** <note>One that must be present for the effect to persist.</note> does not require time. For a branding iron, as soon as it is applied to the flesh, produces pain. Among **preliminary causes** <note>original: "procatarcticis"</note>, some require time until the effect is brought to completion; others do not require time, such as a fall in the case of a fracture. Are these then called "timeless" not because they lack time entirely, but because the time is so small—occurring suddenly—that it seems as though no time passed?

<margin>C</margin>
Every cause that can be understood by the mind as a "cause" is a cause *of* something and exists *in* something. It is the cause of an effect—for instance, the sword is the cause of cutting. It exists in a substrate that is suitable and adapted to it, just as fire exists in wood; for fire will not burn a diamond. A cause is among those things categorized by relationship. For it is conceived in the mind by its habit and relation to another thing. Thus, when two things are applied to each other, we understand the "cause" as a cause. The same logic applies to the craftsman, the producer, and the father. Nothing is its own cause, nor is anyone his own father. For if that were so, the first would also be the second. The cause certainly acts and affects, while that which is produced by the cause is acted upon and affected.

<margin>D</margin>
The same thing, taken by itself, cannot simultaneously act and be acted upon, nor can it be both father and son. Furthermore, that which is the cause of something being made must be prior in time regarding its essence, just as the sword exists before the incision. The same thing cannot be simultaneously prior in time as the material (insofar as it is the cause) and posterior in time as the finished work. There is a difference between "being" and "having been made." So too, a cause is the cause of that which is being made, and a father is the father of a son. It is not possible for the same thing to simultaneously "be" and "be becoming" through the same means. Therefore, nothing is its own cause. Causes are not causes of each other reciprocally, but rather one is a cause to another. For example, a preexisting splenic condition <note>A reference to an enlarged spleen or illness related to it.</note> is not the cause of a fever, but it is the cause *for the fever to happen*; and the preceding fever is not the cause of the spleen, but the cause *for the condition to increase*. Likewise, the virtues are causes of one another so that they are never separated, due to their mutual consequence. And just as the stones in an arch <note>original: "fornice"</note> are causes for each other to stay in place, they are not the causes of each other's existence.

<margin>E</margin>
The teacher and the student are also reciprocal causes of progress. Sometimes they are said to be causes of the same thing, such as a merchant and an innkeeper who are causes of each other’s profit. At other times, they are causes of different things, like the sword and the flesh. The sword is a cause to the flesh so that it may be cut; the flesh is a cause to the sword so that it may cut. "An eye for an eye, and a life for a life." For he who inflicts a lethal wound on someone is the cause of death, or cause for death to befall him. He who is in turn lethally wounded by the other has the other as a cause—not insofar as he was a cause to him, but through another factor. He himself is the cause of death; but death did not in turn inflict a lethal wound on him, rather he was wounded by the person. Therefore, he was the cause of one thing, but had another thing as his cause. And he who commits an injustice is the cause of something to another, namely the one who suffered the injustice.

<margin>F</margin>
The law, however, which commands that he be punished, is not the cause of the injury or the crime, but is the cause of vengeance for one person and the cause of discipline for the other. Therefore, they are not causes of each other *as causes* if they are truly causes. Furthermore, the question is asked whether many causes can produce one effect through **concurrence** <note>original: "congressum"</note>. For when men are joined together...

<summary>Clement provides a detailed logical breakdown of causality, identifying four types (efficient, material, formal, and final) and distinguishing between essential causes and necessary conditions. He explores the relational nature of causes, arguing that nothing can be its own cause and illustrating how multiple factors interact to produce effects in nature, law, and human relationships.</summary>

<keywords>Aristotelian causes, Stoic logic, efficient cause, material cause, formal cause, final cause, synectic cause, procatarctic cause, reciprocal causality, Clement of Alexandria, philosophy of action</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes Clement’s technical analysis of causality in Book VIII. Having previously discussed efficient and material causes, he now focuses on the nuances between "preliminary," "sustaining," and "assisting" causes, utilizing common Stoic and Peripatetic logical distinctions to define how multiple factors contribute to a single result.</meta>

### MISCELLANIES BOOK VIII.

...men are the cause of a ship being pulled, but only in conjunction with others, unless there is also some helping cause, which is called a **co-cause** <note>original: "concausa"</note>. Others say that if many causes exist separately, they each form one cause; for instance, regarding "blessedness," which is a single state, the causes are the virtues, which are many. Likewise, for the state of being heated or being in pain, there are many causes. Is it not therefore the case that many virtues share a single power? And things that heat or cause pain similarly; so that a multitude of virtues, which are one in genus, may be the cause of one thing—namely, being blessed. In reality, however, **preliminary** causes <note>original: "procatarcticæ"; these are the initiating or triggering causes</note> of a single thing are many, both in genus and in species. In genus, for example, the causes of any disease might be cold, exhaustion, labor, indigestion, or drunkenness; but in species, the result is a fever. On the other hand, **sustaining** causes <note>original: "continentes" or "synecticæ"; the causes that must be present for the effect to continue</note> are many only in genus, not likewise in species. For the state of "smelling sweet," which is one in genus, has many causes in species, such as frankincense, rose, saffron, storax, myrrh, and ointment. A rose might not be as fragrant as myrrh.

Furthermore, the same thing may be the cause of contraries, sometimes due to the power and magnitude of the cause, and sometimes due to the suitability of the thing being acted upon. Due to a specific power, the same musical string produces a high or low sound depending on its tension or looseness. Due to the suitability of the subjects, honey affects healthy people with sweetness, but affects those suffering from a fever with bitterness. One and the same wine rouses some to anger but cheers others. The same Sun melts wax but dries out clay. 

Moreover, among causes, some are evident while others are hidden; some are grasped by observation, others by reasoning. Among the hidden causes, some are temporarily hidden—meaning they are concealed for a time but may be seen clearly again later. Others are hidden by nature and can never be made evident. Among those hidden by nature, some can be comprehended (which were called "not-obscure"), which are understood through signs by reflection and reasoning, much like the symmetry of complex arguments that fall under contemplation. Others are incomprehensible, which can in no way be grasped, and these are called entirely obscure.

There are also **preliminary** causes, **sustaining** causes <note>original: "synecticæ"</note>, **co-causes** <note>original: "concausæ"</note>, and **assisting** causes <note>original: "adiuuantes"</note>. Some causes pertain to things according to nature, others to things contrary to nature. Some pertain to disease, some to accidents, some to the affections, and some to the magnitude of those affections. Still others pertain to times and occasions. If preliminary causes are removed, the effect remains. However, a sustaining cause is one where, if it is present, the effect remains, and if it is removed, the effect is removed. By synonym, the sustaining cause is also called "perfect in itself," since it is sufficient on its own to produce the effect. 

If "cause" signifies an operation perfect in itself, then an "assisting cause" signifies a ministry or a service performed with another. If nothing is contributed, it cannot even be called "assisting." But if it is contributed, it is entirely a cause of that to which it contributes—that is, of what happens through its help. Therefore, an assisting cause is that which, when present, allows the effect to happen—an evident cause for an evident effect, a hidden one for a hidden effect. Furthermore, a **co-cause** is also of the genus of causes, just as a fellow soldier is a soldier, and a fellow youth is a youth. An **assisting cause** provides help to a sustaining cause to increase the intensity of what is being produced. A **co-cause** is not conceived of in this way. For there can be a co-cause even if there is no sustaining cause. A co-cause is understood as acting with another which cannot produce the effect by itself; thus, it is a cause alongside another cause. The assisting cause differs from the co-cause in this: the co-cause provides an effect to that which cannot produce it alone, while the assisting cause—though it also does not produce the effect alone—joins with another that *can* produce the effect alone, helping it so that the effect becomes most intense. Most of all, an assisting cause is brought in to increase the power of an effect already set in motion by a preliminary cause.

->THE END.<-

<sig>Aa</sig>

<summary>Clement concludes Book VIII by categorizing causes into preliminary, sustaining, co-operative, and assisting types, explaining how the same cause can produce different effects based on the subject's disposition. This technical discussion serves as a foundation for understanding divine and natural agency in his theological framework.</summary>

## Proverbs

My son, let not sinners lead you into error, nor walk in the paths with them if they should exhort you, saying: Come with us, be a partner in innocent blood; let us hide the righteous man in the earth unjustly without cause, let us take him away from the midst, like the underworld takes the living. *Proverbs 1.* 35.a

<column-break/>

Blessed is the man who finds wisdom and the mortal who sees prudence. *Proverbs 3.* 79.d

There was a certain very rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen <note>Original: *bysso*; a high-quality, expensive flax or silk-like fabric from the ancient world.</note>, who feasted splendidly every day. And there was a certain beggar named Lazarus who lay at the rich man's gate covered in sores, desiring to be filled with the crumbs that fell from the rich man's table. Luke 15. 73.b

## Of John

In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. John 1. 25.e
For that which was made, in him is life. 103.a, 1.15.c, and 66.a.b.
And there shall be all one flock and one shepherd. John 2. 23.b <note>This verse is actually from John 10, but is indexed here under chapter 2 in the source.</note>
He who believes in the Son has eternal life. John 3. 16.d
I have food to eat which you do not know. My food is to do the will of him who sent me. John 4. 21.d
For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments. And his commandments are not heavy. John 4. 105.e <note>This is actually 1 John 5:3, though the index attributes it to the Gospel of John.</note>
Amen, amen, I say to you, he who hears my words and believes him who sent me has eternal life: and he does not come into judgment, but passes from death to life. John 5. 15.c
Eat my flesh and drink my blood. John 6. 18.f, 20.d.
For Moses did not give you bread from Heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread from Heaven. John 6. 21.b.
This is the will of my Father, that everyone who beholds the Son and believes in him should have eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day. John 8. 16.d.
I am the good shepherd. John 10. 23.b
Little children, I am with you yet a little while. John 13. 11.b
I am the true vine and my father is the husbandman <note>Original: *agricola*; a farmer or tiller of the land.</note>. John 15. 26.f
The Father himself loves you, because you have loved me. John 16. 9.e
And you have loved them, just as you have loved me. John 17. 9.e.
That they all may be one, as you, Father, in me, and I in you, that they also may be one in us, so that the world may believe that you sent me. And the glory which you gave me I have given to them, that they may be one just as we are one. I in them and you in me, that they may be made perfect in one. John 17. 28.a
When Jesus stood on the shore he said: Children, do you have any fish? <note>Original: *obsonium*; refers to anything eaten with bread, frequently fish in the context of the Gospels.</note> John, last chapter. 10.f

## Of Acts

It is not good for us to leave the word of God to serve tables. Acts 6. 59.d
And he sees heaven opened and a certain vessel bound at the four corners <note>Original: *initijs*; literally "beginnings" or "ends," referring to the corners of the great sheet in Peter’s vision.</note> let down upon the earth, in which were all the four-footed animals and serpents of the earth and birds of the air. Acts 10. 46.c
It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay no greater burden upon you than the necessity of abstaining from things sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from things strangled, and from fornication. Acts 15. 59.d

## To the Romans

See the severity and the goodness of God. Toward those indeed who fell, severity; but toward you, goodness, if you remain in goodness—that is, in faith in Christ. Romans 11. 27.f
Providing good things, not only before the Lord, but also before men. Romans 12. 106.d
Let us put on the armor of light: as walking becomingly in the day: not in reveling and drunkenness, not in chambering and impurity. Romans 13. 54.c
The kingdom of God is not food and drink. Romans 14. 42.e
Let him who eats not despise him who eats not. And let him who does not eat not judge him who eats. Romans 14. 44.c
I wish you to be wise indeed toward what is good, but simple toward what is evil. Romans, last chapter. 13.b

## To the Corinthians

Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, and let not the strong man glory in his strength, but let him who glories glory in the Lord. 1 Corinthians 1. 18.d, 22.a
Thanks be to God who always makes us triumph in Christ and manifests the odor of his knowledge through us in every place; for we are the good odor of the Lord to God among those who are saved, and among those who perish; to the one indeed an odor from death unto death, but to the others an odor from life unto life. 1 Corinthians 2. 61.b <note>This is actually 2 Corinthians 2:14-16.</note>
Women likewise, not with braided hair or gold or pearls or costly attire: but as becomes women professing godliness, adorning themselves through good works. 1 Corinthians 2. 79.c <note>This is actually 1 Timothy 2:9-10, though the index attributes it to 1 Corinthians.</note>
Milk I gave you as drink as to infants in Christ, not food: for you were not yet able; but neither are you able even now. 1 Corinthians 3. 17.e, 18.b, 22.a
And I, brothers, could not speak to you as to spiritual people, but as to carnal. Ibid. <note>Referring to the same chapter mentioned above.</note>
What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love and the spirit of gentleness? 1 Corinthians 4. 25.e
Food for the belly, and the belly for food. But God will destroy both it and them. 1 Corinthians 6. 42.b
Do not err: neither adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor those who lie with men, nor thieves, nor the covetous, nor drunkards, nor revilers shall possess the kingdom of God. 1 Corinthians 6. 103.e
Food does not commend us to God. 1 Corinthians 8. 43.e
If any such food should offend my brother, I will not eat meat forever, lest I offend my brother. 1 Corinthians 8. 44.c
Do we not have the power to eat and to drink, and to lead about women? 1 Corinthians 9. 43.e
I do not wish you to become participants with demons. 1 Corinthians 10. 43.d
Whether you eat or whether you drink, do all for the glory of God. 1 Corinthians 10. 45.c
Each one takes his own supper first in eating, and one indeed is hungry, and another is drunk. 1 Corinthians 11. 45.a.b
When you come together it is not permitted to eat the Lord's supper. 1 Corinthians 11. 51.f

### To the Galatians

<margin>16.d</margin>
*Before faith came, we were kept shut up under the law, for the faith that was to be revealed; therefore the Law was our tutor <note>Original: *pædagogus*; Clement uses the Greek concept of the household tutor to explain the role of the Law before Christ.</note> in Christ so that we might be justified by faith. But after faith came, we are no longer under a tutor. Galatians 3.*

*You are all children of God through faith in Christ Jesus. For whoever of you were baptized into Christ have put on Christ. There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus. Ibid. e.*

But in all confidence as always, now also Christ shall be magnified in my body, whether through life or through death. For to me to live is Christ and to die is gain. Phil. 1 99.e

### To Timothy

This command I entrust to you, son Timothy, according to the prophecies previously made concerning you, that by them you may wage a good warfare, having faith and a good conscience, which some, having rejected, have suffered shipwreck concerning the faith. 1 Timothy 1. 55.c <note>The letter/number combinations like '55.c' refer to specific pages and sections in this 16th or 17th-century printed edition of Clement’s works.</note>
The law is not made for the righteous. 1 Timothy 1. 113.b
I desire that the younger women marry, bear children, manage the house, and give no occasion to the adversary for the sake of reproach. 1 Timothy 3. 103. d. <note>In modern Bibles, this is found in chapter 5.</note>
In the latter days, some will depart from the faith, giving heed to spirits of error and doctrines of demons, forbidding to marry and commanding to abstain from foods. 1 Timothy 4. 96. e. 104. c
I testify before God and Christ Jesus and the elect angels that you observe these things without prejudice, doing nothing according to partiality. 1 Timothy 5. 2.b
If anyone does not agree with sound words, but is puffed up with some doctrine, knowing nothing; but laboring about questions and disputes over words, from which come strife, envy, railings, evil suspicions, and the contentions of men corrupt in mind and deprived of the truth. 1 Timothy 6. 11.f
O Timothy, guard what has been entrusted to you, avoiding profane novelties of words and the oppositions of what is falsely called knowledge <term>gnosis</term>, which some, promising, have missed the mark concerning the faith. 2 Timothy 1. 61. b <note>This verse is traditionally at the end of 1 Timothy, though the indexer cites it under 2 Timothy.</note>
You therefore, be strong in the grace which is in Christ Jesus, and what you have heard from me through many witnesses, entrust these things to faithful men, who will indeed be fit to teach others also. 2 Timothy 2. 1.f
Study to show yourself an approved workman unto God, who need not be ashamed, rightly handling the word of truth. (the same, in the same place).
